The backend will not register a contract unless the signer matches on-chain owner() and the runtime bytecode keccak matches the live Arc deploy.
Arc is the settlement network. ENSv2 is Sepolia only. We resolve the current resolver before a write, grant authorizeTextRoles for service.metadata, and keep a tab-local secondary key for the allowed text update and the forbidden setAddr check. The Graph Agent0 subgraph is queried server-side. If _meta is older than seven days the agent is exclude. Graph never types an amount. We hit this. The live index is still 4 March 2026, so inclusion is blocked.
Hacky bits worth saying. The payer deployed the contract from MetaMask because this Linux box had no PRIVATE_KEY. A signing state is written before the wallet popup so a second tab cannot send a second batch. Replacement hashes are accepted only after a successful receipt. Demo hosting is Tailscale Serve onto 127.0.0.1, not a public port. Native USDC gas and ERC-20 USDC share the same pool, so spending the whole token balance leaves nothing for the settle tx. The old Yellow and LI.FI path is still in the tree. It is not wired into this payment flow.

name: Sluice
description: Pay-per-call API gateway monetizing AI inference in native USDC settled on Arc.
projectDescription:
Project Overview: Sluice — Pay-Per-Call API Monetization on Arc
Sluice is an autonomous, machine-native pay-per-call API gateway that monetizes digital services and AI inference in native USDC settled instantly on Arc Layer 1. It bridges the critical gap between traditional web APIs and autonomous AI agents by replacing human-dependent SaaS subscriptions with standard HTTP 402 Payment Required challenges and an immutable on-chain UsageVault smart contract.
The Problem
Today, API monetization is fundamentally broken for autonomous machines:
Subscriptions Fail Autonomous Agents: AI agents operate per task or per second. They cannot create accounts, complete KYC, sign monthly subscription contracts, or manage credit card portals.
Credit Card Rails are Too Slow & Expensive: Traditional card rails charge $0.30 + 2.9% per transaction and settle in 2–3 business days, making micro-transactions (e.g., $0.05 per AI inference call) economically impossible.
Private Database Lock-In: Traditional metered API billing records usage inside private off-chain databases (AWS RDS, Stripe logs). Neither the buyer, the autonomous agent, nor independent third-party auditors can verify whether the billing was accurate, transparent, or manipulated.
How Sluice Solves This
Sluice provides a trust-minimized, machine-speed monetization layer where payment, execution, and accounting happen autonomously in a single closed loop:
Standard HTTP 402 Challenge: When an unpaid human or AI agent sends an API request (e.g., to an AI inference endpoint), the Sluice Gateway intercepts the call and immediately returns a standard HTTP 402 Payment Required response with structured JSON containing the price (0.05 USDC), the network (Arc Testnet #5042002), and the target UsageVault contract address.
Sub-Second Native USDC Settlement: The caller transmits a micro-payment transaction on Arc. Because Arc uses native USDC for both transaction value and network gas, agents do not need secondary gas tokens or complex automated swaps.
On-Chain Accounting via UsageVault.sol: The payment triggers recordPayment() on a custom Solidity smart contract on Arc. The contract isolates seller balances, enforces Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) against reentrancy, and emits an immutable UsageRecorded event log.
Autonomous AI Inference Unlocking: The gateway validates the transaction receipt directly on Arc L1. Once verified, the gateway unlocks the protected microservice (powered by live Google Gemini 3.6 Flash neural models) and delivers the result along with verifiable on-chain transaction proof.
Key Technical Innovations
Zero Private Database Dependency: The Arc blockchain is the canonical database. If the API seller's servers go down, their revenue accounting, usage receipts, and withdrawable treasury remain completely intact and provable on-chain.
Customizable Withdrawal Thresholds: To prevent micro-dust fragmentation and optimize gas efficiency, sellers configure custom payout thresholds (e.g., minimum $0.50 USDC) before executing non-custodial batch withdrawals.
Meridian Neumorphic Mission Control: A high-precision tactile dashboard featuring real-time Arc L1 block telemetry, RPC latency ping tracking (~40ms), an interactive 402 visualizer aperture, 1-click prompt presets, and an on-chain audit ledger.
100% Real On-Chain Execution: Zero mocked data. The system is deployed live on Arc Testnet at contract address 0x2fB757b6158320b239a6eC4f7d7A0149D858D890 and is completely scripted for immediate Arc Mainnet deployment.
howItsMade:
How It's Made: Technical Architecture & Implementation Details

Technologies Used
Blockchain & Settlement: Arc Testnet (Chain ID 5042002), Solidity 0.8.20, Hardhat, Foundry, Ethers.js v6.
Partner / Core Network Technology: Arc Layer 1 Network (Native USDC as the gas and execution token, Arcscan Block Explorer).
AI & Machine Intelligence: Google Gemini 3.6 Flash neural inference engine.
Backend & Gateway Layer: Next.js 14 App Router (Node.js runtime serverless API routes, HTTP 402 middleware specification).
Frontend Architecture: React 18, HTML5 2D Canvas for procedural kinetic shaders, Canvas-Confetti, Lucide Icons.
Design & Material System: Meridian Neumorphic Design System v2.0 (Monochrome dark neumorphism, dual-directional tactile lighting, tri-font hierarchy: Fraunces serif for editorial numbers, Space Grotesk for technical controls, and IBM Plex Mono for the ledger).
How the Components Are Pieced Together
The Smart Contract Layer (UsageVault.sol): We wrote a non-custodial smart contract deployed on Arc Testnet at 0x2fB757b6158320b239a6eC4f7d7A0149D858D890. The contract implements isolated balance mappings per seller, enforces strict Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) reentrancy protection (zeroing state balances before external calls), and allows sellers to set automated withdrawal thresholds to batch transactions and eliminate micro-dust gas waste.

The HTTP 402 Payment Interceptor (/api/gate/summarize): Inbound requests hit the gateway. If no X-402-Payment-Proof header is attached, the route immediately halts and returns an RFC-compliant HTTP 402 Payment Required challenge alongside a WWW-Authenticate header containing the price (0.05 USDC), chain ID (5042002), and vault address.
On-Chain Settlement Verification & AI Execution: When the caller submits their transaction hash, the gateway queries the Arc Testnet RPC directly via provider.getTransactionReceipt(hash) and parses the UsageRecorded event emitted by UsageVault.sol. Only upon confirmed Arc L1 finality does the gateway forward the prompt to live Google Gemini 3.6 Flash, returning the inference payload, condense ratios, semantic insights, and a clickable Arcscan verification link.

How Arc Network Uniquely Benefited the Project
Building on Arc was essential for making this project possible:

Native USDC as Gas: On other chains, an AI agent needs two separate tokens: USDC for the API service and ETH/MATIC for network gas. On Arc, native USDC is the gas token. An agent only holds a single balance of native USDC, making automated, friction-free micro-payments possible.
Sub-Second Block Finality: AI agents cannot afford to wait 12–15 seconds for a block confirmation. Arc's sub-second block times allow the 402 payment and AI unlock loop to complete in near real time.
4. Notable Engineering & "Hacky" Solutions
Zero-Database Event Sourcing: We completely eliminated off-chain databases (no MongoDB, Postgres, or Redis). The seller treasury, historical call receipts, and audit trail are reconstructed dynamically on the client by querying event logs (UsageRecorded) directly from the Arc L1 contract. The blockchain is our canonical database.
Forced EIP-2255 Account Re-Selection: Web3 wallets like MetaMask normally cache connected accounts and silently reconnect without prompting. We implemented a cache-clearing routine using wallet_requestPermissions with { eth_accounts: {} } before calling eth_requestAccounts, forcing MetaMask to pop up the account picker on every single connect click so users can switch wallets effortlessly.
Deterministic Number Formatting across Server & Client: In Next.js SSR, system locale differences (e.g., Indian comma grouping 6,12,45,980 on the server vs US standard 61,245,980 on the browser) trigger React hydration mismatches. We implemented a deterministic regex formatter with suppressHydrationWarning to ensure byte-for-byte identical HTML across all locales.
Procedural 60 FPS Canvas Kinetic Wallpapers: Rather than using static CSS or heavy video backgrounds, we engineered a canvas engine (LiveWallpaperEngine.tsx) with 3 interactive mathematical shaders: Hydro (laminar wave deflection), Quantum (3D undulating mesh), and Celestial (gravitational orbit physics), responding in real time to pointer coordinates.

name: Tranched
description: A DeFi product splitting NVDA exposure into Senior and Junior tranches with different risk profiles.
projectDescription: NVDA Tranched Platform lets two investors take different levels of risk in the same NVDA strategy. Senior investors deposit USDC for a target 5% USD yield and receive priority in the settlement waterfall, while Junior investors take the residual risk in exchange for leveraged NVDA exposure. The protocol uses ERC 7540 vaults, a custom Uniswap v4 hook for just in time liquidity, an onchain NVDA price rail, a bounded strategy agent, and an accountant that handles tranche settlement at maturity.
howItsMade: Users deposit USDC into either the Senior or Junior tranche. Senior receives priority and targets a 5% USD yield, while Junior takes residual risk and leveraged NVDA exposure. Capital is deployed through a Uniswap v4 JIT strategy, with oracle checks and bounded agent decisions controlling execution.

name: Attestat
description: Show your EU ID wallet once, prove age in zero knowledge, get approved on chain. No passport copy.
projectDescription:
Exchanges, launchpads and funds keep your passport copy. Attestat lets a token issuer accept the EU digital identity wallet (EUDI) once and apply its approval to the customer's crypto wallet, with no document on chain.
Demo: an investor connects her crypto wallet; her address is not permitted. The official German EUDI test wallet answers: given name, family name, over 18. Her browser tab proves in zero knowledge that it says over 18; only the proof reaches the registry. The issuer approves separately. Door one: the fund token reads the record; she subscribes. Door two: a Uniswap v4 permissioned pool reads the same record; she buys, no second presentation. One revoke closes both doors.
On chain: one record per address and policy (predicate bits, expiry); no name, no document; the address may still be linked to a person.
Limits: test wallet, sample identity; sanctions and other checks simulated; revocation manual; Sepolia. https://attestat.dev, https://app.attestat.dev (read-only today).
Prior work: the builder's public verifier library Klartext-ID/klartext-verifier (pre-event) is used; the Noir circuit adapts eid-privacy's swiyu circuit; see DISCLOSURE.md. Repositories keep the former name Nachweis.
howItsMade:
Contracts (Foundry): AttestationRegistry: one decision per address and policy; evidence and approval separate, isEligible needs both; proof verifiers pluggable per policy; FundToken and the Uniswap checker read it. Tests: forge 155 passed (20 fork skipped), 8 app, 19 automation, 5 Playwright.
Proved: a holder-bound SD-JWT presentation (the wallet's signed credential format) from the pinned issuer key says over 18; its nonce commits to the crypto wallet address.
Browser route: the verifier relays the wallet's encrypted answer unopened; the investor's tab decrypts and proves with Noir UltraHonk (noir_js, bb.js). Sepolia: prove about 11 s, attest about 4.58 million gas.
Fallback: SP1 zkVM, Groth16 wrap; the server proves and submits and saw the presentation; we say so.
Identity: OpenID4VP from the official German test wallet into the builder's public verifier library. Unchecked: x5c chain to a trust anchor, status list, challenge freshness (Noir route).
Uniswap v4: Uniswap's permissioned-pool contracts as deployed on Sepolia, plus the 41-line EudiAllowlistChecker.sol: swap and liquidity allowed iff registry.isEligible. The portal quotes from slot0; the quoter cannot quote a permissioned pool.
eIDAS 2 asks for zero-knowledge proofs in the wallet, none selected yet, so our side proves today; a wallet proof would need a verifier adapter, not built.

name: WorldOnline
description: An application which helps mark attendance for employees in an office.
projectDescription: An application built using World Network's tooling which helps mark attendance for employees in an office. To perform a liveness check, we are using WorldOnline to allow people mark their attendance live. This will ensure fairness, liveness, uniqueness and also help the managers to regulate things properly.
howItsMade: We tried using World Network's tools but did not receive access to their Sandbox. That's bad and shameful to be happening at this stage. We could not use their toolings - have nothing more to add to it. This happened last time as well during ETHGlobal New Delhi - getting access to their toolings is very much tough. Building goes on suepr tough then

name: Indenture
description: A Uniswap v4 hook that stops a hacked AI fund manager from trading outside its mandate, on Hedera
projectDescription:
Indenture is a compliance-enforced, AI-managed investment fund on Hedera - a pool that can say "no."
AI agents are being handed real money, and every one of them can be prompt-injected. Today, if the model is tricked, the funds move. Indenture assumes the AI is already compromised and makes that irrelevant.
The system has three trust tiers:


The Manager (untrusted): an LLM agent that reads the fund's state and proposes trades. It is deliberately treated as hostile - it has a low-privilege key and no ability to enforce anything.


The Validator (independent): a separate service that receives ONLY { poolId, swapParams } — never the prompt, never the AI's reasoning. A strict Zod schema rejects anything else, so injected English has no path to the thing that signs. It re-derives every fact from source (Hedera mirror node, on-chain pool state, Chainlink price feed) and either signs an EIP-712 receipt or refuses with a named reason.


The Hook (on-chain): a Uniswap v4 PolicyHook re-checks the receipt with ecrecover, binds it to the exact swap parameters and sequence number, and runs four fixed integer covenant checks (max position %, max trade notional, etc.) before any swap settles. It makes zero external calls, so it can never be down or manipulated.


Result: even a fully jailbroken AI - or a stolen Validator key - cannot move funds outside the mandate.
Investor access is also gated: fund shares are an ERC-3643 permissioned token, so the pool refuses buyers who aren't verified, not just managers who overstep.
Every approval AND every refusal is permanently journaled to Hedera Consensus Service. Blocked attacks aren't hidden failures - they're a public, auditable part of the product. The web app includes a live Attack Console where you can type your own prompt injection, watch the AI manager fall for it completely, and watch the fund balance not move. The "Blocked" wall currently shows 15 attacks refused and $0.00 lost.
howItsMade:
Indenture is a TypeScript + Solidity monorepo: 8 contracts, 4 services, 4 shared packages and 221 passing tests, running on $0 of infrastructure with no database and no always-on server.
On-chain, we deployed Uniswap v4-core's PoolManager, unmodified, on Hedera testnet. That only became possible once Hedera added transient storage (HIP-865), and as far as we could find nobody had done it before. On top of it sits PolicyHook, a v4 hook that makes no decisions itself: it's a routing table from PoolId to an IPolicy contract. MandatePolicy verifies an EIP-712 receipt with ecrecover, binds it to the exact swap params and a sequence number so it can't be replayed, then runs 4 integer covenant checks (max position %, min cash %, max trade size, daily volume). We check covenants in afterSwap, against the real settled amounts rather than the requested ones, and a revert there still unwinds the whole swap. IndentureVault is the fund and acts as its own v4 router using flash accounting. Fund shares are ERC-3643 tokens, and a custom compliance module freezes transfers whenever the mandate is breached.
Off-chain there are three trust levels. The Manager is an LLM agent (any OpenAI-compatible API, with a pure-math fallback) that runs on a GitHub Actions cron and is treated as already hacked. The Validator is a Hono + Zod service on Cloudflare Workers / Vercel that signs with viem. Its only input is { poolId, swapParams }, parsed with Zod .strict(), so a prompt injection has no way to reach the signer. It re-derives everything else itself and signs or refuses. The Journaler writes every approval and every refusal to Hedera Consensus Service. The frontend is Next.js 15 + React 19 + wagmi + Tailwind with zero API routes, with GSAP, Lenis and OGL for motion.
Partner tech: Uniswap v4 is the one enforcement point an attacker can't route around, because it runs inside the swap. Hedera HCS is our tamper-proof audit log, and the Mirror Node REST API is our entire database: no Postgres, no indexer, no backend. Chainlink Data Feeds give the Validator an independent price that doesn't come from the pool being traded, and it refuses to sign on stale data. Because the hook only trusts a signer address, the Validator can later be replaced by a Chainlink DON without changing any contract.
Hacky bits: Foundry can't talk to Hedera's Hashio RPC relay directly, so we wrote a small Node JSON-RPC shim that rewrites requests between forge and Hashio. v4 hooks store their permissions in the address itself, so we brute-force a CREATE2 salt until the address has the right flag bits. To keep the EIP-712 struct identical across languages, we sign a test vector in TypeScript and recover it inside a Foundry test. Any drift breaks CI. Finally, there's a live attack button (a workflow input and an npm run inject CLI) that fires real prompt injections at the fund. You watch the AI fall for them and the balance stay put.

name: receivable.eth
description: Invoice financing where the invoice stays private: priced in a TEE, named on ENS, logged on Hedera.
projectDescription:
An invoice is a promise that pays in ninety days. A small business that needs the cash today can sell it, but factoring is expensive for one structural reason: the buyer cannot cheaply answer three questions. Is the invoice real? Will the customer pay? Has it already been sold to someone else? Every lender re-underwrites from scratch, and prices the uncertainty in.
receivable.eth removes the uncertainty without publishing the invoice.
A business connects its accounting system. A Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow pulls the invoice inside an AWS Nitro enclave, where the OAuth token, the full invoice, the customer identity and the debtor's payment history are decrypted and scored. None of it leaves. Exactly seven fields cross the enclave boundary — a business label, an invoice label, a keccak256 fingerprint of the document, the face value, the due date, a risk score and a discount rate — and the DON signs that report before anything is written on-chain.
The signed report mints inv-1042.acme.receivable.eth on ENSv2. A permissioned resolver decides who may write each record, so a business cannot name an invoice that was never verified. The name becomes the invoice's public identity: anyone can resolve it and read the score, the fingerprint and the terms, without ever seeing the document itself.
Before it can be financed, the fingerprint is registered on a Hedera Consensus Service topic. That topic is the double-financing registry — an invoice already claimed there is rejected, so the same receivable cannot be sold twice across the market. The financed position is then issued as an ERC-1400/1410 partitioned security through Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio, so investors hold a transfer-restricted instrument rather than a bare ERC-20.
Investors buy units at a discount — $0.968 per dollar of face value on the demo invoice — and the purchase moves USDC from the investor to the business in a single transaction. The market never custodies the cash. When the customer settles, holders redeem at par.
The privacy is the whole point. The lender gets a verified, uniquely-registered, priced claim. The business's customer list, payment history and invoice terms never leave the enclave.
howItsMade:
Monorepo on pnpm 9 + turbo, Node 20, Foundry for Solidity, vitest for TypeScript. Four packages typecheck and lint clean; 31 vitest tests and 32 Foundry tests pass.
Chainlink CRE — the pricing workflow is a Confidential Workflow, not a normal one. It uses cre.handlerInTee against @chainlink/cre-sdk 1.20.1, so the handler body executes inside an AWS Nitro enclave in us-west-2. rt.getSecret() decrypts the accounting-system OAuth token in-enclave, so it is never in node memory, and rt.usingTheDons() has the DON sign the seven-field report on the way out. This is the piece that makes the product possible at all: without a TEE you either publish the invoice on-chain or you ask the lender to trust an off-chain operator.
ENSv2 (namechain) on Sepolia — names are minted into a PermissionedRegistry; each business gets its own UserRegistry deployed as a proxy through VerifiableFactory, and records are written through a PermissionedResolver. Authorization is Enhanced Access Control, where roles are packed as nybbles inside a uint256. Building against it surfaced two real bugs in our role library: ALL_ROLES had been written as type(uint256).max, which sets every bit rather than every nybble, and ROLE_RENEW as 1 << 4 instead of 1 << 16 (nybble 4). Both are fixed with regression tests. All eight ENSv2 beta addresses in contracts/sepolia/deployments/sepolia.json were verified live on-chain rather than copied out of docs.
Hedera — two roles. HCS is the double-financing registry: the invoice fingerprint is submitted to a topic, and a duplicate is a hard rejection, not a warning. HTS is reached through the 0x167 precompile, which returns response codes instead of reverting, so every call site checks explicitly for 22 (SUCCESS); the test mock also has to treat 0 as success, because vm.etch copies contract code but not storage. The security itself is ERC-1400/1410 via Asset Tokenization Studio, with _DEFAULT_PARTITION = bytes32(uint256(1)).
Frontend — Next.js 15 App Router, Tailwind, viem + wagmi v2. We dropped wagmi's connector packages entirely: @coinbase/wallet-sdk drags in @x402/* and broke next build. Instead the app does raw EIP-6963 provider discovery, which is smaller and works with whatever wallet the browser announces.
Adapter service — Hono + Zod, with a file-backed state store that writes to a temp file and renames, so a crash mid-pipeline can't leave a half-written cursor. Every stage is idempotent (hasCompleted / completeStage), so a re-run resumes instead of double-registering an invoice.
Hacky bit worth mentioning: the demo seed generates due dates relative to boot and refuses to start if the seed is stale. An earlier version had every dueDate hardcoded in 2025, which silently made the entire market $0.00 financeable — everything "worked", it just quietly showed nothing.

name: Hardpull
description: Confidentially detects onchain loan stacking without any lender seeing another's book.
projectDescription: This project is a confidential exposure registry that lets undercollateralized onchain lenders detect loan stacking - a borrower drawing simultaneous, uncoordinated credit from several lenders who each believe the borrower is unencumbered - without any lender ever seeing another lender's book. A lender POSTs a subject to /v1/pull and gets back a verdict (CLEAR / WARNING / CRITICAL), an exposure bucket, an inquiry velocity, and a stacking flag - never a furnisher name, an exact amount, or a counterparty. Every pull is gated by borrower consent (a revocable onchain grant, non-transferable between lenders), metered per-inquiry via x402 on Hedera Testnet, and logged immutably to Hedera Consensus Service so the bureau itself cannot quietly edit its own audit trail. The cross-lender join that actually computes exposure runs inside a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow (a TEE), which is the only reason competing lenders are willing to contribute data at all - contributing normally means disclosing your loan book to a rival. Public on-protocol exposure (Aave v3, Morpho Blue, Maple) is normalized into one cross-protocol CreditPosition schema by a Graph subgraph, so the CRE workflow queries one shape instead of three separate protocol integrations. It is live end-to-end on Ethereum Sepolia (5 verified contracts) and Hedera Testnet, not a local demo.
howItsMade: Hardpull is a pnpm monorepo. contracts/ (Solidity 0.8.24, Foundry, OpenZeppelin) holds five contracts on Sepolia - SubjectRegistry and FurnisherRegistry for identity, ReciprocityLedger and ExposureCommitments for the confidential join's inputs, and VerdictAttestations, which only accepts signatures from the CRE workflow's signing key and is covered by a 10,000-run Foundry fuzz test on the disclosure invariant. cre/ (Go, Chainlink CRE Workflow SDK) is a Confidential Workflow that runs the actual cross-lender exposure join inside a TEE, verifies commitments against on-chain state, and strips furnisher identity at the type level before anything leaves the enclave - tested with the CRE SDK's testutils runtime so we can assert plaintext never appears in the verdict or any enclave log. api/ (TypeScript, Hono, Postgres, Redis, Zod) is the bureau surface: it enforces the consent gate before any compute or payment happens, issues an HTTP 402 challenge via @x402/core and @x402/hedera against Hedera Testnet with @hiero-ledger/sdk, prices pulls differentially by reciprocity standing, and writes every inquiry to an HCS topic. subgraph/ (The Graph, AssemblyScript) normalizes Aave v3, Morpho Blue and Maple positions into one CreditPosition schema that both the API and the CRE workflow query - one shape instead of three protocol integrations. mcp/ wraps that subgraph as an MCP server with four credit-file tools. console/ (Next.js 15, wagmi, viem, Tailwind) is the lender console and borrower file viewer, with @worldcoin/idkit wired for World ID personhood checks (built, not submitted as a partner prize). sdk-node/ is a typed client generated from api/openapi.yaml. The gnarliest part was making the TEE boundary honest rather than asserted: the CRE workflow's tests specifically assert that plaintext, furnisher identity, and both private keys never appear in the signed verdict or the enclave's own logs, not just that the workflow runs. Every commit on this repo was pair-built with Claude Code (Opus 5 and Sonnet 5) as co-author - it wrote the initial scaffolding for each package, drafted the Foundry tests and the CRE workflow handler, and helped debug the three integration bugs (documented in docs/DECISIONS.md) that only surfaced once the flow ran against real Sepolia and Hedera Testnet infrastructure instead of local mocks.

name: Reclaim
description: Executable receipts that let buyers cancel, refund, transfer, or dispute onchain purchases.
projectDescription: Reclaim turns payment receipts into executable interfaces for onchain purchases. Instead of a receipt being a passive record, each purchase creates a portable receipt that exposes the rights attached to that transaction, such as cancelling an eligible purchase, requesting a refund, transferring the claim, or opening a dispute. Arc is the canonical settlement layer, where USDC is held and purchase state is enforced by the escrow contract. ENSv2 gives each receipt a portable identity such as order-1.reclaimprotocol.eth, together with records describing its status, amount, merchant, claim owner, deadlines, and available actions. The result is a receipt that acts like a remote control for the purchase while keeping financial authority onchain.
howItsMade:
Reclaim uses a Solidity escrow contract deployed on Arc Testnet with USDC for settlement. The contract manages purchase lifecycle states including PAID, REFUND_REQUESTED, CANCELLED, REFUNDED, FINALIZED, and DISPUTED, and exposes the actions currently available to each user. We built and tested the contract with Foundry and verified a real 49 USDC lifecycle on Arc: approve → purchase → PAID → cancel → CANCELLED → funds returned.
The application is built with TanStack Start, React, TypeScript, Vite, and viem. The frontend independently reads canonical order state from Arc instead of trusting browser state.
For ENS, Reclaim uses ENSv2 Beta on Ethereum Sepolia. reclaimprotocol.eth acts as the parent namespace, with a Permissioned Registry creating receipt subnames such as order-1.reclaimprotocol.eth. A Permissioned Resolver stores receipt metadata including status, amount, Arc chain ID, escrow contract, order ID, merchant, claim owner, deadlines, transferability, and available actions.
A dedicated server-side synchronizer reads the canonical Arc order and updates ENS only after verifying the real onchain state. ENS never authorizes or moves funds. We also use ENSv2 Enhanced Access Control so authoritative receipt fields remain controlled by the synchronizer while the current claim owner can receive narrowly scoped permissions such as editing a customer note.
GitHub Actions is used for contract deployment and real lifecycle verification, and the application is being packaged as a single Vercel deployment with a same-origin /api/receipt-sync server endpoint.

name: Prompt2API
description: AI-powered factory that turns prompts into live, reusable blockchain data APIs.
projectDescription:
Prompt2API turns a plain-English request into a live blockchain data API that AI agents can access and pay for automatically.
Creating a custom onchain dataset normally requires writing event decoders, configuring an indexing pipeline, validating it against blockchain data, operating storage infrastructure, and building an API. Prompt2API turns that process into a prompt-driven workflow.
A user begins by describing the data they need, such as: “Track Deposit and Withdraw events for this ERC-4626 vault on Base and provide raw events and hourly flows.” Prompt2API interprets the request, checks whether it is supported, and creates a reusable data pipeline. If required information is missing, it asks a follow-up question. Requests outside the supported scope are rejected instead of producing an incorrect pipeline.
The hackathon version supports Deposit and Withdraw activity from one to three ERC-4626 vaults on Base. It uses The Graph Substreams to process live blockchain data, normalizes activity from different vaults into one standard format, stores the resulting records in PostgreSQL, and publishes typed REST endpoints for raw events, hourly flows, filtering, pagination, metadata, and indexing health.
Before deployment, the operator can review the interpreted request, selected contracts and events, Substreams module graph, live validation results, and artifact hashes. This makes the otherwise automated build process visible and ensures that the deployed pipeline is exactly the one that was tested and approved.
Once the dataset is live, another AI agent can request data directly from its API. Protected endpoints respond with HTTP 402 and machine-readable payment instructions. The agent validates the payment requirements, pays 0.001 HBAR through Blocky402 on Hedera testnet, retries the original request with payment proof, and receives the blockchain data automatically.
The frontend’s “Pay 0.001 HBAR & load data” button visualizes this autonomous interaction for the hackathon demonstration. It shows the purchased records, payment receipt, Hedera transaction ID, and HashScan verification link. In normal agent-to-agent use, the x402 client performs the same flow without a button or human involvement.
Prompt2API therefore removes two major barriers to agent-accessible blockchain data: creating and operating specialized indexing infrastructure, and managing subscriptions or manually issued API keys. The Graph provides the live, reusable data infrastructure, while Hedera enables agents to purchase that data through fast x402 micropayments.
howItsMade:
Prompt2API is built like a controlled compiler. Gemini interprets what blockchain data the user wants, while trusted backend code decides what is valid and what can run.
The frontend uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, and custom CSS. It provides the prompt builder, structured overrides, pipeline status, live validation results, artifact approval, dataset tables, API examples, and a visual x402 payment demonstration. An Express and TypeScript backend controls planning, builds, validation, deployment, dataset queries, and payment protection. PostgreSQL stores pipeline state, build jobs, indexed blockchain events, and synchronization cursors.
We use gemini-3-flash-preview through Google’s official @google/genai SDK. Gemini converts a natural-language request into a strict PipelineSpec. It can return only one of three results: a ready plan, clarification questions, or an unsupported result.
Gemini is deliberately limited. It cannot return Rust, SQL, shell commands, dependencies, package names, file paths, provider endpoints, or credentials. It only identifies configuration such as the network, vault addresses, Deposit or Withdraw events, starting block, and requested API outputs.
The backend parses the response with Zod and validates every EVM address with viem. It confirms that the request uses Base, contains one to three valid vault addresses, includes only supported ERC-4626 events, and has a valid non-negative start block. The backend then derives event topics, Substreams filters, identifiers, package parameters, schema names, paths, and commands without relying on model-generated executable text.
Every pipeline comes from a reviewed ERC-4626 template. The template contains fixed Rust mapping code, Protobuf definitions, the ERC-4626 ABI, PostgreSQL schema, DatabaseChanges mapper, Substreams manifest structure, dependencies, and pinned toolchain configuration. Only validated parameters are inserted into the generated package.
The generated package composes The Graph’s pinned [email protected] Substreams package. It consumes the reusable filtered_events module instead of rebuilding Base block extraction from scratch. Our Rust/WASM mapper then decodes ERC-4626 Deposit and Withdraw logs and converts them into one normalized event format.
This composition makes the pipeline reusable. Adding another ERC-4626 vault only changes the validated event filter. It does not require another Rust mapper, ABI, Protobuf model, SQL schema, or API implementation. One pipeline can process one to three vaults while returning the same standardized data structure.
The backend runs the Substreams CLI as a restricted child process. It uses fixed executables, argument arrays, canonical artifact paths, reduced environment variables, output limits, cancellation, and timeouts. It never passes model output directly to a shell.
The build process compiles the reviewed Rust mapper into WebAssembly, creates a versioned .spkg, inspects the package metadata, and checks the module graph. Because the executable mapper is shared between pipelines, Prompt2API uses a fingerprinted Cargo target cache. If the Rust, Protobuf, ABI, Cargo files, toolchain, and build script have not changed, it safely reuses the reviewed WASM and repackages it with the new validated parameters. This significantly shortens repeat builds.
Before deployment, Prompt2API runs the package over a fixed 100-block range of live Base data supplied through The Graph Market. It checks the decoded records for allowed vault addresses, supported event types, deterministic event IDs, unsigned raw amounts, block metadata, transaction hashes, and log indexes.
The frontend displays these stages so the hackathon judges can see what is happening. It explains when Prompt2API prepares the mapper, inspects the package, verifies the composed module graph, and validates against live Base data. These intermediate screens provide transparency for operators; an AI agent purchasing data does not need to interact with them.
If the live range is valid but contains no matching events, Prompt2API reports NO_ACTIVITY_IN_SAMPLE instead of treating it as a provider error. The operator can enter another start block and retry the validation without making another Gemini request.
After validation, the operator reviews and approves the exact pipeline. Approval contains SHA-256 hashes of both the generated configuration and compiled .spkg. Before deployment, the backend verifies the reviewed template files again and recalculates the package hash. If anything changed after review, deployment is rejected.
Once approved, Prompt2API creates a separate PostgreSQL schema for the dataset and starts a resumable Substreams PostgreSQL sink. The sink processes historical blocks from the chosen starting block and continues toward the live Base chain head. It stores its cursor so it can resume after a restart. Deterministic event IDs prevent duplicate database rows.
PostgreSQL views calculate hourly deposits, withdrawals, net flows, event counts, and unique owners without requiring the Substreams package to be recompiled. The Express API exposes typed endpoints for metadata, health, schema, raw events, hourly flows, filters, and cursor-based pagination.
The Graph is load-bearing in two ways. First, The Graph Market supplies the live Base data used for validation and continuous synchronization. Second, the composable ethereum-common package provides the reusable EVM event-filtering layer under our standardized ERC-4626 mapper. This supports both composable Graph products and AI tooling that turns one natural-language request into a working Substreams pipeline.
For payments, Prompt2API uses x402 v2 with native HBAR on Hedera testnet. Metadata, schema, and health endpoints remain free. Raw-event and hourly-flow endpoints are protected as paid data products.
When an agent calls a paid endpoint without payment, the API returns HTTP 402 with machine-readable requirements. These specify the exact payment scheme, Hedera testnet, native HBAR, amount, recipient, facilitator fee payer, and requested resource.
A separate TypeScript consumer agent uses the official x402 packages for Hedera. Before signing anything, it validates the x402 version, network, asset, price limit, recipient, fee payer, and requested Prompt2API resource. It then creates the Hedera payment authorization and automatically retries the original HTTP request with the payment proof.
Blocky402 verifies the proof and settles the payment on Hedera testnet. After successful settlement, the API returns the requested Graph-derived data together with a PAYMENT-RESPONSE receipt. The payment produces a real Hedera transaction that can be independently verified on HashScan.
The payer’s private key exists only inside the consumer-agent process. It is never exposed to the browser, Gemini, or the Prompt2API data service.
For the hackathon demo, the frontend includes a “Pay 0.001 HBAR & load data” button. A server-only Next.js route starts the same restricted consumer-agent process, purchases the data, and returns only the dataset response and settlement receipt to the browser. The page then shows the purchased Base events, Hedera transaction ID, and HashScan link.
The button makes the autonomous payment visible to judges. In normal use, an external AI agent performs the complete flow directly:
Request API → receive HTTP 402 → validate and pay in HBAR → retry automatically → receive data
No subscription, manually issued API key, checkout page, or human action is required for the agent’s paid data request.

name: AgentTrust
description: A pay-per-query, manipulation-resistant trust score for autonomous agents.
projectDescription:
AgentTrust is a pay-per-query, manipulation-resistant trust score for autonomous agents. As AI agents increasingly transact with each other on-chain, each carries an ERC-8004 identity with a self-reported reputation, which is trivially gameable. An agent can feed itself glowing feedback from wallets it controls and present a perfect score to whoever it's about to transact with.
AgentTrust reads an agent's on-chain ERC-8004 record and analyzes the structural integrity of its reputation rather than just surfacing the raw average. It detects manipulation such as self-dealing, ungrounded feedback, missing validations, and Sybil rings, then returns a trust score a counterparty can check for a fraction of a cent before transacting. It separates trustScore from confidence, so a brand-new agent is marked UNKNOWN and never punished with a low score.
howItsMade: It composes two of The Graph's products: the Agent0 / ERC-8004 subgraph for an agent's feedback and raters, and the Subgraph MCP to cross-check whether each rater is itself a real, active agent or a throwaway wallet. This enables Sybil-ring detection that no single query exposes. The whole check is sold as an x402-payable MCP tool and Recipe via Bazantic, and scoring is permissionless: any agent can be vetted by its agentId whether or not it has ever heard of AgentTrust.

name: Common
description: Shared spending memory for AI agents: pay once via x402 on Hedera, every agent reuses the evidence.
projectDescription:
Common is a shared spending memory for AI agents: one agent pays for an open-model evaluation, every later agent reuses the result instead of paying again.
How it works: an agent sends a goal and a budget. Common checks memory for a matching, fresh report. If one exists, it's returned with no payment. If not, Common reserves budget on a Hedera smart contract, pays the evaluation service 0.5 HBAR via x402, runs two open Qwen models through five browser tasks on a controlled support-desk app (each task checked against the final page state), and stores the report. If the budget is below the price, the agent rejects the purchase.
Every decision buy, reuse, wait, reject is published to a Hedera Consensus Service topic with the agent's reasoning, and every payment carries a HashScan-verifiable transaction id.
howItsMade:
TypeScript monorepo: orchestrator (API + dashboard), paid evaluation service, Playwright runner, Solidity contract, vanilla-JS frontend. Models run locally via Ollama (Qwen3 1.7B/4B).
Payments use x402 on Hedera: the service answers 402, the orchestrator signs a partially-signed HBAR transfer, and the Blocky402 facilitator settles it. Agents never hold keys; one payment module signs, only against a matching on-chain reservation.
The CommonBudget contract is a ledger, not a vault: one purchase per evaluation configuration, claimed atomically, with payment and delivery recorded separately - a paid job whose report fails is never silently repurchased, and unclear settlements are reconciled against the mirror node, never retried blindly. Decisions are published to HCS.
The buyer agent is gpt-4o-mini choosing only among actions the orchestrator permits; a deterministic policy takes over if it's unavailable, so the money path never depends on an LLM.

name: FairStake
description: Proof of person, not passport — reusable investor credentials for sybil-resistant fair launches.
projectDescription:
Fair launches get sybil-farmed. Full KYC is overkill for small pools. FairStake separates human eligibility from capital commitment.
Investors prove they're a unique live human via World Selfie Check — one nullifier, enforced on-chain. They receive a portable investor passport (ENS-shaped credentials on Sepolia) with max commit and expiry. They then commit USDC into fair-launch pools on Arc Testnet with per-investor caps.
Unverified wallets fail closed. The Sybil Test: verified investor commits → fresh wallet reverts → same passport works on Round 2 without a second selfie.
Proof of person, not proof of passport.
howItsMade:
Built with Scaffold-ETH 2 (Next.js + Hardhat). Smart contracts: FairStakePool on Arc Testnet (USDC commits, nullifier reuse guard, fail-closed gating) and InvestorPassportRegistry on Sepolia (ENS-shaped text records).
World IDKit v4 + RP signing server for Selfie Check; verified nullifiers flow through /api/world/verify → /api/credential/issue, which writes credentials on-chain via the deployer verifier key.
Frontend: Judge Theater with Sybil Attack Theater (50-bot simulation), KYC Treadmill vs Passport contrast, and live commit flow on Arc. Deployed on Arc (0x53fa…3766) and Sepolia (0x53fa…3766). 5 passing Hardhat tests.

name: Vela
description: A spending mandate in a Ledger's Secure Element: one tap per envelope, not one per transaction.
projectDescription:
An agent that spends money needs a credential on whatever machine it runs on, and every guardrail then runs inside the process being attacked: a spend cap in the same memory a prompt injection just reached, an allowlist in a file that process can edit. Hardware custody solves the adjacent problem. It proves you approved, one tap per transaction, and enforces no limit at all. Both assume something an autonomous agent cannot have.
Vela moves the decision instead of the human. A native BOLOS app for the Ledger Flex holds a mandate in the Secure Element: this agent, this budget, this ceiling per payment, these payees, these contracts, this many draws an hour. A human grants it once with a tap. After that the agent runs unattended on a machine with no key on it, and every payment is checked inside a chip no host can read or edit. One tap per envelope, not one per transaction.
Then the refusal nothing on a host can make. A transfer names its payee in the transaction body, so any software policy can read it. A contract call names only the contract; where the value lands is an ABI argument the body never interprets, and under prompt injection that argument is exactly what an attacker rewrites. The chip reads that word out of the calldata it is about to sign and compares it with its own account. On a host, the attacker is already inside the thing doing the checking.
All four agents run on GitHub runners with no USB bus, no seed and no envelope. Each paid inside its own ceiling and was refused above it. Every draw is anchored on Hedera with a 29-byte statement the chip signed, so anyone can check the log from the mirror node in their own browser.
howItsMade:
The Secure Element app is about 5,400 lines of C on BOLOS for the Ledger Flex: NVRAM mandate storage for eight agents, an on-chip Hedera protobuf serialiser so the chip builds the transaction body itself rather than signing bytes it was handed, and ordered refusals on expiry, payee, ceiling, budget, rate, and the recipient argument inside contract calldata.
Payments are x402 over Hedera, signed on-device and settled on testnet. Every draw is anchored to an HCS topic carrying the chip's own signed statement. A Node verifier and a browser verifier both read that log from the mirror node and nothing else, held in step by a parity suite: one that agrees with itself in a terminal and disagrees in a browser would be the worst possible failure for a claim like this.
An agent's toolset is derived from the mandate the chip published, so one whose envelope allows no contract calls is never told that swapping exists. Its capabilities come from a broker whose secrets are sealed under the Ledger Key Ring Protocol, so a host holds a membership rather than an API key. A Chainlink CRE workflow in an AWS Nitro enclave can narrow a mandate and is provably unable to widen it.
The console talks to the Flex over WebHID with nothing installed. macOS gives the HID interface to one process, so the tab lends the device back on the bridge's own port and the gateway never learns a browser is at the other end. The deployed copy has no gateway and still reads your chip, walking the slots itself with a parser pinned field by field against the gateway's.

name: The Solvent
description: One shared maker-liquidity layer for every intent—protocol-agnostic, non-custodial, cross-chain.
projectDescription:
Solvent is a zero-inventory, protocol-agnostic intent resolver built around 1inch Aqua and 1inch SwapVM.
DeFi liquidity is fragmented across pools, price ranges, protocols, strategies, and chains before anyone knows where demand will appear. A maker may have enough assets to fill an order, yet those assets may be in the wrong place or stranded on another network.
R measured approximately $1.84 billion of concentrated liquidity across leading pools and found 29.5% completely outside its fee-earning range. On the measured Uniswap v3-family pools, the broader unused share reached approximately 85% after including in-range liquidity untouched by swaps.
Those assets have not disappeared; they were allocated before demand arrived. A conventional pool deposit can serve only that pool, while concentrated liquidity can trade only inside its selected range. Quoting across markets therefore requires makers to divide capital in advance.
Intent solvers compensate by funding inventories across every supported protocol and chain. This ties up capital, requires continuous rebalancing, and makes new networks and long-tail pairs expensive to serve.
Solvent addresses one question: How can a single non-custodial maker balance safely serve multiple strategies, intent protocols, and chains without requiring the resolver to maintain fragmented, pre-funded inventories?
Solvent is a zero-inventory, protocol-agnostic intent resolver built around 1inch Aqua and 1inch SwapVM.
Aqua lets one maker wallet balance support multiple programmable positions. Tokens remain in the maker's wallet and move only when an authorized swap executes. This is shared liquidity, not leverage: Solvent does not create debt or make the same assets spendable twice. Every execution remains limited by the maker's real wallet balance.
SwapVM lets makers define their pricing strategies. Solvent requests live quotes from those programs and executes without bypassing the maker's pricing logic.
Solvent builds a complete resolution layer around these primitives. It discovers positions, requests quotes, estimates execution costs, constructs routes, reserves balances, submits settlement transactions, and reconciles its local state with the blockchain.
The maker retains custody and controls prices. Solvent discovers orders, calculates routes, coordinates settlement, pays execution costs, and retains the remaining spread from profitable fills. Tokens may temporarily pass through a filler contract, but Solvent holds no inventory before or after settlement.
Protocol-specific adapters normalize formats such as UniswapX and ERC-7683 for Solvent's Rust engine, allowing them to access the same Aqua-backed liquidity while keeping their signatures and settlement interfaces isolated.
The engine validates the order, discovers eligible positions, requests live SwapVM quotes, and checks profitability after maker payments, gas, slippage, protocol requirements, and safety margins.
Solvent's water-fill routing algorithm divides an order among several positions according to marginal price. It combines the competitive portions of multiple curves instead of forcing the complete trade through one increasingly expensive source.
Before execution, Solvent's reservation ledger holds the selected liquidity so simultaneous orders cannot plan against the same maker balance. Aqua supplies the final on-chain balance guarantee.
A thin Solidity filler validates the callback and execution plan, calls SwapVM for the selected positions, and delivers the promised output to the intent protocol's settlement contract.
The same-chain trade is atomic. If a balance changed, a quote became invalid, or the required output cannot be delivered, everything reverts. The Rust engine reconciles the receipt and settles or releases its reservations.
Cross-chain delivery and payment happen on separate networks, so they cannot be completed atomically in one transaction. SolventX separates the lifecycle into four responsibilities: The Compact locks, Aqua fills, Chainlink CCIP proves, and Circle CCTP repays.
The user's source funds enter a non-custodial resource lock through Uniswap's The Compact rather than a Solvent-owned wallet.
Solvent prices the destination fill using its same-chain quoting, routing, and reservation systems. Maker tokens are sourced just in time from Aqua-backed balances and delivered to the recipient, eliminating the need for a Solvent treasury on every destination chain.
After delivery, the destination contract records the fill against a unique order identifier. The record binds the proof to the chains, assets, recipient, delivered amount, and settlement contract, preventing one fill from being reused for another order. Chainlink CCIP carries authenticated proof to the source chain, where the receiver verifies the remote chain, sender, order, and settlement payload before allowing the Compact claim.
Circle CCTP then burns USDC on the source chain and mints native USDC on the destination chain after attestation, providing the repayment asset. CCIP proves delivery; CCTP moves repayment value.
A recoverable Rust state machine tracks the lock, destination delivery, proof, claim, CCTP transfer, repayment, and reconciliation. Delays and temporary failures can be retried without duplicating deliveries, proofs, claims, or repayments.
SwapVM strategies provide on-chain price protection: Solvent cannot force a maker to trade outside the conditions encoded in their program. The reservation ledger prevents off-chain overcommitment, and Aqua remains the final real-balance safeguard.
Solvent also identifies profitable opportunities to restore maker positions after a trade. Part of the surplus remaining after restoration costs can return to the maker as a rebate. This is loss-versus-rebalancing mitigation and arbitrage-value recapture, not protection from every form of MEV.
The Rust engine handles normalization, quoting, profitability, routing, reservations, tracking, retry, and reconciliation. Thin Solidity contracts enforce custody, pricing, callback authentication, and settlement constraints. Protocol adapters let new intent systems reuse the core liquidity engine; not every protocol is already integrated.
Privy provides embedded wallets and email or social authentication for makers and takers. Users receive a familiar onboarding experience while custody and settlement remain enforced by their wallets and the contracts.
The interface lets participants create maker positions, request quotes, submit intents, inspect route allocations, follow same-chain and cross-chain settlement, and view restoration opportunities without hiding the underlying execution stages.
Makers can use one non-custodial balance across more strategies. Takers access routes combining several positions. Intent protocols gain reusable Aqua-backed liquidity, while resolvers can enter new markets without funding a separate treasury for every protocol and chain.
Solvent's distinctive contribution is the non-custodial passive-maker, reservation, routing, settlement, and protocol-adapter layer built around Aqua. It separates the capital provider from the resolver operator and makes externally owned maker liquidity usable across heterogeneous intent flows.
Shared capital follows intent demand instead of remaining fragmented.
One balance. Every intent. Every chain.
howItsMade:
We built Solvent as a hybrid off-chain intent engine and on-chain settlement system. The backend is written in Rust and handles the full intent lifecycle: ingesting orders, discovering eligible maker positions, requesting live quotes, calculating profitability after gas, routing trades across multiple positions, reserving liquidity to prevent concurrent fills from over-committing the same balance, and tracking every order through a deterministic state machine until completion or recovery.
On-chain settlement is implemented in Solidity using thin filler contracts. For same-chain swaps, the filler connects intent protocols such as UniswapX and ERC-7683 to 1inch Aqua. Aqua lets makers keep tokens in their own wallets while exposing programmable virtual balances, and 1inch SwapVM provides the pricing and swap-execution layer. This allowed us to build a zero-inventory resolver: Solvent does not maintain a pre-funded trading treasury and instead sources maker liquidity just in time during atomic settlement.
For cross-chain execution, the taker’s source funds are secured in The Compact while destination liquidity is supplied through Aqua. Chainlink CCIP transports authenticated proof that the destination fill occurred, enabling the source-side claim to be released safely. Circle CCTP then burns USDC on the source chain and mints native USDC on the destination chain to repay the liquidity used for the fill, avoiding wrapped assets and traditional bridge liquidity pools.
Privy provides embedded wallets and a familiar email/social-login experience, removing the need for browser extensions, seed-phrase setup, or manual network configuration. A notable engineering challenge was coordinating systems with very different timing and failure models. We addressed this by representing cross-chain settlement as an explicit, recoverable Rust state machine and separating quoting, liquidity reservation, transaction execution, proof delivery, claiming, and repayment into individually observable stages. The result is a non-custodial architecture in which Solidity enforces atomic settlement, Rust coordinates execution and recovery, Aqua supplies reusable liquidity, CCIP proves delivery, CCTP handles repayment, and Privy makes the system accessible to users.

name: StakeFit
description: Fastest runners on Google Fitbit take the pot over the catalog distance
projectDescription:
Racing costs a day, not a race. You pay the entry weeks ahead, then work moves, travel moves, a knee complains, and the bib goes unused. Even when you show up, the start time rarely matches the shape you were in that month. So people either skip the race and eat the fee, or run it flat and wonder what the money bought. The training was real. The result was not.
StakeFit races the run you already did. Sign in with Google. Google Health is the only session source, so nothing new gets strapped on. An admin opens one distance from a fixed catalog of 50 m, 200 m, 5 k, and 10 k. You pay the HBAR entry from HashPack, then go run whenever the day allows. We do not time the full lap. A Fitbit bout counts if it started on your own civil day and covered the catalog distance, and the score is the catalog distance at that bout's pace. A 200 m effort scores a 50 m race honestly. Sessions keep syncing on their own, so there is nothing to submit.
Other times stay hidden until the race resolves. That keeps the day a pace market instead of a live leaderboard you can chase. When the board opens, the top three split the pot 50 / 30 / 20. A World Selfie Check stands between a result and the money, so one person cannot farm a pot with three accounts. A soulbound HTS run card mints as the receipt. Sepolia holds the market. Hedera holds the pot, the consensus trail, and the token.
Next is more wrists. Apple Watch through HealthKit, Garmin, Strava, and Whoop are the same shape of problem: a session with a start time, a distance, and a duration. One qualification rule already sits behind a single shared function, so adding a source means adding a reader, not a second scoring model. More sources also make richer races possible, like heart-rate-capped efforts or elevation-adjusted pace, without asking anyone to change how they already train.
howItsMade:
Google is the Fitbit pipe. OAuth lands on the orchestrator. Access tokens stay in process memory. Health Connect exercise sessions are pulled after login after pay and on a background tick for anyone who has entered. The web client sends X-Timezone so day bounds are the runner's civil day not the UTC host. That is how we pick the right bout and not yesterday's.
The catalog is a sealed TypeScript table. createMarket will not take a custom meter count. Qualification is one shared function. Start in the local day. Distance millimeters at least the catalog. Score is catalog millimeters at session pace or duration times catalog over distance if pace is missing. CRE is written to emit that duration only. The orchestrator mirrors ingestWorkout so the same number shows without a live TEE.
Entry is x402 v2. HashPack signs the 402 accept. HBAR settles to the Hedera pay-to account. StakeFitMarket on Sepolia is create enter result resolve. HCS is the trail we replay after a restart. HTS mints the soulbound run NFT. World verifies Selfie Check and we keep the nullifier. The Graph is an indexed read of Sepolia. The live board is orchestrator plus the contract plus HCS.
The useful bit is treating Fitbit as an already-run oracle and refusing a public board until resolve so the pot is a catalog-pace market not a live leaderboard.

name: Sovereign
description: Private financial agreements for autonomous agents, enforced onchain.
projectDescription: Sovereign is a privacy-aware financial agreement protocol for autonomous agents. Treasury and strategy agents discover intents, negotiate bounded financial terms, and sign agreements using EIP-712. Sensitive risk policies remain private while cryptographic commitments bind them to onchain agreements. A Chainlink CRE workflow evaluates agreement and position conditions using private policy inputs and publishes only actionable decisions. Our demonstration uses CRE’s simulation workflow with a verified receiver, real Sepolia and Arc Testnet transactions, and a trusted Sepolia-to-Arc relayer for escrow enforcement.
howItsMade: Sovereign combines Solidity smart contracts on Ethereum Sepolia, USDC escrow on Arc Testnet, TypeScript/Bun autonomous agents, SQLite-backed orchestration, EIP-712 signatures, and Chainlink CRE workflows. The agent runtime indexes finalized IntentCreated events, creates idempotent jobs, uses leased execution claims to prevent duplicate work, and runs Treasury and Strategy agents without a browser or per-intent environment changes. Negotiated terms are signed and validated before onchain agreement finalization. CRE receives private policy inputs and authenticated position data, then produces minimal validation or breach decisions. The public-chain demonstration uses CRE’s MockKeystoneForwarder simulation path; finalized Sepolia decisions are verified and relayed to Arc for escrow locking or unwinding.

prizes.rawText: Chainlink -  Best Confidential Workflow

name: Interline
description: Lend in a pool or open a named credit line with other people
projectDescription: Interline is credit in two forms that do not share funds. You can supply or borrow in an isolated pool like a normal market, with collateral and a health factor. You can also open a named agreement with one other address, where that lender puts up the cash, the other side has to accept, borrowed money sits in a restricted vault, and the stress path is a due date or a recall rather than a pool liquidation. Same wallet can be a supplier, a borrower, a lender, and a counterparty at once. Roles come from the agreement, not from a badge on the account.
howItsMade:
Interline is an isolated lending protocol plus bilateral direct credit, live on Ethereum Sepolia. Contracts are Solidity 0.8.24, compiled with Foundry/Forge (via-IR). Each pool is its own LendingMarket with its own oracle, caps, and liquidation params; OTC lines are DirectCreditFacility clones. Factories do not carry market initcode — we split MarketDeployer, DirectFacilityDeployer, and VaultDeployer so factory bytecode stays under EIP-170. Pricing is a ChainlinkPairOracle (collateral/USD, loan/USD, L2 sequencer). On Sepolia, those feeds are mocks; the UI still reads mainnet Chainlink and can push those answers onto the mocks. Interest, LTV, and liquidation math live in a shared TypeScript package so the keeper, indexer, and UI use the same ray formulas as the contracts.
The app is Next.js 15 (Turbopack) + React 19 + wagmi/viem. Writes go wallet → contract. Reads are layered on purpose: a Hono + Drizzle indexer first, then MarketLens RPC, and we never show fake “live” stub loans in production. Activity can come from a Sepolia subgraph on The Graph, then the indexer; balances never depend on The Graph. ENS is mainnet-only reverse/forward lookup so counterparties can be name.eth while the checksum address stays on screen. Wallets are injected (MetaMask, including Ledger through MetaMask) plus optional WalletConnect for Ledger Live.
Partner stack that actually ships: Chainlink for every LTV quote, ENS for human-readable counterparties, The Graph for the activity feed without making it the source of truth for money, Ledger as a first-class connect path, WalletConnect for Ledger Live. Notable hacks: Sepolia builds with optimizer_runs = 1 and stripped metadata to fit EIP-170; a relative viem/utils alias because Turbopack rejects Windows absolute imports of the hoisted workspace viem; mainnet sits in the wagmi config as a read-only chain for ENS, not as a switchable write network.

name: Detent
description: Preview a coupon run line by line, then lock the treasury key to exactly that transaction
projectDescription:
Whoever operates a tokenized security pays coupons, runs court ordered transfers and handles redemptions with a treasury key that can sign anything the contract exposes. The only check before signing is reading an explorer or trusting a script, so a lapsed allowlist entry, a wrong amount or a thin treasury shows up after the transaction lands.
Detent puts one step in that gap. The operator console reads the holder register and compliance state of an ERC-1400 security, replays the corporate action off chain and prints the plan: every holder and amount, every row the compliance module will reject with its reason (expired allowlist entry, overdue KYC, sanctions hold), and the treasury cover and headroom. Two officers approve, which is a key quorum of two. The plan's exact calldata is then compiled into a wallet policy that allows that contract, that function and those parameter bytes, and denies everything else by default.
If anyone edits a single amount and sends it, the key refuses and names the condition that failed and the byte where the payload diverged. The untouched plan still signs with the same wallet under the same policy, and the lock is spent afterwards. Before the policy opens, the plan hash is anchored on a PlanAnchor contract on Hedera testnet, and a permanent record page reads it back with no key.
What is live today: the console, the refusal, the quorum and the on chain anchor on Hedera testnet. The register reads from the cached register snapshot, and the policy is evaluated by a local mirror of the Privy policy engine. The live ATS register read and the Privy server wallet path are implemented and tested against mocks, and switch on with environment variables.
howItsMade:
Frontend: Next.js 16 App Router with the React Compiler, React 19, TypeScript strict, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn on Base UI, Motion (loaded after hydration to keep the first load small) and next-themes for light and dark mode. The app has a command palette, a stepped five section console, and a record route per plan hash.
Hedera and Asset Tokenization Studio: register reads are hand written viem calls over the Hashio JSON-RPC relay (chain 296) to the ATS ERC-1400 facets, balanceOfByPartition and canTransferByPartition, checking each credit from the issuer treasury. We decode the EIP-1066 status byte and the error selector, so a compliance refusal is shown as a named hold reason instead of a revert. ATS gave us partitions, KYC and control list semantics, which is exactly the compliance state the plan has to respect.
Privy: the approved plan becomes a Privy wallet policy on a server wallet owned by a key quorum of two. Conditions use ethereum_transaction for chain id and target, and ethereum_calldata with the ABI for the function selector and partition. Requests carry RFC 8785 canonicalized ECDSA P-256 authorization signatures and idempotency keys, and the policy is detached and revoked on every exit path, including lock expiry. Privy policies cannot pin whole dynamic arrays, so the server also enforces the exact calldata byte for byte and reports the first diverging byte.
Server: a single fail closed route. The server derives the plan itself from the register and the operator's row selection, mints the lock id, checks the quorum against a registered approver list, refuses plan mismatches and rate limits per client.
Contracts: PlanAnchor in Solidity 0.8.24 with Foundry, a one way state machine (anchored, then settled or abandoned) with custom errors and fuzz tests. It is deployed on Hedera testnet at 0x1a393277908834c39D2611Ce9A151474B8Dfea0d and verified on Sourcify. Anchoring reads before it writes, so rehearsing the same demo does not revert.
Notable hack: the keyless demo runs a local evaluator that mirrors the Privy policy semantics, so judges see a real refusal with a real byte offset without any credentials. While deploying we found that a refused edit abandoned the plan on chain, which is terminal, so the approved send could never settle it; the refusal now leaves the row anchored and only an unspent lock abandons it.
Quality: 403 unit tests, 72 Playwright end to end tests including axe accessibility checks in both themes, and 80 visual regression baselines.

name: Rawmarkets
description: RawMarket is a spot trading venue for tokenized representations of US commodity benchmarks
projectDescription: RawMarket is a professional spot trading venue for tokenized US commodity benchmarks, beginning with USDA Class III Milk and expanding to potatoes, tomatoes, wheat, corn, rice, soybeans, and dry beans. Users can inspect source-labelled candlestick history and live order-book depth, fund a test account, place market or limit orders, manage inventory, review fills, and open immutable Hedera receipts from order history. The product separates benchmark data, exchange prices, and blockchain lifecycle state so each remains independently auditable.
howItsMade: RawMarket combines a Next.js and TypeScript trading terminal with a deterministic Rust/Axum central limit order book hosted on AWS. The matcher uses integer ticks, price-time priority, reservations, partial fills, post-only orders, cancellation, and self-trade prevention. Hedera records every accepted order through an EVM receipt contract, with Mirror Node resolving native transaction IDs for HashScan links. The application now includes Hedera’s official Asset Tokenization Studio SDK. RawMarket uses the ATS factory path for governed commodity assets, ERC-1400 partition operations for issuance, holds and redemption, and an ERC-3643-compatible identity/compliance module for transfer eligibility. HTS provides native testnet token identities while ATS supplies the controlled asset lifecycle.

name: Free
description: Any outcome you're exposed to but can't control is a hedge you haven't placed yet.
projectDescription:
If your money, revenue, or plans depend on how some real-world outcome goes, you're carrying that risk unhedged whether you notice it or not.
Parasol turns it into a position: tell the agent what outcome you're exposed to, and it prices and assembles a hedge from live prediction-market odds on exactly that outcome. If things go the wrong way, the position pays out and offsets the loss. This creates a market-priced hedge for any exposure a public source can settle far beyond your typical bespoke insurance product for one narrow case. You sign every transaction yourself; the agent only ever attests to what happened, it never touches your money.
howItsMade:
Agent
Risk elicitation runs as a conversational front-end to 0G Compute's Router, the vanilla OpenAI SDK repointed at the Router's baseURL, so the integration surface is trivially small and swappable. The Router mediates access to whichever underlying model is configured, settling inference cost on-chain per call; those settlement debits against the Router's payment contract are themselves the primary proof of inference, supplemented by raw request/response logs and, where the Router exposes one, a TEE attestation binding a specific model execution to a specific output.
That attestation matters more than it might first appear: it's what lets a "private, verifiable inference" claim survive scrutiny instead of remaining a marketing assertion.
Architecturally, the model is confined to a single, narrow responsibility: producing a schema-constrained risk profile (event, threshold, target payout, a confidence scalar), and nothing downstream trusts it beyond that boundary. Output is validated against a strict JSON schema server-side; a malformed or underspecified response triggers a re-prompt rather than silent coercion. Everything with numerical consequence (pricing, position sizing, order construction, slippage bounds) lives in deterministic, unit-testable code that consumes the model's output as an opaque input, never as an instruction to execute.
This is a deliberate separation of concerns: the stochastic component is quarantined to intent-capture, and the entire financial state machine downstream is reproducible and auditable independent of what the model said. A secondary inference provider sits behind an identical inference(messages) → json interface, so failing over is a one-line baseURL swap rather than an architectural rewrite, demonstrated live, as evidence the abstraction isn't cosmetic.
Execution
The custody boundary is absolute: the backend never holds, generates, or has access to a Polygon private key at any point in the flow. It operates purely as a read/construct/relay service: reading public market state from Gamma and the CLOB order book, constructing unsigned limit orders pinned to the best ask with bounded slippage, and relaying already-signed payloads onward.
Every state transition that touches value. the initial USDC.e approval, the collateral wrap into tradable position tokens, CLOB L1 authentication (an off-chain EIP-712 signature that derives API credentials without costing gas), individual order signatures, and eventual redemption is signed client-side by the user's own EOA. signatureType 0 is used throughout with funder set to the signer itself, so there is no delegated-execution path, no meta-transaction relayer with spending authority, nothing standing between the user's key and the outcome.
Threshold and weather markets settle through a structurally different exchange contract than plain binary markets, the NegRisk exchange, purpose-built for the bundled, mutually-exclusive-outcome markets these products are, which means the negRisk flag has to propagate correctly into the EIP-712 domain the client is asked to sign, or the venue rejects the signature outright. Rather than risk that flag being forgotten at some future call-site, order construction is centralized into a single module that every code path funnels through, with a small integration test firing one minimal real order against it before it's ever trusted at demo scale.
Fill timeouts (roughly ten seconds without a match) trigger an automatic cancel-and-requote against the refreshed best ask rather than leaving a stale order hanging, the system re-derives its own price rather than assuming the world held still.
Indexing (The Graph)
This was built and adversarially verified against live chain state rather than assembled from documentation. Two independently deployed subgraphs: one for Polymarket, one for Azuro, are mapped into a single canonical schema: Market, Outcome, Resolution, and an append-only PricePoint ledger that turns "current price" into an actual time series rather than a single mutable scalar that overwrites its own history.
Polymarket alone decomposes into two structurally distinct on-chain sub-systems, and treating them as one would have been the easiest possible silent mistake. Plain binary markets settle through one exchange contract with OrderFilled events keyed by a token ID derived straight from the Conditional Tokens Framework's getPositionId. Threshold/NegRisk markets, the daily weather buckets this product actually prices, settle through an entirely separate exchange contract and, critically, mint their tradable outcome tokens through a different derivation path, NegRiskAdapter.getPositionId(questionId, outcome), that has no relationship to the plain CTF formula. This was not discovered by reading an interface but by computing the plain-CTF derivation for a real, currently-trading weather market and getting a numeric mismatch against the token IDs Polymarket's own API actually reports for it, which is the only reliable way to know a derivation is wrong before it silently mispricess every weather market in production. The correct call was then located in the NegRisk adapter's interface and substituted in.
Modern Conditional Tokens compounds this further: collection-ID derivation isn't a simple keccak chain anymore but encoded as a point on an elliptic curve (an ecAdd precompile call plus a modular square root over a ~254-bit prime), which means reimplementing the math independently would have been a meaningful cryptographic undertaking with real odds of a subtle, undetectable error. The mapping instead calls the deployed contract's own view function for this derivation at index time: delegating the one piece of logic that's genuinely hard to get right to the only party guaranteed to have it right.
Azuro required a different kind of forensic work. The contract address published in Azuro's own developer documentation, when interrogated with real event logs pulled directly from the chain and matched against every ABI in their public config repository by topic-hash rather than by name, turned out to belong to their live, in-play betting product rather than the pre-match product the documentation implied, two structurally different contracts sharing a naming convention that suggested otherwise.
Once corrected, Azuro's actual pricing signal is decimal odds carrying a bookmaker's margin, not a raw probability, so implied probability is derived via multiplicative de-vigging, inverting each outcome's odds and renormalizing across the full outcome set so the vig cancels out and the resulting number sits on the same 0-to-1 probability scale as Polymarket's direct trade price, rather than a systematically inflated one. Volume and trade-count aggregates accumulate per outcome from the same fill/bet events that drive price, at no additional indexing cost.
The net effect: a pricing engine or a resolution-watcher issues one query shape — implied probability, resolution status, winning outcome — against either venue, and is structurally incapable of knowing or caring which of three incompatible on-chain resolution mechanisms actually answered it. That query happens live against the deployed subgraphs at request time, which is what makes the integration load-bearing rather than a cached decoration sitting beside the real system.
Registry (0G)
