A minimal, purpose-built state machine — Issued → ResolvedYes | ResolvedNo → Paid
deployed on 0G's Galileo testnet with a monotonic status-transition guard and custom errors rather than string reverts — it's already live, already attesting a real first policy on-chain. Inference runs through two tiers on 0G Compute: an OpenAI-compatible Router for drop-in model access, and — for the parts of the flow that need to be provably real — a direct compute-broker integration built on 0G's compute SDK, where each inference request is wallet-signed and settled against an on-chain ledger. The provider doesn't just trust a header claiming the call came from us; it verifies our account against the chain itself before serving the request. That's the actual proof of inference: not a log line we could have written ourselves, but a cryptographic handshake the provider independently checks on-chain.
ENS
On issuance, Parasol mints a real subdomain under parasol.eth and writes the policy's payout, premium, status, on-chain attestation hash, and 0G storage pointer directly into that name's text records, giving every position a human-readable, independently resolvable identity rather than a hex string only a database can explain. Resolution runs both directions: a buyer can hand the interface either a raw address or a .eth name and watch it resolve the other way live against mainnet, and the broker itself carries its own identity, resolved off parasol.eth through ENS's UniversalResolver. Naming and identity resolution deliberately live on different networks, the subdomain is written on Sepolia, where we actually own and can fund the parent name, while personal identity resolution reads mainnet, where the names people actually recognize live.

name: Privet
description: AI treasury agent: proposes payments, policy decides, isolated signer executes. AI never holds keys.
projectDescription:
Privent is a security and execution layer that lets a company give an AI agent bounded access to a treasury — without ever giving the AI a private key.
It is not a trading bot, a wallet, or “an AI that spends crypto.” The product thesis is: AI agents should receive financial authority, not unrestricted access to company funds. The AI decides what it wants to do. A deterministic policy engine decides whether it may do it. An isolated signer decides whether a transaction can actually be authorized. The blockchain decides whether it settles. Humans keep control of anything irreversible or high-risk. Every step is audited.
That split is the whole point. You never trust the model to enforce its own security.
howItsMade: pnpm TS monorepo: Next.js, Hono API, isolated signer. OpenRouter GPT-4o-mini proposes JSON; policy ALLOW/REQUIRE_APPROVAL/DENY. The Graph, Privy, ENS feed live data. Keys live in a separate Node process that re-reads SQLite, re-runs policy, then viem-broadcasts to Sepolia. Hack: signer never trusts the API.

name: gotrade
description: Gotrade: WhatsApp-controlled autonomous DeFi with live wallets, risk limits, and swaps.
projectDescription: Gotrade is an autonomous DeFi agent platform controlled through WhatsApp. Users can register, view live wallet balances, analyze markets, manage AI agents, configure risk limits, and execute blockchain actions using natural-language commands. Gotrade combines conversational AI with deterministic safety policies, live onchain data, user-controlled wallets, Uniswap execution, and MongoDB-backed auditability. It is designed to make DeFi more accessible while ensuring agents cannot exceed user-defined trading limits or silently report simulated success.
howItsMade: Gotrade uses FastAPI and Python for the backend, MongoDB with Motor for asynchronous persistence, Redis for service support, and a Next.js/TypeScript frontend. The WhatsApp gateway uses Twilio webhooks and TwiML, while Gemini interprets natural-language commands with deterministic regex fallbacks. Coinbase Developer Platform wallet infrastructure and an existing EVM wallet provide wallet access, Web3.py reads live Sepolia balances, and Uniswap v3 supplies onchain quotes and execution paths. The architecture is fail-closed: unavailable providers, missing credentials, unsupported services, or failed transactions produce explicit errors rather than fake success. Docker Compose runs MongoDB and Redis, while ngrok exposes the local webhook for live testing.

name: Leash Layer
description: Revocable ENSv2 authorization and scoped credentials for agent software
projectDescription:
Leash is an explainable permission layer for agent software. It identifies an agent wallet
through ERC-8004, reads its capabilities from ENSv2 on Ethereum Sepolia, and decides whether a requested action is allowed. When approved, Leash issues a short lived, singleuse
credential scoped to one capability and wallet address. Before the protected service
executes, authority is checked again against ENSv2, so revoking a role immediately blocks the
next request. The project demonstrates how agents can receive bounded permissions instead of permanent API access.
howItsMade:
Leash is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Bun, and viem. The Next.js dashboard and
server-side API routes use shared authorization logic from the src backend layer. A custom
ENSv2 client reads resource ownership, expiry, and role bitmaps from Ethereum Sepolia.
Capabilities are mapped to required roles, and the gate returns structured ALLOW or DENY
decisions with stable reason codes, block numbers, and latency. Approved requests receive
HMAC-signed credentials containing the agent, wallet, capability, expiry, and nonce. The
protected service validates the credential, prevents reuse, and performs a live ENSv2 re-
check before execution.

name: PolicyProbe
description: Deterministic onchain policy assertions and repair findings for Hedera Harness.
projectDescription:
PolicyProbe extends Hedera Harness with deterministic onchain behavioral verification. Developers can declare what an application is expected to do, execute real actions on Hedera, and compare the observed result against that expectation instead of treating a successful transaction as proof of correctness.
For example, if an unverified investor must not receive a tokenized bond, PolicyProbe can execute that action, detect if it unexpectedly succeeds, capture the resulting transaction and state evidence, and emit a structured finding that Harness can feed back into its existing repair loop. The same probe can then be rerun after the fix to prove that the behavior now matches policy.
The result is a reusable verification layer for AI-built Hedera applications: expected behavior → real execution → observed state → deterministic PASS/FAIL → repair. Our flagship demo uses a tokenized-asset policy scenario to make that loop concrete and auditable.
howItsMade:
PolicyProbe is a TypeScript contribution built on Hedera Harness and exercised against an Asset Tokenization Studio bond on Hedera testnet. It extends the Harness recipe schema with optional chain validation actors and assertions. The assertion runner provisions named signers, executes declared actions, resolves EVM transaction hashes or Hedera transaction IDs through Mirror Node, compares confirmed outcomes and optional exact balance deltas, and emits typed policy or infrastructure findings.
The implementation stays generic and backward compatible: recipes without chain assertions follow the existing Harness flow. The companion fixture uses the same engine to test transfer restrictions, role boundaries, frozen holders, and pause controls. This repository includes focused tests, a reproducible fixture, architecture documentation, and linked HashScan evidence.

name: LEASH - Agent Guard
description: A signed, revocable spending mandate that stops an AI agent from ever paying past its cap.
projectDescription:
LEASH gives an AI agent a wallet with a real budget instead of a prompt that tells it to be careful. A mandate sets the scope, meaning which resources it can pay for, plus a ceiling, a rate limit, and an expiry. Every payment attempt is checked against that mandate's current state before any money moves, so a rejected request never reaches the payment rail at all. The same mandate is enforced the same way across two separate settlement rails, Hedera testnet through a Blocky402 facilitator and Arc testnet through a Circle Developer Controlled Wallet, so the enforcement is not tied to one chain.
Every mandate event, including issuing, spending, rejecting, raising the ceiling, and revoking, is written to Hedera Consensus Service and can be checked independently on the public mirror node. Raising a mandate's ceiling needs signatures from a real Privy key quorum, so one compromised operator cannot widen what an agent is allowed to spend on their own.
Live at leash-kowaipanda.vercel.app
howItsMade:
The frontend is built with Vite, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, deployed on Vercel. The backend is Express and TypeScript on Render, and it keeps mandates in memory with a JSON snapshot for persistence. The core piece is a small guard function that checks scope, remaining ceiling, rate limit, expiry, and revocation before either settlement rail is touched. The x402 v2 spec says budget and session management are out of scope, and its facilitators do not expose a hook for custom checks. So instead of waiting on one, LEASH runs as its own facilitator proxy sitting in front of Blocky402 on Hedera testnet, and settlement only happens after our own check passes.
Hedera's exact payment scheme does not use a signed authorization object the way EVM chains do, so we build and sign a real, partially signed TransferTransaction with the Hedera SDK, and the facilitator adds its own signature and settles it. Every mandate event is sent to an HCS topic, so the audit trail can be checked on Hedera's public mirror node instead of just trusting our own database.
The second rail settles real USDC on Arc testnet through Circle's Developer Controlled Wallets SDK, using createTransaction and then polling until the transfer finishes, and the token id is looked up from the wallet's own balance instead of being hardcoded. The trickiest part was Privy. Privy's policy engine only gates real wallet actions like eth_sendTransaction, it does not have a field for an arbitrary business number like a spending ceiling. So we mirror the mandate's ceiling into the value of a policy rule owned by a key quorum. That rule is never checked against a real transaction, but changing the number still needs signatures from enough Privy authorization keys to meet a 2 of 2 threshold, sent all at once with generateAuthorizationSignature, which skips Privy's support gated approval queue entirely. The Arc rail falls back to a clearly labeled mock settlement if Circle sandbox keys are not set, so the guard logic can still be demoed either way.

name: Leash_dash
description: Keep your AI agents on a leash: bind an agent, set on-chain spend limits, cut it off with one write.
projectDescription:
Everyone is racing to build AI agents that can spend money. The part almost nobody has built is the place you sit and actually govern them once they can. That is what LEASH is. It is a control centre for the AI agents that spend your money, where every agent you run is on a leash you can see and pull.
The problem
Once you hand an agent a wallet so it can pay for things over x402, the only real control you have left is the private key itself. There is no per-call limit, no list of who it is allowed to pay, no hierarchy if you are running a fleet, and no single off switch. The part that actually worries me is revocation, because if a key leaks today, cutting that agent off means going service by service and rotating keys by hand, which is exactly the situation where slow manual work is the last thing you want.
What LEASH does
LEASH gives an organisation one console to run its whole fleet of paying agents. You bind an agent you already run, give it a spending account that you and LEASH co-own, set its limits, fund it, and if you ever need to, you pull the leash and cut it off everywhere. The thing that makes this work is ENS. Each agent becomes a child name like data.acme.leash.eth, and the spend policy for that agent (its per-call cap, the payees it is allowed to hit, its Hedera account, and optionally a rolling daily or weekly budget) lives right there in the name's resolver record. The bit I care about most happens at payment time: a facilitator I run reads that live ENS record before it settles anything, and it only co-signs a payment that is actually within policy. So the moment you clear the record, the very next payment the agent tries just fails. One write on Sepolia and it is done everywhere, with no key rotation and no chasing down services.
How it works
It is five steps end to end. You bind an existing agent whose identity already lives on another chain, say an Arc or Base wallet or an ERC-8004 registration, and LEASH resolves that identity on-chain and then generates a fresh Hedera spending keypair for the agent. The public half goes into a two-of-two Hedera account that you and LEASH co-own, and the private half is shown to you once, right there at bind, and never stored by LEASH. If you would rather bring your own, pasting your agent's own Hedera public key is still supported as an advanced option. Either way LEASH never holds the agent's private key. Then it writes the policy into the agent's ENS resolver record. From there, every time the agent pays, the facilitator reads that live record, checks the cap and the allowlist and the window, and only adds its co-signature if everything passes, settling gas-free on Hedera so the agent spends zero on gas. Every decision, allow or deny, gets logged to a Hedera Consensus Service topic so it is checkable on-chain. And revoking is the whole point: clearing the record is a single Sepolia transaction, and because the facilitator re-reads with no cache right before it settles, the next payment fails closed rather than slipping through.
Being honest about the guarantee
I would rather be straight about how strong this is. The enforcement is facilitator-trusted, not trustless. The facilitator I run is the thing reading your policy and deciding whether to co-sign, and the chain's job is to hold the policy and the revocation, not to physically block a payment. The model I keep coming back to is a corporate card, where the employee is genuinely independent and holds their own card, but the company sets the limit and can freeze it. So control is real and independence is real, but trustlessness is not,for now.  Same spirit on the rolling daily and weekly caps, which are a soft budget rather than an exact one, and on identity, which is on-chain-resolved rather than a proof that the person binding actually controls the address.
Two ways to see it work
The fastest is the sandbox at /demo, which needs no login, no wallet and no ETH. It governs a real agent of mine called SOLV-001, an autonomous agent running on a Circle wallet on Arc (its on-chain-resolved identity is 0x927c1d756d12879aebea0772f3ee220f21f4841a), and it walks you through five moments: meet the agent, watch it pay three dollars inside its cap and settle gas-free, watch it try fifty and get refused, revoke it and watch the same payment fail closed, then watch a leaked key try to over-fund it and get denied by the funding rail. The second way is the real product at /app, where you log in with Privy, spin up your org, and bind an agent you already run by pasting its Hedera public key and its identity. You get the same controls on your own agent, and LEASH still never touches its private key.
What is live right now
Everything below is on live rails. If you only click a few things, click these.

The app: https://leash.ink (sandbox at /demo, proof page at /proof)
The code, MIT and public: https://github.com/dmustapha/leash
Revoking an agent in one write, on Sepolia: 0xf03e14d1c0ed8528d90f9d0e5aa4bc55cb2fe29baedea97596d902c427702293
A gas-free settle where the agent pays zero HBAR, on Hedera: [email protected]

Every headline number here recomputes from committed evidence with npm run verify:claims, and the full ledger is in submission/proof.md. There are 102 unit tests and 8 integration tests behind it, plus the live on-chain runs.
Where it goes next
Right now the actual spend governance runs on Hedera, because the co-signing facilitator I run is the x402 Hedera one, even though binding identity already works across chains and the funding rail is general enough to move. The near-term work is standing that co-signer and policy read up on other EVM chains too. Further out I want to move enforcement from something I am trusted to do toward something the chain checks itself, most likely a contract wallet that mirrors the cap on-chain.
howItsMade:
The frontend is a Next.js app on Vercel, and the two rails behind it, the x402 Hedera facilitator and a small x402-gated resource server, run on Render. There is a Neon Postgres in the stack too, but I want to be clear that it is only an index for the UI and never the thing that decides whether a payment is allowed. It is all TypeScript, with 102 unit tests and 8 integration tests, plus a set of live runs that actually hit Sepolia and Hedera instead of mocking them.
For the ENS side, and I used ENSv2 on Sepolia with a three-level hierarchy: a root, an org under it, and each agent as a child name beneath the org. The spend policy sits in the agent name's resolver record under the key leash.policy, and the facilitator reads it with a single PermissionedResolver.text call right before it settles. Nothing is hard-coded, the caps and the allowlist and the revocation are all real Sepolia transactions, and revoking is just clearPolicy, which is one write. The reason ENS was the right primitive rather than a database is that the record is already a public source of truth anyone can read, so revocation is not a flag I flip in my own system, it is an on-chain fact.
For Hedera I self-hosted an @x402/core plus @x402/hedera facilitator, the same shape as Blocky402, and it settles with the native fee-payer scheme, which is the partner feature that actually matters here: the agent pays zero HBAR and is only debited the USDC it is spending, using its own six-decimal HTS test token. The gate itself is a pure authorize function with no database in it. There are two reads of the ENS record, an advisory one before verify that is allowed a short cache, and the authoritative one right before settle that never caches. That second read is the part I sweated over, because it is what closes the window where a revoke lands in between verify and settle. Without it you could revoke and still have an in-flight payment go through, which would quietly turn the whole promise into a lie. Every decision, with its reason, is written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, all the amounts are compared as BigInt on raw units so nothing rounds, and if the RPC or the mirror is unreachable the gate fails closed rather than defaulting to zero.
The two-of-two account is how I keep the agent genuinely independent while still being able to govern it. When you bind an agent, LEASH generates a fresh Hedera spending keypair for it, puts the public half into a KeyList account alongside LEASH's own co-signer key with a threshold of two, and hands the private half back to the user once, at bind. LEASH never stores that key, so it is not in the facilitator, the database or the env anywhere. If someone would rather supply their own agent public key instead of having one generated, that path is still there as an advanced option, and the invariant holds either way: LEASH never retains the agent's private key. LEASH only adds its signature at settle, after the gate passes, at a single spot in the code. I checked both failure directions on-chain: the agent signing alone gets a clean MISSING_COSIGN and nothing settles, and LEASH together with its own operator key still cannot move the agent's funds. I also assert at startup that the co-signer key is not the same as the gas fee-payer key, so the line about the authority key not being the gas key is literally true in the running process and not just a claim in a README.
Privy is the second, independent rail. The treasury is a P-256-owner Privy wallet driven through @privy-io/server-auth, and its policy caps and allowlists the actual USDC transfer calldata, so an over-cap top-up comes back as FUNDING_DENIED before it ever broadcasts. There is deliberately no on-chain artifact for that denial, the absence is the proof. The hacky detail I did not expect is that a KeyList account has no key-derived EVM alias, so funding has to target its long-zero EVM address, and that took me a while to work out. I kept Privy strictly funding-only on purpose, because the moment it co-signs a payment the honest story falls apart.
Identity uses ERC-8004. On register, LEASH resolves the owner live against the canonical Sepolia registry and writes the agent.erc8004 and agent.address records, and a mismatch just errors instead of registering. I label this on-chain-resolved rather than verified, and that wording is deliberate, because ownerOf tells you who the registry says owns the agent but it does not prove the person binding actually controls that address. A proper signed proof-of-control handshake is something I want, it just is not in yet.
The last thing I would rather disclose than bury is that the rolling daily and weekly caps are a soft budget. They are summed from the HCS topic through the mirror node, which lags, so under enough concurrency you could overshoot by roughly the number of in-flight payments times the per-call cap. The hard bounds are the per-call cap on live ENS and the funding cap on Privy. On top of that the console runs requireOwner on every mutating route, the mutation routes are rate limited, and the replay set is stored in Neon so a replayed payment is still rejected even if the facilitator restarts.
If you want to check the addresses yourself, the policy resolver the facilitator reads is 0xdC460cd7151D679CF5D1e34595e1ac890A5E4978 on Sepolia, the sandbox registry is 0xB45830aeaf0A00367A450635a110cffA6878A679, the org-parent registry is 0xb36e0ede0Ed38653c5aB8222B409a6b2Ba78b409, the canonical ERC-8004 registry I resolve against is 0x8004A818BFB912233c491871b3d84c89A494BD9e, and on Hedera the 2-of-2 spending account is 0.0.10508343 and the audit topic is 0.0.10496492.

name: scout
description: Autonomous DeFi research agent: Graph + OpenSEO scores, x402 micropayments, Privy, ENS identity
projectDescription:
Scout is an autonomous on-chain research agent for Base lending markets. You give it a plain-language prompt and a USDC budget; it discovers live protocol data from The Graph (Messari Lending/CDP subgraphs), enriches candidates with OpenSEO keyword and SERP signals, then ranks them with a deterministic six-dimension opportunity score plus a separate risk score no LLM in the scoring math.
When the top two candidates are too close to call, Scout pauses and asks you to authorize a small, policy-capped x402 micropayment for one extra diagnostics report—paid by a Privy server wallet, never the visitor’s wallet. Results stream live over SSE, and the final status is published to an ENSv2 name (scout-agent.eth) via a Permissioned Resolver. The full decision log, including refused payments or missing evidence, stays with the session.
howItsMade:
Scout is a TypeScript Turborepo monorepo: Next.js 15 + React 19 frontend, Hono API with SSE, and shared packages for the research loop. @scout/graph queries The Graph Gateway; @scout/openseo pulls search signals; @scout/scoring runs the six-dimension model and uncertainty gate; @scout/llm (OpenRouter) only narrates already-computed scores.
When the gate fires, @x402/hono gates a $0.03 USDC deep-analysis endpoint on Base Sepolia; @scout/privy signs with a policy-enforced server wallet (budget cap, per-request cap, recipient allowlist). @scout/ens writes status to ENSv2 text records on Sepolia behind role-gated access control. We also expose the pipeline as an MCP tool and ship a headless scout-agent CLI. Deployed on Render as scout-api + scout-web.

name: Noria
description: From wallet to liquidity: Noria helps users choose pools, reinvest earnings and reduce debt.
projectDescription:
Noria brings the steps of liquidity investing into one application: fund a wallet, research pools, build a position and track the money. Users get an analysis backed by verifiable sources and a path to execute their decisions.
The experience starts with Privy. Users sign in with email or Google, create an embedded wallet and can access a EUR-to-USDC checkout or receive funds from another wallet. They can then deposit USDC into Aave to earn variable interest, make transfers or prepare a liquidity position.
For research, Noria uses The Graph to compare pools, examine price history and calculate a price range and the required amount of each token. Reports explain the selection criteria and why a candidate may not qualify. The same research is available through six tools that external AI agents can call.
For the Aqua strategy, users supply ETH or USDC as collateral on Aave and borrow USDC to provide WETH/USDC liquidity on Arbitrum. The position uses 1inch Aqua and SwapVM. When a completed cycle produces distributable surplus after accounting for borrowing interest and accumulated losses, the policy allocates 50% to debt repayment and 50% to capital for the next cycle.
Users confirm fund movements and track amounts, network fees and transaction receipts in downloadable reports. Noria connects research, execution and capital management so users can understand and follow each financial decision.
howItsMade:
We built Noria with Next.js, React and TypeScript. The interface, analysis services and financial integrations share data validation rules. We use viem to read blockchain state, prepare transactions and verify receipts.
Privy provides authentication, embedded wallet creation and transaction confirmations. We integrated wallet funding, a EUR checkout, transfers and Aave deposits and withdrawals. Each transaction has a review step before signing, and its outcome is checked onchain. Interrupted requests are recorded for recovery.

name: Otter
description: First implementation of a provably MEV-resilient AMM — Uniswap v4 hook + off-chain VCG solver.
projectDescription:
Otter is the first implementation of "Otter: A Provably MEV-Resilient Automated Market Maker via Surplus Redistribution" (Shi, Zhang, Chung & Li — IACR ePrint 2026/1877), deployed as a Uniswap v4 hook on Ethereum Sepolia.
The core problem: every conventional AMM has a queue, and any queue is sellable. A searcher who can see your order and insert before it will front-run you — buying before you drive up the price, then selling after you fill at the worse rate. This is not an edge case. In our harness test, an attacker deploying 5,000 OTB captures 92% of the victim's trade on a plain pool. The victim gets 1.38 OTB instead of 47.6. That loss is the searcher's profit, by construction.
Otter removes the queue entirely. Orders are collected into a 60-second batch window as an unordered set — no first, no second, no sequence position to purchase. The mechanism is dominant-strategy truthful: your best move is always to report your real reservation price, regardless of what anyone else does or what the attacker tries. A searcher who joins the batch clears at exactly the same price as every other participant. The Clarke pivot redistributes any surplus back to the LP rather than to the attacker.
What makes this design novel over existing batch AMMs (CoW Protocol, Angstrom, SPEEDEX, am-AMM, Penumbra) is that it achieves dominant-strategy truthfulness for both regular users and for a builder-acting-as-user simultaneously, via VCG surplus redistribution. Existing batch AMMs clear at a uniform price and are not incentive compatible in this sense. This is the first implementation of a mechanism with that specific property.
The full stack is deployed and verified on Sepolia: OtterOrderBook (escrow and batch commitment), OtterSettlement (VCG outcome verification and v4 pool settlement), and OtterHook (the Uniswap v4 integration). A live demo page walks through a real settled 6-order batch — showing the sandwich comparison, VCG allocation results, individual order fills and refunds, LP surplus redistribution, and Etherscan links to every source-verified contract.
Stated limitation: the mechanism's guarantees assume censorship resilience at the consensus layer (Theorem 23 of the paper). A testnet does not provide this. We say this explicitly in the README, in the demo UI, and here — not buried.
howItsMade:
Stack: Foundry (Solidity 0.8.26), TypeScript solver (Node 22), Vite + React + TypeScript frontend, wagmi + RainbowKit for Sepolia wallet connection. No additional backend — the solver runs as a CLI and the web app is fully static.
SOLVER (solver/)
The two-sided VCG mechanism is implemented in otter.ts. The dominant side is determined by comparing aggregate eligible supply across both directions; ties go to sell-Y (eq. 10 of the paper). The symmetric case reuses the same one-sided code with the token roles swapped and the answer flipped back — one implementation path, no chance of the two branches drifting apart.
The dominant-side allocation uses a layer-cake pivot algorithm extracted from the proof of Lemma 16. The closed form for the Clarke pivot integral has a global zero-crossing (the clearing price, shared by the whole batch) and a per-user lower breakpoint. We implement this, verify it against the naïve O(n²) leave-one-out computation across 4,000 random batches (max relative error 3.8e-10), and benchmark both: at n=1,000 the layer-cake solver runs in 8.8ms vs 233ms naïve — a 27× speedup. Current limitation: the pivot loop is still O(n²) with a small constant because it scans pieces linearly; replacing those scans with binary search plus a prefix-summed antiderivative table is the outstanding optimisation.
Property tests (solver/test/properties.ts §8) independently grid-search the allocation space for n ≤ 4 and confirm that nothing on the grid beats the solver's own output. This is evidence for small instances, not a proof for arbitrary n — the comment in that test says exactly that.
CONTRACTS (contracts/src/)
OtterHook implements IHooks directly. BaseHook was removed from both v4-core (v4.0.0) and v4-periphery with no migration note; every tutorial still references it. Implementing IHooks directly is arguably cleaner for a hook that only needs three callbacks, but we found this out by reading source, not from the docs. The hook's CREATE2 address encodes the beforeSwap, beforeAddLiquidity, and beforeRemoveLiquidity permission bits; HookMiner was vendored from v4-periphery/test/ since it lives under test/ despite being a deployment-critical tool.
OtterSettlement calls poolManager.unlock() to enter the v4 singleton and runs the residual imbalance swap. Before distributing, it verifies: feasibility (pool conservation), individual rationality (no seller underpaid), budget bounds (no overfill), minority pricing, dominance, and that the pool actually yielded enough to cover all obligations.
OtterMath is an internal library compiled directly into OtterSettlement (all functions are internal). Fixed-point arithmetic uses solmate's mulDivDown and mulDivUp exclusively — PRBMath's public API has no mulDivUp, which matters for the one rounding direction that decides whether an invariant flips. The rule throughout OtterMath: amounts a user may receive round down; amounts a user must have earned round up. fTildeDown and fTildeUp are never mixed.
Notable finding during integration: Uniswap v4 executes a swap in two stages on a Q64.96 price grid, rounding in the pool's favour at each. It therefore pays strictly less than the continuous curve predicts. A settlement paying the full theoretical ceiling failed with PoolOutputShortfall by 14 wei in testing. We measured the gap across 512 fuzz runs (it scales with price impact, not trade size — roughly 1 wei per 1.2% of impact) and derived a tight allowance function: ceil((y − M) × 200 / y0) + 2. Critically, fTildeDown is left untouched as a faithful port of the paper's curve. The allowance is a separate function used only in verify — the two are kept distinct in kind because one is the mechanism and the other is a fact about executing it on v4.
GAS & HARNESS (harness/)
Settlement gas is dominated by ERC-20 transfers and ecrecover, not by verification (which is O(n) arithmetic). Measured: ~40,906 gas per order at n=200; block ceiling at 630 orders per block on a 30M gas limit. The sandwich harness runs a vanilla v4 pool vs the Otter pool against the same attacker parameters — the direct swap on the Otter pool reverts at the hook, so the attacker gains nothing.
WEB (web/)
The demo data is not hardcoded — it is inlined from the real solver fixture generated by solver/src/demo-cli.ts. The Sepolia sandbox reads live batch state directly from the deployed OtterOrderBook contract via wagmi. The GasChart renders the measured harness data as an inline SVG. No public solver/relayer is running; this is clearly disclaimed in the UI.
