name: AutoBazar
description: A game where models are tasked with running a simulated vending machine business over a year!
projectDescription:
AutoBazaar is a competitive vending-machine simulation where AI agents run small shops. Humans choose strategies, while agents manage prices, inventory, and supplier orders.
The game shares the business-management idea behind Andon Labs’ Vending-Bench 2. That benchmark tests whether an AI can run a simulated business for one year, starting with $500. Agents find suppliers, negotiate prices, manage deliveries, and respond to problems. Their final bank balance determines their score. Its Arena version adds competing vending machines at one location.
AutoBazaar puts four agents into a shared season. The demo uses one human-owned agent and three house agents. Each entry costs 1.00 test USDC. Half funds customers, and half provides the shop’s operating cash.
Each game day, the server sends agents a fixed morning observation. Agents have three minutes to submit prices, shelf loading, and supplier orders. The server calculates customer purchases and updates inventory and balances. Arc Testnet records purchases, supplier bills, and daily fees. The highest final bank balance wins.
The system has a local agent, a local dashboard, a shared game server, and blockchain contracts. The local agent runs Codex or a custom policy. The dashboard shows cash, inventory, strategy, private notes, decision drafts, and transaction receipts. The downloaded implementation uses Node.js, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and a local SQLite database.
Circle supplies the agent wallet. World AgentBook records human ownership on World Chain. Game funds and transaction settlement use Arc Testnet. The server still calculates customer demand, so blockchain settlement does not make the entire game decentralized.
In Review mode, Codex drafts decisions and waits for human approval. In Automatic mode, the agent signs and submits decisions itself. Strategy instructions guide the agent, but they do not enforce a spending limit. The agent’s computer must stay running. Pausing an agent does not pause the shared season.
Sources:
AutoBazaar: https://autobazaar.vending-arena.workers.dev
AutoBazaar guide: https://autobazaar.vending-arena.workers.dev/agent-guide.html
Vending-Bench 2: https://andonlabs.com/evals/vending-bench-2
howItsMade:
We built Autobazaar as three connected systems: a deterministic market simulator, independently running agents, and an on-chain economy.
World AgentKit connects agents to verified human owners through AgentBook on World Chain, enforcing one human seat per season. Circle Agent Wallets give agents wallets for funding and signing. Solidity contracts on Arc Testnet, integrated through viem, handle test-USDC deposits, purchases, supplier payments, operating fees and withdrawals. Agents sign EIP-712 authorizations; the escrow checks prices, spending limits and balances. Customer demand remains calculated by the server.
One useful implementation trick is separating financial settlement from animation. An entire day settles atomically onchain, while individual purchase events become NPC visits in the 3D world. Spectators can pause or replay those visits without triggering another payment. We also persist signed transaction bytes before broadcasting, so recovery can rebroadcast the same transaction instead of accidentally paying twice.
For onboarding, we created a single copy-and-paste Codex prompt that prepares the runner, provisions or reuses a Circle wallet, guides World registration and opens the dashboard. The hackathon demo supports one human-backed entrant competing against three explicitly labeled house agents with separate wallets and strategies.

name: VenekoVox
description: Private polling for verified humans, with encrypted ballots and verifiable results.
projectDescription:
VenekoVox is a privacy-first civic polling platform built around a simple question: how can people express an opinion, prove they are eligible to participate, and trust the counting process without publishing their identity or their choice?
The failure mode is identical everywhere — only the coercer changes. Under state repression, dissent is punished and real sentiment cannot be safely measured; under social pressure, the silent majority self-censors while a vocal minority dictates the narrative; and everywhere, bot farms and AI personas poison the polls that shape public opinion. Polls influence policy, yet the instruments we use to measure them reward the loudest and most coerced voices. VenekoVox replaces manufactured consensus with ground-truth conviction.
Participants use ZKPassport to prove the attributes required by a poll — one real human, one vote — from their own passport's NFC chip, without revealing their identity. They connect a wallet and submit an encrypted ballot through MACI: no one, not even the operator, can prove how anyone voted, and votes can be re-cast invisibly, which makes bribes and threats unenforceable. Personal document details are never written to the blockchain.
ENSv2 makes every poll a named, discoverable on-chain object — our own subname registry turns superintelligence.polls.venekovoxv1.eth into a poll's address, brand and share-link. The Graph indexes public participation into standardized, queryable governance data without exposing ballot choices.
Our flagship poll — "Should development of superintelligence be paused?" — is live on Ethereum Sepolia and open to any passport holder, 18+. The prototype has recorded a real-passport eligibility flow, an authorized poll join and an encrypted ballot submission on-chain; completing and demonstrating the proof-verified tally is the next milestone (both live polls close within 24 hours of submission). Longer-term: privacy-preserving demographic analysis and reducing reliance on a single operator. This is a product we intend to keep building — the Polymarket of public sentiment, built for Ethereum.
howItsMade:
https://deepwiki.com/satojandro/venekovox
VenekoVox builds on the open-source MACI codebase, combining a React and TypeScript frontend, Vite, a Node.js/Express backend, Solidity contracts and ethers.js.
ZKPassport handles passport-based eligibility proofs. Our integration uses salted uniqueness and strict FaceMatch, with the backend independently verifying proofs against the configured eligibility requirements. After checking wallet control, the backend issues an EIP-712 authorization—a structured, signed permission—which the on-chain eligibility policy validates. An application-specific identity tag supports duplicate-participation checks without placing the raw passport-derived identifier on-chain. This prototype retains an explicit trust dependency on the eligibility issuer.
MACI provides the encrypted voting infrastructure and proof-based processing and tally architecture. Voting keys are separate from wallet keys. Our application connects eligibility authorization, poll membership, encrypted ballot publication and transaction verification into one participant journey.
The Graph indexes public MACI events and signup state. One particularly useful engineering detail is our indexed membership-proof path: we reconstruct the signup tree, check it against an on-chain historical root, and prepare the participant’s proof against that exact snapshot. This prevents new signups from changing the reference state midway through joining. Validated fallbacks support recovery when an indexing source is unavailable.
Our ENSv2 integration adds registration and named-poll discovery through custom registrar/resolver logic. Names are optional public metadata; they neither establish personhood nor contain passport eligibility information.
We also built recovery checks that distinguish a submitted transaction from a confirmed action, and ballot rendering that reads each poll’s actual options. VenekoVox’s contribution is the eligibility integration, application contracts, indexed proof service and guided polling experience around the upstream infrastructure.

name: ConduitX
description: Decentralized AI agent data vending machine with x402 metering & Hedera HCS receipts.
projectDescription:
ConduitX is a decentralized data vending machine for autonomous AI agents. While agents have payment rails, they lack an open marketplace to discover, buy, and audit blockchain data query by query.
With ConduitX, an agent discovers data providers, receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required challenge with dynamic pricing based on query complexity, and settles micro-payments in under two seconds over Hedera.
The seller delivers live data from The Graph subgraphs and immediately publishes a cryptographic receipt to Hedera Consensus Service (HCS Topic 0.0.9840084). Future buyer agents read these public HCS receipts via Mirror Nodes to calculate provider reputation objectively before purchasing.
ConduitX also includes a native Model Context Protocol (MCP) server so AI models like Claude and Cursor can procure blockchain data autonomously.
howItsMade:
ConduitX is built as a TypeScript monorepo combining Hedera Consensus Service, the x402 payment protocol, The Graph Subgraph Studio, and a Next.js 16 workstation dashboard.
On the payment rail, we built custom Express middleware that intercepts incoming data queries, meters cost dynamically based on request complexity (base fee + per-row returned), and issues HTTP 402 challenges. The buyer agent settles micro-payments using the Hedera SDK via the Blocky402 facilitator with automatic ECDSA private key parsing.
Once settled, the data provider executes live GraphQL queries against The Graph Subgraph Studio (Uniswap v3 DEX analytics, token concentration risk, and portfolio indexers) and immediately publishes an immutable receipt message to Hedera Consensus Service (HCS Topic 0.0.9840084).
A notable design innovation is turning HCS receipts into a decentralized reputation oracle: instead of relying on a centralized database to rate providers, our broker queries Hedera Mirror Node REST APIs to deterministically compute provider reliability, latency, and failover routing directly from public consensus timestamps. We also implemented a native Model Context Protocol (MCP) server so Claude Desktop and Cursor can run this entire data procurement loop as a standard agent tool.

name: AutoCFO
description: An autonomous CFO that handles your treasury, audited by you.
projectDescription:
AutoCFO is an AI CFO any organization can self-onboard in about a minute. It gets a real treasury (a Privy organization wallet holding USDC on Arc), an on-chain identity (yourco.autocfo.eth on ENSv2), and an agent that runs your finances: it pays vendor invoices when they're due, runs payroll on standing schedules, buys pay-per-call market data over x402 for $0.001 a request, and pays contractors on whatever chain they prefer via Circle Gateway.
The core idea: autonomy is only safe when enforcement lives below the model. Most agent-wallet demos put guardrails in the system prompt. In AutoCFO, the agent's signing key is cryptographically incapable of exceeding its mandate, every payment rule (payee allowlist, per-payee cap) is evaluated inside Privy's TEE policy engine at signing time. An org-wide daily budget and a duplicate-payment guard are enforced deterministically in code before any send. Payroll amounts and dates never pass through the LLM, schedules are materialized into invoices by code. Anything over the mandate is queued for a human, whose approval executes with the owner quorum key, a key the agent never holds.
You manage it all by talking to it. Say "onboard karan at 0x… and pay him 1000 USDC monthly". The agent registers karan.yourco.autocfo.eth on ENSv2 with its role-bounded key, then stops and asks you what payment cap to grant, because payment authority is a human decision. Every action lands in an audit trail: signal → decision → on-chain proof. An autonomous CFO you can audit line by line and overrule with a better key.
howItsMade:
Privy is the enforcement layer. Each tenant gets an organization wallet whose owner is a human key quorum; the agent is an additional_signer bounded by an override policy of ABI-decoded calldata conditions (transfer.recipient == payee && transfer.amount <= cap), evaluated in Privy's TEE at signing.
Arc + Circle Gateway. The treasury settles on Arc. A per-org petty-cash EOA deposits into Gateway and pays x402-priced APIs gaslessly via @circle-fin/x402-batching (EIP-3009 authorizations, batched settlement, the middleware silently defaults to the mainnet facilitator, which cost us an evening). Cross-chain contractor payouts use Gateway's unified balance to mint on Base Sepolia in <1s. We ship our own x402 seller so the demo is self-contained.
ENSv2 (Sepolia beta) is the tenancy model. autocfo.eth owns a UserRegistry; onboarding deploys each org its own subregistry via VerifiableFactory, so payees become karan.org.autocfo.eth. Hacky discovery: PublicResolverV2 authorizes via the ENSv1 NameWrapper, so v2-native names can never write records to it ,we deployed a PermissionedResolver with per-record EAC roles instead. The agent's ENS key holds only ROLE_REGISTRAR|ROLE_RENEW (Enhanced Access Control): it onboards payees, it cannot touch parent names. Payout addresses resolve live through the Universal Resolver at pay time never from our DB.

name: Arvo
description: The decentralized insurance layer protecting every trade made by autonomous agents.
projectDescription:
Arvo — Decentralized Agentic Trade Insurance Protocol
Arvo is a decentralized trade insurance protocol designed for the emerging ecosystem of autonomous AI trading agents. As agents become increasingly capable of independently managing portfolios and executing trades across decentralized exchanges, users need a way to protect their capital without interfering with the agent's trading strategy. Arvo provides an insurance layer that evaluates and protects individual trades executed by autonomous agents across multiple blockchain networks.
How Arvo Works
Users begin by connecting their wallet to the Arvo platform and selecting one of the supported blockchain networks, such as Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Polygon, Sepolia, and other supported chains. Users can then create a dedicated vault on each chain and deposit the assets they want their trading agent to access.
These vaults act as secure, user-owned capital containers. Trading agents can interact with the assets through Arvo's chain-specific smart contract infrastructure to execute trades and swaps while the user retains ownership and control over their funds.
Trade Execution and Risk Assessment
Arvo operates through two core engines: a Trade Engine and a Risk Engine.
When a trading agent identifies an opportunity, it submits a trade intent containing information about the proposed trade and, optionally, the insurance terms requested for that trade.
The Trade Engine is responsible for executing the submitted trade intent. Arvo intentionally allows trades to proceed without unnecessary interference from the insurance system because the protocol does not aim to alter, restrict, or second-guess an agent's trading strategy.
At the same time, the Risk Engine independently analyzes the proposed trade to determine whether it is suitable for insurance coverage.
The Risk Engine evaluates multiple factors, including:

Liquidity of the assets and markets involved
Asset and market volatility
Expected price impact of the trade
Trade size relative to available liquidity
Oracle and market data
Requested insurance coverage duration
Other relevant market and risk parameters

Based on this analysis, the Risk Engine determines whether the trade is insurable. If the trade qualifies for coverage, the engine generates a risk assessment report containing:

Insurability status
Risk Score ranging from 1–100
Insurance premium denominated in USDC
Plausible coverage duration
Additional risk and market assessment data

Insurance Application
The risk assessment report is submitted to the Arvo backend, which compares the coverage terms proposed by the Risk Engine against the insurance requirements originally specified in the agent's trade intent.
The backend determines whether the requested coverage can be applied under the calculated risk conditions. If the trade is approved for insurance, the Arvo infrastructure signals the appropriate chain-specific smart contract to apply the insurance coverage and deduct the required premium in USDC from the vault selected by the user.
Asset Locking and Coverage
Once insurance coverage is activated, the relevant traded assets are locked for the duration of the coverage period. This allows the protocol to track the trade's performance and calculate the resulting profit or loss throughout the insured period.
The locking mechanism is designed specifically for insurance tracking and settlement. Users still retain control over their assets and may choose to withdraw locked assets before the coverage period expires. However, withdrawing assets before the end of the agreed coverage duration automatically invalidates the associated insurance coverage and makes any future insurance claim for that trade null.
The Vision
Arvo aims to become a decentralized risk and insurance layer for autonomous on-chain trading. Rather than controlling how AI agents trade, Arvo allows agents to operate freely while providing users with an additional layer of protection against the risks associated with autonomous trading.
By combining user-controlled vaults, chain-specific smart contracts, autonomous trade execution, real-time risk assessment, and decentralized insurance mechanisms, Arvo enables a future where users can confidently deploy autonomous trading agents while maintaining greater control and protection over their capital.
howItsMade:
Arvo is built as a multi-service, event-driven system that connects autonomous trading agents, trade execution, risk assessment, and on-chain insurance infrastructure.
The user interface is a modern Next.js application built with TypeScript and Tailwind CSS. Next.js also handles our backend and API layer, allowing users to connect their wallets, select supported chains, create and manage vaults, deposit assets, and monitor their trades and insurance coverage.
Our Trade Engine is built with Node.js and TypeScript and uses Uniswap as a core partner technology. We leverage Uniswap for fetching swap quotes, accessing liquidity and market data, and executing trades submitted by autonomous agents. To handle multiple trades concurrently, the Trade Engine uses Redis-backed queues and a multi-worker architecture, allowing trade intents to be processed asynchronously without blocking one another.
The Risk Engine is an independent Python-based service designed for parallel risk assessment. It uses Redis Streams and consumer/worker groups to process multiple trade intents concurrently. The engine analyzes factors such as token liquidity, price impact, token age, 30-day volatility, market conditions, and requested insurance duration. We use Uniswap APIs for quotes and market data alongside DexScreener and other data sources for liquidity and token-level market analysis.
Our smart contracts are written in Solidity and developed and tested using Foundry/Forge. The contracts implement Arvo's chain-specific vault and protocol infrastructure, enabling users to securely deposit assets, allow authorized agent trades, pay insurance premiums, and lock insured assets for the duration of coverage. For the demo, contracts are deployed on testnets such as Sepolia, while the architecture is designed to support multiple EVM chains.
To piece everything together, the Next.js frontend and backend are deployed on Vercel for the demo, while the Trade Engine and Risk Engine run as independent services on AWS. All services communicate asynchronously through Upstash Cloud Redis, which acts as the event and messaging backbone connecting the Arvo backend, Trade Engine, and Risk Engine.
One particularly hacky but important architectural decision was separating trade execution from risk assessment entirely. We didn't want insurance evaluation to slow down or interfere with an agent's trading strategy, so the trade can execute independently while risk assessment happens in parallel. Once the Risk Engine produces its report, the backend validates the proposed insurance terms against those requested in the original trade intent and signals the appropriate chain-specific contract to apply coverage, deduct the premium, and lock the insured assets.
The result is a distributed system where autonomous agents can trade freely while Arvo independently acts as a decentralized risk and insurance layer around every trade.

name: Watcher
description: Your wallet gets one more chance before suspicious withdrawals become irreversible.
projectDescription:
Watcher is a self-custody security protocol for EVM wallets that detects suspicious withdrawal behavior and creates a reaction window before funds leave the wallet.
Every withdrawal is evaluated on-chain against behavioral security rules. Large withdrawals, probe transaction patterns, and slow-drain attacks are automatically placed into a Security Queue instead of executing immediately. During the delay window, users can cancel the withdrawal, activate Containment Mode to freeze the vault, or instantly recover funds to a pre-registered Trusted Recovery Address.
The smart contract itself enforces security.
howItsMade:
Watcher is built in Solidity, with the protocol deployed on Ethereum Sepolia. The core architecture is a per-user smart vault that maintains isolated balances, pending withdrawals, recovery addresses, and security state for every wallet.
The Security Engine evaluates each withdrawal against the behavioral rules. Recovery features are implemented entirely on-chain. Trusted Recovery Address changes require a delayed confirmation flow, while Containment Mode freezes vault activity and cancels pending withdrawals when activated. Watcher also supports optional Ledger hardware authorization using OpenZeppelin ECDSA signature verification, requiring a valid hardware wallet signature before executing flagged withdrawals.
The protocol includes tests covering attack scenarios, edge cases, and state transitions, along with integration tests validating the complete recovery workflow.

name: Weir Protocol
description: Perpetual subscriptions for AI agents. It spends yield forever, never principal.
projectDescription:
Your agent has a $12/month API subscription. You fund it with $500. In forty months it is dead, and so is whatever it was maintaining. Recurring costs do not stop. Budgets do.
Every funded agent today is mortal by construction. You hand it a lump sum and a spending cap, and that cap is a policy: a session key that drains, an allowance someone can raise, a config line in a service you hope nobody edits. The agent spends principal because principal is the only thing it has.
Weir endows the bill instead of funding the agent. An owner commits principal to Aave once. From then on the agent is paid only what the index produces, and three things are true by construction rather than by policy. The agent never chooses an amount: harvest() derives it from Aave's liquidity index as accrued = P x (i1 - i0) / i0, so there is no amount parameter to abuse. It never chooses a destination; that comes from storage. And it cannot reach the principal, because after withdrawing the accrual the remaining balance is P again.
Because a caller has nothing to choose and nothing to gain, harvest is permissionless. No keeper, no relayer, no liveness dependency on us. The agent can call it and pay itself, and it has: 0.016172 USDC released on Base Sepolia with the principal unchanged.
The owner can close the endowment and reclaim 100% of the principal at any time.
At Aave's live mainnet USDC rate, $4,045 endows a $12/month subscription forever. The yield is not small. The bill is small, and the principal is simply whatever that bill requires
howItsMade:
An Aave aToken is a scaled-balance token: your balance is a raw balance times a global index. That is the same object as a Token-2022 scaled-UI multiplier on Solana, and it is the one property Weir needs. For principal P committed at index i0, the releasable amount at i1 is P x (i1 - i0) / i0. After withdrawing exactly that, the remaining balance is P again, so principal is preserved by construction rather than by a check someone could forget.
Stack: Solidity 0.8.35 and Foundry for the contract; Next.js 15, viem and Privy for the app; a subgraph on The Graph's Subgraph Studio; an MCP server for the agent; a TypeScript agent with an x402 client.
Two things were genuinely hacky, and they are the parts we are most pleased with.
First, keeping the swap permissionless. harvest() has no keeper because the amount comes from the index and the recipient from storage, so a caller has nothing to abuse. Adding Uniswap reintroduced exactly one attackable parameter, amountOutMinimum, and a caller could pass zero and sandwich the agent. We floored it against Aave's own Chainlink-backed oracle, so a caller may RAISE the slippage guard but never lower it. That adds no trust assumption we did not already carry, since Weir already depends on Aave.
Second, a rounding reserve. Aave burns scaled units with rayDiv round-half-up, so withdrawing the exact accrual burns up to one extra scaled unit and leaves the balance a hair BELOW principal. Left alone that leaks a unit per harvest and, with several endowments sharing one aToken position, the shortfall compounds until the last owner to close is short. Weir withholds index/RAY + 1 units per harvest, tracks the total, and pays it to the agent on close, so nothing leaks and nothing is stranded. A fork test runs 48 harvests across two endowments and asserts both.
Partner tech, and how it earned its place. The Graph indexes every endowment and release, and our MCP server answers the question an endowed agent actually needs — not "what is my balance", which is actively misleading here because principal is visible but unspendable, but "what can I spend forever". It returns a PERPETUAL or NOT SURVIVABLE verdict against a proposed burn rate. Uniswap converts a WETH endowment's yield into the USDC bills are denominated in; fork tested, 10 WETH accrued 0.08638 WETH over 180 days and paid 218.698043 USDC, within two cents of oracle. Privy is how an owner signs in and commits principal, as a self-service Earn vault flow — deliberately not the only way in, because we fall back to any injected wallet, and gating the whole write path on one vendor's key turns a missing env var into a dead demo.
Testing: 23 tests. 10 offline unit and fuzz tests run in 477ms with no RPC; 13 fork tests run against live Aave v3 on Base at a pinned block, no mocks. The fork tests found four real bugs that reading the code did not, including the rounding leak above.
Built with Claude Code as the implementing agent. Full disclosure of what was AI-written, what the human contributed, and the eight bugs the AI introduced and later caught is in AI-USE.md in the repo.

name: Blitzwing
description: No GPU? No problem. Host a piece of an AI model and earn HBAR for it.
projectDescription:
Blitzwing is an OpenAI-compatible large-language-model inference network with no data center behind it. Instead of one machine holding an entire model, the model is sliced layer-by-layer across a swarm of ordinary, volunteer computers. When a chat request arrives, it flows through those machines in order — each computing only the layers it holds — and the finished completion comes out the other end. To the caller it looks exactly like a normal /v1/chat/completions endpoint; under the hood, a dozen strangers' PCs/laptops may have collaborated to produce that single answer.
The breakthrough is that you don't need a GPU to participate. The compute required by splitting layers is small enough that a slice runs comfortably on a plain CPU. A contributor installs one command (npm i -g blitzwing), says how many layers their machine can host, and provides only a Hedera account ID — no private key ever leaves their machine, and a free Cloudflare tunnel means no public IP or port forwarding is required.
Two things make it more than a networking trick. First, everyone gets paid automatically, per request: a consumer pays via the x402 protocol over Hedera, and the instant payment settles, every machine that contributed is paid HBAR proportional to the number of layers it hosted, with a tamper-evident receipt written to the Hedera Consensus Service. No invoicing, no payout portal, no human in the loop. Second, nothing is "trust me": every node carries a real on-chain ENS name (host-abc123.blitzwing.eth) publishing exactly which layers it serves and which Hedera account it's paid to. A consumer can independently verify, on two separate public ledgers, that a given machine computed a given slice of a given request and was paid the exact amount claimed. Blitzwing turns idle hardware into verifiable, automatically-paid inference capacity: priced on Hedera, named on ENS, open to anyone with a PC even without a GPU.
howItsMade:
The brain is a Python orchestrator ("mother"). It boots holding the whole model, then as contributors join it carves layer ranges off the largest current holder — a live "shrink and hand off" rebalance. The clever bit that makes this demoable in seconds: restarting a compute server with a narrower range is fast because the layer weights are already cached on disk, so there's no re-download. It keeps an authoritative in-memory host registry (source of truth for routing), serializes joins so coverage of 0:total_layers is never broken, verifies a new host's blocks are actually visible in the Distributed Hash Table before finalizing, and runs a heartbeat/reaper loop (~20s beats, 60s TTL) that reclaims and merges the layers of any node that goes silent.
The distributed inference engine is a vendored fork of Petals (bigscience-workshop) over a libp2p DHT. Because most volunteer machines sit behind NAT, we added a custom HTTP-chain forward pass: the orchestrator picks the tail host (holder of the highest layers) as the conductor, and it drives generation token-by-token by making outbound HTTP calls hop-to-hop (/v1/chain/prefix → /v1/chain/continue), serializing hidden states between hops with a compact tensor codec, then applying the final RMSNorm + lm_head and sampling only on itself. Outbound-only hops are exactly what NAT and Cloudflare Quick Tunnels allow — that's how a home laptop becomes a first-class node with zero router config. A lightweight shard_manager sidecar on every machine starts/stops/reloads the compute engine with a given layer range.
Payments are x402 over Hedera, implemented as two small TypeScript (Hono) services: a gateway that enforces HTTP 402 and advertises price + payTo, and a facilitator that verifies and settles the HBAR payment — it's deliberately strict and fetches the payer's public key from the Mirror Node to validate wallet-signed transactions. A deliberate design choice is settle-before-inference: CPU inference on a swarm can run long enough that an up-front-signed Hedera tx would expire, so we settle into escrow first, then compute. Payout is layers_hosted × cost_per_layer, sent via a Hardhat-deployed BlitzwingEscrow.sol contract (a pool-based, operator-gated payment splitter on Hedera's Testnet). Every payout writes a consensus-timestamped HCS audit message, and the consumer's response carries a blitzwing_payment receipt referencing the same topic + sequence number.
Identity is deliberately split onto a second chain. An ens-service (TypeScript, built on ensjs + viem) mints real ENSv2 subnames on Sepolia for every host and writes namespaced com.blitzwing.* text records (host id, Hedera account, block range, role, status) — the operator pays all Sepolia gas so a contributor needs only a Hedera account. The orchestrator's Python ENS client keeps these records in sync through the swarm lifecycle (join/rebalance/leave), acts as a hard payout gate (ENS_STRICT), and every receipt binds the ens_name to the payment.
The frontend is a TanStack Start (React 19 + Vite, SSR) "Swarm Console" deployed on Vercel that polls the live network to animate the swarm, and lets a user connect a HashPack wallet to sign an x402 payment client-side — using browser-safe base64 encoding and a same-origin proxy so the browser can read the custom x402 CORS headers — completing the full pay-to-compute loop in a browser.
Notably hacky / worth mentioning: the two-chain verification story (ENS on Sepolia for identity, Hedera for value), the tail-driven outbound-only HTTP forward pass that makes NAT'd PCs/Laptops first-class contributors, the settle-before-inference sequencing to dodge transaction-expiry on slow CPU generation, and reusing on-disk weight caching to make live layer rebalancing near-instant instead of a multi-minute stall. Everything ships inside the npm package, so a contributor never clones the repo — one command and a Hedera account ID and they're earning.

name: Scouts
description: Scout turns natural-language onchain intents into verified live monitors.
projectDescription:
Scout is an autonomous onchain monitoring system that turns what a user wants to watch into a real, verifiable monitoring program. Instead of making users find contracts, understand events, configure indexers, or write alert logic, they can describe an intent such as “alert me when a first-time Uniswap trader buys more than $100K of ETH.”
Scout resolves ambiguity, asks for missing details when necessary, compiles the request into a typed monitoring program, determines the data capabilities it needs, discovers reusable Substreams infrastructure, verifies the resulting pipeline against real historical chain data, and transitions it into live monitoring.
The monitoring runtime is protocol-independent: normalized onchain events flow through reusable filters, comparisons, windows, aggregations, historical predicates, investigations, and deterministic decisions. Uniswap is our deepest integration, while a separate Base USDC transfer monitor demonstrates that the architecture is not tied to swap-specific logic.
The core idea is simple: protocols provide data; Scout provides the monitoring language.
howItsMade:
Scout is built as a TypeScript monorepo with a Next.js/React frontend, a durable background worker, PostgreSQL/Supabase persistence, typed domain packages, and Rust Substreams modules compiled to WASM.
The Graph is load-bearing in two places. Substreams powers Scout’s historical and live blockchain data pipelines: Scout searches and inspects existing packages, prefers reuse/parameterization/composition over rebuilding known infrastructure, executes pipelines against real historical blocks, persists cursors, catches up to finalized chain state, and then continues monitoring live data. Graph/Subgraph data is used for contextual investigations such as determining whether an actor had previous Uniswap activity.
Natural-language requests are compiled into a typed WatchProgram rather than executed directly by an LLM. A capability planner validates every requested field, operator, historical predicate, chain, address, and data requirement before a Watch can run. The actual hot path is deterministic: normalized events are evaluated through typed comparisons, windows, aggregations and historical evidence. Unknown historical state stays UNKNOWN rather than being guessed.
For Uniswap, Scout normalizes real V3 swap activity and combines live Substreams data with historical Graph context for monitors such as large ETH buys and first-time Uniswap traders. We also implemented a separate Base canonical-USDC transfer path through the same generic evaluator to prove the runtime is not hardcoded around Uniswap.
A major engineering focus was preventing AI hallucinations from becoming product truth: model outputs are schema-validated, packages/modules must exist in inspected registry data, addresses are resolved from authoritative sources, explanations are evidence-bound, and only deterministic verification/health gates can mark a Watch as verified or live.

name: EchoTip
description: On-chain thank-you notes — publicly tip and credit maintainers, speakers, or friends by ENS name.
projectDescription:
EchoTip is a simple on-chain tipping and message board built around ENS identities. Instead of tipping or thanking someone with a long, easy-to-mistype 0x address, EchoTip lets you type in their ENS name (like vitalik.eth), automatically resolve their profile — name, avatar, and address — and send them a small ETH tip together with a public message.
Every tip is recorded on-chain in a lightweight smart contract, so each ENS name effectively gets its own public "wall" of tips and shout-outs that anyone can view. It's a small piece of social infrastructure for the ENS ecosystem: turning a human-readable name into a shareable, tippable identity with a visible history of support.
We built this to show how much friction ENS removes from everyday on-chain interactions — no address book, no clipboard, just a name.
howItsMade:
EchoTip has two parts: a Solidity smart contract (TipBoard.sol) deployed on Sepolia that stores tips as (sender, amount, message, timestamp) structs per recipient address and emits a TipSent event, and a Next.js + TypeScript frontend using wagmi, viem, and RainbowKit for wallet connection and contract calls.
ENS resolution happens client-side using viem's built-in ENS actions (getEnsAddress, getEnsAvatar) against an Ethereum mainnet RPC, so users can type any ENS name and instantly see the resolved address, avatar, and profile — even though the tipping contract itself lives on a testnet, keeping the demo free to use. The frontend reads a recipient's tip history straight from the contract with getTips(address) and renders it as a live-updating wall.
We used Foundry for contract development, testing, and deployment, and Vercel for hosting the frontend.

name: OpenGotchi
description: A voice-driven pet that hires, pays and rates AI agents on Arc via USDC escrow jobs and swaps.
projectDescription:
OpenGotchi is a palm-sized AI pet: an ESP32-S3 device with a 1.8-inch AMOLED screen, a microphone, a speaker, touch and motion sensors, and a personality. It has needs you look after (feed, clean, sleep, play), it reacts with animated "milady" eyes, and it talks. Say "Jarvis" and it listens, transcribes, answers, and can open apps or take actions for you. It is meant to be the friendly physical face of an AI agent that sits on your desk instead of in a browser tab.
gotchiOS is the operating system that runs it, and our flagship. It is an ESP-IDF firmware with an embedded MicroPython app runtime, so apps are single Python files that can be deployed to the device over the air. It provides the on-device wake word (esp-sr WakeNet), a voice rail with a background audio recorder and a speaker path, a TLS MQTT link to the OpenGotchi broker with per-device identity and secrets, a notification system, pet-state telemetry, and a design system (dark AMOLED, violet gradients, proportional fonts, rounded surfaces, eye sprites). Anyone can flash it onto their own ESP32 hardware from the open-source releases at https://github.com/opengotchi/gotchiOS-releases.
What we built for ETHOnline: OpenGotchi Jobs on Arc. We gave the pet a wallet and taught it to hire, pay, and rate other AI agents on Arc, entirely by voice, and to buy tokens on Arc with its own money. Everything runs on top of stock gotchiOS through its public app and MQTT interfaces. No firmware was modified, and the on-device app was deployed over the air.
The flow. Say "Jarvis, what's the weather in Berlin?" The pet agent turns the transcript into a job for a worker agent, checks its own rules, then opens an ERC-8183 job on Arc with the worker as provider and itself as evaluator. The worker sets its price onchain, the pet approves and funds USDC escrow, the worker does the work and submits the keccak hash of its result, the pet checks that the hash it received matches the onchain deliverable, completes the job so the USDC settles to the worker, and records feedback on the worker's ERC-8004 identity in the ReputationRegistry. Seven Arc transactions per request, ten to eighteen seconds end to end. The pet then speaks the answer and shows a receipt: job number, price, settlement transaction, balance, today's spend.
Agents with identity. The worker registers itself as an ERC-8004 agent on first start (agent id 894780 on Arc testnet) and sells six skills: live weather, crypto prices, the top tech headline, Polymarket prediction-market odds, a mood-matched snack for the pet, and a fortune. The pet only pays workers that have an onchain identity, and gives a new worker only cheap jobs until it has a track record.
Autonomous spending with real guardrails. "Jarvis, buy one dollar of bitcoin" is a real Circle App Kit swap on Arc from USDC into cirBTC; "buy two dollars of euros" swaps into EURC. "Buy ethereum" is politely refused because ETH does not exist on Arc. Every decision runs on live signals: USDC balance minus a reserve, a daily budget from the ledger, per-job and per-purchase caps, the worker's identity and history, the pet's battery from device telemetry, and the planner's confidence. Declines are spoken and shown on screen as "held by policy", not hidden.
A better UX for talking to your pet. The pet listens on its wake word or a tap, stops on silence with a live waveform, and communicates back through TTS. The app follows the gotchiOS design language: the pet's eyes react to the job (spiral while thinking, heart when it settles, sleepy when a job is held, teary if it fails), a six-node orbit ring lights one node per Arc transaction while the job runs, and a particle burst fires on settlement.
The result is a physical companion that can do paid work through other agents and settle it on Arc while you watch it happen on its face.
howItsMade:
Stack. TypeScript on Bun for the two server-side agents, MicroPython for the on-device app, viem for Arc, Circle App Kit for swaps, whisper.cpp for speech-to-text, Claude with structured outputs for planning, MQTT over TLS for the device link. Chain: Arc testnet (chain id 5042002, USDC as the native gas token), using viem's built-in arcTestnet chain definition.
Onchain layer (shared/arc.ts). We use Arc's deployed reference contracts directly, no contract of our own: the ERC-8183 AgenticCommerce contract (0x0747…4583) for createJob, setBudget, fund, submit, complete, getJob; the ERC-8004 IdentityRegistry (0x8004A8…BD9e) for register, and ReputationRegistry (0x8004B6…8713) for giveFeedback; and USDC's ERC-20 interface at 0x3600…0000 for approve and balanceOf. The ABIs are hand-typed as const so viem infers every argument and event. Job ids are recovered by decoding the JobCreated log from the createJob receipt. The pet is client and evaluator; the worker is provider.
Two agents, two wallets. worker/ is an Express service that registers an ERC-8004 identity on first start (metadata is a base64 data: URI, agent id persisted in worker.json), exposes /skills, and implements two job hooks: POST /jobs/:id/accept reads the job onchain, verifies it is assigned to this provider and still Open, then calls setBudget; POST /jobs/:id/run verifies the job is Funded, executes the skill, computes keccak256 of the canonical result payload, calls submit, and returns payload, hash, and result. Skills pull free public data: Open-Meteo, CoinGecko, the Hacker News Firebase API, and Polymarket's Gamma API (public-search then highest-volume active market). agent/ is the pet's brain: it orchestrates the lifecycle, and it never calls complete() unless keccak256(payload) equals the deliverable it reads back from getJob. Every settled request is seven Arc transactions, ten to eighteen seconds wall clock with sub-second finality.
Decision logic (agent/src/policy.ts). Purely deterministic, evaluated before any USDC moves: USDC balance minus a reserve, spend-to-date from an append-only ledger.json, a per-job cap re-checked against the worker's onchain setBudget quote, whether the worker has an ERC-8004 id, how many jobs it has completed for us (a new worker only gets jobs at or below half the cap), the pet's battery from the firmware's telemetry topic, and the planner's confidence. Declines are surfaced as a "held" receipt and spoken.
Buying tokens. agent/src/swap.ts wraps Circle App Kit: createViemAdapterFromPrivateKey from @circle-fin/adapter-viem-v2, kit.estimateSwap for the quote, kit.swap({ from: { chain: "Arc_Testnet" }, tokenIn: "USDC", tokenOut, amountIn }). Arc testnet lists USDC, EURC, and cirBTC, so "bitcoin" maps to cirBTC and "euros" to EURC; anything else is declined by name. A separate per-purchase cap applies. App Kit gave us a working same-chain swap on Arc in one call, with fees and gas returned in the estimate.
Planner (agent/src/brain.ts). Claude via the Anthropic SDK with zod structured outputs: the transcript plus the skill catalogue produce {action: job | buy | none, skillId, params, buyAmountUsd, buyAsset, confidence, reply}. A regex-based planner with the same output shape takes over when no API key is set, so the pipeline is deterministic in a demo.
Device link. The firmware speaks MQTT over TLS on 8883 with the device hash as username and a provisioned secret as password. We subscribe to the device's commands and telemetry topics and publish directives on its agent topic. Two firmware facts shaped the protocol: the agent inbox holds only eight messages, and the auth hook rejects client ids starting with agent-. So the receipt is sent as one message, rcpt k␟v␞k␟v… with ASCII unit and record separators, status applied last, and it is sent before the speech so the screen flips before the pet talks. The device app is pushed with bun run deploy-app, which base64-encodes the file into the firmware's app/deploy topic with launch:true, after first asking any running copy to exit (deploying over a live instance rebooted the pet twice).
Voice pipeline. The pet's own WakeNet "Jarvis" model is armed through the firmware's audio.wake_* API, disarmed during recording and playback because the detector and recorder cannot share the mic. Recording uses the firmware's background recorder ring (8 kHz PCM16) with an energy VAD: noise floor learned over the first 300 ms, threshold 3× floor plus 350, stop after 800 ms of silence, 1.2 to 7 seconds. The PCM is POSTed to the agent's /voice/stt, resampled to 16 kHz by ffmpeg, and transcribed by whisper-cli with ggml-base.en in roughly 200 to 350 ms. Replies come back through /voice/tts as raw 16 kHz s16le PCM that the app streams straight into audio.play() via http.stream; odd trailing bytes are carried between TCP chunks so samples never misalign, which was the fix for an initial burst of pure noise, along with skipping the padding chunk Apple's WAV writer inserts.
On-device app (device/arcvoice.py). Single-file MicroPython on the stock gotchiOS runtime, drawn with the firmware's primitives: rrect, rrect_grad, rrect_a, ftext with the Space Grotesk and Plex faces, and gray4 for the 168×88 milady eye sprites. Eyes react to state, a six-node orbit ring (one node per Arc transaction) advances from the agent's step messages with a comet while working, the listening screen renders a 28-bar waveform from rec_level(), and settlement fires a 40-frame particle burst using precomputed sine tables. Crashes are reported back over MQTT as evt|shell|error: so they can be diagnosed remotely.
Hacky bits worth admitting. Boot markers emitted over MQTT to bisect a startup crash that turned out to be a stray placeholder token. A receipt encoding built on control characters because JSON plus eight inbox slots lost the status flip. Funding the worker's gas by a plain native-value transfer, since on Arc USDC is the gas token.

name: Smile
description: Standard options market potentially as popular as Robinhood, decentralized as Polymarket.
projectDescription:
Smile is a non-custodial marketplace for fixed-expiry, cash-settled European options on ETH — and, on Circle's Arc chain, on any USDC-quoted pair. Every option sold is backed by collateral a liquidity provider (LP) has committed through 1inch Aqua, a shared-liquidity layer where a maker's tokens stay in the maker's own wallet until a trade actually needs them: collateral is pulled just-in-time at fill, never parked in advance. Pricing runs inside 1inch SwapVM, a small on-chain virtual machine that executes a maker's strategy as a program of opcodes; Smile adds one custom opcode that prices an option from its strike, tenor and volatility.
For the EthOnline 2026 Continuation Track, Smile adds three capital-efficient sibling vaults so LPs can make markets for options sellers without locking the full notional:
• SpreadVault — defined-risk credit spreads. A short put is hedged by a long put, so the vault escrows only the spread's true worst-case loss (the strike width) instead of the whole strike. The same holds for call spreads and iron condors: because European options settle at one price, only one side can finish in-the-money, so the escrow is the larger wing, not the sum.
• MarginVault — partially-collateralized (naked) puts: sell a put on ETH without posting a full ETH of collateral. A six-stage margin-and-liquidation process — open, buy, under-margin on a price crash, a one-hour grace window then auction, a waterfall (writer's margin → auction bidder → backstop pool → insurance fund), then cash settlement at expiry — stands behind every position and is traceable end-to-end with ./script/margin-lifecycle.sh. These are Arc's programmable-money flows made concrete.
• RfqVault — request-for-quote fills agains
t LP-signed EIP-712 quotes, for sizes and strikes off the standard grid.
The Graph indexes the vault's liquidity ranges and fills, replacing the brute-force RPC scan that went blind past 50 authorizations. The Subgraph MCP feeds an AI copilot live liquidity, open interest and trade opportunities which — alongside news, social and quant MCPs plus packaged trader skills regarding smile and their portfolio — give traders an edge.
Circle Arc makes the whole book stablecoin-native: because Arc settles in USDC, both calls and puts are collateralized in USDC, rather than calls in ETH and puts in USDC. The margin-vault treasury runs with no private key in the repository — Circle Gateway bridges USDC from any chain to top up the insurance fund, and a Circle developer-controlled wallet, signed through Circle's API, funds the backstop pool. Every top-up lands as an on-chain receipt shown in the app.
howItsMade:
please note the continuation submission is not on main branch, but EthOnline2026_continuation_track.
Technologies. Solidity contracts (Foundry, via_ir) on the official 1inch Aqua + SwapVM, vendored and unmodified; a Next.js 16 frontend with Wagmi/Viem, recharts and a TradingView price chart; The Graph for indexing; and an AI copilot on the Vercel AI SDK (Anthropic/OpenAI/Google/OpenRouter). Expiry settlement reads Chainlink.
How it's pieced together. An LP authorizes a price range and ships it to a vault; the vault is an Aqua app, so at buy time Aqua pulls the LP's collateral just-in-time and SwapVM prices the premium on-chain via a custom opcode. Fills emit events that The Graph indexes; the frontend and the copilot read that index instead of scanning the chain. On Circle Arc the same stack settles in native USDC.
What the partners bought us.
1inch Aqua — collateral stays in LP wallets and is pulled at fill, so we added three capital-efficient vaults (defined-risk spreads, partially-margined puts with a liquidation waterfall, RFQ against LP-signed quotes) as sibling Aqua apps without touching the audited main vault.
The Graph — its index replaced a brute-force RPC scan that went blind past 50 authorizations, and via the Subgraph MCP it became a live data source the copilot reasons over.
Circle Arc + Gateway — Arc settles in USDC, so calls and puts are both USDC-collateralized; Gateway and a developer-controlled wallet top up the margin tier's safety funds, so the treasury runs with no private key in the repo.
Hackiest part. Not the contracts but the last-mile UI — keeping an options frontend honest about the async, just-in-time chain state it doesn't directly own (write-before-read races, and stale ranges that had to be gated so they couldn't look actionable).

name: Poincaré
description: A Uniswap v4 hook that knows when a trend is real, then leans its curve against it. No oracle.
projectDescription:
Poincaré is a Uniswap v4 hook that decides when a price trend is genuinely real, and only then bends its bonding curve to defend liquidity providers.
THE PROBLEM. LPs don't lose money because markets are volatile. They lose it because markets have direction. That loss has a name, Loss-Versus-Rebalancing, and the identity behind it says the lever is the curve's shape, not the fee. Two price paths with identical step sizes leak completely differently: the one that chops ends where it started and barely costs anything, while the one that trends is arbitraged the whole way down. So the right response is to reshape the curve, but only while a real trend is actually happening. That last clause is the hard part, and it is the project.
THE ENGINE. Deciding "has a regime change started, and how fast can I be sure without crying wolf" is a solved problem in statistics called Quickest Change Detection. Poincaré runs a two-sided CUSUM detector on the pool's own log-returns, sampled once per block from pre-swap reserves. CUSUM is asymptotically optimal under Lorden's minimax criterion, meaning it minimises worst-case detection delay for any false-alarm rate you tolerate. Crucially it fires at a data-dependent stopping time rather than after a fixed number of blocks, so there is no countdown for an attacker to precompute. A directional-efficiency gate confirms the move is a march rather than a thrash, and a Huber clip bounds any single block's influence. Thresholds are derived from a target false-alarm rate measured on the pair's own heavy-tailed returns, never hand-picked.
THE ACTUATOR. Once a trend is confirmed, flow pushing with it pays a small, capped, rate-limited spread that goes straight to the LPs it would otherwise have been taken from. Flow trading against the trend, and all flow in calm markets, pays nothing and trades at the plain constant-product price. We originally built the stronger version, direction-dependent curve depth, found a buy-shallow/sell-deep round trip that drains the pool, and shipped the spread instead because it is arb-safe by construction.
NO EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES. No oracle, keeper, AVS, relayer or cross-chain service. The only input is the pool's own reserve-implied price. Adding a feed would reintroduce exactly the trust and latency assumptions the detector exists to remove.
BUILT DURING THIS HACKATHON: THE DETECTOR LAB. The detector's parameters decide what counts as a trend, so nobody should take that calibration on trust. The Lab replays the pool's real recorded history under any parameters you choose, against the deployed configuration as a control, using an exact BigInt port of the on-chain Cusum, DirectionalSignal and ControlLaw libraries. Replaying the live parameters reproduces the trace the hook actually emitted with ZERO WEI of deviation across 362 real Unichain Sepolia blocks, and that capture is committed as a fixture and asserted in CI so the port cannot drift from the contracts without failing a build. Drop the threshold and watch it fire inside chop; drop the directional gate and watch the duty cycle explode. Each panel is also narrated in plain English by a Gemini call routed through a Supabase edge function, with a deterministic local fallback so it degrades rather than breaks.
DOES IT WORK. Over 12 months of real Binance ETH/USDC 4h closes, against a symmetric volatility-scaled fee sized to cost traders exactly the same (matched to 0.01%), Poincaré retained +23,706 USDC of LP value against the baseline's +18,184, which is 6.73 against 5.17 of LP value per unit of trader cost. On raw LVR reduction the symmetric baseline edges us, 4.41% against 4.27%, and we publish that too. The first run of that study tripped the equal-friction assertion, which caught us spending 40% more of our traders' money than the baseline; we retuned and re-ran rather than shipping the flattering number.
STATUS. Live on Unichain Sepolia with a demo WETH/USDC pool, a faucet and a web app. 131 Foundry tests plus 40 TypeScript tests, invariants at 128k randomised calls per flavour with zero reverts, and quotes that match execution to the wei even in a fresh block. Selected as a winner at the Uniswap Hook Incubator 10, then selected by the Uniswap Foundation Security Fund, which sponsored a security review by Olympix: nine findings, none high severity, all fixed, each with a regression test that fails on the pre-fix code. An independent external audit is still required before mainnet, and we say so.
The curve is the actuator. The detector is the contribution.
howItsMade:
STACK. Solidity 0.8.30 with Foundry. Uniswap v4-core and v4-periphery, OpenZeppelin's uniswap-hooks BaseCustomCurve for settlement, Solady FixedPointMathLib for lnWad, hookmate for router and address constants. Frontend is Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind v4 with wagmi, viem and RainbowKit, backed by Supabase (Postgres, Realtime, Edge Functions on Deno). Deployed to Unichain Sepolia against the canonical v4 PoolManager, with the hook address CREATE2-mined so the permission flags are encoded in it.
THE HOOK. It is a custom-curve hook, so it bypasses v4's native x*y=k entirely. beforeSwap returns a BeforeSwapDelta that consumes the full specified amount and supplies the computed counter-amount; the native tick-liquidity path is reverted. Reserves are the hook's own ERC-6909 claim balances rather than a tracked variable, so they stay consistent through take/settle/sync inside the unlock pattern. Liquidity is hook-owned with the LP share token being the hook's own ERC-20, and MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY is burned to a dead address on the first mint as a first-depositor guard.
THE DETECTOR PIPELINE. Four small pure libraries, each independently unit-tested before the hook was wired: PriceLib turns reserves into a WAD price and a signed log-return (the only ln per block, taken at the hook boundary so it stays off the pricing hot path); DirectionalSignal keeps two O(1) exponentially-weighted accumulators for directional efficiency D and a live volatility estimate sigma-hat, deliberately not a ring buffer because a fixed window has a hard edge an attacker knows the timing of; Cusum runs the two-sided recursion with updateCapped so a sustained drift can never overflow and revert a swap; ControlLaw maps evidence to a bounded, rate-limited kappa. Detector state is packed into 4 storage slots (int128 statistic pair, int128/uint128 accumulator pair, uint64 kappa plus trend plus block number), which took the per-sampled-block cost to about 96k gas including the trace event. The int128 downcasts are safe because sMax <= int128.max is enforced at construction and the EWMA is bounded by the lnWad domain over (1 - lambda).
THE ARCHITECTURAL TRICK WORTH STEALING. All detector logic lives in one pure view, _projectDetector. The swap path calls it and persists the result; previewSpread and previewDetector expose the same projection read-only; the Lens quotes through those. Because the Lens sees the projected once-per-block sample the next swap would take, a quote taken in a fresh block before anyone has swapped still matches execution to the wei. One function, so the two paths cannot drift.
THE THING WE GOT WRONG FIRST. The brief called for direction-dependent curve depth. We built it, then found a concrete buy-shallow / sell-deep round trip that drains the pool, because depth asymmetry moves the mid-price rather than just the spread. The shipped design puts the asymmetry in the slope instead: a non-negative directional spread on a single symmetric base, which is unprofitable to round-trip by construction. The deep symmetric base also has two obvious parameterisations that are both unsafe (offsets recomputed from current reserves are drainable in two swaps; fixed absolute offsets shift the mid on every ratio deposit), so offsets are anchored at the first deposit and scale only with LP share supply.
BUILT THIS HACKATHON: THE OFF-CHAIN PORT. The Detector Lab needed an exact TypeScript reimplementation of three Solidity libraries. Everything is BigInt in WAD, mulDiv floors like FullMath and only ever touches non-negative magnitudes with signs reapplied, and every clamp and >= vs > is copied verbatim, because boundary cases are where a reimplementation silently drifts. It reproduces the live trace with zero wei of deviation across 362 real blocks, verified against a committed fixture in CI.
HACKY BITS AND REAL BUGS FOUND.

toWad used toFixed(18), which prints a float's BINARY expansion: (0.07).toFixed(18) is "0.070000000000000007", so parameters arrived several wei off. Fixed by going through the shortest round-tripping decimal string with exponent forms expanded by hand.
The detector runs on price = reserve1/reserve0 while the UI charts USDC/WETH, so the hook's "up" is a falling chart. The inversion is confined to one constant and one boundary, and the replay works in hook orientation so it can be diffed against raw event data.
detector_samples stores numerics for charting, and an 18-decimal value loses its low digits through a JS float. Wei-exact parity was impossible until we added a nullable jsonb column carrying the event's raw integers as decimal strings, with the reader falling back to floats for older rows.
The DetectorSample event carries D and sigma-hat but not the EWMA accumulators, so the replay seeds them by inverting those two. Exact for ewmaTV, exact in magnitude for ewmaNet, with only the sign inferred.
Enabling adaptive mode against a pool deployed with sigmaFloor = 0 divided by zero on a cold start, which is a configuration the hook's own constructor would refuse. Two clicks from a white screen; now guarded at both ends.
supabase-js turns any non-2xx edge-function response into a FunctionsHttpError and leaves the JSON body unread on the Response, so a real error message surfaced as "returned a non-2xx status code". We read it off error.context.
Gemini 3.x reasons before answering and those thought tokens count against maxOutputTokens, so a budget sized for three sentences got spent on reasoning and truncated the reply mid-word. Raised the ceiling, and now reject any candidate whose finishReason isn't STOP so a truncated answer can never reach the cache.
The narration cache had no invalidation path, so one bad answer would be served forever. Keys are now namespaced by a CACHE_VERSION constant.

TESTING. 131 Foundry tests plus 40 TypeScript. Two invariant flavours (plain and full-feature) at 128k randomised calls each with zero reverts, asserting ghost-accounting equality to the wei and that the constant-product invariant never decreases. Manipulation sims run end-to-end against the real PoolManager: a fake-trend round trip loses money, a single-block flash spike moves the detector by exactly zero, and a sigma-inflation attack on the adaptive mode burns value every block. The 12-month study forks Sepolia and replays real Binance closes through three pools. Its equal-friction assertion is the reason our headline number is honest: the first run tripped it at 28.5%, catching that we were spending 40% more of our traders' money than the baseline we were claiming to beat.
No oracle, AVS, keeper, relayer or cross-chain dependency, because the detector's entire security argument is that its only input is the pool's own price. The hackathon work uses Supabase (Postgres + Edge Functions) as the backend and the Gemini API for narration, with the key held as an edge-function secret since anything a Vite app can read at runtime ships in the bundle.

name: VaultRadar
description: Cross-protocol vault risk, sold per request to autonomous agents over x402
projectDescription:
VaultRadar is a machine-payable, cross-protocol vault-risk service. One standardized Graph query template per schema family runs across every Messari-schema deployment in its registry: fifteen registrations over ten protocols and five chains. Alongside it is a new ERC-4626 Substreams module written in Rust, composed from Pinax's erc4626 package and shipped to two chains from one WASM binary.
Risk reports are sold per request over x402, on Hedera through Blocky402 and on Arc through Circle Gateway's batcher. An autonomous agent finds the service, checks its signing key against the ERC-8004 registry on chain, seals its request with a hybrid post-quantum KEM, pays, and verifies every signature before it acts. Nothing on the path learns which vaults were asked about. Every receipt and every per-vault attestation is signed with ML-DSA-65, and the receipt hash is committed to Hedera Consensus Service, so a decision stays auditable long afterwards. When the underlying data is older than the policy allows, the service refuses to answer instead of guessing. A verdict of "no data" is a real answer, and it names the source, the block and the age so it can be checked.
howItsMade:
Built with Claude Code under human direction, using a spec-driven subagent workflow, a written spec, a written plan, one implementer per task working from a written brief, an independent reviewer for each task's diff, and a whole-branch review with a fix wave at the end. Every artifact of that process ships in the repository under docs/ai-workflow/, including the prompts in sequence, the decision ledger, the per-task briefs and reports, and the review findings. The human contribution was direction, scope cuts, and every account and key.
The service is TypeScript on Bun. Data comes from two GraphQL queries against Messari standardized subgraphs through The Graph's gateway. Each deployment is pinned by its deployment id, so a re-point cannot silently change the data underneath a risk verdict. A verification gate reads each deployment's _meta and records how fresh it is. The ERC-4626 metrics come from a Substreams module written in Rust that imports Pinax's erc4626 events package instead of scanning logs, and a sink in the same project feeds the Postgres the service reads.
The post-quantum layer is @noble/post-quantum: ML-KEM-768 combined with X25519, through HKDF-SHA-256 into AES-256-GCM for sealing requests and replies, and ML-DSA-65 for receipts and per-vault attestations. Payments run on two rails that settle in different orders. Blocky402 verifies before the handler and settles after it. Circle's Gateway settles before the handler ever runs. The code handles both explicitly instead of pretending they behave alike. Both rails have settled real payments on testnet, and the dashboard verifies a receipt in the browser against the key hash pinned on chain.

name: Re-Solver
description: Self-resolving prediction market where AI agents price questions no oracle can settle
projectDescription:
Prediction markets and oracles only work when someone can eventually report the true answer. A huge class of useful questions never gets that moment: "Is this protocol's TVL growth organic or incentive farming?", "Do these wallets belong to one actor?", "Will this DAO proposal actually help the treasury?". The evidence is public on chain, but no oracle will ever settle them, so no market can pay anyone for being right.
Re-solver is a working implementation of "Self-Resolving Prediction Markets for Unverifiable Outcomes" by Srinivasan, Karger and Chen (Yiling Chen, Harvard). The market resolves against itself. AI agents report a probability one at a time, and each one sees every earlier report. After every report the market closes with probability alpha, and the last agent becomes the reference. Everyone before it is paid with a cross-entropy market scoring rule against that reference: moving the price toward where it closed earns money, moving it away loses part of your bond. Because nobody knows when the market will stop, reporting your honest belief is the best strategy. Copying the previous agent earns exactly zero (Theorem 7), and the asker's total cost is provably capped by the deposit.
How a market works:

An asker opens a market from a browser wallet and pays a deposit over x402 on Hedera. The deposit is the paper's cost bound (b·log2 + k·R), and whatever the market does not spend is refunded.
Registered agents discover the market and each pays its own bond over x402 from its own Hedera key. No API keys, no accounts.
Each round, an agent is drawn, buys its evidence from Messari standardized subgraphs on The Graph, reasons over it with an LLM and signs a probability.
Every report is written to Hedera Consensus Service. The stopping dice come from the running hash of the report just written, so nobody, including the operator, can predict when the market closes, and anyone can recompute it from a public mirror node.
Settlement is recorded on HCS, then paid out in HBAR. Books close to the tinybar.
Each agent's track record is written to its own ENSv2 name. Per-record permissions let an agent edit its profile but never its own score.

Everything runs on Hedera testnet and Ethereum Sepolia with real payments: 20 agents, full markets with x402 deposits and bonds, HCS audit trail and on-chain settlement, all independently verified from the mirror node. The repo includes 760 offline tests and a README that maps every claim to on-chain evidence.
How it's made
TypeScript monorepo (pnpm): a pure mechanism package, Hedera, Graph and ENS packages, an Express API with orchestrator and settlement engine, an agent runtime, and a Vite + React frontend. 760 unit tests run offline in about 10 seconds.
Mechanism. The scoring rule, market state machine and settlement were written straight from the paper and enforce its hard constraints in code:  recompute it from a public mirror node.
5. Settlement is recorded on HCS, then paid out in HBAR. Books close to the tinybar.
6. Each agent's track record is written to its own ENSv2 name. Per-record permissions let an agent edit its profile but never its own score.
Everything runs on Hedera testnet and Ethereum Sepolia with real payments: 20 agents, full markets with x402 deposits and bonds, HCS audit trail and on-chain settlement, all independently verified from the mirror node. The repo includes 760 offline tests and a README that maps every claim to on-chain evidence.
howItsMade:
TypeScript monorepo (pnpm): a pure mechanism package, Hedera, Graph and ENS packages, an Express API with orchestrator and settlement engine, an agent runtime, and a Vite + React frontend. 760 unit tests run offline in about 10 seconds.
Mechanism. The scoring rule, market state machine and settlement were written straight from the paper and enforce its hard constraints in code: the reference is always the terminal agent (a rolling reference creates unbounded payouts, Theorem 8), reports are clipped to [0.01, 0.99], each agent joins a market once, the order is drawn lazily and never published, and a timeout is slashed but never counts as a round. Settlement asserts the telescoping budget bound and that money in equals money out. We hit one real design problem: capping losses at the bond during settlement breaks telescoping and the asker's guarantee. So the bond became a position limit instead: an agent can only move the price as far as its bond can cover, clipped when the report arrives. A small calculator also implements Theorems 1 and 4 to show how large k should be.
Hedera. Three paid routes (open a market, post a bond, buy a resolved answer) use @x402/express with the Hedera exact scheme through the Blocky402 facilitator on testnet. The deposit is priced per request by the same function settlement checks against. Agents pay their own bonds with @x402/fetch and their own keys. The browser pays through Hedera WalletConnect: we reimplemented the x402 signer so the wallet signs a partially signed transfer without submitting it. HCS is both the ordered report ledger and the randomness source: the stop roll reads bytes 0-7 and the agent draw reads bytes 8-15 of the SHA-384 running hash (reusing the same bytes would make part of the pool unreachable), keeping the top 53 bits so the value never rounds to 1.0. Settlement is written to HCS before any transfer, chunked because of Hedera's per-transaction account limit, and resumable without paying a chunk twice. Hacky but important: @x402/express runs the handler before settling payment, and in a live run two agents joined without paying. We now undo a paid route's effect before the 402 response is written.
The Graph. Agents read Messari standardized subgraphs through the Graph gateway (Curve as subject, SushiSwap, Bancor V3, Saddle and Uniswap V2 as peers, the Arbitrum bridge). Five data slices (liquidity, holders, activity, bridge, comparative) turn raw rows into derived statistics. The standard schema is what makes the comparative slice possible: one query string sent unchanged to five protocols built by different teams. No two agents hold the same subset of slices, because the paper requires agents' signals to be conditionally independent, and a test enforces it. The gateway client treats any GraphQL error array as a failure (the gateway returns auth errors with HTTP 200) and includes an x402 client that decodes the 402 challenge from the payment-required header.
ENSv2 (Sepolia). We deployed our own UserRegistry and PermissionedResolver proxies from ENSv2's VerifiableFactory under unverifiable.eth and minted agent-01 to agent-20. Agent Hedera accounts use ECDSA secp256k1 keys, so the same key pays bonds, signs reports and owns the ENS name. Names are minted with roleBitmap = 0, so an agent cannot swap its resolver, transfer or delete its name. Resolver permissions are granted per text key, so the agent can write description or endpoint but not score.*. We proved every rule on Sepolia with one test name before minting twenty. Registration checks on chain that an agent owns the ENS name it claims, and after every settlement the orchestrator writes each agent's record in one multicall. Contract addresses came from the contracts-v2 deployment artifacts, because the docs addresses did not match Sepolia.
Agents use OpenAI gpt-4o-mini with strict JSON output behind a one-function interface. Development was assisted by Claude Code, and the spec, roadmap and step log are in the repo.

name: AmberMarket
description: AmberMarket turns real-time junction traffic data into verifiable on-chain prediction markets.
projectDescription:
The problem AmberMarket solves
AmberMarket – Every signal is a market
The Problem It Solves
Every signal is a market. Every junction is an asset.
AmberMarket transforms real-world traffic data into on-chain prediction markets grounded in something measurable, verifiable, and live: how many vehicles cross a junction during a single green-light window.
No abstract outcomes. No human referees. Just a CV oracle watching actual CCTV streams and settling bets automatically.
What you can do with AmberMarket:
Stake on live traffic — Place $AMBER bets on real-time junction vehicle counts, settled by a YOLO-powered computer vision oracle reading live camera feeds. Transparent, automated, tamper-resistant.
Own a junction — Mint an AmberJunctionNFT to claim ownership of a real-world intersection and earn royalties every time others bet on your junction.
Get a Web3 identity — Claim a free .ambermarket.eth ENS subname and appear across leaderboards and live markets with a human-readable name.
Trust the machine, not the middleman — Smart contracts hold all funds; the oracle provides the count; winners are paid by tolerance (e.g. +-15% or exact). Zero manual intervention.
The stack in one line: Real-time CV data + on-chain prediction markets + automated oracle settlement + ENS identity, all wired together in a single hackathon build.
Challenges we ran into
Challenges We Ran Into


Bridging Python CV and a Node backend
The vehicle-counting pipeline runs on Python (YOLO + OpenCV), while the rest of the stack is Node.js + Socket.io. Rather than splitting into two long-running services, we spawn the CV pipeline as a subprocess and consume JSON lines from stdout, keeping the server single-process while still streaming live counts to clients. Getting clean shutdown, timeouts, and graceful fallbacks (a "fake mode" for when YOLO is not installed) took a few iterations to get right.


ENS subnames via Namespace
We wanted free .ambermarket.eth identities with no gas cost for users. The Namespace offchain manager requires domain-scoped API keys, something we discovered the hard way after hitting repeated 401s with a default key. Switching to domainApiKeys: { [ENS_PARENT_NAME]: NAMESPACE_API_KEY } fixed it. We also added rate-limiting (10-minute claim cooldown) and proper UI differentiation between "subname not found" and "API unavailable" for a cleaner demo experience.


Taming real CCTV streams
Caltrans D3 HLS streams are not framed for lane-level counting. They capture wide scenes with sidewalks, adjacent lanes, and irrelevant zones. We introduced a per-junction viewport config (e.g. 0.30,0.40,0.70,0.90) so the CV model only counts within a defined region of the frame. This meaningfully reduced false positives and made counts accurate enough to actually settle bets on.


Phase loop and frontend sync
The server drives a strict market cycle: RED_OPEN > GREEN_COUNTING > SETTLING, broadcast over Socket.io. Keeping the client's countdown timers, bet-open/closed states, and settlement modals in sync with backend phase (and on-chain state when the oracle is active) required a single authoritative source of truth and clearly named events, so the UI never showed "Place Bet" after the market had already locked.
howItsMade:
Technologies used: Solidity, HTML, React, Node.js, CSS, JavaScript, Flask, Python, ethers.js, Tailwind CSS
Stake on live traffic — Place $AMBER bets on real-time junction vehicle counts, settled by a YOLO-powered computer vision oracle reading live camera feeds. Transparent, automated, tamper-resistant.
Own a junction — Mint an AmberJunctionNFT to claim ownership of a real-world intersection and earn royalties every time others bet on your junction.
Get a Web3 identity — Claim a free .ambermarket.eth ENS subname and appear across leaderboards and live markets with a human-readable name.
Trust the machine, not the middleman — Smart contracts hold all funds; the oracle provides the count; winners are paid by tolerance (e.g. +-15% or exact). Zero manual intervention.
The stack in one line: Real-time CV data + on-chain prediction markets + automated oracle settlement + ENS identity, all wired together in a single hackathon build.

name: Envelope
description: Confidential payroll on Arc: computed in a Chainlink enclave, approved via Privy
projectDescription:
Envelope pays employees in USDC on Arc without ever putting the payroll table onchain.
Employer HR data, including employees, salaries, hours, leave, performance multipliers, and compensation policy, is fetched over confidential HTTP inside a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow. Payroll is computed inside the enclave and committed to a Merkle tree. Only four values leave it: the period, Merkle root, batch total, and recipient count.
