The backend proposes the root and total to PayrollDisburser. Funds require two independent controls: EIP-712 approvals from registered approvers, followed by a Privy server wallet secured by a 2-of-2 authorization-key quorum. Below the approval threshold, no transaction is built.
Each employee gets a private claim link with only their payroll line and Merkle proof. Their payment becomes public when claimed, but the rest of the payroll table never does.
Envelope is deployed on Arc testnet with the full lifecycle tested. The mainnet address is fixed via CREATE2, and a single command runs 16 local verification checks with no accounts or funding.
howItsMade:
The enclave is a TypeScript CRE workflow registered with handlerInTee. Secrets come from the Vault DON at use, HR data is fetched through confidential HTTP, payroll is computed in integer micro-USDC math, and the result is returned to the backend through a third HTTP call. Capabilities are restricted to exactly those three calls, preventing a tampered workflow from adding another.
The backend rebuilds the Merkle proofs from its own payroll table and accepts the result only when the enclave root matches. The employer already knows its payroll; the enclave protects that data from node operators and the chain.
Since Arc does not yet have a CRE Forwarder, the enclave computes and the backend submits the transaction. The stack is a Next.js app with viem, an ops CLI, and a Solidity contract using OpenZeppelin MerkleProof and ECDSA, claim bitmaps, relayable claims, and CREATE2 deployment through the canonical deployer.
Privy handles both signing paths: secp256k1 embedded wallets for approvers and P-256 authorization keys for the server wallet quorum. createViemAccount from @privy-io/node plugs the quorum wallet into the existing viem flow.
The rough edges are documented too. The CRE simulator drops config during preHook, preventing restricted workflows from completing simulation, so we reproduced and reported it and maintain a control run without that restriction. The simulator also requires a real PTY and window size, so a small Python driver runs it unattended. The only mocked component is the employer HR system, since real salary data is obviously unavailable.

name: Index-Fi
description: Onchain RWA index vaults: deposit USDC, get one share for diversified stock exposure.
projectDescription:
IndexFi is a prototype for turning tokenized stock exposure into a single onchain primitive. Instead of manually buying and managing multiple RWA assets one by one, users deposit USDC into a basket vault and receive one vault share token that represents proportional exposure to the full index.
For the MVP, we built an “AI Leaders” basket (NVDA, MSFT, GOOGL, AMD, TSM) with target weights and live NAV/share accounting. The app lets users deposit, withdraw, and track portfolio value while also showing drift between target and current basket weights. A manager can trigger rebalancing to restore allocations.
The core thesis is simple: move from “tokenized single assets” to “tokenized programmable portfolios” that are composable with DeFi rails.
howItsMade:
We built the protocol side in Solidity with Foundry and deployed it on a local Anvil chain for fast iteration. The contract stack includes: mock RWA ERC-20 tokens, a mock oracle for pricing, a basket vault with ERC-4626-style share accounting, a factory to create vaults, and a rebalancer entrypoint.
On the frontend, we migrated from Vite to Next.js (App Router) and wired wallet/auth + contract interaction using Privy, wagmi, and viem. Privy handles embedded/external wallet onboarding; wagmi + viem handle reads/writes for deposit, withdraw, approvals, manager checks, and rebalance actions.
One hacky but useful move: we kept the whole flow reproducible locally (contracts + UI) with deterministic Anvil deployment addresses and env-based wiring, so judges can run everything end-to-end without external infrastructure. We also intentionally used simulated RWAs/oracles to focus on protocol UX and basket mechanics before adding compliance-heavy real-world issuance layers.

name: Mercury
description: A USDC wallet built around identity, not addresses. Any chain, no gas, ~5 seconds.
projectDescription:
Mercury is a self-custodial iOS wallet (Expo / React Native, Rust signing core) that makes paying in USDC feel like sending a message: you pay a name, not an address; you never bridge and claim; and you never buy a gas token first. Circle Gateway and Arc are what make that literally true rather than a tagline.
One balance, no bridge. USDC is held as a single Circle Gateway balance rather than a dozen per-chain pots. You deposit once — approve, deposit into GatewayWallet, on whichever chain you already hold funds — and it is spendable on every Gateway chain in the wallet's registry (sixteen Circle domains: ten testnet, six mainnet). There is no bridge, no claim, no wrapped asset and no per-transfer wait, because the finality was paid for at deposit time. A send is an EIP-712 burn intent naming the destination and recipient, signed on the device, attested by Circle, and minted on the destination by our relayer. Measured end to end: attested in 1.2s, minted in 1.0s, with the recipient holding no gas token on the destination chain.
Settlement on Arc. Arc is the settlement chain, and USDC is its native gas token — so a balance there pays its own fees and the wallet never has to tell anyone to go buy ETH before they can spend what they were just paid. It is also the fastest door into the balance: Arc reaches finality in about half a second, against 13–19 minutes on the Ethereum-finality chains (Base, Arbitrum, OP, Unichain, World Chain), which is why every testnet deposit routes through Arc rather than through the "obvious" L2. Spending is instant regardless of where the money was deposited, so the only thing the deposit chain changes is how long the top-up takes to land — and we route on that number instead of on familiarity. On mainnet, Gateway lists no Arc domain yet, so mainnet settles through Polygon: 8s finality and the cheapest domain to spend from, ~$0.0015 of gas per transfer against $1.00 on Ethereum.
Money is never stranded mid-flight. Handing an attestation to a relayer is safe by construction — Circle signs it and names the recipient inside the signature, so the relayer cannot redirect, alter or skim it; its only power is whether to submit. What it can do is fail to submit, so the app checks deliverability before it signs: destinations the relayer cannot pay out on are refused, not offered, because a burn cannot be recalled once Circle accepts it. The signed claim is written to disk before the relay is attempted, so a dropped mint is retried rather than lost. We also shipped the unglamorous half of the door — withdrawing from Gateway back onto one chain takes seven days, and readiness is never guessed from block heights (on Arbitrum an in-contract block.number is an L1 approximation while eth_blockNumber is L2 — a bug that would be days wrong on exactly one chain). We eth_call the withdrawal instead: it reverts until the contract's own clock says it is ready.
Identity. Every user gets name.mercurywallet.eth — real ENS, not a database row. We wrote and deployed MercuryNameRegistry.sol (Sepolia, 0xe6967ac719caa21ee46d62ceafa9969f96e9252d) and set it as the resolver on our parent name, so every subname is answered on-chain through ENSIP-10 wildcard resolution. One record holds the owner's EVM, Solana and Bitcoin addresses plus a preferred chain — the routing hint that tells a Gateway send where to land — so a single name routes payments on all three. Claiming is sponsored by our hub, so a brand-new wallet with a zero balance can get a name before it has ever received money. No server sits behind it: any ENS-aware wallet resolves these names, and they keep resolving if every machine we run disappears.
Data: The Graph. Balances and history come from The Graph — the Token API for the major EVM mainnets, and our own subgraph for Arc, which indexes native USDC and EURC transfers because nothing else indexes Arc at all. Both are proxied through our hub, so no provider key ships in the app bundle.
Also in the app. Per-payment stealth addresses (ERC-5564) for private receiving — and Arc is the first chain where that closes end to end, because a note there pays its own gas out, so the consolidating sweep that would tie every note back to one identity is never needed. Cross-chain atomic swaps (Garden on testnet including Bitcoin testnet4; Flashnet Orchestra on mainnet). Uniswap V2 to turn a non-USDC balance into a depositable one. A dApp browser with WalletConnect. A spoof-resistant token registry where a curated seed always beats a downloaded list. Multi-account BIP-32 wallets across EVM, Solana and Bitcoin.
Custody. All keys and all signing live in a Rust core on the phone, behind iOS keychain classes that delete the recovery phrase if the passcode is removed and require biometric auth at the OS level rather than in app code. The hub is one small Node service with exactly three jobs — relay Gateway mints, sponsor ENS names, proxy The Graph — holding a gas-only key bounded by an on-disk spend ledger denominated in ETH with a gas-price ceiling. It never sees a user key and never holds user funds; kill it and the wallet still holds keys, shows balances and sends transactions.
howItsMade:
The stack. Expo / React Native (TypeScript, expo-router) for the iOS app; a Rust signing core exposed as a React Native turbo module for every key and every signature; Solidity for MercuryNameRegistry; a small Hono/Node service ("the hub") in Docker; an AssemblyScript subgraph on The Graph. The app talks to chains over raw JSON-RPC through one hand-rolled eth layer (ethCall / sendCall / waitForReceipt) rather than a full client library — the whole EVM surface this wallet needs is about six methods, and hand-encoding calldata kept the bundle small and the failure modes visible. viem is used on the hub, where bundle size does not matter.
There is no stub for the signing core: without the native module linked, the app refuses to bundle. A wallet that starts without its signer would be worse than one that will not start.
Arc
Arc is the settlement chain, and building on it produced most of the interesting engineering in this project, because USDC being the native gas coin changes things that are normally invariants. Everything below we observed against the live chain; it is all written up in FEEDBACK.md with the commands that produced it.
USDC is the native coin AND an ERC-20, at two different scales. eth_getBalance returns 18dp; balanceOf(0x3600…) returns 6dp; they are the same money. Measured at one block: 10.191319965 native against 10.191319 ERC-20. A naive wallet shows the user two balances for one pot — and a wallet that sweeps "all your USDC" as an ERC-20 has just spent its own gas.
Two Transfer emitters, and the native one is a superset. A plain value send emits one log from 0xffff…fffe. An ERC-20 transfer() emits from BOTH 0xffff…fffe and 0x3600…. We built the subgraph against the ERC-20 contract first and lost every native send; indexing both double-counts. The fix — index the native emitter alone and scale 18dp → 6dp in the handler — we only found by sending one of each and counting logs. It is the highest-risk thing about indexing Arc and it is documented nowhere.
Gas is cheap enough to stop designing around. Measured gas price 21.2 gwei in USDC: a transfer is 0.00045 USDC, an approve 0.00127. So we approve the exact amount being spent instead of the customary unlimited allowance — a trade nobody makes on a chain where approvals cost real money.
Because gas IS the asset, we reserve 0.25 USDC (about fifty transactions) and enforce it at the point of sweeping, not by asking the user to remember. There is no second token to fall back on.
UniswapV2Router02.WETH() on the Arc deployment points at an address with no code, so every ETH-path helper reverts with nothing useful. We use swapExactTokensForTokens exclusively.
Arc is also the reason private receiving works at all. A per-payment ERC-5564 stealth address elsewhere is money that cannot move without a gas top-up that deanonymises the recipient. On Arc the note pays its own way out, so we never sweep, and the consolidating transaction that would link every note back to one identity is never created.
Circle Gateway sits on top: one unified USDC balance, spendable across sixteen Circle domains with no bridge and nothing to claim. Three hacks worth naming. (a) The transfer fee is not knowable up front — maxFee must be inside the signed intent, and Circle only prices it in answer to one. So we submit once with a deliberately low fee to READ the quote out of the rejection ("expected at least 0.0035, got 0.000001"), then re-sign at that exact price: one extra round trip, ~280ms, and an exact fee instead of a guess. (b) burnIntentExpirationHeight from /v1/info is the current height and is already stale by the time you have signed; we add a 1000-block buffer. (c) The Gateway API and the GatewayWallet contract lag in OPPOSITE directions — the contract sees a fresh deposit the block it mines but still counts an attested burn; the API is the reverse. Measured simultaneously they disagreed by $3.00 on $18.72, and both were right about different things. So the contract answers "what do I own", the API answers "what can I spend", and burns our own client issued are discounted locally until the contract catches up. Withdrawal readiness is never computed either: withdrawalDelay() is in the chain's own blocks, and on Arbitrum an in-contract block.number is an L1 approximation while eth_blockNumber is L2, so we eth_call the withdrawal and let it revert until the contract's own clock says yes.
The Graph
Two Graph products composed into one portfolio, over live data, because neither one covers this wallet alone.
Token API for the major EVM mainnets — balances and transfers, eight networks. Our own subgraph for Arc, because the Token API rejects network=arc-testnet outright, Arc is Studio-only on the decentralized network (support level basic, issuanceRewards: false, no Substreams), and Arc has no Blockscout instance either. A subgraph is the only way to see Arc history at all, so we wrote one: two data sources (the native USDC emitter, and EURC as an ordinary 6dp ERC-20, which the native emitter does not mirror), an immutable Transfer entity keyed txHash-logIndex so the indexer can skip load-before-write, and a mutable Account entity carrying running sent/received/txCount totals so history questions do not have to page every transfer. Amounts are normalised to 6dp minor units in the handler regardless of which emitter produced them.
Two field notes that cost us time: on the free tier a Token API limit above 10 does not clamp, it returns ZERO rows — so an activity feed asking for 25 renders as "no transactions" rather than erroring, the worst possible failure mode. We page at 10. And the server_-prefixed key authenticates with X-Api-Key, not Authorization: Bearer, contrary to the docs we were reading; the JWT does use Bearer.
Both products are proxied through the hub's /index route rather than called from the app. EXPO_PUBLIC_* is inlined into the bundle at build time and recoverable from the app package, so a provider key there is handed to everyone who downloads the app and billed to us — ERC-7677 gives exactly this advice for paymaster keys and it applies unchanged here. The proxy forwards a fixed set of shapes with validated parameters; one that passed arbitrary paths through with our key attached would have moved the credential rather than protected it.
ENS
Every user gets name.mercurywallet.eth as a real ENS name. We deployed MercuryNameRegistry.sol to Sepolia (0xe6967ac719caa21ee46d62ceafa9969f96e9252d) and set it as the RESOLVER on our parent name, so under ENSv2 every subname beneath it arrives as resolve(name, data) via ENSIP-10 wildcard resolution — no per-name registry entry, no subregistry, records living in this contract's storage. One record holds the owner, the 0x address (coinType 60, which covers Arc, Base, Arbitrum and every other EVM chain at once from one secp256k1 key), a Solana address and a Bitcoin address as ENSIP-9 addr(node, coinType) records, and a preferred-chain hint that tells a Gateway send where to land.
Lookups go through ENSv2's UpgradableUniversalResolverProxy (0xeEeE…EeEe, the same address on mainnet and Sepolia, so it needs no per-environment config), with DNS wire-format names encoded by hand. We implemented EIP-3668 CCIP-Read ourselves, including the x-batch-gateway:true pseudo-URL — the Universal Resolver offers its own hosted batch gateway, and we chose to unpack the batch and fetch each inner gateway ourselves instead. That removes a third party from the path of every lookup and stops leaking which names our users type into someone else's server.
The deliberate trade: on-chain records cost one transaction per name, where offchain CCIP-Read names are free but put an HTTP service on the critical path of every lookup forever. We took the transaction, and then removed it from the user — the hub sponsors registration, so a zero-balance wallet can claim a name before it has ever received money. The sponsor is the payer and never the owner: the caller signs a message naming the label and every address in it, the registration is made out to the RECOVERED signer rather than to any address in the request body, and we only sponsor a name pointing at the signer's own address (paying to publish an address nobody proved they hold is how you fund a phishing campaign). One sponsored name per address, plus a daily ceiling, both bounded by an on-disk ETH-denominated spend ledger with a gas-price ceiling — counting operations does not bound cost.
Honorable mention: Uniswap
Uniswap V2 is what turns a non-USDC balance into a depositable one: if you hold something else on the chain you want to fund from, we quote and swap to USDC on that same chain first, then deposit. Same-chain by design — Circle credits a deposit made on any domain to the one balance, so there is never a reason to move funds across chains before depositing. The V2 router on Arc is also where the WETH()-with-no-code finding above came from; our FEEDBACK.md carries it.
The rest of the hacky bits
The app checks deliverability before it signs a burn, because a burn cannot be recalled once Circle accepts it. Destinations the relayer cannot pay out on are refused rather than offered, and the signed claim is written to disk before the relay is attempted so a dropped mint is retried rather than lost.
Block-explorer history has a keyless Blockscout first path and an Etherscan V2 fallback — of 22 supported testnets only 5 had a reachable history source when we checked. The fallback learns which chains the key's plan covers from the upstream's own refusals ("Free API access is not supported for this chain") rather than hard-coding a free-tier list that is wrong for anyone who pays and stale the day Etherscan moves a chain between tiers.
The token registry ships a curated seed that a downloaded list can never overwrite. Against CoinGecko's list the guard drops a "UNI" that is really UNICORN and an "ETH" that is really The Infinite Garden — an ERC-20 wearing the native coin's ticker.
The recovery phrase lives under iOS's WHEN_PASSCODE_SET_THIS_DEVICE_ONLY with requireAuthentication, so it is excluded from every backup and device-to-device restore, cannot be written on a device with no passcode, and is DELETED if the passcode is removed. The biometric gate is the keychain refusing to return bytes, not a JavaScript if that can fail open.
One hub process, not two: the mint relayer and the name sponsor spend the same key against the same ledger, with in-flight reservations held in memory so concurrent requests cannot each pass a check none of them could afford together. Two containers would mean two ledgers that cannot see each other. It runs as non-root with a read-only root filesystem, tini as PID 1, and /app/data as the only writable path.

name: Pool Party
description: Pool Party: Cash+ for business treasuries and hookrisk for Uniswap v4 hook security.
projectDescription:
Pool Party connects investment strategy managers with investors through rules enforced by smart contracts. For this continuity submission, we added two products to the platform: Cash+ and hookrisk.
Cash+ is a business treasury investment strategy that combines two sources of return: lending interest on Aave and margins from stablecoin conversions. Eligible capital earns interest while waiting for conversion opportunities. When a conversion takes place, the strategy releases the required liquidity and retains the margin for investors, subject to price, volume and exposure limits. Businesses deposit USDC, track performance and request withdrawals from a dedicated page.
Hookrisk helps managers evaluate Uniswap v4 hooks before opening a position. Hooks are smart contracts that can change a pool’s fees and transaction behavior. They can also introduce undeclared charges, prevent withdrawals or expose callbacks to unauthorized callers.
Integrated into Pool Party’s Tools menu, hookrisk provides findings with references to the affected source files and lines. It also identifies dimensions it could not measure, without treating missing information as an absence of risk. Managers gain evidence for selecting hooks, and investors receive an assessment they can independently inspect.
howItsMade:
We extended Pool Party’s existing frontend using Next.js, React, TypeScript and viem, preserving the platform’s visual design.
For Cash+, Solidity contracts account for deposits, investor shares and withdrawals. Adapters supply eligible assets to Aave, while 1inch Aqua and SwapVM execute stablecoin conversions. A custom pricing extension applies the conversion margin and checks the strategy’s limits using Chainlink price feeds.
The integration withdraws assets from Aave within the same transaction that settles a conversion. Capital can therefore earn interest until it is needed for settlement. If any step fails, the entire conversion reverts. An automated operator manages lending allocations, liquidity buffers and orders.
For hookrisk, we combined Python detectors built on Slither, a TypeScript scoring engine and Solidity tests using Foundry. The tests use Uniswap’s actual v4-core to compare two otherwise equivalent pools: one with a hook and one without. This differential testing can detect behavior such as charges exceeding the declared fee and trapped liquidity. The project also provides an optional integration with BlockSec HookScan.
We translated the Uniswap Foundation’s Hooks Security Framework into executable criteria. Reports distinguish measured results, developer declarations and unmeasured dimensions. Hook permissions are generated directly from v4-core, avoiding a manually maintained copy that could become outdated.
We validated Cash+ through Foundry tests and a complete browser journey using Playwright: deposit, conversion, Aave withdrawal and investor redemption on an Arbitrum fork using the protocols’ official contracts.

name: Refusal.eth
description: Deny-by-default spending firewall: prove policy before an agent can sign.
projectDescription: AI agents can be prompt-injected into unsafe spending when policy is readable context and signing is unconditional. REFUSAL.eth makes refusal the default: an agent identity is resolved, a sealed policy is evaluated, and only an explicit ALLOW receipt can reach a downstream signer. Revocations, allowlist misses, limit breaches, and human denials become named, inspectable refusal proofs instead of silent failures. The public console exposes deterministic allowlist-miss and limit-breach paths, while the repository honesty table separates verified local behavior from sponsor integrations still awaiting live evidence.
howItsMade: The verified build is a Next.js/TypeScript proof surface with viem-based ENS resolution, a Solidity RefusalGateway, and one shared deterministic gate mirrored in the CRE workspace. The contract binds verdicts to deadline and nonce, rejects zero keys and empty names, and prevents case-variant revocation bypasses; parity tests compare the web mirror and canonical gate. The CRE handlerInTee retrieves a sealed policy and private intent inside the TEE, with an official CLI simulation recorded; production deployment is not claimed. Privy remains an adapter boundary until a funded wallet, policy/quorum flow, approval, and Sepolia receipt are evidenced. make verify runs 11 Forge tests, 15 gate assertions, 20/20 parity, ENSv2 checks, and claim auditing.

name: safety
description: ERC-4337 smart wallet owned by a passkey; scoped session keys enable zero-popup transactions
projectDescription: Every wallet interaction today means a signature prompt, which is fine for a rare high-value transfer but kills UX for anything interactive: games, trading bots, subscriptions. This project is a smart contract wallet (ERC-4337 account abstraction) owned by a passkey (Face ID / Touch ID / Windows Hello) instead of a seed phrase or browser extension. The owner can grant a scoped, time-boxed session key: a lightweight keypair generated in the browser that is only allowed to call one specific contract function, until a set expiry, up to a set number of times. Once granted, the dApp can send a burst of transactions signed by that session key with zero further wallet prompts. We demo this with a tiny on-chain clicker game: create your passkey wallet once, grant a session key once (one more Face ID prompt), then click away with no interruptions, exactly like a Web2 app, while every action is still a real, independently-authorized on-chain transaction.
howItsMade: Built from scratch on top of eth-infinitism's reference ERC-4337 EntryPoint/BaseAccount (v0.6) in Foundry. SmartAccount.sol implements a single IAccount whose signature is a mode byte plus payload: mode 0 verifies a WebAuthn/secp256r1 assertion against the owner passkey public key using base-org/webauthn-sol (RIP-7212 precompile with a FreshCryptoLib fallback); mode 1 checks a plain ECDSA signature from a session key against an on-chain SessionKeyPermission struct (target contract, function selector, validUntil, maxUses) so a session key can never be used outside its granted scope. SmartAccountFactory.sol deploys accounts via CREATE2 for deterministic addresses. A GameContract.sol clicker is the demo target. Four Foundry tests drive the whole flow end-to-end through EntryPoint.handleOps: grant, click, hit the usage cap, reject an out-of-scope call, and revoke. The frontend (Next.js + viem + @simplewebauthn/browser) creates the passkey client-side, parses the COSE public key and DER signature manually to build the on-chain WebAuthnAuth struct, and signs UserOperations with either the passkey (owner actions) or a locally generated session key (gameplay). For demo reliability we relay signed UserOperations straight to EntryPoint.handleOps from a Next.js API route acting as a mock bundler against a local Anvil node, rather than depending on a live bundler network.

name: Agent Grove
description: Agent Grove gives AI agents portable ENS identities with scoped control over live profiles.
projectDescription: Agent Grove is an ENSv2 identity studio for AI agents on Sepolia. Teams can issue durable subname identities such as researcher.grove.eth, attach an agent wallet, and grant only the profile-record permissions that agent needs—such as its endpoint, capabilities, or operating status. The namespace owner keeps control of the parent namespace while agents can safely keep their own discoverable profiles current. The app also includes a live ENS resolver that verifies names and agent records on Sepolia, making identities portable across wallets, dapps, and agent directories.
howItsMade: Agent Grove is a lightweight browser application built with vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using Viem for Sepolia RPC access, ENS normalization/namehashing, resolver lookups, calldata encoding, and transaction-confirmation handling. It connects to an injected browser wallet and resolves ENS address, resolver, description, and com.agent.endpoint records live. For profile updates, it discovers the active resolver, encodes setText calls, batches them with multicall, and submits the wallet-signed transaction. A Solidity AgentNamespaceRegistrar integrates with ENSv2’s Permissioned Registry, issuing subnames with a constrained role bitmap. ENSv2 Permissioned Resolvers and Enhanced Access Control enable narrowly scoped record-writing authority without giving agents control of the entire namespace.

name: attesta
description: Marketplace for trading strategies whose returns are attested inside a TEE, not self-reported
projectDescription:
attesta is a marketplace for automated trading strategies where the track record is attested rather than claimed.
The problem it attacks is simple. Anyone can publish a 40% APY. The number is produced by whoever profits from it, and a strategy with a real edge will not reveal the code behind it — so an investor is asked to trust a screenshot. attesta removes the need to trust either side.
HOW IT WORKS
A creator writes a strategy in TypeScript against a fixed six-function contract (describe, onTick, balanceOf, totalAssets, onDeposit, onWithdraw) and submits it in the browser. The platform compiles it and deploys it as a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow, so the strategy's identity becomes its binary hash: binary hash + config hash -> workflow hash, registered on-chain in a StrategyRegistry. Swap the script after building a track record and the hash changes, in public. Creators need no CRE account of their own; the platform deploys under its owner identity, and anyone can recompile the published source and check the hash matches what is registered.
When a tick fires, the strategy does not run on a node — it runs inside a TEE (AWS Nitro Enclaves, us-west-2). It fetches prices over HTTP from inside the enclave, reads its creator's parameters as Vault DON secrets that are released only into an attested enclave, and returns a target allocation in basis points. Risk guardrails are evaluated in the enclave too, so the rules stay private while remaining verifiably applied.
Strategy parameters never reach the platform in the clear. They are encrypted in the creator's own browser before they leave the machine; the backend relays ciphertext, stores it in a table with no plaintext column, and holds no key that opens it. There is no read-back API at all. So a creator can publish a verifiable track record without revealing the thresholds and signals that produce it — which is the thing that makes a real quant willing to list at all.
Investors sign in with a wallet, browse the marketplace, and allocate USDC. Each strategy has its own on-chain vault with ERC-4626 share math. Deposits and withdrawals are signed in the browser and settled on-chain into that vault; the backend records what the transaction receipt says happened, not what the client claims, so a forged or replayed hash records nothing. The strategy page shows NAV per share, the investor's own position series, every trade, every execution log line, total return, max drawdown and — once the history is long enough to state it honestly — APY.
WHY THE NUMBERS HOLD
Nothing about performance is hardcoded; that is the point of the whole build. Each tick runs the real strategy against a live price series, prices the decision it returned (target weights x price delta since the last tick, minus venue cost in bps), and applies the resulting profit or loss on-chain with vault.applyPnl(int256), which emits PnlApplied.
Performance is then read back from the vault's own settlement log — PnlApplied, Deposited, Withdrawn — rather than from a table the backend wrote. The number on the screen is the chain's account of what happened, not the server's, and one getLogs call covers a whole listing. Total return, max drawdown and APY are derived from that series and stored nowhere as inputs.
APY is deliberately withheld until the series is long enough to annualise honestly. Annualising twenty minutes of history turns a 1.4% move into a meaningless exponent and turns every loss into exactly -100%, so below that threshold the metric returns null and the card leads with since-inception total return instead. That is a real figure at any span, and it still separates a strategy down 1.4% from one down 13.4%, which saturated annualisation does not. A strategy that picks badly shows a negative return because its weights lost money, not because a field says so. Three seeded strategies — momentum, mean-reversion, and a deliberately bad overtrader that churns itself into fees — demonstrate exactly that, side by side in the same marketplace.
The verifiable chain runs end to end: TypeScript workflow -> registered workflow identity -> TEE attestation -> signed reports -> on-chain settlement record -> reported returns. Break any link — a different workflow, a different enclave, an unsigned record — and the performance claim stops verifying.
WHAT IS HONEST ABOUT THE LIMITS
This build integrates two partner technologies: Chainlink CRE for confidential compute, and Privy for investor onboarding. Settlement is USDC vaults on a local chain, and a strategy's operator — the only account allowed to settle a tick — is a local EOA. Circle Agent Wallets on Arc are the intended production form for that operator, and the design is written against them: one policy-capped wallet per strategy, its control credential held as a Vault secret so only the attested workflow could direct it. That integration is out of scope here and nothing in the demo depends on it. Saying so plainly matters more than the extra logo would.
Two further limits. CRE Vault secrets are scoped to the owner rather than to a single workflow, so isolation between creators rests on every workflow under the owner being enumerable and hash-verifiable rather than on the Vault itself. And phase 1 does not audit strategy code — "verified" means "this exact code produced these results", not "this code is safe".
All of these are stated in the docs and in the UI rather than glossed over, because a product whose entire claim is verifiability cannot be vague about what is not verified.
Everything runs locally against an anvil chain, which is why the demo link points at the repository: ./scripts/dev.sh brings up anvil, deploys the contracts, seeds the marketplace and serves the backend on :4000 and the frontend on :3000.
howItsMade:
Five packages in one repo: contracts/ (Foundry), backend/ (Fastify + Drizzle + better-sqlite3 + viem), frontend/ (Next.js 15 App Router, React 19, Tailwind v4), chainlink/ (the CRE workflow), and shared/ — two files, types.ts and strategy-contract.ts, that every other layer builds against so the DTOs and the strategy interface can never drift between frontend, backend and enclave.
CHAINLINK CRE CONFIDENTIAL WORKFLOWS — the compute layer
The workflow is TypeScript against @chainlink/cre-sdk 1.18.0, compiled through bun to WASM and driven by the CRE CLI v1.32.0. The cron callback takes a TeeRuntime rather than a Runtime, and that type is what moves execution off the node and into the enclave. Inside it, runtime.getSecret({ id, namespace }) pulls a Vault DON secret that is decrypted at the moment the call runs and only inside an attested enclave, and cre.capabilities.HTTPClient().sendRequest() has a TeeRuntime overload, so the outbound price fetch keeps its request and response payloads confidential from node operators. (ConfidentialHTTPClient is the wrong tool here — it has no TeeRuntime overload and is not meant to be called from a TEE handler; that cost us an afternoon.) Simulation prints "Trigger requested TEE Execution ... AWS Nitro in us-west-2", and that is the only attestation claim this project makes anywhere — no SGX, no MRENCLAVE, no zero-knowledge proofs, in code, copy or docs.
Two CRE gotchas worth passing on. @chainlink/cre-sdk declares engines: { bun: ">=1.2.21" }, and on an older bun the workflow still compiles, then dies at engine start with "wasm trap: wasm unreachable instruction executed" rather than a version complaint — the toolchain goes TypeScript -> JavaScript -> WASM through bun, so an old bun silently emits a broken binary. And the CLI does not read .env on its own: without -e .env, simulation fails with a missing-secret error and silently falls back to a default private key.
CONTRACTS — Foundry, with unit and invariant tests
StrategyVault holds one strategy's capital with ERC-4626 share math, plus applyPnl(int256) and recordTrade(), both restricted to the strategy's operator account, and a reserve prefunded at publish time so a gain is actually payable. The invariant is usdc.balanceOf(vault) >= totalManagedAssets. Four revert cases shaped the whole scheduler, and none of them are visible in the ABI: a gain with no depositors (NoSharesOutstanding — otherwise the next depositor mints 1:1 against zero supply and redeems the stranded amount), a gain larger than the reserve (ReserveExhausted — the vault refuses to promise value it cannot pay), a loss larger than the book (LossExceedsManagedAssets), and settling from the wrong account (NotOperator). So a tick caps its delta at the reserve, caps a loss at totalManagedAssets, and skips settlement rather than losing the tick — the strategy still decides, still records trades and still snapshots NAV, so an unfunded strategy is visibly running rather than silently absent. navPerShare() returns par when totalShares == 0 instead of dividing by zero, so the UI reads NAV as a claim per share and totalShares as the evidence of capital. StrategyRegistry anchors keccak256(strategyId) -> vault + binary hash on-chain; the platform id is a uuid, and the hashing lives in exactly one file with the chain layer taking the bytes32 pre-hashed, so nothing can ever anchor a strategy under keccak(keccak(id)) — a key nothing looks up, with nothing anywhere to report it.
THE SUBMISSION PIPELINE — nine stages, in order, first failure stops the rest
parses -> required-exports (all six) -> forbidden-imports (and no dynamic import()) -> no-side-effects (no forbidden globals, no top-level statements beyond imports, declarations and exports) -> tsc --noEmit against the shared strategy contract -> describe-valid (metadata and declared assets) -> deterministic (onTick twice on an identical context must return identical output) -> cre workflow build, capturing the binary hash -> cre workflow simulate, yielding a parseable decision. Only after stage nine can a submission publish, which deploys its vault, funds the reserve and registers the measurement. Results stream into the create screen as each stage lands.
THE SCHEDULER — where returns actually come from
cre workflow simulate fires a cron trigger once and exits; the CLI has no scheduled mode and rejects --listen for cron, so the scheduler owns the interval (60s default, bounded concurrency). Each tick refreshes a seeded, deterministic price oracle, runs the workflow for that strategy, parses the decision, prices the target weights against the price delta since the last tick, charges venue cost in bps on turnover, sends applyPnl and recordTrade from the strategy's operator account, and writes an execution row. The composition root builds one ChainPort and one OraclePort and is called after listen() — because the enclave fetches prices over HTTP from this same process, so the oracle route has to be answering before the first tick can complete. The whole loop (publish, deposit, four ticks, metrics) is proved end to end by a single npm run verify:loop.
METRICS — read from the chain, not from our own table
Performance is quoted from the vault's own settlement log rather than from a table the backend wrote: lib/chain-metrics.ts reconstructs the NAV series from PnlApplied, Deposited and Withdrawn events and the strategies routes serve that, falling back to the stored snapshots only if a chain read fails. One getLogs covers a whole listing — 63ms cold, 5ms warm. It matters for the product's claim, not just for correctness: the figure on the card is the chain's account of what happened, which is exactly the thing a sceptical investor can independently recompute.
lib/metrics.ts is pure — same series in, same value out, no clock, no database — and returns null rather than zero when history is too short, because zero reads as "flat" when the truth is "unknown". APY is the case that bites: annualising wall-clock over a twenty-minute demo turns a +1.4% move into an astronomic exponent and saturates every loss at exactly -100%. So the annualisation window is passed in through the MetricsOptions parameter the module already exposes rather than by editing the module, APY comes back null below it, and StrategyCard falls back to since-inception total return (headline = apy ?? totalReturn, label flipping to SINCE INCEPTION). A real figure at any span beats a saturated one.
AUTH AND MONEY — the backend never holds a user key
POST /auth/challenge issues a nonce inside a multi-line SIWE-style message whose domain line is derived from CORS_ORIGIN; the browser signs that string verbatim with viem and POST /auth/verify recovers the signer with recoverMessageAddress and compares. Nonces are single-use with a 5-minute TTL. Investing has the same shape: the browser sends approve + deposit itself, waits for receipts, then posts the tx hash, and the backend fetches the receipt, parses the Deposited event and verifies it came from the caller's address and targets this strategy's vault before recording a position. GET /api/chain/config is authoritative for chain id, RPC URL and every contract address — addresses must never live in env, because anvil redeploys move them and a stale .env pointing at a dead address fails in a way that looks exactly like a bug in the contract.
CREATOR SECRETS — the part that took the most research
The production path is TDH2 threshold encryption performed in the creator's browser against the Vault DON's P256 key, fetched from vault.publicKey.get on the CRE gateway, using Chainlink's own pure-JS TDH2 (src/tdh2.js in @chainlink/functions-toolkit) with the envelope matching the Go implementation field for field. Two things make it non-trivial: the toolkit's exported encrypt() hardcodes an empty label, while CRE requires the label to be the owner address left-padded to 32 bytes, so tdh2.js has to be vendored and the internal tdh2Encrypt called directly; and the gateway returns no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header and fails the OPTIONS preflight, so the browser cannot post to it and the backend has to relay. Locally neither the Vault DON nor the gateway is reachable from a machine with no CRE deployment, so EncryptedSecret.scheme is the seam: it carries "local-dev" (AES-256-GCM, key generated and kept in the creator's browser, HKDF-derived per submission) instead of "tdh2-p256-aesgcm", and the create screen states the limitation in plain words rather than glossing it — under local-dev the platform's ignorance of the plaintext is real, but no enclave can read it either. Everything either side of the cipher is already the production path: encryption happens in the browser, the backend stores ciphertext in a table with no plaintext column, and the endpoint accepts nothing else. Swapping schemes replaces one function.
FRONTEND
Hand-written React against Stitch-generated reference screens, in a dark "cryptographic quantitative terminal" system — Inter for text, JetBrains Mono with tnum and zero feature settings for every number, hash and ticker, 4px radii, 1px hairlines, no shadows outside modals. CodeMirror 6 for the strategy editor, Recharts for the NAV and position series, viem for all signing and broadcasting.
TWO PARTNER TECHNOLOGIES, AND WHAT IS ACTUALLY WIRED
Chainlink CRE is fully wired: the confidential workflow builds, simulates in the enclave and returns the decision the scheduler prices, and its binary hash is what lands in the registry.
Privy is the investor surface. The signer sits behind one swappable interface in lib/wallet.ts — SignerKind is a union and BrowserWalletClient is typed over a generic Transport precisely so a Privy embedded wallet drops in where the local key is today without the challenge/verify exchange moving at all; Privy hands you a provider, you wrap it with custom(provider), and signMessage still produces a personal_sign signature that recoverMessageAddress verifies. Along the way we established by probing that Privy's JWKS keys are EC P-256 / ES256 — some Privy docs describe the verification key as Ed25519, and a verifier built on that does not work — and that the JWKS endpoint doubles as an app-id validator, 200 for a good id and 400 missing_or_invalid_privy_app_id for a bad one, which is the fastest way to catch a copy-paste artifact that otherwise presents as a mysteriously broken integration.
Settlement is USDC vaults on a local chain, and a strategy's operator — the only account the vault will accept applyPnl and recordTrade from — is a local EOA. Circle Agent Wallets on Arc are the intended production form for that operator and the design is written against them (one policy-capped wallet per strategy, control credential held as a Vault secret so only the attested workflow could direct it), but that integration is not built here and nothing in the demo depends on it. We are saying so rather than implying otherwise, because the entire claim of this product is that you can check what is true; a project about verifiability does not get to be vague about which of its own parts are verified.
TWO OPERATIONAL THINGS WORTH KNOWING
Only one process may tick a given vault. Run several backends against the same anvil chain and each settles the same vaults on its own timer, so a block ends up carrying more than one PnlApplied and no single database sees the whole series — the stored snapshots then disagree with the chain for reasons that look exactly like a write bug. Related: every backend signs with the same anvil account unless a distinct deployer key is set, so concurrent processes race the same nonce and drop settlements.
ONE LAST HACKY THING
A global gitignore excluding [Ss]cripts and [Ll]ib silently hid scripts/ and src/lib/ from git status — the project .gitignore negates both, and git status -uall is now the rule before committing a new directory. An entire evening went to code that existed locally and simply was not in the repo.

name: POP
description: A Uniswap-like prediction market on Arc, using native USDC and powered by Chainlink CRE.
projectDescription:
POP is an AMM-based prediction market built on Arc. Instead of matching buyers and sellers through an order book, every market has its own liquidity pool where users can trade outcome tokens continuously and prices move with the market.
POP uses Arc-native USDC as the base asset, making markets simple to fund, trade, and settle without introducing another collateral token. Chainlink powers the connection between onchain markets and real-world information, allowing POP to automate market resolution and settlement while also exploring privacy-preserving prediction market flows.
The goal is to make prediction markets feel more like open onchain markets: permissionless to create, continuously liquid, composable, and programmable.
howItsMade:
POP is built on Arc with smart contracts handling market creation, outcome-token accounting, AMM liquidity, trading, resolution, and redemption. Native USDC is used as the collateral and settlement asset across the entire market lifecycle.
When a market is created, liquidity is deposited into an AMM pool and users trade directly against that liquidity. The relative reserves and trading activity determine the market price of each outcome, giving POP continuous onchain price discovery without requiring a traditional order book.
Chainlink CRE is used to connect POP's onchain contracts with external data and computation. A CRE workflow can retrieve the information required by a market, apply its resolution logic, and trigger settlement on Arc once the outcome is determined.
We also experiment with Chainlink-powered privacy workflows for cases where some market inputs, positions, or data should not be publicly exposed before settlement. The final result can still be brought back onchain for transparent settlement.
The frontend connects directly to the Arc contracts, allowing users to create markets, provide liquidity, trade outcomes with USDC, follow changing probabilities, and redeem their positions after resolution.

name: Handshake
description: Deals become verifiable on-chain objects with their own ENS identity and history.
projectDescription: Handshake lets two people make a deal and put real money behind it. Both sides stake USDC collateral, funds lock in an on-chain escrow, and the agreement's full lifecycle — created, funded, active, completed or disputed — becomes a permanent, verifiable object rather than a private off-chain promise. Each deal gets its own ENS identity: <dealId>.handshakedeal.eth resolves live to that deal's current status, straight from the contract, with nothing cached or hardcoded. Instead of a reputation score built on stars and reviews, anyone can inspect a deal's real factual history — a Deal Passport reconstructed entirely from on-chain events. Login uses Privy's embedded wallets, so funding a deal is as simple as signing in with Google and confirming a transaction — no MetaMask install, no seed phrase.
howItsMade: Solidity contracts written and tested with Foundry: a single Handshake.sol contract holds the escrow state machine (no factory/registry split), enforces terms-locking by simply never exposing an edit function once a deal is accepted, and resolves disputes winner-takes-the-full-pot via a fixed per-deal reviewer address. Reentrancy is guarded manually and proven against a malicious ERC20 in the test suite — 18 tests total, all passing. HandshakeResolver.sol is a custom ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver that stores zero deal data: it decodes the DNS-encoded subdomain label into a dealId and calls Handshake.getDeal() live on every query, which is what makes "not hardcoded" a structural fact rather than a claim — verified directly with a raw cast call against the deployed contract on Sepolia, before and after a real state change. The name handshakedeal.eth is registered on ENS's actual ENSv2 beta deployment on Sepolia. The frontend is Next.js with Privy for auth and embedded wallet creation, and wagmi/viem for all contract reads and writes.

name: Glide
description: Self custodial glide path liquidity on 1inch Aqua, reachable through a Uniswap v4 hook.
projectDescription:
Glide lets a wallet rebalance itself without ever depositing into a pool. The maker keeps tokens in their own wallet and publishes a glide path: the value split now, the split they want, and a time window. Glide prices the wallet like a weighted AMM whose weights slide along that path. Whenever the market moves, an arbitrageur can profit by trading against the position, and every such trade walks the wallet toward the target while paying the maker a fee. Instead of paying slippage to sell at once or fees to a bot, the maker collects fees. It is a liquidity bootstrapping pool for a single wallet, with no pool contract holding the money. Positions live on 1inch Aqua, so tokens are pulled only when a trade executes.
A Uniswap v4 pool with a custom hook forwards any Uniswap swap into the position, so routers and aggregators reach it while the pool itself holds no liquidity. Paths can be linear or any piecewise schedule: ease-in, S-curve, hold-then-move. The demo ships a USDC/WETH position on a Unichain fork, an arbitrage loop keeps the pool at the reference price, and the maker's value share tracks the path while fees accrue in their wallet.
howItsMade:
Glide is two new SwapVM instructions in a redeployed router, settling through the official 1inch Aqua registry on Unichain. GlideSwap moves the token A weight in a straight line between two endpoints; GlideSwapPiecewise follows a schedule of up to 20 segments. Both apply a weighted constant-mean curve modelled on Balancer V2 math, using solady's powWad with an upward error bump so every rounding step favours the maker. Schedule and curve had to live in one instruction, because SwapVM instructions can only talk to each other through the four swap registers. In Aqua mode the program is stateless: balances come from Aqua on every quote, and fees land as tokenIn in the maker's own wallet.
The Uniswap side is a v4 hook using beforeSwap custom accounting. It takes the swapper's input from the PoolManager, fills against the Aqua order through the router, settles the output back, and returns a delta that consumes the whole specified amount. Liquidity adds are refused, so the pool never holds tokens.
Tests: fuzz against an unrounded reference, 1inch's CoreInvariants suite at fixed, extreme and mid-glide weights, hook tests on a fresh PoolManager, and a fork test against the real Aqua and PoolManager. 47 green.

name: deCAPTCHA
description: A CAPTCHA that lets real AI agents through with human pre-approval built on World's Selfie Check.
projectDescription:
Your AI agent just got blocked by a CAPTCHA. Again.
Every bot gate on the internet asks one question: are you a human? For an agent booking your flight or grabbing your ticket, there's no good answer. (Because let's be real, it's all going to be automated now.) So it gets treated like a scraper, and you go do it yourself.
deCAPTCHA asks a better question: Not "are you human" but "is a real human accountable for this?"
Here's how it works. You pass World's Selfie Check once - takes a second. That mints a vouch: an ENS subname on Sepolia that says a verified human is standing behind this agent, it can do exactly this much, until exactly this time, and that human can pull the plug whenever they want. Your agent carries that name around like a badge.

No vouch? CAPTCHA. Blocked. Nothing changes for the bots.
With a vouch? Straight through. Instantly. Logged as acting for you.
One claim past what you allowed? Blocked, exactly like a bot.
Agent decides it wants more? It tries to raise its own limit and ENS slaps it down.The agent has zero permission over its own credential.

Then you hit revoke. The transaction lands on Sepolia, you watch it confirm, and the agent's very next request bounces. No waiting for a cache to clear, because there is no cache.
When a vouch is minted, we hand the human write access and then throw away our own. Read the resolver yourself. The agent can't touch it and either can we.
Bots still walk away with nothing, exactly as they should. But an agent working for a real person finally gets treated like one, with access that reaches precisely as far as that person allowed and lasts precisely as long as they're comfortable with it. The second they aren't, it's gone.
howItsMade:
Node and Express backend, ENSv2 on Sepolia, a vanilla-JS embeddable widget, and a Chrome extension as the human's vouch wallet.
The widget is the product. One script tag and one div, and the server-side check is POST /api/siteverify with a secret - deliberately the same shape as reCAPTCHA, because adopting this should be a swap and not a re-architecture. The response carries two fields reCAPTCHA never had: whether a human or an accountable agent passed, and which human is on the hook. It renders in a shadow root so a host page's CSS can't break it and it can't leak styles outward.
ENSv2 does the heavy lifting, and the primitive that makes it work is PermissionedResolver scoping Enhanced Access Control resources to keccak256(node, part) - a name AND a record type. Permission is granted on one specific field of one specific vouch. The human holds ROLE_SET_TEXT on the revocation record. The agent holds nothing, anywhere. When it tries to bump its own scope the chain throws EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles naming the agent's address and the exact role it lacks. That refusal is ENS talking, not us.
Every vouch gets its own resolver, cloned through VerifiableFactory, so its records and permissions belong to it alone instead of a shared table. Minting is three transactions: deploy the resolver with records already baked in, register the subname, then grant the human and renounce ourselves in one multicall. That first one works because PermissionedResolver skips permission checks during init, so records exist before anyone has rights over them.
Authorisation needs no identity provider. The human signs readable terms naming the agent, scope and expiry, and that signature is published on the record. Anyone can recover the signer from chain data alone. Ten tests prove it binds rather than merely exists: change the scope, the expiry, the agent or the name and verification fails.
Expiry is layered. The subname outlives its vouch by a week on purpose. We tried setting them equal and it broke the story - the name stopped resolving before the gate could read the record, so an expired vouch looked identical to one that never existed.

description: AI-powered medical travel with on-chain escrow for safer treatment abroad.
projectDescription:

howItsMade:
built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Supabase, Gemini, Privy, Arc, viem, Mapbox, SerpAPI, and Calendly. Gemini powers the medical-travel AI and report analysis, while Supabase handles journeys, consultations, medical documents, and persistent chat state. Privy provides the embedded patient wallet and a familiar login-to-payment experience.
The key technical piece is a custom Arc escrow smart contract using USDC. When a patient pays, funds move from their Privy wallet into escrow and are released through programmable 20/60/20 treatment milestones, with trustee-controlled release/refund logic and on-chain verification. Live flight and hotel data comes through SerpAPI, Mapbox handles location experiences, and Calendly connects patients to real doctors. The result is a full-stack application where AI, real-world healthcare workflows, travel infrastructure, and programmable money work as one system.

name: The Pit
description: The Pit: a public proving ground where AI trading agents can't fake their results.
projectDescription:
The Pit is a public, adversarial proving ground for AI trading agents. AI trading bots are everywhere now: copy-trading bots, autonomous DeFi agents, Claude-powered trading assistants, but there is no trustworthy way to prove one is actually good before anyone hands it real capital. Backtests get cherry-picked, screenshots get faked, and a claim like "my agent returns 12% a week" is unverifiable because nothing about it is public or tamper-proof. The Pit fixes that by giving any registered agent a fixed stake, a fixed clock, and on-chain rules it structurally cannot get around, then writing every result into a permanent public record.
Any agent can register through the same generic pipeline: fund a backend-managed wallet with a small amount of USDC, register with our contracts, and commit a hashed strategy config before the match starts. Each match runs six fixed-length rounds on a house-seeded Uniswap v3 pool. Agents trade through PitRouter, a custom contract we built that wraps the pool's swap function and enforces on-chain, per round, which wallet can trade, how many trades it gets, and tracks swap fees so they get rebated back into the agents' stakes instead of quietly punishing active trading. Balances are read directly on-chain at each round lock, no oracle needed since USDC is already a dollar. After the match, strategies are revealed and the contract settles: it picks the winner by final balance and pays out the fee rebate.
Every round lock, every revealed trade, and every result gets written into a custom subgraph on The Graph, a permanent, publicly queryable proof layer that outlives the demo. Agents can even query their own subgraph-indexed match history through The Graph's Subgraph MCP before deciding their next move, so their reasoning is genuinely informed by their own track record, not just the current tick.
This is not a mockup: the contracts are deployed for real on Base Sepolia, backed by 51 automated tests including a live fork test against the real Uniswap v3 Factory and PositionManager, and we ran a full real rehearsal end to end (register, six real on-chain rounds of trading, lock, reveal, settle) with three separate agent wallets, confirmed indexed correctly in the live subgraph. At least three agents run through the identical registration pipeline in the demo, two of our own strategies plus one deliberately different one, to prove the proving-ground claim is real infrastructure and not two names hardcoded into a frontend.
howItsMade:
The Pit is a TypeScript monorepo (npm workspaces) with a Foundry project for the contracts, glued together by a shared match-state model so the loop, the board, and both subgraphs never disagree about what a match looks like.
Contracts (Foundry, Solidity 0.8.26, Base Sepolia). PitRouter wraps a single Uniswap v3 pool's swap function and is the entire "structurally cannot cheat" layer: it checks the caller is a registered participant, that match's round is currently live, and the agent is under its per-round trade cap, then forwards to the real pool and tracks swap fee volume per agent. MatchController handles generic commit-and-fund registration, on-chain-enforced round timing (not just a runner promise), reveal, and settlement, and deploys its own CommitReveal contract internally for the hashed strategy configs. We originally scoped this against Uniswap v4 hooks, then pivoted to v3 mid-build since v3 has no hook slot at all, so all enforcement had to move into a router contract we fully own instead, which actually made the fairness logic easier to reason about and test in isolation.
The Graph. A custom subgraph indexes every MatchController and PitRouter event (registrations, round locks, reveals, settlement, trades) into a permanent record, composed alongside a Messari Standardized DEX AMM subgraph over the same pool for the composability track. The agent itself queries its own subgraph-indexed match history through The Graph's Subgraph MCP before each decision, so its reasoning is genuinely grounded in its own track record rather than just displaying a query result.
Agents, runner, board. Each agent runs a tick loop on the Claude Agent SDK across three distinct strategies (momentum, mean reversion, and a passive baseline), submitting swaps through PitRouter with a viem wallet client. A runner package orchestrates the full match lifecycle on-chain (register, start, lock each round, reveal, settle) and pushes live state to Supabase, which a Next.js board subscribes to for a coarse, delayed leader indicator so a live position cannot be reverse engineered mid-round.
The genuinely hacky part. We caught two critical bugs by running an adversarial security review against our own contracts before touching a demo: registration originally pulled each agent's stake into the contract with nothing to ever pay it back out, and settlement could brick itself forever on a misconfigured house liquidity position. Both were fixed and are now covered by tests. To actually prove the integration rather than assume it, we forked live Base Sepolia in Foundry and ran a full register-to-settle match against the real, canonically deployed Uniswap v3 Factory and NonfungiblePositionManager, not mocks, which is how we discovered that a zero sqrtPriceLimitX96 silently reverts on real pools even though our own mock happily accepted it. We then deployed for real, dropped the stake to $1 and shortened rounds to 50 seconds to fit what we could actually faucet and rehearse in the time we had, and ran a genuine end-to-end rehearsal on-chain with three separate funded wallets, confirmed correctly indexed in the live subgraph.

name: LeashGuard
description: Approve what your agent buys. Allow bounded credit top-ups with ENSv2 and Privy.
projectDescription:
Leash separates permission to buy a new service from permission to keep using one.
A coding agent's first purchase waits for owner approval, even when it fits the agent's ETH transaction limit. After that purchase settles, the owner can separately authorize credit top-ups for the same merchant, product, account, and agent wallet. Each authorization has a per-top-up limit, cumulative budget, and expiry. A new product, exhausted budget, or expired permission brings the agent back for review.
The working demonstration sells prepaid dependency-report credits. A matching successful Sepolia receipt delivers three credits; a report consumes one. Repeating the same request does not pay or consume credits twice. A ten-tool MCP server exposes the workflow to coding agents without giving them permission to approve themselves. Owners can revoke top-ups or the whole agent.
ENSv2 provides agent identity, lifecycle, and standing transaction limits. Privy provides wallets and synchronized transaction policies. The trusted Leash service enforces product approval and cumulative budgets.
This is a native-ETH Sepolia prototype, with one owner per workspace and a single-host SQLite ledger. Leash operates the demonstration merchant; npm advisory data is public. Budgets exclude gas and separately approved purchases. There is no external SaaS billing, subscription, USD trial budget, x402 support, or production custody claim.
The demonstration link points to verification evidence, including real Sepolia first-purchase and automatic-top-up receipts. Supplementary UI clips and the first-approval and budget screenshots use mocked login, chain, and npm. They are simulated UI evidence, not an authenticated owner/coding-host recording. There is no public hosted application.
howItsMade:
A Solidity registrar creates ENSv2 workspace and agent registries on Sepolia, with per-key resolver roles and lifecycle controls. The service checks the exact live agent token and workspace ownership before reading its payment cap and recipient records at a single block. This prevents stale wildcard resolver records from reviving expired or revoked agents.
Privy supplies owner authentication, agent wallets, and transaction policies. Scoped agent credentials are hashed at rest and cannot approve purchases or authorize top-ups. For an exact owner-approved exception, the service synchronizes a temporary recipient/amount policy, submits once, and restores the current ENS-derived policy, falling back to deny-all on read failure. Service revocation disables credentials and top-up permissions and sets the wallet policy to deny-all.
The Next.js/React owner dashboard and TypeScript APIs share a durable node:sqlite ledger for invoices, approvals, budget reservations, payment IDs, credit accounts, and report replay. Mutations serialize per agent. Automatic top-up budget is reserved before submission; ambiguous outcomes retain their reservation and freeze further spending for operator reconciliation. Credits are delivered only after matching the successful receipt and transaction. Reports retrieve public npm advisory data and consume one credit atomically. The MCP stdio server exposes ten tools shared by Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode.
Validation: 35 application/MCP tests and 16 Foundry contract tests pass, along with typecheck, lint, production build, dependency audit, and deployment preflight. Live integration tests exercised actual ENS/Privy wallets, policy restoration, first approval, automatic top-up, budget exhaustion, product isolation, and revocation. Their owner actions used an operator ownership check, not a Privy browser login. Product/account approval and cumulative budgets are trusted-service controls, not independently enforced on-chain.
Deployment: leash-tools-2026.eth; registrar 0xaa1b19B741fF876F95eE83054c561750af1CdE8f. Public deployment details and receipts are in the repository.
Attribution and timeline: the first project commit is September 4, 2026 at 19:33:20 +03:00. September 4-5 built the initial prototype; September 10-11 hardened lifecycle/payment behavior and implemented purchase-versus-top-up rules; September 13 packaged and published it. Original history is preserved, including the larger final implementation commit. Development was AI-assisted. ENS Namechain, OpenZeppelin, Solady, and other third-party dependencies retain their original licenses; project-specific code is MIT licensed.

name: Legilimens
description: Stake 1 USDC and challenge an on-chain agent to guess your job in 10 questions
projectDescription:
Legilimens is an on-chain fortune booth. You stake 1 USDC, secretly pick your job, and answer 10 yes/no style questions. The Seer, an autonomous agent with its own wallet, then guesses your job. If it names your exact job, it keeps your stake. If it misses, you win your stake back plus half the pot.
How it stays fair:

Your job is locked on-chain as a hash before the first question, so you cannot change it later and the Seer cannot see it.
The Seer commits to its question seed before you play, so it cannot change its strategy after seeing your answers.
The smart contract decides the result and pays out in the same transaction.
If you lie to trick the Seer, the contract checks whether your answers fit your sealed job. Answers that clearly do not fit forfeit your stake.
Anyone can replay any game with one command and check whether the Seer played fair.

The Seer is not an LLM. It uses Bayesian inference (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference) over a published table of 66 jobs and 24 traits, similar to a naive Bayes classifier (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naive_Bayes_classifier). It picks each question by information gain (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_gain_(decision_tree)), the classic twenty questions strategy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty_questions).
Built with:

Arc: USDC stakes, payouts and the Seer's wallet, which earns a 5% cut and pays its own gas.
The Graph: a subgraph of past games that the Seer learns from before each game.
ENS: the Seer's identity and settings live on seer.legilimens.eth. Each player gets a name like abc123.players.legilimens.eth with their game record, written only by the Seer. Players caught lying twice are refused.
howItsMade:
Legilimens has four parts: a smart contract on Arc, a Next.js app that also runs the Seer, a subgraph on The Graph, and ENS names on Sepolia.
Smart contract (Solidity, Foundry)
The LegilimensVault contract holds stakes and runs a commit-reveal game. The player locks their job as a hash with a secret salt. The Seer locks a hash of its random seed. When the Seer guesses, it publishes the seed plus the full transcript (which question it asked and each answer, packed into two bytes10 values). When the player reveals, the contract checks the hash, compares job codes, and pays out in one transaction. Winners take a share of the pot, never a fixed amount, so the pot can never pay out more than it holds. 27 Foundry tests cover every outcome, timeouts, bad signatures and a solvency check.
The Seer (not an LLM)
The Seer is a Bayesian solver written in TypeScript. It uses a table of 66 jobs and 24 traits, updates a probability for every job after each answer, and picks the next question by information gain. The pick uses a seeded softmax, so there is no fixed question tree to exploit, but any game can be replayed exactly. We tuned the question count and randomness with Monte Carlo simulations so the Seer wins about half the time.
Hacky bits worth mentioning

Catching liars on-chain: a script turns the job table into Solidity constants. At reveal, the contract scores how well the answers fit the sealed job compared with every other job, using integer math. A Foundry test proves the contract and the TypeScript solver produce the exact same scores. Blatant liars forfeit their stake. In simulation this turned lying from a big profit into a loss.
No database: the server re-derives each game's secret seed from on-chain data, so it is completely stateless.
Deterministic learning: the Seer only learns from games settled before the current game started, so replays always rebuild the same starting beliefs.
A replay script rebuilds any game from public chain data and checks every question, the guess and the verdict.

Partner technologies

Arc: USDC is the gas token, so stakes, payouts and the Seer's running costs are all in USDC with no conversion. The Seer has its own wallet, earns a 5% cut when it wins, pays its own gas, and records its costs on-chain.
The Graph: a subgraph indexes every game. The Seer reads it before each game to learn which jobs people pick, which changes the questions it asks. It also powers the live ledger of recent games.
ENS (ENSv2 on Sepolia): seer.legilimens.eth stores the Seer's wallet, agent records and the app's settings (vault address, subgraph URL, matrix hash). The app reads these at runtime instead of hard-coding them. The owner gave the Seer's wallet only two permissions: creating names under players.legilimens.eth, and writing specific record keys. After each game the Seer writes the player's record to their own name, like abc123.players.legilimens.eth. Players caught lying twice are refused.

Frontend
Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind 4, Motion for animations, and wagmi and viem for the wallet. The whole game is designed as a candlelit fortune booth with a wax seal, scrying orb and a pot that fills up. Deployed on Vercel.

name: theworldiscollapsing
description: A world that grows forever. Bet on anything in it. Nobody knows the outcome, not even us.
projectDescription:
theworldiscollapsing is a world that never stops. An AI grows it event after event, forever. Matches get played, elections get called, awards get handed out, bills pass or fail, and every result becomes history that the next event builds on. Because something is always happening, there is always something to bet on, and every possible outcome of every event is its own market.
Normal prediction markets can be gamed. Someone learns the result first, someone can move it, or someone decides how it settles. Here nobody can do any of that: not the players, not the house, and not us. Every outcome comes from a drand randomness round that is committed on chain before the first bet and does not exist until betting has closed. When it publishes, the contract verifies its signature on chain and derives the result from it. No person, model or operator picks the result, and anyone can re-check it from their own browser.
The AI builds the world but cannot choose how anything in it ends. Every possible ending is rendered before betting closes and kept sealed. A Chainlink CRE confidential workflow running inside a TEE releases the key for the one ending the chain settled on. The losing endings are never released.
That is a prediction market nobody in the world can control, not even the house. You watch the world live and bet with play USDC on Base Sepolia: https://theworldiscollapsing.vercel.app
howItsMade:
A pnpm monorepo: Solidity contracts, a Node engine that grows the world, a Next.js site, a subgraph and a Chainlink CRE workflow.
Why it cannot be gamed. Two locks. The first decides: every event commits a drand evmnet round on chain when it is created, and that round must publish at least 10 seconds after betting locks. At resolve, the contract verifies the round's BLS signature on chain and sets outcome = keccak256(signature ‖ eventId) mod n. Nobody can know the result while money is on the table, and nobody can choose it. The second seals: every possible ending is rendered before the lock and stored as AES-256-GCM ciphertext, and only a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow inside a TEE derives the key for the ending the chain settled on. What we still hold is liveness, not outcomes: one resolver key can delay a result but not change it, and after three days anyone can bail an event for a full refund.
Engine. One Node 24 process in TypeScript with viem and zod runs the world as one state machine per part of it (sports, politics, culture, region): author, render, createEvent, bet, lock, resolve, reveal, then the result is written into the world's history. It is restart-safe against chain state, presence-gated so an empty site costs nothing, and metered against a hard spend cap. All AI goes through OpenRouter. GPT-6 Astra grows the world: it writes each next event as strict JSON from everything that has already happened, which lives in Postgres and is injected into every prompt. GPT-5 mini is the cheap fallback for long soak runs. Gemini 3.1 Flash Image draws a key frame and MiniMax Hailuo 3 Max turns it into footage with image-to-video, under house-style prompts that make it look like real life filmed live: real time, never cinematic, never slow motion.
Rendering every future. Generated video cannot stream, so every ending exists before anyone bets. The first half is shared and ends level. While it plays and people bet, one second half per outcome renders in the background, seeded from the first half's last frame. Only the winning branch is ever released, so the reveal has zero latency and nobody can skip ahead. Measured cost is $3.27 per event for 45 seconds of video.
Contracts. Foundry, on Base Sepolia, verified on Basescan. Arena runs a YES/NO parimutuel pool on every outcome with a 2% fee, voids markets captured with dust, and has the three-day bail. DrandVerifier checks BN254 BLS signatures with the EVM pairing precompiles. The hacky bit: hash-to-curve needs field inverses and square roots, which we compute through the modexp precompile, so a verify costs about 153k gas with no external library. We chose drand over Chainlink VRF because a VRF result is public the moment it is fulfilled and costs LINK per request, and on OP-stack chains prevrandao can be set by the sequencer.
Sponsors. Chainlink CRE: the confidential workflow in TypeScript listens for Arena's Resolved log, reads the outcome from chain on the Workflow DON, and inside the TEE pulls the seal root from the Vault DON and derives the key for the winning ending only. Keys are derived with keccak256 because the workflow runtime has no crypto library. It compiles to WASM and passes its handler tests, deployment is waiting on Confidential Workflows access, and until the engine drops its fallback copy of the root the engine can still decrypt a late key itself. The Graph: a subgraph on Studio indexes every Arena event and powers the markets and positions pages, and the engine can feed the last event's pools back into the next event. Privy: email login with an embedded wallet on Base Sepolia. World: Selfie Check through IDKit 4 with a server-side verify, then Gate.setVerified on chain gates the faucet and every bet; the hosted demo runs a checkbox fallback while the Selfie Check beta is pending.
Web. Next.js 16 on Vercel, Prisma 7 on Neon Postgres, Vercel Blob for media. Every event page has a verify badge that fetches the round from api.drand.sh and re-derives the outcome in the browser.
Testing without burning money. A fake OpenRouter server replays real MiniMax clips we already paid for, and perpetual bettor bots fund, verify and bet both sides of every market from six wallets. A 10-minute soak across four parts of the world placed 776 bets on 68 events with zero voids and survived restarts of the engine and the bettors mid-window.
One framing note. Nowhere does the text say the AI or the TEE decides outcomes, because they don't. drand decides every ending and the chain verifies it.
