The AI only grows the world, and the TEE keeps the endings sealed. That split is what makes "not even the house can control it" true, and a judge who reads the code will see it matches.
Three honest status lines are kept inside "How it's made":

The CRE workflow isn't deployed yet, and the engine still holds a fallback copy of the seal root.
The hosted demo uses a checkbox instead of World Selfie Check.
GPT-5 mini is the fallback author, so set the engine to Astra before any live demo.

name: Plumb
description: Lets you or your agent analyze live DeFi data from one GraphQL query across many protocols.
projectDescription:
Plumb is a cross-protocol DeFi copilot for agents (Claude, Cursor, or a small web chat). It answers questions like “where is this wallet’s lending risk?” and “how do comparable markets look ?” by running one GraphQL document against many pinned subgraphs on The Graph, not by hard-coding a single protocol API.
Today that means Messari lending markets: Aave v3 (Ethereum), Spark (Ethereum), and Moonwell (Base). The same MARKETS_QUERY and POSITIONS_QUERY are POSTed to every deployment. Adding another lending protocol is a registry.json row (display name, chain, pinned deployment ID) not a new mapper. The same registry-and-shared-query shape is how Plumb can later grow into other DeFi families (for example DEX) without becoming a pile of one-off integrations.
Honesty is the product. Each protocol is pinned to a subgraph deployment ID. Queries go to The Graph gateway by that ID. If _meta.deployment does not match the pin, _meta.block is more than six hours behind, the call times out, or GraphQL/HTTP fails, the payload is discarded. Tools return structured failures[] and the UI/agent must say unavailable. They must not fill a cell with 0, a cache, or an LLM guess. The demo can break a pin on purpose so judges see that path.
Agents do not just dump JSON. Four reusable MCP tools (list_lending_markets, query_market, compare_markets, wallet_lending) return the same columns across protocols: APYs, deposits/borrows, derived available liquidity, LTV/liquidation fields, and _meta provenance. The model is instructed (tool descriptions + SKILL.md) to reason on those rows: compare borrow APY and liquidity, talk about liquidation risk from schema fields only (Messari has no healthFactor), and always surface failures. A CLI and a local web UI call the same tools.
The Graph API key never leaves the server. There is no swap execution, no fake health factor, and no mocked market numbers in the product path.
howItsMade:
We built Plumb as a TypeScript (Node 22+, ESM) service with pnpm, Zod, and Vitest. There is no Next.js app and no GraphQL client that could cache answers. The product path is: MCP or UI → tools → honest Graph fetch → structured rows and failures.
The Graph is the only partner in the loop. A Subgraph Studio / Network API key lives only in the server process. Every query is an HTTP POST of a shared document to gateway.thegraph.com/api/<KEY>/deployments/id/<PIN> never /subgraphs/id/..., so we do not silently follow “latest.” registry.json maps protocol slug → chain → pinned deployment ID. Enabled protocols are queried in parallel (Promise.allSettled); one dead subgraph does not abort the others.
Two GraphQL templates cover everyone: Messari lending MARKETS_QUERY and POSITIONS_QUERY, both requesting _meta. After a 15s timeout, HTTP/GraphQL errors become QueryFailure. Success still goes through honesty: normalize _meta.deployment against the pin; stale if _meta.block.timestamp lags more than six hours (or is in the future). Failed bodies are dropped—callers never see numbers from a bad pin.
Mapping is schema-faithful, not protocol-specific. Supply/borrow APY come from rates (LENDER / BORROWER, prefer VARIABLE). availableLiquidityUSD is derived as max(0, deposits − borrows) because Messari has no such field. Positions use the intersection of Aave/Spark 3.1.0 and Moonwell 2.0.1 so one document still runs; we do not invent healthFactor. Asset match is inputToken.symbol with case variants; USDC.e is a separate row.
MCP (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk, stdio) exposes list_lending_markets, query_market, compare_markets, wallet_lending. Handlers call the real tools and return JSON text. Logs go to stderr so stdout stays JSON-RPC. A small node:http API and Vite + React UI (and a CLI pnpm compare) use those same tools. Optional in-app chat is Anthropic tool-calling on the server; with no key, the UI is forms only.
Notable hack: --break / a UI checkbox still hits the live gateway with a wrong CID or a mismatched pin. Unavailable is a real HTTP_ERROR or DEPLOYMENT_MISMATCH, not if (demo) return 0.

name: Limit order book
description: fully on chain limit order book built on arbitrum stylus using a novel bitmap algorithm
projectDescription:
We are solving an open problem in DeFi- bringing limit order books on chain.
This was impossible on EVM given its limitations on computation and memory-till now. Arbitrum stylus allows you to write smart contracts in rust unlocking 10x more memory and throughput. We paired it with a novel bitmap based algorithm to make limit orders possible with EVM's 256 bit K-V storage trie structure.
howItsMade:
Tech stack

Smart contract: rust
Chain: arbitrum stylus
Indexing: subtraphs (wip)

The smart contract builds up on a large number of innovations


Bitmap tree: instead of a traditional tree structure to store orderbook nodes, we use EVM's 256 bit key value trie as the store. Encoding a full tree in EVM is wasteful as slot keys store temporary indices and every update forces large rebalancing writes. We structure data as a sparse matrix instead of a tree. The key hash encodes details like price and market ID while the state stores order state.


High througput allows us to market make dozens of orders across multiple markets in a single atomic call. We can beat Uniswap when it comes to gas and market making. Benchmarking is still wip.


The smart contract code acts as the indexer and SDK. We code will be embedded inside a rust WASM subgraph and be used for indexing.

name: Margit
description: Margit is a marketplace for private Github repositories for AI agents to trade.
projectDescription:
Pronounced almost like MARKET (Mar-Git)
Margit is a marketplace for private GitHub repositories, built for humans and AI agents. Sellers connect GitHub, choose a repository, set a price and access terms, and receive payments in USDC or EURC on Arc testnet. Buyers pay to unlock authenticated Git clone or ZIP access.
GitHub does not provide a native checkout for selling private repository access. Margit connects discovery, payment, and code delivery in one workflow, helping developers monetize templates, plugins, starter kits, and complete applications directly from their repositories.
The same workflow is available to agents. Imagine asking your coding agent to build something useful, then authorizing it to list the repository for sale. Another agent can discover it, evaluate whether it fits a project, and purchase access within its user’s budget. Margit makes repository commerce accessible through both a visual interface and agent tools.
Users can browse listings, explore sales activity, and use our Bazantic-powered Repository Advisor to compare options against their requirements and budget.
Think about it this way: You have your agent creating code, next logical step - just Margit! Let it be a verb like just google it, but for putting your code for sale - just marg-it!
howItsMade:
We built Margit with React, TypeScript, and Vite, backed by a Hono API on Vercel. GitHub OAuth connects sellers’ repositories, while Upstash Redis stores listings, sessions, purchase records, and encrypted credentials. After payment verification, our backend issues scoped Git clone or ZIP access without exposing the seller’s GitHub token.
Arc and Circle power payments. Our contract ↗ (0x72c54ecd669acb19d6e6d5b5160f67d03b4d5b7b) handles buyer-bound signed orders, publisher payments, and platform fees. Circle Gateway provides a separate x402 payment path for agents: request access, receive an HTTP 402 challenge, sign payment authorization, and retry to unlock the repository. We support demo and personal agent wallets, Circle-managed wallets, and a 1Claw remote-signing integration. Our payment evidence ↗ documents a successful 0.05 USDC Gateway purchase and authenticated Git delivery.
The Graph makes marketplace activity queryable. Our Subgraph ↗ indexes contract purchase and fee events for catalog statistics, bestseller rankings, and buyer/seller leaderboards. These statistics cover contract checkout activity; Gateway x402 purchases follow a separate payment path.
Our OpenRouter-powered assistant connects discovery and actions. It combines indexed activity with current catalog data, manages authorized seller listings, and executes requested purchases through backend tools. External agents can use our MCP or API ↗ and published SKILLS ↗ to interact with the marketplace.
Bazantic powers our Repository Advisor. We connected Margit’s catalog API and GitHub’s public API through two Bazantic gateways, then published a reusable Recipe that evaluates project requirements against a USD repository budget. For explicitly supplied comparison repositories, it checks GitHub metadata, languages, and releases. The same Recipe serves the Catalog’s advisor form and an optional tool in the agent sidebar. Our guide ↗ includes gateway URLs, tool bindings, the Recipe prompt, and test evidence.

One particularly hands-on part was implementing the Git delivery proxy, which enforces purchased access terms while keeping seller credentials private. Another was handling uncertain payment outcomes: we validate payment requirements before signing, retain purchase records, and block automatic payment retries when the result is unclear. This helps prevent duplicate charges while allowing buyers to recover access after a completed purchase.

prizes.rawText: Bazantic - Agentify a new API 1st place

name: Ratip
description: Ratib is a SvelteKit, Convex, and Privy operations workspace for crypto-native businesses.
projectDescription:
Ratib is a governed finance-operations platform for businesses working with digital assets. It brings wallets, payments, approvals, invoices, automation, reconciliation, reporting, and audit evidence into one shared workspace. Instead of forcing finance teams to coordinate transactions across wallet interfaces, spreadsheets, messaging apps, and accounting tools, Ratib turns each financial action into a structured, traceable workflow.
A team can organize wallets by company, review payment requests, apply internal approval rules, execute deterministic batch operations, monitor transaction status, and reconcile onchain activity with its business context. Every action is scoped to the organization and recorded as append-only evidence, giving operators and reviewers a clear history of what was requested, who approved it, which policy applied, and what eventually settled.
Ratib deliberately separates business permissions from cryptographic authority. Ratib manages roles, workflow approvals, policy previews, and operational records, but those roles never grant signing power. Privy remains the final authority through embedded wallets, owners, signers, quorum rules, MFA-backed approvals, and provider-enforced policies. Transactions currently settle in USDC on Base Sepolia, so the prototype is clearly testnet-only.
The long-term vision is to become the operational layer between programmable money and modern finance teams—expanding into invoice checkout, transaction simulation, recovery and gas management, developer APIs, accounting connectors, forecasting, fiat accounts, global payouts, cards, and qualified custody partnerships.
howItsMade:
Ratib is built with SvelteKit and TypeScript on the frontend, with Convex providing the real-time database, server functions, scheduled automation, and append-only audit history. Privy supplies embedded wallets, verified user identity, owner/signer configuration, policy enforcement, MFA-backed approvals, and secure transaction execution. Transactions settle using USDC on Base Sepolia.
The key architectural decision was separating finance workflow from wallet authority: Ratib coordinates requests, roles, approvals, policy previews, and reconciliation, while Privy remains the final signing authority. Every operation is organization-scoped and follows a strict state machine. Deterministic run keys and idempotent actions prevent duplicate payments, while verified webhooks reconcile onchain results back into Convex.

name: Obscura protocol
description: Shielded prediction markets with zkVM-proven solvency bet privately, prove you were right.
projectDescription: Obscura is a prediction market where your position is shielded end to end, yet every market's payouts are provably correct and solvent no operator is trusted for the numbers. Today's markets (Polymarket, Kalshi) make every bet public, leaking strategy and inviting front-running on correlated markets. In Obscura your side and stake never touch the chain in the clear only a Poseidon commitment does. When a market resolves (via a Chainlink feed, a Graph metric, or a Chainlink CRE workflow), an SP1 zkVM proof establishes the per-outcome totals and the commitments-tree root and proves they reconcile with the escrowed USDC so payouts are correct and solvent by proof, not by trust. Winners then prove in-browser (Noir) that they hold an unspent winning note and withdraw to a fresh address, unlinkable to the deposit. On top of shielded positions it adds Private Parlays, Proof of Foresight (an anonymous, verifiable "I called it" track record), a ZK accuracy reputation badge, and a live AI solvency/risk oracle. Most "private" markets stop at hiding individual bets; the hard, largely unsolved part is proving the aggregate settlement is correct and solvent while revealing nothing about individuals which is exactly what Obscura demonstrates.
howItsMade: Privacy layer: Noir zk circuits for shielded deposit commitments, private claims, Proof of Foresight, parlays, and reputation; claim + foresight proofs are generated in the browser with @noir-lang/noir_js + @aztec/bb.js (UltraHonk) against on-chain verifiers. Solvency proof: an SP1 zkVM program (guest/host/aggregation in Rust) recomputes each market's per-outcome totals + Poseidon commitments root and asserts solvency; PredictionMarket.settleWithProof verifies it via the SP1 gateway before payouts unlock. Poseidon is byte-compatible across Noir / Rust light-poseidon / JS poseidon-lite (pinned test vectors) so every layer agrees on roots. Chainlink CRE: three TypeScript CRE workflows confidential settlement (TEE aggregation reconciled on-chain vs SP1 totals), Graph-metric resolution, and cron auto-resolution (the successor to classic Automation, sunset in 2026) driving an on-chain AutoResolver keeper. Resolution is source-agnostic: Chainlink feeds, The Graph, or CRE. The Graph: a subgraph indexes only public aggregates; an AI risk oracle (MCP server + in-browser port) computes solvency coverage + HHI concentration with a pinned deployment id + freshness gate, benchmarked against a Messari-standardized mainnet subgraph. Circle/Arc: USDC-denominated escrow (ERC-20 + EIP-2612 permit), deployed on Circle Arc testnet (USDC-native gas), with a CCTP entry that bridges USDC Base -> Arc into a shielded position. Client: Next.js 16, Wagmi, Viem, lightweight-charts. Everything is deployed + verified on Ethereum Sepolia and Arc testnet (addresses in the README). Hacky-but-notable: the SP1 EVM/Groth16 settlement proof is memory-heavy, so it runs on prover infrastructure and is verified on-chain by the SP1 gateway the standard production path.

name: Bombus
description: Agents vote in secret. A TEE tallies them. Only the verdict comes out. Paid per query via x402.
projectDescription:
Hear the swarm, never the bee.
DAOs, protocols, and agent networks need collective private signals — votes, risk assessments, price estimates — but today they must either publish every input on-chain (killing the signal's value, inviting front-running and copying) or hand everything to a centralized aggregator (defeating the point of a decentralized swarm).
Bombus is a confidential aggregation substrate for agent swarms. Independent agents each hold a private value; that value is encrypted to a Trusted Execution Environment, combined inside it, and only the aggregate ever becomes public. No individual input is exposed — not to other agents, not to the chain, not to the coordinator operator.
The first use case is DAO deliberation: each agent deliberates with its own persona and an LLM, encrypts its ballot, and submits it to a blind coordinator. When quorum is reached, a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow decrypts the batch inside the enclave, computes a confidence-weighted tally, and emits a signed verdict (pass / fail / contested). The verdict is served per query behind an x402 payment on Hedera — consumers (agents or humans) pay to read it, and anyone can verify the TEE's signature in the browser against a key published on ENS.
The demo runs live: three agents with distinct stances (Growth Hawk, Risk Auditor, Community Steward) deliberate on a real proposal, the quorum fills, the verdict reveals only after its signature verifies, and the paid-access receipt links to a settled Hedera transaction. The absence is the product: the UI shows that agents voted, never how.
Privacy guarantees, stated honestly: individual ballots are visible to no one — coordinator included (it routes ciphertext); participation metadata is public by design; the workflow deployer is a trusted party; and external LLM providers see only public proposal text, never ballots or private strategy.
howItsMade:
Swarm (off-chain): N independent Node.js agent processes, each with an ed25519 keypair and an ENSv2 identity (agent1.bombus.eth) on the hackathon deployment. Each agent deliberates via a hosted LLM (OpenAI-compatible endpoint — NVIDIA Nemotron) with a distinct persona, producing a confidence-weighted ballot, then seals it to the TEE's X25519 key (X25519 + XChaCha20-Poly1305) and signs the envelope. Agents are fully independent — no shared state, no coordination among themselves.
Blind coordinator (Node.js/Express): verifies envelope signatures against the agent keymap, deduplicates and quorums per round, and hands the batch onward. It never sees a plaintext ballot — validation is signature + schema only. Round metadata (who submitted, ciphertext hash) is public; content is not. Tombstones persist closed rounds so replays are rejected across restarts.
Confidential aggregation (Chainlink CRE): a confidential workflow runs inside an AWS Nitro TEE. The handler decrypts each envelope with a Vault-stored key, validates against the use-case schema, computes the confidence-weighted tally (net = (W_support − W_oppose) / total, pass at ±0.5), suppresses detail below N=5 for small-cohort privacy, and signs the result with a TEE-held ed25519 key. Only the signed verdict leaves the enclave. The same handler code runs in cre workflow simulate (both confidential and plain targets) and in the coordinator's local seam, so the demo is resilient while the deployed path fires real DON executions as attestation.
Delivery (x402 + Hedera): the resource server verifies the TEE signature at intake and refuses anything unverifiable, then serves the verdict behind an x402 payment on Hedera testnet via the Blocky402 facilitator (@x402/express + @x402/hedera, x402 v2). A paid request settles a real test-USDC transfer on-chain — receipt visible on HashScan.
Trust layer (ENSv2): agent identities, the enclave encryption key, and the TEE signing key are published as text records on the hackathon ENSv2 deployment (bombus.eth), giving the whole system a tamper-evident, human-readable root of trust. The web UI resolves the TEE key from ENS and verifies every verdict signature in the browser before revealing it.
UI: a Vite + React observatory that polls the coordinator for live round state (dynamic quorum slots, sealed envelopes as hashed cells), reveals verdicts only after in-browser signature verification, and shows the Hedera receipt — never any ballot content.

name: Preflight MCP
description: The check an AI agent clears before it signs. High risk needs a press on your Ledger.
projectDescription:
An AI agent can read a contract, decide it looks fine, and sign against it with no human in the loop. The text it reads to make that decision was written by whoever deployed the contract, for the price of gas.
Here is a real token on Ethereum mainnet. It reports 1.1 trillion dollars of liquidity. Four transactions have touched it in four years. The source is verified and the name is friendly, so an agent reading the contract finds nothing wrong. Preflight scores it HIGH 94, because it asks a different question: not what the contract says, but what it has done.
An agent crosses five boundaries. What it installs, what it reads, what it trusts, what it submits, and what it is allowed to do. Four of those have somebody defending them. The one nobody defends is what the agent reads, and it is the cheapest of the five to attack.
Preflight sits at that boundary. It ships as an MCP server, so the check happens inside the agent that was about to sign. Eleven weighted signals, four of which read Uniswap V3 pool state through The Graph across Ethereum, Arbitrum and Base. Source code tells you what a contract may do. Indexed pool history tells you what it has done, and only one of those predicts a rug.
The score is arithmetic, not a judgement call. The same address in the same on-chain state gives the same answer every time, and the language model in the pipeline writes one advisory paragraph that structurally cannot move the number.
Every on-chain string is treated as hostile. It gets sealed before a model reads it and wrapped in an unpredictable nonce before an agent does. When the verdict is high, the approval leaves software entirely and goes to a Ledger for a physical button press. Unplug the device and the flow breaks. That is the point: the device is the only part of the loop an attacker cannot reach over the network.
This extends Inspector AI, which I built at ETHGlobal Singapore in 2024. Everything after the ethonline-2026-start tag is new. Twenty one hand verified addresses in the repo, zero false positives.
howItsMade:
TypeScript throughout, pnpm workspaces, eight packages. The MCP server speaks stdio and exposes three tools, so an agent in Claude Code or Cursor calls preflight_check before it approves anything.
The Graph is where the project earns its answers. Four of the eleven signals query the official Uniswap V3 subgraphs through the decentralised gateway with a Subgraph Studio key, on Ethereum, Arbitrum and Base. Uniswap ships identical subgraph code per chain, so one query string covers all three and only the deployment id changes. That is the reason this supports three chains instead of one. Pool queries run on both sides of the pair because a Uniswap pair is directional and a token on the wrong side would be invisible. Etherscan V2 supplies source, ABI, proxy resolution and transfer history.
Scoring is noisy-OR over independent evidence rather than a weighted average. Averaging assumes findings dilute each other, and they do not: a pool holding 1.1 trillion dollars that four transactions have touched is damning on its own. Under averaging that address scored 18 and read LOW. It now reads HIGH 94.
Ledger shows up twice. wallet-cli ring is the credential store, so the API keys in the repo are ciphertext and no plaintext exists on disk. And a high verdict blocks on a device confirmation, returned to the agent as an error rather than a warning it could reason past.
The notable hack is why that gate is fast. wallet-cli does not fail quickly when no device is attached, it scans for about a minute, which blew past the MCP client's sixty second request timeout. So the gate reads the USB tree directly first, which answers in 47 milliseconds, and the engine hands the gate only the budget the analysis did not already spend. Unplugged now refuses in nine seconds instead of timing out.
Thirteen hardware test cases on a Nano S Plus found nine defects a passing test suite had not, including a parser that refused every genuine button press because receive --verify reports success as status success with verified and source fields and never emits the ok true we required. Every one of those failures failed closed.
Postgres for persistence with an in memory fallback. Contributed fixes back to both partners while building: Uniswap/v3-subgraph#310 and LedgerHQ/device-sdk-ts#1884.

prizes.rawText: Ledger - Extend to Ledger 2nd place

name: Clearing Bell
description: Batch auctions for tokenized bonds on Hedera, with one clearing price and eligibility checks.
projectDescription:
Putting a bond on-chain is only half the job. The harder question is what happens when its holder wants to sell.
Clearing Bell is a secondary-market prototype for tokenized bonds on Hedera. It brings buyers and sellers together in timed batch auctions: participants submit public limit orders, and the clearing engine determines a single price for matched trades. Eligible orders can fill partially, and an auction with no matching demand closes without forcing a trade.
We chose this approach for assets that may not trade every second. Gathering orders into a shared window gives buyers and sellers a common moment for price discovery, without requiring a continuously funded liquidity pool.
Eligibility is part of the trading process. The contracts check the bond’s configured identity registry when an order is submitted and recheck eligibility before settlement. Matched bond and payment-token transfers execute together in one transaction.
The architecture also supports a curated multi-issuer model. A platform administrator registers bond issuers, while bond-specific permissions govern their auction operations. The frontend brings markets, auction depth, wallet balances, settlement records and issuer controls into one workspace.
Our focus is the gap between issuing a digital asset and giving its holders a usable market. Clearing Bell is currently a hackathon prototype; multi-issuer workflow validation and security hardening remain in progress.
howItsMade:
We built Clearing Bell with Solidity contracts, a React and TypeScript frontend, and Hedera’s EVM-compatible testnet. The frontend uses Vite and viem to read contract state and prepare wallet transactions directly, without a separate application server.
The auction logic is split between AuctionEngine and a pure ClearingLib library. The library evaluates executable demand and supply across submitted price levels, selects a uniform clearing price, and allocates fills using price priority and submission order. Keeping the calculation separate from token transfers makes the matching logic easier to inspect and test.
Settlement uses a collect-and-distribute flow inside one transaction. We also handle token amounts using integer base units, with explicit decimal conversion between bond quantities and payment tokens. This matters because small rounding errors can otherwise leave settlement underfunded or create leftover balances.
Our Hedera integration includes bond-deployment scripts targeting the Asset Tokenization Studio factory and a compliance gate that queries the configured identity registry. One particularly tricky integration detail was matching the deployed ATS factory’s ABI: the scripts explicitly encode its v7 bond-creation structure, whose field order differs from newer versions.
For the interface, we built reusable auction charts from actual order-book data, wallet-session restoration, and separate investor and issuer views. Three.js provides optional spatial visuals, with still-image fallbacks and reduced-motion support.
We use Foundry and Anvil for contract development, alongside frontend tests, TypeScript and ESLint. The repository also includes a Uniswap v4 hook integration, but the current frontend routes directly to the auction engine; real PoolManager integration is not presented as a completed production flow.

name: Sight
description: Sight — selfie-proofed human agents on ENSv2, with on-chain reputations you can graph and trust
projectDescription:
Sight, what we originally called Agent Passport, is an abuse-prevention primitive for the agentic-web era.
The problem we’re trying to solve looks a bit like this: anyone with an automated script and some compute can spin up 50 sock-puppet agents, Sybil an application, and farm reputation or rewards. As autonomous agents increasingly interact with applications, marketplaces, and each other, there is currently very little tying an agent’s identity back to a real, unique participant.
Sight operators on a very simple principle: one verified human ⇒ one wallet ⇒ a set of trusted agents.
Every agent is registered on ENSv2’s Sepolia deployment under the root agentpassport.eth. It is impossible to register one without first passing a live World Selfie Check. There is no CAPTCHA and no KYC involved—only a ZK-backed proof that the wallet belongs to a unique human.
Once verified, a human can register individual agent subnames beneath agentpassport.eth. Each agent identity carries three independent records: who owns the name, whether that owner has been verified as a unique human, and the agent’s reputation score. This separates human provenance from agent reputation: verification establishes that an agent ultimately originates from a scarce human identity, while reputation captures how that particular agent has behaved over time.
All of this state can be indexed through a The Graph subgraph, allowing applications to efficiently query verified humans, registered agents, ownership relationships, and reputation without repeatedly reading raw contract state. On top of this, an MCP server exposes the same trust layer directly to AI systems. An agent can therefore ask questions such as “Is agent-x backed by a verified human?”, “Who controls this agent?”, or “What reputation has this agent accumulated?” before deciding whether to interact with it.
The goal is to give the agentic web something it currently lacks: a lightweight, privacy-preserving way for agents and applications to distinguish persistent, human-backed identities from an unlimited swarm of disposable ones.
howItsMade:
The contracts are written in Solidity, with Foundry, against ENSv2's Sepolia registry. The app itself is a just React + Vite + ethers v6. The backend is an Express verifier uses World's Developer Portal /verify API and calls HumanVerification.
the frontends IDKit widget mints a Selfie Check Proof which the backend validates against World. So now a verified human can register an Agent. This mints a "agent passpot" and configures the EAC role bitmaps and sets the initial records. Reputation writes go through onlyScorer. Everything that emits state is indexed by Graph Node and queried via GraphQL from both the dashboard and the MCP server.
Some of the things we'd love to improve on: the nullifier claim is held in an in-memory set. We'd like to swap that to a store. Right now, since we're based of in India, World selfie checks dont really work. So for the purposes of the video we've set it to testing.

name: ArcSet
description: ArcSet turns a DeFi thesis into a self-custodial portfolio you can review and execute on Arc.
projectDescription:
ArcSet is a self-custodial portfolio app for Arc Testnet. It turns an investment thesis, such as stablecoin yield, Bitcoin income, currency diversification, or cross-chain liquidity, into a basket with clear target weights. Users create a Circle modular wallet secured by a device passkey, fund it with USDC, inspect the assets, protocols, risks, fees, and exit paths, then request a fresh execution plan. Every swap, vault deposit, minimum output, and estimated fee is shown before signing.
ArcSet uses Circle App Kit to swap USDC into EURC or cirBTC and EarnKit to deposit USDC into a screened Morpho ERC-4626 vault. Its experimental cross-chain basket deposits part of the investment on Arc, bridges canonical USDC to Base Sepolia through CCTP, swaps half for WETH, and creates a Uniswap V3 liquidity position. Confirmed steps are recorded, allowing an interrupted route to resume without repeating an earlier transaction or bridge burn.
Assets and positions remain in the user's wallet. ArcSet reads live balances, values holdings, links receipts to each basket, calculates allocation drift, and provides reviewed exit and rebalance flows. Since Arc uses USDC for gas, the same balance can fund investments and network fees. The project also includes a Messari-compatible Graph subgraph for Morpho deposits, withdrawals, TVL, and vault activity.
howItsMade:
We built ArcSet with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, viem, and Circle's Arc stack. The frontend talks to Arc Testnet through viem, with fallback RPC endpoints for balance reads, contract checks, and transaction receipts.
Circle Modular Wallets provide the wallet layer. A device passkey controls a Circle smart account, so users never handle a private key. We wrote a custom EIP-1193 provider that translates standard wallet calls into sponsored ERC-4337 user operations through Circle's bundler and paymaster. It supports wallet_sendCalls, transaction status polling, and regular transaction requests, which lets Circle App Kit work with the passkey wallet on both Arc Testnet and Base Sepolia.
Circle App Kit supplies fresh swap quotes for USDC, EURC, and cirBTC. Each quote includes fees and a 1% minimum output before execution. EarnKit discovers the active Morpho USDC vault on Arc. We then verify the vault ourselves by checking its deployed bytecode and ERC-4626 asset(), decimals(), and totalAssets() responses. ArcSet rejects mock or inactive vaults, non-USDC assets, and vaults with red risk warnings.
Each basket is a versioned set of execution adapters. An adapter must support entry, exit, position reads, and valuation before its strategy appears in the catalog. Composite baskets quote every leg together, then execute the swaps and Morpho deposit in sequence. We record each confirmed transaction separately. If a later step fails, ArcSet keeps the completed receipts and retries only the unfinished steps with fresh quotes.
The cross-chain basket uses Circle CCTP to bridge canonical USDC from Arc to Base Sepolia. It deposits one part into Morpho on Arc, bridges another part, swaps half of the received USDC for WETH, and mints a wide-range Uniswap V3 LP NFT. Exact approvals, minimum outputs, and a Testnet pool-price sanity check protect the Uniswap steps. We persist progress after each stage so resuming the route cannot repeat a completed CCTP burn.
One surprisingly tricky Arc detail is USDC accounting. Arc exposes the same underlying USDC balance through an 18-decimal native interface for gas and a 6-decimal ERC-20 interface for transfers and approvals. ArcSet treats these as one asset, uses the ERC-20 view for portfolio accounting, and reserves the native view for gas and msg.value. This avoids displaying or counting the same money twice.
We also wrote a Messari Yield Aggregator compatible subgraph for The Graph. It indexes Morpho ERC-4626 deposits and withdrawals on Arc and calculates vault activity, TVL, share supply, and user metrics. The portfolio view combines live onchain balances with locally recorded execution attribution, then calculates allocation drift and prepares user-reviewed exit or rebalance actions.

name: Cope Market
description: A social feed where every take is backed by a real USDC position.
projectDescription:
Cope Market is a social feed where every opinion costs something. You post a thesis — an asset, a direction, and your reasoning — and back it with real USDC. Other people can copy your position with one tap, and if their copy closes in profit, you get paid automatically, on-chain, by the contract.
The problem it solves is that financial opinions are free to give and impossible to score. Crypto Twitter is full of calls nobody tracks, from people with no position. Here a thesis without a position is visibly marked as such, every track record is derived from settled trades rather than self-reported, and the incentive to share a good call is paid by the protocol instead of by a sponsorship deal.
Positions are synthetic and oracle-priced. A shared USDC pool is the counterparty to every trade — LPs deposit into an ERC-4626 vault, traders' losses and fees become LP yield, traders' wins come out of the pool. Each position is an ERC-721 you actually hold and can sell; the credit for the call stays with whoever opened it, so buying someone's position doesn't buy their leaderboard rank.
The copy mechanic is where the money flow gets interesting. A copy records which position it followed and the author's fee rate at that moment, so changing the protocol's fee later never rewrites a deal someone already took. On a profitable close the contract pays the original author a share of the profit only — never the notional, and capped at the payout so it can't be funded out of anyone else's collateral. The author never signs that transaction and may not know it happened. There's no invoice and nothing to reconcile.
It runs on Arc, where USDC is the collateral, the quote asset and the gas, so no leg of that settlement touches a second token.
Everything described is deployed and verified on Arc testnet: three contracts, three subgraphs across two chains, an MCP server, and two always-on services. The numbers in our demo were read from the chain, not typed into a slide — the indexed open interest reconciles to openInterest() on the contract to the wei.
howItsMade:
Contracts (Solidity 0.8.36, Foundry). SyntheticVault mints ERC-721 positions and does all settlement; LiquidityVault is an ERC-4626 pool whose totalAssets nets out what it owes open positions, so an LP can't deposit just before traders lose and withdraw just before they win. Entry prices are skewed against the trader by the oracle's confidence interval — a long enters at mid + conf, a short at mid − conf — so the pool never takes the oracle's uncertainty onto its own balance sheet. 166 Foundry tests including fuzz and invariant runs.
Arc / Circle. USDC being native is not a detail here. Collateral, the pool's balance sheet, the author fee, the payout and the gas are one asset, so the conditional settlement has no swap, no wrapped representation and no price risk between the leg that pays and the leg that settles. One thing that catches people: Arc's native currency is USDC at 18 decimals and the ERC-20 at 0x3600…0000 is the same balance at 6. Gas therefore moves your USDC balance, and we had to account for that when reconciling — our liquidation test came out 3,920 units short until we realised the gap was gas.
The Graph. Three subgraphs. One indexes any ERC-4626 vault — nothing about Cope Market appears in its schema, its mappings, or even its ABI, which is hand-written from the standard rather than exported from our vault. We proved that by pointing the same unmodified code at two MetaMorpho vaults on Base from a config file: a 6-decimal-asset vault and an 18-decimal one, priced correctly by the same expression. Then an MCP server on top, seven tools that compute drawdown, windowed rankings and whether copying a given author has actually paid — deliberately no raw GraphQL passthrough, and a test that fails if a tool name ever looks like one.
Privy. X login creates an embedded wallet, and Arc is registered as a custom chain via defineChain so that wallet signs Arc transactions directly — no extension, no seed phrase. The backend holds no key at all: it validates, quotes, simulates the call as you with eth_call, and hands back an unsigned transaction. A compromised API server can lie to a user but cannot move their money.
Backend. Next.js with Postgres holding only social content — theses, follows, comments. Wipe it and every position, balance and copy relationship survives on-chain. Routes are declared once as zod schemas, folded into an OpenAPI 3.1 document, and compiled into a typed client that's vendored into the frontend with a CI check that fails on drift.
Pyth's pull oracle does not work on Arc. We proved it with a cross-chain control: the identical Hermes blob is accepted on Base mainnet and rejected on Arc testnet with InvalidWormholeVaa. Root cause is that Arc's Wormhole receiver holds Wormhole's guardian set (19 guardians) instead of Pythnet's (5) — not our bug, and not fixable from our side. Because the vault only ever knew an IPriceOracle, swapping to a push oracle was a constructor argument plus a service, not a rewrite. So we wrote a price pusher that fetches from Hermes, rescales to 18 decimals in exact BigInt arithmetic, drops feeds whose timestamps haven't moved, and — crucially — judges its own success by reading the oracle back and comparing each feed's age to that asset's maxAgeSec, because a mined transaction is not a usable price.

name: alpha402
description: An on-chain market where AI agents pay for live signals on Hedera and act on Uniswap.
projectDescription:
AI trading agents can't participate in markets on their own. Every API key,
card, and subscription assumes a human is present to buy the data, and placing
a trade still needs a person to click "swap" — so an agent that should run
autonomously ends up needing someone at both ends. The rails for
machine-to-machine commerce, where software pays for a read and then acts on
it, simply don't exist yet.
alpha402 builds those rails. It's a market made for machines: instead of a raw
API, it sells synthesized market alpha — whale flows and volume momentum pulled
live from Uniswap through The Graph, fused with macro news by AI into a single
market read. An agent queries the signals, reads them, and pays for exactly
what it uses, per query, with x402 on Hedera; or it holds an on-chain HTS
subscription pass for the recurring AI brief. Then it acts on the answer: the
agent recommends a Uniswap pool and executes a real swap, with no human in the
loop. Every payment is a genuine on-chain transaction that settles on Hedera
and leaves a verifiable receipt on HashScan, and the whole payment engine ships
as a reusable npm package so any agent can plug in.
The economics are part of the design. Raw signals are metered per query, while
the AI brief runs on a schedule and is cached and gated by a subscription pass
rather than charged on every request — which is the reason the pass exists at
all. You can watch the entire loop end to end: ask a question, subscribe on
Hedera, and the autonomous agent reads the market and pays for the data it
needs on its own, out loud, before recommending a pool and swapping on Uniswap.
Every "paid" line is a real settled transaction you can open on HashScan.
howItsMade:
alpha402 is one pnpm monorepo, and data flows through it Uniswap to The Graph
to AI to Hedera to pay, then back to Uniswap to invest. The reusable payment
engine lives in packages/hedera-x402 and is published to npm as alpha402; it
handles both sides of x402, mints and verifies HTS passes, writes HCS receipts,
and schedules renewals, so any agent can run npm i alpha402 and plug straight
in. On top of it, apps/api is a single Hono server that serves the feed
catalog, gates each feed, runs the signal scheduler and the autonomous agent
loop, and settles payments, while apps/web is a React (Vite) dashboard the same
server serves in production. The whole thing deploys as one Docker image on
Fly.io, with the API and the dashboard on a single port behind an SPA fallback,
so the entire product is one deploy.
Hedera is the settlement core and roughly eighty percent of the build.
Per-query payments run through x402 via the blocky402 facilitator, priced
dynamically rather than flat. Subscriptions mint an NFT pass on the Hedera Token
Service to the agent's wallet, and entitlement is checked against the mirror
node — hold a valid, unexpired pass and the AI brief is served with no payment.
Every payment and subscription writes an audit record to a Hedera Consensus
Service topic, all verifiable on HashScan, and recurring renewals are queued
on-chain with Scheduled Transactions. An autonomous buying agent completes real
paid requests end to end.
The market signals come from live Uniswap v3 subgraph queries on The Graph,
using a real Studio key rather than mocked data: whale swaps above a USD
threshold, and volume and liquidity momentum measured today against the prior
day. A watchlist and a watcher loop turn watched-wallet activity into a
near-real-time smart-money feed, and the AI reasons over all of it, with each
query paid per request through x402. The AI itself is OpenAI, behind a
provider-agnostic llm() function so it swaps to Claude or a local model with one
line, running on a scheduler and cached between requests.
When the agent acts, it executes a real swap on Unichain Sepolia through the
Uniswap Trading API, running the full Permit2 flow: quote, approve to Permit2,
sign a PermitSingle, submit to the swap endpoint with the signature, simulate
with eth_call, then broadcast — verified with live testnet swaps of USDC into
WETH. Two things fought back along the way. The published hak-uniswap-plugin
never signed the Permit2 permit, so swaps reverted with no logs until we rewrote
the swap path to sign the PermitSingle ourselves; and the public Unichain
Sepolia RPCs accepted transactions but never mined them, so tx.wait hung until
we moved to an RPC that actually confirms.
Across the three sponsors it is one product. For Hedera, it is x402 plus HTS
passes plus HCS receipts and real HashScan transactions, with an agent
completing paid requests end to end. For The Graph, it is live subgraph queries
with AI reasoning over them, each one paid per query with x402. And for Uniswap,
it is pool intelligence the agent acts on with a real swap through the Trading
API and Permit2, with our developer notes written up in FEEDBACK.md.

name: zBase
description: zBase enables private x402 agentic payments onchain, using ZK Privacy Pools and sanctions screening.
projectDescription:
zBase is a private payment rail for AI agents on Base. It lets an agent fund a Privacy Pool with USDC, withdraw to a fresh address using a zero-knowledge proof, and pay an x402 API seller without exposing the direct on-chain link between the agent’s original funding wallet and the seller.
zBase is proud to be a Base Batches 003 finalist, selected as one of 12 teams in Base’s Spring 2026 program. The cohort focuses on companies building across AI, DeFi, prediction markets, stablecoins, and agentic payments, with Demo Day held in San Francisco.
base
+1
For ETHOnline, we focused on two things: helping agents make honest privacy decisions and making paid API trials harder to farm.
howItsMade:
Technical implementation
The Graph subgraph
We built the zbase-pool-base subgraph with @graphprotocol/graph-cli 0.98 and AssemblyScript mappings. It uses minimal contract ABIs taken from the vendored 0xbow Privacy Pool contracts, with Base configured as the default network in networks.json.
We identified the correct Base mainnet deployment start block by binary-searching eth_getCode, rather than assuming a block number and risking missed historical events.
The subgraph is deployed on The Graph Subgraph Studio and synced to the current chain head:
h
We verified that the roots indexed by the subgraph match the values returned on-chain by currentRoot() and latestRoot().
pool-state decision tool
We built pool-state as both an MCP tool and a CLI command in run.ts.
It queries the subgraph directly using plain fetch and GraphQL, then passes the result into a pure decidePoolState() function with unit tests. Keeping the decision logic pure and tested makes the payment decision predictable, reviewable, and easy to reuse across agent environments.
Before a payment, pool-state checks for subgraph indexing errors through _meta, reads the current ASP root and leaf count, converts 256-bit root values safely using BigInt, and cross-checks the result with the facilitator.
If the subgraph is unavailable, missing, or returning indexing errors, the tool fails closed. The agent does not attempt a privacy payment when it cannot verify the pool state.
The tool is registered in our MCP server through @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and exposed through the run.ts CLI. SKILL.md documents when an AI agent should call it before making a payment.
World AgentKit integration
We integrated @worldcoin/agentkit 0.2.1 into the x402 seller built with @x402/express 2.11.
The integration uses registerExtension, onProtectedRequest, and createAgentBookVerifier to verify AgentBook-backed identities and enforce human-level free-call limits.
We added a file-persisted AgentKitStorage implementation that stores per-human trial counters and a capped nonce replay-protection window. The cap is important because an unbounded nonce store could be abused to exhaust storage or memory over time.
The stock AgentKit hook does not include a request ID, so we use AsyncLocalStorage to safely associate hook events with the correct incoming request.
The entire World integration is behind an AGENTKIT_ENABLED feature flag. When the flag is disabled, the seller remains byte-identical to the original payment-only implementation.
We added 15 node:test cases covering the key trial, verification, replay-protection, and payment paths. We also built a demo client with a fetch shim to handle the x402 interoperability issue where the payment challenge may be delivered in a response header rather than the response body.
Mainnet safeguards and RPC compatibility
The demo registry stub intentionally throws during startup on Base mainnet. This prevents development-only identity behavior from accidentally being enabled in production.
We also fixed the seller’s eth_getLogs behavior. The original implementation queried a 50,000-block range, but public Base RPC endpoints enforce a 2,000-block cap. The seller now scans logs in ranges compatible with public Base RPC limits.

name: Star Wallet
description: Kids earn USDC-backed Stars while parents save through 1inch Aqua, SwapVM and The Graph.
projectDescription:
Star Wallet helps families turn kids' completed tasks into onchain savings: parents award Stars backed by matching USDC deposits, then manage those savings through 1inch Aqua and SwapVM.
The child sees Stars, quests and goals. A device passkey can sign only those actions; it cannot transfer tokens, withdraw savings, trade assets or call arbitrary contracts. The parent uses a normal Ethereum wallet and retains control over USDC, WETH, savings positions and financial approvals.
When a parent awards five Stars, the same transaction contributes five USDC to the family vault and issues five STAR to the child. If the USDC transfer fails, the STAR issuance also fails.
STAR is a zero-decimal, non-transferable reward token. It is not a stablecoin, a claim on one USDC or a share of the vault. After issuance, the reward and savings ledgers are independent. A child can spend Stars while the original savings remain invested, change in value or are withdrawn by the parent.
Parents can keep the contributed USDC in the family vault or combine it with WETH in a programmable savings position powered by 1inch Aqua and SwapVM. Aqua tracks the position's balances, SwapVM handles exchanges between USDC and WETH, and the vault applies Chainlink-based price and safety checks before any position is opened or changed.
The Graph turns the protocol's Sepolia events into the family data shown throughout Star Wallet, including children, Star balances, quests, goals, requests, savings positions and activity history. Live blockchain reads are still used whenever current balances, permissions or transaction status must be confirmed.
howItsMade:
Star Wallet runs on Ethereum Sepolia. Its Solidity contracts separate the system into family registration, child accounts, quests, goals, STAR accounting and one isolated savings vault per family. STAR is a zero-decimal, non-transferable ERC-20. Issuing a reward atomically deposits one USDC of principal into the family vault, so the deposit and reward either both succeed or both fail.
Parents sign financial actions with their Ethereum wallets and always retain custody. Children use WebAuthn P-256 passkeys through deterministic ERC-4337 smart accounts. Each child operation travels through Alchemy’s Bundler and Paymaster to EntryPoint v0.8. Gas sponsorship gives children a wallet-free experience, while the smart account’s onchain allowlist prevents transfers, withdrawals, arbitrary contract calls and other actions outside Star Wallet.
The savings system integrates 1inch Aqua’s virtual-balance accounting with SwapVM’s programmable execution. The family vault remains the maker and allocates its available USDC and WETH to a concentrated-liquidity strategy. We built an SDK-free viem encoder that reproduces canonical token ordering, maker traits, strategy hashes and SwapVM instruction bytes. Before accepting a position, the vault independently decodes and verifies the maker, token pair, fee, salt, deadline and program structure. Chainlink feeds enforce fresh prices, bounded ranges and maximum USDC/WETH exposure. Positions can be opened, topped up, replaced, safely closed, paused and recovered during emergencies.
The Graph is the system’s read layer. Custom AssemblyScript mappings index Star Registry, STAR, Goals, Quests, family-vault, Aqua and SwapVM events. Dynamic data-source templates start indexing each new family vault and quest contract as it is deployed. Aqua events can occur before the corresponding vault position event within the same transaction, so we queue and replay those events in log order using the maker and strategy hash as the position identity. Subgraph responses are pinned to the expected deployment and verified against Sepolia RPC block state.
ENSv2 provides commit-reveal family namespaces and permissioned child subdomains that resolve to each child’s deterministic smart account. The application is built with Next.js, TypeScript, wagmi and viem, with a Fastify service that verifies deployments, prepares transaction intents and Aqua strategies, validates live protocol state and constrains sponsored RPC requests. Together, these components keep parents in control of funds, limit children to safe family actions and provide responsive indexed data without replacing live onchain verification.

name: Strikeline
description: Name a price to sell your ETH at and get paid to wait. Covered calls on 1inch Aqua.
projectDescription:
Strikeline lets anyone holding ETH name a price they'd sell at, pick an expiry, and earn while they wait, without the ETH ever leaving their wallet. Each offer is a covered call written as a pricing curve on 1inch Aqua. With nothing locked, one wallet can back many offers: in the demo, a wallet holding 10.4 ETH backs offers for 15.4 ETH at once, and every trade checks the real balance so it can never owe more than it holds.
Example: ETH trades at $2,440 and you hold 10 ETH. You'd happily sell 5 of them at $2,600. In Strikeline you pick that price, an expiry one week out and a volatility, then publish the offer in one click. All 10 ETH stay in your wallet. The offer is a quote registered on 1inch Aqua that traders can fill.
Volatility (IV) is how much you expect ETH to move, as a yearly percentage, and it sets the shape of the curve. A higher IV prices each trade further from the market, so trades are rarer but earn more. A lower IV gives tighter pricing and more frequent, smaller trades. The app pre-fills it from how much ETH has actually moved recently.
While the offer is live, nobody pays more than the market price. If ETH moves on other exchanges by more than your offer's spread, 1inch resolvers trade with it. When ETH rises, the offer sells a little ETH. When it falls, the offer buys some back. The spread widens in both directions every day, so small wiggles don't trigger trades. Your result is the P&L of a covered call. It works like selling insurance: you come out ahead if ETH moves less than the volatility you chose, and behind if it moves more.
At expiry, if ETH is above $2,600, whatever remains of the 5 ETH sells at exactly $2,600. If ETH is below, nothing more sells and you keep your ETH.
One wallet, many offers: every trade checks your real wallet balance and your approval to Aqua. A fill on one offer immediately shrinks what the others can deliver, with no keeper, so you can post more offers than you could fill at once and never owe a trade you can't pay. There is no vault, no option token, no oracle and no settlement transaction. There is also a buy side: an offer to buy ETH below today's price with USDC. Every fill pays a 0.10% protocol fee.
The app shows each offer's fill progress and average sale price, how its spread widens over time, and its payoff at expiry compared with just holding. It also notifies you when an offer is filled or withdrawn. Withdrawing takes one click and moves no tokens.
Limits: you earn only when someone trades, and you end up behind holding when ETH moves more than you priced. I replayed a week of real Base ETH prices on a four-offer book of about $50k. It beat holding by $201. When the offers were written far below realised volatility (15% vs 46.6%), a plain 5 bp liquidity pool beat it.
What's next: a mainnet launch on Base with a real audit; more pairs beyond ETH/USDC (cbBTC, LSTs); ladders, where one click writes a spread of strikes and expiries from a single wallet; automatic rolling into the next expiry when an offer ends; and routing so Strikeline offers show up directly inside 1inch swaps for regular traders.
howItsMade:
Strikeline is built on 1inch Aqua and SwapVM. Every offer is a SwapVM program shipped to the official, unmodified Aqua registry (0x1111113CCf1426A8E30e2bfF5E005d929bF6a90a): Deadline, FeeProtocol, Coverage, RmmSwap, Salt. I chose Aqua because the liquidity stays in the maker's wallet and one balance can back many strategies at once. That lets one wallet quote a whole ladder of strikes and expiries. SwapVM doesn't ship an option curve or a check against the wallet's real balance, so I wrote both as custom instructions. Strikeline's offers fill through a redeployed StrikelineRouter that includes them.
RmmSwap (opcode 0x55) implements RMM-01 from Angeris, Evans & Chitra ("Replicating Market Makers", arXiv:2103.14769; "Replicating Monotonic Payoffs Without Oracles", arXiv:2111.13740): Y = L·K·Φ(Φ⁻¹(1 − X/L) − σ√τ). Time to expiry τ comes from block.timestamp, so the curve ages without any transaction. At τ = 0 it becomes a constant-sum order at the strike. The normal CDF and its inverse are fixed-point on Solady, with error around 5e-12.
Why it works: under arbitrage, reserves held on this curve track the value of long spot plus a short Black-Scholes call at strike K and volatility σ. Each trade by an arbitrageur moves the reserves toward the call's delta, so resolver fills perform the delta hedge. As τ shrinks, the curve's no-trade band widens on both sides. That band is how the curve collects the option's time decay (theta) from the traders who fill it. The maker ends up with covered-call P&L: ahead when realised volatility stays below σ, behind when it's above.
Coverage (opcode 0x93) wraps the curve. It prices the trade, then rejects any output larger than the maker's live balanceOf and their allowance to Aqua. Aqua allows a maker to allocate more than they hold, and this check turns that into safe portfolio margin across offers, enforced inside every trade. The 0.10% fee uses SwapVM's own FeeProtocol instruction and is taken from the taker's input, so the curve prices the net amount exactly. The router is 23,851 bytes, under the EIP-170 limit, and a fill costs about 211k gas. The contracts are Solidity 0.8.30 with Foundry.
The frontend is Next.js 16, React 19, wagmi and viem. It uses a TypeScript SwapVM encoder checked byte-for-byte against Solidity. The app has no option maths of its own: every quote and chart point is a call to the router. Positions, fill progress and average sale price come from Aqua's Shipped logs.
The demo runs on an anvil fork of Base mainnet, so it uses the real Aqua registry and the real WETH and USDC contracts. The fork runs on a small Google Cloud VM behind a JSON-RPC relay that forwards only safe methods. Anyone can publish, fill and withdraw offers with a built-in demo wallet and no funds.

name: Transvia
description: Cross-border payments for humans and AI agents — USDC in, local currency out, onchain in seconds.
projectDescription:
Transvia is a cross-border payments platform on Arc, Circle’s stablecoin L1 where USDC is the gas token. Anyone holding USDC can send value to 11 destination currencies — EUR, GBP, MXN, BRL, PHP, NGN, AED, SGD, CAD, AUD, and INR — at a flat 0.50% fee shown upfront, with no hidden spread.
Funds are locked in TransviaEscrow, an open-source, zero-dependency Solidity contract. Settlement executes three atomic onchain legs — FX, payout, and fee split — while recipients claim funds using a gasless EIP-712 signature from an embedded wallet created through email login with Privy. This removes seed phrases and gas-token friction from the receive flow.
The same payment rail is machine-native. Transvia exposes a REST API, TypeScript SDK, MCP server at /api/mcp with six tools for AI assistants such as Claude, and an x402 HTTP payment layer where software pays 0.01 USDC per quote using EIP-3009 signatures.
Automation agents monitor every transfer and record every decision. They purchase FX feeds through x402, apply compliance rules including holds above 5,000 USDC, and can trigger timeout refunds through the escrow contract’s agentFallback. The live system runs on Arc Testnet with real USDC, Neon Postgres persistence, and Vercel hosting. Every transfer has a complete, auditable trail including state transitions, agent decisions, and Arc explorer transaction hashes.
howItsMade:
Transvia uses hexagonal architecture: a framework-free core built from pure TypeScript domain logic, ports, and adapters, wired through a single composition root. The Next.js 16 application, REST routes, MCP server, and TypeScript SDK all call the same underlying services rather than maintaining separate implementations.
Arc’s USDC-as-gas model eliminates the need for users and agents to acquire a separate gas token. Privy handles identity and embedded wallets: email login creates the recipient wallet, which signs the EIP-712 claim. Sessions are automatically restored on page load, with a browser-local demo wallet fallback when Privy is unavailable so the receive flow remains usable.
Settlement is enforced by TransviaEscrow, an MIT-licensed, zero-dependency Solidity contract built without OpenZeppelin. We hand-rolled EIP-712 verification and a 20 Gwei gas floor. We also added AlreadySettled reconciliation after identifying and fixing a double-settlement race between concurrent state-machine advancers.
For x402, we implemented the verification layer ourselves: EIP-3009 TransferWithAuthorization signatures are recovered with viem, checked against the payer, and recorded in a payments ledger. We validated the implementation with an independent client and confirmed that tampered signatures are rejected.
A few deliberately hacky reliability features make the rail resilient: it self-heals the escrow’s maximum USDC allowance when approval drifts, while polling endpoints also advance in-flight transfers, effectively making GET requests part of the settlement state machine. This allows transfers to continue progressing without requiring a separate worker process.

name: Exit Drill
description: Turn treasury liquidity risk into bounded exits and independently verified settlement.
projectDescription:
A treasury balance is not a cash guarantee. A team holding WETH needs to know whether an exit can cover its cash commitments, control how that trade is executed, and prove what actually arrived.
Exit Drill connects those decisions in one product. Users sign in, open a managed Sepolia treasury, fund its displayed address, and choose WETH from their actual balance. Optional risk analysis uses fresh Ethereum liquidity evidence to compare exit routes under a user-selected price shock. A portable risk brief preserves the source block, inputs, cash coverage, route comparison and modeling assumptions.
When the user decides to trade, Exit Drill obtains a fresh Sepolia quote. The user reviews a bounded approval, minimum received and expiry before confirming. Proceeds return to the same treasury. After confirmation, a receipt reconciles settlement against token movements; anyone can independently verify the transaction, plan hash and output without signing in.
The same evidence and analysis engine is available through a reusable, read-only MCP server for external AI hosts. It compares scenarios against a single Graph snapshot and produces structured cash-coverage assessments, while leaving trade authorization to the human.
This release executes actual Sepolia transactions with custom test WETH/USDC and independent Uniswap v3 pools. The assets have no monetary value. Ethereum risk estimates and Sepolia execution quotes are clearly separated. The liquidity model infers full-range pools from live TVL and price.
howItsMade:
Exit Drill uses Next.js, React, TypeScript and viem, with Solidity execution guards and a responsive treasury interface.
The Graph adapter queries Ethereum Uniswap v3 WETH/USDC pools at 0.05% and 0.30% fees, reads liquidity and recent history, and rejects stale data or indexing errors. When a subgraph omits a timestamp, the adapter verifies the exact Ethereum block through RPC. The analysis engine deploys official Uniswap v3 bytecode to ephemeral Ganache chains, calibrates full-range liquidity from that evidence, applies the selected shock, and compares both routes using snapshots and reverts. This is a model, not a mainnet fork.
A standalone MCP server exposes fresh evidence, treasury exit assessments and same-snapshot shock comparisons. It reuses the engine directly rather than calling the website, needs no Privy account, and exposes no signing tools. An external AI host supplies the language model.
Privy verifies access tokens and maps each authenticated account to a managed treasury. Attached signing policies restrict Sepolia, contract addresses and methods. Each backend action verifies treasury ownership. The Solidity executor fixes the router and tokens and enforces the recipient, amount cap, fee allowlist, minimum output, expiry, nonce and reentrancy protection. Router approval is cleared after settlement. Wallets are app-managed rather than self-custodial.
The public verifier reconstructs the plan hash from calldata, checks the executor and treasury, and reconciles USDC transfer logs against the settlement event. A recorded browser exit of 0.01 test WETH settled for 24.984094 test USDC on Sepolia. Unit tests, actual-EVM rejection tests, MCP protocol and stdio checks, and the production build pass in CI.

name: TrustLine
description: TrustLine lets AI agents privately verify solvency and automatically settle deals onchain.
projectDescription: TrustLine is a trust and payment layer for autonomous AI agents. Before an agent pays for a deal, TrustLine privately verifies whether the agent can cover the required amount without revealing its wallet balance. Chainlink CRE handles the confidential solvency logic, while Privy provides a policy-controlled wallet for automated settlement. Bazantic makes the capability discoverable and callable by other agents through an x402-enabled service. If the private check returns SETTLE, the approved wallet can release the exact deal amount to the counterparty; if it returns INSUFFICIENT, payment is blocked. Our MVP demonstrates the complete orchestration on Base Sepolia, with the confidential CRE computation currently simulated locally due to CRE access constraints.
howItsMade: TrustLine combines Bazantic, Chainlink CRE, Privy, and Base Sepolia into one agent-to-agent payment flow. An AI agent calls TrustLine through the Bazantic/x402 interface with a deal amount and reference ID. The backend passes the request to our solvency-check workflow, which determines whether the wallet can cover the deal without exposing its actual balance. A SETTLE result triggers the Privy policy-controlled wallet to authorize the payment, while INSUFFICIENT stops the flow. We use BigInt-based amount handling and reference IDs to prevent rounding errors and duplicate payments. The MVP uses a local simulation of the Chainlink confidential execution environment, while the wallet settlement path is designed for real Base Sepolia transactions.

name: x402-validate
description: Add validation layer to x402, so ai agent don't pay for low effort response
projectDescription:
What this project is
x402_validate is a Chainlink CRE (https://docs.chain.link/cre) (Chainlink Runtime Environment) workflow that acts as a confidential, trust-minimized validation oracle for API responses. A caller asks: "call this API and check whether its response satisfies my
private criteria" — and the workflow executes that check inside a hardware enclave so that neither Chainlink's node operators, nor network observers, nor other callers can see what's being validated or how.
The core flow (main.ts)

Trigger: anyone can fire the public HTTP trigger with a payload of { api: { url, requestType, body }, validationFunction } — an API to call plus an arbitrary JavaScript snippet that must return a boolean verdict on the response.
TEE execution: the handler is registered with handlerInTee, so all logic runs inside an AWS Nitro enclave (Confidential Workflows, private beta), not on regular DON nodes.
Authenticated API call: before calling the target API, the workflow fetches an ed25519 private key (API_SIGNING_KEY) from the Vault DON — released only into attested enclaves — and signs {timestamp, body}. The API verifies this signature against the workflow's
published public key, which proves the request genuinely came from this workflow, inside a TEE (the Vault DON's release policy stands in for raw attestation, since CRE doesn't expose enclave attestation documents to workflow code).
Validation: the caller's validationFunction is eval'd against the response (delivered base64-encoded, since the runtime lacks atob and text() mangles binary) and must return a boolean.
Result: the verdict is returned as the workflow result — note HTTP triggers are fire-and-forget, so callers get results via callback, not the trigger response.

The demo application: color-gated image API
mock-api.js is a stand-in protected API that serves one of two paint images at random (paint_high_small.png / paint_low_small.png), only to requests bearing a valid, fresh enclave signature (401/400 otherwise). The showcase validationFunction (in
payload-color-validation.json) is a self-contained ~35KB PNG decoder: it base64-decodes the response, inflates IDAT chunks with an embedded copy of fflate, reverses PNG scanline filters, computes mean HSV saturation, and accepts only if it's above 0.44 — the
high-color image (0.484) passes, the low-color one (0.402) is rejected. The point: a proprietary, non-trivial algorithm can run as caller-supplied data, invisible to everyone but the enclave.
What the experiments established
• Payloads can be encrypted client-side to a workflow x25519 public key (ECIES: ephemeral ECDH → HKDF → AES-GCM), decrypted only in-enclave via a Vault-DON-held private key (main-tee.ts) — including the validation function itself, keeping it private even from other
callers.
• CRE limitations found empirically: no CSPRNG in the WASM sandbox, no workflow-writable secrets (so no ZK-ceremony-style TEE-born persistent keys), no attestation API, 250KB HTTP response cap, and eval scope leaks that required AsyncFunction isolation.
howItsMade: It uses chainlink CRE to run inside secure TEE to validate the api with validation function, nothing is reveal to either parties. The core is a TypeScript CRE workflow whose HTTP trigger handler is registered with handlerInTee, so the entire callback executes inside an AWS Nitro enclave rather than on Workflow DON nodes; callers POST a JSON payload naming an API (url, method, base64 body) plus a validationFunction string containing arbitrary JavaScript that must return a boolean verdict on the response. Before calling the API, the enclave fetches an ed25519 private key from the Chainlink Vault DON, which threshold-encrypts secrets and releases them only to attested enclaves, then signs the request body and timestamp so the receiving API can verify against the workflow's published public key that the call genuinely originated from this workflow inside a TEE. Because CRE never returns trigger responses synchronously, the workflow calls the API itself and the verdict flows back through the workflow result. The demo API is a small Node server that serves one of two paint images at random only to validly signed requests, and the showcase validation function is a self-contained 35KB string that base64-decodes the image response, inflates PNG

name: BasePetition
description: Create and sign transparent, on-chain petitions on Base with IPFS-powered metadata.
projectDescription: BasePetition is an on-chain petition platform built on Base that helps communities turn public concerns into transparent, verifiable action. Anyone can create a petition with a title, description, image, signature goal, and deadline. Petition metadata and images are stored through IPFS, while petition creation and every signature are recorded on Base through a smart contract. Visitors can browse petitions, review their progress, connect a wallet, and sign without relying on a centralized database. Creators can manage their petitions and track activity from a personal dashboard, while anyone can inspect petition details and signer addresses directly on-chain. The platform also includes petition lifecycle management, deadlines, creator controls, and basic moderation visibility for safer public participation.
howItsMade: BasePetition is built with Next.js 16 App Router, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. The frontend uses Wagmi and Viem for wallet connection, contract reads, transaction submission, chain selection, and receipt tracking, with TanStack Query handling caching and reactive updates. The application runs on Base and interacts with a Solidity 0.8.20 smart contract that manages petition creation, deadlines, lifecycle status, signature uniqueness, signer records, creator dashboards, pagination, and owner moderation controls. Petition text and images are uploaded through a Next.js API route to Pinata/IPFS, with the resulting metadata URL stored alongside the petition on-chain. The blockchain remains the source of truth, while the UI reconstructs progress and status from contract reads and events. We also use ERC-8021 transaction attribution through ox so submitted transactions can be identified as coming from the application. This combination keeps the interface responsive while preserving publicly verifiable petition data.
