name: agent-snapshot
description: Archive and verify off-chain files belonging to ERC-8004 trustless agents.
projectDescription:
ERC-8004 agents publish an off-chain agent-card.json file that on-chain records only reference by URI — so its contents can be silently swapped without leaving any on-chain trace. This site lets anyone browse the crawl history of any registered agent and verify, entirely in-browser, that a given snapshot is authentic and untampered.
For each agent, it shows a timeline of past crawls with drift flagged whenever content changed, and a "no change" state proven whenever it didn't. Clicking any entry runs a full independent verification: it fetches the record's Merkle path and reads the on-chain transaction log directly by RPC (so the indexing subgraph itself is never trusted), reconstructs the Merkle root to confirm the record's inclusion in that batch, checks the TLSNotary proof against its on-chain hash, and finally verifies the proof against the notary's public key to confirm the server genuinely returned that content. All of this runs client-side in WebAssembly — the only party trusted is the TLSNotary notary.
The site also surfaces a direct comparison against Agent0, the standard ERC-8004 subgraph: an agent can look completely normal there while its actual off-chain content has already been swapped, making the blind spot this system closes immediately visible. Where a snapshot is available, the site fetches the real agent-card.json from IPFS/Arweave to show exactly which fields changed and how — the indexing layer itself only ever compares hashes, never raw content.
howItsMade:
This project uses TLSN (ZKTLS library in rust), IPFS, and The Graph fousing on verifiability and decentralized infrastructure. This project also uses Cloudflare and AWS S3 for high availability. https://agent-snapshot.kryor.studio are static, and built using snapshots and hosted on cloudflare. It updates when crawl happens.
The most difficult thing I encounter is the choice of primitives. It actually uses Incremental Merkle Tree (IMT) for storing snapshots (tree of hases) and keccak256, but the existing library in rust uses poseidon as a hash. So I implemented minimal IMT from scratch in rust.
The second problem is discovery and verifiability at scale - The Graph solved both. ERC-8004 has ~500k agents across five chains. Finding which ones have a registration file would have meant scanning the Identity Registry from its deployment block per chain and resolving tokenURI per token. The Agent0 Subgraph already indexes all five against one shared schema, so it collapsed into one GraphQL query — zero lines of discovery logic, multi-chain for free.
Verification was the harder half. Serving Merkle paths from my own API would have made the trust argument circular. With a subgraph, anyone can pull the path, reconstruct the root, and compare it to the on-chain batchRoot read straight from RPC.

name: AgentPermit Delta
description: AI proposes, you approve: delta-neutral Uniswap V3 LP hedged on Hyperliquid, with ENSv2 identity.
projectDescription:
AgentPermit Delta turns a natural-language goal into a bounded, human-approved WETH/USDC strategy. Nothing is ever signed by a model.
You describe what you want. The server then makes three real reads before it will answer. The Uniswap V3 Ethereum subgraph on The Graph returns the 0.05% and 0.3% USDC/WETH pools with exactly seven complete UTC days of TVL, volume, fees and prices, plus the indexed block. Hyperliquid mainnet returns ETH mark price, funding, open interest and order-book depth at plus or minus half a percent. OpenAI then compares the two fee tiers under a strict JSON schema and returns a pick-a-tier, open-or-wait recommendation where every stated reason must cite a metric ID that was actually supplied, with both pools represented. Missing, incomplete or stale data fails the proposal. There is no fabricated fallback. The full GraphQL query, raw inputs, model request and model response are written atomically to a local evidence file with no API keys in it.
The model advises. It never sizes or sends anything. Deterministic code fixes the test limits: 500 USDC total, 300 for the LP, up to 200 of perp reserve, a range of plus or minus twenty percent, isolated 1x leverage. A proposal older than five minutes cannot be approved, so historical evidence cannot be replayed as a current decision.
On approval the executor mints a real Uniswap V3 position against the official Ethereum contracts on a pinned Anvil mainnet fork, resolving the pool through the factory and rechecking both tokens and the fee before minting. It reads the confirmed on-chain LP amounts, then opens a matching ETH short on Hyperliquid testnet with deterministic client order IDs. A ten-second monitor recomputes LP WETH plus free WETH plus pending fees plus perp ETH, and only re-hedges when residual exposure passes twelve dollars. It closes after sixty seconds outside range or when liquidation sits within ten percent of mark.
The interesting part is what happens when things go wrong. Every external intent is persisted before it is sent. A timeout leaves that intent "unknown", and on restart the process looks the order up by its deterministic client order ID and requires a fresh account read before it touches anything. Unknown outcomes block replacement orders instead of double-sending. If initial coverage fails three times, it unwinds both legs. Closing demands the perp position reach exactly zero; residual exposure is not written off as dust.
ENSv2 on Sepolia gives the service a discoverable identity. The owner delegates only the endpoint record to an operator key and keeps payout and protected records, and a wallet-free client resolves the endpoint independently.
This is test funds on a fork, a testnet and Sepolia. Delta neutrality is not a profit promise: funding, basis, range, liquidation and execution risk all remain.
howItsMade:
The whole thing is one TypeScript repo with no build-time framework beyond Vite: a Node 24 server that runs .ts files natively via type stripping, a React 19 client, and viem instead of ethers for every chain call. 33 deterministic Node tests, strict TypeScript and a production build all run under one command.
The Graph leg queries the documented Uniswap V3 Ethereum subgraph on The Graph Network with a server-side API key, pulling two pools plus their poolDayDatas and validating that seven consecutive complete UTC days came back, that the token identities match the real USDC and WETH addresses, and that the subgraph's indexed block is recent. That validation is the point: the AI never sees data the code has not already vouched for, so the model's citations can be checked against the supplied metric IDs after the fact.
OpenAI Responses with gpt-5-nano runs under a strict structured-output schema. The schema forces the model to reference metric IDs from the payload and to cover both fee tiers, and the server rejects the response if a citation does not resolve. The model returns a fee tier and an open/wait call, and that is all it is allowed to influence.
Uniswap execution uses the official V3 SDK for tick math and mint calldata, driving the real NonfungiblePositionManager, SwapRouter and factory on an Anvil fork pinned to mainnet block 25965916. Funding happens by impersonating a USDC whale inside Anvil only. A separate disposable-fork script proves the full lifecycle end to end for both fee tiers: mint, read, remove, collect, burn the NFT, sell the WETH, and assert zero WETH residue.
Hyperliquid uses the nktkas client. Sizes and price precision are discovered from exchange metadata rather than hardcoded, orders go out IOC with deterministic client order IDs, and mainnet is used read-only for analysis while only testnet ever receives an order. The client order ID is the whole recovery story: it is what lets a restarted process ask "did my order land?" without ever guessing.
ENSv2 on Sepolia uses the permissioned resolver so an operator key can write exactly one record, agentpermit.endpoint, and nothing else. The client resolves that endpoint with no wallet at all.
Two hacky bits worth naming. First, persistence is temp file, fsync, rename, directory fsync, so a kill -9 mid-mint cannot produce a half-written ledger. Second, there is a deliberate chaos mode: two env vars make the first hedge order request only 80 percent of the needed size and then throw away a known-good response to simulate a network timeout, which is how the recovery path gets demonstrated live instead of merely claimed. Keys never reach the browser bundle; the client gets an ephemeral session token minted at server startup and writes additionally require a loopback Host and an allowed Origin.

name: Bank Rock
description: A NFC Connected Physical rocks that contains a self-custodial DEFI liquidity
projectDescription:
Bank Rock is a rock with an NFC chip in it. It is the physical interface for a fun, rule-breaking, self-custodial and very giftable DeFi liquidity account. We built it with normal people in mind: someone who has never touched crypto can be onboarded for the first time through this rock. The MCP server helps a lot here. A newcomer can chat with their rock through their favourite AI agent and just ask it stuff (what do I own, what has it earned, who had it before me) and get answers from live chain state, in plain language.
Tap the rock with a phone and its page opens. Anyone can see what the rock holds, which liquidity streams it runs, what it has earned in fees and who has owned it. Sign in with an email code or a passkey through Privy and you get an embedded wallet with no seed phrase. If you are the owner you can fund the rock, start it earning, stop it, or give it away.
Each rock has its own onchain account: a Safe smart account controlled by the owner's Privy wallet. The rock's tokens stay in that account the whole time. Through 1inch Aqua the rock acts as a market maker. It "ships" virtual USDC/WETH balances to one or more constant-product strategies without depositing anything into a pool. Visitors can trade against the rock, and the trading fee stays inside the rock's own reserve. Several streams with different fee levels (Wide 30 bps, Tight 5 bps, Patient 100 bps) can share one reserve, and the UI shows actual, virtual and executable balances separately and never adds them up.
The gift is the core flow. A giver names a recipient and signs once. The recipient taps the rock, signs in on a brand-new account with zero ETH, and claims it. The registry moves ownership and the rock's smart account changes hands with everything in it: balances, live strategies and history. Every operation is gas-sponsored, so nobody ever needs to hold ETH. A rock can be retired and the same chip can awaken a fresh rock into the same funded account.
The NFC tag is an NTAG 424 DNA chip that signs a fresh URL on every tap (this is the magic rock hardware at work!). The server verifies that signature and a strictly increasing read counter before it will attest to a physical tap, so a copied URL proves nothing: paste it into a second browser and the badge reads "unverified". The tag identifies the object. It never holds a key and never authorises a payment. Financial ownership is always the Privy-controlled smart account.
Bank Rock also exposes a read-only MCP server, so an AI agent such as Claude can be asked "what does this rock hold, who owns it and what has it earned?" and answer from live chain state. It never invents a number, and it never moves money: it reads, the owner signs. Super friendly for a newcomer, and safe by construction.
Everything runs on Ethereum Sepolia with Circle USDC and WETH, and the whole story (awaken, ship, visitor swap, gift and claim, archive and re-awaken) has been executed end to end on chain. We show no APY and promise no yield.
howItsMade:
FRONTEND. Next.js 16 (Turbopack) on React 19, Tailwind 4, shadcn/base-ui, framer-motion, and react-three-fiber for the 3D rock on the landing page. Wallets through Privy (@privy-io/react-auth) with wagmi and viem. It is an installable PWA. Deployed as a Cloudflare Worker through OpenNext, with Cloudflare D1 (Drizzle) holding the tap counter store, telemetry and presentation data. GitHub Actions deploys on push to main and applies D1 migrations before publishing the Worker.
CONTRACTS. Hardhat 3, Solidity 0.8, OpenZeppelin 5, unit and fuzz tests, verified on Sepolia Etherscan. BankRockRegistry (Ownable2Step, Pausable, EIP-712) is identity and lifecycle only: it holds no tokens, takes no approvals and has no function that can move money. awakenRock and claimHandover are authorised by an EIP-712 attestation signed by the server that verified the tap, not by msg.sender, so both can be relayed for a user with no ETH. Replay protection is on chain: the tag's read counter must strictly exceed the last one the registry accepted.
1INCH AQUA. We deployed the reference XYCSwap constant-product AquaApp, vendored unmodified, against the canonical Aqua on Sepolia. The Rock Account is the maker: it approves Aqua once and ships virtual balances, and tokens never leave its wallet. The strategy salt is keccak256(domain, rockId, streamIndex), so a rock's streams are addressable from public data alone: recompute the hash for streamIndex 0, 1, 2 and call safeBalances. A revert means "not shipped". No indexer, no database. XYCSwap settles by calling back into its caller, which must answer with Aqua.push, so an EOA or a plain Safe cannot swap against it at all. We wrote XYCSwapTaker, a stateless periphery that pulls the input, calls the app and fulfils the callback, and the visitor's swap is one sponsored approve + swapExactIn batch from their own Safe. Aqua has no fee accumulator, so realised fees are summed from Pushed events, none of which are indexed, so it is a log scan and decode.
PRIVY + ACCOUNT ABSTRACTION. Each Rock Account is a counterfactual Safe 1.4.1 on EntryPoint 0.7 built with permissionless.js, owned by the user's Privy embedded wallet, with saltNonce = keccak256(tag UID). The account follows the tag and the owner, not the rock id, so retiring a rock and tapping again awakens a new id into the same funded account. Pimlico's verifying paymaster sponsors every UserOperation. Approvals and ship go into one atomic executeBatch, and embedded-wallet signing is silent (showWalletUIs: false): the app's own button, which states the exact on-chain effect, is the confirmation. Only receipt.success counts as landed, because ERC-4337 hands back a perfectly good tx hash for an included-but-reverted operation.
GIFTING. The giver's single signature both opens the handover on the registry and pre-signs a Safe.swapOwner UserOperation that the recipient could never produce themselves. On claim our relayer lands the owner swap first (carrying initCode, so the Safe deploys as a side effect), then the registry asks the account isOwner before rebinding it, so a gift never leaves the giver's Safe recorded against a rock they no longer own. Relayer spend is capped per UTC day in D1 and unset means off.
NFC. NTAG 424 DNA with Secure Dynamic Messaging. The verifier is our own implementation from NXP's application notes AN12196 and AN10922: AES-CBC PICCData decryption, SV2 session-key derivation, RFC 4493 AES-CMAC and a 3-byte little-endian counter, tested against NXP's published worked example. The counter is monotonic in D1, so a copied URL reads "unverified" in a second browser and no client code path can paint the "Verified Physical" badge.
MCP. A TypeScript server on @modelcontextprotocol/sdk that reads the registry and Aqua over RPC with viem, plus the same fee route the rock page uses. Every tool returns live data or {status: "unavailable", reason}. It never invents a value.
HACKY BITS. (1) "Balance and ship": most people fund a rock with USDC only and a constant-product stream needs two tokens, so Bank Rock ships its own house USDC/WETH stream on the same app, and the ship UserOperation swaps half of the deposit against it through our own taker periphery before shipping. Five calls, one tap, atomic. (2) A demo-only "magic tap" route forges a genuine SDM pair for a synthetic tag with the real master key, so the whole production verify path could be rehearsed on the live site before physical chips were programmed. (3) A rehearsal script ran the entire demo on Sepolia (awaken, ship, visitor swap, named gift and relayed claim, archive and re-awaken) and committed every hash. (4) Honesty is enforced by CI: a grep fails the build if "APY" appears in any component, and a drift check compares the committed contract addresses against the deploy records. Every value on screen is REAL, UNAVAILABLE or badged SIMULATED, and no catch block invents a number.

name: Alt Agent
description: Pay-per-inference AI on Hedera. x402 micropayments auto-routed to the cheapest capable model.
projectDescription: An agentic AI gateway on Hedera where every inference call is paid per request via the x402 protocol — no subscriptions, no prepaid balances. A prompt classifier automatically routes each request to the cheapest model capable of handling it, and every paid call is settled through Blocky402 and logged to Hedera Consensus Service for a verifiable on-chain audit trail. One endpoint replaces a stack of separate AI subscriptions, and the agent proves what it paid for.
howItsMade:
The project is built on top of Hedera's x402-inference-pay-per-request-poc starter, extended with a custom broker overlay that adds intelligent model routing and on-chain auditing.
The core is split into two packages. packages/router holds a prompt classifier, an offering catalogue (each model tagged with capability and cost-per-call), and selection logic that picks the cheapest model capable of handling a given prompt — so a trivial query never gets billed at frontier-model prices. This is what turns a plain gateway into an actual router. It ships with unit tests, including a word-boundary regex fix that was killing us early on: the classifier was matching substrings inside unrelated words and misrouting requests, so we tightened the matching to whole-word boundaries.
Payments run through the x402 protocol on Hedera testnet, with Blocky402 as the facilitator (X402_TESTNET_FACILITATOR_URL=https://api.testnet.blocky402.com). The flow is genuinely pay-per-request: a call only settles once the request completes, and the gateway won't forward the inference until payment confirms. The model itself is served locally through LM Studio sitting behind the x402 gate, which let us test the full paid loop against a real open model without external API keys.
Every settled call is logged to Hedera Consensus Service via packages/audit — an HCS logger plus a topic-creation script — giving each transaction a tamper-evident, verifiable on-chain receipt rather than a claim in a database.
On the hacky side: because the starter repo wasn't designed to be extended, we kept our overlay as isolated packages and wired them into the agent with three surgical edits documented in INTEGRATION.md, which kept the reused-vs-new boundary clean for attribution and let us iterate on the router without touching the upstream PoC.

name: Mandi
description: Humans set the rules. Agents spend the money — ENS discovery, policy checks, x402 on Hedera.
projectDescription:
Mandi is a procurement layer for autonomous agents. A human signs a spending policy with their own wallet. An agent discovers competing suppliers by name, but it cannot pay. A separate executor — the only module that holds the payment key — re-derives every fact from chain state and either signs an x402 payment on Hedera or refuses with reasons. Both outcomes are public.
Sellers connect their wallet, sign a registration, and get <label>.mandi.eth minted to their wallet on the ENSv2 Sepolia. Price, capability and the x402 endpoint live in the resolver. A Selfie Check in World App, bound to that same wallet, is the only accreditation a policy will accept.
Buyers sign the policy, deposit HBAR from their wallet over Hedera’s JSON-RPC relay, and run a task like “Assess risk of Aave.” The agent ranks suppliers on attestation, then reliability from settled receipts, then price. The executor resolves the name again, checks price, remaining budget, the deposit ledger, success rate, and the verifier-signed attestation, then pays per call through Blocky402. Failures cancel (x402 v2 authorization flow) and the agent falls back. Nothing eligible means nothing paid.
Live console: https://mandi.up.railway.app/
Seller + Selfie Check: https://mandi.up.railway.app/seller
HCS audit trail: https://hashscan.io/testnet/topic/0.0.10454931
ENS Names: https://app.ens.dev/mandi.eth
howItsMade:
One Hono process (server/) and one Vite + React app (web/). No database, no queue.
ENS. server/src/ens.ts talks to the live ENSv2 Sepolia contracts with viem. A UserRegistry subregistry under mandi.eth, a PermissionedResolver, and seller-owned names. Records: ENSIP-26 agent-context and agent-endpoint[x402], plus custom mandi:capability, mandi:price, mandi:chain, mandi:verified, mandi:upstream. The executor re-resolves at decision time. Prices are never hard-coded.
Hedera / x402. @x402/hono gates every supplier route with a per-route HBAR price. @x402/fetch + @x402/hedera sign the transfer only after policy checks, settled through Blocky402 (exact, HBAR 0.0.0). Buyers fund the executor from MetaMask on chain 296. server/src/buyer/funding.ts nets mirror-node deposits against anchored spend. POLICY_ACTIVATED, DECISION, and RECEIPT go on one HCS topic via @hiero-ledger/sdk and join on the transaction id. Reliability is computed from those receipts only. Agent identity is the ENS name, not HCS-14. executor.ts is the only file that reads BUYER_KEY.
World App, selfieCheckLegacy, signal = seller wallet. The server signs RP context, verifies on the v4 endpoint, binds a 90-day attestation to the ENS name, and enforces one accreditation per human via a hashed nullifier. requireVerifiedFor reads the attestation, not the ENS flag.
The Graph. Messari subgraphs (aave-v3-ethereum, compound-v3-ethereum, morpho-aave-v3-ethereum, lido-ethereum) feed the paid risk endpoints. risk-pro does more queries per call than risk-basic — extra work, not a claim of being more correct.

name: usufruct
description: Sell a fixed window of your Uniswap fees upfront. Keep the position, get the same NFT back.
projectDescription:
Three things are deliberately decoupled, and that's the core of the design. Capture happens after the end block, so it collects more than the sold period; the contract reserves the actual USDC received rather than trusting any projection. The residual owner can retrieve the NFT before allocation is resolved at all — that withdrawal cannot touch the protected fee reserve. And settlement is authenticated against historical chain state, with allocation bounded by what was captured. Holders then redeem independently, so one recipient failing cannot block anyone else. Payouts use the immutable original claim count, never the remaining token supply, so somebody else redeeming never changes your fraction.
This ran end to end in public. Series 1 on Sepolia: position NFT 39216 activated at block 11696226, end block N at 11696317, 10,000 claims issued against a 0.25 USDC upfront payment for 2,500 of them. A teammate bought 1,000 claims across three real Aqua trades. Capture collected 1.499999 USDC. The NFT returned at 11696393 while allocation was still unresolved. Allocation at 11696450 separated 0.999999 USDC earned by N from 0.500000 USDC earned after it. 9,010 claims have since been redeemed for 0.900996 USDC across four independent holders.
Every figure shown before allocation is an estimate. Estimates never authorise a payout.
howItsMade:
Contracts are Solidity built with Foundry 1.5.1 (Cancun) and run through Slither. Four first-party contracts: FeeStrip.sol escrows the canonical Uniswap v4 NFT for a fixed window, FeeClaim.sol issues the transferable claims against that window's unpaid native USDC fee income, and market/FeeStripMarket.sol with market/FeeStripRouter.sol provide the claim/USDC market. Coverage is 20 protocol tests plus two invariant campaigns totalling 16,384 calls with zero unexpected reverts, with separate proof and market suites on top.
Uniswap v4 is the substrate rather than a dependency. We work against canonical position NFTs with a native v4 lifecycle, freezing the fixed range for the window. Series 1 ran the complete lifecycle in public on Sepolia against NFT 39216: activation at 11696226, end block N at 11696317, capture, NFT return at 11696393 before allocation resolved, then allocation at 11696450 costing 4,396,570 gas. Settlement authenticates the historical block header, position manager account and pool storage, and an independent native-endpoint oracle on an isolated fork produces 999999 USDC micros matching the authenticated witness.
The claim market runs on official source-pinned Aqua and SwapVM sources from 1inch, extended with a custom two-instruction dispatcher so a fee claim is a first-class position inside Aqua rather than a token bolted on beside it. That's the hackiest and most useful thing we did. In series 1 a teammate bought 1,000 claims across three real public trades of 189, 63 and 748 — genuine FeeClaim and USDC transfers on Sepolia, not a fork. Tests cover both directions, unavailable and shared maker capital, stale lifecycle state, and adversarial callback ordering. That teammate's redemption of 1,000 claims for 0.099999 USDC cost 122,011 gas.
Buyer analytics compose two Graph products. Hosted Substreams joins Subgraph Studio series 1 instrument state at finalized block 11696247, with 22 of 22 observed blocks covered and in range, at zero indexing lag relative to finalized history. packages/data/src/compose.mjs does the join with identity, common-block and hash checks, packages/data/src/store.mjs handles cursor persistence and reorg recovery, and packages/core/src/economics.mjs computes range occupancy and break-even. The snapshot is partial-period and carries no exact-fee or forecast authority. Analytics inform buyers; they never authorise settlement.
The repo is a pnpm 12 workspace on Node 24. The web app in apps/web deploys to Vercel; an operations service runs from Dockerfile.operations on Railway with an api/ surface. The complete browser lifecycle — sale, trade, capture, return, settlement, redemption — runs end to end against a real local chain and reproduces in hosted CI via pnpm test:browser:chain.
Endpoint durability is handled by a dedicated keeper that saved N at N+2. Exact proof was then restored from two remote GETs into a fresh local database and two authenticated copies, with zero remote writes, no RPC witness fallback and no hosted failover. An operations service runs from Dockerfile.operations on Railway; the web app deploys to Vercel; the repo is a pnpm 12 workspace on Node 24.

name: Cadence
description: Cadence makes liquidity scarce, time-bound, and tradable through ERC-1155 slots.
projectDescription: Cadence makes market depth a scarce, priced, time-boxed resource — sold as ERC-1155 slots. A Uniswap v4 hook splits reserves each epoch: 25% active, 75% locked. beforeSwap gates every trade — hold a slot, burn your notional, fill active-only. No slot, no fill; unused slots expire worthless. Includes commit-reveal private intents (size hidden until fill), a slot CLOB, a multi-pool router, a live The Graph index, and a paid Hedera x402 intel call that writes the ask on-chain. LPs earn 90% of slot sales. Live on Sepolia, end-to-end verified.
howItsMade: Solidity v4 hook + ERC-1155 slots, Foundry-tested, deployed via CREATE2 with versioned salts. Next.js + TypeScript frontend with viem and a custom EIP-1193 wallet layer — one reducer mirrors live chain truth, with simulate-first writes that surface decoded reverts before the wallet opens. The v4 hook is the product: beforeSwap enforces slot ≥ size, burns notional, fills active-only. The Graph Studio indexes every event (commit→reveal included); one real Hedera x402 micropayment buys the capacity/toxicity quote that writes the slot price. Notable hackiness: hook address mined to fit v4 permission flags, and a full-audit pass that caught a reducer never receiving the wallet address — silently no-op'ing every UI write.

name: Squash
description: One QR splits any bill. Everyone confirms, then one Hedera transaction settles it all.
projectDescription: Squash is a bill-splitting app where nobody pays until everyone says yes. One person pays the tab, creates a bill in pesos or dollars, and shares a QR code. Guests scan it, join with just their name, and see their exact share update live. Each person signs in with their email through Privy, which creates a real Hedera wallet in the background — no seed phrase, no crypto knowledge required. When the organizer asks for confirmation, every share is frozen and converted to dollars at that day's exact exchange rate, so everyone agrees on the same number. Each guest then taps "Yes, I pay," sending the amount from their own wallet. Nothing moves until the very last person confirms — then every transfer executes together, in one shot, and everyone lands at zero at the same time. The same engine that computes a single bill also solves a whole shared trip: given 15 crossed debts between 6 people built up over several days, it finds the provably minimum number of transfers to settle everyone — 3 transfers, an 80% reduction — instead of naively running every individual debt one by one.
howItsMade:
Squash is a Next.js app on Hedera testnet. The settlement engine is a greedy net-settlement algorithm (net each participant's balance, then repeatedly match the largest creditor with the largest debtor) that finds the minimum number of transfers to zero out a group's debts — for our 6-person, 15-debt sample trip, that's 15 crossed debts collapsed to 3 transfers, an 80% reduction, computed live rather than hardcoded.
The engine isn't free to call: every settlement plan, including a single bill at the table, is bought over x402. The app receives a 402 Payment Required, pays the facilitator (Blocky402) in HBAR based on the size of the debt graph, and only then gets the plan. Every run's inputs and outputs are hashed and published to Hedera Consensus Service (HCS), so anyone can recompute the plan and verify we didn't fudge the numbers — that HashScan link ships right in the product, not just in a slide.
For money movement, we use a Hedera fungible token (tUSD, 1 unit = 1 cent) as the settlement currency; the same code path settles in USDC on mainnet. Privy handles identity and custody: signing in with an email creates a real Hedera account with a real balance, so every participant pays from their own wallet, not a shared pool the app controls — that was the trickiest part, since most bill-splitting demos fake this with a single custodial account.
We also built World ID verification for "no fake guests, no double seats" — it's fully implemented against World's SDK, but it's gated behind partner approval that hadn't come through by submission time, so it's present in the code and disabled in the live demo rather than pretending it works on camera.
The genuinely hacky bit: freezing the FX rate at the moment confirmation is requested (not at bill creation, and not at settlement) so that every participant is cryptographically agreeing to the same dollar figure, without needing an oracle contract on-chain — we treat the rate as an off-chain input that gets hashed into the plan alongside the debts.

name: PayeeLock
description: Recover unpaid invoice balances without rewriting completed onchain payments.
projectDescription:
PayeeLock is a recovery protocol for approved supplier payments. If a supplier's payout wallet becomes unsafe, a constrained guardian can pause the unpaid invoices, but it cannot move funds or choose a new recipient. The supplier proposes a replacement wallet and the buyer accepts the exact same invoice set onchain. Previously paid value stays final, only the unpaid balance moves, and every authorization signed before recovery becomes stale.
Anyone can use it today. Connect a wallet at payeelock-sentinel.vercel.app and the app deploys your own vault where your wallet is the buyer: register a supplier, prefund an invoice, pay it with a signed authorization, pause the supplier, and complete recovery. A separate review mode walks through a completed Sepolia case between Meridian Labs and Harbor Systems, where 2,400 MockUSDC was paid before the incident, 11,600 was settled after recovery, and an old queued payment reverted with zero tokens moved.
howItsMade: I built the PayeeLock vault in Solidity and tested it with Foundry, including replay, expiry, wrong-beneficiary, freeze, exact-invoice-set recovery, fee-on-transfer, partial-payment fuzz cases, and factory ownership isolation. EIP-712 payment signatures bind the beneficiary, supplier epoch, invoice nonce, amount, expiry, chain ID, and contract. A permissionless factory deployed on Sepolia creates a vault and its payout resolver in one transaction with the caller as buyer, so anyone can run their own workspace. ENSv2 on Sepolia is the supplier identity and authority layer: a Permissioned Resolver lets an invoice publisher edit invoice text but not the payout address. A Privy server wallet is the freeze-only guardian under a default-deny policy scoped to one chain, one PayeeLock deployment, and freeze(bytes32). The recovery monitor reads indexed history from a deployed Graph Subgraph, confirms current state through Sepolia RPC, and may request only that freeze call. The Graph also indexes payment, recovery, and ENS events for the case review. The frontend uses Next.js and viem, signs typed data in the browser, and is hosted on Vercel. The repository is a Turborepo with separate web, Foundry, and Subgraph workspaces plus isolated Anvil lifecycle tests.

name: LiquidPay
description: Liquid Pay keeps your positions working until the instant you need to pay.
projectDescription:
Liquid Pay provides just-in-time liquidity for everyday payments. Instead of keeping capital idle in stablecoins, users can remain exposed to assets they want to hold and liquidate only the amount required when a payment is made. Before paying, Liquid analyzes the connected wallet, considers the user’s liquidation preferences, identifies eligible positions, compares available exit routes, accounts for gas and slippage, and presents a controlled liquidation plan. Once approved, the required positions are converted into USDC and the recipient is paid.
This makes capital more efficient: users can preserve market exposure until liquidity is actually needed, while retaining control over which assets may be sold, how much may be liquidated, and where the payment goes.
howItsMade:
Liquid Pay is built with Next.js, TypeScript, React, Convex, The Graph, Privy, OpenAI and viem.
The Graph is the intelligence layer. Subgraphs provide indexed pool prices, liquidity, volume and historical market evidence; the Token API helps discover supported assets held by the wallet; and Substreams supplies recent onchain activity. Liquid composes this information into wallet exposure, sector analysis, exit evidence and route selection context.
Users authenticate and connect embedded or external wallets through Privy. Natural language instructions such as protecting an asset or limiting how much may be liquidated are converted by OpenAI into a structured policy. The AI interprets intent, but deterministic application logic validates and enforces the resulting constraints. A payment is always previewed before execution, and Privy provides explicit wallet approval and narrowly scoped, time limited permissions for supported reviewed transactions.
The liquidation planner checks existing USDC first, then evaluates eligible positions and compares executable exit routes using live Base contract reads. It includes gas reserves, slippage protection, token approvals and minimum-output constraints. viem is used for contract calls, transaction encoding, simulation and receipt verification. Convex privately stores wallet snapshots, signed preferences, payment plans and execution checkpoints so an interrupted multi-step payment can be recovered without blindly sending the same transaction twice.
The result is a controlled just-in-time liquidation workflow: keep capital deployed, liquidate only what the payment needs, and verify that the recipient received the expected USDC.

name: Atlas
description: Autonomous AI trading protocol with EVM escrow caps, Backpack L2 & Hedera audit logs.
projectDescription:
180/200
copy-text185 words
Currently, most autonomous AI crypto trading bots have two drawbacks: they are either perilous black boxes or they require the use of TypeScript or Solidity programming languages to modify a trading rule. Atlas was created to address this trust and accessibility concern in trading.
Atlas enables traders to easily create automated trading logic like Dip Buying, Momentum breakout, and customized price triggers at a visual no-code level. One of their most remarkable features is that every trading event is conducted through smart, agent vault non-custodial contracts (AgentVault.sol). Users impose a number of restrictions on their spending, going from dictating the upper limit on each trade to establishing the maximum amount of money to spend throughout the trading process and involving traders in multiple steps of trading activity.
When using the service, users are able to see the execution of the trading strategy on the shocking depth interest order book from Backpack Exchange and TradingView candlestick charts simultaneously. Moreover, every trading signal and emergency kill switch are being recorded immutably on Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) along with links to HashScan, thus guaranteeing the complete audit trail.
howItsMade: Atlas is built as an autonomous quantitative crypto trading protocol pairing low-latency Backpack Exchange L2 orderbook depth with non-custodial EVM escrow smart contracts (AgentVault.sol). Built using Next.js 14, Foundry, and TypeScript, the platform programmatically enforces lifetime spending caps, per-trade ceilings, and human approval gates on-chain. Every AI trade signal and kill-switch activation is logged immutably onto Hedera Consensus Service (Topic #0.0.48912) for a 100% cryptographic audit trail. Oversized trades pause safely in an EVM pending queue for human owner signature

name: CustodIA
description: Chat-native DeFi agent that proposes; you sign an EIP-712 boundary on ENSv2, policy enforces it
projectDescription:
CustodIA is a runtime, not a bot. You type an intent in a chat (web, Telegram or WhatsApp): "Keep ETH/USDC inside a 5% drawdown", "Protect me if ETH drops 15%", "Buy 500 USDC of ETH". The agent researches with live The Graph data, buys a risk analysis with an x402 micropayment on Hedera, and answers with a generated, schema-validated interface: sliders, toggles and charts whose bounds are clipped to the risk context, never invented by the model.
You adjust the boundary and sign it once as an EIP-712 mandate with typed constraints (max trade, max notional, max drawdown, allowed assets, rebalance permission, expiry). The mandate hash is anchored on an ENSv2 task subname ({task}.{you}.custodia.eth) and the agent receives a role scoped to a single text record on that name. From then on a pure, tested policy engine evaluates every action against the mandate before anything moves, and you can revoke the agent's role on-chain at any moment. After revocation the agent's next write reverts.
When you want real execution, you deploy a TaskVault from the task page and fund it with Sepolia ETH. Orders typed in chat are quoted on Uniswap V3, approved per action by a policy signer, executed by an execution signer that cannot withdraw, and the contract itself enforces the assets, caps, cooldown, expiry and router you signed. The agent can also act alone inside the boundary: it sells to USDC when the drawdown limit is hit and proposes rebalances over chat that you confirm with a YES.
The point is separating intelligence from authority. The LLM only proposes. Bounds come from deterministic risk numbers computed from live market data. The human signs the envelope. The policy engine, the ENSv2 role and the vault enforce it. Requests outside the envelope become a "needs a new signature" screen instead of an execution. Everything runs on Sepolia and Hedera testnet with real transactions, live data and no mocks on the qualifying path.
howItsMade:
pnpm monorepo in TypeScript: Next.js 15 web app, a worker, a Hono risk API, a delegated signer subprocess, and packages for schema (Zod), agent, policy, graph, ens, registry, vault, runtime and db (Drizzle on Neon Postgres, PGlite for tests). Contracts are Solidity 0.8 with Foundry.
The agent is an OpenAI tool loop (chat.completions.runTools with Zod function tools, gpt-5.6-luna). Its only way to produce UI is an emit_ui_spec tool whose output is validated against a frozen Zod schema and then clipped server-side to the RiskContext, so a bound outside the risk envelope is a validation error, not a fallback.
The Graph: market context comes from the Uniswap V3 Messari standardized subgraph through the gateway. Prices are derived from the pool tick (10^(dec1-dec0)/1.0001^tick), realized vol from hourly snapshots, every snapshot carries its block, cached 30 s. The pool constant is verified by name at runtime because the first one we hardcoded was the wrong fee tier.
Hedera: the risk API is gated with @x402/hono and @x402/hedera (pinned 2.25.0), priced in HBAR, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. The Hedera key exists only in apps/signer: the agent sends the payment-required header on stdin and gets a payment-signature back on stdout, calls are serialized, and the policy engine must allow the pay_x402 action before the signer is asked. Receipts are checked against the mirror node.
ENS: each task is a free wildcard subname on a PermissionedResolver deployed through the VerifiableFactory on Sepolia. The operator writes owner, mandate hash, agent and status text records; then authorizeTextRoles grants the agent a role for xyz.custodia.status only. Revoking that role makes the next agent write revert with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles, which pnpm verify:ens proves live. The trap that cost us the most: authorize* takes a DNS-encoded name while setText takes a namehash.
Mandates are EIP-712 typed data bound to an immutable stored proposal (proposalId plus constraints hash), so what you sign is exactly what was rendered. Non-authorizable intents (needs_human, compare_strategies) are refused with a 409.
Runtime durability: every chat turn is a run with an append-only event stream and a job on a Postgres queue leased with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; agent runs are never auto-retried; channel deliveries go through an outbox. Telegram and WhatsApp are transports paired to the wallet, signing always happens on the web.
Hacky bits worth mentioning: a dependency-free Chrome DevTools client drives the end-to-end demo with screenshots across all ten prompt cases; the pre-signature receipt is composed server-side so the UI numbers match the mandate byte for byte; Neon's IPv6 records stalled cold connections on our box, so the db client forces ipv4first; the demo wallet was stocked by swapping through the Sepolia Uniswap V3 pools from a script because the faucets only give ETH.

projectDescription:
SPECTER — The private payments layer for onchain money, built to outlive quantum computers.
"Send to a name. Only the recipient can discover, link, or spend it."
═══════════════════════════════════════════
THE PROBLEM

• Every payment on a public blockchain is a permanent, searchable record — your

• Stealth addresses (Umbra, Fluidkey, ERC-5564) are the current fix: each payment gets a

• This is not theoretical. "Harvest now, decrypt later": adversaries are archiving on-chain

cannot be re-encrypted after the fact.
• NIST finalized its post-quantum standards in 2024 (ML-KEM / FIPS 203) and the migration

name: ChainSentry
description: ChainSentry is an observability and alerting tool for Ethereum smart contract developers
projectDescription:
I come from a backend and DevOps background, and most production issues I have debugged were only possible to understand because of monitoring and observability tools. In backend systems, we have tools like ELK, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, and alerting pipelines. If an external service fails, latency increases, or some unexpected error starts happening, we can look at logs, metrics, traces, and alerts to understand what went wrong.
I wanted to bring that same kind of visibility to smart contracts. Once a smart contract is deployed, it is running in production and interacting with users, tokens, protocols, and other contracts. If one of those dependencies changes, fails, or starts behaving differently, the contract may also behave differently. But unlike backend services, smart contracts usually do not have a proper observability layer around them.
ChainSentry helps developers monitor their smart contracts after deployment. A developer can register a contract, index its on-chain activity, view metrics, inspect event history, create dashboards, and set alerts for unusual behavior. For example, they can monitor event counts, transaction volume, success rate, gas usage, or value transferred. If something crosses a threshold, ChainSentry creates an issue and notifies the on-call person through email or phone call.
The idea is simple: smart contract developers should not have to wait for users to report problems. They should be able to observe their contracts in production, understand what changed, and respond quickly.
howItsMade:
ChainSentry uses The Graph to get blockchain data in a reliable way. Directly hitting RPC endpoints for every dashboard or query is slow, expensive, and not suitable for a monitoring product. So the backend generates subgraph configurations for the smart contract and stores those generated artifacts in Google Cloud Storage. The indexed blockchain data is then ingested into ClickHouse, which is used for fast analytical queries.
The backend is built with Node.js, Express, Prisma, PostgreSQL, and ClickHouse. PostgreSQL stores users, organizations, contracts, deployments, alert rules, on-call schedules, and issues. ClickHouse stores the high-volume event and transaction data that powers dashboards and metrics. The frontend is built with Next.js and gives developers pages for metrics, logs, traces, incidents, alerting, and contract configuration.
I also integrated Resend and Twilio for alerting. When an alert rule is triggered, ChainSentry can send an email or place a phone call to the on-call developer. This was important to me because real observability is not just dashboards. It should also help the right person know when something is wrong.
The project is basically my attempt to bring the DevOps monitoring workflow I use in backend systems into Web3, so smart contract developers can debug and monitor production contracts with the same confidence.

name: Leash
description: The AI agrees to pay, and the chain says no. On-chain spending rules for agent wallets.
projectDescription:
Leash is a permission layer for AI agent wallets. What an agent may spend and who it may pay lives in a smart contract, and the wallet checks it on every payment the agent makes — so you don't have to trust the agent to follow its own rules.**
The problem. An AI agent that can spend money needs a spending limit, and every existing answer puts that limit somewhere the agent can reach: a config file it reads, an API key it holds, a session key whose cap the agent itself enforces. Compromise the agent and the limit goes with it.
There's a second problem that gets less attention and happens more often. Limits given to agents don't add up. Teams don't deploy one agent, they deploy several. At 9am the subscriptions agent renews a licence; at 11 the invoices agent pays a contractor; at noon the account is empty and the payment that mattered fails. Neither agent did anything wrong — each stayed inside the limit it was given. There were two limits and one bank account. No per-agent setting fixes that, because it's arithmetic, not a security failure.
What Leash does. The limit isn't attached to an agent. It's attached to an ENS name. The wallet resolves that name on every single payment to find the policy contract that governs it, and the on-chain ledger of what's been spent is keyed by the name, the token and the day — with no agent in the key. So every agent bound to that name draws down one budget, enforced by the chain, with no shared database, no coordinator, and no message passing between them. The agents don't know each other exist.
What you see in the demo. A four-person studio with two AI agents — one pays invoices, one handles renewals — sharing fifty dollars a day.

You type an instruction in English. Claude turns it into a payment. It never writes an address: it picks a vendor by name, and those names are ENS records — our vendor directory contains no addresses at all, so a hallucinated payee has nowhere to appear. The retainer is paid with no approval and no human click.
A new contractor's first invoice is refused. Nobody caught it — no filter, no review queue. The rule isn't in the agent's prompt or its config; it's on chain, and the agent can disagree with it, ignore it, or be compromised, and the wallet still says no. To widen what the agent may do, a live human scans their face with World ID Selfie Check, and the wallet checks that proof against the one World ID it has registered. No key can do that — not the agent's, not the wallet's own. Then the agent tries again on its own and the answer has changed; nobody told it.
The other agent, on a different key in a different process, is refused a payment its vendor and per-transaction limit both allow — because the first agent already spent the budget. It works that out by reading the chain. And notice what the face scan bought: it added a payee. It did not add a dollar.
Rules are swappable. A second policy a human already approved says small payments to anyone, OR the full original rules — two policy contracts composed with an OR. Point the ENS name at it, and a payment that was refused a minute ago goes through, with nothing retyped and nothing said to the agent.

Refusals are first-class. A blocked payment doesn't revert — it emits an event and returns. That's deliberate: it means every refusal is indexed and visible on The Graph, so you can audit not just what the agents did but what they tried to do. It's also the only reason a refusal exists anywhere at all.
The asymmetry is the design. Expanding what an agent may do costs a live human face. Reducing it — tightening a rule, removing a payee, revoking an agent, pausing the wallet — is free and instant, because when something has gone wrong nobody should have to find their phone before pulling the brake.
What it does not claim. EIP-7702 constrains calls to the delegated account, so the wallet's own private key can always sign a direct transfer. That's both the boundary and the escape hatch: the owner can always retrieve their funds and can never be locked out by a rule they installed. Leash is the agent's only spending path, not the wallet's.
Everything runs on Sepolia against deployed contracts. Every claim in the README has a transaction hash behind it, including the refusals.
howItsMade:
The wallet is an EOA with delegated code. LeashAccount is an EIP-7702 delegate implementation (2,856 lines of Solidity, 260 Foundry tests). Delegation is 23 bytes — 0xef0100 || impl — and the code runs against the EOA's own storage, so state lives in an ERC-7201 namespace at keccak256("leash.account.v1"). Re-delegating to a newer impl reads back identically because every field keeps its slot; ownerNullifier was appended at SLOT+6, which was unused.
spend is the only path an agent has, and it cannot go around the check because the check happens inside its own execution path. Authorise the caller from per-EOA storage → walk ENS three hops to resolve the policy → verify that address against a human-approved list → staticcall the policy under a 200k gas cap → honour the reason code.
ENS is the lookup path, not a label. LeashRegistry implements the ENSv2 IRegistry (getSubregistry / getResolver / getParent + IERC1155Singleton) and is mounted under leash.eth, so resolution is forced through it. LeashResolver implements only ENSIP-10 resolve(bytes,bytes) — measured fact: minimal ENSv2 resolvers have no addr() at all, so a compatibility layer is wasted work. ENS's own UniversalResolverV2 resolves our names. Three things hang off the name and breaking any one stops the system: the policy address, every payee address (agent/vendors.json contains names and zero addresses, so a hallucinated payee has nowhere to appear), and — the part we didn't design and then discovered — the budget. The ledger is spent[node][token][bucket]: three keys, no agent. So two agents bound to one subname share one budget, enforced by the account, with no coordination between the processes. That needed no contract change; it fell out of the storage layout.
The Graph is the agent's only sense organ. A refusal doesn't revert — it emits SpendBlocked and returns — so a blocked payment leaves a status-1 receipt and exists nowhere a getter can reach. That was a deliberate design decision to make refusals indexable, and it means the subgraph is the only place four things exist: the refusal log, the payee allow-list (no contract can enumerate it), the list of approved policies (events, not an array), and the per-agent split of the shared budget. That last one is reconstructed client-side by walking spentAfter backwards from the budget's current total until it reaches zero — which finds the period boundary by arithmetic rather than by assuming 86400 seconds. EIP-7702 delegation emits no log, so the subgraph has no factory event to trigger a template from; LeashAccount emits Leashed on the first bindAgent to be that trigger.
World ID Selfie Check is the asymmetry. Widening costs a live human; reducing is free, because when something has gone wrong nobody should have to find their phone before pulling the brake. WorldAttester verifies an EIP-712 attestation from our RP signer against a digest bound to the exact widening, and LeashAccount additionally checks the nullifier equals the one ownerNullifier it has registered. allowPayeeByFace deliberately has no onlySelf — the wallet's own key gets NotAttested() while a valid face scan relayed by anyone succeeds. The face outranks every key in the system, including the wallet's.
Claude drives the agent. claude -p with a vendor directory of ENS names; the model picks an id and never writes an address.
Three hacky/hard-won things worth naming. (1) @worldcoin/idkit-standalone cannot request a face check at all — we proved it from the published bundle (zero occurrences of "selfie", four verification levels) and migrated to idkit-core's selfieCheckLegacy(). On the wire it's verification_level: "face" — the same vocabulary with a fifth value the widget's switch is missing. (2) Once you store a nullifier, the action stops being a free choice: a nullifier is hash(person, action), so every future scan must reuse the same action or the stored one never matches. Nothing documents that, and the verification succeeds either way — it fails only in your own code. Both are written up in docs/world-feedback.md. (3) PolicySet reaches its members by staticcall, not call, because the account doesn't revert when it blocks — a member that wrote state on the way to a refusal could never be rolled back.
Honestly stated: PolicyApprovals is wired to MockAttester in this deployment, so getting onto the approved list is currently ungated. The account's own attester is the real WorldAttester; the approvals contract's is immutable, so fixing it is a redeploy of two contracts. It's flagged in the README and docs/deployments.md rather than buried.
Foundry, viem, node:test. 260 Solidity tests, 212 JavaScript. Every claim in the README has a Sepolia transaction hash behind it.

name: Carpool
description: AI agents buy research someone already did instead of redoing it. The author gets paid in USDC.
projectDescription:
Carpool is a registry where AI agents buy and sell finished research.
Before an agent spends twenty minutes and a few dollars of tokens on a question, it searches Carpool. If someone has already answered it, the agent pays a small USDC fee over x402, gets the document, and skips the work. Whoever wrote it earns a royalty on every sale.
Each piece of research is addressed by a hash of its contents, so it can't be swapped after it's listed. Search matches on meaning, and ranks answers higher when they're fresher and more thorough. Prices fall as research ages. The author picks a half-life, the price halves on that schedule, and after three halvings the registry stops selling it, because a stale answer sold as current does more harm than having none.
Buyers have a two-minute refund window. The registry holds each payment for that window, then pays authors in batches with HTS transfers and posts a Merkle root of every batch to an HCS topic, so payouts can be audited.
Agents use it through an MCP server with four tools: search, fetch, publish and delist. It installs into Claude Code. Search is free and needs no account. Publishing always asks the user first, and it removes secrets and local file paths before anything is listed. Buyers can rate a purchase as worth it or not, one rating per purchase, signed by the key that paid.
We measured one real case. Redoing an ETHOnline prize analysis cost at least $3.97 in tokens; buying the same document cost $0.44. We also ran every payment path on Hedera testnet: refunds, a 13-author payout split across two transactions, recovering a batch whose receipt was lost, and two settlement processes hitting the same batch at once, which still produced a single transfer.
Authors can also publish under their own ENS name. The name's records hold their Hedera payout account and signing key, and each sale looks up where to pay at the moment it happens, so an author can move payouts to a new account without republishing anything.
howItsMade:
TypeScript monorepo (pnpm and turbo) on Node 20, split into a payment package, a core model, a search package, the registry, the MCP server and a Next.js dashboard.
Payments: the paywall is built on @x402/core and @x402/hedera, and payments are verified and settled by the Blocky402 facilitator on testnet. Buyers pay the registry's account rather than the author's. That was a deliberate choice, since otherwise a refund would have nothing to pull back.
Hedera: settlement uses @hiero-ledger/sdk. Payouts go out as HTS token transfers with at most 9 authors per transaction, because a transfer list caps at 10 entries. Each batch's Merkle root is posted to an HCS topic. The mirror node is used to recover lost transactions by their memo, and a Python script re-checks 60 of our on-chain claims against it without importing any of our code. Money is Circle's testnet USDC.
Registry: Express with SQLite through better-sqlite3, sqlite-vec for the vector index, and MiniLM embeddings running locally through transformers.js. A lease row in SQLite stops two processes from settling the same batch twice. We found that bug in a simulation, where it paid one author twice, and then confirmed the fix on testnet.
MCP server: built on the official SDK. A Claude Code PreToolUse hook blocks publishing unless a person confirms it.
ENS: an author can publish as name.eth on the ENSv2 beta on Sepolia. Reads go through viem's Universal Resolver. The registry trusts the name only when three records agree (Hedera address, coin type 3030; the signing key; and a signature from that key over the name and account), then reads the payout account at purchase time and records how it paid. If ENS is slow or the records don't match, the sale still goes through and pays the backup account the author signed into the listing.
