name: Arbiter402
description: Sub-second conditional micro-escrow & zero-hallucination adjudication for machine commerce.
projectDescription:
Arbiter402 is an autonomous, sub-second conditional micro-escrow and deterministic ground-truth adjudication protocol built for the machine economy. While demonstrated on high-stakes DeFi indexing as its reference implementation, the protocol is fundamentally modular and generalizable to any verifiable machine-to-machine compute task.
Why Human-in-the-Loop Fails for AI Agents:
Traditional escrow and human arbitration (e.g., Kleros, multi-sig signers) are completely infeasible for machine-to-machine commerce:
• Cost Inversion: AI agents execute micro-transactions ($0.05 - $1.00). Paying human jurors $10+ to review a $0.20 dispute is an immediate economic failure.
• Latency Destruction: Human dispute cycles take days or weeks. An autonomous agent making automated market actions needs settlement in seconds, not days.
• The LLM Trap: Using an LLM to judge another LLM introduces stochastic drift, hallucinations, and prompt injection. Machine commerce demands deterministic mathematical ground truth.
How Arbiter402 Solves It:
• Sub-Second Micro-Escrow: Buyer agents lock micro-escrows into ArbiterEscrow.sol on Hedera EVM (~0.84s finality, ~$0.007 gas fee) via HTTP 402 and MCP tool-calling.
• Zero-Hallucination Adjudication: When deliverables are contested, our referee queries The Graph's decentralized indexing network to evaluate mathematical invariants (e.g., Uniswap v3 VWAP over verified block ranges) directly from raw onchain swap logs.
• ERC-8004 Machine Reputation: Lost disputes trigger atomic refunds and slash rogue agents by -50 points onchain, while honest completions award +5 points.
• Immutable HCS Audit Trail: Signed ECDSA audit proofs are anchored to Hedera Consensus Service for public verifiability on HashScan.
howItsMade:
Arbiter402 brings together Hedera EVM, Hedera Consensus Service (HCS), The Graph, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) into a unified, hardened machine-commerce pipeline:
• Hedera EVM Smart Contracts: We developed and deployed ArbiterEscrow.sol (0.0.10520281) and ERC8004ReputationRegistry.sol (0.0.10520278) on Hedera Testnet (Chain ID 296), both 100% verified on Sourcify with Exact Match. Hedera's ~0.84s finality and fixed sub-cent fees enable high-frequency micro-escrow transactions that are cost-prohibitive on L1.
• Hedera Consensus Service (HCS): Every dispute adjudication generates a tamper-proof audit payload containing the job specification hash, deliverable hash, ground-truth value, error delta, and the referee's ECDSA signature, permanently anchored to HCS Topic 0.0.10520952 with nanosecond consensus timestamps and stored in the contract's auditLogUri.
• The Graph Decentralized Oracle: To eliminate subjective LLM arbitration, our referee queries The Graph’s decentralized network for raw Uniswap v3 swap events (amount0, amount1, sqrtPriceX96). It deterministically computes the true Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP) across the requested block window to evaluate deviations against basis-point contract tolerances.
• Bazantic MCP Recipe & HTTP 402: Built with @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, our recipe server exposes standardized tools (adjudicate_escrow_dispute, verify_agent_reputation) allowing autonomous agents in Claude, Cursor, and LangChain to negotiate escrows and trigger dispute settlements natively over standardized HTTP 402 headers.
• Security Hardening: We engineered a cryptographic deliverable substitution defense (pre-flight checks ensure payloads match onchain keccak256 hashes), push-to-pull fallback queues (pendingWithdrawals) that immunize against denial-of-service reverts, and liveness safety valves for uncontested claims and expired deadlines.

name: Intentra
description: Intentra finds the right human. USDC escrow makes sure they get paid.
projectDescription:
Intentra is a decentralized service marketplace , framed as an "AI Commerce Protocol." Here's how it works:
AI-driven matching – you describe what you need and your budget, and an AI parses your intent to find a matching service provider, with the arrangement secured by EIP-712 cryptographic mandates (structured, signed data commitments).
Human verification – providers must prove they're real humans (not bots) using World ID's "World Selfie Check," aiming to eliminate scams and fake accounts.
Escrowed payments
funds are held in USDC via a smart contract escrow on the Arc testnet, only releasing to the provider once the job is completed and approved by the client.
In short, it's a trust layer for hiring freelancers/service providers where an AI agent handles the negotiation/matching, identity is verified cryptographically, and payment is escrowed on-chain until work is confirmed done.
howItsMade:
The backend is a FastAPI modular monolith, organised domain-per-package rather than
by layer: intents, providers, transactions, authorization, payments, fulfillment,
evidence, disputes, identity and audit each own their router, models, schemas and
service. Boundaries are not a convention here, they are CI — 14 import-linter
contracts fail the build if a domain touches another domain's tables, if the shared
kernel imports a domain, if an adapter reaches back inward, or if pure rule code
(money, hashing, state machine, policy) imports FastAPI, SQLAlchemy or web3. The one
deliberate exception is the Transaction aggregate root, and a test walks the source
tree to prove the state machine is its only writer.
SQLModel/SQLAlchemy async over asyncpg, Alembic migrations, 20 tables. Three worker
loops (chain watcher, transaction outbox, reconciliation) run in-process, guarded by
a Postgres advisory lock so only one instance is leader and the same code scales to
several replicas untouched. 572 tests.
ON-CHAIN
IntentraEscrow is Solidity on Arc testnet (chain 5042002), built with Foundry. Two
rules drive the whole design: money states commit only on confirmed chain events,
never on an optimistic write, and settlement needs two distinct signatures from
{customer, provider, AI arbitrator}. The watcher reads eth_getLogs from the escrow's
deploy block, advances a cursor only after every log in a range is handled, and keys
events on (tx_hash, log_index) so a replay after a crash is a no-op. Outbound calls
go through an outbox: rows are claimed with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, the
transaction hash is committed to the database before we wait for a receipt, and one
lock serialises the resolver's nonce.
PARTNER TECHNOLOGIES
Arc — escrow and settlement in USDC, with gas paid in USDC too, which removes the
"buy the native token first" step that kills onboarding for the Nigerian users this
targets. Deterministic finality let us run the watcher at 1 confirmation.
Privy — email login to an embedded wallet, so a customer signs an EIP-712 mandate
without ever seeing a seed phrase; also signTypedData and sendTransaction for the
escrow calls. Access tokens are ES256-verified server-side against the app's
verification key.
World — Selfie Check proof-of-human gates authorisation and complaint, the two
places fraud pays. One nullifier per action per transaction, so a proof cannot be
replayed onto another job.
The Graph — a subgraph over the escrow's own events turns completed, disputed and
refunded jobs into provider trust scores, so reputation comes from chain history
rather than rows we could edit.

name: Althea
description: Althea Care turns independent charitable funds into a programmable relief network
projectDescription:
Althea is a patient financial-assistance platform and programmable charitable relief network built to intervene before an unaffordable hospital bill becomes medical debt.
A patient starts with their hospital, bill amount, household size, income, and insurance status. Althea converts the hospital's Financial Assistance Policy into structured, explainable rules and shows whether the patient may qualify for free or discounted care. It then helps prepare the application, surfaces required documents and important timelines, and tracks the hospital's decision. The hospital—not Althea—makes the final eligibility determination.
But hospital assistance does not always eliminate the entire bill. That is where the Althea Care Network begins.
When a verified residual balance remains, Althea searches available charitable funding programs and assembles eligible relief across independently governed pools. For example, a $500 grant can combine $250 from the Althea General Medical Hardship Fund with a $250 matching grant from a partner foundation.
Foundations, employers, and charitable organizations can create rules-based USDC relief programs with defined budgets, grant caps, matching ratios, expiration dates, and settlement restrictions. Althea's Care Agent evaluates the verified case state and available programs, then routes approved capital through a programmable settlement flow on Arc.
Funds are first reserved and only released toward the verified medical obligation when the required settlement conditions are satisfied. Unused or expired reservations can return to the charitable pool instead of being stranded.
In our demo, an $18,420 hospital bill receives $15,950 in simulated hospital financial assistance, leaving $2,470. Althea then assembles a $500 charitable grant from multiple funding sources, reducing the remaining balance to $1,970.
Patients never need to understand wallets, gas, bridges, or crypto, and sensitive information such as names, diagnoses, income, medical records, and hospital bills remains offchain.
Althea's goal is simple:
The financial help may already exist. Althea makes it usable.
And when that help stops short, Althea turns independent charitable capital into a programmable relief network.
howItsMade:
Althea is built as two connected systems: an offchain patient financial-assistance navigator and an onchain charitable relief network.
The patient experience is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. Hospital Financial Assistance Policies are converted from unstructured documents into a structured policy schema. AI assists with policy extraction and plain-language explanation, but financial calculations are intentionally deterministic: household income, Federal Poverty Level thresholds, policy rules, estimated discounts, and relevant timelines are calculated in code rather than delegated to an LLM. Every result can be traced back to the underlying policy source.
Sensitive patient information stays offchain in our application/database layer. The blockchain never receives the patient's name, diagnosis, income, insurance information, medical record, or hospital bill.
After the hospital assistance process, Althea switches into the Althea Care Network.
World Selfie Check is used as one liveness and abuse-prevention signal before a patient can access Althea's separate, limited charitable Care Fund. We intentionally do not use World to gate hospital financial-assistance rights; a patient can search policies, estimate assistance, and prepare an application without completing a biometric check.
Privy is the institutional wallet and control layer. Althea and participating foundations can operate organization-controlled wallets with policies restricting which contracts, networks, amounts, and financial actions are permitted. This lets a foundation commit capital to a Althea matching program without giving our agent unrestricted access to its treasury. Privy also lets us hide normal crypto complexity from fund administrators and donors.
On Arc, we deploy programmable USDC care pools. Each funding program can define a budget, per-case grant cap, matching rules, and other restrictions. Rather than performing a simple token transfer, Althea supports a multi-step settlement flow:
verified case → funding programs matched → USDC reserved → approval conditions satisfied → provider settlement confirmed → USDC released
Our new multi-funder flow allows several independently governed programs to contribute toward one verified medical obligation. In the demo, Althea contributes $250 and a foundation's 1:1 matching program contributes another $250, assembling a $500 grant automatically.
The Althea Care Agent, built with Circle Agent Stack, reads structured case and program signals such as the hospital decision, verified residual balance, World verification state, available program liquidity, grant limits, and approval status. The agent can discover the appropriate funding route and orchestrate settlement, but it cannot change grant rules or freely move treasury funds. Deterministic rules, Privy wallet controls, and Arc smart-contract limits constrain what the agent is allowed to do.
Our Arc smart contracts include protections such as authorized executors, program-level grant caps, duplicate-case protection, settlement-address validation, available-balance checks, and pause controls. We use USDC as the dollar-denominated settlement asset.
The result is a system where the patient sees a simple financial-assistance experience while the infrastructure underneath coordinates multiple charitable organizations, programmable wallets, autonomous agents, and conditional stablecoin settlement.
In our demo:
$18,420 original bill
− $15,950 hospital assistance
= $2,470 residual
Althea then finds:
$250 Althea General Fund

$250 Foundation Match
= $500 programmable relief

After settlement:
$1,970 remains.
We don't tokenize the patient, and we don't tokenize their medical debt. We use blockchain where it adds real value: coordinating independent charitable capital, enforcing funding rules, and making the movement of relief funds verifiable without exposing the person who needed help.

name: PROVE Protocol
description: PROVE verifies AI agents did what they were paid for on-chain, via Chainlink CRE + ENSv2 reputation.
projectDescription: PROVE protocol verifies that AI agents actually did what they were paid to do. A requester posts a task on-chain with a spec and an ETH reward. An AI agent picks it up, executes the described action on-chain, and submits proof. A Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow — running in a TEE — compares the agent's actual on-chain execution against the original spec and produces a pass/fail verdict. If it passes, the reward is released automatically and the agent's trust score is updated live on its ENSv2 identity (agent1.prove.eth), building verifiable, publicly-readable reputation for AI agents.
howItsMade:
STACK

Contracts: Solidity 0.8.28, Foundry (forge/cast), OpenZeppelin v5. Three contracts: TaskRegistry (task lifecycle + ETH escrow), VerificationOracle (receives the verification verdict, triggers settlement), AgentRegistry (trust score + ENS writeback). 44 tests, including a live Sepolia fork test.
Identity/reputation: ENSv2 (beta, live on Sepolia) — real subname registration under prove.eth, real text records.
Verification engine: Chainlink CRE (Confidential Workflow / TEE), written in TypeScript against @chainlink/cre-sdk, with an automatic Node.js/viem watcher as the settlement path.
Frontend: Next.js 14 (App Router), wagmi v2 + viem, Tailwind, a single scrollable dashboard (create task -> live task feed -> agent trust score, read from both AgentRegistry and the live ENS resolver side by side).

HOW IT'S PIECED TOGETHER

A requester calls TaskRegistry.createTask(agentENSNode, taskSpec, deadline) and deposits ETH as the reward, which is held in escrow.
An agent watcher (agent/agent.js) polls for TaskCreated events targeting its ENS node, executes the described on-chain action, and calls submitResult with the result tx hash.
That ResultSubmitted event is what a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow (cre-workflow/verify-task/workflow.ts) consumes: it reads the task spec on-chain, pulls the agent's actual transaction data, and compares spec vs. reality inside a TEE handler (handlerInTee) — so the comparison and the agent's raw execution data stay confidential from node operators until a verdict is final.
The pass/fail verdict is posted to VerificationOracle.postVerification, gated to a single CRE-DON-equivalent address. A pass atomically releases the escrowed reward via TaskRegistry and bumps the agent's trust score in AgentRegistry; a fail refunds the requester and penalizes the score.
AgentRegistry mirrors that trust score live to the agent's own ENSv2 subname (agent1.prove.eth) as a com.prove.trustScore text record, so anyone can read an agent's reputation independent of our own frontend, straight from ENS.
In the running demo, an always-on watcher script runs both the "agent" loop and an "oracle" loop that reuses the exact same comparison logic as the CRE workflow, so pressing Create Task in the dashboard settles the task to Paid automatically with zero manual steps.

name: QWitness
description: Portable signed evidence and independent verification for onchain AI agents.
projectDescription: QWitness turns live onchain research evidence into portable, independently verifiable JSON receipts. Its shared TypeScript core queries The Graph for Aave V3 USDC and DAI reserves on Ethereum, calculates utilization with exact integer arithmetic, attaches structured deterministic analysis, and signs the complete canonical protected header and payload with ML-DSA-65. The public web flow and an actual MCP SDK client have successfully acquired live data, created receipts and verified them with a separately supplied signer pin. The Tamper Lab detects altered values and claims, and distinguishes a mathematically valid signature from an unexpected signer. Bundled HTML and Node verifiers work offline. This targets reusable AI tooling; deterministic analysis is labelled and no actual LLM call is claimed. Signatures do not prove provider honesty, analysis correctness or quantum resistance of Ethereum. The prototype is unaudited. The participant approved the review and reported no issues. Human narration and final submission remain pending.
howItsMade: Created in a new repository using TypeScript, Next.js, React, the official MCP SDK, canonicalize and @noble/post-quantum 0.7.1. The bounded Graph adapter pins the Aave V3 reserve query to one indexed block and retains query text, variables, responses and deployment metadata. Token amounts remain integer/decimal strings. Actual provider responses revealed that number-pinned _meta can omit optional hash and timestamp; these stay unknown while conflicting known metadata, deployment IDs and block numbers are rejected. Web and MCP call the same acquisition, analysis and signing service. The complete canonical protected header and payload are signed with ML-DSA-65 and domain separation. Independent signer fingerprints establish the chosen trust input; embedded keys are not automatically trusted. All 77 unit tests and CI pass. Live Graph, real MCP client issuance and public browser tampering/key-substitution checks have succeeded. Codex assisted the specification, implementation, tests, documentation and video preparation. The participant supplied the AI-assisted brief, completed account connections and performed Graph key regeneration. The participant approved the review and reported no issues; no detailed manual-test observations are inferred. A 170.5-second live recording and clearly labelled synthetic-voice review were generated. Human narration is still required for the submission video.

name: Receipt
description: A drop-in x402 facilitator that pays the seller only if the response passes the buyer's checks
projectDescription:
Receipt is a working x402 facilitator with conditional settlement, live on Hedera testnet. 54 real deals have gone through it: 22 released to the seller, 26 refunded to the buyer automatically, and 6 where the seller never answered and the money became claimable by anyone. All 48 verdicts it has published reproduce exactly when an independent implementation recomputes them from the public log. Zero mismatches.
The gap it closes: when an agent pays for an API call over x402, the money moves the moment the payment is verified. If the API returns garbage, the agent has paid for garbage. x402 has no refund primitive and no dispute step anywhere in the stack.
Receipt closes it without adding a judge. The buyer writes down what a good answer looks like, signs those terms, and only then pays. The payment sits in escrow on Hedera instead of going to the seller. When the response arrives, seven checks run against it: HTTP status, content type, body size, required JSON paths, JSON schema, freshness of the snapshot, and an optional exact-hash match. All seven pass and the escrow releases. Any one fails and the refund is automatic. If the seller never answers at all, the deadline passes and any stranger can call claimExpired to return the buyer's money.
Having no judge is the innovation, not a limitation. Every check is a pure function of (terms, response), and that single property buys three things at once that nothing else in this space has together. The buyer can compute the verdict. The seller can compute it before answering and decline a sale it knows it cannot earn, which no evaluator-based design can offer, because you cannot consult an external evaluator before the work is delivered. And a stranger can recompute it afterwards and check it against what was recorded on chain.
The counter-example is worth stating, because it is why we built it this way. Virtuals Protocol's Agent Commerce Protocol shipped escrow with Client, Provider and Evaluator roles, went live on Base, and accumulated over 12 million commerce memos. It now runs at roughly five unique senders a day. The evaluator is what broke it: nobody could answer who judges, who pays the judge, and why the verdict should be trusted.
You do not have to trust us either. Every terms document, every raw response body and every verdict is published to a public Hedera Consensus Service topic, hashed with JCS (RFC 8785) plus keccak256. The live ledger is a static page with no backend of ours behind it: it rebuilds all 54 deals in your browser directly from the Hedera mirror node and recomputes any verdict locally, in front of you. If the public log did not carry what that page claims, the page could not exist. One command, pnpm verify --all, replays every verdict ever published. And a second implementation in Python, written from the spec rather than from our code, with zero dependencies and its own keccak and JCS, reaches identical verdicts.
We are as strict about what we cannot prove as about what we can. Response latency is our own stopwatch and no third party can recompute it, so it is recorded, displayed, and gates nothing. The verdict splits into reproducible checks, which move the money, and attested ones, which do not.
The seller in the demo is a stock x402 resource server selling live token data from The Graph, composing the Token API with a subgraph. Making it settle through Receipt means changing one URL. That is the drop-in claim, and it is a claim a judge can diff.
CHECK IT ON CHAIN
Escrow contract: 0x3483B3761ebe3C2fC2eB3EfE8215a7CF90634071 (Hedera id 0.0.10485798, verified on Sourcify, full match)
Audit topic: 0.0.10495465
Hosted ledger: https://receipt-ledger-zeta.vercel.app
Three deals, one of each outcome, all on Hedera testnet. Every hash below opens on hashscan.io/testnet and returns SUCCESS.


All seven checks passed, escrow released 0.5 HBAR to the seller
deal      0x0aa1e03afb0bf9e2472d60390bf8128e443a53dc671a27c0115fd42f17027623
release() 0x8e4805f761c73814512bc1ce54ffcd506462628733ae74525432caa2849e1aaa


Seller answered HTTP 200 with an error blob, requiredPaths failed, buyer refunded automatically
deal      0x55e54e954c4c2f32738b878408809d81d05cdc1aaa16835dbb1e468999c55411
refund()  0xdc71a23dab3f6566d0e6a6d6ce8ececdf993b61315b53c98c34e29ea45a2a2a5


Genuine Graph data, correct shape, every field valid, but the snapshot was hours old. Only the freshness check caught it, buyer refunded automatically
deal      0xe17dcdc8eb7307a0d47a22af290590ac5cdc9035f0a5b896b2742ea12accd7bc
refund()  0x43eb94f56c3adda7a92487192df8a2024a3c5dcfec1f77b8ff496d3c6253dbb3


That third one is the case worth opening. Nothing about it looks wrong and a human reviewer would approve it. Each of these three also has its terms, its raw response body and its verdict published on topic 0.0.10495465, which is what lets anyone recompute the verdict with no cooperation from us.
howItsMade:
Monorepo in TypeScript with pnpm workspaces. The centre of it is packages/core, where the adjudicator is a pure function from (terms, response) to verdict: no clock, no network, no randomness. That purity is the product, because it is what lets a buyer, a seller and a stranger each compute the same answer independently. It was built test first and the repo runs 307 tests, including ones that assert the adjudicator imports nothing impure, so the guarantee cannot rot.
HEDERA. The escrow is a Solidity contract on Hedera testnet (chain 296), deployed with Foundry. It holds the HBAR between payment and verdict, verifies the buyer's EIP-712 signature on chain, and exposes release, refund and a permissionless claimExpired that lets any stranger return a buyer's money when a seller goes dark.
Hedera Consensus Service is what makes the whole thing auditable at x402 prices. Every terms document, every raw response body and every verdict goes to topic 0.0.10495465, chunked on write and reassembled byte-wise on read. Publishing complete response bodies for every single transaction is only economically possible because HCS is cheap and final in seconds, and at a median x402 ticket well under a dollar nothing else we evaluated came close.
The mirror node then does something decisive: it serves permissive CORS headers. That is why our hosted ledger is a static page with no backend of ours behind it. It rebuilds all 54 deals in the visitor's browser directly from Hedera and recomputes any verdict locally. A judge never has to trust our server, because there is no server. Hedera is what made the strongest version of this project possible.
One piece of hard-won Hedera knowledge worth passing on: msg.value on the Hedera EVM is denominated in tinybars, not weibars, so the x402 valueScale must be 1. Every EVM tool you arrive with assumes 18 decimals.
BLOCKY402. Settlement runs through Blocky402 as the x402 facilitator underneath ours, and Receipt implements the identical /verify, /settle and /supported surface. That is what makes it genuinely drop-in rather than a fork: an existing x402 seller changes one URL and gains conditional settlement. The payment itself is a partially-signed Hedera TransferTransaction carried in the PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header, so the buyer signs and pays no gas.
THE GRAPH. The seller sells something real. It returns live token holdings from the Token API composed with the liquidity pools those holdings trade in from a subgraph, both products in one response, fetched together so a failure in either half fails the sale rather than half-answering it. This matters because the acceptance terms are written against the true shape of Graph data, and it is what makes the sharpest scene in the demo possible: a genuine, correct Graph response whose only defect is a stale snapshot. Nothing about it looks wrong and a human reviewer would approve it. Only the freshness check catches it, and the buyer's money comes back automatically.
BAZANTIC. Two Recipes are published so an agent can buy verified data through the gateway without knowing that x402, escrow or Hedera exist. The second Recipe composes both sponsors: it buys Graph data through Receipt and proceeds only when the escrow verdict passes, which makes conditional settlement the control flow of the recipe rather than a detail inside it. An MCP server exposing buy_verified_data, verify_deal and get_deal does the same job for agents that speak MCP.
TWO IMPLEMENTATIONS, ONE VERDICT. Hashing is JCS (RFC 8785) canonical JSON plus keccak256, chosen so an independent implementation can agree byte for byte. We proved that rather than asserting it: verify-py is Python with zero dependencies, its own Keccak-256, its own JCS canonicaliser, its own JSON Schema subset and its own JSONPath, written from SPEC.md rather than from our TypeScript. It reads the public topic and prints the same verdictHash the escrow recorded. Writing it also sharpened the spec, by surfacing that human-readable detail strings sit inside the hashed document and so must be pinned exactly for two implementations to agree. That is now specified in SPEC.md and asserted in CI, and it is precisely the class of ambiguity only a second implementation can find. The escrow itself is verified on Sourcify with a full match, so the deployed bytecode provably matches the published source.
THE HACKY PART. The demo film has no video editor behind it. demo/film.html is a page where the entire film is a pure function of time: seek(ms) computes every pixel of state from the clock and returns a signature of what it painted, so the renderer captures a frame only when that signature changes and turns the rest into a longer duration in an ffmpeg concat list. A scene that holds still for twelve seconds costs one screenshot instead of three hundred and sixty. It drives headless Chrome over the DevTools Protocol using the WebSocket client built into Node, with no dependencies at all. The narration is generated the same way, timed from the same schedule the renderer wrote, so the script and the film cannot drift apart. The same determinism the project claims for its verdicts is what makes the film cheap to render and impossible to fudge, because every figure on screen is pulled from a real captured run rather than typed in by hand.

name: Remate
description: Secondary market for a tokenized bonds and its KYC'd users. Bid and buy.
projectDescription:
Remate is a secondary market for a tokenized bonds and its KYC'd users. A holder auctions an exit; only wallets already KYC'd for that bond can bid and buy.
It is a first-price exit auction, started by the holder, on an ATS hold with no live quote: sealed reserve, USDC on Arc, award in a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow, compliance enforced by the token at delivery.
How it works. The seller lists by placing an ATS hold with ExitAuction as escrow. The bonds never leave the seller's wallet and keep earning the coupon. The reserve is sealed — only its hash is on-chain. Eligible investors approve and placeBid in USDC into BidEscrow on Arc testnet. A wallet without KYC for that bond is blocked in the app; executeHoldByPartition would revert anyway.
After the deadline a Chainlink CRE handlerInTee is built to read the sealed reserve and a confidential compliance screen and to write a DON-signed report to BidEscrow. The highest eligible bid at or above reserve wins and pays its own bid.
The operator then executeHold on Hedera and confirmDelivery on Arc. USDC is released to the seller; losers withdraw. Hedera holds the ATS bond (whitelist, internal KYC, coupon) and ExitAuction. Arc holds native USDC and BidEscrow. Chainlink holds the confidential award.
howItsMade:
Remate is a secondary market for a tokenized bond and its KYC'd users. A holder who has no live quote auctions an exit. Only wallets already KYC'd for that bond can bid and buy. We built the rails so that constraint is the token's, not a checkbox in our UI.
Issuance stays in Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio (web app): whitelist, internal KYC, coupon, holds. We did not rewrite the bond. Our Hedera contract is ExitAuction.sol — Foundry, Solidity 0.8.26, evm paris. The seller lists with createHoldByPartition, ExitAuction as escrow, then createAuction. The bonds never leave the seller's wallet and keep earning the coupon — the holder can seek a price without giving up the asset or its yield. Delivery is executeHoldByPartition: KYC and whitelist run at that instant. A wallet that is not KYC'd for that bond is blocked in the app; the token would revert anyway.
The cash leg is BidEscrow.sol on Arc testnet. Buyers approve native USDC (0x3600…0000) and placeBid. That is the business of the auction: public bids, dollar settlement, pull withdrawals for losers. confirmDelivery pays only the registered seller.
The award must not be a venue operator picking a friend. packages/cre-award is a TypeScript CRE workflow with handlerInTee (@chainlink/cre-sdk). Inside the confidential handler it fetches Vault secrets, the sealed reserve and a compliance screen over authenticated HTTP, checks keccak256(reserve, salt) against the on-chain commitment, and computes a first-price award. Only winner, price, commitment, outcome and digest leave. Confidential Workflows are in private beta; we simulate with the CRE CLI. The simulator is not a hardware TEE. BidEscrow also has a documented awardByOperator fallback (visible as source=Operator).
The app is a Next.js 15 monorepo (apps/web, apps/landing) with wagmi, viem and React Query: market, sell, auction, operator. Route handlers and a JSON store index auctions. An operator key mirrors the auction to Arc, triggers close, executeHold on Hedera, and confirmDelivery on Arc. Two chains, coordinated steps — not one atomic settlement. The operator can stall, void or cancel. It cannot redirect USDC or deliver to a non-compliant wallet.
What was hard, and why it matters: holds instead of approve/transferFrom (the ATS approve path needs a whitelisted spender; holds keep coupon entitlement). Arc's 20 gwei fee floor. The CRE forwarder address — sources disagree on simulation vs production; BidEscrow.setForwarderAddress exists for that. The hederaTxHash stored on Arc is a pointer for humans, not a proof.
Hedera is the compliant asset. Arc is the USDC cash. Chainlink CRE is the award the operator does not decide. The product is the exit: bid and buy, only if you are already allowed to hold the bond.

name: hedera-harness-go
description: Harness for the Hedera ecosystem: an agent builds your dapp, hh checks it on chain in code
projectDescription: hh(hedera-harness-go) is a harness for the Hedera ecosystem, written in Go and inspired by hedera-dev/hedera-harness. You describe a dapp in one sentence and hh starts from scaffold-hbar with the official Hedera skills. The agent writes the contracts, deploy scripts and frontend, but it never holds a private key. After every attempt hh compiles, type checks and deploys to testnet with your connected wallet. It also runs YAML scenarios that make real transactions and check the result on the mirror node. Any failure goes back into the same agent conversation until everything passes. The same scenarios run on a built-in mock network in milliseconds, on a local Solo network, or on testnet.
howItsMade: The whole thing is Go on top of hiero-sdk-go. Scenarios are strict YAML with actors, steps and assertions, checked offline with line numbers. There are 20 step types covering HTS tokens, NFTs, custom fees, airdrops, HCS topics and multisig schedules. Assertions are plain code that polls the mirror node REST API and verifies the HCS running hash chain. The hacky part is the mock network: it's a fake gRPC consensus node plus a fake mirror node running in the same process, so the real SDK client talks to it with no Docker. The agent loop drives the Claude CLI over stream-json and resumes the same session for repairs. Judge files are pinned by hash so the agent cant edit them to pass. The TUI is built from Charm libraries (bubbletea, lipgloss), the demos are recorded with VHS and releases ship with goreleaser.

name: TrulyOpenRouter
description: Like OpenRouter, except open on Crypto Rails powered by x402 payments
projectDescription:
TrulyOpenRouter is actually OpenRouter, on crypto rails. We bring together two groups: the ones that want inference, and the ones with spare compute sitting idle. Your company has a floor of desktop machines that do nothing from 6pm to 9am? Run TrulyOpenRouter on that hardware and those idle hours turn into revenue, paid per request.
For the user, nothing changes. It's the classic Claude or OpenAI experience: you pay a normal subscription, open a chat or point your OpenAI-compatible client at an API key, and get an answer. What changes is underneath. Every request is routed to whichever host wins on price, latency, stake and reliability, and that host is paid per call over x402 on Hedera.
On top of that, team plans built for how organizations actually buy compute, managed by our AI compute wallet. An org sets the requirements: which models are allowed, a daily spend ceiling, per-seat caps, which routes and which geographies are acceptable, and which hosts are approved.
As tokens are the new currency and highly valuable, TrulyOpenRouter supports tightly scoped keys with hard limits. An agent that hits its ceiling doesn't quietly spend more. It stops and asks for approval, and a human raises the limit by signing the exact terms on a Ledger.
howItsMade:
Next.js on Vercel for the frontend, a TypeScript/Express gateway over Postgres, Solidity contracts on Hedera testnet (chain 296).
Hedera + x402. Paid requests use @x402/core, @x402/express and @x402/hedera (2.25.0). Hosts run a guard that puts an x402 paywall in front of Ollama and quotes $0.001 on hedera:testnet; the gateway takes the 402, checks the terms, and pays. We settle through Hedera's own Blocky402 facilitator. On-chain: SubscriptionVault (subscribe → credits, gateway-only debit split 90% host / 10% fees, withdraw, refund), HostRegistry (permissionless register with a 4 HBAR stake, heartbeat, deregister → release behind a 24h timelock), HTS test USDC for host payment, and HCS as the audit log, where the receipt id is the topic message.
Privy is how a business manages their new "currency" compute. We use an organization wallet as our AI compute wallet: the one account a company's inference runs on, where you manage who holds a seat and what their role is, and set the rules and requirements every inference request has to meet. Per-seat caps, the daily spend ceiling, which models are allowed, which routes and geographies are acceptable, which hosts are approved, and cutting off a member. Finance gets a single place to see and cap what the business spends on AI, and those rules are synced to the gateway and checked before a host is chosen. Buying credits or paying out a host runs as a Privy intent. Approving an intent returns 428 approval_signature_required with the exact bytes; the approver's browser signs those bytes and posts them to /intents/<id>/authorize.
Ledger. Key custody is built on wallet-cli's Key Ring: tor-agent seal pipes an API key in on stdin into ring encrypt, so only ciphertext ever touches disk and the key never reaches shell history or ps. The hacky part: Ledger's CLI has no primitive for enrolling a machine with no device attached, so we wrote one. tor-agent enroll --docker copies this Mac's Key Ring membership into a container's own keychain over stdin, and that container (with /dev/bus/usb empty, no Ledger can ever be plugged in) then opens its sealed key with no device present. Delete one keychain entry and it can open nothing, every file intact. This allows safely sharing of secrets for remote hosts/agents. Agent approvals are EIP-191 personal_sign on 44'/60'/0'/0/0 over a message binding agent, payer, model, request hash, credits, the limit hit, nonce and expiry, claimed once within five minutes. The same approval works in a browser over WebHID via the Device Management Kit.

name: Strata402
description: x402-powered pay-per-request DeFi service on Hedera — AI agents pay HBAR automatically, no API keys.
projectDescription: Strata402 is a pay-per-call service on Hedera built on the x402 payment standard. When an AI agent requests analysis without payment, the service responds with HTTP 402 and a signed payment requirement. The agent constructs a Hedera transaction, signs it, and resubmits the request with a PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header. The Blocky402 facilitator verifies and settles the payment on Hedera testnet, and the service returns the paid result — no API keys, no subscriptions, just metered payments settled in HBAR with sub-cent fees and fast finality.
howItsMade:
Strata402 is a Bun monorepo with four workspaces: an Express-based api-gateway, a TypeScript consuming-agent, a shared x402-sdk package, and a placeholder ai-engine. The gateway implements the x402 v2 "exact" payment scheme for Hedera using the official @x402/core, @x402/hedera, and @x402/express packages, so the protocol layer is never hand-rolled — payment requirements, headers (PAYMENT-REQUIRED, PAYMENT-SIGNATURE, PAYMENT-RESPONSE), and signature verification all go through the SDK.
The single MVP endpoint, POST /v1/strategy/yield-risk, returns HTTP 402 with a base64-encoded PaymentRequired object when called without payment: network hedera:testnet, asset 0.0.0 (native HBAR), amount expressed in integer tinybars (never decimals), and a payTo pulled from HEDERA_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID. The consuming-agent discovers the service catalog, decodes and fail-closed validates every field of that challenge (12 distinct rejection codes — wrong network, wrong asset, payTo equal to 0.0.0, non-integer amount, missing feePayer, etc.) before doing anything else. Only once a challenge passes validation does it build a partially-signed Hedera TransferTransaction with @hiero-ledger/sdk, wrap it into a PaymentPayload via ExactHederaScheme/createClientHederaSigner, and resubmit the request with a signed PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header.
Settlement runs through the public Blocky402 facilitator (verify + settle against hedera:testnet), and the resulting transaction is independently verifiable on HashScan and via the public Hedera Mirror Node REST API — no mocked or fabricated payment data anywhere in the flow. Every payment attempt is also logged to an HCS topic for an on-chain audit trail.
Development followed strict phase gates: each unit was built, tested (bun test, live integration tests against a running gateway), and reviewed before merging, with branch protection on main requiring pull requests. Yield/risk analysis is intentionally sourced only from the keyless, real Hedera Mirror Node account API — no SaucerSwap/Bonzo data is claimed live unless independently verified, in line with the project's no-fabrication policy.

name: Lamplighter
description: Lamplighter watches your lending position and defends it before liquidation hits.
projectDescription: Lamplighter is an agent that keeps watch over leveraged lending positions so they don't get liquidated while you're not looking. It pulls live health-factor data from Aave, Compound, Spark and a few other protocols through the Graph, using one shared query since they're all built on the same standardized schema underneath. When a position it's watching crosses a risk threshold, it repays part of the debt automatically using USDC that's been pre-approved, capped by limits the owner sets themselves so it can never spend more than they're comfortable with. It's meant to be the thing that reacts in the ten minutes you're asleep or away from your screen, not a replacement for actually managing your own risk.
howItsMade: The contracts are Solidity, built and tested with Foundry — a vault contract holds each user's USDC and only lets an authorized agent spend it if the owner's own preset caps and health-factor threshold actually allow it. The risk-scoring side is a TypeScript service that queries Messari's standardized lending subgraphs on The Graph — the same GraphQL query works across Aave v3, Compound v3, Spark and more, since they all share the same schema, which is really the whole point of using The Graph here instead of hitting each protocol's own API separately. The decision of when and how much to defend lives inside a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow, so the trigger threshold stays private instead of sitting in a public contract where it could get front-run. Once it decides to act, it settles the defense on Arc using Circle's USDC-native chain. The hackiest part is probably the demo fixture: we deployed our own tiny mock lending pool on testnet just so we could force a live liquidation scenario on stage, since you can't exactly crash real Aave on command.

name: AI Clearing Desk
description: AI clearing desk for tokenized fund trades, paid and settled on Hedera.
projectDescription: The Conformance Desk clears secondary-market trades in tokenized private-credit fund units. A seller locks the exact units in a Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio hold. Before the trade can clear, a Privy-controlled buyer agent pays 0.01 testnet USDC through Hedera x402 for an independent data-quality verdict. The service checks six live lending deployments through The Graph, signs an APPROVE or DENY decision, and binds it to that exact trade. The ClearingEscrow contract then executes or releases the hold. The result is verified through Hedera Mirror Node and anchored to Hedera Consensus Service for public replay.
howItsMade:
We built the asset and settlement layer with Hedera ATS, an EVM ClearingEscrow contract, Mirror Node, and HCS. ATS issues the fund units and locks them in a buyer-specific hold, which prevents the units from being spent twice while a decision is pending.
The buyer is an Ethereum server wallet managed by Privy and paired with a Hedera ECDSA account. Privy signs the Hedera transaction-body hashes remotely, so the buyer’s payment key is never exported into our application. A local policy checks the network, USDC token, recipient, fee payer, and maximum price before allowing the wallet to pay.
The verdict endpoint uses Hedera x402 and Blocky402 to charge 0.01 canonical testnet USDC. Payment verification happens before any data work, and settlement happens before the signed verdict is returned.
The Graph is the evidence layer. One standardized Messari Lending v3.1 query checks six pinned deployments across Aave, Compound, Morpho, and Spark. We combine live Gateway data with Subgraph MCP schema inspection, then run deterministic checks for indexing errors, freshness, schema agreement, deployment identity, and market invariants. Missing or invalid Graph evidence fails closed, so no verdict means no trade.
The final authorization commits to the asset, seller, buyer, amount, hold, policy, payment reference, action, expiry, and one-use nonce. After settlement, the agent confirms the contract event, ATS balance change, consumed nonce, Mirror Node finality, and HCS audit record. Our completed testnet run passed all 11 replay checks and transferred exactly one SPCF unit to the Privy-controlled buyer.

name: Graph Trail
description: A ledger of large stablecoin transfers where every number traces back to its onchain source.
projectDescription:
Graph Trail is a compliance-officer's ledger for large USDC/USDT/PYUSD transfers.
Ask a plain-English question and Claude resolves it into a filter, real transfer data comes from The Graph's Token API, and an AI-generated summary sits alongside a sortable table.
Every row links straight to its transaction on a public block explorer, so nothing shown is asserted without a source you can independently check yourself.
Note: this is my first project in blockchain. I hacked solo for a few hours, only to built something and having fun doing it. No rocket science here!
howItsMade:
Backend: FastAPI, with Pydantic models (Transfer, QueryFilter, FlagResult) as the single schema contract the whole app is built around.
Data sources sit behind one interface (TransferDataSource) chosen by a DATA_SOURCE env flag (fixture or token_api). The real data source calls The Graph's Token API directly for USDC/USDT/PYUSD transfers on Ethereum.
NL layer: a natural-language question ("USDC transfers over $1M last week") gets turned into a structured filter via a single forced tool (call to Claude Haiku 4.5). A second Claude call turns the resulting transfer list into a short plain-English summary.
Frontend: Streamlit, using its native column_config.LinkColumn and row-selection (on_select).
All fixture data is real, currently-existing on-chain transactions — pulled live via a public RPC (eth_getLogs). The NL layer is tested against the real Anthropic API, not just mocks. ruff and ty (types) stayed clean throughout.

name: KEEL
description: Liquidation protection whose strategy is sealed in a TEE — and provably never changed.
projectDescription:
Every on-chain liquidation-protection bot has a secret: the health factor at which it acts. That trigger is the most valuable number in the whole setup, and today it leaks by default. Collateral, debt, and wallet balances are public, so every action or inaction the bot takes at a given price is one bit of a binary search over its trigger — three well-placed price pushes locate a fixed threshold to ±0.005 HF. A located trigger plus a public reserve is a drain plan: push price to the line, force a defensive spend, repeat until the reserve is empty, then push through it. Whale positions get hunted like this in the real world (Hyperliquid's $521M short, Solend's $170M seizure panic).
Putting the bot in a TEE does not fix this. Hidden code still produces visible behavior, and the behavior is what leaks.
KEEL is a liquidation-defense agent whose trigger cannot be located from its behavior — and whose honesty can be independently verified afterwards. Three mechanisms:


The tripwire moves. trigger = clamp(base + k·σ + jitter(HMAC(salt, price-level))). One fresh, deterministic-but-secret jitter draw per price level, shifted only upward — randomness can make Keel act earlier, never later, so it never costs survival. No sequence of observations narrows the base below the jitter width.


The sealed envelope. Before the market moves, the enclave commits keccak256(policyHash ‖ salt) on-chain. Every defense carries an EIP-712 receipt signed by a key derived from the salt inside the enclave. Afterwards, reveal(policy, salt) lets anyone recompute every round's trigger from public PriceUpdate logs and check every action matched the policy that was sealed before anything happened. Private during, provable after.


Survival by construction. A hard floor trigger and an emergency override sit under all the cleverness; the clever part can only ever move action earlier.


We also shipped the attacker: a real Bayesian Hunter that watches public (HF, acted?) streams. Against the fixed-threshold starter it collapses to a point estimate in ~3 observations; against Keel its uncertainty is floored at the jitter width no matter how long it watches. The live app runs the replay, the Hunter, a full stop-hunt attack simulation, and a /verify page that reconstructs everything from Sepolia events — commitment block before scenario start, receipt signature recovery, reveal preimage check, per-round trigger audit.
howItsMade:
The core is a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow: a handlerInTee woken by two triggers (60s cron heartbeat + a PriceUpdate log trigger for instant reaction) that runs the entire protection loop inside the enclave and returns a single status word — IDLE / SAFE / DEFENDED — so nothing numeric ever leaves the TEE. Chainlink CRE is what makes the thesis possible at all: Vault DON secrets released only to the enclave mean the salt (which drives the jitter, the receipt-signing key, and the commitment) genuinely never exists outside it.
How the protection loop actually works, tick by tick. The enclave is stateless, so every tick it rebuilds the world from public data: one batched read (≤5 HTTP calls, quota-compliant) fetches vETHPrice, the position struct, scenarioStartTime, all PriceUpdate logs since the scenario started, and its own past Repay/Deposit logs. The price-update count is the round number — the clock everything else runs on.
From collateral × price × 0.78 / debt it computes the health factor in basis points, using the contract's own integer math (the on-chain hf is a floored ×100 integer, so true HF 1.009 already liquidates — Keel treats HF 1.01 as the real liquidation line, not 1.00). Then it builds this round's trigger from three layers:

Volatility term — an EWMA over log-returns of the price series (half-life ~4 updates) scales the trigger up when the market moves fast, capped at +0.02 so an attacker who manufactures volatility can't drag the trigger up indefinitely.
Jitter — HMAC-SHA256(salt, round) mapped to a uniform draw in [0, jmax), added upward only. One fresh draw per price level; re-used while price sits still, so camping at one level leaks nothing new. Upward-only is the survival proof: randomness can only make Keel act earlier, never later.
Hard floor + emergency override — the base trigger is the floor under everything, and if HF ever drops below the emergency line the controller acts immediately, ignoring jitter, cooldown, and per-action caps. Survival never depends on the clever part.

If HF ≤ armed trigger (and a one-price-level cooldown has passed), a cost solver decides what to do, not just that it acts: it prices repay vs deposit in expected score points — repay lifts HF ~35% more per dollar but forfeits debt-time score, so deposit wins early in the scenario and repay wins late — and solves for the exact amount that restores HF to a jittered target (an independent draw, so even the level Keel restores to leaks nothing). Then it signs the defend tx inside the enclave, signs an EIP-712 receipt with a key derived from the same salt, and sends both — action at nonce n, receipt at n+1, same EOA, so the binding is checkable on Etherscan.
The controller is one pure, integer-math package (contract-exact arithmetic, no boundary mismatch), and the exact decide() that runs in the enclave is the exact function the replay and the Hunter's attack simulator import — one source of truth, no demo-vs-prod drift.
On-chain: PolicyCommit (one-shot commit, reveal verifies keccak256(policyHash ‖ salt)) and Receipts (EIP-712, ecrecover must equal the committed signer), plus a byte-for-byte copy of the official ChallengeLending — proven identical to the deployed bytecode by a fidelity script (metadata stripped), then property-tested against a real local deployment over 200 random action sequences so our scoring mirror is trusted, not assumed. The policy commitment includes a reproducible keccak hash of the controller source tree, so the reveal binds the algorithm, not just the numbers.
The statelessness is also what makes verification possible: because the jitter round is just the public price-update index, anyone holding the revealed salt can replay every round's trigger from logs alone and audit every action and every inaction. The verifier does exactly that — it never trusts a receipt's self-reported HF, it recomputes it independently from PriceUpdate logs and flags mismatches.

name: MeterX402
description: Turn any API, dataset or AI agent into a pay-per-use Hedera x402 service in seconds
projectDescription:
MeterX402
Turn any API into a metered x402 API. Buyers pay for exactly what each call returns, not a flat price per request.

The Problem
x402 enables APIs to charge per request, but a request is often the wrong unit of pricing.

A 5-word AI response and a 5-page response cost the same.
A 1-day weather forecast and a 7-day forecast cost the same.

Sellers therefore have to price for the worst case, and light users overpay. This is especially painful for AI agents, which make many small API calls.

One npm Package
npx mx402 publish <url> --wallet <account>

MeterX402:

Calls the API once and reads its response.
Automatically determines what should be metered:

Tokens for LLMs
Rows for lists
Entities for GraphQL


Suggests a price based on the measured unit.
Starts a payment gateway in front of the API.
Registers the service in a searchable registry for agents.

No code changes required. Your upstream API key never leaves your machine.

Pay for Exactly What You Get
The gateway:

Runs the API request.
Measures the returned units.
Holds the response.
Returns 402 Payment Required with the exact price.
Ties the price to a hash of the response.
Lets the buyer's wallet verify the price against its budget.
Releases the response after payment.
Returns a receipt that anyone can verify on-chain.


Sell Datasets Too
npx mx402 data file.csv

Turn a CSV, JSON, or JSONL file into a queryable API priced per cell.

Schema is free.
Row count is free.
The original file stays on your machine.


Sell AI Agents
Point mx402 publish at an LLM or your own agent endpoint.

Price the agent per token.
Stream responses through Metered Tabs.
Generate an A2A agent card.
Create a Hedera HCS-14 identity.


Multi-Chain Settlement
One flag determines where payments settle:
| Hedera | Base Sepolia | Solana Devnet

One Dashboard
The Deployer page shows:

Income, paid calls, and units sold.
Price of every call.
How much buyers saved compared with flat pricing.
Every payment with its blockchain explorer link.
A service registry with reputation scores based on real settlements.

Reputation data is anchored to Hedera Consensus Service.

Onchain Data
The Graph

One query across 15 standardized DEX subgraphs.
One query across 15 lending subgraphs.
Arbitrary GraphQL queries against any subgraph.
Payment per result.
No Graph API key required.
Failed queries cost nothing.

Uniswap

Uniswap Trading API quotes are sold per call.


The DEX Analyst
An AI agent that pays for its own research.

Performs four paid research steps.
Returns four payment receipts.
Only reports numbers that it actually paid to retrieve.
Can build a Uniswap swap transaction for the user's wallet without ever submitting the transaction.


Use It From the AI You Already Have
MeterX402 connects to:

Claude
VS Code — Copilot or our extension
ChatGPT

Setup takes only a few steps.
Each AI agent pays using the user's own testnet account, directly from their machine and within their configured budget.

The Vision
Machines pay machines directly.
No signup. No API key. No human approval for every call.
howItsMade:
MeterX402 — How It Works
Flow

Publish. The seller runs npx mx402 publish <url> --wallet <account>. It calls the API once, reads the response, and detects what to meter — tokens, rows at a JSON path, cells, entities, bytes — along with a starting price.
Gateway up. It starts a gateway in front of the API. The seller's upstream key is injected server-side and never reaches buyers. mx402 data file.csv does the same for a dataset, priced per cell.
Meter, then quote. When a buyer calls, the gateway runs the request first, counts the units, holds the body, and replies 402 Payment Required with the exact price and a SHA-256 of that body.
Pay. The buyer's client checks the price against its budget and signs one x402 payment. A settlement adapter sends it to the right facilitator for the chain.
Release. After settlement the same body is released with a receipt. Every event streams to the hub, which runs the registry, reputation scores, analytics, and the web app (marketplace, Try it, Playground, Deployer dashboard).
Plug in. AI clients connect three ways: an MCP server with 12 tools (Claude, Copilot, Cursor) via the mx402 connector; a REST API with an OpenAPI spec behind a bearer token (ChatGPT Custom GPT Actions); and a VS Code extension. All of them sign with the user's own key, never a shared wallet.


Partner Technologies
Hedera (default settlement)

Payments settle through the blocky402 facilitator in HBAR or HTS tokens.
Hedera Consensus Service stores a public receipt for every payment and anchors reputation evidence, so the dashboard is auditable.
Native allowances power Metered Tabs: a buyer approves once and an LLM answer streams token by token, settled in batches.
Scheduled transactions power cancellable subscriptions.
Every service gets an HCS-14 agent ID.
The mirror node verifies every transfer.

The Graph

Messari's standardized schemas let one query cover 15 DEX subgraphs and another cover 15 lending subgraphs, across chains, in one shape. That is what makes the analyst's "lend or provide liquidity?" comparison possible.
A circuit breaker drops slow indexers, and Uniswap's own v3 subgraph answers when a standardized one fails.
Any subgraph can be queried and paid per entity, with no Graph key for the buyer.
4 MCP tools and a SKILL.md make it usable by any agent.

Uniswap

Trading API /quote, /check_approval and /swap are sold per call.
Our swap builder turns a quote into the approval, a signed Permit2 message, and swap calldata (classic routes and UniswapX) — never broadcast.

Base and Solana

USDC through x402.org: EIP-3009 on Base, SPL transfers on Solana.
--- when used, so npx mx402 starts fast.

name: Agent Allowance
description: An agent shouldn't hold keys. It should get a revocable allowance to pay for its own data.
projectDescription:
AI agents can now decide to spend money, but today you either hand them a wallet with everything in it, or they cannot pay at all. Allowance is the middle option.
An agent watches a real Uniswap v3 position on Base and warns when it deteriorates. Every piece of data it needs costs money and is paid per request. The agent spends from an allowance with a limit and an expiry: before each query a deterministic rule decides whether the data is worth its price, so the agent refuses to pay when its data is still fresh or the query no longer fits the budget. When the allowance runs out, it stops by itself. The owner can revoke it in one click, which burns the allowance token on-chain.
A Claude analyst reads the paid data and raises OK / WATCH / ACT alerts, but it never decides spending.
howItsMade:
TypeScript end to end.

The Graph: data comes from a Messari Standardized Subgraph (DEX AMM Extended schema) for Uniswap v3 on Base, queried with a Subgraph Studio API key; one query shape reads both the position and token USD prices. The same priced tools are exposed over MCP.
Hedera: each query sits behind an x402 payment gate built on @x402/hono, charging USDC (HTS 0.0.429274) per tool and settled through the Blocky402 facilitator; settlement only happens when data is delivered. The allowance itself is a bond issued with Asset Tokenization Studio contracts, allocated to the agent, and burned with controllerRedeemByPartition on revoke.
Arc + Circle: each paid query is settled in USDC on Arc testnet from a Circle Developer-Controlled Wallet via the Circle SDK, with an idempotency key derived from the payment so it can never settle twice.
A live panel (Hono + SSE) shows each sponsor step lighting up, budget, prices, decisions, refusals, the analyst alert and the revoke button, with HashScan and Arcscan links.
Hacky bits found on real testnet: Hedera hollow accounts cannot send tokens until they pay a fee themselves, so the agent account is completed first; ATS factory and resolver must be called by their EVM aliases, not long-zero addresses; the relay's gas estimate for the burn is too low, so the burn sets an explicit gas limit; Circle native USDC transfers need the wallet's tokenId, not an empty token address.
All payments in the demo are real testnet transactions, linked in the README.

name: ACR
description: Every desk runs TCA. No AI agent ever has. Now one does, on Arc: public on The Graph, human-backed.
projectDescription:
Every institutional trading desk runs transaction-cost analysis on its fills: did I pay more than the market at the moment I traded, and to whom? No AI agent has ever been able to ask that, because there was no benchmark to ask it against. Agents pay per call for inference, GPU time and data at whatever that seller quotes that hour, and nothing tells them they overpaid.
ACR is the benchmark. It is a live, on-chain reference rate for machine compute on Arc (ACR-INF, ACR-GPU, ACR-DATA), recovered hourly from Arc's own USDC payment exhaust by a manipulation-resistant estimator, signed by a Circle custody wallet, and published with a confidence interval and the USDC an attacker would have to burn to move it one basis point. That existed before ETHOnline. It is the frozen baseline and claims no credit here.
What was built during the event is Machine TCA, the first transaction-cost analysis for AI agents, in four parts.
Benchmark, in public. Every x402 nanopayment settlement on Arc is benchmarked inside a subgraph mapping against the ACR print the payer could have seen at the block it traded (the arrival-price convention, the standard implementation-shortfall measure). The slippage in basis points is computed by The Graph, not asserted by us, and anyone can query it. make recompute re-derives the index from the indexed tape and checks it against the chain.
Rate. Sellers get A–D grades from the same tape (fairness, cleanliness, human depth, attestation freshness), with the sample size and the synthetic share printed on every card, so a reroute points somewhere actually fair rather than merely cheap.
Humans, not wallets. Wallets are free; people are not. HumanIdMirror records, per week, which wallets act for one verified human as a rotated cluster id, never a World ID nullifier, so the manipulation bound can be denominated in people. ACROracleV2 posts that human-adjusted bound beside the wallet-denominated one. An agent can present a proof and get one TCA across every wallet its human owns, and the API gate meters all of a person's keys as one budget: ten wallets, one bill. A human claim the chain cannot confirm is a 401, not a downgrade.
Reach. Six read-only MCP tools (my_tca, reroute_suggestion, seller_rating, benchmark_price, get_rate, query_tape) put TCA inside any agent host, and an "Ask the Tape" skill lets a judge interrogate the live subgraph in plain English through The Graph's own Subgraph MCP.
The loop closes in CI and on camera. The buyer agent reads its own TCA, sees which seller it overpaid, and moves its next Circle Gateway nanopayment to the one it overpaid least; that settlement is indexed with its own slippage, so the agent's TCA improves from public data. Three such reroute settlements are archived from CI's own buyer, and a drivable version lives at arc-compute-rate.vercel.app/loop.
Stated plainly: this is a Continuity project. Baseline tag v1.0-submission; 45 commits and 41,200 insertions since, 91.6% of them in files that did not exist before, 0.7% baseline churn, all re-derivable from CONTINUITY.md. The testnet tape is partly our own flow, flagged synthetic on chain and disclosed on every card. Demo identities are World ID Sandbox identities, flagged the same way. Arc mainnet opens Sep 16: ACR is deployment-ready with a chain-id-checked runbook and a dry run of all five deploys, not deployed. Seven contracts are live on Arc testnet, three of them new. 677 Python, 156 Foundry, 159 terminal and 31 agent tests are green, and a CI audit re-measures every number in the docs, including these.
Live: arc-compute-rate.vercel.app · API acr-api-1fto.onrender.com · Subgraph Studio ethonline v0.2.0 on arc-testnet · github.com/kaustubh76/ACR---Arc-Compute-Rate
howItsMade:
The stack, layer by layer. The estimator is Python: a Kalman-class state-space deconvolution of Circle Gateway's batching operator (payments arrive batched, so a naive VWAP measures the scheduler, not the market), a Louvain-clustered sybil and wash cleaning stage, an α-trimmed volume-weighted median, and a hedonic regression that strips seller quality to leave a constant-quality rate, with a manipulation-cost bound published beside every print. Contracts are Solidity on Foundry, live on Arc testnet: ACROracle, ACROracleV2, AttestationRegistry, ACRFutures, FeedAccessAttestor, ReceiptMirror and HumanIdMirror, with unit and invariant suites. The x402-gated API is FastAPI, the terminal is Next.js, the buyer agent is TypeScript on Circle's @circle-fin/x402-batching, the subgraph is AssemblyScript on Subgraph Studio, and the MCP server is TypeScript. Everything runs credential-free against a calibrated simulator; every live path is additive.
Arc. USDC is the gas token and fees are deterministic, which is the only reason "attack cost per basis point" is a number rather than a distribution. Three contracts were added during the event. ReceiptMirror puts every x402 settlement on chain as raw features only (unit, quantity, synthetic flag) so the subgraph can benchmark it. HumanIdMirror records weekly human clusters. ACROracleV2 extends the print with a cleaning-policy hash and the human-denominated bound, keeping v1's six signed fields as a strict typehash prefix so the immutable ACRFutures.oracle is never orphaned. Mainnet: make deploy-mainnet-dry simulates all five deploys with a chain-id preflight.
The Graph is load-bearing, not decorative: the slippage number is computed in the mapping. The hard part was timing. The arrival price must be the print at the trade block, but the quantity needed for a unit price arrives in a later ReceiptMirror block. So the Gateway settlement handler writes a mutable PendingSettlement that snapshots the LatestPrint at the trade block, and the ReceiptMirror handler reads that snapshot, computes unit price and slippageBp, and creates the immutable Settlement. The keeper never supplies an arrival price, so it cannot flatter one. Daily seller and payer roll-ups are maintained in the mapping with a seven-bucket slippage histogram (the schema deliberately avoids @aggregation and says why), and the p50 is interpolated from the histogram because there is no median in a sum. Studio on arc-testnet indexes about three seconds behind head. acr recompute --rederive-cleaning re-clusters from on-chain funding edges under the policy hash each print carries and reports whether its exclusions match the keeper's, so the one keeper-authored step is re-derivable rather than trusted. The acr-analyst skill carries the schema map, unit conventions and six canned questions so The Graph's Subgraph MCP can answer a judge in plain English.
World. HumanIdMirror stores keccak256(nullifier, salt, window), never the nullifier, and the salt commitment is an immutable constructor argument, so the resolver cannot retroactively regroup wallets into whichever clustering flatters a number. Every cluster carries a sandbox flag from the signed message through the event into every rating, because every demo identity is a World ID Sandbox identity and the reader should not have to take the README's word for it. The proof path is a 401 challenge, a CAIP-122 signature, then /tca/human with the nonce spent on use; make prove-human runs it end to end with nothing secret. The API gate has three tiers: anonymous shares a host ceiling, carded gets a per-key bucket via an EIP-712 agent card, and human gets a per-person bucket because the card's cluster claim is checked against HumanIdMirror.clusterOf on chain. The card's domain deliberately names no verifyingContract, which is what permissionless means here: no registry, no allowlist, the gate believes the key.
Circle. Gateway x402 nanopayments gate the API at $0.0001 a query on both sides, developer-controlled wallets sign every print, and the buyer uses the Agent Stack SDK. Two things cost real time: EIP-3009 needs a signature ecrecover can verify, so the hedger's smart account trades while its backing EOA pays; and circle wallet execute cannot build a transaction carrying a negative int256, so an agent on that path can open a position but never close one.
One guard is not from any sponsor and is named rather than folded in. Agent-to-agent traffic (the carded subgraph read) passes Google Cloud Model Armor in both directions, fail-closed, from asia-south1. On 2026-09-12 it refused a prompt injection by name (pi_and_jailbreak) over the public internet, driven through the real endpoint rather than by calling the module. /armor/info reports which backend answered, because an offline pattern floor and Model Armor look identical from outside and only one of them is a screen.
The hacky bits worth admitting. CI runs with zero secrets and stands up its own anvil, and a dedicated step fails the build if the on-chain suites skip, because a skipping test looks exactly like a passing one and that is how a real regression once stayed green for a day. scripts/verify_claims.py re-measures every count, address and diff statistic against the documents that state them, and CONTINUITY.md's numbers are anchored to a named commit range at both ends, because a statistic measured against HEAD goes stale the moment the commit correcting it lands. The free-tier API host pings its own public URL from its 60-second loop so the hourly press does not fall asleep with it. Arc's eth_getLogs has a hard cap near 15,000 blocks and separate 429 throttling, and a reader must never treat a throttle as a range error, because backing off the range once collapsed a 7.9-hour walk to eleven minutes. And a bare-digit find-and-replace on a test count once nearly rewrote an on-chain settlement price in the docs, so every count edit is anchored on its neighbouring words.
