name: Wifiproof
description: Private proof of presence using venue WiFi, World ID, and zero-knowledge location proofs.
projectDescription: WiFiProof is a privacy-preserving alternative to visitor books and public attendance lists. It lets someone prove they were physically present at an event without publishing their name, wallet address, IP address, or exact GPS coordinates. A valid check-in combines four signals: World ID for unique-human verification, the venue’s approved internet connection, a rotating QR code displayed at the venue, and a zero-knowledge proof that the attendee is within the event radius. The final result is an event-specific proof of attendance rather than a record of the person’s identity. WiFiProof is designed for conferences, schools, coworking spaces, and buildings that need reliable attendance without collecting more personal data than necessary.
howItsMade:
The frontend is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The proximity circuit is written in Noir, and Barretenberg generates an UltraHonk proof directly in the browser, so the attendee’s coordinates never leave their device. The proof shows that the coordinates fall within the venue’s radius and binds the result to one event. A generated Solidity verifier checks the proof on Base, while EAS records the attendance receipt.
World ID is the unique-human layer. The app verifies the World ID proof and creates an event-scoped identifier, preventing one person from checking in repeatedly without revealing who they are. Browsers cannot reliably expose or prove a WiFi SSID, so I used a practical workaround: the server checks whether the request came through the venue’s registered public network range and also requires a short-lived rotating QR challenge. These checks are combined into a signed EIP-712 authorization, and a CDP-managed relayer submits the transaction without exposing the attendee’s wallet on-chain. Supabase stores event configuration and manages idempotent relay jobs. The public prototype is deployed on Base Sepolia, and the V2 contracts add anonymous sponsored claims and stronger event binding.

name: PartyBid
description: A social music queue where partygoers bid to decide what the DJ plays
projectDescription:
PartyBid is a social music bidding app that turns the party song queue into a live priority market. Guests join a party, request songs, and bid for the songs they want the DJ to play. If another guest wants the same song more, they can outbid the current bid, automatically moving the request higher in the queue. The DJ gets a clear, real-time priority queue instead of having to choose between competing requests.
Once a song is played, the guest can like or dislike it, and the commitment can be settled based on the outcome. PartyBid uses Privy for frictionless social login and embedded wallets, while 1inch Aqua provides the shared liquidity layer for committing and settling bids. The result is a fun consumer experience that hides the complexity of Web3 while demonstrating a real on-chain lifecycle: join, bid, outbid, commit, play, react, and settle.
howItsMade:
PartyBid is built as a full-stack Web3 application using Next.js, React, MongoDB Atlas, Ethers.js, Solidity, and Privy. The frontend provides the party experience: DJs create and manage parties, while guests join, request songs, place bids, outbid other guests, commit their winning bids, react after a song is played, and settle the final outcome.
Privy powers frictionless authentication through social login, including Google, while creating and managing embedded wallets behind the scenes. This lets users interact with on-chain functionality without starting with a traditional crypto-wallet onboarding flow.
The backend uses Next.js API routes and MongoDB to maintain authoritative party, song request, bid, and settlement state. We deliberately don't trust client-provided settlement details. Instead, the backend derives the maker, bid amount, outcome, recipient, identifiers, and strategy data from server-side records, then generates an EIP-712 authorization signed by a dedicated settlement signer.
The core Web3 integration is built around 1inch Aqua on Arc Testnet. When a guest commits a bid, the client receives canonical strategyBytes from the backend and uses them to create an Aqua ship() position. The corresponding strategyHash is cryptographically bound to the settlement, so the commitment and later payout reference the same liquidity context.
We built a custom PartyBidAquaApp Solidity contract that validates the EIP-712 settlement authorization, enforces WUSDC-only settlement, restricts outcomes to player or platform payouts, binds platform payouts to the configured recipient, checks deadlines and signatures, and prevents replay attacks. On settlement, the contract consumes the Aqua virtual balance through pull() and routes the WUSDC payout to the authorized recipient.
One particularly hacky part was making the whole flow feel like a normal consumer app while preserving the full on-chain lifecycle underneath: Google login → embedded wallet → bid → outbid → Aqua commitment → DJ plays → guest reacts → EIP-712 authorization → on-chain settlement. We also built blockchain-first confirmation: MongoDB only marks a settlement as COMPLETED after the backend independently verifies the real transaction receipt and SettlementExecuted event, rather than trusting the frontend.

name: Covenant
description: A bonded watch over a lending position, sold per evaluation and paid for in both directions
projectDescription:
Covenant sells a bonded obligation to watch a DeFi lending position. One x402 payment on Hedera opens a watch, evaluations are billed per subgraph deployment actually read, and a 1 HBAR bond moves to the borrower the moment a promised evaluation fails to land. It reads Aave v3, Aave v2, Spark, Compound v3, Compound v2, Morpho Blue, Morpho Aave v3, Moonwell, Venus, MakerDAO, BENQI, Iron Bank and Sonne through one unchanged GraphQL query against Messari standardized subgraphs, measures which deployments actually conform before trusting any of them, and repays debt on Aave v3 Sepolia when a health factor crosses the mandate.
Every claim here is a transaction you can open. The service is live at https://covenant-x402.vercel.app, registered on-chain as ERC-8004 agent 120 on Hedera testnet, and its entire billing history is a public Hedera Consensus Service topic (0.0.10510015) that anyone can replay from a free mirror node.
THE PROBLEM. A borrower who sleeps through a move gets liquidated. Today they pay for that risk in over-collateralisation, because every alternative is a monitor: it tells you something and owes you nothing. A monitor that misses your liquidation loses nothing. Covenant is the first version of this that is exposed when it fails.
THE PRODUCT. The seller posts a bond, the terms live on consensus, and the borrower adjudicates from the public journal without asking the seller for permission or for data. Both outcomes are proven on testnet: a breached covenant moved 1 HBAR to the borrower, and a kept one moved nothing. That single property, a promise with a price and a consequence, is what separates this from every liquidation dashboard in the category.
A MACHINE BUSINESS WITH REAL UNIT ECONOMICS. Covenant sells evaluations over x402 on Hedera and buys its own evidence over x402 from The Graph's gateway on Base. Revenue and cost of goods are both on-chain, so the margin on any individual call is recomputable by a third party. It is an agent that runs a business, not an agent that spends an allowance.
IT KNOWS WHAT IT DOES NOT KNOW. A $57M Aave position scores 0.821 from the standardized fields, which reads as already liquidatable. It is not: the collateral is sUSDe, whose base maximumLTV is 0, so the position exists only inside e-mode and the real threshold is not in the schema. Covenant names the cause and declines, because a confident wrong number at 3am costs a borrower more than silence. Judgement about when not to answer is the hardest thing to build into a risk service and it is built into this one.
ONE QUERY, THIRTEEN PROTOCOLS, ZERO PER-PROTOCOL CODE. Adding a lending market is a single line in a registry. Schema CID QmNnWjciPb8 is byte-identical across five deployments spanning three protocols and four networks: one content hash, one query shape, whole ecosystems of collateral.
AND IT ACTS. When the mandate is crossed the guard signs and broadcasts a protective repay, then asserts the health factor actually rose: 1.105 to 1.350, on chain, verifiable.
howItsMade:
THE DATA LAYER IS ONE QUERY. packages/schema/src/query.ts holds a single GraphQL document that runs unchanged against Messari Lending Protocol schema 2.0.1, 3.0.1 and 3.1.0 across 19 deployments. packages/schema/src/registry.ts is the only file in the repository that names a protocol. There is no per-protocol code anywhere else, so onboarding a new lending market is one line in an array. The proof that the standard earns its keep: schema CID QmNnWjciPb8 is byte-identical across Aave V2 Ethereum, Aave V3 Ethereum, Aave V3 Polygon, Aave V3 Avalanche and Spark Ethereum.
RISK BRANCHES ON ONE STANDARDIZED FIELD. LendingProtocol.riskType decides whether an account's positions net together (GLOBAL: Aave, Compound, Spark, Venus, Moonwell) or are scoped per market (ISOLATED: Morpho Blue, MakerDAO). That single field is the entire protocol-awareness of the engine, which is why the thirteenth protocol costs the same as the second.
CONFORMANCE IS MEASURED, NOT ASSERTED. scripts/conformance.ts probes every registered deployment for schema coverage and lag against chain head on every run. It caught Spark Lend on Gnosis answering every query correctly while indexing 86.5 days behind, which a hand-written registry would have happily used to price live collateral. The oracle re-measures per request and names anything it excludes.
PAYMENTS. @x402/express with ExactHederaScheme, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet. Price is a function of the request line: 0.0575 HBAR for the full 19-deployment index, 0.025 HBAR for two protocols, quoted in the 402 before the buyer signs anything. The middleware only ever sees the URL, which is precisely why the quote is knowable in advance.
RECEIPTS CLOSE THE LOOP. Every settled request writes an HCS message carrying its own settlement transaction id, so the whole bill replays against the ledger from a free mirror node. Receipts record deploymentsQuoted alongside deploymentsDelivered, so the buyer can audit the meter rather than trust it.
THE BOND HAS NO DATABASE. Terms, evaluations and settlements are all messages on one HCS topic, folded into state on read. GET /v1/covenant/:id is free and unauthenticated, because the borrower must be able to check the seller's promise without asking the seller. Adjudication runs on the public journal, so both parties reach the same verdict from the same bytes.
IT EXECUTES. scripts/guard-act.ts repays debt on Aave v3 Sepolia through viem, simulating first and then asserting the health factor actually rose. A receipt proves a call landed; only the post-condition proves the position is safer, so the script exits non-zero if it is not.
IDENTITY AND DISCOVERY. Registered as ERC-8004 agent 120 on Hedera testnet, with the agent id learned by eth_call against register() before writing so the document is complete in a single transaction. It is stored as a data: URI, so the identity resolves with no hosting dependency at all. GET /v1/catalog is free and unauthenticated, so an agent that has never met the service reads what it sells and what it costs before spending anything.
BUILT FOR THE PLATFORM IT RUNS ON. HBAR is absent from @x402/core's DEFAULT_ASSETS, so client spend controls silently reject every HBAR payment until the asset is allowed explicitly. The settlement header decodes to transaction while the SDK calls it transactionId. Serverless freezes the instance the moment a response is sent, which kills any receipt written in res.on('finish') unless it is held open with waitUntil. Each of these is handled in code, and each is the kind of thing that only shows up under real traffic.

name: RWA Outlet
description: Instant RWA liquidity through 1inch Aqua, Uniswap v4, and ERC-7540 queues
projectDescription:
RWA Outlets is an instant-liquidity market for tokenized real-world assets. Tokenized T-bills and private credit (~$33B) redeem on issuer timelines — T+2 up to 180 days — so holders needing cash either wait or dump at unpredictable discounts.
With RWA Outlets, holders exit to USDC in one transaction through three risk-tiered pools built as 1inch Aqua strategies with SwapVM programs: Express (NAV minus 5–25 bps), Patient (onchain Dutch-decay auction that discovers the fair discount), and Market (two-sided AMM, so buyers can enter too). Pricing plugs into the unmodified official 1inch router via a custom NavExtruction instruction; KYC is a soulbound NFT checked by stock opcodes. Patient holders instead queue through an ERC-7540 redemption vault and collect full NAV plus accrued yield. That instant-vs-patient gap (~2.5%) is the profit motor: makers buy below NAV and redeem at NAV.
Retail LPs deposit USDC into ERC-4626 curator vaults run by an AI agent that reads only our live Graph subgraph and logs every decision as query → reasoning → transaction. A Uniswap v4 lane (custom compliance + TWAP hook) provides fallback routing and price sanity, and the router always executes the user's best quote. Live on Sepolia: contracts, subgraph, faucet, app, and agent.
howItsMade:
CONTRACTS (Foundry, Solidity 0.8.30 + 0.8.26)
The swap engine is the official 1inch stack: Aqua + AquaSwapVMRouter vendored and redeployed to Sepolia as untouched bytecode — never reimplemented. Settlement safety (per-order reentrancy lock, pull/push verification) is inherited from 1inch's audited router, not our code.
Custom pricing enters through the one official extension point: NavExtruction implements the IExtruction/IStaticExtruction duals as a single function branching on isStaticContext, so quote() and swap() return identical amounts. Three modes: fixed NAV spread (Express), Dutch decay (Patient — onchain replacement for RFQ bidding), NAV band post-check on the xyc AMM (Market). Handles exactIn/exactOut, both directions, 18d/6d decimal scaling, maker-favoring rounding.
Each pool is an Aqua strategy: an order template with useAquaInsteadOfSignature, so shipped virtual balances replace EIP-712 signatures — which is exactly what lets our ERC-4626 CuratorVault be a contract maker. Fills are hard-capped by shipped balances (no invalidators needed); one USDC treasury concurrently backs every pool it ships to.
RedemptionQueue: ERC-7540 + ERC-7575 async vault with an external share — share() returns the RWA token itself, the vault mints nothing, deposits are disabled, requestId = issuer batch epoch, FIFO claims, solvency structural (pays only from received settlement cash).
CuratorVault: sync 4626 deposits, async 7540 exit epochs (closes the classic stale-price 4626 arb), mandate-scoped createPool()/recycle() for the AI curator.
Uniswap v4 lane: RWAGateHook (CREATE2-mined address) gates swaps/liquidity on a soulbound KYC NFT with the real user forwarded via hookData, and doubles as a cumulative-price TWAP oracle in afterSwap. V4Venue settles swaps in its own unlockCallback and quotes through the official V4Quoter (revert-simulation, called via eth_call). OutletRouter arbitrates Aqua pools vs v4 and enforces a TWAP sanity band on program quotes.
KYC is a soulbound ERC-721 checked by stock SwapVM opcodes — no custom compliance opcode needed.
93 forge tests (unit/fuzz/invariant, incl. the quote==swap duals against the real vendored router), plus a standalone Foundry simulation repo: 180-day time-warped queue lifecycle, CSV → matplotlib PnL report, and an anvil demo where the issuer window is enforced onchain at compressed timescale (60 s ≙ T+90d — provable, not narrated).
THE GRAPH
graph-cli/AssemblyScript subgraph indexing both the official Aqua/router events and ours: strategies with decoded pool params, per-pool virtual balances, queue/vault epochs, NAV history, TWAP observations, day rollups. Published to Studio and the decentralized network.
Hacky: the hook ABI carries two ObservationRecorded signatures so pre- and post-upgrade hooks index together, and a Legacy router data source keeps pre-migration swap history after a state-carrying router redeploy.
AI CURATOR AGENT (Node 22 + Express + MongoDB)
An OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions facade; behind it an LLM (Groq or Claude) runs a tool-use loop against an in-process MCP server (in-memory transport, no extra process) exposing get_subgraph_schema + query_subgraph. The subgraph is the agent's ONLY chain view — every curator decision is logged as query → reasoning → tx. The MCP server also runs standalone over stdio for Claude Desktop.
FRONTEND (React 18 + Vite, wagmi v3 + viem, TanStack Query, Framer Motion)
Live reads of the Sepolia contracts (NAV oracle, Aqua shipped balances, router best-of quotes incl. v4, queue epochs).
Uniswap Trading API as the secondary execution rail: check_approval → quote → swap with CLASSIC vs UniswapX (Dutch v2/v3, gasless) response normalization and EIP-712 permitData signing. Each demo RWA maps to a mainnet twin (rwaTBILL→USDY, rwaCREDIT→USDe) and every trade is priced against the Uniswap route side-by-side, in bps.
Hacky: the API has no CORS, so a same-origin proxy injects x-api-key server-side — the key never reaches the browser.
ONBOARDING & INFRA
Faucet dApp (React + viem + Foundry) whose drip() mints demo tokens AND the soulbound KYC NFT in one tx — one click to become a compliant demo user.
Terraform on DigitalOcean App Platform; Dockerized frontend/backend, secrets injected as TF vars.

name: AquaQoS
description: Protected-capacity scheduling for shared maker inventory on 1inch Aqua and SwapVM.
projectDescription:
Aqua lets independently-accounted strategies share a maker’s liquidity, but virtual balances do not reserve the same real ERC-20 inventory. AquaQoS adds protected-capacity scheduling: a custom SwapVM CAPACITY_GUARD instruction admits a fill only when configured capacity for sibling strategies remains covered.
The app includes a replayable comparison workspace, reproducible tests and benchmarks, and public Sepolia receipts showing protected rejection, successful sibling fills, replenishment, and real token transfers. AquaQoS is a bounded v0 protocol prototype, not a production or external-audit claim.
howItsMade:
AquaQoS is built on the official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM contracts. Aqua remains load-bearing for virtual accounting and final settlement. We added a restricted maker vault and a custom SwapVM instruction, CAPACITY_GUARD (opcode 0x05), which evaluates configured protected and burst capacity before canonical fee-free XYC settlement. AquaQoS changes fill admission; it does not replace Aqua’s settlement model.
The protocol is written in Solidity 0.8.30 and tested with Hardhat. We reproduced the shared-inventory failure first, then added deterministic regression tests, adversarial cases, three fuzz properties, a bounded capacity model, transaction replays, and A/B/C/C100 benchmark fixtures. A public Sepolia deployment provides exact Sourcify source matches and 22 retained transactions, including ERC-20 transfer receipts, guarded rejections, sibling fills, replenishment, reverse-direction settlement, and maker exit.
The product surface is a static Next.js and React app deployed on Vercel. It provides a capacity workspace, public onchain evidence, proof mapping, and curated technical documentation. Etherscan and Sourcify links let judges independently inspect deployed contracts and transactions.

name: Aqua Funds Manager
description: Pre-built liquidity management strategies on Robinhood adapted to risk tolerance using 1inch Aqua.
projectDescription: Aqua Funds Manager is a 1inch Aqua app built on Robinhood. It offers 3 x pre-defined fund allocation strategies (Conservative, Balanced, or Aggressive) to liquidity providers, tailored to their level of investment risk tolerance. Pick one of the three risk profile, the app will allocated your funds accordingly across three SwapVM XYC strategies — USDG/WETH, WETH/1INCH, and USDG/TSLA — then ships them on-chain to the official Aqua registry. The dashboard shows your funds allocation and simulate how funds are rebalanced in a scenario when one of the price goes up (e.g: TESLA stock price pump). Another page allows traders to swap USDG for WETH against the low-risk sleeve, with real ERC-20 transfers. Demo txs run on an Anvil snapshot of Robinhood mainnet fork pre-loaded with chain state that already contains Aqua, SwapVM, and the token contracts.
howItsMade:
Built as a Next.js App, UI components with shadcn/ui, and viem + 1inch SDKs (Aqua + Swap VM) to interact with the Aqua contracts, build the strategies, ship, dock, create concentrated liquidity, quote and swap orders. The connected wallet signs ERC-20 approvals and Aqua.ship() for each allocation sleeves. Strategies are AquaXYCAmmStrategy programs from @1inch/swap-vm-sdk, encoded as SwapVM orders, and shipped with @1inch/aqua-sdk to AquaSwapVMRouter on the official Robinhood Aqua contracts. The demo app runs on a local Anvil fork of Robinhood mainnet. After ship, the trader desk quotes with SwapVM.quote(), then MetaMask signs SwapVM.swap() to perform a USDG → WETH. The UI decodes Swapped, Pulled, Pushed, and ERC-20 Transfer logs as on-chain proof.
A faucet API impersonates whales on Robinhood to distribute and transfer tokens from them to test and demo the app. Sleeve weights follow the chosen risk profile. Asset prices in USD are hardcoded here for simplicity.

name: AmanaScore
description: An AI guardrail blocking non-compliant Hedera transfers with on-chain HCS audit logs.
projectDescription:
Islamic finance has very little on-chain compliance infrastructure. Most payment flows do not check whether a transfer is acceptable before executing, and they rarely preserve an auditable trail of that decision.
AmanaScore is a Hedera testnet demo that blocks non-compliant transfers with a custom Sharia policy and logs every decision to Hedera Consensus Service (HCS).
howItsMade:
AmanaScore is a Node.js agent built on Hedera Testnet that enforces Sharia-compliance rules before executing any HBAR transfer. I used the Hedera SDK (@hashgraph/sdk) for native CryptoTransfer transactions and Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) for immutable audit logging, plus Hedera Agent Kit to wire the agent's decision-making flow.
The architecture is intentionally simple but powerful: a custom ShariaCompliancePolicy module sits as a middleware gate between the agent intent and the Hedera network. Every transfer request first hits the policy lookup — if the recipient is tagged as interest-lending (riba), the transfer is blocked before any network call is made. If the recipient is asset-backed and compliant, the agent signs and submits a live CryptoTransfer to testnet. Unknown recipients fall back to dry-run mode, allowing safe exploration without spending HBAR.
For auditability, every decision — allowed, rejected, or dry-run — is serialized to JSON and submitted to a dedicated HCS topic. If no topic ID is configured, the app auto-creates one on first run, making deployment frictionless. I used dotenvx for encrypted secret management and built the entire flow as a single-file demo (demo.js) that runs three scenarios end-to-end in under 10 seconds.
The hacky part: I treated the compliance policy as a pre-flight middleware rather than a post-transfer filter. This means non-compliant transactions cost exactly zero HBAR — they never touch the network — while still producing an immutable HCS audit trail of the attempt. This pattern could plug directly into custodian wallets or payment rails that need provable compliance without wasting gas on rejected transactions.

name: AgenIPO
description: Startup fundraising where the investor is an AI agent bound by a human mandate
projectDescription:
AgentIPO is a fundraising platform where the investor is an AI agent, not a person.
We are trying to solve two problems at the same time:

Founders get funding from verified investors
Investors can run their own AI agent that analyzes and verifies data (onchain & offchain), with the ability to close deals autonomously.

How does this work:


A founder lists a startup with links, contracts, token, and all data they think is important, such as MRR, DAU, growth, etc. They can gate it and send it upon request from an agent


Investor run their own AI agent, based on their investing rules - thesis, sectors, minimum
diligence score, max ticket, per-round share, daily budget, risk tolerance.


Agent working in the background and does the research for every new startup on the platform, then shows investors good matches. It has two modes: fully autonomous, where the agent tries to send money ASAP, and human-in-the-loop, where investors can review data themselves and proceed with investing.
howItsMade:
pnpm monorepo: NestJS 11 API, Next.js 16 dashboard, a zod contract package shared by
both, and Foundry contracts. Every module is ports & adapters, every source file is
capped at 100 lines by ESLint and a CI script, and the domain layer — evaluators,
mandate gate, spending policy, approval policy, growth math is framework-free pure
functions with Vitest specs.
The Graph is load-bearing, not decorative: agents cannot decide without it. Three Graph
products compose in one pipeline — the Token API for holders, top-10 concentration,
30-day transfers and treasury stables; a Messari standardized DEX subgraph so one query
works against any DEX by swapping the subgraph id; and the Agent0 / ERC-8004 subgraph,
whose reputation for the agent's own identity is fed back into its decision prompt.
Every signal carries a provenance badge in the UI, and fixtures are labelled as
fixtures rather than passed off as live.
Arc is where money moves. RoundEscrow.sol (Solidity 0.8.24, 52 Foundry tests) is a
milestone escrow settled in USDC — which on Arc is the native gas token, so the same
asset pays fees and fills the round. createRound sells equityBps; invest is
target-or-refund; releaseMilestone pays tranches; settleExit(kind, valuation,
proceeds, evidenceUri) pays a liquidity event into the claim pool, callable only by the
platform or the round's founder. Claims are floored per investor so the sum can never
exceed the pool. Agents hold their own wallets — HD-derived from one mnemonic, or
Circle developer-controlled wallets on ARC-TESTNET behind the same SettlementRail port.
Hedera carries the audit trail: data access requested and granted, decision made,
approval, settlement, exit, claim — each written to an HCS topic with sequence numbers.
Agents also get their own Hedera accounts and ERC-8004 identities.
Two decisions worth naming. First, we removed our own x402 paywall on the diligence
report. Charging agents to read public on-chain evidence is the wrong product, and it
broke every run without Hedera keys; x402 survives as an opt-in flag
(X402_GATE_REPORTS), with the real scarcity moved where it belongs — the founder's
private numbers, gated by the founder and opened per agent. Second, missing data is
never zero: a withheld metric, an unreadable index and a single reading with no
trajectory all land as "unknown", which lowers the report's data coverage instead of
inventing a score. The mandate gate then refuses low-coverage rounds before any LLM
call or any signature.
Hacky bits worth mentioning: Prisma's engine binaries were blocked by our network, so
the whole app runs on Prisma 7 with the Rust-free @prisma/adapter-pg and hand-written,
transaction-safe migrations. For offline development and for the hosted demo we run a
local Arc stand-in — anvil on Arc's chain id with MockUSDC injected at Arc's native
USDC address — so the entire escrow lifecycle, including exits and claims, executes as
real EVM transactions with no testnet funds. Sign-in is Privy, and when no Privy app is
configured the same screens run on a local session that is labelled "demo" in the nav,
on the sign-in step and in the stored account record, so a screenshot can never imply a
verified login.

name: ETH Arcade
description: Trading was boring. So we built a handheld arcade where ETH price becomes the game, plus an SDK.
projectDescription:
ETH Arcade is an open-source handheld console and SDK for games powered by live financial markets. It turns the ETH price chart into something you can physically interact with: a screen, a rotary knob, two buttons, and a speaker, all housed in a custom enclosure powered by a Raspberry Pi.
Our first game is Box Run. The player turns the knob to position a box on the price chart and presses a button to commit a stake. Each round lasts ten seconds. If the ETH price finishes inside the box, the player scores a hit and receives the corresponding payout; otherwise, the stake is lost. The market supplies the movement, making every round different.
We built ETH Arcade to explore what happens when interacting with crypto becomes tactile, playful, and social. Instead of watching charts across multiple monitors, players can pick up a handheld, learn the controls, and pass it to a friend.
Three integrations power the experience:
The Graph supplies the live market data. We compose Uniswap v3 and v4 Substreams packages into a reusable price pipeline that runs across Arbitrum and Base. Standardized subgraph queries discover supported liquidity pools, while the price consumer filters outliers and calculates a liquidity-weighted ETH price. This connects actual onchain trading activity to gameplay.
Circle’s Arc provides USDC session settlement. On Arc testnet, players fund a session with USDC. An escrow contract locks the player’s funds alongside a house reserve, and cashing out settles the final session balance back to the player. Gameplay rounds run offchain, keeping the controls responsive, while session funding and settlement happen onchain. Gas is also paid in USDC. The designated device reports the final balance; the contract enforces authorization, payout limits, and refund conditions.
ENSv2 provides player identity and the leaderboard. On Sepolia, players receive wallet-owned subnames under tick.eth. ENSv2’s Enhanced Access Control separates profile permissions from score permissions: players can update their profiles, while a scorekeeper updates designated statistics after observing settled sessions on Arc. The handheld reads names and statistics from ENS records to construct the leaderboard, without a separate leaderboard database.
ETH Arcade also includes a Python SDK that packages reusable components for price feeds, rounds, odds, wallets, settlement, physical inputs, and sound. Developers can scaffold a game and build their own market-driven experiences using these building blocks. Box Run demonstrates the concept; the SDK makes it extensible.
The website brings everything together with an interactive 3D hardware walkthrough, a playable browser version of Box Run, hosted SDK documentation, integration explanations, source links, and our launch video. The browser demo uses simulated prices and paper balances; the integrated onchain flow currently uses testnets.
ETH Arcade combines hardware, live blockchain data, stablecoin settlement, and programmable identity into a working arcade experience—and opens the tools for others to build what comes next.
howItsMade:
We built ETH Arcade from the hardware up. We wanted to take a live ETH chart off a trading dashboard and put it into something you could hold, play, and pass to a friend. That meant building a physical console alongside the game, contracts, data pipeline, and SDK.
Building the handheld
We borrowed a friend’s 3D printer to make the enclosure. That was a very hands-on part of the project: translating a digital design into a shell that had to fit the electronics, expose the controls, and feel comfortable to use.
Inside is a Raspberry Pi Zero W connected to a 3.5-inch 480×320 display, a rotary encoder, two buttons, and a rear speaker. The hardware design also includes a lithium-ion battery and charging circuit. We had to account for mounting points, component clearances, display connections, and space for wiring—not just how the outside looked.
The controls shaped the game itself. Turning the knob positions a box on the price chart; pressing a button commits the stake. We wanted the interaction to be understandable through your hands, with sound and immediate visual feedback making each action feel like an arcade input.
Firmware and game software
The Python firmware brings together rendering, physical inputs, sound, networking, and the different screens: funding, gameplay, cash-out, receipts, and the leaderboard.
Our first game, Box Run, uses ten-second rounds. Players position a price interval and commit a stake. If the ETH price finishes inside the box, they receive the corresponding payout; otherwise, they lose the stake.
A key architectural decision was keeping the game loop local. Individual rounds do not wait for blockchain transactions. Funding and settlement happen at session boundaries, so the controls stay responsive while the money flow remains connected to onchain contracts.
The Graph: making the market move the game
We compose Pinax’s Uniswap v3 and Uniswap v4 Substreams packages into a custom map_pool_prices module. This reuses existing event decoding and produces a common representation of pool price, liquidity, and block time.
The same compiled module runs on Arbitrum and Base with different pool configurations. We also use a shared Messari standardized DEX subgraph query to discover pool metadata for supported Uniswap v3 and SushiSwap v3 deployments.
A relay sends live updates to the price consumer, which rejects outliers more than 0.5% from the weighted median and calculates a liquidity-weighted aggregate. This helps keep one thin or stale pool from dominating a round. The Graph is effectively the connection between onchain trading activity and what moves across the handheld’s screen.
Circle and Arc: replacing arcade coins with USDC
We wrote a Solidity escrow contract, TickEscrow, and deployed it to Arc testnet. The player funds the device with USDC, and the device opens an escrow session in the player’s name after retaining a configured gas allowance. The contract locks the session funds alongside a house reserve.
Rounds execute offchain. At cash-out, the device submits the final balance and the contract settles to the recorded player address. The contract enforces authorization, payout limits, reserve constraints, and a timeout-based reclaim path.
Arc lets us use USDC for both session balances and gas. The device is trusted to report the final session balance; the contract does not independently verify every gameplay round.
ENSv2: an arcade identity that holds your score
On Sepolia, we deployed an ENSv2 UserRegistry under tick.eth and a shared PermissionedResolver through ENS’s VerifiableFactory.
Players receive wallet-owned subnames. Enhanced Access Control separates permissions: players can edit their profile records, while the scorekeeper can update seven designated tick.* statistics records.
A deterministic Python scorekeeper watches settled sessions on Arc and writes the resulting statistics to ENS. The handheld discovers registered names and resolves their records through the Universal Resolver to construct the standings.
One particularly unusual choice is that the leaderboard has no separate application database. ENS stores the player statistics, including a reference to the latest Arc settlement, connecting the payment flow to the player’s arcade identity.
Making the hardware reusable through an SDK
We packaged reusable game infrastructure into a Python SDK: price feeds, rounds, odds, wallets, settlement, physical inputs, and sound. Developers can start with tick new mygame and build their own market-driven games.
The goal is for someone else to spend their time designing a game rather than rebuilding the connection between a knob, a price feed, a wallet, and a leaderboard.
The website uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, and React Three Fiber to show the hardware through an interactive 3D walkthrough. It also includes a simulated browser version of Box Run, hosted SDK documentation, and our launch video. Firebase Hosting serves the website, and Firestore stores email signups.
The most memorable part of building ETH Arcade was bringing all those layers into one physical object: borrowing a friend’s printer, fitting electronics into a custom shell, wiring real controls, and making a live market respond on a tiny screen.

name: Alive402
description: One selfie-verified AI trial. Then agents pay per call on Hedera.
projectDescription:
Alive402 makes AI free trials fair and turns the moment after a trial into a native agent-payment flow.
AI APIs commonly offer free credits, but email addresses, browser cookies, and wallet addresses are easy to rotate. Alive402 gives a person one promotional API call after they complete World Selfie Check. The backend verifies the World proof, uses its scoped nullifier as a privacy-preserving continuity signal, and atomically records the entitlement for that provider campaign.
The next request reaches the same protected inference endpoint and receives a real HTTP 402 Payment Required response. A budgeted agent reads the x402 payment requirements, pays 0.001 test USDC on Hedera through Blocky402, retries the original request, and unlocks the AI response. The app then shows the execution receipt and Hedera transaction.
The result is a reusable access pattern for AI inference, data APIs, developer tools, and other metered HTTP services: let a real person try once, then let humans or agents pay per request without subscriptions or API keys.
howItsMade:
Alive402 is built with TanStack Start, React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind. The application uses Supabase Postgres for persistent provider campaigns, World enrollment records, one-time proof-signal hashes, opaque server sessions, access decisions, and sanitized payment receipts.
For World, we use the IDKit Selfie Check legacy preset. The browser never receives the RP signing key. Instead, the server creates a short-lived random signal, stores only its hash, signs the RP context server-side, and sends the completed IDKit result unchanged to World’s backend verification API. After verification, Alive402 normalizes the scoped nullifier and grants one promotional entitlement per provider campaign. Selfie images are never stored.
For paid access, the protected OpenRouter inference endpoint uses x402 v2 with canonical PAYMENT-REQUIRED, PAYMENT-SIGNATURE, and PAYMENT-RESPONSE headers. We use @x402/core, @x402/hedera, @x402/fetch, and the Blocky402 facilitator to build, verify, and settle an exact payment in test USDC on Hedera Testnet. The demo agent is server-side and constrained to one network, one USDC asset, one merchant account, a maximum payment amount, and a daily spend limit. A HashScan-linked receipt proves the settlement. Vercel hosts the application and Vercel Analytics measures real product traffic.

name: Xenia
description: Slashable-stake trust for AI agents: ENS identity, Graph standing, Hedera x402 pay-per-check.
projectDescription:
Xenia is slashable-stake infrastructure for AI agents, named after Greek guest-friendship. Agents register as *.xenia.eth (ENS namehash on Sepolia). A host locks ETH behind an agent and sets a premium; the agent pays that trust fee to keep coverage live. If the agent defaults, stake can be slashed to the victim after a dispute window.
The Graph indexes registry events into standing scores (premiums up, defaults/slashes down). Hedera is not the stake ledger — it meters API access: POST /xenia/check returns HTTP 402 until ~0.001 HBAR settles via x402/Blocky402, then returns standing. Live demo theater runs mint → stake → premium → default → slash → Pay HBAR → decide (transact vs refuse).
howItsMade:
Xenia is a pnpm monorepo: Foundry Solidity for XeniaRegistry on Sepolia; Next.js + wagmi/viem/RainbowKit for apps/web and the CRT-style apps/demo theater; Fastify for apps/api; AssemblyScript subgraph; optional MCP standing tool.
ENS gives each agent a *.xenia.eth handle. Registration stores the namehash on-chain; scripts set backing text records (xenia.host, stake, premium) and demo host-only EAC so non-hosts can’t rewrite trust metadata.
The Graph indexes registry events into standing: clamp(50 + 10×premiums − 25×defaults − 40×slashes). Product UI and the demo Decide step read Studio GraphQL — not raw RPC — so scores stay queryable after slash.
Hedera is only for API metering. Stake never leaves Sepolia. POST /xenia/check returns HTTP 402; the client signs an exact HBAR transfer with @x402/hedera, Blocky402 settles ~0.001 HBAR, then standing is returned. Demo Run requires pnpm dev:api after the slash path.
The demo orchestrator mints fresh agent wallets each Run, funds them from a host key, and streams NDJSON over SSE into the theater. Notable hack: payer ≠ payTo (self-transfer nets to 0 under x402), so we auto-provision a distinct testnet payer and cache it; Decide also polls the subgraph so A’s ~60 isn’t race-zeroed like B’s post-slash 0.

name: DeFi-Risk-Sentinel
description: AI-powered DeFi liquidation risk monitor for Aave V3 on Ethereum
projectDescription:
Detailed Description
What It Does
The Sentinel continuously monitors DeFi lending positions on the Aave V3 protocol (Ethereum mainnet) and answers one critical question: "How close is this wallet to liquidation?"
It fetches real user reserve data — collateral balances (aTokens), stable/variable debt, per-asset liquidation thresholds, and oracle prices — directly from a live The Graph subgraph via GraphQL. No mocks, no hardcoded data. Every number originates from on-chain state.
How It Works

Data Layer (src/data/)
graphClient.js
— A GraphQL transport client that queries The Graph's decentralized gateway (gateway.thegraph.com), with built-in retries and rate limiting.
aaveQueries.js
— Aave V3-specific GraphQL queries to fetch user reserves, price oracles, and active users. Parses raw subgraph responses into a normalized position format.
Risk Engine (src/engine/)
riskEngine.js
— Core computation module. Calculates the health factor using the formula:

Health Factor = Σ(collateral_i × price_i × liquidationThreshold_i) / Σ(debt_j × price_j)
Classifies positions into three risk tiers:
Level	Health Factor	Meaning
🔴 DANGER	< 1.05	Imminent liquidation
🟡 WATCH	< 1.20	Elevated risk
🟢 SAFE	≥ 1.20	Healthy
Also identifies the weakest collateral (the asset whose price drop has the largest marginal impact on health factor) and the largest debt position.
scenarios.js
— Scenario simulation engine. Can:
Simulate arbitrary price changes and recompute health factors
Analytically solve the exact liquidation price for any collateral asset (not just brute-force search)
Run multi-drop stress tests (e.g. 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, 50% simultaneous crashes)
Handle correlated assets via aliases (WETH/stETH/cbETH all track ETH; USDC/USDT/DAI all track USD)
3. AI Reasoning Layer (src/reasoning/)
nlGenerator.js
— Generates rich, natural-language risk reports from computed data. Not template-filling — produces context-aware narratives explaining why a position is risky, what the weakest link is, and what actions to take. Supports an optional OpenAI GPT-4 integration for even deeper analysis and a conversational Q&A interface.
4. Alerting System (src/alerts/)
poller.js
— Configurable polling loop (default 60s) that re-fetches positions and detects when a wallet transitions from SAFE/WATCH into DANGER.
webhook.js
— Sends alerts to Discord, Slack, or any generic webhook endpoint.
5. Interfaces
REST API (
api.js
) — 12 endpoints covering health checks, watchlist CRUD, risk assessments, simulation, stress testing, and natural-language queries.
Web Dashboard (
public/
) — Premium dark-themed glassmorphic UI with animated backgrounds, real-time risk tables, an AI chat panel, per-wallet stress test controls, and auto-refresh.
CLI (
cli.js
) — Interactive terminal interface for all features.
Tech Stack
Component	Technology
Runtime	Node.js 18+ (ES Modules)
Data Source	The Graph (Aave V3 Ethereum Subgraph, decentralized network)
Server	Express.js
HTTP Client	node-fetch
AI (optional)	OpenAI GPT-4 for enhanced NL reasoning
Frontend	Vanilla HTML/CSS/JS (glassmorphic dark theme)
Agent Integration	MCP config + SKILL.md for AI agent compatibility
Key Design Decisions
Protocol-agnostic engine: Only src/data/aaveQueries.js is Aave-specific. The risk engine, simulation, reasoning, and alerting layers operate on a normalized position format — swapping to Compound, Morpho, or any lending protocol only requires a new data adapter.
No mocks: Every data point is fetched live from Ethereum mainnet via The Graph. The app works against real positions with real risk.
Analytical liquidation solving: Instead of binary search, the scenarios module solves the liquidation price algebraically for O(1) precision.
Graceful AI degradation: Works fully without an OpenAI key (rule-based NL generation), but produces richer output when one is configured.
howItsMade:
We built the Sentinel as a from-scratch Node.js (ES Modules) application with a clean five-layer architecture: Data → Engine → Reasoning → Alerts → Interface. Each layer only depends on the one below it, making the whole system protocol-swappable — only one file knows anything about Aave.
The Graph (Partner Technology) is the backbone. Every number in the app — collateral balances, debt amounts, liquidation thresholds, oracle prices — comes from live GraphQL queries to the Aave V3 Ethereum subgraph (GQFbb95cE6d8mV989mL5figjaGaKCQB3xqYrr1bRyXqF) on The Graph's decentralized gateway. No RPC calls, no mocked data, no indexing infrastructure of our own. We fire two parallel GraphQL queries per wallet: one for userReserves (positions, collateral flags, reserve config) and one for priceOracles (live USD pricing). The Graph handles the heavy lifting of indexing Ethereum's state into a queryable schema — without it, we'd need our own indexer, archive node, and weeks of setup. We also ship an mcp_config.json for @thegraph/subgraph-mcp, so AI agents can query the same subgraph through the Model Context Protocol.
The trickiest engineering problems:
Parsing Aave V3's on-chain encoding. Balances come as raw BigInt strings scaled by token decimals (6 for USDC, 18 for WETH, 8 for WBTC). Liquidation thresholds are basis points (8250 = 82.5%). Rates use ray precision (1e27). Prices use a double-indirection: a priceInEth field scaled by 1e18, plus a separate usdPriceEth oracle value you invert and multiply. We wrote a parseTokenAmount() function using JavaScript BigInt to split integer and fractional parts without floating-point loss, and a multi-fallback pricing pipeline that tries the USD oracle first, then falls back to priceInEth × ethPrice.
Analytical liquidation price solving. Instead of binary-searching for the price drop that pushes health factor to 1.0 (which is what most tools do), we derived a closed-form solution: dropFraction = 1 - (totalDebt - effectiveOther) / (balance × price × LT). This gives O(1) exact answers and lets us compute liquidation prices for every asset in every wallet on every poll cycle without blowing up compute.
Correlated asset aliasing in simulations. When a user asks "what if ETH drops 20%", we need WETH, stETH, wstETH, cbETH, and rETH to all move together — they're the same underlying exposure. We built an alias map that groups synthetic/wrapped variants under their base asset (ETH, BTC, USD), so one simulation input cascades correctly through the whole portfolio.
Graceful AI degradation. The NL reasoning layer works in two modes. Without an OpenAI key, it uses a rule-based engine that pattern-matches user questions with regex (price drop queries, stress test requests, wallet lookups, portfolio summaries) and generates reports by computing real numbers — collateral shares, repayment amounts to reach target HF, margin-to-liquidation percentages. With an OpenAI key, it injects the full position dataset into GPT-4o-mini's context as a system prompt and lets the LLM reason over actual numbers. If the LLM call fails, it silently falls back to rule-based. Zero-config, always works.
Tech stack: Node.js 18+, Express for the REST API (12 endpoints), vanilla HTML/CSS/JS for the frontend (glassmorphic dark theme, animated gradient background, custom markdown-to-HTML renderer for the chat panel), node-fetch for HTTP, dotenv for config. Four total dependencies. The frontend auto-refreshes every 60 seconds, the backend polls The Graph on a configurable interval, and the alerting layer detects risk-level transitions (SAFE→WATCH, WATCH→DANGER) and fires Discord/Slack/generic webhooks with auto-detected payload formatting.

name: MeteredSignal
description: Arc agent pays Hedera x402 for live Graph DeFi signal, then spends USDC on GO.
projectDescription:
MeteredSignal is a pay-per-call intelligence market for agents that move capital in DeFi. You do not buy a monthly Graph API seat or dump a single subgraph into a prompt. You buy a metered signal. Before the agent spends, the product only exposes a catalog of priced routes: lending compare or wallet risk, HBAR price, and a freshness contract so you know the data is live. The capital move stays locked until the verdict is GO. That gating is the product. Raw subgraph access is free but hard for agents to budget, and blind USDC transfers treat every call like a green light. MeteredSignal flips both sides at once. Merchants sell standardized Messari lending intelligence as an HTTP 402 service instead of a subscription. Agents get live multi-protocol risk they can afford per call, with a policy so Arc USDC only moves when the signal is fresh and actionable.
The agent journey is built around that meter. An Arc-side wallet discovers the free catalog, hits a paywalled merchant route, settles Hedera x402 through Blocky402 without an API key, then receives a paid JSON signal built from Messari Standardized Subgraphs on The Graph — Aave v3, Compound v3, and Spark under one query shape. The merchant runs a freshness gate on _meta.block; fewer than two fresh sources means UNAVAILABLE, not a soft maybe. The agent reasons to GO, NO_GO, or UNAVAILABLE, ranks venues by TVL and utilization on lending-compare, and scores cross-protocol borrow exposure on wallet-risk. Only on GO does Circle Agent Stack settle a nanopayment on Arc to the GO-action seller. Identity of the human operator never has to sit in the payment path; the economic actor is the agent wallet. Settlements can append to a Hedera Consensus Service topic so payment is auditable on HashScan, not just logged in memory.
Merchants get the other half of the loop. An Express service lists metered routes, challenges unpaid GETs with an exact-scheme Hedera 402, queries live GraphQL after settle, and sells a separate Arc USDC GO-action behind Circle Gateway batching. Treasury agents, lending desks, and autonomous spenders all hit the same inventory: one Messari template, two prices (compare cheaper than risk), one freshness policy. Demand can arrive through the demo console or a headless agent, while supply still publishes once.
Agent loop: discover → 402 → settle → Graph → freshness → decide → USDC or refuse. Merchant loop: catalog → challenge → query → signal → HCS audit. Arc loop: GO-only nanopay with a spend cap. The whole point is one market that meters truth for buyers and liquidates intelligence as a payable service without spoiling either side.
Less noise. More signal.
howItsMade:
MeteredSignal was built from scratch during ETHOnline as an npm workspaces monorepo. The demo console is a Vite React app with a live SSE pipeline rail. Express owns the merchant and agent surfaces; on Vercel they mount together as one serverless app so /, /demo, /api, and /v1 ship from a single deployment. A shared packages/graph registry pins Messari Standardized Lending deployments and runs the freshness-gated queries. Partner tech is not bolted on for a checklist: each one sits on a critical path in the decision loop.
The UX is intentional about failure modes, not just happy paths. The console streams Discover → 402 → Settle → Paid → Graph → Fresh → Decide → USDC → Receipts so judges can watch the meter in real time. A labeled Simulate indexer lag toggle still pays for a live Messari query, then injects tip ahead of _meta.block so sources go stale, the verdict becomes UNAVAILABLE, and Arc policy refuses spend — the demo beat that proves the gate is real. Wallet presets drive high-borrow NO_GO versus clean GO without mocking Graph. ArcScan, HashScan, and HCS topic links land next to decoded PAYMENT-RESPONSE payloads so receipts are evidence, not decoration.
Money runs through Hedera x402 and Arc Circle rails, not a custom auth stack. On the intelligence leg, @x402/express plus Blocky402 as facilitator challenges unpaid routes; the agent signs with ExactHederaScheme and settles HBAR — about 0.001 for lending-compare and 0.0025 for wallet-risk. On the capital leg, @circle-fin/x402-batching GatewayClient pays the merchant’s Gateway-batched GO-action on Arc Testnet (eip155:5042002), capped by ARC_SPEND_AMOUNT_USDC. Missing Arc keys yield an explicit dry_run instead of a panic spend; an optional native USDC fallback stays behind a flag if Gateway fails. The UI and receipts treat HBAR meter cost and Arc USDC spend as separate ledgers on purpose, because agent demos often die when one rail is funded and the other is not.
The signal layer is The Graph. One Messari query template covers Aave v3 (Ethereum and Arbitrum), Compound v3, and Spark; the agent ranks and decides rather than dumping raw JSON as the product. Freshness requires _meta block number and timestamp against GRAPH_MAX_BLOCK_LAG. Without Graph there is no evidence and no verdict. Without Hedera and Blocky402 the merchant is not a payable agent service. Without Arc and Circle nanopayments the loop never closes from intelligence to capital under Agent Stack rails.
The audit trail is Hedera Consensus Service. After a paid settle, the merchant can append settlement metadata to an HCS topic so HashScan shows more than a transfer — a verifiable payment history for the metered route. HCS is best-effort: if topic or creds are missing the response still returns, and that is disclosed.
The hacky but useful glue is shipping merchant and agent in one Vercel function with a long maxDuration, plus demo tip-lag and wallet presets that keep the video cinematic while every Graph query and 402 settle stay live. Mainnet for Arc is an env flip when Circle publishes RPC and chain ID — same GO-only policy, documented in ARC_MAINNET.md for the Launch track unlock. Put together, The Graph supplies the evidence, Hedera meters and audits the call, Arc moves USDC only on GO, and the product in the middle stays what it claims to be: less noise, more signal.

name: Pocket
description: Spending limits for AI agents. Each agent gets its own wallet and a cap it cannot raise.
projectDescription:
Everyone who has handed a task to an AI agent has had the same small moment of hesitation. You are about to let it run on its own, and somewhere in the back of your mind is the question: what if it doesn't stop?
We are comfortable letting agents write code, book things, and read half the internet. We are not comfortable handing one a credit card. And that is the thing standing between where agents are now and where they are obviously going, because almost everything useful an agent needs is sold per call. Search results, market data, compute, other agents' output. Someone has to pay for it, and right now the only options are to do it yourself in advance or to give the agent your card and hope.
Pocket is the third option. Give the agent its own wallet and a limit it cannot raise.
WHAT THAT LOOKS LIKE
→ You create an agent in a dashboard and you set the rules in plain terms. How much it can spend a day. How much on any one purchase. How much on a particular job. Who it is allowed to pay. And the amount above which you want to approve things yourself.
→ Then you let it go. Every time it tries to buy something, Pocket checks the purchase against those rules before any money moves. If it passes, the payment goes through in about a second and nobody is interrupted. If it fails, the purchase is refused and written down along with the exact rule that stopped it, so you are never left guessing why your agent did not do something.
→ The agent cannot change any of this. It does not hold the key to its own wallet, and it cannot raise its own limit. Those are set by you, and the agent only ever spends against them. The limit is not a suggestion it agrees to follow. It is a wall.
And everything is written down. Every purchase, every refusal, every change you make, in a record that cannot be edited after the fact. If you want to know what your agents spent last week and why, the answer is one page.
HOW IT IS PUT TOGETHER
→ Agents pay sellers using x402, an open payment standard that lets a website charge for a single request without the buyer ever opening an account or holding an API key. It is what makes an agent buying one search result for one cent actually practical. We built Pocket to sit inside that exchange: the seller names its price, Pocket decides whether that money may be spent, and only then is anything signed.
→ The wallets are held by Privy, so no private key ever touches our servers. We also set a second, independent limit inside Privy itself, which means even if Pocket were compromised, the wallet would still refuse to overspend.
→ Payments settle on Hedera, which is fast and cheap enough that buying something for one cent is not absurd, and every settled payment links out to a public block explorer so any number on the screen can be checked against the chain.
→ The Graph prices the limits you set in dollars. We deliberately ask two independent Graph sources for every price and require them to agree. If they disagree, Pocket refuses the purchase rather than guessing, because a limit enforced with a wrong price is not a limit.
→ Agents connect through MCP, the standard Claude and other assistants already use for tools. There are eight of them (tools), and only one can actually spend money. The other seven let an agent check what it is allowed to do before it tries, so it can ask "would this be approved?" without moving anything.
TRY IT


Dashboard: https://www.pocket-app.xyz


Documentation: https://docs.pocket-app.xyz/docs


API: https://api.pocket-app.xyz


MCP server: https://mcp.pocket-app.xyz


An example seller, with six live data feeds priced from one cent to seventy-five: https://pay.pocket-app.xyz


That last one is worth a click. It is a genuinely separate business that knows nothing about Pocket and has no account with the buyer. It states a price, gets paid, and serves the data. We built it so the demo is a real purchase from a real counterparty rather than Pocket paying itself.
How the whole exchange works: https://docs.pocket-app.xyz/docs/how-it-works
howItsMade:
WHERE THIS STARTED
Making an agent spend money took an afternoon. Making it refuse to took the rest of the build.
That is the honest summary. The happy path here is genuinely easy: a seller asks for payment, a wallet signs, the data comes back. The hard part, and the only part that matters, is everything that has to be true before the wallet is ever asked. So we built the refusal first. The very first thing that worked was an engine that said no and explained itself, with nothing behind it that could actually pay. Spending came later.
See: https://docs.pocket-app.xyz/docs/how-it-works
THE SPINE
Every purchase runs as a single call, in a fixed order that never varies.
→ Read the seller's 402 terms. Price it, if the limit is written in dollars. Check it against the daily budget, the task budget, the per-transaction cap, the recipient list and the category rules. Ask for a signature, but only if every check passed. Settle. Record the outcome either way.
→ The order is not an implementation detail, it is the product. Nothing is signed before the decision, so a refused payment leaves no signature lying around for a later request to replay. And the agent never holds a payload of its own, so there is no policy step for it to skip.
WHAT THAT TURNED INTO


Dashboard (https://www.pocket-app.xyz), where a human sets the limits and reads the record. Signing in starts a setup guide that takes you from an empty organization to an agent that has bought its own data.


API (https://api.pocket-app.xyz), the decision, the ledger and the audit trail across 35 endpoints. Open the root and it describes itself: every endpoint, which vendor is answering for each slot, and which build is running.


MCP server (https://mcp.pocket-app.xyz), how an agent actually reaches Pocket. The root lists the transport, the credential it wants, and all eight tools with whether each one can spend.


Example seller (https://pay.pocket-app.xyz/catalog), an x402 business we built specifically so we would have someone real to pay. Its catalogue is public and quotes every price without charging.


Documentation (https://docs.pocket-app.xyz/docs), with screenshots of every screen and every state, refusals included.


That fourth one deserves a sentence. We could have faked the seller. We built it as a genuinely independent service with six live data feeds instead, because a payments demo where both sides are yours proves nothing.

PRIVY (https://docs.pocket-app.xyz/docs/stack/privy)

Privy custodies every agent wallet, so no private key ever touches our servers. The same application also signs operators into the dashboard, which saved us building a second identity system.
The part we are proud of is that we did not trust our own engine alone. When a wallet is created, Pocket installs a Privy-side policy capping transfer value and denying key export. That is a second ceiling underneath the first: if Pocket itself were compromised, Privy would still refuse the transaction. One lock is a single point of failure, and this is money.

HEDERA (https://docs.pocket-app.xyz/docs/stack/hedera)

Payments settle on Hedera through the x402 exact scheme and a facilitator. Hedera earned its place by being cheap and fast enough that buying something for one cent is not absurd, which is the entire premise of paying per call. Every settled payment carries a public explorer link, so any number on the dashboard can be checked against the chain.

THE GRAPH (https://docs.pocket-app.xyz/docs/stack/the-graph)

Two jobs, and only one of them needed keys.
(i) Pricing came from a problem we did not see at first. A limit written in tokens is not a limit on money: an agent allowed two HBAR is allowed unbounded value if HBAR moves. So dollar ceilings are priced by two Graph products that check each other, the hosted Token API and a subgraph on the decentralized gateway. If they disagree beyond a tolerance, or if fewer than two answer, Pocket returns no price and denies the purchase. It never guesses. A price feed that decides whether money moves should not be one thing that can be wrong.
(ii) Reconciliation needed no keys at all, because The Graph does not support Hedera and there was no endpoint to paste. So we ship our own subgraph and Graph Node setup that indexes transfers, and Pocket checks its own ledger against what actually settled on chain.

MCP (https://mcp.pocket-app.xyz)

Eight tools, and exactly one can spend. The other seven exist so an agent can find out what it is allowed to do before it tries, including a preview that returns the real decision without moving anything. The server holds no credential of its own: every caller brings its own key, which is what stops a hosted endpoint becoming an open door onto someone else's agents.
THE HACKY BITS
→ x402 on Hedera addresses accounts by native ID, but wallets are provisioned by EVM address. Rather than have someone paste the ID into config and get it wrong, the seller looks up its own payee through the mirror node at startup.
→ The seller warms every feed before it opens its port. A feed whose upstream is unreachable is simply not offered, because nothing should quote a price for something it cannot deliver. Stale data is served and labelled stale rather than failing a request somebody already paid for.
→ 686 tests, including the policy engine against every refusal path and the API against a real database rather than a mock.

name: Tempo
description: A SwapVM instruction that gives a 1inch Aqua strategy memory of its own fill history
projectDescription:
Tempo is a custom instruction for 1inch's SwapVM. A maker ships a bytecode program that prices their swaps; Tempo hooks in through the Extruction opcode as a separately deployed contract, tracking per-strategy fill velocity in persistent storage and widening the spread as velocity rises, saturating at a bound. It runs against the already-deployed Aqua registry and AquaSwapVMRouter on Base with no changes to 1inch's contracts.
The question was whether a strategy that remembers its recent fill history prices better than one that doesn't. To answer it I built a replay harness: real hourly ETH/USD price tapes, an arbitrageur sized endogenously from the pool's own quotes rather than a scripted trade list, and price-sensitive organic flow that walks away from bad execution. The control is Tempo against itself configured with a constant spread — same contract, same placement, same rounding, same gas shape — bracketed around Tempo's own realised average spread.
The result is negative. Adaptiveness does not beat a matched constant spread in any of nine tape and flow-mix combinations. An earlier version of this measurement reported the opposite; that finding came from a control with structural disadvantages and did not survive a fair one. The diagnosis is in ANALYSIS.md: in every configuration tested the decay window was shorter than the interval between trades, so the velocity ramp only ever activated on fills sharing a timestamp and was never exercised across ticks.
Also shipped: an HTTP API that encodes SwapVM programs and replays Tempo's pricing offline, live at https://tempo-ysu3.onrender.com with an OpenAPI spec at /openapi.json, exposed through a Bazantic x402 gateway.
howItsMade:
Solidity 0.8.30 and Foundry, tested against pinned Base mainnet forks using the live deployed Aqua registry (0x1111113ccf1426a8e30e2bff5e005d929bf6a90a) and SwapVM router (0x111111338c5091e8440b67b168bae16a668ac0de), verified byte-identical to swap-vm v1.0.1 and aqua v1.0.0 via Sourcify before building against them. Only my own contracts are deployed; 1inch's are consumed as pinned git submodules, never vendored.
Tempo is an Extruction target implementing IExtruction and IStaticExtruction, placed after XYCSwap in the program. It keys velocity state on orderHash, packs volume and timestamp into one slot, and takes a genuinely read-only path under isStaticContext — the router issues a STATICCALL to the target whenever quoting, so a write there reverts at the EVM level.
The replay harness runs both arms over identical tapes and seeds, with paired per-seed differences and a measured noise floor established against a pass-through stub before the real logic existed.
Four bugs worth naming. The deployed router's opcode dispatch has an off-by-one: _opcodes() reuses the fixed array's memory as the returned dynamic array's length word, shifting every opcode index down by one, so XYCSwap is 17 and Extruction 32 rather than 18 and 33. That only surfaced by executing against the real contract. The gas measurement was biased by EIP-2929 warm/cold leaking between sequential swaps in one test function. The harness never advanced block.timestamp, making the decay window inert. And the first control arm used swap-vm's own Fee instruction, whose pre-curve placement was itself a confound — replacing it with constant-spread Tempo reversed the headline result.
The API is Python stdlib only, Dockerised, with the program encoding byte-matched against fixtures captured from real Foundry output.

name: Stylus Hook
description: Uniswap v4 hooks written entirely in Rust on Arbitrum Stylus
projectDescription:
This continues a project from ETHGlobal Scaling Ethereum 2024, built when Stylus was still
testnet-only and Uniswap v4 was still in development. Back then the contract v4 actually called was
a Solidity proxy, forwarding every callback to the Rust code behind it. It was never Stylus end to
end, because a hook must sit at an address whose low 14 bits encode its callbacks, and Stylus could
not deploy to a mined one.
Both have shipped since. Stylus is on mainnet and CREATE2s through StylusDeployer, so we finished
it: the contract the PoolManager calls is now the Stylus contract itself, with no Solidity in it.
The other half is finding out whether that is worth doing. Entering a Stylus contract costs ~7,900
gas more, storage is identical, and arithmetic is 3-640x cheaper. So most hooks should stay in
Solidity, and we publish that: a counter hook costs 2.8x more in Rust.
Where it pays, it pays widely. Against the TWAMM live on Base and Unichain, at 32 concurrent order
streams, Solidity spends 2,849,561 gas per swap and Rust spends 1,891,213. Replaying v4's swap math
is 7.1x cheaper per tick. And a post-quantum signature check is 11.3M gas in Solidity against 33k
in Rust, because SHAKE is not reachable through the EVM's keccak opcode.
Porting v4-core also found a failing input in Uniswap's own TickMath fuzz test. The fix is one
character.
howItsMade:
Rust on stylus-sdk 0.10.9, compiled to wasm32 and run on Arbitrum Stylus. stylus/base-hook is
BaseHook.sol's counterpart: the v4 types, the permission flags, all ten IHooks callbacks, and the
calls back into the singleton. A test pins all ten selectors against the compiled IHooks.sol.
Solidity's onlyPoolManager can't be forgotten because BaseHook is abstract; Rust has no abstract
types, so a proc macro inserts the guards instead. And hook-miner reimplements StylusDeployer's
salt derivation, keccak(salt || initData), to find an address carrying the declared flags.
Two things worth stealing. The SDK has no immutable, so build.rs bakes the pool manager in as a
Rust const rather than paying a cold SLOAD per callback: 2,568 gas a swap. And rustc at opt-level 2
or 3 emits a DataCount section ArbOS refuses to activate, so Stylus looks capped at size-optimised;
--llvm-memory-copy-fill-lowering fixes it. Both builds pass cargo stylus check and only fail at
deploy. Every ratio here doubled when we found it.
Forge can't run WASM, so the Solidity twins are tested through a real local v4 stack and the Rust
side against TestVM, cross-pinned to the same values. Every gas figure is a receipt from an
Arbitrum Nitro dev node, not an estimate.
Hackiest bit: the TWAMM is 41 KB, so it needs ArbOS 61 code fragments, but cargo stylus
get-initcode refuses fragmented contracts. We deploy once with --wasm-file, read the root back off
chain, re-wrap it in the EVM prelude, mine against that, and hand it to StylusDeployer ourselves.

name: Recourse
description: x402 pays before delivery. Recourse escrows it and refunds you when the API breaks its SLA.
projectDescription:
When an agent pays for an API call with x402, the money moves before the response exists. If what comes back is empty, stale, or quietly wrong, it's already gone. A person notices and stops buying from that seller. An agent making a thousand calls an hour doesn't notice, and has no refund path to reach for.
Recourse changes one thing. The payment goes into an escrow contract on Hedera instead of straight to the seller. Before any money moves, the seller publishes an SLA: a short list of checks a machine can run on the response, like "bid must be greater than zero" or "the spread must be within 50 basis points". The 402 response carries the hash of that document, and the buyer refuses to pay if the terms don't hash to what was advertised.
The seller returns the data along with a signature over what it sent. If the response breaks one of the published checks, the buyer disputes and posts a bond worth 10% of the payment. A Chainlink CRE workflow running inside an AWS Nitro enclave then reads the response, checks it against the SLA, and rules on it. The payload never goes on-chain and no node operator sees it. That matters, because the thing being argued over is usually the exact thing the buyer paid to keep private.
The verdict arrives back on Hedera carrying a reason code that names the clause that failed. Reason 102 means clause 2 broke. So a refund points at a specific promise the seller made and didn't keep, rather than at somebody's opinion about data quality.
If nobody disputes, none of that happens. The window closes, the seller withdraws, and the whole exchange costs one extra contract call with no oracle involved. Disputes are the exception, and only the exception pays for the machinery.
It runs end to end on testnet today. In one run the seller returned a negative bid, and the buyer got 0.11 HBAR back: the payment plus the bond. In another the seller behaved and was paid 0.1 HBAR with no adjudication at all.
howItsMade:
The escrow is Solidity on the Hedera testnet EVM, built with Foundry, with 40 tests including a fuzz test on the accounting. The SLA checker is a small TypeScript package with canonical JSON hashing so the buyer, the seller and the enclave all agree on what a document hashes to. The adjudicator is a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow. The site is Next.js, and it reads the chain directly rather than from a database, so nothing on it can drift from what actually happened. Payments settle through Blocky402 on Hedera.
Three things forced the design into a shape we didn't expect.
First, Hedera doesn't run contract code on a plain transfer. A native TransferTransaction credits a contract's balance without ever calling receive() or fallback(), and the x402 facilitator settles that way. So the escrow can't be told about its own funding. We split it into two steps: the facilitator settles, then anyone calls bind() to attach terms, and the contract only commits money it can prove it already holds by checking its balance against what it has already promised out. One deposit can never back two payments. That invariant is the thing the fuzz test protects.
Second, CRE can't write to Hedera. It isn't in the 57 chains a tenant can target, so there's no forwarder for writeReport to reach. The enclave writes its verdict to a relay contract on Ethereum Sepolia instead, where the KeystoneForwarder checks the DON signatures, and CCIP carries it the rest of the way to Hedera. The escrow only accepts a message from the CCIP router with that relay as the sender. We confirmed the lane by calling isChainSupported on the live Sepolia router, which was necessary because Chainlink's own docs leave Hedera off the destination list.
Third, we wanted an LLM to judge disputes and couldn't. The enclave result is attested and verified by DON consensus, which needs the same input to produce the same output every time, and a model doesn't. So the model moved upstream to help sellers write the SLA, and the enclave enforces a contract both sides already agreed to. There isn't even a clock read in the handler, because Date.now() would break consensus. Freshness is judged against a deadline that's already on-chain.
The most expensive bug: our first live verdict reached Hedera and did nothing. CCIP said the message was delivered, the OffRamp transaction succeeded, and the escrow never moved. Our trimmed CCIP receiver was missing supportsInterface. The router staticcalls it before delivering, and an address that reverts gets treated as a normal account, so the router skips the receiver and still records the message as executed. Nothing reports a failure anywhere. The verdict just disappears. Two tests now pin that, including the literal interface id the router looks for.
Two smaller ones worth passing on. Blocky402 answers HTTP 200 for a payment that failed, with the real result in the body, so our gateway gated on the status code and briefly gave away paid work for free. And cre workflow simulate --broadcast submits real transactions without needing deployment access, which is how we produced genuine on-chain state while our CRE org was still gated.

name: Matoi
description: A working economy where AI agents price information, buy what they need, and prove every payment.
projectDescription:
Matoi is an agent-to-agent market for paid intelligence.
Provider agents collect and evaluate information from sources such as Telegram, RSS feeds, market APIs, protocol data and other live streams. They decide what is useful, price their output, and publish it for other agents to buy.
A BuyerAgent searches the market for information relevant to its task, compares available providers, evaluates quotes against its budget and risk policy, and pays for the sources it chooses. Circle Developer Controlled Wallets and testnet USDC handle agent spending, while paid requests are settled through a Hedera x402 flow using a Blocky402-compatible facilitator.
Each completed call produces a receipt and an audit trail. Payment records are kept in the app ledger, and proof is anchored to Hedera Consensus Service so the full mission can be reviewed afterwards.
One of the working providers reads a live Telegram news stream, evaluates incoming messages and sells the resulting signal per request. The same model can be extended to video analysis, policy speeches, market data, security events, onchain activity, or any other source an agent can evaluate and price.
The product is a Next.js control room, an in-process BuyerAgent, a provider marketplace, a Hedera payment signer, an Arc spend ledger and an HCS audit topic — all wired into one A2A transcript.
howItsMade:
I built Matoi as one Next.js app that talks to two rails.
Frontend is plain Next.js with TypeScript. A control room page lets you pick a buyer scenario and click RUN. There's a Blocky402 toggle that decides which payment rail gets used.
Backend lives in the same repo. /api/mission/run is the single entry point. It runs a BuyerAgent in-process, asks provider agents for quotes, picks the ones that fit the budget, and writes the whole interaction as an A2A transcript.
Providers are small modules. TelegramPulse uses a local Telethon bridge that reads a public Telegram channel and turns the messages into a paid signal. The other providers hit CoinGecko, DefiLlama, RSS feeds and GitHub directly through their public APIs. No keys needed for the demo.
When Blocky402 is ON, the mission endpoint calls /api/x402/blocky402/pay. That route uses @hashgraph/sdk to build and sign a Hedera USDC TransferTransaction off-chain, encodes it as an x402 payment header, and posts it to my self-hosted /settle route. The route acts as a Blocky402-compatible facilitator, opens a challenge, settles the receipt and returns an HMAC-signed envelope with a receiptId.
Arc/Circle side: the BuyerAgent authorizes spend through Circle Developer Controlled Wallets. There are three role wallets on ARC-TESTNET — Trader, ArcResearch, Risk. Authorization goes through an Arc spend ledger on disk with idempotency keys so nothing double-pays. Real ARC-TESTNET transfers are gated behind two env flags that have to both be true.
