Nanopayments: every accepted call appends a meter entry (base price + costPerCall × calls). HCS: receipt hashes and the mission summary land on topic 0.0.10426202 on Hedera testnet. Allowlisted payloads only.
Partner tools that actually matter:

Circle Developer Controlled Wallets — the agent's identity and treasury
Hedera x402 + Blocky402-compatible facilitator — the pay-per-call rail
HCS — the public proof layer

name: Receivables Flow
description: The capital flywheel for invoice receivables: source, fund, resell, repay, and reprice capital cost
projectDescription:
Business App:  https://business-production-0df2.up.railway.app
Investor App:   https://investor-production-d938.up.railway.app
A business is owed $50,000 on an invoice and has to wait 60 days for it. Payroll does not wait. Invoice factoring/financing exists to bridge that cashflow gap, but it has two problems: the investor's money is locked until the customer pays, and nobody outside one lender can see whether the business pays on time.
Receivables Flow fixes both. Two of three business directors approve the invoice sale through a Privy key quorum, and the invoice is minted on Hedera as a token that only KYC-approved investors can hold. For example:

Day 0: an investment fund buys it for $47,990, a 4.02% fee priced off the business's public repayment record.
Day 20: the fund sells half of the invoice to another investor for $24,330 on the secondary market, so the fund gets liquidity before the invoice is due.
Day 60: the business repays $50,000 on-time and each holder is paid $25,000. The first fund made $1,340, the second $670, and the whole $2,010 of return is the fee the business paid.

Then the loop closes. The on-time repayment is written to the business's ENS name (ironline.business.receivablesflow.eth) and its credit score rises from 83 to 86 — so in the next round of financing, the business gets a lower cost of capital because of its own timely repayment behavior.
howItsMade:
This project has two Next.js apps: a business portal for Ironline Freight and an investor portal for Woodgrove Capital. They share three workspace libraries: the Privy layer, the Hedera contracts, and the ENS registry code.
Hedera settles the full lifecycle of the receivable. The invoice is issued with Asset Tokenization Studio as a whitelist-only security: $50,000 face value, 60-day maturity, one unit per dollar. Payment is in mUSDC, a mock dollar deployed for the demo because Circle's testnet faucet caps at $20. A delivery-versus-payment contract settles each sale by moving the mUSDC and the token in one atomic transaction. The same transaction also books the day-60 repayment on Hedera's schedule service. KYC is enforced by the invoice token itself. Only wallets on its approved list can hold the security. Every step of the lifecycle runs on Hedera: issuing the token, the sale to the fund, the day-20 resale on the secondary market, and the day-60 repayment to each holder.
ENS holds a business's creditworthiness in public, under its own name. On the ENSv2 hackathon deployment on Sepolia, receivablesflow.eth issues ironline.business and woodgrove.investor, so both portals show a readable name instead of a wallet address. A Permissioned Resolver lets only the platform key write the fields that matter. The investor's KYC pass is a wallet record plus the name's expiry. The business's repayment history is five counts on its name: financed, paid on time, paid late, defaulted, and outstanding. The fee on every invoice is computed live from those counts by a published formula, so each on-time repayment raises the score and lowers the cost of the next invoice. In the demo the score rises from 83 to 86 and the fee falls from 4.02% to 3.84%.
Privy provides the controls a B2B financial product needs. Both portals sign in with email OTP, with no extension or seed phrase. On the business side, tokenizing an invoice requires two of the company's three directors to sign, enforced by a Privy key quorum on the company wallet. For the demo, the first signature is made automatically by the app backend, and whoever signs in as demo user is seated as a director so their approval is the second.  On the investor side, the fund's wallet is governed by a Privy policy that enforces its mandate: no payment above $100,000, and no payment to a business that is not on the approved list. Anything outside the mandate is refused by Privy, not by application code. Both wallets transact on Hedera through Privy's EVM RPC.

name: Orbit
description: A DeFi collectible economy where trading fees fund rewards and liquidity stays permanently locked.
projectDescription:
Orbit is a DeFi collectible economy on Base that connects liquid tokens, permanent collectibles, and rewards funded by trading activity.
FUEL is the tradable side of a 4,444-identity collection. Gaining a whole FUEL unit triggers a random Discovery that reveals a Grounded Craft, including its rarity and reward track. Collectors can keep trading or choose to Launch a favorite: permanently burn one FUEL to turn that craft into an Orbiter. The Orbiter keeps its identity, becomes reward-eligible, and no longer depends on a FUEL balance. Unclaimed rewards belong to the collectible and transfer with it to its next owner.
The economy runs through a canonical Uniswap v4 FUEL/WETH market. A custom hook charges 3% on WETH-side trading volume: 2% funds stock-reward conversion, 0.85% builds permanently locked protocol liquidity, and 0.15% goes to the creator. Reward cycles split the available budget across AAPLc, GOOGLc, METAc, and NVDAc tracks. Ordinary Orbiters share their track's allocation by rarity weight; three Stations and an Observatory receive allocations across all four tracks. Rewards depend on actual activity and successful conversions.
Uniswap's Continuous Clearing Auction distributes 4,000 FUEL, discovers the opening price, and combines auction proceeds with 444 reserved FUEL to seed permanently locked market liquidity.
Privy lets a collector start with email or an existing wallet and use the same account for funding, trading, Launch, and claims. The Graph integration makes pooled fee allocations and completed reward conversions inspectable.
The working demo is deployed on Base Sepolia. Settlement and stock-reward tokens are valueless test assets, demonstrating the mechanics rather than live stock ownership or guaranteed returns.
howItsMade:
Orbit combines Solidity contracts tested with Foundry, a Next.js/React/TypeScript frontend, and Effect-based TypeScript services with SQLite persistence.
The protocol pairs ERC-20 FUEL with ERC-721 collectible identities. Whole-unit acquisitions create pending Discoveries. Chainlink VRF supplies a verifiable seed; separate, retryable finalization applies identity draws in acquisition order. Launch burns exactly one FUEL and activates permanent collectible reward accounting. The reward ledger accrues rewards to identities and checks current ownership when a wallet claims.
Uniswap is the market and launch infrastructure. CanonicalRouter settles swaps through the official v4 PoolManager, while CanonicalFeeHook enforces the registered FUEL/WETH market and collects the WETH-side fee using hook deltas. The initial distribution integrates the official Continuous Clearing Auction and Liquidity Launcher with wallet-bound bidder escrows. A launch coordinator verifies pool initialization and permanent liquidity custody before enabling trading. EpochConverter processes four fixed WETH-to-USDC-to-reward-token routes independently; failed tracks keep their reserved budgets for retry.
Privy's React SDK and wagmi adapter support email-created embedded wallets and external wallets on Base Sepolia. The same connected account signs the faucet proof, approvals, trades, Launch, and claims. A bounded testnet faucet supplies gas and test WETH. Saved transaction evidence and receipt reconciliation recover interrupted wallet responses without automatically replaying a trade.
The Graph subgraph preserves the Messari DEX AMM 1.3.2 schema and adds v4 hook-fee, reward-funding, and auction lifecycle entities. Standard pool/token/swap fields support reusable market queries; custom entities expose exact fee allocations and successful conversion spending. Live Studio integration evidence and reproducible queries are included in the repository. The frontend requests funding analytics through a cached, budgeted API. Direct contract reads serve current balances and ownership; a separate SQLite index serves protocol history.
Two subtle integration challenges were separating PoolManager swap deltas from the user's total payment after hook fees, and checking actual auction-to-pool readiness because a successful migration transaction can still contain an internal migration failure. Both are covered by contract checks and lifecycle tests.

name: VendingAgent
description: Autonomous pay-per-call API proxy using Hedera x402 and Chainlink CRE for agentic workflows.
projectDescription: This project is an autonomous pay-per-call API proxy (VendingAgent) designed for the emerging Agentic Economy. It solves the problem of AI agents needing rigid subscriptions or hardcoded API keys to access premium Web2 data. Using Hedera's x402 standard, it gates a premium data endpoint, requiring autonomous agents to stream sub-cent micro-transactions in HBAR to unlock the payload. Furthermore, to protect the upstream Web2 API key from being exposed on-chain or leaked in the logs, the project utilizes Chainlink's CRE Confidential Workflows (running inside a hardware TEE enclave) to securely fetch and return the data. We also integrated Bazantic MCP Recipes so other autonomous agents can easily discover, understand, and autonomously interact with the service.
howItsMade: We built the backend API proxy using Node.js and TypeScript, integrating the @hashgraph/sdk to verify x402 micropayments on the Hedera testnet via the Blocky402 facilitator. The core data fetching logic is handled by a Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE) handlerInTee script. This script securely decrypts the upstream Web2 API key exclusively inside a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) enclave, ensuring the secret never leaks to the public while executing the confidential workflow. To make the service discoverable, we created a Bazantic Model Context Protocol (MCP) server alongside a recipe.json file that instructs any consumer LLM on exactly how to construct the HBAR transaction and request the data. Finally, a separate autonomous client agent script was written to simulate the end-to-end HTTP 402 payment negotiation and successful data retrieval loop.

name: BO-Sealed-Bid
description: Agent-to-agent commerce has a bad default: to negotiate its price
projectDescription:
Agent-to-agent commerce has a bad default: to negotiate, an agent either reveals its reserve price
(and gets priced at the edge of it) or trusts a middleman who sees both numbers. We remove the
middleman with a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow.
Agent A and Agent B each hold a private reserve. A CRE Confidential Workflow reads both as Vault secrets inside a Nitro enclave and returns only SETTLE @ midpoint or NO_OVERLAP. SETTLE is written to a receiver on Base Sepolia; NO_OVERLAP writes nothing. Third-party vetting via x402.
Both reserve prices and two commitment salts are CRE Vault secrets. Inside a handlerInTee handler
running on AWS Nitro, the workflow makes one getSecrets call, computes whether the bands overlap,
and produces exactly one of two outputs: SETTLE @ clearing (the midpoint) or the literal
NO_OVERLAP. Alongside it: two salted commitments sha256(reserve‖salt) and a run id, so either
party can later prove what it bid without the enclave ever having published it. Nothing else crosses
back to the DON — not the reserves, not the gap, not which side was higher. That property is tested at
every layer, with deliberately leaky implementations kept in the suite as negative controls.
On SETTLE, the DON writes the attestation through the CRE Forwarder to SealedBidReceiver on Base
Sepolia, a contract that records only SETTLE outcomes and reverts everything else — so even a
misbehaving workflow could not leave a NO_OVERLAP trace. Agent A then pays Agent B the clearing amount.
On NO_OVERLAP, no transaction is sent at all.
Settlement is not self-certified. Before bidding, each agent vets the other through BlindOracle, a
public pay-per-call API settled over x402 in USDC on Base mainnet; a trust badge opens the bracket, a
reputation lookup closes it, and a process-followed attestation can be bought over the hash-chained,
signed evidence of the run. Every one of those payments is a USDC transfer anyone can check on Basescan.
The one thing SETTLE does reveal is A_max + B_min. That is the standard sealed-bid trade-off and
we state it rather than hide it.
howItsMade:
Chainlink CRE (CLI v1.31.0, @chainlink/cre-sdk 1.18.0, TypeScript). cre.handlerInTee with a
Nitro/us-west-2 constraint; one getSecrets call for four Vault secrets (a measured runtime limit —
a second call fails); usingTheDons().report(...) with an ABI-encoded attestation; EVMClient.writeReport
on SETTLE only. 34 bun tests. Deployed live to the on-chain registry on 2026-09-11; one DON execution settled through the real Forwarder, the next was refused as a duplicate run. Measured along the way: cre workflow simulate --broadcast writes through
the simulator's own mock forwarder as a placeholder owner, so a receiver built for the production
Forwarder correctly rejects it — hence two deployed receivers, one per forwarder, documented in EVIDENCE.md.
Solidity / Foundry. SealedBidReceiver implements CRE's IReceiver; forwarder-only, optional
pinned workflow owner, SETTLE-only state, ERC-165. 13 forge tests including a fuzz over the midpoint.
Base. Settlement on Base Sepolia (receiver + the A→B transfer); BlindOracle payments on Base mainnet.
x402. The x402 Python SDK signs EIP-3009 TransferWithAuthorizations; the facilitator settles
gaslessly. 42 real payments across 4 SKUs during the build ($4.02), every one a USDC transfer on Base mainnet listed in bo_calls.jsonl.
Python. bo_client.py (client + the reserve-never-leaves-the-parties rule), scripts/demo.py
(the whole protocol in one command, producing a hash-chained evidence bundle in the RAP-1 wire format,
signed with ed25519 — public key at evidence/signing-key.pub; HMAC only as the keyless fallback), scripts/skucheck.py.
Process attestation. The signed bundle is bought against BlindOracle's security.process-attestation
SKU: conformant, signature_binding: attributable (tx 0xa562f6f7…a1fc, USDC on Base mainnet). The first
run came back non_conformant and is recorded as such in EVIDENCE.md — the fix was matching a published
wire format and switching to an asymmetric key, not rewording the claim.
AI assistance. Built with Claude Code from this repository's own SPEC.md, after kick-off, from a
minimal CLAUDE.md that forbids reading anything outside the repo. See DISCLOSURE.md.

name: Proof of Attraction
description: A dating app where real human verification is built into every interaction.
projectDescription:
PROOF OF ATTRACTION
Detailed Project Description
ETHOnline 2026 — World Track
===============================================================================
THE ONE-LINE IDEA
A dating app where every single profile is a verified, unique, living human —
no bots, no catfish, no duplicate or throwaway accounts — and where an optional
human-backed AI agent can act on your behalf in a way the person you are talking
to can actually trust.
Human verification is not a badge bolted on at the end. It is the foundation the
whole product stands on. If you cannot prove you are a real, unique person, you
do not get in.
===============================================================================
THE PROBLEM
Every mainstream dating app has the same three rotten foundations:


Bots and scammers. A large share of "people" on dating apps are automated
accounts, romance scammers, or paid engagement farms. Users waste time,
lose money, and lose trust.


Fake and duplicate identities. One person can spin up ten profiles. Banned
users return instantly under a new email. There is no notion of "one real
human = one account."


No trust in AI. AI is flooding these apps — auto-swipers, script-written
openers, ghost-written conversations. When a message feels too smooth, you
cannot tell if a human is even involved. AI is treated as something to hide.


The result: matching feels like gambling against machines, and the moment AI
enters the chat, trust collapses entirely.
===============================================================================
THE CORE INSIGHT
The scarce, valuable thing in online dating is not looks or wit — it is the
guarantee that there is ONE REAL, UNIQUE HUMAN on the other side.
World ID can prove exactly that, anonymously, without collecting your identity
documents or selling your data. So we built a dating app where that proof is the
entry ticket, the trust signal on every screen, and — crucially — the thing that
makes AI safe instead of scary.
Instead of hiding AI, we make it accountable: an agent may act for you, but every
action it takes is cryptographically tied back to a verified human via World's
AgentBook. The other person sees "this was sent by a verified human's agent,"
not "you might be talking to a bot."
===============================================================================
HOW IT WORKS FOR A USER (THE EXPERIENCE)


PROVE YOU ARE HUMAN (onboarding)
You open the app and verify with World ID. This is a real, anonymous proof of
personhood — one account per unique human, enforced at the protocol level. No
email/password, no phone number. The proof itself is your identity.
Because World ID 4.0 nullifiers are one-time-use, we also create a World ID
"session" during signup so you can log back in later with a single tap,
without re-proving from scratch. On a new device you just enter your handle
and approve the login in the World App.


LIVE SELFIE ESTIMATE (optional, clearly labelled)
A quick two-frame front-camera check. It confirms you are a live person in
front of the camera (not a photo of a screen) via a small liveness challenge
— "turn your head", "smile" — and records an ESTIMATED gender presentation.
This is shown everywhere as an estimate, never as "verified." World does not
verify gender and we never claim it does. It is a third-party vision-model
guess, kept honest and separate from the real human-verification badge.


BUILD A PROFILE
Handle, photos, bio, interests, self-declared gender, who you are looking for,
and location. Photos are stored privately and served through short-lived
signed links, never as permanent public URLs.


DISCOVER REAL HUMANS ONLY
You swipe through other verified humans. Each card shows a humanity badge
(Orb / Selfie tier), an "Agent enabled" badge if that person authorized an
agent, and a compatibility match score computed from shared interests, age,
distance, verification tier, and on-chain reputation signals. A "Verified
humans only" filter is always available.


THE AGENT ACTS FOR YOU (the AgentKit part)
You can register a personal agent. It genuinely acts on your behalf:

"Ask my agent about her" — pre-screens a profile and gives you a take
before you even match.
Auto-suggested opener — when you match, your agent drafts a first message
in your chosen tone (warm / witty / direct). You can send via the agent,
edit it, or dismiss it.
Reply drafting — mid-conversation, it drafts your next reply from the
thread.
The recipient always sees a disclosure: "sent by a verified human's agent."
Nothing is hidden.



TRUST GATES ON HIGH-STAKES MOMENTS
First message and event RSVP are the moments abuse actually happens, so
human-verification is required there — a bot cannot send the first message or
claim a limited event seat.


AN ACTION LOG YOU CONTROL
Every action your agent takes is recorded and shown to you, each tagged with
whether it was cryptographically verified through AgentBook. You can revoke
any action. You always know what your agent did in your name.


===============================================================================
WHY THIS IS DIFFERENT


Verification is the product, not a feature. The entire funnel is gated on
proof of a unique human. This is Sybil resistance applied to dating.


AI is disclosed and accountable, not hidden. Most apps pretend AI is not
there. We surface it and make it provably human-backed. That flips AI from a
trust-destroyer into a trust signal.


Privacy-preserving by construction. World ID proves personhood without
revealing who you are. We store an anonymous nullifier, not your identity.


Gender is handled honestly. It is an ESTIMATE from a live selfie, always
labelled as such, always separate from the real human badge. We refuse to
launder a guess as a verified fact.


===============================================================================
THE PRIZE ANGLE (ETHOnline — World Track)
The build targets both World prizes at once, and they reinforce each other:


AgentKit Continuity: a human-backed agent acts in chat and discovery, and
every action routes through a real AgentKit-protected backend that resolves
the agent to a human through AgentBook on World Chain. A durable, per-human
free-trial quota (keyed to the verified human, not a device or wallet) demos
real continuity, with an on-chain testnet top-up when the trial runs out.


Selfie Check / Proof of Human: human verification is used as a risk,
eligibility, fairness, continuity, and abuse-prevention signal at the two
highest-stakes moments — first message and event RSVP — not as a one-time
checkbox.


===============================================================================
ONE-SENTENCE PITCH
Proof of Attraction is a dating app where you can finally be certain the person
you match with is a real, unique human — and where AI is allowed to help, but
only when it is provably backed by one.
howItsMade:
PROOF OF ATTRACTION
How It's Made — Deep Technical Description
ETHOnline 2026 — World Track
===============================================================================

HIGH-LEVEL ARCHITECTURE
===============================================================================

Three moving parts:
[ React Native app ]  --HTTPS-->  [ Hono API on Vercel ]  -->  [ Neon Postgres ]
(Expo)                          (serverless)                (Drizzle ORM)
|                                |  --> Upstash Redis (quota/nonces)
|                                |  --> AWS S3 (private photos)
|                                |  --> Ably (realtime chat)
|                                |  --> Groq LLM (OpenAI-compatible)
|                                |  --> World Chain (AgentBook, reputation)
|                                --> developer.world.org/api/v4/verify
--> WebView -> IDKit (World App) for World ID proofs
--> Privy embedded wallet + viem for testnet top-ups

Client: React Native via Expo SDK 57, Expo Router for navigation. Standalone
app (not a World Mini App), built as an Android dev/release APK.
Backend: Hono, deployed to Vercel serverless (local dev via @hono/node-server).
Stable public alias: server-two-steel-51.vercel.app.
Repo split: /app and /src (client), /server (backend), /docs (submission +
feedback docs). Drizzle migrations in /server/drizzle.

===============================================================================
2. IDENTITY, AUTH, AND SESSIONS (the hard part)
There is no "Sign in with World ID" session product — IDKit produces a one-shot
proof, not a session. So we own the session lifecycle.
WORLD ID 4.0 SPECIFICS THAT SHAPED THE DESIGN

We use idkit-core 4.2.4 and verify against developer.world.org/api/v4/verify/{rp_id}.
v4 requires a signed rp_context: the backend signs a short-lived request token
with an RP signing key (signRequest from @worldcoin/idkit-core/signing) before
the widget can open. App ID + RP ID + signing key are the three portal values.
v4 uniqueness nullifiers are ONE-TIME per (rp, action). Re-verifying the same
action returns nullifier_replayed. There is no "max verifications" toggle on a
v4 action page. This is why naive "verify again to log in" does not work.

THE FLOW WE BUILT

Signup: proofOfHuman uniqueness proof (Sybil check, action from
EXPO_PUBLIC_WORLD_ID_ACTION) -> backend verifies -> issues our own HS256 JWT
keyed to the anonymous nullifier -> upserts a users row. Immediately after, we
run IDKit.createSession and store the returned session_id on the user
(users.world_session_id) and in SecureStore.
Login: IDKit.proveSession(session_id) -> POST /auth/session/prove -> new JWT.
No uniqueness re-proof, so no replay. On a fresh device with no stored session,
the user types their handle -> GET /auth/session/lookup?handle= resolves the
session_id -> proveSession.
The WebView page (server/public/verify.html) takes a mode param:
uniqueness | create-session | prove-session, and drives IDKit accordingly.
A native bridge (WorldIdProvider / WorldIdModal, react-native-webview) returns
the proof to the app.

TOKEN HANDLING

JWT (7-day) stored in expo-secure-store, attached as a Bearer token by
authedFetch, which transparently retries once via POST /auth/refresh on a 401
before signing out.
The derived humanId (from the nullifier) is the exact key the AgentKit quota
counts against — tying agent continuity to the verified human.

===============================================================================
3. THE AGENT — REAL AGENTKIT, NOT A COSMETIC CHATBOT
What makes it a genuine AgentKit integration: every in-chat/discovery agent
action routes through an AgentKit-protected backend endpoint, and the server
verifies the caller against AgentBook on every call.
CLIENT SIDE (src/agent/agentkit.ts)

Uses @worldcoin/agentkit createAgentkitClient + declareAgentkitExtension.
CRITICAL: the extension is declared with network 'eip155:4801' (World Chain
Sepolia). Without the network, supportedChains is empty and createHeader throws
"Signer eip155:4801/eip191 is not supported" — the bug that silently dropped to
the fallback gate. The signer is the Privy embedded wallet (eip191, signMessage).

SERVER SIDE (server/src/agentkit.ts + agentGate in index.ts)

Real verify path: parseAgentkitHeader -> validateAgentkitMessage (maxAge 300s,
nonce replay set) -> verifyAgentkitSignature (RPC) -> AgentBook lookupHuman.
Fallback gate: if no/invalid AgentKit header, resolve via x-agent-wallet against
a homegrown registry. The response carries a "gate" field: "agentkit" or
"fallback: <reason>", surfaced in the app ("Last call: agentkit").
AgentBook is read on World Chain mainnet (eip155:480) — a free eth_call,
no funds, no tx. Our agent signs on Sepolia (eip155:4801). Single deliberate
mainnet touch, flagged; the fallback covers it if unavailable.

AGENT ENDPOINTS (all pass through agentGate)
POST /agent/context     pre-screen a profile or read match context (generateTake
for discovery, generateContext for a match)
POST /agent/icebreaker  draft a first message in a chosen tone
POST /agent/reply       draft the next reply from the last ~8 messages
POST /agent/send        send a message as the agent (viaAgent=true)
GET  /agent/actions     action log + quota { used, freeTrial, credit, remaining }
DELETE /agent/actions/:id  revoke a logged action
Every call records an agent_actions row (kind, detail, agentBacked, registered),
shown in the Agent tab and revocable.
CONTINUITY QUOTA + x402-STYLE TOP-UP

FREE_TRIAL_CALLS per verified human, stored in Upstash Redis (durable across
serverless cold starts). Exhaustion returns HTTP 402 with a top-up target.
On-chain settlement (testnet only): the agent settles a native ETH transfer on
World Chain Sepolia (chain id 4801) from the Privy embedded wallet via viem.
Client reports the tx hash to POST /agent/topup; verifyTopUp
(server/src/payments.ts) waits for the receipt and checks recipient, minimum
value, and unused hash (replay protection), then credits N calls in Redis.
The wallet defaults to World Chain Sepolia (Privy supportedChains) and calls
wallet_switchEthereumChain to 4801 before sending; the signer pre-checks
balance to give a clean "wallet has 0 ETH" message instead of a viem stack dump.
A "Credit from transaction" fallback lets any wallet's tx hash be pasted to
settle, since a keyless exchange wallet cannot sign on a custom chain.

===============================================================================
4. LIVE SELFIE GENDER ESTIMATE (vision + liveness)

Client (src/verification/GenderEstimateCapture.tsx): expo-camera front camera,
two frames — neutral then a challenge (turn head / smile / raise eyebrows).
Capture quality is stepped down in a loop until each base64 frame is small
enough to fit Vercel's ~4.5MB request cap (the FUNCTION_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE issue).
Server: POST /me/gender-estimate (GET .../challenge issues the challenge).
llm.ts estimateGenderFromFrames calls a Groq VISION model (qwen/qwen3.6-27b;
Llama-4 vision is deprecated on Groq) with JSON mode, checking live /
samePerson / challengePassed plus an estimated label + confidence.
Result stored in users.gender_estimate. Frames are held in memory only — never
written to S3 or the DB. Soft signal only: it never blocks, and the profile
shows a private "estimate differs from what you declared" note, never exposed
to other users as verified.

===============================================================================
5. DOMAIN MODEL, MATCHING, AND REALTIME
REPO PATTERN (server/src/repo/{types,memory,pg}.ts)

getRepo() returns PgRepo when DATABASE_URL is set, else an in-memory MemoryRepo
(used for local dev and stub mode). Same interface for both.

DRIZZLE SCHEMA (server/src/db/schema.ts)
users (nullifier_hash, handle, tier, gender_estimate, wallet,
world_session_id, likes_everyone), profiles, likes, matches, messages,
events, rsvps, push_tokens, agent_actions.
DOMAIN ROUTES (server/src/routes.ts, all behind requireSession)
GET  /me                    user + profile (photos presigned)
PUT  /me/profile            requireOrb
PUT  /me/handle             unique handle
POST /me/wallet             link agent wallet -> human
POST /me/photo              multipart upload
GET  /discovery             ranked deck (verifiedOnly filter)
POST /likes                 like/pass, auto-match, push
GET  /matches, /matches/:id/messages, POST .../messages
GET  /realtime/token        Ably token
GET  /events, POST/DELETE /events/:id/rsvp   (RSVP requires human tier)
POST /push/register
MATCHING (server/src/matching.ts) — pure weighted scorer
interest Jaccard 0.34, distance (haversine) 0.14, tier 0.14,
agentBacked 0.14, age 0.12, reputation 0.12; top candidates enriched with
on-chain reputation signals (onchain.ts: viem publicClient — tx count, balance
band, AgentBook registration; null-safe).
REALTIME + MEDIA

Chat over Ably websockets (src/realtime/ably.ts) with a polling fallback and a
"loaded" flag used to trigger the agent's auto-suggested opener exactly once.
Photos: private S3 objects (server/src/s3.ts) returned as 12-hour presigned GET
URLs; blob.ts routes to S3 when configured, else a data-uri/Vercel Blob fallback.
Push via Expo push tokens.

===============================================================================
6. STACK SUMMARY
CLIENT
React Native 0.86 / Expo SDK 57, Expo Router
@worldcoin/agentkit 0.2.1
@privy-io/expo 0.73 + viem 2.56 (embedded wallet, testnet signing)
expo-camera 57 (live selfie), react-native-webview (World ID widget)
ably 2.28 (chat), expo-secure-store (JWT + session), expo-notifications
BACKEND
hono 4.6 on Vercel serverless
@worldcoin/idkit-core 4.2.4 (v4 verify + signing)
@worldcoin/agentkit 0.2.1 (AgentBook verify)
drizzle-orm 0.45 + @neondatabase/serverless (Neon Postgres)
@upstash/redis 1.38 (durable per-human quota + nonces)
@aws-sdk/client-s3 + s3-request-presigner (private photos)
ably 2.28 (chat), openai 7.15 -> Groq (LLM text + vision)
viem 2.56 (World Chain reads + testnet receipt verification)
CHAINS
World Chain mainnet eip155:480  — AgentBook resolution (read-only eth_call)
World Chain Sepolia eip155:4801 — agent signing + testnet top-up settlement
===============================================================================
7. NOTABLE ENGINEERING DECISIONS / GOTCHAS SOLVED

World ID v4 replay: solved with createSession/proveSession instead of
re-running uniqueness proofs; login is a session proof, not a new nullifier.
AgentKit header: must declare the extension on eip155:4801 or createHeader
rejects the Sepolia signer.
Vercel payload cap: selfie frames are downscaled client-side until under the
request limit; non-JSON error bodies (413) are handled instead of JSON.parse.
Node/undici picks broken IPv6 routes to Neon on some networks; db/client.ts
forces IPv4 (dns ipv4first + undici Agent family:4), escape hatch NEON_FORCE_IPV4=0.
Privy provisioning failures were swallowed; useWallet now surfaces the real
error (e.g. invalid_native_app_id) with a retry, deduped across call sites.
Everything on-chain is testnet only, never mainnet — the one mainnet touch is a
free AgentBook read, explicitly flagged, with a fallback gate.

name: Blockhead 2026
description: Explore and interact with the decentralized web in a modular, plug-and-play local-first client!
projectDescription:
In early 2026, after five years iterating on the same codebase over dozens of hackathons, I decided to dive headfirst into the world of agentic software factory engineering and rebuild Blockhead from scratch. The result: a local-first interface with a highly accurate, irreducible, internally consistent ontology capable of modeling integrations with any decentralized protocol, blockchain ecosystem, wallet, node or data source.
Browse artifacts across the decentralized web, connect existing wallets across any ecosystem, interact with protocols of all shapes and sizes, and plug and play with your own nodes and data providers leveraging Blockhead's extensive library of adapters.
howItsMade:
Blockhead's codebase models every stack layer explicitly and modularly. Provider sources handle external requests and data queries. Resolvers map responses into native entities. Selectors uniquely identify entities and route URLs with distinct sets of fields. Local-first collections cache data and feed the UI views.
For ETHOnline 2026, I extended its native data model with Messari Standardized Subgraphs and adding Ledger support to its wallet interface.
The Graph integration queries live Messari Standardized Subgraphs. Protocols, pools, block observations, and ordered pool assets use native selectors. Historical requests preserve the deployment and block hash. Reported schema versions remain separate from the versions expected by our deployment configuration. Missing data is an error, not an empty result.
Ledger uses Device Management Kit, Ethereum Signer Kit, and the official Speculos transport. The wallet adapter checks signing authority and verifies message signatures. Browser tests exercise device approval, rejection, and persisted request history.
In the demo, I have an automated harness drive a browser to demonstrate data queries and local-first client side caching. It also drives an instance of Ledger's Speculos emulator, clicking through screens to connect to Blockhead's UI and facilitate a signing request.
Uniswap V3 and Sushi V3 financial observations use the same view and query pattern. Each observation retains its exact values, source deployment, schema version and block. Reloading an observation requests that block, rather than silently replacing it with current data. A separate Uniswap view interprets pool state, including its raw token ratio, fee configuration and oracle capacity.
The Ledger flow reviews a message on the official Speculos emulator, signs it and saves a request that can be reopened after reload.
Once I have the stack layers, data modeling and automation harnesses fully nailed down, I plan to continue building out the UI layer and implement immersive graph visualizations on top of the client-side cache.

name: Reveal
description: Buy a sealed mystery night. You know the vibe, the experience stays secret until you shake
projectDescription:
Reveal is a two-sided marketplace for sealed mystery nights. You do not book a named show or pick a venue from a list. You buy a crate. Before you pay, the product only shows the vibe: category, neighborhood, time window, mystery USDC price, and a value floor so you know the deal is real. The actual experience stays locked until after checkout. That secrecy is the product. Empty seats an hour before showtime are almost worthless, and public discounts train people to wait while bots scoop the good inventory. Reveal flips both sides at once. Merchants quietly clear leftover capacity as sealed crates instead of training the market to delay. Buyers get the thrill of not knowing what they pulled, with guardrails so the surprise stays fair.
The buyer journey is built around that mystery. Guests browse constraints-only cards, sign in with Privy, prove they are a live human with World Selfie Check, pay USDC on Base, then shake the crate open. Only then do title, details, and a door pass appear together. One crate per verified human per drop: the nullifier is unique for that night, so a second selfie cannot double-dip. Identity never goes to the merchant. After payment, a non-transferable Hedera Reveal Pass is minted with a QR for check-in; because it cannot be transferred, the night cannot be scalped after reveal. If a drop never reveals, payment can refund.
Merchants get the other half of the loop. A cinema, theatre, or dining room lists leftover seats as a sealed crate, watches a dashboard, and scans the guest QR at the door to redeem the pass and settle the seat. There is also an AI concierge path: an agent pays an x402 availability API on Hedera via Blocky402, then reads which mystery nights are still open by area without scraping the consumer UI. So demand can arrive through the app or through chat, while supply still publishes once.
Consumer loop: auth → selfie → pay → shake → pass. Merchant loop: create → dashboard → scan. Agent loop: 402 challenge → settle → availability. The whole point is one marketplace that protects the mystery for buyers and liquidates expiring inventory for merchants without spoiling either side.
Both sides win.
howItsMade:
Reveal was built from scratch during ETHOnline as a pnpm monorepo. The consumer, merchant, and agent surfaces live in a Next.js app. An Express service stays up as the x402 availability API. Drizzle owns the schema for PGlite locally or Postgres in production. A shared Hedera package handles Reveal Pass issue and redeem. Partner tech is not bolted on for a checklist: each one sits on a critical path in the mystery loop.
The UX is intentional about spoilers. Drop cards show category, area, time, and price only. Venue and title stay blurred until the shake animation finishes. Rarity heat is computed from deal quality, face value versus mystery price, so a stronger discount feels rarer without revealing what you bought. After unbox, XP, streak, and badges land on the player profile, and a public board shows live pulls without unsealing other buyers’ crates. That keeps the demo cinematic while the fairness rules stay real.
Money and auth run through Privy embedded wallets plus viem on Base Sepolia. On login, users without wallets get one automatically. Buyers transfer USDC into escrow from the buy flow; if the night never reveals there is a refund path. The UI tracks USDC and gas as separate balances on purpose, because hackathon demos often die when someone has faucet USDC but no Base Sepolia ETH. Merchant routes are allowlisted by Privy DID so venue tools stay gated without a custom auth stack.
Fairness is World IDKit v4 Selfie Check. The server signs the RP request, the widget collects the proof, and we post the payload to World’s v4 verify endpoint. We store action plus nullifier plus dropId so a second selfie cannot buy the same mystery night, and we never forward identity to the merchant. Selfie Check is still beta-gated, so we kept a labeled Demo verify path that still hits our verify and uniqueness APIs rather than silently mocking pay, reveal, and pass. That let us record the full stack while waiting on Portal enablement.
The night itself is tokenized on Hedera. After USDC payment confirms, we mint a non-fungible Reveal Pass with the Hashgraph SDK over HTS, associate and transfer it, surface HashScan links, and redeem it when the merchant scans the door QR. ATS factory addresses are documented for Tokenization of Anything alignment; the live hackathon path is HTS because the full Equity.create diamond was too heavy for the event window. Consumer Hedera keys are operator-custodied for mint on the demo path, and that is disclosed.
The agentic path is Hedera x402. GET /availability returns HTTP 402 with an exact-scheme Hedera challenge and Blocky402 as facilitator. The /agent console settles that challenge, then reads remaining mystery inventory by area. That is how AI chat can discover sealed nights without scraping the consumer UI, and how the same inventory serves both the human UI and the agent.
The hacky but useful glue is an in-process Next.js store that auto-seeds a demo crate so recording does not depend on a cold database, while Drizzle remains ready for durable Postgres. Put together, Privy moves money, World enforces one human per crate, Hedera carries the pass and the paid availability API, and the product in the middle stays what it claims to be: a sealed mystery night for both sides of the market.

name: AgentAlpha
description: Agent marketplace that grades what it sells — DeFi forecasts via x402 on Hedera.
projectDescription:
AgentAlpha is a verifiable DeFi signal market built on Hedera testnet. It solves a fundamental problem in the emerging agent economy: when Agent A pays Agent B for a prediction, how do you know the prediction was any good?
Today's A2A protocols (Google A2A, ACP, etc.) give agents an "Agent Card" and let them self-describe capabilities, but they have no mechanism to objectively measure output quality after the fact. An agent can claim 99% accuracy with zero verification. Crypto trading signal groups operate the same way — Chainalysis estimates 87% of crypto signal providers show no verifiable track record, and CoinTelegraph reports that "premium" signal groups routinely delete losing calls.
AgentAlpha introduces three innovations that go beyond existing A2A paradigms:


COMMIT-REVEAL VERIFICATION: Every forecast is hash-committed on-chain before its target time, then publicly revealed and graded against Pyth oracle prices. No backdating. No selective disclosure.


QUALITY ≠ COMPLETION: Most A2A protocols measure "did the agent respond?" — we measure "was the response actually correct?" using oracle-backed directional accuracy, MAE in basis points, and grade coverage as separate public metrics.


REVEAL COVERAGE AS A FIRST-CLASS METRIC: A provider's willingness to publicly reveal predictions after the alpha window expires — proving trust in their own track record — is measured independently. Buyers filter on reveal_pct alongside accuracy, creating market pressure for transparency without slashing or staking.


The system uses x402 v2 micropayments settled through the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera. Buyers sign exact HBAR transfers (0.001 HBAR per forecast), with per-request caps, kill switches, and bounded wallets. Payments are final — a bad forecast doesn't trigger a refund, but it does tank your public metrics.
Two real paid requests have been completed end-to-end with on-chain commitments, HCS audit receipts, and public reveals. The buyer agent autonomously discovered the provider, verified its Agent Card, enforced spend policy, and completed the purchase without human intervention.
Designed but not yet built: a Subscription Vault using HIP-1215 scheduled transactions for recurring payments, and multi-provider/multi-horizon support. These are documented as P1 scope — we're transparent about what's live vs. what's designed.
howItsMade:
SMART CONTRACTS (Solidity, Hedera testnet):

AgentRegistry: On-chain identity, gateway/payee binding, metadata hash, active flag. Owner-authorized lifecycle management.
SignalLedger: Commitment storage, permissionless reveal, oracle-backed grading using Pyth price feeds. Emits grade events, never moves money.

Both contracts are deployed and verified on Sourcify.
BACKEND (TypeScript, Node.js ≥22):

x402 Gateway: Generates schema-valid forecasts, validates Blocky402 payment, persists before settlement, commits to SignalLedger, returns response with salt for buyer-side verification.
Indexer: Reads Mirror Node events, reconciles payment references against actual transfers, computes rolling discovery metrics from public evidence.
Worker: Restart-safe background loop for HCS audit receipts, reveal submission after target time, grade retries with Pyth Hermes historical data.
Store: SQLite with durable WAL mode, process lock, forward-only projections.

BUYER AGENT (TypeScript CLI):

Autonomous discovery → policy filter (5 eligible samples, 80% reveal coverage) → quote validation → exact HBAR signing → commitment verification → resume recovery.
Kill switch, per-provider daily cap, global daily cap, token/network allowlist.

FRONTEND (Vanilla HTML/JS):

Discovery dashboard, seller profiles with raw metrics, signal evidence pages with transaction links, buyer activity view.
No framework, served by the same Express instance.

KEY INTEGRATIONS:

Blocky402: x402 v2 payment verification and settlement on Hedera testnet
Pyth/Hermes: Historical price data for oracle-backed grading (currently blocked by InvalidWormholeVaa on testnet — reveal works, grade is evidenced as oracle_unavailable)
Hedera Mirror Node: Event indexing, transaction evidence, payment reconciliation
HCS: Append-only audit receipts (no secret data before target time)

All code is TypeScript with 94.57% test coverage (46 unit tests + 13 contract tests). CI passes on GitHub Actions.

name: Wikshi
description: Give your agent an inbox, a voice, and a face. Paid per use with x402 on Hedera.
projectDescription:
Imagine your agent finding business contacts, sending emails, making phone calls, and hosting video meetings for you, then bringing the answers back.
AI can do a lot of research, but when getting an answer means actually talking to someone, you're still doing the work yourself. Wikshi gives your agent its own inbox, a voice for phone calls, and a face for video meetings, along with the research and contact data to reach the right people.
Wikshi provides 14 services through x402 on Hedera. Your agent discovers a service, gets a quote, and pays per use in native HBAR or HTS USDC through Blocky402. You don't need separate provider accounts, API keys, or subscriptions.
Your agent can:

Research people and companies: Search the web, discover businesses and professional profiles, and read source pages for details.
Find business contacts: Look up available business emails and phone numbers, identify someone by email, or find relevant contacts at a company.
Maintain its own inbox: Create an email address, receive responses, and keep conversations together.
Send emails and follow up: Contact people, read their replies, and continue the conversation from its inbox.
Call someone: Ask your questions, follow up on their answers, and return the call transcript.
Host a video meeting: Send a guest link for an AI-led conversation of up to five minutes. Your agent asks the questions and retrieves the transcript. You don't need to attend.

Calls and meetings are metered by the second, with unused prepaid funds refunded on-chain to the original payer. Signed receipts record usage and charges, and receipt hashes are anchored to Hedera Consensus Service. External agents can buy services directly or delegate tasks through A2A. Wikshi's hosted agent has completed a real paid A2A research request within an approved budget, with settlement and receipt verification on Hedera testnet.
For example, you ask your agent to find a manufacturer that can deliver 500 custom bags before an event. It researches suppliers, finds their business contacts, creates an inbox, and emails for quotes. As replies arrive, it follows up on missing details. It calls one supplier to confirm delivery and invites another to a video meeting to discuss your requirements. Each paid step goes through x402 on Hedera. You get a shortlist backed by quotes and conversation records, with receipts showing what your agent spent.
howItsMade:
Wikshi uses x402 to quote and collect payment before an agent's request runs. Payments settle through Blocky402 as native HBAR or HTS USDC transfers on Hedera testnet, without a custom settlement contract. Blocky402 pays the purchase's network fee, so a buyer paying in USDC doesn't need HBAR for gas.
Each payment memo binds the transfer to one operation. We check Mirror Node records and reject reused payments. For calls and meetings, the backend meters seconds used, calculates the final charge, and refunds the unused prepayment in the original asset.
Signed receipts record usage and billing. Their hashes are anchored to Hedera Consensus Service, allowing a verifier to check the receipt, arithmetic, and payment trail without exposing private results.
One important detail: we save refund transactions before submitting them. If a network response times out, we check the existing transaction rather than send another refund. Persistent operation state also lets agents resume work without purchasing it again.

name: AgentPass
description: AgentPass: a human-backed AI agent that pays to check your DeFi risk.
projectDescription: AgentPass is a web app for safely getting an actionable DeFi risk check. A user verifies that they are human with World ID, then gives a named agent its own limited spending budget. The agent queries live lending positions across Aave and Compound through The Graph, computes a reasoned risk score and recommendation, and returns the result with a verifiable payment receipt. Instead of trusting an API key or a black-box dashboard, users can see the agent identity, activity, budget, payment, and analysis in one continuous flow. The same service can also be discovered and called by other agents.
howItsMade: We built AgentPass as a pnpm TypeScript monorepo with a Next.js dashboard, a Hono API, and reusable packages for identity, data, payments, verification, and discovery. The Graph Subgraph MCP and Messari standardized lending schema provide live Aave V3 and Compound V3 positions; a risk engine converts those positions into factors, a 0-100 score, and a recommendation, with 60-second caching to protect the free tier. The API is protected by x402: an unpaid request returns 402 pricing metadata, the agent checks its HBAR session budget, signs a Hedera testnet payment through the Blocky402 facilitator, retries with X-PAYMENT, and receives a receipt. World ID gates spending authority, ENSv2 on Sepolia gives the agent a permissioned onchain identity, and Bazantic exposes it for agent discovery. A notable implementation detail is that every sponsor integration is a step in the same user action rather than a collection of disconnected demos.

name: Arc Reserve
description: Tokenize green projects and assets with a real price floor and stablecoin yield
projectDescription:
Arc-Reserve enables tokenized investment in green and renewable energy projects via blockchain technology. For example we have project features Solar Indonesia 01 (SOLAR01), a 50 MW solar installation located in Indonesia.     Operational Architecture: Project owners list eligible renewable initiatives on the Arc-Reserve platform. KYC-verified investors purchase asset-backed tokens using stablecoins. Tokens do not mean as equity or corporate ownership; rather, they grant holders a proportional right to underlying real-world cash flows generated by the energy assets.   Revenue Cycle: Revenues are routed on-chain and distributed programmatically: the majority is disbursed as yield to token holders, while remaining allocations fund a protected reserve, operator compensation, and protocol fees. Investors maintain continuous exit liquidity through automated stablecoin redemptions backed directly by reserve capital.     Liquidity & Price Protection: A portion of capital raised during offerings is locked into active Uniswap V3 liquidity positions, establishing a fully backed price floor that prevents catastrophic downside volatility. When revenue profit are distributed, the liquidity baseline are increased, so it will raise the token price. And we ensure with this feature the token price will not fall below the baseline price and rugpulled.   This application operates across three testnets: Base Sepolia, Hedera Testnet, and Circle Arc Testnet. We also use stablecoin, in here we mock USDC so people can invest to the renewable project / assets using USDC and enable save investment.

howItsMade:
Smart Contracts & Compliance: Smart contracts were authored in Solidity and validated using Foundry. Token transfers are strictly restricted to KYC-compliant wallets through integrated IdentityRegistry and Compliance modules. The Vault contract segregates funds across five discrete accounting buckets: issuer proceeds, protected reserve, market liquidity, revenue, and protocol fees.
Market Management & Yield: The Market Manager governs concentrated Uniswap V3 liquidity positions under strict immutable constraints: token minting is prohibited, and execution is restricted to explicitly allocated inventory. Trading surplus automatically flows into the reserve vault, systematically raising the asset price floor over time.
Application Layer & Multi-Chain Deployment: Off-chain infrastructure comprises a real-time event indexing service, a RESTful API backend, and a React frontend for asset discovery and analytics. The complete architecture is deployed across Base Sepolia, Hedera Testnet, and Circle Arc Testnet. On networks lacking canonical Uniswap V3 deployments (Hedera and Arc), official Uniswap V3 factory and pool contracts were compiled and deployed directly.
For infra and deployment we’re using docker, nginx, aws. And for AI code we use opencode, claude code, and open spec for specs management. We also use google stitch for visualizing the UI and application flow.

name: Scenario Engine
description: SCENARIO: hedera-harness runs native multi-actor Hedera plans and checks the public mirror
projectDescription:
This is an open-source improvement to hedera-dev/hedera-harness, the CLI that drives a coding agent to build Hedera apps and then decides whether the work passed.
The harness already had CHAIN: one throwaway testnet wallet injected into the generated app. That is the wrong layer for two-party transfers, HTS airdrops, or HCS messages. People were left hoping Playwright clicked Transfer, or trusting a toast after the agent wrote 40 to 80 lines of SDK boilerplate. A toast is not proof. The agent does not get to grade itself.
This project adds SCENARIO, an opt-in fifth stage. You write a short YAML plan with named actors (alice, bob), steps (transfer HBAR, create a token, associate, airdrop, create an HCS topic, submit a message), and asserts. The harness funds those actors from your testnet operator, sends real transactions with the official @hiero-ledger/sdk, then polls the public testnet mirror until the effects are visible: Bob's HBAR, Bob's token balance, the topic text. The coding agent does not run this and does not declare success.
Stage order is GENERATE, ASSERT, SCENARIO, SMOKE, EVALUATE. A failed native plan skips the browser, so you do not pay for Playwright when the chain work already failed. A mirror or SDK outage is treated as infrastructure, not as an app failure.
There is also hedera-harness validate-scenario, which runs the plan alone with no agent. That is the demo path. Testnet only. Mainnet is rejected. Actor keys are never committed.
howItsMade:
Built in TypeScript on top of hedera-harness 2.0 (schema v3, their dev branch). The new code lives in src/scenario/: a YAML plan parser, operator env reuse from chainValidation, real AccountCreate / AccountDelete for named actors, an executor that uses the @hiero-ledger/sdk already shipped with the CLI, and a small REST client that polls https://testnet.mirrornode.hedera.com for HBAR balances, token balances, topic messages, and pending airdrops.
Steps map to real SDK transactions: TransferTransaction, TokenCreateTransaction, TokenAssociateTransaction, TokenAirdropTransaction, TokenClaimAirdropTransaction (PendingAirdropId built from the mirror, not a fake fromString), TopicCreateTransaction, TopicMessageSubmitTransaction. Later steps can refer to earlier ones by id (token: gold, topic: chat).
The stage is wired into attemptStages so it runs after ASSERT and before SMOKE. sessionRunner provisions actors once per run and sweeps leftover HBAR at the end (best effort: a token treasury cannot be deleted). doctor checks operator env and plan shape. CLI help and validate-scenario call the same executor as a full run. harnessGit treats scenario-actors.json as a secret.
No in-process fake ledger. No simulated consensus. Tests cover plan parsing, recipe load (inline and file:), mainnet rejection, CLI wiring, and cleanup of actor keys. Docs are in docs/scenarios.md plus the README stage table. The skeleton ships a two-actor HBAR / HTS / HCS example.
