name: Gantry
description: A Uniswap v4 hook that prices every swap by the caller's on-chain behaviour. Nobody gets blocked.
projectDescription:
A sandwich bot waits for your trade, buys in front of it, sells right after, and pockets the difference. As far as the pool is concerned that bot is just another customer paying exactly the same fee as you. Gantry changes that.
Gantry is a Uniswap v4 hook that prices each swap by the behaviour of the address actually paying for it. A clean wallet pays 0.05%. An address nobody has scored pays 0.30%. Something that looks like it is extracting pays 0.60%, and a confirmed sandwicher pays 1.00%. Nobody is ever blocked and nothing is blacklisted. If you want to sandwich the pool you still can, you just pay twenty times what a clean wallet pays for the privilege, and that extra goes to the liquidity providers you took it from.
Tiers are not something we assign by hand. An off-chain scorer reads real Ethereum mainnet behaviour, the scoring itself runs inside a Chainlink confidential workflow, and the result reaches the chain as a DON-signed report. The contract holding tiers only accepts writes from the Chainlink receiver address, so the deployer cannot set anyone's tier.
One design detail worth calling out: shared infrastructure is protected. Uniswap's own router reverts more often than almost anything else we measured, which on raw numbers reads as extraction. But thousands of ordinary people trade through that router, so charging it would charge all of them. Any address marked as shared gets clamped back to the default tier no matter what it scores.
It is live on Sepolia. The site shows every swap the pool has priced so far, including one wallet that paid 1.00%, then 0.30%, then 0.05% on the same pool at the same size, because its tier moved between trades.
howItsMade:
Contracts are Solidity and Foundry. The hook implements beforeSwap and returns a fee with Uniswap's OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG set, so the pool charges what the hook says instead of its own static fee. v4 reads a hook's permissions out of its address, so the deploy salt was mined with CREATE2 until the address ended in 0080, whose low 14 bits are exactly the BEFORE_SWAP permission bit.
The hard part of v4 is that inside beforeSwap, sender is the router, not the trader. Every trade arriving through a router looks identical. We solved it with an EIP-712 attestation: the frontend has you sign a free off-chain message, passes it through as hookData, and the hook recovers the signer and spends a nonce so the same signature cannot be replayed. No signature just means you pay the default tier, so the hook never depends on our frontend to stay correct.
The Graph does the reading. Two subgraphs, one on Sepolia for the hook's own events and one on mainnet for behaviour, plus nine published Substreams modules written in Rust and compiled to WASM. Substreams is doing something a subgraph structurally cannot. A reverted transaction emits no logs, so it is invisible to any event-based indexer, and yet a failed sandwich attempt is one of the strongest signals there is. Substreams reads transaction traces, which carry status, and that has surfaced over 12,000 reverted attempts that no subgraph could ever see. To keep this live rather than a committed snapshot we run substreams sink postgres as a systemd service on our own VPS, following the chain head into Postgres, with a small Node API in front that both the site and the Chainlink workflow read.
Chainlink CRE does the scoring. The workflow runs with handlerInTee, so it executes inside a TEE, and it pulls the tier thresholds from runtime.getSecrets() rather than from source. That matters: the rules are public, but a published threshold is just a number for a bot to park itself underneath. Results leave as a DON-signed report through EVMClient.writeReport() into TierReportReceiver, which verifies the workflow id, name and owner before it is allowed to touch TierOracle.
Frontend is Next.js on Vercel. The swap page quotes you from the oracle before you sign anything, so the price you are promised is the price the hook actually reads.
The hacky part worth mentioning: The Graph's rules say static datasets do not qualify, and the textbook fix, a Substreams-powered subgraph, turns out to be dead for EVM chains now. The error text says so outright. Rather than ship a snapshot and call it live, we stood the real sink up ourselves. It runs in 24MB of RAM with a 20MB API next to it, and the committed snapshot survives only as a fallback for when the box is unreachable.

name: GraphMind
description: Natural language DeFi research assistant powered by The Graph's Subgraph MCP
projectDescription: GraphMind is a DeFi research assistant I built for the ETHGlobal hackathon. Instead of digging through dashboards or writing GraphQL by hand, you just ask plain-English questions, like "what are the top lending pools by TVL on Aave?" and it queries live onchain data through The Graph's Subgraph MCP, reasons over the numbers, and answers back with tables and risk callouts instead of raw JSON.
howItsMade:
Frontend: a simple chat UI (HTML/CSS/vanilla JS) where you type a question.
Backend: a small Express server hat receives the question via a /api/chat endpoint.
The agent (agent.ts): sends your question to OpenAI along with a system prompt describing its job (DeFi research assistant) and a list of tools it's allowed to call.
The tools are provided by The Graph's Subgraph MCP server a hosted service that exposes real blockchain data through the Model Context Protocol. The model can call tools like "search subgraphs by keyword," "get GraphQL schema" or "execute a query."
The MCP client (mcpClient.ts) forwards those tool calls to The Graph, which runs GraphQL queries against indexed onchain data (e.g., Aave's subgraph) and returns real numbers.
The model can call multiple tools in sequence (search → get schema → query → maybe compare), each time getting real data back, until it has enough to answer.
Instead of raw JSON, the model writes a natural-language summary with a table and risk callouts.

name: HederaTube
description: Pay-per-second video on Hedera. Lock a few cents in USDC, watch, get back what you did not use.
projectDescription:
Ads and subscriptions exist for one reason. Payments could never be small enough to charge for a few seconds of video. So platforms charge for a month and sell your attention to cover the rest.
HederaTube is what a video site looks like when payments can be that small. A video costs a few thousandths of a dollar. You press play and that amount is deposited into an escrow contract on Hedera. As you watch, every 5 second chunk is paid with a signed voucher that never touches the chain. When you leave, whatever you did not watch is refunded in one transaction, and a receipt shows exactly what you paid and what came back. The creator gets everything they earned in a single settlement that can cover thousands of viewers.
Three things had to be true for this to work, and none of them existed when we started.
First, streaming payments on Hedera. x402 has a batch-settlement scheme for EVM chains, but nothing for Hedera. We wrote the Hedera binding, contracts, SDK, facilitator, spec and examples, and opened it as a PR against the x402 repo (x402-foundation/x402 #3466). It is deployed on testnet and verified on Sourcify.
Second, no wallet prompts. A five minute video is about sixty signatures. No one will click approve sixty times. With Privy's embedded wallet we sign every voucher silently, so the viewer presses play once and the stream just pays.
Third, real creators. A platform that pays anyone per second watched will be farmed with junk channels and self viewing loops. Creators verify once with a World ID Selfie Check. One human, one channel. Viewers stay anonymous and never verify.
The result is a site where the price of a video is the price of a video, not the price of a month, and the creator gets paid for exactly what people watched.
howItsMade:
The stack is a Vite and React 19 frontend, an Express backend with Drizzle on Postgres, Redis for channel state and BullMQ queues, ffmpeg for transcoding into HLS, Garage as S3 storage, and a standalone x402 facilitator. Everything runs on Hedera testnet at hederatube.xyz.
The payment layer is the x402 batch-settlement scheme, which did not exist for Hedera, so we built it and opened PR #3466 upstream. The EVM version verifies signatures with ecrecover and funds channels through Permit2. Neither works on Hedera. Permit2 is not deployed on mainnet, and Hedera accounts can have ED25519 keys that ecrecover cannot check. So the escrow contract, x402BatchSettlementHedera, sends every signature (vouchers, claim batches, refunds, deposit authorizations) through the Hedera Account Service system contract, HIP-632 isAuthorizedRaw, which verifies against the account's current key on the network itself. Deposits go through a new HederaAllowanceDepositCollector that pulls USDC with an HTS transferFrom under an allowance the viewer granted once, plus a per deposit signed authorization with nonce and deadline. The facilitator submits with the Hiero SDK and reads through the Mirror Node, simulating every call before sending. 32 Foundry tests with mocked system contracts, 337 unit tests in the TypeScript package, and a live testnet integration test that locks, pays three chunks, refunds, claims and settles.
Pricing is integer math on USDC base units. Segments are 2.5 seconds, chunks are 5 seconds, the deposit is exactly the video price, and the cumulative charge after k chunks is floor(price × k / chunks), so watching to the end pays exactly the price and never more. A custom hls.js fragment loader routes only the first segment of each chunk through x402 with a fresh cumulative voucher. The second segment is free, but the server refuses it unless the first was paid, so a client cannot skip vouchers. Vouchers are verified locally against Redis, never through the facilitator, which is what makes playback feel instant.
Privy is what makes any of this usable. External wallets are deliberately not offered because they cannot sign without a prompt. The embedded wallet runs with showWalletUIs off, Hedera registered as a custom EVM chain (296, Hashio RPC), and we sign the raw 32 byte EIP-712 digest through Privy's secp256k1_sign RPC instead of personal_sign, because the EIP-191 prefix would break on chain verification. Each signature is recovered and checked against the wallet address before it leaves the browser. Onboarding is a faucet drip of HBAR that creates the hollow account, then a USDC association, then one approve. Those are the only transactions a viewer ever pays gas for.
World ID gates creation, not viewing. The backend signs a relying party context with the portal key, IDKit shows the QR, World App returns a Selfie Check proof (credential 11, World ID 3.0) with the wallet address as signal, and the server verifies it against World's endpoint. The nullifier is stored under a unique index, so a second wallet from the same face gets a 409, and the upload API returns 403 for any wallet without one. We treat Selfie Check as an abuse prevention signal rather than identity, and its 90 day validity doubles as a continuity check for silent channels. Our integration feedback for World is in the repo.
Hacky parts worth mentioning. The Mirror Node lags consensus by several seconds, and the facilitator was polling it after every deposit, which made play take 8 seconds. Our server never needs that read, so we made the poll configurable and set it to zero. Play now starts in about 4 seconds, all of it Hedera consensus. Vite's dependency pre-bundling broke IDKit's WebAssembly load, so a small dev plugin serves the wasm from the right path. An approve on a Hedera account that has not associated USDC reverts silently and burns the faucet gas, which cost us an afternoon before we reordered onboarding. And the settlement batch used to run on a 60 second timer, so receipts sat on Settling for a minute. Now every close schedules a batch 4 seconds later and closes inside that window share one job.

name: Hello Bounty
description: Open marketplace where AI agents compete for bounties, paid from escrow once work is verified.
projectDescription:
Hello Bounty is an open marketplace built for the emerging agent economy, where people and businesses can post real tasks and have AI agents compete to complete them. Instead of hiring a single freelancer or manually prompting an AI yourself, you post a bounty describing exactly what you need done, your deadline, and how much you're willing to pay. Qualified AI agents then review the brief and submit their proposed approach, competing on quality and reliability rather than just price.
The core innovation is the payment model: funds are deposited upfront in USDC and held in escrow rather than paid directly to an agent. Once an agent submits completed work, it goes through a verification step — only if the work actually meets the bounty's requirements does the escrow release payment to the agent. If the work fails verification, the funds are automatically refunded to the person who posted the bounty, removing the risk of paying for subpar or incomplete work.
The platform also includes agent and requester profiles, a public bounty board for browsing open tasks, and a reputation system built from completed jobs and reviews, so trust in the marketplace compounds over time. In effect, Hello Bounty positions itself as trusted infrastructure for a world where AI agents are treated as legitimate workers: it gives people a straightforward way to delegate work to AI systems with accountability built in, and gives capable agents a transparent way to find work and get paid fairly for it.
howItsMade:
Hello Bounty is built on the Arc testnet, with a smart-contract escrow system at its core. When someone posts a bounty, the funds are locked into an on-chain escrow contract rather than sent directly to an agent. AI agents can browse open bounties and claim the ones they're capable of completing, then submit their finished work back to the contract.
Verification is handled by Chainlink CRE (Chainlink Runtime Environment), which checks whether the submitted work actually satisfies the bounty's requirements. If CRE confirms the work is done correctly, the escrow automatically releases the locked funds to the agent; if the work fails verification, the funds are refunded back to the person who posted the bounty. This removes the need for a trusted middleman or manual dispute resolution — the release logic is enforced entirely by the contract and oracle network.
For identity, every agent on the platform is issued its own subname using ENS V2, giving each agent a persistent, human-readable, verifiable identity on-chain. This ties an agent's track record and reputation directly to its ENS identity rather than to a centralized platform account, so its work history travels with it.
Together, this stack — Arc testnet for execution, escrow contracts for trustless payment, Chainlink CRE for automated work verification, and ENS V2 for agent identity — lets Hello Bounty function as a fully on-chain, trust-minimized marketplace where neither the requester nor the agent has to take the other's word for it.

name: Revoke.eth
description: Grant, limit, or revoke an AI agent's spending through ENS — instantly, no key rotation.
projectDescription: Revoke turns an AI agent's ENS name into its authorization. A parent grants an agent a narrow, expiring, revocable capability recorded on ENSv2 - a delegated right, not a handed-over key - and services check that capability before honoring a paid request. A subgraph indexes the full delegation tree and verifies freshness on every read, refusing to authorize against stale data rather than guessing. Payments settle over x402 on Hedera, and every HCS receipt is bound back to the ENS name that permitted it, so the full chain - who allowed this, when, and what happened - is publicly auditable. The result is a kill switch for agent access: revoke the name, and the agent's spending stops everywhere at once, with no key rotation and no service-by-service cleanup.
howItsMade:
ENSv2 on Sepolia is the source of truth. Each agent gets a Permissioned Resolver with Enhanced Access Control, defining exactly which records it can modify. A registrar built around ETHRegistry handles subname issuance. The contracts are written in Solidity with Foundry, deployed and verified on Sepolia.
The Graph indexes every grant, revocation, and expiry through a subgraph with AssemblyScript mappings. Every query returns a provenance envelope containing the deployment ID, indexed block, live chain head, indexing lag, and authorization verdict. The service refuses to authorize against stale data rather than guessing. Freshness is a security control, not a UX feature.
Hedera handles payments. An x402-gated service checks the agent's live capability before accepting a request, settles payment through a real ContractExecuteTransaction using EIP-712 transferWithAuthorization, and writes an HCS receipt bound to the ENS name that authorized it. The receipt can be independently verified through the Hedera mirror node.
One of the key security challenges was establishing a trustworthy chain head. An initial high-water-mark approach could silently report data as fresh after a cold start. This was replaced with a real eth_blockNumber RPC call on every authorization check, ensuring freshness is independently verified before a payment is allowed.
The system was built with contracts and shared types defined first, followed by parallel ENS, Graph, Hedera, and UI implementation against those interfaces, then integrated and re-verified against live Sepolia and Hedera testnet data. Planning documents, implementation specs, and fix history are included in the repository.

name: Countersign
description: An agent's Hedera treasury cannot move until an independent guard, paid per decision, countersigns.
projectDescription:
Autonomous agents are being handed treasuries. The usual protection is a policy check inside the agent's own code — which a compromised agent simply skips.
Countersign removes that assumption. The treasury account holds a native Hedera key tree: 1-of[ownerKey, 2-of[agentKey, guardKey]]. The owner can always recover funds alone. The agent alone satisfies neither branch — when it signs a transfer by itself, the Hedera network rejects it with INVALID_SIGNATURE. Nothing inside the agent's process can talk its way past that.
So the agent proposes instead. It publishes the transfer it wants as a Hedera Scheduled Transaction — public, and unexecuted, carrying only its own signature. It then pays an independent guard to review it. That guard is a live service at https://countersign.gudman.xyz. It answers HTTP 402 Payment Required, quotes its price in HBAR, and settlement goes through the Blocky402 x402 facilitator on Hedera testnet.
Only after payment does the guard do any work. It resolves the ScheduleID from consensus — it never trusts a summary the caller sent it — and checks 48 decoded fields against a mandate the treasury owner signed: recipient allowlist, amount cap, asset, fee, expiry, who created the schedule, who pays for it, and that its own key is not already on it. If every check passes it adds its signature and Hedera executes the transfer. If one fails it refuses, and the schedule simply never executes.
The caller pays either way. A refusal is a delivered service, not a failed request.
Refusal has no state of its own on Hedera, so it is proved by absence: the schedule exists, its executed_timestamp is null, only the agent's key prefix appears in signatures[], and the treasury balance is unchanged. Every verdict is also written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic. All of it is readable from the public mirror node without running any of my code.
You can pay the guard yourself. curl https://countersign.gudman.xyz/guard returns its public key and HCS-14 identifier for free, and npm run hosted-review in the repository sends a real paid review request to it from your own machine. The approved and refused runs linked in the README were made exactly that way, from a separate machine, against that endpoint.
Honest limits, also stated in the README: these are my own operator runs, not external users, and testnet payments are paid protocol trials, not revenue. One guard process authorizes exactly one treasury, so this is a deployed service and not a marketplace — a second treasury needs a second guard. HTS token approval is deliberately disabled, and every token proposal is refused.
howItsMade:
TypeScript on Node 24, and no Solidity anywhere — Hedera native services only, through @hiero-ledger/sdk.
The treasury is a nested KeyList, 1-of[ownerKey, 2-of[agentKey, guardKey]]. Hedera evaluates it at consensus, which is what makes the guarantee structural instead of procedural. Scheduled Transactions are the product mechanism rather than decoration: they are how a second signature arrives asynchronously. The agent's ScheduleCreate publishes the exact transfer; the guard's ScheduleSign completes the threshold.
Payment is x402 through @x402/core and @x402/hedera, settled by the hosted Blocky402 facilitator on hedera:testnet. Hedera's x402 is exact-scheme only, so the price is one known check-unit quoted up front in the 402 challenge — not post-usage metering, and the README says so. The fee is paid from a separately keyed operational account, so no treasury authorization key ever enters a payment payload; startup asserts that separation and refuses to run otherwise.
The validator is a pure function, and the subtle part is what it is allowed to trust. ScheduleInfo returns an already-decoded body, and a protobuf decoder silently drops fields it does not know. So the guard pins the exact HAPI protobuf and services versions, reads them from the same consensus node both before and after resolving the schedule, and refuses on any mismatch — a schema change makes it fail closed rather than approve something it cannot see. It also rejects any body carrying a field outside the audited schema.
Mandates are RFC 8785 JCS-canonicalized, domain-separated and Ed25519-signed by the owner, so the agent cannot rewrite its own policy. They are single-use: the nonce is atomically reserved in SQLite before approval, and only the request that wins the reservation may submit ScheduleSign. Participant identity is HCS-14 for both agent and guard, and verdicts go to immutable, submit-key-protected HCS topics with custom fees rejected at startup.
360 tests across 15 files, all offline. One defect the offline suite could not have caught surfaced on the first live run: the mirror node returns signatures[].public_key_prefix as base64 and three code paths expected hex. The fixtures used "a".repeat(16), which is itself valid base64, so they passed while asserting nothing about the real encoding. The regression tests now run against verbatim mirror-node responses captured from that run.
The build briefs each task was run from, and a full AI usage disclosure, are published in the repository.

name: WorldMod
description: Anyone with a phone records short real-world tasks for robot training and gets paid in USDC.
projectDescription:
Go in as much detail as you can about what this project is. Please be as clear as possible! (min 280 characters)
World Mod is a permissionless network for physical-world data. Anyone with a phone opens a web page, does a short physical task while the camera watches, and gets paid in USDC once the recording is accepted. A buyer posts what they need and escrows what it pays. Nothing to install, no hardware to buy, no gas to hold.
Why this exists. Robots cannot learn from the internet the way language models did. They need first-person video of humans handling objects, and the datasets that exist today were collected by expensive, centralised research programs with recruited participants and custom hardware. The scarce resource is not storage or compute. It is someone doing a physical thing while a sensor is pointed at it. World Mod makes that contribution nearly frictionless and pays the person who made it.
How an episode earns


A buyer posts a bounty ("15 seconds of keyboard typing, hands in frame") and escrows the full budget in real USDC. A bounty is only listed once it is funded.
A contributor opens the app inside World App. Their World wallet is their identity, and a one-time Selfie Check keeps one person from farming payouts across many devices.
They record a 15-second task on their phone. A head strap gives the best first-person footage but is optional; holding the phone works too. The app shows a live hand skeleton so they can see they are in frame.
The recording is sealed on the device before a single byte leaves it: hashed, signed with the contributor's key, and queued so going offline mid-task loses nothing.
The server scores every frame. Are the hands in frame? Does the camera motion agree with the gyroscope (a screen replay fails this)? Is it a near-duplicate of something already submitted? We measured the replay check against real recordings: genuine takes correlate at 59% on average, replays at 24%.
The buyer's acceptance threshold is checked inside a TEE by a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow, so the bar a buyer sets is never visible on-chain or to the operator. A pass is written on-chain as a DON-signed report. A rejection makes no on-chain call at all.
The contributor is paid from escrow in real USDC, into a balance only they can withdraw. They never need gas.

What accepted episodes become. Episodes are bundled into a licensed dataset with a real IPFS content address and an on-chain registry entry. A buyer can tokenise that dataset as a KYC-gated Bond on Hedera, mint licence seats to the dataset's creator, and pay licence-fee coupons in USDC. Meanwhile a world model trains over the episodes and runs live during the next take, showing the wearer what it thinks happens next. A second Confidential Workflow settles each contributor's share of model improvement on-chain.
What is real today. All six registry and escrow contracts are deployed on both Ethereum Sepolia and Hedera testnet, using Circle's testnet USDC on both, not a mock token. Real episodes from three contributors have been captured, scored, anchored, paid and tokenised. A real Selfie Check has completed end to end against World's sandbox.
What we say plainly. A browser has no secure enclave, so every episode carries a "heuristic" trust level in the UI: the checks measure whether a capture is plausible, not that pixels came from a real camera. With five episodes the world model does not yet beat a "predict no change" baseline, and the buyer dashboard shows that curve rather than hiding it. We would rather ship a real pipeline that improves with every episode than a mock that looks finished.
howItsMade:
The phone. A Next.js PWA, installable on iOS and Android. Capture is getUserMedia plus MediaRecorder with per-browser codec negotiation recorded into the manifest, DeviceMotionEvent for 60Hz IMU, and TensorFlow.js hand-pose detection with self-hosted 4MB lite models for the live skeleton. The manifest is canonicalised with RFC 8785 and the IMU is hashed as a binary stream, because float formatting across two runtimes is where byte-exactness dies. Scoring used to run on the phone too. We measured it dropping capture to 26.9fps with 818ms gaps during movement, so it moved to the server; a client-computed score was never authoritative anyway.
The server. ffmpeg decodes every frame. Optical flow is correlated against the gyroscope with lag estimation, because the frame and IMU clocks are offset and a zero-lag correlation scored a genuine capture below a spoof. Fixing that took one episode from 5.2% to 59.6%. Perceptual hashing catches duplicates. Episode bytes and dataset metadata are pinned to IPFS through a local kubo node.
Contracts. Foundry. EntityRegistry, AssetRegistry, EpisodeRegistry, BountyEscrow, DatasetRegistry and FederatedRound, plus a native WMOD token whose one shipped function is a ValidatorBond that stakes and slashes validators. Contributors sign EIP-712 payloads that a relayer submits, so nobody needs gas. Escrow credits a pull-based balance so nobody else can redirect a payout. The same contracts are deployed on Ethereum Sepolia and Hedera testnet, switched by one environment variable.
Chainlink CRE. Two Confidential Workflows, both registered with cre.handlerInTee. The episode validator fetches the buyer's minimum framing and plausibility thresholds with runtime.getSecrets so they are only ever decrypted inside the enclave, pulls scored episodes over HTTPClient, compares in-enclave, and on a pass calls donRuntime.report then evmClient.writeReport into a consumer contract registered as an EpisodeRegistry validator. The utility oracle holds the utility weighting exponent as a secret, computes normalised basis-point shares in-enclave, and the DON co-signs them into a second consumer that is now BountyEscrow's registered oracle. Both consumers follow Chainlink's ReceiverTemplate and accept the production Sepolia KeystoneForwarder. This replaced the product's biggest trust assumption: one EOA acting as validator and oracle.
Hedera. The core contracts call the HTS precompile in their constructors to self-associate with Circle's HTS USDC. Forge's local EVM has no HTS precompile, so those three had to be deployed via raw viem over Hashio instead of forge script. On top, a licensed dataset becomes an Asset Tokenization Studio Bond: the app reads the DatasetRegistry live, maps it through a tested dataset-to-bond mapping with a valid ISIN, issues via Bond.create, grants KYC with a real Terminal3 Verifiable Credential, mints licence seats to the dataset creator, sets a 5% coupon, and distributes it in real USDC. Four Bonds are source-verified on Sourcify for chain 296.
World. The app is a MiniKit mini app. MiniKit.walletAuth gives contributors a recoverable identity, and MiniKit.signTypedData signs the same EIP-712 payloads the previous Privy signer did, a transport swap rather than a redesign. Selfie Check uses IDKitRequestWidget with the selfieCheckLegacy preset and a server-signed RP context. The verify route calls World's production v4 verify API and only records a verification when World says success.
World model. A PyTorch encoder plus GRU dynamics head, exported to ONNX and checked against the PyTorch graph over an eight-step recurrent sequence (worst-case difference 2.5e-5). During capture the phone streams a cropped frame and motion sample twice a second, the server keeps the GRU hidden state per session, and returns the nearest-neighbour frame from the same take.
Hacky things worth mentioning. The Hedera ATS SDK has no raw-key signing path; its public wallet list is MetaMask, WalletConnect and enterprise custody only. We wired an ethers.Wallet directly onto its transaction adapter and stubbed the hard global.window gate. That stub then broke Next.js server rendering across the whole app, because React checks typeof window in its own internals, so ATS issuance now runs in a short-lived child process that starts, issues one Bond, prints one line of JSON, and exits. Granting KYC and setting coupons both revert on a fresh Bond because the diamond owner does not receive _KYC_ROLE or _CORPORATEACTIONS_ROLE automatically; we found that by decoding reverts on the mirror node, and in the process discovered our own account-id and private-key pair had been mismatched from day one. Nobody had verified the ATS ResolverProxy on Hedera testnet before, so we recovered the compiler version from the on-chain metadata CBOR and rebuilt 153 source files to a byte-exact match.

name: Nametoll
description: Agents pay a desk they found by name. TEE gates spend. Hedera bills on HCS.
projectDescription:
If an agent needs live lending data today, somebody hands it a URL, an API key, and a monthly bill. There is no name you can pass to another agent. The spend limit sits in a config the buyer can read. And when the payment goes through, there is no receipt a stranger can check.
Nametoll is a desk for that job. You find it by a name. A spend rule the desk itself cannot see decides whether the buyer may pay. If they may, they pay only for what came back, in HBAR, and the bill is written where anyone can recompute it. The public origin is https://nametoll.run.place. You paste a parent such as nametoll.eth on /desks, or a child such as desk.nametoll.eth on /app. The happy path does not ship a name. The name resolves to an HTTP origin, who to pay, what it costs, and where the receipt will be written. Two protocols cost two hundred thousand tinybars against a secret cap of one hundred fifty thousand, so the desk refuses and Pay stays locked. One protocol is one hundred thousand, which is allowed. Unpaid traffic is still HTTP 402. After settle you get live rows, and the same numbers show up on HashScan and on HCS topic 0.0.10464309.
What you buy is two things on the same meter. A snapshot is priced by how many protocols you asked for: Aave v3 and Compound III, one Messari-shaped query, fail-soft if an indexer is down. A risk score is one unit. You pass a wallet; the desk computes a health factor, distance to liquidation, and the worst market from those same markets. If the indexer has positions it uses them. If not, it builds a deterministic book from live TVL ratios. The wallet never goes into the spend check. Positions on a public chain are not private, and we do not sell them as if they were. The Graph is the data you pay for. We used it. We did not apply for its prize.
The name lives on ENS, version two, on Sepolia. nametoll.eth is the parent. desk.nametoll.eth and agent-02.nametoll.eth are children under that UserRegistry, each with its own Permissioned Resolver. Three documented text keys (url, agent-context, agent-endpoint[web]) carry the origin, the Hedera pay-to, the price rule, the HCS topic, and HBAR asset 0.0.0. The operator can edit those keys and cannot transfer the name. /register issues a new child that resells this desk: the label and endpoint vary, price and pay-to stay this origin. Optional expiresIn writes a bounded expiry. gone.nametoll.eth was registered for ninety seconds; on-chain state is now AVAILABLE and /desks marks it unresolved. npm run agent -- nametoll.eth discovers a live child and pays it.
The spend rule is a Chainlink confidential workflow, handlerInTee from their official scaffold. Before Blocky402 settles, the desk asks nametoll-brain. getSecret loads SPEND_CAP and, if set, BUYER_ALLOWLIST and RATE_LIMIT inside the enclave. The public reasons are under cap, over cap, buyer not allowlisted, or rate limited. Deny, or a skipped TEE, is HTTP 403: no settle, no snapshot, no bill. Four cre workflow simulate logs in the repo show AWS Nitro in us-west-2 for allow, over-cap deny, allowlist deny, and rate deny. The same handler can emit unsigned join() calldata for the official ChallengeLending contract on Sepolia; that join is already on-chain. Functions and Automation are not used. CRE deploy is still enrollment-only, so the public desk uses attested simulate, caches a good verdict per amount, payer, and hour-count, re-warms the two pinned amounts so a cold click does not sit for nine seconds, and kills a hung simulate at sixty seconds. Missing simulate fails closed.
Payment is Hedera. Unpaid GET /desk/snapshot and GET /desk/risk are HTTP 402, x402 v2, exact, tinybars, asset 0.0.0, fee-payer 0.0.7162784 read live from Blocky402 GET /supported. We do not hold a facilitator key. An operator buyer or a guest session (POST /desk/session creates a Hedera ECDSA account and faucets 0.05 HBAR; the key never appears in JSON) completes a real paid request. If an indexer is down we charge only what arrived and refund unused prepaid on a seller TransferTransaction. Those prepaid, owed, and refund amounts sit on the same HCS topic. A stranger GETs the Mirror Node, decodes each message, and checks units times price. TOLL (0.0.10483302) is an HTS token with a custom HBAR fee, and two wait_for_expiry slots have executed and been claimed. Snapshot 402 stays HBAR because Blocky402 does not advertise an HTS asset. The guest faucet closes with HTTP 503 if the seller is under 5 HBAR or sixteen guests are already live. /health shows that runway.
Live evidence: TEE-gated settle https://hashscan.io/testnet/tx/[email protected]. Remainder refund https://hashscan.io/testnet/tx/[email protected]. HCS topic https://hashscan.io/testnet/topic/0.0.10464309. Parent register https://sepolia.etherscan.io/tx/0x28ab9c164cca6f967413f944a3ef1f81ca3ef86f7e1620fdc5b7a57d8d7a8a96. Sibling https://sepolia.etherscan.io/tx/0xd1f6f4faa9f11636fb64673ddfe6d458285e6cbf6ea79631c0d017c528c10454. Expired child https://sepolia.etherscan.io/tx/0x44bbbd33adc88b3fb103eec45e2941ee4ad9eb14d8a0f446f738c7c2ac20d3ac. ChallengeLending join() https://sepolia.etherscan.io/tx/0x980aaffe6d62561964a42675f7831adbca09cf442c7db0cede9255e2ed5e3086. Repo https://github.com/shreyas-sovani/Nametoll
howItsMade:
Nametoll is one Node and TypeScript Express app, not a collage of demos. Six modules share stable interfaces: Directory (resolve a pasted name, list children, register a constrained child, guest session), Gate (402, Blocky402 verify and settle, refuse a TEE deny), Brain (CRE handlerInTee verdict), Merchandise (live Graph snapshot, desk-side risk score, billable units), Ledger (HCS bill, optional HTS and schedules), Buyer (resolve, ask TEE, pay, print HashScan and topic). Tests assert those observables. CI is .github/workflows/test.yml. The UI is /, /desks, /register, /app, and /docs. Official partner skills, MCP ids, and llms.txt were the only APIs; if a symbol was not in a skill or the live docs it was not invented.
Directory is ENSv2 on Sepolia, not mainnet v1. Writes use the official ens-cli ABIs and addresses; ens-cli emits unsigned {to, data, value} and npm run ens:sepolia broadcasts. The owner Permissioned Resolver was deployed before register so the name never sat on a zero resolver. EAC authorizeTextRoles is scoped to the three desk text keys. Catalog prefers the hosted Omnigraph at api.v2-sepolia.ensnode.io. That host currently serves a Railway certificate Node refuses, so resolve falls through to the official Sepolia Universal Resolver (0xeEeEEEeE14D718C2B47D9923Deab1335E144EeEe) and listChildNames walks getSubregistry plus LabelRegistered logs on the parent UserRegistry. That fallback is why /desks still lists children when the indexer TLS dies. /register calls the same issueDeskChild path; expiresIn becomes register(..., expires). After expiry, getState is AVAILABLE.
Gate never holds a Blocky402 facilitator key. It reads the fee-payer from live GET https://api.testnet.blocky402.com/supported, returns x402 v2 PAYMENT-REQUIRED, then verify plus settle. payTo is a Hedera account id (0.0.10463755), not an EVM address. Amounts are tinybars. @hiero-ledger signs AccountCreate (guest buyer), TransferTransaction (0.05 HBAR faucet and unused-remainder refund), HCS submit, HTS token create, and ScheduleCreate wait_for_expiry. Guest keys stay in process memory; JSON never includes them. POST /desk/pay is rate-limited with /desk/session and /desk/register, optionally gated by DESK_PAY_SECRET, and pinned to PUBLIC_DESK_URL when that is set. Before a guest is funded, the desk reads the seller balance from Mirror Node. Below 5 HBAR, or at 16 live guests, POST /desk/session returns 503 and tells the judge to use operator pay. /health.runway exposes that floor so a human can check before recording.
Brain lives in cre/nametoll-brain, scaffolded with cre init -t hello-confidential-workflows-ts. The HTTP trigger runs inside TeeRuntime. Secrets come from runtime.getSecret. HTTP inside the TEE uses HTTPClient only; ConfidentialHTTPClient is not mixed into a TEE handler (that mix is a documented DQ). Live CRE deploy is private beta, so the public desk runs cre workflow simulate against staging-settings and caches a successful verdict per amount plus payer plus hour-count. Failures and timeouts are not cached. Boot warms the 1-unit and 2-unit amounts. A keep-warm interval re-decides those two amounts every half TTL (VERDICT_TTL_MS, default 60s; set 1800000 for judging day) so the cache does not expire while the process lives. cre workflow simulate is mutexed — one child at a time — and killed at 60 seconds so a hung CLI fails closed instead of hanging the desk. Policy evidence is four redacted Nitro us-west-2 logs: simulate-allow.log, simulate-deny.log, simulate-allowlist-deny.log, simulate-rate-deny.log. The same handler accepts { action: join } and returns unsigned join() to official ChallengeLending 0x88574e7Cc0027afd04951daa09B64d4441931ba1 (the live challenge contract; the ETHOnline scrape address is a dead older deploy). npm run join broadcasts that calldata. Selector 0xb688a363; isUser is true.
Merchandise is one Messari-shaped lending query across two pinned Studio deployments (Aave v3 Ethereum JCNWRypm7FYwV8fx5HhzZPSFaMxgkPuw4TnR3Gpi81zk and Compound III AwoxEZbiWLvv6e3QdvdMZw4WDURdGbvPfHmZRc8Dpfz9). Schemas were fetched through The Graph Subgraph MCP, not invented. Units billed equal delivered protocols. Fail-soft returns the live rows and lets Ledger refund the rest. The risk SKU reuses those markets: if Account positions exist, score them; if not, build a deterministic book from TVL weights and score that. The wallet never touches Brain, so scoring a second address does not spawn another simulate. Graph stays off the form.
Ledger appends JSON to HCS topic 0.0.10464309. Recompute is units times priceTinybarsPerUnit (100000). Remainder fields (prepaidTinybars, refundTinybars, refundTx) follow the Pinout metering shape on one topic, not dual-topic HIP-991. Risk bills carry sku: risk-score. Subscribe and claim are a side rail: TOLL 0.0.10483302 (custom 100000-tinybar HBAR fee) plus two executed wait_for_expiry slots that delivered live Aave and wrote subscribe bills. Snapshot 402 stays asset 0.0.0 because Blocky402 /supported lists Hedera exact with no HTS asset list.
Notable and slightly hacky, on purpose. Hosted ENSNode TLS forced the Universal Resolver plus LabelRegistered catalog fallback so discovery did not depend on a broken cert. Unused remainder is a seller CryptoTransfer, not a second 402 scheme, because Blocky402 testnet is exact-only. The public-desk TEE is attested simulate, not a mainnet DON deploy (Confidential Workflows deploy is still enrollment-gated); missing simulate fails closed with HTTP 403. We opened hedera-dev/hedera-harness pull request 59 after in-place init adopt planted Yarn and Next into this npm Express app; Nametoll has no .harness folder. We did not build ERC-8004, HCS-14, A2A, World Selfie Check, or a Graph prize SKILL. Those would have been stickers. The product is the loop a judge can paste, pay, and recompute.

name: Mycelium
description: Connect devices to run verifiable distributed inference of open source models, get paid with x402
projectDescription:
Mycelium connects multiple devices into cooperative networks that run open-source AI models through distributed inference. Instead of relying on a single centralised AI provider, people can pool their hardware to jointly host models, users can discover and pay per request whilst the system stochastically ensures that the advertised model is the model they requested inference from. While one user may be unable to wrong the open source model they want to use, in a swarm each individual needs to have less compute power. Together, more powerful models can be run.
The long term goal being that people can function both as users and providers, with the system either handling or integrating routing through services like open router, compared to the current provider self-selection.
The application brings that infrastructure into a practical flow: choose a model and provider, receive a request-bound quote, authorize an x402 payment, stream the response, and keep a signed receipt. Hedera provides the payment rail, ENS gives providers human-readable identities, and The Graph makes published receipt history queryable to inform future provider selection.
Our verification design separates the machines doing inference from the checker. We utilise model-specific statistical screening and private reference spot-checks, with the checker being run inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) so users can ensure the checker is behaving honestly. The aim is to detect model substitution and forgerys without requiring every inference device to have confidential-computing hardware, or needing to trust in any centralised service or even a quorum of verifiers. Dishonest providers have their staked bond slashed, and the system is designed to ensure that it is economically unfeasible to run inference that is not the model the user requested. In the future we aim to have a system that allows users to also serve as verifiers for inference.
Mycelium is designed for both people and software agents, with browser, SDK, CLI, and MCP access. The goal is an open decentralised inference marketplace where users can choose who serves their models, hardware owners can offer underutilised edge compute(phones, laptops, desktop PC's, small Racks), and provider history helps give both humans and agents the information they need to make informed decisions based on the inference providers past history. A system that benefits humanity as a whole and not just people owning data centers.
howItsMade:
We built the hackathon application around the existing Mycelium distributed-inference project. We built model integrations for Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and a 4-bit Qwen3.8-27B model. The demonstrated 0.5B and 27b routes splits one model across two physical Apple Silicon Macs: MLX executes most transformer layers, while a NumPy worker executes the final layer and output head. The architecture of Mycelium is designed for heterogeneous hardware, although these demonstrated execution paths are Mac-based for simplicity purposes.
The application uses Node.js, JavaScript modules, versioned JSON contracts, SQLite-backed state, and a shared HTTP API for browser, SDK, CLI, and MCP clients. Execution, payments, discovery, indexing, and assessment are separate components. Ed25519-signed receipts bind the provider, requested model profile, request, and output.
For payments, we integrated native Hedera x402 through Blocky402. The service returns an HTTP 402 challenge containing the payment requirements; the client authorizes the quoted payment, and the application verifies and settles it before admitting the job. Persisted payment-attempt state allows interrupted requests to be reconciled without blindly paying again. ENSv2 records on Sepolia provide human-readable provider identities and discovery. To provide inference, providers must put up a stake. Payments are settled only after verification has occured, and if inference providers are found to be dishonest they are slashed to a mathematically determined degree (based on stake amount, inference price, chance of being audited etc.) to ensure it is not economically viable to serve a different model than the one the user requested.
The Graph provides the application’s queryable provider history. Solidity registries on Sepolia emit receipt and assessment events, which custom AssemblyScript subgraph mappings turn into immutable claims, daily activity records, and provider metrics. A reputation formula combines a smoothed assessment pass rate, capped receipt volume, and recent activity. The application uses indexed history to compare providers, while preserving separate counts for mismatches, inconclusive results, and unavailable checks. This makes The Graph part of provider selection rather than just a transaction dashboard, as it allows humans and agents to make informed decisions on where they wish to get their inference from.
Our verifier uses two complementary mechanisms. First we have model-specific binary classifier screening ordinary response text: a TF-IDF/LinearSVC model captures lexical patterns, while a trained RoBERTa detector captures learned text features. They are combined in an ensemble and return a likelihood that the respective model was served. Separate trained bundles exist for 0.5B and 27B. Screening runs asynchronously, outside response delivery, and is a monitoring signal as well as a requirement for inference providers to be paid for their inference (withdrawal of attached x402 payment can only be made after verification has occurred).
Second, the checker conducts private reference audits. An independent random policy selects observations for auditing (utilising some information from TheGraph to analyse all inference provider swarms and ensure they are roughly all selected at the same rate, 10% uniform per request, given their current uptime, with higher likelihood assignment to new providers, overdue checks and mismatched histories, with the aforementioned classifier triggering audits for three consecutive negatives. The checker sends a new challenge containing exact input token IDs and pinned generation parameters to the provider. It then compares the native output token sequence, output length, and EOS-versus-length termination against a private, profile-bound reference bank. Expected answers remain checker-side.
The TEE design places the classifiers, private reference bank, audit scheduler, and comparison logic inside confidential computing on a GCS, while the large generative models remain on providers’ ordinary hardware. With this architectural split, the verification is quite lightweight compared to the actual inference, and even with the auditing it still makes it far easier to do verification than inference. The fees for upkeeping the verification TEE are paid for by a 5% fee on all inference payments, with the remaining 95% going back to the inference providers.

name: Warrant Protocol
description: Warrant Protocol - My bot acted. I fired every agent under me. Nobody learned who I was.
projectDescription:
Warrant is a permission slip for AI agents. You keep your wallet key. Your bot gets a time-limited warrant instead of your identity. It can call services, leave a public note, even hire a helper. Whoever it called still cannot tell who authorized the request. When you are done, you Fire in the tab and every agent under that warrant stops.
The problem is simple. Today, if you want a bot to act, you hand it a key or an account. Then whoever the bot called can name you. If it hires helpers, you often lose the ability to shut the whole chain down. Warrant splits those jobs. MetaMask authorizes. The bot carries only a bearer. Hedera pays when a shop requires x402. Fire takes the warrant back.
On the hosted product at warrant-beta.vercel.app you authorize a guest warrant (about 30 minutes). Install the skill once into Hermes or another HTTP agent. Paste the warrant. The bot POSTs to Warrant’s agent API. Warrant’s prove worker builds a Groth16 hop proof over Baby Jubjub mandates in a LeanIMT on Base Sepolia (MandateRegistry). The bot never sees the witness or the zkey. The shop verifies the proof and learns a context-scoped nullifier, not you.
For the memo demo, Hermes posts to /api/agent/memo. The memo shop on Railway returns 402 until ExactHedera payment settles via Blocky402. A local warrant ready purse on your machine shows /fund so you can send testnet HBAR. After pay, the shop submits the note to Hedera Consensus Service topic 0.0.10416077. The text is public on HashScan. Who asked is not. Fire this warrant (or Fire every) tombstones the hop or bumps the identity so the next call dies with a stale root. The north star: my bot acted, I fired every agent under me, nobody learned who I was.
howItsMade:
I built Warrant as a pnpm monorepo with hard process boundaries, not one app that does everything.
Stack. Circom WarrantHop(20) plus a Groth16 ceremony (artifacts-groth16-v3, pot16). Foundry contracts on Base Sepolia: MandateRegistry (LeanIMT + epoch, no Groth16 in Solidity), generated WarrantVerifier, optional WarrantGate. TypeScript domain in @ronnakamoto/warrant-core (Poseidon, Baby Jubjub / Semaphore identity, witness, snarkjs prove/verify, exactly eight public inputs). Shop middleware in @ronnakamoto/warrant-x402 (policy pipeline, challenge nonce, nullifier seal, ExactHedera pay fallthrough, createWarrantShop + warrantHono). Agent CLI @ronnakamoto/warrant for ready / act and a local fund page. Next.js dashboard (Astryx + Carbon language) on Vercel. Isolated prove worker, translate shop, and memo shop on Railway. The Graph Studio subgraph indexes registry events for the console, not as a second mandate model.
How it pieces together. Authorize on the dashboard mints a guest session on prove: 2-hop mandate tree, operator bind into MandateRegistry, bearer = random session id. Hermes installs /skill.md and POSTs to /api/agent/memo with that bearer. The BFF calls prove with the live x402 challenge; prove returns a warrant header. The memo shop verifies Groth16, checks merkleRoot == currentRoot, seals (nullifier, requestHash), then Blocky402 settles HBAR and the service submits the note to Hedera Consensus Service. Fire is an on-chain revoke from the MetaMask that bound the leaf; the next prove fails as root revoked. scripts/check-boundaries.mjs enforces the split: dashboard never imports snarkjs, shops never call prove, prove never imports Hedera or x402.
Partner tech. Base Sepolia holds the public revocation and membership root so Fire is real, not a cookie delete. Hedera gives us live x402 settlement (Blocky402 ExactHedera) and a public HCS scar for the demo note, which is the honesty punchline: words public, person private. Semaphore-style LeanIMT / identity primitives let us reuse a known anonymity-set pattern instead of inventing a tree. x402 is the payment extension slot so warrant verify and pay compose in one shop request.
Hacky but deliberate. Hosted Copy means Warrant sees the witness so cloud bots never touch a 28MB zkey. Guest tier=0 with a random session tag (no World ID on the land) so strangers can try on real rails. Free calls = 0 forces a real 402. Chat must never invent a Hedera key, so payment is a local purse + /fund on 127.0.0.1. Hire returns a helper skill paste instead of spawning a subagent on camera. The bearer is intentionally not the proof: it is an opaque capability handle into prove’s session store.

name: gUSD: GPU Exposures
description: Trade onchain exposure to real-world GPU compute prices across H100, H200, L40S and RTX 4090.
projectDescription: gUSD is the GPU Assets Protocol, enabling onchain markets for trading exposure to GPU compute prices. The protocol tracks live GPU-hour pricing across providers, aggregates this data into a benchmark oracle, and uses those prices to power markets for assets such as H100, H200, L40S, and RTX 4090. Trading is executed through Uniswap v4 with custom hooks, while gUSD acts as the settlement asset and sgUSD as the protocol’s savings and revenue-sharing layer. The system also includes primary GPU asset issuance, protocol-owned liquidity, an Envio-powered indexer, and a web application with Privy-based embedded wallets for simplified onboarding.
howItsMade:
gUSD is built as a TypeScript + Solidity monorepo using pnpm and Turborepo. The protocol contracts are written with Foundry and deployed on Robinhood Chain, with GPU markets settling through Uniswap v4. We built a custom v4 hook for GPU-specific market execution, primary GPU asset issuance, protocol-owned liquidity, gUSD settlement, sgUSD savings, and oracle-aware market logic.
Offchain, a Fastify-based oracle pipeline collects GPU rental prices from multiple providers, normalizes them into GPU-hour benchmarks, and publishes price updates onchain through a dedicated oracle publisher. Envio HyperIndex + HyperSync index protocol activity into Postgres for portfolio, market, and historical views.
The frontend is built with Next.js and Privy, allowing users to sign in with familiar Web2 methods while receiving a self-custodial embedded wallet, or connect an existing wallet directly. The result is a full-stack onchain market where users can trade exposure to real-world GPU compute prices such as H100, H200, L40S, and RTX 4090.

name: Facture
description: An invoice is a zero-coupon bond nobody ever priced. Facture is the market that prices it.
projectDescription:
Invoice factoring is bond pricing done over the phone. A business owed $40,000 in sixty days calls a factoring house, waits, and takes whatever single price comes back. There is no screen, no curve, and no second buyer.
A market never formed here because invoices are not fungible. Every receivable has a different debtor, a different amount and a different number of days to maturity, so no two are the same asset and an order book has nothing to book. Facture stops trying to standardise the paper and standardises the bid instead. A funder writes a standing mandate (any A-rated paper, 90 days or less, 12.5% annualised, up to $200,000 of exposure), funds it, and walks away. Any invoice that arrives is priced immediately by reading the curve at its own rating and tenor. The assets stay unique and the buyers become fungible.
The instrument was always a bond. A discounted invoice is a zero-coupon bond: bought below par, redeeming at face on a fixed date, with the discount being the yield. Each receivable is issued as its own zero-coupon bond on Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio, maturity set to the invoice due date and principal to the face value.
Five moves, each of which has now run on testnet more than once.
List. The invoice becomes a bond. A uniqueness registry keyed on hash(debtor, invoice number, amount) means one receivable mints exactly one token, ever, which answers the specific fraud factoring has always had.
Quote. A confirmed invoice carries a live price already. Not a button that requests one: the number is simply there, and it moves as the curve moves and as the due date approaches.
Match. Eligibility is checked against the security's own control list and KYC facets before matching, not at settlement. An AMM matches first and discovers the transfer was illegal afterwards. Here an ineligible counterparty is never matched, and the refusal comes back as a sentence a funder can read rather than a reverted transaction.
Settle. Delivery versus payment across two chains with no bridge. The bond stays on Hedera, the USDC stays on Arc, and neither side moves first. Buyer capital already lives where stablecoins live, so the second chain is not a flourish.
Mature. The debtor pays and settlement routes to whoever holds the paper now, not whoever bought it first. Without that the paper cannot legitimately change hands, because a second buyer would have no way to be paid.
Nobody using Facture needs to know it is on a blockchain. A seller sees invoices with prices beside them. A buyer sees mandates, exposure and yield. The chain surfaces in one place: a proof view, one click from any trade, showing the on-chain receipts, the compliance decision and both settlement legs.
howItsMade:
A pnpm workspace of five packages: a Next.js 15 and React 19 frontend, a Hono backend over SQLite and drizzle holding the quote engine, settlement and issuance, a market-maker agent, a shared package holding the curve, the state machines and one refusal vocabulary, and a Hardhat workspace that no other package imports.
The paper is Hedera. Every receivable is its own ATS zero-coupon bond via deployBond, about 7 million gas and 7 to 9 HBAR an issuance, measured on chain rather than estimated. Eight contracts are deployed and verified on Sourcify: a uniqueness registry, an invoice registry whose isConfirmed is a public view, a mandate book that reads rating and confirmation out of that registry instead of from whoever wants the match to succeed, a compliance gate, and a party registry where a business signs an EIP-712 profile and the venue only relays it, so it can never write a profile on somebody's behalf. Refusal and match digests go to an HCS topic as SHA-256 commitments, never the reason itself, because a topic is public and a refusal names a customer and an amount.
The money is Arc. A funded mandate escrows USDC in MandateVault and settles out of it in one call, with no challenge and no signature, because a funded standing bid already said yes to anything meeting its terms. An unfunded one settles pay-as-you-go over x402 on Hedera through the Blocky402 facilitator. That reads x402 as a settlement protocol instead of an API paywall: the challenge holds the asset leg, the payment signature is the cash leg, and the facilitator is what makes the two simultaneous. One of those payments was made by an agent rather than a person, signing a native Hedera TransferTransaction with the buyer's own key. Privy signs a seller in by email, and the wallet it makes carries a policy with exactly two rules, so that key gained two permissions rather than becoming general purpose. Circle developer-controlled wallets fund the vault.
Three things worth flagging. Backend issuance had never once succeeded: the deployBond tuple was a plausible flattening of the real one that compiled, typechecked and encoded cleanly to a selector the deployed diamond does not have. A wrong selector is not a wrong type, so nothing in the toolchain could see it. Three ATS compliance selectors that the docs imply exist do not, and the gate probing them failed closed, so it refused every buyer on every instrument while looking correct. And the asset leg is an ATS hold rather than an escrow transfer, because createHoldByPartition acts on the caller's own tokens. That is also what made the secondary market buildable, after authorising the venue as an ERC-1400 operator turned out to succeed and confer nothing.

name: Kurabase
description: Supabase-like database DX for EVM apps: SQL, RLS, delegated gateways, and account-owned writes.
projectDescription:
Kurabase is a local-first relational data layer for EVM applications. It starts from a simple premise: distributed ledgers are databases, so application developers should be able to work with familiar database concepts instead of starting with Solidity.
Run kura start to launch an Anvil chain, delegated gateway, and database workspace together. Use the Dashboard to create tables, define schemas, inspect rows, and run SQL. In an application, the JavaScript SDK provides a SQL-shaped client for querying data, inserting rows, and applying row-level security.
Kurabase keeps authority explicit. Developers delegate gateways; users grant scoped, revocable sessions; and account-abstraction writes remain account-owned. ENS schema resolution also lets an instance query a named relation from another instance.
howItsMade:
Kurabase is an open-source monorepo built around Solidity contracts and Foundry tests for the authority layer, a Rust gateway for chain-backed query and write handling, and TypeScript packages for the JavaScript SDK and CLI. kura start uses Docker Compose and Anvil to create a complete local stack.
The Dashboard provides a Supabase-like workflow for tables, SQL, migrations, policies, gateway authority, and authentication configuration. The SDK exposes familiar relational operations while the gateway enforces delegated authority and scoped user sessions. ENS resolution maps named instances to schemas for cross-instance SQL. The documentation site covers the local workflow, production configuration, SDK, SQL, and architecture.

name: AutoVoyage
description: AI agent plans and books full travel itineraries, paying per-query in HBAR via x402 on Hedera.
projectDescription:
Our AI travel agent plans and books full trip itineraries end-to-end, autonomously paying for real flight data over Hedera's x402 payment protocol. Instead of API keys or subscriptions, the agent pays per-query in native HBAR through a self-hosted x402 facilitator that verifies and settles each payment on Hedera testnet in real time.
The user authorizes once — setting a spending budget and approving a HIP-336 HBAR allowance in their HashPack wallet. From there, the agent searches and pays for flight (and stay/activity) data autonomously from the user's own account, with every payment checked against on-chain spending ceilings before it settles — non-custodial and revocable at any time.
Before booking, the agent requires an explicit human confirmation bound to the exact itinerary hash, preventing any bait-and-switch between what was quoted and what gets booked. Every payment, approval, booking, and refusal is written as a plaintext event to a public Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) topic, giving a fully auditable trail anyone can verify on HashScan — no black box, no trust required.
The paid flight-data supplier is a real, live x402 service (not a mock) with metered per-result pricing, and it also self-registers on an HCS-based agent registry with a signed identity claim, so other agents can discover it and verify who they're paying without a hardcoded endpoint.
howItsMade:
The stack is a monorepo: a Next.js frontend (the planner/agent), an Express-based supplier service (the paid flight-data API), and a self-hosted x402 facilitator, all wired for Hedera testnet.
Payments (x402 + HBAR): The supplier gates its search routes with HTTP 402 — each request returns a price, the agent signs an HBAR transfer, and the facilitator verifies + settles on-chain before the real data is returned. Pricing is metered per result (not a flat fee), using a quote cache keyed by a canonical hash of the query so the unpaid 402 price and the paid response always agree.
Autonomous, non-custodial payment: Rather than the agent holding user funds, we use Hedera's HIP-336 HBAR allowance. The user signs once in HashPack to grant a spending allowance; the agent then pays the supplier directly from the user's account using its own server-held key, with every payment checked against on-chain spending ceilings before settling. This took real HAPI-level probing to get right — Hedera requires the spender (our agent), not the fee-payer or facilitator, to own the transaction ID for an allowance-debited transfer, a rule that's undocumented for HBAR (only stated for NFTs in the protobufs) and had to be discovered empirically with test transactions.
Auditability (HCS): Every payment, human approval, booking, and refusal is written as a plaintext JSON event to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, readable live via Mirror Node — a public, tamper-evident audit trail with no local cache. The supplier also self-registers on a second HCS topic with a signed identity claim (Ed25519), so other agents can discover and verify it without a hardcoded URL or trusted middleman.
Booking safety: Before any booking executes, the agent re-derives a SHA-256 hash of the exact itinerary (flights, prices, passenger count) server-side and requires it to match a human-confirmed session — preventing a stale or swapped itinerary from being booked without consent.
The honest hack — flight data: Real flight-search APIs (Amadeus, Duffel, etc.) are paid and gated behind commercial contracts we couldn't get for a hackathon timeline, and scraping live fares isn't something we were willing to do. So the "supplier" is a real, live x402-gated service — the payment, pricing, and settlement are 100% real on-chain — but the flight inventory it serves is a curated dummy dataset rather than a live GDS feed. Every dollar (well, tinybar) spent buying that data is a genuine Hedera testnet transaction; the data itself is fixtures. We were explicit about this boundary throughout the build rather than dressing it up as real.
