name: Aquastack
description: One balance, two yields: Aave lending + 1inch Aqua liquidity, with automated depeg exit
projectDescription:
In normal DeFi, a dollar can only do one job at a time: it's either lent out on a money market like Aave, or it's paired into a liquidity pool on a DEX. You have to choose, and whichever you don't choose sits there earning nothing. AquaStack removes that choice by making a single stablecoin deposit do both jobs simultaneously, without ever splitting or moving the underlying funds.
The mechanism relies on a property of 1inch Aqua, a shared-liquidity layer where a liquidity provider registers a "virtual balance" with the protocol instead of transferring tokens into a pool. Aqua only ever touches the real tokens at the exact instant a swap settles, pulling from the maker's wallet and pushing the counter-asset back. Because the tokens sit in the wallet the entire time rather than being locked in a pool contract, they are free to simultaneously be something else: a rebasing Aave v3 aToken, quietly accruing lending interest every block. Nothing is double-spent, since Aqua can never pull more than the registered virtual balance allows.
The full flow: you deposit two stablecoins (USDC and USDT on our Base Sepolia deployment). Both are supplied to Aave v3, minting rebasing aUSDC and aUSDT directly into your wallet. Those aTokens are then registered with Aqua as a pegged, narrow-band automated market maker strategy. From that point on, the aTokens keep rebasing with Aave yield in the background, while real swaps route through the pegged pool and pay the position a small spread on top — two independent income streams from one balance.
Because pegged pools carry depeg risk, every position carries a protective rule you configure at deposit time: a peg-deviation limit, a take-profit target, a stop-loss, and a max-drawdown limit, any combination of which can be active. An automated keeper runs a pass over every open position on a schedule, reads its live on-chain state, evaluates the rule, and either holds, raises an alert, or executes a full unwind: docking the Aqua position, repaying any variable debt left by an asymmetric swap, and withdrawing both legs from Aave back to your wallet as plain stablecoins plus yield. This happens automatically, even if you are offline, without ever taking custody of your funds. The keeper only ever holds a Privy session signer scoped to exactly two functions, dock() and withdraw(), on the one position it was delegated for.
howItsMade:
AquaStack is a Next.js (App Router, TypeScript) app with the entire chain-facing layer built as Server Actions, so none of the 1inch SDK code or RPC logic ever ships to the browser. The client only ever receives pre-built, ready-to-sign transaction plans and read-only position state.
The stack: wagmi + viem for chain reads and transaction sending, Privy for wallet auth (both a plain browser-wallet fallback and Privy's embedded wallets with delegated session signers), Tailwind for styling, and Upstash Redis for the position/rule store in production — it falls back to a local JSON file in dev, since a serverless deployment's filesystem doesn't persist between invocations but a long-running dev server's does.
The core partner technology is 1inch Aqua, via the official @1inch/aqua-sdk and @1inch/swap-vm-sdk. Aqua's key property a maker registers a virtual balance and the underlying tokens only move at the instant a swap settles  is what makes the whole product possible: it lets the same aToken be Aave-earning and Aqua-liquidity at once, since Aqua never actually takes custody. Aave v3 supplies the lending side for real, live yield rather than a simulated APY.
The most notable hacky bit: neither 1inch Aqua nor SwapVM has an official Base Sepolia testnet deployment, so we redeployed both ourselves  opcode-identical to the official SDK builds — and verified the whole flow end-to-end against our own deployment, which the 1inch bounty rules explicitly allow. Close behind that: the 1inch SDKs ship a broken ESM build (extensionless relative imports that Node can't resolve), so we had to add the packages to Next.js's serverExternalPackages config to force it to fall back to native require() and pick up the working CJS build instead  without that, the build silently fails at import time.
Another deliberate design choice: a deposit ships min(suppliedLegA, suppliedLegB) to Aqua so the pegged curve always starts exactly at 1:1, leaving any small remainder from an unbalanced deposit sitting in the wallet, still earning Aave yield, just outside the Aqua position. And the keeper itself only ever holds a Privy session signer scoped to exactly dock() and withdraw() for one position at a time a deliberately narrow blast radius instead of a general-purpose delegated signer.

name: Maqam Protocol
description: Discover agents with The Graph. Authorize one exact USDC payment on Arc.
projectDescription:
Maqam Protocol connects live agent discovery to exact, single-use payment authorization. The Graph supplies ERC-8004 registrations on Base Sepolia. The app screens declared capabilities, active status, indexed agent wallets and distinct non-owner feedback reviewers, explaining which candidates can proceed to human review and which are held. A real recorded model analysis uses a fresh Graph snapshot to recommend a candidate, with its complete input and output preserved.
For a selected agent, the wallet review refreshes Graph data and binds the agent ID and snapshot hash into the exact payment evidence. The owner independently verifies the invoice and recipient, then signs the token, amount, recipient, executor, expiry, nonce and revocation epoch. A Solidity executor on Arc Testnet enforces those terms and transfers USDC once. Changed recipients or amounts, replay and revoked approvals fail.
The demo shows live Graph screening, recorded model reasoning, and a separate mined Arc payment fixture with controlled owner, executor and recipient accounts. The receipt viewer verifies that real payment against live Arc RPC. We do not claim the Graph-discovered third-party agent was hired or paid. Registry claims and feedback do not prove trust or an Arc payment agreement.
This is a new ETHOnline application using the existing public MIT [email protected] npm library as a disclosed dependency. Its contracts, UI, APIs, Graph integration, assets and tests were created during the event. The initial Continuity classification was corrected to Building from Scratch based on the public-library exception; see BUILD-PROVENANCE.md. This is an unaudited testnet prototype.
howItsMade:
The Graph is the live data backend for agent selection. A server-side GraphQL request reads the Agent0 ERC-8004 Subgraph on Base Sepolia. Deterministic screening checks active registration, an explicit agent wallet, task keyword matches and a configurable distinct-reviewer threshold. Index errors or data more than 15 minutes behind halt discovery. We retain exact snapshots and hash them; a selected candidate is queried again during payment review, and the snapshot commitment is included in the signed evidence. Packet import checks the snapshot and recipient linkage. A separate real model adapter uses live Graph results for a candidate recommendation; the hosted model panel clearly labels that preserved call as recorded.
The Solidity executor uses OpenZeppelin EIP712, SignatureChecker (including ERC-1271), SafeERC20 and ReentrancyGuard. Owner nonces are consumed atomically with transferFrom. Cancellation and epoch invalidation revoke pending approvals. An ethers 6 browser client verifies runtime bytecode, manages exact token allowances and requests typed signatures.
The public Cloudflare Worker serves Vite assets and bounded policy/discovery APIs. [email protected] is an existing MIT public library used for proposal policy, not claimed as newly authored code. Graph credentials remain server-side. The initial demo uses documented public read-only gateway access distributed by Agent0's SDK; a dedicated Graph Studio key is configurable. Thirty-two automated tests cover contracts, policy, Graph screening and evidence integrity, plus the real UI handlers against a local EVM: exact allowance/signing, settlement, replay, revocation, wallet changes and separate-executor packet import. Clean Linux CI and the production build pass. Pending wallet or input changes invalidate stale reviews; imported packets undergo onchain signature, nonce and epoch validation. Public Chrome checks verify live Graph results, the Arc receipt and a narrow-screen layout.
Arc USDC is the settlement asset and gas currency: ERC20 amounts use six decimals, native gas uses eighteen. The fully verified contract and retained 1 USDC fixture prove exact authorization and replay protection. That fixture is separate from Graph-discovered third-party agents. A second Chrome test connected the participant’s MetaMask wallet and settled a 0.10 test-USDC self-payment on Arc (block 61761093). The participant confirmed wallet prompts while Codex operated the app; recipient/amount tampering and replay were rejected through eth_call simulations. Public receipt and consumed-nonce verification are retained in evidence/participant-wallet-test.json. This second test is not a separate-executor or third-party agent payment.
AI assistance: OpenAI Codex assisted research, implementation, tests, UI and documentation. Specifications, model prompts, live-query evidence and incremental commits are retained. Participant direction, automated tests, scripted signing, human wallet testing and narration are distinguished honestly in AI-ASSISTANCE.md.

name: product tracker
description: Transparent USDC grants on Arc — one-sig contribute + ERC-8004 agent IDs.
projectDescription:
Open Treasury is a transparent public-funding vault on Arc Testnet. It is built for NGOs, DAOs, grant programs, and anyone who needs to collect USDC and later pay it out as grants — with every contribution and allocation visible on-chain.
The problem. Typical treasuries are opaque: money goes into a wallet or multisig, and the public cannot easily see who funded it, how much is still free to grant, or what has already been promised to recipients. Open Treasury separates who paid from what the vault holds, and it keeps grant state on-chain.
How funding works. A contributor connects a wallet (MetaMask, Rabby, Coinbase Wallet, Trust, or Phantom) on Arc Testnet, gets test USDC from Circle’s faucet, and submits an amount plus a short reference (for example a campaign or grant name). That reference is hashed with keccak256 and stored in a ContributionRecorded event. Approve and contribute happen in one signature using Arc’s Multicall3From, so the recorded contributor is the user’s wallet, not a helper contract. The same Arc USDC balance pays both the donation and gas.
How the vault works. Funds sit in TreasuryVault. Operators (role holders) can create grants, approve them, and recipients can claim (including partial claims). The UI today focuses on connect, inspect balances, register an agent, and contribute. Grant create/approve/claim is already in the contracts and is planned for the UI next.
Agents. On Arc, actors can have a portable ERC-8004 identity (an NFT ID on Arc’s shared Identity Registry — we did not deploy our own). Users can register an agent, then optionally tag a contribution as agent:{id}|their-reference. That does not move money by itself; it lets funding be attributed to an on-chain agent, not only a bare address. Reputation and ERC-8183 jobs (for example agent-assisted grant review) are the next step.
What you can see. The app shows wallet USDC, vault total, available (unallocated) and allocated balances, transaction finality with Arcscan links, recent contribution history, and in-app docs from the project README.
howItsMade:
Open Treasury is a transparent USDC grants vault on Arc Testnet. Contracts are Solidity 0.8.20, built and tested with Foundry (unit + invariant tests) and OpenZeppelin (AccessControl, Pausable, SafeERC20).
The protocol is split on purpose: TreasuryVault holds tokens and grant state (Pending → Approved → Claimed); a thin TreasuryFundingRouter pulls USDC and emits ContributionRecorded so the vault never stores who paid. Contributors get one wallet signature by batching USDC.approve + router.contribute through Arc’s Multicall3From (aggregate3 + CallFrom). That preserves the original EOA as msg.sender — a normal multicall would record the batcher as the contributor. We always use Arc USDC’s ERC-20 6-decimal interface for amounts; the same USDC balance also pays gas (native 18-decimal).
The frontend is Vite + React + TypeScript, wagmi / viem, and TanStack Query. Wallet connect uses explicit injected targets (MetaMask, Rabby, Coinbase Wallet, Trust, Phantom) so providers don’t race on window.ethereum. History prefers Arcscan’s logs API because Arc RPC caps eth_getLogs at 10k blocks. A known router ABI typo (refrenceHash) is kept so event topics still decode.
For Arc’s agentic stack we did not deploy a private registry: we call register(string) on the shared ERC-8004 Identity Registry. Contributions can optionally hash agent:{id}|reference so funding is attributable to a portable agent ID. Docs in the app are the root README parsed into sections at build time.
Hacky-but-necessary bits: Multicall3From sender preservation, USDC 6 vs 18 decimals, chunked/Arcscan log fallbacks, and collapsing huge wallet-reject hex dumps behind Details. Hosted on Vercel from the frontend/ app.
That’s about 1,600 characters. If the form has a tight max, use this shorter cut (still well over 280):
Built on Arc Testnet with Foundry / Solidity / OpenZeppelin: a TreasuryVault plus a thin TreasuryFundingRouter. Contributors approve + contribute in one tx via Arc Multicall3From, so ContributionRecorded still names the real wallet. The app is Vite + React + wagmi/viem; we use Arc USDC’s 6-decimal ERC-20 for transfers (same USDC pays gas). History uses Arcscan logs because RPC eth_getLogs is capped at 10k blocks. Agents register on Arc’s shared ERC-8004 Identity Registry and can tag contributions as agent:{id}|ref. Notable: sender-preserving multicall, decimal split, and truncated wallet-error dumps.

name: Mandate Run
description: Give your agent a mandate, not a credit card. It refuses what it can't justify.
projectDescription:
An agent handed a wallet will spend it. Mandate is the layer that decides whether a purchase is worth making at all.
Give it a purpose, a budget, and hard constraints. It sends each x402 seller the real request to collect a live 402 quote, then competes three plans over the remaining work: staged evidence, a hybrid, or one bundle. It picks the lowest expected cost among plans whose worst case still fits the budget at full coverage, reserves the final step so it can always finish, and pays one signed Hedera transfer per purchase.
When no plan can guarantee coverage, it refuses before spending a cent and says what completion would have cost. That refusal is the product, not a failure mode.
The worked example investigates Uniswap v3 liquidity. It screens five pools, finds the one that moved, buys transaction-level evidence for that pool alone, and writes an explanation in which every number is checked back against purchased facts. A model only writes prose; the runtime computes every claim itself.
Settlement is proven from the Hedera mirror node's records for the runtime's own transaction id, never from an HTTP response. A lost response is recovered with the original signed payment rather than a second one. A crash costs at most one attempt. Every decision writes a receipt to Hedera Consensus Service.
Payment behavior is verified by Proctor, a harness in the same repo. Its task contracts have two halves: one reads the buyer's own report, the other reads what Proctor measured independently from the seller's journal and the buyer's ledger. A check passes only when both agree, because an application is never its own oracle. Proctor caught a real double-payment bug during development from the journal, not from anything the buyer said about itself.
howItsMade:
The buyer runtime is Rust, edition 2024 on 1.98.1, with its own x402 types and an exact-scheme Hedera signer built on the Hedera Rust SDK. State lives in SQLite as a recovery ledger: signed payment bytes are persisted before anything leaves the process, so a crash or a dropped response never costs a second payment. A single ledger invariant (settled + outstanding + held <= budget) is enforced on every transition and tested across 200 randomly interleaved operations.
The sellers are TypeScript on Node 24: four x402-gated endpoints with published tariffs, priced per pool, per pool-window, and per input KB rather than a flat rate. They serve evidence from the Uniswap v3 subgraph on The Graph Network (5zvR82QoaXYFyDEKLZ9t6v9adgnptxYpKpSbxtgVENFV) through the gateway with a Subgraph Studio key, reading token-denominated TVL at the window's two observation blocks, hourly volume, and the largest events above a materiality threshold. Every response states its block range, coverage, truncation, and indexing status, so the buyer can tell thin data from no data.
Payments settle on Hedera testnet through the Blocky402 facilitator, which acts as fee payer and co-signs. The asset is a field of the mandate, so one code path settles HBAR and any fee-free fungible HTS token. Circle's testnet faucet never delivered USDC to us after four attempts, so rather than fake it we made the runtime mint its own HTS token and proved settlement in that instead.
Two things worth calling out. First, HTS custom fees: a token can carry a fee schedule that debits the payer beyond the payment, so the runtime checks mirror-node token metadata before signing and settlement reconciliation independently rejects any extra debit. Second, the harness. Proctor reads a SQLite ledger and a JSON-lines journal as plain files and links to nothing, so it tests any service that writes those two artifacts. Its bounded agent loop hands failing checks to a coding agent and retries, but never while a payment is unresolved: with money neither spent nor free, editing code and re-running could sign a second payment against the first, which is exactly the failure the harness exists to catch.
The whole thing runs from a clean clone with one setup script that creates its own HCS topic, pins the served manifest hash into the example mandates, and starts the sellers with canned Graph facts so no API keys are needed. Verified end to end on testnet: 175 Rust tests, 83 seller tests, 10 Python tests, 87% coverage.

name: Aether Credit
description: Evidence-aware AI treasury for policy-constrained USDC payments on Arc.
projectDescription: Aether Credit is an agent-native treasury platform that helps organizations manage USDC spending without surrendering control to an AI model. Employees submit expenses, managers approve an exact immutable version, and an evidence-aware analyst compares lending markets using The Graph. The agent can recommend, abstain, or require review, but it can never authorize a transfer. Every payment must independently pass deterministic rules covering recipients, per-payment limits, cumulative budgets, reserves, expiry, pause state, approvals, and replay protection. Eligible payments are executed through Circle Agent Stack against a customer-owned vault on Arc and reconciled into an inspectable audit trail. Privy provides organization authentication, wallets, role-bound approvals, and constrained funding controls.
howItsMade:
Aether Credit is a TypeScript monorepo with separate Next.js consumer and admin applications, a Fastify API, PostgreSQL and Drizzle ORM, and durable analysis and payment workers backed by pg-boss. Shared Zod contracts keep validation consistent across the browser, API, and workers. The analyst is a typed Vercel AI SDK harness that queries standardized lending data through The Graph, records deployment IDs, query parameters, freshness, block height, response hashes, citations, calculations, model metadata, and failure states, and fails closed when its evidence is stale or incompatible.
Privy authenticates three organization roles, binds users to wallets, captures exact EIP-712 approvals, and constrains treasury funding with a deposit-only signer policy. Payments are submitted by Circle Agent Stack on Arc Testnet to a non-upgradeable Solidity vault whose customer wallet is the immutable owner. The vault rechecks allowlists, caps, budgets, reserves, expiry, pause state, signatures, and replay protection onchain. The payment worker uses idempotency keys and independently reconciles transaction receipts and decoded events, treating timeouts as unknown outcomes instead of blindly retrying.
One particularly hacky integration detail came from Circle Agent Stack CLI 1.0.0 rejecting the vault’s original nested-tuple ABI before broadcast. We added scalar contract entry points while preserving the same policy checks, then covered the adapter with regression tests. The result is deliberately split between probabilistic advice and deterministic authority: AI explains what should happen, while application and contract policy decide what is permitted to happen.

name: GaussVM
description: Gaussian prediction-market liquidity, powered by 1inch Aqua and SwapVM.
projectDescription:
GaussVM brings Gaussian prediction-market liquidity to 1inch Aqua, using SwapVM to turn a research pricing curve into executable onchain trades. It builds on the pm-AMM research by Ciamac Moallemi and Dan Robinson and connects it to a working application where users can trade YES/NO outcome tokens, create liquidity positions, and inspect transaction receipts.
Aqua’s approach to liquidity is central to the project. Makers authorize trading strategies while keeping their outcome tokens in their wallets until a trade executes. A single wallet can support both GaussVM’s static and experimental time-scaled strategies without making separate token deposits for each position. Actual execution still depends on the wallet’s balances and allowances.
SwapVM provides the other essential piece: programmable execution. GaussVM implements Gaussian pricing as a custom SwapVM instruction, while the surrounding engine handles order validation and settlement through Aqua. Together, these 1inch technologies provide a practical foundation for taking a specialized market-making idea from a paper to a usable trading experience.
The live Sepolia demo asks a simple, slightly self-referential question: “Will this project win ETHOnline 2026?” Users can obtain free test tokens, swap between YES and NO, and follow confirmed transactions on an explorer. Liquidity controls support creating and removing positions, while the market contracts handle merging complete sets and redeeming outcomes after resolution.
GaussVM demonstrates how Aqua and SwapVM can support a pricing model tailored to binary outcomes. It is currently an unaudited testnet prototype with worthless test assets and manual resolution. Its time-scaled mode is an experiment, rather than a claim to reproduce the research paper’s complete economic result.
howItsMade:
The project is built around two complementary pieces of 1inch infrastructure: Aqua for liquidity accounting and token transfers, and SwapVM for programmable trade execution. GaussVM extends the official SwapVM base with a custom Gaussian instruction, opcode 0x80, and uses an unmodified deployment of official Aqua source.
When a maker creates a position, the application encodes the market, liquidity scale, timestamps, and strategy mode into a SwapVM order and authorizes it through Aqua. During a swap, the custom instruction reads that strategy’s current allocations and calculates how many outcome tokens the trader receives. SwapVM then applies its execution checks and settles the transfer through Aqua. This division lets GaussVM focus its custom logic on prediction-market pricing while using 1inch’s infrastructure for the surrounding execution flow.
The mathematical implementation uses signed 18-decimal fixed-point arithmetic, bounded Gaussian cumulative-distribution and density calculations, and a bisection solver with conservative output rounding. One useful optimization computes the density once and shares it between the calculations that need it. Regression tests compare the optimized and earlier implementations, including returned values, rejected inputs, and complete swaps.
Separate Solidity contracts provide test collateral, ERC-20 YES/NO tokens, collateral-backed splitting and merging, manual resolution, and timeout cancellation. Positions support either a static liquidity scale or an experimental scale based on the square root of the remaining market lifetime.
The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and viem. It reads balances and allocations, obtains quotes through contract simulation, requests limited token approvals, and links confirmed transactions to Sepolia receipts. Submitted hashes are preserved when confirmation is unavailable so users can recheck the same transaction. The public interface is hosted on GitHub Pages without a hosted backend or database.
The repository includes numerical tests, contract integration tests, Playwright browser tests, and a standalone Hardhat lifecycle demo. That demo exercises two Aqua strategies sharing one maker wallet, executes trades, checks actual balance changes and Aqua events, removes the positions, and completes merging and redemption. A separate fork demo runs the same lifecycle against 1inch’s canonical Aqua deployment, with all writes confined to a local Ethereum fork.

name: LockENS
description: ENSv2-powered NFC access passes with wallet proofs and resource-level authorization.
projectDescription:
LockENS turns wallet-held ENSv2 identities into access credentials that can be presented over NFC. The final demo uses one Android holder and three Android gate stands representing a Front Door, Lab and Server Room.
A user selects a pass in the LockENS Android app and presents it through Android HCE/NFC. The holder signs a fresh proof with a Privy embedded wallet. A local verifier checks holder control offchain and reads the current credential state and resource permissions from ENSv2 on Sepolia before returning ALLOW or DENY.
This means the same credential can remain owned by the same wallet while its global access, validity or permissions for individual resources change independently. The demo shows real NFC grant and denial flows, wallet switching, suspended credentials and resource-specific authorization. The gates are virtual interfaces rather than physical lock actuators.
howItsMade:
LockENS is built as an Android + NFC + Node.js authorization stack backed by ENSv2 on Sepolia.
The holder app is written in Kotlin and uses Android Host Card Emulation to present the selected credential over NFC. Privy provides embedded wallets and signs a fresh resource-bound EIP-712 holder proof. On the gate side, Android devices act as persistent NFC Gate Stands for the Front Door, Lab and Server Room.
A local Node.js verifier uses viem to validate the holder proof offchain and then reads the current ENSv2 state on Sepolia. ENSv2 UserRegistry establishes registration and ownership, while PermissionedResolver data provides global access and resource-level policy. The verifier only returns ALLOW when holder control and the current ENSv2 policy both pass; errors and denials fail closed.
For the final four-device demo, each Android gate reaches the same local verifier through ADB reverse. We also built and validated an experimental ESP32-S3 + PN532 route during development, but the final submission uses the more reliable Android gate architecture.
The notable part is that NFC presentation, wallet control and ENSv2 authorization are separate layers: possession of the phone or credential alone is not enough to open a gate. The verifier evaluates fresh holder proof plus current onchain policy for the specific resource being requested.

name: Bloom
description: The Bloomberg terminal for trading with AI agents — chat to buy, sell, and track assets live
projectDescription:
A smart helper answers you and at the same time builds clear, live pictures on the screen for you price charts, market lists, your money balances, and simple trade boxes with a Confirm button.
You can watch live prices move second by second, pause or switch what you are watching, and see a full history of all your past trades in one small floating box. For safety, there is a practice mode where you start with play money.
In short, it turns confusing trading work into a calm conversation with live pictures, a practice playground, and one-click real actions.
howItsMade: This project used privy wallet for auth, sub-graph for sub second real time data and uniswap api for trading and executing trades. And open ai, openUi for agents and real time UI generation for interaction and agents trade. Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS frontend.   Substreams for live prices. PostgreSQL + Redis for state and caching.

name: Plimsoll
description: Tokenised notes the network refuses to settle once their real backing falls below the line.
projectDescription: Every tokenised asset today prices itself with a number its issuer typed in, and a market that trusts that number has no way to stop trading when it stops being true. Plimsoll is a market for tokenised notes backed by real ERC-4626 vault positions, where coverage is computed continuously from the vault flows themselves and never taken from the issuer. Nothing in the calculation is typed in: the note's obligations are read from its own supply and nominal value on Hedera, the holder is the note's own on-chain issuer, and we value what that address actually holds in the nominated vaults on Base, so a claim of backing larger than the real balance has nowhere to go. When coverage falls below the note's load line, the network refuses: transfers revert with a typed reason, coupons stop settling because the cash leg is frozen at consensus, and a paid request for a coverage attestation returns a signed refusal that is never charged. Moving the load line or halting a market requires a human to approve it on a Ledger device, and a refusal on the device produces no signature at all. The name comes from the Plimsoll line, the mark on a ship's hull made law in 1876 after ships were deliberately overloaded and sunk for the insurance: a visible limit past which the authorities will not let a vessel sail.
howItsMade: Plimsoll is five pieces that each own one job. The truth layer is a Rust Substreams package (packages/substreams) that imports Pinax's ERC-4626 extractor by pinned URL, so its module hash and server-side cache are unchanged, and adds what they deliberately left out: a vault registry resolved by an asset() probe instead of topic0 matching, entry and exit rates kept apart so a fee spread cannot hide in one blended number, a consistent() check that refuses a zero or out-of-band share price, per-holder positions read with batched eth_calls inside the stream (map_positions), and Messari Yield Aggregator v1.3.1 entities, all from one spkg that runs on Ethereum and Base and is published to substreams.dev as v0.2.0; a cross-check script compares the stream against independent archive nodes wei for wei, and check_package.py refuses to release a package whose embedded README names a module the package does not contain, a check that exists because we shipped exactly that mistake once. An MCP server (packages/mcp, Streamable HTTP plus an A2A card) serves that feed with the package hash, module hash and block on every answer and refuses rather than serve a stale figure. The attestation service (packages/attestor, TypeScript with viem and the Hedera SDK) values the issuer's positions on Base with eth_call pinned to a block hash and corroborated by a second RPC, reads the note's supply, par, issuer and load line from Hedera so no number in the ratio is configured, and signs EIP-712 over CoverageOracle's own domain and types, with a test that hashes the same payload in TypeScript and in Solidity; it is sold per call over x402 through Blocky402, where the exact scheme settles only after the handler succeeds, so any refusal returns a 4xx and settlement is never called, which makes a refusal free by construction rather than by refund, and every verdict is anchored to an immutable HCS topic so verify-charge can check from public data that a charge exists if and only if an attestation was warranted. The contracts (packages/contracts, Foundry, 201 tests, Sourcify-verified on Hedera testnet) put a coverage gate in front of an order book built on ATS's non-reverting canTransferByPartition pre-flight and holdByPartition escrow, pay coupons in an HTS cash token whose freeze key is a contract key with no admin key, and re-arm coupons with HIP-1215 scheduleCall; moving a load line or halting a market needs a mandate approved on a Ledger device through the Device Management Kit, the contract rebuilds the displayed text from typed arguments rather than parsing it, and the verifier answers only to its adapter while the adapter answers only to LoadLine, so a signed mandate cannot be spent through a side door. One command (packages/verify) checks all of it from public endpoints with no keys. The hackiest part: the Ledger Ethereum app reflows newlines into spaces and wraps at about nineteen characters, so a market code containing NONCE: 9 could make a human approve what reads as a mandate with two nonces; we found it on the emulator and closed it with a charset rule enforced identically in TypeScript and Solidity. The most humbling part: our own checks caught an attestation we had submitted from test fixtures while the real backing was zero, and the deployment record now says so beside the stored number instead of letting it read as a measurement.

name: Private Hire
description: Hire agents for private work, verify their deliveries, and settle payments onchain
projectDescription:
PrivateHire is a platform for hiring agents to perform private work with verifiable delivery and onchain payments.
A buyer chooses an agent, defines a task, and funds an escrowed request. The agent receives the inputs needed to complete the work, while the buyer’s evaluation policy remains separate. An evaluator checks the committed delivery against that policy and produces a decision used to resolve payment.
The goal is to verify work without publishing its underlying inputs, full results, or evaluation policy onchain. Public records contain participants, payment amounts, lifecycle events, and cryptographic commitments. Inputs and results are stored encrypted and exposed through authenticated routes. The current backend operator remains trusted and can access the stored data.
Our first integrated agent is Portfolio Calculator. It processes a synthetic portfolio and returns deterministic position values, portfolio weights, and concentration. It provides a concrete example of the hiring flow: request an analysis, agree on its price, fund it, receive a report, and evaluate the delivery.
PrivateHire brings together ERC-8004 agent identity, A2A communication, Chainlink CRE evaluation, and ERC-8183 contracting on Arc Testnet. The prototype integrates one agent; onboarding additional agents is the next step.
howItsMade:
PrivateHire is built as a TypeScript monorepo using pnpm workspaces and Turborepo. The frontend uses Next.js App Router, deployed to Cloudflare Workers through OpenNext. Browser wallets connect through wagmi and RainbowKit, with viem for contract interactions and Sign-In with Ethereum for authenticated sessions.
Cloudflare D1 stores request correlations, task states, and processed events. Private payloads are encrypted with AES-GCM and stored in a private R2 bucket. Conditional writes and task reservations prevent concurrent requests from replacing an existing delivery. Recovery retrieves the same persisted artifact and commitment rather than silently generating a new result.
Portfolio Calculator communicates through A2A. Its calculations use BigInt, explicit decimal representations, and deterministic rounding. The buyer’s evaluation policy is not included in the agent request. A separate provider service is implemented to confirm budgets and submit deliveries, with restricted transaction construction and a durable journal that preserves signed transaction bytes across retries.
Chainlink CRE connects private evaluation to onchain settlement. The workflow checks request funding and commitments, retrieves the A2A delivery, evaluates it against the private policy, and constructs a public report for an evaluator receiver. The confidential path uses handlerInTee and Vault secret references. Our demonstration uses CRE simulation; deployed enclave execution is not claimed.
On Arc Testnet, we reuse an existing ERC-8183 deployment for the request lifecycle and USDC payment escrow. ERC-8004 supplies the agent’s registered identity. The evaluator receiver is configured specifically for simulation reports and validates report context, state, expiry, and replay before resolving a request.
A key engineering challenge was coordinating browser transactions, encrypted offchain artifacts, agent delivery, and evaluation without treating client-side assertions as truth. Receipts and RPC reads establish onchain state, while transport or integrity failures leave evaluation pending instead of turning technical failures into business rejection.

name: Priime
description: The vault structuring platform to compose, test & distribute vaults; in one verifiable venue.
projectDescription:
The vault structuring platform to create, test & distribute vaults; in one verifiable venue.
Problem
The chain can hold a vault. It cannot run one.
A vault has an infrastructure problem: a smart contract cannot react to markets, and it cannot compute the math a strategy needs, so the work that actually operates a vault sits on private servers, and that breaks composability, growth and trust. That server is a legal entity to structure, a breach waiting to be disclosed, and a centralized dependency no other protocol can build on.
Solution
Priime is where a strategy becomes a verifiable, automated onchain vault.
So we built the infrastructure and the killer app on top of it. A strategy is composed on a canvas, backtested and launched as a vault, and the off-chain work it needs runs as decentralized compute on our own Trustless Execution Network. Sophistication, efficiency, security and reach all go up without giving up decentralization. That is what lets DeFi products get better now, and what will let TradFi products be built onchain tomorrow.
Discover what we built during ETH Online hackathon here: https://priime.finance/ETHOnline-Priime-Hackathon
howItsMade:
The chain can hold a vault. It cannot run one. A contract cannot react to a market or compute what a strategy needs, so the work that operates 7.5 billion dollars of curator-run vaults runs on someone's private server. Nobody outside can check it.
The Priime canvas replaces the company with modules. A Liquidity source pins the venue and the market; Dynamic leverage holds the position inside a published health band; Auto-compound puts the earnings back to work. Every number is modeled from live market data before publish.
Corrupt one operator and the chain still takes the honest number. Publishing hands the composition to the Trustless Execution Network, where operators each re-execute the same deterministic WASM component against the same pinned input block, and only a quorum of identical signed results settles. In our sabotage strike the honest operators reported 500.000000 USDC and the corrupted one reported 750.000000. The lie never settled.
A quorum-signed plan cannot drain the vault. Settlement is an ERC-4626 vault on Base with an ERC-7540 redemption queue, one per strategy. Operators sign a plan and the vault executes it against a whitelist of target and selector pairs in which every address argument is decoded and pinned to the vault itself, so no foreign receiver and no rogue approval spender can be named. The operators never touch funds.
Every dependency a strategy touches gets a watcher. A vault does not have to be exploited to lose money, it only has to hold something that was: of this year's 165 DeFi exploits, 44 ran through a bridge, a cross-chain message or a price feed, and cost 405.3 million dollars. They are watched as one stack, every block.
The Graph gives one schema across protocols, so a single query spans many of them and a strategy becomes backtestable before it ships. Wallets, policies and quorum approvals run through Privy, and the depositor keeps ownership of the position. Uniswap is the trading engine on every entry and exit, with v4 hooks at the edges.
Discover what we built during ETH Online hackathon here: https://priime.finance/ETHOnline-Priime-Hackathon
