name: Levee
description: An on-chain wallet that turns planned spending into time-locked funds
projectDescription:
Freelancers and gig workers rarely experience income as a steady stream. Three weeks can pass with nothing, followed by two invoices at once. Yet rent, subscriptions, and bills arrive on fixed dates regardless. The real problem is knowing what is genuinely safe to spend today without spending tomorrow's rent.
Most financial tools are advisory. They warn you, and you dismiss the warning and spend anyway. The failure is not the maths. It is that nothing stands in the way at the moment the decision is made. An actual levee, the embankment kind, does not persuade water to stay back. It simply does not let it through. This one works the same way with money.
People with irregular income already do a version of this by hand, with separate accounts, cash set aside, or fixed deposits. Those work right up until the moment you decide to override them. And no bank budgeting tool reaches on-chain income at all.
Define an obligation, such as rent, 0.006 ETH, due on the 25th, and those funds move into a contract that will not release them early. Not to the app, not to an agent, not to you. Your home screen shows one number: what is actually free to spend right now. Try to spend past it and Levee declines, names the obligation protecting the money, and tells you when it unlocks. No transaction is sent.
An in-app assistant answers questions about your position in plain language. It reads live contract state for what is spendable right now and indexed history for what has happened over time. It answers only from data it has, and never invents a figure.
The same guarantee extends to software. Subscription bots and payment agents do not know what you have set aside, so Levee publishes a spend-check service they can call before spending. They get back a verdict and the specific obligation standing in the way.
Every budgeting tool asks you to be disciplined. Levee makes discipline a property of the system instead.
howItsMade:
Levee is built around a Solidity smart contract deployed on Ethereum Sepolia through Remix. The contract implements four core operations: "deposit", "commit", "spendFree", and "release". "commit" earmarks a portion of the user's balance against a Unix timestamp and label. "release" reverts before the unlock date, making early release impossible regardless of caller, while "spendFree" can access only uncommitted funds. A read-only "canSpend" check runs before spending and returns whether an amount is allowed, along with the earliest-unlocking commitment blocking it. This enables deterministic refusal without submitting a transaction that would revert.
Everything else hangs off that one function. "canSpend" drives three separate surfaces: the refusal screen in the app, the assistant's answer when a user asks why they are blocked, and the public endpoint an autonomous agent calls. All three read the same verdict from the same source, so a bot and a human are never told different things about the same wallet. The frontend uses Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind, and viem.
Privy handles email and social authentication while creating embedded wallets automatically, so users never need to manage seed phrases or connect external wallets. External wallet connection is deliberately disabled. Without embedded wallets this would be a dapp for people who already own MetaMask, which is the opposite of the intended user.
Subgraph Studio indexes the "Deposited", "Committed", "Released", and "Spent" events. Live contract reads answer what can be spent right now; the Subgraph answers what has been committed over time. Without that indexed history the assistant could only read a balance back to you, rather than reason over commitments made and released.
The in-app natural-language assistant combines both feeds to answer real-time and historical questions. It operates strictly on supplied data and never fabricates figures. The same pairing powers a public agent endpoint, whose responses include a "sources" field identifying the origin of each result. The endpoint is documented through OpenAPI and published through a Bazantic gateway with a Recipe explaining when and why an autonomous agent should call it, which turned a plain endpoint into a discoverable service rather than something only I knew existed.
Two things were genuinely painful to get working. Privy's RPC rejects "wallet_sendTransaction", which is exactly what viem defaults to when the wallet client is created without an explicit account and chain, so every write failed with an opaque "unsupported method" error until both were passed into "createWalletClient" directly. And the Gemini model catalog is inconsistent with its own serving endpoint: "gemini-2.5-flash" is listed as healthy with "generateContent" supported, but calling it 404s, and the error body redirects to a different model. Trusting the error over the catalog was the only way through.

name: Plimsol
description: Proof of enough, not proof of how much: a confidential credit check for autonomous agents.
projectDescription:
Two agents want to do a deal on credit. The buyer wants the goods now and will pay later. The seller has to decide whether the buyer is good for it. Right now the buyer has two ways to answer, and both are bad. It can show its whole balance sheet, in which case the seller knows exactly how hard to squeeze it. Or it can say "trust me", which is worth nothing.
Plimsoll is a third option. The seller pays a few cents to ask one question, "is this agent above the line?", and gets back one signed bit on chain. We call that a Mark. It says ABOVE, BELOW, or INDETERMINATE, plus a timestamp and an expiry. That's it. No balance, no amounts, no price. Not even the reason if it failed.
The reading happens inside a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow running in an AWS Nitro enclave. The enclave fetches the buyer's private holdings with a key only it can see, prices them at Chainlink, applies a haircut, and compares to the threshold. Only the verdict comes back out.
The privacy comes from the structure, not from asking nicely. The buyer decides in advance which thresholds it's willing to be asked about (we call that the ladder). Nobody can ask anything finer, so the most you can ever learn is "somewhere between two rungs", and the buyer picked the rungs. Requests are rate-limited per counterparty so you can't just ask every rung. And because a "no" leaks more than a "yes", publishing a no is opt in per rung. One good answer can be faked with a flash loan, so lenders look for Standing: three yeses spread over a day.
Bazantic is how an agent actually uses this. Two live gateways and a published Recipe that an agent calls as one tool: price the deal at Chainlink, pick the rung, ask, read the Mark, decide. The Recipe also carries the rule that matters most: if the answer is no, don't ask again at a lower rung.
Everything is live on Sepolia. Real Marks have been posted by the workflow, and the dashboard lets anyone request one and watch it land.
howItsMade:
We started with the contracts. PlimsollRegistry (Foundry, Sepolia) holds subjects, their ladders, survey requests and Marks. It's a CRE receiver, so the Forwarder calls onReport and the contract decodes the six fields and checks them the same way it would a hand posted Mark. Lines are stored as structs rather than hashes so one Mark can serve any counterparty whose exposure it covers. CreditDesk is the reference lender and won't pay out without Standing. 42 tests.
The Survey is a CRE workflow in TypeScript. An EVM log trigger fires on SurveyRequested and the handler is registered with handlerInTee, so it runs inside AWS Nitro. In there it pulls the Hold credential from the Vault DON, makes three HTTP calls (the ladder, the Chainlink price, and the buyer's holdings), does the valuation in plain integer math, and crosses back to the DON with only the verdict and its provenance. Debug logging is off in every shipped config because logs leave the enclave too. We simulated it with the CRE CLI against real Sepolia transactions, then left it running in listen mode so new requests get answered on their own. The transcripts are in the repo.
The API is a Next.js app on Vercel with route handlers for price, line derivation, ladder, requests, Marks and Standing, all reading the chain with viem. The Hold adapter lives there too, behind a shared key that only the enclave presents, and it's deliberately missing from every public spec.
For Bazantic we served two OpenAPI specs, registered two gateways with x402 settlement (sandbox, test USDC on Base Sepolia), and published two Recipes from JSON definitions with Claude Sonnet as the model. We ran the composed Recipe end to end with paid calls.

name: Heirloom
description: Non-custodial HBAR inheritance: an allowance, not a deposit, released by the chain itself.
projectDescription:
Every crypto inheritance product today is a vault: you hand your savings to a contract and hope it gives them back later. Heirloom does the opposite. The owner grants our contract a native HBAR allowance (HIP-906) from their own wallet. No money moves. They keep spending normally. The allowance lies dormant until the switch fires, and then a single HTS cryptoTransfer with isApproval=true moves the HBAR directly from the owner's account to the beneficiary's. Our contract's balance never changes. This is only possible on Hedera: Ethereum has no allowance mechanism for its native asset.
There is also no server, keeper, or cron job. The vault schedules calls to itself with HIP-1215 scheduled contract calls. It wakes up, checks whether the owner is alive, and reschedules. The interval tightens as the deadline approaches (30 days, then 7, then 1), so the system watches harder the closer it gets to acting.
Liveness is detected passively. Every transaction the owner signs costs a fee, so any activity lowers their balance, and only the key holder can cause a decrease. The heartbeat sees that and resets the timer. The owner never has to open our app. A one-tap "I am alive" covers the rest. Before releasing, the vault re-checks liveness one last time and reads the allowance live from the ledger; if the owner has been active, it resets instead of releasing. It fails toward not releasing.
The beneficiary needs no setup and need not know the vault exists. The factory indexes vaults by beneficiary, so connecting a wallet is enough to find one. The owner can revoke at the ledger level at any time by setting the allowance to zero, with no cooperation from our contract.
This is running on Hedera Testnet. We watched a scheduled self-call release 100 HBAR from the owner's account to the beneficiary's, three times, with nobody clicking anything. The vault's balance only ever moved by its own heartbeat fees.
howItsMade:
Contracts are Solidity 0.8.24 with Foundry, tested against mocked Hedera system contracts etched at 0x167 (HTS), 0x16a (HAS) and 0x16b (HSS), 63 unit tests plus fuzzing on the timer maths. Three Hedera primitives do the real work: HIP-906 HBAR allowances (the owner calls hbarApprove on the Hedera Account Service; the vault reads hbarAllowance live, never cached), HIP-206 atomic cryptoTransfer with isApproval=true to spend that allowance, and HIP-1215 generalized scheduled contract calls for the vault to schedule its own heartbeat(). The scheduler never reverts: failures are emitted, and a permissionless poke() restarts a dead chain.
The frontend is Next.js 16, Tailwind 4, wagmi and viem, with MetaMask over the Hedera JSON-RPC relay. The activity log is built entirely from mirror-node event queries; no subgraph. Deploy and lifecycle scripts are TypeScript with viem and the Hedera SDK.
We spent the first hours on verification spikes before writing production code, and they earned their keep. Two findings overturned our plan. First, inside the Hedera EVM every value (msg.value, address.balance, call{value}) is already tinybars; the relay presents weibars. Our spec assumed weibars in the contract and would have released 10^10 times too little. The contract now does zero unit conversion. Second, a scheduleCall costs about 1.5M gas, so our planned 400k heartbeat budget would have killed the chain on its first link, and each heartbeat costs about 1.75 HBAR, which we surface as runway in the dashboard.
Hacky bits worth admitting: liveness by balance decrease is a heuristic, and we saw it bite us in a good way. Calling release() from the owner's own wallet aborted the release, because paying the fee proved the owner alive. Only a non-owner can trigger a release now. We also drained the fee reserve exactly at the finish line in one test run (INSUFFICIENT_PAYER_BALANCE on the final scheduled call), which is why the reserve is refundable, runway is shown, and anyone can restart the chain. And MetaMask refuses to send calldata to one of its own accounts, so the allowance grant goes through the Account Service system contract instead of the HIP-906 own-address redirect.
Nothing is faked: the demo runs on testnet with compressed timings (3-minute timeout, 15/10/5-second heartbeats) using the same code path as production.
Two things to adjust before submitting: swap the project name if you've picked a different one, and if the form asks for team or partner technologies separately, the partner technology is Hedera (HIP-906, HIP-206, HIP-1215, the JSON-RPC relay, and the mirror node).

name: Signa Covenant
description: An FX coverage gate on Arc: USDC drawdowns are refused onchain when the hedge stops covering them.
projectDescription:
A credit originator owes investors USDC while its loans repay in euros. The loan book lives in a servicing system, the hedge lives at a bank, and the capital sits in a vault that cannot see whether that hedge is current, sufficient, or even matched to this facility.
The covenant meant to govern all of this is checked by operations on a calendar, while capital moves on demand.
Signa Covenant puts the covenant in the money path. The servicer and the hedge provider each sign an EIP-712 credential: one states what is owed, the other what is hedged. A coverage engine on Arc computes how much of the outstanding USDC obligation the hedge actually covers, after a haircut.
Every drawdown asks the gate first, and when coverage falls below the facility's minimum, the vault refuses the draw onchain.
It is live on Arc Testnet and proven with receipts. The same draw, with byte-identical calldata, was sent three times to the same vault: accepted at 100% coverage, refused at 68.4% with DrawNotAllowed(CURE), and accepted again once a fresh hedge credential restored coverage. Nothing changed between the three calls except the evidence underneath them.
Overriding the covenant is governed too. The facility admin is a Privy 2-of-2 key quorum, fixed at creation, so a waiver needs two named approvers, and the wallet's policy only lets it call createWaiver on this vault on Arc.
Boundary: signatures authenticate who asserted what. They do not prove a hedge legally exists. The hedge feed in the demo is a labelled mock, and no bank has signed anything.
howItsMade:
Contracts are Solidity, built and tested with Foundry: FacilityRegistry, CredentialRegistry, CoverageEngine and CovenantVault, deployed to Arc Testnet (chain 5042002) and verified on Arcscan. The product is one small interface, ICoverageGate.assess(facilityId, amount). CoverageEngine implements it. CovenantVault is the reference host: every draw is ruled by assess and reverts with a typed reason when coverage is short.
The offchain side is TypeScript and viem, using arcTestnet from viem/chains. A credentials package builds and verifies the EIP-712 exposure and hedge credentials, and the registry only accepts a sequence number higher than the last one for that trade, so a stale credential cannot be replayed. A scenario runner drives the acceptance sequence against Arc and writes every hash, receipt and block reference to a JSON evidence file. A Vite dashboard reads the deployment manifest, simulates before any write, and explains a refusal in plain language.
Arc made us careful about money. USDC is the gas token with 18 decimals, while its ERC-20 view has 6: one balance, two views, 10^12 apart. Every amount crossing into a credential goes through a single decimals module. And cast send exits 0 even when the transaction reverts, so every step asserts its receipt status in the direction it expects: the refusal has to be a failed receipt carrying the DrawNotAllowed selector, not just any error.
Privy governs the override. A server wallet owned by a 2-of-2 key quorum is the facility admin, and each approver holds a non-extractable P-256 key in their browser. The hacky part: authorizing a Privy intent needed two fields the docs don't mention, intent_id and timestamp, signed over Privy's normalized request body (RFC 8785 canonical JSON, ECDSA P-256). Privy's managed broadcast isn't enabled for Arc on our app yet, so Privy signs the transaction and we broadcast it ourselves. The wallet policy restricts the key to createWaiver on this vault on Arc. It can't cap the waiver's uint32 duration, so the contract enforces that cap.
64 TypeScript and 31 Solidity tests run in CI. A local Anvil replay covers the states the testnet run doesn't reach: breach, cure expiry, and repayment during breach.

name: Riptide
description: An AMM that charges a volatility-indexed fee and auctions stale-price arb back to LPs.
projectDescription:
RIPTIDE — an AMM on 1inch Aqua + SwapVM that prices and reclaims the money LPs lose to arbitrage
The problem
A normal AMM quotes a price from its reserves and collects a swap fee. That quote lags the rest of the market. When ETH moves on a CEX, the pool still quotes the old price until someone trades against it. The trader who does that is usually an arbitrageur, and the profit comes from the LP.
This is called Loss-Versus-Rebalancing (LVR). Since 2022 there has been a closed-form expression for it. For a constant-product pool it is σ²/8 of pool value per unit time. At 100% annualised volatility that is one eighth of the pool per year, paid to arbitrageurs, before fees.
Two consequences:

A fixed fee does not match the cost. LVR scales with σ². A flat 30 bps overcharges on quiet days and undercharges on volatile ones.
The arb profit can be auctioned instead of left to the mempool. When the pool is stale, the size of that profit is known. Today it goes to whoever pays the highest priority fee. It can instead go to whoever pays the LP the most for the right to take the trade.

What RIPTIDE is
A RIPTIDE strategy is a constant-product pool (x · y = k) with two extra layers: a fee that moves with volatility, and an auction for the right to reprice the pool when it is stale. The curve itself is unchanged.
Mechanism 1 — a fee that tracks volatility. An on-chain controller reads a live volatility estimate and moves the fee toward the break-even point where expected fee revenue covers expected LVR: φ* = (σ̂²/8)/λ, clamped into the maker's [feeMin, feeMax] band, approached by a clamped PI controller with anti-windup. Higher volatility, higher fee; lower volatility, lower fee. To a trader this is an ordinary protocol fee. It is delivered through 1inch's existing fee instruction — no new fee opcode. SwapVM already staticcalls an IProtocolFeeProvider; RIPTIDE answers that call with a contract that reads an on-chain EWMA volatility estimate. Because it is a staticcall, the fee a quote shows and the fee a swap charges are the same number.
Mechanism 2 — a Dutch auction for the rebalance. When the external price moves, the strategy opens a declining-price auction for the right to rebalance the pool. Resolvers compete on time priority. On settlement the contract measures surplus S on-chain, pays the resolver ⌊(1−β)·S⌋, and leaves at least β·S with the LP. With β = 0.95, at most about 5% of the arb value leaves. A reverse swap immediately afterwards is penalised, so the rebalance cannot be sandwiched. If S is not positive the trade reverts, which also stops a resolver from filling at a loss.
The loop between them. A resolver only settles when the rebalance is profitable, so the price they pay is a traded price, not just an oracle print. That price is written into the volatility oracle and moves the next fee target. This is a design property, not a theorem.
The research this is built on
Nothing in the economics is invented. Three papers, all included in the GitHub Repo

arXiv:2208.06046 (Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden, Zhang) — the definition and closed form of LVR, and the identity that decides everything: LP value − rebalancing value = fees − accumulated LVR.
arXiv:2210.10601 ("Diamond", McMenamin, Daza, Mazorra) — the recapture result: auction the rebalancing right and retain β, and the LVR escaping to arbitrageurs is bounded by E[LVR] ≤ (1−β)·L. Their simulations use β = 0.95.
arXiv:2305.14604 (Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden) — the fee is the instrument that offsets LVR, with an interior optimum. We take the principle, not a closed-form constant.

EWMA/Garman–Klass volatility estimation and the PI controller come from outside that set and are labelled as engineering mechanics, not economic claims. Papers we deliberately did not use are listed with a written reason for each.
How it uses 1inch
This is built on Aqua and SwapVM, not merely alongside them.
Aqua is the custody layer. Makers keep tokens in their own wallets. Aqua holds an allowance record, not the money — so there is no vault to trust and no LP share token. RIPTIDE's routers are registered as Aqua apps that pull/push against a maker's ledger entry. No RIPTIDE contract ever holds inventory. All five Aqua primitives (ship/dock/pull/push/safeBalances) are load-bearing.
SwapVM is the execution layer. A strategy is a bytecode program. RIPTIDE emits two: a 41-byte swap program built entirely from upstream opcodes (Deadline → aquaDynamicProtocolFee → XYCSwap → Salt), and a 66-byte rebalance program that adds two RIPTIDE instructions — the declining-price schedule and the β-split. A 226-byte policy payload (fee band, auction policy, oracle config, salt) rides in the same order via the MakerTraits program slice, which is what lets a strategy's full policy be committed in Aqua's immutable strategy hash.
Everything compiles against [email protected] and [email protected] — the releases 1inch has actually deployed to mainnet, never main — and @1inch/aqua-sdk builds all Aqua calldata in production. We deploy two slimmed routers rather than the all-opcodes SwapVMRouter (which does not fit EIP-170) because RIPTIDE needs a custom instruction; the resulting swap program is still a plain Aqua-AMM program, and a fork test ships it to a stock, unmodified AquaSwapVMRouter and asserts it prices identically to ours, to the wei. Integration against the real 1inch mainnet Aqua registry is proven by a separate mainnet fork test.
Who gets what

Liquidity providers — tokens stay in your wallet; no vault, no LP token. Your fee rises when volatility rises, so you charge more precisely when you are losing more, and when the price gaps, most of the re-pricing profit comes back to you instead of going to a searcher. The dashboard shows the number that matters: cumulative value recaptured.
Traders — a quote that shows the applied fee and the σ that produced it, before you sign. Orders are split across makers by a solver and settle atomically: if any fill fails the whole route reverts and you keep your funds.
Resolvers / searchers — a legible source of flow instead of a mempool race. See open auctions with their live declining price, preview your exact take ⌊(1−β)·S⌋ before committing, and settle through a permissionless entry point from any wallet.
Analysts — every headline number links to the on-chain event that produced it, with the indexed block stated and an honesty panel marking which claims are verified on-chain versus validated by simulation.

What is actually deployed
Fourteen contracts live on Base Sepolia with three seeded strategies running different fee bands and β values (0.90 / 0.95 / 0.97), a six-page web app (one per persona: explainer, maker studio, swap terminal, resolver board, positions, analytics), a subgraph on Graph Studio indexing six contracts into thirteen entities, and four off-chain services (solver API, resolver bot, volatility indexer, and an MCP server exposing executable-liquidity tools).
The off-chain layer is untrusted and replaceable — none of it signs for a user, and none of it can move maker inventory, settle a loss-making rebalance, or make the settled fee differ from the quoted fee. The contracts recompute everything.
How we verified it
120 Solidity test functions across 45 files. Five named protocol invariants, each shipping a negative control — a deliberately broken variant that must make the test fail, so a green suite is evidence the tests can fail. Plus 10 fuzz tests at 10,000 runs, 12 differential tests against a committed Python oracle, atomic-rollback and reentrancy tests, and fork tests against the canonical 1inch mainnet Aqua deployment.
On top of that, a scripted end-to-end run against the live deployed app — it generates two wallets, funds them from the faucet, and walks every persona (ship → swap exact-in → swap exact-out → skew the oracle → preview → settle → dock → read analytics) through the same HTTP endpoints the browser uses. Nothing pre-approved, no fixtures. The most recent run: 20 transactions, 41/41 assertions, every hash linked to BaseScan in docs/E2E_RUN.md. in our Github repo. It observed σ move from 0 to 0.1124 after a settlement, with the fee target shifting to 15954 against a reported 10892 — the loop closing, measured rather than asserted.
howItsMade:
RIPTIDE is a constant-product AMM that runs as SwapVM programs over 1inch Aqua. The curve is ordinary x · y = k. Around it sit two control layers: a fee that tracks realized volatility, and an auction that sells the right to reprice a stale pool and keeps most of the surplus with the maker.
The repo is a pnpm monorepo. Contracts are Foundry (Solidity 0.8.30, via_ir, 700 optimizer runs, Cancun — the same settings as pinned SwapVM, because opcode-table layout is build-dependent). Everything else is all-ESM TypeScript. The subgraph is AssemblyScript. The app is Next.js 15. Python is used only as an independent math oracle.
Aqua holds allowance records. Maker tokens stay in maker wallets until a trade pulls them. Two slim SwapVM routers execute the programs — one for taker swaps, one for rebalances. Behind them sit a volatility oracle, a fee provider the VM staticcalls mid-swap, and a stateless kernel that does the surplus and β split. Periphery is a quoter that prices through the real VM, a lens, a permissionless auction settler, and a batch executor for atomic multi-maker routes. Off-chain (solver, resolver bot, vol indexer, MCP server, subgraph, web app) is untrusted: none of it signs for a user, and none of it can move maker inventory, settle a loss-making rebalance, or make the settled fee differ from the quoted fee. The contracts recompute from live state.
We compile against SwapVM v1.0.2 and Aqua v1.0.0 — the releases 1inch has actually deployed, never main. GitHub main has a different fee-provider signature that does not exist in any published release; we implement the v1.0.2 one, getFeeBpsAndRecipient → (uint32, address), which Fee.sol decodes as exactly 64 bytes. @1inch/aqua-sdk 0.3.4 builds all ship/dock calldata in production. @1inch/swap-vm-sdk is installed and unused. OpenZeppelin 5.4.0 and Solady 0.1.26 (ln/exp/pow/sqrt, wrapped with explicit domains) fill the rest. 1inch has no Aqua on Base Sepolia, so the demo deploys an unmodified official Aqua v1.0.0 instance; integration against the real registry is a mainnet fork test that ships WETH/USDC into the canonical Aqua address.
Aqua
Aqua is a shared-liquidity registry. A maker approves it once and distributes virtual balances across strategies. RIPTIDE's routers register as Aqua apps, which is what lets them pull and push against a maker's ledger.
ship is called from the maker's own wallet — no RIPTIDE contract ever calls it — and commits strategyHash = keccak256(abi.encode(order)). safeBalances is read on every quote and every swap; SwapVM seeds balanceIn/balanceOut from it before running the program, never from a cache or an indexer. pull sends swap output to the taker, the β rebate to whoever is settling a rebalance, and the protocol fee (that last one pulled by SwapVM itself). push credits taker input into the maker's strategy. dock cancels and releases balances.
There is no RIPTIDE vault and no LP share token. The same tokens can back several strategies at once because Aqua distributes allowance, not capital. A docked strategy cannot execute even if router runtime is stale. Fee collection on the swap path is best-effort by upstream design: SwapVM wraps the fee pull and emits a skip rather than reverting, so a one-sided maker position stays tradable.
SwapVM
A strategy is a bytecode program: [opcode:1][argsLength:1][args:N]. RIPTIDE emits two. Mechanism 1 uses only upstream opcodes. Mechanism 2 adds two RIPTIDE instructions. Reserves are not loaded by a balance opcode — the Aqua trait makes the router seed registers from safeBalances before runLoop. Emitting DynamicBalances would overwrite those Aqua-seeded registers, so it is absent.
Aqua stores no policy, and neither does either router. The full policy has to be immutable at ship time, so it goes in the order: order.data = [226-byte payload][program bytes], order.traits = (1 << 254) | (226 << 208). Bit 254 tells SwapVM to authorise via Aqua and seed from safeBalances. 226 << 208 writes the program start into MakerTraits slice index 3 (bits 208–223), so the VM sees data[226:] and never the payload. On-chain resolution honours this packing; the SwapVM SDK normalises it away. Re-encoding a live order through that SDK returns 224 bytes instead of 448, drops the payload, and orphans the Aqua position — which is why order construction stays with our codec. The Aqua SDK produced byte-identical calldata to what we had hand-rolled, so it replaced that code. The SDK's ESM build is also broken (a deep import with no exports map), so it cannot be imported from this workspace anyway.
Because the Aqua trait is set, SwapVM's order hash is the same value Aqua computes as strategyHash. Any change to payload, program, or auction start is a different Aqua position. The payload is packed big-endian, magic RPT1: tokens, salt, reserve snapshots, fee band, PI gains, auction parameters, oracle config, fee-provider address. maker is deliberately not in it. Decoding is never authorisation — every runtime path re-reads live Aqua balances. The codec exists in Solidity, TypeScript, and Python, held identical by committed vectors.
Four identifiers are never interchangeable: policyHash = keccak256(payload), strategyHash = keccak256(abi.encode(order)), strategyKey = keccak256(abi.encode(maker, salt)), and marketId of the ordered pair. Aqua events speak in hashes; router and fee-provider events speak in keys. The subgraph is what reconciles them.
SwapVM dispatches on an index into a function-pointer array. Aqua's opcode set builds a fixed array and converts it to a dynamic one by writing the length into slot 0 with assembly, which overwrites element 0. Every runtime index is therefore one less than its source position — XYCSwap dispatches at 17, not 18. A test resolves the indices from the live table so a silent upstream renumber fails the build instead of swapping in the wrong instruction. We do not repeat that assembly write when extending the table; we allocate a new array and append at 34–37. Opcode 37 (OraclePriceAdjuster) is reserved and unused: it rewrites swap amounts toward a Chainlink price, which would fight Mechanism 1 rather than observe volatility.
1inch's all-opcodes router does not fit EIP-170, and the stock Aqua AMM router has no slot for a custom instruction. We deploy two slimmed routers on the same SwapVM base, each with a reduced opcode table at the canonical Aqua indices. Mechanism 2 is further split into a router and a module. The swap router is 24,548 bytes against the 24,576-byte cap — 28 bytes of headroom, asserted in CI. To check it is still a real Aqua AMM program, the Mechanism 1 program is shipped to a stock unmodified AquaSwapVMRouter and asserted to price identically, to the wei.
Mechanism 1
The swap program is 41 bytes: Deadline → aquaDynamicProtocolFee → XYCSwap → Salt. Every opcode is upstream. The dynamic fee needed no new opcode — SwapVM already staticcalls a provider; we answer with a contract that returns a committed, volatility-indexed rate.
The fee instruction wraps the rest: save amountIn, subtract the fee, run the swap and salt on the net input, restore, then try to pull the fee. Volatility is estimated on-chain (EWMA of log returns, optional Garman–Klass range term, clamped, stale-frozen). Only the rebalance router and a governed indexer key may observe; quoting is static and writes nothing. The controller targets φ* = (σ²/8)/λ, clamps into the maker's [feeMin, feeMax], and steps with a PI loop and anti-windup. The maker sets the band and the gains, not the fee.
The provider is view and returns the already committed feeReported. The controller advances only after a swap or a rebalance, so within a block the quoted fee and the charged fee are the same number. RIPTIDE denominates fees at 1e7 = 100%; SwapVM v1.0.2 uses 1e9. We initially returned the wrong scale, so the VM charged 100× too little, silently, with every test still green because they shared the bug. The conversion now lives at the one provider return (×100). Setting the scale back to 1 breaks five tests.
Mechanism 2
The rebalance program is 66 bytes: Deadline, then a declining-price instruction that scales balanceIn by decay^(now − start), then wrapping Decay (anti-sandwich), XYCSwap, the custom rebalance instruction, and Salt. Deadline is first so an expired auction reverts before any balance is touched.
SwapVM's DutchAuction lives in the limit-order opcode group, not the AMM group. Rather than borrow across that boundary, the schedule is a RIPTIDE instruction that only scales a reserve register. XYCSwap still prices from the constant-product curve. Shrinking balanceIn reduces what the resolver must pay over time, so surplus decays toward zero and they race to be first at a still-profitable price.
On settlement the module decodes (beta, staleInWad) from 24 bytes of args, takes the rebate recipient from the VM taker (not from the args), measures S = executedIn − staleIn, reverts if negative, and pays ⌊(1−β)·S⌋ via Aqua pull. The retained remainder stays in the maker's Aqua balance. The split also runs in static context, so a quote of a loss-making rebalance reverts the same way settlement would. The price written back to the oracle is the auction-clearing price, which moves σ and therefore the next fee target. That loop is a design property, not a theorem.
The rebate recipient used to be encoded in the program args. The program is part of order.data, which is part of the strategy hash, so an address in the args pinned the order to one resolver. On a live deployment only the pre-designated wallet could settle, which also breaks the auction: a monopolist waits until the price decays to wherever their margin is fattest. Args are now beta ‖ staleInWad, and the recipient is ctx.query.taker. That immediately showed a second bug: the settler is the VM taker, so the bought base landed on the settler and was never forwarded. It now sweeps both legs — unspent quote plus rebate, and the base — back to msg.sender. Anyone can call it; protection is the surplus check, not an allow-list.
RebalanceSettled names the VM taker, which on this path is the settler contract. AuctionSettled names msg.sender. The subgraph joins them in the same transaction so attribution is per wallet rather than one contract address forever.
Math
WAD fixed point, explicit rounding, revert on zero denominator or overflow. amountIn ceils, amountOut floors, the β rebate floors — all three favour the maker. SwapVM registers are output-per-input; the UI shows quote-per-base; conversion happens only at the market boundary.
The Graph
RIPTIDE is single-maker micro-pools: each maker ships their own strategy, and there is no on-chain registry to enumerate them. Aqua is keyed by hash and exposes balance getters only. So the taker path is discover off-chain, verify on-chain. The subgraph answers what exists; the contracts re-derive every number that matters. A stale snapshot can make a route revert. It cannot authorise a bad fill. It also gives the time series (fees vs σ, recapture vs payout) that an RPC node does not.
Six datasources, including 1inch Aqua. Lifecycle and inventory are Aqua's Shipped/Docked/Pushed/Pulled, filtered to the RIPTIDE app. The rest are our router, fee provider, batch executor, rebalance router, and settler. A fill on our router resolving to a strategy created by an Aqua Shipped is a cross-contract join, which is why this is one subgraph.
The load-bearing field is orderBytes. Policy lives only in the 226-byte payload inside the Aqua order. Aqua has no getter for it; neither router stores it. The only place those bytes appear is Aqua's Shipped event. The mapping keeps them; the solver decodes them and rebuilds a priceable strategy. Without that field, anything a real maker ships through the UI is invisible to takers. No RPC call recovers it.
Aqua events carry strategyHash; our events carry strategyKey. A secondary index maps key → strategy. The fee-provider handler returns early when the index is missing rather than inventing a dangling row. For settlement, the rebalance handler writes a join keyed by txHash-strategyKey; the later AuctionSettled in the same transaction rewrites settledBy and rolls amounts into a per-wallet Resolver aggregate. That is why the Rebalance entity cannot be immutable.
Every quote carries subgraph lag (_meta.block vs chain head). The UI shows the indexed block and a stale badge. If no subgraph is configured, reads fall back to getLogs from the deploy block: the app still works, but maker-shipped strategies stop being routable, freshness becomes unknown, and aggregates are rescanned on every request.
Off-chain and the app
The solver discovers candidates, draft-optimises, refreshes live Aqua balances over RPC, re-optimises, stamps each fill with a version token, builds orders, eth_call-simulates the whole batch, and returns unsigned calldata targeting the batch executor only. Simulation is the gate. It originally priced against reserves committed in the order bytes — those are the strategy's initial inventory, frozen for the life of the order — while the VM prices against live Aqua balances. Multi-fill routes overshot slippage and reverted. It now prices against live balances; quoted output matches realised output to the wei.
The resolver bot previews on-chain and settles when the rebate clears a threshold; the no-surplus guard is the real protection. The vol indexer pushes prices and computes no volatility — EWMA and clamps are on-chain. The MCP server exposes executable size (quoter as ground truth) and recapture stats.
The web app is Next.js 15, viem/wagmi, Reown AppKit. Six routes (landing, make, swap, resolve, positions, analytics). The browser holds no RPC secrets; addresses come from one deployment manifest, and CI fails on hardcoded ones. Writes are server-built transaction plans walked by a stepper, so approve-then-execute is one click. Quotes show the fee and the σ that produced it. There is no in-place strategy edit: change means dock and ship a new salt.
Verification
A Python Decimal oracle (120 digits, no Solidity imports) emits committed JSON vectors. Solidity and TypeScript consume the same files. 120 test functions; five named invariants each with a negative control so a green suite is evidence the tests can fail. Fork tests cover the canonical 1inch Aqua registry, the stock AquaSwapVMRouter, and permissionless settlement. A live-app script walks every persona through the same HTTP endpoints the browser uses: 20 transactions, 41/41 assertions. After one settlement σ moved from 0 to 0.1124 and the fee target shifted with it.
Base Sepolia, deployed at block 46742718, with a Graph Studio subgraph and the web app on Railway building from committed ABIs (no Foundry in the container).

name: Zuno.fun
description: A community-governed launchpad that recycles liquidity from inactive tokens into active projects.
projectDescription:
ZUNO is a liquidity-recycling token launchpad on Arc Testnet. Creators launch tokens on a bonding curve; traders buy and sell until the graduation target is hit. Instead of burning LP forever, ZUNO locks LP in a vault when the token lists on Uniswap V2 so liquidity stays recoverable.
If a graduated pool goes quiet, ActivityMonitor flags it as inactive. The community can then propose healthier listed tokens, stake USDC to vote, and execute a recycle: dead LP is removed and redeployed into the winning pool, then locked again.
The app covers the full loop Explore, Launch, Trade, Lifecycle (list / vote / recycle), charts, and recent trades with native USDC gas on Arc.
howItsMade:
Contracts (Solidity + Hardhat): Core bonding curve (Core, BondingCurveFactory), local Uniswap V2 stack, DexRouter, LPRecyclingVault, ActivityMonitor, and RecyclingGovernor. Deployed stepwise on Arc (chain id 5042002) after a one-shot deployer hit Arc’s initcode size limit a practical hack we worked around with scripted multi-step deploys and wiring.
Indexing: A The Graph Studio subgraph on arc-testnet indexes Create / Buy / Sell / Listing / Swap into tokens, trades, and 1m candles for Explore, charts, and trade feeds.
Frontend: Next.js + wagmi / ethers / Privy for wallet + Arc network. Token lists prefer subgraph → Mongo → short RPC lookback so the UI stays snappy. Mongo stores lifecycle state (phase, progress, vault, proposals); post-trade soft-refresh updates mcap, progress, chart, and trades.

name: PrivyShild
description: AI-powered DeFi agent with Privy-secured wallets and policy guardrails
projectDescription: PrivyShield AI is an autonomous DeFi agent designed to let users perform on-chain actions while keeping wallet operations within strict security boundaries. The project combines Privy Server Wallets and the Privy Policy Engine with an AI agent, allowing the agent to execute approved DeFi actions while enforcing transaction limits, destination restrictions, and chain restrictions. It also includes a Red-Team simulator that demonstrates how a malicious transaction can be rejected by the policy layer
howItsMade: PrivyShield AI was built with Next.js 14, React, TypeScript, Solidity, and Base Sepolia. Privy is the core of the wallet and security layer: we use Privy Server Wallets for programmatic transaction signing, Privy Policy Engine to enforce spending and destination rules, and Privy Embedded Auth for user authentication. The AI agent uses a tool-based execution flow to understand user intents and prepare blockchain actions. Viem and ethers.js handle EVM interactions, while our AgentVault smart contract manages the on-chain DeFi logic. We also built a Red-Team simulator to demonstrate how the policy layer blocks unauthorized transactions

name: Gifty
description: Give a friend ETH and an ENS name with one link. Privy signup faster than fintechs, 0 crypto jargon.
projectDescription:
Gifty is a social wallet for sending ETH to people who do not have a wallet yet. You lock some ETH into a gift, get a link, and send that link the way you already talk to them. They open it, sign in with Privy (email or Google), pick a free username, and claim the money. After that, friends send to eg. "vitalik" (vitalik.gifty.eth), not a hex address.
The gift is ETH behind a secret. Signup always includes a free ENS subname on gifty.eth (vitalik resolves to vitalik.gifty.eth). Full names like vitalik.eth still resolve through ENS. Raw 0x addresses still work.
Money lives on Base. Usernames live on Sepolia, because ENS v2 beta is Sepolia-only. The app never asks the user to switch networks. We sponsor Sepolia gas for every username so a new account can get a name before it holds any ETH.
Once you are in: live Privy onramp from fiat into Base USDC, live Privy swaps, balances, contacts after someone claims your gift, and more gift links. The spend card is in the dashboard; the full issuing flow is mocked because we do not have KYB and Bridge fully set up on Privy yet.
Claims are on-chain. The contract stores a hash - Poseidon(code), not the code, and a browser PLONK proof authorizes release. If the claimant has no Base ETH, the operator pays gas and takes a small fee from the gift. If they already have gas, they claim with no fee and pay the tx themselves, seamless, easy.
Login, a real ENS name, money in, money out, and a way to pull the next person in, without teaching anyone a seed phrase.
howItsMade:
Production Next.js app (Bun) with Privy for auth and embedded self-custodial wallets, including Google OAuth. Privy wallets stay on Base. Fiat top-ups use Privy’s live useAddFunds onramp. Swaps are live Privy swaps into Base ETH or USDC. Card UI talks to Privy cards and stops at a demo path; live issuing needs KYB we do not have.
ENS v2 on Sepolia: parent gifty.eth, plus GiftyRegistrar on the ENSv2 UserRegistry and Permissioned Resolver. Register is free and one username per wallet. An operator key always submits the Sepolia tx (/api/operator/register) so the user’s Base wallet never needs Sepolia ETH. No-dot labels resolve as label.gifty.eth. Dotted names go through the Sepolia Universal Resolver.
Gifts on Base: GiftyClaimer stores Poseidon(code) and the locked ETH. The secret is packed into two BN254 limbs. Circom circuit gifty_claim Poseidon-hashes those limbs, range-checks the claimant to 160 bits, and exposes codeHash and claimant as public signals so a proof for address A cannot be replayed for address B. Prove in the browser with snarkjs PLONK. Verify on-chain with the snarkjs EVM verifier (GiftyVerifier). Sender always pays createGift. Claim is either claim() (user pays gas, fee 0) or operator claimFor() (sponsored gas, small operatorFee capped at 0.00075 ETH). The app picks based on whether the wallet can cover the tx.
The awkward bit we leaned into: two chains, one session. Alchemy RPCs are proxied server-side. Operator routes exist only for register and sponsored claim. code → amount is not trusted to our database.

name: Ladder
description: CEX-style WETH/USDC grid on 1inch Aqua + SwapVM. Custom opcodes; rungs re-arm in-wallet.
projectDescription:
Ladder is a CEX-style grid we shipped as maker liquidity on official 1inch Aqua. The pair is WETH/USDC on Base. You approve Aqua once; the tokens never leave the wallet. We did not redeploy Aqua - that registry is 1inch's. What we built is LadderRouter (SwapVM pointed at that Aqua), GridManager to ship discrete rungs, and LadderLens so the UI can tell which rungs would actually quote. A rung is a price, not a curve. When a bid fills, Aqua push() flips inventory and the ask on that same rung is live with no extra maker transaction. WalletGuard caps each quote to a live share of the real wallet at quote time. CoverageGuard stops the quote if coverage is below the maker's floor. Both sides have already filled on Base through LadderRouter.swap.
Here is the contract - https://basescan.org/address/0xD810CD7E5Aa03848596a86277fffc6a50DA1121b
howItsMade:
Contracts are Foundry, Solidity 0.8.30. We left official 1inch Aqua in place and subclassed 1inch SwapVM as LadderRouter.
LadderOpcodes extends AquaOpcodes so 1inch's stock instructions still run; we added five of our own, then fall through to theirs.
OracleEnvelope reads Chainlink ETH/USD. WalletGuard, CoverageGuard, RungQuote, and ProtocolFee sit in the same table.
GridManager builds every rung as one program - envelope, WalletGuard WETH, WalletGuard USDC, CoverageGuard, fee, RungQuote, salt and ships it through Aqua.
Takers call LadderRouter.swap.
The UI is Next.js, viem, wagmi, and RainbowKit. A small TypeScript resolver quotes those rungs and hedges leftovers through the 1inch Swap API.
https://basescan.org/address/0xD810CD7E5Aa03848596a86277fffc6a50DA1121b

name: Vaultara
description: Private file storage with onchain, revocable ENS sharing and live access logs.
projectDescription:
Vaultara is a privacy-first decentralized drive: each file is encrypted in the browser before its ciphertext is stored on IPFS. File ownership and every sharing decision live in a Base Sepolia smart contract, giving users a verifiable audit trail rather than trusting a storage provider.
Owners share files to an ENS name or address through a revocable onchain grant. Recipients see the file in Shared with me and can decrypt it; owners can revoke future access and both sides see the change in a live access log indexed by The Graph. Privy provides email/social onboarding with an embedded self-custodial wallet.
Vaultara is a testnet hackathon reference implementation. Revocation prevents future access but cannot revoke a file someone has already downloaded; device-to-device owner key sync and key-layer revocation are future work.
howItsMade:
Vaultara is a monorepo with a Next.js frontend, a Foundry Solidity contract, and a The Graph subgraph. The DriveRegistry contract on Base Sepolia records file ownership plus grant and revoke events; it never stores plaintext or holds funds. The Graph indexes those events for the UI's live, two-sided access log.
In the browser, WebCrypto encrypts each file with AES-GCM before upload. Only ciphertext is pinned to IPFS through Pinata. File keys are wrapped for recipients with a secp256k1 ECIES envelope using @noble tooling; an owner derives their deterministic key from a wallet signature. ENS resolves human-readable recipients and reverse-resolves them in the interface. Privy supplies embedded wallets with an injected-wallet fallback.
The project includes Foundry tests for the contract and Vitest coverage for crypto and sharing helpers. The deployed Base Sepolia contract is verified, and the hosted Vercel app uses security headers plus server-side upload controls.

name: AgentDock
description: Policy controlled AI agents that buy risk data without exposing keys or private policy.
projectDescription:
AgentDock is a policy-controlled workflow platform for organizations that want AI agents to purchase specialist services and produce recommendations without receiving unrestricted credentials, treasury access, or private policy data.
Its first workflow is a private treasury-risk assessment: a delegated agent discovers and pays for an independent risk report, evaluates it against an organization’s confidential risk policy, and produces a minimal verifiable receipt. The project combines scoped, expiring agent identity, metered service payments, confidential policy evaluation, and auditable workflow events. The goal is to make AI agents useful in high-trust financial workflows while preserving human control, revocation, spending bounds, and privacy.
howItsMade: AgentDock is built as a TypeScript pnpm/Turborepo monorepo with a Next.js/React dashboard, a Fastify workflow orchestrator, and a separate Fastify x402-gated Risk API. ENSv2 on Sepolia provides organization, agent, and service identities with scoped capabilities, expiry, and revocation. The agent uses Hedera x402 to obtain a paid risk report without receiving unrestricted treasury authority. A Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow evaluates the paid report against private organizational thresholds inside handlerInTee, returning only a decision and decision hash. The orchestrator persists immutable, idempotent workflow events and writes a minimal Sepolia receipt containing hashes, ENS references, payment reference, CRE decision, status, and timestamp. The dashboard supports onboarding, workflow creation, live event inspection, evidence links, approval/rejection, and agent revocation. Private keys, policy inputs, and service credentials remain outside the agent context and source repository

name: Harness
description: Every AI agent gets a container with limits your Ledger sets and ssh to it by its ENS name.
projectDescription:
Harness gives every AI agent its own machine, its own name, and a spending limit it cannot go past.
Right now, giving an agent money means giving it a key. Once it has the key, it can spend everything, and the only thing stopping it is the agent's own judgement. We think that is backwards.
With Harness you tap your Ledger once. That creates a container for the agent, mints it an ENS name like runner.acme.harness.eth, and writes a daily spending limit on chain. The agent gets a shell, tools, and whatever credentials you sealed for it.
Inside its limit the agent acts on its own, with no approvals and no waiting. Past that, a human has to sign. There is no server deciding any of this. The contract enforces it.
The name is real ENS, so you just ssh to it. No wallet, no plugin, no copied IP address. The same name that resolves for DNS is the one sshd checks your key against.
Revoking is one transaction. The name stops resolving, the shell stops opening, and the money stops moving, all at once, because all three were reading the same record the whole time.
howItsMade:
Ledger Key Ring, on a machine with no USB port
The host is a VPS. There is no device attached to it and there never will be, so the ring has to be joined over the network without a key ever crossing it.
The host generates its own member keypair and keeps it. The browser opens a relay session and does nothing but forward bytes between the Ledger over WebHID and the ring flow running on the host. It never holds a key and never sees one. One confirmation on the device admits the host as a member of the tenant's ring.
Once that is done we write the trustchain and the member credentials into wallet-cli's state directory, so wallet-cli ring encrypt and ring decrypt work on the VM from then on with no device present. That is how the ring ends up usable directly inside the machine.
We use it to hold the agent's credentials. Model keys and service tokens are sealed under the tenant's ring and sit on disk as ciphertext. They are opened at container start, in memory, and only if the chain still says the agent is live. A revoked agent does not get them back the next time it starts. The agent never sees a private key at any point.
The fiddly part was the transport. LKRP's SDK speaks hw-transport-webhid and the Device Management Kit speaks its own, and only one of them can hold the HID handle at a time. So a session is something we open, use, and explicitly release, and the device is passed back and forth between the two as the flow moves from Ledger Sync to the Ethereum app. WebHID permission is per origin and per device and it persists, so the handover is invisible to the person holding the Ledger.
The Ledger signs a grant that says what the agent may spend and over what period. Inside that permission the agent acts on its own, whether that is an x402 call or any other transaction. Anything outside it is pushed back to the Ledger for the person to sign, so they stay in the loop for what they did not already allow. The registry enforces it by measuring the tenant's balance before and after the batch and reverting if the difference is over the allowance.
Payments use EIP-3009 out of the tenant's account, the one the Ledger controls. We use @x402/express and @x402/core, so none of the payment code is ours and it works with any x402 seller.
EIP-7702
Setting up a machine needs four transactions. We batch them with 7702 so it is one confirmation on the device instead of four.
ENS
We deployed our own registry on the ENSv2 Sepolia contracts, using PermissionedRegistry and EnhancedAccessControl. Each tenant's registry roots its own subtree. harness.eth holds acme.harness.eth, and acme's registry holds runner.acme.harness.eth. EAC is what stops one tenant writing into another's subtree, and it is also why the agent cannot rewrite its own records, so it cannot change the key or the fingerprint it is admitted by. None of that is us checking it in application code.
AgentResolver answers for those names. It resolves the machine's address, the agent's key, and the ssh host key fingerprint, computed from the grant when you ask rather than written in as separate records.
Both are fine to have in public. An ssh host key fingerprint is meant to be published, which is what GitHub does with theirs. The address is a Tailscale mesh address, so it only means anything to a device already in the tailnet.
We run a nameserver in front of it that answers .eth over DNS. That is what makes ssh runner.acme.harness.eth work with no wallet and no plugin. On the machine, sshd's AuthorizedKeysCommand asks ENS whether the key being offered is allowed in, and known_hosts comes from the same name.
Revoking is one transaction. It unregisters the name, so resolution, ssh access and spending all stop together.
