name: Carrentic
description: Own a share of a real car as an ERC-3643 token on Hedera, and earn its rent on-chain.
projectDescription:
A car is one of the most expensive things a person ever buys, and it sits
parked most of the time. Ownership is all-or-nothing: you can't buy a slice of
a car you like, and you can't earn from a car you don't fully own. The rent a
vehicle could generate goes entirely to whoever holds the title, and there's no
simple, compliant way to split that asset — and its income — across several
people.
Carrentic turns a real car into shares. The car becomes an ERC-3643 security
token on Hedera: people buy a share, the car is rented out, and the rent flows
back to every owner on-chain, pro-rata to what they hold. An AI fleet manager
watches the car, explains how it's performing, and drafts the on-chain actions —
paying out this month's rent, marking the car's value — while the car's worth
and the rent owners receive are priced against a live market through the Uniswap
stack rather than a hard-coded number. Tokenizing a car is a single click: no
wallet, the platform signs as the issuer the way a real securities issuer does,
and every step settles on Hedera testnet with a verifiable receipt on HashScan.
You can watch the whole loop end to end. Tokenize a car and one click deploys a
real ERC-3643 token and mints its 1,000 ownership shares to the treasury. Open
the fleet to see that live token, its co-owners and their pro-rata positions,
and the car's value marked through Uniswap. Then ask the AI fleet manager to pay
out the rent, and it drafts the on-chain payout for the owners. Every figure on
the dashboard — the car's worth, the treasury, the rent — is read live, and the
tokenization itself is a genuine on-chain transaction you can open on HashScan.
howItsMade:
Carrentic is one pnpm monorepo (turbo), with a Next.js app in apps/web and the
chain, pricing, and agent logic split into packages (hedera, uniswap, agent,
fund). Data flows one way: a car is tokenized on Hedera, its value and rent are
priced through Uniswap, and an OpenAI agent reasons over the result and drafts
the next on-chain action. The 3D fleet is react-three-fiber with real GLTF car
models, and the whole app deploys as a single project on Vercel.
Hedera is the core, and roughly eighty percent of the build. A car is issued as
an ERC-3643 security token through the Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS) — the
same factory/resolver ATS uses — and the entire deploy-and-mint chain runs
server-side, operator-signed, over the Hashio JSON-RPC relay with ethers v6:
deploy the token, grant the KYC / issuer / SSI-manager roles, register the
issuer, grant KYC to the treasury, and issue the 1,000 shares. There is no
wallet in the flow — the platform signs as the issuer, which is how a real
issuer actually works — and every transaction is verifiable on HashScan
(example car token: 0.0.10478278 on testnet).
Uniswap is the pricing layer. The car's NAV and the rent owners are paid are
computed through the Uniswap Trading API (computeNav, priceUsd, and a
quoteRentPayout that quotes a WETH-to-USDC rent swap), so the value on the
dashboard and the rent a co-owner receives are marked to live market prices
instead of a fixed figure. Treasury holdings are valued the same way, live per
request.
OpenAI is the fleet manager. A LangChain agent (gpt-4o-mini, behind a
provider-agnostic model layer) sits beside the dashboard: it reads the car's
position, answers questions about value, owners and rent, and drafts the on-
chain actions — the rent payout, the valuation — for the owner to approve.
Two things fought back along the way. The ATS deploy kept reverting with no logs
until we stopped feeding it Hedera "long-zero" addresses (toSolidityAddress) and
switched to the canonical EVM addresses from the mirror node — after that the
deploy and mint went through on the first try; and the factory also rejects an
ISIN with a bad check digit (WrongISINChecksum), so the demo uses a
checksum-valid ISIN. We also pivoted the tokenization off the browser
MetaMask/WalletConnect ATS SDK — which needs a human to sign every step — to the
server-side operator-signed flow above, which is what makes "tokenize a car" one
click. Finally, react-three-fiber wouldn't render inside the app's async-streamed
page (the Canvas got starved of its render loop), so the 3D car runs in an
isolated /showcase route embedded as a transparent iframe.
Across the sponsors it is one product. For Hedera (Tokenization of Anything), a
real-world asset — a car — becomes a compliant ERC-3643 token via ATS, deployed
and minted server-side and verifiable on HashScan. For Uniswap (Best Uniswap
Stack Contribution), the car's value and the rent paid to owners are priced live
through the Uniswap Trading API, with developer notes in FEEDBACK.md. And OpenAI
is the fleet manager that reads the car and drafts the on-chain actions owners
act on.

name: PayPilot
description: PayPilot — B2B treasury: invoice emails in, quorum-approved payouts onchain, bank-grade controls.
projectDescription:
PayPilot is a B2B treasury and payout platform built on Base, where companies run payroll, vendor and bounty payments from multi-signature organization wallets. Anyone can sign in with Privy and self-serve create their own organization with named wallets (Treasury, Payroll, Bug Bounty Rewards, Ops) — each wallet carries its own onchain policy: a vendor address allowlist plus a per-transaction spending cap that Privy enforces inside the signing enclave, not in our app code.
The core workflow is a real dual-control loop: a vendor simply emails an invoice (e.g. "Please pay 0xAbC… 0.02 USDC") to our receiving address — a Resend webhook parses the recipient and amount, checks the vendor against the allowlist, and creates a payout request backed by a Privy intent on the org wallet. The request needs quorum approval: an authorized team member clicks Approve, and the app's quorum signing key submits a real ECDSA authorization signature to Privy — when the threshold is met, Privy broadcasts the transfer onchain and the payout flips to Executed with the transaction hash.
On top of that, PayPilot ships: role-based access (Owner, Treasurer, Finance Officer, Viewer), amount-tiered approvals (small payouts route to a single-approver Ops wallet, larger ones require the full quorum threshold), pre-generated employee wallets by email, scheduled recurring payments, and balance-condition automations. It's a finance team's controls — allowlist, caps, quorum, roles — running onchain instead of in a bank's database.
Stack: Next.js, MongoDB, Privy (auth, organizations, wallets, key quorums, policies, intents, authorization signatures), Resend for the email pipeline, deployed on Vercel and live on Base Sepolia testnet.
howItsMade:
PayPilot is a Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind) app deployed on Vercel, with MongoDB Atlas as a pure UI-state mirror — deliberately. Every money-critical operation runs through Privy: @privy-io/node drives organizations, wallets, key quorums, policies, condition sets and intents server-side, while @privy-io/react-auth handles embedded email auth in the browser. The architecture's core principle: authority lives in Privy, never in our database. Even a fully compromised app server can't move funds — quorum thresholds, policy gates and intent execution all live in Privy's enclave.
The genuinely hacky/notable bits:

Amount-tiered approvals done wallet-level. A quorum has exactly one threshold, so instead of bolting logic on top, each org runs two quorums: a main quorum (owner-settable 1-of-N…N-of-N) governing Treasury etc., and a single-signer ops quorum governing an Ops wallet whose Privy policy cap equals the org's amount tier. Payouts ≤ $300 auto-route to Ops; bigger ones need the full quorum. The tier is enforced at signature time by the policy, not just by routing logic.
Governance that can't change itself solo. Once the main threshold is ≥2, adding a signer or changing the threshold is itself an async Privy intent that the quorum must approve — the same signing pipeline as payouts.
Vendors as condition sets. Onboarding a vendor adds their address to a Privy condition set that every wallet policy references — allowlists enforced in the enclave. (We store both checksummed and lowercase forms after discovering calldata comparisons are case-sensitive.)
Pregenerated employee wallets. Inviting by email creates the employee's Privy user + embedded wallet up front, so it's waiting the moment they first log in.
Email-triggered payouts with policy replies. Resend webhooks carry metadata only, so we fetch the full email body via resend.emails.receiving.get, regex-parse the invoice, create the payout, and reply to the vendor — "received, pending approval" or "blocked by policy" for a spoofed address. The fraud-beat plays out in email, fully automated.
Automation with human rules. Scheduled sends (daily/weekly/monthly) and balance-condition rules (sweep excess, notify on thresholds) fire through the same pipeline as manual requests — policy gates apply to automation exactly as they apply to humans, and a policy failure pauses the automation with an audit trail.
Sponsored gas everywhere — org wallets never hold ETH, every transfer is Privy-sponsored.

Partner technologies: Privy (the entire security story), Resend (inbound invoice inbox + outbound approval emails), Vercel (deploy + cron), MongoDB Atlas (org-scoped app state), viem (calldata encoding, balance reads).
The build also taught us the hard way: Privy's env vars are newline-sensitive, its intent members report user IDs without the did:privy: prefix, and its webhook secrets are base64 — all three are now documented in the repo and handled.

name: rehold
description: REHOLD is a repoplatform which lets institutions post bonds as collateral for short-term cash loans
projectDescription:
REHOLD is a repo-financing platform built on Hedera, on top of the Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS). It lets institutions post tokenised treasury bonds as collateral for short-term cash loans — with pricing, margin monitoring, and liquidation all running as smart contract logic instead of manual back-office reconciliation.
The name comes from the core technical insight the platform is built around: collateral is never moved into a separate custody wallet, it is placed on Hold — locked in place under ATS's own native escrow primitive, in the investor's own compliant identity, until it's released or executed.
The Problem
Institutional finance runs on repo. Every day, trillions of dollars change hands in short-term loans secured by high-quality collateral — mostly government treasuries — because it's one of the safest, most liquid ways for cash-rich institutions to earn a return and for asset-rich institutions to access cash without selling what they own.
But the mechanics behind that trade haven't caught up with what's possible today.
A repo trade has two "legs": the cash leg (money moving from lender to borrower) and the collateral leg (the bond moving from borrower to lender, as security). The cash leg is often fast — but the collateral leg still runs on a parallel paper-and-legal process: custody agreements, manual valuation checks, phone calls and faxes to confirm a margin call, and overnight batch reconciliation to make sure both sides agree on who holds what. It's slow, it's manual, and it's opaque outside of the two counterparties involved.
Tokenising the collateral changes what's possible. If the treasury itself is a compliant, programmable token, the collateral leg can become a provable, automatic, on-chain state change — the same trade, but the slow half disappears.
What REHOLD Does
REHOLD is a full repo desk for tokenised treasuries:
Issuers create tokenised, KYC-gated treasury bonds through ATS, with real lifecycle features — coupons, maturity, redemption.
Investors buy those bonds, then pledge them into REHOLD as collateral to raise cash without selling — the token gets locked in place, not moved to some separate custody wallet, so their compliance status and ownership record never leave their own identity.
Lenders supply the actual cash liquidity that funds these trades, earning a return for taking on well-collateralized credit risk — the same economic role played by money-market funds and cash desks in the real $4-trillion-a-day repo market.
A live price oracle continuously values the pledged collateral. If its value falls too far relative to the loan, the system automatically issues a margin call, and — if unaddressed — force-liquidates just enough collateral through REHOLD's own secondary market to restore safety, without anyone needing to notice, call, or intervene manually.
At the end of the trade, either the borrower repays and gets their bond back, or — if they don't — a Hedera Scheduled Transaction fires automatically at maturity to settle the position, redeeming the bond at face value from the issuer rather than dumping it into a possibly depressed market.
Every transfer anywhere in this flow — issuance, trading, pledging, liquidation, redemption — passes through ATS's own compliance machinery: KYC verification, freeze/blacklist enforcement, and pausability. None of it is bypassed or reimplemented;
REHOLD is built to work with ATS's compliance layer, not around it.
howItsMade:
REHOLD is a repo desk that sits next to a live Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio bond. This repo is the cash/risk layer: Solidity on Hedera testnet (chain 296) plus a Vite desk..
Stack. Solidity 0.8.28 (Hardhat, OpenZeppelin, Hedera HTS precompiles). Four contracts: BondPriceOracle, RepoVault, SecondaryMarket, MarginEngine. Cash is Circle testnet USDC (HTS). UI is Vite + React + wagmi/viem against Hashio; MetaMask. Event tape comes from the Hedera Mirror Node. A Node keeper heartbeats NAV. Market view uses lightweight-charts.
Architecture. Two layers, one chain. ATS owns the bond: KYC, allowlist, coupons, Hold, maturity redeem. ReHold never copies that. The vault is bond-agnostic: it takes a diamond address, looks up a per-bond NAV oracle, and lends from one USDC pool.
The trade is a Hold, not a transfer. The investor authorizeOperators the vault. originateRepo locks units in place under their identity (createHoldFromByPartition), then sends USDC. Title never leaves them, so coupons still accrue. Repay pulls principal + fee, releaseHoldByPartition, done. Term is on the vault (termEnd), not hold expiry.
Risk is a separate contract. MarginEngine.evaluate is permissionless: mark collateral with the 8-decimal NAV, then healthy (≥110%), issueMarginCall (102–110%), or liquidatePartial (<102%). Liquidation executes the hold, ships bonds to SecondaryMarket.sellOnBehalf, and sells only enough to restore 110%. Peer trades use the same book; ATS compliance still reverts ineligible transfers.
ow it is pieced together. The investor stays the bond holder. RepoVault.originateRepo calls ATS createHoldFromByPartition as an operator, then wires USDC from the lender pool. Repay calls releaseHoldByPartition. If NAV falls under 102%, MarginEngine.evaluate (permissionless) executes the hold and SecondaryMarket.sellOnBehalf sells just enough to restore 110%. ATS still owns KYC, control list, freeze, coupons, and fullRedeemAtMaturity. We only vendor ABI shims that match the diamond’s selectors.
Partners that actually matter. Hedera gives HTS (bond + USDC), HIP-719 association, and cheap marks. ATS Hold is the whole product: collateral locks in the investor’s identity instead of moving to a vault. Circle USDC is the cash leg. HashScan is the explorer we verify against.
The hacky bits, all real: ATS rejects hold expiry 0 (WrongExpirationTimestamp), so we set expirationTimestamp = type(uint256).max and enforce term on the vault, not the hold — otherwise borrowers could reclaim via reclaimHoldByPartition. Creating a hold also burns ERC-20 allowance to the vault, so the desk has a separate Approve Vault step. HTS needs HIP-719 associate() on every EOA before approve/transferFrom; contracts associate in the constructor. Hashio wraps ATS AccountIsBlocked as RPC 0x128, so the UI pattern-matches both. Liquidation has no bid book — we scan asks and treat the seller as the cash-paying counterparty (demo-scale, O(n)). The NAV oracle is a single updater with a 30% circuit breaker; the keeper re-pushes the same price every 5 minutes just to refresh updatedAt. After every vault/market redeploy we must allowlist and KYC those contract addresses on the bond, same as people.

name: Horizon
description: A prediction market humans and AI agents pay to ask: curve orders, shared USDC liquidity, no fees.
projectDescription: Every AI model is trained on the past; the data that matters most is about the future, and nobody has it yet. Prediction markets are where people put real money on what happens next. Horizon is a binary prediction market on Ethereum Sepolia built so that a person or an AI agent can ask the world any question and pay for the answer. Creation is a paid service over Hedera x402; a verified World credential tells humans and agents apart, at half price; 1inch Aqua puts real USDC behind every quote, with one balance shared across markets; executable pricing curves let people and agents rest orders that reprice themselves; The Graph and Substreams keep the page true to the chain; and Hedera Consensus Service records the whole creation flow. The rest of this description is how each of those works. Makers publish executable pricing curves instead of resting single-price orders. A curve is a start price, an end price and a size; the chain evaluates it on every fill, so a BUY curve declines as the maker accumulates and a SELL curve rises as inventory leaves. Equal endpoints are just a fixed-price limit order. Fills are partial, exactly accounted, and cancellable at any time. One USDC balance backs quotes in every market at once. Maker funds sit in the wallet and are drawn through 1inch Aqua only at fill time, so a small maker can express views across several markets without pre-funding each one. Within a market, an on-chain per-market budget stops a maker's resting orders from ever committing more than the wallet can currently spend. Markets bootstrap themselves: a YES buyer paying 0.60 USDC and a NO buyer paying 0.40 USDC mint a fully backed pair in one transaction. Nobody has to seed inventory. An off-chain allocator picks up to four fills across direct and complementary legs, and RouteExecutor settles the whole route atomically or reverts it. Stale state, drained balances and slippage produce a clean rejection, never a partial trade. Trading carries no fee of any kind: no maker, taker, routing or protocol fee. The only charge is market creation, offered as a paid service to people and agents alike. A drafting step grounded on live indexed markets from The Graph proposes the question, outcomes, close time and resolution rules and warns about duplicates by market id; the requester approves a hash of the draft before anything is charged. Payment runs over Hedera x402, settled through Blocky402, and is resumable: a retried request never charges twice and never creates two markets. A verified World credential halves the price, at most once per credential per day. Every approved draft, settled payment and deployed market is then stated on a Hedera Consensus Service topic, in order, with a consensus timestamp anyone can read back from a mirror node. Markets, curves, fills, routes, collateral and resolutions are indexed by a Subgraph, mirrored into PostgreSQL for fast reads, and overlaid by a Substreams-fed live layer so a fill or a new market shows up in the open browser tab seconds after its block, before the indexer has it. Several binary markets can be grouped as an event under one review and one payment, optionally importing definitions (question, outcomes, criteria, dates; never prices or liquidity) from a Polymarket page. After close, a disclosed resolver submits YES, NO or INVALID once, with an on-chain evidence reference. Winning tokens redeem 1 USDC; INVALID pays 0.50 per token. Resolution and creation authority are deliberately centralized and stated in the UI; neither role can spend from a user wallet, withdraw collateral or mint unbacked outcomes. Demonstrated live: an atomic two-curve route on Sepolia and its indexed result, an agent completing a paid creation end to end (1 HBAR on Hedera testnet, then a market on Sepolia, then indexed by The Graph), a human verified through World Selfie Check paying the discounted 0.5 HBAR, and the creation audit trail on HCS topic 0.0.10473191 (62 statements at submission) verified byte for byte against the mirror node.
howItsMade: Contracts (Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry, Cancun). Horizon extends the pinned, unmodified official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM sources; all 329 vendored files are hashed in vendor-lock.json and re-verified in CI. HorizonSwapVM overrides SwapVM's _runOpcode hook to add two application-local instructions in the reserved opcode range, 0xf0 (fixed-price BUY) and 0xf1 (curve). Each reconstructs and hashes the maker's canonical Aqua order against the MarketRegistry, refuses any order the router has not admitted, prices it (the curve through CurveMath: an exact rational integral of p(x) = start + (end - start) * x^alpha, alpha in {1,2,3}, BUY rounds down, SELL rounds up) and tracks filled shares. RouteExecutor performs up to four fills per transaction with a spend limit, a deadline and full rollback; for complementary legs it escrows 1 USDC per pair into BinaryMarket inside SwapVM's pre-transfer-in callback and mints YES to one side and NO to the other. OrderBudget is a ledger the router deploys and owns. The Foundry suite is 54 tests including three fuzz properties, and an Anvil test cross-checks 44 contract vs. TypeScript curve results. Backend (Node 24, TypeScript, Express, Prisma, PostgreSQL 18, pg-boss). The API returns prepared unsigned transactions only; the worker is the sole process holding a key, for createMarket and resolve. Every quote re-reads balances, allowances, fill counters and market status over RPC at a single block, rejects an indexed snapshot more than 64 blocks behind or on a reorged hash, and simulates the full route before returning calldata. AdminJS sits on top for record inspection. Drafting goes through a MarketDraftProvider interface with an Anthropic-backed provider and a deterministic development provider; both read the same live Graph data. The Graph. A Subgraph in Studio (horizon/0.3.2) indexes markets, curves, fills, routes, collateral and resolution, and validates Aqua Shipped bytes against the deployed router rather than trusting them. On top of that a Substreams package (horizon_events, Rust compiled to WASM) extracts the same events per block for a stream consumer that writes a live overlay into Postgres, one block per transaction with the cursor included, and wakes the API through pg_notify. The API exposes a POST /api/live SSE endpoint with Last-Event-ID replay, and reads apply only live changes whose block is newer than the snapshot's, so a lagging sweep can neither hide a market nor duplicate a fill. BlockUndoSignal handling marks trades reverted rather than deleting them. Hedera. Creation is an x402 v2 resource: the server answers 402 with scheme exact, network hedera:testnet, a per-request nonce and the facilitator's advertised fee payer (read from Blocky402's /supported endpoint, never assumed); the signed payload is checked field by field against what was issued before the facilitator is contacted. Browser payers sign over Hedera WalletConnect, agents with their own key. Audit statements (horizon.audit.v1) are written to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the workflow transition, then published to an HCS topic by the worker in sequence, so Hedera being unreachable can never cause a second payment or deployment. Unknown outcomes are reconciled against the mirror node by event id before any resubmission. World. IDKit Selfie Check verifies server-side and lowers the 402 amount from 1 to 0.5 HBAR, once per credential per UTC day; the server re-checks action, environment and signal_hash against the request id before contacting World, and stores only the nullifier. Sandbox access arrived late in the hackathon; a credential has since been verified in Sandbox against the production deployment and a creation was then paid at the discounted price over Hedera x402. Frontend. React 19, Vite, viem, @x402/hedera, served by the API process. Deploys on Railway as three processes (API, worker, stream consumer) and one database. Hacky bits worth mentioning. Aqua's ship has no application callback, so publication is two transactions, Aqua.ship then HorizonSwapVM.admitCurve, and the router refuses to fill anything it has not admitted; a strategy shipped straight to Aqua is inert and filtered from discovery. Aqua's default dispatcher does not enable LimitSwap, so the probe harness overrides _runOpcode to permit it. Idempotency on the paid path comes from deriving creationId = keccak256("horizon-creation:" + requestId) and checking marketByCreationId before every broadcast. INVALID payouts of half a base unit are carried per holder in invalidRemainder so combining or splitting claims never changes total payout.

name: ArcFlow
description: Cross-chain intent protocol — interact with Arc DeFi from any EVM chain, no bridging needed.
projectDescription:
ArcFlow is a cross-chain intent forwarding protocol that lets users interact with Arc-native DeFi applications directly from any supported EVM chain — Somnia, Base Sepolia, Monad Testnet — without bridging or switching networks.
Users sign a single transaction on their preferred source chain. ArcGateway emits an intent event, a permissioned relayer picks it up and executes it on Arc Testnet via ArcExecutor, which maps each external wallet to a Universal Arc Account. The result is seamless cross-chain DeFi: one wallet, any chain, instant execution.
The primary feature is an Arc-native Stablecoin Vault — users can deposit, withdraw, and harvest yield on Arc USDC through intents submitted from any supported source chain. Counter and Todo demos are included as live testable examples of the intent pipeline in action.
howItsMade:
ArcFlow is built on a three-layer architecture: source chain contracts, an off-chain relayer, and Arc Testnet execution contracts.
On the source side, ArcGateway.sol (deployed on Somnia, Base Sepolia, and Monad Testnet) accepts user-signed intent transactions and emits IntentForwarded events with nonce-based replay protection. No state is stored — it's a pure event emitter.
The relayer is a TypeScript/Node.js service that polls source chains for events, validates intent targets against an allowlist, and submits execution transactions to Arc Testnet via ArcExecutor.sol. It handles retries, duplicate protection, health reporting, and writes intent history to a JSON endpoint consumed by the frontend.
On Arc, ArcExecutor.sol verifies relayer authorization, maps each external wallet address to a deterministic Universal Arc Account, and calls the target contract — Vault, Counter, or Todo — with a try/catch wrapper so failures are handled gracefully.
The frontend is built with Next.js 15, wagmi v2, RainbowKit, and TailwindCSS v4. Multi-source chain selection, intent submission, real-time status polling, and history are all handled through custom React hooks (useIntent, useVaultIntent, IntentFlowContext). The dark/lime RemitStar visual system is applied throughout.

name: flowfi.finance
description: FlowFi: an AI-powered DEX aggregator on Arc  swap, bridge, launch tokens in native USDC
projectDescription: FlowFi is a stablecoin interface on Circle's Arc Testnet (chain 5042002), with an AI Copilot reading live on-chain data across Portfolio, Dashboard, and Analytics views. Gas and balances are both USDC: native units are 18 decimals, the ERC-20 contract (0x3600...) is 6 decimals — one asset, two interfaces, handled explicitly in code. What works today: browser wallet or Circle Developer-Controlled Wallet (no seed phrase); USDC/EURC swap; USDC bridging Sepolia↔Arc via Circle's CCTP V2 (burn, attestation, mint); curated liquidity pools; an ERC-20 launch tool with permanent-liquidity locking. FlowFi does not custody funds or market-make: on testnet, thin pools are flagged rather than quoted as live prices. After Arc mainnet, the same UI is meant to route swaps through real external liquidity (Uniswap, LI.FI) and earn an interface fee, not hold reserves itself.
howItsMade:
Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, viem. Wallets are EIP-1193 in the browser, or Circle Developer-Controlled Wallets through a backend so the seed never sits in the client. Same-origin proxies sit in front of Arc RPC and Arcscan because public eth_getLogs and explorer rate limits fail under load.
Contracts: Solidity 0.8.19 factory + constant-product pool, shipped in several testnet revisions as bugs showed up. One revision called addLiquidity with a deadline on a v2 pool that had no deadline and the tx reverted. Later pools pull both tokens with SafeERC20, record reserve deltas from balanceOf, and (in the newest code) match Uniswap-style amountAMin / amountBMin so a skewed deposit is not silently donated. Pause, where it exists, is queued for two days; unpause is immediate. None of this is audited; it stays testnet infrastructure
Integrations that actually move value: Circle CCTP V2 (burn on Sepolia, attest, mint on Arc) and Circle wallets. USDC on Arc is one balance, two interfaces — eth_getBalance / gas at 18 decimals, ERC-20 0x3600… transfer / approve at 6. We hardcode 6 on the ERC-20 path instead of trusting decimals() on that precompile.
What we refused to ship as product: quoting a residual pool (cents of USDC/EURC) as a live FX price. A constant-product pool only knows its reserve ratio. FlowFi is an interface; after Arc public mainnet the same screen is meant to route to an external venue and take a fee, not to market-make.

name: Proctor
description: An AI agent stops mid-payment and pays a live, verified human for permission to continue
projectDescription:
Proctor is a human-oversight gate for AI agents, built on x402. When an autonomous agent is about to take a consequential action (releasing funds, executing a trade, anything past a policy threshold) it stops on an HTTP 402 instead of proceeding. The agent then pays a small fee to ask a real, live human for permission to continue.
That human is a witness, deliberately distinct from the agent's operator. The witness answers on their own phone through a single-use link, proves liveness with World ID's Selfie Check (bound to that one decision via a signed nonce, so the proof can't be replayed elsewhere), and approves or refuses within a short deadline. No answer before the deadline is a hard refusal, not a default approval, the system fails closed.
Every decision produces an attestation written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic with no admin key, so the record can't be edited or deleted after the fact, by us or anyone else. The attestation states exactly how the human was authenticated and whether their independence from the operator is cryptographically provable or only policy-asserted, so a third party auditing the log doesn't have to take our word for it. Anyone can verify the evidence directly on HashScan.
The gate itself is x402-native: agents pay per-interrupt to escalate, then pay again per-second of actual human review time on release, settled over Hedera and Circle Gateway rails. Proctor ships as an installable MCP server (proctor-mcp on npm and in the official MCP Registry), so any MCP-capable agent, Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or a custom client, can add real human-in-the-loop oversight with one command, without building the escalation, identity-proofing, or evidence-logging infrastructure itself.
howItsMade:
Backend
Bun and Fastify, with Prisma 7's new driver-adapter mode (@prisma/adapter-pg, no native query-engine binary, so the Docker image stays small and boots fast on Railway). The gate speaks x402 v2 (@x402/core, @x402/fastify, @x402/hedera) against the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet, with Circle Gateway (GatewayEvmScheme) as a second settlement rail and its own capability cache with retry/fallback so a facilitator outage degrades gracefully instead of failing every request. Every decision is a state machine (OPEN -> DISPATCHED -> APPROVED/REFUSED/EXPIRED) persisted in Postgres (Supabase), with a TTL sweeper that fails a decision closed the instant its deadline passes, evaluated inside the same SQL statement that performs the write so there's no check-then-act race window.
Identity and liveness
The witness proves they're a live, present human via World ID 4.0's Selfie Check, requested through IDKit and verified server-side with a signed RP (Relying Party) nonce minted fresh per decision and bound into the World signal, so a proof from one decision can never be replayed against another. Getting this genuinely working end-to-end meant independently re-implementing World's RP signature algorithm (secp256k1 + EIP-191, not ES256 as commonly assumed) to diagnose a stale signing key after a Portal key rotation, and excluding just @worldcoin/idkit-core (not its React wrapper) from Vite's dependency optimizer, since the wrapper's WASM binary was 404ing under default pre-bundling.
Evidence
Every resolved decision is attested to a Hedera Consensus Service topic created with no admin key, so nobody, including us, can alter or delete the log after the fact. The attestation body states plainly how the human was authenticated and whether their independence from the operator is cryptographic (a separate World ID nullifier scope) or only policy-asserted, so a skeptical third party can verify the actual guarantee on HashScan rather than trust the UI.
Frontend
TanStack Start (React 19, SSR), Tailwind 4, GSAP and Lenis for the landing page and floating glass-effect nav, and a live operator console that drives an on-camera countdown/meter over Server-Sent Events. That stream now has a polling fallback for resilience: a long-lived SSE connection is powerful for a live "on-camera" feel, but a production demo can't depend on one persistent connection behaving perfectly for its entire lifetime, so the same evidence record is also polled every two seconds as a safety net.
Distribution
proctor-mcp is published to npm and registered in the official MCP Registry (io.github.louissarvin/proctor), so any MCP-capable agent gets real human-in-the-loop oversight with one claude mcp add` command instead of building escalation, identity-proofing, and evidence-logging from scratch.
Notable hacky bits, honestly stated
The SSE stream writes straight to Fastify's raw response to control chunk timing precisely, which turned out to silently bypass @fastify/cors's header injection, fixed by reflecting Origin manually before the raw writeHead. And more than once during deployment, Railway's GitHub webhook went stale after a force-push and needed an empty commit to re-trigger a deploy; Supabase's free-tier pooler needed a project-level restart (paired with a Railway app restart, since a stale Prisma pool otherwise reuses dead sockets) after connection-heavy testing exhausted its pool. Neither is glamorous, but both are the kind of infrastructure reality a real deployment surfaces that a purely local demo never would.

name: arcsignal
description: AI-powered prediction markets with transparent signals, market consensus, and settlement evidence.
projectDescription: ArcSignal is an AI-powered prediction market platform where users can explore crypto and event-based markets, compare AI confidence against market consensus, and make more informed predictions. The project focuses on a proof-first experience: clear market rules, resolution sources, cutoff times, settlement status, transaction history, and transparent AI signal reasoning. Instead of only showing odds, ArcSignal gives users a structured intelligence layer around every market so they can understand why a prediction may be valuable, risky, or disputed.
howItsMade:
ArcSignal is built as a web application with a modern frontend for prediction market discovery, AI signal cards, market analytics, and user-facing settlement information. The frontend uses React/Next.js-style components, wallet-ready UX patterns, and a proof-first market interface. The AI layer is designed to compare agent confidence with market consensus and explain the reasoning behind predictions. The project also plans support for oracle-based resolution, settlement receipts, explorer links, and transparent market metadata so judges can clearly verify how each market moves from prediction to final outcome.
AI tools were used as development assistants for planning, UI copy, implementation guidance, and technical research, while the project direction, product decisions, integrations, and final submission are directed by the team.

name: proofads
description: Ad inventory as revocable ENSv2 rights. Pay only for delivery proven in a Chainlink enclave.
projectDescription:
ProofAds turns advertising inventory into a revocable ENSv2 rights hierarchy, and settles payment against delivery verified privately inside a Chainlink Confidential Workflow.
Two pieces of the ad supply chain are assertions nobody can enforce: who may sell a placement, and what was actually delivered. Today the first is ads.txt — a plaintext file, domain-wide, never checked at transaction time. The second is a number produced by the party who benefits from it being large, computed over data the buyer never sees. Publishing that data on-chain doesn't fix it; it publishes a viewing log. Delivery has to be verifiable without being public.
The ENS layer. Each ad slot is a name the publisher owns: hero.ads.proofads-pub.eth. AdInventoryRegistry extends ENSv2's real PermissionedRegistry, and the right to sell a slot is ROLE_SELL_SLOT — an application-defined Enhanced Access Control role in an unassigned nybble (1 << 40), living alongside ENS's own roles. The marketplace calls hasRoles() at listing and again at auction finalization, never a cached copy, so revocation takes effect on the next block. The payout address is registry.getOwner(labelhash), read live from ENS — a delegated agency can sell a slot but can never redirect the money.
The Chainlink layer. A browser SDK measures a view: ten seconds at ≥50% of the viewport, foregrounded, with the creative's bytes hashed against the creativeHash committed on-chain at bid time. Raw events are frozen into an immutable batch, then read inside an AWS Nitro enclave by a CRE Confidential Workflow (cre.handlerInTee). The enclave holds the collector's token, released by the Vault DON, and recomputes the batch digest to catch tampering. Five scalars leave — campaignId, cumulativeVerifiedUnits, batchDigest, windowStart, windowEnd — signed by the DON and delivered through the Keystone Forwarder. Session ids, visibility traces and per-view timestamps never cross the boundary.
Settlement is cumulative and idempotent: the workflow reads what the chain says is already paid rather than trusting the collector's arithmetic, and each batch digest applies once, so retries can never double-pay. Escrow is unitPrice × targetUnits USDC, released as delivery is verified, with the undelivered remainder refunded at close.
Live on Sepolia. Contracts deployed and verified; proofads-pub.eth registered on the ENSv2 beta with ads, hero and sidebar beneath it; an auction listed by a delegated agency, bid with escrowed USDC, measured in a real browser, and settled by the confidential workflow in tx 0x320ea411…36e29b — 20 raw events in, 1 verified unit out, 0.11 USDC paid to the publisher. The agency sold it; the publisher got paid.
howItsMade:
Contracts in Foundry/Solidity 0.8.30, built against ensdomains/contracts-v2 compiled from source — ENS is real here, not mocked, and the local test chain stands up the actual ENSv2 hierarchy. AdInventoryRegistry extends PermissionedRegistry, so authorization and the payout address both come from a registry we don't control: revocation is protocol-level, and we never had to build a permission system. ROLE_SELL_SLOT squats an unassigned Enhanced Access Control nybble (1<<40) beside ENS's own roles, and the marketplace re-reads hasRoles() at listing and again at finalization.
Chainlink CRE is what makes private verified delivery possible at all — without a TEE the raw measurement data would have to be either public or trusted. The workflow is TypeScript on bun, running under cre.handlerInTee in an AWS Nitro enclave: the Vault DON releases the collector's API token inside, DON consensus signs the aggregate, and the Keystone Forwarder delivers it on-chain.
Rest of the stack: Next.js 15 + wagmi/viem, a Fastify + Postgres measurement collector, browser SDK in TypeScript.
Hackiest bit: ENSv2 re-mints an ERC-1155 token id on every role change, so slot identity had to become keccak256(registry, labelhash) rather than the token id. Runner-up: our first real settlement was a transaction with status: success that paid nobody — the receiver ran out of gas inside Circle's USDC and the Forwarder swallowed the revert. Every local test was green; they all settle against a mock token.

name: Hark Protocol
description: An open intent layer for ads. Platforms publish intent. Agents pay to reach it on Hedera.
projectDescription: Hark Protocol is an open intent advertising protocol with on-chain machine payments on Hedera. Platforms such as search apps, social feeds, shopping apps, or AI assistants detect that a user has a temporary commercial interest, for example wanting a laptop, and publish that intent to Hark as a normalized, anonymous, short lived signal, without exposing the user's identity. Autonomous advertiser agents discover these anonymous opportunities, use an LLM to decide for themselves whether the opportunity is relevant to their campaign and budget, and if it is, pay Hark programmatically through the x402 protocol on Hedera testnet, settled via the Blocky402 facilitator, to earn the right to reach that user. The human never pays, and their identity, wallet address, and browsing history never leave the publisher. Hark's core paid endpoint, POST /v1/reach, is protected by x402. An unpaid request returns HTTP 402, the agent signs a real HBAR payment, and Blocky402 settles it on Hedera testnet, after which Hark queues the ad delivery for the publisher to show. Advertiser agents can see the publisher's identity, the placement, the topic, a sanitized summary, and the price, but never the user's name, email, IP address, or any stable cross platform identifier. Beyond the mandatory paid flow, the project also implements a publisher revenue share so publishers earn a portion of every payment, an HCS based audit trail for every settled payment, and HCS 14 based advertiser agent identity. Everything described here is live and deployed, not simulated. There is a published npm SDK and protocol package, a working web demo covering the publisher experience, an agent dashboard, and a system explorer, plus real, independently verifiable Hedera testnet transactions backing every claim.
howItsMade:
Stack

TypeScript monorepo using pnpm workspaces and ESM.
apps/api: Express, Zod, Drizzle ORM, PostgreSQL, deployed on Railway, database hosted on Neon.
apps/web: Next.js, Tailwind, shadcn/ui, deployed on Vercel. Covers the Demo Publisher screen, an Agent Dashboard, and a Hark Explorer.
agents/runner: a CLI advertiser agent (discover, score relevance, decide, pay).
Two published npm packages: @hark-protocol/protocol (shared Zod schemas and topic taxonomy) and @hark-protocol/sdk (publisher and advertiser clients).

Payments (the core of the project)

x402 protocol v2, using @x402/core, @x402/express, @x402/fetch, and @x402/hedera.
POST /v1/reach is protected by x402 on the API side. An unpaid request returns a real HTTP 402.
The agent side signs and retries automatically, paying in native HBAR.
Settlement runs through the Blocky402 facilitator against Hedera testnet.
Every settled transaction shown in the app and pitch deck is independently confirmed against the public Hedera testnet mirror node, not just Hark's own API response.

Why Blocky402 and Hedera mattered here

Blocky402 is the actual value add of the project. It lets an autonomous agent sign and settle a real payment inline in a single HTTP request response cycle, with no manual invoicing or offchain reconciliation.
Hedera testnet gives fast, cheap settlement, which fits a per-request micropayment model like this far better than a slower or more expensive chain would.

Relevance reasoning

Uses the Vercel AI SDK with an OpenAI model.
Wrapped behind a RelevanceScorer interface, with a deterministic fallback scorer, so the demo never silently breaks if a key is missing or a network call fails.
The LLM only recommends relevance. Budget and price limits are enforced entirely in code, never by the model.

name: Jenny Builds
description: AI agents pay only when answers pass a public deterministic check.
projectDescription:
Verity is a pay-per-correct-answer protocol for AI agents on Hedera. Existing x402 services settle as soon as a provider delivers a response, even when that response is wrong. Verity reverses the flow: the buyer receives the real response first, checks it against a versioned deterministic , and only then settles the signed payment through Blocky402.
The live reference market uses FX rates and entity resolution, where correctness has objective ground truth. When a buyer rejects an answer, Verity requires a bond and a verified human root. Independent checkers compare competing provider responses under a strict-majority rule. The result, content hashes, votes, bond resolution, and reputation evidence are anchored to Hedera through HCS and can be independently replayed.
Providers earn reliability standing, buyers earn honesty standing, and reputation follows durable human identity rather than disposable wallet addresses. The public demo is live on Hedera testnet.
howItsMade:
Verity was built from scratch as a TypeScript monorepo with independent HTTP provider processes, a deterministic buying agent, a Solidity bond escrow contract, and a two-entry-point SDK. Providers use the SDK to protect existing x402 handlers with a price and published verifier rule. The FX provider supports a real DEGRADE_MODE that returns an incorrect rate without using a mock, while the entity-resolution provider charges according to observed cached or fresh usage.
The payment path uses the Hedera SDK, Blocky402 x402 v2, runtime capability discovery, HCS settlement and dispute topics, Mirror Node verification, and Hedera testnet consensus. HCS receipts are compact and content-addressed so replay never stores response bodies on-chain. A separate Go checker provides an independently implemented adjudication vote. World ID verifies the human-root input, while ERC-8004 and Agent0 provide the portable identity and reputation model. The public explorer reads live hosted Graph data and exposes the real Hedera purchase flow.

name: Lute
description: Build, independently verify, and deploy AI-generated Graph infrastructure.
projectDescription:
Lute is an AI-native build, verification, and deployment layer for The Graph. It lets AI coding agents build Graph infrastructure, but it does not let those agents approve their own work.
AI can now generate Subgraphs, schemas, mappings, tests, and other indexing infrastructure in minutes. The problem is that code can compile, sync successfully, and answer GraphQL queries while still indexing the blockchain incorrectly. A mapping can silently miss an event, duplicate one, store the wrong value, or produce data that no longer matches what actually happened onchain.
Lute adds an independent verification step before deployment.
A developer can ask an agent to build a Subgraph, but before that candidate is allowed to ship, Lute independently reconstructs the blockchain facts it should represent from canonical chain data and compares those facts against the indexed output. The verifier is deliberately separated from the generated mapping logic, so a mistake in the code being tested cannot automatically reproduce itself inside the system judging it.
When Lute detects a disagreement, it does more than return a failed test. It identifies the first divergent block, transaction, log, event, field, and expected-versus-observed value. Deployment is immediately blocked.
That evidence can then be passed to a coding agent such as Claude Code or Codex to repair the candidate. The repaired candidate receives a new cryptographic hash and must pass the same independent verifier again before Lute allows it to deploy.
This creates a simple trust boundary:
The AI can build it. The AI cannot approve its own work.
Lute's first verification standard is an ERC-4626 Integrity Pack, which verifies observable vault activity such as Deposit and Withdraw events, assets, shares, ownership fields, event presence, duplicate records, and blockchain provenance. Integrity Packs are designed as reusable verification specifications so the same system can later support additional standards and protocols.
Lute also supports auditing compatible existing Graph deployments, not just projects originally generated through Lute. A supported Subgraph can be checked against historical blockchain evidence to determine whether its indexed representation agrees with the underlying chain.
The core lifecycle is:
BUILD → VERIFY → DEPLOY
If verification fails:
VERIFY → DIAGNOSE → REPAIR → REVERIFY → DEPLOY
And for deployed infrastructure, the same verification model can be reused to detect integrity drift over time.
Lute is ultimately building a trust layer between autonomous software and blockchain data infrastructure: AI remains responsible for generation and repair, while deterministic evidence decides what is safe to ship
howItsMade:
Lute is built around a deliberately separated verification architecture.
At the center is a deterministic verifier written in TypeScript. For EVM-based Subgraphs, Lute independently reads canonical blockchain events from the source chain using standard JSON-RPC calls such as eth_getLogs. Events are decoded from the contract ABI and normalized into canonical records containing information such as block number, transaction hash, log index, contract address, event type, and event parameters.
Separately, Lute queries the corresponding indexed data from The Graph through GraphQL. That data is normalized into a second representation.
These two paths are intentionally kept independent:
Blockchain → independent decoder → canonical facts
and
Subgraph mappings → indexed entities → GraphQL
A reconciliation engine then compares them.
For supported Integrity Packs, Lute can check whether expected events exist, whether records are missing or duplicated, whether indexed values match their onchain values, and whether transaction, block, contract, and log provenance agree.
When a mismatch appears, Lute searches for the earliest deterministic divergence instead of simply reporting that two totals differ. A failure can therefore be reduced to evidence such as:
block → transaction → log → decoded event → expected entity → indexed entity → failed check
That structured evidence is also what Lute provides to a coding agent during repair.
The first implementation uses an ERC-4626 Integrity Pack. The pack defines which Deposit and Withdraw properties can be independently reconstructed and verified. Lute explicitly distinguishes between claims it can verify, claims that are only conditionally verifiable, and properties it cannot independently prove. Unsupported properties are never silently converted into a successful result.
Every candidate also receives a deterministic cryptographic hash derived from its execution-relevant source. A Verification Run is bound to that hash. If the candidate changes after verification, the previous result becomes stale and the deployment gate rejects it. This prevents a dangerous workflow where one version is verified and a different version is deployed.
The deployment gate therefore checks both the verification result and candidate identity before permitting deployment to The Graph.
Lute also exposes its capabilities programmatically so coding agents can request actions such as auditing, verification, evidence retrieval, repair context, and deployment checks without gaining control over the actual verdict.
The Graph is the core infrastructure behind the project: Lute works around Subgraphs, GraphQL data, Graph deployment tooling, and reusable Graph data products. Where included, Substreams provide another independently implemented data-processing path that can be compared against both raw blockchain events and Subgraph output.
Hedera extends Lute into an agent-to-agent verification service: an external agent can pay for a verification job through an x402 flow, after which Lute performs the actual audit and returns the resulting evidence and verdict. Compact verification attestations can also be anchored through Hedera Consensus Service. Bazantic exposes Lute's API as reusable agent tooling and allows the verification step to participate in a Verify Before Trust Recipe, where another autonomous workflow can continue only if Lute's policy requirements are satisfied.
The result is not another AI-generated testing dashboard. Lute deliberately separates generation from approval: agents can write and repair infrastructure, but only independently reconstructed evidence can unlock deployment.

name: Reality Bridge
description: Privacy-preserving citizen data layer bridging recorded stats & lived reality using EAS & World ID.
projectDescription:
Socioeconomic circumstances can shift rapidly due to economic shocks, employment changes, or health events, but official welfare and statistical databases ("Recorded Reality") often take years to update. This creates a critical gap between recorded data and citizens' actual circumstances ("Lived Reality").
Reality Bridge is a privacy-preserving citizen data-quality layer that empowers citizens to report changes in their socioeconomic status and generate verifiable on-chain proof without exposing sensitive personal information.
Key Features & Workflow:

Unique Human Verification: Integrates World ID to prevent duplicate submissions while preserving participant anonymity.
Cryptographic Commitments: Sensitive household data remains strictly off-chain. A salted SHA-256 cryptographic commitment binds the submission on the client side, producing a downloadable JSON receipt.
On-Chain Attestation: Uses Ethereum Attestation Service (EAS) to log lightweight attestations containing only the commitment hash, schema version, region code, and a privacy-preserving "Reality Signal" (classified as LOW, MEDIUM, or HIGH severity based on directional indicators).
Public Observatory: Displays aggregated, real-time insights, category trends, and regional distributions without revealing individual household data.

By adhering to the principle: "We don't put citizens' data on-chain; we put proof that their voice was counted," Reality Bridge provides a verifiable, citizen-controlled bridge to improve public data quality and social safety net responsiveness.
howItsMade:
Reality Bridge was built using Next.js (App Router, React 19), Tailwind CSS, Wagmi/Viem, and Recharts, combined with privacy and Web3 primitives to create a secure citizen data layer.
Technologies & Partner Integration:


World ID Integration (@worldcoin/idkit):
Used for Sybil resistance and Proof of Personhood. World ID ensures each unique human can submit socioeconomic data signals without linking their on-chain wallet address to their real-world identity.


Ethereum Attestation Service (EAS):
On-chain attestations are generated using @ethereum-attestation-service/eas-sdk. The schema records non-sensitive metadata: the salted commitment hash, signal level (LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH), schema version, region code, and timestamp.


Client-Side Zero-Knowledge Privacy & Canonical Cryptography:
All sensitive responses remain strictly on the user's browser. We use the Web Crypto API (crypto.subtle) to canonicalize JSON payloads with sorted keys, append a 32-byte cryptographically secure random nonce, and generate a SHA-256 commitment hash. The raw data is saved directly to the user's device as a downloadable JSON receipt.


Viem-to-Ethers Adapter:
Because the EAS SDK expects an Ethers.js signer while Wagmi v3 uses Viem WalletClients, we built a lightweight client-side bridge (walletClientToSigner) that maps Viem transports directly to Ethers JsonRpcSigner interfaces without requiring a heavy full Ethers setup.


AI Agent Engineering with Matt Pocock Skills:
Development and codebase architecture were designed and refined using Matt Pocock's Agent Skills framework (mattpocock/skills). We leveraged TDD (Test-Driven Development with Vitest), domain-driven modeling, deep-module architecture, and strict TypeScript patterns to ensure rapid, clean, and verifiable implementation.


Dynamic Observatory & Heuristic Engine:
We designed an illustrative Weighted Severity Scoring algorithm across six weighted domains (employment=3, housing=2, health=1, etc.). The Observatory operates on a pre-seeded synthetic dataset of 2,500 records and dynamically injects new user attestations in real time using client-side immutable state reducers.

name: LATCH
description: Authorization and access control for AI workers inside organizations.
projectDescription:
LATCH is an authorization and access control system for AI workers inside organizations. It helps companies give AI agents specific jobs without giving them unlimited access to company tools and services.
Each AI worker gets its own verifiable identity and specific capabilities through ENSv2. For example, a Procurement Agent can handle purchase requests, while a Research Agent can search for information. One agent cannot simply use another agent’s permissions.
Before an AI worker can perform an action, LATCH checks who the agent is, whether it has the right capability, and whether the exact action follows the organization’s policy. Companies can use normal server side policies or Chainlink Confidential Workflows when sensitive rules, such as spending limits or approved vendors, need to remain private.
LATCH can also be used by other AI workflows. Through Bazantic, I created a reusable procurement Recipe that combines Exa for product sourcing with LATCH for authorization. LATCH also uses Tavily for authorized research tasks.
The main idea is simple: AI agents should be able to work for organizations, but only within the authority they have been given. Give AI workers a job, not the keys to everything.
howItsMade:
LATCH is built as an authorization layer that sits between an AI worker and the tools it wants to use. When a user gives an agent a task, Gemini first turns the request into one structured action. It can only choose from capabilities that LATCH supports, such as procurement.purchase or research.search. Gemini only understands and proposes the action; it never decides whether the action is allowed.
Each worker has an ENSv2 identity under its organization’s namespace. LATCH reads fresh ENS records to verify the worker’s wallet, role, status and capabilities before every protected action. This means permissions are tied to an onchain identity instead of only being stored in a normal application database, and an organization can revoke a worker’s authority.
After ENS verification, LATCH checks the exact proposed action against the organization’s policy. Organizations can use normal server side policies or Chainlink Confidential Workflows. With Chainlink, sensitive rules can be loaded and evaluated inside a TEE, while the agent only receives a simple approved or denied result instead of learning the private policy itself.
For execution, the Procurement Agent handles authorized product sourcing, while the Research Agent uses Tavily only after receiving the research.search authorization. I also exposed LATCH through a Bazantic Gateway and built a reusable procurement Recipe that combines Exa for real product sourcing with LATCH for authorization.
A key security detail is that LATCH binds authorization to the exact proposal. An agent cannot get one product, quantity or capability approved and then execute a different action with that approval.
The application is built with Next.js and TypeScript on the frontend, with a NestJS API and MongoDB for application data and audit records. Overall, ENSv2 handles worker identity and capabilities, Chainlink handles private policy evaluation, and LATCH connects those checks to external tools so an AI worker only gets the authority needed for its specific job.

name: fly402
description: An autonomous travel agent that watches flight fares and holds your seat while you sleep
projectDescription:
Web3 doesn't meet in one place. ETHGlobal, Devconnect, Token2049, EthCC — a different country every time, and if you build here you're on a plane six times a year. Every trip goes the same way: you know weeks ahead, you book days ahead. Not because you forgot — watching a fare is a job, and you already have one. By the time you open that tab the good flights are gone: the direct one, the sane hour, the price you saw first. You book when you're free, which is never when it's best.
What Fly402 does
Describe the trip once — where, when, your budget, and how much the agent may commit for you. Then close the tab.
The agent watches real fares. When one fits, it doesn't just tell you the good option exists —
it takes the seat off the market, then emails you. You open the link whenever you get to it.
The price is still there. The seat is still there. Confirm, or walk away.
What we actually built
A price hold today is free and therefore worthless, or it doesn't exist at all. Fly402 makes it a
real product: an option on a seat, with a price and a lifecycle.
One payment, two kinds of money. A small fee buys the time and is gone — that's what the seller
earns for pulling inventory. The ticket money goes into an escrow contract instead of the seller's
pocket, and leaves by exactly one of three doors: you book and it pays for the seat, you pass and
it comes back, you forget and it comes back anyway.
"We'll refund you" is a promise; a contract isn't. Once the hold expires, anyone can trigger the refund — the seller doesn't have to cooperate, or even be online. No owner, no pause button, nobody who can change the rules once your money is in. That's why a traveller will pay for a hold, and why a seller can finally charge for one.
Fly402 is an agent with its own wallet and a spending limit you set once. It pays for each search as it goes, and your money sits in a contract — the seller can't take it, and neither can the agent. The same pattern fits anything that sells out before you're ready to decide: hotels, conference tickets, limited drops.
howItsMade:
Fly402 is a React frontend, an Express 5 TypeScript seller, and a Solidity escrow on Hedera
testnet. Two endpoints are x402-gated: POST /holds and POST /booking, priced in HBAR and quoted in tinybars under the exact scheme on hedera:testnet. The seller registers ExactHederaSchemeon an x402ResourceServer pointed at the Blocky402 facilitator, so calling either endpoint without paying gets you a real 402 back.
The buyer is an agent running in the browser. It holds an ECDSA Hedera key, and
wrapFetchWithPayment does the rest — 402 → sign → retry, all inside one ordinary fetch. Booking a flight is a single function call. The payment is the transport.
The fun part is what a seat hold actually is. It's an option on a seat, so one atomic x402 payment
has to become two different kinds of money: a fee the seller keeps, and a deposit it is only
holding. The seller splits them on arrival and forwards the deposit into HoldEscrow.sol with a
ContractExecuteTransaction, keyed by a SHA-256 of the hold id so off-chain ids stay opaque
on-chain.

The escrow has no owner. No pause, no upgrade, no admin key. settle() works only for the payer, and only before expiry. After expiry, refund() is open to anyone — a seller that
disappears can't strand a traveller's deposit.
TVL is a chain read. The dashboard calls the contract's stats() instead of counting
locally, and every settlement and escrow call resolves to a real HashScan link.
The agent can't overspend. Auto-hold, max fee and max deposit are checked before a 402 is ever answered, so it runs unattended inside limits the traveller set once.
Real fares, not fixtures. Live Google Flights data via server-side SerpApi, cached 12h and
served stale if the upstream dies. Match emails go out through Resend and deep-link straight back into the booking page.

name: PayGate
description: Team payments with built-in approval rules, settled instantly in stablecoins.
projectDescription: PayGate is a treasury and spend-management tool for companies that pay  contractors, vendors and staff in stablecoins. Today most teams route every  payout through one person with wallet access — a bottleneck, a single point of  failure, and an approval trail that lives in email. PayGate replaces that  with a shared company treasury where every payment carries an enforced rule:  who can approve it, how many of them, and up to what amount.  A company signs up with an email and gets a Privy organization wallet as its  treasury — no seed phrase, no key for anyone to lose. Admins then define  approval groups, each backed by its own Privy key quorum and spending policy:  "Payroll — HR, one approval, up to 10,000 USDC", "Grants — the four-person  committee, two approvals, up to 50,000", "Vendors — finance, two approvals, no  ceiling". Groups attach to the treasury as scoped additional signers with  override_policy_ids, so Privy evaluates only the policy of whoever actually  signs. That's what lets one wallet enforce genuinely different limits per team  instead of needing a wallet per budget.  Any team member raises a payment — payee (an external address or a teammate by  name, resolved to their Privy embedded wallet), amount, asset and an attached  invoice. Before submitting they see exactly which rule will govern it and who  must approve. Payments under a group's threshold clear on the requester's own  signature; larger ones wait for a second approver. Approvals are signed in  each approver's browser with their own Privy key via  useAuthorizationSignature() — PayGate only relays the signature and never  holds signing material, so even a fully compromised backend cannot manufacture  an approval. Once enough signatures exist they're submitted together and  Privy verifies them against the treasury's key quorum before anything moves.  The treasury holds multiple assets — USDC, EURC, WETH and native ETH — with  per-asset balances and per-asset limits, handling both native value transfers  and ERC-20 calldata. Changing the rules is itself an approved action:  attaching a group is owner-level at Privy, so it requires the same sign-off as  a large payment. Everything lands in an audit trail recording who acted,  when, and the on-chain transaction, exportable to CSV with approvers included.  Settles in USDC on Base Sepolia. Live at usepaygate.xyz.
howItsMade: Stack: Next.js 16 (App Router) with React 19 and TypeScript, Tailwind 4,  Prisma 7 against Postgres (Neon, provisioned through Vercel), and viem 2 for  chain reads and calldata encoding. Privy via @privy-io/react-auth 3 in the  browser and @privy-io/node 0.34 on the server. Deployed on Vercel at  usepaygate.xyz, settling on Base Sepolia.  How the pieces fit. Org setup runs a fixed sequence against Privy: create  users → create key quorums → create a spending policy → create the  organization → create the treasury wallet with entity: {type: 'organization'}  and the member quorum as an additional_signer carrying override_policy_ids.  Approval groups are the same shape — each one is a quorum plus a policy,  attached as another scoped signer, which is what lets a single wallet enforce  different limits depending on who signs. Payments store the exact transaction  at submit time so every approver signs identical bytes; signatures are  collected and submitted together, comma-delimited in the  privy-authorization-signature header. Prisma holds what Privy doesn't know  about: invoices, memos, roles, group membership and the audit trail.  The notable hacky parts:  @privy-io/[email protected]'s public client is missing methods the docs show —  users.create, keyQuorums.create, and the entire organizations service exist  only on a private underlying client. I reach it through one narrow cast that  names exactly the surface used, typed with the SDK's own param types, so an  SDK change surfaces as a type error rather than at runtime.  I built the whole approval flow on Privy intents first, then had to tear it  out. intents.authorize() doesn't exist on either client — only the  IntentAuthorizeInput type ships — and the REST endpoint rejected signatures  built to the documented payload spec across eleven variants, including the  intent_id and timestamp fields that appear in the browser SDK's types but not  the server's. Separately, POST /v1/wallets/authenticate rejects valid Privy  access tokens on this app, so no server-side user signing key can be issued at  all. The way through was to sign in the browser with  useAuthorizationSignature() and have the server merely relay — which turned  out to be the better architecture, since PayGate then never touches signing  material.  additional_signers is replaced wholesale on a wallet update. Attaching a new  group by sending just that group would have silently detached every other one,  including the original member quorum and its capped policy — it would have  demoed perfectly and quietly broken every other rule. desiredSigners()  rebuilds the complete list every time.  Smaller things that mattered: invoice types are sniffed from magic bytes  rather than trusting Content-Type or the extension, and stored as Bytes in  Postgres because Vercel's filesystem is ephemeral. Money is integer base units  as BigInt everywhere with per-asset decimals — which caught a real bug where  the dashboard was adding micro-USDC to wei. Balances are cached server-side  for 10s after the public RPC started throttling under polling. Privy caps  display_name at 50 characters, which silently broke org creation for longer  names until I truncated.
