name: REPAYD
description: Deposit insurance for AI agent wallets . It pays you back when prompt injection slips through
projectDescription: REPAYD is deposit insurance for AI agent wallets: a protected account that holds suspicious transactions for two minutes while a sealed, tamper-proof verifier checks them against the owner's rules, blocks outright violations, cryptographically proves who actually issued each instruction (so no one can fake an attack to collect a payout), and — for whatever slips through, like a prompt-injection attack that tricks an agent into transferring funds — pays the owner back automatically in the same block, no claims process required; it prices each agent's coverage based on its real behavior over time so safer agents get cheaper every week, and sells the whole system as an API to the platforms launching AI agents, so that instead of competing with the firewalls and prevention tools already on the market, REPAYD sits behind all of them as the layer nothing else has: guaranteed recovery, the same force that scaled banks (deposit insurance), cars (liability insurance), and credit cards (chargebacks), now built for the agent economy.
howItsMade:
How we built REPAYD — the nitty-gritty
Stack. Solidity ^0.8.28 on Foundry (5 contracts: GuardAccount, PolicyRegistry, VerdictContract, MutualPool, Blocklist + a deploy-seeded USDCMock), a Bun workspaces monorepo (engine, sdk, api, demo, dashboard, pricing, record, hedera, subgraph) in strict TypeScript,
viem for all chain I/O, and a Next 16 + React 19 frontend (authored pages synced from the dashboard HTML, anime.js transitions, lenis scroll). 102 forge tests including 1000-run fuzz invariants; 200+ JS tests; CI runs contracts, tsc per-package, every runner, and both
subgraph builds.
How it's pieced together. The classification decision is deliberately tiny and on-chain: _classify() is a pure function of policy × transfer × daily-state — hard caps (per-tx/daily/velocity/blocklist) revert before broadcast, allowlist-absence/curfew/strikes route to a
funded hold with a releaseAt window, everything else executes instantly. Verdicts are EIP-712 signatures over a domain that embeds block.chainid + contract address + salt, so a signature can't be replayed on another deployment, and every verdict pins an exact
policyHash so it can't be replayed against a different rulebook. A covered verdict calls MutualPool in the same transaction as the payout. The off-chain half (pricing engine, alibi SDK) mirrors the on-chain logic function-for-function — same inputs, same verdict —
which is what makes the payout parametric rather than an opinion. The Risk Subgraph (38 events, 12 entities) is not decoration: the live AI pricing consumer queries the Studio endpoint and computes the premium multiplier (2.7×, $135/mo) from indexed
claims/attempted-breach data with zero hardcoded inputs.
Partner technologies. Arc made the demo moment possible — USDC-native gas and fast blocks meant "payout in the same block as the verdict" is a literal transaction, and gas-priced-in-USDC let us measure real deployment cost (~0.36 USDC per fresh stack). The Graph Studio
(free tier) gave us a public, standard-schema memory layer for ~$0. Hedera contributed the x402 machine-payment rail through the Blocky402 testnet facilitator — two real 0.001ℏ settled requests, HCS topic receipts, and a ScheduleCreate demoing recurring-premium draws.
Circle Agent Stack gave authenticated wallet-set/Gateway-balance reads across 12 domains. ERC-8004 canonical registries (agentId 894341) gave us a standards-compliant reputation mirror with fail-closed posting (frozen holds post nothing).
The hacky parts worth admitting.

Our own demo narrative lied to us: the "look-alike address one hex off Alice" was narrated as bypassing the firewall, but exact-match allowlisting means an off-by-one address is just a new recipient — held, not executed. We rewrote the beat as a labeled controlled
watcher false-negative (benign facts → score below threshold → signed clean release → verified real $150 out → then the covered verdict pays $135). A parametric product can't fake its own loss.
demo.ts called main() twice. Duplicate payroll spends blew the $1,000/day cap in ways we initially blamed on RPC races — the actual cause only surfaced when we ran a one-second dailyState monitor loop against the live chain.
Run integrity is now a server-owned RunManager: the child signs against its own fresh deployment, emits structured @@DEMO_TX@/@@DEMO_RESULT@ markers, and "Complete" requires verified receipts + balance-delta checks on all six story beats — exit code 0 alone fails
the run.
Crash-safety hack we're weirdly proud of: an OS-scoped SQLite BEGIN EXCLUSIVE connection held for process lifetime as the signing lock (the OS releases it even on SIGKILL; you must never unlink the lock inode — our first PID-file scheme had its own check-then-unlink
TOCTOU race), plus a Bun IPC channel where the worker exits on parent disconnect so a killed dashboard can never leave two processes spending the same funded testnet keys.
Honest labeling as architecture: every displayed fact is VERIFIED or COMPUTED, never INFERRED; the UI states "local demo signer (not a live TEE)" because the watcher key is scripted for the hackathon and CRE/TEE hosting is the documented production path; the Circle
endpoint refuses dashboard GETs with a 405 because the legacy route could provision/spend — you must POST an explicit confirmation.

name: Adaptive Hook AMM
description: Uniswap v4 dynamic-fee hook that neutralizes sandwich attacks & LVR via intra-block MEV dampening.
projectDescription:
AdaptiveVol AMM is a Uniswap v4 Hook that protects liquidity providers (LPs) from MEV bots and market volatility.
Normally, dynamic-fee pools only look at old price data. Because of this, MEV bots can easily predict the fees and run sandwich attacks, causing LPs to lose money (known as LVR).
Our hook solves this problem with two features:

Volatility Fees: We index swap history with The Graph and calculate market volatility using Chainlink Functions. The hook changes the fee tier (0.10%, 0.30%, or 1.00%) based on how calm or wild the market is.
MEV Defense: The hook checks the pool price at the start of each block. If a sudden intra-block price spike is detected during a sandwich attack, the fee immediately jumps to 5%. This makes the attack unprofitable for the bot while keeping regular gas costs very low (~16.7k gas).

We also created an interactive web interface where users can simulate swaps, test volatility changes, and see the MEV protection in action.
howItsMade:
We built this project using Solidity, Foundry, Uniswap v4, The Graph, and Chainlink Functions. Here is how the different parts work together:


Uniswap v4 Hook (Solidity & Foundry):
We developed a smart contract called AdaptiveFeeHook. Inside the beforeSwap function, the hook checks the swap price. It remembers the pool price at the start of each block. If a swap causes a sudden, abnormal price jump in the same block (which is how sandwich bots attack), the hook immediately increases the fee to 5%. This stops the bot from making any profit and protects regular traders and liquidity providers.


Indexing Swaps with The Graph:
We created a custom Subgraph in AssemblyScript. It listens to Uniswap v4 PoolManager events (Initialize and Swap) and stores recent pool prices and swap history in real-time.


Volatility Bridge with Chainlink Functions:
We wrote a JavaScript script that runs on Chainlink Functions. It fetches the recent swap history from our Subgraph, calculates the price volatility (standard deviation), and sends the result back onchain. The hook then adjusts the pool fee between Low (0.10%), Medium (0.30%), and High (1.00%). If the oracle ever stops responding, the contract safely switches to the High fee tier automatically.


Testing & Web Sandbox:
We wrote 32 unit and invariant tests in Foundry. Our tests prove that the hook only adds about 16.7k gas overhead and successfully causes sandwich attackers to lose money. Finally, we built an interactive web dashboard using simple HTML, CSS, and JavaScript so anyone can easily test the swaps and simulate MEV defense in their browser.

name: PayMe
description: Verified marketplace where creators earn when people or AI agents unlock their sources.
projectDescription:
PayMe is a marketplace for human-made knowledge in an AI-driven world. Creators can publish original articles, documents, transcripts, tutorials, skills, or research notes, then set a price for access. The app hashes each source to create a verifiable fingerprint, stores the full content behind a locked preview, and preserves the creator’s wallet-based attribution.
Readers or AI agents can browse sources, view previews for free, request a Hedera x402-style payment quote, and unlock the full content after payment verification. Each unlock records the buyer, creator, source, amount, currency, and transaction metadata, giving creators a basic earnings and usage history.
The goal is to create a simple payment and attribution layer for original human knowledge, so creators can prove ownership, control access, and get paid when their work is used by people or software agents.
howItsMade:
PayMe is built as a React + Vite frontend with a Python FastAPI backend. The frontend lets a creator enter a wallet-style identity, publish a source, browse the marketplace, preview locked content, request a payment quote, unlock a source, and test an AI-style citation flow.
The backend uses FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, and SQLite for the MVP data layer. When a source is created, the backend generates a SHA-256 content hash, stores the full content, creates a short preview, and exposes only the preview until the unlock endpoint verifies payment. Purchases are recorded with buyer wallet, creator wallet, amount, currency, and transaction metadata.
For Hedera, I implemented an x402-style exact-scheme payment quote using hedera:testnet, HBAR-to-tinybar conversion, a configurable pay-to account, and a verification layer with demo mode and strict mode. This makes each source unlock behave like a paid API request. I also added The Graph-ready analytics endpoints for marketplace stats and Bazantic-style manifest/recipe endpoints so agents can discover, unlock, and cite paid human-made sources. The hacky part is the demo verification mode, which lets the full product flow work locally before wiring in real facilitator settlement.

name: NotWallet
description: Turn any everyday contactless card into a $0 seedless hardware wallet with ENSv2 & World ID.
projectDescription:
Over $2.14B was drained in Web3 exploits recently, with >68% stemming from private keys compromised on internet-connected disks. While hardware wallets prevent this, less than 8% of users own one because of high costs ($150+), charging cables, and fragile 24-word seed phrases written on paper.
NotWallet solves this crisis by turning any contactless card you already carry—a metro card, gym ID, arcade token, or Visa debit card—into a bank-grade, air-gapped hardware wallet with $0 extra equipment.
Using Multi-Factor Key Derivation (MFKDF), NotWallet reads the card's physical NFC UID as an uncloneable hardware salt and combines it with a secret memory passphrase. In just 38 milliseconds, it deterministically computes your Ethereum private key in volatile RAM, signs the payload, and instantly wipes the key from memory. Zero private keys or seeds ever touch disk. If your phone is stolen, the attacker has no keys. If your card is lost, it is just inert plastic without your passphrase.
NotWallet pairs with any dApp via WalletConnect / Reown and features offline clear-signing that decodes transactions into plain English, flags infinite approvals, and forward-resolves counterparty addresses against ENS to eliminate copy-paste phishing.
howItsMade:
NotWallet was built as a native Android app (React Native + Expo dev-client) coupled with Foundry smart contracts and a Vite presentation dashboard.
Key Architectural Components & Partner Integrations:


Cryptography & NFC Layer:
We utilized Android NFC Reader Mode (react-native-nfc-manager) to read raw NFC tag UIDs directly from everyday plastic cards. For key derivation, we implemented MFKDF using scrypt via native QuickCrypto primitives. The key exists strictly as an ephemeral in-memory buffer during signing and is zeroed out immediately via garbage collection hints.


ENS (ENSv2) Hierarchical Account Architecture:
Instead of raw hex addresses, NotWallet builds on ENSv2's hierarchical registry live on Sepolia. We deployed our custom NotWalletRegistry (0x6ab7F8D372c3a12bF3267B49754bFF661329FB87) under notwallet.eth. Calling claim() mints user.notwallet.eth on-chain. Users can spawn arbitrary sub-wallets (e.g., bot1.agent.user.notwallet.eth) as distinct EOAs with bounded daily spend allowances, ideal for scoping autonomous AI agents. ENS also stores guardian pointers for our emergency recovery sweep.


World ID (Selfie Check Beta):
To protect unlocked devices from unauthorized physical sweeps, we integrated @worldcoin/idkit-react-native. Irreversible actions—like lifting the 0.05 ETH transaction limit or triggering an emergency sweep—require an interactive 3D selfie liveness check via the World ID bridge protocol (policy-override-guard), proving genuine human presence with Zero-Knowledge proofs without needing an Orb.


Reown / WalletConnect:
Integrated Reown WalletKit to provide universal QR pairing and air-gapped clear-signing with any mobile or web dApp.


Notable Hacks & Engineering Challenges:

NFC Normalization: Everyday contactless cards use varied UID lengths (4-byte single, 7-byte double, 10-byte triple). We engineered a normalization pipeline that cleans standard EMV/MIFARE cards into deterministic entropy salts.
High-Performance Presentation Engine: For our live presentation deck, we eliminated GPU-heavy CSS blur convolution filters in favor of pure radial-gradient falloffs and concurrent framer-motion transitions, ensuring buttery 60/120fps navigation across all devices.

name: RingTree
description: A Ledger-secured trust layer where autonomous agents operate without surrendering human control.
projectDescription:
RingTree is a Ledger secured trust layer for autonomous agents. It allows agents to run on remote infrastructure without receiving raw API keys or unrestricted wallet access. A trusted broker protects credentials using the official wallet-cli ring and gives each agent only signed, time-limited capabilities, call quotas, and spending budgets.
Ledger Flex keeps the user in control of high risk actions such as authorizing a host, granting permissions, revoking access, and signing payments. Agents can pay for services through capped x402 flows, while host binding, nonces, cascading revocation, and audit history prevent replay and silent permission escalation. RingTree enables useful autonomous agents without surrendering control of secrets, permissions, or funds.
howItsMade:
RingTree is built with TypeScript, React/Vite, Node.js, Express and SQLite. A local broker protects OpenAI, Graph and payment credentials using Ledger’s official wallet-cli ring. The React dashboard connects to Ledger Flex through DMK and WebHID for readable permission approvals and transaction signing.
Agents run on AWS EC2 (VPS) and reach the broker through a private AWS SSM relay with no inbound ports. The broker enforces signed capability scopes, expiration, shared quotas, spending limits, host binding, replay protection and cascading revocation.
The Graph Agent combines our live Base Sepolia USDC Subgraph with Subgraph MCP queries for blockchain analysis. A separate Key Ring-protected wallet makes capped x402 payments for Graph queries, while mission rewards require an exact Ledger-signed Base Sepolia transaction.

name: Ringo
description: Tweet-native challenges in USDC. The agent reasons over The Graph. World ID guards the credit.
projectDescription:
Ringo turns a tweet into a real-money challenge. Someone replies to a post, another person takes the opposite side, and it settles in USDC on Polygon through an order book and the RingoManager contract. That platform has been live since September 2025 and is closed source. None of it is submitted for judging.
This is a Continuity entry, and two things were built during the hackathon.
The first is an index of Ringo's own contracts. Until this week the agent could answer questions about a single position but knew nothing about the history it had created. A subgraph now indexes every creation, resolution and fee transfer on Polygon, and a new agent tool answers questions from it in natural language. It also gives the agent a base rate: when someone opens a new challenge, the agent looks up how comparable questions actually resolved and suggests a price from that rather than from nothing. The public dashboard reads every figure it shows from that index, with no database fallback, so if the index is wrong the page is visibly wrong.
The second is proof of personhood in front of free money. Ringo gives new users one free credit. One human with three accounts was getting three credits, and no email or wallet check can fix that. A World ID verification service now sits in front of the grant, and a unique index on the nullifier makes a second claim by the same person a no-op rather than a payout.
howItsMade:
The subgraph indexes RingoManager and USDC fee transfers on Polygon, and it exists because the private ABI never arrived. We recovered it from the chain instead: matching keccak256 of each candidate signature against the topic0 the contract emits, then reading the LOG opcode after each of those constants in the unverified implementation's runtime bytecode to learn which parameters are indexed. Three of our four guesses were wrong. Deploying the guess would have decoded every amount one word off, producing plausible numbers that were all incorrect.
One consequence shapes the schema. ringoId is an indexed dynamic bytes, so the event topic holds keccak256 of the value and never the value itself, and it cannot be recovered from calldata because every Ringo transaction is an ERC-4337 UserOperation. Entities key on the topic hash, and callers hash before querying.
The World ID service has zero runtime dependencies: node:sqlite for the nullifier store, node:test for its 43 tests. It fails closed on every path, including a redirect from an upstream that answers yes, and it takes the nullifier from World's verification response rather than from the client payload, because a client controls its own request body and not what World says back.
The most useful thing we found is a documentation bug. World's published personhood example uses a preset that returns World ID 3.0 proofs only, and a v3 proof carries a different nullifier than a v4 proof for the same person. An integrator following that page and building a uniqueness guarantee on the result gets a guarantee that is silently absent, with every check still reporting success. We only caught it by reading the shipped type definitions instead of the page. Our gate now pins verification to exactly one protocol version rather than widening to accept both, which is the safe configuration nobody documents.

name: Spigot
description: Pay-per-call API marketplace over MCP, settled in USDC on Arc Testnet.
projectDescription:
Spigot is a marketplace for paid APIs where every call is billed individually in USDC on Arc Testnet. The core idea is that if you've built an API and want to charge for it, you shouldn't need to set up Stripe, manage API keys, or lock people into monthly plans. You just list your endpoint, set a price per call, and that's it. On the consumer side, you top up your balance once and start calling APIs right away. There are no minimum commitments, no monthly fees, and no overage charges. You pay exactly what you use.
Under the hood, Spigot acts as a reverse proxy. When someone makes a call, the platform verifies payment using an EIP-3009 nanopayment, which is a gasless signature-based USDC transfer on Arc Testnet. Once verified, it forwards the request to the publisher's upstream server and streams the response back. The caller never sees a wallet popup or has to manually sign a transaction for each request. Everything settles on-chain but the UX feels like calling any normal API.
I'm also building MCP (Model Context Protocol) integration so that AI agents can discover APIs on the marketplace and pay for them on their own. The goal is that an agent should be able to find a tool it needs, check the price, and just use it without a human having to approve every single payment. This turns Spigot into infrastructure for agent-to-API commerce, where machines can autonomously buy and consume services.
The backend is built with Express and SQLite, the frontend is Next.js, and all on-chain settlement uses EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization on Arc Testnet so there's no gas cost for the end user.
howItsMade:
The backend is an Express server written in TypeScript that handles API registration, user accounts, credit management, and the payment proxy. All state lives in SQLite, which keeps things simple and means there's no database server to manage. When a publisher registers an API, they provide the upstream URL and set a per-call price in USDC. The backend stores this and exposes it through a REST API that the frontend consumes.
The payment flow is where it gets interesting. I'm using EIP-3009 (transferWithAuthorization) on Arc Testnet for nanopayments. This is a standard that lets a user sign a USDC transfer off-chain, and then anyone can submit that signature on-chain to execute the transfer. The benefit is that the caller doesn't pay gas and doesn't see a wallet popup on every API call. They sign once when they top up, and from there the platform handles settlement per request. The backend acts as a facilitator that verifies the payment authorization, forwards the API call to the publisher's upstream server, and streams the response back to the consumer. It's essentially a paid reverse proxy.
The frontend is a Next.js app with Tailwind CSS. It talks to the backend through Next.js rewrites so the browser only ever hits the Next origin, which keeps the httpOnly session cookie same-site and avoids CORS issues entirely. The marketplace page lets consumers browse and search APIs, and the sidebar shows their live USDC balance on Arc Testnet. Authentication is handled through Google Identity Services.
For MCP integration, the plan is to expose the marketplace as a set of MCP tools so that AI agents can discover available APIs, check pricing, and make paid calls programmatically. This means an LLM agent could autonomously find and pay for a tool it needs without human intervention.
One thing that's a bit hacky but works well is how the payment verification and API proxying happen in a single request cycle. The consumer makes a normal HTTP call to Spigot's gateway endpoint, the server checks their balance, deducts the cost, forwards to the upstream API, and pipes the response back. From the consumer's perspective it looks like a regular API call, but there's a full payment settlement happening in between.

name: Swap
description: Unlock under-collateralized DeFi loans using The Graph and ENS for verifiable on-chain reputation.
projectDescription:
Passport DeFi: Verifiable On-Chain Reputation for Capital Efficient Lending
Currently, decentralized finance suffers from massive capital inefficiency. Because smart contracts have no concept of "trust" or "credit," almost all DeFi lending protocols require users to over-collateralize their loans (often locking up 150% of the value they want to borrow). This severely limits the growth and real-world utility of Web3 finance.
Passport DeFi solves this by introducing verifiable, on-chain credit scores that dynamically adjust a user's Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio. If a user has a proven history of good financial behavior, they can unlock under-collateralized loans.
Our architecture achieves this by seamlessly integrating three core technologies:


Data Indexing (The Graph) We utilize a Subgraph to index a user's historical DeFi activity, specifically tracking loan repayment history across protocols. This raw data is synthesized into a single, verifiable "Passport Score."


Decentralized Identity (ENS on Sepolia) An arbitrary score isn't useful if smart contracts can't reliably read it. We bind this Passport Score directly to the user's decentralized identity using ENS Text Records on the Sepolia network. Every user receives a mathematical subname (e.g., score-0x...getpassport.eth) where their reputation data lives permanently on-chain.


Capital Execution (Arc Testnet) The actual financial execution happens on the Arc Testnet. We deployed a custom Lending Pool smart contract (PassportLendingPool.sol) that natively reads the user's verified ENS identity. Standard users are capped at an 80% LTV, but users with a Passport Score of 70 or higher unlock a 150% under-collateralized borrow capacity.


Autonomous AI Agents To tie it all together, we built a Node.js AI Agent that acts as an autonomous portfolio manager. The agent independently queries The Graph for the latest scores, cross-references them against ENS on Sepolia to verify identity, and then automatically executes risk-adjusted deposit and borrow strategies on the Arc Testnet on behalf of the user.


By combining The Graph's data layer, ENS's identity layer, and Arc Testnet's execution layer, Passport DeFi bridges the gap between traditional credit dynamics and decentralized finance.
howItsMade:
How it's made
We built Passport DeFi using a multi-chain architecture that separates data indexing, identity storage, and financial execution across different layers.


Smart Contracts & Execution (Arc Testnet & Foundry) The core lending protocol (PassportLendingPool.sol) and our test tokens (MockWETH, MockUSDC) were written in Solidity and compiled/tested using Foundry. We deployed these contracts to the Arc Testnet because of its fast finality and L2 scaling benefits. The lending pool is mathematically hardcoded to check external identity parameters before granting 150% under-collateralized loans.


Data & Identity (The Graph & ENS on Sepolia) We used The Graph's GraphQL API to query historical loan repayment data. However, the most interesting technical challenge was getting this data into a format that the Arc Testnet contracts could trust. We chose to use ENS Text Records on Sepolia as our identity layer.


The Notable Hack: During development, we realized that the official ENSv2 PublicResolver enforces strict ownership checks, which blocked us from dynamically writing subnames (like score-0x...getpassport.eth) off-tree without setting up a complex CCIP-read gateway. To solve this quickly for the hackathon, we built and deployed a custom MockResolver on Sepolia. This acted as a test-double that bypassed the strict ownership checks, allowing our backend scripts to dynamically mint and update ENS text records for any wallet address on the fly.


Frontend (React, Vite, Wagmi) The user interface is a responsive React application bundled with Vite. We utilized Wagmi v2 and viem for wallet interactions. Because our architecture spans multiple chains (Sepolia for Identity, Arc Testnet for Execution), we heavily utilized Wagmi's useSwitchChain hooks to ensure the user is seamlessly routed to the correct network before signing transactions. The UI features a custom "Cyber-DeFi" aesthetic built with vanilla CSS.


Autonomous AI Agent (Node.js & Ethers.js) Finally, we built an autonomous agent using Node.js. The agent is a standard script powered by ethers.js and dotenvx for secure environment variable injection. It runs a 3-track loop: querying The Graph's endpoints via fetch, reading the ENS MockResolver on Sepolia via an RPC provider, and mathematically calculating the risk-adjusted strategy before signing and broadcasting the actual borrow transactions to the Arc Testnet using a private key.

name: SubStrat
description: Delegate DeFi strategy, not custody. Manage Aqua positions with ENSv2 permissions.
projectDescription:
SubStrat is a non-custodial strategy-delegation protocol for 1inch Aqua positions. It lets a client or organization give a strategist narrowly scoped authority to manage a DeFi liquidity strategy without handing over custody of the underlying funds.
A client’s StrategyController becomes the Aqua maker and holds the required Aqua approval, while the strategist can only call a guarded rebalance function. Because Aqua strategies are immutable once shipped, tuning a position means docking the existing strategy and shipping a new one with a fresh strategy hash and updated parameters.
ENSv2 provides the delegation layer. A client grants a strategist a scoped role through Enhanced Access Control, tied to a specific name and strategy resource. The controller checks that role onchain before allowing a rebalance. If the client revokes the role, the strategist’s next attempt fails immediately, without changing the controller or relying on the strategist’s cooperation.
Privy provides the client-side ownership and governance layer. Its wallet and policy controls protect principal-changing actions such as emergency closure, reassignment, and future organization-level approvals. The result is a clear separation between tuning and taking: a strategist can operate within an approved strategy boundary, but cannot withdraw the client’s funds or override the owner.
SubStrat turns Aqua’s self-custodial liquidity into a delegatable primitive: delegate strategy, not custody.
howItsMade:
SubStrat is built with Solidity 0.8.30, real 1inch Aqua contracts, 1inch SwapVM strategy data, ENSv2 Enhanced Access Control, Privy’s server SDK, Hardhat, ethers v6, OpenZeppelin contracts, and a standalone solc compilation script.
The core contract is StrategyController. It acts as the Aqua maker rather than relaying calls from the client wallet, because Aqua keys ship() and dock() accounting from msg.sender. The controller therefore holds its own Aqua approval. A strategist never receives that approval and never directly handles the client’s tokens.
A rebalance follows Aqua’s immutable-strategy model. The strategist calls rebalance(), the controller checks the ENSv2 permission, the controller docks the old strategy, and then ships a new strategy. Aqua records a new strategy hash. The old strategy is marked as docked, while the replacement receives a new hash and updated parameters. The owner retains an independent emergencyDock() path.
ENSv2 is integrated as an execution permission, not as display metadata. The controller calls hasRoles() against a resource derived from the ENS name and strategy key. The resource calculation, role bitmap, and ROLE_SET_TEXT value were aligned with the real ENSv2 Permissioned Resolver implementation. We also created a Sepolia wiring script using a minimal ABI to call authorizeTextRoles() and verify permissions on the live resolver without compiling ENSv2’s entire dependency tree locally.
Privy is used on the owner side. The real Privy server SDK creates a wallet, attaches a policy restricting calls to the controller’s owner-only functions, and can submit an emergencyDock() transaction. Privy Key Quorums provide the upgrade path for 2-of-3 organizational treasury control, while the current MVP focuses on the SDK-manageable policy layer.
The build used several practical workarounds. Foundry and direct Solidity compiler downloads were unavailable in the sandbox, so we used the solc npm package with a custom compiler script. We pinned Solidity 0.8.30 to match Aqua’s exact pragma and normalized Windows path separators so nested imports compiled correctly on both Linux and Windows.
The most important validation was reproduced on two machines against real Aqua contracts. An unauthorized strategist is rejected, an ENS-authorized strategist can create a new strategy, revoking the ENS role makes the next rebalance revert, and the owner can still emergency-dock independently. This demonstrates the core property of SubStrat: strategy authority can be delegated and revoked without transferring custody of the position.

name: BlockTerms
description: Pay AI agents for data they can verify. Purchase live blockchain data through x402
projectDescription: BOUND is an agent-native protocol for buying live blockchain data with explicit, machine-readable delivery terms. Instead of treating an HTTP response as sufficient proof of delivery, BOUND binds each order to a specific provider, source chain, block, query scope, selected fields, payment amount, deadline, and warranty commitment. The provider reserves collateral before payment, the buyer agent pays through x402, and the returned result is checked against the agreed delivery terms. If the final delivery is invalid or late, the original payment is not reversed; the order follows a separate warranty path backed by the provider’s reserved collateral. The current demo uses live Uniswap data from two standardized Graph deployments, a bounded Ethereum state witness, and a real Hedera x402 payment settled through Blocky402. The goal is not to prove every property of a protocol, but to make a narrow paid data request verifiable and economically accountable.
howItsMade:
BOUND is an agent-native protocol for buying live blockchain data with explicit, machine-readable delivery terms. Instead of treating an HTTP response as sufficient proof of delivery, BOUND binds each order to a specific provider, source chain, block, query scope, selected fields, payment amount, deadline, and warranty commitment. The provider reserves collateral before payment, the buyer agent pays through x402, and the returned result is checked against the agreed delivery terms. If the final delivery is invalid or late, the original payment is not reversed; the order follows a separate warranty path backed by the provider’s reserved collateral. The current demo uses live Uniswap data from two standardized Graph deployments, a bounded Ethereum state witness, and a real Hedera x402 payment settled through Blocky402. The goal is not to prove every property of a protocol, but to make a narrow paid data request verifiable and economically accountable.
How it's made *
BOUND is built as a TypeScript monorepo around a single durable BlockTermsService runtime that owns validation, order state transitions, adapter selection, policy enforcement, and persistence. The same runtime is exposed through four interfaces: a TypeScript SDK, REST API, CLI / npx flow, and an MCP stdio server, so agents can integrate directly without depending on the web UI. Orders move through explicit states such as quoted, reserved, payment-pending, paid, and accepted, with atomic JSON persistence and compare-and-set revisions to avoid unsafe duplicate execution.
For the data layer, we deployed two separate subgraphs on Ethereum Sepolia for Uniswap V2 and Uniswap V3. Both expose a normalized schema so BOUND can send the same query shape to different protocol deployments instead of hardcoding protocol-specific logic into the agent. The runtime queries both deployments at a common block, checks schema/version compatibility, validates returned token and balance arrays, and rejects malformed or mismatched responses.
For state verification, BOUND uses an EVM JSON-RPC provider with eth_getProof and eth_getBlockByNumber to inspect a bounded set of account/storage fields at a pinned block. The system deliberately limits the proof scope to selected fields and does not claim full Graph query completeness or general financial correctness.
Payments use x402 v2 on Hedera testnet through Blocky402 with the exact scheme. The payment adapter is built with @x402/core, @x402/fetch, and @x402/hedera, and only accepts configured network, payee, asset, and budget constraints. In the live demo, buyer account 0.0.9695366 paid 0.01 HBAR to seller 0.0.10524176, while Blocky402 facilitated the network fee. After settlement, the paid request was retried and returned live standardized data from both Graph deployments with matching schema versions. The runtime writes payment-pending before invoking the irreversible payment step and stores the settlement receipt immediately afterward, so a crash cannot blindly trigger a second payment.

name: Speakeasy
description: Non-custodial 1inch Aqua trading for agents while Ledger holds the keys
projectDescription:
Speakeasy is a non-custodial trading backend for AI agents on 1inch Aqua / SwapVM. An agent talks to a local MCP stdio bridge (request_trade, post_trade, and related tools). That bridge handles OAuth and Ledger FIDO2 login, then asks our Bun HTTP API for an immutable five-minute trade preview. The API never receives a private key and never signs with the user’s wallet. Agent, facilitator, keeper, and PASETO material live in a Ledger Key Ring (wallet-cli ring). A secret-broker process decrypts over a Unix socket only when something must be signed. Humans keep hardware custody; the chain stays the source of truth.
Settlement is official Aqua plus SwapVM, not a custom AMM. Limit flow uses a pinned five-instruction SwapVM program on LimitSwapVMRouter. Funding uses x402 v2 exact Permit2 on the deployment chain (any standard ERC-20 sell token). Canonical Permit2 and the x402 exact proxy are the usual mainnet addresses. Conditional orders (stops, trailing, OCO, brackets) go through our Foundry contracts: AquaIntentController, vault factory, and BoundedMatcher, which may call at most eight allowlisted target/selector pairs.
Off-chain, Postgres plus workers rebuild the book from confirmed Aqua and SwapVM events and poll ERC-20 transfers (no websocket). Keepers can only hit manifest-allowlisted functions. Local demo is Anvil 31337 with fixture aUSD/aETH. Live explorer demo is Ethereum Sepolia (11155111). Physical Ledger (Sync, Ethereum blind signing, Security Key) is the real path; Speculos is for protocol tests only and is not a Secure Element claim.
The API is a strict language recognizer: unknown JSON keys and non-canonical amounts are rejected. OpenAPI lives at /docs. Cubane is the first-party EVM stack (no first-party viem/ethers/1inch SDK). Bazantic catalog discovery exists; a public paid Agentify gateway is out of scope until we have HTTPS OpenAPI. Hosted Vercel can serve read/health routes; hardware-bound trades stay on the local MCP bridge.
howItsMade:
We built Speakeasy as one Nix flake so the toolchain is locked: Bun, Aube, Foundry, Postgres, Process Compose, and (on Linux) Speculos plus pinned Ledger Sync / Ethereum / Security Key ELFs. There is no first-party viem, ethers, or 1inch SDK. Cubane + Noble do RPC, ABI, EIP-712, and txs. Zod 4 owns every HTTP body; OpenAPI 3.1 and Swagger are generated from the same routes. Errors are RFC 9457. Amounts are canonical decimal strings turned into bigint with maker-favouring rounding.
Custody is the hard split. wallet-cli ring encrypts agent, facilitator, keeper, and PASETO keys (LKRP). apps/secret-broker only decrypts over a Unix socket. The HTTP API never sees plaintext. Physical mode is node-hid, Device Management Kit, and on-device confirmations (quit Ledger Live). Emulated mode is Speculos + AQUA_E2E=1 and a wallet-cli adapter. Those keyrings are not interchangeable: a coworker with a real Nano cannot decrypt Speculos ciphertext, and Sepolia AquaIntentController.operator is immutable, so a new device means a new deploy.
The agent path is MCP stdio (apps/mcp-bridge): OAuth 2.1 + PKCE, Ledger FIDO2 (Security Key / CTAP), then request_trade → five-minute preview hash → post_trade. First POST /v1/trades returns x402 v2 PAYMENT-REQUIRED; retry is exact Permit2 on the deployment chain. The local facilitator settles Anvil/Sepolia. Quotes are SwapVM eth_call against pinned 1inch Aqua + LimitSwapVMRouter / AquaSwapVMRouter. Workers poll logs and ERC-20 transfers into Postgres (no websocket). The keeper may only hit manifest-allowlisted selectors on the intent controller, vault factory, and BoundedMatcher (max eight hops).
Partner tech: Ledger is the actual KMS and the login authenticator (amr: ["fido2","hwk"] on PASETO v4.public). 1inch Aqua/SwapVM is the matching and limit bytecode, not a wrapper AMM. Uniswap Permit2 and x402 exact (0x402085c2…) are the payment rail. Optional 1inch spot prices are a keyed add-on and are not required to quote.
Hacky / notable: Windows had to clone onto WSL ext4 because Anvil Unix sockets and chmod die on /mnt/e. Nix needed filter-syscalls = false. We patched Linux LD_LIBRARY_PATH so node-usb could load libudev/libstdc++ in e2e. Pocket’s Sepolia RPC answered eth_getCode but often returned “method not found” for Foundry EIP-1559 and even eth_sendRawTransaction depending on User-Agent; we signed with cast mktx and broadcast through a second RPC, and skipped genesis-hash checks on pruned nodes. Compose on Mac maps Speculos to host 15000 so it does not steal port 5000. dev/start refuse to serve until the runtime manifest’s code hashes, Aqua bindings, and matcher allowlists verify. Incomplete .data/keyring is never overwritten. Arbitrary Aqua programs are rejected on purpose because SwapVM instruction order is load-bearing.

name: Human-Gated Copilot
description: An AI copilot that can't spend without a Selfie Check bound to the exact action.
projectDescription:
Human-Gated AI Copilot (EchoBrief) is an AI agent for on-chain actions that can read, analyse and prepare — but cannot execute anything consequential until a real human approves that exact action with a World ID Selfie Check.
Most agentic apps verify a person once, at login, then let the agent act with the human's authority for the rest of the session. We bind the proof to the action instead of the session: the World ID signal is the keccak256 hash of the canonicalised action payload. The resulting receipt authorises one action, expires in five minutes, and stops validating if a single byte of the payload changes.
How it works: you ask the copilot about a wallet or a transfer. It pulls the wallet's live history from The Graph (Uniswap V3 on Ethereum mainnet), and a deterministic risk engine scores it with cited reasons — computed server-side from the data, never taken from the LLM. If the action is risky or costs money, a human gate appears: the user scans a QR code with World App, completes Selfie Check, and our server verifies the proof with World before issuing a single-use receipt. Only then is execution unlocked; an attempt without a receipt is refused by the server.
The same gate is offered to other AI agents as a paid service on Bazantic: an agent pays $0.05 in USDC on Base via x402, receives a live risk assessment and an approval link — and can prepare the action, but never approve it. The console shows provenance for every decision (live subgraph ID and query time) and an append-only receipt trail that also tracks continuity, recognising returning humans.
Verified live at echobrief.online: Selfie Check completed end-to-end in production with the standard World App, and a paid x402 call settled through the Bazantic gateway.
howItsMade:
I was single girl hacker)
Next.js 16 (App Router), TypeScript and Tailwind 4, deployed on Vercel at echobrief.online, with Upstash Redis for shared state (Vercel's filesystem is read-only and requests land on different instances).
The Graph: a Gateway GraphQL client queries the canonical Uniswap V3 mainnet subgraph for a wallet's swaps, and a pure, unit-tested risk engine turns them into a score whose reasons cite the numbers and the subgraph ID. The agent also uses the Subgraph MCP server for its own subgraph discovery. We packaged the data layer as a SKILL.md in The Graph's official skills format.
World ID: IDKit 4 with the selfieCheckLegacy preset. The signal is keccak256(canonicalJson(payload)); the canonicaliser sorts keys and rejects ambiguous values (NaN, -0, undefined, BigInt), so a hash can't be matched by reformatting the payload. RP contexts are signed server-side with World's official signRequest. Two traps worth mentioning: IDKit's signal_hash is hashSignal(signal), not the signal itself — a naive comparison rejects every genuine proof, and it bit us twice — and verification is pinned to our own rp_id, so a proof requested by another app can't open our gate. Receipts are claimed atomically (Redis SET NX), so they can't be replayed even under concurrent requests, and a test proves the gate fails closed.
Agent: Gemini with function calling. propose_action can only prepare, never execute; the server recomputes the risk score so the model can't talk it down, and a code-level honesty check rejects replies that claim an action was prepared when none exists.
Bazantic: we published our OpenAPI spec as the EchoBrief x402/MPP gateway (an MCP server with four tools) and a recipe, eth-transfer-risk-check-with-human-approval, that feeds a 1inch swap quote into our gate. Bazantic's v1 402 challenge sends a relative resource and omits fields, so our x402 client normalises it before the standard x402-fetch library validates it.
32 automated tests. The code was built in parallel workstreams against a frozen shared type contract, each in its own git worktree.

name: Swan
description: Swan gamifies compliant repo funding, margin management, and bond liquidation on Hedera.
projectDescription: Swan is a collateral and repo arena that gives ATS-issued tokenized bonds a practical financing use case. Institutions assemble compliant bond baskets, optimize borrowing capacity under haircut and concentration rules, and compete for USDC funding from KYC-approved lenders. After funding, Swan monitors oracle prices, triggers margin calls when collateral value falls, supports repayment and collateral substitution, handles coupon obligations, and returns collateral when the repo closes. If the borrower defaults, the collateral enters a KYC-gated auction that repays the lender and returns any surplus to the borrower. The gamified interface rewards efficient collateral selection, competitive rates, quick margin responses, and successful repo completion.
howItsMade: Swan is built inside the Asset Tokenization Studio monorepo using Solidity, Hardhat, TypeScript, React, Vite, RainbowKit, wagmi, and ethers. Its contracts are deployed on Hedera Testnet and integrate with four ATS-issued demonstration bonds and Hedera testnet USDC. RepoLifecycle manages collateral locking, lender offers, margin calls, substitution, repayment, maturity, and default. SignedPriceOracle verifies signed price observations and enforces freshness. ComplianceAuction handles voluntary and liquidation sales with delivery-versus-payment settlement, while KycAccessRegistry provides an on-chain KYC request and approval queue without storing personal information. ATS pause, freeze, balance, KYC, and transfer restrictions are checked throughout the lifecycle. The frontend connects through RainbowKit-compatible EVM wallets and presents the institutional workflow as a timed, score-driven arena.

name: Rubh
description: Rubh tokenizes verified infrastructure cash flows into Sharia-compliant investments from $10.
projectDescription: Rubh turns physical, fast-moving SME inventory and revenue-generating business assets into fractional, yield-bearing digital assets. By replacing self-reported financial data with Chainlink CRE's tamper-proof verification — pulled directly from point-of-sale systems, ERPs, and IoT devices — investors can see exact business performance rather than relying on static financial statements. Rubh gives SMEs a choice of Sharia-compliant financing structures matched to their actual capital need, while offering global retail investors fractional, asset-backed opportunities starting at $10. Beyond the initial financing product, Rubh's long-term direction is to grow into a full neobank with multiple revenue streams built on the same verified-performance infrastructure.
howItsMade:
Rubh is built on an Ethereum Layer-2 mainnet, utilizing EVM architecture and Yul assembly to optimize our core smart contracts for high execution efficiency and security. To manage the compliant fractionalization of real-world assets down to $10 ticket sizes, we rely on the ERC-3643 token standard.
Our primary partner integration—and biggest technical moat—is Chainlink CRE. Instead of relying on easily manipulated, static PDFs, Chainlink acts as a decentralized data pipeline. It pulls live commercial telemetry directly from merchant Point-of-Sale (POS) APIs, inventory ERPs, and physical IoT hardware sensors. This cryptographically verified "Proof of Sale" data is then anchored on-chain to trigger our event-driven smart contracts. These contracts automatically read the telemetry, calculate the exact profit share or fixed markup, and settle investor yields instantly in USDC, bypassing manual reconciliation entirely.

name: TradeTokenStocks
description: Our App sits between the intersection of Traditional and Tokenization of Stocks.
projectDescription:
Stock ownership is splitting in two. People hold shares at a regular brokerage, and more and more they also hold tokenized versions of the same company onchain, such as NVDAx from xStocks or NVDAon from Ondo. No app shows both side by side, and only the onchain half can actually be put to work.
TradeTokenStocks is one portfolio across both. You sign in with Privy and get an embedded wallet. You link your brokerage through SnapTrade, which is strictly read-only: those shares count toward your total exposure and nothing more, and the SnapTrade keys never leave our server. The tokens in your wallet are the allocatable side. You can commit them to a 1inch Aqua liquidity strategy without them ever leaving your wallet. The app keeps that line visible everywhere, because the difference between observed and allocatable is the whole point.
The strategy we focus on pairs two tokens of the same stock, such as NVDAx and NVDAon. They should trade close to 1:1, so we use Swap-VM's PeggedSwap curve instead of a constant-product pool. In our model, swapping 10 NVDAx into a 100 + 100 position returns about 9.96 NVDAon, while a constant-product pool with the same balances pays about 9.07.
The hard problem is corporate actions. Under ERC-8056, a tokenized stock handles a split or a reinvested dividend by changing a multiplier instead of minting new tokens. After a 10-for-1 split, one raw token stands for ten shares instead of one, but ERC-20 transfers still move raw amounts. Issuers don't apply these changes at the same moment or in the same way. As soon as one token's multiplier moves, a pegged position still quoting the old ratio is mispriced, and the first arbitrageur drains it. Aqua strategies are immutable, so the position can't correct itself. That is a big part of why AMM liquidity on tokenized equities is so risky today.
So we forked 1inch's Swap-VM and added a new instruction, CheckStockMultiplierRange, at opcode 0x24. Every position we ship runs this guard on both tokens before the fee and the PeggedSwap curve. On every quote and every swap, the VM reads each token's live multiplier onchain and reverts if either one has left the band the maker signed (±5% by default). The position halts itself the moment the underlying changes, instead of quietly bleeding out. The app surfaces the halt, and the maker can dock the stale strategy and ship a replacement at the corrected figures. Multiplier update events are indexed with Envio and shown in the app's activity.
The whole lifecycle runs onchain: mint the stock tokens, approve, ship the guarded PeggedSwap strategy to Aqua, fill swaps against it, push a multiplier outside the band and watch the next swap revert, restore it, and dock the position to withdraw.
TradeTokenStocks is a Bun and Turborepo monorepo with a Next.js web app and an Expo mobile app. Both share one platform-neutral domain package for the strategy math, Swap-VM program building and contract calls. Privy provides embedded wallets and signing, SnapTrade provides read-only brokerage data, and Envio indexes multiplier events. Everything runs on Ethereum Sepolia: 1inch Aqua, our forked Swap-VM router, and NVDA and AAPL test tokens modeled on xStocks and Ondo.
Live Sample Transactions:
