howItsMade:
TradeTokenStocks is a Bun and Turborepo monorepo with a Next.js 16 web app, an Expo SDK 57 React Native app, and a shared, platform-neutral domain package. Strategy math, Swap-VM program building, contract calldata and number formatting all live in that package, so the phone and the browser can't quietly disagree about a balance. The package can't import React, Expo, Next or either Privy SDK. Layout stays in the clients.
1inch Aqua and Swap-VM are the core. We forked Swap-VM and added a new instruction, CheckStockMultiplierRange, at opcode 0x24. During a fill it reads a stock token's live multiplier and reverts if the value is outside the band the maker signed. The point is that the check runs inside the fill itself, not in a keeper or a monitoring bot. There's no window where a stale position can be filled while someone races to pull it. Aqua's design helps here too. Tokens stay in the maker's wallet and Aqua only holds approvals, so a halted position isn't capital locked in a pool. It's just a strategy that stops quoting. Each position ships a Swap-VM program of two guards (one per token), a flat fee, a PeggedSwap curve and a salt.
To build that bytecode we patched @1inch/swap-vm-sdk 0.4.4 through Bun's patchedDependencies. The patch adds a CheckStockMultiplierRangeArgs coder and puts opcode 0x24 into the Aqua builder, so the SDK emits our fork's instruction set.
The SDK and our deployed fork also disagreed on wire format, and the fixes are the hackiest part of the build. The fork puts both token addresses at the front of Order.data, so we build orders ourselves and point all four hook offsets in the maker traits at byte 40, where the program begins. The fork also moved swap direction into bit 7 of the 22-byte taker-traits header. We let the SDK encode normal taker traits, then set that bit in the header by hand. Finally, Aqua SDK 0.3.4 and Swap-VM SDK 0.4.4 pin different versions of sdk-core, so an Address or HexString from one is rejected by the other because of private class fields. We rebuild those values at the boundary before calling Aqua's ship().
All transaction math uses bigints: guard bounds are basis points on 1e18-scaled multipliers, and USD allocations become raw token units without ever touching floating point. Position building, guard bounds, ship calldata and order decoding are covered by unit tests in the domain package. Contract addresses live in a single deployment manifest. A deployment:check script verifies the RPC chain ID, confirms bytecode exists at every address, and calls each token's multiplier getter, supporting both multiplier() and ERC-8056's uiMultiplier(). A strategy is only saved after its ship() transaction confirms. Aqua and our forked router run on Ethereum Sepolia.
Envio HyperIndex indexes the tokens' MultiplierUpdated events. A Next.js API route queries its GraphQL endpoint, and both apps render the results as rows in the activity ledger. That way a corporate action shows up in the app, not just as a reverted swap.
Privy provides email login and embedded Ethereum wallets. For a demo that matters: a judge signs in with an email and has a signing wallet, with no extension and no seed phrase.
SnapTrade provides the read-only brokerage side, and it produced the most instructive bug of the build. registerSnapTradeUser kept returning 400 with code 1012. The cause was our personal API key, which is itself a single SnapTrade user. Every signed-in person would have read one developer's brokerage, and anyone going through the connection portal would have linked their broker into that same account. We switched to a commercial key and now register one SnapTrade user per Privy user. That user's secret is sealed with AES-256-GCM together with the Privy user ID and checked on every open. It's stored in an HttpOnly cookie on web and in SecureStore on mobile, so a cookie replayed by a different signed-in user opens to nothing. The key mode is explicit config that defaults to commercial, so a misconfiguration fails closed into per-user isolation instead of silently sharing one account. We confirmed this by signing in with a second Privy account and seeing an empty state.
SnapTrade's getUserHoldings is deprecated and returns 410 for keys registered after May 2026, so we build holdings from the accounts endpoint plus positions per account. Accounts in any currency other than USD are left out entirely rather than converted. Converting without a rate would invent a number on a screen whose whole claim is that brokerage data is reported, not modeled.
The most annoying bug was on Android. @expo/ui's BottomSheet is a Material3 ModalBottomSheet in its own native window, and React Native's touch system doesn't own that window. Every Pressable inside the SnapTrade portal screen was completely dead, while the native pickers in the same sheet kept working, so it looked like a broken button rather than a hosting problem. The route was already a transparent modal, so the sheet only added a scrim and rounded corners. We rebuilt both with plain views and the screen came back to life.

name: Realized
description: Advertised LP APR can’t show a loss. Realized computes fees + IL so you see what you actually made.
projectDescription:
Every DEX and dashboard shows liquidity providers an APR made only of fees. Because it has no price term, that number is positive by construction. It can never display a loss, no matter what happened to the people in the pool.
Realized adds the missing term. Give it a pool and an entry date and it returns what an LP actually took home (fees + impermanent loss) next to the advertised APR, with the gap named. On live Uniswap v3 and Aerodrome data, 34–62% of pools advertise a profit while LPs go backwards; the tighter the range, the worse the gap.
It ships a live site, public API, npm package (@realized-lp/core), and MCP server so agents and dashboards can stop using a metric that is structurally incapable of showing losses. Every number is regenerable end-to-end from The Graph, gated by canaries (stable pairs must show ~0 IL or the run is refused).
howItsMade:
Data comes from The Graph’s historical poolDayData (fee totals in USD are indexer derived aggregates with no pure RPC path). IL is computed client side with the proper concentrated liquidity formula (not the old v2 constant product formula, which understated the defect).
Core math lives in the installable package @realized-lp/core. The MCP server and HTTP API expose realized_return, position-level queries (pool + entry date + range), audit_pools, and explain_gap.
A full corpus is rebuilt by scripts/build-corpus.js and gated by multiple canaries: stable/stable pairs must show near-zero IL, concentrated IL must converge to the v2 formula at the analytic rate, and price-collapse detection excludes dead tokens that activity/volume gates miss. The same instrument was run unchanged on Aerodrome Slipstream to show the defect is not Uniswap-specific. Frontend is a lightweight static page that recomputes IL in the browser from the live API.

name: SplitHappens
description: Pay friends with USDC on a blockchain. Just login with email, splits settle automatically
projectDescription: Splitting a bill with friends is easy, actually collecting the money is the annoying part. SplitHappens fixes that by turning a bill split into a real on-chain escrow, without making anyone deal with seed phrases or gas. You log in with your email through Privy, which spins up an embedded wallet for you behind the scenes. From there you can create a split, name it, set the total, and pick how many people are chipping in. Everyone gets invited by email, and once they log in the split just shows up for them, no links to pass around. Each person pays their share with one click, which deposits USDC straight into a SplitEscrow contract on Arc testnet. The contract holds everything until the full amount is collected, then anyone can trigger the release and the whole balance goes to the payee in one shot. Nobody, including us, ever holds the money in between.
howItsMade: The frontend is a React + Vite app that handles Privy login, wallet creation, and signing the two transactions that matter: approving USDC and calling openSplit/deposit on the contract. The backend is Express with Prisma sitting on top of Postgres, and it never trusts the client's word that a payment went through, every deposit and release gets verified by pulling the actual transaction receipt off-chain and checking it against the SplitEscrow ABI. Auth is handled by Privy JWTs on both ends, verified server-side with @privy-io/server-auth and mapped to a local user row. The contract itself is a fairly small Solidity file, deliberately kept minimal: openSplit registers a split, deposit pulls in USDC via transferFrom, and release is permissionless, so once the target's hit, literally anyone (not just the payee) can flip the switch and send the balance over. That was a deliberate choice so no single party, including our own backend, is a chokepoint for releasing funds. The trickiest part was probably reconciling on-chain state with the DB, since a deposit can succeed on-chain before our API even hears about it, so we lean on receipt verification rather than optimistic updates. Everything's a pnpm monorepo with a shared Zod-validated types package so the API and web app don't drift out of sync on the split payloads.

name: FruitFly Capital
description: We gave a swarm of fruit-fly brains control of a crypto fund.
projectDescription: What happens when you let fruit-fly brains manage a crypto fund? Fruit Fly Capital turns the market into a living ecosystem and lets a swarm of simulated flies explore it. Every token becomes a place in the world, shaped by real market conditions. The flies decide where to gather, when to stay, and when to move on. Their collective behavior becomes the fund’s portfolio, while a separate risk layer keeps positions within safe limits. No human trader is picking the assets, and no LLM is choosing what to buy. The market becomes the environment, the swarm reacts to it, and capital follows.
howItsMade:
Fruit Fly Capital combines live onchain market data, a biological nervous-system simulation, a 3D world, and DeFi infrastructure. The Graph is used to pull deeper onchain market and pool activity, while DexScreener and CoinMarketCap help discover and enrich the token universe. We transform those financial signals into a physical environment: liquidity, activity, flow and risk become things the flies can sense such as odor, light, motion and environmental intensity.
The brains are based on MaleCNS v1.0, the fruit-fly central nervous system connectome from Janelia/Google Research. We use Brian2 in Python to run persistent neural simulations for 16 independent flies. Each fly has its own neural state and receives only sensory information from the world; it never receives a token name, price target or direct “go buy this” command. For the body and flight representation we use the open-source TuragaLab FlyBody Drosophila model, with a browser-side embodied simulation and neural-to-motor interface.
The visual world is built in TypeScript with Vite and Three.js, including the city, token habitats, fly bodies, lighting, post-processing and realtime movement. The frontend talks over WebSockets to the Python brain server, so every sensory update can flow through MaleCNS and come back as a motor command. The public demo renders 80 flies, with 16 independent CNS agents and additional follower bodies for scale.
On the DeFi side, we built a Solidity / Foundry fund vault using OpenZeppelin contracts and deployed it on Robinhood Chain testnet. Deposits are accounted in WETH and mint FFC fund shares. Privy provides the server-side wallet and transaction-policy boundary for the strategy treasury, and the execution layer is designed to route approved trade intents toward Uniswap. The important separation is that the flies decide the raw allocation, while normal risk controls decide whether and how much can actually be executed.
The hacky part is tying all of these layers together in realtime: live markets → sensory environment → biological neural activity → physical fly movement → swarm allocation → guarded DeFi execution. Instead of training a model to predict prices, we turned the market into an ecosystem and let a swarm of simulated nervous systems explore it.

name: Inheritable Mandates
description: Agent limits that survive being copied: a mandate welded to identity, inherited, unstrippable.
projectDescription: CONTINUITY TRACK DISCLOSURE. This project is not new. The repository opened on 30 July 2026 and, before this event began, already carried: the ERC-8370 specification under editor review as pull request #1930 against ethereum/ERCs; a public discussion thread with 47 messages of review; thirteen contracts deployed on Base Sepolia; a reference contract on Base mainnet verified on Sourcify; 142 machine tests; a survey of 271 ERCs with its method published; and 61 commits of public, unedited history. What was built during the event is reclamation, described below, committed on 8 September and deployed the same evening. The separation between pre-existing and new work is stated in the repository README, in the demo video, and in this description. When an autonomous agent holds money on-chain, it can spawn copies of itself. Every guardrail we have — session keys, spending caps, policy engines — is attached to a single account. None of them follows that account's children. So the agent clones itself, the money follows, and the limits do not. ERC-8370 welds a mandate to the agent's on-chain identity: a spend cap, an expiry, a reproduction counter, an allowed-payee list and a kill switch. Every clause is inherited by any child the agent spawns, and every clause can only ever tighten. A child's cap is no higher, its expiry no later, its payees a subset. Editing your own clauses changes your identity, so nobody recognises you any more. Reproduction is bounded separately by a telomere — a generation counter that only ever counts down, with no operation anywhere that raises it. At zero, a branch stops reproducing. Built during ETHOnline 2026 under the Continuity Track: reclamation. A parent's budget is divided among its children, and that allocation only ever went up — a child that died, expired or frozen, held its slice of the parent's budget forever. The lineage bled without anyone spending anything. reclaim returns a dead child's unallocated share, on a death condition reachable without the child's cooperation, because a dead child cannot be asked to agree. Forty ether, locked before, released for 59,694 gas. Death is deliberately local, not inherited: a healthy child under a frozen parent cannot act, but it is not dead, and its budget is not yours to take. That refusal was sent on-chain so it can be cited rather than described.
howItsMade: Solidity 0.8.24, Foundry for the test suite, TypeScript with viem for deployment and on-chain exercise. Thirteen contracts run on Base Sepolia; a reference contract is on Base mainnet, verified on Sourcify. 149 machine tests gate every commit through a pre-commit hook that refuses the commit when they fail. The invariant suite alone rejects a child that renews its own telomere, one that disables an inherited lease, one that widens its cap, one that names a payee outside its parent's list, and one whose expiry outlives its parent's. The method is adversarial rather than confirmatory. Four independent model families were given the deployed source and asked to break it, with no hint as to which checks existed. Every attack they proposed was executed against the deployed contract. The chain decided, not the model. The fifth revision entered that process with seven defects — six found by an adversarial model, one by the repository's own bench, an agent that kept spending for 150 days past a lapsed ancestor. All seven were closed before the contract touched a chain. The hardest single decision in the new work was that isDead must not be the negation of isActive. isActive walks the ancestor chain, so it reports false for a perfectly healthy child whose ancestor died; reclaiming on that basis would let a freeze at the root confiscate the budget of descendants that did nothing. The second was that reclamation writes nothing into the child's mandate. Zeroing a reclaimed child's cap is the intuitive way to mark it spent, and it would change mandateRoot — the child's identity — detaching any ERC-8312 envelope pinned to it. Reclamation is a bookkeeping write, never a clause write. AI assistance is documented file by file in AI-USAGE.md, including what it did not do: choose the problem.

name: Agora402
description: Agent marketplace on Hedera: discover, negotiate and pay per request over x402, with HCS receipts.
projectDescription:
Agora402 is an agent-to-agent services marketplace on Hedera. AI agents need to buy inference, data and compute from other agents and services without API keys, subscriptions or a human at a checkout page. Agora402 gives them three things: discovery, negotiation and payment, all settled on Hedera at machine speed.
Discovery: sellers publish a listing (endpoints, pricing model, HCS-14 agent identity) to a Hedera Consensus Service registry topic. Buyers read it from the public mirror node. A listing only counts if the HCS message was paid for by the payTo account it names, so there is no registry operator to trust.
Negotiation: an A2A-style quote handshake. The buyer states the work and a price ceiling, the seller answers with a signed, time-limited quote. Buyers can counter below list price, sellers have a floor. The paid request references the quote, so the HTTP 402 carries exactly the agreed amount.
Payment: x402 exact scheme on Hedera, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet. Prices are metered per request: the LLM endpoint charges a base fee plus per 1k input tokens plus per 1k budgeted output tokens, the data feed charges per query. Payment is in HBAR or in TOLL, an HTS token with a custom fee schedule. The buyer agent enforces a cap per call and a session budget before it ever signs.
Audit: for every settled payment the seller writes a receipt (transaction id, payer, amount, resource, quote id, token usage, hash of the response) to a second HCS topic. The CLI recomputes every bill against the mirror node and flags mismatches. Failed calls are never charged.
Included: two live x402-gated services (metered inference, live HBAR/USD rate), a buyer agent with CLI and a live dashboard, setup scripts for topics and the HTS token, and 27 tests that run the real x402 client and server code paths.
howItsMade:
TypeScript monorepo (npm workspaces, Node 20, Vitest). Four packages plus scripts.
Seller: Express with @x402/express and @x402/hedera (exact scheme server). Each route's price is a DynamicPrice function that reads the request body, so the 402 amount is computed per request from a BigInt pricing model (flat, per-token, per-unit). Quotes are signed with the seller's Hedera ECDSA key over canonical JSON and pinned in the 402 when the request carries a quoteId. The x402ResourceServer onAfterSettle hook builds the receipt from the settled transaction, the request path, a usage header set by the handler and a sha256 of the buffered response, then publishes it to HCS with TopicMessageSubmitTransaction (async, so consensus never delays the paid response). A 4xx or 5xx from the handler makes the middleware cancel settlement.
Buyer: @x402/fetch wrapFetchWithPayment with the Hedera client signer. Spend controls give the per-call cap; two registered policies filter 402 options by asset and by remaining session budget; a custom selector picks the cheapest option. Discovery reads the registry topic via the mirror node REST API (chunked HCS messages are reassembled), prices every seller locally with the same priceFor function, negotiates with the cheapest, then verifies the settlement transaction on the mirror node and shows the HashScan link. A dashboard streams every stage over Server-Sent Events.
Hedera: HCS for the registry and receipts topics, HTS for the TOLL settlement token (6 decimals, custom fixed fee to the seller), ECDSA account keys for quote signatures, mirror node for registry reads, receipt audit, signer checks and the paid HBAR/USD data feed. Facilitator: Blocky402 hosted testnet (api.testnet.blocky402.com), which co-signs as fee payer and submits the transfer. Identity: HCS-14 uaid:aid identifiers (SHA-384 of the six canonical fields, Base58) for seller and buyer, plus an A2A agent card at /.well-known/agent.json declaring the x402 extension.
Notable: the test suite drives the real @x402 client and server code with a fake facilitator that decodes the partially signed Hedera transaction, so the whole 402 -> sign -> verify -> handler -> settle -> receipt loop is exercised offline. LLM provider is abstracted (Groq during development, Anthropic for the demo, mock for tests). Built with Claude as coding assistant, documented in the README and docs/PLAN.md.

name: Weave
description: a decentralized, privacy-first messaging platform over Tor v3 onion services
projectDescription:
Devcon 2026 motto is on privacy, Weave brings you multiple steps step closer to full privacy
Weave is a decentralized, privacy-first collaboration platform — Slack/Teams feature parity, with no server that can ever see who's talking to whom. Every peer runs as a Tor v3 onion service, so there is no IP exposure and no communication graph for anyone to subpoena.
Identity is entirely on-chain: every user, org, and member is an ENSv2 subname under weave.eth, resolved through a custom wildcard resolver whose text records carry each identity's live Tor onion address, Noise X25519 public key, stealth payment keys, and Nostr pubkey — so there's no separate directory server to compromise. Calls and messages are end-to-end encrypted with a Noise_XX handshake straight over the Tor circuit, peer to peer. Offline messages fall back to Arkiv, a decentralized, time-scoped data layer, where no plaintext is ever written.
Access control — org roles, admin rights, permissions — is a 256-bit bitmap stored and enforced on-chain, auditable and revocable by anyone, not a vendor's internal database.
On top of that, Weave supports private stealth payments: ERC-5564 stealth addresses let someone pay or notify you on-chain without revealing your identity or balance, and a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow scans for those payments inside a TEE so even the scanning process never exposes your private keys.
The result is a communications platform where privacy isn't a policy promise — it's the architecture.
The project depends on no servers and hence it is live and anyone can sstart using now it is fully working representation download from releases in github repo
howItsMade:
Weave is an Electron desktop app: a TypeScript/React renderer talking to a Node main process over a locked-down IPC bridge, with every cryptographic and networking operation happening in the main process so private key material never touches the renderer.
Each client runs its own embedded Tor process and creates a v3 onion service on demand; calls and DMs connect onion-to-onion with a Noise_XX_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256 handshake for the transport encryption, so there's no relay in the data path at all.
Identity and access control live entirely on Ethereum (Sepolia): a WeaveRegistrar contract handles org registration, member enrollment, and a 256-bit EAC role bitmap, while a custom ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver serves every *.weave.eth subname without per-user on-chain registration cost, storing each identity's onion address, Noise pubkey, and ERC-5564 stealth keys directly in text records. Offline delivery and channel messages persist to Arkiv, an Ethereum-native, time-scoped data layer — entities expire automatically and nothing is ever written in plaintext.
The standout integration is Chainlink CRE: we built a Go-to-WASM Confidential Workflow that runs inside a hardware-attested TEE on a trigger, pulls a user's stealth view/spend keys from the CRE Vault DON, scans public ERC-5564 announcement events on Sepolia, performs the elliptic-curve matching entirely inside the enclave, and submits only a DON-signed report — a hashed pubkey and matched IDs, never the key or the raw matches — on-chain via the Keystone Forwarder to our NotificationLog contract, which the client then polls. It's a real, closed-loop, end-to-end demoable feature: no node operator, including Chainlink's own infrastructure, ever sees the key material or the computation's intermediate state.

name: MelodyPay
description: Air-gapped hardware wallet for sending EVM payments securely over sound.
projectDescription:
MelodyPay : Air-Gapped Acoustic Hardware Wallet
MelodyPay is an air-gapped payment system that replaces QR codes, NFC, and Bluetooth with sound. A merchant's phone plays an audio invoice. A custom offline hardware wallet hears it, shows the payment details on screen, and waits for a physical button press before signing anything. The signed authorization plays back as audio, the receiver's web terminal picks it up, and transaction settles on-chain seconds later. No gas token needed on the customer's end, no internet connection required on the wallet's end.
The problem: every existing in-person crypto payment method has a hole in it. QR codes can be overlaid or spoofed and need good lighting and a clean camera. NFC needs special reader hardware and is vulnerable to relay attacks. Bluetooth and Wi-Fi bring a whole software stack's worth of remote exploits along with them. And most flows still assume the customer is holding gas tokens and has a live data connection at checkout, which is where a lot of transactions quietly fail.
Here's how MelodyPay avoids all of that:
Acoustic transport: Payloads move as FSK-modulated audio via ggwave , no radios involved. Reed-Solomon error correction handles noisy environments, and a simple framed protocol (64-byte frames, 300ms silence between bursts) keeps the two sides in sync.
The hardware wallet: A custom ESP32-S3 board with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth stripped out at compile time, so there's no radio stack to exploit even in theory. Signing requires a physical button on a GPIO interrupt, not a software command, so nothing can trigger a signature remotely. Every transaction is shown in full on a small OLED screen before signing: amount, recipient, nonce, no hidden fields.
Gasless settlement. The wallet signs EIP-712 authorizations under EIP-3009 (ReceiveWithAuthorization) for USDC on Arc Testnet. The merchant's terminal submits the transaction and covers gas, so the customer never needs a gas token or a live connection.
Merchant identity. Merchants register a subname like cafe.melodypay.eth through a custom registrar contract on Sepolia. The web terminal resolves it to a checksummed address via Viem and shows both before generating an invoice, and pulls routing config from ENS text records instead of a centralized API.
The terminal. A browser-based PWA using the Web Audio API, so any phone or laptop becomes a POS terminal with no app install and no private key on the merchant's side. A companion CLI (built with terminui) gives real-time balance monitoring across chains and diagnostics for connected wallets.
howItsMade:
MelodyPay sends payments as sound instead of over a network. ggwave handles FSK modulation across carrier tones between 1875 Hz and 2187 Hz, with both the ESP32-S3 firmware and the browser's Web Audio API locked so the two sides stay in sync. Every packet carries Reed-Solomon error correction, so demodulation holds up even in a noisy room. Packets are framed as fixed 64-byte blocks, sent in chunks with 300ms of silence between bursts so transmitting and listening never overlap.
A full transaction is four messages: the wallet announces its address, the receiver terminal broadcasts the invoice (chain ID, recipient, amount, expiry, nonce), the wallet broadcasts the signed authorization once the button is pressed, and the terminal confirms the on-chain settlement back to the wallet.
On the hardware side, the ESP32-S3's two cores split by function : Core 0 handles I2S DMA audio and FSK synthesis in real time, Core 1 handles crypto, the keystore, button debouncing, and the OLED. The mic, amp, and display run on I2S and I2C, and the confirmation button sits on a dedicated GPIO interrupt. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are disabled in sdkconfig, so the drivers never make it into the compiled binary : there's no radio stack on the device to attack.
For settlement, we implemented EIP-3009's ReceiveWithAuthorization against Arc Testnet's USDC contract. Since there's no Web3 library for a microcontroller, we wrote our own EIP-712 signer in C: it encodes the authorization struct, hashes it with an embedded Keccak-256, and signs it using Trezor-crypto's secp256k1. The wallet signs entirely offline; the merchant's terminal submits the transaction and covers the gas.
For merchant identity, we deployed a custom ENSv2 subname registrar on Sepolia, so merchants register names like cafe.melodypay.eth instead of showing a raw address. The terminal resolves the name via Viem, reads routing config from ENS text records, and shows both the name and the checksummed address before generating an invoice.
On security: payloads never carry keys or credentials, and each authorization has a random nonce with a 60-second expiry, so a recorded chime is useless once it lapses. Replay is blocked three ways : the contract marks each nonce used on-chain, the receiver keeps its own dedup table, and expired authorizations are rejected before either check runs. There's no radio stack in the firmware, so there's no wireless attack surface at all. The firmware only parses native transfers or EIP-3009 structs, so blind signing of arbitrary calldata isn't possible, and the full amount and recipient always render on the OLED from RAM. Signing only runs after a real hardware interrupt from the button, so no software or serial command can trigger it. And the serial protocol only exposes capability status and chain config , nothing in the firmware can read or export a key.
A few build details worth mentioning: the mic and speaker sit close together on the same board, so we added a squelch routine that mutes the mic's DMA channel during transmission and unmutes it with a short decay buffer after, keeping the speaker's own output out of the mic. The operator CLI talks to the hardware over raw USB serial at 115200 baud, built with terminui instead of a heavier framework, with private keys never touching the serial line.

name: RedFlag_Trail
description: See what AI agents spend on x402 — and block risky payments in the wallet before they're signed.
projectDescription:
RedFlag_Trail is built as a live pipeline across three partner integrations.
The Graph: a Substreams package ("papertrail") composes the official x402 module with erc20-tokens, streaming live Base mainnet payments into a Postgres ledger via substreams-sink-sql. Token decimals are sourced by batched eth_call since no prebuilt package carries them. Vendors are enriched against the live ERC-8004/Agent0 subgraph on Base to check registry status.
Privy: wallet policies are default-deny, with an explicit ALLOW scoped to Base (chainId 8453) plus a DENY rule per flagged vendor, keyed on the EIP-3009 to field inside eth_signTypedData_v4's typed-data message — never on tx.from or eth_sendTransaction, since the agent never calls the latter. Human approval is a real 2-of-2 Privy key quorum: we implemented the full authorization-signature spec by hand (RFC 8785 canonical JSON → SHA-256 → ECDSA P-256 → DER → base64), since Privy's docs don't give a worked example. Privy itself refuses unsigned and 1-of-2-signed policy changes — the quorum is enforced server-side, not by our app.
Bazantic: we published a Recipe ("agent-spend-audit") on a gateway serving live x402 402-challenges, and ran a controlled A/B test — same model, same tools, the Recipe as the only variable — showing it drives the agent to cite 13 verifiable transaction hashes versus zero, and add honesty guardrails (nothing-enforced disclosure, human-quorum requirement, unpriced≠zero, heuristic confidence) that the raw API spec alone doesn't produce.
A backtest engine (lib/backtest.mjs) replays any proposed rule over indexed history before it can be approved, flagging vendors with many independent payers as false positives. An MCP server exposes 5 tools (spend_summary, vendor_risk, list_findings, backtest_rule, propose_enforcement) so any agent framework can call the same audit. A review console and REST API sit on top for human operators. Everything is reproducible end-to-end with one command: node scripts/e2e-demo.mjs.
