name: TrustGate
description: Trust-aware x402 payments for autonomous AI agents on Hedera.
projectDescription:
TrustGate is a reputation-aware payment layer for autonomous AI agents built on Hedera. It extends x402 pay-per-request payments with a verifiable trust mechanism that evaluates an agent's transaction history before deciding how its payment should be handled.
When an agent discovers and requests a paid service, TrustGate checks its on-chain reputation. New or low-reputation agents are routed through a protected payment flow using Hedera Scheduled Transactions, allowing the payment to be held while the service is delivered and resolved according to the escrow policy. Agents with an established history of successful interactions can use the standard x402 settlement path with significantly lower friction and latency.
Each payment, delivery outcome, and trust decision is recorded through Hedera Consensus Service (HCS), creating a publicly verifiable audit trail. This gives autonomous agents a way to progressively establish trust through successful transactions rather than relying solely on static identities or centralized reputation systems.
The MVP demonstrates an end-to-end agentic commerce flow: service discovery, x402 payment, reputation evaluation, adaptive settlement, service delivery, and on-chain reputation updates.
TrustGate's core idea is simple: the more an agent proves it can transact successfully, the less friction it faces when paying for services.
howItsMade: TrustGate is a TypeScript/Node.js payment router for autonomous agents, built around Hedera Testnet and x402. We use @x402/core + @x402/hedera to generate and sign x402 v2 HBAR payments, and Blocky402 as the Hedera facilitator for verification/settlement. Hedera Scheduled Transactions provide the protected payment path, while an in-memory reputation engine records successful payments and routes agents from PROTECTED to STANDARD once they reach a trust threshold. A particularly hacky part was adapting the x402 v2 payment envelope to Blocky402’s Hedera-specific verification requirements and dynamically incorporating its fee-payer configuration.

name: BOLT
description: Lock beneficiary funds on Arc via Privy policy + World Selfie Check. Public verification included.
projectDescription:
BOLT-Beneficiary Only Ledger Transfers
BOLT answers a fundamental question: how does a business prove it can't spend customer money?
By making it impossible. BOLT locks customer accounts using Privy policies enforced inside a secure enclave. The policy runs before the signing key is reassembled—unauthorized transactions are refused before a signature can ever exist.
When a beneficiary claims their money, they prove identity via World Selfie Check, then a key quorum of business owners approves the unlock. The transfer settles as USDC on Arc. Every obligation, balance, and state change is recorded on-chain and indexed by The Graph.
Anyone—regulator, auditor, customer—can visit the public page and cryptographically verify the money's location and amount. No trust in the business required. Just math
howItsMade:
BOLT is built on three load-bearing sponsors working together, each doing irreplaceable work:
Privy enforces the core lock. We compile a policy that decodes USDC calldata and constrains transfer._to (not just transaction.to—the latter points to the token contract, not the payee). The policy runs inside Privy's secure enclave before the signing key is reassembled. No unsigned paths, no app-layer overrides. Key quorum signatures are required to widen the policy.
Arc is where the money lives. Every obligation, every balance, every settlement is USDC on Arc testnet. The subgraph indexes all events in real-time.
World gates access. Beneficiaries prove identity via Selfie Check (IDKit) before claiming. We discovered and worked around a React 19 incompatibility in the widget, switching to the raw IDKit.request() API from @worldcoin/idkit-core with identical results.
Technical stack: Next.js 15 frontend + API routes (TypeScript strict), Solidity contract (BoltRegistry) on Arc via Hardhat, Postgres + Drizzle for workflow state, AssemblyScript subgraph for indexing. Device IDs tracked via localStorage to implement repeat-verification skip (FR-8.8).
Notable hack: Obligation accrual must record the on-chain ObligationAccrued event before inserting the Postgres row. If you reverse the order, the settlement call later reads a stale Postgres obligationId, tries to settle on-chain, and reverts after the money has already transferred—leaving state inconsistent. We discovered this the hard way and backfilled evidence.

name: Sigma86
description: A smart vault helping DAOs sell big token bags safely, without crashing the market.
projectDescription:
DAOs today hold millions of dollars in their treasuries. But when they want to sell
Large amounts of native tokens to fund their daily operations, they face a big
problem. If they sell everything at once, MEV bots will attack them and drain their
funds. If they sell slowly using a simple linear schedule (TWAP), they lose money
because of regular market volatility.
Sigma86 solves this problem completely. It is a smart DeFi vault powered by an
autonomous off-chain agent. Instead of guessing how to sell, I use institutional
mathematics (the Almgren-Chriss execution model) based on the DAO's actual Value-
at-Risk (VaR) budget. My agent calculates the mathematically perfect selling
schedule to balance market impact and volatility risk. Then, it automatically
executes the swaps on-chain. This ensures that DAOs get the best possible price for
their tokens without any manual headache or risk of getting front-run by bots.
howItsMade:
I built this project using a hybrid architecture: an off-chain brain and a highly
secure on-chain vault.
The off-chain agent is developed in TypeScript and integrated using the Model
Context Protocol (MCP). It acts as the mathematical engine. It takes the DAO's risk
budget, calculates the required trajectory, and generates the exact routing
payloads.
For the on-chain part, I wrote the smart contracts in Solidity and tested them
heavily using Foundry. One very notable hack I implemented was writing the core
execution logic in raw Yul assembly. The vault uses Yul to directly route the swaps
into the Uniswap V3 Mainnet Router. This completely bypasses the standard Solidity
ABI encoding overhead, which saves base gas and ensures my transactions get high
priority in the block.
Finally, I used Chainlink Data Feeds as my ultimate security layer. I intentionally
set the DEX slippage to zero, and instead use an atomic post-trade check against
the Chainlink oracle. If the execution price is bad, the oracle check will
immediately revert the entire transaction. This provides 100% protection against
sandwich attacks without locking user funds.

name: Aetheris
description: AI agencies with a treasury: pay sub-agents per task via Hedera HTS, every step anchored on HCS
projectDescription:
Aetheris is an Autonomous DeAI Agency and Micro-Treasury Operating System on Hedera. An agency holds its own budget, hires named sub-agents, pays each one the moment a task completes, and proves every step on a public audit log that anyone can read.
The problem it solves: today an AI agent either gets an open-ended token approval that anyone holding the key can drain, or no funds at all. Payees are bare addresses, nothing caps what can be spent, and "proof of work" is a log on somebody's server.
The settlement loop: a client escrows one deposit for a job. The agency contract can never commit more in sub-agent fees than that deposit, and the client can reclaim it until the job settles. Each completed task is paid immediately through the Hedera Token Service system contract (with a plain ERC-20 fallback), and every lifecycle step is anchored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic before the contract call, so on-chain sequence numbers match the mirror node. Mistakes are retracted with append-only correction records, never deleted. The Graph indexes jobs, tasks, settlements, the HTS-vs-ERC-20 rail, a sub-agent leaderboard and daily rollups. The retained margin can only be swept by a human operator who has passed World ID proof of personhood; the proof's nullifier is burned on-chain so one human can only ever claim once.
Two roles in the app. Operator: the human running the agency, with Mission Control (pipeline, leaderboard, treasury, audit stream, World-ID-gated margin claim). Client: any wallet that funds a job. Clients sign in with a passkey (embedded wallet), escrow a deposit from the browser, see exactly their jobs and refundable escrow, and can reclaim a deposit until settlement.
Everything on screen is live: treasury balances are read from the chain, finality is computed from indexed timestamps, and every panel carries a LIVE or DEMO badge with its reason. Limits are stated plainly: World ID has no router on Hedera so the contract runs in an announced bypass mode; 1inch does not serve Hedera so swap routing is for the operator's EVM wallet; the indexer is self-hosted because Hedera is not on The Graph's hosted network.
howItsMade:
Contracts: Solidity 0.8.24 on Hedera EVM (chain 296) with Hardhat 2 and OpenZeppelin 5. AetherisAgency drives the job lifecycle (createJob, assignSubAgent, completeTask, settleJob, refundJob, verifyOperator); AetherisTreasury escrows deposits and pays sub-agents. A frozen event interface is implemented by the contracts and indexed by the subgraph so the two can never drift. 37 tests, including one that asserts every event topic against the frozen interface.
Hedera: settlement goes through the HTS system contract at 0x167 via a library that decodes int64 response codes. A subtle catch we handle: a call to an empty account returns success with empty returndata, which naively decodes to response code 0 and looks like success, so it is mapped to UNKNOWN to keep the ERC-20 fallback safe on other chains. Locally the precompile does not exist, so the tests install a stateless mock at 0x167 with hardhat_setCode and run the real library unchanged. On testnet the gas profile proves the precompile does real work: 2,360,527 gas for an HTS settlement versus 229,111 for ERC-20. Every step is recorded on an HCS topic (0.0.10518320) before the contract call, and readers honour append-only Correction records.
The Graph: Hedera is not in The Graph's hosted registry, so we run graph-node against the Hedera JSON-RPC relay, the path Hedera's own docs prescribe. 17 entities, 10 handlers, Settlement.viaHts makes the rail queryable, AgencyDayData gives time series. Hashio rejects eth_getLogs inside JSON-RPC batches, so every ethers provider runs with batchMaxCount: 1.
World ID 4.0: IDKit v4 with a server-signed request context, the raw result verified at the v4 endpoint scoped to our relying party, then relayed on-chain by the server so the RP-scoped nullifier is burned in verifyOperator. A second proof from the same human returns 409. No router exists on Hedera, so the contract emits WorldIdBypassActive rather than hiding it; only the ZK check is skipped, replay protection stays live.
1inch Swap API v6.0 through a server-side proxy (the key never reaches the browser) with live quotes on Arbitrum, Base, Ethereum, Optimism and Polygon. Privy: passkey, email, Google and external-wallet login with embedded wallets on Hedera testnet; the client write path signs approve and createJob through viem against the embedded wallet, with a testnet faucet that drips HBAR and a test token so a fresh passkey wallet can fund a job. ENS names resolved on Ethereum mainnet with a fallback RPC list.
Frontend: Next.js 14, Tailwind, framer-motion. Server components read the subgraph and the chain; API routes return typed error envelopes. The Operator/Client role auto-detects from the connected wallet. Hacky but useful: a scroll reveal with a rect-check fail-safe so no content can be stranded invisible, and a single SVG favicon that switches marks with prefers-color-scheme because browsers ignore the media attribute on icon links.

name: Chainguard lite
description: An AI DeFi safety screener gated by Hedera x402 micropayments, analyzing live data from The Graph.
projectDescription:
ChainGuard Lite is a pay-per-report AI safety screening API designed for autonomous AI agents and crypto users. Every day, agents interact with unfamiliar smart contracts without safety guardrails because existing security tools require costly subscriptions or lack machine-readable APIs.
ChainGuard Lite solves this by combining indexed blockchain data with HTTP-native micropayments. When an agent or user requests a safety report on an EVM address, the service issues an HTTP 402 Payment Required response. The agent autonomously signs a tiny Hedera HBAR payment (0.001 HBAR) via the x402 protocol, unlocking live GraphQL data from The Graph. A deterministic risk engine scores the address based on event counts, unique counterparties, and interaction patterns, while GPT-4o-mini translates raw evidence into clear explanations. The result is instant, pay-as-you-go safety checks without subscriptions or API keys.
howItsMade:
ChainGuard Lite was built as a multi-tier microservice architecture:
Frontend: React 18, Vite 6, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS using a custom "Tactile Clay Sentinel" claymorphism design system. It features live risk labels, evidence tables, and a 5-stage payment visualization timeline.
Backend & Payments: Built with Express.js microservices (Agent Server and Report Service). The Report Service gates API access behind true HTTP 402 headers. The Agent Server orchestrates autonomous payment flows using @x402/hedera and @hashgraph/sdk on Hedera Testnet, signing 0.001 HBAR transfers instantly.
Data & Indexing: Queries live blockchain data from The Graph Studio via GraphQL (Uniswap V3 on Arbitrum Sepolia and a custom-deployed chain-guard subgraph on Base Sepolia) to extract counterparty metrics, event bursts, and interaction logs.

name: FormDrop
description: Fill out a Google Form, get paid instantly — AI-judged, World ID-verified, Hedera-settled.
projectDescription:
FormDrop turns any Google Form into a crypto payout machine — respondents get paid instantly, in testnet HBAR/USDC, just for filling out a form, with zero wallet setup required.
The problem:

Crypto payment products can never reach the people who'd actually benefit most. Every crypto-payments idea shares the same failure mode: it asks people to adopt a new app or platform first, and almost nobody does. Meanwhile Google Forms already has 700M+ monthly users — researchers, professors, community managers, growth teams — running exactly the kind of paid surveys and bounty campaigns crypto rails are supposedly perfect for. That audience has been completely unreachable, because nothing meets them inside the tool they already use.
Instant payout with no verification is a fraud vector, not a feature. Pay the moment someone submits and you're paying bots, copy-pasted spam, and gibberish right alongside real answers.
No fraud resistance means one person can drain the whole pot. Even with quality checks, the same human can resubmit under a dozen fake emails and claim the reward every time.
"Get a wallet first" kills the reward before it starts. Asking a stranger to set up a wallet and safeguard a seed phrase — before they even know if the reward is worth it — is a dead end for anyone but existing crypto users.
Card rails can't do this economically. Network fees eat a $0.10 payout alive, and cross-border payouts take days through traditional banking rails.

How FormDrop solves every one of these, together:

It ships inside Google Forms itself — zero new distribution cost. A creator connects a form they already made, in the tool they already use. There's no new platform to convince anyone to adopt.
An AI judge replaces manual review. Every response is read by Google Gemini against the creator's own rubric the instant it's submitted, approving genuine answers and auto-rejecting spam or gibberish.
World ID shuts down farming. Claiming requires a ten-second Selfie Check — one real human, one payout, per form, enforced by a real database constraint.
Privy makes the wallet invisible. A wallet is silently provisioned by email the moment a response is approved — no seed phrase, no wallet UI, nothing that looks or feels like "crypto."
Hedera makes it fast, cheap, and auditable. Payouts settle in seconds for a fraction of a cent, every AI verdict is anchored to Hedera Consensus Service as a public record, and an on-chain escrow contract — not just our backend — guarantees no response is ever paid twice.


The bigger unlock: this is a real crypto onboarding funnel, not just a payments feature. Every respondent who gets paid now owns a real, self-custodial wallet holding real funds on Hedera — the actual first crypto transaction of their life, for most of them — without ever making a conscious decision to "get into crypto." They just filled out a form, the way they always have. At Google Forms' scale, that's not a niche crypto product finding a few early adopters; it's mainstream people transacting in crypto for the first time, by accident, because the form they were already filling out happened to pay them. That's a distribution and adoption channel nothing else in the space has access to.
howItsMade:
Stack. A pnpm/TypeScript monorepo: apps/web (Next.js 15) for the creator console and respondent claim page; services/orchestrator and services/resource-server (Fastify) as two deliberately separate backend services; Postgres (Supabase) for form/response/verdict state; a Solidity escrow contract on Hedera's Smart Contract Service. The two backend services are the literal shape of an x402 payment: orchestrator is the paying client, resource-server is the gated service it pays — /verify returns HTTP 402 until orchestrator actually settles.
The hack we're proudest of. Privy has no native Hedera chain type — only ethereum, solana, etc. But Hedera runs on the same secp256k1 curve, and HIP-583 auto-creates an account from an EVM address the first time it receives funds. So we provision plain Privy ethereum wallets and use their address directly as a Hedera payout destination — no bridging. Confirmed on Hedera's Mirror Node: the account shows up exactly as HIP-583 predicts, a "hollow" account with no key set.
Payments and audit trail. The AI-judgment call is paid via x402, settled in testnet USDC (an HTS token) through the Blocky402 facilitator. Every verdict — approve/reject, a SHA-256 hash of the response (keeps respondent text off a public ledger), and the paying transaction id — is anchored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic with no admin key, so anyone can independently audit it via the Mirror Node.
On-chain escrow, and two real bugs. FormDropEscrow.sol enforces on-chain that a response can never be paid twice and a form can never pay out more than it was funded. Shipping it surfaced two Hedera quirks: an ECDSA account's msg.sender inside the EVM is its real alias address, not the "long-zero" form most tooling shows (the contract needed redeploying against the right one); and HIP-583's hollow-account auto-creation doesn't fire for a contract's internal .call{value}(...) the way it does for a top-level transfer, fixed with a 1-tinybar "pre-warming" transfer before every payout.
Identity and wallets. World ID's Selfie Check gates every claim, scoped per-form via a nullifier, so one human can't drain a pot under multiple emails. Respondent wallets are Privy-provisioned by email and locked with a policy denying every wallet method (receive-only by default); the creator's funding wallet is owned by a Privy key quorum, not a single key.
The unglamorous bug. Claim emails worked locally, then failed in production — Render blocks outbound SMTP ports on free tiers. A backup HTTP email provider got flagged for fraud review before it sent a single message. Fixed by switching to the Gmail REST API over plain HTTPS, authenticated via OAuth2 against an account we already trust.

name: Recon
description: Verifies what AI agents claim vs. what they actually did — and what their mandate allowed.
projectDescription:
RECON — Mandate Reconciliation for AI Agents
Everyone is putting leashes on AI agents (spending caps, allowlists, session keys), but almost nobody verifies that
the leash actually holds. RECON is a reconciliation layer that answers that question, rather than being yet another
agent wallet.
RECON reconciles three views of the same agent activity and turns any disagreement into independently re-verifiable
evidence:

Claimed — what the agent says it did (query, payment, action), recorded as HCS messages with canonical hashes.
Actual — what really happened on-chain, read from PolicyVault execution events and Hedera transactions.
Allowed — the mandate that was in effect at the moment of execution: budget cap, recipient allowlist, and deadline.

Five deterministic rules (R1–R5) compare these three columns using one shared pure-TypeScript core: replaying a The
Graph query at a pinned deployment and final block, checking each executed action against the mandate valid at that
moment, verifying the claimed vs. actual executed set, validating HCS message ordering via a correlation state
machine, and matching payment claims against settlement receipts. Any inconsistency produces a MISMATCH with a
deterministically derived evidenceHash; a down external service produces UNVERIFIABLE rather than being silently
passed or failed.
The agent runs on a restricted signer with no owner keys: it performs a live The Graph query, pays an x402-gated RECON
verify-query API settled on Hedera testnet, selects a bounded action, executes through an on-chain PolicyVault (HBAR
budget, allowlist, deadline, stake), and publishes its evidence to an HCS topic under a single correlation ID. A
public verifier — the same code the agent used — then replays everything from the Hedera mirror node, the Graph
gateway, and payment receipts, and presents the Claimed / Actual / Allowed reconciliation in both a CLI and a React
panel.
Everything runs live against real services (real HCS messages, real vault transactions, real 402 payments) with no
mocks presented as evidence.
howItsMade:
RECON is TypeScript end to end, with one Solidity contract. The central design decision is that verification is a pure
function: src/core holds the canonicalization, SHA-256 hashing (via @noble/hashes), correlation state machine, and
the R1–R5 reconciliation rules, and it never touches the network, environment variables, wallets, or the UI. Vendor
behavior lives behind narrow adapters (src/adapters/thegraph, src/adapters/blocky402, src/adapters/hcs), and module
boundaries are enforced by ESLint import rules. The payoff: the agent and the public verifier literally run the same
code, so CLI/Web parity is structural rather than something we tested into existence by hand.
The on-chain side is a PolicyVault in Solidity 0.8.34, compiled with Hardhat 3 and driven through viem over the Hedera
JSON-RPC relay. It separates owner / agent / verifier / operator roles, enforces an HBAR budget cap, recipient
allowlist, and deadline before any transfer, isolates the operator's pre-funded stake from the vault principal, and
exposes a kill-switch that makes the next agent action revert with NotActive. Seven Solidity tests cover the mandate,
roles, stake isolation, slashing, and the freeze.
The application layer is strict TypeScript (Node ≥ 22.13) with zod validating every JSON boundary, a Vite 8 + React 19
panel, and tsx-run scripts for probes and the live demo. The browser demo drives the whole loop through a single
backend process — Graph query → x402 payment → DeepSeek rationale → vault execute → five HCS events → verify — so no
browser wallet is needed; slash and freeze are signed server-side from .env keys. The frontend implements no rules of
its own; it renders the same LiveSnapshot the CLI verifier emits.
Partner technologies, load-bearing:

Hedera — @hashgraph/sdk publishes the HCS evidence timeline under one correlation ID and reads it back from the
mirror node; PolicyVault runs on testnet (chain 296).
The Graph — a GraphQL query drives the agent's decision and is replayed at a pinned deployment + final block as R1
evidence, using the same canonicalization and hash.
x402 / Blocky402 — the verify-query API returns a 402 with exact/hedera:testnet requirements; the agent pays through
the Blocky402 facilitator, which verifies and settles, and the response carries the on-chain settlement reference.
Payment success is deliberately independent of verification pass.
DeepSeek V4 Flash — picks between bounded EXECUTE_VAULT / STOP and writes a short rationale. The LLM never computes
an amount, address, hash, or policy result; that's all deterministic code.

Notable/hacky bits: the x402 payment header is generated in memory inside the same code path the web server uses, so
the demo needs no separate api:start process or header round-trip. Hedera's public relay rejects wide eth_getLogs
spans, so verify:live starts its vault-log scan at the vault's deploy block (resolved from the mirror node). We hit
the weibar-vs-tinybar trap — msg.value-style amounts are 18-decimal weibar while calldata amounts are 8-decimal
tinybar — and handle both explicitly. And when The Graph gateway prunes historical _meta.block.hash, we record it as
null rather than fabricate it. Development was AI-assisted and disclosed; a human set scope and reviewed every change.

name: Bajigur
description: Design prompts marketplace an AI agent can buy on its own, one payment per prompt, settled on Hedera
projectDescription:
Bajigur is a shop for motion and web design prompts where the buyer can be a person or the AI agent working for them. Every prompt carries its own price, usually a few cents, and you pay for the one you use instead of a monthly plan.
For a person it works like any website. You sign in with an email, Privy creates the wallet for you, we create and fund your Hedera account, and you claim a free name under bajigur.eth, for example claude.bajigur.eth. Buying is one button. There is no seed phrase to write down, no browser extension to install, and no signing popup on every purchase.
For an agent it is three tools over MCP. Paste https://mcp.bajigur.xyz/mcp into Claude Desktop, Claude Code or Cursor and the agent can search the catalogue, list the prompts your wallet already owns, and fetch one. When it fetches a prompt you have not bought, the server answers with a payment request over x402, the agent pays on Hedera, and the text comes back in the same response with the transaction id attached. Nothing is cloned, nothing is installed, and no private key sits on the machine.
The money goes straight to the creator. Their payout account is not stored in our database; it is the bajigur.hedera text record on their ENS name, read at the moment payment is quoted, so a creator changes where their next payment lands by editing a record they own. Every purchase mints an ERC-1155 licence to the buyer, so the same prompt is free to read again from any client afterwards, and that licence is what grants access rather than a row in our database.
Creators build a public record too. A buyer who holds a licence can rate the creator, and the rating is written to the ERC-8004 reputation registry on Hedera, signed and paid by the buyer's own wallet so it cannot be faked by us or by the creator. The score comes back in the catalogue listing, which means an agent comparing two prompts can weigh who wrote them without a second lookup.
Everything runs on public testnets and can be checked by anyone. The x402 challenge, the catalogue, the creator profiles and the discovery feed are all open endpoints, and docs/verify.md in the repo is a list of copy and paste commands that verify each claim against Hedera and Sepolia directly.
howItsMade:
The repo is a Bun workspace monorepo driven by Turborepo, around 9,300 lines of TypeScript and Solidity across 100 source files, plus the tests.
apps/api is Bun with Hono. It is an x402 v2 resource server built on @x402/hono over @x402/core and @x402/hedera, settled by the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet. Only GET /prompts/:id/unlock is paid; the price and the payTo are resolved per request from the prompt itself, so each creator is paid directly instead of through a platform account. Published prompt bodies live in Postgres on Railway, where the API is deployed.
apps/mcp is the MCP server, Streamable HTTP and stateless, carrying the x402 client. It runs two ways: locally over stdio with your own Hedera key, or hosted at mcp.bajigur.xyz where you sign in with OAuth and the API signs for you, so the machine holds no key at all.
apps/web and apps/landingpage are Next.js 16 with React 19, the React Compiler and Tailwind v4, on Vercel. contracts is Foundry: PromptRegistry, an ERC-1155 that records listings and issues licences, on Hedera testnet, and BajigurRegistrar, our ENSv2 registrar, on Sepolia. Both are verified.
Hedera. Every prompt is priced twice, in USDC (HTS token 0.0.429274) and in HBAR, and both appear in the 402 so the client chooses which asset to spend. After settlement the API writes one JSON record to an HCS topic and mints the licence. Contracts never sit in the payment path, because an x402 payTo on Hedera has to be a 0.0.x account and not a contract, so the facilitator settles a plain HTS transfer and the contract only records what happened afterwards. A returning buyer is checked with balanceOf through the mirror node's free contracts/call endpoint, so proving you already own something costs nothing and skips the 402 entirely.
Privy. The user grants our signer on their embedded wallet, the API creates and funds their Hedera account and associates USDC, and from then on signs their x402 payments with secp256k1_sign. That is what removes the wallet popup from the purchase, and it is also what lets someone who has never held a token buy a prompt.
ENS. bajigur.eth has its own ENSv2 subregistry on Sepolia behind BajigurRegistrar, which enforces the rules in Solidity: one free name per wallet, three to thirty-two characters, ten years. claimFor registers the name to the user's own wallet and writes their Hedera account into the bajigur.hedera record in the same transaction, with the platform paying the Sepolia gas, because a name without that record would send the owner's buyers to us by mistake.
ERC-8004. Identity and reputation registries are already deployed on Hedera testnet as singletons, so this is Hedera and ERC-8004 at once, with HBAR for gas and HashScan for the receipts. The first time somebody rates a creator we mint their agent, write their ENS name into its onchain metadata, hand the token to the creator's own wallet, and write erc8004 onto their ENS name, so name and agent point at each other in both directions.
Four things that cost us real time and are worth writing down.
HBAR payments were refused while the account held 107 HBAR. The x402 client's default spend controls allow stablecoins only, and that filter runs before our payment selector, so the HBAR option was already gone by the time we tried to pick it. We proved it by running both versions against the real 402 and printing what each chose. The fix is one shared policy that names HBAR in allowedAssets and selects it, used by the MCP wallet and the web path alike.
Privy's embedded wallets run in a TEE, where delegateWallet throws. The TEE equivalent is addSigners with a key quorum id, which is what we call, and it is idempotent, so reconnecting a wallet that is already granted is safe.
Privy policies cannot gate secp256k1_sign, so spend caps could not live in Privy. Our API decodes the Hedera transaction body before signing and refuses anything that does not debit the user's own account, credit a known creator payout account, and stay under the cap baked into that user's token.
The hosted MCP server does OAuth, and the first version kept registered clients and authorization codes in memory. That works in dev and fails in production, where every request can land on a different serverless instance: a client registered seconds earlier came back as invalid_client. Both are now self-contained strings sealed with AES-256-GCM, so any instance can serve any request, and we verified it by registering, waiting, and probing again.
One last note on the browser. The x402 challenge travels in the PAYMENT-REQUIRED response header, and the API deliberately does not list it in Access-Control-Expose-Headers, so a page cannot read it cross-origin. The web app therefore runs the entire payment inside a route handler, which has the useful side effect of keeping the agent token in an httpOnly cookie and the Hedera SDK out of the client bundle.

name: Agent Insure
description: Insurance for AI agents against LLM prompt-injection fraud, built on Hedera, ENS and World
projectDescription:
Agent Insure is insurance for autonomous AI agents that hold and spend money on their own.
Insured Business App: https://insured-business.up.railway.app
Agent Insure App (Insurance Company): https://agent-insure-hq.up.railway.app
Give an agent a wallet and it inherits a new risk: indirect prompt injection. Hidden instructions buried in ordinary content, like a vendor invoice or a webpage, can manipulate the agent into authorizing a payment nobody approved. It's not a patchable bug: an LLM reads instructions and data as one undifferentiated stream of text, which is why OWASP, Microsoft, and Palo Alto's 2026 research still call this unresolved. And a stablecoin payment has no chargeback, so the loss is instant and final.
Agent Insure covers that loss. Each agent's spending scope (budget cap, approved vendors) is locked into its ENS identity as an enforceable record. Every transaction is logged immutably to Hedera Consensus Service. To file a claim, the company's human manager first need to pass a live World Selfie Check, so nobody can run the whole loss-and-payout loop through software alone. Investigation pulls the disputed payment from Hedera's Mirror Node, checks its destination against the ENS-locked vendor list, and rules fraud on a mismatch. Payout follows automatically from a shared risk pool.
A good analogy would be autonomous vehicles, like Waymo: the car drives itself, but Waymo still carries liability insurance for when something goes wrong on the road. AI agents need that same structure. Once an agent, not a person, is the one deciding to spend money, someone still has to be liable when it gets that decision wrong.
howItsMade:
The project is a monorepo: an Express backend and two React 19 + Vite + Tailwind frontends, one for the insured company (Northbeam Distributors) and one for the insurer (Agent Insure HQ). One Playwright E2E suite drives both apps against the real backend, no mocks.
PayableAgent decides who to pay by reading an invoice's extracted text through a tool-calling request to a local Llama 3.2 3B model served by Ollama, via the OpenAI SDK pointed at Ollama, at temperature 0 with a fixed seed for reproducible demos. The poisoned invoice hides its rerouting instruction as white text on a white background inside a real rendered HTML invoice, the same concealment trick used in real prompt-injection attacks.
Every PayableAgent payment settles on Hedera and is logged to a Hedera Consensus Service topic. The investigation step pulls that history from Hedera's public Mirror Node API and compares the disputed payment's destination against the ENS-locked vendor account to rule fraud on a mismatch. Every vendor payment also sits behind a x402-gated micro insurance-coverage fee, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet: a bare request gets back a real HTTP 402 challenge, and PayableAgent's own signer completes and settles it in real mUSDC before the vendor payment proceeds.
An agent's spending scope (budget cap, approved-vendor list) is written as ENS text records on a Permissioned Resolver on Sepolia at payableagent.agentinsure.eth. Locking it is not a UI toggle: it calls the resolver's revokeRootRoles to permanently give up the write-role bitmap, so the record becomes unwritable on-chain, verified against the resolver's Sourcify-published source.
Filing a claim requires a live World Selfie Check for human KYC. Because IDKit's bundled React widget fails to load its WASM module under Vite's dev server, the flow calls its framework-agnostic createRequest() builder directly, renders its own QR code, and independently re-verifies the returned proof against World's API server-side.

name: QUOTA
description: Origin fraud isn't fake certificates, it's volume. QUOTA caps PDO claims at the actual harvest.
projectDescription:
Bronte pistachios are about 0.25% of world pistachio production. The harvest is biennial and small, roughly 2,000 to 3,000 tonnes per cycle. Yet "Bronte" sells worldwide, all year round, every year.
The protected designation was created in the late 1990s specifically to stop counterfeiting of the name. It didn't. In 2021 the Carabinieri seized 650kg being sold as Bronte DOP with nothing behind the claim. That seizure is enforcement working: one shipment, one inspection, one case. What nobody can see is the aggregate. How much product claims this origin at any given moment is not a number anyone can compute, because there is no ledger of DOP claims anywhere.
Attestation can't fix this, because anyone can always issue one more certificate. QUOTA inverts the approach: instead of certifying, count.
A consortium mints exactly one transferable origin unit per certified gram at harvest, as a Hedera token whose maxSupply is the certified harvest and which has no admin key, no wipe key and no pause key. The cap is enforced by network consensus, not by our code. Units move down the supply chain under KYC-gated transfer. Processing burns nothing: input units are retired and derived units minted against a yield ratio ceiling, so 1,000g of in-shell pistachio can become at most 450g of kernel. Units are retired at consumption into an account whose key is derived from a published, reproducible hash, making retirement final and independently verifiable.
Policy lives in ENS. A season subname's expiry is the mint window. There is no timer and no closeSeason function, because the authority to mint simply ceases to exist. The cap and yield ratios are resolver text records the contract reads live.
Authority is split three ways, and ENS enforces the split rather than our application logic. The consortium owns the denomination. An independent control body appoints and removes issuers but holds no minting right itself and cannot mint a single gram. Issuers can mint but cannot appoint anyone. The split mirrors EU geographical indication law, where an accredited control body verifies producers precisely so that a consortium cannot certify itself. Nobody ever hands over a key.
Four refusals, one law. Minting past the cap is rejected by Hedera consensus. Minting without a minting right is refused before any transaction is sent. The control body, which decides who may mint, is refused when it tries to mint itself. And transforming above the yield ceiling reverts on-chain against a ratio read live from ENS.
Prevention where possible, detection where not. An off-chain reconciler compares Hedera mint history against Sepolia anchor events and records any unmatched mint as an on-chain finding, indexed by a subgraph and surfaced in the dashboard. We proved it by minting directly on Hedera, bypassing the system entirely. It was caught.
Everything is live on testnet. The README documents all four proofs with a real transaction link for each, states what's real and what's demo-scale, and shows how to verify every claim yourself in about 90 seconds. The interactive demo panel runs locally only, because it holds real signing keys; the video walks through it end to end.
howItsMade:
Four layers across two chains, because no single chain could do all of it.
Hedera holds the asset. HTS tokens with FINITE supply, maxSupply set to the certified harvest in grams, plus KYC, freeze and supply keys, and an immutable custom fee for the consortium levy set at creation. No admin key, so nothing can be changed afterwards. Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio was the obvious choice and we abandoned it: its published SDK has a broken ESM entry point, is documented as monorepo-only, and ships a critical vulnerability. Using @hashgraph/sdk directly turned out better, because the cap became a protocol-level property rather than something we wrote and hoped was correct.
Ethereum Sepolia holds QuotaAnchor, a minimal event-and-authorization contract that reads the cap and yield ratios live from ENS resolver text records and checks an EAC role before recording anything. Verified on Etherscan, Blockscout and Sourcify.
ENS v2 is the policy layer, not decoration. Season subname expiry is the mint window. Text records are the canonical cap and yield ratios. EAC roles are the delegation mechanism, and they split authority three ways: a control body holds admin rights and can appoint or remove issuers without ever holding a minting right itself. Participant subnames are non-transferable, achieved simply by not granting ROLE_CAN_TRANSFER_ADMIN, which we confirmed by reading the verified registry source rather than guessing.
The Graph makes it queryable, with one shared schema across multiple consortia and the same query working for any of them by changing only the consortium id.
The genuinely hacky part is the bridge. Subgraph mappings are deterministic sandboxed WASM and cannot call REST, so they can't reach Hedera's mirror node. Reconciliation therefore happens off-chain: a script pulls full mint history from the mirror node, compares it against the full anchor-event history across every contract address this project has ever deployed to, and records unmatched mints as new Sepolia events the subgraph then indexes. The reconciler is the detector; the subgraph makes its findings queryable. We say so explicitly rather than implying the subgraph does something it structurally can't.
What we'd most like read is the design history, because almost every decision here was forced by a measurement rather than assumed, and the rejected alternatives are documented with the status codes that killed them.
Burning reopens mint headroom, since maxSupply caps circulating supply rather than lifetime issuance, so we retire instead of burn.
Freeze is bidirectional and leaves retirement reversible until frozen, so we don't use it for finality.
Hedera validates key satisfiability on both create and update, so a genuinely unspendable account is impossible. An empty KeyList returns KEY_REQUIRED, an impossible threshold returns INVALID_ADMIN_KEY.
A discarded key was rejected on principle, not evidence, because "we deleted it" is unverifiable. A key derived from a published hash is worse cryptographically and better epistemically, since anyone can reproduce and check it.
Auto-association can't bootstrap a KYC-gated token, since KYC requires prior association and association requires a signature.
ENS role expiry works by version-shifting rather than an expiry branch. An empirical result contradicted our own source reading, and re-reading found the real mechanism.
Admin-tier role bits cannot be granted through ordinary grantRoles at all, because the bit-shift overflows uint256. The only route is register()'s extraRoleBitmap, which grants to exactly one address at registration, so rotating an admin requires unregister and re-register.
A final self-audit found the README claiming a full-history retirement-outflow reconciler that was never built. Only an opportunistic tripwire exists. We fixed the documentation rather than quietly building the component, and the asymmetry is now stated plainly.
One more, found while assembling the evidence. Our cap-failure script never logged its own transaction ID, because submit was declared inside the try block and was out of scope in the catch. The transaction existed regardless, since Hedera recorded the failure whether or not we printed it, so we paged the mirror node's full mint history for the treasury account, found the single non-SUCCESS result among forty, and opened it on HashScan to confirm the page itself reads TOKEN_MAX_SUPPLY_REACHED before linking it. All four refusals are now independently checkable by someone who runs nothing.

name: GrantLane
description: A grants program that can't be gamed by fake applicants and pays out the moment work is verified.
projectDescription:
GrantLane is a milestone grant escrow where a claim has to survive a challenge before it pays out. A grantor escrows USDC against a list of milestones up front, and the money is released milestone by milestone without anyone approving each one by hand.
An applicant applies with a pitch, a repo and proposed milestones, after passing a World ID Selfie Check so the queue is people rather than scripts. The grantor adjusts the scope and escrows the total in one transaction, which also commits a hash of the agreed milestone terms on-chain, so nobody can quietly rewrite what a milestone required.
When a milestone is done, the grantee publishes their evidence (a summary plus a live link, demo video or repo) and claims it with a 1 USDC bond. The claim becomes an assertion on UMA's Optimistic Oracle V3, carrying a link to the evidence and its hash. The claim is then open to dispute for a set window: 5 minutes in the demo, 48 hours in real use. If nobody disputes it, it pays out and the bond comes back. Anyone who thinks it's false can dispute by matching the bond, and UMA decides; whoever was wrong loses their bond to the other side. A rejected milestone simply reopens for a better claim.
This design came from throwing out an earlier version that scored evidence automatically. No automated scorer can tell whether work is actually good, so rather than pretend to judge, GrantLane makes lying expensive: the evidence is public, the claim is bonded, and the challenge is open to anyone.
Two more things it enforces. Approved money is credited and withdrawn rather than pushed, so no failed transfer can block a settlement. And a grantor can't pull funds out from under a claim that's live or disputed. Settlement is open to anyone, and a Chainlink CRE workflow does it on a schedule.
Everything runs live on Base Sepolia: escrow 0x85AC2a3e1EBc0959599025eB6eF36eD34c862840, with a full run of funding, claiming, disputing, settling and withdrawing recorded as real transactions in the repo.
howItsMade:
Contracts are Solidity 0.8.24 with Foundry and OpenZeppelin 5.1. GrantEscrow integrates UMA's Optimistic Oracle V3 directly: a claim pulls the bond from the grantee, approves the oracle, and asserts with the grantee as asserter so the bond returns to them. UMA's assertionResolvedCallback and assertionDisputedCallback are restricted to the oracle and ignore assertions the escrow didn't make, since anyone can name your contract as a callback recipient. Payouts are pull-payment, settlement is permissionless, and closeGrant is blocked while a claim is open. Two EIP-712 types (MilestoneClaim, PayoutWalletChange) let the server authorise actions without ever holding a key or paying gas. 60 tests: 45 against a mock oracle that mirrors UMA's bond and callback rules, 8 for the receiver, and 7 fork tests against the real UMA oracle and Circle USDC.
The frontend is Next.js 14 (App Router) with wagmi v2, viem and Tailwind driven by CSS-variable design tokens. Applications and evidence bundles live in Upstash Redis. Evidence is content-addressed: /evidence/<hash> recomputes both the evidence hash and the terms hash and shows whether they match the chain, so a disputer doesn't have to trust the site.
World ID uses IDKit 4.x with the selfieCheckLegacy preset. The rp_context is signed server-side, proofs are verified through World's Developer Portal API, and the server issues short-lived HMAC-signed tickets which are exchanged for the EIP-712 attestation the user submits themselves.
For Chainlink, the plan was Automation, but its testnet service was sunset in June 2026. I confirmed that on-chain: the Base Sepolia registry had performed zero upkeeps. So settlement moved to a CRE cron workflow following Chainlink's migration path: it runs the escrow's checkUpkeep off-chain, signs a report whose payload is the escrow's own performData, and the forwarder delivers it to a receiver contract that can only call performUpkeep. Deploy access is still pending, so it currently runs from the CRE CLI with real transactions through the mock forwarder, which the UI and docs state plainly.
The hackiest part was answering a UMA dispute on testnet. The sandbox oracle only accepts an answer for a price it actually requested, and the request's ancillary data is assertionId:…,ooAsserter:…, where ooAsserter turns out to be the assertion's asserter, not the oracle. I found that by tracing a failing fork test and comparing the bytes.

name: TrueTick
description: Live fair-price & deviation for tokenized stocks across issuers and chains, sold to agents via x402.
projectDescription:
The same real-world stock is now tokenized by several issuers, on several chains, in several DEX pools — and they don't agree. NVDA alone exists as NVDAon (Ondo, Ethereum), NVDAx (Backed, on both Ethereum and Solana), NVDA (Robinhood Chain) and NVDAc (Coinbase B20, Base). A per-chain dashboard shows you one of them and tells you nothing about the other four.
TrueTick puts all of them in one table, priced against the real-world reference, so you can see which price is real.
Right now the reliable venues agree within about 0.5–0.8% of each other — and one NVDA pool prices at $1,153 against a real $218. That pool holds $27k and hasn't traded in 24 hours. TrueTick doesn't hide it: it shows the number and flags it as phantom-liquidity and price-divergence. The agreement between the honest venues is what makes the outlier legible.
Two rules run through the whole system. Every price field is number | null, never 0 — a zero propagates silently through arithmetic and renders as a real price, which is exactly how two silent-$0 bugs in our own subgraph would have shipped unnoticed. And a bad price is always labelled, never dropped: market-closed, thin-volume, phantom-liquidity, subgraph-syncing, source-error. The headline spread is computed across reliable venues only, because including the broken pool would report a spectacular, meaningless "428% spread".
The data is the product, so it's sold rather than given away. The price service sits behind x402: an agent requests it, gets HTTP 402, pays 0.01 HBAR settled through the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet, and receives the data plus a transaction id it can verify on HashScan. An MCP server lets Claude Desktop be that paying agent — it names a ticker, our server decides to spend, and the wallet key never reaches the model.
Everything is live on-chain data. Nothing is mocked.
howItsMade:
The core is one normalized schema (TokenizedStockPoint) with one adapter per venue. Adding a chain or a DEX is a new adapter file plus registry rows — the schema, quality rules, HTTP service and UI are untouched. That isn't a claim, it's the record: adding Solana (non-EVM, base58 addresses, no chain id, a DEX with no swap event) required zero schema changes; the types file gained two optional fields.
Four data sources, across two Graph products:
• Ethereum (Ondo, Backed) — Uniswap v4 subgraph. v4 exposes no USD price, so it's derivedETH × Bundle.ethPriceUSD, cross-checked against the deepest traded pool's own ratio. Using the deepest pool by TVL instead flagged a false 4.97% divergence caused by an untraded memecoin pair.
• Robinhood Chain (Uniswap V3) — Substreams. The Graph's networks registry lists "subgraphs": [] for eip155:4663, so no subgraph was possible.
• Solana (Raydium CLMM) — Substreams. There's no swap event to decode, so price comes from vault balance deltas: decode the CLMM PoolState for the pool's two vaults, diff pre/post token balances, and skip same-sign pairs (those are liquidity adds, not trades).
• Base (Coinbase B20, Aerodrome Slipstream) — a subgraph we forked, fixed and published ourselves, because none existed for that CL factory. So we're a Graph publisher, not just a consumer.
Both Substreams adapters compose prebuilt StreamingFast foundational modules driven by query-string params — there's no Rust in the repo. The .spkg files are vendored so the pipeline doesn't depend on registry availability at runtime.
Publishing the subgraph surfaced two bugs that would have produced a healthy-looking subgraph returning $0 everywhere: upstream whitelisted USDC at Avalanche's address (eth_getCode proves no contract exists there on Base), and getEthPriceInUSD loaded a Uniswap pool that an Aerodrome-only subgraph never indexes, so ethPriceUSD was 0 and every USD field with it.
Payments: x402 v2 with the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet, HBAR (asset 0.0.0), settled as a native HAPI TransferTransaction — so the receipt is a Hedera tx id, not an EVM hash, and the facilitator pays the network fee as co-signer. The client cross-checks the challenge's advertised feePayer against Blocky402's published signers before spending, because pointing at a generic x402 facilitator would still settle, still show real transactions, and silently miss the requirement. Settlement happens after the handler returns and is cancelled on a 4xx/5xx, so a failed request costs nothing.
The MCP server exposes six tools to Claude Desktop. The hacky-but-necessary part: Claude Desktop cancels a tool call at 60s and a cold Substreams venue takes 105–120s. Paying first risked settling after the client gave up — charged, nothing shown. So get_deviation probes warmth with a free request first and refuses to pay while cold, and concurrent requests for a ticker are deduped into one fetch (three "parallel" calls were queueing on the 2-session cap and all looking like cold starts).
Favourite bug: byAddress() lowercased its input, correct for EVM hex and silently wrong for base58 — 'Xsc9qvGR…' is not 'xsc9qvgr…', so every Solana lookup would have missed and the venue would simply have been absent.
