name: DEADMAN
description: An x402 escrow whose refund is executed by the Hedera network itself. No keeper, no arbiter.
projectDescription: Every x402 payment on Hedera eventually asks the same question: what happens if the seller just goes silent? Usually the answer is someone has to step in — the buyer, an arbiter, a hosted watchdog service — and now you're trusting that someone to notice, to act, and to stay online. DEADMAN removes that someone entirely. The moment a buyer pays into escrow, the contract schedules its own refund using Hedera's HIP-1215 (scheduleCall) — in the same transaction, before anything can go wrong. If the seller delivers and reveals the right key, they get paid and the scheduled refund cancels itself. If they never respond, nothing needs to happen — the network just executes the refund it already scheduled, on its own, with zero signatures. We proved this isn't theoretical by literally killing our own server mid-flow: the process holding the decryption key was gone, and the refund fired anyway, right on schedule. Built for a world where the buyer paying is an AI agent, not a person who can chase down a refund manually.
howItsMade: DEADMAN is a HoldEscrow contract on Hedera, EVM-equivalent, wired into an x402 payment flow. The trick that makes the whole thing possible is HIP-1215 — Hedera's scheduleCall — which lets a contract arm a future call to itself inside the very transaction that accepts payment. No cron job, no relayer, no keeper bot polling a database. The network is the keeper. On top of that sits a hash-commitment scheme: before payment is even accepted, the seller commits to hashes of the key, the ciphertext, and the underlying message. Payout only unlocks by revealing a key that matches — and a mismatch is provable on-chain, not just taken on faith (see verify.ts). We spent most of our time not on the happy path but breaking it: fifteen adversarial spikes against real testnet behavior — gas floors that silently ate transactions, revert edge cases around scheduled calls, a mirror node that occasionally lied about its own state. We kept the ones that failed in the docs instead of hiding them. The live board and server are both deployed and talking to real testnet transactions, not mocked — including the demo where we kill the server mid-flow and the scheduled refund still fires with zero signatures.

name: GroupBet
description: Private prediction markets for small groups to create personalized events.
projectDescription: We built private prediction markets that let small groups bet on events that cannot be covered by traditional prediction markets. The way it works is someone in the group can create a market with a description describing anything they want to bet on. Then, the members of the group can purchase contracts betting on a certain outcome, and once the outcome has happened someone can submit a photo as "proof" of the outcome. If the photo proves either the "Yes" or "No" decisions on the market the market will resolve and the bettors will be paid out.
howItsMade: We used Privy to allow for easy onboarding by automatically creating and funding wallets for our users, and we used Bazantic to seamlessly integrate API calls from Privy and our own app. This allows humans and agents alike to use our platform. We built our own prediction markets from scratch on Solana, with pricing determined by an AMM with an LMSR algorithm. We used the OpenAI image API to create a description for the submitted resolution image, which is sanitized and passed back into the API to create a resolution for the market with a confidence level. We also support notifications through Telegram to notify users of important shifts in their predictions and groups.

name: Repo Shield
description: Know what a GitHub repo does before you run it, a  scanner for fake-interview malware.
projectDescription:
Fake recruiters send developers "take-home assignments" as GitHub repos. Opening the folder in VS Code or running npm install is enough to steal your SSH keys and drain your crypto wallet — the code looks completely normal. This is the Contagious Interview campaign (attributed to the Lazarus Group), and it's hitting engineers now: our submission includes real LinkedIn posts from people it happened to.
Every existing scanner (Socket, Snyk) is built for the repo owner and needs an app or CI action installed. But when a "recruiter" invites you to a private repo as an outside collaborator, you have read access and nothing else — so you clone it blindly or walk away.
RepoShield is the first candidate-side scanner. You paste a repo (public with no sign-in, or private via GitHub OAuth) and it reads what the code actually executes — install hooks, editor auto-run tasks, obfuscated payloads, credential-access patterns, typosquatted dependencies — using a two-phase pipeline: 38 fast static rules find the risky files, then an LLM reads only those and explains the execution flow in plain English. You get a 0–100 threat score, a verdict, and a copy-pasteable plan to inspect the repo safely without ever running it.
Two things make it more than a linter: it can run the entire analysis inside a Chainlink CRE enclave, so a private/company repo is scanned without our servers or a public AI ever seeing the source; and it publishes verdicts to an onchain registry indexed by The Graph, which the LLM reads back — so a repo whose owner has a pattern of flagged repos is caught before its code is even read.
howItsMade:
The core is a TypeScript analysis engine (38 heuristics + a classifier + a Gemini phase-2 pass) inside a Next.js 16 app on Vercel. A key design choice: the engine is a pure function with zero I/O, so the exact same analyzeRepo() runs in the browser and inside a hardware enclave.
Chainlink CRE (Confidential Workflows): the workflow is a handlerInTee running in an AWS Nitro enclave. It fetches the developer's GitHub OAuth token and the Gemini key from the Vault DON, reads the private repo over the confidential-HTTP capability (token never leaves the TEE), runs the full scan, and returns only a 7-field aggregate verdict to the DON — the findings quote source code, so they stay inside. Making the engine run in CRE's WASM runtime meant it couldn't use fetch, crypto, Buffer or setTimeout — all banned — so we hand-wrote SHA-256/base64/UTF-8 and inject an HttpClient. It compiles to WASM and simulates end-to-end via the cre CLI. We also implemented the ETH-signed JWT (alg: ETH) the gateway needs to trigger a deployed workflow.
The Graph: a ScanRegistry contract (Foundry, on Sepolia) emits ScanPublished; a subgraph on Subgraph Studio indexes it. Before analysis, the app queries the subgraph live for prior verdicts on the repo AND its owner (name_starts_with), and feeds that into the LLM's prompt and the score — making The Graph a load-bearing decision input, not a display.
Hacky bit worth mentioning: repos are fetched as one gzip tarball via GitHub's archive endpoint, which 302-redirects to codeload — unmetered against the API rate limit. A whole scan costs ~2 API calls instead of 15+, so we read 100% of a repo's files instead of a sample. Contracts use Foundry; the app and gateway signing use viem.

name: NanoAffliate
description: Affiliate payouts by the second, not the month — verified human, settled on Hedera.
projectDescription:
NanoAffiliate is a pay-per-second affiliate marketing platform built natively on Hedera. Instead of the usual pay-per-click model — where creators wait 30–90 days for commissions and sellers pay for traffic that's often fraudulent — we meter and pay out real, verified human attention in 5-second intervals, settled instantly on-chain.
At the center is our Attention Trust Oracle: a real x402-gated service on Hedera that scores every 5-second interval of a reader's session — tab activity, interaction patterns, scroll behavior, device signals, and cross-session diversity — and returns a trust verdict. Our Hedera Agent calls it autonomously, pays for every call via x402, and when a session is verified, pays the creator directly through a native Hedera transfer from the seller's on-chain escrow. Sessions that stay ambiguous get escalated to a Selfie Check, a biometric liveness proof that also unlocks a premium, verified-attention pricing tier.
Every affiliate link is its own dedicated Hedera Consensus Service topic — the same identifier a creator shares as a link is the identifier anyone can paste into a public Hedera explorer to see that link's complete, tamper-proof history of clicks, attention ticks, and trust decisions. Both the Oracle and the Agent carry portable HCS-14 identities, so the service relationship being paid for is provably real, not just an account number paying another account number.
The result: creators get paid in real time instead of months later, sellers only pay for attention that's actually verified rather than guessed at, and the entire system is independently auditable by anyone — not because we ask you to trust our dashboard, but because you don't have to.
howItsMade:
NanoAffiliate is built entirely on Hedera's native services, deliberately avoiding smart contracts since none of the logic requires on-chain computation — the Consensus, Account, Crypto Transfer, and Schedule services do everything needed.
The core loop: every affiliate link is its own dedicated HCS topic, created at link-generation time — the topic ID doubles as the shareable URL, so pasting a link into a browser redirects to the product, and pasting the same ID into HashScan shows that exact link's full, tamper-proof click/attention/trust history. Every 5 seconds a reader is on the page, our Hedera Agent (built on Hedera Agent Kit, running autonomously) calls our Attention Trust Oracle — a stateless Express service scoring tab state, interaction recency, scroll naturalness, device fingerprinting, and cross-session diversity. That call is gated by @x402/hedera, settled through the Blocky402 testnet facilitator — a real, metered, pay-per-call service, not a free internal function dressed up as one. When a tick passes, the Agent fires a separate, plain Hedera TransferTransaction from the seller's escrow to the creator — deliberately not x402, since there's no resource being gated on a push payment, just a payer and a payee.
Identity: the Oracle and Agent each carry an HCS-14 UAID — a SHA-384 hash of six canonical fields (registry, name, version, protocol, native Hedera account ID, skills), deterministic and independently recomputable by anyone, with HCS-11 profile documents published to a shared identity-registry topic.
Escrow: every seller gets their own distinct Hedera account, but all of them share one key — the Agent's own — so payouts need no per-seller secret lookup, while balances stay individually verifiable on Mirror Node.
Partner tech: Blocky402 for x402 settlement, World ID's Selfie Check for the one fraud signal that's a genuine hard stop rather than a heuristic — a bot farm can defeat IP diversity with rotated residential proxies, but it can't hold a real face to a camera. Redis + BullMQ drive the 5-second tick scheduler and a rolling session-diversity aggregate.
The hacky bit worth admitting: for the hackathon build, Amazon products are supported via manually-entered product data rather than the Product Advertising API, since PA-API now requires 10 qualifying sales in a trailing 30 days just to keep access — impossible for a fresh project. Purchase confirmation for those links is honestly self-reported, not webhook-verified, because Amazon exposes no real-time conversion API to third-party affiliates at all — a platform limitation, not one we could engineer around.

name: Covenant_Hedera
description: Covenant is a lending console for private credit where a program sets the collateral value
projectDescription:
you would not lend someone money against their house and also let them tell you what the
house is worth. private credit runs close to that: a fund holds a pile of loans, values them
itself, and borrows against its own number. the Financial Stability Board found that the same
loan gets different marks at different managers, because the judgement behind the mark is the
manager's own (FSB, Report on Vulnerabilities in Private Credit, 6 May 2026, section 3.3).
covenant takes that valuation out of self-marking. a confidential compute engine reads the
underlying borrower's revenue, EBITDA, total debt, cash and interest expense, and returns two
things only: a covenant pass or fail, and a haircut. both sides read the program before the
facility is struck. the lender never sees the financials behind the number, and can still
check that the published program produced it.
what is live: a real note issued on Hedera testnet through the Asset Tokenization Studio,
against its deployed resolver and factory, no new Solidity and no contract deployed. the full
lifecycle runs: issuance, a transfer blocked by a compliance gate then granted then permitted,
a coupon priced and distributed, and a collateral hold created, released, created again and
executed on default. 21 transactions, signed by a human in MetaMask throughout, four gates
independently re-verified against Hedera's mirror node and the testnet json-rpc relay. every
hash is in EVIDENCE.md in the repository.
howItsMade:
Hedera testnet, the Asset Tokenization Studio SDK (@hashgraph/[email protected])
against its already-deployed resolver 0.0.9212226 and factory 0.0.9213391. we deploy no
contracts and write no Solidity: issuance, the KYC compliance gate, the coupon and the
collateral hold all run on ATS's own diamond, through the SDK. the benefit is concrete: a
compliance-gated, coupon-bearing, hold-capable security token is not something we built, it is
something ATS already gave us, correctly, on testnet, and we spent our time on the
confidential leg instead of reimplementing a compliance facet.
Next.js 16 and React 19 for the console, with the confidential compute engine built as a plain
local service behind one swappable interface, CovenantEngine (lib/engine/types.ts). the entire
surface for a different implementation is one file, lib/engine/registry.ts: no caller names a
concrete provider. that is the shape a Chainlink CRE handlerInTee needs to drop into without
touching a single route or component, and we proved the swap. we did not ship it live inside
the build's timebox, and we say so rather than imply a deployment that did not happen: what
shipped is the interface a real handlerInTee would sit behind, not a running enclave.
the hacky part, and it is the most interesting thing we found. ATS's own
Bond.createKpiLinkedRate cannot work on the deployed factory: it calls a factory function that
exists only in MockFactory.sol, a test-only contract, and the KPI-linked bond configuration is
registered in the deployed resolver but unreachable by any working path. we root-caused this
from source and on chain, filed it as B1, and routed around it by issuing on the working
variable-rate configuration instead, then driving the coupon rate through
setCouponRateType(FIXED) and a role-gated setRate, both called directly against the deployed
contract because the SDK exposes neither method. that single workaround is what makes the
coupon's rate provably token-enforced rather than caller-supplied: the token refused a rate
handed to it at setCoupon and stamped the value FixedRate.setRate had written 33 seconds
earlier instead, checkable on HashScan without trusting us.
fifteen defects surfaced by building a working flow against the SDK, not by auditing it for
faults, filed in BUG.md as B1 through B15, two of which we investigated and withdrew after
finding the actual cause was ours, not the SDK's.
the confidentiality boundary is enforced by a committed script, npm run scan:disclosure, which
builds the console for production and scans every asset the lender's and holder's pages ship
for the borrower's raw financial fields and figures. it was tested on itself: we deliberately
introduced a leak, confirmed the script failed on it, then removed the leak and confirmed a
clean pass, so the check is proven to fire rather than assumed to.
built by one person, hao, directing a team of AI agent configurations running on Claude. the
agent definitions and the specs and prompts that drove this build are committed in the
repository, in .claude/agents/ and specs/, not written after the fact. every one of the 21
transactions on chain was signed by a human in MetaMask: ATS SDK v8 ships no local-key signer
(SupportedWallets.CLIENT is disabled in its source), so no agent could have signed any of
them, and this is independently checkable on Hedera's mirror node, not asserted. full account:
AI_USAGE.md.

name: Conduit
description: Buy AI inference from a peer's GPU, paid per answer in USDC on Arc. No server, no cloud.
projectDescription:
Conduit is a serverless, peer-to-peer marketplace for AI inference. You buy an answer directly from someone else's GPU and pay them per answer in USDC. There is no server in the middle, no account on either side, and your prompt never touches a cloud  peers find each other over a DHT and the model runs on the seller's own machine.
The core idea is that the payment is the access handshake: a seller's inference runtime sits behind a firewall that only opens for a buyer who has settled. A freeloader connecting without paying is refused at the handshake and gets zero bytes.
PRE-EXISTING (built June–July 2026 for QVAC Hackathon I): the P2P marketplace itself — Hyperswarm discovery, the payment-gated provider handshake, the on-device capability prober that decides what a machine can sell, the ConduitEscrow payment-channel contract, and the Electron desktop app.
NEW THIS HACKATHON (Continuity track):
• Migrated settlement to Arc Testnet (chain 5042002), where USDC is both the gas token and the token answers are priced in — so a seller earns and spends one asset instead of earning one and paying fees in another.
• Built a subgraph on The Graph indexing every channel the escrow has ever opened, so a first-time buyer can see how a seller treated everyone, not just themselves. Crucially it classifies withdrawals rather than counting them: probes and session renewals are indexed and visible but excluded from scoring, because a naive settled/withdrawn tally is trivially gamed.
• Added a World personhood gate via AgentKit. A seller can require that a buyer is a verified unique human; the wallet resolves to an anonymous human id in AgentBook on World Chain - never an identity. This is what makes the reputation layer expensive to forge: buying a reputation now costs a person, not gas.
• Removed the free local-answer tier entirely. Every answer is bought from a peer, so the market is never invisible.
Demonstrated end to end across two machines: a Mac buyer is refused as an unverified human, verifies by scanning a QR in World App, then buys answers from a Linux GPU - settling six answers in two on-chain transactions
howItsMade:
Stack: TypeScript throughout. Hyperswarm/HyperDHT handles serverless peer discovery and NAT hole-punching. QVAC, Tether's on-device runtime, runs the models: Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B/4B and Llama 3.2 1B. Inference is delegated over an end-to-end encrypted Noise link, so model weights never leave the seller and prompts never reach a cloud service. ethers v6 handles signing, Solidity + Hardhat handles the escrow, React + Electron powers the desktop app, and node:test runs the suite with 79 tests and zero new test dependencies.
ARC: settlement. ConduitEscrow (0xdC48E5e5c3Cf91b6db9ec0f329a14188174632C2) is an EIP-712 payment-channel contract. A channel is opened once with a deposit, then every answer gets an off-chain signed voucher containing a cumulative total. The seller can redeem everything in a single claim.
The reason Arc worked particularly well here is that USDC is both the gas token and the settlement token. A seller earns and spends the same asset, which makes sense for a machine selling compute. One subtle issue took some debugging: Arc exposes the same balance through two views, native at 18 decimals and ERC-20 at 6. The ERC-20 view is a floored projection, so gas accounting has to happen in native units or you can lose a base unit on each reading.
THE GRAPH: reputation. AssemblyScript mappings index Opened, Settled, and Withdrawn events from the escrow. The interesting part is the classification, not just counting events.
On the original Sepolia deployment, both real Withdrawn events came from the same buyer reopening 24 seconds later. That is loyalty, but a naive counter would classify it as abandonment and give the seller a 0.0 score.
So withdrawals are split into qualified abandonment, probes, and renewals. Probes are sessions that were too short, too small, or came from a buyer with no settlement history. Only qualified abandonment affects the reputation score.
The UI shows both the naive score and the hardened score, so the difference is visible instead of just being claimed.
WORLD: personhood. AgentKit's createAgentBookVerifier resolves a wallet to an anonymous humanId through AgentBook on World Chain.
There were two gotchas worth calling out. lookupHuman(0x0) returns a NON-ZERO id, so the zero address has to be rejected before the lookup. Otherwise, an unfunded wallet could appear to be a human.
The second issue was validateAgentkitMessage. It compares only the URI host, not the path. That meant a proof issued for one seller could validate for another seller. We added an explicit seller binding check.
Registration happens directly in the app. The engine spawns the AgentKit CLI as a managed child process. Since the CLI only draws an ASCII QR code to a TTY, the QR is generated client-side from the link emitted by the CLI.
A few other hacky bits were needed to make the desktop builds actually work.
npm does not preserve the executable bit inside published packages, so the bundled Bare runtime was shipped as 0644. The app then failed with EACCES inside a squashfs AppImage and EROFS on a read-only DMG. An afterPack hook now restores the executable bit.
The macOS prebuild of the llama.cpp addon links Homebrew's OpenSSL using an absolute path. The same hook vendors the required dylibs into the bundle, rewrites the load commands to @loader_path, and ad-hoc re-signs the binaries. install_name_tool invalidates the signature, and without re-signing, Apple Silicon refuses to dlopen the addon.
The runtime also cannot restart a provider inside the same process. So the seller proves it can actually serve by launching its own binary in a child process, loading the model, and exiting. The exit code becomes the answer.
Finally, the firewall allow-list could not be amended once the provider was running. That meant a seller could only serve the first buyer who paid. The allow-list is now accumulated before the provider starts, so multiple buyers can connect.

name: Veritas_IITD Markets
description: On-chain prediction markets for campus events — real stakes for students, real signal for colleges.
projectDescription:
Veritas (IITD Markets)
For students: put your money where your prediction is. Pick a side in any inter-hostel event — cricket finals, sports championships, any competition with a real outcome — and stake USDC on it. Win, and you don't just get bragging rights: you claim a proportional share of everyone who backed the losing side, after a 10% platform fee. It turns campus rivalry into something with actual stakes, and gives you a live, crowd-priced read on who's actually favored before the event happens.
For institutions: Veritas isn't just a betting app for students — it's a plug-in engagement and insight layer for the college itself. Student councils and event bodies get a transparent, on-chain gauge of real sentiment (backed by real money, not casual polls) around their own events, which drives attention and participation toward those events in the run-up. It's a product a college can point to as infrastructure it runs, not just something students happen to use.
Two sponsor integrations are load-bearing, not decorative. Resolution is handled by a Chainlink CRE workflow that fetches the official result through a confidential-compute step and writes it on-chain via a DON-signed report through a Forwarder → Receiver contract, rather than a plain script or a trusted admin key. Uniswap V2 is used two ways: users can swap ETH for USDC and place a bet in one transaction if they don't already hold USDC, and every bet mints a transferable ERC20 "position token" that's listed on its own Uniswap pair — so a user can exit a position before resolution, or someone else can buy into a position on the open market and later claim the payout themselves, never having placed a bet at all.
Payouts are claim-based rather than pushed to avoid unbounded gas costs as the number of bettors grows. The full stack — Solidity contracts, the CRE workflow, and a React/wagmi frontend with market list, betting, and results/claim screens — is tested end-to-end, including a headless-browser verification of the actual wallet-connected UI against a live local deployment.
howItsMade:
The stack is Hardhat + Solidity 0.8.24 for the contracts, a two-agent split repo (Chainlink resolution side / Market+Uniswap+frontend side, coordinated via AGENT_COORDINATION_*.md docs), and a React + TypeScript + Vite frontend using wagmi/viem for wallet and contract calls.
Contracts: Market.sol owns the OPEN→CLOSED→RESOLVED lifecycle: USDC-denominated createMarket/placeBet/closeMarket, and a claim-based (never looped) payout so gas cost stays flat regardless of how many people bet. resolveMarket is gated to a single resolver address, designed from the start to eventually be CREMarketResolverReceiver rather than an EOA.
Chainlink CRE: the resolution side is a Chainlink CRE workflow with a confidential-compute step that fetches and validates the official competition result, then writes on-chain via a DON-signed report through a Forwarder → CREMarketResolverReceiver.onReport → Market.resolveMarket. We built a mock resolver first (same validation logic, plain EOA signer) so the market side could be built and tested against a real call path before the CRE deployment existed, then verified the real receiver contract against it with a dedicated integration test.
Uniswap: two integrations, both load-bearing. placeBetWithETH swaps ETH → USDC through a real Uniswap V2 Router and bets the actual received amount in one transaction. More ambitiously, every bet also mints a transferable ERC20 "position token" (OutcomeToken, 1:1 with USDC staked) that createMarket lists on its own Uniswap V2 pair against USDC — a genuine secondary market, not an internal ledger. claim() was reworked to pay out (and burn) whoever currently holds the winning token, not whoever originally placed the bet, since that's the entire point of making it tradeable.
Notably hacky bits:

Vendoring the real Uniswap V2 Factory/Router locally for tests hit the classic gotcha where UniswapV2Library's hardcoded CREATE2 init-code-hash only matches Uniswap's original 0.5.16 build — a different Hardhat/solc/optimizer config produces different UniswapV2Pair bytecode, so every swap silently resolved to the wrong (non-contract) pair address. Fixed by vendoring a patched copy of the library with the hash recomputed from our own build (scripts/lib/computeInitCodeHash.js), and wrote a script to regenerate it if compiler settings ever change.
Listing an OutcomeToken on Uniswap at market-creation time had to degrade gracefully — a call to a Router with no code "succeeds" at the EVM level with empty returndata, and Solidity's try/catch can't catch the resulting ABI-decode failure (it's an uncatchable revert), so we added an explicit code.length check before attempting the call, so the stretch goal never blocks core market creation.
Pulling in OpenZeppelin's Strings (for token symbols) transitively requires the MCOPY opcode, which isn't available under the default paris EVM target — had to explicitly set evmVersion: "cancun" in the Hardhat config.
For frontend verification without a real wallet extension, we drove the actual UI in a headless Playwright browser using a ~40-line fake EIP-1193 provider that forwards eth_sendTransaction etc. straight to a live local Hardhat node (which auto-signs for its own known accounts) — this caught a real bug where the UI's "transaction confirmed" indicator flipped invisible the instant an approve transaction landed, before the user ever saw it.

name: AgentGate
description: Privacy-first payment gateway that lets AI agents make stealth transactions.
projectDescription: AgentGate is a privacy-focused payment gateway built for AI agents. It lets an agent initiate USDC payments using only a recipient’s normal wallet address, while AgentGate resolves the recipient’s registered stealth identity and generates a fresh ERC-5564 stealth destination for each payment. The system is built on Base Sepolia and exposes an agent-friendly MCP interface through Bazantic, while keeping transaction signing isolated from the agent-facing API.
howItsMade: AgentGate is built with TypeScript, Node.js, a REST API, Supabase/PostgreSQL, and Base Sepolia smart contracts. The payment engine prepares USDC transfers and integrates ERC-5564 stealth payments through a custom helper contract that calls the canonical ERC-5564 Announcer. Bazantic provides the agent-facing Gateway, MCP server, and Recipe, allowing Codex and other agents to interact with AgentGate using natural-language payment requests. A separate signer handles transaction execution so private keys never enter the Gateway or MCP layer. The frontend is built with React, Vite, and Tailwind for wallet connection and payment-plan testing.

name: WalletOS
description: WalletOS an AI companion for w3 wallets makes your autonomous workflows smarter, safer, and easier!
projectDescription:
WalletOS is an agentic intelligence layer for crypto wallets. It gives users a way to connect their existing AI agent, such as Codex or Claude Code, to their wallets and dApps so the agent can understand context, investigate on-chain activity, recommend actions, and prepare transactions for user approval.
Instead of building another wallet with a closed AI assistant, WalletOS turns the user’s own agent into the intelligence layer of the wallet. The agent can use installable WalletOS Skills for tasks such as transaction security, portfolio analysis, protocol research, risk management, and rebalancing.
Our first skill focuses on transaction safety. When a user interacts with an unfamiliar dApp, WalletOS can provide the agent with the page context, contract interaction, calldata, and wallet request so it can compare what the website claims will happen with what the transaction will actually do. This helps users understand risky approvals, deceptive signatures, phishing flows, cloned protocols, and potential wallet-drain behavior before they approve anything.
WalletOS also supports proactive financial workflows. An agent can analyze positions across wallets, identify concentration or idle capital, research protocols, recommend a rebalance, and prepare the required transactions for the user to review and approve.
Sponsor technologies extend the agent’s capabilities: The Graph provides on-chain intelligence for protocol and wallet research, Ledger strengthens the security and trusted signing workflow, and Privy enables agentic wallet and execution use cases.
The long-term vision is an open marketplace of Web3 agent skills, similar to extensions for an IDE, where developers can publish reusable capabilities and the user’s AI agent decides when and how to use them.
Your wallet provides custody. Your agent provides intelligence. WalletOS connects both.
howItsMade:
WalletOS is built as a browser extension + local desktop runtime. The extension captures dApp and wallet context, while the desktop companion runs local agents such as Codex and gives them access to WalletOS Skills.
The key idea is the runtime: instead of hard-coding every blockchain integration into the app, WalletOS loads plugins/skills that tell the agent which tools to use for a task. A skill can combine CLIs, MCPs, APIs, and scripts, so new capabilities can be added without changing the core app.
For example, our security skill uses Foundry tools such as Cast and Anvil to decode and simulate transactions. The Graph is used by research and portfolio skills to query on-chain protocol and wallet data. Ledger is integrated into the security and signing flow, including local testing with Speculos. Privy is used for agentic wallet and execution workflows.
The most hacky part is that WalletOS does not run its own AI model. It launches the user’s existing local agent and turns it into a wallet-specialized agent by giving it runtime context plus installable Web3 skills. This lets us keep the core lightweight while making the system extensible across many protocols and partner technologies.

↓
AGENT RUNTIME
↓
PLUGIN MARKETPLACE
↓
WALLET ACTIONS

name: Sigil
description: Skills for AI agents, backed by staked USDC and verified on-chain, licensed per use via x402
projectDescription: Sigil is a trust layer for AI agent skills. An agent extends itself by installing skills (small tools, MCP servers, snippets of code), and one bad skill can leak a cloud key or drain a wallet. Today an agent has two signals about a skill, the author's description and a scanner's opinion, and neither costs anything to be wrong. Sigil makes being trustworthy cost money. Anyone lists a skill for free; the gateway hashes its source into the skill id, pins the bundle on Hedera as an HCS-1 file and announces it on an HCS registry topic. A staker then locks USDC on Arc behind one machine-testable predicate about the skill: it reads no env var, opens no network connection, reads or writes no path outside an allowlist, starts no subprocess, runs no dynamic code. An agent buys the skill's source per request over x402 on Hedera, gets an HTS licence NFT, and runs the skill in a deterministic sandbox that records every env, file, network, subprocess and eval event and hashes the canonical trace. If the trace breaks the claim, anyone can dispute with a counter-bond and the trace; an independent verifier re-runs the exact bundle from the pinned source, and the contract pays stake plus bond to whichever side the evidence supports. A World Selfie Check nullifier is stored on every claim and dispute so one person cannot hold both sides of a stake. No model adjudicates anything: the only thing behind a claim is capital at risk, and anyone can re-run the evidence. Everything is live on Hedera testnet and Arc testnet: 17 skills listed, real x402 settlements through Blocky402, real USDC escrow on Arc, disputes settled both ways, and the whole loop (register, claim, probe, dispute, resolve, settle) works from the browser.
howItsMade: A pnpm monorepo in TypeScript. The gateway is Express: a JSON index for skills, claims, disputes, resolutions and payments, with Hedera HCS as the audit log. Every event is an HCS message on the registry topic and on a per-claim topic; skill sources and dispute evidence are pinned as HCS-1 files; each buyer gets an HTS licence NFT minted on settlement; the agent carries an HCS-14 identity. Paid access is x402 via @x402/core, @x402/express and @x402/hedera, settled by the Blocky402 facilitator in HBAR or HTS USDC, priced per kilobyte of source; a licence gate reads NFT ownership from the mirror node so holders read free. The sandbox runs the skill in a scrubbed Node child process with an interposition shim that wraps process.env, fs, net.Socket.connect, dns, child_process and eval (the child also runs with --disallow-code-generation-from-strings); canary env vars are planted so a leaking error handler is caught red-handed; the trace is canonicalised and sha256'd, and we verified byte-identical hashes across processes, working directories and a Docker container. Stake custody is a Foundry/Solidity contract on Arc (SigilStake: openClaim, dispute, resolve; DisputeResolver records verdicts), and the agent signs every approve, dispute and resolve as an ERC-4337 user operation from a Circle Agent Stack wallet. The web app is Next.js 16, React, TanStack Query, wagmi/viem and Tailwind, designed as a printed ledger rather than a dashboard. Hacky and worth mentioning: the gateway exposes POST /claims/:id/probe, which runs the claim's skill in the same sandbox on the server, so a browser user gets dispute evidence without the repo; a headless agent cannot open the World widget, so its operator verifies once and lists the nullifier; and the same skill.json folders feed both the UI's example picker and the CLI registration script.

name: Bond Desk
description: Compliant bond desk on Hedera: KYC-gated order book, scheduled coupons, TEE risk monitor
projectDescription:
Bond Desk is a compliant corporate bond market on Hedera testnet, watched by a confidential Chainlink CRE enclave.
The bond is a real Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS) token, created through the live ATS factory on testnet, so it carries its own KYC list, freeze list and transfer rules. An on-chain order book trades it against USDC and asks the token's own compliance check (canTransferFrom) before every fill: KYC is enforced by the contract, not by the UI. Three bonds with different coupon schedules trade on the desk today, each with its own book.
Coupons are paid by the Hedera Schedule Service: the lifecycle contract calls HIP-1215 scheduleCall, Hedera executes it at the due time, and the executed call schedules the next coupon from inside itself. Collateral is native HBAR held in a vault and valued against the live Chainlink HBAR/USD feed on Hedera.
Risk is handled by a Chainlink CRE workflow running inside a TEE. It reads the coverage, compares it with thresholds that never leave the enclave, and signs an EIP-712 verdict (OK, WARN, FREEZE, DEFAULT). Anyone can relay the verdict; the RiskGate contract checks the signature and the nonce, not the sender, and a FREEZE halts trading for that bond only. The policy is private, the verdict is public and verifiable.
The same desk is a web app (a dense trading terminal with full keyboard control), a public OpenAPI service, a paid Bazantic gateway with an MCP server, and a Bazantic Recipe that chains three gateways (Hedera Mirror Node, Bond Desk, Bank of Canada Valet) so an agent can find the best bond a wallet is allowed to hold and whether its coupon beats the sovereign benchmark.
Everything ran on Hedera testnet with verified contracts and a receipt for every step: issuance through ATS, KYC grants, a rejected non-KYC fill and an accepted KYC fill, coupons paid by the Schedule Service on their own, WARN and FREEZE verdicts relayed, a fill rejected while frozen, an unfreeze. Both CRE workflows are deployed on the CRE network: the bond monitor runs hourly against Hedera, and the liquidation-protection workflow defends our position in Chainlink's Sepolia challenge every 30 seconds.
For Hedera's harness track we also opened PR #62 on hedera-dev/hedera-harness, which makes the harness prove that a scheduled transaction executed and that its child transaction succeeded.
Live app: https://wd6nrvmajt.ap-south-1.awsapprunner.com · Docs: https://bond-desk.mintlify.site
howItsMade:
Contracts: Foundry, Solidity 0.8.28, OpenZeppelin v5. Six contracts (BondRegistry, BondMarket, CollateralVault, NavOracle, BondLifecycle, RiskGate) around ATS v8 bond tokens created through the existing testnet factory. ATS is treated as a black box behind its canTransferFrom, KYC, snapshot and freeze facets; we did not fork it. BondLifecycle is the Schedule Service payer: it calls scheduleCall on the 0x16b system contract and each executed coupon arms the next one. We hit the out-of-gas nested schedule and a block.timestamp lag on testnet and fixed both (4M schedule gas, a 10 s lag margin). RiskGate verifies EIP-712 verdicts: trusted signer, strictly increasing nonce per bond, freshness window.
Chainlink CRE: TypeScript SDK, handlerInTee pinned to AWS Nitro, one batched JSON-RPC read per run because Hedera is not a CRE-supported chain, viem signing inside the enclave, secrets in the Vault DON. The same decide.ts policy module drives the Sepolia liquidation-protection workflow, which probes the challenge contract's onlyActive gate inside its read batch so it never spends gas outside a scoring window. The relayer (Node, viem) verifies the signature locally before paying gas; the deployed workflow can also deliver verdicts to Hedera itself.
API and app: Hono on Node 22 with mirror-node history plus eth_call state, an OpenAPI 3.1 document that renders as an interactive reference in a browser and stays JSON for programs, served from one AWS App Runner image together with the Vite/React/wagmi app. The app is a trading terminal: sortable desk, depth ladders, keyboard for everything (j/k/Enter, b/s, arrows to nudge price), a compliance page that shows the token's own decision, a coupon page with the pending schedule, a risk page where anyone can paste and relay a verdict. Every write is simulated first, so a revert is decoded into a sentence before the wallet signs. Testnet self-service KYC works through EIP-191 signed messages and an officer key on the API.
Bazantic: three gateways (Bond Desk API, Hedera Mirror Node testnet, Bank of Canada Valet, the last one written from scratch as an OpenAPI spec) and a Recipe with seven tool bindings, published through Bazantic's control MCP and tested on a KYC wallet and a no-KYC wallet.
Hedera harness: our own Foundry harness with mocks for the 0x16b and 0x167 system contracts, a base test that fires due schedules, and doctor/verify/validate-schedule scripts (42 tests). Upstream, PR #62 on hedera-dev/hedera-harness adds a CHAIN-stage check that reads the scheduled child transaction at its execution timestamp on the mirror node, because the schedules endpoint cannot tell an executed-and-succeeded schedule from an executed-and-reverted one. We exercised the upstream branch end to end on testnet with real reverted fixtures.
Hacky and notable: explicit gas overrides where hashio's estimator is wrong, the scheduling lag margin, splitting CRE secrets across two files to fit a 10-id cap, and discovering that cre execution logs returns confidential-handler logs once per DON node.

name: Zikibols
description: Fund real-world cashflows on Hedera: agent pays for diligence via x402, backers pledge with email.
projectDescription:
A backer should be able to fund an invoice bond or harvest share without a seed phrase, without trusting a screenshot of "DeFi history," and without receiving a meme ticker.
Zikibols is that product: a crowdfunding app for tokenized real-world cashflows, built from scratch for ETHOnline 2026. One app, three load-bearing sponsor integrations — Privy for login and the pledge, The Graph for live diligence, Hedera for paid risk notes, an HCS audit trail, and the token lifecycle.
It is not a general crowdfunding clone. A founder starts a campaign — a diligence-gated listing for invoice receivables or revenue-share assets. After funding, the campaign becomes a restricted token with a coupon that needs two people to release.
Due diligence has two layers:

The campaign (free). When a founder starts a campaign they publish the story, creator name, optional email, and Ethereum wallet. That is the public brief anyone can read without paying.
Paid due diligence. Before pledging, a backer can Check this creator. The agent queries live DeFi books, searches the public web for that name and email, pays Hedera x402 for a written risk note, and hashes the result onto HCS.

A backer can:

Read the campaign, then Check the creator (live Graph + founder research + paid note) before sending money
Pledge HBAR after logging in with email or social (no seed phrase)
See the campaign turn into a restricted Hedera token, then a coupon that needs two people to release
howItsMade:
Zikibols is a Next.js 16 / React 19 app for tokenized invoice and harvest-share campaigns. The stack is three sponsor pipes, not a pile of demos: Privy gets a backer in, The Graph is the only on-chain source the diligence agent is allowed to trust, and Hedera is where money, the audit trail, and the security actually live.
A founder publishes a free campaign brief (story, name, optional email, Ethereum wallet). A backer clicks Check this creator, which hits POST /api/agent. That agent queries Aave v3, Compound v3, and Spark Lend with one Messari lendingProtocols query and one account(id) query through the Graph Gateway. Same schema, three books; one subgraph can 500 without killing diligence. Adding a protocol is one subgraph id. There is no mocked Graph fallback — missing THEGRAPH_API_KEY fails on purpose.
Those live books then become paid compute. The agent pays two x402 services on Hedera testnet through the Blocky402 facilitator: founder OSINT (Tavily, priced per query: name vs name+email) and a written risk note. wrapFetchWithPayment signs HBAR from the agent key, retries on HTTP 402, and we publish both settlement tx ids plus SHA-256 of the note and profile onto an HCS topic. Without Tavily we skip and label the profile; we never invent a biography.
Privy is the only auth. Email/social login creates an embedded EVM wallet (createOnLogin: "users-without-wallets"). The app registers Hedera testnet (chain 296) as the sole chain, switchChains, and sendTransactions HBAR to the campaign treasury. No extension, no seed phrase; HashScan is the receipt. After funding, the Operator desk issues an Asset Tokenization Studio bond (@hashgraph/asset-tokenization-sdk v8): Bond.create clones factory 0.0.9213391, mints one unit to the backer’s Privy 0x, Security.pause is the compliance op, then ICoupon.setCoupon plus a tiny HBAR coupon after a 2-of-2 (Privy founder + treasury). Campaign book, approvals, x402 receiver, and topic id live in .data/state.json — on-chain txs are the source of truth.
What the partners actually unlocked: Blocky402 made a real pay-per-call agent path possible on testnet in days. Messari’s shared lending schema is why three protocols are one query. Privy’s embedded wallets are why a judge can pledge HBAR without MetaMask.
The hacky bit worth mentioning is ATS. The published SDK is MetaMask-first (“only metamask is compatible right now”). We load the CJS build with createRequire so Next doesn’t double-bundle ethers, stub window only around Network.connect({ debug: true }), and inject an ethers Wallet signed by the operator ECDSA key. Internal KYC is on at Bond.create because deployBond encoding requires it, then we deactivateInternalKyc so minting does not need a Terminal3 VC. The SDK’s Coupon.setCoupon sent empty calldata under Next, so we call ICoupon.setCoupon on the diamond ourselves. Coupon size is a lifecycle proof (tinybars), not yield.

name: Agentis
description: Complete financial infrastructure for AI agents, usable via SDK, CLI, MCP or its dashboard
projectDescription:
Agentis gives AI agents wallets and the ability to pay for things—with spending controls set by their owner. Instead of handing an agent an unrestricted private key or manually paying for every request, users create named agents with separate wallets, budgets and permissions. Agents can operate automatically within those limits or request owner approval for each payment.
A shared backend handles authorization, spending reservations, execution and transaction receipts across the dashboard, SDK, CLI and remote MCP. Hosted wallets use Privy, while Agentis enforces per-transaction, hourly, daily and total USD limits across each agent’s networks, including fees. Agents can send funds and access paid APIs through x402 and MPP without managing individual subscriptions or API keys for those services.
For users who prefer local custody, the CLI also supports multichain wallets with keys kept on their own machine rather than in Privy. Local wallets support transfers, x402/MPP payments, shared USD spending limits and transaction history. They use owner-only file permisisons and do not require a hosted Agentis account.
Optional capabilities are enabled per agent. The Uniswap integration adds swaps, manual portfolio rebalancing, recurring purchases, gas refill and swap-to-fund x402 payments—buying only the missing payment-token amount. The current implementation targets testnets across Base, Arc, Tempo and Solana, with Uniswap execution on Base Sepolia. The goal is practical financial autonomy for agents, with clear owner control and a traceable record of what was spent.
howItsMade:
Agentis is a TypeScript monorepo with a Bun/Hono backend, PostgreSQL and Drizzle for persistence, and Zod for input validation. The dashboard uses Next.js, React, Tailwind and TanStack Query. The SDK, CLI and remote MCP server all call the same backend operations rather than implementing separate payment logic. MCP uses the official protocol SDK and OAuth with PKCE; browser consent grants access only to explicitly selected agents and networks.
Privy handles authentication and hosted wallet keys. Wallets use a user/server 1-of-2 ownership quorum, allowing server-authorized execution without a wallet-signature popup for every payment. Agentis—not the quorum itself—enforces spending rules. PostgreSQL transactions and owner-level locks reserve the payment amount plus maximum fees before execution. Amounts use bigint arithmetic and decimal strings, with fresh server-side prices for shared USD budgets. Approvals bind to the exact operation, and signed transaction data is persisted before broadcast so uncertain submissions can be reconciled instead of blindly resent.
Viem handles EVM interactions, while Solana uses its own transaction adapter. x402 and MPP connect agents to paid HTTP services: discover payment requirements, authorize payment, retry the request and retain the payment record even if the service response fails. Local-custody CLI wallets use locally derived keys and a separate local policy ledger, without routing signing through Privy.
Uniswap provides the trading layer on Base Sepolia. One practical workaround was using its deployed V3 Quoter and SwapRouter02 directly after the hosted Trading API returned upstream errors. We compare quotes across four fee tiers and construct bounded calldata ourselves, including exact token allowances, minimum outputs and native-token wrapping/refunds. Swap-to-fund buys only a payment's shortfall using exact output. PostgreSQL-backed schedules run through the existing worker and approval pipeline, so recurring purchases do not require an always-online AI agent or a separate scheduling service.

name: StablePay
description: WakaPay demo store for crypto checkout, webhooks, and merchant payment automation.
projectDescription: This project is a demo merchant storefront built for the ETHGlobal hackathon to showcase how WakaPay can power real-world crypto commerce. It simulates a modern online store where users can browse different product types, add items to a cart, and complete payment through a secure WakaPay checkout flow. Behind the scenes, the app creates signed checkout sessions, redirects users to hosted crypto payment, and listens for payment webhooks to confirm transactions and trigger customer notifications. For a competition jury, the key idea is that this is not just a static UI demo, but an end-to-end proof of how merchants can integrate WakaPay into a production-style e-commerce experience for digital goods, subscriptions, services, tickets, and physical products.
howItsMade: It is built as a Next.js web application with a marketplace-style frontend and a lightweight backend layer inside the same app. The frontend handles product browsing, filtering, cart management, and the checkout trigger, while the backend exposes API routes that prepare payment requests for WakaPay. When a user starts checkout, the server signs the payload with HMAC using the merchant credentials, sends it to the WakaPay/Wakari checkout API, and receives a hosted checkout_url for redirection. The project also includes a webhook endpoint that verifies Wakapay signatures, processes payment status events, and sends confirmation or reminder emails through SMTP. In short, it combines a modern React-based storefront, secure server-side payment integration, webhook handling, and email automation into one end-to-end merchant demo.

name: Trelp
description: Tranched Uniswap v4 liquidity, with a 1inch Aqua buffer that never leaves the vault.
projectDescription:
Trelp splits a single Uniswap v4 liquidity position into two tradeable claims with
different risk profiles.
THE PROBLEM
Being an LP is one blended bet. You earn trading fees, you lose money when the pair
moves against you, and you find out the net at the end. There is no way to buy only
the steady part or only the levered part. So two kinds of capital stay out: treasuries
that need predictable yield will not accept a position that can be down 20% because ETH
moved, and traders who want leveraged exposure to fee income have to borrow it elsewhere
and manage that separately. Both want the same position. They want different slices of it.
HOW IT WORKS
Depositors choose a side. Senior is paid first at settlement and earns a capped return,
protected by junior's capital sitting underneath it. Junior absorbs losses before senior
feels anything, and in exchange keeps the entire upside above senior's capped claim.
Both sides hold ERC-20 claim tokens, so a position can be sold before the epoch ends.
Senior's rate is not configured in advance. It is derived when the deposit window closes,
from how much of each side actually arrived. More junior capital means a thicker cushion,
so senior needs to be paid less for the risk. The derivation requires junior to beat an
unlevered LP at any fee yield, which makes the fee term cancel out, so the bound holds
regardless of how the epoch performs. Past roughly 50% junior there is no rate that leaves
both sides better off than simply LPing, and the vault refuses to start rather than sell
terms that do not work.
A curator manages the position: picks the price range and moves it as the market moves.
Those powers are deliberately narrow. The curator never holds depositor funds, cannot
change terms once the epoch starts, is rate limited by a cooldown, and is blocked from
moving the range at all once the position is under stress. Every move has its cost
measured and recorded.
The protocol never computes impermanent loss. At settlement it holds one number, the cash
balance after unwinding, and pays senior first up to its claim. Everything (fees, IL,
adverse selection, unwind cost) is already inside that number. Attributing it per user
would need path-dependent accounting and a counterfactual price oracle, and would change
nobody's payout.
THE TWO INTEGRATIONS
Uniswap v4: a custom hook gates the pool to the vault's own position, overrides the LP fee
from a live solvency reading, and refuses swaps that would push more of the falling asset
onto the vault while still accepting trades that reduce risk. A dynamic fee is symmetric
and cannot skew, so a directional refusal is the only way to decline one side. A normal
pool has no way to say no, which is exactly how an LP ends up buying all the way down.
1inch Aqua: part of junior's capital works as a standing bid below spot. Aqua takes no
custody, so that capital is still sitting in the vault backing senior while it quotes. It
buys at a discount in calm markets, widens as the cushion thins via an Extruction target
that reads vault solvency at swap time, and stops bidding entirely when coverage breaks.
Anyone can then revoke it permissionlessly, turning it back into pure loss absorption.
Both venues read the same coverage number from the same contract. One view of risk,
applied in two places.
WHAT IS BUILT
Full protocol in Solidity with 98 tests across 11 suites, plus an opt-in mainnet fork suite
that runs the whole stack against the real v4 PoolManager and a real Aqua registry. Live
deployment on Base Sepolia with a working frontend: deposits, claim balances, live coverage,
on-chain event history, and redemption.
A full epoch on a mainnet fork, with ETH falling 45%: coverage goes from 42.9% to negative,
the pool fee widens 30 to 90 bps, the hook refuses a swap, the buffer is revoked, and the
vault settles. Junior loses everything, senior finishes down 0.98%. That is the honest
shape of the product. Junior is a cushion, not a guarantee.
KNOWN LIMITS
Senior's coupon is paid from realised gain, so a flat epoch returns principal and nothing
else. A CLO-style interest waterfall is the fix and is not built. There is no hedge during
a drawdown and no early settlement. One position per vault.
howItsMade:
UNISWAP V4 HOOK
The hook is what makes the pool defensible. Gates liquidity so only our vault can LP in,
overrides the LP fee live off the vault's solvency, and refuses swaps that would dump more of
the falling asset on us while still taking trades that reduce risk. A dynamic fee is
symmetric and can't skew, so a directional refusal is the only way to decline one side. A
normal pool has no way to say no, which is how an LP ends up buying all the way down.
v4 encodes hook permissions in the address, so we mine it with CREATE2 until it ends in
0x880. Pool also needs DYNAMIC_FEE_FLAG or the fee override is silently ignored.
1INCH AQUA
ship() takes no custody, the tokens stay in your wallet. That's the whole reason this works:
junior's capital is a live standing bid and a loss-absorbing reserve at the same time,
because it never leaves the vault.
The buffer is a SwapVM program, quote only. A two sided maker would hold inventory correlated
with the exact drawdown the buffer exists to survive. XYCConcentrateSwap derives virtual
reserves from its bounds, so a zero risky balance still quotes a working bid.
Aqua strategies are immutable once shipped, so a spread tracking live coverage can't be a
strategy parameter. Extruction fixes that: it hands the swap registers to any contract mid
program, so our adjuster reads the vault at swap time and rewrites the output. Coverage-aware
pricing against the officially deployed SwapVM, no redeploy.
We also had to anchor the bid to an oracle. With an unanchored curve the risk policy made
senior worse off (-15.43% vs -15.50%), because it underpaid for the risky asset so refusing
fills gave up as many gains as losses. Anchored, the same crash went -1.24% vs -15.44%. Those
two demo paths differ by one constructor argument.
THE ANNOYING PART
v4-core pins solc 0.8.26, Aqua and SwapVM pin 0.8.30. No single file can import both. The
vault talks to both through hand written interfaces, every test suite takes one venue real
and mocks the other, and the one place both run together uses deployCode so no type crosses
the version line. activate() ships to Aqua and mints the v4 position in the same call, and
that path had never actually run until we wrote a combined test for it.
STACK
Solidity, Foundry, Next.js 16, viem, Privy. Live on Base Sepolia, verified against forked
mainnet with the real PoolManager and a real Aqua registry. 98 tests.
TWO THINGS THAT BIT US
Asset ordering. Pool price is currency1 per currency0, so which range bound exposes you to
the risky asset flips with token ordering. We had it as a constructor bool. Get it wrong and
the halt inverts silently, refusing the safe side and allowing the dangerous one. Derived
from the pool key now.
settle() needed the risky balance at zero, but unwinding an in-range position returns both
tokens and nothing could convert them. redeem needs Settled, cancel needs Subscription. Funds
would have been stuck permanently. Tests missed it because the harness was impersonating the
vault to dump inventory. Added liquidate(), permissionless and floored against the oracle.

name: Opaque
description: Quantum-safe private USDC— from chain to IP. Still private when elliptic curves fail.
projectDescription:
Opaque is a post-quantum private payments rail for USDC on Arc, built for the confidential-payments market.
Current systems can hide a transfer while leaving the authorization key, payment timing, RPC activity, or IP origin exposed. Opaque addresses these leak paths together while providing post-quantum security end-to-end.
Users control ERC-4337 smart accounts whose authority comes from FORS+C, a hash-based post-quantum signature scheme. Keys are generated and protected locally in the browser, while PQKeyRegistry and the account validator enforce key use, rotation, and bounded authorization on Arc. USDC is deposited and split into shared fixed-denomination pools—1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 USDC—so payments use interchangeable notes rather than a wallet-specific balance, which allows ring signatures to work.
For a payment, the wallet forms an eight-member same-denomination ring: one owned note and seven real decoys. A hash-based MPC-in-the-head proof shows ownership of one eligible note without revealing which member was spent. A one-time nullifier prevents double spending, while the pool enforces real deposits, denomination, recipient binding, and post-quantum attestation before releasing funds.
Opaque also protects the network layer. Wallet payments and wallet-specific RPC/Graph queries travel through a three-hop ML-KEM onion mesh with authenticated encryption, padding, batching, delays, and operator-diverse relays. The first hop sees the connection but not the request; the exit can submit the request but cannot identify its origin.
The Graph is Opaque’s privacy coordination layer, the brain of the privacy mechanism. Its Arc subgraph indexes aggregate pool and relay conditions that help the wallet choose stronger decoys and better relay paths, so it allows the client to select the decoys while being network aware to provide stronger cover. A typed Graph Client composes this operational state with an independent standardized Arbitrum USDC context, and Privacy Sentinel exposes the combined public context through MCP.
Finally, each payment can settle immediately or wait for stronger privacy conditions. The payer’s recipient, threshold, and latest-settlement deadline are sealed to a Chainlink CRE workflow running inside an AWS Nitro confidential environment. CRE releases the payment when the privacy policy is satisfied, or when the deadline arrives. Opaque therefore protects authorization, payment linkage, timing, and network origin as one coordinated, quantum-resilient settlement system.
howItsMade:
Opaque is a modular TS, Solidity, and Rust system. The web wallet and chrome extension use Vite and TypeScript, with shared packages defining notes, ring inputs, relay messages, sealed intents, and typed module interfaces. Arc contracts are developed with Foundry and use ERC-4337 v0.7 for smart account execution.
The account layer replaces a conventional ECDSA owner with a FORS+C hash-based key. PQKeyRegistry stores the current-key commitment, next-key commitment, usage budget, and rotation state. PQAccount and PQValidator connect that authority to EntryPoint UserOperations. Key material is generated and encrypted in the browser; only commitments and bounded authorization state are published on chain. Rotation is pre-committed and accepted only under the current post-quantum key.
USDC is held by shared denomination pools for 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 USDC. The wallet decomposes deposits with a greedy denomination algorithm and submits the resulting notes in one account operation. Each note is represented by a commitment while its spending secret remains local. For a payment, the client selects one owned note and seven eligible same-denomination deposits, ranking candidates using freshness, reuse, activity, and coarse funding-concentration signals.
The ring proof uses a hash-based MPC-in-the-head construction. It proves knowledge of one note-opening secret among eight commitments without revealing which signer was used. A one-time nullifier prevents reuse. The attested spend path then enforces real ring membership, denomination, nullifier uniqueness, recipient binding, and post-quantum authorization before the pool transfers USDC.
The central design principle is that privacy is network-adaptive. The Graph continuously observes public conditions, and Opaque adapts as those conditions shift: the wallet dynamically re-ranks decoys as pool composition changes, while the mesh updates relay choices as reliability, occupancy, selection pressure, and operator diversity change. CRE uses the same versioned readiness signals to decide whether a payment can settle early or should wait until its deadline. Privacy is therefore not a static setting; every payment responds to the current network state.
The network layer is a reusable anonymizing transport. Requests are wrapped in three ML-KEM-768 onion layers, encrypted with AES-256-GCM, padded to fixed sizes, batched, and delayed. The same mesh carries payments and wallet-specific RPC/Graph queries, creating cover traffic and preventing query patterns from trivially identifying payment intent. Six registered relays are available and three operator-diverse hops are selected per request. Large proof payloads are chunked, transported, reassembled, and integrity-checked at the exit.
The Graph integration has two products. The Arc Subgraph Studio deployment indexes aggregate pool, ring, and relay events for the operational intelligence layer. A typed Graph Client composes that state with an independent standardized Arbitrum USDC source. Privacy Sentinel exposes the combined context through MCP so judges, agents, and developers can inspect the same public signals used by the system. The index publishes aggregates only; it never records a user’s selected note, final ring, route, recipient, or IP.
Chainlink CRE runs the confidential release policy. Each payment’s recipient, credential, privacy threshold, and latest-settlement deadline are sealed to a CRE key. A scheduled workflow reads pending envelopes and public Graph aggregates, then decides WAIT, RELEASE, or DENY. Vault DON secrets hold compact seeds and MAC material, while the enclave derives larger cryptographic keys internally. The executor stores ciphertext, checks the released authorization, and submits the Arc settlement without being able to rewrite the sealed terms.
"Hacky stuff" (more of creative) we did:

We turned Graph telemetry into a local Markov-chain route policy. Each relay is a state, and transition weights incorporate reliability, batch occupancy, recent selection pressure, and operator diversity. The wallet chooses the next hop dynamically from those weights, discouraging overused or correlated paths while preserving three-hop anonymity. This makes the relay mesh adaptive to live network conditions instead of relying on a static route list.
We turned the relay mesh into a general privacy transport by adding a QUERY message type, so wallet-specific Graph and RPC reads receive the same anonymity treatment as payments.
We packaged the Graph signal model as an aggregate-only Substreams module, making the privacy coordination layer reusable by other EVM pools and relay networks.

Arc and Circle complete the money path: USDC is both the settlement asset and gas currency, while CCTP V2 provides Sepolia-to-Arc onboarding. Together, these components form a network-adaptive, post-quantum private payment system rather than a collection of isolated privacy features.

name: Sotto
description: Sotto is a request-for-quote block-trading venue built on Hedera for ATS-issued securities.
projectDescription:
ATS, which is Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio, lets an issuer mint a compliant bond. It does not let anyone trade one. Sotto is the missing secondary market.
A bondholder escrows a block of an ATS-issued security and puts it up for bid. Dealers compete under commit–reveal: during the quote window only keccak256(price, quantity, nonce, dealer) reaches the venue, so nobody, including us — can read a price before the window closes. The window closes on a Hedera Consensus Service timestamp rather than our clock, so the venue cannot quietly extend it for a favoured dealer. Dealers then reveal, and each price is recomputed against its commit and must match exactly or the quote is void.
The book is allocated on strict price priority across several dealers at once. In a live testnet run, a 30-unit block filled 3 units at 98.80 to one dealer and 20 at 98.55 to another, leaving 7 unfilled — each dealer paying its own quoted price, never a rival's and never a uniform clearing price. Every fill is a separate EIP-712 Trade with its own signatures, its own nonce and its own firmness deadline, and a dealer's firmness bounds its own settlement deadline on-chain rather than merely in our engine.
Settlement is atomic delivery-versus-payment in a single transaction. Cash moves by transferFrom; the security moves by executeHoldByPartition on the ATS diamond, which runs compliance at the transfer itself. Any failure reverts both legs. There is no window in which the buyer holds the security and the seller has not been paid, and a revoked-KYC buyer fails inside the delivery call, taking the payment back with it.
Compliance is enforced by ATS, not bolted on by the venue. A NAV band guard inside the settlement contract additionally refuses any trade priced more than 5% from an on-chain reference, with a staleness bound so an unmaintained mark blocks settlement rather than being trusted.
Every stage — the request, the escrow, each sealed commit, the close, each reveal, the award and each fill — is timestamped on HCS topic 0.0.10383803. The venue is auditable after the fact without being transparent while the auction is live.
The bond's whole lifecycle is on-chain too: coupons the contract schedules for itself through HIP-1215 scheduled calls, and redemption at maturity through the ATS Bond facet.
Live on Hedera testnet at https://sotto-tau.vercel.app. Every claim in the README links to HashScan or to the HCS topic, so none of it has to be taken on trust.
howItsMade:
Hedera testnet throughout, against the real Asset Tokenization Studio diamond (factory 0.0.7708432) and real Circle USDC (0.0.429274),  not a mock token.
Contracts are Solidity 0.8.24 under Hardhat, all verified on Sourcify as exact_match:
• SottoSettlement — EIP-712 verification of both parties, nonces consumed inside the settling call so a signature cannot replay, hold validation (escrow is self, amount sufficient, not expired), then transferFrom and executeHoldByPartition in one call. Every guard is a custom error, and the API decodes those four-byte selectors back into sentences for the UI.
• SottoNavOracle — administrator-published NAV with a staleness bound, behind an IPriceSource seam.
• ChainlinkPriceSource — reads live Chainlink AggregatorV3 feeds on Hedera testnet through that seam, so an asset with a real market price overrides the administrator's mark. A bond's NAV is not on a price feed and never will be, which is why the administrator path is primary and the feed is the override rather than the reverse.
• SottoCouponScheduler — schedules its own coupon payments using HIP-1215 scheduled contract calls via the Hedera Schedule Service system contract at 0x16b.
• SottoDealerBond — a dealer posts a bond and forfeits it to the seller, not to the venue, for failing to reveal.
Two settlement paths, both live:
Path A is EVM-native. The buyer approves exact USDC and anyone at all can relay the fully-signed trade, because the authorisation is the two signatures rather than the sender.
Path B grants no allowance anywhere. The buyer signs a native HTS transfer of their own cash with a HIP-820 wallet session, the venue batches it together with the delivery call as a HIP-551 atomic batch, and the network provides the atomicity instead of a contract. The relay verifies the inner cash leg before batching — correct token id, exact debit and credit, exactly two transfers, no hbar movement, our batch key, already frozen — because without that check a buyer could sign a one-unit transfer and take the whole block.
Backend is Fastify with ethers 6: the RFQ engine and allocator, an HCS audit writer, and the batch relay. Auction windows are judged against HCS consensus timestamps rather than the server clock. Frontend is Next.js 15 with Reown AppKit, wagmi and @hashgraph/hedera-wallet-connect, so a single ECDSA account serves both the EVM and Hedera-native namespaces from one wallet connection.
The most useful thing we learned is in docs/ATS-SPIKE.md and is absent from Hedera's published docs: ATS v3.1.0 as deployed uses different role hashes from repo HEAD. Grants made with HEAD's constants land on hashes the deployed contract never checks — hasRole returns true and every guarded call still reverts, with no useful error. Only DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE is stable across the two versions, which is what let us repair it from outside.
One more that cost us a live trade: Hedera's JSON-RPC relay attaches no revert data to the error from a sent transaction, so a custom error's four bytes never reach the caller. Recovering them needs an eth_call replay against the same block, which the venue now does automatically whenever a revert comes back unexplained.

name: Levantate Bridge
description: AI agents post tasks; verified humans bid, deliver work, and get paid in USDC on Arc.
projectDescription:
Levantate Bridge is an agent-to-human task marketplace where AI agents autonomously post work, hire verified humans, and settle payment in USDC on Arc testnet—without a human operator in the loop on the agent side.
When an agent hits a task it cannot complete alone (e.g. collecting neighborhood complaints, subjective judgment, or physical-world steps), it posts the task with a max budget and bidding window. Human workers browse open tasks, link a wallet they already control, and place bids. Every bid requires a fresh World ID Selfie Check bound to that task, round, and amount—identity comes from the proof, not the client, and each proof is spent once to block bot/sybil bidding. One World ID nullifier maps to one payout address.
The agent selects a winning bid using live historical data from The Graph (completion rates, missed deadlines, typical payouts). Funds lock in a TaskEscrow smart contract on Arc funded by a Circle Developer-Controlled agent wallet. A separate Circle relayer wallet submits placeBid and submitWork for workers so they never need gas. Workers submit proof before a submission deadline; the agent evaluates it and calls approveWork, which releases USDC directly to the worker’s self-custodied wallet. If a worker misses the deadline, the agent can reclaim the task for a new bidding round—recorded on-chain and indexed for future scoring.
All eight escrow events are indexed by a subgraph on Arc testnet. The agent uses that data for budgeting and bid scoring; write confirmation uses Arc RPC receipts. Settlement is USDC on Arc via Circle throughout—no bridging or swapping.
howItsMade:
Overview
Levantate Bridge is a monorepo: contracts/ (Solidity escrow on Arc), backend/ (Node 22 API + agent + relayer), frontend/ (Next.js worker UI), subgraph/ (AssemblyScript indexer). Supabase Postgres stores workers, bids, proofs, and relayed tx state. One root .env.local configures everything. The agent chat, winner loop, and REST API all call the same escrow operations module.
Circle + Arc
Circle Developer-Controlled Wallets on Arc testnet (chain 5042002, USDC 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000).
Two wallets:
Agent 0x42472b448b6ba8bb654483d4773db715901a64a7 — funds escrow, posts tasks, selects winners, approves/rejects work, reclaims, cancels
Relayer 0xd055b6cee7d72bc5111119ec7beb8c56b2f61ae1 — submits placeBid and submitWork so workers never hold gas
Escrow contract: 0xc8F1db364B14D7Aa4ea620bF9f649Ef3D7F14d52 (deploy block 61231705)
Explorer: https://testnet.arcscan.app/address/0xc8F1db364B14D7Aa4ea620bF9f649Ef3D7F14d52
Every write: Circle SDK → wait for tx hash → Arc RPC receipt (success = confirmed, revert = failed). Relayer uses a serialized nonce queue + idempotency keys so concurrent bids don’t race nonces.
Benefit: Autonomous USDC settlement on Arc; workers paid to self-custodied wallets—the backend never holds worker keys.
World ID (Selfie Check)
Every bid requires a fresh Selfie Check via @worldcoin/idkit (selfieCheckLegacy, sandbox World App). Backend signs mandatory rp_context, verifies at developer.world.org/api/v4/verify/{rp_id}.
Signal per bid: bid:{taskId}:{round}:{amountMicro}. Nullifier comes from the proof, not the client. Each proof is spent once; fingerprints tied to task_id, cleaned up after pay/cancel/reclaim.
Workers link a payout wallet with a free off-chain personal_sign before bidding. First bid binds one nullifier → one address.
Benefit: Gates economic participation—blocks scripted bid floods without custodial worker wallets.
The Graph
Subgraph slug levantate-bridge, network arc-testnet, indexes all 8 escrow events from the contract above.
Published links:
Subgraph Studio: https://thegraph.com/studio/subgraph/levantate-bridge/
Graph Explorer: https://thegraph.com/explorer/subgraphs/Fnr7E8tC1HbD1bvdAsTXMwe5R5kZdx98pH1bhmcWWGeL
Query gateway: https://gateway.thegraph.com/api/subgraphs/id/Fnr7E8tC1HbD1bvdAsTXMwe5R5kZdx98pH1bhmcWWGeL
Agent uses live indexed data for:
Budget — median historical payout + submission window before postTask
Bid scoring — completion rate, missed deadlines, price vs median
Benefit: Winner selection and budgeting use real on-chain history, not hardcoded rules.
Stack & notable details
Next.js 16, viem, RainbowKit, Supabase, OpenAI agent at /agent. LLM proof review on submit. Two deadlines: bid (auction) vs submission (delivery); reclaimTask reopens bidding if a worker ghosts.

name: PinTool MM
description: Sell your market-making strategy without showing it. Makers run it on Aqua with their own funds.
projectDescription:
PinTool Market Making removes the trust barrier between strategy creators and capital owners on 1inch Aqua. A Strategy Provider publishes a market-making strategy while keeping its activation rules, thresholds and sizing logic private. A Maker picks a strategy and sets private risk limits: total budget, maximum inventory share, per-fill caps and authorization lifetime. Neither side ever sees the other's inputs.
A Chainlink Confidential Workflow intersects both policies inside a TEE (handlerInTee). Provider policies are Vault DON secrets; Maker limits are sealed in the browser and opened only inside the enclave. The workflow publishes only the minimal authorization the chain needs, a Guard report with allowed directions, per-swap caps, inventory caps and expiry, and it can only make the Maker's limits stricter, never looser.
PinTool Guard sits behind SwapVM's Extruction instruction and checks every Aqua fill against that authorization, reverting anything outside it, so a strategy halts the moment the workflow stops renewing it. Funds never leave the Maker's wallet; one balance can back several strategies with at most one active at a time. Strategies are published under ENSv2 names on Sepolia so Makers pin a verified, immutable release.
Everything runs end to end on Ethereum Sepolia with canonical WETH and Circle USDC: a public run of 40 transactions shows guarded swaps on two strategies plus an expected on-chain rejection, and the mandate service independently verifies every Guard report and Aqua receipt before the app shows it.
howItsMade:
