Confidential workflow (workflow/, TypeScript, Bun, @chainlink/cre-sdk): a cron- or HTTP-triggered handlerInTee callback fetches the Provider strategy and the Maker limits with getSecrets(), reads live ETH/USDC market data from Kraken, runs a pure intersection function (the stricter side wins on every cap; inventory caps are derived from budget × share at the mid price; paused reports zero every cap), ABI-encodes the Guard report and crosses back with usingTheDons() so the DON signs it and the forwarder delivers it to PinTool Guard's onReport(bytes,bytes). The encoding is golden-tested byte for byte against the fixture the Solidity side decodes, and a leak-check script diffs every secret value against the simulation output. Local CRE CLI simulation broadcasts real reports through Chainlink's Sepolia simulation forwarder.
Contracts (contracts/aqua-executor/, Solidity, Foundry): the official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM sources are built unmodified at pinned commits. PinTool Guard implements the Extruction interface and is the terminal instruction of every Maker-approved program, so each fill is validated before any token moves. It enforces direction, per-swap amount, post-swap inventory and expiry per (maker, strategyHash), with strictly increasing nonces and standing authorizations the Maker can revoke. Official Aqua deployments require a KycNFT, so we redeployed Aqua and the SwapVM router on Ethereum Sepolia.
Mandate service (orchestrator/, Node, Railway): validates requests, signs CRE HTTP-trigger calls, runs the confidential runner and independently verifies every Guard report and Aqua receipt from Sepolia RPC before the web app shows it, with a durable event outbox, serialized deliveries and restart recovery.
Web app (frontend/, Next.js 15, React 19, Privy, viem, static export): marketplace, Provider Studio with an AI-assisted strategy builder (Vercel AI SDK + OpenAI), a Maker mandate flow that seals limits in the browser with noble ciphers, an activity monitor, and ENSv2 strategy names on Sepolia (namespace registrar, delegated version pointer, Maker-pinned releases).
Hard parts: EVMClient has no TeeRuntime overload, so on-chain writes must cross out of the enclave; SwapVM's Extruction has no try/catch, so a veto must revert; the SDK's opcode table lagged the contract; and Extruction args are capped at 235 bytes, so the Guard report lives in PinTool Guard's storage and only a public envelope goes into the bytecode. Codex and Claude Code were used heavily across contracts, workflow and frontend, with the team owning product, privacy model and verification (see AI_USAGE.md).

name: cackpass
description: A decentralized event ticketing platform with USDC payments on Arc and on-chain proof of purchase.
projectDescription:
CACK-pass is a Web2/Web3 hybrid event ticketing platform that lets organizers
create events, sell tickets, and settle revenue in USDC on Arc. We originally
ran on Lisk with a Paystack fiat rail, but Lisk Mainnet is being deprecated, so
we are migrating the whole platform to Arc — an EVM chain where USDC is the
native gas token and Circle-native rails are first-class.
Buyers can pay two ways:
• Fiat via Flutterwave (card, USSD, bank transfer, mobile money)
• Native USDC on Arc via Circle App Kit, using a Privy embedded wallet
Every crypto payment is written on-chain by our CackPassArcPayment contract,
which records the payer, amount, reference, event ID, ticket quantity, and
status (Pending → Confirmed → Failed). That gives organizers and attendees a
shared, tamper-proof audit trail for every ticket sale.
Buyers without crypto can buy real USDC with a card through Privy's Fiat
Onramp (NGN / USD / EUR / GBP), delivered to their embedded wallet on Base
Mainnet. Tickets are stored on IPFS, verified by signed QR codes, and emailed
to the customer after purchase — no login required for guest checkout.
howItsMade:
CACK-pass is a Next.js 16 (App Router) + TypeScript app deployed on Vercel.
Auth and embedded wallets come from Privy — users sign in with email, Google,
or Twitter and get a wallet with no seed phrase to manage.
Payments — Fiat: We migrated the old Paystack rail to Flutterwave v3. The
Flutterwave verify and webhook routes validate verif-hash signatures, create
Order + Payment + MyTicket records in MongoDB, and trigger a shared ticket
email. Card, USSD, bank transfer, and mobile money are all supported.
Payments — Crypto (the hackathon core):
• Contracts: A new Hardhat project (arc-contracts/) holds
CackPassArcPayment.sol, deployed and verified on Arc Testnet
(0x084622e6970BBcBA510454C6145313c2993ED9E4). It exposes
initializePayment / confirmPayment / failPayment and emits
PaymentInitiated / PaymentConfirmed / PaymentFailed events.
• Server side: lib/arc/client.ts wraps the contract with ethers v6 —
provider, signer, generatePaymentId, paymentIdToBytes32,
initializeOnChainPayment, confirmOnChainPayment, and getOnChainPayment
(with proper PaymentStatus enum decoding).
• Client side: lib/arc/app-kit.ts wraps Circle App Kit —
sendUSDCWithAppKit(provider, contractAddress, amount) uses the Privy
embedded wallet's EIP-1193 provider to move USDC on Arc. Ticket price
and gas are both paid in USDC because USDC is the native gas token.
• UX: components/payments/ArcPaymentButton.tsx orchestrates it —
gets the Privy provider, calls /api/payments/arc/initialize,
invokes sendUSDCWithAppKit, then redirects to
/payment/success?provider=arc&transaction_id=<hash>. Includes
double-click guards, wallet-not-ready state, and insufficient-funds
messaging.
• Verification: /api/payments/arc/verify polls the contract, calls
confirmPayment as the platform owner, retries until the status is
Confirmed, mints MyTicket records, and sends the ticket email via
a shared /api/email/ticket-confirmation endpoint.
• Fiat → Crypto onramp: The wallet dashboard uses Privy's
useFiatOnramp().fund() to buy real USDC with a card (NGN / USD / EUR /
GBP) on Base Mainnet. Base and Arc balances are shown side by side in
a dual-network dashboard so buyers can see exactly where their funds
live.
Partner tech benefits:
• Arc — native USDC gas means zero-gas UX for buyers.
• Circle App Kit — the fastest way to move USDC into a contract-driven
payment flow.
• Privy — passwordless auth + embedded wallets + fiat onramp in one SDK.
• Flutterwave — reliable African fiat rails (card, USSD, bank, mobile money).
Hacky bits worth mentioning: We solved a Mongoose strict-mode gotcha by
resolving the buyer email from multiple fallbacks (Order → Payment →
metadata.userEmail → User) so ticket emails never get dropped. We also
made the Arc verify step idempotent — if a payment is marked completed but
no ticket exists, we self-heal and re-process instead of silently failing.

name: arbiter
description: Arbiter lets clients escrow USDC on Arc for well defined tasks.
projectDescription:
Digital work often ends with a subjective dispute: was it delivered, did it meet the agreed criteria, and who should get paid? Arbiter turns that question into a fixed, inspectable agreement.
A client commits the scope, acceptance criteria, worker, resolver, payment amount, and deadlines before the worker accepts. The scope can describe research, a website with required pages and performance characteristics, a copywriting brief with tone and messaging constraints, or a marketing campaign with agreed KPIs and reporting requirements. The client then deposits USDC into a non-upgradeable escrow on Arc. The worker submits an immutable Markdown deliverable or delivery record and commits its exact content hash onchain.
Arbiter evaluates the committed work against the agreed rubric. Deterministic checks can cover required sections, word limits, links, or other committed requirements. Semantic evidence records a pass, failure, or inconclusive result with criterion-level explanations and supporting excerpts. In this MVP, website and marketing work is assessed through the worker's submitted Markdown delivery record; independent URL crawling and KPI-provider integrations are future work. A pass proposes full payment; a failure proposes a full refund. Either party can challenge during the review window, which freezes automatic settlement and sends the agreement to the resolver. The resolver can pay, refund, or split the deposit. If the resolver times out, the pre-agreed testnet rule splits funds 50/50.
The deployed MVP uses public sample material and one Markdown submission per agreement. It makes deadlines, evidence commitments, transaction states, and resolver powers visible to both parties.
howItsMade:
The core is a non-upgradeable Solidity escrow deployed on Arc testnet. It commits the
client, worker, resolver, USDC amount, research brief hash, source hash, evaluation-policy
hash, and separate submission, evaluation, challenge, and resolution deadlines. The contract
handles funding, report-hash submission, proposed outcomes, challenges, payment, refund,
resolver splits, and timeout settlement.
The web app uses React and viem for browser-wallet transactions. A Bun API stores immutable
Markdown reports and agreement material in SQLite, authenticated with wallet signatures and
one-time nonces. It hashes the exact submitted content before the worker commits it onchain.
Evaluation is implemented as a TypeScript Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow. Its
handlerInTee processes the agreed rubric, supplied sources, report, model credential, and
structured model response. Deterministic checks validate sections, word limits, and source
references; semantic results include criterion-level outcomes, short reasons, and report
excerpts. Invalid or uncertain evaluation never triggers automatic payment and instead
routes the agreement to human review.
The public MVP is deployed on Fly.io with an encrypted SQLite volume. It runs on Arc testnet
and uses USDC for escrow settlement.

name: Vesta
description: Vesta utilizes a portion of CCA commitments for launch LP liquidity, by rewarding invested bidders.
projectDescription: Vesta is a token launch strategy for CCAs. The auction discovers the launch price, then bidders can opt to escrow ETH plus a percentage of their allocation for for locked liquidity position using vesta. The team strengthens launch liquidity, and in return, bidders get rewards set by the team.
howItsMade: The contracts are built with Solidity and tested with foundry, locally and on Sepolia testnet. uniswap v4 and CCA repos are used to implement the vesta strategy and vault contracts, the frontend allows a launch team to manage any of their CCA launches directly from the site, and any participants to manage their CCA bids and their vesta commitments. The frontend uses React for the UI, wagmi and ethers for wallet connections and onchain calls/reads.

name: x402 Work Receipts
description: Signed work orders and receipts between two agents, paid with x402, verified by a stranger
projectDescription:
When two companies let agents act for them — one ordering work, one accepting and doing it — the record of what was ordered, agreed and delivered ends up inside one company's system, which can edit it, lose it, or simply be believed less than the other when the two accounts differ.
x402-work-receipts is a working instance of the alternative: no single party owns the authoritative audit trail; a shared ledger records signed evidence of which agent, holding which mandate, received, accepted and executed which command. A customer agent turns a story card into a signed work order and pays an intake fee; a contractor agent verifies the signature, anchors the order's fingerprint on a Hedera consensus topic, and returns a signed acceptance. When the work exists, the customer pays the balance and collects a signed delivery receipt carrying both payments. Six anchors go on the topic — only hashes, no content — and a stand-alone verifier reaches the same verdict either party would, reading nothing but the public mirror node.
Built for two organizations that already argue about what was agreed — an agency and its client — and, longer term, for any pair of agents transacting without a platform both of them trust.
What the chain proves (wording taken from the source protocol spec §4.2): a sealed mandate with envelope hash eh existed at the sender no later than consensus time T1 and was accepted by the contractor, whose receipt with hash eh2 is fixed no later than T2; the counterparty's signature verifies independently. It does not prove the mandate's content (only its fingerprint), the quality or the fact of the work, or that a key belongs to a person. The payment profile adds: the intake and balance transfers exist on the ledger with the stated payer, payee and amounts.
Try it without installing anything: https://x402-work-receipts.zeabur.app/verify loads the demo run and re-checks it against the public mirror node in the browser, with links to every anchor and payment on HashScan.
This is not only a hackathon demo: two real companies have run the same signed work-order and receipt format in a private pilot since 8 September 2026 (their public audit topic on Hedera testnet: 0.0.10226839). The hackathon build is the open, self-contained slice of that format with x402 payment added.
howItsMade:
Node/TypeScript. Both agents speak x402 with the exact scheme on hedera:testnet, settled by the Blocky402 facilitator (api.testnet.blocky402.com) — not a payment demo, a real settled HBAR transfer per paid route, using the upfront flow so the handler can anchor the payment id inside the receipt it signs. Every step — order received, both payments, acceptance, delivery, receipt — is anchored as a hash-only message on a Hedera Consensus Service topic; a stand-alone verifier (verifier/) reads only the public mirror node, seven checks, three exit codes (0 verified, 1 failed, 2 could not check). The contractor publishes an agent card at /.well-known/agent.json, so a customer agent discovers the service and pays for it with x402 without any API key.
Envelopes are Ed25519-signed RFC 8785 canonical JSON; mandate.v1 and receipt.v1 are byte-identical copies of a pre-existing protocol (drift-tested by sha256), so the project extends a schema it does not own rather than inventing its own. Extras shipped after the base flow verified end to end: HCS-14 uaid identifiers so the verifier can tie a signature to a stable id instead of only a handle; a Scheduled Transaction retainer the customer authorises up front and the contractor releases after delivering; an MCP server exposing order/collect/verify as tools for any MCP-speaking agent runtime.
The hacky bit: the base protocol schemas forbid any field that looks like money (hour, rate, amount, usd, price, cost), so payment.v1 is generated by a Python script that flattens the base schema's keywords into a new, self-contained schema, because JSON Schema 2020-12's unevaluatedProperties: false makes a plain allOf+$ref extension impossible. Claude Code wrote the modules under protocol/, anchor/, contractor/, customer/, verifier/ and demo/ from a written design and task-by-task plan kept in the repo; every task was reviewed, tested and checked against the public mirror node by hand before merging (see the "AI collaboration" section of the README).

name: Roll Call
description: Every protocol has a pause button. Roll Call tells you whether anyone is still holding it.
projectDescription:
Every protocol has a pause button, an upgrade path, a multisig. Almost none can tell you whether anyone is still holding it. Roll Call derives that from onchain history instead of reading the claim.
Paste a protocol contract. Roll Call resolves the Safe above it, recovers which owners actually signed each transaction from the execTransaction calldata, tests whether those signers act independently or as one party, dates every signer's last onchain signal, and reads what the contract holds. Out comes the number that matters: the honest quorum, how many independent, awake parties are really required to move the money, against the threshold the protocol declares.
Base's L1 Portal holds $1.92B. It can be upgraded by a 2-of-2 with zero margin and no timelock. Mantle's L1 Portal holds $411M behind a declared 6-of-14 that resolves to an honest quorum of 2, with 7 of its 14 signers showing no onchain signal in 180 days. Across 47 protocol contracts worth $4.82B, $2.38B sits behind a signer set with zero margin. Every number was read from chain state.
Every number carries its tier: observed (chain state), tested (a calibrated permutation test with a published false positive rate), or inferred (the effective quorum curve). Nothing is a made-up score; the calibration endpoint is public.
Ask it a question. "Who can freeze Mantle, and how many of them are asleep?" and an agent resolves the protocol to its keys, prices the report by the work it takes, reads what money sits behind those keys through The Graph, pays for the report over x402 on Hedera with its own wallet, and answers in plain English from the numbers, every step on screen. Every report also comes back as sentences, one per number, and as a path from the money to the people.
It is a service agents pay for: metered by work, settled in HBAR or in RCC, an HTS token with a 2% fee schedule the network enforces; prepaid credits for runtimes that cannot sign; renewals by Hedera Scheduled Transaction; every report attested to HCS, and that archive doubles as the shared cache behind the enclave's signal. Roll Call is a registered ERC-8004 agent on Hedera testnet and Sepolia, with a discovery manifest at /.well-known/x402.
Two Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflows turn the measurement into action inside an enclave. One watches a private list of protocols and reports breaches. The other defends a live lending position in the official liquidation protection challenge on Sepolia, with a trigger no other protection has: if the market's own control surface degrades, it de-risks regardless of price. Both run end to end in the CRE simulator against the live contract.
The Graph carries the population: a subgraph of Safe executions and approvals, and a registry of 84 verified Messari standardized deployments across 12 networks queried with one query string, every answer stamped with its deployment and indexed block. Seven MCP tools and a SKILL.md let any agent ask the same questions.
Live: https://rollcall-pi.vercel.app
Repo: https://github.com/divyanshkhurana06/rollcall
Hedera Harness PR: https://github.com/hedera-dev/hedera-harness/pull/53
Harness before/after video: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1cqjV9rzSAkYKB_b_eQtC0rDgDpGZ_vvM/view?usp=sharing
howItsMade:
The load-bearing primitive is signature recovery. A Safe's execTransaction calldata carries a packed signature blob. Roll Call splits it by v-type (contract signature, approved hash, eth_sign, EIP-712), recovers each signer against the safeTxHash, and reconstructs who approved what, including nonce-zero signers that no explorer shows. Validated at 100% on every recoverable transaction in the test set.
Independence is a permutation test: for each pair of owners, the observed co-signing count against a null that preserves the threshold (Efraimidis-Spirakis weighted sampling), a co-submission artifact filter, and an empirical p-value with +1 smoothing. Calibration runs on synthetic signer sets and is published: 0% family-wise false positives at alpha 0.01, 100% power. Liveness is a binary search on eth_getTransactionCount over block history, with an explicit indeterminate state rather than a silent "never signed". Authority resolution walks EIP-1967 slots, Ownable and AccessControl grants; time to harm comes from timelock delays. Readers fail over across RPC providers and across the Safe API and its gateway, and a read that fails everywhere is reported as unreadable, never as an empty slot.
Hedera: x402 v2 with strict PaymentRequirements through the Blocky402 facilitator; two settlement assets (HBAR, and RCC, an HTS token with a 2% fractional fee assessed by the network on a real settlement); a bearer credit store bought over x402; renewals by Scheduled Transaction verified on the mirror node; HCS attestations that double as the shared signal cache, which is what makes the serverless deployment stateless; ERC-8004 registration with the agent card inline as a data URI; and a PR to the Hedera Harness that makes doctor verify operator credentials against the mirror node.
Chainlink: two Confidential Workflows on the TypeScript SDK. The liquidation strategy is written in the challenge contract's own integers, because at $1,800 the starting position has a health factor of 1.0029, which the contract truncates to 100 and liquidates; walked through the five published scenarios under both orderings of price update and liquidation check. One tick() engine runs inside the enclave, from a laptop, and in tests against an in-memory model of the contract that decodes every signed transaction. The hacky part: the simulator trapped for three days on every workflow including Chainlink's own scaffolds; the cause was the Bun version the SDK bundles with, isolated by reinstalling the old one and reproducing the trap. The enclave's plain HTTP budget is ten seconds, so the governance signal is served warm from HCS rather than computed on request.
The Graph: a Safe subgraph in Studio, the Messari standardized deployments probed into a registry with per-deployment provenance, an MCP server with seven tools, and the Ask agent using the gateway as a step in a paid workflow. Web is React and Vite, API is Express bundled by esbuild into one Vercel function with a 300-second budget, web and API on one domain. Everything is testnet.

name: Bridle
description: x402 payment gateway for AI agents on Hedera. Blocks overspend, logs proof to HCS.
projectDescription: Bridle is a deterministic policy firewall and hardware-confirmed trust layer designed to eliminate the "Soft Guardrail Fallacy" in autonomous agent payments. As LLMs gain the autonomy to procure compute, data, and APIs using crypto wallets, existing security models rely on system prompts like "do not spend over $10" or unconstrained private keys stored in .env files. These approaches fail when faced with prompt injection, context drift, or recursive loops. Bridle resolves this through a dual-rail economic architecture. Micro-payments of 1.0 HBAR or less settle autonomously at machine speed using the x402 protocol and the Blocky402 facilitator, enabling sub-cent, sub-second API access without pre-funded subscriptions. Whenever an agent attempts a high-value payment exceeding 1.0 HBAR, execution is instantly paused by hardcoded Python logic rather than probabilistic LLM prompts. The transaction parameters are routed to a Ledger hardware wallet—emulated via Speculos—requiring physical operator confirmation on the OLED screen before any funds move. Every operational decision, whether settled autonomously, signed via hardware, or vetoed by an operator, is immutably recorded to Hedera Consensus Service Topic 0.0.10474223 for verifiable auditability.
howItsMade: Bridle is built across five interconnected layers spanning Python, Solidity, and Hedera native services. The cognitive engine runs on Google's Gemini 3.6 Flash within a Python agent that discovers endpoints, evaluates task relevance, and responds to standard HTTP 402 Payment Required challenges served by a FastAPI gateway. Rather than delegating spending guardrails to prompt engineering, the gateway and agent enforce spending limits strictly in Python runtime logic. For transactions exceeding 1.0 HBAR, execution is suspended and handed off to our custom Speculos emulator bridge (server/ledger_client.py and server/speculos_emulator.py), which exposes an interactive Web GUI and REST endpoints on port 5000 that emulate the Ledger Nano S+ chassis, OLED display, and APDU button flows. Approved transactions are broadcast to Hedera EVM Testnet (Chain ID 296) and settle against our Hardhat-tested BridlePaywall.sol contract deployed at 0x5442A862d2B11709045BE15015368c7dD6B9cfd8, which utilizes cryptographic nonces to prevent replay attacks. To solve asynchronous latency between EVM RPC transaction broadcast and Hedera Mirror Node indexing, the gateway integrates resilient exponential backoff polling (5 retries with 1.5s delay) to verify receipts reliably. Finally, the system leverages the Hedera SDK to commit structured audit messages directly to Hedera Consensus Service Topic 0.0.10474223, taking advantage of fixed USD-pegged fees and immediate ABFT consensus.

name: citable
description: Prove you quoted correctly — per-paragraph position proofs on chain, ENS-named, any language.
projectDescription:
Citable is a provenance register for language. It does not try to answer "is this quote real?" — that question has no denominator, because nobody knows what share of everything a person ever said is available to check against. Citable inverts the burden of proof and answers a question that is actually decidable: "here is the proof that I quoted correctly."
An author registers a statement. The text is split into paragraphs at blank lines, each paragraph is bound to its position and hashed into a merkle tree, and only the 32-byte root goes on chain — together with the author address, an ENS node, a timestamp, and the IPFS CID of a bundle holding the full text. The index sits inside the leaf: leaf = keccak256(keccak256(abi.encode(uint256 index, string segment))). That detail is the entire point. Sibling pairs get sorted when the tree is built, which discards their order, so without the index in the leaf a proof would show membership but not position — and position is what quoting out of context destroys.
Verification runs as a cascade of three stages, and the interface never lets them blur into each other:

Wording — is this paragraph in the statement, and where? A merkle proof, verified by the contract. Paragraph 5 of 7, with the neighbouring paragraphs shown next to it. Change a single character and the proof fails.
Excerpt — is the fragment cut out of a registered paragraph? A fact, checked locally, with the full paragraph displayed beside the shortened quote. This is the common case of honest-looking distortion: the words are real, the meaning is not.
Coverage — is the claim covered by the text, in another language or other words? A measurement, explicitly labelled as one, never as a proof.

Stage 3 exists because a translation shares no bytes with its original. It runs entirely in the browser: embeddings (multilingual-e5-small) pick candidate paragraphs, a deterministic value check throws out claims that assert numbers or persons the paragraph never mentions, and an NLI model (mDeBERTa-v3-base-xnli) judges whether the claim is actually entailed by the text. Typing "Revenue rose by four percent last quarter." against a German paragraph scores 0.8253 entailment and reports paragraph 3 of 6. Changing one word to "forty percent" is not scored at all — the value check sees a 40 in a paragraph that says four and never lets the model near it.
That design came out of a measurement, not a preference. Plain semantic similarity rated an invented confession ("Roth admitted the figures were manipulated") at 0.880 — higher than a faithful English translation of the same paragraph at 0.877. Similarity models measure what is being talked about, not what is being claimed. Built on similarity, the percentage would have endorsed the disinformation in exactly the case the project exists for. Entailment plus the value check separates the strongest false quote from the threshold by 0.235 instead of 0.072.
A percentage from stage 3 means "no distorted quote in our 16-case test set reached this score" — not "83% true". The paragraph is always shown in full next to the number, so the reader judges, not the model.
Identity comes from ENS. A signature alone is anonymous, and "key 0x7f3a… said this" convinces no reader. registerRoot is gated by an INameGuard, implemented against the real ENSv2 registry on Sepolia: the name holder may publish, and so may anyone the holder granted the publish role to — which is what a newsroom actually looks like, a volunteer publishing under the paper's name without owning it.
The limits are on the landing page, not behind it. Stage 3 can be wrong. Spanish scores 0.562 against 0.821 for English and would be rejected at threshold 0.80. Irony and quote-within-quote are not handled. "Not registered" does not mean "fabricated" — and when nothing matches, the app says so with its denominator visible, naming how many statements and paragraphs it compared against.
howItsMade:
Contracts in Solidity with Foundry. CitableRegistry stores one record per statement — root, author, ensNode, timestamp, CID, segment count — and verifies position proofs on chain. Registration is gated by an INameGuard interface; ENSv2NameGuard implements it against the live ENSv2 registry on Sepolia. Both are deployed and verified on Etherscan, and all three registered statements went out with the guard armed.
The single biggest technical risk is that the JavaScript and the Solidity disagree about a hash. If they ever drift, every statement already registered becomes unverifiable. So there is no hardcoded fixture anywhere: test/Leaf.t.sol shells out via Foundry FFI to script/js/leaf.mjs and compares the result against Leaf.leafOf, and test/ProofBridge.t.sol lets the JS segment a text, build the tree and produce a proof, then hands that proof to the contract. Segmentation, tree shape, pair sorting and the leaf formula are proven identical by forge test, not assumed. 55 Solidity tests, 60 JS tests for the client library.
The client library (lib/citable/) is plain ESM on viem and merkletreejs, and the frontend imports it through an alias rather than copying it — a second copy of the leaf formula is exactly the drift the bridge test exists to prevent.
Frontend is Next.js 16 with Tailwind 4, exported as fully static routes. There is no database, no server, no indexer: search by ENS name reads logs by the indexed ensNode topic straight from an RPC endpoint, the bundle is fetched from IPFS, and the tree is rebuilt in the browser. Verifying requires trusting no service at all.
Three things were harder than expected and are worth naming:
ENSv2 token ids are not labelhashes. The registry keeps a tokenVersionId in the lower 32 bits of the id, so ownerOf(labelhash(name)) returns 0x0 for every name that exists — a live Sepolia name currently sits at version 9. The guard therefore never derives an id; it asks the registry, which resolves the version itself. script/js/ens-probe.mjs proves this against names discovered from mint events, and a Sepolia fork test asserts the delegation path rather than assuming it. Registering the name itself was a second detour: the ENSv2 registrar on Sepolia prices in a test USDC that has a public mint, which is why wochenzeitung.eth could be acquired properly and the guard never had to be switched off. script/js/ens-register.mjs makes that path reproducible.
transformers.js cannot be bundled here. env.js reads fs at import time to decide whether it is running on a server; Turbopack compiles a bare node builtin in a browser bundle to void 0, and Object.keys(void 0) kills the library before the first model byte arrives. resolveAlias does not help — the substitution happens before resolution. So stage 3 loads the library from jsDelivr and the weights from huggingface.co at runtime, about 400 MB on first use and only after the button is pressed. That is a real third-party dependency and it is stated on the page. Stages 1 and 2 depend on nothing but the chain and the bytes.
CIDs are computed without kubo. A bundle below the chunk size is a single raw block, so its CID is sha256 with a four-byte header — verified against kubo 0.43.0, with its own vectors in the test suite. Above that size it throws rather than guessing a CID that points nowhere. publish.mjs refuses to broadcast until the CID this repo computes equals the one kubo computes, the bytes read back out of IPFS rebuild the root, and the deployed contract accepts a proof at the right index while rejecting the same segment at a different one.
Availability is treated as a race, not a hierarchy. Public gateways, a Pinata dedicated gateway, and the app's own copy are all tried at once, and the first source whose bytes rebuild the on-chain root wins. A source serving anything else loses the race instead of being believed — which is why the app may ship its own copy at all: it buys reachability, not trust, and the screen names which source answered. Outage and forgery stay separate: "nobody answered" proves nothing, "someone answered with wrong bytes" is an accusation.
One deliberate exception to the no-server rule: a browser must not hold a pinning key, so api/pin.mjs is a Vercel function that pins on the author's behalf before the transaction is offered. The order is the whole fix — earlier, the screen asked authors to download the bundle and pin it by hand, and nobody does that, which is how three statements ended up on chain with CIDs no node serves. The function accepts a bundle only if it rebuilds the root the client states, using the same verifyBundle a verifier runs, and pins the received bytes verbatim rather than a re-serialised object, because a round trip through an object could move the CID. The browser then compares the CID it gets back with the one it computed itself and refuses to register if they differ. It is a second point of centralisation next to the registry owner: it can refuse, it cannot forge.
Partner technologies: ENS (ENSv2 on Sepolia) supplies the identity layer without which a proof of authorship convinces no reader; IPFS holds the full text addressed by its own hash, so the chain only has to carry 32 bytes; Vercel hosts the static export plus the single pinning function.
AI usage, declared honestly: contracts, frontend and tests were developed with Claude Code. Architecture, design decisions and verification by me.

name: Allowance
description: A spending limit for AI agents — signed by a human, enforced before payment, and receipted forever.
projectDescription:
AI agents can spend money autonomously now. The x402 standard lets an agent hit an API, get told it costs a cent, pay, and carry on — no card, no human. That works beautifully, and it's the problem: x402 answers how money moves, and nothing answers whether it should. An agent reads a poisoned webpage and sends 500 HBAR to an attacker. Or it loops overnight and buys the same call four thousand times. Every one of those payments is correctly signed and correctly settled. The money is just gone.
Spending limits do exist — Hedera's Agent Kit ships policies, x402 ships SpendControls — and they solve real problems. But in every case the limit is a setting the agent itself can reach. The thing being restricted holds the restriction. That's not a limit; it's a suggestion.
Allowance is the layer that fixes it. A human writes spending rules — per-payment cap, rolling hourly budget, which counterparties are acceptable — and signs them as an EIP-712 message. The agent receives a sealed envelope it can read but cannot rewrite; change a digit and the signature breaks. Before every payment a guard checks the amount, the running spend, and the recipient's on-chain reputation from the ERC-8004 registry.
Every decision is written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic — including the refusals. That's the part everyone skips. If your agent is attacked at 3am and the guard holds, a success-only log shows you nothing, and nothing looks exactly like no attack happened. At $0.0001 per message, logging every denial is free, so the trail is complete instead of sampled.
In the live demo the allowlist is deliberately empty. The agent pays an account its owner has never approved, because three independent reviewers on-chain rate it 910/1000 — then gets refused on the fourth call when the hourly budget is spent. The run finishes by replaying the topic from a public mirror node and recomputing the spend from scratch: it matches. The audit trail isn't a log kept beside the system; it is the system's memory.
howItsMade:
TypeScript monorepo, npm workspaces, no build step — tsx runs sources directly. 94 tests, none requiring a network, because the evaluator is a pure function: no I/O, no clock, every fact passed in as an argument.
Hedera does settlement, evidence, and reputation. HCS is the reason the project works at all — our claim is a complete audit trail, and on an EVM chain each log line is a gas-costing contract event, so denying a $0.002 payment would cost more than the payment. You'd batch or log off-chain, and the verifiability claim collapses. HCS is a native service at $0.0001/message and 10,000+ TPS, so recording every refusal stops being a cost decision.
x402 — we didn't wrap the library. It publishes an async BeforePaymentCreationHook that runs before a payment payload is built and can abort with a reason; that signature is almost exactly our evaluator's, so our guard is an x402 hook. Settlement goes through the Blocky402 facilitator, which co-signs and submits every transfer — which is why our payment requirements advertise their fee-payer account.
ERC-8004 answers "should we pay this stranger?" The registries turned out to be deployed on Hedera testnet at the same deterministic CREATE2 addresses used everywhere else, so reputation and settlement share a chain — no cross-chain hop on the payment path. We count distinct clients, not feedback entries: fifty five-star ratings from one address is one endorsement.
Three things worth flagging as hard-won. ExactHederaScheme exists three times on different subpaths — /exact/client, /server, /facilitator — and the bare import gives you the client one, which fails on a server with a useless error. Two Hedera SDKs coexist (@hashgraph/sdk for receipts, @hiero-ledger/sdk transitively via x402), and instances can't cross that boundary. And a Hedera transfer can pass execute() and still fail at consensus, so the ALLOW receipt is written in onPaymentResponse after settlement confirms — writing it at authorization time would put a payment on a permanent audit trail that never happened.
We also rewrote the reputation layer once. It originally scanned NewFeedback logs, on the belief getSummary() couldn't aggregate without a client list. getClients() returns exactly that list — and Hedera's mirror node caps topic-filtered queries at a 7-day window, so the log approach would have meant ~30 windowed queries per lookup on the payment path. Two eth_calls replaced all of it.
The console is a single self-contained HTML file — no framework, no backend — so a judge can double-click it and see live receipts without running an install.
Not finished: the owner's key still lives in .env, so "human-authorized" currently means a string on the same machine as the agent — the same weakness we criticise above. LedgerTrustRoot is written against Ledger's Device Management Kit and typechecks against their real packages, but never ran: no physical device, and Ledger's own Ethereum app doesn't build against their own SDK (C_chain_1_14px_bitmap undeclared, reproducing on both Nano targets). Details and the full error are in the README.

name: Securtxn
description: SecurTxn is control layer that verifies identity before money moves
projectDescription:
THE PROBLEM
About $226 billion a year moves in B2B stablecoin payments, and none of it can
be recalled. When a payout goes to the wrong recipient, there is no chargeback
and no reversal. What exists instead is a recovery industry: Binance processes
roughly 4,000 deposit-retrieval requests a month, and Kraken charges $200 to
$500 per attempt. Recovering a misdirected payment is a support ticket. Not
sending one is a control.
Traditional banking solved this in 2020 with Confirmed Payee, which checks the
name on the account before a transfer goes out. Stablecoin rails have no
equivalent. A wallet address carries no identity, so nothing on the payment
path can answer the only question that matters: does this address actually
belong to the vendor on the invoice?
https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbestechcouncil/2026/08/06/why-stablecoins-still-have-a-payment-recovery-problem/
SecurTxn is that missing control layer.
WHAT IT DOES
SecurTxn sits in front of a stablecoin payout and refuses to let it proceed
until three independent questions are answered:

Is the payee who they claim to be?
Is a live human approving this specific payment?
Is this address allowed to hold the asset at all?

Each is answered by a different system, and none of them can be satisfied by
the person trying to get paid.
HOW IT WORKS
Onboarding. A vendor connects a wallet and completes a real DigiLocker consent
flow, which returns their Aadhaar and PAN documents with a verifiable XML
signature. They then sign an EIP-712 wallet control proof and an identity
binding that ties the DigiLocker subject to that specific address. Only the
combination makes a wallet CONFIRMED. Identity documents are encrypted at rest
and reduced to HMAC digests for matching.
On-chain KYC (Hedera). The platform issues a verifiable credential for the
confirmed wallet and calls grantKyc on a tokenised bond deployed with the
Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio (security 0.0.10444329, internal KYC
activated). This is the control that cannot be talked around: the token itself
rejects transfers to addresses that were never granted. An unverified wallet
does not fail our validation, it reverts on chain.
Consent before matching. When a payment is raised, the payee is notified and
must accept it with an EIP-712 signature before any identity check runs. This
ordering is deliberate. Running a match without consent would turn the product
into a lookup service that tells a stranger whether a given address belongs to
a given PAN.
The match (Chainlink CRE). The identity comparison runs inside a Confidential
Workflow on a Chainlink DON, in a TEE. The enclave never sees a name or a PAN.
It receives HMAC digests, compares them as opaque bytes, and returns one of
four verdicts: MATCHED, IDENTITY_MISMATCH, WALLET_NOT_ON_FILE or
VENDOR_NOT_FOUND. There is a single reason code for any identity failure,
because reporting which field mismatched would hand a prober a second bit of
information. The enclave has no crypto library and does no name scoring, so
there is nothing in it to leak.
Proof of personhood (World ID). The sender passes a World ID Selfie Check on
every payment, unconditionally. The payee is challenged only when the risk
engine asks for one: a first payment from this sender, an amount above their
tier ceiling, a recently rotated wallet, a stale check, or a recent identity
mismatch. Signals are role-qualified as sender:<paymentId> and
payee:<paymentId>, so one human acting as both sides of a payment cannot
satisfy both checks with the same proof.
Settlement. The payout moves as an HTS token through an HTLC on Hedera testnet.
The payee claims it by revealing the preimage from their own key, which makes
the reveal itself the receipt. Nobody can produce it on their behalf, and an
unclaimed payment returns to the sender after the timelock.
Evidence. Every decision writes an evidence record. Records are batched into a
Merkle tree and anchored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic (0.0.10454706).
Each anchor reads itself back from a mirror node after writing, so an anchor is
verified against the public record rather than merely submitted. Any single
record can produce a standalone inclusion proof, and altering a record after
anchoring makes its proof stop matching.
Exception desk. A refusal is not a dead end. Blocked payments open a case with
the reason code, the evidence trail, and a path to resolution, because the
finance team still has an invoice to pay.
WHAT IS REAL
This is deployed and runs end to end at https://www.securtxn.com with no mocks
in the path. Two people have completed the full flow with their own DigiLocker
identities, their own World ID enrolments, a verdict from the deployed TEE
workflow, and a real token transfer on Hedera testnet.
One thing stated plainly: the asset moved in the demo is stUSDC, a test
stablecoin we issued on Hedera testnet, not Circle's USDC. The mechanics are
identical, an HTS fungible token moving between KYC gated accounts through the
escrow contract, but it should not be described as transferring USDC.
TECH STACK
Hedera: Asset Tokenization Studio bond with internal KYC, HTS token, HTLC
escrow contract, Hedera Consensus Service for evidence anchoring, mirror node
verification.
Chainlink CRE: Confidential Workflow with a TEE handler, deployed to a DON,
secrets held in the Vault DON, digest-only matching.
World ID: Selfie Check proof of personhood, role-qualified signals, nullifier
continuity enforced against enrolment.
Identity: DigiLocker via the Sandbox aggregator, Aadhaar and PAN with XML
signature verification.
Application: TypeScript, Fastify, Prisma, PostgreSQL, Next.js, viem, EIP-712
throughout.
howItsMade:
ARCHITECTURE
A pnpm monorepo. Fastify and Prisma over PostgreSQL (Supabase) for the API,
Next.js for the web app, viem for all chain work, Zod at every boundary, and a
shared package holding the EIP-712 struct definitions. Chain, compliance,
anchoring and identity are interfaces with a real and a mock implementation
selected by env var, so the test suite never depends on a public network being
up while the deployed instance always uses the real one. API and web run on
Render, the database on Supabase, the workflow on a Chainlink DON, the
contracts on Hedera testnet.
CHAINLINK CRE, AND THE CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPED THE DESIGN
The identity match runs in a Confidential Workflow on a TEE. The obvious design
was "encrypt the vendor record, decrypt inside the enclave, compare it." That
is impossible. The CRE SDK bans node:crypto outright, and the declared globals
are only TextEncoder/Decoder, Buffer, atob/btoa, URL and console. No
crypto.subtle, nothing. There is no primitive inside the enclave to decrypt
with.
So we inverted it. At onboarding we store HMAC(pan, pepper) and
HMAC(normalise(legalName), pepper). At match time the API hashes the sender's
typed values the same way, and the enclave compares digest against digest. No
crypto is needed inside because the hashing already happened outside. The
pepper never leaves our server and the enclave never sees an identity. It is
not that the enclave is trusted with PII, it is that there is no PII in it to
leak.
The cost is real and worth stating. Exact digests remove the near-miss band, so
a typo is now a flat mismatch rather than a 0.95 similarity score. We think
that is a net gain, because fuzzy name matching is precisely how a lookalike
payee slips through. Normalisation does the work instead: "MERIDIAN COMPONENTS
PRIVATE LIMITED" and "Meridian Components Pvt Ltd" reduce to the same digest.
The second CRE problem is that the HTTP trigger is fire and forget.
workflows.execute returns an execution id and nothing else, and there is no API
to read a workflow's return value, so a workflow cannot be called as a
synchronous "is this payee verified?" RPC. The workflow POSTs its verdict to a
callback endpoint and the caller awaits the database row. That suits the
confidential design rather than fighting it, because the verdict is exactly the
one value that is supposed to leave the enclave.
The callback has to be idempotent. In DON mode every observing node runs the
handler and every node POSTs the same verdict, so five callbacks arrive for one
logical answer. In TEE mode exactly one does. Both are correct, so later
callbacks are accepted and ignored.
One trap worth naming: a CRE execution reaching SUCCESS only means the handler
did not throw. A matcher that always answered MATCHED would look identical
across every case. Our end to end script therefore asserts the verdict for five
different inputs rather than the execution status. The enclave authenticates to
the vendor lookup with a JWT held in the Vault DON and released directly into
the attested enclave.
HEDERA
Three separate uses, each doing something the others cannot.
The tokenised bond is deployed with the Asset Tokenization Studio with
internalKycActivated set to true. That single flag is the integration: false and
the token enforces nothing, leaving grantKyc with nothing to gate. The issuing
account holds the KYC_MANAGER, INTERNAL_KYC_MANAGER and SSI_MANAGER roles and is
registered as an issuer, without which grantKyc reverts with AccountIsNotIssuer.
The demonstration that matters is the failure: a transfer to a wallet that never
went through grantKyc reverts on chain, not in our validation.
The cash leg is an HTS fungible token moving through an HTLC contract. HTS
tokens answer the ERC-20 interface at their long zero address, 0x followed by
the token number in hex padded to 40 characters, which is how viem can talk to
them at all. Accounts are created with maxAutoAssociations set to -1, because a
receiver with no free association slots rejects an incoming token transfer. The
balance card surfaces that field for exactly this reason.
Evidence anchoring uses the Consensus Service. Records are batched into a Merkle
tree and the root is submitted to a topic. Anchoring then reads itself back from
a mirror node and compares the published root against the recorded one. Mirror
nodes lag consensus by a few seconds, so the read back retries briefly, but a
root mismatch throws immediately and is never retried away: a disagreement
between our row and the public record is the one failure this whole mechanism
exists to surface.
WORLD ID
Selfie Check, with signals role qualified as sender:<paymentId> and
payee:<paymentId>. This is not cosmetic. The nullifier uniqueness index is
(nullifier, action, signal), so a bare payment id means one human acting as both
sides of a payment collides with their own earlier proof. The asymmetry is
deliberate too: the sender is checked on every payment unconditionally, while
the payee is challenged only on risk, because the payee is the counterparty and
friction there costs you the payment.
HACKY AND NOTABLE
The EIP-712 structs live in one shared package imported by the signer, the
verifier and the tests. A second copy that merely reorders two fields produces
signatures that fail with no useful error, because the recovered address is
simply a different address.
Next.js rewrites default to afterFiles, which runs only when no page matched. We
had pages at /vendors and /payments, so the API proxy was silently shadowed:
calls returned 200 with Next's HTML, JSON.parse produced a string, and the first
visible symptom was an undefined id three steps later. beforeFiles fixes it.
The API's token minting endpoint is registered only when NODE_ENV is not
production, deliberately, because an approver token is what stands between a
payment and a human agreeing to it. That broke the entire deployed app, since
the web console minted its own tokens. The fix is a Next route handler signing
HS256 tokens server side for two roles only, agent and approver, never issuer or
bridge. The JWT is hand rolled with node:crypto rather than adding a library,
because the payload is two claims and a new dependency means a lockfile change
on a deployment that installs with a frozen lockfile.
grantKyc is idempotent. The chain outlives our database and the wallet key lives
in the browser's localStorage, so a reset database plus a reconnected wallet
asks the chain for a state it is already in. The contract answers with a bare
custom error revert that surfaces as an unhelpful 500. A grant is a state, not
an event.
Every foreign key is onDelete: Restrict, so evidence is never silently orphaned.
Even wiping the demo database has to be done in strict reverse dependency order.
DigiLocker returned a 403 whose body we were deliberately withholding from logs
to avoid leaking PII. The actual message was "Insufficient credits." We now
surface the message and transaction id only, never the data. Separately, a user
who grants Aadhaar consent but not PAN produced an opaque 400 much later, so
there is now a pre-flight scope check naming the document that is missing.

name: NotYet
description: Scheduled agent authority — spend keys, API keys, any secret — that doesn't exist until its time.
projectDescription:
NotYet gives an autonomous agent a budget on a schedule — without ever handing it a key it can drain early.
The problem:
• Hand the agent the whole budget up front → one hack or prompt injection drains it all.
• Run a key server that releases keys just-in-time → that server is a honeypot holding every future key.
• Session keys solve expiry; nothing solves start — authority always exists the moment it's issued.
Why it matters — every one of these was a key that existed before it was needed:
• Grok / Bankr wallet drain — May 2026, ~$175K.
• Lobstar Wilde trading bot — Feb 2026, ~$250K.
• Malicious LLM routers — Apr 2026, ~$500K.
How NotYet fixes it:
• Each period's key is timelock-encrypted (drand/tlock) to a future round — before its time it doesn't exist in usable form, not even for the owner. Ask early → NOT_YET.
• Not just payments — the same lock seals ANY secret (an API key, a credential, a token): the agent holds only ciphertext up front and gets it at its time, not before. No key server to breach or coerce.
• Spends settle as real x402 pay-per-call on Hedera, gated on-chain by a PeriodVault (window + budget + per-tx cap) and audited on HCS.
• Hacked today = one period's budget. Never the treasury, never a future period.
howItsMade:
• Issuance: each period's spend key is generated in software, its EVM address committed to a PeriodVault contract, then tlock-encrypted (tlock-js) to a future drand quicknet round and the plaintext wiped. The agent holds only ciphertexts.
• Unlock + spend: the agent calls withdraw(i, amount, sig); the vault enforces on-chain the time window (useless before AND after its period), ecrecover identity, per-period budget, and a per-tx ceiling. A real x402 pay-per-call then settles via the keyless Blocky402 facilitator; encrypted receipts land on HCS.
• Hedera: PeriodVault runs on Hedera EVM via @hiero-ledger/sdk (no ethers) — money, x402, HCS audit, and an optional HIP-423 scheduled-tx mode, all on one chain, no bridge.
• Ledger: the schedule is signed on-device via the Device Management Kit (headless on Speculos, RFC 6979, ERC-7730 descriptor); the device also co-signs over-cap spends and holds the audit view keys the agent can never reopen.
• Bazantic: wrapped as an MCP server + a published recipe chaining two services (NotYet + Hedera Mirror Node) — any agent integrates in one line.
• Stack: TypeScript ESM, viem, tweetnacl, drand-client, solc. Also an npm SDK: @keccak002/notyet.
