name: Wallet Vitals
description: Aave risk copilot with health factors, stress tests, and verifiable onchain evidence.
projectDescription:
Wallet Vitals is a read-only Aave V3 Ethereum risk copilot. Paste a public address without signing in, connecting a wallet, or signing a message. The app returns a reconstructed health factor, liquidation buffer, fixed 5%/10%/20% collateral stress scenarios, and changes between comparable snapshots.
The Graph supplies indexed positions, reserve indices and rates, liquidation parameters, and block metadata. The backend reads Aave oracle prices and the pool's account data at that same block hash, and cross-checks the reconstructed account before producing a report. Stale blocks, indexing errors, negative balances, unsupported eMode, and inconsistent accounts stop analysis instead of producing an unverified score.
Every report carries an Evidence Receipt: subgraph and deployment identifiers, block number and hash, timestamps, calculation rules, assumptions, position references, oracle/pool addresses, and the contract cross-check. An optional AI layer explains precomputed facts; critical liquidation-boundary answers remain deterministic. Warning and danger labels are not presented as liquidation.
The application is publicly deployed on Cloudflare with independent D1 storage, server-side API keys, expiring report links, explanation caching, and bounded public-demo usage. Live Graph/RPC/AI integration has been verified and all 50 tests pass in GitHub Actions. The video shows genuine public-deployment captures with English synthetic narration.
This is a historical evidence snapshot, not a guarantee of current safety or financial advice. It never signs or executes transactions. The repository transparently discloses its retained upstream baseline and all new work in PRE_EXISTING.md. AI assistance was used during development.
howItsMade:
The implementation uses FastAPI and strict Pydantic contracts with deterministic Decimal/RAY math. A server-side GraphQL adapter queries the Aave V3 Ethereum Subgraph through The Graph Network and reconstructs accrued balances from scaled balances, reserve indices, rates, and source-block time. The Graph is load-bearing: without it, new analyses cannot discover positions.
A notable integration finding was that indexed prices could be frozen even when the indexed block was current. We therefore obtain Aave's own oracle values using EIP-1898 eth_call requests pinned to the exact evidence block hash, resolve the oracle and pool from Aave's Ethereum addresses provider, and compare the reconstructed totals and health factor against the pool. There is no latest-block or fixture fallback. Unsupported eMode and material discrepancies fail closed.
The local app runs on Python 3.12 with SQLite; production runs as a native Cloudflare Python 3.13 Worker with D1. A Fetch-backed httpx transport supports the same shared application code without sockets. The responsive UI uses server-rendered HTML, CSS, and dependency-free JavaScript. Production includes atomic request quotas, cached explanations, and 24-hour report links.
OpenAI Responses receives precomputed structured facts. Numeric and identifier guards constrain narration, and deterministic explanations remain available. The boundary-critical 'What breaks first?' response is always deterministic. Keys never enter browser JavaScript.
uv, Ruff, Pytest, GitHub Actions, and Docker support reproducibility; 50 tests cover risk math, data validation, oracle/account checks, API behavior, storage and quotas. Code was developed with AI assistance.
Provenance: the repository retains the MIT-licensed dorukyy/telegram-wallet-tracker baseline under the upstream-baseline tag. The legacy Telegram bot is not the running product. The web app, Graph integration, Aave risk engine, same-block contract checks, tests, and Cloudflare deployment are new work in event-period commits. PRE_EXISTING.md describes the boundary; we do not claim the upstream code as original.

name: DeDNS-over-DeVPN
description: DDoV: anonymous browsing via attested, no-log relays - paid per-session on Arc via x402.
projectDescription:
DDoV (DeDNS-over-DeVPN) is a marketplace for anonymous internet access with enforceable, revocable permissions. A user pays for a time-boxed session at a chosen bandwidth tier (Lite/Standard/Turbo), and their device opens an encrypted tunnel to an authorized relay operator. That operator's tunnel-termination, DNS-resolution, and outbound-proxy logic runs inside a Chainlink CRE confidential handler, so the operator's own machine cannot read or log the user's traffic - attested and independently verifiable, not just promised.
Which relays are currently authorized lives in an ENSv2 registry (hierarchical subnames like bob.dvod.eth) that separates the operational key (updates endpoint/capabilities) from the payout address (where earnings go), so a compromised operator key can't redirect funds. A permissionless watchdog contract - not a human admin - automatically revokes any relay whose attestation report stops matching its published, audited build hash, and the client fails over to a healthy relay within seconds.
When you pay for a VPN with a your card, the payment itself ties your name to the service - you're exposing exactly the identity a VPN is supposed to protect. Paying in crypto avoids that: no card, no name, no linkage back to you, which is why DDoV settles exclusively through Arc/x402 rather than any card rail. Since payment is x402-gated and settles in USDC on Arc, as a single batched per-session purchase - never a per-packet or per-DNS-query transaction, so the latency budget for live browsing stays intact.
The one-line pitch: browse without your ISP, your relay operator, or the sites you visit ever being able to link "who" to "what" — provably, not on our word. It's a full VPN-shaped privacy layer, not DNS-only, and the README states plainly which pieces (ENSv2, Chainlink CRE, Arc/x402, automatic vs. manual revocation) are genuinely live versus honestly labeled as simulated at demo time.
howItsMade:
DDoV is a pnpm + Turborepo TypeScript monorepo, built spec-first: the architecture, phase plan, and design system are laid out up front and drive implementation phase by phase, with small feature-branch commits merged into dev and tagged phase-completions merged into main -never a single end-of-day dump.
The shared type layer (packages/session-spec) uses Zod to define the session, tier, and ENSv2 capability-record schemas, plus an explicit session state-machine transition table (BROWSING → QUOTED → PAID → TOKEN_ISSUED → TUNNEL_OPEN → ACTIVE, with RELAY_REVOKED/RELAY_UNREACHABLE both routing through an automatic FAILOVER_SELECT) so every transition is validated in code, not just diagrammed.
Four partner technologies each do one job, deliberately non-overlapping: ENSv2 hierarchical subnames + permissioned resolvers register relay operators and separate their operational key from their payout address, so a compromised operator key can never redirect earnings; Chainlink CRE runs the tunnel/DNS/proxy logic inside a confidential, attested handler so the operator's own machine can't read traffic; Arc settles USDC; x402 gates session purchase/renewal only - never per-packet - to keep DNS/browsing latency real.
The design system enforces its own discipline in code: an --accent token is reserved by convention to exactly three UI moments (countdown, tier highlight, failover/revocation), documented alongside the token values themselves rather than left to hope.

name: Credence
description: Onchain credit bureau giving autonomous agents identity, reputation, and financing.
projectDescription: Credence is an onchain credit bureau for autonomous agents. It gives each agent a persistent ENSv2 identity, connects that identity to human-backed verification, and builds a transparent credit history from completed jobs. The CreditBureau contract records outcomes, calculates a score and spend limit, and freezes agents after repeated defaults. CreditEscrow enforces those limits at settlement time, so creditworthiness is not merely displayed in a dashboard. The Graph indexes registrations, outcomes, score changes, and limit updates for a live analytics experience. Once an agent proves its reliability, its receivables can be priced and tokenized through Hedera. The result is an end-to-end trust layer for agents: identity, verification, reputation, controlled credit, and financing.
howItsMade: The core contracts are written in Solidity and tested with Hardhat. CreditBureau stores agent profiles, human-backing status, outcome history, score snapshots, spend limits, and freeze state. CreditEscrow checks the bureau before allowing settlement and records the outcome afterward. ENSv2 is integrated through a separate Foundry project because the ENSv2 contracts are distributed as a Foundry dependency. Our custom AgentSubnameRegistrar creates non-transferable agent subnames under a project-owned ENSv2 namespace, deploys per-agent resolver and registry proxies through the ENSv2 Verifiable Factory, and uses Enhanced Access Control role bitmaps to scope CreditBureau’s permissions. World provides the human-backing signal, while The Graph converts contract events into queryable entities consumed by the frontend and credit analyst. Hedera’s Asset Tokenization Studio is used to issue receivables whose pricing reflects the agent’s onchain score. The notable design choice is treating every boundary as enforceable infrastructure: ENS identity prevents ambiguity, EAC limits who can update records, escrow prevents unauthorized settlement, and indexing makes the full decision trail auditable.

name: harbor
description: Harbor: instant liquidity for redeemable assets and pending withdrawal rights.
projectDescription:
Harbor is an onchain redemption-liquidity market connecting users who need liquidity now with capital willing to wait.
Across DeFi, redeemable does not always mean immediately available. Yield-bearing assets can involve withdrawal queues, cooldowns and delayed settlement. Once a
user requests redemption, they may receive a pending withdrawal right instead of spendable funds. Harbor makes that waiting period tradable.
Users can swap supported redeemable assets, sell eligible pending withdrawal rights for immediate liquidity, or buy available rights from pool inventory.
Liquidity providers deposit into a shared vault that supplies capital across approved strategies. The pool can resell acquired assets and claims or hold them
through redemption, sharing the resulting gains and losses with LPs.
Harbor’s pricing engine considers expected recovery, remaining settlement time, operating costs and the pool’s existing exposure. It does not treat every claim
as guaranteed cash or assume every withdrawal takes the same time. As exposure grows, inventory-sensitive pricing makes further purchases more conservative and
adjusts resale prices to encourage reducing exposure.
Ordinary token trading supports buying and selling with both exact-input and exact-output execution through Aqua and SwapVM. Eligible withdrawal NFTs trade as
whole rights through direct settlement using the same Book, pricing and risk accounting. Approved integrations do not require fresh governor approval for every
NFT.
The Graph powers transaction-linked views of trading activity, strategy exposure, deposits, withdrawals and realized results. Privy provides embedded-wallet
onboarding alongside external-wallet support, with capability-aware batching and ordinary transaction flows.
We also evaluated four pricing policies against frozen historical withdrawal data: fixed-delay pricing, age-based pricing, queue-aware valuation and Harbor’s
capacity-adjusted model. The presentation distinguishes simulated results from actual protocol activity and makes the assumptions and maker-versus-seller
tradeoffs explicit.
The current demonstration runs on Hoodi. Harbor’s contracts are unaudited, and immediate liquidity depends on supported assets, valid pricing and available
capital.
The core idea is simple: a user should be able to sell the right to wait, while the buyer receives a clearly priced and verifiable obligation.
howItsMade:
Harbor is built with Solidity and Foundry, integrating official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM contracts, Solady and OpenZeppelin primitives, The Graph, and a Next.js
frontend with Privy.
The contracts separate economic responsibilities. HarborVault holds pool funds, issues LP shares and manages withdrawal liabilities. HarborBook owns portfolio
accounting, acquisition basis, exposure limits, pricing policies and settlement rules. A shared Executor coordinates trades across registered Book/Vault pairs.
Issuer adapters verify asset conversions, withdrawal ownership, claim status and actual recovery.
A central accounting distinction runs through the system: nominal entitlement, estimated portfolio value and spendable cash are different quantities. A pending
claim can contribute to portfolio backing without becoming cash available for another purchase or an LP payout.
Harbor combines discounted recovery valuation with an inventory-capacity adjustment. In simplified form:
recovery_value =
nominal_entitlement
× sum(
scenario_probability × recovery_fraction
/ (1 + annual_funding_rate × remaining_days / 365)
)
pool_bid =
recovery_value − operating_cost − buy_margin
− increase_in_capacity_penalty
pool_ask =
recovery_value + operating_cost + sell_margin
− decrease_in_capacity_penalty
The capacity penalty is zero below a utilization threshold and grows cubically above it. Its change across a trade adjusts the price according to how much
exposure the pool acquires or releases. Requesting redemption does not free that exposure merely because the asset changes representation.
Authorized publishers provide reusable, bounded and expiring recovery-discount parameters. Contracts combine them with verified live state to calculate
executable amounts. Quotes do not depend on a backend signing every individual fill. Independent valuation remains responsible for LP accounting; publishing a
trading price cannot manufacture NAV.
For ordinary ERC-20 swaps, Harbor builds a canonical SwapVM program using the official instruction set. Extruction invokes Harbor’s Book pricing logic, while
FeeProtocol handles the configured VM fees. The Vault is Aqua’s maker and publishes its strategy allocations. Aqua allocations and token approvals do not
replace Harbor’s cash, reserve and exposure constraints.
Execution opens a shared operation lock, calculates the trade through the VM, authenticates callbacks, measures token movements and commits accounting only
after settlement checks pass. Exact-input and exact-output modes use explicit integer-rounding rules. Transient storage carries transaction-local authorization
and callback state, while fixed linked libraries keep substantial execution logic outside the Book’s runtime without introducing upgradeable dispatch.
Raw withdrawal NFTs use direct settlement through the same Book because Aqua’s ERC-20 transfer path does not carry NFT IDs. The adapter verifies each claim’s
ownership, status and entitlement under an approved issuer policy. This avoids deploying a wrapper and publishing a separate Aqua strategy for every withdrawal
ID.
The Graph indexes economic events into trade history, strategy-level activity, LP flows and realized results, with transaction hashes for verification. The data
layer also includes reusable standardized external-vault queries and a historical issuer pipeline. Historical finalizations use inclusive ranges and prefix
accounting to keep indexing work bounded. Exported research datasets carry provenance and reconciliation checks, and simulated pricing results remain separate
from live Harbor events.
Privy manages embedded-wallet onboarding and connected external wallets. The transaction layer checks wallet capabilities before requesting atomic batches or
EIP-7702 authorization, with ordinary transactions available when batching is unsupported. Harbor’s Periphery handles native-token wrapping, unwrapping and
measured refunds without taking ownership of users’ signing keys.
Foundry tests cover accounting lifecycles, all four trading modes, fee rounding, withdrawal funding, claim recovery, callback rollback and pool isolation. Fork-
based tests exercise real issuer and Aqua/SwapVM dependencies, while the Hoodi deployment demonstrates actual token and withdrawal-right transfers.

name: ARC MAP
description: Investigate Arc activity with sourced reports and a baseline you can revisit.
projectDescription:
ARC MAP turns activity on Arc into questions you can test. Start with a sourced signal on Today, run a read-only Hunter, inspect the transactions, then save a thesis with a fixed baseline and a finite check budget. Return later to see what changed without rewriting the original observation.
In the recorded demo, The Graph returns 200 SUN transfer events, all from one transaction. ARC MAP reports that limit instead of treating the event count as independent activity. When the index advances but the transfer evidence stays unchanged, the thesis stays unchanged too.
The current source also supports sharing one completed investigation: a contributor adds a public source and counterevidence, the owner reassesses, and revocation removes access while preserving the original report and contribution. This sharing flow was tested separately and is not shown in the recorded demo.
The Graph supplies indexed transfer evidence; Arcscan and GitHub remain separate, labelled sources. You can explore without a wallet. Built-in analysis is rules-based; external agents can use the same bounded research operations through MCP.
howItsMade:
Next.js 16, React 19 and TypeScript serve the browser and the research API. Node 22 workers run three loops: a public-source collector, an Arcscan radar, and a finite thesis checker with lease-fenced checks. SQLite stores observations, radar entries, private missions and theses; reports are immutable and comparisons are pinned to the baseline observed when the thesis was saved.
The Graph supplies the transfer evidence. We deployed an ERC20 Transfer subgraph for the SUN token on Arc testnet (chain 5042002) in subgraphs/arcmap, and the Hunter queries it with bounded, dated samples. Arcscan and GitHub are separate, separately labelled evidence sources. A Graph outage is shown as a Graph error, never relabelled as an explorer result.
Privy is wired for wallet login and viem for chain reads, but the submitted journey is read-only and performs no transaction. Contracts in contracts/ (Foundry) are the research-payment escrow developed during the event and are not exercised by this demo.
Oscar set the product direction, workflow, visual direction, priorities and acceptance requirements. Codex and Cursor wrote most of the implementation and tests under his review, and Claude and Fable did source reviews. The product analysis is rules-based and does not call an LLM.

name: Tabir
description: Graduated liquidation protection with a policy no one can see. not even the node operators.
projectDescription:
Tabir protects a leveraged ETH/USDC position from liquidation without giving away how it does it.
Most liquidation bots work off a single visible threshold: when health factor drops below some level, repay the debt. That survives the first shock, but it burns the borrower's emergency capital and closes out a position they wanted to keep. Worse, a public rule is a rule an adversary can probe, nudge the price just far enough to trigger a costly defensive action, repeat, and drain the protection budget without ever needing to liquidate anything.
Tabir does two things differently. It responds in proportion to the actual threat rather than to a fixed level, using the rate of change in health factor to estimate time-to-breach and intervening only when a breach falls inside the reaction window. And it rations the emergency budget across the whole price path, holding reserve for a second shock it cannot see coming, so it survives multi-leg drawdowns that exhaust a naive strategy on the first dip.
The protection policy itself, thresholds, buffers, sizing, budget caps, never leaves a hardware-isolated enclave. Observers see the action taken. They never see the reasoning behind it, or how much capital is left.
The name is Indonesian for veil.
howItsMade:
Tabir is a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow in TypeScript, compiled to WASM with @chainlink/cre-sdk. It protects a leveraged vETH/vUSD position on Sepolia.
A log trigger on PriceUpdate (with a cron fallback) calls handlerInTee. Inside the enclave, the workflow pulls the signer key, the RPC URL, and the policy from the Vault DON, then reads the position over JSON-RPC and rebuilds the price history from logs. It then runs decide() and signs the deposit or repay transaction with viem. The DON publishes a receipt with a salted hash of the policy, so we can later prove which policy ran without revealing it.
decide() is pure bigint TypeScript, shared by the enclave and our rubric simulator, so the simulated scores describe the code that ships: 89.65 average, 0 of 11 scenarios liquidated.
Why CRE: a public policy can be attacked by pushing the price just past its thresholds. The TEE keeps every threshold sealed, and only the action comes out.
Hacky: the EVM write capability has no TEE support, so we send raw JSON-RPC and sign transactions inside the enclave. Every tick also runs the same path whether it acts or holds, so timing can't leak the thresholds.

name: Superposition
description: Aqua strategies backed by yield tokens: underlying asset discoverability, atomic re-deposit on fill.
projectDescription:
Superposition-Liquid is a meta-layer for 1inch Aqua that lets liquidity providers earn yield on 100% of their capital without giving up fill readiness.
Today, when a maker ships a strategy on 1inch Aqua, their tokens sit idle in their wallet — Aqua is pure virtual-balance accounting and never takes custody. Superposition changes what backs that strategy. The maker points a per-token config at a yield venue (Aave v3, any ERC-4626 vault like Morpho or Euler, Stargate V2 pools, Pendle PT, or a Uniswap v4 hook), and every fill cycles that capital inside the swap transaction itself: a preTransferOut hook JIT-withdraws/redeems/unstakes exactly the delivery amount and hands it to the taker; a postTransferIn hook re-deploys whatever the taker paid back into the protocol. The maker's wallet holds tokens only for the duration of one transaction, idle balance stays zero, and the position earns protocol yield on top of swap fees. To routers and aggregators it reads as an ordinary ETH/USDC pool.
It deliberately ships no pricing curve. Superposition wraps whatever SwapVM program the maker already writes — xyk, curved, flat-price, or a third-party curve — via two append-only meta-opcodes: YieldAdjustedRateXD (scales swap registers by the live exchange rate so quotes stay accurate while capital sits in yield tokens) and MakerCapitalGuardXD (makes quote() a complete fill-oracle: it reverts unless a real withdrawal of the delivery amount would succeed right now, so a passing quote is a strong fillability signal and a failing one returns the exact on-chain revert reason). Capability is abstracted behind one ILendingAdapter interface, so a new protocol is a single registry entry, not a router change. The adapters are pull-less: the router executes each adapter's pullPlan with its own allowance, so the maker approves once per token and never re-approves when switching protocols.
Beyond supply, a side can be borrow-sourced: MakerConfig.BorrowConfig lets an Aave side quote an asset the maker doesn't hold, borrowing it against yield-bearing collateral, with the matching in-fill repaying the debt first — turning the same adapter into a delta-neutral/short inventory profile. Superposition also reaches into Uniswap v4: the SuperpositionUniAdapter exposes a concentrated-liquidity hook (which itself keeps 100% of pooled capital in ERC-4626 vaults between swaps) as just another yield venue the Aqua router can back a position with.
howItsMade:
Stack: Solidity 0.8.30 + Foundry for the contracts; Next.js (App Router) + wagmi/viem + react-web3-icons for the landing page and a live maker console. Dependencies are pinned hard: 1inch/swap-vm v1.0.2, 1inch/aqua v1.0.0, OpenZeppelin v5.4.0, @1inch/solidity-utils 6.9.7.
Piecing it together. The core is a modified redeploy of the SwapVM router (explicitly allowed by the 1inch rules). We append two custom opcodes to the end of the dispatch table — the deployed v1.0.2 has reserved no-op slots, so appending is append-only and never renumbers existing instructions. Around that we built ILendingAdapter and five implementations (Aave v3, generic ERC-4626, Stargate V2, Pendle PT, Superposition v4 hook), plus a MakerConfig registry mapping (maker, token) → adapter, and two router hooks (preTransferOut, postTransferIn) that orchestrate the JIT cycle. Each adapter resolves per-fill via one registry lookup, so routing never touches pricing math.
Partner tech and why it helped. 1inch Aqua is the substrate: ship() allocates virtual balances with no token movement, and pull()/push() move real tokens only when a fill happens — exactly the seam we needed to swap "idle wallet" for "yield position" without changing the pool surface. Chainlink Data Feeds are our MEV guard: a price-sanity opcode reverts a fill if the implied swap price deviates beyond the maker's tolerance band from ETH/USD or USDC/USD (with per-feed staleness checks), so manipulation is rejected on-chain before execution. Uniswap v4 supplies a second engine entirely — the Superposition concentrated-liquidity hook — which we expose as a yield venue through the same one-token adapter interface.
Notable, slightly hacky bits. (1) SwapVM hooks don't receive the final recipient and the default transfer always runs, so direct-to-taker delivery is impossible — we designed a "JIT-unwrap" pattern: the hook withdraws into the maker's wallet as preTransferOut, and SwapVM's own transfer delivers. (2) Aave tokens rebase, so shipping virtual balances in share counts while fills move underlying units produced a real unit mismatch; we fixed it by shipping in aToken count units and scaling quotes by rate(now)/rate(ship) on both quote() and swap(). (3) Borrow mode is implemented as the inverse of supply in the existing adapter (borrow on out-fill, repay-first on in-fill) rather than a new contract, keeping one code path and one source of truth. (4) The generic ERC-4626 adapter covers Morpho, Euler, Spark, and Yearn with zero protocol-specific code.
Testing is where the design was validated. Real-vault fork tests caught two bugs mocks missed — the aToken unit mismatch above, and Pendle's callback conventions. The suite is 101 tests: unit + invariant fuzzing (256 runs over randomized fill sequences) + fork suites against live Base, Ethereum, and Arbitrum state. The whole stack is deployed to Ethereum Sepolia and verified via Sourcify (no Etherscan key), with an on-chain OrderBuilder so the console can ship() a real strategy through a browser wallet.

name: Peaje
description: The payment rail for AI agents: your site charges them, your agents buy for you.
projectDescription:
Peaje is the cash register of the agent economy: it lets any business charge AI agents per request, and lets any person run a buyer agent that spends from the same balance, with no payment code and no crypto knowledge required.
Selling side: a business registers with an email and a URL, sets prices on links or API routes (or imports its sitemap), and gets a hosted gateway that answers HTTP 402 payment challenges via MPP, the machine-to-machine payment standard from Tempo and Stripe. Agents pay on their own in stablecoin (pathUSD on Tempo, USDC on Arc) and the gateway proxies the paid request to the original site. Peaje also makes the site discoverable to agents: agents.md, llms.txt, ard.json, an enriched openapi.json, an api-catalog, JSON-LD, Link headers and a paid-tools MCP server, all generated from the database and anchored at the business's own domain. The demo site's agent-readiness score (Ora) went from 40 to 73 after installing Peaje with a single prompt. The gateway also speaks the emerging agent-commerce protocols: UCP profile, ACP checkout sessions, and AP2 cart mandates signed with ES256.
Buying side: every account gets one buyer agent with its own wallet. You type what you need in plain language ("this week's weather in Bogotá, three lines"), the agent searches roughly 15,000 real paid services across three sources (Peaje's own directory, Coinbase's x402 Bazaar, and the ERC-8004 identity registry via The Graph) and shows you what it would buy, at what price, and why, before spending a cent. A language-model veto rejects services that would not answer the request: buying nothing beats buying garbage. On approval it pays (MPP on Tempo/Arc, x402 with real USDC on Base mainnet), translates your request into the service's actual query parameters, reads what it bought, and returns a short human-readable answer with the on-chain receipt behind it. The agent's wallet balance is its budget: it physically cannot overspend. Peaje takes a 2% fee per transaction on the selling side.
The full loop is live: an external agent paid for content on the demo business, that revenue funded the owner's buyer agent, and the buyer agent purchased real weather data and returned a three-line answer, every step with an on-chain receipt.
howItsMade:
Monorepo with three pieces: a multi-tenant Hono gateway (Railway) that does the charging, proxying, discovery generation and the whole buyer-agent engine; a Next.js dashboard (Vercel) with email-only onboarding; and a shared db package over Supabase. Wallets for businesses and agents are Privy server wallets, created invisibly at signup, exposed to code as viem accounts.
Charging uses mppx (MPP's reference implementation): the gateway issues 402 challenges offering two rails per request, Tempo (pathUSD) and Arc (USDC via EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization), verifies receipts, credits a per-tenant ledger net of the 2% fee, and proxies to the origin. Discovery files are not static: they are generated per tenant from the database and served through the business's own domain via a reverse-proxy kit installed by pasting one prompt into any coding assistant, so the docs self-name at the business domain and agents never get pointed at our infrastructure.
The buyer agent composes three discovery sources: our own directory, the full Coinbase x402 Bazaar index (~15 pages of 1,000 services, cached an hour: with the default 100 the agent only ever saw 0.7% of the market and bought junk), and ERC-8004 identity plus reputation read from Agent0 subgraphs on The Graph, which feeds on-chain reputation into every scoring decision. Deterministic keyword scoring picks a shortlist; Claude then acts as a veto gate ("does this service actually deliver the requested data?"), fills the winning API's query string (city coordinates, forecast variables, date ranges) and synthesizes the purchased content into a plain-language answer. Purchases pay via mppx on Tempo/Arc and via x402-fetch with real USDC on Base mainnet, from the same Privy account.
Notable hacky bits: the agent's spend cap is not an accounting entry, it is the wallet's literal balance, so no bug can overspend; structured outputs silently reject open JSON schemas, so the query-builder had to move from a record type to closed key/value pairs (before that fix every purchase went out with an empty query and we paid for weather APIs that returned nothing); sweeping a Tempo wallet needs a fee buffer because gas is paid in the same token you are sweeping; and pending withdrawals are reconciled lazily against chain receipts from the scheduler tick, so the ledger heals itself.

name: teecash
description: User-friendly trustless privacy mixer combining TEE and cryptography
projectDescription: This project combines blind signatures with TEE signing workflow to create seamless user experience while enabling trustless security, adding money and withdrawing are as simple as making regular wallet transactions and outputs are actual single-use wallets so long-term security of the funds does not depend on protocol details or additional at all (only mixing stage is dependent on that) and any functionality of a regular wallet is possible without extra engineering - if multiple outputs need to be combined to make a particular transaction those transfers are managed in the background USDC is used for gas on Arc avoiding any complexity with gas management.
howItsMade: Chainlink confidential TEE workflow is used to trustlessly sign blind BLS signatures turning classic Chaumian eCash into fully-trustless construction. TEE-based Privy wallets complement it by providing managed output addresses with no need for client-side secret management (beyond the mixing operation). Arc is perfect chain for this type of service, using USDC for gas is essential for making withdrawals seamless and so it EIP-2537 precompiles support.

name: ProofOfHack
description: ProofOfHack ensures hackers are not incentivised to hack platforms and then hold them to ransom.
projectDescription:
ProofOfHack bridges the gap between protocol teams needing verified evidence before paying
bounties and security researchers needing payment certainty before disclosing findings.
• Funded Bounty Escrows: Protocol teams create and fund immutable, fixed-reward USDC
bounties locked in onchain escrow contracts.
• Confidential Claim Submission: Researchers submit encrypted evidence packages that are
hidden from the protocol team prior to payment.
• Exclusive Claim Reservations: Submitting an active claim places a temporary, exclusive
hold on the bounty reward so multiple submissions cannot fight over the same reserved
funds.
• Confidential Verification: An isolated verifier service evaluates the claim against the
bounty policy and issues an onchain signed verdict without public disclosure.
• Permissionless Payouts: Qualifying claims credit the researcher directly in the escrow.
The researcher can collect USDC funds at any time without requiring protocol approval.
• Post-Payment Report Delivery: The private vulnerability report is released to the
protocol team's security reviewers only after payment finality is confirmed onchain.
• DeFi Vault Coverage & AI Assistant: Indexes live ERC-4626 vault deployments via The
Graph and uses a source-aware coverage assistant to recommend funding for uncovered vaults.
• Bounded Funding Automation: Enables automated policy funding via Circle Agent Stack
subject to strict onchain budget limits.
howItsMade:
Core Technologies Used
• Frontend: React 19, Vite, TypeScript, viem for chain reads/encoding, and Lucide UI icons.
• Backend & Database: Fastify, Node.js (>=22.14), PostgreSQL with Drizzle ORM, and pg-boss
for durable PostgreSQL-backed background job queues.
• Smart Contracts: Solidity 0.8.28, Foundry (forge), and OpenZeppelin ERC-20 / Merkle /
ReentrancyGuard standards.
• Cryptography: libsodium-wrappers-sumo and Web Crypto API for client-side envelope
encryption and verifier signatures.


Partner Technologies & Sponsor Integrations


-> Arc (Settlement & On-Chain Escrow)
• Role: Arc testnet serves as the primary financial settlement layer.
• How it helped: Arc's near-instant finality and native stablecoin architecture enabled
atomic USDC bounty funding and payouts.
• Benefit: Ensures low gas fees and deterministic transaction finality for automated
report releases.
-> Privy (Auth, Wallets & On-Chain Policy Controls)
• Role: Powers identity for protocol teams and researchers, embedded wallets, and smart
contract access rules.
• How it helped: We integrated Privy’s policy engine to enforce programmatic treasury
constraints (e.g., rejecting unauthorized funding actions or capping daily spending
limits).
• Benefit: Smooth Web3 onboarding without friction, paired with robust server-side wallet
management.
-> The Graph (Live Vault/Cont Coverage Indexing)
• Role: Indexes ERC-4626 vault and general smart contract deployments across target EVM networks using custom GraphQL subgraphs.
• How it helped: Queries real-time vault TVL, asset balances, and contract metadata to
calculate which registered vaults/contracts lack funded bounty coverage.
• Benefit: Gives protocols an automated, data-driven view of their security coverage gaps.
-> Circle Agent Stack (Autonomous Bounded Funding)
• Role: Powers an autonomous operations agent that monitors coverage gaps and top-ups
bounties.
• How it helped: Interacts with our BudgetController smart contract on Arc to execute
programmatic bounty deposits within daily budget caps.
• Benefit: Allows protocol treasuries to set rules once and let AI/agents handle routine
security top-ups automatically.

How The Pieces Fit Together (Data & Control Flow)
Discovery & Recommendation: The Graph indexes vault data → Circle Agent or Coverage
Assistant detects missing coverage → Recommends an approved policy.
Escrow Funding: Protocol owner approves transaction via Privy → USDC is deposited into
the Arc Escrow Contract.
Encrypted Claim Upload: Researcher selects a bounty → Encrypts evidence payload in-
browser using Sodium / WebCrypto → Ciphertext stored in object storage.
Isolated Verification: Verifier Service (running in an isolated container context with
isolated keys) verifies the evidence payload against the target condition → Signs an on-
chain verification proof.
Settlement & Report Release: Verifier proof is posted to Arc → Escrow pays USDC
directly to researcher's Privy wallet → Report Release Service captures the
PaymentFinalized block event on Arc → Unlocks decrypted report access to the protocol
reviewer.

Hacky & Notable Implementation Highlights

Cryptographic "Pay-Before-Reveal" Gate:
The report-release service enforces a cryptographic barrier: the server refuses to serve
the report decryption keys until it performs an independent RPC read verifying that the
payout transaction has achieved block finality on Arc.
Isolated Verifier Sandbox vs. Trojanized Exploits:
To solve the issue of trojanized PoCs (where malicious exploit scripts target protocol
reviewers), we designed the verifier service as a headless, zero-trust runner. Proofs are
evaluated in isolated memory without human reviewers ever touching raw executable code on
local machines.

name: OAO
description: An AI agent that leverages The Graph and LangGraph to optimize your portfolio.
projectDescription: This project automates the process of finding lending protocols, comparing markets and optimizing yield for the onchain assets in your portfolio. It leverages a LangGraph pipeline to orchestrate LLM discovery, The Graph onchain data and deterministic Python functions to analyze an Ethereum wallet and come up with a recommendation based on blockchain data.
howItsMade: The project consists of a React frontend where the user can input their wallet address. This sends a request to the FastAPI backend which invokes the LangGraph graph (a pipeline of nodes with each their own functions in the process). The first step of the LangGraph graph is to analyze the wallet and its token holdings, it does so through The Token API from The Graph Protocol. Then it engages the LLM (Claude Sonnet 5) to discover relevant lending protocols for the assets in the wallet. Then the LangGraph graph engages the Subgraph MCP server to find subgraphs for the discovered protocols. The subgraphs are then queried to get real market data from the protocols, so that the optimizer node can use that data to make a decision based on yield and TVL. Finally the decision gets handed back to the LLM to create a human-readable recommendation. Each step of the process is being communicated back to the React frontend in real time through LangGraph streams and FastAPI Server-Sent Events.

name: Retainer
description: Your agent's access renews itself on-chain at 3am, with nobody awake.
projectDescription:
An agent can pay for something. An agent cannot subscribe to something.
Every payment rail built for agents charges per request: 402, sign, retry, pay, repeat. That works for one call. For anything an agent needs continuously, a human keeps re-authorising it — by clicking, or by operating a cron job somebody has to keep alive. There is always a person behind the subscription.
Retainer removes that person. It is a live x402-gated service on Hedera testnet, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. An agent pays once. The server forwards that settled payment on-chain into a contract, which opens a subscription and arms a scheduled renewal through the Hedera Schedule Service (HIP-1215, the system contract at 0x16b). When the access window closes, the network itself calls renew() on the contract. No user. No server job. No cron.
The network has renewed access 55+ times across 3 deployments with nobody awake, and is still doing it hourly.
What it cost to learn, said out loud rather than hidden:

The network charges the CONTRACT for each scheduled call, so the contract must hold gas to pay for its own future execution. Retainer books three separate pots: refundable to the subscriber, earned by the seller, and gas reserved for the next renewal.
A renewal that re-arms the next one costs ~1.55 HBAR; one that does not costs ~0.05. Re-arming is ~97% of the cost, so at 1 HBAR per period this loses money on every renewal. That is the real economic constraint of on-chain self-renewal.
One scheduled renewal reverted with our own Insolvent() guard when the three pots came within ~2.4 HBAR of the account balance. The contract correctly refused to spend money it had already promised elsewhere. It is disclosed as a limitation on /judge.

Live: https://retainer.edycu.dev · For judges, 30 seconds: https://retainer.edycu.dev/judge Contract 0.0.10415845 / 0x433050c9bd203FBdd49FAB6b5E20eD3E1FB2a931
howItsMade:
Solidity contract (RetainerAccess) on Hedera testnet, a Next.js 15 App Router front end, and a TypeScript agent script, from the Scaffold-HBAR template as boilerplate.
The engine is the Hedera Schedule Service. The contract books its own next execution through HIP-1215, the system contract at 0x16b, using three of its methods: scheduleCall arms the next renew() at the exact second the window closes, deleteSchedule releases the booking on cancel so reserved gas returns rather than being stranded, and hasScheduleCapacity asks the network whether the slot can be booked before committing — without that pre-check a full network turns a clean lapse into a revert. Tested locally against @hashgraph/system-contracts-forking, which is what made a system contract testable in CI at all.
Payments are x402 over HBAR via @x402/core and @x402/hedera, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. Blocky402 advertised hedera:testnet with scheme exact and x402Version 2 on the standard /supported contract, so it dropped into the template's HTTPFacilitatorClient with no adapter — the swap was one environment variable — and it supplies its own fee payer, which removed a whole account from our setup. Wallet connection is native Hedera through @hashgraph/hedera-wallet-connect and Reown AppKit on the hedera namespace, not an EVM-address shim, so the account a user sees is a real 0.0.x id.
The hacky parts worth naming:


The agent signs exactly once. Rather than have it sign again to subscribe, the resource server takes the payment it just received and forwards it on-chain itself, so one signature becomes a self-sustaining subscription. Two transactions come back: the payment, and the subscription it became.


Two different units for the same money. HBAR value on the wire is weibar (1e18) while the EVM sees tinybar (1e8), and getting that boundary wrong silently mis-prices everything. It is pinned by property tests that check every tinybar amount from 0 to 100,000 exhaustively, plus 100,000 randomised amounts across the whole uint64 range.


A contract that pays for its own future needs an accounting model, not a balance. Three pots — refundable, earned, gas reserve — because "the contract has money" and "the contract can afford its next scheduled call" are different questions. We learned that from a live revert.


The payment and the access it buys are two unrelated rows on the ledger. An x402 settlement is a CRYPTOTRANSFER and the subscribeFor it pays for is a CONTRACTCALL; nothing on Hedera ties them together. Both are now written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic (0.0.10440194, immutable, no admin key) sharing a settlement id, so the join is public. Writing it surfaced the hacky bit: the two records for one request can reach consensus in either order, so the verifier joins on settlement id rather than sequence number. It is off unless configured and can never reject a payment — an HCS outage must not cost a paying agent its access.


The mirror node cannot see the thing being verified. Schedules a contract creates via scheduleCall do not appear under /api/v1/schedules, and /api/v1/contracts/{id}/results omits scheduled executions entirely — the first version of our verifier queried that endpoint, reported no renewals found, and looked entirely correct while doing it. Read the account's transactions, not the contract's results.


64 contract tests, 258 app unit tests including the property suite, and 58 end-to-end tests. The punctuality is measured rather than claimed: yarn bench needs no keys and reports that across all 30 renewals this deployment had armed as of the dated run on 2026-09-09, the network executed the scheduled call a median 64 ms — p95 151 ms — after the second it was asked for.

name: beanie
description: A multichain, non-custodial, permissionless stablecoin payment gateway.
projectDescription:
A multichain, non-custodial, permissionless stablecoin payment gateway. A merchant registers ONE destination address and ONE blockchain network to get dedicated, merchant-bonded non-custodial receivers on all supported blockchains; deposits settle through these receivers without Beanie ever having custody of users' funds. Incentivized keepers consistently call sweep() on pending balances to earn 0.05% of volume MEV reward.
All chains share one pattern:

A single factory deploys non-custodial receivers whose destinations are pinned to the merchant for good at deploy time.
Receiver addresses derived from the merchant address. Funds ALWAYS sweep to the merchant
Universal Beanie Webhook Registry, KV store for merchants' URL (as a 20-byte EVM address)
Optional Stealth Account: Provides protocol-agnostic privacy on Beanie using PassKey Stealth Account Abstraction
howItsMade:
At its core, Beanie is a private intent layer. It allows anyone to announce an intent and uses JIT deployment to trigger actions when onchain conditions are met; in this case, it settles transfers.
The exposed single function of the receiver is basically a deterministic turnkey and would do exactly the actions embedded without accepting external parameters.
Beanie is grounded in efficient stablecoin infrastructures. Near-zero overhead of compute, network, or storage beyond the call function used to dispatch the announce events for direct wallet transfers using Chainlink CRE.
No external ACID storage beyond the contracts deployed onchain, enabling a network of API providers and Keepers to serve as a convenience layer over Beanie contracts, without a privileged party.
Starting beanie_api brings up the convenience layer; including the API, the workers, and the customer/merchant-facing UI.
Receiver initialization is bundled with the first sweep() following a deposit; subsequent sweeps are cleared as a single transaction, ensuring that spam is a losing game for spammers
On EVM, automations are orchestrated from Chainlink's CRE to ensure fast onchain delivery of assets, and signed webhooks are optionally delivered.
UI and server authentication are through passkeys, and neither merchants nor users need native gas to make payments or receive payments on Beanie. Beanie processes direct transfers and gasless payments.
Beanie abstracts all its complexity behind a single link that renders a payment widget for end users. Developers, merchants, and ordinary users can use any chain from any wallet.
Zero sign-up friction during onboarding, merchants authorize with their passkey. The same PassKey is essential for Stealth Account Abstraction on Beanie

name: Portcullis
description: A security firewall that authenticates cross-chain settlement messages before value moves.
projectDescription: Portcullis protects inbound cross-chain settlements at the receiving contract. Before an adapter transfers a token, PortcullisGuard verifies the signing authority, token and recipient allowlists, value bounds, replay protection, nonce order, per-source rate limits, and volume or policy conditions. Invalid messages are rejected before receiver state changes. The circuit breaker only latches on authenticated anomalies: a rate-limit breach, a volume spike, or an explicit policy denial. The project runs across Arc testnet, ENSv2 identity on Sepolia, Chainlink CRE private policy checks, and a Graph subgraph for inspection history and configuration.
howItsMade: Portcullis is built in Solidity 0.8.36 with Foundry, Solady OwnableRoles, and OpenZeppelin. PortcullisGuard keeps the settlement state, while the inlined PortcullisChecks library evaluates six checks before an adapter can transfer value. The message digest binds block.chainid, the guard address, and the settlement payload; an ECDSA signature from the resolved authority proves the sender. EnsIdentityRegistry resolves guardian-allowlisted ENS names through ENSv2’s UniversalResolverV2. A Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow runs policy checks in a TEE and reports ALLOW, DENY, or MANUAL_REVIEW to CrePolicyConsumer. The Graph indexes guard and receiver events for the static Next.js guardian dashboard, built with viem and Privy. The project also includes Foundry unit, fuzz, invariant, and exploit-replay tests.

name: Dry Powder
description: Shared-reserve dip-buying strategies powered by 1inch Aqua and SwapVM.
projectDescription: Dry Powder is a DeFi prototype for coordinating multiple buy-the-dip strategies from one shared stablecoin reserve. A maker can allocate one 10,000 mUSDC budget across ETH, WBTC, and LINK strategies, while each strategy remains independently fillable through Aqua. When one leg fills, the shared reserve state updates, reducing capacity and repricing sibling strategies automatically. This prevents overcommitted strategies from spending more than the maker’s real budget while still letting the maker express broader intent across multiple assets.
howItsMade: Dry Powder is built with Solidity, Hardhat, TypeScript, 1inch Aqua, and 1inch SwapVM. The core is a custom DryPowderRouter with a custom SwapVM opcode that reads shared reserve state before settlement. Aqua handles strategy shipping and virtual balances, while the Dry Powder opcode enforces reserve budget, per-leg caps, maker wallet balance, tranche boundaries, and dynamic price multipliers. The demo deploys to Ethereum Sepolia using the official Aqua registry, mock ERC20 assets, and scripts for deploy, setup, quote, fill, and sibling repricing. The hacky/fun part is using independent Aqua strategies that appear overallocated, while one shared onchain reserve makes them collectively safe.

name: Verdikt
description: x402 marketplace: delivery verified per call in a TEE, auto-refunded on-chain, no disputes.
projectDescription:
Verdikt is a marketplace of x402-gated API services whose delivery is verified per call — not just self-reported at listing time.
A proxy sits between a paying agent and an x402 provider at <slug>.verdikt.bond. When a payment header is present, the proxy recovers the payer from the payment signature and hands the call to a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow, which:

Replays the payment against the provider from inside a TEE — once, because an x402 payment settles once
Evaluates the response against the provider's own declared SLA
Writes a PASS/FAIL/DOWN verdict to the on-chain registry on Arc

If the SLA isn't met, the paying agent is auto-refunded from the provider's bonded deposit — capped at what was paid, booked as a credit rather than pushed, with no dispute or arbitration step.
The SLA lives as a text record on the provider's ENSv2 subname (<slug>.verdikt.eth), scoped with per-key access control so only the provider can write it and only the verifier can write the derived reputation scores. An hourly workflow publishes conformance and availability ratios back to the same subname, and the marketplace ranks on them.
It runs for real. Providers register self-serve through the dashboard: the wizard mints the ENS subname, publishes the SLA and posts the bond on Arc. The services listed front real third-party x402 providers (Alchemy, Allium, Syntalic and others). A Circle agent wallet has paid them through Verdikt, each call was judged inside the workflow, and the FAIL and DOWN verdicts drew real refunds out of the providers' bonds — all of it readable off Arc Testnet and Sepolia.
Because verification is deterministic and code-enforced, consumers can pick a service based on its real track record instead of a provider's own marketing.
howItsMade:
Arc holds the registry, escrow, verdicts and refunds. USDC is Arc's native gas token, so bond, payment and refund are one asset moving as msg.value, with no approve/transferFrom. VerdiktRegistry is an IReceiver: verdicts arrive as DON-signed reports through the KeystoneForwarder, and a refund is booked as a credit the payer withdraws, or claims by an EIP-712 signature anyone can relay, never pushed, so a reverting payer can't erase its own FAIL.
Ethereum Sepolia holds ENS: each provider's SLA lives only as the sla text record on <slug>.verdikt.eth, using ENSv2's Permissioned Resolver for per-key access control. The provider writes sla/url, the score writer writes conformance/availability, and cross-writes revert. VerdiktSubnameRegistrar mints subnames with exactly those roles; VerdiktScoreWriter is the IReceiver the hourly workflow reports to.
Payment verification covers both exact transfer methods a real x402 challenge offers, plain ERC-3009 and Circle's GatewayWalletBatched, through one verifier that recovers the payer from the signature rather than reading it out of JSON. A contract-account payer is asked via ERC-1271 on the chain it paid on.
Verification runs inside a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow (TEE): it replays the paid call once, evaluates the response with a pure SLA engine, and writes the verdict to Arc. A 402 on the replay writes nothing, since the provider is saying it wasn't paid. A second, separate CRE cron workflow reads public VerdictWritten events and publishes trailing-window conformance/availability ratios to ENS, kept apart so the confidential path never depends on aggregate traffic timing.
Deployment. The proxy is a Cloudflare Worker on *.verdikt.bond, with Durable Objects for the pending-verification rendezvous. The dashboard is a Lit + Vite static app reading Arc and ENS straight from the browser via viem, live at verdikt.bond.
Workaround. Production CRE deployment access wasn't yet enabled, so we ran the confidential and cron workflows entirely through cre workflow simulate --broadcast, fronted by a small runner container that plays the role of Chainlink's gateway. It forwards the proxy's trigger into a long-lived simulate verify --listen process and runs the hourly aggregate as a scheduled job. Everything on Arc and Sepolia in this submission, every verdict, refund and published score, was produced by that simulator against the real live contracts, not mocked.

name: Arx
description: Arx is a programmable transaction firewall and policy engine for on-chain AI agents.
projectDescription:
An AI agent that can move money needs authority. The usual way to give it
authority is a private key or an API credential, which grants everything that
credential can do, for as long as it exists.
That is a poor fit for a system whose behaviour is steered by text it did not
write. A poisoned invoice tells a payment agent the supplier's banking details
have changed. The agent believes it — it is not malfunctioning, it was convinced
— and signs. Better reasoning does not fix this, because the model is the part
that can be talked into things.
The problem is not intelligence. The problem is authority.
Arx sits between the agent and the signer and answers one question: is this exact
transaction inside the authority this agent was actually granted? It normalizes
the transaction, resolves the agent's capability, evaluates policy, inspects the
transaction bytes, scores risk from explainable signals, and produces one of four
outcomes in Ledger's own vocabulary — ALLOW, DENY, ESCALATE, or ABORT. Only an
approval cryptographically bound to those exact bytes can reach the signer, and
the Ledger device remains the final boundary.
What makes it more than an allowlist is the set of checks a naive policy layer
gets wrong:

The agent's own numbers are claims, not facts. An intent declares amountUsd;
Arx prices the actual transaction bytes through a Chainlink feed and refuses
the mismatch. An agent declaring $1 while moving 1000 ETH is caught.
The recipient is often inside the calldata. In an ERC-20 transfer the payee is
an argument, not the to field, so an allowlisted token contract is otherwise
an open payment channel.
A standing allowance is authority. An approve moves nothing now and lets the
spender move everything later, so the USD ceiling applies to it.
Dependency failure is never permission. Every external adapter distinguishes
"checked, clean" from "could not check". Unknown resolves to DENY or ESCALATE,
never ALLOW. Silence is never approval.

Arx also solves the credential half of the problem. Using the Ledger Key Ring, a
capability broker seals upstream secrets and hands the agent a short-lived token
bound to a hash of the policy in force — never the API key. The agent cannot leak
what it does not hold, and tokens die the moment an operator narrows the policy.
Fourteen adversarial scenarios run as assertions, not printouts: prompt
injection, declared-value lies, calldata smuggling, address poisoning, a
double-sign race, replay, revocation mid-flight, and audit tampering. The suite
exits non-zero if any behaves differently from the documentation. A separate demo
drives a real AI agent that is genuinely prompt-injected, alongside an
unprotected control case that signs the attacker's transaction — because the
contrast is the argument.
howItsMade:
TypeScript on Bun, Fastify, Zod, SQLite via bun:sqlite, viem for EVM primitives.
The authorization kernel makes no network calls and runs no model on the decision
path, so there is no prompt in it to inject into. Every decision is a pure
function of the capability, the intent, the transaction bytes and an injected
clock, which is what makes decisions reproducible from the audit log.
Ledger is the core. The Device Management Kit (1.9.0), the Ethereum signer kit
(1.18.0), the first-party Speculos transport (1.2.1) and context-module (2.5.0)
are all pinned exactly, because the @ledgerhq packages publish a develop build
daily and a caret range drifts mid-event. Alongside the SDK path I implemented
the app-ethereum APDU protocol directly from its published specification and the
app's own C source, so the signing path is transparent and auditable rather than
opaque: BIP-32 path packing, 255-byte chunking, the EIP-2718 type-byte framing,
and the typed-transaction parity convention. Signatures are not accepted, they
are verified — the signer address is recovered from the exact signed digest and
compared to what the device reported.
Because Docker was unavailable on the development machine, I built an in-process
implementation of the app-ethereum protocol that drives the same codec and is
keyed from the published Speculos test mnemonic. It derives
0xDad77910DbDFdE764fC21FCD4E74D71bBACA6D8D — the address Ledger's own fixtures
expect for that seed — which cross-checks the request encoding, BIP-32 packing
and response parsing against an external value. That mode produces real secp256k1
signatures that verify by address recovery, so the full pipeline is demonstrable
on any machine with no hardware, while reporting emulated: true and refusing to
start in production.
The Ledger Key Ring CLI (wallet-cli ring) backs the capability broker. Its key
property is that after ring init, encrypt and decrypt need network but not the
device — which is what makes the "hosts with no USB port" story work: provision
once on a laptop, then unseal on a VPS with no hardware attached.
Integrations plug into named seams — PriceOracle, NameResolver,
RiskSignalProvider, SignerAdapter, HumanVerifier, ExecutionVenue — and every one
returns an Availability<T> that keeps "checked, clean" distinct from "could not
check". ENSv2 on Sepolia resolves allowlist entries during authorization and
binds the resolved address, so a name re-pointed between approval and signing
aborts rather than redirecting funds. Chainlink aggregators are read directly
rather than through a convenience API, because latestRoundData returns updatedAt
and that lets Arx enforce its own staleness bound.
The parts I would highlight as hacky or hard-won: hashing goes through an
RFC 8785-style canonicalizer rather than JSON.stringify, because otherwise a
digest depends on key insertion order and a reordered payload could be shaped to
match an approval bound to different bytes. Claiming an approval for signing is a
SQL compare-and-swap performed before any bytes reach the device, which is what
makes double-signing impossible under concurrency — verified with eight parallel
requests. The audit log is hash-chained so editing any historical decision
invalidates every hash after it, and GET /audit/verify recomputes the chain and
names the first break.
An adversarial audit of this repository found six real defects during the build —
including a $100M standing allowance passing a $500 ceiling, and one agent being
able to sign another agent's approval. All six are fixed, each with a test, and
they are listed in the README rather than quietly patched.

name: Faregate
description: Policy-governed AI agents autonomously transact for onchain data with human-in-the-loop controls.
projectDescription:
Faregate is a permission and payment gateway that lets AI agents autonomously purchase paid onchain data while keeping humans in control of what agents can access and spend.
A human defines an agent's capability, including its allowed data scope, maximum cost per query, daily spending limit, and the amount above which human approval is required. The agent can then request blockchain data using natural language. An LLM interprets the request and produces a structured query, but it never makes the authorization decision.
Faregate uses a deterministic policy engine to validate the structured query against the agent's capability, current spending ledger, query price, and approval rules. Requests can be denied, automatically approved, or paused for human approval. Once authorized, the agent pays for the query through x402 on Hedera using USDC, and Faregate retrieves the requested data from The Graph using the Messari standardized lending schema.
The resulting data can be analyzed by an LLM, but the analysis is grounding-checked against the retrieved dataset so unsupported addresses or hashes are not presented as facts. Agent identity and capabilities are represented through ENSv2 passports on Sepolia, with live revocation checks on every request.
The key idea is to give an AI agent a controlled capability instead of an unrestricted API key, wallet, or payment credential. Humans define the boundaries, deterministic code enforces them, and the agent operates autonomously within those boundaries. If the human revokes the agent, that revocation takes precedence even if the agent already holds an approved payment quote.
howItsMade:
Faregate is built as a TypeScript monorepo with an Express/TypeScript gateway, a Next.js dashboard, a separate demo agent, and shared domain logic. The gateway coordinates identity resolution, natural-language request interpretation, deterministic policy evaluation, pricing, payment, data retrieval, AI analysis, spend tracking, and audit logging.
The agent sends a natural-language request to the gateway. OpenRouter with a structured-output LLM interprets the request into a validated query, but the model is deliberately excluded from the authorization path. A pure deterministic policy engine evaluates the agent's ENS capability, requested scope, query cost, daily spend, existing ledger, and human approval threshold. Pricing uses integer micro-USD values, avoiding floating-point rounding problems.
For payments, Faregate integrates x402 with Hedera testnet and USDC, enabling machine-to-machine, per-query payments without API keys or subscriptions. ENSv2 subnames on Ethereum Sepolia act as agent passports, with capabilities stored in ENS text records and resolved through the Universal Resolver. The Graph is used as the data layer, with Messari's standardized lending schema allowing the same query documents to fan out across multiple protocol subgraphs.
The project also includes several security-focused implementation details: policy is re-evaluated before quoting and again at payment release, payment nonces are single-use, requests are idempotent, human actions use wallet signatures, structured queries are validated and clamped, agents are rate-limited, and the gateway fails closed when identity resolution fails. AI-generated analysis is checked against the retrieved data to catch unsupported claims.
The most notable design choice is the separation between AI reasoning and authorization: the LLM can interpret what the agent wants, but deterministic code decides whether it is allowed. ENS revocation is also checked live, so an agent can be rejected even after receiving an approved quote. The gateway never holds the user's funds or private keys; the agent pays from its own account.

name: Mandate Agents
description: Agent executes real on-chain financial actions for you, inside limits you set, with a ledger
projectDescription:
Mandate is bounded delegation for AI agents. You control what contracts an agent can call, how much USDC it can move, and which actions need your Ledger approval. The smart account enforces these limits on-chain, not the AI.
Tell it: “Get me 100 USDC on Arc by Friday to pay Acme. Don’t sell my ETH.” It checks your positions, compares borrow rates, creates and simulates a plan, then executes safe steps on its own. For irreversible actions like bridging via CCTP, it pauses for a plain-text Ledger approval. The contract verifies the exact approval on-chain before executing.
Everything is enforced on-chain: spending caps, allow-lists, replay protection, and guardian approvals. The agent never sees your keys or writes calldata.
howItsMade:
Built with Solidity + Foundry + OpenZeppelin, with a TypeScript/viem SDK powering deterministic action adapters and agent tooling.
The core idea is bounded, verifiable execution: the AI only creates an intent; deterministic code builds the actual calls, while the smart account enforces allow-lists, per-tx/daily caps, replay protection, and guardian approvals.
We use Circle CCTP v2 for Base Sepolia → Arc transfers and The Graph for standardized lending-rate data across protocols. Safe steps execute automatically; irreversible steps trigger a plain Ledger approval that the contract reconstructs and verifies byte-for-byte on-chain.

name: Rug Radar
description: Autonomous agent that pays per call for live DeFi drain and whale intelligence
projectDescription:
Rug Radar An autonomous agent that pays per call for live DeFi drain and whale intelligence — settled on Hedera with x402, computed from The Graph's standardized subgraphs and Substreams, discovered through ENSv2. "Is the WETH/USDC pool being drained right now?" → the agent resolves api.rugradar.eth, hits a 402, signs a 0.03 HBAR payment, gets a risk score with evidence, and every payment plus the final decision lands on a Hedera Consensus Service topic you can audit on HashScan. Built from scratch at ETHOnline 2026 for three bounties: | Bounty | What in this repo satisfies it | |---|---| | Hedera — AI & Agentic Payments (x402) | Live x402-gated service on Hedera testnet settled through the Blocky402 facilitator (packages/service), and an agent that pays for it (packages/agent). Extras: metered pricing (per protocol, per lookback day, per 15 s stream window), streamed micropayments, HTS USDC as an alternative asset, HCS audit trail of every settlement and every agent decision, ERC-8004 registration file, discovery directory via ENS. | | The Graph — Composable / Standardized Graph Products | Every endpoint runs one query string across many protocols using the Messari Standardized Subgraphs (dex-amm schema: Uniswap v3, Uniswap v2, SushiSwap, Curve; lending schema: Aave v3, Compound v3, Spark). The live whale wire composes Substreams (ethereum-common package, filtered_events) with a standardized subgraph for pricing. All data is live from The Graph Network gateway; nothing is mocked. | | ENS — Best Use of ENSv2 (Sepolia) | The namespace rugradar.eth owns its own PermissionedRegistry and own PermissionedResolver (deployed through the VerifiableFactory). Services are expiring, non-transferable, revocable subnames; their x402 endpoint, price list, pay-to account and audit topic are text records (ENSIP-26 agent-endpoint[x402] + agent-context). Enhanced Access Control delegates exactly one text key (x402.pricing) to the service's own key. The agent discovers services by walking the registry and resolving through the Universal Resolver; nothing about the paid API is hard-coded in the agent. Agents get their own identity subnames too. | Demo UI — everything from one tab pnpm ui # → http://localhost:3001 One page, four panels, every button does the real thing and streams what happens over Server-Sent Events: Discover — resolves api.rugradar.eth live through the ENSv2 Universal Resolver, shows the records and the registry hierarchy (ETHRegistry → our registry → our resolver, expiry, non-transferable), and a Prove Enhanced Access Control button where the service's own key edits x402.pricing and is refused on any other record. Pay per call — one-click paid requests: the 402 quote (HBAR and USDC options, pay-to, fee payer), the Hedera settlement id linked to HashScan, then the result summarized (risk score, whale list, lending stress). Plus a Whale wire button that pays for one 15-second SSE window. Ask the agent — the LLM run as a live feed: tool calls, quotes, payments, budget meter, then the verdict with a risk gauge, evidence, the payments list, and the HCS-anchored decision. One query, every protocol — the same standardized query fanned out to all seven protocols with timings. demo.md is the recording runbook; slides.html is the four-slide pitch (arrow keys). A real run (Hedera testnet + ENSv2 Sepolia + The Graph Network) 🛰 Rug Radar agent · wallet 0.0.10372230 on hedera:testnet · budget 1 HBAR · model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B ❓ Is the WETH/USDC pool on Uniswap v3 being drained right now? Should an LP exit? ⚙ discover_services({}) ENS discovery: 1 service(s): api.rugradar.eth ⚙ read_catalog(...) → GET https://…/v1/catalog (free) ⚙ pool_risk({"tokens":["WETH","USDC"]}) paid 0.03 HBAR · settlement [email protected] · HCS [email protected] ⚙ scan_whales({"protocols":["uniswap-v3"]}) paid 0.015 HBAR · settlement [email protected] ⚙ pool_risk({"protocol":"uniswap-v3","pool":"0xe0554a47…"}) paid 0.03 HBAR · settlement [email protected] **Verdict: Watch (not critical)** — the Uniswap v3 WETH/USDC 0.01% pool shows heavy LP churn but no drain: 24h withdrawals $2.49M (68% of TVL) are offset by $2.51M deposits (net +$22.9k), outflow is spread across many addresses, large swaps run both ways. Recommended action: no exit needed. 💸 Spent 0.075 HBAR of 1 across 3 paid call(s) 🧾 Decision anchored on HCS: https://hashscan.io/testnet/transaction/0.0.10372230%401788663436.746860424 Architecture flowchart LR subgraph Agent["packages/agent · LLM agent (Qwen 3.8) with a Hedera wallet + demo UI"] A1["discover_services"] --> A2["read_catalog"] A2 --> A3["pool_risk · scan_whales · protocol_health · watch_whale_wire"] A3 --> A4["budget guard + HCS spend ledger"] end subgraph ENS["ENSv2 · Sepolia"] E1[("ETHRegistry
rugradar.eth")] --> E2[("our PermissionedRegistry
api · scout")] E2 --> E3[("our PermissionedResolver
agent-endpoint, x402.*, hcs.* records")] end subgraph Service["packages/service · x402-gated API on Hedera (Render)"] S1["GET /v1/whales"] S2["GET /v1/pool-risk"] S3["GET /v1/protocol-health"] S4["GET /v1/stream/whales (SSE)"] S5["onAfterSettle → HCS audit"] end subgraph Graph["The Graph"] G1[("Messari standardized subgraphs

"token prices" .-> G1 S5 --> H2 A4 --> H2 One paid request, end to end sequenceDiagram participant Agent participant ENS as ENSv2 (Sepolia) participant Svc as Rug Radar service participant Fac as Blocky402 facilitator participant Hedera participant Graph as The Graph Agent->>ENS: getEnsText("api.rugradar.eth", "agent-endpoint[x402]") ENS-->>Agent: https://…/v1 (+ x402.network, x402.payTo, x402.pricing, hcs.audit) Agent->>Svc: GET /v1/pool-risk?tokens=WETH,USDC Svc-->>Agent: 402 · PAYMENT-REQUIRED (0.03 HBAR or $0.003 USDC, payTo, feePayer) Note over Agent: budget guard checks the quote before signing Agent->>Agent: sign Hedera TransferTransaction (ECDSA) Agent->>Svc: GET … · PAYMENT-SIGNATURE Svc->>Fac: /verify Svc->>Graph: liquidityPool + snapshots + withdraws (standardized query) Svc->>Fac: /settle Fac->>Hedera: submit transfer Svc-->>Agent: 200 · JSON risk score · PAYMENT-RESPONSE (tx id) Svc->>Hedera: HCS x402.settled {path, payer, amount, tx} Agent->>Hedera: HCS x402.paid {url, amount, tx} Agent->>Hedera: HCS agent.decision {verdict, payments} If the upstream data fails (every protocol query errors, or the stream has no source), the handler returns a non-2xx status and the x402 middleware cancels the payment — the agent is never charged for nothing. What's metered and how much | Endpoint | Price (HBAR; USDC quoted alongside) | Data | |---|---|---| | GET /v1/whales?protocols=…&minUsd=&lookback= | 0.01 + 0.005 × protocols | Largest swaps and LP withdrawals per DEX, one standardized query per protocol | | GET /v1/pool-risk?tokens=WETH,USDC or ?protocol=&pool= | 0.03 + 0.01 × extra lookback days | Drain score 0–100 with factor evidence (7d TVL drawdown, 24h withdrawal pressure, withdrawer concentration, abnormal swaps, age) | | GET /v1/protocol-health?protocol=aave-v3 | 0.02 | Lending stress: utilization, hot markets, liquidations | | GET /v1/stream/whales?seconds=15..120 | 0.02 per 15 s window | Server-Sent Events whale wire; re-request to extend = streamed micropayments | | GET /v1/catalog, /.well-known/agent-registration.json, /health | free | Discovery surface (also linked from ENS records) | Prices are computed per request (x402 dynamic pricing), so a one-protocol scan and a four-protocol scan produce different 402 quotes. The Graph: what the standard bought us packages/shared/src/protocols.ts — seven protocols, one registry of subgraph IDs from Messari's deployment manifest, all verified at chain head. (Messari's Balancer v2 and PancakeSwap v3 Ethereum subgraphs are currently unhealthy on the network and were left out; re-adding one is a single JSON entry.) packages/shared/src/graph.ts — three query strings (whales, pool-risk, lending-health) serve seven protocols. The only divergence we hit between schema majors is the event actor field (from in 1.3, account { id } in 4.0), handled by a one-line switch. Pool search uses the standardized inputTokens_contains filter with canonical token addresses on every DEX. packages/service/src/substreams.ts — the live wire composes the reusable ethereum-common Substreams package (filtered_events with an evt_sig: query string) with the standardized Uniswap v3 subgraph for lastPriceUSD. Set SUBSTREAMS_API_TOKEN (Pinax or StreamingFast) to enable; without it the stream polls the standardized subgraphs so it is still live data.
