name: VibeDesk
description: A security-first desktop app: AI trading agents, local wallets, live multi-source data — all local
projectDescription:
Wallet (account) + Data + AI = Agentic Trading

A local-first desktop application where your AI agents read live multi-source market data, analyze the news, and — with your wallet's explicit approval — execute real on-chain trades. Your wallet, your AI, your data: nothing leaves your machine except signed transactions. Out of the box — the agent runtime ships inside the app, no server to install or run yourself.

01 · Safe Account
Your keys. Your rules.

Local-first wallet vault — manage multiple wallets on your own machine; seed phrases and private keys are generated locally and never shown in plain text
Per-wallet agent approval — grant an agent access to a specific wallet with one click, revoke it anytime
Process isolation — the agent and the wallet live in separate processes; the agent can only request signatures over IPC and can never read your secrets

02 · AI
Agents that actually do things.

Multi-agent by design — run a general chat agent, a trading agent and news bots side by side, each with its own context, tools and memory
Powered by the Pi engine — a full agent runtime with persistent context and tool-calling built in
Pluggable skills — extend any agent with data-source skills, strategy skills, or skills the agent builds for you on the fly (partially implemented)

03 · Data
Every price. Every signal. One desk.

Unified multi-source prices — Hyperliquid, Binance, Robinhood and more in a single view, refreshed in real time
News & social feeds — watch the price and the narrative at the same time, on one screen
AI-driven analysis — agents turn raw prices and headlines into actionable recommendations
howItsMade:
How it's made
VibeDesk is an Electron + React desktop app with a hand-rolled Windows 95-style shell — a custom window manager with draggable multi-window layering, taskbar, start menu and desktop shortcuts built on top of React95. The whole "local OS" feel is just our own React state machine over DOM windows, which let us ship a demo where a trade agent window, a chat window and a live markets window all run side by side.
Architecture: the wallet and the agents are strictly separated. The wallet vault lives in the Electron main process — keys are AES-encrypted on disk, decrypted in memory only, and never leave main; agents can only request signatures over IPC, they can never read the keys themselves. Agents are built on the mature Pi engine (the harness from the OpenClaw ecosystem), giving us a production-grade multi-agent runtime out of the box — persistent per-agent context, tool-calling, and a pluggable skill system we'll keep extending with more data sources, strategies, and agent-created skills.
The data layer is also main-process-bound: a multi-source aggregator fetches live quotes from Robinhood, Yahoo Finance, Hyperliquid and Binance. We deliberately fetch from Electron main instead of the renderer, because public endpoints like Robinhood and Yahoo throw CORS errors in the browser — running Node fetch in main completely sidesteps that. Every tick is written into a local SQLite store (one point per symbol/provider/minute) so the price-history charts overlay multiple sources on the same time axis. One hacky note: better-sqlite3's native prebuild hung inside the Electron main process, so we swapped to sql.js via WASM, which turned out to be more reliable across rebuilds. LLM access is OpenAI-compatible — any base URL + key works, plus Ollama for fully local inference, plus a deterministic rule mode that runs with zero API keys (great for demo machines with no network key).
Partner technologies. Arc (Circle) is our execution chain: real swaps run on the Arc testnet against the Minara deployment of Uniswap v4 — we call the V4 Quoter (quoteExactInputSingle) for live quotes including pool/hook fees, handle Permit2 dual approval (token → Permit2 → Universal Router), sign locally with viem, and broadcast; gas on Arc is native USDC, which makes the demo feel like a real agentic-trading OS. The same module already has mainnet placeholder configs for switching networks.
The agentic trading loop. In the trade agent, a user can simply type "buy 1 USDC worth of ETH"; the Pi agent quotes, checks the authorized wallet, executes the swap in the main process, and returns the tx link while the balance panel refreshes live. Data + AI + Wallet = Auto Trading, all local-first.

name: perjury
description: AI agents post bonded claims; VRF peers verify them in a TEE. Lying costs ENS standing.
projectDescription:
We trust what AI agents tell us about their own work. An agent says "Compound v3 utilization is 64.66%", another party acts on it, and nothing ever re-derives it. Logs do not help, because the agent writes its own logs. As agents start acting on each other's output, that gap becomes structural.
Perjury closes it. An agent posts a claim with an economic bond; only the hash of the exact sentence goes on chain, so the claim cannot change once the money is down. The protocol assigns a random peer as witness — submitClaim has no witness parameter, so there is no code path to ask for one. The witness never sees the claimant's reasoning and independently re-derives its own answer from the same block. A Chainlink CRE confidential workflow opens both sealed submissions inside an enclave, recomputes each value from raw rows rather than trusting either stated conclusion, and publishes only a verdict and a commitment hash — never the evidence, never either methodology, never the disputed numbers. On a mismatch the claimant forfeits its bond and its stake, and its ENS standing drops, which makes it ineligible to audit anyone else in the next block.
The forfeited ETH is paid to nobody. Not the witness, not the protocol, not us. The witness earns a flat fee whichever way the verdict goes. Paying the forfeit to the witness is exactly what would make fabricating disagreement profitable, and that is the single most important design decision in the project.
Three constraints drive the rest, and each rules out a simpler approach:
A claimant who picks its own auditor can always buy a pass, so assignment must be verifiably random.
An adjudicator that publishes evidence leaks each agent's methodology and hands future claimants a rubric to game, so the comparison must happen where the inputs stay sealed.
Reputation the subject can write is not reputation, so the record must be writable only by the adjudicator.
howItsMade:
Contracts (Solidity, Foundry, Sepolia). ClaimRegistry escrows bonds and runs the claim lifecycle. WitnessRoster handles registration and assignment. VerdictSink is the only door a verdict can walk through. PerjuryStandingWriter is the only thing holding the ENS write role. No contract has an owner, a pause, an upgrade proxy, or an address setter — the claim "operators cannot influence a verdict" has to survive someone grepping for an escape hatch. 69 Solidity tests and 110 TypeScript tests, most of them asserting that things fail: a verdict from an EOA or the deployer reverts, assignment is unreachable except through the VRF callback, an agent cannot write its own reputation.
That immutability is not free, and we paid for it three times. Each contract holds the next immutably and the registry's pointer at its verdict sink locks on first wiring, so a four-line change to the sink means redeploying everything and claim ids restart at 1. The site reads all three cascades rather than deleting the evidence of the earlier two.
Chainlink. The CRE workflow is the tribunal — there is no second code path that produces a verdict. It is deployed to the DON and adjudicates inside an AWS Nitro enclave, not only in the simulator. Each scheduled run reads ClaimRegistry.pendingForTribunal() to find its own claim, fetches both sealed submissions over Confidential HTTP, opens them with an envelope key the Vault DON releases into the enclave and nowhere else, recomputes both values, and writes (kind, claimId, verdict, evidenceCommitment) through the production Forwarder. A verdict it settled: 0xf8dd4d0219ccfd9a723409fbd8d19c88a87c91547c123805e6ff16f3d1c657c5.
VRF v2.5 draws every witness and every appeal panel. The callback walks the roster from seed % agentCount, skipping the claimant and anyone ineligible. On the claim the demo replays, the seed landed on the claimant itself and the walk stepped straight past it.
The Graph. The facts under dispute. Live Gateway only, nothing mocked: 13 pinned deployments across 2 Messari schema families and 5 chains, all served by one standardized query pattern, so adding a protocol is a line in a config file rather than code. Where a subject has a second independently-indexed deployment we query both and require agreement — a deployment id is a hash of the mapping code, so two agreeing means something two RPC nodes agreeing does not. Divergence returns Unverifiable rather than a judgement. Every read is pinned to a block and the served block must equal the requested one, because state that legitimately moved between two honest reads is otherwise indistinguishable from disagreement.
ENS. Each agent owns a real subname of perjury.eth, issued from a subname registry we deployed through the Verifiable Factory. Standing is a text record on a Permissioned Resolver, and Enhanced Access Control scopes the write per record key: the tribunal holds SET_TEXT on exactly two keys and has no grant on the issuance record, because the contract that can lower an agent's standing must not also decide whose standing it is. The operator that deployed everything and owns the name reverts when it tries to write standing. Agents get RENEW on their own subname and nothing else — an agent holding SET_RESOLVER could repoint its name at a resolver it controls and write whatever standing it liked.

name: Tessera
description: Tessera: An MCP marketplace where AI agents pay for API tools per-call using Hedera & x402.
projectDescription: Tessera is a decentralized, per-use tool marketplace built specifically for autonomous AI agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Today, the infrastructure of the web is stuck in human-centric patterns; when an AI agent needs to access a paid data source or run an API calculation, it cannot autonomously create a SaaS account, agree to a subscription, or enter a credit card. Tessera solves this by creating a true machine-to-machine economy. Instead of human signups, an agent connects to the Tessera MCP gateway, programmatically requests a tool, receives a per-invocation price quote, and instantly streams a micro-payment using the x402 protocol settled on Hedera. Once the payment is verified, Tessera securely executes the API call and feeds the clean data payload back to the agent in milliseconds. We chose Hedera because its fixed, ultra-low transaction fees make sub-cent micro-payments economically viable, unlocking a highly composable, zero-friction web where agents can seamlessly buy exactly what they need, one API call at a time.
howItsMade: Tessera is built as an extensible Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway using Node.js and TypeScript. At its core, we mapped the standard JSON-RPC tool-calling cycle of MCP directly onto the open x402 payment standard. When an AI agent invokes an MCP tool, the Tessera proxy intercepts the request, assesses the metered cost, and intercepts the flow to throw a standard cryptographic payload via the x402 scheme. We deeply integrated Hedera as our foundational settlement layer, leveraging the @x402/hedera reference packages alongside the open-source Blocky402 facilitator on the Hedera Testnet. Hedera provides immense benefit to this architecture; its fixed, predictable, and ultra-low $0.001 network transfer fees are what actually make sub-cent micro-payments economically viable for rapid-fire API inference. A particularly notable, "hacky" engineering choice was how we bypassed traditional web authentication. Because AI agents lack persistent browser sessions or traditional Web3 extension injections (like MetaMask), we built a lightweight transport middleware that wraps the x402 402 Payment Required header challenge into an inline MCP error response framework. This allows the client-side agent framework to catch the payment request, sign an off-chain transaction authorization autonomously via its private key, and pass it back to the facilitator, completing the entire transaction, validation, and API data delivery natively within a single, continuous command-line routine without breaking the LLM’s execution context

name: ProofOrder
description: Verifiable task results and conditional payments for AI agents.
projectDescription: AI agents can agree on a task and escrow payment onchain, but escrow alone cannot determine whether an offchain result satisfies rules fixed before payment. ProofOrder connects a deterministic work order, encrypted delivery, independent re-evaluation, and fixed-payee settlement in one reproducible workflow. A buyer freezes the task, input snapshot, acceptance rule, verifier, chain, contract, deadline, payment amount, and payee before funding. The provider computes the result and submits an HPKE-encrypted delivery bound to that order. A designated verifier decrypts the committed ciphertext, independently reruns the fixed rule, and signs evidence bound to the order, ciphertext, chain ID, and settlement contract. Any relayer can then settle to the immutable payee without redirecting funds. The demo also shows fail-closed rejection of a tampered order digest. The current prototype uses a trusted verifier; it is not a zero-knowledge proof, does not establish full fair exchange, and has not received a production security audit.
howItsMade: We built ProofOrder as a public monorepo using Solidity, Foundry, Anvil, Node.js, and ethers.js. The buyer, provider, and verifier run as separate CLI processes and persist checkpoints between steps. A canonical OrderSpec and SHA-256 commitments bind the task and input snapshot. The provider encrypts the complete result with HPKE using X25519, HKDF-SHA256, and AES-256-GCM. The verifier decrypts the same committed ciphertext, reruns the deterministic evaluator, and creates an ECDSA attestation bound to the order ID, ciphertext commitment, chain ID, contract address, and evidence digest. The Solidity contract enforces the designated verifier, fixed payee, settlement state transitions, refund deadlines, grace periods, and replay protection. A separate relayer can execute settlement while the buyer remains offline. We added adversarial tests for mismatched context, tampering, duplicate settlement, reentrancy, refunds, and offline recovery. The reproducible local workflow passes 198 JavaScript tests, 38 Foundry tests, five separate-process CLI tests, both demos, and npm audit with zero reported vulnerabilities. Codex and Hermes-family AI agents substantially assisted implementation, tests, documentation, and reproduction; human team members defined the scope and trust boundaries, reviewed outputs, narrowed unsupported claims, and are responsible for final acceptance and presentation. No partner technology is claimed as integrated.

name: AgentGuard
description: Policy-gated agent commerce with verified Arc USDC settlement.
projectDescription: This submission is entered in ETHGlobal’s Continuity Track. AgentGuard extends an existing policy-controlled agent commerce prototype with new ETHOnline work: live The Graph provenance feeding YieldScout decisions, Privy-authorized Arc Testnet wallet execution, Arc USDC escrow, independent verification, and public VERIFIED, BLOCKED, and FROZEN evidence. The repository history predates the event because this is an explicit continuity submission; the new integrations and evidence workflow are documented in the repository and demo.
howItsMade: We built the workflow in TypeScript with Solidity escrow contracts and a deterministic independent verifier. The Graph adapter records the query, response, timestamp, and provenance hash; that observation becomes a policy input and is bound into the task intent. Privy provides a policy-controlled buyer wallet restricted to Arc chain 5042002, zero native value, and the escrow/USDC targets. The Arc ERC-20 escrow implements identity registration, policy limits, task creation, seller submission, verifier-gated release, refunds, and frozen containment. The browser demo separates safe replay from live transaction evidence.

name: SwapGuard
description: Task-level cost accounting and RPC receipt checks for Uniswap agents, via a local advisory MCP.
projectDescription:
SwapGuard adds task-level cost accounting and original-condition checks to existing Uniswap swap agents. One swap task may include approval, a failed transaction and a retry. A refreshed quote should not erase gas already spent or silently lower the user's original minimum output.
Through a local advisory MCP interface, agents retain the original output floor, cumulative gas budget and deadline, check each proposed attempt, and keep a ledger across retries and restarts. The ledger separates approval, failed-swap and successful-swap gas. Unfinished tasks retain their costs without being shown as zero-cost successes. Optional RPC receipt verification reconciles supported WETH-to-USDC transactions and distinguishes receipt-derived observations from unverified caller reports.
We tested a project-authored deterministic reference agent on a local Ethereum fork using fake funds and the same four scenarios under three policies. Per-attempt budgeting completed four tasks with two budget overruns; independent cumulative budgeting and SwapGuard MCP each completed three with one overrun. Only two tasks per policy met both output and budget requirements. These results demonstrate reusable accounting and reconciliation, not superior routing or guaranteed savings.
The website also retains manual read-only analysis and clearly labelled synthetic examples. SwapGuard is an advisory prototype, not a trading router or wallet-enforced spending cap. The reference agent is not a third-party or LLM integration, and the tests are not live mainnet trading.
howItsMade:
SwapGuard is built with TypeScript, React, Vite and viem, with a Hono API deployed on Cloudflare Workers. A separate local stdio server uses the official MCP TypeScript SDK, exposing four accounting tools and an optional swapguard_verify_receipt tool.
Strict schemas, bigint arithmetic, immutable task terms, pending-operation checks and idempotent recording support the ledger. A private single-writer journal persists costs and restores task state after restart. Agents keep their own execution channel; SwapGuard does not sign or broadcast transactions.
Uniswap v3 Factory and QuoterV2 provide read-only quotes. Receipt verification supports narrowly defined WETH approvals and deadline-bound SwapRouter02 WETH-to-USDC swaps. It checks the bound wallet, chain, transaction parameters, receipt identity, canonical block and confirmation threshold, then reads actual gas usage and recipient transfer logs. Receipt-block Chainlink ETH/USD and USDC/USD feeds convert gas into USDC-equivalent while preserving native values.
An Anvil local-fork harness restores the same snapshot for each policy run and publishes tool calls, receipts, restart records, outcomes and source fingerprints. Synthetic examples, live reads and local-fork execution are labelled separately. Verification trusts configured RPC data; it is not a cryptographic proof or enforced wallet budget. AI-assisted development and review limits are disclosed in docs/AI_USAGE.md.

name: Assay
description: Assay verifies agent reputation before payment—and makes good reputation unfakeable.
projectDescription:
ERC-8004 gives AI agents on-chain identity and reviews so they can pick trustworthy counterparties. But reviews are free to write, so they're worthless: the #1 agent on Base by review count has 309,734 reviews — 95% from one wallet, every score identical, all inside one day, none backed by a payment. Independent research (arXiv:2606.26028) found 98.7–100% of all ERC-8004 feedback carries no proof of payment.
Assay is a paid pre-flight for agent payments. Before your agent pays a counterparty, it asks Assay over x402: is this agent's reputation real? Assay reads the registries live through The Graph across six chains and returns VERIFIED, UNPROVEN or WASH_REPUTATION_DETECTED with the evidence, what would change the verdict, and the exact subgraph deployment and block it was read at. If the source can't prove where the data came from, Assay refuses to answer rather than guess. Confidence is earned only from reviews backed by real payments from independent addresses — eleven detectors catch both the obvious farm and the sybil farm that concentration analysis alone would pass.
Then the write side: after an agent pays through Assay, it writes the one review that can't be faked — ERC-8004 feedback whose file carries the settlement as proofOfPayment. That's how a good agent earns its way to VERIFIED, and how a farm can't buy its way there for pocket change. Every UNPROVEN report ends with the priced path to VERIFIED.
Live today: one 402 that settles on three rails — Hedera via Blocky402, Arc via Circle Gateway, Base Sepolia via x402.org — with every settlement leaving a receipt on Hedera Consensus Service (the only store; no database). Assay is itself registered as ERC-8004 agent #9200 on Base Sepolia, and its own first payment-backed review is on-chain. A Privy treasury wallet enforces the mandate's allowlist and spend cap, refusing anything else before it's signed; raising the cap needs a live human via World Selfie Check. Exposed as REST, OpenAPI 3.1, and an MCP server with paid tools so any Claude or Cursor agent can call it. Built on Next.js 16, deployed on Vercel.
howItsMade:
One repo, one deployable. A Next.js 16 App Router app on Vercel is the only server: the console UI, the paid REST API, the MCP endpoint and the World step-up page share one origin. Underneath is a framework-free TypeScript engine (src/engine) that never imports Next, so the same code runs in the CLI, the route handlers and the MCP tools. Node 24, strict TypeScript, node:test, no ORM, no database.
Reading — The Graph. The engine queries the Agent0 ERC-8004 subgraphs on The Graph's decentralised network — Ethereum, Base, BSC, Polygon, Base Sepolia, BSC Chapel — through one shared schema, so adding a chain is a row in registry/chains.json. Every query carries _meta; a response without a pinned deployment hash and block number is refused, not returned. From up to 1,000 reviews it computes reviewer concentration and HHI, payment-proof coverage, self-issued feedback, distinct score values, the densest 24-hour window, validation-registry entries and registration completeness; eleven named detectors turn that into a verdict, and every report ends with what would change it. Concentration detectors only apply above a ten-review floor — a lesson learned when the engine called our own first review a farm.
Selling — x402. Paid routes are wrapped per handler with @x402/next (never in middleware — Edge can't run the Hedera signer), which settles only after the handler succeeds, so nobody pays for an error. The resource server has three facilitators, so one 402 offers three rails: Hedera testnet through Blocky402 (@x402/hedera, HBAR, the facilitator pays the network fee), Arc testnet through Circle Gateway (@circle-fin/x402-batching, off-chain signatures batched, no gas), and Base Sepolia through x402.org (@x402/evm). Prices are metered by work: a six-chain corroboration costs four single reads. The MCP endpoint wraps the same tools with @x402/mcp, so the payment rides in the tool call's _meta.
Remembering — Hedera Consensus Service. The deploy is serverless, so nothing lives in process memory. A settle hook writes a receipt for every paid call — rail, payer, amount, settlement tx, verdict, deployment, block — to one HCS topic, and human approvals go to the same topic. Everything is read back over the free mirror node, so the action trail is on a public ledger, not in our database. The handler and the settle hook never share a request object; the verdict crosses over keyed by the signed payment itself and is dropped once consumed.
Writing — the receipt. The reference paying agent signs only; after a 200 it writes ERC-8004 feedback about the provider with viem on Base Sepolia. The feedback file — with proofOfPayment pointing at the Hedera settlement, chain id 296 — is pinned to The Graph's own IPFS node, because the Agent0 subgraph reads feedback only through file/ipfs data sources; an https URI would never be indexed. Assay registered itself as agent #9200 under the service key; the agent key writes the review, because the spec forbids an owner reviewing itself. The subgraph indexed the review in under a minute and the engine reads it back as 100% payment-proof coverage.
Bounding — the mandate. mandate.json sets per-payment and run caps, allowed verdicts and a step-up line; the caps are enforced inside the x402 client's onBeforePaymentCreation hook and its spend controls, so an over-limit payment is aborted before it's signed. Privy's server SDK holds the other half: a treasury wallet bound to a policy (allowlisted recipients, value ceiling) owned by a P-256 key quorum, so raising the cap is a quorum-signed change. When the mandate says step-up, the agent prints an /escalate link and polls the ledger; a live human approves with a World Selfie Check (RP signature minted server-side, proof forwarded byte-for-byte to World's verifier), and the approval lands on HCS keyed by the nullifier.
Around it. OpenAPI 3.1 at /api/openapi (Redocly-clean) feeds a Bazantic gateway; a second gateway fronts Sourcify for the "is the counterparty's contract verified?" step; a Uniswap Trading API quote prices the payment. A stdio MCP server runs on the judge's machine for Claude Desktop and Cursor. The Hedera Harness got a PR adding an x402-facilitator preflight to doctor — the check that would have saved us an afternoon.
Hacky bits worth admitting. The Circle package inlines drifted core types, so its facilitator is cast at one boundary. Its default Gateway URL is mainnet-only and doesn't list Arc testnet; the testnet URL is set explicitly. Bazantic's CLI can't read a v2 402 (it wants x402Version in the body) and its gateway hosts 404 at Fly's edge — both reported. The landing page's glass blur over a patterned background stalled a low-end GPU once; the dot grid is now a tiled SVG and cards get their own compositing layer.

name: Crew AI
description: Hire AI agents that pay per call in USDC, each with an ENS name and a budget it can't raise
projectDescription:
Crew AI lets you run a crew of AI agents that spend real money without ever holding a key. Every agent you hire gets its own ENS name under yours (researcher.alex.crewai.eth), a budget it cannot raise, and a workspace on your machine. Every reply shows what it cost.
How it works:

Install with npm install -g @harsh132/crew-ai and run crew.
Log in with Privy and sign twice. Your crew's key is derived from that signature, so the same wallet restores the same crew on any computer. There is nothing to back up.
Claim you.crewai.eth, owned by your own wallet.
Send USDC on Arc. It is deposited into Circle Gateway automatically.
Hire agents and give them tasks. Every model call is paid for over x402, and charged only for the tokens it actually used.

Budgets are enforced by the side holding the money. Agents hold capability tokens, not keys, and a local authority refuses to sign once an agent's budget is spent. An agent can ask for more, and a human approves an amount. Revoking an agent clears its ENS address record, and the authority checks that name before every payment, so revocation is on chain, verifiable by anyone, and stops an agent mid-task.
Organizations get their own .eth name, owned by a Privy key-quorum wallet that only its owners control. Owners and managers invite members by their Crew name, and each member accepts in their own app and gets a name under crew.<org>.eth issued to their own wallet.
howItsMade:
Four pieces, TypeScript throughout.


x402 gate (Cloudflare Worker). An OpenAI-compatible endpoint in front of OpenRouter, limited to three cheap models for testnet use for now. Payments settle through Circle Gateway nanopayments on Arc testnet. x402's exact scheme can only charge a fixed price, so we built prepaid tabs: a Durable Object per payer holds a balance, each call reserves a ceiling with an EIP-712 voucher, and the gate meters OpenRouter's reported cost from the stream and settles only what was used. The receipt rides in an SSE comment, so streaming still works.


Budget authority (packages/core + sdk). Macaroon-style capability tokens that can only be narrowed, plus a spend tree held in the one process that has the key. Sub-agents get a capability, never a key; every payment is charged to their node, and an ENS name guard re-checks the agent's name before each signature.


Crew runtime and UI (published to npm as @harsh132/crew-ai, plain Node). Agents run on the pi agent loop with tools for their workspace and for requesting more budget. The React, Tailwind and shadcn UI is served by the runtime. The crew key is derived from two EIP-712 signatures, checked for determinism so smart and passkey wallets are refused. Wallet USDC is auto-deposited into Gateway.


Crew backend (Cloudflare Worker, D1, Durable Objects). Privy access-token auth and Privy key-quorum wallets for organizations. Names live on ENSv2 on Sepolia: each user and org name gets its own registry and resolver, deployed through ENSv2's VerifiableFactory, with role bitmaps that let the crew signer only register, revoke and write records for its agents.


Hacky bits worth mentioning: a user's whole name setup (deploy registry, deploy resolver, register, set address, fund the signer's gas) is one EIP-7702 batch through our own Batch7702 delegate, in one block. The batch needs contract addresses before they exist, so we simulate each factory deployment first to learn them. ENSv2 token ids carry a version in their low 32 bits, so reads have to clear them, and the deployed resolver only accepts DNS-encoded setAddress.

name: Warranty Pass
description: WarrantyPass is a consumer app for keeping portable digital records of product ownership
projectDescription:
WarrantyPass is a consumer app that helps people keep track of product receipts, warranty coverage, and purchase history in one place. Instead of losing a paper receipt or digging through old emails months later, users can upload a receipt, have AI extract key purchase details such as the product, retailer, purchase date, and price, review the information, and create a digital WarrantyPass for the item.
Each WarrantyPass shows important warranty information, including the coverage period, expiration date, remaining time, retailer, and whether the warranty is transferable. Receipt images and sensitive purchase information stay private in secure storage rather than being published onchain.
For added integrity, WarrantyPass can create a tamper-evident proof on Ethereum Sepolia. The original receipt file is cryptographically hashed, and only the hash, an opaque product identifier, warranty dates, transferability information, and the wallet that registered the proof are recorded in the smart contract. WarrantyPass then reads the record back from the blockchain and verifies that it matches the locally stored receipt and warranty data.
The goal of WarrantyPass is to make warranties easier to manage today while creating a foundation for portable product history in the future. When products are resold, their purchase history, repair records, and eligible warranty rights could move with them, giving buyers more confidence in secondhand purchases while keeping private information offchain.
howItsMade:
WarrantyPass is built as a React + Vite + TypeScript application with Tailwind CSS for the UI. Supabase powers the backend, including anonymous authentication, Postgres, Row Level Security, and private Storage for receipt images. Users can either enter product details manually or upload a receipt. Receipt images are sent through a Supabase Edge Function, where a vision-capable AI model extracts structured product information such as the brand, model, retailer, purchase date, and price. The user always reviews and confirms the extracted information before a WarrantyPass is created.
Sensitive data stays offchain. The original receipt file is stored privately in Supabase and is never exposed publicly. For the blockchain layer, WarrantyPass hashes the exact original receipt bytes using keccak256, then stores only the resulting hash and minimal warranty metadata in a custom WarrantyPassRegistry smart contract deployed on Arc Testnet.
The contract records an opaque product key, receipt hash, purchase date, warranty expiration, transferability flag, and the wallet that registered the proof. It intentionally does not store serial numbers, personal information, receipt images, or other sensitive data onchain.
The frontend uses wagmi and viem for wallet connection, Arc Testnet network handling, contract reads, transaction simulation, writes, and confirmation tracking. Before submitting a transaction, the app checks whether the product has already been registered to avoid duplicate proofs. After confirmation, WarrantyPass reads the contract record back from Arc Testnet and compares it against the local receipt hash and warranty data. The UI only shows the proof as verified if the values match.
One of the more important design choices was keeping Supabase identity and wallet identity separate. Supabase controls access to private user data through RLS, while the connected wallet is only used to sign blockchain transactions. This avoids treating wallet connection as application authentication and keeps private consumer data protected.
The result is a hybrid architecture where AI makes receipt onboarding fast, Supabase handles private user data and application state, and Arc provides the tamper-evident onchain proof layer without putting personal information onchain.

name: FaceGate
description: Stop credential sharing with privacy-preserving face auth. Zero biometric data stored. 3-line SDK.
projectDescription: FaceGate is a credential sharing prevention SDK for subscription platforms, powered by World ID Selfie Check. It treats face identity as a continuity and abuse-prevention signal,, confirming the same person returns on every login, not just the same password. Streaming platforms lose $9.1 billion annually to credential sharing. FaceGate fixes this with three lines of integration. Zero biometric data stored anywhere, only cryptographic nullifiers. One API key powers multiple platforms with full nullifier isolation across apps.
howItsMade: Built with Next.js, MongoDB, and Privy auth for the server, deployed on Vercel. The SDK is published as @facegate/sdk on npm. World ID Selfie Check handles liveness detection and ZK proof generation entirely on-device. FaceGate's server holds the World ID RP credentials, generates RP signatures, verifies ZK proofs with World's API, and stores only nullifiers in MongoDB, no biometric data. Each developer gets a unique action string for nullifier isolation across platforms. Demo integration built as a Netflix-style app showing full signup and login flow with Selfie Check.

name: Leashh
description: Agents fix prod, pay over x402 on Hedera, and can't spend a cent past their ENS limits. That's it.
projectDescription:
Leash solves a massive problem with AI agents: how to let them spend money without letting them empty your wallet. Right now, if an agent needs to pay for a server or an API, you hand over a private key, and it has unlimited access.
With Leash, every AI agent gets an ENS name with strict, on-chain spending rules. You can definitively state: “This agent has $5, can only buy AI services, and expires in 30 days.”
How It Works:

The Family Tree: Agents form a hierarchy (e.g., parent -> child). A parent can give a child a slice of its budget, but the child never gets more money or a longer timeline than the parent. Smart contracts enforce this.
The 6-Step Check: Before any payment happens, Leash checks the agent (and its parents) for: name existence, remaining budget, per-request limits, allowed services, allowed currencies, and expiry. If one check fails, the payment is blocked. No money moves.
The Kill Switch: One on-chain transaction revokes an agent. Every child under it stops instantly, and rented servers shut down within 20 seconds.

What Agents Can Actually Do:

Buy AI: Agents pay per token (via x402) using USDC on Hedera—no subscriptions or API keys needed.
Rent Servers: Agents can request infrastructure (like a Redis cache) and pay per minute.
Auto-Fix Apps: A team of agents can monitor a web app, diagnose issues, and pay for simple fixes (like restarting a service) within their limits.

Every single action is logged publicly on Hedera. It's built on ENSv2 (using Ethereum Sepolia) for permissions, proving agents can be useful and financially constrained.
howItsMade:
Leash is an AI agent framework built on a simple split: the rules live on ENS (Sepolia), and the money moves on Hedera.
The Rules: Every agent gets an ENSv2 subname. We store their limits—like budgets and allowed services—as simple text records. Because of how ENSv2 works, revoking a parent name instantly shuts down all its child agents. We even restricted transfers so agents can't go rogue and sell their names.
The Money: Our Rust backend uses the x402 protocol to settle micro-transactions in USDC on Hedera. Hedera’s tiny fees make paying a fraction of a cent per AI request actually viable. Before any money moves, a policy engine verifies the agent's ENS rules, and it only pays for successful LLM responses.
Look, Ma, No Database: We ditched traditional databases entirely. Instead, Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) acts as our audit log, service directory, and cross-provider spending ledger.
What it does: Agents can rent Docker containers by the minute or fix broken apps. In our "autopilot" setup, three agents team up: one monitors the system, one pays an LLM (like Llama or Qwen) to diagnose issues, and the third pays to execute a fix from a strict, pre-approved menu.
The Setup: Our React frontend reads directly from Sepolia and Hedera mirror nodes, so it works even if our own backend goes down.
The Coolest Hack: If you revoke an agent's name on Sepolia, our cleanup loop catches it and literally kills that agent's Docker containers on a completely different server within 20 seconds. It’s real-time, cross-chain mandate enforcement.

name: Herit
description: On-chain inheritance with ENSv2 subnames & World ID. Owner aren't alive, heirs gain access.
projectDescription:
THE PROBLEM:
When a crypto holder dies or becomes incapacitated, their assets are often permanently locked on-chain without a documented plan. No bank, no password reset, no next-of-kin override.
THE SOLUTION:
Herit, a crypto inheritance platform, uses ENS subnames as heir slots and a role-based permission system to enforce the inheritance lifecycle without any off-chain coordination.
Herit combines Solidity contracts on Ethereum Sepolia, a World ID verification backend, and a browser frontend to let someone pass their crypto to their next of kin without ever handing over a seed phrase. Herit is a dead-man's switch, but it replaces the two parts of that pattern that are usually fake: proof that the owner is still alive, and the heir's identity.
Ordinary dead-man's-switch contracts treat a timestamp as proof of life. Any transaction refreshes it, which means a bot on a schedule refreshes it, and so does the thief who stole the key. The contract concludes the owner is fine while the estate drains.
Herit instead requires a World ID Selfie Check to check in, which is a live biometric liveness and uniqueness proof. World ID returns a nullifier that is stable for one human and different for everyone else, and the backend salts that into a commitment and signs an EIP-712 attestation that a LivenessAttestor contract on Sepolia verifies. The first check-in binds the estate to that commitment permanently, and every subsequent CONTINUITY check-in must match. A stolen key can sign anything, but it cannot pass a liveness check, so the thief produces a different nullifier, and the transaction reverts.
Selfie Check is used because an inheritance switch needs to know the owner is alive today, not merely that they are a unique person.
The second replacement is the heir. Most inheritance contracts store heirs as addresses in an array, which have no verifiable link to a real person and nothing stopping one human from occupying several heir slots. In Herit, each heir is given a genuine ENSv2 subname, such as son.alice.herit.eth, inside a registry deployed for that one estate through the Verifiable Factory.
The subname carries public text records of the relationship and the share in basis points, so an heir can see their inheritance and read its terms years before they can act on it. What keeps it dormant is a withheld permission rather than a flag in our own database. Herit claims a free slot in ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control role bitmap as a claim role and deliberately does not grant it when the subname is created, so canClaim reads false. Unlocking the estate is a grantRoles call on the real ENS registry, and the claim gate is a hasRoles call, which means anyone can read an heir's permission directly from ENS without touching Herit at all.
Using it works as follows.

The grantor opens an estate under herit,  which is free and avoids making every user buy a .eth name first
The grantor registers their heirs with shares, and deposits ETH or ERC-20 tokens into an opt-in vault rather than exposing their whole wallet.
Then, they pass a Selfie Check to start the clock. Each interval, a continuity Selfie Check resets it. If the interval lapses, anyone at all can poke the contract, and the estate enters a grace period.
The grace period is a real second stage and not a formality, because a single Selfie Check inside grace returns the estate to active. Someone who was simply traveling with no signal can undo the whole thing by proving they are alive.
If grace also lapses, another poke unlocks the estate, and in one transaction the vault freezes its balances so a later deposit cannot change what a share means.
Afterward, the estate name is renewed so no permission lands on an expired name, and each heir's subname is granted the claim role.
Each heir then passes their own Selfie Check, proving they are a distinct living human, and withdraws their share.
One human gets one claim per estate; the grantor cannot claim from their own estate, and the same person cannot claim twice under two different heir names.

Everything described is deployed and verified on Ethereum Sepolia against the frozen ENSv2 hackathon deployment: AccessControlGate, HeritRegistry, HeritVault, ClaimManager, and LivenessAttestor, with herit.eth registered and a grantor registry attached beneath it.
Because Herit targets that frozen hackathon set rather than the regular Sepolia beta set, the names don't appear in the official ENS app and must be read directly from the registry or the dedicated hackathon ENS Explorer(https://hackathon-deployment-portal-app.ens-cf.workers.dev/).
Lastly, in line with Security-minded development, there are 45 passing tests, including fork tests that run against the live ENSv2 registry rather than mocks.
The frontend is a Next.js app using IDKit, wagmi and viem, and the full path runs end to end on Sepolia: open an estate, fund it, check in, miss the window, unlock, and claim.
The Graph makes Herit's history visible. Herit runs a subgraph over all five of its Sepolia contracts, indexing fourteen events across the gate that opens estates and mints heir subnames, the registry that holds the check-in clock, the vault, the claim manager, and the attestor that verifies each Selfie Check.
The subgraph exists because there is no "list every estate" getter on-chain, because an unbounded array in contract storage is gas-intensive. The subgraph builds that list from the EstateOpened event instead: every estate anyone has ever opened, with its label, its grantor, the ENS registry deployed for it, and when it was opened, newest first.
The Graph replays everything that has happened to one estate: configured, checked in, entered grace, unlocked, deposited, withdrawn, claimed, settled, and every Selfie Check attested along the way.
howItsMade:
The contracts are Solidity 0.8.30, built with Foundry and deployed to Ethereum Sepolia. The app is a Next.js 16.3.4 frontend on React 19 using wagmi 3, viem 2, ensjs, and Tailwind 4, with the World ID integration through IDKit 4.2.3.
There are five contracts:

AccessControlGate deploys a per-estate ENS registry and is the only thing allowed to touch ENS roles.
HeritRegistry is the estate state machine holding the check-in clock and the heir list.
HeritVault is the escrow, ClaimManager is the heir-facing payout path, and LivenessAttestor verifies the backbackend's-712 attestation before anything else can run.

Every dependency between them is immutable with no setter, so a compromised or mistaken address cannot be repointed later.
That decision created the most interesting problem in the build. The five contracts reference each other in a ring, so none of them can be deployed first, and CREATE2 does not solve it because a CREATE2 address depends on the creation code, which carries the constructor arguments, so predicting the vault would need the registry's address and predicting the registry would need the vault's. However, plain CREATE does solve it, because a contract address is only the hash of the deployer and its nonce, and the constructor arguments aren't part of it. So the deploy script computes all five addresses from the deployer's before deploying anything, passes the predicted addresses into the constructors, and asserts after each deployment that the real address matches the prediction.
It then walks the finished ring and checks that every contract agrees with every other one, which is the test itself.
The ENS integration took the most reading. ENSvENSv2'sanced Access Control packs 64 roles into a uint256 as nybbles, where a role at nybble N sits at bit 4N and its admin counterpart 128 bits higher. ENS's RegistryRolesLib occupies nybbles 0 to 9 and 30 to 31, so Herit claims nybbles 10 and 11 for its claim role and its registration marker, sitting alongside ENS's rather than in a parallel system.
That is what makes unlock a literal grantRoles call on the real registry and the claim gate a hasRoles call. Because hasRoles requires the whole bitmap, checking both bits at once asks "has this estate unlocked for you" and "did Herit create this subname at all" in a single call, and the second bit stops a name that acquired the claim role by some other route.
We had to find three ENSv2 behaviors the hard way and handle them in code. A role granted on an expired name writes to a resource ID that nothing reads, so the grant appears to succeed and silently does nothing; unlock has to renew the heirheir'sname before granting anything. Every grant and revoke burns and re-mints the subname token, so any cached token ID is a bug waiting to fire, and names are addressed by labelhash throughout.
And renewing an already-expired name takes a revival path that needs a root-level renew role on that specific registry, which the deploy has to grant explicitly. On top of that, the deployed ENSv2 hackathon contracts are newer than the pinned submodule, and one signature differs exactly where it matters: the deployed user registry takes initialize as an array of account-and-role pairs. In contrast, the submodule declares it as a single pair. I
Importing the submsubmodule'serface would have compiled, deployed, and reverted on Sepolia with no error to explain why, so every function Herit calls was checked selector by selector against the deployed bytecode, and a minimal local interface was declared instead.
The World ID side has one design decision that quietly decides whether the whole thing is secure. A World ID action string is the namespace that scopes the nullifier, so the same human verifying against two different action strings produces two unrelated nullifiers.

The first design used a per-heir claim action, which reads correctly and is wrong: one person registered as two heirs of the same estate would have produced two different nullifiers, two different commitments, and been paid twice, with every individual proof valid.
Collapsing check-in and claim into one action per estate and moving the heir label in proof's final fixed it, and it also turned on a second check that had been dead code — because a grantor's check-in and a claim on the same estate now share a namespace, the contract can compare the two commitments and refuse a grantor trying to claim from their own estate.
Selfie Check is a World ID 3.0 credential, so legacy proofs have to be explicitly allowed and results can arrive in the older shape. The nullifier has to be read from the IDKit result rather than the Cloud Verify response, whose success shape isn't documented anywhere.

The backend is two Next.js route handlers.

One signs the relying-party request server-side, since that key proves a proof request came from Herit. It can never reach the browser, and it has to remap four of the five fields the signing helper returns into the names the widget expects, across a JSON boundary where nothing type-checks it.
The other verifies the prooWorld'srld'sud Verify, salts the nullifier into a commitment, and signs the EIP-712 attestation the contract will check. Before signing, it runs read-only preflight calls against Sepolia that mirror each revert the transaction would hit, so it refuses a doomed attestation with a readable sentence instead of costing the user gas; those checks fail open if the RPC is unreachable because the contract enforces every rule regardless.

The frontend never hand-writes an ABI; a script generates it from Foundry's output, and it caught a stale copy missing the two main write functions. The tests run against a Sepolia fork with the real ENS registry rather than mocks, including the two that matter most: proving a stolen key cannot check in, and the same human cannot claim twice.
The subgraph uses graph-cli 0.98.1 and graph-ts 0.38.2 to index five Sepolia contracts from their deployment blocks. Fourteen handlers cover estate creation and heir subname minting, check-ins, vault activity, claims, and World ID attestations.
ABIs are generated directly from Foundry artifacts, preventing contract changes from leaving the indexer with outdated interfaces. The schema has two entities: a mutable Estate, keyed by grantors'aby grantors', and an immutable ActivityEvent, keyed by transaction hash and log index. Shared mapping logic populates common fields and rejects events for estates the gate never opened, avoiding dangling relationships.
Events include a sequence number calculated as block number × 1,000,000 + log index, enabling accurate chain-order sorting in GraphQL's single orderBy field. Data remains typed rather than pre-rendered, leaving token formatting and heir-label display to the application.
The frontend sends GraphQL requests with fetch and uses TanStack Query for caching and retries. To stay within StudStudio's00-query daily limit, it polls every 30 seconds and pauses in hidden tabs. After a user transaction confirms, it stores its block number outside TanStack Query. The feed compares that block with the subgraph's block, polls every four seconds while the indexer catches up, and stops after two minutes to avoid hammering a stalled indexer.
The chain remains the source of truth for live state. The subgraph records what happened, while the interface reads countdowns, statuses, and balances directly from Sepolia so it never shows stale time-sensitive data.

name: Catenor One
description: Tokens prove who holds. Catenor proves who may be paid today — one DID, checked confidentially.
projectDescription:
Catenor One is the first reference implementation of Catenor Protocol, an open protocol for canonical identity and verifiable authority for humans, organizations and agents.
The problem: tokenized assets prove who holds them, not who may be paid today. A wallet is not an identity, a relationship is not a capability, and a validly signed credential is not current eligibility.
Catenor gives every subject a persistent did:catenor identity that is independent of wallets and identity providers. Organizations become Trust Anchors through a confidential admission. Authority flows as explicit, scoped capabilities that can be delegated but never exceed the delegator's. Investors hold W3C Verifiable Credentials. Every payout is gated by a confidential decision about current eligibility.
The live demo ran end to end on testnet (24/24 stages). A Trust Anchor is admitted by a deployed Chainlink Confidential Workflow and authorizes a Sponsor. The Sponsor tokenizes a synthetic real-estate SPV on Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio and issues 600 and 400 units to two investors whose KYC passed in the Sumsub sandbox. A dividend is declared, with entitlements of 6 and 4.
Then one investor is sanctioned. He still holds his 400 units and a valid credential, but the TEE re-checks today's evidence and decides HOLD. A Privy-controlled Distribution Agent, authorized only through delegation, pays the eligible investor 6 HBAR and never even requests a signature for the other.
Every DENY path is part of the demo:
a capability used outside its scope;
an agent with a wallet but no capability;
a relationship without a capability;
a non-delegable action.
Everything is verifiable: the CRE execution IDs, the HashScan transactions, the Privy policies and a hash-chained audit log.
Honest labels: the Sumsub sandbox uses synthetic applicants, the company KYB in the admission is a synthetic mock, and Hedera runs on testnet.
howItsMade:
Architecture.
A TypeScript monorepo built as spec-driven vertical slices against a pinned protocol baseline.
Framework-free domain packages: identity, credentials, authority, policy and audit.
An API and a clean-room stage runner of 24 numbered scripts.
Postgres through Prisma on Railway, used only as an index. The proofs are the signed documents and a hash-chained audit.
Identity and credentials.
Random did:catenor identifiers, with DID Documents that carry Ed25519 verification methods.
W3C VC 2.0 with Data Integrity eddsa-jcs-2022 (RFC 8785 JCS).
Verifiable Presentations bound to a challenge and a domain, checked by seven named checks.
Issuer-signed status statements.
Authority.
A Trust Anchor admission whose bootstrap configuration is pinned by hash, decided by a deterministic policy and endorsed by a separate bootstrap key.
Relationships kept apart from capabilities.
Delegation chains checked for scope, delegability and validity windows.
Chainlink CRE. One Confidential Workflow, identity-confidential, runs five operations with cre.handlerInTee: admission, investor eligibility, credentials, offering eligibility and the pro-rata PAY/HOLD distribution.
The Sumsub API keys come from the Vault DON, and the signed Sumsub calls are made inside the enclave.
The trigger context is sealed with AES-256-GCM, using HKDF-derived keys, so the trigger payload carries no plaintext.
Only facts, decisions and commitments come out, through an HMAC-authenticated callback.
It was deployed to the private registry twice; the second deploy pins the Trust Anchor's key as the only accepted issuer.
It is triggered through the gateway's JSON-RPC with an ETH-signed JWT, paced to respect the rate limit.
The notable part: a store-and-forward relay on our Railway API lets a local runner receive TEE results. We also found that the documented private-registry gateway answered "Workflow not found" for our org, and proved with a control workflow that the CLI's gateway works.
Privy. Every key is a Privy server wallet under a Catenor-created policy.
Management-owner keys stay outside the runtime, and the runtime signers are override-scoped key quorums, so the service can never loosen its own limits.
The credential-signing wallets allow signMessage only.
The SPV wallet may only call the ATS Factory on chain 296. Then owner-authorized calldata rules pin issueByPartition, grantRole and setDividend to the new equity.
The Distribution Agent may only pay the two investor wallets, up to 20 HBAR.
The investor wallets are receive-only.
Transactions are signed with eth_signTransaction for Hedera's EVM, behind a signer-boundary check that the signed transaction equals the prepared one.
Hedera ATS. The official ATS v8 contracts on testnet, driven through their typechain bindings with ethers v6.
deployEquity through the Factory.
issueByPartition, only for the exact units approved by a TEE-backed ALLOW decision.
grantRole and setDividend, with the entitlements read on-chain.
The payout, as an HBAR transfer from the Agent.
A public verification script that uses only the JSON-RPC relay and the Mirror Node.
Front end. A static site on Vercel: a landing page, a click-through replay console of the recorded run (with live Mirror Node checks) and the full evidence history.
AI. Built with Claude Code, with project subagents for CRE, Privy and Hedera. Every prompt, plan and provenance entry is in the repo.

name: Beast
description: Give AI agents onchain identity and spending limits, backed by a verified human.
projectDescription:
Beast is a human-controlled treasury for AI agents. It gives each agent an ENSv2 identity and a policy-bounded Privy wallet, while World Selfie Check provides a renewable signal that a human controller is still present.
An agent’s ENS name acts as its expense card. Its addr record identifies the paying wallet, while agent.merchant and agent.cap define the permitted recipient and maximum transaction amount. Before every payment, Beast resolves
these values through the real Universal Resolver and verifies both the registrar binding and the wallet’s Enhanced Access Control role. The wallet and merchant are never supplied by the payment request, so a missing, expired or
revoked ENS name prevents the transaction from being constructed.
World proofs are checked for credential type, action, environment, completed user presence, single-use nonce, controller-bound signal and same-human continuity. A successful check creates a ten-minute presence lease; payments
above 3 USDC require a check-in from the previous two minutes.
Privy provides the financial enforcement layer. Each organization agent has a routine signer for autonomous payments, a two-person approval signer for elevated payments and a three-key owner quorum for administrative changes.
For example, an agent may spend up to 3 USDC autonomously, require both the owner and an approver between 3 and 25 USDC, and be refused above the ENS-recorded 25 USDC maximum. Privy policies independently constrain the token
contract, decoded ERC-20 recipient and amount.
Beast is live on Sepolia with dedicated Permissioned Resolver instances, ENSIP-25/26 agent-discovery records, real EAC grants and revocations, real USDC payments, browser-held P-256 approval keys, and adversarial Foundry and
integration tests.
howItsMade:
Beast is built with Solidity, Foundry, Node.js/Express, viem and a browser-based JavaScript dashboard. It runs on Sepolia and combines ENSv2, World IDKit, Privy server wallets and OpenAI’s GPT-4o-mini.
For ENSv2, we deployed a custom AgentSubnameRegistrar over our own PermissionedRegistry. Every agent receives a subname under beast.eth and its own PermissionedResolver proxy, deployed through VerifiableFactory. The resolver
stores the agent wallet, permitted merchant, spending cap and ENSIP-25/26 discovery records. Payments use ENSIP-10 resolve(bytes,bytes) through the Universal Resolver to retrieve these values live. The gateway also verifies the
registrar’s wallet binding and the agent’s Enhanced Access Control role before proceeding. Foundry tests exercise expiry, role administration, revocation and re-registration against a real PermissionedRegistry, not a mock.
World Selfie Check supplies renewable human presence. The backend creates signed RP requests and verifies seven properties: selfie credential, expected action, production environment, completed user presence, single-use
session-bound nonce, controller-bound signal and same-human nullifier continuity. Successful verification creates a ten-minute lease. A tiered freshness rule requires payments above 3 USDC to use a check-in less than two
minutes old.
Privy provides policy-enforced EIP-7702 wallets. Organization agents use three P-256 key quorums: a 3-of-3 administrative owner quorum containing the backend, owner and approver; a backend-only routine signer; and a 2-of-2
human approval signer. The human private keys are generated with WebCrypto and remain in their respective browsers. Two Privy policies inspect decoded ERC-20 calldata to constrain the token contract, recipient and amount. Small
payments execute autonomously, larger payments collect signatures over one frozen transaction payload, and over-cap payments are rejected.
An OpenAI-powered procurement agent can choose between vendor packages, but it receives no wallet authority or trusted payment parameters. It submits only its label and selected amount; the gateway obtains everything security-
sensitive from ENS and server-side state.

name: Ulysses
description: Get paid for a zero-day without anyone, including us, ever seeing it
projectDescription: Get paid for a zero-day without anyone, including us, ever seeing it. Researchers submit a live exploit encrypted. A Chainlink enclave replays it, proves the real damage, and releases the bounty, then reveals nothing until the patch ships. Not private finance. Private disclosure. First on CRE.
howItsMade:
The trick is that we built ourselves out of the loop on purpose. The researcher seals the exploit in the browser, encrypted (X25519 → HKDF-SHA256 → XChaCha20-Poly1305) to a public key only the enclave can open. It reaches us as ciphertext we can't read, and the plaintext never touches a server, the wire, or the sponsor.
A Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow runs it inside an AWS Nitro TEE. Only the sealed enclave holds the decryption key. There it unlocks the exploit, replays the attack against the live target via eth_simulateV1, and measures the exact drain straight off the Transfer logs. What leaves the enclave is only a verdict: an EIP-712 signature over {severity, lossAmount, exploitHash, researcher, programId, target}. A price and a commitment hash, never the payload. The raw attack never crosses out.
The DON verifies a cryptographic attestation proving a genuine enclave ran the genuine code, then the verdict settles on-chain. BountyEscrow checks the attestor signature and releases the tier reward from escrow, with no arbiter and no disclosure. The same sealed exploit is replayed later against the patched contract to confirm the fix before anything is ever revealed. Pure-JS @noble crypto so it runs in the WASM enclave, and nothing is logged inside the box.

name: Botanica
description: SimCity for AI agents. Plug in any model. They earn. You own the swarm.
projectDescription:
Botanica (agent-town repo) is SimCity for agents. The bet is that agent work only becomes an economy if people can see it, understand it, direct it, and own it; a gamified agentic economy system. Wonder if people would watch their agents? People watch fly brains trade crypto with millions of views in a 24hr period; imagine watching your agent do work in a SimCity like game!
Currently, you watch a town of named agents earn/lend/borrow/repay USDC (agentic DeFi rails), but eventually your agents could step in and create any part of the virtual world to earn money, be social, trade, lend/borrow, create compute tasks, etc. The ultimate vision is allowing a user to plug their own agent with MCP from Claude/GPT/Grok/Hermes and open up aspects within the economy with what's possible such as different services, bartering, and more.
botanica.eth is live on Arc. Eight agents have ENS names and Circle wallets. They pay each other, take loans, default, and pick up credit scores on their names. You can mint your own name in the UI, fund it, and tell it to deposit. That name can spawn subagents as well, allowing for swarms. The eight town agents are still rule-bots to ensure the POC and onchain backend worked. Next a user can plug in their agent behind a name and wallet. Then the swarm is something they can sell, rent, or license.
Live: https://agent-town-eight.vercel.app
howItsMade:
We built Botanica (agent-town repo) as a TypeScript monorepo with pnpm. Next.js 16 and PixiJS draw the town you actually look at. A Hono API sits behind it, with REST for snapshots and a live event stream for ticks, payments, and speech. Contracts are Foundry. The agents today are a tick loop of role rules, with shared zod types as the contract a future model would hit.
We ended up on two chains because ENS provides the credit, wrapper and naming convention that can be owned/leased/transferred in economy, while Arc provides settlement layer cross chain. ENSv2 for this hackathon is on Sepolia. USDC and Circle wallets are on Arc. Each agent name stores its Arc wallet address, which is how a Sepolia identity keeps pointing at Arc money.
On the ENS side we registered botanica.eth, stood up a town registry, and mint names like ada.botanica.eth for example. After a repay or a default, the treasurer writes a credit score onto the name. Visitors mint from the UI, and a name can mint subdomains under itself, like scout.you.botanica.eth. ENS published the hackathon contract addresses but not the ABIs, so we pulled nearby source and checked each function ID against the bytecode on chain until the calls matched.
Every agent is a Circle developer-controlled smart wallet: the eight town agents, the mayor, and anyone who mints in. TownTreasury is our first bank on Arc Testnet. Agents hire each other through ERC-8183, an escrow job contract on Arc: post the work, lock USDC, deliver, get paid. Arc uses USDC for gas as well as transfers, but the token is 6 decimals and the gas balance is 18, so you have to convert at the edge or you send the wrong amount. We compile Solidity as paris because Arc does not support the newer PUSH0 opcode. We also used Circle Gateway once to move Sepolia USDC into the Arc treasury; that inbound is already settled.
For data we wrote an agent-town subgraph on Arc that indexes the bank and jobs, so the UI and the agents read the same loan book. Each tick we also query public Aave V3 and Uniswap V3 subgraphs and price the town rate off live market APY. Studio rate-limited us, so we keep the last good response and back off.
Tick history lives in Supabase. The site is on Vercel. Anything that spends money stays off until we flip a flag, so the public demo cannot drain the treasury by accident.

name: Cyberattack Sunday
description: Turns a live cybersecurity news feed into a deduped, evidence-linked weekly incident report.
projectDescription:
Cyberattack Sunday, chain-first: The Graph as the detector for the crypto lane, the newsletter as the consumer, the incident feed sold per query over x402 on Hedera, and graph-evidence packaged as an MCP server so it lands in The Graph's tooling pool.
A secure, read-only Google Sheets connector is live-verified against the authorized Cyberattack Sunday workbook. It inventories historical structure without exposing content or modifying the source. Automated row ingestion remains a post-inventory implementation step.
Goal was to train it with ~90 weeks of previous content, but ran out of time. Will continue as I do intend to use this daily.
I do a Cyberattack Sunday run down on my Substack every single week, that takes me eight hours to manually compile. But my RSS feed can't sort out the cyberattacks from regular cyber news, so I decided to build my own dashboard that could. Goal is to add more filtration to help manage my news channel.
The system includes deterministic classification, incident clustering, evidence correlation and drafting, with chain evidence from The Graph and an MCP interface. I also built a secure, read-only Google Sheets connector and verified it against my authorized 83-tab historical workbook. The 23,910-row corpus validates cleanly, although completing its production ingestion remains the immediate post-submission infrastructure step.
howItsMade:
pnpm & Turborepo monorepo
Next.js dashboard
Node.js & PostgreSQL
deployed on Railway
mapped out the architecture, then divided the project into audited sprints (don't laugh, I just found out how to make a proper Sprint thanks to this so... thanks!)
first sprints established the repository, threat model, data lineage and PostgreSQL foundation
then I started on the classification engine, which still needs calibrating
The system includes deterministic classification, incident clustering, evidence correlation and drafting, with chain evidence from The Graph and an MCP interface. I also built a secure, read-only Google Sheets connector and verified it against my authorized 83-tab historical workbook. The 23,910-row corpus validates cleanly, although completing its production ingestion remains the immediate post-submission infrastructure step.
The Graph became the chain-first detector for the crypto lane. I used it to collect standardized protocol observations across Ethereum and Base while preserving the provider, deployment, block and query provenance. I then packaged the graph-evidence layer as a bounded, read-only MCP server so the same incident and anomaly tools can eventually participate in The Graph’s tooling ecosystem. The commercial destination is to make the reviewed incident feed available per query through x402 settlement on Hedera, although that payment layer remains future work.
The Google Sheets integration was added last because I wanted the application connected to exactly one workbook, not my entire Google Drive.
(Second last. These login creds are driving me insane, making a last minute switch to no logins!)
The development process deliberately alternated implementation with adversarial review. Claude built each bounded sprint, while Codex independently reproduced failures against compiled commands, disposable PostgreSQL databases and hostile inputs before a sprint was accepted. That cycle uncovered issues including stale database snapshots, mutable completed records, search-path shadowing, path traversal, symlink races, cancellation leaks, redirect handling and secret-encoding leaks. Fixes were regression-tested through offline suites, PostgreSQL integration tests, browser tests, network-denial tests, migration rollback checks, CodeQL and continuous integration.
I did not finish training or evaluation against approximately 90 weeks of published Cyberattack Sunday material before the deadline. What I completed is the foundation: traceable inputs, deterministic decisions, incident construction, evidence-aware drafting, human review, a production dashboard and a live-verified connection to the historical workbook. I intend to continue building it because it is designed around a workflow I perform every week and a tool I genuinely plan to use daily.

name: ATLIS
description: Laddered, time-decaying automated trading strategies that are intended to grow "HODL" stacks
projectDescription:
This project is a rebalancing trading bot leveraging 1inch Aqua. It purchases WETH with USDC and then attempts to sell it for a higher price.
The strategy begins by defining a price ladder, where each price is roughly 2.5% higher than the one below it on the ladder. The protocol will create "buy"and "sell" orders as concentrated liquidity positions on 1inch Aqua. For example, the strategy will create a sell order ranging from roughly 5% above the average purchase price to 20% above the average purchase price. Similarly, a standing "buy" order will exist below the average buy price.
The concentrated liquidity setup is used because it allows us to scale into positions proportional to price movements. When WETH dips heavily, we buy more, and when it goes up quickly, we sell proportionally more.
The strategy will leave some USDC initially un-deployed, and then over time it will deploy more capital. Every "period", the strategy rebalances, deploying more capital into the "buy" side based on user configuration.
during each rebalance, the "time decaying" nature of the system may occur. If the current spot price of WETH is higher than the average buy price, the system will sell some pre-defined portion of the held WETH on Uniswap. This will be repeated every time a rebalance occurs while the system is in profit. This way, we capture profits every time we are able, while not completely exiting the trade immediately.
Finally, during a rebalance, we may also purchase some WETH (on Uniswap) if the spot price is lower than the average entry price of the strategy. The amount of "dry powder" USDC that is used for a direct buy during a rebalance is based on user defined parameters.
Every rebalance, buying or selling may occur if the spot price differs from the entry price. Then, the average entry price is recomputed, buy and sell liquidity ranges are recomputed, and a new set of Aqua strategies are shipped.
The system redirects proceeds from sales into a "tax" and "profit" wallet, such that the profit wallet will passively grow in USDC value over time.
howItsMade:
This project uses 1inch Aqua, Uniswap v3, and Chainlink oracles on Base Mainnet.
The general structure of the project is centered around a "Manager" contract, which is the owner of two "ladder proxies". These ladder proxies hold the funds and are the addresses associated with the "buy" and "sell" Aqua strategies.
The Manager contract computes the values of the ladder rungs, as well as tracking average entry price for all WETH purchased. Average entry price is the universally used value for profit accounting, and by doing this we can ensure that purchasing new WETH at a low price helps to bring the average purchase price down.
The Manager holds the "amount spent on WETH" and uses the WETH balance held by itself and strategies to compute the average entry price.
On every rebalance, which must be triggered manually by the Manager's owner, the manager will call into the proxies, having them dock their aqua strategies and transfer all funds into the Manager contract. The Manager will first tabulate profit from any WETH sold, then proceed to sell more WETH if the spot price is high enough. This does not change the average entry price. Profit and "taxes" will be redirected to two separate wallets, and the principle USDC will be re-invested in the strategy. After tabulating profit, the manager will tabulate the new average entry price based on any new WETH purchased from the buy side. Then, the manager will compute the new amount of USDC to make "active", and potentially purchase some WETH if the spot price is low enough. Finally, new buy-band and sell-band price limits will be computed based on the spot price and average entry price (the bands must not include either). These price limits will be passed into the buy and sell proxies, along with USDC for the buy side and WETH for the sell side, and then the proxies will use these amounts and price boundaries to construct an Aqua concentrated liquidity position, and then call ship in Aqua to make the strategy live.
At any point, partial fills can be "harvested" to prevent selling WETH at a low price or buying it at a high price. A harvest simply transfers purchased WETH out of the buy-side, or transfers USDC out of the sell-side, and into the Manager. The manager will include these in its rebalance computations. If harvest is not called in a timely manner, the ATLIS system still benefits in the form of trading fees.
The ATLIS system also has a simple emergency withdraw functionality, which allows the Manager to pull funds into its own address from the proxies. This is great in the case that a strategy cannot easily be docked via the proxy functions. Aqua allows the proxies to retain custody of their funds. If there is ever an emergency, funds are transferred directly back to the manager, which does not possess an Aqua strategy, at which point those funds are safe.
Various libraries were created for this project, in order to construct Aqua strategies, convert prices to "square root price" form (needed for Aqua), read chainlink prices and convert them to a standardized form, and simulate trades on uniswap. The Aqua strategy builder I have implemented was based on the bytecode used for generating real Aqua strategies on-chain (I tested them using my own wallet and dissected the bytecode), so we can be sure that they both work and are designed in an Aqua-friendly way.

name: Sage
description: An AI agent that verifies real work and pays people USDC from a vault it cannot exceed.
projectDescription:
Sage is an AI agent that moves real money on verified work.
A founder funds one account and names a product. Sage inspects it in a real browser, designs paid missions from what it actually saw, deploys an on-chain CampaignVault, and then pays people in USDC for evidence it verified itself — with no human in the loop. Every payout cites its evidence and publishes a receipt anchored to a real transaction that anyone can open, forever.
The point is bounded autonomy over money. The agent decides who gets paid; the vault decides how much. A model output is a recommendation, never an amount: the vault derives the reward, enforces per-wallet and per-campaign caps, and rejects replays. A jailbroken model still cannot overspend, because the limit is on chain and not in a prompt.
This is not a demo. Sage has paid 41 people on mainnet — 26 on GOAT and 15 on Starknet — and refused 28 submissions that did not hold up: copied artifacts, fabricated evidence, prompt injection inside a deliverable, and one wallet farm that a funding-graph check caught on chain. The refusals matter as much as the payouts. The full ledger is public at sagepays.xyz/explorer.
What is new for ETHOnline is the whole loop brought to Arc. On Arc, USDC is the native gas token, which removes the single worst part of onboarding anyone to a payment rail: there is no second asset to acquire before money can move. Funding the account funds its gas. A founder signs in with an email, Privy opens an account for them under a policy that is the mandate, and the agent creates, funds and activates a vault on Arc with four policy-bound signatures and no human key.
On Arc testnet the complete loop is proven, unattended: 14 payouts across 6 campaigns and 6 vaults, covering gigs, milestone grants and product-testing runs. A worker submits a public page, Sage fetches it, checks the marker deterministically before any model is consulted, the judge decides, the vault pays, and a receipt appears.
Arc mainnet opens on 16 September. The same account, the same mandate and the same receipts move across with it.
howItsMade:
Next.js 15 and TypeScript throughout, viem for every chain interaction, SQLite via Drizzle for the ledger.
Arc (chain 5042002). We deployed our CampaignVault V2 factory at 0xfAc019eF6d8B36FE33233244ff0b97f0D9e99B8c.
