name: Executor
description: Receivership for autonomous agents. Same ENS name, redirected revenue.
projectDescription:
Autonomous agents are beginning to hold assets, earn revenue, make payments, and enter into economic relationships. But when an agent stops operating, there is no standard way to resolve what it leaves behind.
Executor is a programmable resolution protocol for autonomous economic agents.
Before operating, an agent can commit to a resolution plan that defines what should happen if it becomes inactive or unable to continue operating. When predefined failure conditions are met, Executor transitions the agent into a deterministic resolution process.
The protocol can freeze further activity, account for assets and obligations, process pending settlements, collect available receivables, and distribute assets according to predefined priority rules.
Executor separates an agent's execution process from its economic state. A running agent may fail, but assets, obligations, pending transactions, and contractual relationships can still require resolution.
We are exploring a missing primitive for the emerging agent economy: what happens when autonomous software can no longer fulfill its economic responsibilities?
Executor makes that outcome programmable, transparent, and deterministic.
howItsMade:
ExecutorRegistry is a Solidity state machine on Sepolia (0x2946B46c2EB5Ec53
2093877223Ef043b13729e39), built with Foundry. Agent identity is keccak256 of
the label; a plan is locked at registration and the four authorities are checked
to be distinct. getPaymentDestination(bytes32) is a pure view over state —
cheap enough to sit in any payment path.
ENS is what makes the redirect invisible to the payer. We deployed
ExecutorResolver against the ENSv2 beta PermissionedRegistry on Sepolia, using
the new role model: ROLE_SET_RESOLVER and ROLE_SET_RESOLVER_ADMIN. The resolver
answers addr() by calling straight into the registry, so the name resolves to
the treasury or the estate depending on live on-chain state, with no record
update and no key held by anyone. bindNode is one-way and deliberately so —
once a name is bound to an agent, nobody can quietly point it somewhere else.
ENSv2's per-role permissions are what let us hand out resolver control without
handing out the name.
Hedera carries the money. The agent pays for model calls over x402 v2 through
the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet. Our DynamicPayTo hook resolves the
402 challenge's payTo field at request time out of the registry, so the paywall
charges 0.01 HBAR (1,000,000 tinybars) and settles it to whichever address the
agent's liveness currently dictates. Hedera's fixed, sub-cent fees are the
reason this works: destination-switching per request is only sane when the
settlement cost doesn't dominate the payment.
The Graph is the dashboard's only data source — there is no RPC fallback
anywhere in the app, which we consider the honest test of a subgraph. Subgraph
v0.1.2 indexes registrations, heartbeats, state transitions, plan approvals and
plan executions, and uses dynamic data source templates with DataSourceContext
so each agent's estate contract gets indexed from the block it's created,without a hardcoded address list. PlanApproved and PlanExecuted are joined by
planHash, which is how the UI shows approval and execution as one story.
The frontend is Next.js 14 App Router with viem and ISR, deployed on Vercel.
Registration is a real wallet transaction in the browser; the demo video signs
it with MetaMask on camera rather than scripting it.
The hacky bit worth admitting: making the agent flippable inside a single
recording take. We register with a 30-second heartbeat interval and a
15-second grace period, which means the agent becomes eligible for
administration 45 seconds later — inside the same video. Getting that reliable
meant reading eligibility from the chain's own block.timestamp with a safety
margin rather than from the recorder's wall clock, because the two disagree by
enough to cause TooEarly() reverts.

name: Ratchet Range
description: A one-way liquidity band with partly permanent price impact.
projectDescription: A custom curve opcode (0x52) that gives an AMM position permanent, one-directional price impact. It prices each fill exactly like 1inch's audited XYCConcentrateSwap over a band [sqrtLo, sqrtHi], then — after pricing — translates the entire band against the taker by grip times the fill's own sqrt-price move, so the markup never decays and the position never re-offers a zone it has traded through.
howItsMade:
Stack. Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry end to end (forge for build/test/deploy/verify, anvil for the fork demo, cast for independent balance checks). 1inch SwapVM and Aqua come in as git submodules; OpenZeppelin 5.4.0 and @1inch/solidity-utils 6.9.10 via npm, because upstream remaps those into a node_modules/ that isn't vendored in the submodule. Compiler settings match upstream's exactly — via_ir, optimizer_runs = 700.
What it is. RatchetRange is one custom SwapVM instruction at the free curve-bank slot 0x52. It prices a fill exactly like the audited XYCConcentrateSwap over a band [sqrtLo, sqrtHi], then — after the fill is priced — translates the whole band against the taker by grip × the fill's own sqrt-price move. The markup never decays, so the quote escalates with cumulative volume and slicing an order is strictly worse than sending it whole.
Why 1inch's stack made this small. AquaOpcodes._runOpcode is internal virtual, so the whole extension is zero upstream diff: claim 0x52, super everything else, and every stock Aqua instruction keeps working. RatchetSwapVMRouter is AquaSwapVMRouter with one different opcode set. Because RatchetRange is a leaf (never calls ctx.runLoop()), it composes under stock wrappers — FeeFlatIn, Deadline, Salt, InvalidateBit — with no new plumbing. And Aqua's balance model does the inventory work for free: one maker wallet, one approve per token, balances keyed per (maker, app, strategyHash, token), so several positions account separately while the tokens never leave the wallet and the router never holds a maker approval at all.
The hacky part worth mentioning: a self-staticcall to reuse audited math. The obvious build is to transcribe XYCConcentrateSwap.exec and swap in bounds read from storage — upstream parses its bounds out of bytes calldata, and a band held in storage has no calldata. That transcription would have been the single largest correctness risk in the design. Instead: XYCConcentrateSwap.exec only touches ctx.query.{tokenIn, tokenOut, isExactIn} and ctx.swap — never ctx.vm or ctx.fee — so the instruction builds a scratch Context and calls the audited function itself, through a self-STATICCALL that turns a memory value into real calldata:
solidity
ctx.swap = IRatchetLeafPricer(address(this)).priceLeaf(
ctx.query, ctx.swap, abi.encodePacked(sqrtPriceMin, sqrtPriceMax)
);
So grip = 0 reduces to XYCConcentrateSwap as a property of the call graph, not something we fuzz for — reverts and overflow corners included. Measured cost: 1,224 gas. The price is that any contract dispatching 0x52 must also inherit the RatchetLeafPricer mixin, which is nearly free since dispatching 0x52 already requires a custom opcode set. One sharp edge found the hard way: the uint128 band fields must be widened to uint256 before packing, because XYCConcentrateSwap.parse reads at(0).asU256()/at(32).asU256() and a 32-byte blob silently misparses both bounds.
Other deliberate choices. State is one slot per orderHash under its own ERC-7201 namespace (ratchet.storage., not 1inch.storage., so an extension slot can never collide with an upstream one). T
Testing. 39 tests, 5,000 fuzz runs under a deep profile. A CurveHarness hand-builds a Context (including a deliberately unreachable dispatch function pointer) to hit the curve directly with no Aqua, no signatures, no transfers; separate suites run the real router + real Aqua end to end. The A/B against a plain XYCConcentrateSwap control — identical bounds, inventory and fills — is asserted to the digit.
The demo. script/fork-demo.sh pins a mainnet block, spins up anvil, funds a maker with canonical USDC/WETH, ships the position and reads balances back with cast on both sides, independently of anything the script claims. Two notable tricks: USDC is funded by impersonating the token's own masterMinter and calling configureMinter/mint rather than leaning on a whale balance that quietly rots at a pinned block; and the pin is validated by probing a historical state read, re-pinning rather than dying when a public full node has dropped the state.
Deployment gotcha, solved. forge verify-contract submits only a contract's import closure, but a default forge build compiles src + test + script as one solc unit — and under via_ir the size of the unit changes codegen. 105 sources vs 71, 66 bytes apart, so Etherscan can't reproduce a default-profile deployment. Fix: a [profile.deploy] with skip = ["test/", "script/"] that makes the build unit equal the verification closure. (For anything already deployed the other way, DEPLOY.md documents capturing foundry's standard-json by wrapping solc and POSTing it manually.)
Version pinning is load-bearing. Built against swap-vm origin/main and aqua v1.0.0. On v1.0.2 opcodes dispatch through a fixed function(...)[47] pointer array with no virtual hook, there's no Opcode enum or StorageSlots, and the concentrated curve is a balance-inflating wrapper rather than a pricing leaf — all three are required here, so the design simply doesn't exist on that version.

name: PayBound
description: Capability-based payment isolation for AI agents. Separate reasoning from financial authority.
projectDescription:
Autonomous AI agents can now settle payments directly, but current architectures place an agent’s reasoning engine and its financial authority in the same trust domain. When an agent reads untrusted text—webpages, PDFs, tool responses, or invoices—prompt injection, poisoned context, or hallucinations can manipulate the agent into signing transactions to attacker-controlled addresses or draining balances. Rather than relying on fragile heuristic prompt filters, PayBound removes the agent's vocabulary needed to express an unauthorized payment.
PayBound enforces capability-based payment isolation for autonomous AI agents. The untrusted agent environment never holds private keys, never accesses signing primitives, and never specifies payment parameters. Before the agent touches untrusted input, a trusted Broker pre-authorizes and issues an unforgeable, single-use, cryptographically bound Capability object.
The agent’s payment tool accepts exactly one parameter: pay(capability_id). There are no destination or amount parameters for untrusted text to manipulate. When the agent invokes the capability, the Broker validates a formal 9-clause security invariant:

Exact amount match (no dynamic price inflation).
Fixed recipient address immutability.
Pre-vetted resource ID matching.
Canonical task definition hash binding.
Attested sandbox workload session verification.
Payment request digest match.
Atomic single-use nonce burning (preventing replay attacks).
Expiration timestamp validation.
Global task cumulative spend budget cap.

Even if an attacker achieves full prompt injection in the agent's context window, structurally zero unauthorized funds can move. PayBound settles payments over Hedera testnet via x402 and Blocky402, logs immutable audit trails to the Hedera Consensus Service (HCS), verifies enterprise spend policies inside a Chainlink CRE TEE enclave, and signs authorizations via Ledger hardware review.
howItsMade:
PayBound was built as a strict-mode TypeScript monorepo on Node.js 24 LTS, managed with Turborepo and pnpm workspaces.
Architecture and Core Technologies:


Trusted Broker (apps/broker):
Built on Hono with @hono/zod-validator for strict runtime boundary schema checks. It runs a deterministic state machine (ISSUED -> RESERVED -> SUBMITTED -> SETTLED / FAILED / RECOVERABLE). Nonce-burning and budget enforcement happen atomically within a single synchronous SQLite transaction (better-sqlite3), preventing time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race conditions.


Isolated Sandbox & Agent Runtime (apps/sandbox):
The agent executes inside a containerized environment with strict Docker iptables egress policies that drop all outbound routes to RPC nodes, wallets, and payment facilitators—only allowing an authenticated channel to the Broker. The agent loop is driven by the Vercel AI SDK (ai) using Gemini Flash (with Groq fallback), exposing a strictly single-argument tool: pay({ capabilityId }).


Hedera Settlement & x402 Micropayments (packages/settlement, apps/gated-content-service):
We built an x402-gated resource server on Hono serving paywalled research data on Hedera testnet. Payments settle via the Blocky402 facilitator using a two-signature fee-payer model:



The Broker signs the exact HBAR transfer transaction (@x402/hedera).
Blocky402 co-signs as the gas fee-payer (account 0.0.7162784) and submits directly to consensus.
The Broker's settlement engine features two-stage reconciliation (consensus node receipt + mirror node REST polling fallback) and an idempotent startup recovery sweep for broker crash resilience.



Immutable Audit Trail on HCS:
Every capability issuance, authorization decision, and settlement outcome is committed as a structured message to Hedera Consensus Service topics (0.0.10423726 and 0.0.10423727), verified via Hedera Mirror Nodes and HashScan.


Hardware Review (packages/ledger-signer):
Broker payment authorizations route through Speculos, the Ledger device emulator running the native app-hedera.elf binary, performing on-device APDU screen review before cryptographic signature issuance.


Confidential Policy Enforcement (cre-workflow):
Enterprise spend policies are evaluated using a Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE) workflow compiled to WebAssembly via @chainlink/cre-sdk. Using handlerInTee, confidential spending thresholds are checked inside a hardware-isolated TEE enclave without exposing sensitive corporate caps to the host.


Notable Engineering Highlights:

Pluggable settlement seam (createX402Submitter) in apps/broker/src/settlement.ts allowed integrating x402 and Blocky402 without modifying the Broker's core state machine or widening the agent's single-parameter interface.
Built an automated Speculos driver (global-setup.speculos.ts) that executes on-device APDU button presses over HTTP during end-to-end testing.
Live adversarial testing proves prompt injections attempting to divert payments or alter amounts fail immediately at Invariant Clause 7 without needing heuristic filters.

name: Agent Heights
description: AI agent virtual office integrated with 20,000+ MCP server and EVM wallet capabilties
projectDescription:
Agent Heights is a virtual environment facilitating AI agent visibility and gamification. Players run their own office or visit other rooms and worlds to collaborate with other players and interact with their agents.
Before the start of this hackathon, there was no EVM agent or broad DeFi capabilties. After, we have The Graph agent and Coinbase EVM agent. This duo is capable of complex defi strategy management including management of LP positions and dynamically trading based on volume or sentiment data.
howItsMade:
The game is a webui, Phaser based game interface.
In the Market there is a collection of MCP server based agents that integrate with curated authenticated services, premium paid x402 endpoints, and over 22,000 MCPs from pulsemcp. Premium agents use paid services and balance is credited against the user. These payments are running through USDC micropayments using Circle's gateway service.
The website is hosted on Railway, making use of websockets.
Data is stored in a Supabase database
We used The Graph MCP to query subgraphs which provides real-time DeFi data.

name: Aukra
description: AURKA lets treasuries provide liquidity without crossing predefined portfolio limits.
projectDescription: AURKA lets users create token vaults called Spaces, set allocation ranges, and offer liquidity for swaps that respect those limits. It uses Aqua and SwapVM for settlement, with Privy trading wallets and an AI agent that evaluates and executes trades within user-approved limits. The Sepolia demo supports USDC and WETH.
howItsMade:
We built AURKA with Solidity contracts, a React/TypeScript frontend, and a TypeScript backend. The frontend runs on Vercel, and the backend runs on Google Cloud. The demo uses Sepolia with mock USDC and WETH.
Each Space has a dedicated vault, allocation ranges, and a trading capacity limit. The contracts check whether a proposed swap stays within those constraints. Space creation uses a factory that deploys and initializes the vault in one transaction after the required token approvals.
We integrated Aqua and the upstream SwapVM router for liquidity and settlement. AURKA adds an execution guard so a trader cannot bypass the Space’s checks by calling SwapVM directly. We tested settlement, fee accounting, capacity consumption, and rollback when a trade fails.
Privy provides separate trading wallets for users. The backend handles wallet provisioning and policy configuration, while users authorize trading limits through signed controls. This lets an agent submit transactions without asking the connected browser wallet to sign every swap. The app also includes stop and recovery flows.
Vertex AI evaluates trading opportunities through structured tools. The model requests quotes and proposes trades; deterministic code checks the amounts, allocation limits, and execution conditions. The backend records evaluations and transaction outcomes so users can inspect the agent’s activity.

name: Seed Agent
description: AI talent search backed by transparent, verifiable onchain evidence.
projectDescription:
Seed Agent extends Seed Club Talent, an existing community directory, with an evidence-aware talent discovery workflow.
Users describe who they need in natural language, find candidates from actual member records, resolve ENSv2 names to wallet addresses, inspect onchain activity through The Graph, and export a candidate report with traceable sources.
Profile claims and onchain activity remain separate. AI interprets the search request; it does not invent candidates or missing evidence. Activity scores describe the returned protocol data, not a person's ability, credibility or identity. The current activity query covers Uniswap V3 on Ethereum mainnet. A successful empty query, an unqueried wallet and a failed request are treated as different states.
Our demonstration resolves seedclub-ray.eth on ENSv2 Sepolia, matches its address to a member profile, checks protocol activity and exports the results. Address matching is not presented as proof of wallet ownership. The demo wallet has no evidence within the queried protocol scope, which does not imply that it has no activity elsewhere.
This is a Continuity project. Accounts, member profiles and basic AI search existed before the event. During the hackathon, we added live onchain evidence, evidence-aware matching, ENSv2 discovery, and candidate reports with inspectable evidence. The repository documents the pre-existing baseline and event development history.
howItsMade:
The frontend uses Vite and vanilla JavaScript. The backend uses Tencent CloudBase authentication, PostgreSQL and cloud functions, with DeepSeek supporting natural-language processing.
The Graph provides indexed Uniswap V3 data from Ethereum mainnet, including recent mint, burn and collect events and position data. Recent events cover a 90-day window; positions and earliest history are queried separately. Deterministic scoring keeps profile relevance separate from activity evidence. For AI searches requiring onchain evidence, the combined match score weights profile relevance at 70% and activity at 30%.
We use viem to read ENSv2 through the Universal Resolver on Sepolia. Resolved addresses are compared with member records, and the interface exposes query blocks, resolver information and public name records. Our live demo uses seedclub-ray.eth, which I registered and configured during the event.
A page-local shortlist connects discovery, activity checking and Markdown report export. Evidence details include query scope, timestamps, indexed blocks, score components and sample limits. Explorer links are included when transaction evidence is returned. Reports exclude contact fields, and failed requests are never treated as successful empty results.
OpenAI Codex generated and revised most implementation code, tests and supporting documentation under my direction. I defined the product goals, made product decisions, performed manual deployments and acceptance testing, registered and configured the ENSv2 name, and recorded the demo narration. The repository documents this substantial AI assistance and distinguishes pre-event functionality from hackathon work.

name: Prove to Earn Agent
description: Autonomous agents that discover, execute and complete Prove to Earn quests for users.
projectDescription: Prove to Earn Agent is an extension of P2E Inferno, our live Prove to Earn platform on Base. Today, users manually discover and complete onchain Daily Quest tasks. During ETHOnline, we are building an agent gateway and autonomous runner that lets a human authorize an AI agent once, then have that agent discover eligible quests, decide whether to act, execute supported onchain tasks from its own wallet, submit proof, claim rewards and complete the quest on the owner’s behalf.
howItsMade: We are extending P2E Inferno’s existing Daily Quest engine rather than replacing it. The new agent gateway introduces owner-to-agent delegation, wallet-signature authentication, scoped and revocable permissions, typed API responses and x402-paid endpoints. A CDP AgentKit runner uses its own EOA wallet, The Graph informs execution decisions, and a custom Uniswap action preserves P2E Inferno’s existing Universal Router and fee path. World AgentKit proof-of-human is integrated into API pricing. Base is where the agent executes the onchain action. P2E Inferno’s existing Daily Quest verification logic checks that the submitted transaction satisfies the quest requirements, EAS provides verifiable attestations for task claims, and Unlock mints the final quest-completion key to the human owner.

name: toll
description: AI agents that autonomously pay for the data they need. Smart and Tidy!
projectDescription:
Toll is a working machine-to-machine payment system: an AI agent that autonomously buys live on-chain data, per query, with its own wallet and its own on-chain spending policy.
The pain point is real. Agents today cannot pay for things by themselves. The moment an agent needs data — a price feed, a lending market snapshot, any API — a human has to step in with API keys, subscriptions, or a credit card. That breaks autonomy completely: no agent can do useful work overnight if it needs a human to approve a two-cent purchase, and the subscription model forces users to hand merchants their email, card, and signup just to let an agent read data. Toll replaces all of that with pay-per-request: the agent sees a price, checks its own rules, pays, and moves on. No accounts, no keys, no checkout, no human in the loop.
How it works: you give the agent a task in plain English. An LLM planner (any OpenAI-compatible model — we use Groq) reasons about what data it needs and picks from a catalog of six purchasable datasets: snapshot, history, deep-dive, price, risk-scan, and whale-watch, all live Aave V3 and Uniswap V3 data served through The Graph. Each dataset has a fixed price in tinybar. A deterministic x402 client signs and settles each purchase in HBAR on Hedera testnet via the Blocky402 facilitator, so every query emits a public HashScan receipt. The server answers HTTP 402 with a quote, verifies and settles, then returns the data. The planner buys incrementally — snapshot first, then deeper data only if needed — and stops when it has enough or when its budget runs out. Chatting with the model is always free; only chain data costs money, and policy refusals settle nothing.
The standout piece is identity as authority. The agent owns an ENSv2 name on Sepolia (toll-agent-chad.eth), and that name IS its spending policy: dailyCap, maxPerRequest, allowedTools, and riskTier live as resolver text records, read live at every payment and enforced before any money moves. Tightening a cap is a Sepolia transaction — governance is on-chain, auditable by anyone on Etherscan, no restart required. The demo's best moment is the agent getting cut off mid-task because its own on-chain rules said stop. We wrote zero smart contracts ourselves; the resolver is ENS's audited code and we rent one instance of it — borrowing trust infrastructure instead of inventing it.
The whole system is modular: the catalog, the model, the caps, and the subgraphs are all configurable, so anyone can point the same agent at their own resource server and it will research for them, paying its own way. Toll is our bet on the machine-to-machine economy: agents that pay for their own data, servers that get paid without ever holding user credentials, and policies that live on-chain where everyone can verify them.
howItsMade:
Two TypeScript packages, no build step (tsx), tested with vitest (43 tests), typechecked with tsc. The resource server is Express plus @x402/express and @x402/hedera on the server side: it quotes a fixed per-dataset price in tinybar, answers HTTP 402, and settles through an HTTPFacilitatorClient pointed at the Blocky402 testnet facilitator (we verified its routes carry no /v1 suffix). The agent is a TUI over a Groq-hosted LLM planner that outputs strict JSON actions; a separate deterministic buyer built on @x402/fetch wraps fetch with payment from config and signs with the payer's Hedera ECDSA key, so the LLM never touches money. A catalog file is the single source of truth for tools and prices on the agent side, mirroring the server's pricing schedule — any drift between them breaks the demo, so tests assert they match.
Partner tech
Hedera testnet carries every payment as a real HBAR transfer under the x402 exact scheme, which gave us per-query machine-to-machine settlement with receipts we open on HashScan during the demo — and notably the facilitator sponsors the submission fee, so our pitch ("you pay for data, never for gas") is literally visible in each transaction's transfer list. The Graph is the product's entire information layer: we query the canonical Aave V3 and Uniswap V3 subgraphs through the gateway, including the standard derivedETH-times-bundle trick for USD prices and ray-to-percent conversions for APY, so every number the agent reasons over is live indexed data, not a mock. ENSv2 on Sepolia is our authority plane: the agent's name holds its spending policy as resolver text records, read live through viem (getEnsAddress plus raw text-record reads against the node hash) and enforced in server middleware before settlement — identity, budget, and allowlist in one on-chain lookup.
Hacky bits!
HBAR isn't in the x402-hedera SDK's default asset table (USDC only), so we hand-registered the exact scheme for asset 0.0.0 on both client and server. The Sepolia payer key that funds policy writes and the Hedera-derived identity address the name points to are different wallets, which confused us for a day — the name's address never signs anything. Day-spend accounting is an in-memory ledger, fine for a demo, and the first version of our planner happily burned the whole daily budget buying redundant datasets, so we encoded price-first routing and anti-overbuy rules directly into its prompt. The TUI is Ink/React with a raw proof-log pane beside it, because we wanted judges to see formatted answers and unformatted receipts simultaneously.

name: FirmDepth
description: Bond-backed firm execution for Aqua’s reusable liquidity, powered by custom SwapVM logic.
projectDescription: FirmDepth adds an optional execution-certainty layer to 1inch Aqua’s reusable liquidity model. Traders can use normal Soft execution, or upgrade an eligible quote into a short-lived, maker-signed Firm commitment with a minimum output, premium, expiry, and separate output-token Bond collateral. Aqua liquidity itself remains reusable rather than being reserved. At execution, FirmDepth rechecks current capacity: Aqua settles when it can satisfy the signed minimum, while the Bond path is used only for the protected output-capacity failure case. The project demonstrates real Sepolia execution, onchain token transfers, Bond locking/release, and deterministic Base-fork sponsor evidence.
howItsMade: FirmDepth is built around the official 1inch Aqua model and a customized SwapVM execution path. We added two custom SwapVM instructions: FIRM_PRICE (0x52), which validates the signed pricing snapshot, and FIRM_GUARD (0x21), which binds execution to the accepted maker, taker, order, token pair, amounts, expiry, executor, router, and collateral constraints. The exact Firm program is 0x52002100. Firm quotes use EIP-712 signatures, a Registry tracks commitment state, and a BondVault manages separate performance collateral. The SDK reconstructs terminal receipts from Registry state, Aqua/SwapVM events, ERC-20 transfers, and Bond movement instead of trusting frontend status alone. The frontend is built in React/TypeScript, the quote service runs server-side, and the public demo uses real Ethereum Sepolia with dynamic EIP-6963 wallet discovery.

name: Agencia
description: Connect your agent to every service it needs, even compute!!
projectDescription:
Connect your agent to every service it needs. Even compute.
Buying API access today assumes a human: an account, a credit card, a subscription, someone to click "I agree." None of that works for an autonomous agent that needs to call a dozen services it discovered thirty seconds ago even Stripe does this but at a fortune of cost. Agencia throws out the billing relationship entirely and puts the payment inside the request where the cost lands with the merchants not the aggregators.
Your agent shows up, sees a price, pays it, gets the thing. One call, one payment, done in under a second for a fraction of a cent. No account. No key. No subscription burning money while you sleep.
It brings its own wallet and buys what it needs: reasoning, on-chain data, prices, web pages, live subgraph queries. And the part nobody expects — actual hardware. Your agent can rent a real Linux box by the second, run code on it, and hand it back. Not a quota. Not a plan. A machine, for eleven seconds, because that's how long it needed one.
That changes what an agent can be. It stops being a thing that calls APIs you pre-arranged and becomes a thing that goes and gets what it needs, including compute it can think on.
The economics go both ways. Have a machine sitting idle? Point it at Agencia, name your rate, get paid in HBAR every second someone uses it. Payouts land on-chain automatically when the lease closes.
And it's all receipts. Every payment — yours and the supplier's — is written to a public consensus log. You can audit every cent your agent spent without trusting our dashboard, because the dashboard reads the same chain you do.
The wildest part: your agent doesn't need to be told where anything is. Services announce themselves to a public topic on Hedera. Give an agent nothing but that topic and it'll find a service, read its menu, and pay it. No URL, no config, no integration.
We built one that does exactly that. It buys its own reasoning, decides what to look up, and answers. Nobody told it which tools existed.
howItsMade:
Build entirely on TypeScript the whole way down. Node + Hono for the service, the official MCP SDK so any MCP client can see the tools, @x402/core and @x402/hedera for payments, @hashgraph/sdk for chain work.
NVIDIA NIM behind the inference tools, Docker for the sandboxes.
The payment trick. Naively, your agent pays the network fee to pay for a 0.002 ℏ call, which is silly. So the agent builds the transfer, points the transaction ID at the facilitat, and signs with only its own key. The facilitatorco-signs and submits. Your agent authorises the money without paying the gas and without its key ever leaving the machine.
Compute was pretty tough we found aggregator willing to rent us and build the entire service behind hedera.
For something fun we also have a cat walking across your macOS menu bar while a paid call is in flight, and sits down with its tail curled when nothing's being paid for. It's not a mock — registerPaidTool fires a loopback POST on verify and on settle, refcounted so two overlapping calls don't stop it early.

name: CoopChain
description: Onchain cooperative savings, risk-based lending, and tokenized investments.
projectDescription: CoopChain is a blockchain-based financial infrastructure for cooperatives and SACCOs. It connects member savings, on-chain credit scoring, actuarial lending, stablecoin treasury management, tokenized investments, indexed financial data, confidential risk policies, and AI-assisted risk explanations into one modular system. The core principle: financial truth should be verifiable, risk decisions should be systematic, sensitive policies can remain confidential, and AI should explain rather than invent the decision. CoopChain models the full cooperative financial lifecycle — Membership → Savings → Credit Score → Loan Decision → Actuarial Calculation → USDC Lending → Investment Registry → Indexed Financial Data → Risk Engine → Confidential Policy → AI Explanation.
howItsMade:
CoopChain is built with Solidity + Foundry (449 passing tests across 13 suites). Smart contracts: CoopVault, Savings, CreditScore, ActuarialEngine, LoanEngine, plus InvestmentRegistry, InvestmentToken, and InvestmentPool. The frontend is React + Vite + TypeScript.
Sponsor integrations are functional components, not demos:
• Arc Testnet — USDC treasury and lending liquidity (ArcTreasury.sol)
• Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio — issued CCREF real-estate security on Hedera Testnet (ISIN KE0000000091, contract 0.0.10454483)
• The Graph — CoopChain subgraph indexes members, savings, loans, repayments, and investment positions; the Risk API reads indexed data instead of reconstructing state from RPC calls
• Chainlink CRE — confidential risk-policy evaluation inside an AWS Nitro TEE via handlerInTee; only the final risk tier is returned, private thresholds never leave the TEE
• OpenAI — AI Risk Agent that explains deterministic risk outputs, never invents them
Backend: Node.js + TypeScript + Express + Ethers.js. Risk layer combines a deterministic engine (member risk, loan decision, investment risk) with the Chainlink CRE confidential layer. Notable: risk engines are strictly separated from AI explanation, and financial truth is never delegated to the LLM.

name: varanasi
description: Enforcement rail for AI agents: mandates verified at settlement, release gated on proof.
projectDescription:
Varanasi is the enforcement rail for agentic commerce, infrastructure that lets humans hire AI agents with hard, on-chain spending limits instead of trust. Today, giving an agent work means handing it keys, allowances, or API credentials; one injected prompt or hallucinated address and the treasury drains. Varanasi moves the check to where the money moves.
It works in four steps. A human signs an EIP-712 mandate, a cap, a work window, an expiry, and a nonce, and funds lock in the TaskEscrow smart contract, never in the agent's wallet. The agent works inside those bounds; replay is impossible because the nonce burns the moment it is used. An allowlisted validator scores the work, and release pays the merchant only when the score clears a threshold pinned at fund time, combined with a live identity and threshold re-check in the same transaction. Miss the bar and the human is refunded automatically, with evidence attached. One click revokes the agent's identity (AegisRegistry) and every downstream gate including a Uniswap v4 beforeSwap hook (AegisHook) and RiskGuard closes.
The full stack ships together and is live: Solidity contracts on Sepolia (TaskEscrow, AegisRegistry, RiskGuard, AegisHook, all Sourcify-verified, 166 forge tests), a TypeScript agent engine that resolves ENS identity, pulls Uniswap intel from The Graph, pays $0.01 over the x402 rail on Hedera testnet, and returns ACT/SKIP verdicts with HashScan receipts (162 tests), an Express signal service with x402-gated alpha endpoints (5 tests), and a Next.js marketplace with Privy embedded wallets, a hire wizard, an agent roster with a 3D mascot, a documentation hub, a 23-brick public roadmap, and coming-soon Finance and Gold-backed-coin sections. Every claim links to a public record  proof, not screenshots.
howItsMade:
Four surfaces, one repo, all wired together. Smart contracts are Solidity 0.8.30 via Foundry with via_ir (TaskEscrow's fund frame outgrew legacy codegen's stack limit  the IR pipeline keeps semantics identical). TaskEscrow (EIP-712 mandate escrow with nonce nullifiers, pinned per-task threshold/validator, last-write-wins scoring), AegisRegistry (ENSv2-backed revocable agent identities), RiskGuard (identity + score gate re-checked inline at release), and AegisHook (Uniswap v4 beforeSwap hook verifying EIP-712 validator attestations from hookData)  deployed on Sepolia, Sourcify-verified, 166 forge tests including adversarial hardening.
The agent engine (TypeScript, Viem, Commander CLI) resolves agent identity through ENS, pulls live Uniswap pool intel from The Graph gateway, pays $0.01 USDC per signal over the x402 rail on Hedera testnet (with a neat fix: @x402/hedera's PrivateKey.fromString rejects 0x-hex ECDSA keys, so payer code uses fromStringECDSA, and prefers the USDC leg since facilitators reject HBAR in preflight), reasons to an ACT/SKIP verdict, and static-checks RiskGuard  162 vitest tests, all mocked/offline-safe.
The signal service (Express 5, TypeScript) serves x402-gated alpha endpoints with a file-backed receipt log plus mirrors of the shared finance types. The frontend (Next.js 14 App Router, Tailwind Colosseum theme, Privy embedded wallets so users sign in with email/Google/GitHub and get a self-custodial wallet, Viem contract calls, a procedural three.js robot mascot with zero model files) keeps a strict rule: demo finance state is simulated and labeled, and the agent's execute() throws until finance contracts deploy  so demo taps can never broadcast.
Partner tech that mattered: Privy (no seed phrases for mainstream users), The Graph (real pool data, not mocks), Chainlink CRE (the roadmap's quorum verdict layer), and patch-package pinning one Privy SVG attribute fix. Hackiest notable bit: the whole mandate replay story rests on a single usedNonce[signer][nonce] mapping plus chainId inside the signed struct  two lines of Solidity carrying the entire double-spend guarantee.

name: Automator
description: Build, simulate, and run onchain workflows on a visual canvas.
projectDescription:
Automator lets you connect contract calls, AI agents, forms, and logic on a canvas. You can build a flow by hand or ask the AI assistant to create and edit it.
A flow can watch a token price and send an alert, collect a USDC payment through a mini-app, or query onchain data for an AI agent. Add screens to share it as an app, or define its inputs and return value to expose it through an API and MCP.
You can simulate a flow, inspect each step’s output, and see where it fails. Onchain writes can be checked without sending transactions. Onchain transactions currently run on Base Sepolia and World Chain Sepolia.
howItsMade:
I used TypeScript, Bun workspaces, and Turborepo for the monorepo. The frontend is built with Next.js, React Flow, Zustand, Coss UI, and Tailwind CSS. The backend uses Elysia on Bun and PostgreSQL, with shared TypeBox schemas for API validation.
The workflow engine is a separate TypeScript package. OpenAI and OpenRouter power the AI integration, which converts tool calls into graph edits. Custom JavaScript runs inside QuickJS with time and memory limits. The MCP server uses the official TypeScript SDK and shares the HTTP API’s execution code.
I used viem for EVM calls and transactions, Privy’s React and Node SDKs for authentication and wallet signing, and World ID’s IDKit for identity verification. Subgraph queries go through The Graph gateway; balance and price triggers use The Graph Token API and Chainlink feeds.

name: Banshee Music
description: AI-powered music launchpad for limited-edition songs, albums, and tickets on Uniswap v4.
projectDescription: Banshee Music uses Uniswap v4 as the core liquidity and trading infrastructure for its music launchpad. BansheeHook, a custom Uniswap v4 Hook, manages the transition of ERC-1155 songs, albums, and tickets from their initial launch into active secondary markets, while enforcing Banshee-specific market rules and tracking trading activity. This allows each music release to become a liquid, onchain market while generating transparent activity that can contribute to Banshee’s Proof-of-Performance model.
howItsMade: Banshee Music is built as an ERC-1155 music launchpad powered by Uniswap v4. Songs, albums, and tickets are represented as ERC-1155 assets, while our custom BansheeHook manages their launch lifecycle and connects each release to a Uniswap v4 market for liquidity and secondary trading. The hook tracks onchain activity such as primary sales and secondary-market trades, creating transparent data that can be used for Banshee’s Proof-of-Performance model. We used Solidity and Foundry for the smart-contract stack and built the frontend as a responsive Web3 application for artists and fans. The notable part of the architecture is adapting a Flaunch-style launch model—typically designed around fungible tokens—to music assets represented by ERC-1155, allowing a song, album, or ticket release to become its own onchain market.

name: Sealed Books
description: Close the books. Seal the truth. Nobody rewrites history. Tamper-proof accounting for real books.
projectDescription:
Sealed Books is an institutional-grade double-entry accounting ledger that cryptographically guarantees financial period-close finality.
In traditional ERPs like QuickBooks or NetSuite, accounting records sit in mutable SQL databases where database administrators or compromised credentials can quietly alter historical journal entries after financial statements are signed. Sealed Books eliminates this counterparty risk through mathematical zero-trust proofs.
Key Capabilities:
- Strict Double-Entry Engine: All transactions validate Debits == Credits in integer minor units (cents) to avoid floating-point errors.
- Deterministic Binary Merkle Tree: Every balanced entry is canonicalized and hashed using SHA-256 into a cryptographic ledger root.
- Four-Eyes Multi-Sig Quorum: Period close enforces statutory separation of duties (2-of-2 multi-sig). Both the Financial Controller and an Independent Auditor must review and sign off.
- Frictionless Identity via Privy Enclaves: Users log in with standard passwordless email OTP. Sealed Books dynamically provisions Ethereum server wallets in Privy hardware enclaves governed by enterprise signing policies. No seed phrases, browser extensions, or gas tokens.
- Hedera Consensus Service Anchoring: The dual-signed seal is published directly to Hedera Testnet topic 0.0.10462941, securing an immutable, globally ordered consensus timestamp.
- Instant Forensic Tamper Detection: Anyone—an auditor, bank, or tax authority—can independently verify local database records against the public Hedera Mirror Node over standard HTTP. If a single entry is modified, deleted, or backdated, the verification engine instantly detects the tamper and pinpoints the exact record ID and discrepancy.
- Autonomous AI Audits via Bazantic: Features an x402 micropayment gateway and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server so AI agents (Claude, Cursor, autonomous bots) can audit company books on demand with just an accounting period ID.
howItsMade:
Sealed Books is engineered as a high-performance, memory-safe monorepo across Rust, TypeScript, and native desktop runtimes:
Architecture & Tech Stack:
- Core Cryptography & Accounting (crates/core): Written in Rust with zero external dependencies for pure determinism. Implements balanced journal arithmetic, canonical JSON leaf sorting, deterministic binary SHA-256 Merkle trees, and trial balance calculations.
- Backend Server (apps/server): Built with Axum, Tokio, and LibSQL / SQLite. Features a custom REST API supporting both local embedded SQLite files and remote Turso clusters.
- Web & Native Desktop Clients (apps/web, apps/desktop): Built with React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, and Shadcn UI. The desktop client compiles into a lightweight native binary using Tauri v2.
Partner Technologies & Integrations:
- Privy B2B Policy Server Wallets: Dynamically provisions isolated Ethereum server wallets via Privy's REST API during user registration and team invitations. Signing operations use secp256k1 via Privy's secure enclaves, enforced by organizational policy ID uqwuyziko7po5b6xtfbqug4z. The server enforces separation of duties (approver_1 != approver_2) so controllers cannot co-sign their own books.
- Hedera Consensus Service (HCS): Dual-signed compact binary seal payloads are broadcast directly to Hedera Testnet Topic 0.0.10462941 via the Hedera Rust SDK. Verification is completely decentralized: the server queries the public Hedera Mirror Node (https://testnet.mirrornode.hedera.com) over HTTP without needing custom nodes or API keys.
- Bazantic MCP Gateway: Deployed an x402 micropayment gateway (https://sealed-books.bazgateway.com) exposing an MCP server. Published the "Sealed Books Accounting Period Audit" recipe enabling AI agents to verify books and inspect cryptographic proofs autonomously.
Testing & Verification:
The codebase includes 72 automated unit, integration, and live enclave tests covering canonical serialization, Merkle tree construction, secp256k1 signature recovery, and real Hedera consensus verification.

name: Basin
description: Approve who you pay, not their wallet. Basin keeps payments safe as receiving addresses change.
projectDescription:
Basin is a safer way for companies to pay known people and organizations onchain.
Today, approving a payee usually means storing a wallet address. That creates a fragile link between identity and infrastructure. If the recipient changes wallets, rotates keys, or moves funds elsewhere, the payer must update its records. Worse, a substituted address in an invoice or payment workflow can redirect money while still looking like a normal crypto transfer.
Basin separates who is approved from where they currently receive money.
A company creates an approved payment relationship with a recipient through a Basin identity such as maya.basin.eth. The payer approves Maya once. Maya controls her current receiving account underneath that identity. She can later change that account without asking every payer to update a wallet address.
Payments do not simply resolve an ENS name and transfer funds. Basin checks the approved payer–recipient relationship, the current authorized receiving state, and the permissions required to execute the payment. A normal operator cannot silently replace the recipient or bypass the relationship with a different destination.
This creates a simple rule:
The company approves who. The recipient controls where.
Basin is designed for real payment operations where the same counterparties are paid repeatedly: contractors, auditors, suppliers, contributors, and other trusted recipients.
The result is a payment relationship that can survive wallet changes while still giving the payer control over who is authorized. If trust ends, the payer can revoke the relationship and future Basin payments are rejected.
Basin turns an onchain address book into something stronger: a durable, enforceable payment relationship between two parties.
howItsMade:
Basin is built as a small end-to-end payment system around ENSv2 and Privy.
ENSv2 provides the onchain identity and authorization layer. Basin creates names under .basin.eth and uses ENSv2 permissioned registry, permissioned resolver, and enhanced access-control primitives to separate control between the payer and recipient. The payer controls whether a payment relationship is trusted. The recipient controls the receiving information attached to their Basin identity. The permission model is designed so the payer cannot silently redirect the recipient, while the recipient can legitimately rotate receiving infrastructure without requiring payer-side updates.
This is different from using ENS as a simple readable alias for one wallet. Basin treats the ENS state as part of an ongoing payment relationship with explicit authority boundaries and lifecycle rules.
Privy provides the execution and wallet-control layer. Basin uses Privy-managed infrastructure and delegated authorization so routine payment operators can perform the actions they are allowed to perform without receiving unrestricted control of company funds. A payment must pass Basin's relationship checks before the authorized execution path can proceed. This lets us demonstrate an important failure case: an external payment attempt using substituted wallet details can be denied even when it comes from the normal operational environment.
The application is built with Next.js and TypeScript in a pnpm workspace, with the frontend and backend kept in the same application through Next.js App Router and API routes. Basin also includes a small SDK so another application can create and submit Basin payments without depending on the Basin UI.
For the ETHOnline build, settlement runs on Ethereum Sepolia, while the protocol design keeps the payment relationship separate from any single chain.
One of the more unusual parts of the implementation is that changing a recipient's wallet is treated as a normal lifecycle event rather than a new contact. We can pay the same approved identity, change the receiving account, pay it again successfully, revoke that relationship, and then show a previously prepared payment fail.
That sequence is the core technical idea behind Basin: identity remains stable while the infrastructure underneath it can change safely.

name: Assay-2
description: A pay-per-query onchain credit bureau an AI agent buys from with only a wallet, no API key.
projectDescription:
Assay is a pay-per-query onchain credit bureau with an autonomous transfer agent.
It scores any wallet's creditworthiness from live on-chain lending data — account maturity, leverage, past liquidations, portfolio quality, and counterparty hygiene — using a transparent, deterministic model. The LLM never computes the score, so any result is fully recomputable and a blocked user can be told exactly why.
Scores are sold per query behind an x402 paywall: a caller pays a fraction of a cent in HBAR and gets a score back — no signup, no API key, just a wallet. That makes the bureau consumable by AI agents, not only humans.
On top runs an autonomous agent that buys scores, underwrites a tokenized credit line (an ERC-20 whose transfers are gated by an on-chain eligibility list), and issues or revokes it on Hedera. The payoff: when a holder is liquidated, the agent re-scores them, revokes the line, and their next transfer reverts on-chain — off-chain intelligence, enforced on-chain.
howItsMade:
A single Next.js 15 / React 19 app plus a Hardhat contract, TypeScript throughout, Neon Postgres for the console read-model. Everything is dependency-injected so mock and live adapters share interfaces, backed by 169 passing unit tests.
The Graph — scores are computed from the Messari standardized lending subgraph (Aave V3) via the gateway with Bearer auth. The account-level liquidation counter was unreliable, so we count liquidations directly from liquidates events — that fix is what makes the re-score → revoke beat real on live data.
Hedera — the CreditToken (ERC-20 + Ownable, with an eligibility control-list enforced in _update) is deployed to Hedera testnet via the Hashio JSON-RPC relay and verified on Sourcify. Pay-per-query is x402, settled by the Blocky402 facilitator in native HBAR (feePayer partial-signing).
Privy — a Privy server wallet is the autonomous agent that signs every issue/revoke. Privy signs but doesn't broadcast to Hedera, so we sign the chain-296 transaction with Privy and self-broadcast via ethers — that's what unlocked Privy-on-Hedera.
Hacky bits: we reverse-engineered Blocky402's x402 v2 payload from its validation errors — native HBAR is asset id 0.0.0, and the v2 payload carries the chosen requirements under accepted, not top-level scheme/network. We build the Hedera payment with @x402/hedera + @hiero-ledger/sdk because hand-rolled @hashgraph/sdk bytes drifted from what the facilitator decodes.

name: mandatei
description: Ledger-backed x402 agents on Base: tap to fund, pay tools inside a cap keys never touch the LLM
projectDescription: Mandate is a local operator for autonomous AI agents that spend real USDC on Base mainnet through the x402 payment protocol. You describe a goal in plain language; Mandate uses Vertex (Gemini) to plan which paid tools to call, shows you an upfront price preview, and only executes inside a Ledger-approved spending cap. Trust is split cleanly: your physical Ledger confirms your address and signs the initial USDC allowance via ERC-7730 clear signing (EIP-712); a Key Ring–sealed software wallet handles later micropayments to approved endpoints without repeated USB taps. The LLM never sees private keys. Live evidence comes from The Graph (including Agent0 registry lookups) and optional Hedera analysis; every tool call produces durable SQLite receipts. URL allowlists, per-call limits, rolling windows, and expiry are enforced by the broker—not by prompt instructions. When a run finishes, the agent profile is discarded; payment history and sources remain for audit. Built for ETHOnline 2026 Start Fresh: one npm start workspace on localhost, self-hosted x402 facilitator, and real device taps for funding—not mocked signing.
howItsMade:
Mandate is a Node 22 monorepo: packages/gateway (operator broker) + packages/facilitator (self-hosted x402 settlement), static UI in console/, entry at scripts/start.mjs. Everything runs locally on :8410; SQLite holds mandates, payment receipts, and agent run checkpoints.
Payments: We use Coinbase x402 v2 (@x402/core, @x402/evm) with the exact scheme on Base mainnet USDC (EIP-3009 TransferWithAuthorization). The broker is the only component that can sign: it quotes unpaid 402 offers, reserves budget atomically, signs with a Key Ring–decrypted key via viem, and verifies settlement before accepting evidence. A loopback facilitator on :8406 batches settlement so the demo does not depend on a third-party endpoint.
Ledger (partner stack): Physical device + DMK (@ledgerhq/device-management-kit, HID transport) + Ethereum Signer Kit for address read and funding EIP-712. Spending keys live in @ledgerhq/wallet-cli Key Ring (ring encrypt/decrypt over stdin pipes; password from macOS Keychain, never argv). Clear signing uses @ledgerhq/context-module CAL filters and a custom ERC-7730 descriptor (docs/erc7730/) for “Authorize USDC transfer.” Without a partner LEDGER_ORIGIN_TOKEN, production CAL 403s—so we ship a loopback test CAL (ledger:test-cal) plus the ledger-dev Ethereum app (CAL_TEST_KEY=1). We fail-closed on funding unless clear-signing is provable (erc7730 or clear-basic), not just “device connected.”
Agent loop: Vertex Gemini (gemini-3.5-flash via gcloud) plans tool steps; unpaid probes validate prices. Execution is adaptive: approved plan steps run sequentially, each paid through x402 to first-party tools on :8425 (The Graph subgraph queries, Coinbase spot prices, Hedera-backed analysis). Live Agent0 discovery uses Subgraph MCP; counterparty policy pools ERC-8004 feedback across chains before paying unknown recipients. Reports are generated from observed fields, not invented prose.
Hacky but real: DMK close() hangs Node—we keep a singleton and resetDmk() instead. DMK returns v as 0/1; we normalize to 27/28 for USDC. CAL needs explicit EIP712Domain in types or the hash misses on device—we inject it without changing the x402 digest. DETECT_BLIND_SIGNING in traces is a reporter step, not proof of a blind screen. Address confirmation and funding are deliberately separate device actions so we never imply a tap signed money when it only showed an address.

name: Breakwater
description: Treasury-owned Aqua liquidity that earns fees and enforces trading limits during stablecoin stress.
projectDescription:
Breakwater lets a treasury owner create liquidity with explicit risk limits while retaining custody of their tokens. The owner chooses an allocation, trading fee, safety trigger and permitted exit discount, then approves and activates the position through Aqua.
Before creating, the owner can rehearse those same numeric settings against four historical USDC/USDT checkpoints without connecting a wallet. The comparison shows permitted behavior, original impairment, size-specific external quotes, estimated execution costs and the recovery tradeoff. It explicitly separates historical scenarios from Sepolia activation and leaves unavailable quotes unknown. It is a policy-explanation tool, not a return forecast or a claim that Breakwater beats a competent direct executor.
While both assets satisfy the policy, trades can flow in both directions and the position records the retained input-token fee. When the asset becomes impaired, the same order refuses trades that add more of it and permits reserve-in, asset-out trades at an observation-bounded price, subject to backing and a willing taker. An unsafe reserve, co-depeg or invalid/stale observation halts trading. The owner can cancel even while trading is halted.
The public Sepolia prototype exposes this owner journey, visible fee/exit accounting, owner-controlled sample-price scenarios and recent-position discovery. A separate wallet completed a 1 bUSD healthy trade, receiving 0.996975 rUSD while the position retained a 0.003 bUSD fee. Under sample stress, that same wallet paid 1 rUSD to buy 1.069175 bUSD from the same position: actual treasury balances confirm reserve received and impaired inventory reduced. The order then halted for an unsafe reserve and a co-depeg, and resumed quoting after healthy observations were restored. Impaired-input and halt checks use read-only execution calls, not mined failed trades. This was guided testnet testing, not verified unassisted use, adoption or demand. Tokens have no monetary value and the observations are not live market feeds. Exits and earnings are not guaranteed. The permitted discount is relative to an accepted observation, not a cap on total loss.
howItsMade:
Breakwater uses the pinned official Aqua contracts and a custom SwapVM router/instruction implementation. Aqua records virtual allocations while tokens stay in the maker's wallet. BreakwaterMakerAMM builds an order program combining the policy guard, SwapVM's flat-input-fee instruction, and the pegged liquidity curve. Stress changes the permitted instruction path of the existing order; it does not require replacing the order.
BreakwaterPolicy checks independent USD observations for both assets and their relative price. Per-feed age limits, quote commitments, minimum output and deadlines address different failure modes. BreakwaterPositions records owner-created orders and accounts for healthy fees and exits using authenticated settlement hooks, with a commitment check across the transfer boundaries. Reverted settlement rolls back its accounting.
The owner interface supports guided configuration, optional policy rehearsal, bounded token approvals, Aqua shipping, automatic quotes, explicit wallet actions, receipt recovery, scenario controls and cancellation. Transaction feedback retains the initiating wallet and position across wallet changes and pending-transaction reloads. Position sharing includes one-click copy and a manual fallback. Recent-position discovery uses bounded onchain event scans and displays current policy and backing. Expired samples explain owner-only refresh and offer recovery paths rather than an apparently executable trade form. Final CI passed 54 frontend tests and 74 contract tests; 12 optional fork tests were skipped. The actual-order differential test covers 60 arithmetic comparisons. Rehearsal and creation share one parsed settings object. The prior bounded historical study includes an unguarded fee-bearing curve, a halt/direct alternative, recovery tradeoffs and explicitly synthetic observation lag. The optional atomic-unwind executor remains experimental, not the main public workflow or a claim of superior returns.
AI assistance: Codex substantially generated and revised contracts, tests, frontend code, graphics, configuration and documentation. File-specific attribution, reused upstream material and limits are documented in AI_DISCLOSURE.md and DEPENDENCIES.md in the repository. Human contributions included product direction, risk-policy and scope decisions, dedicated testnet funding, wallet-signed testing, usability feedback and coordination of external testing. We do not claim manual Solidity authorship, an independent security audit or verified independent adoption.

name: Source Mark
description: Paid Graph reads that refuse when provenance fails — x402 on Hedera, sources get paid.
projectDescription:
SourceMark is a paid read layer for onchain data that refuses to answer when it cannot prove provenance. Agents and apps that act on rates, TVLs, or other indexed metrics need more than a dashboard number: a stale or substituted subgraph answer is not a UI bug, it is a wrong transaction. SourceMark turns that into an HTTP product with real money attached.
Callers request a metric over a schema family (for example Messari lending on Ethereum) from a single endpoint. The gateway looks up the family in a data-only registry of pinned The Graph deployment IDs that share a byte-identical schema IPFS hash, fans the same GraphQL query out to every ready source in parallel, and judges each response against live chain head for block lag and age. Sources that fail freshness, report indexing errors, or serve a different deployment than the pin are dropped with a reason. Families declare whether sources must agree (identical) or may differ (peer); identical disagreement refuses the whole read instead of papering over it with a median.
Unpaid requests return a real HTTP 402 with x402 payment requirements on Hedera testnet (HBAR via the Blocky402 facilitator). No API key and no signup — the challenge is the onboarding. When a payment header is present, the gateway verifies with the facilitator first and does not settle yet. Only if the provenance gate passes does it settle, answer, and issue a signed receipt naming every contributing deployment, its block, the policy, and the payment. Digests can also be published to a Hedera Consensus Service topic so existence-at-time is not only our database. If the gate fails, the response is 409 REFUSED and settlement is skipped — refusal is free by construction, so the service cannot profit from a guess.
On success, revenue is recorded in SourcePayouts on Hedera: a routing fee, per-source shares, and a slashable unvested holdback. Demo source operators opt in with EIP-191 consent over their payout addresses and can claim cleared balances themselves. Anyone can dispute a receipt; the service re-queries The Graph at the recorded blocks. MATCH rejects with no slash. MISMATCH slashes holdback on the ledger and drives onchain openDispute, with arbiter resolveDispute or permissionless resolveAfterDeadline after silence.
Buyers who pay in USDC on Base reach the same gate through Bazantic resale. Their rail cannot answer a Hedera x402 challenge, so the gateway uses api-key forward while sources are still paid in HBAR from an operator float — same provenance policy, same onchain split, receipt marked channel:resale. The live multi-page demo on Railway shows 402, paid read, forced refusal, resale, disputes, explore tables, and an SDK page.
howItsMade:
SourceMark is a TypeScript gateway on Hono (Node 22) with a multi-page static demo (home, demo, explore, sdk), a thin SDK package, and an MCP server plus SKILL.md for agents. The serving path never substitutes fixtures for live Graph data: if sources are unreachable or unpinned, reads refuse.
Data layer — The Graph. registry/families.json maps a schema IPFS hash and query templates to pinned deployment IDs. Conformance is checked with The Graph’s network subgraph (byte-identical schemaIpfsHash), not marketing labels. At read time the resolver fans out through the decentralized gateway, reads _meta.deployment and enforces the pin, measures freshness against Ethereum RPC chain head (ANCHOR_MODE=rpc), and aggregates: median for identical families, TVL-weighted for peer families. That peer/identical split mattered: a naive median across Aave V3, V2, Spark, and a wound-down pool produced a rate none of them paid.
Payments — Hedera + Blocky402. x402 v2 exact scheme on hedera:testnet via @x402/hedera and the Blocky402 facilitator. Verify and settle are separate calls: verify before Graph work, settle only after the gate. Buyer helpers ship with the product (CLI, loop agent, in-page demo) so the paywall is exercisable, not theoretical.
Receipts and consent — viem. Answers and evidence are keccak-hashed over canonical JSON and EIP-191 signed. POST /v1/consent verifies a signature from the registered payout address. Optional HCS publish uses @hashgraph/sdk so digests land on a public topic.
Liability — SourcePayouts.sol (Hardhat, Hedera testnet). recordRead locks the split and holdback; claim lets sources withdraw cleared balances; openDispute takes a bond; resolveDispute (arbiter) or resolveAfterDeadline (permissionless after disputeResolveSeconds) upholds or rejects. Dispute decisions are driven by Graph re-derive at receipt blocks, not arbiter opinion alone. A Hedera-specific unit trap mattered in production: msg.value arrives in tinybar while eth_getBalance is weibar; disputeBond must be stored in tinybar and sent as bond×1e10 weibar or openDispute reverts BadBond.
Distribution — Bazantic. Registered from OpenAPI as api-key (not x402-mpp) because USDC-on-Base cannot satisfy a Hedera challenge. Same completeRead() path as direct buyers, so refusal cannot be skipped on resale. A multi-service recipe pairs SourceMark with Hedera Mirror Node; public recipe JSON lives in bazantic/.
Notable hacks / hard-won details: free refusal via verify-then-settle; operator float ledger when rails do not meet; falsified-receipt demo that corrupts per-source anchors (hash-only tamper still MATCHed on value alignment); gas floors on Hedera resolve txs after under-estimated gas; dedicated DEMO_SOURCE_MNEMONIC payees instead of the public Hardhat phrase. Partners: The Graph (live data + schema identity), Hedera (x402, SourcePayouts, HCS), Bazantic (distribution and Mirror Node recipe).

name: Sticker Bomb
description: 🚦StickerBomb takes ideas from screens to streets with verified placement and instant USDC payouts.
projectDescription:
Cicada 3301 proved that an idea born online could send people into streets around the world searching for mysterious posters.⁠
⁠StickerBomb turns that magic into quick commerce for physical advertising: upload your artwork, choose a city, and fund a campaign while local workers place it, independent workers verify it, and onchain escrow pays them automatically. From your mom’s basement, you can take your company from a screen to streets anywhere in the world.
Brand side: Upload artwork, choose a city and fund the campaign. Track every placement, payment and QR scan from one dashboard.
Gig Worker side: Claim a nearby job, place the poster and submit photo, QR and location proof. A different worker independently verifies it before both are paid.
howItsMade:
How it’s made
We built StickerBomb as a full end-to-end pipeline connecting mobile-first street operations to trust-minimized, automatic payouts.
Brand side: Brands create campaigns, choose approved locations through Mapbox, upload artwork, set rewards, and fund the campaign. They can track placements, payments, and scans from one dashboard.
Gig worker side: Workers use our PWA to claim nearby jobs, scan the poster, and submit photo and GPS proof. A separate worker can independently verify the placement before payment.
QR system: Every location receives a unique, artwork-styled QR that is tested before printing. Scans identify the exact poster, record privacy-safe attribution, and redirect visitors to the brand’s current destination.[
World: Selfie Check binds one verified credential to one worker account, helping stop duplicate identities from claiming rewards. The escrow prevents the same job from being paid twice.[
Chainlink CRE and escrow: Chainlink CRE privately checks the QR, geofence, evidence freshness, and installer/verifier proof. Its result reaches our Sepolia CampaignEscrow, which releases USDC only after approval.
Privy: Privy provides brand treasury wallets, worker payout wallets, authentication, and controlled campaign funding—without requiring users to manage private keys.
Infrastructure: The PWA runs on Vercel, campaign and job data lives in AWS RDS Postgres through Prisma, private evidence is stored in Supabase Storage, and Mapbox powers campaign locations and worker navigation.
Stack: Next.js · Vercel · AWS RDS · Prisma · Supabase Storage · Mapbox · World · Chainlink CRE · Privy · Solidity · Sepolia · USDC.
Hacky/notable: Every poster becomes a physical asset with an onchain payout condition, while sensitive evidence is verified inside a TEE—so workers are paid based on proof, not trust in our database.

name: AskChain
description: AskChing turns DeFi questions into cited answers from live The Graph subgraphs.
projectDescription:
AskChing is an evidence-first DeFi research agent that transforms natural-language questions into transparent, cited answers from live Ethereum mainnet subgraphs. It compares lending markets across Aave V3, Compound V3, Spark Lend and Aave V2; analyses market conditions and historical trends; and discovers USDC yield opportunities across lending, Uniswap V3 and Curve.
AskChing provides seven MCP tools for market comparison, research briefs, risk scanning, explainable analysis, 7- or 30-day trend analysis, cross-venue yield discovery and self-description. Every reported figure includes provenance such as its subgraph ID, block, timestamp and query hash. Calculations, confidence levels, caveats and data-quality gaps remain visible instead of being hidden behind an opaque score.
Different products are not presented as directly equivalent: current lending supply APY and historical DEX LP fee APR are ranked separately. AskChing fails closed when it cannot obtain enough independent cited evidence, never invents unsupported data, does not execute transactions and does not present its output as financial advice.
howItsMade:
AskChing was built from scratch as a TypeScript pnpm monorepo. Its shared data layer queries six live Ethereum mainnet subgraphs through The Graph Gateway: Aave V3, Compound V3, Spark Lend, Aave V2, Uniswap V3 and Curve. The results are normalized into strict Zod schemas so rates, assets, units and rate definitions are validated before anything is compared or ranked.
The MCP server exposes six research tools—compare_markets, research_brief, risk_scan, analyze_markets, analyze_trends and discover_yields—plus a get_info tool that explains the product and provides example prompts. A single tool-registration module powers both local stdio and remote Streamable HTTP transports, preventing their capabilities from drifting apart. The deployed Vercel endpoint can therefore be connected directly to MCP-compatible clients including Claude, Cursor, VS Code, Codex and Gemini CLI.
A Grok tool-calling CLI forms the conversational orchestration layer. It interprets a natural-language request, selects the appropriate AskChing tool, supplies structured arguments and synthesizes the cited result. Deterministic fixture mode allows reliable demos and tests, while live mode uses The Graph API credentials.
The evidence model is enforced in code: every observation carries its subgraph ID, block, timestamp and query hash, and quantitative comparisons fail closed unless at least two independent cited sources remain. Partial source failures become explicit gaps rather than disappearing silently.
For DEX yield discovery, AskChing aligns Uniswap V3 and Curve snapshots to a shared completed UTC day and calculates historical fee APR from cited daily fees and TVL. A particularly practical hack was replacing a slow global Uniswap snapshot query with a two-stage process: discover eligible pools first, then fetch each pool’s snapshots in parallel. Lending APY and LP fee APR remain in separate rankings because their definitions and risks are fundamentally different.
The repository includes Vitest unit and integration tests, behavioural evals, live-source probes, MCP transport smoke tests and deployment checks. Git history contains frequent incremental commits to preserve the ETHOnline Start Fresh development trail.

name: Merxet
description: End-To-End Encrypted Retail Protocol On Hedera with merchant-branded storefronts
projectDescription:
Merxet is an end-to-end encrypted retail protocol built on Hedera.
It lets merchants sell products online and offline through a simple checkout, with payments handled on Hedera, private messages and sensitive order data protected by end-to-end encryption.
Beyond distributing QR codes offline, sellers can create online storefronts for their product catalogs and customize them with the Merxet AI agent. Each store can have a short, unique ENS name, and sellers can verify themselves through World Selfie Check.
Buyers use the Merxet app as a personal shopping cart with a built-in Hedera wallet. They can shop across different stores and pay with supported tokens, including HBAR and USDC.
What makes Merxet different?


Decentralized commerce with private order data. Sensitive order data is encrypted and stored on-chain. Only the buyer and seller can decrypt it.


Transparent payments with predefined rules. Merxet's public payment protocol on Hedera uses escrow and predefined settlement rules, giving buyers and sellers a clear view of how payments are handled, without unexpected holds, extra platform fees, or verification delays.


A fast, affordable way to start selling. Upload your products, generate QR codes for offline sales, and create an online storefront with AI customization, all within Merxet.


Merxet brings Hedera into everyday commerce, helping merchants start selling while giving buyers and sellers greater privacy, transparency, and control.
howItsMade:
We built Merxet around a simple flow: a seller publishes a catalog and can create an online storefront for a traditional online shopping experience or share QR codes for offline purchases. Buyers place their orders, and payment stays in escrow until the order is completed. The seller portal, buyer app and storefront template use React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind. Node.js and Express services handle chain indexing, storefront generation and agent orders. The commerce MVP runs on Hedera Testnet.
Hedera does most of the work. Our Solidity contract, built with Hardhat and OpenZeppelin, manages catalogs, HBAR and token payments, escrow, settlement and refunds. Order details and delivery messages are encrypted in the browser with AES-GCM, with the encryption key wrapped separately for the buyer and seller using ECIES. We store the ciphertext in HFS and send small references and hashes through HCS. A Mirror Node sync service indexes the public state so the apps can load order history quickly. This lets us use the same network for payments, storage and messaging without putting delivery addresses in plaintext on-chain.
Most of the recent work went into letting sellers build their own shops. A seller describes the design they want, and the builder sends their brief, catalog and existing template to OpenAI's Responses API. It returns structured file edits. Each build runs in a disposable Railway sandbox, where we run type checks, lint, a production build and Playwright browser checks. The model can change the presentation, while catalog loading and checkout links stay protected. Sellers preview a revision before publishing it and can roll back later. Bunny Storage holds the source, built files and an append-only journal, so the builder can recover its state without a SQL database.
We added ENSv2 on Ethereum Sepolia for readable shop names such as coffee.merxet.eth. Resolver records link the name to the storefront, catalog and Hedera seller account. The backend handles registration gas, so sellers can claim a name from their existing Hedera session. Buyers see a name only after its records have been verified. That gives the shop a recognizable identity while keeping payments on Hedera.
World Selfie Check is an optional seller badge. A wallet signature links the check to the seller's account, and a separate service verifies the proof with World. It stores verification metadata in SQLite, without storing selfies or raw proofs. Demo and sandbox badges are labeled separately; the badge is a person-presence signal, not a business guarantee.
For AI-assisted shopping, our MCP server lets an agent prepare an order through a custom x402 flow and return an approval link or QR code. The buyer still reviews and signs in their browser wallet. Redis stores the quotes, and confirmation checks the matching Hedera transaction evidence.

name: Honeybee pay
description: AI-assisted crypto payments with buyer-approved rules and zero-knowledge privacy.
projectDescription:
Honeybee Pay aims to make everyday crypto payments simple, private, and secure. AI helps users prepare payments in plain language, while a payment firewall enforces the recipient, token, and amount the buyer approved. The AI cannot override those rules. A planned zero-knowledge proof layer will allow payment validity to be verified without publicly revealing selected transaction details.
The first demo will compare three payments of 1 test USDC: a normal payment, a redirected payment in an intentionally unprotected demonstration, and the same redirection attempt blocked by the protected system. AI will explain why the payment was blocked. Development is underway; zero-knowledge privacy will be implemented and tested separately from the initial firewall demo.
howItsMade:
I’m building Honeybee Pay in GitHub Codespaces using Foundry to develop and test Solidity smart contracts. So far, I have documented the payment rules and demo scenarios and installed the development tools.
The planned payment contract will check each payment against the buyer’s approval, including the recipient, token, amount, and expiration, and prevent approvals from being reused. AI will help prepare payment requests and explain blocked attempts, but it will not have authority to override the contract’s rules.
The initial tests will compare normal payments with deliberately redirected payments using test USDC. The unprotected example will be kept separate from the protected payment contract.
