name: Melt
description: Gift cards without stores. Send purchasing power for a purpose; let their AI choose the card later.
projectDescription:
Gift cards make you choose a store too early. Cash gives up the reason you sent it. Melt sits between them.
A sender locks ETH in an envelope for a promise like “mobile data for your trip, up to $20.” The vault enforces the budget, expiry, and fixed recovery address onchain. Melt applies the purpose, category, deny list, and price cap before any purchase can be quoted.
The recipient opens a shareable gift page or asks ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, or Grok to find something that fits. AI ranks the choices; deterministic checks decide what money can move. The model can interpret intent, but it cannot raise the budget, rewrite the gift, or invent a transfer.
At redemption, Melt converts only the card amount from ETH to USDC through Uniswap and prepares the Cryptorefills order. On testnet it performs the swap and validates the order without pretending test funds bought a real card. There is no cash-out or generic transfer tool. Unspent funds remain in the vault, and recovery always routes to the sender.
The same primitive also powers agent jobs: one instruction, one budget, one deadline, a live browser you can watch or take over, and a recovery path that survives the worker. Melt give people and agents purchasing power without handing them an unrestricted wallet.
howItsMade:
Melt is a React and Vite frontend backed by Fastify, SQLite, viem, and a Solidity TaskVault.
Privy handles email or wallet authentication and embedded wallets. A separate Privy-managed signer submits the outer transactions and pays gas. Every envelope deploys its own vault with an immutable owner, agent, cumulative ETH budget, and expiry. The contract blocks common approval and transfer selectors, accounts for spending onchain, and keeps closure and recovery available even if Melt’s API or browser worker disappears.
The semantic policy is deliberately separate from the model. Melt derives a purpose, category, deny list, dollar cap, partial-use rule, and return destination, then records a hash of that policy. Discovery combines Cryptorefills’ live catalog with built-in options. A configured model can rank already-approved candidates or audit an item proposed by an external assistant, but deterministic TypeScript checks enforce category, denied uses, price, and remaining funds again before a quote is created. AI can narrow the choices; it never gets final authority over the money.
When a quote is redeemed, Melt calls Uniswap V3’s QuoterV2, builds an exactInputSingle call, and has the vault send only the quoted ETH through SwapRouter02. The resulting USDC returns to the vault without an ERC-20 approval being granted to the agent. Melt then validates or creates the corresponding Cryptorefills order. Testnet runs stop at validation and clearly state that test funds cannot purchase a live card.
External agents can use Melt through hosted Streamable HTTP MCP, stdio MCP, REST, OpenAPI, or a dependency-free JavaScript client. Their keys are displayed once, stored as hashes, scoped to existing envelopes, metered, and revocable. They can list gifts, search, propose, and redeem, but cannot create an allowance, increase its value, change its recovery address, or make an unrestricted transfer. HMAC-signed webhooks and a complete event timeline make the lifecycle
inspectable.
The hacky part was making one vault work for two kinds of hands: a recipient’s assistant spending a gift and an owner’s browser agent completing a task. Browser agents run in isolated Playwright contexts behind an EIP-1193 provider that only forwards vault-permitted calls. The owner can watch the browser, pause it, take over, close the session, and recover remaining ETH plus discovered ERC-20 or ERC-721 assets. Solidity, API, SDK, browser, and restart-recovery tests cover the failure paths as well as the happy path.

name: Pgas.me
description: Fund a new EVM wallet without linking it to your old one. Any token in, unlinked gas out.
projectDescription:
Every fresh wallet has a birth certificate: the transaction that funded it. Send gas from your main wallet to a new one and the two are linked forever. Every protocol you touch, every position you open, every payment that arrives at that "new" address is attributable to you, your balance and your whole history. On a public ledger there is no way to start clean, which is why most people keep using one doxxed address for everything.
pgas.me funds new wallets with gas without creating that link. Connect any wallet, pay with any token you already hold on any supported chain, and the deposit is routed to Ethereum and locked into the Beam bridge. The value settles on Beam, a confidential ledger with no per-address balances and blinded amounts, where it is held as bETH, bDAI or bWBTC. Later, whenever you choose, you list the wallets to fund, the amounts and when they should arrive. Each payout crosses back through the bridge and is signed from a fresh Beam address created for that single order, so on Ethereum the funded wallet's history begins with a bridge payout and nothing points back at your deposit.
Two details make the unlinking real rather than decorative. First, every deposit names a different receiver key on Ethereum. We rebuilt the Beam bridge's wallet-side application so keys are derived from the contract id plus an index rather than the single constant key the stock build derives, so two deposits from the same payer no longer share the 33 bytes that identify them. Second, every payout is signed from a single-use Beam address, so nothing on the Beam side resembles an account either.
Where this goes, and the actual point of the project:

Run it yourself. A standalone app you download from GitHub, launch on your own machine, point at your own Beam wallet and use to fund as many wallets as you want. No operator, no custody, no trust in us. The service you can try today is the hosted demonstration of that app.
Max privacy mode. Beam's Lelantus shielded pool, so value is not merely confidential but drawn from an anonymity set. The code exists and is deliberately disabled today because the pool's unlock timer would strand user funds; it ships when the set size and the timers make it honest.
Instant payouts from a rotating distributor pool. Each distributor is funded independently across the bridge, spends a fixed budget and is retired, so the transaction graph stops at a wallet with no relationship to any deposit. Built and tested, currently flag-off.
Funding for AI agents. An agent that needs gas for a fresh account calls the same API, or runs the local app, and funds itself without exposing the operator's treasury or reusing one hot wallet for every task.
Non-custodial settlement. A BeamVM contract holding balances against keys in the user's browser, so the operator cannot move funds at all.
howItsMade:
The backend is FastAPI with MongoDB; the front end is React, TypeScript and ethers v6. Sign-in is SIWE("Sign-In with Ethereum"), there are no accounts and no email, and the whole thing is in the public repository.
Ingress: on Ethereum a deposit is a direct call to the Beam bridge's pipe contract. From any other chain we ask a cross-chain intent router to fill an order on Ethereum and attach the pipe call as the fill's hook, so the user signs once, on the chain where their money already is. For token-to-ETH on Ethereum we shipped a Uniswap V4 route: a Universal Router swap priced by the V4 Quoter into the user's own wallet, then the direct deposit.
On Uniswap specifically, we first built the atomic version: a zero-liquidity gateway pool whose hook takes the entire input in beforeSwap, routes it through the canonical hookless pool for the real price, floors the output onto the bridge's 8-decimal grid and calls sendFunds in the same transaction, with our own router exposing msgSender() for attribution. It is in the repo with 76 offline tests and 9 mainnet-fork tests after two adversarial review rounds, and we chose not to deploy it. FEEDBACK.md explains why: permission bits in the address mean salt mining on every bytecode change, a hook that takes 100% of the output forces amountOutMinimum to zero at the router so slippage must be enforced inside the hook, router and sender semantics are not discoverable from the interface, and the same atomic post-swap effect is a single field on a cross-chain intent order. That comparison is the most useful thing we can give the Uniswap team.
Beam side: our backend runs its own Beam node and wallet-api, claims each bridge message, and books every movement through an append-only ledger, so a balance is always a sum over movements and never a raw wallet read.
The part we are proudest of is the shader rebuild. The bridge's wallet-side application derives exactly one receiver key per wallet per pipe, so every deposit would have named the same 33 bytes on Ethereum. We patched it: a packed KeyID of contract id plus index is passed to Env::DerivePk, the same blob is handed to SigRequest when the claim is signed, and the incoming-message view derives a bounded window of keys and reports which index a message matched. It compiles to wasm32 with clang in a pinned Docker image, rebuilds byte-for-byte identically, and was proven against the live wallet read-only before deployment: the legacy key is unchanged on all three pipes, indexed keys are distinct and stable, the claim data for an existing message is byte-identical to the stock build's, and a wrong index is refused before anything is signed.
Because this moves real money, the engineering is mostly about evidence. A delivery is proven by identity rather than a balance guess, the pipe's balance falling and the destination's rising in the same block. Every irreversible step checks a kill-switch file. A retry never re-signs, so one nonce means at most one fill. The relayer fee is charged at cost with headroom and the unused part is refunded when the crossing settles. Chain reads walk the whole endpoint pool, because one endpoint's refusal is not evidence of anything. Statuses never say "failed" for an internal cause; an order that cannot move says what it is waiting for and when it will retry. There are 1,134 backend tests and 209 browser tests, all offline.
Operationally it is one VPS: systemd units for the API, the Beam node, the wallet-api and the payment services, nginx behind Cloudflare, and a deploy script that builds locally and ships.

name: Flint
description: Flint is a trustless disbursement protocol for open source contributors and grants.
projectDescription:
Flint is a trustless disbursement protocol for grants and open source. You lock USDC, work gets verified from GitHub, a human signs, and the payout plus a soulbound receipt go out on Arc. Contributors do not fill a Flint form. They update a file in the repo and keep shipping PRs. No spreadsheet in the middle. No bank wire.
The hole is simple. Too many grants are vision based. A team sells the story, takes the money, stops shipping, and the product dies. Or they actually ship and the committee never signs. Both sides ghost. Funds sit or already left, and there is no trail that says which goal was met. Uniswap Foundation committed $26M in grants in 2025 and paid out $11M. A lot of that still moves through forms and a Safe. Open source has the same wait. GSoC has paid 18,000+ people. LFX, Outreachy, Mozilla still use bank wires. If you are overseas that is 3 to 5 days and $25 to $45 on SWIFT, plus paperwork, before you see a cent.
Flint makes the grant goal based. A maintainer opens a flint issue for a grant. A contributor adds one row to CONTRIBUTORS.md with their wallet. That is the whole signup. Grant mode escrows the full amount, writes milestones on chain, and releases a slice when the linked PRs check out. Open mode puts up a pool, scores a GitHub cycle, and splits with sqrt or proportional. Scoring runs in a Chainlink CRE TEE with gpt-oss-120b on Groq. Only the score leaves the enclave. The maintainer or committee still has to sign. If they disappear, 14 days on a grant or 30 days on a pool and it pays anyway. The Graph Studio indexes every pool, grant, and receipt so a committee can query it later.
Work in the repo. Wallet in a markdown file. USDC and a receipt out.
howItsMade:
Flint is a GitHub App wired to escrow on Arc. You work in the repo like you already do. The app watches issues and merges. The chain holds the USDC and pays when the work checks out.
The App posts flint issues (milestones, grantee, deadline). A webhook verifies that and lists them as pending grants. Contributors put their wallet in CONTRIBUTORS.md. When PRs merge, the keeper and the App see it. That same event is what the scorer uses.
On the other side, nine contracts do the money. Grant escrow for tranches. Pool escrow for a cycle. Policy contracts turn a score into an amount. A batch pay sends USDC. A soulbound receipt is minted so the work stays attached to the wallet. You fund and sign from the site. Privy can make the wallet from email. Circle CCTP can bring USDC over from Base. Gas on Arc is USDC.
The two sides meet in a Chainlink CRE TEE. It pulls GitHub from inside the enclave, runs gpt-oss-120b on Groq, and only the score comes out. DON consensus writes that score on the contracts. The Graph Studio indexes every pool, grant, and receipt so the site is reading the chain, not a spreadsheet.
What that gives you in practice: the repo is the source of truth, and the money cannot move until that repo’s work is scored and someone signs. If they never sign, the contract still pays. Fourteen days on a grant, thirty on a pool. The person who shipped is not waiting on a wire or an inbox.

name: LP Copilot
description: An AI liquidity copilot powered by Privy wallets, Uniswap, and The Graph.
projectDescription: LP Copilot helps users understand and manage liquidity through a conversational AI assistant. Privy provides the wallet and transaction approvals, Uniswap powers liquidity positions and adjustments, and The Graph supplies indexed onchain data for monitoring and AI analysis. Users can explore price ranges, track positions, and approve a bounded adjustment plan. The current prototype runs on Base Sepolia, with both manual operations and delegated execution tested onchain.
howItsMade:
Privy: Embedded wallets handle login and user-approved transactions. Temporary delegated signers let an approved plan execute within token, recipient, chain, and expiry limits; the server additionally checks the exact transaction and range.
Uniswap: The SDK and deployed contracts support position math, adding or removing liquidity, collecting tokens, and repositioning into a new range.
The Graph: A custom subgraph indexes pool events. We cross-check indexed data against RPC for freshness and consistency before using it in position monitoring and AI assessments.
React, Node.js, and SQLite connect the interface, monitoring, and execution history. DeepSeek powers the conversational assistant. Development was AI-assisted, with human product direction and testing.

name: Nameslots
description: Earn tax revenue with your subnames and guarantee their productive use
projectDescription:
Nameslots turns the subnames of any ENS name into a market.
Own l2beat.eth, open base.l2beat.eth to anyone. Whoever holds it sets its own price, pays tax on that price continuously, and can be taken out by anyone willing to pay it. Stop paying and you lose it.
One number does three jobs: what you say the name is worth, what you pay tax on, and what anyone can buy it from you for. There is no number that lets you sit on a good name for free. That's the anti-squat part.
The name itself never moves. addr() returns whoever holds the slot right now, so a turnover writes nothing to the registry. Records are scoped to the tenancy and leave when you do. And both control and income follow the .eth name: sell it and the market underneath moves to the buyer, no transaction needed.
Built on ENSv2 and 0xSlots, live on Sepolia.
howItsMade:
Solidity and Foundry. A factory opens one SlotNamespace per parent name, as a beacon proxy so they all upgrade at once. Factory and resolver are UUPS. Each opened label gets a 0xSlots slot, which does the pricing, the escrow and the buyouts.
ENSv2: every namespace gets its own UserRegistry through ENS's VerifiableFactory. A NameSlots contracts (one per name) is granted registrar roles in order to be able to register/slot subnames. It also hold text records (so that when owner changes they're not carried over). Then the UserRegistry create is set as sub-registry on the PermissionedRegistry (.eth)
Resolution is plain ENS, getEnsAddress and getEnsText, no SDK.
Frontend is Next.js 16, wagmi, viem, Turborepo

name: Tremor
description: Two-sided continuous ETH realized-variance receipts hedging LVR on 1inch Aqua & SwapVM.
projectDescription:
Tremor is a continuously priced market in ETH realized variance. It is a way to take a position on how violent the next week is, rather than which direction it goes.
Volatility is one of the largest risks in crypto and almost nobody can trade it directly. You can bet on direction all day. But an LP bleeding to loss-versus-rebalancing, a desk short gamma, a treasury sizing its risk: none of them can take a clean position on variance itself without an options book and a counterparty to face.
Tremor turns realized variance into an instrument. Each market is one observation window on the Chainlink ETH/USD feed carrying two complementary claims:
LONG VARIANCE pays S × min(V / V_cap, 1)
SHORT VARIANCE pays S − LONG
where V is the annualized realized variance actually observed and S is the cap payout. The two sides always sum to exactly S, which is $1.00, to the integer, in every state, because SHORT is computed by subtraction from LONG rather than rounded independently. Buying the pair can never win; selling the pair can never win.
Settlement is computed, not quoted. At expiry anyone calls finalize, and the contract replays Chainlink's own round history on chain to compute realized variance and fix both payouts in a single call. There is no oracle write, no price feed of our own, and no privileged actor. The same is true of checkpointing the observation window: permissionless, bounded per call, and cheap. Anyone who wants a quote can make the call, because a market that is behind refuses to price.
Prices move continuously, and every price the UI presents as executable is executable. This is not an order book. The market quotes off projected variance, meaning what has actually been realized so far blended with a forward for the time remaining. That is displaced by inventory skew and sits inside a spread that tightens as the window closes and the outcome becomes less uncertain. A fill is priced as the integral over a rising ask, so size pays impact honestly. The number on screen is read from the on-chain lens for that exact size, not estimated by the frontend. The indicative mark is shown separately and labelled an estimate, never offered as a cashout value.
Both sides share one pot of collateral. Every claim is fully collateralized before it is sold, and the writer cannot withdraw what backs a live claim. Because long and short cannot both pay out, the market locks ceil(max(long, short) × S) rather than long × S + short × S. The saving is min(long, short) / (long + short) — up to half the capital for the same open interest when the book is balanced — and the terminal shows the actual figure read off the contract rather than a headline. That is the 1inch Aqua contribution: one vault, one reserve, two instruments.
A built-in hedging tool sizes the position for the most concrete buyer: an LP's expected LVR is proportional to realized variance (E[LVR] ≈ P·σ²·T/8, for pool value P), so pool value and horizon in gives units and premium out, priced through the same lens.
howItsMade:
Contracts: Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry. TremorPortfolioMarketV4 holds the accounting and the fill legs; TremorPortfolioLensV4 is a separate read model, split out because the combined contract exceeded the EIP-170 24,576-byte limit by 746 bytes. PortfolioPricing is the whole pricing change and deliberately owns no new arithmetic: every integral, spread and clamp is the v2 VariancePricing library already pinned to reference vectors at 60 decimal digits. The bridge that let two generations compose with no seam is deriving the cap payout S = floor(unitNotional × capVariance / 1e18), which makes v2's perUnitPrice(V) and v3's S × min(V/cap,1) the same function of V.
1inch Aqua + SwapVM is the execution layer, not a wrapper. Each market ships six strategies, issue, exit and settle for both sides, and each one is a SwapVM program built from stock instructions: Salt · Deadline · Extruction. They run on the unmodified official AquaSwapVMRouter; we forked no router and added no opcode, which means this deploys against real Aqua today with no new audit surface and nobody's permission. The interesting part is where the pricing lives: the Extruction instruction calls back into the market mid-swap, so the curve is evaluated inside the swap itself. That is what makes preview and execution provably the same number. The frontend re-quotes through router.quote, which is the exact code path router.swap runs, immediately before signing. The vault ships each strategy hash-pinned, and the market verifies the returned hash matches what it built, so a fill cannot execute against a program the market did not author.
Collateral sits in the writer's own TremorMakerVault, which grants Aqua an allowance the writer does not control the code of; the router pulls against that allowance when a leg fills. It is an allowance model, not escrow — which is exactly why a capped payoff fits it and a perp would not. Maximum liability is fixed at issuance, so a position is fully reserved from t=0, there is no leverage, and there is nothing to liquidate by construction. That is also what lets one reserve back two instruments.
Chainlink is used as a historical record, not a price feed. The accumulator walks AggregatorV3 round history phase-aware, absorbs samples on a fixed per-market grid (sampleInterval, floored at 300 seconds; the demo markets use ten minutes, because the grid must be coarse enough that repeated rounds do not bias realized variance downward), and stores progress so checkpointing is idempotent and bounded. A market refuses to price against a window with unstored samples, so a stale quote reverts CheckpointsStale rather than filling at a number the feed has already moved past.
All arithmetic is integer. WAD for variance, 6-decimal for USDC, bigint end to end with no floats anywhere in the stack. Rounding direction is chosen deliberately in every operation to favour the collateralized maker: takers pay ceil and receive floor, and the complement inherits that direction because it subtracts a floored term from a ceiled one.
Backend: Rust, axum, alloy, sqlx/SQLite. An indexer plus an exact replica of the Solidity pricing, which is what lets the API serve history and previews without a chain round trip per request. The replica is pinned against the contracts' own vectors — 144 portfolio cases for the Rust replica, 60 series cases for the web replica, all generated at 60 significant digits — so a divergence fails a test rather than reaching a user. The API reconstructs price history per sample, on the window's own clock rather than the keeper's transaction time, and reports the anchor drift against on-chain state in ppm. A subgraph (The Graph, tested with Matchstick) mirrors the events.
Frontend: Next.js 16, wagmi v3 / viem, Recharts, Playwright. The terminal is the product: chart with the executable band, an on-chain activity tape, a ticket that prices your exact size, and a collateral panel showing the shared-reserve saving against the separate-cap equivalent. The rule the whole UI obeys is that the Lens is the authority and the backend is a replica. Chain state is merged over API state, never the reverse, and an estimate is never rendered where a user will read an executable price. An oversized order is presented as a partial fill — the ticket prices what the router will actually sell, not the size that was typed.
Notable details. Inventory skew is stateless: rather than storing a decaying signed skew with a half-life and a last-updated timestamp, the forward is displaced by impact × (long − short) derived from outstanding inventory, so it cannot drift from the book and reverses exactly on an exit. The E2E suite drives a real fill against an anvil fork through an EIP-1193 shim that forwards to the node under --auto-impersonate, so transactions are genuinely signed and mined, and the test asserts on the buyer's own receipt balance on chain rather than on the DOM. It also covers a refused signature and a slow wallet, and asserts that a quote which moves between display and signing stops the flow and asks for consent rather than signing the new number. To stress the design we built a harness that funds 1,000 scripted accounts on a local fork, against an earlier deployment of the same contracts, and runs each through the same call sequence the trading panel uses; the P&L report is reconstructed entirely from chain state, from USDC transfer logs and receipt balances, not from the harness's own memory.
Verification: 290 contract tests across 26 suites including two Base-fork E2Es, 86 backend tests, 85 web unit tests, and 34 fixture-driven browser tests plus a live-fill suite that connects a wallet, signs and mines against a fork. A dedicated test decodes the shipped program bytes and asserts the opcode set, so the "stock instructions only" claim is enforced by CI rather than by a README.

name: Sowee
description: Waiting 90 days to get paid? Get cash today. Investors fund invoices at a discount.
projectDescription:
Sowee helps small businesses get paid sooner by turning unpaid invoices into bonds investors can buy. A business gets most of the money upfront, while investors receive the full invoice amount when the customer pays. The bond itself enforces KYC, so only verified wallets can hold or trade it.
The flow is simple. A business submits an invoice and only its digital fingerprint leaves the browser. Sowee lists it as a bond, investors complete World Selfie Check and Sumsub KYC, then fund it with USDC. Investors can also trade the bond with other verified users before maturity.
Everything runs on public testnets. Hedera provides the blockchain and public record, while Asset Tokenization Studio supports regulated securities. AI agents can also buy market data through x402 and fund bonds themselves, as long as their wallets pass the same checks. The same finance core also runs on Arc.
howItsMade:
Sowee has four main pieces that work together. The smart contracts handle the rules, turning each invoice into a bond token that checks KYC on every transfer. The web app lets businesses submit invoices and investors buy bonds, while the invoice itself stays in the browser and only its fingerprint is stored.
The server handles the things a browser shouldn't, including signing quotes, running Sumsub KYC, verifying World Selfie Check, and providing market data to AI agents. Our agent can pay 0.01 USDC for the data, read it, and fund a bond on its own.
Hedera provides USDC and HCS, which we use instead of a database to store and replay the system's records. Asset Tokenization Studio lets us issue regulated securities, Blocky402 handles agent payments, World Selfie Check adds an anti sybil layer, and the same finance core also runs on Arc. One of the more unusual parts is that there is genuinely no database, even issuer logos are stored on Hedera. We also spent a day chasing a vague World generic_error before finding that our own security settings were blocking the SDK.

name: Tappy
description: Tap to approve. An AI agent wallet where every onchain transaction needs a physical NFC tap.
projectDescription:
Tappy is a wallet for AI agents that the agent cannot drain.
People are starting to hand real money to AI agents so they can buy things, pay for services, and move funds without being asked every time. But an agent can be talked into anything. A prompt injection hidden in a product listing, a web page, or an email can convince it to send the whole balance to an attacker, and it will do so confidently and immediately. The current answer is a policy file: a spending cap, an allowlist, a daily limit. Those help, but they are rules written in advance by someone guessing what will go wrong, and a policy file is not a person.
Tappy puts a person back in the loop, physically. The wallet has two keys. The agent holds one. A human holds the other on a device they can put in their pocket, in our case a Flipper Zero. The smart contract executes a transaction only when both keys have signed the exact same transaction. The agent can propose anything it likes and can sign its half instantly, and none of that moves a single wei on its own.
You chat with the agent in a normal web app and ask it to buy something, send money, or swap tokens. The agent works out what it wants to do and creates a proposal. That proposal appears on the Flipper's screen with the action, the amount, and who is receiving it. Press OK and the transaction goes to the chain, with the chat updating when it lands. Press Back and nothing happens at all, and the agent is told it was refused.
The demo turns on what happens when the agent is compromised. A shop listing in our mock store contains a hidden instruction telling the agent to transfer the entire balance to an attacker's address. The agent does what it was told and proposes the transfer. The proposal shows up on the Flipper like any other, reading SEND, the full balance, to an address the human has never seen. The human presses Back, and the money stays where it was.
The agent has exactly three abilities: propose a send, propose a swap, propose a purchase. There is no fourth tool that executes anything, so there is nothing an injection can talk it into that a human does not personally see and approve first. We did not add prompt-injection defenses to the agent, because whether the agent gets fooled does not change what can happen to the money.
Around this we built a working demo economy: a chat interface, a wallet dashboard showing both keys and the live balance, a mock shop with items to buy, and a mock exchange to swap against, all deployed on testnet so the transactions are real on-chain calls.
A physical NFC tag starts the purchase flow. Tapping a phone to a sticker opens the shop inside the app, so the interaction feels like paying for something in a real place.
We chose a Flipper Zero because it has a screen, a button, and a radio, and because many people in this community already own one and enjoy hacking on it. Nothing in the design is tied to it. The same approval step could run on a phone, a hardware wallet, or a keyring NFC tag costing about a dollar.
In this version the human key is stored on the laptop that talks to the Flipper, so the Flipper is the physical approval step and not yet the place the key lives. Moving the key onto the device itself is the obvious next step, and we have measured that the hardware can handle the cryptography, but it needs a toolchain we chose not to take on during a one-week build. Everything runs on testnet.
howItsMade:
Tappy is a 2-of-2 wallet for AI agents. The agent holds one key, a human holds the other, and nothing moves until both have signed the same transaction. Other agent wallets stop a runaway agent with a policy file, and a policy file is not a person.
The contract is the whole security model in about eighty-five lines of Solidity, built with Foundry on OpenZeppelin's typed-data and signature-recovery libraries. Its one function takes a call plus two signatures, recovers both against a fixed agent address and a fixed human address, and reverts if either fails. Replay protection comes from a monotonic nonce combined with the chain ID and the contract's own address, and every proposal carries a deadline ten minutes out. Anyone can relay the call and pay the gas, because authority lives in the signatures and not in the sender. We left out spending limits and allowlists on purpose. Every competing product has those already, and none of them has a hand.
The web app is a T3 stack: Next.js on the App Router, tRPC, Drizzle over Postgres, hosted on Vercel with Supabase behind it. Inside it a model tool-calling loop gives the agent three tools, one each to propose a send, a swap, or a purchase. It has no way to execute anything. Proposals enter a state machine as pending and sit there until a human decides. One library handles typed-data hashing and signing across the server, the laptop bridge and the tests, so the digest comes out the same way everywhere.
What made a three-person week work was putting a single interface in front of the human approver, with one method that takes a summary and a timeout and returns a decision. Three things implement it: a mock that auto-approves or asks yes/no in a terminal, the real Flipper, and a future on-device signer. Two thirds of the project was built against the mock, so only one person ever needed the hardware, and plugging the device in changed nothing above it.
The hackiest part is how the laptop talks to the Flipper. Its JavaScript engine cannot reach USB at all, since the serial module is wired to the GPIO pins rather than the host connection, so there is no socket to open and no way for a script on the device to receive anything from a computer. The bridge instead drives the Flipper's own command-line interface over the USB virtual COM port and uses its file commands to drop small JSON files onto the SD card. The app on the device polls for an inbox file three times a second, renders four short lines on the 128x64 screen, and writes the answer back to an outbox file. A sequence number makes it idempotent, so re-reading a file cannot double-approve. File-based IPC tunnelled through a serial terminal is an ugly way to do this, and it has been reliable.
The hosting forced a similar inversion. Vercel cannot hold an open websocket, so the laptop polls upward twice a second and dials out instead of the server pushing approvals down. That also removes any need for an inbound tunnel to a laptop on hotel wifi. The endpoint takes a bearer token, and it separately recovers the submitted signature against the known human address, so a leaked token still cannot approve something the human never saw.
NFC is how a purchase starts. A sticker carries a URL that opens the shop inside the app. Getting it readable on iPhones cost us an hour of confusion. The tag looked correct by every check we knew, Android read it instantly, and iOS did nothing at all. Dumping the raw pages by hand showed the stored address had two schemes in it: the encoding already carries a byte meaning "https", and we had typed the prefix in as well. iOS validates the address before it will show anything, and it reports no error when it throws one away. We now build the payload from the prefix code and a bare hostname.
The risk we took most seriously was a byte-level disagreement between the TypeScript and the Solidity over how the signed message is encoded. One wrong hash and every transaction reverts with nothing useful to debug. We froze a shared test vector on day one and made both test suites check it, and nothing merged unless the two languages agreed.
We built against a Flipper Zero, though nothing in the design depends on it. The second factor only has to do three things: show a human what is about to happen, take a yes or a no, and produce a signature. The Flipper is a convenient body for that because it has a screen, a button and a radio, and because a lot of this audience already owns one. The same interface could sit behind a phone, a hardware wallet, or a cheap NFC tag on a keyring, where tapping the tag replaces the button press. A tag has no screen, so you lose the ability to see what you are approving before you approve it. That trade buys a second factor costing about a dollar per user.
The human key still lives on the laptop in this version, so the Flipper is the physical approval step and not yet the place the key is stored. Signing on the device is feasible, and we measured the curve maths at roughly a tenth to a quarter of a second per signature, but it needs a C toolchain we chose not to fight mid-build. Testnet only.

name: Solvent
description: Solvency-aware market making for 1inch Aqua: quotes widen as wallets thin and refuse past a floor
projectDescription:
1inch Aqua lets a market maker commit liquidity to a strategy without depositing it. Tokens stay in the maker's wallet and Aqua pulls them only when a taker fills, so one balance can back many strategies at once. The catch is that no strategy knows about the others. SwapVM prices each one as if it owned the whole wallet, Aqua's ship() never checks the total against the balance, and the whitepaper says it plainly: the AMM keeps quoting on virtual balances without checking real balances or allowances. The documented fix is for makers to watch their wallets and dock strategies by hand.
We measured how often this happens. We rebuilt every maker's balance sheet across Aqua's entire history on Base from primary data, reading each wallet's balance and allowance from an archive node. 115 makers shipped 443 strategies. 78 of the 88 books that ever held more than $100 were under-backed at some point, and 89% of all material observations were under-backed. One book advertised about $51,000 of USDC while holding nothing, for weeks, and every taker who tried it paid gas for a revert. The same pipeline, pointed at the identical Aqua contracts on Arbitrum and Optimism, finds 123 of 138 material books under-backed across the three chains.
Solvent makes an Aqua position aware of its own balance sheet, inside the strategy bytecode:

SolvencySkew, a new SwapVM instruction. The maker's utilisation (total committed across all strategies, divided by what the wallet holds and has approved) feeds into price. Below a threshold the quote is unchanged; above it the spread widens, because the last unit of a shared balance is worth more than the first.
SolvencyFloor, a new SwapVM instruction. Above a maker-chosen utilisation the strategy declines at quote time, with a reason, instead of reverting at settlement after the taker has spent gas. It lives in the program bytes, so any taker can read the covenant before trading. It is the automatic version of the whitepaper's manual docking.
The balance-sheet index. Both instructions need a maker's aggregate commitment, and Aqua cannot compute it on-chain. A subgraph maintains every maker's live book on Base, Arbitrum, Optimism and Base Sepolia, published on The Graph Network. A keeper publishes each maker's numbers to an on-chain oracle, SolventBook, where the instructions read them during the quote. Anyone can recompute the same numbers from the public index.

The live demo has five views. Mainnet shows every real Aqua maker's book on Base, Arbitrum and Optimism right now, each capsule filled green only as far as the wallet can settle. How it works shows the deployed system, every component linked to its verified contract or logs. Quote desk runs live quotes from the deployed router on Base Sepolia: step through a healthy book, a wallet that drains (the spread widens from 3,106.67 to 3,202.86 at 87% utilisation) and a book past its floor (every quote declines with SolvencyFloor's reason), or connect a wallet and take a quote for real. Balance sheets and Settlement ledger show the numbers every quote reads and what actually settled, failed fills included.
Makers get automated risk management instead of watching a wallet. Takers and agents get a pre-trade answer to whether a quote will fill. Aggregators can rank quotes by reserve ratio with one query and stop routing to phantom liquidity. The SDK, @aqua-solvent/core on npm, gives any app the same balance sheets on all four chains.
howItsMade:
Contracts (Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry). SolvencyFloor and SolvencySkew are custom SwapVM instructions. We followed upstream's own extension pattern: each takes a reserved placeholder slot in the opcode table (Floor at 0x22 in the guards bank, Skew at 0xb5 in the rate-tuning bank), so no official opcode moves and stock Aqua programs run unchanged on our router. SolventRouter is the official AquaSwapVMRouter shape carrying the extended set, running against a pinned, unmodified deployment of the official Aqua contract on Base Sepolia. Floor is validation-only (no register writes, safe under staticcall), so a decline happens inside a free view call. Skew wraps the rest of the program and mirrors upstream's FeeFlatIn arithmetic branch for branch, so a skewed quote equals a stock program carrying the equivalent flat fee, and below its threshold it is a provable no-op. Both read SolventBook, a small oracle holding each maker's committed and backing per token, with a timestamp so consumers can judge staleness. Two more instructions (ReputationGate and ReputationPriceAdjuster) read SolventScore, a counterparty score built from what actually settled. Tests include differential suites for the book and score math, invariant tests, a regression suite from upstream 1inch running on our router, and a test that reproduces the core failure against the real contracts: one wallet holding 10 WETH ships three strategies advertising 30, each passes a backing check on its own, and the second taker reverts.
The Graph. This is the piece that makes the rest possible. Aqua stores balances per (maker, app, strategyHash, token) with no enumeration and no per-maker total, so no contract call can tell you a maker's aggregate commitment. The subgraph handles Shipped, Docked, Pulled and Pushed. Instead of replaying deltas, every touch re-reads Aqua.rawBalances for that strategy and token at the indexed block and folds the difference into the maker's book, which is exact by construction and immune to event ordering and wrapper edge cases. Backing is min(balanceOf, allowance to Aqua), read in the same handler, because a revoked allowance fails a fill just like an empty wallet. Ship calldata is decoded only to learn a strategy's token list; strategies shipped through wrappers are picked up on their first Pulled or Pushed, which covers 442 of 443 real strategies. One schema ships as four manifests (Base Sepolia, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism), all published on The Graph Network. A parity check rebuilds the largest books on each chain from an archive node and requires agreement to the wei.
The keeper. Wallets drain through plain transfers that Aqua never sees, so the index alone goes stale. The attestor reads every book from the index, re-reads each wallet on-chain, diffs against SolventBook and writes only what changed, so a quiet market costs no gas. It runs on GitHub Actions about once a minute: each run does eight passes and triggers the next run only on success, with a 15-minute cron as a backstop. Its key holds ATTESTOR_ROLE and nothing else.
The console is Vite, React, viem, wagmi and RainbowKit on GitHub Pages. The quote desk simulates every fill before sending and decodes the revert, so a floored book shows SolvencyFloor's reason before any gas is spent. It reads the published subgraphs through The Graph's gateway with a per-request fallback to Studio, pauses polling on hidden or idle tabs, and caps each browser's daily gateway use to protect the query budget. The SDK (@aqua-solvent/core on npm) exposes the same books on all four chains and encodes Solvent strategy programs.
Notably hacky:

A reverted fill erases its own logs, so no subgraph can index a broken promise. SwapVM's transfer functions are private and swap() is not virtual, so a router cannot catch and re-emit the failure either. SolventRecorder records it from outside: a taker contract can try/catch its own swap and report the failure, or the attestor finds failed receipts aimed at the router and records them, citing the reverted transaction hash so anyone can check it on the explorer.
The mainnet numbers came from a one-off analyzer that decoded every ship() transaction, applied every Pulled and Pushed as a delta, and read backing from an archive node at 34 heights plus each book's peak.

Partner technologies:

1inch Aqua and SwapVM. Aqua's shared liquidity is what creates the problem, and SwapVM's instruction set is where the fix lives. Adding two opcodes put solvency inside the quote itself, with no change to Aqua.
The Graph. The aggregate balance sheet cannot be computed on-chain, so an index is the only place it can exist. The Graph let us maintain it on four chains from one schema, publish it on the decentralized network for anyone to query, and feed it back on-chain through the keeper.
