name: FindETH
description: Brands/creators launch internet treasure hunts with on-chain prizes and collectibles.
projectDescription:
FindETH is a Web3 treasure-hunt platform where businesses and creators turn their websites, products, and campaigns into interactive onchain discovery experiences. Creators/brands use AI to generate branded hunts with clues, locations, difficulty, prizes, and answer hashes. The AI workflow queries live The Graph analytics before generation, using historical completion rates, prize sizes, clue counts, and category performance to recommend better hunt designs.
Hunts are published through smart contracts on Sepolia, with clue answers protected as hashes and winners receiving verifiable NFT trophies. The platform combines wallet-based participation, Chainlink-powered mystery rewards, and backend metadata storage without exposing plaintext answers.
FindETH also uses ENSv2 to create hierarchical namespaces for creators, hunts, and AI agents. Each hunt can receive an ENSv2 subname containing metadata records, while Permissioned Resolvers and Enhanced Access Control allow creators or delegated AI agents to update only the records they are authorized to manage.
howItsMade:
FindETH is built as a full-stack Web3 application. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Wagmi, Viem, and RainbowKit for the interface, wallet connection, contract interaction, ENS resolution, and Sepolia network support. Foundry and Solidity power the TreasureHunt and TreasureNFT contracts, including hashed clues, creator verification, prize handling, and Chainlink VRF-based mystery rewards.
The backend is a FastAPI service using SQLAlchemy and Alembic with PostgreSQL/Supabase support. Gemini generates hunt drafts from real business content, while The Graph provides live onchain analytics before each generation so prize sizes, difficulty, and clue counts are informed by previous hunt performance.
ENSv2 is integrated at the namespace level: creators receive hierarchical subnames for hunts and AI agents, with metadata stored in resolver text records. Permissioned Resolver and Enhanced Access Control enable delegated, record-specific updates. A notable security decision is that plaintext answers are never persisted in the backend. Only normalized answer hashes are stored onchain, while answers exist temporarily in the creator’s browser before publication.

name: ENStrology
description: AI horoscopes from your ENS name's onchain birthday the agent writes, but can't rewrite   you.
projectDescription:
Every ENS name has an onchain birthday. ENStrology turns that real, verifiable date into a
playful AI horoscope and uses it to demonstrate a serious problem: how do you let an AI
agent create onchain content for someone without handing it control of their identity?
A user signs in with Privy, links the wallet that controls their ENS name, and ENStrology verifies both the name's control and its real registration date. After paying 0.01 demo USDC on Sepolia, the ENStrology Oracle generates a horoscope and stores it in real, expiring ENSv2 subnames.
The permission model is the point. Verified facts  source name, creation date, owner,  payment proof  live on a name the Oracle has no rights to at all. The horoscope lives on a sibling name where the Oracle holds a single scoped role. It can write the reading. It  cannot rewrite the facts, the owner, the resolver, or the expiry, and the user can revoke  its access at any time. All three cases are demonstrated as real Sepolia transactions,  including the one that reverts.
Readings can stay private or be published to the Cosmic Feed, a discovery page built entirely from contract events and ENS records — no database. Every result clearly separates verified onchain facts from AI-generated entertainment. This is entertainment, not prediction or financial advice.
howItsMade:
ENStrology is a Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS app. Privy provides email and
social sign-in, embedded wallets, and external-wallet linking, so a user with a mainnet ENS
name can prove control of it from any linked wallet. viem handles all chain access: ENS
ownership and registration data are read from mainnet via The Graph's ENS subgraph with an
RPC fallback to registrar events, while every write happens on Ethereum Sepolia — the app
never sends a mainnet transaction.
A Solidity payment contract, built and tested with Foundry, accepts 0.01 demo USDC, prevents
replay, and emits purchase and visibility events. The Cosmic Feed is built from those
events plus ENS resolution, so the contract — not a database — is the source of truth for
what is public.
ENSv2 does the security work. Each reading is created as an expiring, non-transferable
subname in the Oracle's own namespace using the Permissioned Registry, with records stored
on a Permissioned Resolver. Because Enhanced Access Control scopes roles per name rather
than per record key, verified facts and AI content are deliberately split across two sibling
names: the Oracle is granted the Set Text role, as Manager only, on the horoscope name
alone. It holds no role on the facts name and no Admin rights anywhere, so it cannot grant
itself more. Attempting to write outside its scope reverts onchain, and the owner can revoke
the role at any time. The Oracle publishes its own purpose and endpoint as agent-context
and agent-endpoint records on its ENS name, following the ENS agent-record convention.
Horoscope text is generated with the Vercel AI SDK from verified structured facts only — the
model never chooses the name, the date, the payment, or the owner.

name: Web3WAGMI Terminal
description: A crypto terminal whose on-chain desks run on The Graph, with an assistant that shows its work.
projectDescription:
Web3WAGMI Terminal is a live crypto market terminal: around thirty desks covering price, funding, open interest, options, exchange flow, on-chain liquidity, ownership, fees and revenue, yields, unlocks and gas. It is public, free, and needs no wallet or login.
The Graph runs the on-chain half, and every reading it powers answers a question no aggregator already answers.
The flagship one is absorption. Exchange netflow is a standard metric that everybody publishes. Nobody publishes whether the market can actually absorb what just arrived. The deposits come from the Token API as indexed balance history across fourteen labelled exchange wallets. The liquidity that would have to take the other side comes from a Uniswap v3 subgraph through the decentralised gateway. Two Graph products, and neither answers the question alone.
The second is composability shown rather than described. One literal GraphQL string is sent unchanged to nine Messari standardized subgraphs and every one of them answers, because they share a schema: a lending market, a DEX and a staking protocol all reply to the same request. The same string sent to Uniswap v3, which does not share it, is rejected by the gateway, and the panel shows that rejection as the measured cost of a bespoke schema. That shared schema also yields a reading no fee aggregator publishes, because only a shared schema defines supply side and protocol side as separate fields: the share of fees each protocol keeps rather than pays out. Aave v3 keeps 12%, Curve 52%, MakerDAO 88%.
The fee board extends that to the whole market, and opening a row shows ninety days of fees, the chains they actually came from, and who holds the protocol's token, read from the Token API. Uniswap v4 took $107m in fees over thirty days and kept none of it. Lighter's token is 65% held by ten addresses; Aave's is 43%.
An assistant answers in plain language using tools that read the terminal's own routes, so it cannot quote a figure the terminal cannot show, and it names which desks it read so the answer can be checked. It describes conditions and never recommends a trade.
howItsMade:
Next.js 16 App Router, React 19, TypeScript strict, Tailwind v4, standalone output on CapRover behind Cloudflare. Every upstream is read server side and cached per route, so traffic never multiplies cost: a route with a revalidate window costs the same for one visitor as for a thousand.
Seven Token API endpoints. Historical balances and native balances drive the exchange flow desk. Holders and tokens give ownership concentration, since ten addresses holding a large number is not concentration until you divide by circulating supply. Hyperliquid open interest, liquidations and platform volume give the on-chain perp venue. Open interest is taken in contracts rather than dollars, because notional rises with price and would label every rally as new longs.
The decentralised gateway serves a Uniswap v3 subgraph for pool liquidity, and nine Messari standardized subgraphs for the cross-protocol panel. Adding a tenth standardized protocol is one line: an id.
The AI layer is an OpenAI-compatible tool loop with a primary gateway, a fallback, and key rotation. The hard part was never wiring up a model. It had a sign convention backwards twice. A coin arriving on an exchange is bearish and a stablecoin arriving is bullish, and it had that inverted; separately it called short covering downward pressure, when shorts buying back is upward. Both fixes were the same. Every reading now carries its interpretation decided in code and handed to the model with the number, so the model composes the sentence and never the conclusion.
Details worth mentioning. The Token API's canonical host is unreachable from some regions, so the client resolves between it and the Pinax host at runtime and the payload names which one answered. The holders endpoint returns 500 intermittently on the largest tokens, so it retries three times, because losing the ownership read to one unlucky request wastes the most valuable thing the Token API gives this terminal. Multichain flow was built, measured and deliberately not shipped: on Base those labelled wallets hold airdrop dust, on Arbitrum only four of fourteen hold anything material, so the desk states its single-chain scope in its own header instead of implying coverage it does not have.
With no Graph key at all the app still runs. The flow desk falls back to archive JSON-RPC and the payload says which source answered.

name: Envoyage
description: Hire a Uniswap v4 keeper without handing it your position. Scoped permission, not blanket approval.
projectDescription:
To let a bot compound your Uniswap v4 position today, you call approve(keeper, tokenId).
That says WHICH position the keeper may touch. It says nothing about WHAT it may do.
v4 makes this sharper than it sounds. Liquidity management goes through one entrypoint,
modifyLiquidities(bytes actions), and that bytes payload is an action array — a small
language with 26 opcodes. Restricting a keeper to "may only call modifyLiquidities"
restricts nothing, because that function is itself an interpreter. We traced all 26
opcodes to file and line: four of them (TAKE_PAIR, TAKE, SWEEP, MINT_POSITION) take a
recipient address straight from the caller. So an approved keeper can assemble
DECREASE_LIQUIDITY + TAKE_PAIR(..., its own wallet) and nothing on chain objects. That
is the Code4rena Revert Lend H-04 class, and the shape behind the ~$17M Aperture
Finance drain.
Envoyage inverts who writes the instructions. The keeper never sends calldata — it
calls compound(mandateId, minFee), two integers. Envoyage assembles the v4 action array
itself, with the recipient as a constant in code. Misuse is not rejected by a check;
there is no field in which to express it.
A mandate carries what an approval cannot: a fee cap in basis points of harvested fees
(never of the position), a fee recipient pinned at grant time, a cooldown, an expiry,
and a check that the position has not changed hands. Revocation is immediate.
Each mandate is also published as an ENSv2 subname, so anyone can resolve it in any ENS
client and read the exact scope — without visiting our app or trusting our frontend.
howItsMade:
Solidity 0.8.26 on Sepolia, Foundry throughout. The contract is immutable by
construction: no proxy, no admin, no upgrade path, no delegatecall, and no function
that accepts bytes or an address target. That is a security property, not an omission —
a contract aggregating many owners' approvals is a more attractive honeypot than those
approvals left scattered, so we assert it against the DEPLOYED BYTECODE rather than the
source: the runtime contains no DELEGATECALL, SELFDESTRUCT or CALLCODE, and no
arbitrary-call selector resolves. The opcode scanner skips PUSH immediates so a
constant containing 0xf4 isn't misread, and it carries a negative control that runs the
same scan over a contract which does contain DELEGATECALL — a scanner that finds
nothing proves nothing until you know it can find something.
We started with an integration spike against real v4-periphery before writing any
protocol code, which is how we learned INCREASE_LIQUIDITY rejects a caller without
ERC-721 approval. That failure is the architecture: the authority has to live
somewhere, so the question is never whether someone holds it but who. Envoyage holds
it, and Envoyage cannot be told what to do with it.
There is deliberately no swap leg, for two independent reasons: PositionManager does not
dispatch swap actions at all, and without a swap compound has no price, so no value can
leak through one. Uniswap reached a related conclusion itself, deprecating the
FROM_DELTAS variants as "vulnerable to sandwich attacks".
Testing is 38 tests. The exploit replay is paired: every attack runs against NaiveUtils,
a comparator built vulnerable exactly as Revert V3Utils was, AND against Envoyage —
because a test showing we merely lack the vulnerable function is a tautology. The same
H-04 back-run steals 4.757902903361556095 token0 from the comparator and cannot be
encoded against us. The invariant suite fuzzes the keeper as an adversary over 12,800
calls; its anti-vacuity guard sits in a deterministic test rather than in
afterInvariant(), because Foundry evaluates invariants against the initial state and
afterInvariant reads handler counters at their post-setUp values — both placements
would have passed while proving nothing.
ENSv2 (Sepolia beta) is where a mandate becomes publicly readable. We registered
envoyage.eth through the ETH Registrar's commit-reveal flow, deployed our own
UserRegistry via VerifiableFactory, and pointed the parent at it. A separate
EnvoyageNames contract mirrors mandates into subnames — separate on purpose, since
Envoyage is already deployed and immutable, and a mirror must never require edits to
what it mirrors. Every function on it is permissionless because it reads the truth out
of Envoyage rather than taking it from the caller, which is the same shape as the
contract it mirrors. The keeper is granted authorizeTextRoles on exactly one text key,
envoyage:lastRun; writing any other key reverts EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles. That is
the same division the contract's gate enforces — the owner sets the scope, the keeper
touches only what cannot change it — expressed on a second substrate.
Everything ENSv2 was transcribed from verified Etherscan ABIs, not from tutorials, and
that mattered: findTokenId is NOT keccak256(label) — the registry masks the low 32 bits
for versioning, so a locally computed id addresses a name nobody resolves through, and
it fails silently rather than reverting.
Also shipped: a subgraph indexing the granted scope alongside actual behaviour (most
tooling can only index what a keeper did, because what it was allowed to do doesn't
exist on chain), a reference keeper bot verified compounding unattended on Sepolia, and
a web UI reading live state over two independent RPC operators with no backend or
indexer — two operators rather than several keys from one provider, because keys from a
single provider share a failure domain and the fallback never actually fails over.

name: DeSci Proof Notebook
description: Privacy-first research proof tool anchoring local file fingerprints on Base Sepolia.
projectDescription: DeSci Proof Notebook is a privacy-first research proof tool for students, scientists, and independent researchers. It computes a SHA-256 fingerprint of a research file locally in the browser, then anchors that fingerprint, the creator address, a timestamp, and only the user-selected public title and note on Base Sepolia. The original CSV, image, or experiment file never leaves the user's device. Anyone can later upload the same original file to verify that its fingerprint matches the onchain proof, while the public history view lets people inspect available proof records without connecting a wallet.
howItsMade: DeSci Proof Notebook is a bilingual web application hosted on GitHub Pages. It uses the browser Web Crypto API to compute SHA-256 locally, so the original file is never uploaded. The frontend connects to MetaMask on Base Sepolia and calls a Solidity smart contract that stores each fingerprint with the creator, block timestamp, public title, and optional public note. Read-only RPC calls allow verification and public proof-history lookup without a wallet. The contract source is verified on Base Sepolia. A Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow was built and successfully simulated with synthetic data to produce a commitment for a public file hash and private policy label. ChatGPT/Codex assisted implementation, documentation, bilingual copy, debugging, and UI iteration.

name: OECL
description: Verified evidence infrastructure for Ethereum agents and protocol composition research.
projectDescription: OECL is an evidence infrastructure layer for Ethereum protocol research. It turns standardized live blockchain observations into machine-readable EvidenceReceipts that downstream agents, research systems and composition engines can admit or reject deterministically. During ETHOnline, OECL extended its pre-existing scientific laboratory with a standardized ERC-8004 observation pipeline powered by The Graph across Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain, Polygon and Monad. Each observation is independently checked against chain state before OECL classifies it as ADMISSIBLE, REJECTED or INCOMPLETE. Verified protocol presence is deliberately kept separate from compatibility or composition claims.
howItsMade: OECL’s ETHOnline extension is built primarily in TypeScript with Next.js and React. A single standardized GraphQL query is reused across five Agent0 ERC-8004 mainnet deployments through The Graph. For each observation, OECL preserves indexed-block provenance and independently queries the corresponding chain through JSON-RPC, checking chain identity, block hash, Identity Registry runtime code and sampled agent ownership. A pure deterministic admission engine then maps available evidence to VERIFIED/ADMISSIBLE, MISMATCH/REJECTED or INCOMPLETE. Each result is exposed as a machine-readable EvidenceReceipt through an API and the web interface. The existing OECL V2.1 scientific corpus remains separate and deterministic; live evidence does not rewrite prior conclusions.

name: DeFiCat
description: DeFiCat: Telegram ENS agent. The Graph lookups, buy now or on drop, pay with x402.
projectDescription:
ENS data is public, but acting on it from chat is still painful: is kikoulol.eth free, who owns degen.kikoulol.eth, when does a name expire, can I buy it now, or sit on a taken name until it drops?
DeFiCat is a Telegram agent for that loop. You ask in chat. The Graph is the read path: owner, expiry, and grace, for second-level names and subnames. ENS is the write path: if the name is available, the agent quotes then registers it (commit/reveal) from its own mainnet wallet, under a budget cap and a chat allowlist. If it is taken or over budget, you can arm a watch: Temporal waits until the name is eligible and the worker buys it without asking again.
Lookups and quotes stay free. Spending is gated: Sign-In with Ethereum binds your Telegram chat to a wallet, you confirm an exact phrase, then you pay a service fee with x402 (1 USDC to buy now, 10 USDC to schedule the drop). The fee is USDC on Base Sepolia; the registration gas is ETH on mainnet from the agent. After payment, the agent auto-runs the intent: register now, or start the watch.
This ETHGlobal Online 2026 demo targets The Graph and ENS. Paid DeFi services (swaps and the rest) are the same payment rails later, not this build.
howItsMade:
Two packages: a NestJS agents process (Telegram + HTTP + Temporal worker) and a Next.js UI for SIWE and x402.
The bot is hexagonal. Domain rules (ENS label policy, budget, payment SKUs) never import Nest, viem, or LangChain. Telegram is a driving adapter; The Graph ENS subgraph is the lookup adapter (including subnames with no registrar row); viem talks to ETHRegistrarController for quote, commit, wait, re-quote, register. LangGraph tools (lookup_ens, purchase_ens, schedule_ens) cannot skip the gate: the LLM never chooses who may spend.
Scheduled buys cannot live in bot memory. A second process polls Temporal. The bot only arms/cancels; the worker signs months later. Same EOA, so one worker (one nonce). Dev default is an in-memory scheduler that records watches and buys nothing.
Telegram has no HTTP 402, so payment mirrors SIWE: the agent issues a one-shot token, the UI pays, the agent verifies with the public x402 facilitator, then replays the paid intent. Split-chain on purpose: SIWE + ENS on mainnet (CHAIN_ID), USDC x402 on Base Sepolia. Treasury is the same EOA as AGENT_PRIVATE_KEY. Hacky-but-intentional: exact confirmation phrases, fail-closed payment (the UI never tells the agent “paid”), and Temporal memos as the source of truth for watches instead of a second database.

name: NameGate
description: Tokenized bond on Hedera using ENSv2 subnames (roles, expiry, resolver records) as its KYC layer
projectDescription:
NameGate is a tokenized bond on Hedera where an investor's ENS name is the compliance layer, not a database entry. Each investor holds a subname on ENSv2, Sepolia. The issuer writes their KYC status, jurisdiction, accreditation expiry, and lock-up date onto that name as permission-scoped resolver records, not plain text anyone could edit. A permissionless beacon contract reads the name on-chain and ships the state to Hedera over Chainlink CCIP, where the bond's control list checks it before every transfer and coupon payout.
Investor A gets paid. Investor B's transfer reverts with a reason string pulled straight from their ENS record, so you can point at the name and see exactly why. The issuer can't forge either side: they hold exactly one key on the name, the investor holds the rest, and one investor's KYC field is permanently locked against the issuer to prove that actually holds.
Keeping compliance data outside the token isn't new; ERC-3643 and ONCHAINID already do versions of it. What's different here is the identity substrate: a human-readable, user-held name with role-scoped write access instead of an opaque identity contract, checkable by anyone who knows how to read an ENS record.
howItsMade:
Identity lives on ENSv2 (Sepolia): a custom UserRegistry issues non-transferable investor subnames pointing at a Permissioned Resolver, with Enhanced Access Control scoping exactly who can write which field. authorizeTextRoles grants the issuer a per-key role instead of a blanket write role, and ROLE_SET_RESOLVER is withheld so an investor can't repoint their own name to forge a record.
A permissionless beacon contract on Sepolia reads the resolver's text records on-chain and forwards them to Hedera in the same transaction over Chainlink CCIP, so there's no off-chain relayer asserting what a record says. On Hedera, a Mirror contract implements Asset Tokenization Studio's own IExternalControlList extension point, plugged into the bond through its factory, not a fork.
ATS's bond can declare and calculate a coupon but has no payout function at all, so we wrote a roughly 60-line CouponDistributor gated by the same control list the bond checks for transfers, plus a Hedera Schedule Service integration (ScheduleCreateTransaction with waitForExpiry) so a coupon can settle itself with no keeper.
Privy runs the operational side: investors connect through embedded wallets with no seed phrase, and the issuer's own automation runs through an organization wallet whose policy restricts it to exactly two contract addresses, backed by a 2-of-3 key quorum in front of it.
The most notable hacky bit: HBAR is 8-decimal tinybar inside the EVM, not the 18-decimal weibar the JSON-RPC relay reports externally, a documented 10^10 gap a local Hardhat network can't reproduce. Our first live payout reverted because of it; we now assert that exact gap in a regression test. Two more real bugs turned up the same way: an orphaned control list from a prior redeploy that silently blocked every transfer, and a stale per-key grant that survived a lock/unlock cycle. 194 tests total, 49 of them running live against Sepolia and Hedera testnet.

prizes.rawText: Hedera -  Tokenization of Anything

name: PayRail
description: AI accounts-payable agent that verifies suppliers and pays invoices in USDC on Arc
projectDescription:
PayRail is an agentic accounts-payable rail for wholesale B2B.
An invoice arrives the way it does today, as an EDI 810 or a PDF. The buyer's AP agent parses it, three-way matches it against the purchase order and goods receipt, and resolves the supplier from an ENS name whose text records hold the supplier's USDC address on Arc, payment terms, and early-pay discount. Before the first payment, the agent checks that the supplier's agent is backed by a verified human through World ID.
Payment runs from a Privy server wallet with policies set by the finance team: a recipient allowlist derived from ENS, a per-invoice cap, a daily cap, and a 2-of-3 human approval for anything above the cap. Small invoices pay themselves. Large ones wait for two signatures in the dashboard.
On the supplier side, every approved invoice becomes a receivable token on Arc. A supplier waiting on net-60 terms can sell it into a USDC early-pay pool at a discount priced by days to due date and get paid today. Pool depositors earn the discount when the buyer settles.
The whole rail is exposed as an MCP server, so any agent can submit, approve, pay, or finance an invoice with a single tool call.
Built by a team that ships B2B order and invoice integrations for a living. The fixtures, the matching rules, and the payment terms are the real thing, not a toy.
howItsMade:
One monorepo, four packages.
Contracts are Solidity with Foundry, deployed to Arc testnet where USDC is the native settlement asset. InvoiceRegistry tracks the lifecycle from Submitted through Approved to Paid or Financed to Settled. ReceivableToken is an ERC-721 minted to the supplier on approval; owning the token is the right to be paid. EarlyPayPool is a USDC vault that buys receivables at a discount and collects face value when the buyer pays, with the registry forwarding payment to whoever holds the token.
The agent is Node 22 and TypeScript. Invoice parsing uses Claude with structured output to turn X12 810 segments and PDF text into a canonical invoice JSON, followed by a deterministic three-way match. Supplier resolution reads ENSv2 subnames and text records on Sepolia with viem. Human verification checks a World ID Selfie Check proof stored at supplier onboarding. Payment goes through Privy server wallets: the policy engine enforces allowlist and caps before signing, and an approver quorum handles anything above threshold. The supplier's agent runs on a Circle Agent Wallet so two companies with two wallet stacks can share one rail.
The dashboard is Next.js with Privy React for buyer login and World IDKit for supplier onboarding. The MCP server exposes six tools over stdio and is published as a Bazantic recipe. A Graph subgraph indexes registry and pool events so the agent can answer questions like what is due this week without scanning the chain.
Hacky bit worth mentioning: the ENS text records are the policy source. The Privy allowlist is regenerated from resolved ENS records, so adding a supplier is a name registration, not a config change.

name: Batas
description: An agent runs your 1inch Aqua position under limits it cannot widen and a name you can revoke.
projectDescription:
1inch Aqua is a shared liquidity layer where the maker never deposits anything. Tokens stay in their own wallet, Aqua keeps a ledger of allowances, and it pulls directly from that wallet at settlement. That removes custody risk and concentrates a different one, because Aqua.pull() checks nothing beyond msg.sender. Whichever app the maker ships to may take their tokens. The entire security model is one sentence: you trust the app you ship to. Hand that app to an autonomous agent and the question gets sharp — what stops it, and where is the stop enforced? Most agent tooling answers "in the application layer", which means nowhere, because anyone can call the contract directly and skip your checks.
Batas answers with a mandate: a size cap, a floor price, and an expiry.
The mandate IS the Aqua strategy. Aqua.ship() hashes the strategy bytes you hand it, and Batas passes the encoded mandate as those bytes, so the mandate hash and the strategy hash are the same value. The terms are not metadata attached to the position — they are its identity. An attacker can compile a program with the limits removed, but that is a different strategy hash, and the maker never shipped a token to it.
The limits are checked in the two places that gate the money. BatasApp validates them before AQUA.pull(), because after pull() the tokens have already left. And PolicyEnvelope, a new SwapVM instruction at third-party opcode slot 0x21, wraps the rest of the program: it delegates to runLoop() and inspects the settled registers when that returns. Placed first it is the outermost frame, so a fee appended behind the curve cannot push the amounts back out of bounds after the guard has passed, and in exactOut mode — where the input is only final once the curve has run — placement stops being something a program author can silently get wrong. It costs 975 gas.
What that is worth, measured rather than asserted: the same attacker against the same reserves, twice. Under a mandate, two trades at an average rate of 1.662 and 83% of the position still there. With no mandate, sixty-four trades at 0.270 — a seventh of where the pool opened — and it is gutted. Every one of those was an ordinary constant-product swap that no application-layer check was there to stop.
A second instruction at slot 0x22 makes the kill switch binding. The agent's authority is an ENSv2 subname: expiring, with the expiry compiled into the program's own deadline; revocable, because the grantor keeps ROLE_UNREGISTER; soulbound, because ROLE_CAN_TRANSFER_ADMIN is withheld. MandateName reads that registry during settlement, so revoking the name reverts the swap for every caller rather than only stopping an agent polite enough to ask. agent/killswitch.mjs --prove demonstrates it live: quote the position, revoke, quote again and get MandateNameNotHeld from a caller that has never heard of ENS, re-grant, and the position comes back at the same price.
The agent reads the live position, derives its floor from measured price movement rather than a constant, compiles the SwapVM program itself, checks its bytes against the deployed router's hash before shipping, and publishes the grant to Hedera Consensus Service. Run with --watch it keeps running the position: it renews inside the expiry window, docks the mandate it replaces, and stops acting the moment the name is revoked without needing to be restarted by the person who just stopped it.
A paid x402 endpoint on Hedera sells the one answer a counterparty cannot assemble alone: the decoded terms, the consensus timestamp on which those exact bytes became public, and the ERC-8004 identity behind the position with a check that it is held by the address that granted the mandate. Three of the four questions are free, deliberately — an agent should be able to refuse a position for nothing. agent/counterparty.mjs is that second agent: it finds the service through the host's own x402 discovery manifest, asks the free questions, walks away for free from a position it does not like, and pays a tenth of a cent only when a real doubt remains. Then it trades, and writes what it saw into ERC-8004's reputation registry — sixty basis points above the floor the mandate advertised. The registry refuses feedback from the agent's own owner, which is what makes that number worth reading.
Everything is live on Sepolia and Hedera testnet, and the repository is held to it: a README suite walks the document and asks the chain about every address, transaction, topic and timestamp it points at, and a deployment check compares the bytecode on Sepolia against this repository's build byte for byte.
howItsMade:
Solidity 0.8.30 with Foundry, via_ir, pinned to forge 1.8.0. Contracts: a Mandate struct and library, BatasApp (an Aqua application), PolicyEnvelope and MandateName (two new SwapVM instructions), and BatasRouter, a redeployment of SwapVM carrying both. Nothing in node_modules/@1inch/** is edited; the 1inch track permits redeploying a modified SwapVM. Off chain it is Node 24 and viem, an Express service on Vercel Functions, and an MCP server over stdio.
Two things about extending SwapVM that were learned the hard way. Extend AquaOpcodes, not Opcodes: the full set carries 24 instructions an Aqua strategy never reaches for, including every balance instruction, because in Aqua mode balances come from Aqua rather than from bytecode — carrying them puts the router at 28,618 bytes against EIP-170's 24,576 and it cannot be deployed at all. And not OpcodesDebug either, which overrides _runOpcode without re-declaring it virtual, so it is terminal: you can have custom opcodes or debug opcodes, not both.
The hacky part worth mentioning is the guard's own argument handling. InstructionArgs.at is a raw calldataload and 1inch documents plainly that the library does no bounds validation. For a fee or a curve that is a fair trade, because a misparse produces a visibly wrong price. For an instruction whose job is to refuse it produces a guard that passes, which is silent by construction: a PolicyEnvelope declaring sixteen argument bytes instead of thirty-two reads its floor out of the next instruction's bytes, and one that is last in the program reads past order.data entirely. Both instructions check their length. That finding is written up in UPSTREAM.md as a documentation suggestion for swap-vm.
A fuzz of 2000 runs compares the two enforcement surfaces on all five terms — it used to hold expiry and feeBps fixed, which excused the two most able to disagree, and unfixing them found a real one-second disagreement at the expiry boundary: SwapVM's Deadline is block.timestamp <= deadline and BatasApp was <, so for one second a mandate authorised a trade through the VM and refused it through the app.
Hedera: x402 through the Blocky402 facilitator, priced in HBAR first because an HTS token must be associated with an account before it can be received. A caller already associated with the project's HTS token, Batas Inspection Credit, can pay in it instead, and that settlement assesses the token's fixed custom fee on the ledger; a 1% fractional fee was tried first and assessed nothing, because Hedera does not charge a fractional fee on a credit to the fee collector. Note that the official Hedera x402 proof of concept points its testnet config at x402.org and reaches for Blocky402 only on mainnet; Blocky402 does serve hedera:testnet, at api.testnet.blocky402.com, whose /supported sits at the root rather than under /v1. Copy the PoC as-is and you settle through the wrong facilitator with everything appearing to work. Grants and revocations are both published to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, readable by anyone with no account, because a ledger carrying only grants is the optimistic half of the story.
ENSv2 on Sepolia, through a UserRegistry proxy deployed by ENS's own VerifiableFactory. The registry's token id is the labelhash with its low 32 bits cleared — those hold a version counter it bumps on re-registration — so a plain keccak256(label) asks about a token that does not exist, and the zero address that comes back reads as revoked rather than as a wrong question. The off-chain reader calls findTokenId instead; the on-chain instruction hands keccak256(label) to getState, which strips the version bits itself — and getState is where the previous router was wrong: its interface listed the registry's State struct in documentation order rather than declaration order (status, expiry, latestOwner, tokenId, resource), so every settlement against a named mandate reverted while every test passed, because the mock matched the interface. A fork test now asks the deployed registry, and the router was redeployed. Revocation also sets a name's expiry to the moment it happened rather than zeroing it, so a name the owner pulled and one that ran out are indistinguishable by timestamp; ownership is checked before expiry, because burning clears the owner and lapsing does not.
ERC-8004 identity and reputation, both on Sepolia. Two addresses circulate for these registries and the ones in most write-ups hold code on mainnet only, reading as empty on Sepolia — which looks exactly like a correct address for an unregistered agent. The reputation registry needed the same care: the address that circulates begins 0x8004B663056e9e57 and the live one begins 0x8004B663056A597D. What settles it is that getIdentityRegistry() on it answers with the identity registry this project already uses. The registration is a data: URI rather than a hosted link, because the point of an identity registry is that the answer survives.
The service is described in formats other software already reads, all generated from one route table: /openapi.json (OpenAPI 3.1, with the free/paid split as an x-cost per operation), /.well-known/agent-card.json (an A2A Agent Card), and POST /mcp (the same four tools over Streamable HTTP). With BATAS_ATTEST_KEY set, the paid answer carries an EIP-712 attestation over its own canonical JSON. GET /v1/position/health joins the live position to its mandate — headroom to the floor, every settlement since the ship, and alert codes — and the page shows it as a "This morning" panel.
Two implementation notes on reading chains that cost real time. Aqua's Shipped event indexes nothing at all — maker, app, strategy hash and strategy bytes all sit in the data — so a node cannot filter it and every consumer sifts client-side. And ethereum-sepolia-rpc.publicnode.com fronts a pool whose backends do not all hold the same receipts: asked eight times for a transaction demonstrably on the canonical chain, it answered seven, which turned the README suite red with a false claim about the chain. Measured five calls each before switching to rpc.sepolia.ethpandaops.io, which was 5/5 up at 532ms against publicnode's 4/5 at 1680ms.

name: Karwan
description: An open trade market with reputation, protected USDC payments and trade finance.
projectDescription:
Karwan helps freelancers, businesses and clients trade with people they meet online. Users can find opportunities in its marketplace or bring an agreement from a conversation on WhatsApp, Instagram, X or another platform.
A deal brings together the agreed terms, delivery milestones, counterparty history and payment status. Buyers fund protected USDC payments, sellers submit their work, and both parties can follow the agreement through delivery and settlement. Completed trades contribute to a verifiable track record that users can share with future counterparties.
The problem extends beyond payment. Someone finding a client through social media often has little evidence to judge whether that person will deliver or pay. Karwan connects that evidence to the actual agreement and its outcome. Its trade-finance direction builds on these records to help businesses seek funding against invoices and purchase orders.
The current application runs on Arc Testnet. Imported ratings from freelance platforms and unrestricted access to financing are not claimed as available features.
howItsMade:
Karwan uses Next.js, React and TypeScript for the interface, a Hono backend, PostgreSQL for durable workflows, and Solidity contracts for USDC escrow and milestone settlement on Arc Testnet. Circle wallet infrastructure supports email-based accounts, while external wallet users can connect their own wallets. CCTP handles supported cross-chain USDC routes.
The existing marketplace, settlement contracts and reputation system form the foundation. Our ETHOnline work extends it with shareable deal invitations, explicit acceptance of versioned terms, human-linked agent research allowances, and delivery-evidence checks.
The World AgentKit integration uses signed challenges and AgentBook lookups to associate research access with a human identity. Switching agents does not create a fresh allowance. A Chainlink CRE workflow checks GitHub delivery against agreed criteria, including the exact commit, merge status and required checks from a trusted GitHub App. Its report targets a separate evidence registry that holds no funds.
Delivery evidence and payment authority remain separate. An evidence result does not itself authorize payment. Durable invitation claims, replay checks and payout reconciliation address duplicate requests and interrupted operations.

name: AgentProof
description: AgentProof is a developer SDK and safety runtime that sits between an AI agent and execution layer.
projectDescription:
AgentProof — a spending limit an AI agent cannot talk its way around.
The problem. People are starting to give AI agents real wallets — trading bots, treasury agents, autonomous buyers. An agent is not a program you can audit ahead of time; it decides what to do at runtime, and anything it reads can change its mind. A web page, a tool response, a token's own metadata can carry a hidden instruction ("send everything to 0xattacker") and the agent will follow it politely. It can also just be wrong: hallucinate a price, misread a field, swap 250 USDC when you said 100.
Today "agent safety" almost always means a wrapper — code in the agent's own process that looks at what the agent says it wants to do and refuses the bad ones. That fails exactly when it matters, because the thing being restrained is the same process doing the restraining. If the agent is compromised, it skips the wrapper and signs directly.
What we built. AgentProof splits enforcement into two layers that fail independently.

An SDK and HTTP API (npm i @agentproof/sdk, or POST /v1/verify from any language). Three lines in your agent: describe the transaction, get a verdict, stop if it's denied. Seven policy types run per action — allowlist, max per transaction, daily spend, minimum balance, approval threshold, pool liquidity, and unlimited-approval detection. It decodes real Uniswap v4 Universal Router calldata down to worst-case outflow, so a swap that advertises 1 USDC but authorises 250 is priced at 250. Anything it can't decode returns UNBOUNDED and is blocked rather than guessed at. When a transaction is large enough that the owner wanted a say, the HTTP request is held open until a human answers — the agent is genuinely stopped, not notified — and if nobody answers, it's denied. Silence is never consent.
An on-chain hook (ERC-7579 module inside the agent's own smart account). This is the part that actually holds. It re-checks the limits inside the wallet at signing time, so it applies whether or not the agent ever called us.

The point of the whole design: the SDK is advice and we assume it will be bypassed. The hook is the guarantee. Our headline test involves no SDK at all — it installs the hook on the ERC-7579 reference account, sends a validly signed UserOperation through a real EntryPoint v0.8, and the account refuses it. No funds move.
Who it's for. Anyone shipping an agent that can move money: DeFi trading agents, x402-paying agents that buy API calls, treasury automation. The owner writes the policy once; the agent inherits limits it cannot remove — we found that out the hard way when we tried to uninstall our own hook during development and couldn't.
Everything is deployed and links to a block explorer: the hook on-chain, the agent's limits published under its ENS name so anyone can verify them without asking us, a subgraph of what the chain actually admitted, and an x402-gated API where every verification is a real settled payment.
howItsMade:
Stack: TypeScript SDK (zero runtime dependencies on the decision path), an HTTP verification API, Solidity + Foundry for the on-chain hook, solc's SMTChecker for formal verification, Next.js for the demo console. Partner tech: Uniswap v4, ENS v2, The Graph, Hedera (x402 payments).
The design rule throughout: anything off-chain is advice, and the only thing that actually stops a transaction is on-chain.
The decision path has zero dependencies. Every read the policy engine needs is an eth_call issued with fetch. viem is an optional peer dep, dynamically imported, and only if you sign — so you don't take a wallet stack's supply chain into the code that decides whether an agent may spend your money. Seven policies run per action: allowlist, max transaction, daily spend, minimum balance, approval threshold, pool liquidity, and unlimited-approval detection.
Decoding is where the real work is. A policy is only as good as its understanding of the calldata. decode/uniswapV4.ts walks a Universal Router command stream and returns worst-case outflow per currency. The trap is exact-output swaps: the interesting number is amountInMaximum, not the quote, and reading the wrong field lets a 250 USDC swap look like a 1 USDC one. Anything undecodable returns UNBOUNDED rather than a guess, and unbounded always blocks. We pinned the decoder against six real Sepolia transactions — the first run decoded all six as UNBOUNDED, because of an off-by-one in the action bytes and a wrong struct word, invisible until real calldata replaced our own self-encoded fixtures. That bug is the argument for the whole approach.
Uniswap v4 is therefore load-bearing rather than decorative: the Universal Router and PoolManager are the allowlisted targets, and a second public Uniswap subgraph feeds a pool-liquidity policy — bounding spend and bounding loss are different problems.
The hook is an ERC-7579 module on an MSAAdvanced account (reference implementation v0.3.1) driven through EntryPoint v0.8.0. The version is pinned deliberately: v0.7 predates ISenderCreator, and v0.9 gates handleOps behind tx.origin == msg.sender. We also had to match the account's actual postCheck(bytes) — selector 0x173bf7da — not the draft postCheck(bytes,bool,bytes) from the spec. That one is worth dwelling on: the mock-only version of our test suite hid it for weeks. The hook would have installed cleanly and reverted on first real execution. The mocks agreed with each other while both disagreed with reality. There is now an integration test that installs the hook on a real 7579 account and drives it through a real EntryPoint to prove it.
Formal verification with solc's SMTChecker proves MAX_TRANSFER and DAILY_SPEND hold over PolicyLib for all inputs, in about 1.3 seconds. We also compile a deliberately broken spec, PolicySpecBroken, which must produce a counterexample — that's how we know the solver is actually looking rather than trivially passing. The hook itself is fuzzed and invariant-tested, not proven, and the UI says which is which. Missing artifacts report NOT_RUN instead of passing silently.
ENS v2 carries the agent's identity as a namespace: addr to the smart account, plus text records for policy hash, hook address, and status. The EAC roles encode the trust split precisely — the owner holds ROLE_SET_POLICY_RECORD, and the agent's session key holds only ROLE_SET_STATUS_RECORD, so an agent can suspend itself and nothing else. The SDK does a three-way binding check at startup: local file, ENS record, and the hook's stored hash must agree, or it refuses to run.
The Graph indexes the hook's own SpendRecorded events, so spend history reflects what the chain admitted rather than what an agent intended. A pre-aggregated DailyAggregate entity is what keeps a policy decision fast enough for an agent's hot path. Subgraph reads are reconciled against a direct on-chain accumulator read — whichever source permits less wins — and if both are unreachable the SDK fails closed.
Hedera makes the verification service the paid product. POST /v1/verify returns 402 with payment requirements; the client partially signs a transfer; the Blocky402 facilitator co-signs as fee payer and settles; then the verdict comes back. Verify before work, settle after — callers are never charged for failed requests. Each settlement is written to an HCS topic, so an audit trail exists on infrastructure we don't control. The loop closes nicely: the payment itself is a policy-checked action, so an agent can't be talked into paying a thousand dollars for a data query by a service that simply asks for it.
Hacky bits worth mentioning
The browser can't pay, so the server pays for it. The demo console needed the x402 gate switched on to be honest, but a browser has no wallet — every check just came back 402. The console's verify route now answers the payment challenge itself with a Hedera signer, so the gate stays on and every click in the demo is a real settlement with its transaction id linked to HashScan. Nothing in the demo path is a mock or a bypass; the UI pays for its own verifications like any other caller.
We couldn't uninstall our own hook. Updating the policy on a live account means executing against the account itself, and the hook rejects any target that isn't on the allowlist — including the account. uninstallModule is withHook on MSAAdvanced, so calling it directly re-enters the same check. The agent's session key cannot remove its own guardrails, which is exactly the property we wanted, with a consequence we hadn't planned: on this account the policy is fixed for the life of the account. We shipped it that way rather than weakening the check, and wrote up both escape routes in docs/future-work.md along with why neither is free.

name: Genie Markets
description: Genie Markets is a house-funded, $USDC-denominated number prediction market.
projectDescription:
Genie Markets is a house-funded, $USDC-denominated number prediction market where users wager on digit outcomes derived from Chainlink VRF v2.5 randomness. The protocol eliminates traditional Web3 friction via Privy with gas-sponsored transactions and allows users to sign in with a Google account or email, creating a seamless Web2-like experience for non-native crypto users.
When signing in, users have to choose either a Google account/email or an external wallet. The difference is that signing in via external wallets (e.g., MetaMask) will require users to pay their own gas fees.
After users deposit $USDC funds, they can participate in five prediction types across two daily market windows:
*Market Windows:


Open Market: The open market window runs for 18 hours, allowing users to wager on Open Single, Pair, and Open Trio.


Close Market: The close market window runs for 6 hours. Users can wager on Close Single and Close Trio during the Open market window, but the window to wager on Open Single, Open Trio, and Pair officially closes at the end of the Open market window and the start of the Close market window.



Why open and close market? The open and close market allows for fun game types like the Pair.
The whole market runs for 24 hours (Open 18 hours + Close 6 hours). The market windows can be adjusted according to user preference.

*Prediction Types:


Single Digits (0–9): Derived via (digit1 + digit2 + digit3) mod 10 for a 9x payout.
E.g., 1, 2, 3 = Single 6 ((1+2+3) % 10 = 6)
Single digits are of two types: Open Single and Close Single.
Single digits are derived from Trios. (123 in the above example is a trio; more on this below).


Two Digit Pairs (00–99): Formed by combining the Open Single and Close Single outcomes for a 90x payout.
E.g., 1, 2, 3 = Open Single 6 ((1+2+3) % 10 = 6)
4, 5, 6 = Close Single 5 ((4+5+6) % 10 = 5)
The Pair becomes 65 (Open Single 6 & Close Single 5).


Three Digit Trios (000–999): High-tier jackpot markets sorted canonically under Genie Ordering math (1 < 2 < 3 < 4 < 5 < 6 < 7 < 8 < 9 < 0). While there are 1,000 raw permutations from 000 to 999, enforcing canonical sorting reduces the pool to exactly 220 unique trio combinations. These offer tiered returns across three categories:




Unique Trio (3 distinct digits, e.g., 123): 140x


Twin Trio (2 identical digits, e.g., 100): 280x


Jackpot Trio (3 identical digits, e.g., 000): 600x
There are only 10 Jackpot trios, 90 Twin Trios, and 120 Unique trios adding to 220 unique trios out of three digit trios from 000-999.
Trios are of two types: Open Trio and Close Trio. The Open Single and Close Single are derived from the Open Trio and Close Trio.


Hence, the five prediction types are: Open Single, Close Single, Open Trio, Close Trio, and Pair.


*Genie Market Round Flow

Users wager on singles, trios, and pairs.
First, the Open market is settled by Chainlink VRF. It returns a 3-digit number (e.g., 123)—this is the Open Trio. Based on this, the Open Single is derived (e.g., 6 in this case). In this step, the Open Single and Open Trio are settled.
Secondly, the Close market is settled as well by Chainlink VRF. It returns another 3-digit number (e.g., 456)—this is the Close Trio. Based on this, the Close Single is derived (e.g., 5 in this case). In this step, the Close Trio and Close Single are settled, along with the Pair (derived from Open Single + Close Single, e.g., 65).


The round settles as follows:
Open Trio 123, Open Single 6, Close Trio 456, Close Single 5, and Pair 65.

*All wagers are locked in a non-custodial smart contract escrow. Payouts are pull-based and can be claimed within 30 days of round finalization. If a randomness request hangs past a 24-hour window, a permission less emergency recovery mechanism allows any user to trigger 100% wager refunds.
howItsMade:
Genie Markets is built with a modern Web3 stack combining Solidity smart contracts, Chainlink VRF, Privy for gas sponsored transactions and sign in via google/email, and a Next.js prediction terminal.
*Smart Contracts (Solidity + Foundry):

The core protocol lives in two contracts;


"GenieMarkets.sol" is a a 5-phase round state machine (Open Betting → Open Pending → Close Betting → Close Pending → Settled) that handles betting, Chainlink VRF draw requests, settlement, claims, refunds, and bankroll management.


All $USDC interactions use Open Zeppelin's "SafeERC20" and external transfers are guarded by "ReentrancyGuard".
Winners pull their own payouts via "claimWinnings()" with in 30 rounds of round settlement.


"GenieMath.sol" is a pure library that implements the custom Genie ordering math (1 < 2 < ... < 9 < 0), canonical trio sorting, single digit derivation via modular arithmetic, and trio type classification (Unique/Twin/Jackpot).

*Frontend (Next.js + React):

The frontend uses Next.js App Router with wagmi and viem for all smart contract reads and writes. Custom React hooks encapsulate contract interaction logic. The UI is built with Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui components, and Lucide React icons.

*Chainlink VRF:

Each round makes two VRF calls; one for the Open draw, one for the Close draw. The contract extends VRFConsumerBaseV2Plus and uses VRFV2PlusClient to request randomness with 3 block confirmations. A 24-hour staleness check lets anyone call cancelStaleRound() to refund players if VRF never responds.

*Privy (Embedded Wallets + ERC-4337 Gas Sponsorship):

This was the key integration for UX. Privy creates embedded smart accounts for users who sign in with Google or email; no MetaMask, no seed phrases. All transaction gas is sponsored through a custom use-smart-transaction hook that detects embedded vs. external wallets and routes transactions accordingly. Privy is wired into 14 components/hooks across the frontend for auth gating, wallet detection, and funding flows. External wallet users (MetaMask, etc.) are also supported but pay their own gas.

*Partner technologies; Chainlink helped with VRF and Privy helped with UX.

name: Mandate
description: On-chain spending limits for autonomous DeFi agents that hold even when the agent is compromised
projectDescription:
Imagine you hire an AI agent to trade for you and tell it "only use Uniswap, and never risk more than $10,000 at a time." Normally that rule lives inside the agent itself, in its config or instructions. That's a problem, because if the agent gets hacked, tricked, or just makes a mistake, nothing stops it from breaking its own rule. This already happened in real life. In 2026 a compromised agent wallet lost about $150,000, twice. Another sent 1000 times more than it meant to after a crash. A wave of memory poisoning attacks drained an estimated $45 million from trading agents on Solana.
Mandate moves the rule outside the agent's control entirely. The owner writes the agent's limits once, as a record on ENS. The agent can read it but cannot change it. A background service copies that record onto a smart contract so it can be checked instantly. Every time the agent wants to trade, the system checks the published limit and the agent's live reputation, pulled through The Graph. Only if both check out does the trade go through, settling in real USDC on Arc. If not, no money moves. The outcome writes back to the agent's public reputation either way, so its track record builds over time instead of being guessed at.
We also built MandateGate, using 1inch's SwapVM. Instead of only checking permissions before a trade, this opcode checks them inside the swap itself, so the rule can't be skipped even by a bug elsewhere. We proved this with four real Sepolia transactions: one allowed trade that went through, one blocked trade that reverted on chain, one that only worked because we changed permissions after the contract was already live, and one against a real concentrated liquidity position instead of a simple swap. All contracts are verified and publicly viewable.
Nothing here is simulated. The agent is really registered on Sepolia, the data feeds are live, and our public server returns real answers to anyone who queries it. We've completed 9 real settlements on Arc worth $12.71, and 10 real reputation entries written by a second account, since an agent can't rate itself. One honest gap: our dashboard still uses the simpler off-chain check for its own trades. MandateGate is proven on chain but not wired into the main app yet, a real capability sitting ready rather than something clickable today.
Built for ETHOnline 2026. Submitting for ENS, The Graph, and 1inch.
howItsMade:
The app runs on Next.js and TypeScript, talking to the blockchain through Viem. The contracts are written in Solidity and built with Foundry. We run our own subgraph on The Graph, and also read from a separate public ERC-8004 subgraph on Base.
The flow: an owner writes an agent's permission limits into an ENS text record on Sepolia, using ENSv2's newer per-name resolvers. A relayer copies that record into a contract called PermissionMirror, so it can be checked instantly on chain. When a trade is proposed, we combine two live signals into one trust score, our own subgraph's sync history and the agent's real ERC-8004 reputation. No reputation yet is treated as unknown, never as zero. If the trade passes, it settles in real USDC on Arc, whose native currency is USDC itself, so it's a plain value transfer with no token contract or approval step. The result then writes back to the agent's reputation from a second account, since an agent cannot rate itself.
The part we're proudest of is "MandateGate", a custom opcode built on 1inch's SwapVM. Normally our check runs before a trade is attempted. MandateGate moves that same check inside the swap itself, so it cannot be skipped. We built it by reading the real SwapVM source directly, since the pattern we were originally told to follow does not actually exist in the codebase. We found the real one ourselves and extended 1inch's official router in code, without editing any of their files.
To prove a blocked trade really reverts on chain, we had to broadcast a transaction we already knew would fail. Foundry's own tool refuses to send anything its simulation shows will revert, so we pulled the exact transaction data it had prepared and sent it manually with a fixed gas limit, skipping that check. That got us a real, mined, failed transaction instead of just a simulated one.

name: Onchain Heartbeat
description: Live blockchain pulse narrated by an AI agent that pays for its own data over Hedera x402
projectDescription:
Onchain Heartbeat turns blockchain activity into a vital sign, and gives the AI narrating it a wallet and a name.
A circle beats in the centre of the screen. Its rhythm, amplitude and colour are driven by live Uniswap v3 swap flow on Base a slow cyan swell when the chain is quiet, fast crimson thumping when it's busy. You read the state of the chain from across the room, before anyone tells you what the numbers mean.
Every 18 seconds an AI agent buys a fresh reading and calls the play in one line of commentary. It doesn't authenticate with an API key it pays. The reading sits behind an x402 paywall: the agent gets a 402, signs an HBAR transfer, Blocky402 settles it on Hedera testnet, and only then does the data come back. One payment per narration, never batched, each individually auditable.
And it signs what it says. The narrator owns onchain-heartbeat.eth on the ETHOnline ENSv2 deployment, with avatar, description and url as text records an identity, not a label. When the chain's mood shifts, that call is published as its own subname, carrying the comment, the reading behind it, and the Hedera transaction that paid for it. Resolve any narration and you can check what the agent claimed, what it was looking at, and what that claim cost.
It addresses two gaps. Chain data is a wall of numbers you have to read to understand. And AI agents can't sign up for API keys, can't hold subscriptions, and can't prove they said anything their output is unattributable by default. This is a small, complete demonstration of the alternative, running live rather than described.
Verifiable settlement: [email protected]  confirmed on the Hedera mirror node.
howItsMade:
Stack. Next.js 16 (App Router), TypeScript, Tailwind 4, OpenAI gpt-4o-mini, viem, and the x402 v2 packages (@x402/hedera, @x402/next, @x402/fetch). Nine runtime dependencies total.
The seam. Every data source returns the same { activityLevel, label }, so the visual never knows where its number came from. That contract absorbed three swaps during the build  mock to RPC, RPC to The Graph, and one ENS deployment to another and PulseVisual.tsx never changed once. The pulse itself maps 0–100 onto three CSS custom properties (--beat, --amp, --hue) and lets CSS keyframes animate, so the heartbeat runs on the compositor rather than in JS, with @property registrations easing amplitude and hue between readings.
The Graph. A Messari standardized subgraph for Uniswap v3 on Base, queried server-side so the API key never reaches the browser. Swaps-per-minute is derived from the timestamp span of the last 500 swaps 500 rather than 100 because over a handful of integer seconds the rate quantises into coarse jumps (429, 600, 750, 1500). Thresholds were calibrated by sampling, not guessed: 341–652/min in the daytime, but 121 overnight, so the scale is logarithmic rather than linear. A linear window pinned half the day at zero and flatlined the pulse.
Hedera x402. /api/chain-data is a real metered resource behind @x402/next, and the thing it sells is the subgraph reading so the payment buys indexed data, not a receipt. The client sets a hard 0.01 HBAR per-payment ceiling, because an agent paying on a timer should have one. scripts/buy-reading.mjs lets any third party with a funded testnet account buy a reading, so the endpoint isn't a private arrangement.
ENSv2 and the hacky part. The hackathon's ENS app couldn't complete a registration, so we went straight at the contracts. None of the deployment is verified on Etherscan or Sourcify, so the ABIs were recovered by scanning PUSH4 selectors out of deployed bytecode and resolving them against a signature database, then cross-checked against a registration that had already succeeded on-chain argument order copied from a working call rather than guessed. That also isolated the app's defect: it encodes initialize's first argument as address,uint256 where the implementation expects (address,uint256)[], producing a selector that matches no function. Reported with a keyless repro (docs/ens-app-bug-report.md).
Registration is commit-reveal paid in ERC-20, not ETH. Records live on a per-name Permissioned Resolver keyed by DNS-encoded name the shared PublicResolverV2 rejects the owner for every node derivation. The per-narration subnames need no registration at all: writing records on the parent's own resolver is enough for ENSIP-10 wildcard resolution to reach them, so no CCIP-Read gateway.
Verification discipline. Every on-chain write is simulated before it's sent, and multi-step flows are checked together with eth_simulateV1 against one projected post-state which is the only way to verify a call against a resolver proxy that doesn't exist yet. Each dependency degrades instead of breaking: kill the subgraph, the facilitator, the LLM or the resolver and the pulse holds its last rate and keeps beating.

name: LP Terminal
description: Uniswap V3 LP scanner — track every position's range, status, and owner, plus pool balances.
projectDescription:
This is a Uniswap V3 liquidity position scanner built for Robinhood Chain, focused on
solving a specific gap: there's no built-in way to see every LP position in a given
pool at once. The NonfungiblePositionManager tracks positions globally by tokenId, not
per-pool, so the project builts a data pipeline that scans NFPM event logs (Transfer,
IncreaseLiquidity, DecreaseLiquidity) alongside the pool contract's own Mint events,
correlates them by transaction hash to recover tick ranges, and reconstructs each
position's price range and current owner entirely from on-chain history — no
subgraph or archive node required.
The frontend displays a live pool header (current price, token balances), a
paginated table of every position in the pool with its range and status (active
in-range, out-of-range, or closed), and a detail view for inspecting individual
positions with a visual range indicator. Data is fetched from the chain, written to
Supabase, and served to the frontend as a read-only snapshot — the UI shows exactly
which block range the data was scanned from, so it's transparent about being a
point-in-time view rather than claiming real-time accuracy it doesn't have.
howItsMade:
The stack is Next.js (React/TypeScript) for the frontend, Supabase (Postgres) for storage, ethers.js for all on-chain interaction, and uniswap-v3 sdk, targeting Uniswap V3 on Robinhood Chain.
The core technical challenge was position discovery: Uniswap's NonfungiblePositionManager tracks positions globally by tokenId, with no built-in way to query "every position in pool X." The project solved this by scanning NFPM Transfer events (filtered on mint transfers from the zero address) to enumerate all tokenIds, then reading positions() to filter by matching token0/token1/fee for our target pool.
The trickier problem was historical accuracy: calling positions() or slot0() at a specific past block requires an archive node, which our RPC provider didn't support (the project hits a "metadata not found" error mid-build). Rather than switching providers, the project rebuilts the data layer around pure event-log replay — summing IncreaseLiquidity and DecreaseLiquidity deltas to compute net liquidity per position, and correlating each NFPM mint's transaction hash with the pool contract's own Mint event to recover tickLower/tickUpper (which aren't included in any NFPM event directly). This means the entire position dataset is reconstructed from raw logs, with no archive node or subgraph dependency.
The project used @uniswap/v3-sdk for tick-to-price conversion (tickToPrice) to display human-readable price ranges instead of raw tick integers, which handles the precision/decimal-scaling correctly rather than us re-deriving the 1.0001^tick formula by hand.
Data is fetched via a standalone Node/TypeScript script (separate from the Next.js app, using a Supabase service_role key) and written to Postgres. The most "hacky but necessary" decision was scoping to a fixed, prefetched block range rather than live-fetching on every page load — this trades real-time freshness for demo reliability, and the UI is explicit about this by displaying the exact block/timestamp range the data was scanned from.

name: Botvue
description: Catches sites that answer AI crawlers with a 200 OK and nothing in it, then proves it.
projectDescription: Botvue reports when a website serves AI crawlers a different, often empty, page than it serves browsers and Googlebot, while still returning HTTP 200, so the agent has no reason to doubt it succeeded. It fetches one URL six ways at the same moment: a browser, Googlebot, and four real AI crawler user-agents (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, OAI-SearchBot). It compares the responses and classifies any difference on a five-level severity scale, from cosmetic markup residue up to prompt injection: text addressed directly to the AI reading it. Every finding carries a SHA-256 hash of the actual response body, so it can be independently re-verified rather than taken on trust. We measured 131 findings across a 567-property corpus of real news sites; the rest are clean or refuse crawlers honestly with a real 4xx, which isn't a problem since an agent that gets refused already knows it got nothing. Paid checks settle via x402 on Hedera testnet, and that settlement is independently re-confirmed against Hedera's public mirror node rather than trusted from the payment facilitator alone.
howItsMade: The core is a Python/FastAPI gateway that fetches a URL as a browser and as five bot user-agents via httpx, extracts text with trafilatura, and classifies differences with a rule-based taxonomy before mapping the worst match to a pass/flag/block decision. Paid requests are gated by x402: a 402 response carries Hedera testnet payment terms fetched live from the Blocky402 facilitator's own endpoint, never hardcoded, and after settlement we independently re-verify the transaction against Hedera's public mirror node instead of trusting the facilitator's word alone, the same verify-don't-trust discipline as the content check itself. A second adapter, an MCP server, exposes identical logic as three tools for AI agents directly, including fetch_url, a drop-in fetch-tool replacement that withholds content when it doesn't match what a human would see. A GitHub Actions cron re-scans the full corpus daily. A third-party gateway, Bazantic, independently discovered our OpenAPI spec and now prices /check on Base and USDC as a second payment rail.

name: ZubiDubi
description: Self-custodial early exit liquidity for maturing DeFi assets, priced by time, risk, and exposure.
projectDescription:
ZubiDubi is self-custodial early exit liquidity for locked, delayed redemption DeFi assets like Pendle PT tokens, LRT receipts, and vault withdrawal shares. These assets are worth full value at maturity but illiquid before it, and today holders either wait or sell off-chain at an opaque discount. Generic AMMs cannot price this correctly because they have no concept of time to maturity.
Built by modifying SwapVM itself, not wrapping it: a reusable instruction library adds oracle validation, exposure limits, and term-discount pricing as native opcodes.
Many DeFi assets are transferable but not instantly redeemable: Pendle-like Principal Tokens, LST/LRT withdrawal receipts, vault withdrawal claims, bridge receipts, and other maturing positions. Holders who need liquidity early often must wait, sell into thin markets, or accept opaque OTC/RFQ pricing. ZubiDubi creates a programmable early-exit market for those assets.
Makers publish liquidity strategies from their own wallets instead of locking funds into isolated pools. Sellers bring a maturing claim, and ZubiDubi routes the sale across makers who can actually deliver liquid USDC/WETH at that moment. The maker pays liquid tokens now and receives the maturing claim now, taking on duration and redemption risk in exchange for a discount.
The core idea is a programmable term-liquidity book: makers define risk curves based on oracle-backed value, time to maturity, inventory, liquidity depth, risk tier, and exposure limits. The route executor checks real deliverable liquidity onchain, skips insolvent makers, splits fills across the best executable strategies, and reverts if the requested trade cannot fully settle.
ZubiDubi also introduces shared term-risk budgets. A maker can assign sibling Aqua strategies to one global receipt/quote budget, so when one strategy fills, the rest lose capacity and start quoting worse prices as utilization rises. This turns wallet-held liquidity into a coordinated term-liquidity book rather than isolated strategies racing the same balance.
The deployed demo includes verified Sepolia contracts, real Sepolia WETH/USDC/LINK-backed PT-style receipt assets, Chainlink oracle pricing, a deployed Graph subgraph, a hosted solver API, and a frontend for markets, selling, making strategies, portfolio issuance/redemption, and playground proofs.
howItsMade:
ZubiDubi is built on the official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM codebases, with SwapVM extended for term-liquidity markets.
On the contract side, we modified the Aqua SwapVM router and added a reusable instruction library instead of one app-specific mega-opcode. The library has three modular instructions:
BACKING_ORACLE_CHECK: validates the receipt/quote pair, reads oracle-backed par value, enforces stale-oracle protection, maturity bounds, and optional secondary-oracle deviation haircuts.
EXPOSURE_CAP: enforces maker max receipt exposure, max quote-token notional, available liquidity, and inventory limits.
DISCOUNT_CURVE_1D: computes the executable quote using base discount, annualized term rate, convexity, risk tier, inventory pressure, and liquidity-depth penalty.
We also built ZubiDubiRouteExecutor, which is the onchain settlement layer. It receives candidate Aqua/SwapVM strategies from the solver, calls the router for quotes, checks deliverable maker liquidity as min(Aqua virtual balance, wallet balance, allowance), applies shared term-risk budget caps, sorts/fills routes, charges a DAO fee, and executes atomically. If the full route cannot be filled, the transaction does not partially settle.
The instruction library and route executor are covered by Foundry invariant and fuzz tests proving discount never goes negative or above par, payout is monotonic in time to maturity, convex discount is always at least linear discount, maker payout never exceeds the minimum of wallet balance and allowance, routes settle atomically, fees are conserved, and no maker's liquidity is double counted across sibling strategies sharing a budget.
The live Sepolia book includes multiple independent maker wallets, not just one maker publishing sibling strategies. We funded two additional maker EOAs and shipped six more live strategies across different receipt assets and payout tokens, all indexed as active on the subgraph, with the hosted solver actually routing a real request across three independently owned strategies at once. This proves genuine multi-maker competition and routing on real deployed contracts, not a single wallet simulating multiple counterparties.
For demo assets, we deployed PT-style receipt contracts on Sepolia. These are real ERC20 receipt contracts backed by real Sepolia WETH, USDC, and LINK. Users can issue claims by depositing backing assets and later redeem after maturity. For production, the same flow maps to real delayed-redemption assets such as Pendle PTs, withdrawal receipts, vault claims, or bridge receipts.
We used real Chainlink feeds and onchain ratio adapters for pricing, plus an optional Pyth adapter path for dual-oracle validation. We also added a mainnet-fork Pendle benchmark test using a real Pendle PT market, so we can compare ZubiDubi's maker curve against Pendle's implied PT pricing and show inventory-aware repricing after maker exposure changes.
The Graph is the market reconstruction layer. Our deployed Subgraph Studio endpoint indexes Aqua strategies, SwapVM fills, routed fills, skipped makers, shared term-risk budgets, receipt issuance/redemption, maker exposure, market volume, and DAO fee accrual. This lets the solver and frontend discover the live term-liquidity book without scanning raw logs.
The solver API is a hosted Node service on Railway. It queries The Graph for active strategies, decodes executable SwapVM order bytes, calls Sepolia RPC for fresh quoteExactIn checks, returns route splits and budget-pressure metadata, and builds maker strategy payloads for the frontend. The frontend is deployed on Vercel and uses Privy for wallet connection, Viem for contract calls, The Graph for indexed state, and the Railway solver API for executable quotes.
The frontend includes live markets, a swap-style sell page, maker strategy creation with an interactive curve editor where makers drag discount, cap, convexity, and exposure handles directly on the chart, backed by the same pricing math used onchain so the chart and the shipped transaction can never drift apart, portfolio issuance/redemption, and a playground page with proof panels, route-split visualizations, pressure-budget badges, test commands, and live Graph-backed state. Everything is deployed: verified Sepolia contracts, Graph subgraph, Railway solver API, and Vercel frontend.

name: Vouch
description: Identity and reputation for AI agents: ENSv2 names, indexed evidence, x402-priced lookups.
projectDescription:
Vouch makes AI agents prove what they’ve done, not just say it.
Right now any AI agent can claim anything about itself. "I’m fast. I’m reliable. I’ve done 10,000 jobs."
With Vouch, an agent can’t lie about its track record because it doesn’t control the score.
Here’s how it works:

Every agent gets a real name
When an agent registers with Vouch it gets a name under vouch.eth. It’s a real ENSv2 subname.
It can’t be sold, it expires, and it works like a credential — not an asset you flip.Tied to that name are records. But not all records are equal.
Who can write them is what matters.
The agent controls its claims. We control the proof.
The agent’s own key can update things like:
agent:endpoint, agent:capabilities, agent:price

That’s what it says about itself. But it can’t touch: agent:score, agent:disputes, agent:volume.
Only the Vouch scorer can write those. And the score isn’t made up. It’s pulled from real activity:  jobs settled, feedback from counterparties, disputes filed. All of that is indexed on-chain from Ethereum using a Graph subgraph built on the ERC-8004 registry.
And this isn’t enforced by some backend we control. It’s enforced directly by ENSv2’s Enhanced Access Control. The permission is set on each record in the agent’s own resolver.
