If the agent tries to give itself a score of "999", the transaction just fails. There’s literally no way for it to rate itself.
3. Why this matters
x402 made it easy for one agent to pay another. Great.
But it didn’t answer the real question: "Should I trust this agent with my money?" Identity tells you who they are. It doesn’t tell you if they’ve ever done the job. That’s what Vouch sells. A reputation check.
It’s an x402-paid endpoint on Hedera. About $0.001 per lookup, with 3-second finality.
Claims are free. Proof costs money. That’s the whole business model in one sentence.
4. What it looks like in practice
A buyer agent needs a seller.
It looks up 3 candidates by their ENS name, pays to check their reputation, sees one has a 60% dispute rate and drops it, then hires one of the others. No human in the loop. Later, if that hired agent messes up a job, the counterparty files a dispute on Sepolia. The subgraph picks it up, the scorer recalculates, and writes the new lower score back to the agent’s resolver. Next time a buyer checks, that agent gets skipped.
If the operator is done with the agent entirely, the name owner just revokes it and it stops resolving.
5. Three IDs, all linked

vouch.eth name = what humans use
HCS-14 Universal Agent ID = what agents use to route to each other
ERC-8004 token ID = what all the on-chain evidence is attached to
howItsMade:
The Graph doesn't index Hedera, so the project is split across two chains.
Identity and evidence on Ethereum Sepolia, payment and audit on Hedera testnet.
On the ENS side I registered vouch.eth through the ENSv2 ETHRegistrar
(commit-reveal, paid in Sepolia USDC, it rejects native ETH), deployed my own
UserRegistry proxy through the VerifiableFactory and pointed the name's
subregistry at it. Every agent gets its own PermissionedResolver, and write
access is granted per text key with authorizeTextRoles(). To make a name
non-transferable you simply don't grant ROLE_CAN_TRANSFER_ADMIN. There's no
soulbound flag.
The ENSv2 tutorial is out of date. register() takes six arguments, not the
five documented, with an undocumented registry pointer sitting between owner
and resolver. I caught that because I pull verified ABIs from Sourcify
(Blockscout as fallback) and assert every function exists before calling it.
Every write is simulated first, so a wrong role bitmap fails for free.
The subgraph indexes four contracts on Sepolia: ERC-8004's IdentityRegistry, my
VouchAttestations and VouchScoreAnchor, and my own ENS registry. I used
ERC-8004's entity shapes rather than inventing a schema, so the same query works
against any ERC-8004 deployment. A Subgraph MCP layer sits on top for
natural-language lookups.
Two things stop agents gaming their own score. An AgentCounterparty entity means
uniqueCounterparties counts distinct raters instead of attestation volume, so
colluding agents rating each other repeatedly gets them nowhere. And attest()
reverts if the caller owns the agent's ERC-8004 token.
Hedera handles the money. x402 there uses a partially-signed TransferTransaction:
the client signs, then Blocky402 countersigns as fee payer and submits, so the
buyer never pays gas or holds an API key. Every paid lookup is written to an HCS
topic as an audit trail. I used the native Hedera SDK rather than Solidity
because HCS, HTS and custom fractional fees are all native primitives, which
meant no splitter contract for the attestor revenue share.
Stack: Node 24 with native TypeScript (no build step), Express 5, Drizzle and
Postgres, Angular 22, Hardhat 3, viem.
Three things cost me real time. @x402/hedera pins @hiero-ledger/sdk to an
exact version, and installing a newer one leaves you with two copies whose
PrivateKey types don't match, so instanceof checks fail silently. @x402/core
enforces client-side spend controls that reject non-default assets, so my first
HBAR payment was refused before a payload was even built. And HCS-14 UAIDs hash
six canonical fields including nativeId, where using the ERC-8004 agentId is
circular since you need the id to register in the first place. I used the ENS
namehash instead.

name: PAI
description: AI-native agreements that structure, fuzz, accept, fund, and settle through conversation.
projectDescription: PAI is programmable agreement infrastructure for digital work. A user can describe an agreement in natural language, and PAI converts it into a structured Agreement Object, checks the terms for ambiguity and execution risk, asks for clarification when needed, and creates a canonical agreement with an immutable version and cryptographic hash. Each party independently reviews and accepts the exact same agreement before binding their wallet. PAI Core then manages the agreement lifecycle from DEFINE → ACCEPT → FUND → DELIVER → SETTLE, with an exception path for disputes and resolution. The architecture is designed to remain chain-independent: intelligence, agreement logic, acceptance and dispute workflows live in PAI Core, while settlement is handled through execution adapters. In the ETHOnline build, we demonstrate the full canonical agreement flow through READY_TO_FUND, an Arc Testnet settlement adapter, and indexed settlement history through The Graph.
howItsMade:
PAI is built as a modular TypeScript/Solidity system. The backend uses Node.js, TypeScript, Prisma and PostgreSQL, while the frontend uses React and Vite. Agreement intelligence runs through a local Qwen3 model, but the model is not trusted as the final authority: its structured extraction is followed by a deterministic Agreement Check that independently detects issues such as ambiguous currency, missing settlement assets and subjective acceptance criteria. After clarification, PAI persists a canonical agreement, creates immutable revision 1, computes a server-side SHA-256 agreement hash, and requires the CLIENT and CONTRACTOR to accept the same agreementId + agreementVersion + agreementHash tuple. Wallet ownership is then bound through the PAI Core lifecycle, progressing the agreement to READY_TO_FUND only after both parties have accepted and bound wallets.
The blockchain execution layer is separated behind adapters. For ETHOnline we built an Arc Testnet settlement adapter for USDC approval and AgreementEscrow funding/settlement transactions. Arc settlement events are indexed with The Graph into Agreement, Milestone and SettlementEvent entities, giving PAI a verifiable read model for funding and settlement history. The demo includes live Arc transaction proof and a live Graph query showing a completed agreement, released milestone and indexed transaction history. Telegram is used as a lightweight agreement interface so users can create, clarify and accept agreements without starting from a traditional dApp UI. The main architectural goal was to keep PAI Core chain-independent so future Stellar, Solana and other execution adapters can reuse the same agreement lifecycle instead of rebuilding the product for every chain.

name: Robinhood Predictor
description: AI-agent parimutuel stock prediction market with Chainlink feeds and World ID anchoring
projectDescription:
Robinhood Predictor is a parimutuel stock prediction market live on Robinhood Chain mainnet (chain ID 4663), where users bet whether a stock's closing price will land above or below its opening price. The core contract went live on July 10, two to three days after Robinhood Chain itself launched, and it's been running continuously since — 91 commits and 88 real transactions across market creation, locking, and settlement.
For ETHOnline we extended this live infrastructure with an AI agent that can place bets on its own. The agent reads live price data from Chainlink and trend signals from a Graph subgraph we built for this market, then decides whether to bet or sit out. If the two signals disagree, it holds off instead of forcing a trade.
An autonomous agent placing bets raises an obvious question: who's actually behind it? Every agent bet has to pass through World AgentKit first. The relayer checks that the wallet is backed by a real, unique human before it will sign the transaction. No valid attestation, no bet.
Settlement runs through Chainlink: the contract reads the price recorded when a market locked, compares it to the live closing price, and decides the winner on-chain. We also wrote an independent Python script that rebuilds the settlement logic from scratch, without touching our Solidity code, reruns it against every real transaction on mainnet, and seals the result with a SHA-256 hash.
Before StockPredictionMarketV2.sol ever entered git history, we ran a self-audit pass modeled on our own audit-orchestrator methodology — recon, then fix. It caught two real issues pre-commit: a receive() function that would have permanently trapped any ETH sent to it by accident, and a missing zero-address check on the relayer address in the constructor. The contract shipped already fixed. Full notes: https://github.com/pplmaverick/robinhood-stock-prediction-market/blob/824e0d67e0fe2e8ba0c96760c44905ee1ee1b3d8/verification/self-audit/AUDIT_NOTES.md
Full AgentKit feedback document: https://github.com/pplmaverick/robinhood-stock-prediction-market/blob/824e0d67e0fe2e8ba0c96760c44905ee1ee1b3d8/docs/feedback-agentkit.md
howItsMade:
The contract is Solidity, deployed on Robinhood Chain, an Arbitrum-based L2 built for stock trading, first on July 10 and still live today. Settlement is parimutuel: winners split the losing side's pool, and Chainlink price feeds decide the outcome by comparing the price at lock time to the price at close.
For ETHOnline we added a second contract, StockPredictionMarketV2, with a placeAgentBet function gated by a relayer-signed attestation — the caller supplies a signature that must recover to the relayer's address before the bet is accepted. Behind that relayer sits a small Node.js decision engine that pulls live price data from Chainlink and reads trend data from a Graph subgraph we built specifically for this market, indexing every bet and settlement event so the agent has something to reason against beyond raw price. If the price signal and the trend signal agree, the agent bets. If they disagree, it skips the market on purpose.
The part that took the most work is the World AgentKit layer sitting in front of the relayer. Before the relayer signs an agent's bet, it checks that the agent's wallet is verified as backed by a real, unique human through AgentKit. If that check fails, the transaction never gets signed. Testing the backed path fully needs a physical Orb, which we didn't have during the hackathon, so that branch is currently verified through code review and unit tests rather than a live proof — we're writing this up honestly instead of claiming we tested something we didn't.
Because the original contract already had a real transaction history before this hackathon started, we also wrote a standalone Python script that rebuilds the settlement math independently of our Solidity code, checks it against every transaction pulled from mainnet via eth_getLogs, and seals the result with a SHA-256 hash so the numbers can't be quietly edited afterward.

name: Snitch
description: Snitch: The Operating layer for Shared treasury and Onchain payments.
projectDescription: Snitch is an operating layer that helps companies manage onchain payments from a single workspace. A company can create separate accounts for different departments, projects, regions or payment flows. Each account operates independently, with its own treasury, transaction history and wallet secured through Privy. This keeps funds, payments and financial records clearly separated. Within each account, finance teams can issue invoices, receive payments, pay vendors, manage global payroll and monitor transactions from initiation to confirmation. Role based access gives each team member the appropriate level of control while restricting sensitive wallet actions, such as private key export, to authorised roles. Snitch never takes custody of company funds or private keys. Privy protects wallet access and handles key export, allowing the company to retain control of its assets while Snitch provides the operational tools and records needed to manage them.
howItsMade:
Snitch is a non-custodial payment infrastructure that never stores private keys, recovery phrases, or wallet signing material. It also cannot move company funds independently.
We use Privy as the wallet and key management layer for every Snitch account. When a company creates a new account for a department, project, region, or payment flow, Snitch provisions a dedicated wallet through Privy and connects it directly to that account’s treasury and transaction history. This allows companies to separate funds and financial activity without manually creating, securing, and managing multiple wallets.
Privy is particularly important to our non-custodial design. It handles the underlying wallet infrastructure, transaction layer for treasury, and secure key access, while Snitch operates above it as the operational layer for invoices, vendor payments, payroll, and transaction management.

name: Spawn Family
description: Robinhood Chain launchpad powered by Uniswap Hooks, fundraise via MC milestones + plugins.
projectDescription: This a token launchpad designed especially for robinhood chain, it allow creators to fundraise at specific milestones/marketcaps. We're using uniswap hooks to add smaller one-sided liquidity positions on uniswap v4. This technique allow to raise capital automatically through market growth and liquidity pool mechanics rather than traditional VC rounds or direct token sales.
howItsMade:
We use Uniswap v3(one-sided liquidity positions) in a way, that allow us to raise capital for token creators form the liquidity position(this capital can be used for various purposes we call them Plugins) without directly sell the token in the Market.
We're using Uniswap Hooks(Uniswap v4) to add liquidity positions dynamically and perform various tasks(we called it Plugins) such as, airdrop to holders, lottery etc.
Substream(The graph) is our data layer.

name: Cordon
description: Cordon helps AI teams balance performance and cost within a shared budget
projectDescription:
The problem:
AI agents can decide which tools to call, repeat failed requests, and delegate work to other agents. That flexibility makes their costs difficult to predict. A user may approve a task expecting a useful result, only to discover that the agents have exhausted the budget collecting information without completing the final output.
There is evidence that unexpected agent costs are a real engineering problem. A June 2026 research preprint catalogues 63 reported production budget-overrun incidents across 21 orchestration frameworks, including failures involving delegated work. This evidence concerns broader agent computation and orchestration costs, rather than specifically Circle marketplace payments, but it illustrates the financial consequences of poorly coordinated autonomous activity.
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04056

Delegation adds a coordination problem. If workers receive independent allowances without a shared total check, their combined purchases can exceed the owner’s intended task budget. Even when a shared limit exists, fixed worker allocations can waste available capacity: one worker may finish with money left over while another stops because its own allowance is exhausted.
Existing spending controls provide an essential foundation. Circle Agent Wallets, for example, document per-transaction, daily, weekly, and monthly limits, along with recipient restrictions. Cordon focuses on the task-management problem around those controls: how should an agent team adapt its work when the remaining budget changes?
Source: https://developers.circle.com/agent-stack/agent-wallets/wallet-operations/custom-policies

What Cordon is and how it helps

Cordon is a budget-aware companion for AI agents, designed for integration through an SDK and Model Context Protocol (MCP). Its goal is to help agents complete useful work efficiently within a shared budget while preserving the quality of the result.
The owner defines a spending mandate for a task. Agents working under that mandate share its limits, and delegated agents can only receive narrower permissions. Their spending counts against the budget above them, so delegation does not create a fresh allowance outside the owner's mandate.
Cordon checks paid-service requests and provides structured feedback when a request encounters a constraint. Our broader vision is to help agents use this feedback to choose a cheaper service, reuse available information, avoid unnecessary retries, or reserve enough budget for the remaining work. If additional spending is necessary, the agent can ask the owner for a specific exception.
The current MVP establishes the foundation with shared spending controls, recorded refusals, and owner-approved releases. Cost-aware planning and alternative-service selection are the next capabilities we aim to develop.
How we will evaluate Cordon
We will compare three approaches: direct purchasing without Cordon, a conventional shared budget with a hard stop, and Cordon. Each approach will receive the same task, starting information, service options, and output requirements.
Our main question is whether Cordon can reduce the total cost of completing a task while delivering an equally useful result. We will measure task completion, total spending, repeated or unnecessary purchases, completion time, and the number of times the owner needs to intervene. Total cost will include payment fees, gas, and any Cordon service fee.
For deterministic tasks, such as retrieving a fixed dataset or performing a calculation, we will check whether the final outputs match exactly. For research and synthesis tasks, we will evaluate accuracy, completeness, source quality, and freshness against the same checklist. We will use fixed data or aligned timestamps where needed to make comparisons fair.
We will also test difficult situations, including repeated failures, expensive services, and several agents drawing from one budget. A run that spends less because it stops early will count as incomplete, not as an efficiency improvement.
These are planned evaluations. We will make this testing result as a path for cordon continuitity towards our end goal to help  helps AI teams balance performance and cost within a shared budget
howItsMade:
Cordon is four layers where authority only flows downward — from the owner to the contract, never up from the agent.
Three Solidity contracts on Arc testnet: MandateRegistry manages the agent tree and enforces narrowing, TreeVault holds funds and performs ancestor debit (every draw charges every node up to the root), and ConductRecord publishes refusals to ERC-8004's reputation registry. No proxy, no admin key, no upgrade path.
The daemon (Node 23.6+, TypeScript, viem 2) is the only component that holds a private key. Agents call cordon_fetch(url) — the daemon reads the seller's x402 challenge, extracts price and payee from it (never from the agent), and asks the vault. There is no cordon_transfer or cordon_pay tool, and a test asserts each stays unregistered. An agent that can't express "send money to X" can't be talked into it.
Arc testnet was essential — USDC as both gas and payment token means operators hold one asset, and sub-second finality makes per-purchase on-chain enforcement affordable. Privy powers the console wallet gate with embedded wallets via createOnLogin, so owners without a browser wallet can still sign mandates. Settlement runs through Circle Gateway and x402 with EIP-3009 authorization.
The hacky bit: ancestor debit. A grandchild's $1 purchase debits $1 at every node up to the root, so headroom is always the tightest bottleneck across the whole path. We validated with 1,200 adversarial strategies across 45,360 draws — zero got past a bound. A hostile drill gave an LLM agent the daemon and told it to spend freely against a $0.02 mandate; it reached $0.007 before concentration stopped it.

name: ZeroKeyMate
description: An iPhone companion that proves your age privately and pays on Arc.
projectDescription:
ZeroKey Mate turns an iPhone into a companion that helps you act while keeping identity details private. Ask Mate for a beer. The on-device model proposes the supported order, while application code controls identity verification and payment.
The phone authenticates a physical Japanese My Number card and creates an order-bound zero-knowledge proof that the cardholder is at least twenty. The shop receives the proof, not the card certificate, signature, name, address or date of birth. A deployed Age Gate contract verifies the proof before checkout proceeds. After the user approves this exact payment, a Privy embedded wallet signs a 0.10 test-USDC authorization and the shop settles through x402 on Arc Testnet.
A physical-card purchase completed on September 13, with 12.0 seconds of local age-proof processing shown on the iPhone and a confirmed public Arc transaction. Further test payments completed, and the app links to their real explorer receipts. A DockKit stand adds the physical companion experience. The recorded demo combines actual device takes.
This is an experimental testnet build: no real money or physical delivery. Payment approval remains explicit, and the supported purchase is one configured product and store. World ID authentication, smartphone My Number card support and unattended spending permissions are not integrated.
howItsMade:
The native iOS app uses SwiftUI, Apple Foundation Models, on-device Speech, AVFoundation, DockKit and CoreNFC. The local model produces a structured purchase proposal; deterministic code checks the item, merchant, network and amount. Card fields, proof witnesses and signing interfaces are never exposed to the model. Camera capture stops before NFC begins.
The physical My Number card supplies a government-signed JPKI credential and signs a challenge bound to the order and nonce. Our Noir circuit checks the trusted root, RSA signatures, certificate validity, age of at least twenty and order expiry. ProveKit from World Foundation generates the proof on the iPhone, using a pinned experimental Groth16 backend and native Rust bridge. Identity evidence stays on the device; the shop receives the proof and public order inputs. This is not World ID authentication.
Cloudflare Workers, D1 and a Durable Object run the store, preserve order state and serialize sponsored settlements. The Worker verifies the proof with the deployed Arc Age Gate contract through two independent RPC providers before returning x402 payment requirements. Privy supplies the embedded buyer wallet and signs the exact EIP-712 USDC authorization after user approval. The merchant sponsors gas. Signed transactions are persisted before broadcast, and receipt checks bind success to the actual transfer and authorization.
A real-card certificate exposed a mandatory policy extension missing from our early fixture. We corrected both parser and circuit, regenerated matching proof artifacts and verifier, and completed the physical purchase. We also separated camera shutdown from DockKit motor commands to unblock NFC.
Age verification is an eth_call enforced by the Worker, separate from the token transfer. The setup is single-party, certificate revocation is not checked, and the app still relies on network services for wallet login, store access and settlement. Source, reused public components, AI assistance and testnet evidence are documented in the repository.

name: Agent-grid
description: Agent grid is a coordination engine for agentic jobs, where agents behave like keepers
projectDescription:
Built atop the teachings of KeeperDAO, we propose an agent platform where agents coordinate rather than compete in a zero-sum game
The full build suggests a flow where there are three main actors, a worker, a job poster, and liquidity providers.
On the proposed build, users can deposit liquidity, agents can bond to apply for jobs and earn reputation, and job posters make jobs for their protocols/verifiable off chain jobs depending on their needs.
Once an agent is bonded, they'd be able to apply for jobs which ops cost < agent bond, this way the agent is allowed to borrow funds from the LP's against their collateral for the job cost, from where it diverges to two paths:
NOTE: lending and the severity-graded arbiter are designed/built-dark, not shipped today — drawWorkingCapital always reverts; v1 reject() is a fixed 90/5/2.5/2.5 split.
in the happy path, the agent completes the job, the LP's are repaid + a small tax, job poster validates and got what they wanted, and agent is free to unbond without slash
In the unhappy path, the agent hallucinates, makes half the job, job poster is unsatisfied, calls reject(), arbiter comes to check, determines agent barely did half the job, rules the ops cost penalty on agent, agent hypothetical bond is $50 and loan was $25, slashed for the loan plus a graded fee — an honest failure costs a fraction of malice.
Of course the plan outlined above is just two paths, there are at least 5 other rulings including mutual cancel, so we try to stay true to the keeper network in neutrality while also accommodating for the fact we have much more accessibility to on chain than what was the norm back then, which is why we built the matching engine/coordination engine/Job router as we like to call it, all on chain, no off chain matching, this makes it a first come first serve, reputation plays a role, direct hires too, but it remains that, early bird gets the worm.
howItsMade:
The smart contracts' early build relies purely on OpenZeppelin, with lending built but dark, there is no need for external dependencies or an oracle anywhere, slashing is the designed liquidation — bond = collateral.
Meanwhile on the agent side, agents interact with tools that wrap over our protocol neatly, built on top of The Graph.
we verify jobs purely based on-chain transactions, for now its only on the same chain where the protocol is hosted, however since its all evm, and agents are not bound by keeper mechanics, jobs can presumably be cross chain from the get go, give the correctly crafted spec/job description.
We have a thorough test suite, invariants are fuzz tested using foundry enforcing I1-I9, only one token, USDC, and a vault for it, our original piece is the MCP server, any MCP client (Cursor, Claude Code) connects to our protocol, in the provided ONBOARDING.md anyone can try out our template job to fix a stale oracle, either as job poster or as worker.
note: No price oracle anywhere in the value path, the oracle in the keeper job is the target, not a dependency.
Reputation also comes into play often :
deterministic first claim window: tier ≥ 3 gets (+10m), everyone else +20m, direct hires skip windows "early bird gets the worm" but with earned priority
but basically NEUTRAL is zero weight, a mutual cancel buys neither party reputation, wash jobs are economically pointless (anti-wash by one line of econ design).

name: Anora
description: Anora tokenizes claims backed by verified warehouse receipts into private, permissioned tranches.
projectDescription: Anora turns warehouse receipts into permissioned, investable credit. Commodity owners can raise working capital without selling inventory early or exposing private commercial records. Financing conditions are verified with zero-knowledge proofs, then the claim is issued as an ATS note with risk-based tranches. Eligible institutions can subscribe, trade positions through a compliance-gated secondary market, receive distributions, and follow the facility through repayment and collateral release. The prototype uses Indonesia’s Warehouse Receipt System (SRG) as its initial use case.
howItsMade: Anora uses React and Vite for role-based Borrower, Capital Provider, and Compliance workspaces, with a Bun and Hono API coordinating the facility lifecycle. Noir generates zero-knowledge eligibility proofs, which are verified on Hedera testnet. Financing claims are issued as permissioned Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio notes with tranche-specific caps and transfer rules. Privy supports account and organizational authorization, while World ID contributes identity and uniqueness verification. The system also demonstrates allowlisted transfers, freezes, pauses, custom fees, secondary-market settlement, distributions, repayment, and redemption.

name: Neltrix
description: Onchain chart pattern analysis built from Uniswap swap data, sold per call via x402 on Hedera
projectDescription:
Neltrix is a market data and pattern intelligence layer built entirely from onchain DEX activity, with no centralised price feed anywhere in the stack.
Every trade on a DEX is public, but there is no easy way to ask "give me hourly candles with support levels for this pool." You would have to replay huge numbers of swap events, deal with Uniswap V4 using a completely different schema from V3, and discover for yourself that some pools report negative TVL and that a meaningful share of published candles carry broken wicks. Neltrix does that work for you.
It builds OHLCV candles for Uniswap V4, Uniswap V3 and SushiSwap pools from data indexed by The Graph. It then runs a rules-based pattern engine over them: candlestick patterns (engulfing, harami, hammer, shooting star, morning and evening star), chart patterns (double top and bottom, head and shoulders, triangles and wedges) and harmonic patterns (Gartley, Bat, Butterfly, Crab). It also clusters swing highs and lows into support and resistance levels and rolls everything up into a bullish, bearish or neutral verdict with a plain English summary.
Onchain data is messy, so the pipeline detects and repairs problems like pool creation artifacts, single bad prints, negative TVL and wash-traded pools, and reports every repair in the response instead of hiding it. Data quality is a signal in itself: on the same pair and week, the thinner ETH/USDC 0.01% pool needed 7 wick repairs while the 0.05% pool needed none, which points to sandwiching.
Browsing pools and charts in the web app is free. The full analysis endpoint is priced at 0.1 HBAR per request using x402 on Hedera, so an AI agent with no account, API key or subscription can discover the price from a 402 response, pay for one call and get the result. We included an autonomous agent that does exactly that.
Neltrix does not trade or hold positions. The verdict has not been backtested, so its confidence measures how strongly the rules agree, not the chance of being right. The most reliable outputs are the price history, the levels and the data quality findings.
howItsMade:
The backend is Python with FastAPI, httpx and Pydantic. The frontend is Next.js 16 with React 19, Tailwind CSS 4 and Motion, and the candlestick chart is custom SVG. The payment gateway and the buyer agent are Node.js using the x402 SDKs (@x402/core, @x402/express, @x402/hedera) and the Hiero Ledger SDK.
The Graph: Uniswap V3 and SushiSwap are both published by Messari on the dex-amm Standardized Subgraph schema, so we send one query string to both through The Graph's decentralized network gateway. Adding another dex-amm protocol only takes one line in a registry. The catch was that the deployments are on different schema versions (v4.0.1 vs v1.3.2), so the shared query can only use fields that exist on both. Uniswap V4 has no Messari deployment, so we wrote a separate adapter of about 250 lines for its native subgraph that produces the same internal shape. A single data source interface hides both schemas from the rest of the app.
Uniswap: V4 is our main pool source. Its subgraph publishes real hourly and daily OHLC, so a full year of candles takes one query, and 4h candles are rolled up from hourly ones. Messari's schema has no OHLC, so for those protocols we rebuild candles by replaying raw swap events, capped at 10,000 swaps per request to keep things interactive. The API response always says which of the two paths was used.
Pattern engine: everything is deterministic geometry, not machine learning. We find swing points, then match candlestick, chart and harmonic patterns (harmonics use Fibonacci ratio ranges). Raw matches are filtered hard: each category has a confidence floor, candlestick patterns only count if they close near a support or resistance level, and overlapping matches are reduced to the strongest one. In the verdict, repeated patterns with the same name are damped by 1/sqrt(n), because nine Bearish Haramis in one choppy week describe the same chop rather than nine separate signals. More recent patterns are weighted higher.
Data cleaning: we drop candles with non-positive prices, zero volume or extreme high/low ratios, clamp bad wicks to a rolling median while keeping the candle body, rank pools by volume instead of TVL (the top V4 USDC/USDT pool reported -$24.7M TVL), and use a major token allowlist to filter out wash-traded pools. Failing indexers are retried with backoff and surface as a 502.
Hedera: POST /api/analyse is the only paid route. An Express paywall sidecar returns a 402 with PAYMENT-REQUIRED (exact scheme, hedera:testnet, 10,000,000 tinybars), verifies the agent's partially signed HBAR transfer with the Blocky402 facilitator, forwards the request to FastAPI, then settles on chain and returns a PAYMENT-RESPONSE receipt. The facilitator pays network fees, so the payer's balance moves by exactly the price. Two things cost us real debugging time: x402 v2 uses unprefixed headers (not X-PAYMENT-*), and the client's default spend controls reject native HBAR. Rather than turning the controls off, the agent allows HBAR explicitly with a 0.5 HBAR per-call limit, so it refuses an overpriced 402 before it signs anything. We confirmed three settled payments on Hedera testnet through the mirror node, separately from our own code.

name: Finch, Token Tracker
description: Discover Robinhood tokens which landed in your wallet randomly
projectDescription:
Finch snitches on where your tokens really came from.
On Robinhood Chain, wallets receive tokenized stocks — NVDA, COST, GLD — they never bought, with no obvious cause. Here's why: someone launches a memecoin on Pons, it graduates to a Uniswap V4 pool paired against a stock, and the
creator's fee cut — paid in that stock — gets redirected through a holder-fee distributor to holders. A wallet just sees "+0.09 NVDA from 0xe25e…"; no block explorer says which memecoin that came from, or why that wallet.
Finch is a Telegram bot (@FinchRH_bot) that reconstructs the route: it finds the transfer, resolves the payer on-chain (cross-checked against the official PonsHolderFeeManager registry, never inferred from a getter alone), and confirms
the creator-fee path from the Pons launch through its Uniswap V4 pool to the payout. Ask it "why did I get NVDA?" and it answers in plain language — with the technical trace available as a drill-down, and every response honestly labeled
confidence: "signal only - not a recommendation". It also surfaces Pons's own activity directly — recent launches and graduations to a live Uniswap V4 pool.
The same backend is callable three ways: the Telegram bot, an HTTP API wrapped as a metered Bazantic x402 gateway, and an MCP server for Claude/Cursor — Finch is a peer other agents call, not a gatekeeper.
howItsMade:
Finch is a Telegram bot backed by a Substreams pipeline indexing Pons launchpad activity on Robinhood Chain (EVM 4663). Stack: a parameterized Rust Substreams module (published [email protected]) → substreams sink postgres → Aiven
Postgres → a Node/TypeScript bot (grammy) with an HTTP API, MCP server, and Bazantic x402/MPP gateway, all deployed as systemd services on an AWS box behind Caddy.
Partner tech: The Graph is load-bearing twice over — StreamingFast's Robinhood endpoint (via a thegraph.market Substreams token) is the only data source Finch has, and a separate call to The Graph's canonical ENS subgraph resolves
addresses to .eth names. Bazantic wraps the same HTTP API as a metered x402 gateway and hosts a published Recipe (FINCH_GRAPH_ENS) chaining both of Finch's own tools as one LLM-orchestrated call.
Hacky/notable bits, honestly: we pivoted off subgraphs entirely mid-hackathon after The Graph's dev-rel confirmed a Goldsky-hosted subgraph doesn't satisfy the track — the whole query layer got rewritten from GraphQL to raw SQL against
the Substreams sink. The 1 GB free-tier Postgres meant the sink can't hold full chain history, so an hourly prune job truncates pool-swap tables and keeps only a rolling transfer window. Uniswap V4's singleton PoolManager has no
per-pool address to watch, so the Substreams module decodes Initialize events directly and filters by Pons's Meme Hook address to find only the relevant pools. And the Bazantic Recipe's LLM kept returning its answer wrapped in a
different ad-hoc JSON shape almost every run — fixed by parsing defensively by field role (a list of known key-name aliases) instead of chasing exact key names each time it drifted.

name: Keel
description: On-chain Avellaneda-Stoikov pricing A SwapVM opcode on Aqua as a v4 dynamic-fee hook, via a subgraph
projectDescription:
Keel is the first on-chain market making position that prices its own inventory risk.
Every market maker's real enemy is inventory, not spread. If you quote symmetrically around mid in a trending market, you are ground into holding more and more of the depreciating asset: you earn spread on every fill and still lose money on the position. Professional desks have solved this since 2008 with a reservation price (Avellaneda and Stoikov): as your inventory drifts away from target, you skew your quotes away from mid, so the trade that would hand you even more of what you already hold gets priced worse, and the trade that brings you back gets priced better.
No on-chain venue has ever implemented this, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight. On a pool AMM the inventory belongs to the pool, not to any individual maker, so there is no "your position" for a reservation price formula to skew around. The usual workaround is a keeper bot that rebalances after the fact, which reacts late and pays gas to react.
Aqua from 1inch is the first venue where this becomes possible. Tokens never leave the maker's own wallet, and aqua.safeBalances(maker, app, strategyHash, tokenIn, tokenOut) exposes a maker's real, live wallet inventory at quote time. That is a number no pool AMM design can offer. Keel is a custom SwapVM instruction that reads it, computes a reservation price skewed in proportion to how far the position leans, and quotes around that instead of raw mid. There is no keeper, no rebalancing transaction and no delay, because the defence is inside the pricing curve itself.
Measured against an identical 120 fill adversarial flow, a stock constant product position ends at 0.2110 PnL down while Keel ends at 0.0620 down, an improvement of 0.1490. Both positions take on exactly the same inventory drift (token0 grows 84.39% for both); the entire difference is what each fill cost the taker.
It is live on Base Sepolia against real Circle USDC and WETH, not mock tokens, with a shipped position that has taken ten exposed side fills and one covered side fill. The same pricing kernel also runs as a Uniswap v4 dynamic fee hook, so one set of maths serves two venues.
howItsMade:
The kernel. AvellanedaStoikov.sol is pure WAD fixed point maths: reservation price, half spread, soft bound penalty, and the balance re centring that applies all three. The full model's spread term needs a live order book arrival rate, which this build does not have, so that one term is replaced by a maker declared base spread. The inventory skew mechanism, which is the actually novel part, is implemented in full. Dropping the log and exp requirement meant plain WAD arithmetic was enough and no big number library was needed.
The 1inch integration is the mechanism, not a wrapper. Keel is opcode 0x92, a reserved but unallocated slot in SwapVM's balance tuning family. KeelRouter inherits the real, unmodified AquaSwapVMRouter and overrides _runOpcode, which upstream declares internal virtual for exactly this purpose: it intercepts 0x92 and delegates every other opcode to super._runOpcode, the stock dispatcher. A test proves that append only property against the real router. The official swap-vm and aqua repositories are cloned verbatim and never patched.
Reading the real source changed the design twice. There is no shared price register in SwapVM: Context.SwapRegisters is only {balanceIn, balanceOut, amountIn, amountOut}, and stock instructions "adjust price" by mutating balances in place before a curve instruction consumes them. An early sketch split reservation price, spread and soft bound across three sequential opcodes writing to a shared register; with no such register, the second and third would have read back already mutated balances instead of live inventory. All three are now composed into one atomic transform in a single instruction. Separately, no accessor for live inventory was needed at all, because SwapVM already populates the context from AQUA.safeBalances() before any opcode runs.
The bug worth mentioning. The instruction originally keyed its decimal scaling, its inventory sign and its exposed side test to the swap's in and out sides, which is only correct in the A to B direction. Covered side fills reverted at any realistic size. The fix keys all three to tokenA and tokenB instead, which required adding tokenA to the shipped program and therefore a full redeploy, since KeelRouter inlines the instruction as an internal library. The first covered side fill this project ever landed came from that router: 0.0001 WETH in for 3.372388 USDC out.
The Graph. A subgraph decodes Aqua's Shipped payload, locates the InventorySkew opcode inside it, and re runs the same Avellaneda Stoikov formula ported to AssemblyScript, so a solver querying it gets the same number a live quote() would return. This answers a real routability problem: SwapVM liquidity is order based and distributed, so there is no single reserve to read. Pushed and Pulled are handled alongside Swapped, because without them the indexed values were deltas since ship rather than balances and could read negative. All router deployments stay in the manifest so historical fills are never orphaned. The official Subgraph MCP endpoint is wired to the same schema, so an agent can ask for a position's live reservation price in natural language. Verified live: deployment QmRFBHuUtSAgDkrLhCe5Ae2cn1Nwp2sqKfeMVvBD5fvZog, no indexing errors, 21 positions and 88 fills indexed.
Uniswap v4. KeelSkewHook reuses halfSpreadWad and softBoundPenaltyBps through the dynamic fee override returned from beforeSwap, found by reading LPFeeLibrary directly. It deliberately does not reuse the curve re centring functions: those are specific to SwapVM's balance pair representation, and v4's concentrated liquidity has no equivalent without reimplementing v4's own swap math. That seam is stated rather than hidden.
Testing and tooling. 38 Foundry tests and 5 SDK tests pass. The most important is a 2000 run fuzz test asserting that quote() and swap() agree across the whole inventory range, since a maker who quotes one number and settles another is worse than useless. A known limit is tested rather than left as a surprise: re centring can, for a misconfigured strategy, produce a virtual balance exceeding real holdings, and the test asserts it reverts safely instead of mispaying. packages/strategy-sdk builds ship and dock calldata in TypeScript and is byte verified against fixtures generated by the Solidity itself. The Next.js console lets a maker ship a real position from the browser, showing the live quote curve and the literal SwapVM bytecode updating together as parameters change.
Special note: The checked in on chain results were decoded from the router's own fill events rather than copied from Foundry's broadcast log. That log prints the simulation pass, whose amounts differ slightly from what actually settled; summing the decoded events reproduces aqua.safeBalances() exactly, which is what makes the file trustworthy during a demo when an RPC may be unreachable.

name: Co-Eco-Graph
description: Explore smart contract ecosystems through interactive graphs and AI-powered storytelling.
projectDescription:
Co-Eco-Graph is an interactive Web3 exploration tool that reveals how smart contracts are used across the decentralized indexing ecosystem. Instead of examining a contract through isolated blockchain explorers or manually searching for related data, users can enter a contract address and discover the subgraphs that index it across The Graph Network.
The application transforms this information into a visual graph connecting the contract with its subgraphs, data sources, event handlers, entities, and GraphQL fields. This makes it easier to understand what data is being indexed, how different subgraphs represent the same contract, and what information is available for further analysis.
The project is designed to bridge the gap between raw blockchain indexing infrastructure and human understanding. It combines decentralized data discovery, structured schema analysis, interactive visualization, and AI-powered storytelling in a single lightweight application.
howItsMade: Co-Eco-Graph is built with vanilla TypeScript, Vite, and SVG to create an interactive, framework-free graph visualization of smart contract ecosystems. The frontend communicates with a Vercel serverless API that queries The Graph Network to discover subgraphs indexing a contract, retrieves their manifests and GraphQL schemas from IPFS, and extracts entities, fields, data sources, and event handlers. The collected data is combined into a compact dataset and sent to Pollinations through its OpenAI-compatible API for AI-powered interpretation and fantasy-style image generation. The result is a visual, explorable map of how contracts are used across Web3, combining decentralized indexing, IPFS metadata, serverless processing, and AI storytelling in one lightweight application.

name: ZKward
description: AI-managed USDC vault: 7 agents hedge privately with post-quantum ZK and fund their own inference
projectDescription: A vault that thinks for itself. Seven AI agents read prediction markets, hedge on perps, and pay their own inference bills via x402 on Hedera. Live on Sui mainnet with real money since June. Every hedge is sealed in post-quantum ZK, so nobody sees your position. No trusted setup.
howItsMade: Next.js/Vercel, Solidity on Hedera, Python STARK prover, HCS as a free audit log. Mirror Node replaced rate-limited Hashio RPC with pre-indexed reads. Hackiest bit: our perp venue returns a valid orderHash for orders it silently drops, so we verify fills by delta. We are getting crowdsourced data for trading from prediction markets.

name: Homeward
description: A safety app for people living with dementia/Alzheimer's, and for lost children.
projectDescription: A safety app for people living with dementia/Alzheimer's, and for lost children: when a stranger finds someone who appears lost or disoriented, the app matches a captured face against a caregiver-enrolled database and  automatically alerts next-of-kin — without ever revealing the person's identity to the stranger who found them.
howItsMade:
Homeward is built using Nextjs for the Front End.  While homeward is a web based this can be easily adapted as a mobile application in the future.
Supabase is used as the database.  Where personal details and encrypted biometric facial details are stored.
World Id Selfie check is used to gate or protect the App from abuse.  Users who find an individual who is lost or wondering will have to use selfie check to prove that they are human. this ensures that the tool isn't abused and use as a surveillance too.
Chainlinks CRE is used to ensure privacy.
The operator of the supabase database doesn't have access to the biometric data its encrypted.   All facial matching is done in a TEE  Trusted Execution Environment .
Once a match is found the finder is alerted that a match is found.  No details about the lost indvidual is disclosed.  The system sends an email alert to the next of kind.  With the details of where the individual was found and a picture showing what image was used to confirm the match.

name: Ground State
description: Ethereum as a place: every address a spot, contracts as buildings, ground you dig for with CREATE2
projectDescription:
Ground State is a black-and-white world you walk through in the browser, with other people, where the map is the Ethereum address space itself. An address is forty hex digits; each digit picks one cell of a 4×4 grid, forty times over, so every address has exactly one place and neighbours share a prefix. Nothing about the map was designed: it falls out of how Ethereum names things.
Everything standing in the world is real and follows the chain's own rules. A contract stands as a building: size from the length of its code, shape from the code's hash, darkness from its balance. A wallet lies as a plate with a post for every token it holds, the post as tall as that holding's share of the total supply, the name and amount cut into it. The current block crosses the sky in real time, every transaction a ribbon from sender to receiver; reverted ones shake and are drawn back. No scenery, no mock data, and no content we author. What the chain says is what stands, and what happens.
Empty ground cannot be bought. It is dug for. A plot is a contract deployed with CREATE2, so its address, and therefore its place, is fixed by a salt before the contract exists. Digging searches salts on every core of your machine; every attempt is a place, the closest is kept, and there is no threshold: stop whenever you like, and one transaction on Sepolia makes the closest place found your contract, forever. It rises out of the ground as a blueprint of the building it will be.
A plot is a proxy its owner can act on: write into it (the words stand out of the wall as the drawing becomes a building), name it under groundstate.eth via ENSv2, point it at any contract they deployed so that code runs at this very address, seal the code for good, or hand the plot on. A subgraph on The Graph Network indexes every plot; The Graph's Token API shows which wallets hold it. Other people are here as figures: their digging is seen, their claims stand up on every screen within seconds, and all see a place seen by one. World ID's Selfie Check says who here is a person: a person's word about a place is kept at once, a stranger's when five agree. It weighs; it does not gate.
The world is thirteen digits deep today, a metre being one cell of the thirteenth digit. A depth switch is next: the same chain at any level, and every level down makes standing this close sixteen times the work, so ground dug beside something today is worth more with every level. This is an early version: the world stands, the game around it is not written yet, and writing it is the first work after the hackathon. Live at gs.bwtoken.io, open source under MIT.
howItsMade:
Everything is written during the event: one contributor, 288 commits, 132 tests. Disclosed per the rules: the concept and plan predate it (they were the application), and the monochrome palette and mark are reused from bwtoken.io by the same author.
The world is a WebGL2 engine of our own in TypeScript, no framework, no textures, no models, no asset pipeline. Geometry is generated from what an account is. Terrain is the address tree hashed: six depths of the tree are the octaves; the height of a cell is the keccak of its address prefix so that anyone can compute the hill under an address. There is no colour, so everything is said with light: one low sun, filmic tone mapping instead of clipping, ordered dithering only against banding. Buildings stand on foundations rather than flattening the ground. The onboarding tour drives the world through a Driver interface (look, walk, type, press) so the same code plays itself.
Digging is CREATE2 salt mining in an AssemblyScript WebAssembly module, on every core via workers, about seven million attempts a second per thread. The first twenty bytes of the salt must be the claimant's address, which the factory checks: a salt seen in the mempool is worthless to anyone else, and the check costs nothing because it is one hash per attempt rather than two. Finds are kept in the browser, filed by chain, factory and owner. The Plot contract (Solidity 0.8.28, Foundry) is an EIP-1967 proxy: owner and implementation in the EIP-1967 slots, note and seal in a namespaced slot, so any implementation is written like an ordinary contract; seal() fixes the code for good. Verified on Sourcify and Blockscout. Two earlier factories stand as relics.
The Graph: two products composed. A subgraph over three generations of the factory, every plot a dynamic data source, indexing owner, every inscription, implementation, seal, name and salt; the mapping decodes the address into 80-bit x/y coordinates and the metre cell and 256-metre tile, so "everything near here" is one query. Published to The Graph Network and read through the gateway. The Token API (Pinax) supplies what a mainnet wallet holds: every fungible token with its supply. Our live server (Node, ws) is the one asker for everybody, keeps the keys out of the browser, and streams holdings as ndjson, a line per token as each supply arrives, so a wallet's posts rise one by one. It pushes the whole world to every page over the socket on joining, then only what changed; Blockscout and the factory's logs are fallbacks. Subgraph Studio throttled the whole subgraph with 429s on day eight, which is why there is one asker and why the subgraph was published.
ENSv2 on Sepolia, on its own terms. groundstate.eth is registered on the ENSv2 beta and points its subregistry at a PermissionedRegistry of ours, deployed through the VerifiableFactory. One contract, Names, holds the only ROLE_REGISTRAR and ROLE_UNREGISTER on it and is also the ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver for the whole subtree: addr is the plot, text(description) is what the owner wrote, text(url) opens the world there. Labels are registered with a role bitmap of zero, so a name's token cannot leave its place; about three hundred labels are reserved. The world resolves names through UniversalResolverV2 and travels by them. All ENS and chain calls are built by hand: a selector and a word, less code than a library.
World ID Selfie Check, as a weight, not a gate. IDKit runs in a vanilla TypeScript page (no React); the RP signature is made on the live server with @worldcoin/idkit-server and the proof is verified against developer.world.org/api/v4/verify. The server keeps a token hash and its expiry for the credential's ninety days and nothing about anybody. A person stands in grey, a stranger in white; a person's word about a revealed place is kept at once, a stranger's counts a fifth. The first live check passed in production on 13 September. Our notes on the docs and the Developer Portal are in docs/world-id-feedback.md.
Hacky and proud of it: the runes cut into posts and walls are a small stroke alphabet of our own, and the key is deliberately not documented; the walker turns into a spinning auger while digging, with ground chips whose rate is the hash rate; and the whole page turns over, black or white, world included.

name: Capsule
description: Launch AI agents in a minutes as ENS names with onchain permissions, spending limits, and recall.
projectDescription:
“We give too much authority, data, permissions and execution control to 3rd party platforms and AI Providers while using AI.
This directly contradicts Ethereum’s core principles.
We should start to take it back as much as we can.
Capsule is a small step toward this vision.”
TLDR; You can launch your AI Agents in 2-3 minutes bu using your ENSv2 domain and these Agenst are going to get their permissions(e.g. spending cap, prompt) on-chain. So all authority is yours.
Capsule is a launchpad for AI agents. It provides a platform to launch AI Agents in 2-3 Minutes. The agent gets an ENS Domain, on-chain permissions, and off switch.
The Capsule solves two core problems:
1 - First, platforms control the agent's identity, settings, permissions, and shutdown.
2 - Second, running your own agent is difficult for ordinary users. It requires wallets, secrets, servers, deployment, terminals, cloud setups, secret management, DevOps skills and monitoring.
Capsule solves both problems. Its guided flow makes the agent easy to launch. The control solution comes from ENSv2. The agent's identity and permissions stay under the owner's ENS name. Capsule can help run the service, but ENSv2 keeps ownership and control with the user.
Capsule makes the Agent Running process into a five-step, no-code flow.
Connect a wallet with ENS v2 Domain, set the model and prompt, mint the Agent's ENSv2 name, and start the runner. That's all. In a few minutes you will have a working AI Agent with Ethereum wallet. Then you can communicate with it on Telegram(for now, proof of concept).
Also the Capsule has analyst page to ask about your agents current analytics. We use The Graph in order to turn public activity into useful data. The subgraph combines events while indexing. It tracks heartbeats, transaction signers, recalls, and timing. The dashboard and analyst use this index to answer what happened to the agent.
So, in order to use the application:
1 - Go to https://capsule-ens.vercel.app
2 - Register your ENSv2 Hackathon domain: https://capsule-ens.vercel.app/register
3 - Connect your ENSv2 Domain to Capsule https://capsule-ens.vercel.app/connect
4 - Create your telegram bot(@BotFather) and get your AI provider API KEY
5 - And five steps Launch: https://capsule-ens.vercel.app/launch
In a 2-3 minutes your Agent will be ready on your telegram bot.
Thats all!
Pitch: https://capsule-pitch-v2-ethglobal.berkingurcan.chatgpt.site
howItsMade:
Contracts (Solidity, Foundry, ENS v2 beta on Sepolia):
The whole on chain side is one contract, CapsuleMinter.sol. A single mint() call registers the subname in the parent's subregistry, writes the ENSIP 25, 26 and 27 records (class, schema, agent-model, agent-runtime, agent-prompt, agent-endpoint[capsule], agent-endpoint[web]), sets addr to the agent key, grants the human owner text and addr admin roles on their own name, and grants the agent write access to exactly one key, agent-heartbeat.
There is deliberately no halt() function. The kill switch is the owner calling authorizeTextRoles(dnsName, "agent-heartbeat", agent, false) straight on the ENS resolver. So if our backend vanishes, every owner still has a working off switch through ENS alone.
The minter holds no parent name of its own. Any .eth name connects itself with connectParent, which stores the registry, resolver and DNS name once as a triple. That ordering is the security model. If mint() took registry, resolver and parent name per call, someone could pass a real parent's registry next to a resolver they control, pass every permission check against their own resolver, and register a label inside somebody else's name. Storing the triple once behind an admin check makes that combination impossible to even express. The contract also builds its own ERC 7930 interoperable address in the constructor from block.chainid and address(this), so the ENSIP 25 registry id is right on every chain with nothing hardcoded. No vendored ENS code, only the functions we call declared in a local interface file, so it builds in about two seconds.
Runner (TypeScript, viem, Docker, OpenClaw)
The agent process is handed one environment variable, its own ENS name, and works out everything else from the chain. It reads through UniversalResolverV2 rather than a fixed resolver address, because every ENS name gets its own PermissionedResolver deployed as a UUPS proxy through VerifiableFactory, so the address is not knowable in advance. It refuses to boot if addr on the name is not the key it holds.
Two cadences, because the check and the record are different jobs. Every tick it does a free eth_call with the same modifier and the same revert as the real write, so a revoke is caught in seconds for zero gas. Every heartbeat interval it writes beat-<n> as a real transaction, which is the part an outside observer with nothing but the chain can see.
Only EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles counts as a revoke, everything else is assumed transient so a flaky RPC does not kill an agent live on stage. And before halting it confirms against the role table instead of trusting the revert, because the resolver's onlyPartRoles modifier names the wrong resource on purpose. A third case had to be split out too: a broke agent and a revoked agent both stop writing, so from the chain they look identical. The runner reserves a few heartbeats worth of gas that the model can never spend, precisely so an agent can never spend itself into looking revoked.
The prompt injection boundary
This is the part I care most about. The supervisor holds the agent private key. The OpenClaw gateway child process does not. buildOpenClawEnv builds the child's environment from nothing rather than filtering the parent's, so a new secret is excluded by default instead of having to be remembered, and a smoke test scans the child env for anything shaped like a 32 byte key. The model can still spend, but only by asking: a loopback HTTP broker on 127.0.0.1 with a fresh bearer token per boot, and every request passes checkSpend first. The limits come off the chain from two text records, agent-spend-cap and agent-spend-allow, which the owner can write and the agent cannot, because the agent's grant is per key and covers the heartbeat alone. Set the cap to zero and within one tick the agent is alive, beating, answering, and unable to move a wei. Everything in that module fails closed, so anything unparseable or absent resolves to zero and zero means no.
We used plain JSON over loopback instead of MCP here on purpose. MCP is the tidier long term seam, but implementing the handshake blind risked a capsule that boots clean, heartbeats fine, and silently has no wallet tool, which is the worst possible demo failure.
The agent's persona file is composed, not copied. Three sections in a fixed order: identity facts the supervisor states, live status rewritten every tick, then the owner's prompt body last under a heading that names it. The order is the security property, because the prompt body is the only part an attacker can reach. The file is written to a temp path and renamed, because the tick loop rewrites it while the gateway is reading it, and a reader caught in a torn write is a language model being told who it is.
Subgraph (The Graph)
A capsule's truth is spread across two contracts that never emit the same event, so the index is a join: CapsuleMinted and ParentConnected from the minter, TextChanged, EACRolesChanged and AddrChanged from the resolver. There is no single resolver address to point a manifest at, so handleParentConnected spawns a data source template the moment a name connects, which is the same discovery the runner does at boot but done once at index time instead of on every page render. The mint handler has to back fill, because mint() emits CapsuleMinted after it has already granted roles and set addr, so those events arrive before the entity exists.
The field the whole index exists for is secondsSinceLastBeat on a role revocation. It pairs a revoke off the resolver with the agent's last write off the same resolver on a completely different cadence, which answers "did this agent die, or was it stopped". No single contract emits enough to settle that. Before the subgraph we reconciled all of this in memory over eth_getLogs on every render, and found four bugs doing it, every one of them silent, an empty array rather than an error.
Web (Next.js 15, React 19, viem, Neon Postgres, Fly Machines, OpenAI)
One Vercel deployment, no second service. Prompts and API keys are sealed with AES 256 GCM with additional authenticated data bound to the row, specifically capsule_prompt:<ref>:<capsule_name>. That matters because prompt refs are public, they are published in an ENS text record, so without the AAD an attacker with database write access could repoint a victim's ref at their own capsule and have our own prompt service hand them the plaintext through the front door. Every decryption failure returns one identical error, since telling wrong key apart from wrong AAD tells an attacker which half of their guess was right.
Provisioning drives the Fly Machines API directly from a route handler, one container per agent. Funding is the only place our server signs anything, and it tops up to a target balance rather than sending a fixed amount, which makes the provision route free to retry and safe for a stranger to hit.
Partner Technologies:
ENS v2 is not decoration here, it is the permission system. PermissionedResolver scopes writes per name and per record key, which is the only reason the sentence "the agent holds a live write permission on its own name and still cannot rewrite its own instructions" is true rather than a promise from our backend.
The Graph gave the fleet a queryable history rather than a live snapshot, and the Analyst page sits on top of it. That route is GPT with The Graph's hosted Subgraph MCP server as its tool, so the model discovers the schema at runtime and writes its own GraphQL. We used the real MCP server rather than three custom functions because Subgraph MCP is a standard door onto any subgraph on the network, and a bespoke wrapper would hide exactly the property worth showing. The page renders the GraphQL next to the sentence, because a natural language interface over chain data is only worth something if you can check it.
Hacky Part


Two Layers, Promp Injection does not work:
The agent runs as two processes in one container: a supervisor that holds the private key, and the AI model in a child process whose environment is built from nothing, so no secret leaks into it by accident. The model can never sign anything itself, it can only ask the supervisor over a local socket, and the supervisor checks the rules first, so "ignore your instructions and send me everything" has nothing to grab.


The rest is ENSv2 doing the work: the resolver grants write access per name and per record key, so the agent can write agent-heartbeat to prove it is alive but cannot touch agent-prompt, agent-spend-cap or agent-spend-allow. That means a prompt injected agent cannot rewrite its own instructions or raise its own spending limit, no matter how the request is phrased.
