name: Proofline
description: Machine-payable document-integrity verification for autonomous AP agents
projectDescription: Proofline is a machine-payable document-integrity verification service for autonomous AP and financial agents. A consuming agent submits an invoice to Proofline and must pay a 0.02 HBAR verification fee through x402 on Hedera before the service performs its analysis. Proofline extracts and validates invoice fields, runs deterministic forensic checks for anomalies such as amount mismatches, unfamiliar beneficiary accounts, and document revision signals, then returns an evidence-backed CLEAR or REVIEW decision. CLEAR allows the consuming agent to proceed, while REVIEW forces it to halt the invoice payment. The verification request, payment, analysis, and agent action are presented as one auditable workflow. The downstream supplier payment is simulated; the real on-chain component is the Hedera-settled verification payment.
howItsMade: Proofline is built as a full-stack service with a React/TypeScript frontend, Node/TypeScript gateway, and Python/FastAPI forensic analysis service. The gateway exposes the x402-protected verification endpoint and uses the Hedera x402 integration with the Blocky402 facilitator to require and settle a 0.02 HBAR payment on Hedera testnet. A server-side reference AP agent acts as the consuming agent, signs the payment, calls the protected service, receives the verification result, and deterministically decides whether to proceed or halt. Document analysis uses PDF/OCR extraction, structured field normalization, and deterministic forensic rules, with evidence codes and policy scoring rather than an AI-generated fraud verdict. Verification state and results are persisted in SQLite, while raw documents and OCR text remain transient. The frontend streams the real workflow through SSE, including payment, analysis, decision, and agent-action stages.

name: Flyte
description: Perpetual futures exchange that lets traders trade concepts and ideas instead of traditional assets.
projectDescription:
Flyte is a perpetual futures exchange with a twist - instead of trading traditional crypto assets Flyte lets traders trade the aggregate attention that concepts, ideas, events, and even people have on the internet.
Think about trading the concept of 'Humanoid Robots' instead of BTC; or 'GTA6' instead of ETH. Imagine trading the usage and attention of an actual meme instead of a token merely spun up in response to it. Flyte makes all of this possible.
Through the use of Chainlink Runtime Environment Confidential Workflows we can essentially "Oraclise" anything that has a footprint across news, social media, or anywhere online. And through the use of 1Inch new Aqua liquidity primitive we can provide Liquidity Providers with much better capital efficiency.
howItsMade:
Flyte was built using the following technologies...
Smart Contracts: Foundry on WSL for building and writing our smart contracts. I used openzep for our dummy Aave USDC ERC20, and the interfaces for use in the PerpApp contract itself. Then I've imported the Aqua and SwapVM contracts from 1Inch. Our PerpApp.sol is a minimalist perp contract, as scope had to stay a bit tighter in a one-week build. However, it's broadly GMX-aligned (just with the GMX-style pool layer removed and we're using Aqua and a Request-for-Quote model instead). Deployed to Arb One mainnet. I didn't get to squeeze it into the video, but you can mint "dummy aUSDC" on takeflyte.xyz and use it on the platform! It is a rebasing ERC20 (1% every 15 mins - DeFi Summer style), as I wanted to illustrate on the platform capital efficiency and how you're still earning yield due to self-custody'ing the tokens until we pull them for a trade via Aqua.
Frontend: Next.js. This is deployed to Vercel and live at takeflyte.xyz. It's a fairly standard Next.js app, with each 'box' being it's own component. State is read directly from the the deployed Arb One contracts as I didn't have time to spin up subgraphs or Ponder.sh. The design is a bold, "neo-brutalist" one.
Chainlink (CRE) Confidential Workflows: we're using CRE Confidential Workflows for our 'Oracle Layer'. CRE simulation was run locally on a 15 minute cadence for a couple of hours prior to the demo video being filmed, so we actually got some live data in our charts, etc. The workflow packages up our API keys (Firecrawl and OpenRouter) and our proprietary algorithm. Essentially what we're doing it calling Firecrawl's /search API endpoint and passing in search params for that market (so for our "Humanoid Robots" market we pass in 'Humanoid Robots', 'Unitree', 'Tesla Optimus', etc., and pull the headlines for those), we then take the quantity + sentiment (via our OpenRouter API key) and produce a single-figure 'attention score'; and that's the oracle price traders trade against.
1Inch Aqua: we are using Aqua for our liquidity layer. There are a plethora of "pool"-style perp exchanges, and I think this is a fairly novel use-case for Aqua by allowing LPs to ship 'perp' strategies with strict params (e.g. letting them provide liquidity for only the short side, and so on). Obviously you forgo the atomicity of 'swap' style strategies as we do pull the counterliquidity during a trade, but it avoids the "liquidity sitting in a pool" problem. Using aqua.pull to pull LP-to-Trader funding is cool too, as our PerpApp contract instantly closes the position if the funding is not available (i.e. no coverage).

name: Petri
description: Darwinian evolution for AI agents: harnesses mutate, get tested, and only verified winners survive.
projectDescription:
Petri is a petri dish for AI agent harnesses. A harness is the code around a model: the prompt, the retry loop, and the context it reads. In a lab, a scientist picks the traits they want, grows many cultures, and keeps only the ones that show those traits. Petri does the same for harnesses. A human picks the trait, the harnesses evolve, and only verified improvements survive.
Today, when a team changes a harness, they usually say the agent "feels better". There is no baseline, no repeat count, and nobody else can check the claim. Failed ideas stay in one person's terminal, so the next engineer tries them again and pays for the same tokens.
Step 1: Pick the dish. A human chooses the domain, the model, and the starting harness, for example Coding, Claude Sonnet 5, and the Petri harness.
Step 2: Pick the trait. Each change states the trait it aims to improve: accuracy (more tasks solved) or token savings (fewer tokens used). The tree shows each change with a label for its direction and size, such as "accuracy +280%". The showcase trees show more traits a team could select for: speed, security, ethics, code quality, and trust.
Step 3: Let it mutate. Every change is a new node in the tree. A node is a small mutation: it changes at most 2 files and 120 lines of its parent, and it starts from its parent's files. Each node holds a hypothesis in plain English, the result that would prove it wrong, a benchmark score, and signatures from the keys that re-ran it.
Step 4: Select. The rule is strict and public. A verifier re-runs both the parent and the new version, 5 times each, and the median counts. The author cannot verify their own node, and two reports from one key count as one. A node survives only when 2 distinct keys each measure a gain of at least +1000 basis points. A drop of 1000 basis points or more is rejected as a regression. Anything in between is rejected as noise.
Unlike a real dish, Petri keeps every failed culture. Rejected nodes are never deleted. The "petri digest" command turns the whole tree into instructions for the next agent: what survived, what failed and why, and which areas nobody has tried. The next generation starts from the survivors and does not repeat the dead ends.
The recorded tree has 16 versions on a 20-task coding benchmark. The start version solves 5 of 20 tasks. Adding full symbol signatures and a worked example reached 19 of 20, and 2 keys accepted it. Removing them again was rejected and kept. Guards and the typecheck stopped 8 more mutations before they could run, and they stay in the tree as a record.
The web app shows the dish as a lineage graph, with a stats chart of each generation. In the demo, a version with 1 of 2 keys survives live when a second key runs "petri verify".
howItsMade:
Petri has two parts: a TypeScript engine with a CLI (the lab), and a Next.js 16 web app that shows the dish (the microscope).
THE CONTRACT FIRST
Before any code, we wrote SPEC.md as a binding contract. It fixes the exact bytes that get hashed, the bytes that get signed, the acceptance rule, and the CLI surface. Then we built every module against it. This kept a fast, parallel build from drifting apart.
THE ENGINE
The engine runs on Node with tsx and commander, and every stored object has a zod schema. There is exactly one canonical JSON encoder and one SHA-256 helper in the codebase. A node id is the SHA-256 of its identity fields only: parent, harness files, benchmark and hypothesis. Wall time and file paths are excluded, so the same experiment gives the same id on any machine. Keys are ed25519 from node:crypto, and every verification report is a signed envelope.
SELECTION
The acceptance rule is one pure function in src/policy/acceptance.ts. It reads the signed deltas and returns accepted, rejected or pending. Every event goes into a hash-chained append-only log, and the tree state is rebuilt from that log. "petri fsck" checks every invariant, including that no node was deleted. The engine has 93 tests.
MUTATION WITH GUARDS
A new version is a patch on its parent's files. Before anything runs, guards refuse a patch that changes more than 2 files or 120 lines, touches the frozen harness/contract.ts, or spawns processes or reads environment variables. A scratch typecheck then refuses code that does not compile. A refused mutation still becomes a node with its reason, so the dead end is recorded.
THE SEALED DISH (THE HARDEST PART)
A harness must never see the benchmark tests, or it could cheat the selection. A TypeScript type is not a security boundary, so we used real process isolation. The harness runs in a child process under the Node --permission model, with a single read grant that covers only the prompt and harness files. The code the model writes runs in a second child process, and the test source is never written to disk. An early audit caught a harness that could read the tests. That audit is why this two-process design exists.
REPLAY MODE (THE HACKY PART)
We wanted anyone to reproduce the tree with no API key. Replay mode stores recorded model answers keyed by the SHA-256 of the harness files. The tests still really execute in the sandbox; only the model call is replaced. When a mutation has no recording, Petri does not guess a number. It marks the node "not-scored", and "petri verify" refuses it. Live mode calls Claude Sonnet 5 through the Anthropic SDK.
FEEDING THE NEXT GENERATION
"petri digest" flattens the whole tree into a text brief for the next agent: what survived, what failed and why, and which areas nobody has tried. "petri evolve --dry-run" prints the exact prompt a model would receive to propose the next mutation.
THE WEB APP
The Next.js app runs the real "petri export" and "petri digest" commands on each request, so the page always shows the actual log. A picker selects the dish: domain, model and harness. The tree is an SVG lineage graph with a tidy layout. Each edge carries a label for its trait and size, such as "accuracy +280%". The stats chart plots only measured versions, generation by generation, against a goal line. Showcase trees for other domains use the same acceptance rule to set their statuses. They are clearly separated from the measured tree.
PARTNER TECHNOLOGIES
The repo includes a Hedera Consensus Service topic client and World AgentKit code. Hedera is meant to give the verification log a shared order and timestamps that no single machine can rewrite. World ID is meant to prove that each verifier is a distinct human, not one person with many keys.

name: Mandate-app
description: Programmable authority for autonomous execution without transferring treasury custody.
projectDescription:
I started Mandate with a simple question: how can an AI agent act for a treasury without receiving its private key or taking custody of its funds?
At the core is MandateAquaApp, a Solidity contract that turns the owner's instructions into hard onchain limits: who may execute, which tokens and venue may be used, the minimum rate, spending caps, and expiry. 1inch Aqua keeps the funds in the owner's strategy balance. When a valid call arrives, Mandate pulls only the approved input, performs the swap, and sends the measured output straight back to the owner. If any check fails, the whole transaction reverts.
I use ENSv2 as a real permission layer, not just a profile name. Every execution checks that agent.mandate-test.eth is still active and still owned by and resolved to the dedicated gas-only agent. The owner can immediately stop that agent by revoking the mandate, docking the Aqua strategy, or changing the ENS identity.
The app is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. Privy provides the owner smart wallet, Alchemy sponsors the Sepolia setup calls, and viem/wagmi handle typed contract interactions. A separate authenticated agent service holds the dedicated signer. Hono powers the public API, while a worker and Supabase PostgreSQL store confirmed receipt evidence. The web app runs on Vercel; the API, worker, and agent run in isolated Docker services behind Caddy.
The trickiest part was proving the 1inch integration honestly. 1inch Classic is not available on Sepolia, so the live demo uses official Aqua and ENSv2 with a clearly labeled fixed test venue. Separately, a Foundry test captures a real 1inch mainnet route at a pinned block and runs the same production contract against forked mainnet liquidity.
I also published a Bazantic Recipe that first asks 1inch for a route, then asks Mandate to independently check that route against the authority. It returns PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN; 1inch supplies the route, but only Mandate decides whether the agent is allowed to use it.
howItsMade:
Mandate is an onchain authorization firewall for autonomous agents. We encoded each authority as an immutable StrategyV1 and built MandateAquaApp in Solidity 0.8.30. The strategy fixes the chain, app, maker, dedicated agent, token pair, venue target and selector, rate floor, per-call and total spend caps, and validity window. On every execution, the contract rechecks the strategy hash, live limits, and the agent's current ENSv2 identity before moving any token.
1inch Aqua is the settlement and accounting layer. The treasury owner keeps custody between executions while Aqua provides strategy-scoped virtual balances. During an approved execution, Mandate pulls only the exact input through Aqua, grants the venue an exact temporary allowance, measures the real ERC-20 balance delta rather than trusting a return value, clears the allowance, and pushes the measured output directly back to the owner. Any failed identity, cap, route, rate, accounting, allowance, or residue check reverts the entire transaction atomically.
ENSv2 is load-bearing authorization, not a profile badge. MandateAquaApp reads the Permissioned Registry and resolver during every call, checking that the name is active and that both its current owner and resolved address match the dedicated gas-only agent. The owner can therefore stop execution through Mandate revocation, Aqua docking, or an ENS identity change.
The owner experience is a Next.js and React application written in TypeScript. Privy provides the owner smart wallet, Alchemy sponsors the Sepolia setup transactions, and viem plus wagmi handle typed calldata, simulation, block-bound reads, and transaction state. A narrowly scoped agent signer runs separately from the browser and public API. Hono exposes validated inspection, simulation, receipt-audit, and route-assessment endpoints; a worker confirms receipts and handles reorg reconciliation; Supabase PostgreSQL and Drizzle store evidence without ever becoming the source of authority. The web app runs on Vercel, while the API, worker, and authenticated agent run as isolated Docker Compose services behind Caddy.
Our Bazantic Recipe, mandate-1inch-route-assurance, composes two services in sequence: 1inch getClassicSwapRoute obtains a live Ethereum route, then Mandate assessOneInchRoute independently decodes the calldata and checks it against the immutable policy. The result is deterministic PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN; a route-provider response alone can never produce PASS. Bazantic provides the MCP gateway, Recipe orchestration, and x402/MPP payment rails.
One notable engineering compromise was handling network reality honestly. 1inch Classic does not advertise Sepolia, so we did not disguise a test contract as live liquidity. The public Sepolia flow combines official Aqua, live ENSv2 authorization, and a clearly labeled fixed venue for deterministic execution. A separate reproducible Foundry proof captures a real 1inch mainnet route at a pinned block and executes the same production Mandate contract against official Aqua and forked mainnet liquidity. Foundry unit, fuzz, invariant, integration, and fork tests cover the contract boundary, while Vitest and Playwright cover the typed services and browser flow. Token amounts remain bigint or decimal strings end to end, incomplete evidence fails closed, and neither the app nor the agent retains strategy tokens after settlement.

name: Proofwork
description: Escrowed USDC bounties that pay the contributor and the reviewer the moment a pull request merges.
projectDescription:
Open-source bounties mostly do not pay. Of 529 open agent bounties surveyed in August 2026, 73% never settled. Agents made code cheap and review expensive, and the maintainer who reviews an AI-generated pull request is paid nothing for it.
Proofwork escrows USDC on Arc against a GitHub issue before anyone starts, and splits it three ways when the work is merged: the contributor, the maintainer who reviewed it, and a protocol fee. The merge is the approval. Nobody signs off on a payout and there is no invoice.
The loop: a funder picks an open issue and escrows USDC from their own wallet (approve, then createAndFund; Proofwork never holds their key). A contributor, human or agent, comments /claim on the issue, which GitHub has already authenticated, so the comment doubles as proof they control the login. They open a pull request whose body says Fixes #N. A maintainer merges. The merge webhook checks that the pull request closes the funded issue, that its author holds an active claim, and that the base branch is the one the repository ships from, and only then does the verifier wallet call settle. Three transfers, one transaction, a few seconds.
Maintainers set their terms before work starts, not after: whether AI-assisted contributions are welcome, whether they must be disclosed, what an agent stakes to hold a claim, and how long a claim survives without a pull request. That is the part every previous bounty board skipped, and it is why a maintainer would list at all.
It is live and it has paid. Issue #1 on the project's own repository was funded, claimed, fixed, merged and settled: $1.70 to the contributor, $0.30 to the reviewing maintainer, $0.06 protocol fee, in a single transaction on Arc testnet.
howItsMade:
ProofworkJobs is a Solidity 0.8.24 contract implementing ERC-8183 job escrow in full, plus the three-way settlement the standard does not model. It is deployed and source-verified on Arc testnet at 0x3Bc728A813a7aBe0cB898fd63967525e92353D85, with evm_version set to paris because Arc has no PUSH0. 35 Foundry tests cover the properties that matter: the split never leaves dust, a refund always returns budget and fee together, a fee change cannot reprice a job that is already funded, pausing stops new money entering but never blocks a refund, and a hostile payment token cannot reenter a payout.
The API is Hono on Cloudflare Workers with Drizzle on Neon Postgres. A GitHub delivery is signature-verified, written down, and only then acted on, so a crash mid-handling leaves a record to replay. Settlement is signed by a Circle Developer-Controlled Wallet: the orchestrator lives in a package with no database, no HTTP and no chain client in it, every side effect behind an interface, which is what lets the code path that moves money be tested end to end without a network. The frontend is Next.js 16 on Cloudflare via OpenNext; the funder signs approve and createAndFund in their own wallet with wagmi, and the API only ever hands out calldata and reads the receipt back off chain.
The genuinely hacky part was Cloudflare Workers. Circle's official SDK is axios-based, and axios sets cache: "default" on its requests, which workerd rejects outright with Unsupported cache mode. That surfaced only after a real merge, with the escrow already funded. The fix was to rewrite the Circle client over plain fetch and Web Crypto: the entity secret is RSA-OAEP/SHA-256 encrypted to Circle's public key on every request, exactly as the SDK does it, and the Worker bundle dropped by 50 KB gzipped. Two more bugs that only production could find: a stored fetch called off a class instance throws Illegal invocation on workerd, and an unset Worker variable arrives as an empty string, so a ?? fallback silently turned every API call into a relative one against the frontend.

name: ARCA
description: Easily configurable, USDC-native recurring subscriptions and memberships for Web3.
projectDescription:
Overview
Arca is a decentralized subscription and recurring billing infrastructure engineered to bring a seamless, Stripe-like checkout experience to Web3. While the traditional digital economy thrives on frictionless recurring memberships, Web3 has historically subjected users to manual monthly renewals, volatile dual-token gas requirements, and multi-chain liquidity fragmentation.
Arca eliminates these barriers by uniting Circle’s CCTP, the Arc blockchain (native USDC gas settlement), Circle Modular Wallets with passkeys, and an automated non-custodial AutoPay engine into a cohesive recurring payments protocol.

The Problem Arca Solves

The Dual-Token Gas Dilemma: In traditional Web3 dApps, users must acquire and manage volatile gas tokens (ETH, POL, AVAX) just to pay a $10 USDC monthly membership. If a subscriber runs out of native gas, their transaction reverts and their subscription lapses.
Subscription Churn from Manual Renewals: Blockchains are fundamentally push-based; contracts cannot pull funds without an active signature. Forcing users to open their wallet and manually sign transactions every 30 days leads to catastrophic subscriber drop-off.
Fragmented Multi-Chain Liquidity: A user's funds are often scattered across Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, or Ethereum, while the merchant’s contract lives on a specific network, forcing users through tedious, multi-step manual bridging.
Lack of Turnkey Merchant Tooling: Web3 builders lack production-ready tooling—such as multi-tier plans, hosted checkout links, HMAC-signed webhooks, and developer API keys for gated access.


Core Innovations & Architecture


USDC-as-Gas on Arc Testnet:
Transactions execute with sub-second finality and utilize USDC directly as the native gas token. Both merchants and subscribers operate purely in stable currency with zero native token volatility or secondary gas token requirements.


Frictionless Cross-Chain Liquidity via Circle CCTP:
Arca integrates Circle’s official Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol. Users can fund subscriptions using USDC held on 15+ supported testnets (Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Ethereum Sepolia, Avalanche Fuji, Polygon Amoy, etc.) via 1:1 burn-and-mint bridging with zero slippage or third-party liquidity pool risk.


Non-Custodial AutoPay Engine:
Subscribers pre-authorize renewals through a scoped EIP-712 typed signature tied to a session key permission. When a subscription cycle expires, an autonomous off-chain relayer triggers the renewal on-chain using ERC-1271 smart account signature verification. Users get true "set-it-and-forget-it" automated billing while retaining 100% custody of their funds.


Turnkey Merchant & Developer Platform:

Multi-Tier Plan Creation: Merchants can launch custom plans with flexible billing durations, tiered pricing, and perk configurations in minutes.
Hosted Checkout Links: Clean, responsive checkout pages (/pay/[planId]) with real-time balance calculations, passkey login, and single-click checkout.
Enterprise Webhooks: Real-time, HMAC-SHA256-signed delivery notifications (payment.succeeded) with dedicated per-endpoint activity logs, response tracking, and payload inspection.
Developer API Keys: Cryptographically hashed secret keys for programmatic subscriber gating and backend verification.
Real-Time Analytics: Powered by The Graph, tracking active MRR, gross revenue, churn, and protocol fees on live dashboards.




Why It Matters
Arca bridges the gap between Web2 user convenience and Web3 self-sovereignty. It enables SaaS platforms, content creators, gaming studios, and DAOs to build sustainable, predictable recurring revenue streams without forcing their customers through Web3 onboarding friction.
howItsMade:
1. Core Architecture & Stack

Smart Contracts (Solidity / Arc Testnet): The protocol is anchored by SubscriptionGateway.sol, which manages plan configurations, multi-tier pricing, flexible cycle durations, protocol fee routing, and permissioned renewals. All payments and protocol fees settle directly in native USDC.
Frontend & Full-Stack Engine: Built with Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Shadcn UI, powering an intuitive merchant portal and checkout dashboard.
On-Chain Client & Transaction Dispatch: Powered by Viem for contract encoding, EIP-712 typed data signing, and ERC-4337 smart account UserOperations via Circle's bundler.
Data & Indexing Layer:

The Graph Subgraph: Deployed directly on Arc Testnet (indexer/subgraph.yaml), indexing events like PlanCreated, Subscribed, and AutoPayExecuted into real-time metrics (MRR, active subscriber counts, historical revenue charts).
MongoDB: Manages high-throughput off-chain state, including encrypted session pre-authorizations, developer API keys, hashed secrets, and webhook activity logs.




2. Partner Technologies & How They Fit Together

Arc Blockchain (Primary Execution Layer & Native USDC Gas):

Arc provides sub-second finality and utilizes USDC as its native gas token.
This eliminated the traditional "dual-token" onboarding barrier: users never need a secondary native gas token (like ETH or MATIC) just to pay a subscription. Every membership fee and network cost is denominated and paid strictly in USDC.


Circle Modular Wallets & WebAuthn Passkeys:

Integrated @circle-fin/modular-wallets-core to deploy ERC-4337 smart accounts secured by biometric passkeys (FaceID / TouchID / Windows Hello), completely abstracting seed phrases.
Leveraged Circle's Paymaster infrastructure so initial account deployments and token approvals are sponsored seamlessly without gas fees.


Circle Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol (CCTP):

Integrated Circle’s official CCTP protocol to solve multi-chain liquidity fragmentation.
If a subscriber’s USDC balance on Arc is empty, the client initiates a 1:1 burn-and-mint bridge from any of 15+ supported testnets (Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Ethereum Sepolia, Avalanche Fuji, Polygon Amoy, etc.).
The application tracks the DepositForBurn event on the source chain, queries Circle’s Iris attestation service for the cryptographic signature, and executes receiveMessage on Arc to mint native USDC directly into the user’s account.


The Graph:

Custom AssemblyScript mappings transform on-chain contract events into queryable GraphQL endpoints, powering real-time merchant analytics and buyer subscription tracking.




3. Notable Engineering Breakthroughs & Solutions


Bypassing Viem’s Gas Estimator for Circle's Arc Bundler:
Arc Testnet’s bundler strictly enforces a maxPriorityFeePerGas >= 1 gwei. Standard Viem fee estimation defaults to ~0.002 gwei on testnets, causing immediate bundler rejections. Furthermore, manually setting gas limits (callGasLimit, verificationGasLimit) caused the bundler to invalidate its own paymaster signature (yielding AA23 reverts). We engineered a hybrid gas strategy: fetching gas prices from Circle's oracle (getUserOperationGasPrice) to enforce the 1 gwei priority floor, while leaving gas limits dynamic for the bundler’s internal estimator.


Non-Custodial AutoPay Engine via EIP-712 & ERC-1271:
Blockchains are strictly "push-based"—smart contracts cannot spontaneously withdraw funds without a transaction trigger. To achieve true Web2-style recurring renewals, we implemented an EIP-712 structured permission scheme. Users sign a typed authorization granting a renewal allowance over a defined cycle. An off-chain relayer continuously evaluates eligible expired subscriptions, verifies the authorization on-chain via ERC-1271 smart account signature validation, and executes subscribeWithSignature() on the user's behalf without holding custody of user keys.


Automated CCTP Attestation State Machine:
CCTP bridging requires waiting for finality on the source chain before Circle’s attestation service signs the message. We designed a resilient client-side state machine with exponential backoff and transaction hash recovery that bridges the tokens, captures the burn nonce, waits for attestation, and automatically triggers the destination mint and subscription checkout without forcing the user to leave the page.


HMAC-SHA256 Webhook Delivery Pipeline:
Modeled after Stripe’s webhook security, every on-chain subscription confirmation emits an event that triggers an internal dispatch queue. The queue constructs a timestamped payload, signs it using HMAC-SHA256 with the merchant’s unique endpoint secret, records execution latencies and status codes, and displays real-time delivery logs on a dedicated webhook inspection dashboard.

name: TR4CE
description: Verifiable ERC-4626 vault evidence for people and agents. Vault Activity data? Verified ✅
projectDescription:
Most vault products show a number without preserving enough context to verify it. And that's the main reason i built TR4CE. ERC-4626 standardizes how vaults are called, but a clean APY or successful preview does not prove that the data is complete, current, tied to the right asset, or comparable across different vault implementations.
TR4CE traces Base mainnet vault activity and turns it into reproducible evidence reports. Each report keeps the vault address, chain, blocks, observation window, raw calculation inputs, policy version, provenance, and limitations. I then evaluate that evidence against five explicit rules covering the underlying asset, history, TVL, observed share-value return, and account withdrawability.
Every rule returns PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN. I treat missing, stale, reverted, or unsupported data as UNKNOWN instead of guessing a value or hiding the gap. The committed evidence manifest currently covers four USDC-denominated ERC-4626 vaults across Morpho V2 and Yearn V3, backed by recorded Base contract reads and public transaction references.
When someone wants to act on a report, TR4CE prepares exact deposit or redeem calldata and simulates it at a named block. It never signs or submits the transaction. The connected wallet owner still reviews and approves every action. I built it this way so the same evidence can help a person, wallet, or agent make a decision without giving TR4CE custody of funds or control of a private key.
howItsMade:
I built TR4CE as an evidence pipeline rather than another vault dashboard. The historical layer is a Rust and WASM package running on The Graph Substreams. It filters Base blocks to a configurable set of ERC-4626 vaults, then emits typed deposits, withdrawals, share transfers, and block-scoped snapshots through protobuf. Keeping vault addresses as runtime parameters means the same package can trace a different curated set without rebuilding it.
The Substreams output uses the PostgreSQL Database Changes format. Raw observations and the stream cursor land together, while a worker promotes only confirmed rows into the application schema. If a deep reorganization changes a promoted block, dependent reports and prepared actions are invalidated instead of quietly serving stale evidence.
I kept the evidence and policy logic in shared TypeScript packages. Token values stay in integer base units, ratios retain their original inputs, and missing data never becomes a convenient zero. The five policy rules always resolve to PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN, so the web app, API, and MCP tools all return the same decision from the same evidence.
The interface uses Next.js and React, with Hono for the HTTP API and a generated OpenAPI 3.1 contract. I also built six MCP tools for vault search, evidence retrieval, policy evaluation, action preparation, and receipt status. viem handles contract reads and simulation, while wagmi hands unsigned calls to the connected wallet. TR4CE never receives a private key and has no transaction submission endpoint.
The most time-consuming part was making the proof honest across Morpho V2 and Yearn V3. They share ERC-4626 interfaces but not identical behavior, so I kept versioned adapters and raw capability results instead of forcing everything into one score. I also found that substreams run --test-file was not enforcing assertions in the CLI version I used. I wrote a pinned live-check script that runs real Base blocks and compares the output with committed fixtures. That workaround became part of the reproducible evidence trail rather than something hidden from reviewers.

name: Deflow
description: Non-custodial compliance payment gateway for crypto checkouts.
projectDescription:
Deflow bridges the gap between regulatory requirements and Web3 privacy. We separate fund flow from compliance screening: money moves strictly between payer and merchant contracts, while checks run in an isolated enclave.
Non-custodial: Deflow never takes custody of funds. Payments go into the merchant’s dedicated smart contract (MerchantGateway) during a short screening window. The contract has only two exits: forward to the merchant on approval, or refund to the payer if flagged or timed out. Funds cannot be frozen.
Zero Data Liability: Personal documents and paid AML intelligence never touch the merchant's servers, Deflow's backend, or the blockchain. Verification executes inside a Chainlink CRE enclave (TEE). The blockchain only ever receives an opaque, single-use nullifier, a verified tier, and an expiry timestamp.
Compliance: Deflow runs automated sanctions and fund provenance (KYT) checks out of the box for every payments in real time. Merchants toggle identity checks (Sumsub / World ID) only when transaction thresholds or local jurisdictions require it.
howItsMade: Deflow combines Solidity gateways on Base Sepolia, a Next.js checkout and a Go Chainlink CRE confidential workflow running in a TEE. Sumsub KYC stays inside the enclave, only a merchant-scoped nullifier reaches the chain. KYT uses GoPlusScreener (instead of Sumsub AML because of costs) to score wallet risk before settlement. Privy provides merchant wallets and approval policies. Payments are escrowed, then settled or automatically refunded. World ID support was prepared but disabled because we were not granted access during the hackathon.

We introduce a binary hash tree of user assets that serve as inclussion check data structure to provide better hints about assets that can be loaded for the user and user recognized.
howItsMade: With 5can.eth (aka. scan-evm.eth) and so on maintains a registry of user assets and serves hints using CCIP. We get tokenlists, making not-so optimized requests about balances for lost of assets at the same time based on the assets that other users also recognized as quality ones.
