name: Ottopus
description: Stop juggling wallets to get one thing done. Let your agent plan; you review and sign.
projectDescription:
You have assets spread across wallets and chains. Doing one thing onchain means remembering which wallet holds what, then comparing dapps/ protocols for a route, then reading calldata you can't read or using other simulation tools.
Ottopus hands that work to your agent and keeps the decision with you. Link your wallets once, point any MCP-capable agent at Ottopus, and say what you want "Buy 500 USD worth Spacex token." Ottopus looks across every linked wallet, picks the one that makes the action cheapest, builds the route, decodes it, and hands back a review link with a one-sentence reason:
"Recommended Trading wallet (…7A21) — already holds USDC on Base, avoids a bridge and an approval, saves about $4."
You open the link, see in plain language what will happen, simulate it against live chain state, and sign it in your own wallet. The agent never holds a key and never sends anything tool calls produce plans, not transactions.
It works with the wallets you already have: hardware, hot, or a multisig like Safe. Ottopus is not a wallet and takes no custody. It plans, explains and
simulates. You stay the signer.
howItsMade:
A pnpm workspace with two deployables from one commit: a Next.js web app on Vercel and a Node service on Railway, over Supabase Postgres.
The service holds everything that matters — the plan engine, the calldata decoder, external decoders, connectors to services like swap, earn protocols, simulation, and a remote MCP server (Streamable HTTP + OAuth 2.1) that
any agent host can add by URL. The web app renders what the service verified; it never computes a plan or touches the database. Auth is Privy.
Plans are append-only and bound to an immutable hash, so a plan can't change between what you review and what you sign. Simulation runs through a provider
independent of whoever built the route.

name: Agentic EMS
description: Empower EMS with agentic layer for fixed income strategies safely and like a pro.
projectDescription:
Institutional-grade DeFi lacks a unified intelligence and execution layer. While traditional fixed-income traders rely on Bloomberg to monitor macro liquidity, assess underlying credit risks, and execute structured instruments, DeFi equivalents are forced to manually cross-reference fragmented data silos—DefiLlama for TVL, L2Beat for roll-up security, governance forums, and disparate on-chain analytics.
This operational fragmentation makes sizing large allocations across liquidity pools, money markets, and yield protocols inefficient and structurally risky and time consuming.
The Solution: welcome the  Agentic Execution Management System (EMS)
This project rebuilds the Bloomberg terminal kind of experience for fixed-income and yield-focused DeFi allocators, powered by an autonomous, dual-agent architecture accessed through a natural language interface:
Macro & Market Ingestion: An automated ETL engine aggregates real-time macro indicators across DeFi sectors ( using theGraph, defillama and other data providers): scraping TVL flows, fee yields, protocol governance shifts, and underlying L1/L2 systemic risk vectors.

Predictive Intelligence: By pairing transformer-based language reasoning with time-series forecasting models, the system evaluates protocol counterparty risk and models multi-chain yield projections.

Institutional-Grade Execution The agent synthesizes trader intent into an optimized execution strategy, deconstructing large capital allocations into multi-leg routing transactions using bridging solutions like CCTP, lifi, layerzero, OneInch SwapVM to minimize slippage and MEV exposure and can convert positions to stablecoin in less time risk.
Continuous Portfolio Management:  Once on-chain legs settle, the platform tracks positions autonomously, surfacing dynamic hedging recommendations and automated rebalancing alerts.
howItsMade:
The platform is organized within a modular TypeScript-first Turborepo monorepo comprising five distinct applications:

The Trading Desk UI: A high-performance dashboard that guides allocators through intent capture, visual portfolio payoffs, quantitative risk simulation parameters (vega, alpha, beta, gamma which are generated by the AI agent pipeline) and live execution tracking across categories of DeFi protocols (LP, lending, prediction markets, etc…).

Serverless Inference Microservice: A dedicated engine hosted on Google Cloud product running multi-agent workflows that stream typed, step-by-step reasoning events directly to the interface.


Predictive Risk & Indexing Service: An analytical back-end integrating temporal data retrieval, automated market indexing, and quantitative yield projections.


Execution & Settlement Engine: A venue-agnostic transaction compiler that turns strategic goals into concrete on-chain routing instructions across standard bridging protocol (layerZero), standard bridge aggregators (Lifi), and CCTP.


Chain Validation Harness: An automated environment that tests and verifies execution scenarios against live network state forks to ensure deterministic gas fees and possibility of other challenges like MeV sandwich attacks, etc.


Partner Integrations:


Data & Risk Aggregation: Instead of building ad-hoc indexers, we leveraged The Graph alongside Messari’s standardized subgraphs across ~200 deployments to normalize liquidity, lending, and derivative protocols. Macro risks and protocol vulnerabilities are sourced directly from DeFiLlama, L2Beat, and governance hubs.


Sovereign Custody & Approval: We combined Privy (embedded wallets), Ledger (hardware clear-signing), and Safe (multi-sig smart accounts) so institutions retain total sovereignty: agents propose allocations, but devices approve them.



Cross-Chain Settlement & Liquidity: Circle Arc and CCTP v2 provide native cross-chain settlement with zero bridge friction, while 1inch and Uniswap v4 serve as our programmable routing layer for deep liquidity and custom pool hooks.

Inference layer: it runs on Google Vertex AI based Gemini-3.1 / 2.5 models for multi-step reasoning, orchestrated with LangGraph (as the multi-agent system doing custom analysis across the DeFi data analysis pipeline and order execution setup based on the risk parameters), traced via LangSmith (in order to provide the observability), and paired with TimescaleDB and Google’s TimesFM3 open source for continuous time-series yield forecasting.
Resolutions to the challenges I faced during developing the app:


Bypassing Ingestion Bottlenecks: Institutional governance forums and analytics dashboards aggressively rate-limit scrapers. We engineered a stealth Python worker running specialized browser virtualization to scrape critical governance signals, backed by cross-language schema tests to prevent data drift.


Robust error / hallucination handling: That these AI / RAG agents are famously bad news when it comes to hallucination and lack of attribution of data. We have been very strict in terms of detecting all those generated hallucinated patterns, and we have defined very strict guardrails. Either the AI agent will generate the correct response (that is, the predictions for investment into a strategy) or generate the ER EIP-712 transaction typed data structure correctly, or it will give null as an error. We handle the AI agent orchestration and its reliability very seriously.


Simulation of the APY’s of yields: To provide more comprehensive analysis for the fixing traders to define their backstops and other rebalancing strategies. The Times FM3 model provides them with the possibility to predict the potential API/APY yield for the future. It is a state-of-the-art model that can start predicting any time series data, provided it is sufficiently fine-tuned, starting from 10 time series data points of lending protocols, it will be able to do a simulation perfectly.

name: BONE DRY
description: A promise that can't bounce: cross-chain solvency for 1inch Aqua via Opcode 35 & Uniswap v4
projectDescription:
Bone Dry: a promise that can't bounce
Bone Dry makes sure a market maker on 1inch Aqua can't sell the same money twice. If a maker is promising more than their wallet can pay, their quote gets worse, and past a limit the trade is refused, on-chain, before anything breaks.

The problem

On 1inch Aqua, market makers don't lock their money in a pool. It stays in their own wallet, and they just publish a promise: "I'll trade up to this much."
That's efficient, but nothing stops a maker from promising the same balance again and again. When several traders try to use those promises, the first trade goes through and the rest fail, because the money isn't there.
We measured it. 7 of the 12 largest maker positions on Base were promising money they didn't hold. On Ethereum, about 102,000 WETH was advertised, but only around 4 WETH could actually be delivered.

The fix: opcode 35

1inch Aqua strategies run on a small program called SwapVM. We added a new instruction to it, opcode 35. A maker can add it to any strategy, and every time someone trades against it, it:
Checks what the wallet already owes to the maker's other strategies.
Widens the price as the wallet gets stretched. The more of the wallet is already promised, the less generous the quote.
Refuses the trade past a limit the maker chooses, for example 80%, so a promise the wallet can't cover never gets filled.
Makers can still withdraw a promise at any time, in one transaction.

Swapping through Uniswap v4

We built a Uniswap v4 hook called Tap. Its pool holds zero money. When someone swaps, the hook fills the trade straight from Aqua makers' wallets in the same transaction.
If a maker refuses, the hook doesn't fail the swap. It records the refusal on-chain and fills the trade from the next maker that can pay.

One wallet, two chains

Bone Dry is live on Base and Ethereum, and the same wallet can make promises on both.
For traders: before you sign, the app quotes your trade on both chains. It shows the price you'd get and how much of your trade each chain can actually fill, so you can choose.
For makers: the app shows your whole book across both chains, promised against what your wallet holds, and warns you before you publish a strategy that would be refused.

The Graph

Our Aquifer subgraph on Base reads every strategy as it's published. It spots the ones using opcode 35 and checks whether each one's list of the maker's other strategies is complete. It also records every opcode-35 fill and every refusal the hook catches, so the app can show what happened to each maker's strategies, with links to the transactions.

Proof it works

Live on Base mainnet and Ethereum mainnet (router and Uniswap v4 hooks on both).
First real trade through opcode 35 on Base: the quote was cut by 2.98% because the wallet was 60% committed (tx 0x95aab656…).
First real refusal on Base: a strategy at 90% committed was turned away against its 80% limit, and the swap still completed from another maker (tx 0xe29c843d…).
56 contract tests and 15 subgraph tests, all passing.
howItsMade:
Built with: Solidity and Foundry · 1inch Aqua and SwapVM · Uniswap v4 (hooks and PoolManager) · The Graph (AssemblyScript subgraph) · Next.js 16, React 19, viem, wagmi and RainbowKit · Postgres for an Ethereum strategy index · deployed on Vercel.

Opcode 35, added to 1inch SwapVM without forking it

Extending, not copying: 1inch's opcode table is overridable, so our BoneDryRouter extends it and adds one new instruction at slot 35. The original opcodes 0–34 are untouched, so every existing 1inch strategy still runs on our router.
What a strategy carries: its settings are packed into its program as [declared total][sibling count][sibling hashes][max utilisation][widen bps]. On every trade the instruction:
reads the maker's other strategies on-chain (up to 6);
rejects a declared total lower than what it finds;
reads the wallet's real balance and allowance;
then widens the price or refuses.
Safe maths: it uses mulDiv so huge numbers can't overflow. The whole router is 19,793 bytes, under Ethereum's 24,576-byte contract limit, with nothing removed.
Events only on real trades: it emits EncumbranceApplied only on a real trade, never during a price quote, so the index only records trades that happened.

A Uniswap v4 hook with an empty pool

Mining the address: a v4 hook's permissions live in the last bits of its address. Our Foundry script searches salts until the address carries exactly "before swap" and "return a delta".
Filling the swap: the hook takes each swap in beforeSwap and fills it maker by maker. It pulls tokens from each maker's wallet through Aqua and settles with the PoolManager in the same transaction, so the pool never holds a balance.
Catching refusals: each maker's quote and fill is wrapped in try/catch. A refusing maker becomes a MakerSkipped(maker, strategy, token, amount, reason) event, and the trade moves on to the next maker. Normally a revert leaves no trace; this turns it into a record.
Two bugs we hit and fixed:
Rounding remainder: splitting a trade across makers left a few units unfilled, which made multi-maker swaps fail. The remainder now goes to the first maker.
Partial fills: in an empty pool, a partial fill would push the price to its limit and break the pool. Swaps are now all-or-nothing.

The Graph: reading strategies as they're published

No extra events needed: when a strategy is published, the subgraph walks its program bytes the same way the VM does. It finds opcode 35 and decodes its settings from the bytes alone.
Completeness check: it compares each strategy's list of siblings with the maker's actual live strategies and flags lists that are incomplete.
Fills and refusals: it indexes our router's EncumbranceApplied and both hooks' MakerSkipped, and collapses a refusal the hook retried within one swap into a single record. Mappings are covered by 15 Matchstick tests.

The app

Two books, never mixed: Aqua keeps balances per router, so 1inch's makers and our opcode-35 makers are separate books. The route API plans each one, re-checks every maker's real balance live, drops makers whose quote would fail, and picks the better book.
Both chains compared fairly: the same trade is quoted on Base and Ethereum and compared by price per unit actually filled, plus how much of the trade each chain can take.
Always a current quote: browsing uses a 20-second cache, so repeat quotes come back in about 36 ms. Pressing Swap always re-quotes fresh and stops if the price moved.
Your book on every chain: the maker book comes from the subgraph on Base, and from our Postgres index plus on-chain logs on Ethereum, with every amount re-read live.
Honest declarations: the strategy builder works out the declared total on the server from live balances, so a maker can't under-declare by mistake.

Things we're proud of

Refusals you can see: the hook turns a failed quote into an on-chain event, and the subgraph makes it searchable. The first real refusal on Base is indexed and shown in the app.
Cross-chain without a bridge: opcode 35 only rejects a declaration that's too low. So a maker can include what they owe on another chain, and the strategy will refuse when their whole book is overstretched.
Rehearsed before sending: every mainnet script ran on a fork first, with safety checks that abort rather than over-promise. The full Ethereum deployment cost about 0.0004 ETH, and our tests swap against the live Ethereum contracts.

name: ALFQuote
description: Hook-aware discovery, assessment, quotes, and protected Uniswap v4 swap dry-runs.
projectDescription:
ALFQuote is a hook-aware integration toolkit for discovering, assessing, quoting, and safely simulating swaps through Uniswap v4 DualPool hooks on Ethereum.
DualPool hooks can keep assets in external ERC-4626 vaults and return liquidity to Uniswap only when a swap occurs. As a result, the standard PoolManager liquidity value can be zero even when the hook has usable capacity and can provide a quote. Integrators that inspect only vanilla PoolManager liquidity can incorrectly reject these pools.
ALFQuote provides a reusable TypeScript library and an alfquote command-line interface with four commands:
discover enumerates factory deployments or reconstructs a hook’s pools from onchain Initialize events.
assess reports compatibility, provenance, routing requirements, and upgradeability as four independent, evidence-backed fields. It never compresses them into a misleading “safe” verdict.
quote checks hook and pool liveness, applies the hook’s advertised gas bound, reads vanilla liquidity, reserves, and effective liquidity separately, and produces a hook-aware indicative quote.
swap builds protected Universal Router v2 calldata and performs a read-only simulation. It reports slippage protection, gas, decoded reverts, balances, ERC-20 allowances, Permit2 allowances, and all execution blockers. It never signs or broadcasts a transaction.
Every command supports readable terminal output and a stable JSON envelope for coding agents. Results include schema version, chain and block context, input data, warnings, status, and structured output or errors. Zero quotes, unavailable evidence, failed liveness, and identity mismatches fail closed rather than becoming usable prices.
The project includes live Ethereum mainnet verification, a successful protected swap on a controlled Tenderly mainnet fork, reproducible evidence, 235 automated tests, package-boundary checks, and no-send safety gates.
howItsMade:
ALFQuote is an npm workspace written in TypeScript. It contains a reusable alfquote library, a Commander-based CLI, separate read-only verification scripts, and isolated Tenderly fork-evidence tooling. The onchain integration uses viem for Ethereum RPC reads, ABI encoding and decoding, event parsing, storage access, calldata construction, and transaction simulation.
The discovery service reads the official DualPool factory registry at an explicit block. For each deployment, it verifies provenance in both directions: the factory must recognize the hook, and the hook must report the expected factory. Pool discovery scans PoolManager Initialize logs, filters by the exact event signature, reconstructs every PoolKey field, and derives the PoolId to check it against the event. Explicit fixtures remain clearly labeled and never inherit a factory claim.
Assessment is deliberately conservative. ERC-165 support and required IALFHook views establish compatibility. Provenance, routing policy, and upgradeability remain independent. Proxy detection checks EIP-1967 implementation, beacon, and admin storage slots, plus EIP-1167 minimal-proxy bytecode. Failed or incomplete reads produce unknown or unverified, never a favorable guess.
The quote service checks isLive() and livePools(poolId) before quoting. It reads maxGas() and uses that value as the quote call’s gas bound. It then reports three different liquidity signals:
Vanilla PoolManager liquidity
Total DualPool reserves
Effective liquidity currently usable for swaps
The mainnet proof showed why this distinction matters: the selected PoolManager position reported zero vanilla liquidity while the DualPool hook had positive effective liquidity and returned a non-zero quote.
Protected swaps are encoded for Universal Router v2 using V4_SWAP, SWAP_EXACT_IN_SINGLE, SETTLE_ALL, and TAKE_ALL. The release path always uses empty DualPool hookData. amountOutMinimum is calculated from the quote and an explicit slippage value. Simulation checks the sender’s token balance, ERC-20 approval to Permit2, Permit2 approval to Universal Router, and Permit2 expiration. Reverts are decoded and classified conservatively. The public library contains no wallet client, private key, signer, approval transaction, or broadcast function.
Tenderly was used as a controlled mainnet-fork environment because a read-only mainnet address did not have the balances and Permit2 approvals needed to prove successful execution. A fresh evidence run funded an isolated test address, submitted normal approval transactions, and executed a protected 1 USDC swap. The quote, minimum output, actual output, gas, balance changes, and hook events were reconciled. Mainnet remained read-only, and the successful fork simulation remains the primary execution proof.
The CLI uses Commander 15 and exposes injectable arguments, environment variables, and output sinks so command behavior can be tested without spawning processes. Human and JSON output come from the same structured result. Big integers are serialized as decimal strings, RPC credentials are redacted, and long calldata is preserved without truncation. Exit codes distinguish success, typed skips, invalid input, unavailable evidence, swap blockers, configuration problems, and internal failures.
The repository uses Vitest for unit and integration coverage. CI performs a clean install, type-check, build, 235 tests, package-boundary checks, and no-send scans. An offline end-to-end test drives all four commands through one mocked transport. An opt-in integration script verifies the complete journey against live Ethereum mainnet.

name: Helico
description: An agent trades and grows your idle capital without ever taking token custody.
projectDescription:
Helico lets an AI agent manage your capital without ever taking custody of it.
Instead of granting an open-ended token approval to an external bot, you receive a counterfactual smart contract account at a precomputed address, allowing it to receive funds before deployment. You name Helico's agent — a contract, not a key — and explicitly whitelist allowed markets. The agent cannot call functions that transfer tokens elsewhere or specify arbitrary recipients—it can only allocate capital across your approved venues. Capital recovery is permanently guaranteed: the emergency escape hatch resides directly in the proxy rather than the implementation contract, meaning no upgrade can alter or remove it. Even when tested against a hostile implementation, the account owner retains full clawback authority.
Execution is a Chainlink CRE workflow that registers handlerInTee — the handler is declared for the AWS Nitro enclave the network provides — and runs on Chainlink's DON. Every five minutes, it scans every account, evaluates real-time yields across four lending markets, and balances idle liquidity against active allocations. Strategy thresholds are secrets the Vault DON releases only to that handler; what leaves is only the final rebalancing decision — as a report the DON signs and writes to Arbitrum One through Chainlink's KeystoneForwarder, into the agent contract your account named. No key of ours is in that path: the forwarder is the only address that can reach the agent's onReport, a DON transmitter pays the gas, and the agent can only call the two functions your account lets an agent call. In practice it moves capital to whichever pays most — Morpho at 4.32%, Compound USDC at 2.83%, Aave at 2.69%, Compound ETH at 1.26% as of today. Fifteen such moves are on chain across five owners' accounts, sent by nine different DON transmitters under one policy hash, each with the account's own event confirming what moved; the latest landed 23 seconds after a fresh wallet's single signature.
Allocated funds remain fully liquid and spendable. Through a 1inch Aqua mandate, your tokens never leave your wallet — the app holds a ledger entry, not money. When a taker executes a swap, the app unwinds the exact deficit from the lending venue mid-transaction, eliminating the traditional tradeoff between earning yield and staying liquid. Three such fills are on Arbitrum One: each one spent the account's idle cent first, redeemed exactly the shortfall out of Morpho inside the swap, paid the taker, and left the rest earning — and within two runs the network had restored the floor and lent out the ether the taker paid.
A dedicated subgraph, published to The Graph Network, provides visibility across the system. Because Aqua balances are nested multiple layers deep without indexed event parameters, querying active mandates for a wallet is impossible directly on-chain; the indexing layer bridges this gap to surface full portfolio activity. The chat reads that index through The Graph's Subgraph MCP, so a question about your position is answered from the data, with the queries shown beside the answer.
howItsMade:
Three partner integrations perform critical on-chain work rather than serving as passive marketing additions.
Chainlink CRE
Rebalancing decisions are computed by a workflow that registers handlerInTee — the handler is declared for the AWS Nitro enclave the network provides — and runs on Chainlink's DON, deployed to the WorkflowRegistry on Ethereum mainnet (workflow id 0x00fa897bf0b15b8f108f18499ec76ed0817ffac1a06fac02d6e2a8814339b14c), executing every five minutes on DON zone-a against Arbitrum One. Its production configuration matches the repository's config.production.json byte-for-byte, confirmed by identical SHA-256 hashes. The rebalancing policy is injected from the Vault DON as a single JSON secret per execution; an LLM only explains the verdict afterwards and has no influence over it.
The verdict leaves as a report the DON signs and writes to Arbitrum One through the KeystoneForwarder (0xF8344CFd5c43616a4366C34E3EEE75af79a74482, confirmed by typeAndVersion() before anything was pinned to it) into HelicoAgent (0x98c3979358A4e5086Da432CfE91F45aE2A854463), an IReceiver behind a UUPS proxy that the account names as its agent. The forwarder and Helico's workflow-owner key are immutables of that contract; any other sender or workflow owner is refused, and a move past its deadline is dropped rather than made late. A DON transmitter pays the gas, no Helico key signs anything on the way, and the agent can only call supplyIdle and withdrawIdle on the account — neither takes a recipient.
Fifteen moves have been carried this way across five owners' accounts, by nine different DON transmitters under one policy hash (0x84e5626f4fce38e751648d10b37c972d2e1833a8cb2abe9287332894e0ae5363). The first, on 11 September, supplied the first account's idle USDC to Morpho (0x0668c698cf3d396e622a97bfa3e21016de44fb41863fa7cb69b47bd126f9ed27). On 12 September it withdrew that position a minute after an Aqua mandate was shipped from the account (0x6b37141bf0357a7c7b16d7288336bebdb1c091f3f5e40901addfc421fe7fb1b5) — the enclave read the mandate as a claim on the wallet — and after we taught it which apps cover a fill from a venue (coveringApps) the next run supplied it back with the mandate still live (0x0beffeee97ad8a0f11e19af59e763394d4838440796967357ef578299e1d3435). On 13 September a second owner, from a wallet holding 0.001 ETH and nothing else, typed "swap $1 of ETH to USDC and put it all to work" and signed once — the batch opened the account, swapped through 1inch with the account as receiver, named the agent, permitted four markets and shipped a mandate (0x2742cb300e00e8345b5fb395c6732de9fcb4a1911c2b6de7b71d34b4e77f4814) — and three minutes later the DON supplied the USDC to Morpho (0xa99162965825d575b30809c2b073eac53079e3ac573bb732da6f695fb7a9866e). A third owner put both assets to work in one sentence (0xf10298a158159d53b76fbe00b7ffe9c3c63c2db3f457c361ce497aefa1ab278f); the DON placed them one per run, five minutes apart (0x9484d76177ef7a0994f524185786141987e1b74a8755857b993829db0fa57cbc, 0x98bd82ef069c8370be2a334fe492037623d8fed3953c045ba4142e2b73e0a82f), because HelicoAccount.nonce is strictly sequential and one signed statement authorises one call. A fifth owner, on camera: "swap $10 of ETH to USDC and put it all to work", one signature (0x3e12b4fd710b332fda1ec713a30920652edde4ba151e63df80e233af356da25e), and 9.96 USDC was in Morpho 23 seconds later (0xb1f4d9bf239faceda9251747bde970a228b5843a9b757426b7c481221663bf6f). Each time a taker filled against a lent-out position, the network restored the account's floor and lent out the ether the taker paid within two runs.
The portfolio line values an ether position at Chainlink's ETH/USD feed at each hour, read from the aggregator's own round history (getRoundData) — the same feed the app sizes dollars with — so the chart moves when the market did.
Standardizing three distinct lending protocols required bridging major interface differences. Because ILendingVenue adopts Aave v3's native function signatures, Aave connects directly while Compound and Morpho use custom adapters. Both Aqua applications query receipts for UNDERLYING_ASSET_ADDRESS(); Compound's Comet uses baseToken(). To streamline integration and grant native burn authority without external approvals, our custom venues serve as their own receipt tokens. Yields are normalized from three distinct representations into a single metric before entering the enclave: Aave uses an annual ray, Compound uses a per-second wad, and Morpho's unlisted rate is derived by sampling its share price against a 1e27 probe.
1inch Aqua
HelicoMandateSwap (0x0524a353dfab33CD362593ae8e97707764Fb6041) operates as an Aqua application where the mandate defines the entire execution strategy: expiration, designated agent, fee parameters, and permitted venues. User funds remain in their own wallets. If a trade requires more capital than the wallet currently holds idle, the contract pulls the receipt token via Aqua and redeems only the necessary balance before finalizing the swap. A taker of this app must be a contract, since the app pays first and calls back for payment, so HelicoTaker (0x7A52bfD7EF1b4D0345d6e76deD649FC05208DD58) is deployed for any wallet to take through; three fills are on chain — 0xd8dc7dfdfce77c83ea79c9e6eb683cb013939a5f8113af5a10d6936212ff7310, 0x05cad1f5ae7c6c02588b0227d7d165de4ef2224aca2720ec0ae2063629e5afb2, 0xfb15dd01efa9aca0a8e11d05a94a831f07e25008e0e620056a75a5a8725184d1 — each spent the account's idle cent first, redeemed exactly the shortfall out of Morpho inside the swap, and left the rest earning. Additionally, we added an on-chain instruction to a fork of 1inch's SwapVM—returning opcode 34 for AQUA_YIELD_COVER_OPCODE()—letting a concentrated position pay a taker directly out of an active lending position.
The Graph
A custom subgraph indexes both Aqua and our account factory. This indexing layer is essential: because the three-state sentinel distinguishing a docked mandate from an empty balance emits no event, the indexing handler queries the chain directly for each balance. The frontend queries this index through an intermediate Go caching service with operation-name whitelisting to protect API quota limits.
Two Graph products, composed. The subgraph is published to The Graph Network (id 7Qw2zNn9recjF81BVL), and the chat backend composes it with The Graph's Subgraph MCP server: a status question —"why has nothing moved?" — opens an MCP session, hands the model the subgraph's schema, and lets it write its own GraphQL against our subgraph, at most five queries, pinned to that one id. The answer comes back as the last step beneath the reply, with every MCP call shown as a step above it — initialize, schema, each qhether the schema accepted it — so the reads that produced the sentence are visible beside it.Asked what is left in a mandate a taker had just filled against, it answered the ledger's figure to the micro-unit. The enclave keeps its direct GraphQL read; the composition lives in the natural-language interface.
Engineering Highlights

Declared Asset Scope: The enclave batches every market and asset into a single eth_call, and a venue reverts when asked about an asset it does not list, so one refusal would fail the whole run. Markets now declare which assets they list, and a market that declares none serves them all. Declared rather than inferred ropped call, a paused venue, and a market that genuinely does not hold the asset all arrive as thesame silence.
Precise Share Conversions: A share count is not an amount of money, so conversions go through tdeem rather than arithmetic copied out of it. Copied arithmetic works today and drifts from thecontract that actually burns the shares.
Upgradeable Proxies: Both Aqua contracts and the agent sit behind the same lightweight 163-byteintegration tests proving active mandates persist across implementation upgrades and that areplaced agent implementation brings its own forwarder and workflow owner with it.
Verification & Transparency: Testing spans 178 Solidity tests, 74 of them on an Arbitrum One fothe deployed MorphoVenue through the live account from the real forwarder's address, five moredriving HelicoTaker against the live two-sided mandate's bytes, alongside a live-address suite of 46 checks that drives the deployed contracts themselves on a fork of Arbitrum One. AI assistance is logged in AI-USAGE.md, each entry naming what was asked for, what changed, and what was verified, and implementation plaplans/ before the code, 41 of them.

name: WayFare
description: Agents with hardcoded endpoints aren't a market. Wayfare's agent finds its providers at runtime.
projectDescription:
Every agentic-payments demo hardcodes its endpoints. The agent already knows every service it will ever call, which means there is no discovery, no choice, and no market — just a scripted workflow with a payment attached.
Wayfare removes the config file. Its agent starts a run with a task, a budget, and no tools. It resolves an ENS parent name to enumerate providers it has never seen, reads each one's agent-context record to learn what it does and what it costs, and decides which are worth paying for. Payment happens per call over x402 on Hedera, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. Every settled call is anchored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, so the record of which provider was paid, how much, and for what is publicly verifiable rather than self-reported.
Because nothing is hardcoded, the agent's behaviour changes with its environment. Add a provider while the demo is running and the agent finds it on the next run with no code change. Cut its budget and it makes a different choice — cheaper provider, fewer calls, or it declines to proceed. Providers cannot write their own reputation records; that permission is held separately, so track record is something earned rather than claimed.
Wayfare is infrastructure, not an app. The agent is the demonstration; the discovery, settlement, and receipt layer underneath is the product.
howItsMade:
Wayfare is a TypeScript monorepo: an agent runtime, three independent x402-gated provider services, an ENS identity package, and a React frontend streaming over WebSocket.
Hedera handles settlement. Each provider returns 402 PAYMENT-REQUIRED with its price; the agent constructs a transfer transaction, signs it with its own key, and deliberately leaves it incomplete so the fee payer can finalise it. That partially signed transaction goes back as proof of intent, and the provider forwards it to the Blocky402 facilitator, which verifies it, adds its own signature to cover gas, and submits it. No provider in the system ever pays gas or settles on-chain itself. Pricing is metered per call rather than flat, so cost scales with the work requested. Every settled call writes a receipt to an HCS topic — provider name, amount, transaction id, result hash — confirmed via Mirror Node and linked to HashScan in the UI.
ENS is the discovery layer, not decoration. Each provider is a subname carrying ENSIP-26 records: agent-context describing its capability and pricing in a form an LLM reads directly, and agent-endpoint[mcp] pointing at its callable interface. The agent has no provider list; it resolves one. Enhanced Access Control is what makes the reputation record trustworthy — the role permitted to write it belongs to the settlement recorder, not to the provider being rated.
Bazantic sits between the agent and the providers. Each provider's API is registered as a gateway with a Recipe explaining when it's useful, what it needs, and how to read the result, exposed through Bazantic's MCP server. We ran the same task with the same model and settings against raw API specs versus Recipes, changing nothing else, and measured the difference in success rate and malformed calls.
The hackiest part is the guardrails. Spend ceilings are enforced server-side before every payment rather than requested in the prompt, because an agent told to stay under budget will not. A recorded-run replay endpoint re-emits a real run's events for demo resilience against testnet latency and cold starts.

name: VaultBreaker
description: AI agent capability broker protecting private keys via Ledger seed & Hedera on-chain spend limits
projectDescription:
Vaultbreaker is a scoped-capability broker designed to solve the single biggest security threat in autonomous Web3 AI agents: raw private key exposure.
Today, any AI agent executing autonomous micropayments for pay-per-call APIs or services either holds a raw private key in memory (allowing prompt injections or compromised agents to drain the wallet) or a static API key (exposing credentials with no spend limits). There is no standard pattern for giving an agent narrow, expiring, spend-limited, and non-exfiltratable payment authority.
Vaultbreaker solves this by combining Ledger hardware seed protection with Hedera on-chain budget enforcement and tamper-evident audit logging:


DEVELOPER POLICY REGISTRATION: A developer registers a metered pay-per-call service (e.g., an AI inference endpoint) and defines a spend policy specifying maximum price per call, daily budget ceiling, and token time-to-live (TTL).


LEDGER-PROTECTED CAPABILITY ISSUANCE: When an agent requests authority for a task, the Vaultbreaker broker invokes the Ledger Key Ring CLI (wallet-cli ring) to encrypt the underlying settlement credential using Ledger seed-derived hardware protection. The broker issues a short-lived, scoped capability token to the agent. The agent NEVER sees or holds the raw private key at any point.


x402 METERED SERVICE EXECUTION: The agent presents its capability token + payment header to the x402-gated metered service. An x402 facilitator adapter validates the scope and remaining budget against the deployed smart contracts on Hedera Testnet (CapabilityRegistry.sol), decrementing the budget on-chain per call.


REAL-TIME ON-CHAIN REJECTION (THE DEMO MOMENT): If the agent attempts a call after its budget is exhausted, expired, or explicitly revoked, the transaction is rejected ON-CHAIN in real time. The raw credential was never exposed, proving that limits are cryptographically and on-chain enforced rather than just a UI promise.


HEDERA CONSENSUS SERVICE (HCS) AUDIT FEED: Every capability issuance, successful spend, on-chain rejection, and revocation event is written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, producing an immutable, judge-legible audit trail rendered in real time on the frontend timeline.
howItsMade:
Vaultbreaker is built as a three-plane architecture spanning smart contracts, a hardware-secured broker backend, and a cybernetic Next.js frontend:

SETTLEMENT & ENFORCEMENT PLANE (Smart Contracts):
Built with Solidity 0.8.20, Foundry, and OpenZeppelin Contracts.


CapabilityRegistry.sol: Deployed on Hedera Testnet (EVM Chain ID 296). Tracks capability policy hashes, remaining budget accounting, expiration timestamps, and revocation state. Reverts transactions on budget exhaustion (InsufficientBudget), expiry (CapabilityExpired), or revocation (CapabilityRevokedError).
X402FacilitatorAdapter.sol: Serves as the thin adapter between x402 payment callbacks and CapabilityRegistry, ensuring payment settlement occurs only if capability spend checks succeed.
Tested using a complete Foundry test suite (8/8 tests passing) covering time-warped expirations (vm.warp), budget exhaustion, and exact arithmetic.


ISSUANCE & HARDWARE ENCLAVE PLANE (Broker Backend):
Built with Node.js, TypeScript, Express, Ethers.js v6, and Vitest.


Ledger Key Ring Integration: Integrates the Ledger Wallet CLI (wallet-cli ring) as the root of trust to encrypt underlying settlement credentials. Includes a seed-derived AES-256-GCM fallback keyring to guarantee zero credential exposure across all environments.
Policy Engine: Generates cryptographic policy hashes (keccak256) and signs scoped, short-lived JWT capability tokens for the agent.
Vitest Suite & E2E Runner: Includes 4/4 Vitest unit tests and an automated end-to-end integration test (scripts/e2e-demo-test.ts).



AUDIT PLANE (Hedera Consensus Service):
Integrates @hashgraph/sdk to submit structured JSON audit events (CAPABILITY_ISSUED, CAPABILITY_SPENT, CAPABILITY_REJECTED, CAPABILITY_REVOKED) to a Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) topic. The backend auto-polls the Hedera Mirror Node REST API (mirrornode.hedera.com) to populate a live timeline with HashScan verification links.


FRONTEND & UX:
Built with Next.js 16 (App Router + Turbopack), React 19, Tailwind CSS, and Lucide React. Features a Developer Console (policy registration & revocation), an Agent Terminal (simulated x402 micropayment runner with real-time budget gauges), a prominent "REJECTED ON-CHAIN IN REAL-TIME" Cyber-Alert modal for over-budget calls, and a live HCS Audit Feed timeline.

name: ARCANUM
description: Governed USDC wallets for AI agents on Arc, now with signed, offline-verifiable payment receipts.
projectDescription:
Arcanum is a wallet layer for AI agents that have to spend money. Instead of handing an agent a normal wallet and hoping the prompt holds, each agent gets a GuardedWallet contract on Arc with a policy attached by the owner: how much it can spend per payment, per day and per month, which vendor categories it can pay, whether the destination has to be on an allowlist, and the amount above which a human has to look at it. The contract checks all of that inside the same transaction that moves the USDC. Small routine payments just go through. Anything over the review threshold gets held on chain until someone on the council approves or rejects it. Unknown destinations get denied. There is nothing to bypass because the rule lives in the same place as the money.
I have been building this for a while and the app was already live before ETHOnline, so this is a Continuity entry. The repo has a tag marking where the event started, and PRE-EXISTING.md in the root walks through what was there before and what I added during the event, commit by commit.
What I added is payment decision receipts. The idea came from a gap I kept running into. The wallet enforces policy and the indexer shows what happened after the fact, but there was no way to prove what the policy said about one specific payment at one specific moment, especially for a deny, which reverts and leaves nothing on chain. So now, before an agent pays, it can ask for a receipt. The API evaluates the exact signed payment intent against the wallet's policy at one pinned block and signs the result. The receipt has the verdict (allow, escalate, deny or freeze), the reason code, the caps and spend counters it looked at, the vendor entry, whether the signer was authorized, the block number and hash, and the agent's own signature over the request. You can verify it offline against a published issuer registry, no account, no API call. There is a public verify page on the site that does it in the browser.
The receipt id also goes into the calldata of the transaction that acts on it. Afterwards the API links the transaction back to the receipt as evidence: executed, escalated, reverted, and later the council's outcome. An auditor can put the decision next to what actually happened and see whether the chain agreed. One thing I want to be clear about: a receipt never authorizes anything. The contract has no idea receipts exist and evaluates policy again when the transaction lands. The receipt is a record of a decision, not a permission slip.
Everything for this sits on the ethonline-2026 branch: the receipt format and verifier, issuance and evidence linking in the API, the SDK methods (requestPaymentReceipt, executePaymentIntentWithReceipt and attachPaymentReceiptEvidence, and the SDK verifies every receipt before it acts on one), the receipts pages in the dashboard with an evidence timeline, the public verify page, a Circle signer so the agent can sign from a Circle developer-controlled wallet instead of a key file on its own machine, and an inbound CCTP V2 funding flow so a governed wallet on Arc can be topped up from Sepolia USDC.
howItsMade:
The base is what Arcanum already was: Solidity 0.8.24 contracts built with Foundry (GuardedWallet, WalletFactory, PolicyEngine, VendorRegistry, EscalationManager, AnomalyOracle, all on Arc Testnet), a TypeScript monorepo with a Next.js 15 app, tRPC with SIWE sessions, Supabase for the read models, a Ponder indexer feeding them, viem and wagmi on the client, and a TypeScript and a Python SDK. I did not touch the contracts during the event. Receipts live next to them.
The receipt body is a strict schema. Unknown fields are rejected, addresses are lowercased, anything that can exceed 2^53 is a decimal string. It gets serialized with a subset of RFC 8785 (sorted keys, no whitespace, no floats) and hashed with SHA-256, so the digest comes out identical in TypeScript, Python or anything else. The issuer signs that digest with a plain EIP-191 personal signature over a fixed prefix plus the digest. Issuer keys are published in a registry with validity windows, per chain, so verification works offline and I can rotate keys later without breaking old receipts. The API refuses to issue if its configured key is not an active registry entry for the chain it is running on.
To issue one, the API reads the wallet, the policy engine, the vendor registry and the escalation manager with normal eth_calls, all at the same pinned block. The annoying part was the spend windows. The contract rolls the daily and monthly counters over based on block timestamp, so the receipt has to do the same math at that block's timestamp or it would show numbers executeUSDC would never see. After the last read it checks the block hash again; if it changed, that is a CHAIN_READ_FAILED, not a wrong receipt. Envelopes are stored in a Supabase table with a trigger that blocks updates and deletes. Issuance is idempotent per intent reference, so asking twice gets you the original back flagged as replayed. Nothing goes on chain to issue a receipt.
For evidence, the agent puts the receipt id inside the reason string of executeUSDC. To link, the client only sends a transaction hash. The API pulls the transaction and its logs from the Arc RPC itself, requires exactly one matching event from that wallet, notes whether the calldata actually names the receipt, and appends a row: executed, escalated, frozen or reverted, then later the escalation status, each with a flag for whether the chain agreed with the verdict. A denied executeUSDC reverts and emits nothing, so a deny only exists as a receipt, and a revert is evidenced from the transaction status alone. One transaction can only ever link to one receipt.
In the SDK, verifyPaymentReceipt runs four separate checks: format, digest, issuer signature, and the agent's request signature. executePaymentIntentWithReceipt will not submit unless all four pass and the receipt actually answers the intent it just signed. It also will not act on a replayed receipt by default, because the earlier attempt may already have paid and the contract does not dedupe references, so a second executeUSDC is simply a second payment. The dashboard and the public verify page run the exact same verifier in the browser. Verification never talks to the API.
The Circle piece is a viem local account whose signMessage, signTransaction and signTypedData get forwarded to a Circle developer-controlled wallet, so the agent's key lives in Circle's MPC setup and never on the agent's box. I treat Circle as a signing oracle, not something to trust: every signature has to recover to the wallet address, a signed transaction gets parsed back and compared field by field against what I asked for, the entity secret gets re-encrypted for every single request because Circle rejects reused ciphertext, and the SDK does gas estimation and broadcasting to Arc on its own. The thing that cost me the most time: the wallet has to be created on Circle's generic EVM-TESTNET identifier. Named chains like ARC-TESTNET do not support transaction signing, and it took a while to work out that this was what the error meant. The governed wallet, the policy and the receipts have no idea Circle is behind the signer.
CCTP funding burns native USDC on Sepolia with CCTP V2 and mints straight into the governed wallet on Arc. I request Circle's Forwarding Service for the destination mint and keep a separately approved, gas-capped manual relay for when forwarding does not finish. Settlement is checked strictly against the attestation, the nonce and the MessageReceived log on Arc. One detail worth knowing on Arc: USDC is also the gas token, native balances are 18 decimals while the ERC-20 side is 6, and the funding code has to keep those apart or the amounts are off by a lot.
On process: most of the event code, tests, the migration and the docs were written by an AI coding agent working from my written plan, with a second AI reviewing each slice. Design decisions, deployment, the testnet runs and the video are mine. No new npm dependencies were added. It is all written up in PRE-EXISTING.md.

name: AgentARC
description: Agent to agent commerce on ARC: Identity,policy, nanopayments, and escrow.
projectDescription:
AgentARC lets one agent pay another agent in USDC on Circle Arc. I built it around four problems in agentic commerce.
Who to trust: every agent has a Circle wallet, and we only pay sellers we can identify.
What to buy: the agent reads your prompt, finds our seller on Arc, and checks Circle’s marketplace so we don’t overpay.
Whether to pay: small instant jobs go out right away; big or risky jobs hold the money first; bad identity or overspend never pays.
How to settle: we hold USDC, check the delivery, then pay the seller or send it back. After it’s paid, it stays paid, no chargebacks.
Circle Agent Stack in the demo: Agent Wallets, USDC on Arc, Agent Marketplace, Nanopayments, and AuthCapture escrow.
howItsMade:
I built AgentARC as a TypeScript app running on Node 20 with two lightweight HTTP processes: a buyer orchestrator on port 5180 and an independent x402 seller on port 5181. I used Node’s native http module, vanilla HTML/CSS/JS, and Vitest to keep the stack simple.
The flow is: user intent, discovery, ERC-8004 trust signals, deterministic policy, Circle Agent Wallet, USDC on Arc, x402 seller, verification and then receipt.
I used Circle’s developer-controlled wallets for keys and transactions. USDC is both payment and gas on Arc Testnet. x402 gates paid seller APIs using HTTP 402. ERC-8004 data from 8004scan provides identity, feedback, validations, and x402 support as separate signals. CoinGecko provides live ETH pricing and OHLC data, while OpenAI is optional for intent parsing with a regex fallback.
I kept payment decisions deterministic with a rules engine. It fail-closes when identity is missing or failures are high. Small objective jobs use direct nanopayments, while larger or subjective jobs use protected escrow-style flows.
The hacky part was making this reliable on Arc testnet. When Circle’s x402 settlement and contract execution APIs failed, I implemented controlled USDC transfer and AuthCapture fallbacks. I also split the seller into a separate process after discovering that internal API calls could deadlock the original server.

name: Maneki
description: Web3 job board for AI agents: open MCP + AgentKit-verified AI matching. Discover free, act human.
projectDescription:
Maneki (maneki.work) is a live Web3 job board — thousands of active roles scraped nightly from 60+ sources, browsed daily by human candidates. Job-hunting AI agents are coming, and recruiting spam from unverified automation is already here. This project gives agents a first-class way in, with World ID deciding who gets it for free.
The Maneki Agent Gateway exposes two surfaces. Discovery is open, like the web: an MCP server (search_jobs, get_job, list_hiring_companies) that any AI assistant can use with no signup and no API key — just per-IP rate limits. Actions are human-verified: full search results with salary data and AI matching against a real CV sit behind x402. An agent registered on AgentBook — meaning a real, unique, Orb-verified human stands behind its wallet — gets a free quota tied to the anonymous human id, not the wallet address. Spinning up fresh wallets doesn't reset it: Sybil-resistant rate limiting with no accounts, no cookies, no API keys. Everyone else pays $0.01 USDC per request on World Chain or Base.
The payoff: on the website, AI matching requires an email signup gate. For agents, proof of personhood replaces the account entirely. A verified agent posts a CV and gets back scored, ranked matches (23 matches judged from 1,940 candidates in our live demo) — and every application will carry proof that one real human is behind it. That's the spam filter recruiters actually need, and the foundation for continuity: a quota, a match history and a reputation that follow the human across wallets, agents and services.
Live: https://maneki-agent-gateway.vercel.app (MCP at /api/mcp) · https://maneki.work/agents
howItsMade:
The gateway is genuinely registered — agentkit-cli + World App, transaction on World Chain — and the E2E demo runs a real PDF CV (pdf-parse) through agentkit.fetch.
The job data never leaves as a dataset: the gateway queries a private, key-authenticated API on the Maneki Next.js app query-by-query (no bulk export, capped results, links point to Maneki job pages only — anti zero-click by design). The matching endpoint reuses Maneki's production pipeline: deterministic gates first, then LLM judging of shortlisted candidates against the CV.
The hacky bit worth mentioning: @worldcoin/agentkit 0.2.1's client parses the 402 payment-required payload from the response body, but x402 2.25 servers emit it as a base64 response header with an empty body — the reference stack can't complete its own handshake. We ship a response middleware that mirrors the header payload back into the body so both client generations work, and documented it (plus Developer Portal and Sandbox access friction, and a facilitator cold-start timeout we hit in production) in FEEDBACK.md in the repo. Deployed on Vercel via the Hono framework preset after discovering the Node adapter buffers responses and kills MCP streaming — that migration story is in the commit history.

name: HoldBook
description: A prototype for tokenized asset issuance, KYC, and hold workflows on Hedera.
projectDescription: HoldBook is a secondary-market prototype for fictional equity on Hedera Testnet. Eligible users sign NOVA/HBAR orders, which are matched by price-time priority. Sellers lock tokens through ATS Holds, and buyers pay for atomic delivery and settlement. Recorded tests cover normal trades, reverse trades, cancellation and expired-Hold recovery. KYC is synthetic, and reviewers can explore the demo without a wallet.
howItsMade: Built with React, TypeScript, Hedera ATS SDK and MetaMask. A Go service authenticates signed orders, matches trades and stores results in PostgreSQL. A Solidity contract executes ATS Holds and HBAR payments atomically. GitHub Pages, Cloud Run and Neon host the application. AI assistance is documented, wallet actions require manual approval, and original software is MIT-licensed.

name: Arbitra
description: The AI-operated escrow court and reputation protocol for the agentic economy.
projectDescription: Arbitra is a trust-minimized, auditable AI escrow and arbitration protocol for autonomous agents. Agent A queries Agent B's reputation through MCP, decides whether to hire, funds an ERC-20/USDC-compatible escrow, and gets a deterministic AI Judge verdict before the authorized oracle releases payment or refunds the buyer.
howItsMade:
We built Arbitra using a tri-layer architecture: EVM Smart Contracts, a Node.js AI Oracle, and an MCP Reputation Agent.
Think of the protocol like a high-tech courtroom: the Smart Contract acts as the impenetrable vault holding the funds, the MCP Server is the private investigator running background checks, and the Node.js backend is the active judge rendering the final verdict.
Technologies & Partner Integrations
Arc Testnet & Circle: We deployed our ArbiterEscrow.sol contract to the Arc Testnet using Hardhat Ignition. Arc was incredibly beneficial because it treats USDC as a native system-level gas token (0x360...000) while remaining completely EVM-compatible. This allowed us to use standard OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 interfaces without rewriting any Solidity logic for custom token behaviors.
The Graph: To satisfy the AI tooling track, we built an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that acts as an autonomous risk assessor. It seamlessly queries The Graph's Uniswap V3 and Aave V3 subgraphs to pull a seller's DeFi history. By combining live Graph data with our backend's escrow history, our AI can contextually reason about a wallet's risk profile—such as warning a buyer if a seller has zero escrow history but is heavily gambling capital on highly volatile meme coins.
Backend Oracle: The core engine is a Node.js backend using Prisma and Ethers.js v6. It listens for DeliverableSubmitted events on-chain, fetches the associated work, evaluates it using Gemini 2.5 Flash, and signs a resolveEscrow transaction to release funds or issue a refund.

name: T3 Trade
description: An agentic trading environment for your existing AI subscriptions, with enforced risk limits.
projectDescription:
T3 Trade is an open-source agentic trading environment. It gives coding agents a trading workspace with charts, market research, backtests and missions that have a strategy, an expiry and a maximum-loss budget. You can use supported agent providers through their existing CLI logins.
An agent can read the market, publish a plan and wake when a price level or candle condition changes. The server checks every proposed order before signing. Position increases require an exchange-native stop, retries use deterministic order IDs, and the user can pause, reduce, close or revoke a mission even when the agent is offline. Perpetual-futures execution is restricted to Hyperliquid testnet. Research works without a signer.
T3 Forge extends this workflow to Ethereum research. Agents can build typed detectors that combine external sources with onchain swap facts from The Graph. Generated code must pass typechecking, tests and host-reviewed acceptance cases in an isolated container before installation. Each detector retains its evidence and can be armed or disarmed without granting permission to spend. The repository also contains a fixed Uniswap v4 fee hook for a dedicated Sepolia testnet pool, with expiring policies and an owner-controlled pause.
T3 Trade is an alpha built on the open-source T3 Code workspace. The contribution is the trading and research system around that workspace, including deterministic risk checks, market-data recording, event-driven missions and sandboxed detector development. It does not promise returns or offer unattended trading with real funds.
howItsMade:
We forked T3 Code to reuse its agent conversations, repository workflows and desktop shell, then added the trading domain. The web client uses React and TypeScript, the desktop app uses Electron, and the server uses Effect services with SQLite persistence. Typed WebSocket contracts connect the client to server commands. Persisted events drive read models and queued side effects, so the UI sends intent while server-side services enforce policy.
The Hyperliquid adapter owns exchange reads and local signing. A 17-check preview validates mission authority, sizing, leverage, market freshness, risk reservations and stop requirements before an order can proceed. Reconciliation treats exchange positions, orders and fills as authoritative. Pure accounting rules and property tests cover budget exhaustion and reservations.
For Ethereum research, The Graph provides indexed Uniswap swap facts. Source adapters verify deployment identity, indexing errors and freshness before evidence can count as current. The repository includes a Rust Substreams package and a cursor-based ingestion path for pool observations. T3 Forge compiles agent-authored TypeScript detectors in a digest-pinned Docker image with no network, a read-only root and a non-root user. Generated tests and separate host-reviewed acceptance cases gate installation. Missing or stale evidence produces an unknown reading.
The Solidity Uniswap v4 hook is fixed code. It binds to one pool, supports expiring fee policies and falls back to its baseline fee when a policy expires or the owner pauses it. Its authority is separate from Hyperliquid signing. General Uniswap swap drafts currently stop with an explicit broadcaster-missing refusal; a draft is not presented as an executed trade.
The difficult part was separating what an agent may propose from what the host may execute. We kept permissions, spending limits, idempotency and reconciliation in typed services rather than prompts, and made the user's reverse actions work without a running model.

name: SUBFLOOR
description: A signed price floor enforced inside 1inch SwapVM settlement, so an agent cannot sell below it
projectDescription:
SUBFLOOR is a vault where an autonomous agent trades your whole portfolio and one thing is impossible by arithmetic: a fill below the worst price you signed. The floor is not enforced by the strategy, the agent, or anyone watching the mempool. It lives in the settlement function itself, the code no program can reach around, and a machine-checked proof covers every program that could ever run, not just the ones we tested. The authority to set the floor sits on a hardware device in your hand, so the machine that trades is never the machine that defines "worst." A public index recomputes every fill against every floor, so the guarantee is not our claim about our own execution, it is anyone's query. It runs live on mainnet with our own money. A detector can be wrong. A bound cannot.
Prior art, named because it is real: CoW Protocol's settlement contract already enforces on-chain that no order clears worse than what it specifies. But that is taker-side and per discrete order, one signed order at a time. Nothing covers a delegated maker running continuous two-sided programmatic strategies on standing inventory, which is exactly what an agent-run book is. This property exists for taker orders. Nobody gives it to delegated makers.
SUBFLOOR implements ERC-8377 (Reference-Relative Slippage Bounds), a draft standard I authored (ethereum/ERCs PR #1935, public since Aug 2026). The specification is public prior art; every line of implementation here was written during the event, and none of the ERC's reference implementation is reused.
