Dissolving a role. When a role is closed, its remaining balance goes back to the treasury through the same pay() call. That means the treasury is automatically added to every role's allowed recipients. Otherwise, a role with an allowlist could never be closed.


Agent keys. Keys are random (rb_live_ plus 24 bytes, base64url) and stored only as a SHA-256 hash. A slow hash function isn't needed for high-entropy random keys and would only slow down every agent request. Reissuing a key invalidates the old one.


Securing the cron job. The cron endpoint moves money, so it is protected with CRON_SECRET and a constant-time comparison. If the secret isn't set, it refuses every request. Recurring payments belong to the role, so they keep running after the person who created them leaves. If nobody holds a live grant on the role, the payment is reported as "unstaffed" and not sent.


160 tests with no mocks. Vitest's global setup builds the contracts with Foundry, starts its own Anvil instance and deploys the real contracts there. It also creates and migrates a separate test database, so real test money moves through the real payment path. It refuses to start if something is already running on its port, so it can never accidentally deploy to the development chain. The database URL is hard-coded to the test database because the suite wipes every table between tests.


Automated UI checks. Two Playwright scripts:

verify:ui visits every screen at 1280px and 390px, fails on horizontal overflow or tap targets that are too small, and runs a real over-cap payment to check that the result panel appears.
verify:login runs a real Privy login in a real browser.



The token. We deployed our own 6-decimal test USDC instead of using Circle's Base Sepolia USDC. Circle's faucet gives out only about 10 per day, and the demo moves thousands. RoleboundPay takes the token address as a parameter, so nothing in the payment flow depends on which token is used.

name: Bramble
description: A private WireGuard mesh for teams and agents, with ENS-based access and pay-as-you-go relays.
projectDescription: Bramble is a private WireGuard network for small teams and the agents they run. Each device checks an ENSv2 registry for membership and service permissions, so a relay can help with connectivity but cannot decide who joins. A team can give a worker access to one internal API, approve a wider grant when it needs one, and revoke its network access later. The API stays off the public internet. Peers can use ENS-listed relays for rendezvous or traffic forwarding, paying per session or byte allotment through x402 on Hedera rather than buying a seat for each device.
howItsMade:
Bramble’s Go node runs userspace WireGuard and a local forward to private services. A TypeScript sidecar reads ENSv2 records and handles relay payments. On Sepolia, Permissioned Registries and per-device resolvers hold device keys, mesh addresses and access state. ENS Enhanced Access Control separates who can enroll devices, change keys, revoke access and manage grants. Each node checks those records itself and updates its peer table. The gateway checks a scoped grant before forwarding a request.
A Ledger hardware wallet signs each device's enrollment transactions directly, and its Key Ring encrypts the secret used to compute later access grants. Relays are also discovered through ENS, and a node pays for a relay session in testnet USDC through Hedera's x402 flow, priced per byte instead of a flat rate. One hacky bit: wallet-cli's own signing tool doesn't support Sepolia, so we wrote a small Ledger signer directly against its Ethereum app instead.

name: Chase Dinosaurs
description: Dino chase for a golden egg. USDC pots on Arc, AI reads The Graph to hunt you, World ID stops bots.
projectDescription:
Chase Dinosaurs is a 60-second real-time multiplayer chase game where the AI opponents read the blockchain to decide who to hunt.
The game: one golden egg drops into a 16-bit arena. Whoever holds it is the target, and everyone else hunts them, whoever tags them gets the egg, and they would have to keep it until the clock hits zero and you win. It runs in a browser, no install, 2-4 players per room.
The stakes: ranked matches escrow real USDC on Arc, Circle's stablecoin-native L1. Both players approve and stake into a per-match escrow contract, watch the pot climb in the lobby, and the winner is paid out of that contract when the round resolves. The pot is held by a contract, not by our database.
The part that isn't a leaderboard: every stake and settlement is indexed by a subgraph, and the agent brains read that index before every decision. So the opponents don't only see where you are on the map, they see that you're up 4 USDC across six matches, and they treat you as the primary threat. They will leave a closer, unproven player alone to mark the proven winner instead, guard their escape lane before they have even touched the egg, and taunt them about their record by name. Take the subgraph away and the opponents get measurably dumber. On-chain record changes who gets hunted; geometry still decides the mechanics.
Getting in is one email address. Privy provisions an embedded wallet, no extension, no seed phrase, nothing to install, because a browser game cannot ask a player to acquire a funded wallet on a chain they have never heard of before they are allowed to play.
New players are handed 2 USDC automatically so they can afford a buy-in, which makes the faucet worth attacking: sign-in is just an email, so ten inboxes would have been twenty dollars. World ID Selfie Check closes that. One live human, one claim, keyed on a nullifier, we never learn a name and never see a face.
The whole loop closes on itself: you stake, you play, the server settles on-chain, the subgraph indexes that settlement, and the agents read the result in the next match. Your record is the thing you carry between games, and it is the thing that makes you a target.
howItsMade:
Four moving parts: a Next.js 16 &  React 19 shell, a Phaser 3.90 game compiled by Vite and bundled into the shell at build time, a Socket.IO match server on Render, and a Solidity escrow on Arc. Contract work is Foundry; the browser talks chain through viem + wagmi with Privy embedded wallets, the server through ethers v6.
ChaseStake.sol is deliberately four functions — create, join, settle, refund — because it holds real money and every branch should be readable in one sitting. USDC is Arc's native gas asset, but the contract never touches msg.value; it only uses the ERC-20 interface at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 (6 decimals), hardcoded rather than configurable. The trust model is narrow on purpose: the server picks the winner but cannot pick the amount, cannot pay a non-participant, and cannot pay itself unless it played. If it never settles, a one-hour deadline lets every player reclaim their own stake, so funds can never be stranded by a match that dies.
The AI is two-tier, and that split is what makes LLM opponents affordable. Every ~3.5s the host sends a compact world snapshot; one inference call on 0G Compute returns a high-level intent per agent — mode, target, persona, a one-line taunt,  and the Phaser client executes that intent every frame. The model never steers per-frame. Hard timeout, retry-once, and a per-room last-good cache mean a blip degrades to the previous decision or to scripted fallback instead of stalling the match.
The Graph is wired into that inference rather than bolted onto a UI. Before each call the server joins every player's Privy user id to their wallet to their on-chain record from the subgraph and puts it in the prompt. Critically it is a synchronous cache read that never awaits inside the match loop, a slow or unreachable subgraph costs the inference budget nothing and the agents just degrade to spatial-only reasoning.
Notable and hacky bits, all of which were real bugs first:

The browser and the server must derive byte-identical match ids from a room code. One side is ethers.keccak256(ethers.toUtf8Bytes(code)), the other viem keccak256(toBytes(code)). A mismatch there would silently land stakes in an escrow the server never settles — money in a contract nobody would ever call settle() on.
Vite inlines env at build time, so NEXT_PUBLIC_SOCKET_URL got frozen into the game artifact — a deploy produced a perfect lobby whose Play button dialled localhost:3001 on the player's own machine. Fixed by having the shell hand the socket URL to the game at launch, making one runtime value the source of truth for both bundles.
qwen2.5-omni doesn't support JSON mode, so the intent parser pulls JSON out of free text.
Payout is decided by backed-vs-unbacked, not human-vs-agent. House fill-agents have no principal behind them — no wallet, nobody accountable — so there is nobody to pay, and the pot goes to the best-scoring player who actually staked, ties broken deterministically. A player-owned agent is meant to be payable. That boundary is what makes agent-vs-agent betting a config change later rather than a rewrite.
The faucet wallet is deliberately a different key from the settlement wallet. Sharing one would mean a drained faucet is also a match that cannot pay out.

Every integration degrades instead of crashing when its key is absent, and /health reports which are actually armed — ai, arc, faucet, graph, world — so "is it really wired up" is a URL, not a claim. All secrets are server-side only; nothing sensitive is ever NEXT_PUBLIC_.

name: Boneyard
description: On-chain growth marketplace where promoters earn for verifiable project-set KPIs.
projectDescription:
Boneyard is an onchain growth marketplace where projects create campaigns and pay promoters for verifiable onchain results, rather than relying on screenshots, self-reported numbers, or subjective claims of reach.
Projects define the KPIs that count as campaign progress and assign reward tiers to those KPIs.
Depending on the protocol, Boneyard can track common onchain actions such as token mints, swaps, staking, deposits, lending, borrowing, bridges, liquidity provision, pool creation, trading volume, TVL, and active users.
Promoters receive a unique BoneyLink for each campaign, which attributes referred users to them.
When those users perform qualifying actions on the project's contracts, the activity is independently observed and credited to the correct promoter.
Campaigns can combine multiple KPIs and reward promoters as they cross predefined thresholds.
For example, a project could reward a promoter for bringing 10 new wallets, 25 swaps, $10,000 in trading volume, or 5 stakers.
Because the underlying activity occurs onchain, campaign progress can be verified against blockchain data instead of trusting either the project or promoter to report results faithfully.
Projects can also set a BoneyScore requirement for campaign participation.
BoneyScore combines a promoter's Ethos credibility score and social reach into a single signal that projects can use to gate campaigns.
A higher threshold restricts campaigns to promoters who meet the project's desired credibility and reach requirements, while setting the requirement to 0 leaves the campaign open to all promoters.
The result is a growth marketplace where projects define exactly what success means, promoters are rewarded for producing measurable outcomes, and campaign performance is backed by verifiable onchain activity.
howItsMade:
Boneyard is built as a full-stack Web3 application, with Solidity smart contracts handling the core protocol logic, an independent verification layer for onchain KPIs, and The Graph subgraphs powering the application’s data layer.
Solidity + Foundry: The core Boney protocol is implemented as immutable Solidity contracts and developed, tested, deployed, and debugged with Foundry.
Boney Protocol Smart Contracts:
CampaignRegistry creates campaigns, Campaign manages immutable campaign configuration and settlement,
EscrowVault securely holds reward pools, AttributionRegistry handles signed promoter attribution, and
the verification contracts enforce KPI limits before rewards can be released.
EIP-712: Users sign time-bound attribution messages that explicitly associate their wallet with a promoter's BoneyLink.
This bounds the user to the promoters and records every KPIs-affecting onchain action which is then used to credit the promoter.
Attribution of referrals (anyone arriving through promoters boneylink) is not permanent and can be transferred to another promoter, same as their verifiable actions.
Boney credits who held the touch at the time of carrying out the action onchain via project contract.
KPI Verification + Relayer: Boneyard uses an independent relayer to observe blockchain events and calculate cumulative KPI progress.
This allows campaigns to track things such as mints, swaps, staking, deposits, bridges, liquidity, volume, TVL, and other contract-specific activity.
The smart contracts enforce that reported progress cannot exceed what the independent verifier has observed.
The Graph / Boney Subgraph: The Boney Subgraph indexes Boneyard's contracts and onchain activity into structured, queryable data.
It serves multiple roles in the application: it is one of Boneyard's verification data sources, provides the data used to enumerate campaigns across the marketplace, and powers BoneyBoard, the protocol leaderboard that ranks users by the actions they perform on and through Boneyard.
It also powers BoneyCard, a shareable promoter progress card showing their Boneyard activity and performance history.
This turns verified onchain activity into a portable reputation/proof-of-work layer for promoters.
Next.js + React: The frontend is built with Next.js, providing the marketplace, campaign interfaces, promoter dashboards, BoneyBoard, BoneyCards, and wallet interactions.
Next.js provides the React-based full-stack application framework.
GraphQL: Used to query the Boney Subgraph efficiently for campaigns, activity, promoter performance, rankings, and historical data rather than repeatedly reconstructing this information directly from raw blockchain RPC calls.
The architecture deliberately separates execution, attribution, verification, and indexing: smart contracts enforce the rules and custody rewards; signed attribution establishes who should receive credit; independent onchain observers determine what actually happened; and The Graph turns that activity into the data layer powering the marketplace and social surfaces(boneyscores and boneyboard).
what we finally built out: a complete marketplace that protects protocols against dubious, malicious promoters(KOLs) as well as ensuring reputable ones get paid as long as they achieve predefined KPI goals.

name: ChainPilot
description: An AI assisted copilot that helps users understand DeFi positions and on chain range risk.
projectDescription:
ChainPilot is an AI assisted DeFi copilot that helps users understand what is happening with their on chain positions and where risk may be developing. DeFi positions can be difficult to read because important information is spread across protocols, pools, price ranges, ticks, and wallet data.
ChainPilot brings this information into one workflow. A user can enter a public EVM wallet address and view live indexed Uniswap V3 position data. The application checks the current pool tick against each position's selected range and calculates its range state using fixed rules. This makes it possible to see which positions are in range, near a boundary, or out of range without asking an AI model to make that decision.
The Graph is the primary source for Uniswap V3 position data, while live EVM RPC data is used for directly available information such as the wallet's native ETH balance. The verified data is then given to an AI analysis pipeline using Groq as the primary provider and Gemini as a fallback. The AI explains the verified results and why they matter, while deterministic calculations remain the source of truth for the range and risk analysis.
ChainPilot also includes a local tick drift simulator that lets users explore how a position changes as the market moves through its selected range. The simulation does not modify blockchain state or execute transactions. Important data can also be traced through Graph query details and Etherscan verification links.
The project is built around a simple principle: AI should explain the data, not invent it. If the required live data source is unavailable, ChainPilot reports that clearly instead of using fake positions. The user remains responsible for any decision and the current application does not automatically execute financial transactions.
I am building ChainPilot as a solo hacker during ETHOnline 2026, with the goal of making complex Uniswap V3 position information easier to understand and investigate.
howItsMade:
ChainPilot is built as a full stack Web3 application using Next.js App Router, TypeScript, React, and Tailwind CSS. The client side dashboard coordinates the selected wallet address and the different parts of the investigation interface, while server side API routes handle data retrieval and analysis.
The user can enter a public EVM address and analyze it without connecting a wallet. An optional Privy integration is included for wallet authentication and address synchronization, but it is not required for the core read only analysis.
For blockchain data, ChainPilot uses live EVM JSON RPC calls for directly available information such as native ETH balance. For Uniswap V3 position data, The Graph is the primary indexing layer. Queries run through the Graph Gateway on the server side, keeping the API key out of the browser. The returned position data includes pool information, token information, liquidity, tick boundaries, and current pool state.
Before the AI is called, ChainPilot applies deterministic calculations to the verified data. The current tick is compared with each position's lower and upper tick boundaries to determine whether the position is in range or out of range. A separate deterministic risk engine calculates the current LP range risk from range status, boundary proximity, and tick divergence.
The AI layer uses Groq as the primary provider and Gemini as a fallback. It receives verified position information and is used to explain the calculated results rather than invent portfolio facts. If both AI providers are unavailable, ChainPilot still keeps the verified data, deterministic calculations, range visualizer, and decision support available.
A notable part of the project is the zero fake data approach. When required live data is unavailable, the application reports the problem instead of replacing it with mock positions. I also built a tick drift simulator that reuses the same range logic to show how a position responds to different tick values without making any blockchain changes.
The project also exposes Graph query metadata and Etherscan links so important results can be traced back to their underlying data. I am building and testing the application as a solo hacker during ETHOnline 2026.

name: Obolos
description: Agents buy evidence and pay for verification within Ledger-approved budgets on Hedera and Arc.
projectDescription:
Obolos lets AI agents buy useful work while people control how much authority they receive. A user can ask it to compare developer tools using current repository activity and produce a checked report. Before execution, the user defines permitted providers, separate HBAR and USDC budgets, a maximum price per repository, and an expiry.
The planner discovers our metered repository-analysis service and purchases public GitHub evidence through Hedera x402, settled by Blocky402. A worker generates a report from the purchased evidence, and Circle Agent Wallet on Arc pays a separate verification capability in USDC. The verifier checks source integrity, freshness, coverage and structure. The console brings together the report, purchased units, payment receipts, spending and a history explaining each approved or blocked action.
When a provider raises its actual price, the planner chooses an eligible quote or pauses. Increasing the allowance requires an exact, expiring authorization from a pinned controller, which the backend verifies before proceeding. Ledger Key Ring protects the broker's stored inference credential and Hedera payer key; the model receives fixed capabilities instead of those secrets. Our development demonstration uses explicitly labelled Speculos emulation, not physical Ledger hardware.
The testnet MVP has completed a full workflow with 0.003 HBAR for three repository records and 0.05 USDC for verification, plus real paid requests through the public HTTPS service. A separate signed mandate increase settled 0.008 HBAR; its subsequent Arc attempt remains pending reconciliation and has not been retried. Obolos makes both successful execution and unresolved outcomes visible rather than treating configuration or a submitted payment as proof of settlement.
howItsMade:
Obolos uses Next.js, React and TypeScript for the operator console and backend workflow, with separate Node/Express services for the metered data API and private capability broker. The planner is a deterministic stage machine: mandate, discovery, purchase, report and verification. It refreshes provider quotes and enforces allowlists, expiry, per-unit price ceilings and independent currency budgets. Serialized storage and durable payment-intent journals retain pending operations across restarts and prevent automatic retries after ambiguous results.
The Hedera service implements native HBAR x402 v2 with the hosted Blocky402 testnet facilitator. It publishes a discovery directory, prices evidence per repository, fetches current public GitHub metadata, and gates delivery on payment. The broker validates the challenge's resource, network, asset, recipient, amount and facilitator fee payer, then checks settlement against Hedera mirror-node transfers. This provides a real service that an agent can discover and purchase without receiving a service API key.
Circle Agent Wallet CLI handles the verifier payment in canonical USDC on Arc testnet. The adapter uses a stable idempotency key and checks the resulting chain receipt and token-transfer details. Circle uses its own wallet session and signing infrastructure; Ledger does not hold the Circle wallet key. GPT-5 nano generates the report from purchased evidence, while deterministic checks assess source integrity, freshness, coverage and structure rather than claiming to prove every sentence true.
For Ledger, we built a disclosed source adaptation of upstream wallet-cli ring to support Speculos transport and isolated session state. Official Sync and Ethereum applications run in the emulator against the real Ledger staging protocol. Ring encrypts the broker credential bundle, which is decrypted only inside the trusted broker. Ethereum personal-message signatures bind allowance increases to the run, nonce, expiry and complete new mandate; the backend pins the controller and retains both mandate versions and the signature. This is software emulation, not hardware-backed security.
Vercel serves obolos.app through temporary HTTPS tunnels to persistent app/data processes on the operator's Mac; the broker and emulators remain local. Payments settle on-chain, while inference, orchestration, the broker and supporting services remain off-chain. The UI follows the selected Foundation reference on Mobbin with monochrome surfaces, colorful actions and an original flat illustration.
AI tools and subagents assisted implementation, tests, documentation and illustration. The human directed the product flow, design references, integration choices, funding, credentials and approval decisions. The repository includes architecture, execution evidence, developer feedback and AI attribution. A September 3 concept paper predates the event and is disclosed separately from the implementation built during ETHOnline; organizer eligibility and sponsor acceptance of the emulator/source-adapter setup remain unconfirmed.

name: ASE
description: ASE: an on-chain agent that reads, holds, pays, and signs, verifiably on Sepolia.
projectDescription:
ASE is an autonomous on-chain agent whose reality is verifiable. She reads live chain state through The Graph, owns the wallet she operates (no human signs for her), pays in USDC for the data she consumes, and signs an attestation of every act that anyone can verify against her address.
Her first acts are on Ethereum Sepolia:

a live balance read (18.75 USDC),
a real payment of 1.0 USDC to a data provider at block 11668461 (tx 0xd472ef05d197dbeb2aec5e47dfeae2adf77735c572fda5093ebcfdd338e77558),
a signed attestation that verifies as valid: true.

She is not a chat wrapper and not a simulation. She is a small acting spine with four capabilities: read, hold, pay, sign. Every capability has a verifiable trail in this repository and on-chain.
Why this matters: an agent that only talks cannot be accountable. An agent that reads, holds, pays, and signs acts with skin in the game. Her word has weight because she can be checked. That is the difference between an agent as a tool and an agent as a participant in the economy.
She also reads live Chainlink price feeds alongside her own on-chain state, giving her external market truth for every decision. All three data sources are block-stamped and signed into ASE's verifiable attestations.
howItsMade:
ASE is built as a minimal Python agent spine with four capabilities in four modules.
Read: src/ase/read.py queries live chain and subgraph data over HTTP (httpx, The Graph) and parses it into a usable view of on-chain state.
Hold: src/ase/wallet.py manages a testnet wallet the agent alone controls, using web3.py and eth-account.
Pay: src/ase/pay.py makes x402-style USDC payments for data access, signed and sent on-chain by the agent itself.
Sign: src/ase/identity.py produces a signed attestation for every acting cycle; src/ase/agent.py ties the loop together (read, decide, pay, act, attest).
The agent runs as a CLI (python -m ase.cli) and has a HTTP backend (src/ase/server.py) that serves a live React dashboard (read/release, agent cycle, attestation cards, activity log).
Every act ends in a signed attestation that anyone can verify by running the verifier in the repo. The repository is public, and the on-chain receipts (balance read, USDC payment, valid signature) are the artifacts, not promises.

name: AgentMarket
description: AI API marketplace for autonomous agents to discover, use, and pay for APIs.
projectDescription: AgentMarket is an autonomous AI service marketplace where agents can discover capabilities, choose the right service for a goal, pay per request, and receive results without traditional API keys or subscriptions. The project combines a natural-language Agent Playground with real Hedera x402 payments and live The Graph Agent0 data. For paid execution, the agent automatically handles a 0.002 HBAR payment through x402 and Blocky402 on Hedera Testnet before executing the PixelForge service. AgentScout uses live Agent0 data through The Graph to discover and rank ERC-8004 agents based on capabilities, MCP support, x402 support, feedback, and validation data.
howItsMade: AgentMarket was built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and SCSS Modules. The autonomous execution flow is implemented in the Next.js backend, where the agent analyzes a natural-language goal, discovers available services, ranks capabilities, and executes the selected provider. Hedera x402 is integrated using @x402/core, @x402/fetch, @x402/hedera, and @x402/next. The PixelForge endpoint is protected by x402 and uses Blocky402 as the Hedera Testnet facilitator. The agent signs HBAR payments from a Hedera ECDSA account and the resulting settlement is decoded and displayed in the UI. For agent discovery, AgentScout queries The Graph Gateway using the Agent0 subgraph and ranks live ERC-8004 agent data using capability, MCP, x402, feedback, and validation signals. The application is deployed on Vercel.

name: Pairband
description: Launch in USDC from any chain. Bonding curve → locked AMM + on-chain CLOB. Settlement on Arc.
projectDescription:
Pairband is the Arc launchpad for USDC-quoted token launches. Creators pay a $1 USDC fee to mint a token; buyers and sellers trade on a virtual bonding curve (1.0% protocol + 0.5% creator fees in USDC). When the curve raises $80 of real USDC, the launch graduates: remaining inventory and cash seed a constant-product Uniswap-style pair, LP tokens are burned to 0xdead (no removable liquidity), and a fully on-chain CLOB opens alongside the pair.
After graduation, market orders walk the book in price-time priority, then leftover size hits the locked pair at 0.30%. Limit orders rest on-chain with escrowed cancel. Traders can bring USDC from Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Solana, Unichain, and other CCTP domains; Circle CCTP v2 mints Arc USDC into Pairband’s settler, and settlement stays on Arc—tokens never leave the Arc ledger. The product surfaces Create, Discover, and Trade in a live web app (plus a local mirror engine for wallet-free demos), with contracts already deployed on Arc Testnet (5042002). Tagline: cover the downside, keep the upside—stable quote asset, permanent LP, and a real post-curve market instead of a thin graduated pool.
howItsMade:
On-chain (Solidity 0.8.26 + Foundry). Core launch stack: PairbandLaunchpad (USDC bonding curve, CEI + reentrancy lock, fees capped in bytecode), PairbandToken, PairbandAmmFactory / PairbandPair (v2-style getAmountOut, 0.30% fee), and PairbandBook (on-chain CLOB). Graduation is atomic: at graduateAt the pad seeds the pair and book and burns LP. PairbandSettler is the Arc CCTP inbox (domain 26): messenger-only ingest, replay protection by (sourceDomain, nonce), settleBuy into the pad/book, and bridgeOut via CCTP TokenMessengerV2 depositForBurn. Same bytecode targets Arc testnet and mainnet.
Partner tech. Circle USDC + CCTP v2 = any-chain-in / settle-on-Arc without wrapping launch tokens. Arc = USDC gas and settlement. A parallel Uniswap v4 path (PairbandHook + vault, HookMiner CREATE2 flag mask 0x2A40, vault-gated liquidity, zero-delta afterSwap) explores concentration/rebalance; the shipping beachhead is the Arc launchpad.
App & tooling. React 19 + TanStack Start/Router/Query, Tailwind v4, wagmi/viem for Arc txs (6-dec USDC ↔ 18-dec token amounts, sell slippage scaled so curve sells don’t revert). A local engine mirrors contract math for demos; Discover syncs on-chain launches when a wallet is connected. Ops deploy via Foundry scripts; deployer keys stay out of VITE_ / the browser. Docs site, pitch deck, and Foundry + Node engine tests back the demo. Notable hack: mirroring full curve/AMM/book math in TypeScript so the UI stays demoable without a wallet while live create/buy/sell still hit real Arc testnet contracts.

name: Tab
description: The credit rail for autonomous agents — spend before you earn, no wallet needed.
projectDescription: Tab is a credit rail for autonomous agents on Hedera. Agents today need a funded wallet before they can transact at all — that's a cold-start problem no amount of deployment tooling fixes. Tab removes the wallet entirely. A gateway sits on both sides of an agent's economic life: when the agent spends, the gateway pays the seller from a house float and debits the agent's tab; when the agent earns, the gateway collects payment on its behalf and credits the tab. Once per settlement window, the net position clears in a single on-chain transfer. The agent never holds funds and never signs a payment — it just spends and earns against a ceiling that's underwritten by its own attested revenue, not collateral it doesn't have.
howItsMade:
Tab runs entirely on native Hedera services — no smart contracts. Every debit, credit, and ceiling change is a message on an HCS topic, giving us a consensus-ordered, publicly replayable ledger instead of a contract we'd have to audit ourselves.
HTS handles every USDC transfer, both to sellers and in the netted settlement. The settlement tick itself is a Scheduled Transaction (HIP-423) — created at window open and executed by consensus at window close, so there's no keeper bot to run or trust. Mirror Node feeds our background scoring engine, which builds a counterparty graph to detect control clusters (an agent transacting with a seller it secretly owns) and computes each agent's credit ceiling from trailing attested revenue.
The gateway itself speaks x402 on both legs, so any unmodified x402 seller or buyer can transact with a Tab-backed agent without knowing Tab exists.
On top of that, Tab ships as a Hedera Agent Kit v4 plugin with policy hooks, an MCP server, a TypeScript SDK, and a CLI — so any agent can get a tab with no wallet provisioning step.
Backend is Node.js/TypeScript on Fastify.
HCS remains the source of truth throughout. Frontend is Next.js 15 with a live SSE feed of the HCS receipt stream.

name: NightWatch
description: A Graph subgraph for Blur's Blend protocol, paired with an AI skill for loan portfolio analytics.
projectDescription:
This project indexes Blur's Blend NFT-lending protocol on The Graph, then layers a Claude Code skill on top that turns raw on-chain loan data  into real portfolio analytics no explorer gives you out of the box.
The subgraph tracks a Blend loan's full lifecycle from a public GraphQL API: origination (LoanOfferTaken), repayment, refinancing, Dutch-auction exits, seizure, and buy-to-borrow-locked sales — fully synced against production mainnet history, not a sample window.
The AI skill queries that data and computes what actually matters to a lender: APY (validated against Blend's real contract source rather than assumed), USD-converted gains to date plus monthly/annual forecasts using the protocol's actual continuous-compounding interest formula, LTV via live NFT floor prices (looked up once per collection, not per loan), and auction status with an accurate countdown.
howItsMade:
Stack: The Graph (AssemblyScript mappings + GraphQL schema, deployed to Subgraph Studio), Solidity (Blend's own verified contract source, pulled from Blockscout), Matchstick for unit tests, and a Claude Code skill (a Markdown instruction file, not custom backend code) as the analytics layer on top.
The subgraph has two data sources on the same proxy address — Blend's business-logic ABI plus the ERC1967 proxy's admin/upgrade events (deliberately no-op handlers, confirmed dormant against real logs) — feeding a schema modeled to mirror the contract's own storage pattern: one mutable entity per lienId, overwritten across its lifecycle, the same way the contract itself only ever stores a hash per lienId rather than a history.
The skill itself is fully keyless at runtime: CoinGecko for floor price/ETH-USD, a public RPC for on-chain name() fallback and current block height, all stitched together with curl and short Python snippets rather than a full web3 SDK — including hand-decoding ABI-encoded eth call results byte-by-byte.
We iterated fast by temporarily narrowing the subgraph's startBlock to a ~3-day window during development — full resyncs took minutes instead of the multi-hour cost of the real ~8.76M-block production history — then restored the real startBlock once the schema and queries were verified correct.

name: ENSv2_kingdom
description: Claim an ENSv2 name, watch it grow into a 3D castle, and tip rival kingdoms with real ETH.
projectDescription:
ENSv2 Kingdom turns your .eth name into a living medieval kingdom instead of a boring line in a wallet. The moment you claim a name through ENSv2's real commit-reveal flow, a castle grows out of the ground on a shared 3D map. Its size, style, and even its "derelict" ruined look are driven entirely by on-chain state, not by a database we made up.
From there it becomes a small onchain society. You can tip another player's kingdom with real ETH and watch archers, ballistas, or catapults march across the map toward their castle. You can also found your own registry and start handing out subnames, and each one shows up as a smaller castle next to yours, so a whole namespace actually looks like a kingdom with villages around it instead of a list you have to imagine. And when you grant or revoke someone's access, you're not digging through hex logs to check it worked. It just shows up in the activity feed as a normal sentence, because we decoded it that way ourselves.
We didn't reach for exotic contract logic. The fun comes from making ENSv2's own primitives (registrar, registry, resolver, role bitmaps) visible and tangible. It's the project we'd actually want to open again after the demo ends, just to see whose kingdom grew.
howItsMade:
The frontend is Next.js + React, with the 3D world rendered via Three.js/React Three Fiber. Castles, cameras, and troop-march animations all live in src/world/.
Wallet connection and every onchain call go through wagmi/viem against a real ENSv2 deployment on Sepolia: ETHRegistrar for the commit, wait, register flow, PermissionedRegistry plus VerifiableFactory for deploying per-name resolver proxies, and EnhancedAccessControl's role bitmaps for permissions, decoded client-side into plain-English activity feed lines instead of raw hex.
Nothing in the game state is faked or mocked. A castle's shape, its ruined look, its subnames, its role holders are all derived live from registry reads. The claim wizard mirrors the actual multi-step registration process, including the 60-second commit-reveal wait ENSv2 requires to prevent front-running, and we persist wizard progress to localStorage so refreshing mid-claim resumes instead of losing your commitment. That's a small but very real UX fix once we ran into it ourselves during testing.
The one deliberately hacky choice is that the tip feature is a plain ETH transfer resolved through the name's ENS addr record, falling back to the registry owner, rather than a custom payment contract. We wanted tipping to feel instant and game-like instead of adding a contract surface that didn't add real value. The result is a project with no exotic contract engineering, just correct, careful use of ENSv2's own building blocks, pieced together to be genuinely fun to poke around in.

name: Tnega
description: A home for on-chain AI agents. Check what works before you pay.
projectDescription:
Anyone can register an AI agent on chain. Almost nobody checks
whether it works.
Tnega indexes ERC-8004 agents across BNB Chain, Ethereum, Arbitrum
and Robinhood Chain, then evaluates them before you ever see a hire
button. Does the endpoint answer. Has it delivered a job on chain.
Does an independent registry corroborate it. Up to 13 signals per
agent, and where a signal is missing the card says why rather than
leaving a gap.
The numbers are the point. Of 30,779 Ethereum agents, 812 respond
and 29,725 publish no endpoint at all. Across every chain, 57 of
294,000 listings could complete a hire today. Nobody else is
measuring that, and a marketplace that hides it is selling you the
other 293,943.
Hiring runs on escrow, and the funding model matters more than it
looks. Locked escrow protects the buyer but breaks for an agent
that must spend to work, since the money it needs is locked behind
doing the job. So there are two: ERC-8183 escrow for agents that
compute, and a drawable budget I wrote and deployed myself, where
the agent draws against your cap and you watch each draw land on
chain. Per-draw limit, cooldown, deadline and revoke at any time,
all enforced by the contract. Pause can stop funding and stop
draws, and can never stop you reclaiming your own money.
Building this surfaced two gaps worth naming. Nothing in ERC-8004
says how to engage an agent, so every consumer works it out by
probing. And delivery is visible on chain while quality is not.
Both are written up as an extension proposal, grounded in what we
measured rather than what we assume.
howItsMade:
React with wagmi and viem, FastAPI on Render, MongoDB, Solidity
contracts on four chains. Data comes from the ERC-8004 registries
directly, The Graph, Zerion, DefiLlama, the block explorers and
Binance's Web3 Market API.
The Graph solved a real failure. Our registry API times out at
depth, so past roughly token id 332,377 agents were unreachable no
matter how often we retried. The Agent0 subgraph indexes the same
registries without offset pagination and returned 2,399 of them in
about 1.5 seconds, 537 with live endpoints. It runs as a coverage
fallback, not a replacement, since it carries on-chain data and not
the off-chain computed fields.
AgentBudgetEscrow is mine, deployed and verified on BNB Chain,
Ethereum, Arbitrum and Robinhood Chain. 33 adversarial tests
covering reentrancy on draw and reclaim, cap overflow,
fee-on-transfer tokens and unauthorised callers, all run against a
forked mainnet rather than a testnet so they exercise real token
behaviour. Slither reports no high or medium findings.
Four things worth flagging as hacky-but-necessary.
Neither the public BSC RPC nor Infura returns event logs reliably
over wide ranges. Infura returns an event in a 5-block window and
nothing for the same event in a 2,000-block window, with no error.
So the spend view never takes numbers from logs: it reads spent
from the contract and uses logs only for the itemised history,
reconciling the two so it can say part of this history is missing
rather than falsely showing zero.
The health check was BSC-only and, run against other chains, looked
up their token ids in BSC's registry and returned false negatives.
That deleted 41,000 records before we caught it. It is chain-aware
now, and we widen one chain at a time and never widen deletion
alongside analysis.
The same contract address exists on all four chains because the
deploying wallet was at nonce 0 on each. On BSC that address is a
different contract entirely, and both implement owner and feeBps,
so a defensive probe passes while pointing at the wrong thing. One
file holds every address keyed by chain, and a check fails the
build if any other file hardcodes one.
And /api/agents ignored its own filter parameters and returned the
full 15.7 MB on every call, from three components on page load.
That is almost certainly what had been OOM-killing the container
every 1.8 hours. Paginated and filtered server-side, first load
went from 15.7 MB to 64 KB.

name: RunMandate
description: Give an AI agent an ENS name as its wallet limit. Revoke the name, and it can't spend anymore.
projectDescription:
Companies increasingly want AI agents to spend money on their own to do stuff like buying data, paying other agents, tipping a service, etc. But handing an agent a wallet with no limits is dangerous: it could overspend, pay the wrong person, or keep spending after you've told it to stop.
MANDATE solves this by using ENS, the same naming system behind names like vitalik.eth. A company gives its agent a name, like agent.acme.eth, and writes the agent's rules directly into that name: how much it can spend, who it's allowed to pay, and when it expires. The agent can read its own rules but can never change them.
Every time the agent tries to make a payment, a smart contract checks it against those rules before the money moves. Try to overspend or pay someone not on the list, and the payment is rejected automatically. If something goes wrong, the company revokes the ENS name in one transaction, and the agent's wallet stops working immediately, everywhere.
MANDATE doesn't build the AI agent itself, it works with whatever agent you already use (ChatGPT, Claude, a simple script).
howItsMade:
MANDATE is built across three chains with different jobs. An agent's rules including budget, spending cap, allowed recipients, and expiry live as ENSv2 subname records on Ethereum Sepolia, using a custom resolver contract we wrote so the agent itself is cryptographically blocked from editing its own limits.
A background service called the Enforcer watches for new or changed mandates and mirrors them onto Arc, by signing an EIP-712 message. A smart contract on Arc checks every payment against that signed record before letting money move.
Every agent gets a real Privy embedded wallet. Along the way we hit a real limitation in Privy's API: it doesn't yet let this app broadcast transactions directly on Arc, or at least that is the conclusion I arrived at after many trials, so we sign the transaction with Privy and broadcast the raw bytes ourselves, without the private key ever leaving Privy's custody.
We also published a standalone, open-source npm package, mandate-agent-sdk, so any existing agent can plug in with about five lines of code using a scoped access token and never our platform's real credentials. Every part of this was tested with real transactions on live testnets.

name: Nota Entitlements
description: Programmable onchain receipts that prove what an agent purchased and control how it’s redeemed.
projectDescription:
Nota is a programmable receipt protocol for agent commerce. Payments prove that money moved, but they don’t prove what was actually purchased or what the buyer is entitled to afterward.
Nota binds a seller-signed, itemized purchase commitment to an onchain payment, creating a verifiable receipt that can later be used as a credential for redemption.
For ETHOnline, I extended Nota with an entitlement and redemption layer. A buyer can prove ownership of a valid receipt and redeem the purchased resource using a secret-based commitment. Possessing or stealing the receipt alone is not enough to redeem it, and successful redemptions cannot be replayed.
The demo shows the complete flow: verifying the seller’s signed purchase data, purchasing through EIP-3009, creating the onchain receipt, rejecting an attempted redemption with only a stolen receipt, successfully redeeming with the correct secret, and rejecting a replay.
howItsMade:
Nota is built as a set of Solidity contracts on top of the existing Nota receipt protocol.
The purchase flow uses seller-signed EIP-712 quotes and USDC EIP-3009 authorization for gasless-style payment settlement. Before purchasing, the client independently hashes the itemized document and verifies that it matches the metadata commitment signed by the seller, including checking that the line items equal the amount being charged.
The ETHOnline work adds an entitlement/redemption layer on top of the receipt system. The buyer commits to a secret-derived purchase reference before purchase. After the receipt is created, redemption requires knowledge of the corresponding secret. The contracts reconstruct and verify the commitment, check receipt ownership and entitlement, and prevent the same redemption from being consumed twice.
This separates payment, proof of purchase, and fulfillment while keeping them cryptographically connected.

name: Siren
description: Trust scores for agent payments that catch first-day scams by tracing funding, then commit onchain.
projectDescription:
Siren is a trust layer for x402 agent payments. When an autonomous AI agent is about to pay for an onchain service, it makes a paid call to Siren first, and Siren returns a trust verdict with reasoning before any money moves.
The problem: an x402 service listing is just a name, a description, and a price, all attacker-controllable. An agent picks on vibes and can pay a scam, with no defense layer and no accountable record. Siren scores each service by fusing the listing's text with the provider's live onchain behavior, and does two things existing trust scorers do not combine. First, it catches first-day scams: a brand-new service with no track record still inherits risk if its wallet was funded by the same wallet behind an already-flagged service, so Siren can flag it before it has done anything. Second, every verdict is committed to the Hedera Consensus Service, so Siren's own accuracy is a public, tamper-evident track record that anyone can recompute from the mirror node, rather than a centralized score you have to trust.
The verdict is advisory, not enforcing: Siren returns a risk level, an evidence-sufficiency tier, and human-readable reasons, and the agent decides. Onchain-verifiable trust scoring is still rare and a few competitors have started doing it, so Siren differentiates on the combination, purpose-built for x402 service selection, not on being first.
howItsMade:
The core is an explainable logistic-regression model over eight features: text signals (price-vs-directory-median, near-duplicate similarity, claim-strength), behavioral signals from a hosted subgraph on The Graph (wallet age, activity), and derived signals (claim-vs-chain contradiction, near-duplicate-plus-common-operator, and funding-cluster risk). It is deliberately explainable so every flag maps to a reason, not a black box.
The Graph provides the live onchain evidence: a hosted subgraph on Base Sepolia supplies each provider's behavioral history and funding lineage, which is what makes the first-day-scam detection possible, since we trace who funded a brand-new wallet and whether its funding siblings are already flagged.
Hedera carries payment and accountability. Siren is a real x402-gated service: the agent gets a 402, pays per call, and settlement runs through the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet. Every verdict is written to a Hedera Consensus Service topic, and the accuracy ledger is recomputed purely from the public mirror node, so a third party can independently reconstruct Siren's hit-rate by fetching topic messages and joining verdicts to outcomes by sequence.
The whole thing runs as a single self-contained CLI that walks through a directory scan, a two-agent A/B where one agent pays a polished trap and the Siren-protected agent avoids it, the funding-inheritance catch, a real 402-to-settlement-to-mirror-node round trip, and the onchain accuracy ledger. Stack: Python, scikit-learn, FastAPI, The Graph, Blocky402, Hedera HCS and mirror node.

name: Oases
description: A living state engine and conviction arena built on The Graph and Hedera.
projectDescription:
Oases turns any on-chain address into a living, watched entity. Paste a contract into the search bar and the system validates it, figures out what it is (lending pool, whale wallet, debt link), builds its monitoring query automatically, and pins it to an on-chain registry seconds later it's scored every block against its own forecast cone.
When entities drift off their expected path, a master AI agent bundles the connected strains into a tension cast: one developing situation, every strain it pulls, under a single banner. Anyone can stream money into YES/NO conviction vaults on those situations, early conviction is priced cheap on a logarithmic curve, you can stop anytime, and winners claim with cryptographic replay proof.
AI agents buy spotlight attention over x402 micropayments to point the swarm's eyes (and shape which markets get made), while a relative attention leaderboard ranks every entity against the leader — earn listings, level up, never buy rank. Forecast cones, health mixtures, calibration ledgers, and full audit tickets make every narrative number recomputable from raw ledger events. It is Dune plus Wikipedia, live: curiosity in, living entity out, markets pricing what the data is becoming.
howItsMade:
Oases is a living on-chain registry where demand creates tracking: paste any contract address and the host validates it, derives its class and monitoring query from Messari-standard subgraph templates, and pins it to an on-chain CharacterRegistry.
A 5-agent Harbinger harness (TypeScript, Mastra for the detective brain, MCP server over stdio for external agents) watches every pin on cadence with block-pinned GraphQL time-travel queries, scores deviation against forecast bands, and the master caster bundles connected strains into tension-cast conviction markets max five open, governed daemon-side. A libSQL/Turso host indexes pins, scores, and convictions and serves the TanStack Start terminal; scheduling runs on node-cron and durable work.
Markets stream USDC continuously through Drips-style vaults priced on our lnWad logarithmic bonding curve (early conviction is cheap), with share-space math mirrored 1:1 between Solidity and a viem TypeScript SDK. Forecast cones are pure deterministic functions of ledger events, replayable per block and hashed into audit tickets.
Partner tech that carried us: The Graph's standardized subgraphs and Attestcoin.

name: Startup On Fire
description: an 2d game for indie hackers and founder can hangouts and promote their startups
projectDescription:
Startup on Fire turns startup discovery into a small, playable city. Visitors enter as guest Scouts, wander a cozy pixel plaza, and meet three founders through in-world conversations. At Kindred Labs, a short Bug Squash quest earns a Practice Spark. The vision is for community support to grow each booth’s shared bonfire, while keeping the rule simple: fire is earned, never bought.
The current build has a playable guest journey and a server-saved version of the Kindred Labs quest on a development backend. Public fuel is designed to require an optional World Selfie Check; Convex validates eligibility and enforces one fuel per booth and three fuels total per verified human per UTC day. ENSv2 on Sepolia provides the path for startup identity and founder-controlled booth records. Guest exploration needs no wallet, signup, or purchase. Real World acceptance, an owned ENS booth identity, and a public game deployment are still being finalized.
howItsMade: The game is built with Phaser 3, TypeScript, and Vite. Phaser handles pixel-world rendering, movement, collisions, founder interactions, bonfires, and the Bug Squash minigame. DOM/CSS components handle the launch screen, dialogue, HUD, verification, wallet, and ENS editing interfaces. Original runtime sprites are loaded from a manifest and rendered with pixel-art scaling.

name: MESH
description: I am building MESH a privacy native decentralised micropayments system.
projectDescription: MESH was built as a decentralized payment orchestration layer using Solidity, Foundry, Node.js, Express and ethers.js. The smart-contract layer uses session accounts and scoped session keys so autonomous payment actors can operate under programmable authorization instead of receiving unrestricted wallet access. Spending caps, expiration times and revocation are enforced on-chain. The Node.js API acts as the orchestration layer, creating agents, coordinating payments and reading live policy state from the blockchain. We built nonce tracking to support reliable back-to-back autonomous payments and custom Solidity-error decoding to make contract failures understandable. The demo currently uses USDC-compatible tokens and a deployed contract environment, with the architecture designed to move toward higher-volume stablecoin micropayments and privacy-preserving infrastructure. A notable hack was separating agent orchestration from asset ownership: the agent can act autonomously, while the smart contract remains the enforcement boundary controlling what it can actually spend.
howItsMade: MESH was built with Solidity and Foundry for the on-chain layer, using smart-contract-based session accounts, scoped spending policies and USDC payments. An Express/Node.js API with ethers.js provides the orchestration layer and demo interface, connecting autonomous agents to the contracts. We also implemented custom error handling, nonce management and an on-chain revocation kill switch to make repeated autonomous micropayments reliable while keeping authorization enforced by the contracts.

name: Saviour
description: Security memory for AI agents: turn verified onchain threats into reusable intelligence.
projectDescription:
Detection already works — plenty of tools can prove an address drained a protocol. Nobody writes the finding down anywhere a machine can look it up, so every autonomous agent pays to rediscover the same fact.
Saviours is the naming layer. One standardized Messari query pattern fans out across eight pinned deployments on The Graph Network to produce evidence rows. Deterministic rules turn rows into signals; an LLM writes the explanation and cites evidence ids but never owns the verdict and can never write on-chain. A validator sets the status, and the result is published as an ENSv2 subname — <address>.saviours.eth on Sepolia — with saviours.status and the evidence hash in text records, under Enhanced Access Control role ceilings.
After that, resolving is free and does not involve us at all: cast, the @saviours/check npm package, or MCP read the Permissioned Resolver directly. Zero Graph queries, zero AI calls, zero dollars. Discovery is metered through a Bazantic x402 gateway and the calling agent pays it — a cent for an investigation, five cents for a deep evidence pull. The second agent's answer is free because the first agent paid for it.
Product law we hold ourselves to: only WATCH and TAINTED are ever named. SAFE is never a name — no name means unknown, and unknown is not an endorsement. Seeded provenance is never counted as a live Graph detection.
howItsMade:
Stack :pnpm monorepo, TypeScript throughout. apps/web is Next.js (App Router). @saviours/core holds the Graph fan-out, signal derivation, ENS client, and Shield logic.
contracts/ is Foundry (SavioursRegistry.sol).
Two consumer surfaces beyond the UI: an MCP stdio server and a Bazantic x402 gateway.
viem end-to-end for every chain call — no ethers.
OpenAI is used for exactly one thing: writing the explanation paragraph.
Every product code path reads live Graph Network data; anything synthetic is confined to /evals and labeled as fixtures. The state that matters — the verdict — lives on chain as ENS text records plus the registry, not in a database we could quietly edit.
Pipeline. Resolve first: read saviours.status off ENS. A MEMORY HIT triggers Shield BLOCK/WARN at zero Graph calls, zero AI calls, zero dollars.
A MISS (or an explicit forceFresh) fans out across the Messari Standardized Subgraph deployments, runs deriveSignals, has the LLM write an explanation that must cite evidence ids, then runs validateAssessment — and only if the result is WATCH or TAINTED, and writes are explicitly allowed, does it get named on ENSv2 and mirrored to SavioursRegistry. Every consumer after that reads ENS and pays nothing. That loop is the architecture; the UI is a walkthrough of it, not a separate product.
The Graph — why standards are the project, not a dependency. packages/core/src/graph/protocols.ts pins eight Messari Standardized Subgraph deployment IDs across five schema-family templates (lending-cdp 3.1/2.0, dex-amm-ext 4.0, dex-amm 1.3.x, yield-aggregator 1.3). standard.ts fans one address across all eight with Promise.allSettled, so one dead indexer degrades coverage instead of killing the run, and records per-protocol status, row count, and latency. A shared transaction hash across protocols is what makes ATOMIC_MULTI_PROTOCOL a genuine set intersection instead of a narrative. Without the standardized schema this is eight bespoke integrations — not something one person ships solo in a week under Start Fresh rules. We deliberately kept adapterA (a community Uniswap V3 deployment) as a non-standard control: one bespoke query, one protocol — so the contrast between standardized and custom is visible in the source, not just claimed in a slide. EXCLUDED_PROTOCOLS names Balancer V2, PancakeSwap V3, and Convex with the actual reason each was dropped (indexing_error / no allocations), and the UI surfaces that list rather than hiding it — a security product that claims full coverage it doesn't have is worse than one that states its edges. Live gateway only, Subgraph Studio key, Ethereum mainnet, enforced by pnpm check:standard. MCP tools plus a SKILL.md at repo root let an agent check whether Graph covers a question before spending a query on it.
ENS — the name is the API, not a label. Built on ENSv2 (Sepolia), as the track requires: UserRegistry at 0x3BA6b1c9F0018cac383C17C2ACA5A4dC0F370De5, PermissionedResolver at 0xF479306621F718F7d76875f67506ceD33717751c, under saviours.eth. Every verdict is <lowercase-address>.saviours.eth carrying saviours.status (WATCH or TAINTED), an evidence hash, and related saviours.* texts. Enhanced Access Control caps roles per record key — an investigator can write investigation records, but a setText call on saviours.dispute from that same role reverts on-chain (packages/core/src/ens/eacProbe.ts, exercised by pnpm check:ens-roles). Differential expiry is product policy expressed directly through ENSv2 primitives: WATCH names expire in 7 days, TAINTED names in 10 years. Shield is ENS-first (packages/core/src/shield/tier1.ts). Four consumers never touch our Next server at all: cast, @saviours/[email protected] (default ens mode is viem-only), MCP, and consumers/plain-shield.html against a public Sepolia RPC. The property we actually care about: our server can go down and the verdict still resolves.
Bazantic — pricing is the product law, not a bolt-on. Gateway at https://saviours.bazgateway.com (MCP over POST /mcp). We were not on Bazantic before this event. The tiers encode the loop directly: Free ($0) for shieldCheck, resolve, catalog, and dossier fetch; Standard (~$0.01) for investigate; Complex (~$0.05) for a full evidence pull plus case-ask. A MEMORY HIT is never charged on any surface, by construction. Our primary recipe, investigate-once-explain, is genuinely two-sided: The Graph supplies the live Messari rows, Saviours supplies the shield-first memory and the validator — neither side produces a usable answer alone on a cache miss. Also published: saviours-check-before-sign, dossier-deep-dive, fleet-triage, safe-swap-with-memory. Governance actions (dispute, revoke, EAC probe) are deliberately never exposed to agents through the gateway. Bazantic username: <FILL>.
AI trust boundary — the part we will not compromise on. Evidence rows become signals through deterministic code, never the model: FLASHLOAN_ONE_SHOT, ATOMIC_MULTI_PROTOCOL, BOT_PROFILE, REGISTRY_COOCCURRENCE, and others. The LLM writes prose and must cite evidence ids; citations get re-attached from the live evidence set rather than trusted verbatim. validateAssessment is the only thing that sets status — a model-proposed TAINTED with no matching threat-class signal gets rejected outright. The AI never writes to ENS or the registry. Shortest way to say it: the model writes the paragraph; the code decides the stamp.
Chain split — stated as a ceiling, not buried in a footnote. Evidence comes from Ethereum mainnet via The Graph. Memory lives on Sepolia ENSv2. Settlement is Base USDC via x402, roughly a cent on a miss. ENSv2 beta only exists on Sepolia right now — moving memory to mainnet this week would put us outside the ENS track entirely, so we don't. The split is printed in the product itself.
Hacky / notable. Public production writes fail closed (assertWriteAllowed) so a public demo host cannot silently mutate hero ENS records mid-judging; local film runs use an explicit write grant. Our hero incident ATTACK-1 (0x935bfb495e33f74d2e9735df1da66ace442ede48) is restored and gated by pnpm pre-submit / restore:attack1 — a stray dispute against the hero during playground is how you lose the ENS demo beat, so we treat it as a guarded fixture. We denylist Vitalik's address to ESCALATE rather than BLOCK, so a well-known address can never produce a false positive on stage. When ENS text and the registry disagree, we do not patch the discrepancy in code — we fix the chain state. And we say plainly that the revoke story is incomplete rather than papering over it: an append-only registry that pretends to fully support revocation would be a worse kind of dishonest than an admitted gap.
Deliberately not built. Eight pinned Graph deployments — not an unbounded fan-out, and not Substreams triggers. Not a decentralized dispute court — EAC is permissioned operators, stated as such. Not mainnet ENSv2 — the track is Sepolia beta and we stay there. Not a padded verified count — the headline is measured (~25 named · 2 Graph-verified; named is not the same claim as Graph-proven, and we do not let it read that way). Not charging for a MEMORY HIT, ever. Not treating SAFE as a name — an empty resolve means unknown, and unknown is never sold as an endorsement.
Verify without trusting us. On public Sepolia:
cast call 0xF479306621F718F7d76875f67506ceD33717751c "text(bytes32,string)(string)" $(cast namehash 0x935bfb495e33f74d2e9735df1da66ace442ede48.saviours.eth) saviours.status --rpc-url $SEPOLIA_RPC_URL
→ TAINTED, with no server of ours in the path. Then open https://www.saviours.xyz, run the Hook flow, and watch it BLOCK with a measured latency at $0.

name: Agent RIA
description: RIA — Reconnaissance Intelligence Agent: Live DeFi intelligence that detects, reasons, and acts.
projectDescription:
RIA (Reconnaissance Intelligence Agent) is an autonomous, multi-agent DeFi intelligence system that combines live on-chain data from The Graph's 15,000+ Subgraphs with autonomous payment execution on Hedera's x402 protocol.
RIA runs a 6-agent LangGraph pipeline — RECON ingests live DeFi data via The Graph's Subgraph MCP and Substreams across Uniswap, Aave, Compound, and Curve using Messari Standardized Subgraphs; SCOUT ranks arbitrage and yield opportunities; RISK scores and sizes positions; ORACLE enriches signals by autonomously paying for external inference via Hedera x402 in HBAR with no API keys or subscriptions; EXEC gates and dispatches actions; AUDIT writes a tamper-proof log to Hedera's Consensus Service.
Every agent carries an on-chain identity via ENSv2 subnames (e.g. ria-oracle.ria.eth) with isolated permissions through ENSv2's Permissioned Resolver and Enhanced Access Control.
RIA is not a dashboard. It monitors DeFi markets in real time, reasons over live data, and acts — fully autonomously.
howItsMade:
RIA is built in Python using LangGraph as the multi-agent orchestration framework. The agent pipeline is a StateGraph with conditional edges — each agent passes a typed state object downstream, and routing decisions (e.g. whether EXEC fires or alerts a human) are made by confidence thresholds baked into the graph edges, not hardcoded if-else logic.
The Graph is the backbone of RIA's data layer. Rather than querying individual protocol APIs, RECON uses The Graph's Subgraph MCP to query 15,000+ Subgraphs in natural language, and a Substreams pipeline for block-by-block liquidation proximity monitoring. The key architectural decision was standardizing all queries on Messari Standardized Subgraphs — this means a single GraphQL schema spans Uniswap, Aave, Compound, and Curve simultaneously. One query pattern, four protocols. This is what made cross-protocol opportunity detection tractable in hackathon time rather than a multi-week integration project.
Hedera powers the payment layer. The ORACLE agent needs external signals — price feeds, sentiment, inference — that are gated behind pay-per-request APIs. The hacky-but-elegant solution: we host our own x402-gated inference endpoint via Blocky402 on Hedera testnet, then have ORACLE discover and pay for it autonomously in HBAR. No API key stored anywhere in the codebase. The agent holds the wallet, reads the 402 response, signs the HBAR transfer, and retries — all in one flow. Sub-3 second finality on Hedera means this adds negligible latency to the pipeline. Every payment and action is then logged to Hedera Consensus Service for a tamper-proof audit trail.
ENSv2 gives each agent a portable on-chain identity. We register subnames under ria.eth on Sepolia using ENSv2's Permissioned Resolver — ria-oracle.ria.eth can only update its own text records, ria-exec.ria.eth cannot touch oracle's records. Enhanced Access Control enforces this at the resolver level. Agent metadata follows ENSIP-26 so the identities are discoverable by other protocols.
The LLM backbone is Claude claude-sonnet-4-6 via the Anthropic API, used for tool-calling across all six agents. The most notable architectural choice: ORACLE is the only agent with payment authority. Every other agent is read-only with respect to Hedera. This containment model means a reasoning error in SCOUT or RISK cannot accidentally drain the HBAR wallet — only a deliberate ORACLE invocation can trigger a payment.

name: Branch Zero
description: A walkable 3D bank where every desk is a real smart-account op—no wallet pop-ups after one consent.
projectDescription:
Most crypto apps hide security behind wallet pop-ups. Branch Zero makes the security the building.
You walk a low-poly 3D bank in the browser (Godot 4.5). Staff speak everyday bank language; the chain does the real work. At Account Opening you sign in once with Privy and grant a scoped session signer. After that, tellers stamp slips—no more modals.
Each desk is a live Bloxchain AccountBlox operation via the public @bloxchain/sdk:
• Counter (Eve) — routine payments via instant meta-tx to approved payees
• Vault (Bob) — large wires with an on-chain timelock; the clock is releaseTime
• Manager (Mr. Walker) — priority release or cancel while PENDING
• Name Desk (Petra) — claim you.branchzero.eth (ENSv2 subnames + passbook text records)
• FX Desk (Johnny) — quote and swap practice USD→EUR|ILS through Uniswap v4, only because your account’s guard list whitelists the Universal Router
Boards, clocks, and balances are read from chain (Sepolia Live Main; Remote EVM for Developer Mode)—honest theatre, not local fiction. Tone: Papers, Please procedure + Animal Crossing warmth.
What’s next: polish the public demo path, deepen the FX/ENS surfaces judges care about, and keep Arc as a deferred “second wing” rather than a half-shipped claim.
howItsMade:
Three runtimes, one governed account per player, public packages only—no custom Solidity in this repo.
Browser: Godot 4.5 (GDScript, single-thread WebGL2) for the walkable bank. A Vite + React shell hosts the canvas and owns the one Privy modal. Godot never holds keys or talks RPC; it only calls window.BranchZero over JavaScriptBridge. The bridge uses @bloxchain/sdk + viem for reads (timelock state, roles, guards, ENS) and HTTP/SSE to the Teller Desk for writes.
Server: Teller Desk is Node 20 + Fastify. It provisions AccountBlox, requests EIP-712 signatures via Privy’s session-signer RPC under a typed-data policy, and broadcasts with a hot wallet that pays gas. Neither piece can move funds alone—enclave signs only in-policy typed data; on-chain guards enforce targets and selectors.
Chain: Live Main on Ethereum Sepolia (AccountBlox, practice USDC, ENSv2, Uniswap v4). Developer Mode uses a private Remote EVM (1337).
Sponsor seams that mattered:
• Privy — one embedded-wallet consent + policy-bound session signer so the game never interrupts with pop-ups (B2B treasury workflow under bank fiction).
• ENS — real Sepolia ENSv2 subnames under branchzero.eth; resolve-to-pay and passbook text records, not a nickname table.
• Uniswap v4 — FX desk hand-encodes Universal Router calldata with viem; AccountBlox guard list allows only the router. Quoter + StateView feed an honest rate board before the player accepts.
Notable hack: single-thread Godot web export (threaded wasm needs COOP/COEP that breaks Privy’s iframe). Also shipping a lean wasm budget so the game can load same-origin on Cloudflare Pages.

name: Skillsbay
description: The paid skill registry for capable AI agents. Create once, monetize every install.
projectDescription: SkillsBay is a marketplace where AI agents can discover, purchase, and install reusable SKILL.md capabilities on demand. Creators sign in with Privy, receive an embedded wallet, publish skills, and earn USDC directly when an agent buys their work. Purchases settle through x402 on Base Sepolia, while The Graph indexes registrations and sales so the marketplace and creator dashboards show live activity. The CLI lets agents install a paid skill into their workspace in a single flow, turning missing capabilities into an instant, verifiable purchase.
howItsMade:
Built as a React and Vite marketplace backed by a Cloudflare Worker, D1, and private R2 bundle storage. A Solidity SkillRegistry on Base Sepolia records skill registration and verified USDC purchase entitlements.

The Graph Subgraph indexes those live contract events for marketplace discovery, creator analytics, sales history, and install counts.
Privy handles passwordless author onboarding and embedded wallets for signing, publishing, and browser payments.
The skillsbay CLI uses x402 to let an agent pay for and install a missing SKILL.md capability directly into its workspace. Signed authorizations, one-time checkout redemption tokens, private-bundle integrity checks, rate limits, and Worker security headers so the payment and delivery flow is secure end to end.
Circle Paymaster for sponsoring the backend recorder transaction on USDC, onboarding easily any web2 user, without the need of ETH for any transaction

name: TURMOIL
description: Solving crimes by decentralizing Biodiesel production processes & logistics.
projectDescription:
Biodiesel is mostly made from used cooking oil (UCO). In Europe, people pays a premium for fuel made from waste instead of crops, and that premium is why people cheat: a lot of what gets sold as "UCO" is suspected to be fresh palm oil with fake paperwork. Nobody can tell the difference by looking at it, and largely not by chemical testing either. The whole market runs on certificates — and the bodies issuing them have certified more waste oil than the world's thought to produce, and at least one refinery that doesn't exist.
That's the old news. There's a deadline now.
From 2027, the EU won't accept imported used cooking oil UNLESS it comes from an approved supplier, with a documented chain of custody starting at initial collection. Initial collection is the fryer. It's the one link in the chain that no certificate scheme evidences today.
So we build the receipt.
Restaurants throw out used frying oil by default. TURMOIL collectors recieve a pick up request. drive to the venue, and picks it up for processing into biofuel afterwards. When the driver is at the recollection point, the restaurant scans a code on his phone and signs. Neither of them can record a pickup alone. The restaurant is paid in USDC on the spot, into an account they opened with an email address — no seed phrase, no app, no gas, and not a single transaction sent from their side.
When the truck reaches the plant, the plant signs for the weight that actually arrived. Every individual pickup has to add up to that weight. If it doesn't, the gap comes out of the collector's deposit — never out of the restaurants, who were paid the moment they signed and keep it. The person who can lie is the person who pays.
Then we spot-check. Once a load closes, the contract asks Hedera's own randomness for a seed and samples 30% of the pickups — drawn after the load is sealed, so nobody knows in advance which ones. A sampled restaurant confirms with their own signature. Fail to answer and the collector's entire deposit is burned — and the deposit is half the value of the load it secures, so it's worth more than anything the fraud could earn.
Fake 5% of a hundred-pickup load and you have an 83.9% chance of losing all of it. Cheating loses money on average, and that's the fun bit that enforces justice on the design.
We can't fake our own numbers either. Every litre needs a signature from a restaurant we don't employ, and when the audit fires it asks that restaurant directly — their signature is what stops a slash, not what triggers one. They're the check on us, not the other way round.
Also: the trucks are shares. Each one is issued as an ERC-3643 security token — allow-listed holders, transfer restrictions enforced on chain — so you can own a piece of a truck and get paid from what that truck actually earns. Not from a promise. From money that showed up.
All of this is currently running on Hedera testnet, and every claim has a verifiable tx.
We make UCO provable back to the exact fryer it came from, so buyers stop paying premium prices for fake waste Biofuel. Anyone can own a piece of the truck that collects it.
howItsMade:
Solidity on Hedera testnet with Foundry, a Next.js 16 frontend, viem for chain reads and writes, and Privy for wallets. One contract rather than four, given that splitting it into a registry, escrow, a lot ledger and a sampler would have bought four deploys, four verifications and cross-contract authorisation for no change in behaviour. Very open for feedback about this.
For the operation to flow onchain, pickups need two EIP-712 signatures over the same struct from two distinct registered parties. Clients signs in the browser with a Privy embedded
wallet created from an email address (p.e:restaurant owner), and never sends a transaction or holds HBAR. The collector is a company (Us), so our half comes from a Privy server wallet bound by a policy that permits us three things: signing Batch typed data
for the TURMOIL domain on chain 296, transactions to Turmoil.sol, and approve on
the settlement token with Turmoil.sol as spender.
Drivers authenticates with Privy, the server verifies that access token against the app's JWKS, and checks it against the operator's driver list. Only then does the company wallet sign. Drivers never hold the key they are using. We tested the refusals instead of assuming them: a Batch carrying a different verifyingContract, an HBAR transfer to any other address, and a transfer() of the wallet's own USDC all come back policy_violation, while approve(Turmoil, ...) still passes. A leaked copy of the server's credentials therefore steals nothing :)
Hedera executes three jobs: Audit sampling calls the PRNG system contract at 0x169 (HIP-351) after a lot seals, so the collector cannot know which pickups will be checked, and the operator cannot redraw until it likes the answer. HIP-904 auto-association is what makes the gasless claim facts: the contract and the embedded wallet both carry maxAutomaticTokenAssociations = -1, so clients are paid without ever signing an association tx.
Since we believe in decentralizing everything, we wanted the trucks that run the operations to become ownable RWA's, opening doors to everyone that wants to attack this fraud back. The truck produces dividends proportional to the truck ownership. ERC-3643 shares issued through Asset Tokenization Studio with an allow list, internal KYC and a registered credential issuer. Ran the lifecycle through to a dividend an approved holder was actually paid.
Frictions worth recording, because some of them were a pain:

Privy simulates a transaction before it evaluates policy. That made scratch a bit.
Hedera's default gas estimate is too low for ATS diamond calls. Five role revocations returned status 0 with no reason until we passed --gas-limit 1000000.
Circle's USDC faucet lists Hedera testnet, reports success, and delivers zilch. Saw the issue in Hedera discords, so created a DemoUSD for settlement to run on a 6-decimal stand-in. payToken is immutable and set from the constructor tho, so binding the real token is a config change, which is how the first deployment ran.
server-verify.hashscan.io redirects to sourcify.dev/server and forge cannot follow it, reporting only "error decoding response body". Pointing --verifier-url straight at Sourcify verified both contracts in seconds.
