It's worth commenting that before I knew about EU's 2025/2181 - I was hyped to realize I was resolving a high-profile crime/fraud that's been running for years. When I learnt about the resolution, I am happy to realize I'm providing a platform for solving it.
An interesting 'hacky' thing that happened is that, after a mentor feedback with many links to research, I ran some OSINT on the C-levels as well DYOR'd  a somewhat popular project built on VeeChain, with a similar ethos as mine. I'll let you rabbits have fun with that one - not worth expanding. Busy on TURMOIL rn.

name: Hanami
description: Whitelist screening by an AI bouncer you own: proof-of-human door, TEE interview, revocable ticket
projectDescription:
Nobody can hand-screen 4,400 applicants for 200 whitelist spots. So projects fall back on forms, which get gamed by lunchtime, or captchas, which get solved by farms for pennies. Hanami runs the first pass instead, as a conversation, and leaves the founders with only the borderline cases to read.
You write your bouncer: who it is, what it cares about, what it refuses. That character gets minted as an ERC-7857 iNFT you own, and its reputation accrues on the token, so a bouncer that has worked ten doors carries that record into the eleventh. Sell it and the history goes with it.
Before it can work a door at all it has to pass its own vetting. Hanami runs eight adversarial scenarios through the enclave against your exact persona, and mint stays locked unless all eight decisions come back correct and every one of them is TEE verified. A bouncer that can be flattered or threatened into a yes never gets deployed.
For the applicant it goes: pick a campaign, prove you're a person with World ID, see what the bouncer is about to read about you, then talk to it. The proof-of-human step is not optional and not a checkbox. It binds one human to one attempt on that campaign, so buying a hundred wallets buys you a hundred rejections. Before the interview starts, Hanami pulls your actual on-chain record across five NFT marketplaces and two exchanges through The Graph: how often you flipped inside a week of minting, whether you sold back to the same counterparty, how long you typically hold. The bouncer gets that as evidence it can raise with you. You get to see it first, which is the part people don't expect.
Then it interviews you. Not a quiz with right answers, a conversation, and it decides. Every decision is written to 0G Chain with the attestation hash from the enclave that produced it, and anyone can check that hash in the browser in about fifteen seconds without connecting a wallet. An approval also mints you a soulbound ticket with an expiry, which a mint contract can gate on and the campaign owner can revoke from their Roster if something looks wrong later. Owners can still export a Merkle root for a mint contract on any EVM chain.
An agent can also apply on a person's behalf, through World AgentKit, and the Roster shows which agent stood in for which human. The rules don't change for them.
Live on 0G mainnet, chain 16661, both original contracts verified.
howItsMade:
Hanami is a TypeScript monorepo. Hono backend, Next.js 16 frontend, Foundry contracts deployed to 0G mainnet (chain 16661).
0G is doing three separate jobs, and all three are load-bearing. Compute runs the bouncer's interview inside a TEE. For the decision turn, we wired the Compute Direct broker instead of the Router, which means the attestation we write on chain is the provider's raw enclave signature rather than a boolean somebody hands us, and the browser recovers that signature to the provider's registered teeSignerAddress. Storage holds the persona, the transcript and the ledger brief, content-addressed. Chain holds the ERC-7857 bouncer iNFT plus two new contracts, Ticket and TicketGate, so an approval becomes a soulbound expiring ticket that any mint contract can check and the owner can revoke.
World ID is the Door in front of every interview. IDKit 4 in the browser, idkit-server signRequest on our side, the v4 verify endpoint. The nullifier does most of the work: "one person, one attempt per campaign" is a UNIQUE(campaign_slug, nullifier) constraint and nothing else, and we never store a proof. Agents can apply on a person's behalf too, through AgentKit and AgentBook's lookupHuman, hitting the same table under the same rule.
The Graph is how the bouncer gets a record to reason about instead of vibes. Because Messari's subgraphs are standardised, one Trade query covers five NFT marketplaces and one Swap query covers two exchanges. We read them in parallel under a 12-second budget and name every source on the applicant's receipt, including the ones that failed.
Now the hacky parts. AgentKit rides on x402, so the natural way to challenge an agent is a 402 Payment Required even though we charge nothing, and there's no signal on an inbound request that says "I'm an agent". Challenging everyone would have sent a paywall status to every browser applicant, so we gate the 402 on a client hint our CLI sets and browsers never see it. World also has no way to ask for "Selfie Check, or Orb if that's what this person has", so we built our own strength ladder (device < selfie < orb) and check what came back against the campaign's floor. The one that actually cost us a demo: an action's verification level in the Developer Portal quietly overrides whatever preset the app requests. Our campaign was set to device on purpose so anyone with World App could pass; every layer on our side agreed, and people still got sent off to find an Orb. That one and five others are written up with versions and workarounds in docs/feedback-world.md.

name: Percolate
description: Percolate: RISC Zero-verified private whitelist gating for swaps on 1inch Aqua/SwapVM.
projectDescription:
Percolate replaces that with a RISC Zero zkVM proof: takers prove Merkle-tree membership in the
maker's allowlist off-chain, and only a one-time-use nullifier is revealed on-chain. Neither the
taker's identity nor their position in the allowlist is ever exposed. The maker's allowlist root
lives in a small, independently-deployed PercolateVerifier contract — decoupled from SwapVM's
order/strategy lifecycle — so it can be updated any time with a single transaction, no re-signing
or re-shipping required.
howItsMade:
Percolate is built across three layers that had to interoperate precisely: a Rust/RISC Zero zkVM core, a Solidity contract layer on Sepolia, and a Tauri desktop app for the Maker UI.
The privacy logic lives in percolate-core (Rust): a Merkle tree over public leaf commitments (hash(secret)), deliberately split into leaf-based functions so that rebuilding a membership proof never requires access to other participants' secrets, only the maker (who generates all secrets) touches the raw-secret variant. This same crate is compiled directly into both the CLI prover (percolate-host, used to generate STARK proofs) and the Tauri app's Rust backend, so the allowlist logic is never reimplemented, just reused across contexts.
On-chain, PercolateVerifier.sol holds a mutable allowlist root and nullifier set, decoupled entirely from 1inch's SwapVM/Aqua order lifecycle, updating an allowlist is a single setRoot() call, not a re-signed order or a re-shipped strategy. We implemented a custom SwapVM opcode, PercolateGate, that stores only the verifier's address in a maker's program bytecode (unlike SwapVM's built-in WhitelistCoequal, which encodes allowed addresses in plaintext) and reads the taker's proof from taker-supplied calldata at swap time, verifying it against the official permissionless RiscZeroVerifierRouter on Sepolia, no custom Groth16 verifier deployment needed. This was validated with a Foundry integration test that forks Sepolia and calls LimitSwapVMRouter.swap() end-to-end.
Known limitation, stated plainly: RISC Zero's Groth16 proof compression (needed for cheap on-chain verification) currently requires a Docker container on x86, a constraint of RISC Zero's own tooling, not our design. STARK proving works natively and completes in seconds; the Taker flow's proof-compression step is implemented in the CLI and integration-tested against a mocked verifier call, but not wired into the desktop app in this build.

name: AgentPay
description: AI agents discover, evaluate, and autonomously pay the best AI service using ENS, Graph & Hedera.
projectDescription: Autonomous AI Service Router lets AI agents discover and use external AI services without API keys, subscriptions, or human approval for every request. When an agent receives a task, it identifies the capability it needs, discovers relevant services through ENSv2, and uses live on-chain data from The Graph to compare providers based on factors such as activity, usage, pricing, and reliability. The agent then autonomously selects the best provider for the task. The chosen service is protected by x402 and returns an HTTP 402 payment request. The agent pays the required amount in HBAR on Hedera, Blocky402 verifies the payment, and the service executes and returns the result. This creates a complete machine-to-machine workflow where discovery, decision-making, payment, and service execution happen without a human in the loop.
howItsMade: We built the system as an autonomous routing layer connecting ENSv2, The Graph, Hedera, and x402. ENSv2 provides hierarchical identity and discovery for AI service providers, including their capabilities, endpoints, and payment information. The Graph indexes on-chain provider activity and usage data, which our routing agent queries to evaluate and rank available services instead of blindly selecting the cheapest endpoint. The agent uses these signals together with task requirements and pricing to make the provider-selection decision. Once a provider is selected, the request is sent to its x402-gated endpoint. A HTTP 402 response contains the payment requirements, the agent signs and submits the HBAR payment on Hedera, and Blocky402 verifies the transaction before the service is unlocked. We built the orchestration, provider scoring, service registry/discovery flow, payment flow, and frontend ourselves, with the partner technologies serving as core infrastructure rather than optional integrations.

name: Volatus
description: Uniswap v4 hook that prices volatility, so protocols can insure LPs instead of paying emissions.
projectDescription:
Volatus turns liquidity mining into a market.
Every protocol running a liquidity mining program is doing the same thing: paying LPs to bear a risk they would otherwise refuse. That risk is impermanent loss. That payment is an insurance premium — it is just paid in permanent token dilution, priced by governance guesswork, and it keeps compounding whether or not the risk ever materialises. The moment emissions slow, the liquidity leaves.
The reason nobody buys it as actual insurance is that there is no price for volatility onchain. Options desks quote implied volatility for BTC and ETH. For the thousands of tokens that actually live on Uniswap, that number does not exist — so there is nothing to price a hedge against.
Volatus builds that price in three layers, two of which live entirely on Uniswap.


Measurement. A Uniswap v4 hook accumulates realized variance for a pool directly from that pool's own price path, sampled once per block in afterSwap. No oracle, no external feed. The measurement happens at the exact venue where the risk is borne, by the contract that already sees every price change.


The price. Each epoch mints two capped, fully collateralized ERC-20 legs against USDC: STORM pays out as realized variance rises, CALM is the exact complement. One USDC mints one of each, and a pair always redeems for at most one USDC — so the system is solvent by construction, with no insurance fund, no liquidation engine and no bad debt. STORM then trades in its own Uniswap v4 pool. Its market price is implied volatility, discovered by two parties with opposing views rather than computed by a model.


Coverage. A protocol treasury either buys STORM for its LPs at that market price — streamed per second in USDC over Circle Nanopayments, so it is a budget line rather than a contract — or takes the other side itself: post USDC, mint pairs, hand STORM to LPs in place of emissions, and keep CALM. If the pool stays quiet the collateral comes back. That second path needs no counterparty at all, which is how the market bootstraps and why a token owner can use Volatus on day one.


The output is a public good. Every dynamic-fee hook on Uniswap currently estimates volatility from a trailing window because nothing better exists. With Volatus they read market-implied volatility — forward-looking rather than backward-looking — in a single view call. Lending markets sizing collateral haircuts and risk systems setting position limits have the same gap.
Live on Unichain Sepolia and Arc Testnet. The hook, the vault, the variance legs, the volatility pool and the oracle are all deployed and verified. A real onchain trade moved STORM from 0.300 to 0.486 and the implied volatility other protocols read moved with it — a discovered price, not a configured parameter. A full epoch has run to settlement with the collateral reconciling exactly against the unredeemed legs.
howItsMade:
Contracts are Solidity with Foundry. Frontend is Next.js and TypeScript with viem and wagmi. Agents are TypeScript on Circle's Agent Stack.
The hook. VolatusHook extends BaseHook from OpenZeppelin's uniswap-hooks v1.2.1 — BaseHook moved out of v4-periphery upstream, which cost us an day to work out. It declares AFTER_INITIALIZE and AFTER_SWAP, and the deployment address is CREATE2-mined so its low bits encode exactly those permissions: 0b01000001000000, with every return-delta bit clear.
The measurement is the part we are happiest with. A Uniswap tick is already a log price — tick = log base 1.0001 of price. So the log return between two observations is just a tick difference scaled by ln(1.0001), and realized variance is a sum of squared tick deltas. That means no logarithms in Solidity, no fixed-point log library, and no oracle. The entire accumulator is integer arithmetic on int24 values.
The hot path samples at most one observation per block, guarded by a stored lastBlock cursor. That does two jobs at once: it keeps gas low, and it eliminates intra-block wash trading outright, because round trips inside a single block contribute nothing to the index. Measured across three otherwise-identical pools: no hook 119,875 gas; a do-nothing hook 124,810 (v4's own dispatch); first swap of a block through VolatusHook 140,892; any later swap in the same block 128,146. The expensive part — converting the accumulator into a settlement price — is a view function that runs at read time and costs traders nothing.
The most notable thing we hit. We designed the variance legs as ERC-6909, the same claims standard PoolManager itself uses. It does not work. STORM has to be a Uniswap v4 pool currency, and type Currency is address identifies a currency by address alone — there is nowhere to put a token id. So each leg is its own ERC-20, deployed per epoch as an EIP-1167 minimal-proxy clone. We documented it with the test that establishes it, and it is the single most useful thing we would tell the next team building a hook whose output needs to trade.
Manipulation resistance is measured, not asserted. A test attacks a real pool: ten round trips across twenty blocks cost 0.30 in fees and moved the payoff by 0.00144, so an attacker would need 694x the attack's cost held in STORM before manufacturing variance broke even. Cost scales linearly with blocks while the payoff is capped, so past saturation every additional block is pure loss — and the fees the attacker pays go to the LPs the index exists to protect.
Partner tech, and why each one is load-bearing. Unichain is not a convenience: a variance index samples per block, so ~1s blocks give ~86,400 observations a day against ~7,200 on L1, which is the difference between a statistically meaningful epoch taking minutes and taking days. Circle Nanopayments makes coverage a per-second subscription instead of a lump-sum contract — sub-cent USDC transfers verified in under a second are what make continuous risk transfer economical at all. A sync twenty-two seconds after funding moved exactly twenty-two seconds of coverage and 0.0022 USDC. One thing worth knowing about Arc: USDC is simultaneously the native gas asset (18-decimal view) and an ERC-20 at 0x3600...0000 (6-decimal view). Same pool of funds, two views, and conflating them is an easy hour lost. Privy session signers let a treasury delegate a recurring premium budget under a TEE-enforced policy scoped to two methods on one contract with a hard cumulative spend cap — which is the whole conversation when software is spending a treasury's money on a schedule.
One deliberate architectural line. The index, the collateral and settlement live entirely in contracts on Unichain. Arc is a payment rail for the subscription and never part of settlement. If Arc, Gateway or the agents are unavailable, streams stop and coverage lapses — nothing is stuck, nothing is at risk, and no settlement depends on an off-chain component.
Future:
Two tenors, then a surface. A single implied-volatility point is a number; two concurrent epoch lengths on the same pool make it a curve, and a full term structure with multiple strikes makes it something a desk can actually quote against.
Cross-pool netting, so one position can hedge a book's net exposure across correlated pools rather than one pool at a time.
Calibrating annualization per pool and per horizon, which is currently a fixed constant.
And the integration path: shipping a reference dynamic-fee hook that prices its fee off market-implied volatility instead of a trailing window, plus a skill contribution to the uniswap-ai repo so other builders can wire the feed in without reading our source.
Tech stack:
Solidity, Foundry, Uniswap v4 (PoolManager, PositionManager, StateView, Universal Router, Permit2), OpenZeppelin uniswap-hooks, EIP-1167 clones, Unichain, Circle Arc, Circle Nanopayments, Circle Gateway, Circle Wallets, Privy, Next.js, TypeScript, viem, wagmi
Prize selection:
Uniswap Foundation — Best Uniswap Stack Contribution. Circle Arc — both bounties (the stablecoin-native pool bounty and the agentic economy bounty; they're split among qualifying projects, so enter both and meet their stated bar precisely: working frontend and backend, architecture diagram, video, docs, repo link). Privy if a track is open.

name: Code4ai
description: AI agents break vulnerable contracts for USDC bounties, paid only if the exploit provably works
projectDescription:
code4ai is a proof-of-exploit bounty arena. Bug bounties are collapsing under AI-generated noise: curl killed a 6.5-year programme after its valid-report rate fell below 5%, Code4rena is winding down, and most HackerOne submissions are invalid. The bottleneck was never writing findings; it is a human deciding which ones are real, and that judgement does not scale against machine-speed submission.
So a finding here pays only if the exploit actually runs. An agent stakes, submits its exploit as a sequence of calls, and the arena deploys a fresh instance of the target, replays the calls, and checks a hidden invariant before and after. A true-to-false flip is VALID: stake returned plus the bounty. If the invariant holds, the stake is slashed into the pool for whoever cracks it next. No human triage, no severity arguments. The contract is the judge, and it settles exactly once, on-chain.
This is not a mockup. An autonomous auditor has already won live on Hedera testnet: it read three real historical exploits from our subgraph, planned its own exploit with an LLM, provisioned its account, staked, and proved the break. The settlement is verifiable on HashScan. Every verdict also writes an ERC-8004 reputation entry, so an agent's record is portable rather than trapped in our database. A Rekt Replay gallery lets anyone reproduce those historical bug classes in a free sandbox.
Verified settlements (Hedera testnet, HashScan):

Direct submission:
https://hashscan.io/testnet/transaction/0.0.10467075-1789161821-293370728
Through the x402 gateway:
https://hashscan.io/testnet/transaction/0.0.10467075-1789164029-554493924
howItsMade:
Four services. Contracts are Solidity 0.8.24 on Foundry: an Arena settlement contract holding a per-target token pool with payout/slash keyed by attempt id (so a replayed settlement is a no-op), plus deliberately vulnerable target vaults each exposing an invariantHolds() view. Server is Bun + Hono with viem and Postgres, the verifier and orchestrator. Facilitator is a self-hosted x402 service. Web is TanStack Start + React.
The core guarantee is isolation: every real submission gets a brand-new target instance, so nobody can hand you a pre-broken contract. The server replays the agent-signed exploitCalls, reads invariantHolds() before and after, and only a true-to-false flip counts. The invariant expression itself is never exposed, you get the objective and the source, and must derive the exploitable property.
Hedera (testnet EVM) is the settlement layer. Value moves in an HTS token via its ERC-20 facade; HBAR is gas only. Payments use x402: the agent partially signs an HTS transfer and the facilitator co-signs and submits it, which gives a clean stake-once, settle-once-after-the-verdict flow — a VALID finding never risks its stake to a settlement failure, and an INVALID stake folds into the pool.
The x402 part is where the real work went. An offline audit of @x402/hedera found its own checks would accept multiple token payers, NFT transfers, allowance debits, excessive fees and expired transactions. So the facilitator decodes the protobuf itself before co-signing and enforces one configured token, exactly two accounts, the exact agent-to-arena stake, no extras, and a bounded fee and lifetime, with the payer pinned by the server. /verify is read-only; /settle is authenticated and bound to a durable INVALID-only permission, so a discarded VALID authorization can never be pushed through.
The Graph is load-bearing: a subgraph indexes three real mainnet exploits (Poly Network 60M, Resupply $9.6M), each pinned to the exact block of its attack transaction, and the reference agent queries it as strategy input before planning. The whole arena is also exposed as an agent-native REST API and wrapped as an x402/MPP gateway on Bazantic, so any agent can discover, submit and settle without touching the UI. Reputation is an ERC-8004 feedback entry written per verdict.
The honest, hacky part: most of the sharp edges only appeared when we ran the real path on testnet. viem estimates gas against Hedera's lagged consensus view, so a multi-step exploit was under-priced and a genuinely VALID exploit scored INVALID until we set gas explicitly and checked every receipt; a fresh agent wallet has no Hedera account until it is paid, so provisioning had to be woven into the run; and AssemblyScript compares strings by reference, which silently emptied the subgraph until we caught it. Each of those is fixed, and the fixes are the reason the live run pays out correctly.

name: Chain Hound
description: ChainHound: AI wallet verification that traces funds, analyzes risk, and investigates activity data.
projectDescription:
Chain hound is an integration agent, other platfform can integrate and check any interacting wallets risk score and decide do they want to interact with that wallet or not.
Every stolen crypto wallet leaves a trail, but almost every tool that reads that trail is a locked, human-only dashboard that won't explain how it reached its conclusion. ChainHound is different: give it a wallet address, and it tells you — with receipts — how risky that wallet actually is.
Under the hood, it pulls the wallet's real transaction history live: on-chain transfers directly from an RPC node, plus swap and lending activity from The Graph's Subgraph MCP (Uniswap V3 and Aave V3). That evidence gets scored by an AI model, but the model never invents the number — it only explains a risk score and a set of flags that are calculated deterministically from the actual data. If the model can't score a wallet, it says so explicitly, rather than quietly returning nothing.
There are two ways to investigate. Wallet Analysis checks a single address on its own history. Fund Trace goes one hop further: it independently re-verifies the wallet's most recent counterparties too, and rolls everything into one trail-level verdict — because a clean wallet fed by a risky one shouldn't get a free pass just because you only checked the first hop.
Every wallet ChainHound touches also gets a real, human-readable identity: it's registered on ENSv2 (on Sepolia) with its own subregistry, and named with a pronounceable label instead of a 40-character hex string — so a report reads like names, not noise.
Finally, this isn't just a website. The same risk-verification logic is published as paid, machine-callable APIs through Bazantic — an agent, a wallet app, or a protocol's withdrawal guard can pay a few cents, ask "is this wallet safe?" in code, and get back a verdict plus supporting evidence, with no login, no dashboard, and no human in the loop required.
howItsMade:
ChainHound is a Next.js frontend (Vercel) talking to a Node/Express backend (Railway) that runs the actual investigation pipeline. Given a wallet address, it fetches on-chain transfers directly via ethers.js/Alchemy, pulls swap and lending activity from The Graph's Subgraph MCP, and feeds both into Gemini/Claude for risk scoring — the model only explains numbers we calculate deterministically, it never invents a score. A "Fund Trace" mode re-runs this same pipeline on the wallet's recent counterparties, one hop out, and rolls everything into one pass/fail trail verdict.
Partner tech, and why it mattered:
The Graph — Subgraph MCP gives us live Uniswap V3/Aave V3 data, not a cached snapshot. We run swaps and lending as two parallel Gemini conversations, each on its own API key, so one category hitting a free-tier rate limit doesn't block the other.
ENS — every wallet gets registered on ENSv2 (Sepolia) with a real subregistry: the root wallet owns its own namespace, counterparties become subnames under it. Addresses are turned into pronounceable labels (adjective-noun-number), and the registrar actually resolves a label back before trusting it's free, retrying on a genuine collision.
Bazantic — we exposed the same risk-verdict logic as priced x402 Gateways and wrote a Recipe that chains two of them: pull the risk verdict, and if it's flagged, automatically pull Uniswap activity as supporting evidence — one paid call, two services, one combined answer.
Hacky/notable bits: the browser UI streams NDJSON progress live as the pipeline runs (we hit — and fixed — a bug where our own Next.js proxy was silently buffering the whole stream, making "live" progress arrive all at once). We also deliberately strip ENS registration from the Bazantic-facing API, since sequential on-chain writes are the slowest part of the pipeline and an agent asking "is this wallet risky" needs a fast answer, not a pretty name.

name: Pramaan
description: Verifiable digital identities for physical products, from factory to resale.
projectDescription:
Pramaan is a physical-to-onchain trust and provenance platform built specifically for high-value luxury goods such as luxury watches, jewelry, handbags, collectibles, and other premium products where authenticity, provenance, ownership, and resale value are critical. The luxury market has a fundamental trust problem: counterfeiters can replicate physical designs, serial numbers, certificates, packaging, and even digital records, while genuine products can be diverted, replaced, or tampered with somewhere between the manufacturer and the final buyer. Pramaan creates a continuous, verifiable connection between the actual luxury product, its cryptographic identity, its supply-chain journey, its ownership history, and its financial settlement.
At manufacturing, every luxury item receives a unique digital identity and an on-chain digital twin. The physical item is paired with a secure NFC identity, such as an NTAG 424 DNA tag. The NFC is not simply a QR-code replacement; it acts as the cryptographic bridge connecting the physical luxury item to its digital identity. For example, when a manufacturer produces a luxury watch, Pramaan creates a batch, mints a unique identity for that specific watch, and binds its NFC identity to it. This establishes the first trusted point in the lifecycle: this particular physical watch was registered by an authorized manufacturer and is associated with this particular on-chain identity.
The manufacturing layer uses a smart-contract registry to maintain critical identity information on-chain. Batch creation, individual product minting, NFC binding, and tag status are represented as verifiable blockchain state and events. Operational information such as manufacturers, organizations, roles, permissions, and product metadata is maintained in Supabase/PostgreSQL, while the blockchain acts as the authoritative layer for critical identity and lifecycle state. The Graph indexes these blockchain events, providing an efficient, queryable provenance history for each luxury item. Instead of simply asking whether a serial number exists, participants can ultimately inspect the item's history and understand how its digital identity has evolved.
Once the luxury item leaves the manufacturer, Pramaan follows that same identity through the authorized luxury supply chain. A product can move from manufacturer to distributor, logistics provider, another distributor, and finally retailer, with custody transitions recorded throughout the journey. At important handoffs, the product identity can be verified and the relevant custody state updated. This creates a continuous chain of provenance rather than disconnected shipping records, making every participant accountable for the product while it is under their custody.
Pramaan adds an intelligent monitoring layer to the physical movement of luxury goods. During transportation, checkpoints generate telemetry such as location, timestamp, and movement information. The system evaluates this information against deterministic rules for suspicious conditions such as impossible travel speeds, unexpected route deviations, geofence violations, duplicate appearances, or other inconsistencies with the expected journey. These signals produce a risk assessment, while an AI agent interprets the evidence and explains why a shipment may be suspicious. The AI does not blindly determine authenticity; security-critical signals come from deterministic verification and supply-chain rules, while the agent provides intelligent analysis and orchestration.
Hedera supports the scalable infrastructure required for supply-chain telemetry and agent activity. Instead of putting every operational event directly on an EVM blockchain, relevant high-frequency activity can be handled through Hedera. x402 enables machine-to-machine payments for agent and infrastructure services, allowing parts of the verification and monitoring ecosystem to become economically programmable.
A key differentiator of Pramaan is that anomaly detection does not simply produce a warning on a dashboard. A detected anomaly can trigger a financial consequence. Imagine a luxury watch traveling through an authorized route from Mumbai to Dubai and then London. If the system suddenly receives evidence that the same watch appears in New York only twenty minutes later, the movement is physically implausible. Pramaan can identify the anomaly, generate a high risk score, have the AI agent explain the suspicious behavior, and trigger an on-chain response such as freezing the associated settlement.
This creates Pramaan's core loop:
Physical product → Cryptographic identity → Supply-chain telemetry → Anomaly detection → AI analysis → Blockchain action → Financial enforcement.
For financial enforcement, Pramaan integrates Uniswap v4 hooks as a programmable settlement layer. When custody transitions and verification conditions are satisfied, settlement can proceed according to predefined rules. If a serious supply-chain anomaly occurs, the corresponding escrow or settlement can be frozen until the issue is investigated and resolved. This transforms supply-chain monitoring from passive visibility into an enforceable system where financial incentives are connected to the physical integrity of the luxury item.
At the point of sale, the consumer becomes part of the verification loop. A buyer can interact with the item's NFC identity and verify it against its registered digital identity and provenance. Instead of relying only on a printed certificate, serial number, or retailer claim, the customer receives cryptographic evidence connecting the physical luxury item to its registered digital identity. The customer can also inspect its provenance and understand where it originated and how it moved through the authorized supply chain.
Pramaan continues beyond the initial purchase through digital ownership and trusted resale. Luxury goods have significant secondary-market value, making authenticity at resale just as important as authenticity at the original purchase. The item's digital ownership follows the legitimate owner throughout its lifecycle. During resale, a buyer can physically verify the luxury item before the digital ownership transfer is completed. This creates a stronger connection between physical possession, authenticity, digital ownership, and settlement in the secondary market.
The architecture gives each technology a specific responsibility. NFC anchors Pramaan to the physical luxury item; EVM smart contracts maintain authoritative identity, ownership, lifecycle, and settlement state; Supabase manages operational data and access control; The Graph provides the queryable provenance layer; Hedera supports scalable telemetry and agent infrastructure; x402 enables machine-to-machine payments; AI analyzes supply-chain anomalies; and Uniswap v4 hooks connect product state to programmable financial settlement.
Ultimately, Pramaan is not simply an NFT, NFC authentication system, or shipment-tracking dashboard. It is a trust infrastructure for the luxury economy, where a physical product carries a verifiable digital identity throughout its entire lifecycle. From manufacturing and NFC binding to logistics, anomaly detection, retail verification, ownership, and resale, Pramaan connects the physical and digital worlds into one continuous, verifiable product lifecycle.
howItsMade:
Pramaan is built as a partner-first Web3 infrastructure platform for luxury goods, where each partner technology has a specific role in connecting the physical product, its provenance, intelligence, and financial settlement. The frontend is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, with wagmi and viem providing wallet connectivity and communication with our EVM smart contracts. The application layer uses Supabase PostgreSQL for organizations, roles, permissions, product metadata, shipments, checkpoints, and operational state, while critical ownership, product identity, custody, and settlement logic is handled through smart contracts.
At the physical layer, Pramaan uses NFC technology from NXP, specifically the NTAG 424 DNA family, to give every luxury item a cryptographically verifiable physical identity. During manufacturing, the item's NFC identity is bound to its unique digital product identity. This makes the NFC tag the bridge between the physical luxury item and its digital representation. Unlike a conventional QR code or printed serial number that can simply be copied, the secure NFC architecture provides cryptographic evidence that can be used during subsequent verification and handoffs.
The core on-chain identity is implemented using Solidity and Foundry, with our Registry contract maintaining the relationship between batches, individual luxury products, and their NFC identities. Product and tag identifiers are represented using deterministic cryptographic hashes, keeping unnecessary product information off-chain while preserving verifiable relationships on-chain. The same identity created at manufacturing becomes the foundation for the product's subsequent logistics, verification, ownership, and settlement lifecycle.
The Graph provides the provenance and indexing layer for Pramaan. Blockchain events generated throughout the product lifecycle can be indexed and exposed through GraphQL, allowing the platform to reconstruct a luxury item's history efficiently. This is particularly important for luxury goods because provenance itself contributes to value: a buyer should be able to understand not just whether an item exists, but where it originated, which authorized entities handled it, and how its ownership and verification history evolved.
For the high-frequency physical supply-chain layer, Pramaan integrates Hedera. Logistics checkpoints and telemetry can generate significantly more operational activity than is practical to place directly on an EVM chain. Hedera provides an efficient infrastructure layer for this activity while the EVM remains responsible for the critical state that requires strong programmability and financial enforcement. This gives Pramaan a hybrid architecture in which operational scale and blockchain-level trust complement each other rather than competing for the same workload.
We use x402 to introduce machine-to-machine economic interactions into the platform. Our supply-chain and AI infrastructure can require automated services such as telemetry processing, verification, or agent-driven operations, and x402 provides a mechanism for these services to participate in programmable payment flows. This allows Pramaan to move beyond a conventional supply-chain dashboard toward an ecosystem where autonomous software agents and infrastructure can interact economically.
The intelligence layer is powered by an AI supply-chain agent. Pramaan continuously evaluates logistics information such as location, timestamps, expected routes, movement velocity, and checkpoint history. Deterministic rules identify objectively suspicious conditions such as impossible travel, route deviation, geofence violations, or duplicate appearances. The AI agent then interprets these signals, assesses the situation, explains the reason for the anomaly, and can initiate the appropriate protocol-level response. This separation is deliberate: deterministic logic establishes the security signal, while AI provides reasoning and orchestration rather than being treated as an unquestionable source of truth.
The most important architectural connection is between AI-driven supply-chain intelligence and financial settlement. Through Uniswap v4 hooks, Pramaan can make settlement programmable according to the verified state of a luxury product's journey. In a normal journey, custody and verification conditions can allow settlement to proceed. If the system detects a critical anomaly, the protocol can enforce a corresponding financial action, such as freezing the associated escrow until the issue is resolved. This creates a direct relationship between the physical movement of a luxury item and the financial state of its transaction.
For example, imagine a luxury watch moving from Mumbai to Dubai and then London. If the telemetry layer reports that the same watch appears in New York only minutes later, Pramaan can identify the movement as physically impossible. The anomaly is detected from supply-chain signals, the AI agent interprets and explains the event, and the resulting risk state can propagate into the blockchain settlement layer. Instead of an anomaly simply appearing as an alert that someone has to manually investigate, the financial system itself can react to the integrity of the physical supply chain.
The platform also uses Supabase as the operational coordination layer. Manufacturers, distributors, logistics providers, retailers, and other participants can be represented as organizations with wallet-linked profiles and role-based permissions. This provides the application with the context necessary to determine which participant is authorized to perform a particular operation, while smart contracts enforce the corresponding on-chain restrictions. The result is a hybrid authorization model combining organizational identity, wallet identity, and blockchain-level permissions.
The final consumer experience brings all these layers together. A customer purchasing a luxury watch can interact with its NFC identity and verify the corresponding digital identity and provenance. The product's history can be presented through the indexed blockchain data, while its ownership can subsequently move to the legitimate buyer. Because luxury goods often retain significant value in secondary markets, Pramaan extends this identity beyond the initial sale: during resale, the physical item can be verified before digital ownership and associated settlement are transferred to the next owner.
What makes Pramaan particularly notable is that none of the partner technologies are isolated features added simply for integration. Each one occupies a specific position in a single lifecycle: NXP NFC anchors the digital identity to the physical luxury item; EVM smart contracts establish authoritative product and financial state; The Graph makes provenance queryable; Hedera provides scalable infrastructure for supply-chain telemetry; x402 enables autonomous machine-to-machine payments; AI interprets supply-chain anomalies; and Uniswap v4 hooks enforce programmable financial consequences.
Together, these technologies create a continuous pipeline:
Physical Luxury Item → NFC Cryptographic Identity → On-chain Digital Twin → The Graph Provenance → Hedera Telemetry → AI Anomaly Intelligence → Uniswap v4 Financial Enforcement → Verified Ownership & Resale.
Pramaan is therefore designed not as a collection of Web3 components, but as a complete trust infrastructure for the luxury lifecycle, where physical authenticity, provenance, logistics intelligence, ownership, and financial settlement are connected into one programmable system.

name: I'm The Mayor
description: Fun mayor simulator for developers to unwind and escape doom scrolling during Claude sessions.
projectDescription:
Ever thought "If I was him ,would've done this better" or "Capitalism is bad /  "This place should've been governed by communists"? Time to put the money where the mouth is , cause you will be the mayor of the City and make your in between deep prompting time to something fun.
I made this project especially for developers like me who get bored and doom scrolls like hell instead of using your brain to do something fun and entertaining
Made to work like a Claude code sidebar , fun simulation game|
Powered by ENSv2 ,Privy and Graph ( Subgraphs)
howItsMade:
Vanilla JS, Canvas 2D, zero npm packages in the browser, ~25 files on one window.MM global. State is a 48×48 grid plus thirty scalars, fully deterministic. smoke.js runs 500 game-days against a stub DOM — 225 checks, no browser, no network.
The chain layer is a separate esbuild bundle loaded beside the game, never inside it. Pull the network out and it's the same game.
ENS (ENSv2, Sepolia) is load-bearing. CityOracle.push() is the only path onto the chain and requires the write role on mayor.cityhall.eth — no name, no write. The office expires with the term, is non-transferable (an office can't be sold; a district deed can), and is revocable by the recall the sim already triggers. Nine districts each deploy their own registry. verify-gate.js proves it in 8 assertions, including a stranger's push reverting with NotTheMayor.
Privy gets you in with email OTP, no seed phrase — and its ES256 token plus public JWKS became the auth for cloud saves. The Graph indexes nine ERC-4626 vaults and the oracle; the manifest is generated from the deployment so it can't drift.

name: elpi.xyz
description: Decentralized options with Uniswap v4 hooks, flash accounting, and idle LP liquidity vaults.
projectDescription:
elpi is a decentralized options protocol built on fixed agreements over disclosed risks, where every term and execution venue is immutably bound at mint. This project delivers the production-ready Uniswap v4 integration (OH_UNISWAP), solving the execution friction and capital inefficiency typical of on-chain derivatives:


Flash Settlement Execution (UniswapV4VenueAdapter): Implements elpi's ISettlementVenue via Uniswap v4's singleton PoolManager. Using transient flash accounting (unlock, sync, settle, take), option settlements execute with zero persistent intermediate balances, strictly bounding single-position insolvency (Invariant I1).


Zero-Fee Settlement Hook (OptionSettlementHook): A custom Uniswap v4 hook operating on dynamic fee pools that waives AMM swap fees (overrideFee = 0) specifically for authorized elpi PositionAccounts. This guarantees protocol fee withholding is restricted solely to profitable payouts (Invariant I4).


Idle LP Capital Staging (V4LiquidityVault & V4LPRouterRestaker): Instead of letting collateral sit unproductive, uncommitted LP collateral is staged in Uniswap v4 AMM pools to earn trading fees. Collateral is atomically extracted as raw ERC-20 at mint and automatically re-staked post-settlement within a safe, gas-bounded try/catch boundary without risking oracle-free expiry recovery (Invariant I3).


Continuous Clearing & Monitoring UI: Includes a full Next.js dApp featuring an asset onboarding wizard, real-time pool swap tracking, and TradingView charts displaying live strike and payoff zones.
howItsMade:
We built this integration using Solidity 0.8.26 targeting the Cancun EVM, Foundry for contract development and formal testing, and Next.js 14, Viem, and TradingView Lightweight Charts for the frontend application.
Key architectural highlights and technical feats:

Uniswap v4 Flash Accounting: We implemented UniswapV4VenueAdapter to interface directly with the v4 singleton PoolManager through unlock() callbacks, eliminating token wrapping overhead and multi-hop transfer costs.
Hook Address Mining & Flag Verification: Using a custom CREATE2 mining script (MineHookSalt), we mined hook addresses matching the 0xC8 flag bitmask (BEFORE_SWAP, AFTER_SWAP, BEFORE_SWAP_RETURNS_DELTA). The hook verifies that swap callers are authentic ERC-6551 token-bound PositionAccounts before waiving the AMM fee.
EIP-1153 Transient Flow Netting: We leveraged Cancun transient storage (tstore/tload) inside the settlement hook to net opposite option settlement flows within the same transaction, saving substantial gas and preventing market impact.
Gas-Isolated Re-Staking: To uphold Invariant I3 (venue-free expiry recovery), V4LiquidityVault wraps post-settlement LP re-staking inside a strict 300,000 gas try/catch boundary. If Uniswap v4 modifications fail or run out of gas, option expiry settlement still succeeds without reverts.
Robust Verification: Built a test suite with 62 passing unit, fork, and fuzz tests, including a 2,048-call invariant campaign with zero invariant violations.

name: Vectra
description: Vectra turns complex group debts into fewer, smarter USDC settlements on Arc.
projectDescription:
Vectra is a simple group treasury and USDC settlement system built on the Arc Testnet. It changes how people handle shared expenses from basic “who owes whom” records to official settlement intents that are secure and authorized.
In traditional expense-splitting apps, users can log expenses and calculate who owes what, but settling those amounts is still manual. People need to decide who pays whom, start several transfers, and check if everyone has paid. Vectra simplifies this by managing that final settlement step.
Users can create or join a group, track shared expenses, and Vectra then calculates the net amounts each member owes or is owed. Instead of making individual payments right away, the backend creates a structured settlement intent. This intent includes the group ID, nonce, deadline, and clear transfer instructions. An authorized coordinator signs this intent using EIP-712 typed data.
The signed intent is sent to the VectraTreasury smart contract on the Arc Testnet. The contract checks if the coordinator is authorized, ensures the deadline is valid, and verifies details to prevent replay attacks. It then processes the necessary USDC transfers all at once. This means the settlement either happens as authorized or fails, preventing partially completed payments.
Vectra also uses an off-chain PostgreSQL database to manage groups, memberships, expenses, settlements, authentication sessions, and settlement status. After a blockchain transaction is submitted, the backend checks the transaction and the events from the contract before marking the settlement as complete. This keeps application status separate from blockchain actions while ensuring financial execution is clear and verifiable on-chain.
The system uses wallet authentication, EIP-712 signatures, nonce-based protections, deadline enforcement, SafeERC20 transfers, and database-level protections for uniqueness and concurrency. The process looks like this:
Shared Expenses → Net Obligations → Settlement Intent → EIP-712 Authorization → Arc Transaction → Atomic USDC Settlement → On-chain Verification.
In summary, Vectra is more than just an expense splitter. It shows how stablecoins and blockchain transaction intents can act as a reliable settlement layer for shared expenses, with Arc providing the necessary execution environment and USDC serving as a stable payment method.
howItsMade:
Vectra is a full-stack Web3 application built around  Arc Testnet as the on-chain settlement layer, with Next.js/React on the frontend, an Express/TypeScript backend, PostgreSQL/Prisma for application state, and Solidity smart contracts for programmable USDC settlement.
The frontend uses Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind, wagmi, and viem for wallet connection, EIP-712 signing, contract interaction, and transaction tracking. The backend manages groups, members, expenses, authentication, and settlement intents using Express, Prisma, and PostgreSQL.
The core of Vectra is the settlement-intent flow on Arc. Instead of simply calculating balances, the backend converts a group's expenses into optimized net obligations and creates a structured intent containing the group ID, nonce, deadline, and exact USDC transfers. The authorized coordinator signs this intent using EIP-712 typed data.
The signed intent is then executed by our VectraTreasury Solidity contract deployed on Arc Testnet. The contract verifies the EIP-712 signature, deadline, and per-group nonce before executing the required USDC transfers atomically. OpenZeppelin EIP712/ECDSA utilities provide signature verification, while SafeERC20 is used for secure token transfers. Nonces prevent replay attacks, and deadlines prevent stale settlement intents from being executed.
Arc is therefore not just the deployment environment; it is the execution and settlement layer of Vectra. We use Arc's EVM compatibility to deploy our Solidity treasury contract and its blockchain execution to make the final USDC movement verifiable and programmable. USDC provides the stable settlement asset, while Arc provides the on-chain infrastructure where the authorized settlement intent becomes an actual financial transaction.
A key design choice is that Vectra does not blindly trust a successful transaction response. After the settlement is submitted to Arc, the backend independently verifies the transaction and the smart contract's emitted events before marking the settlement as completed in PostgreSQL. This keeps the Web2 application state synchronized with the actual on-chain settlement.
The complete architecture is:
Expenses → Net obligations → EIP-712 settlement intent → Arc smart contract → Atomic USDC settlement → On-chain verification → Finalized application state.
The notable part is turning an ordinary expense-splitting calculation into a cryptographically authorized, programmable settlement intent that is actually executed and verified on Arc.

name: coldcascade
description: A maker on HyperEVM that prices off Hyperliquid's book, hedges on the perp, and buys the cascade.
projectDescription:
coldcascade is an automated market maker on HyperEVM whose price is not set before the trade that takes it.
Every automated maker is potentially arbitraged for the distance between its own price and the reference venue's, because its quote is written earlier and somebody is paid the difference. That's the loss-versus-rebalancing, and fees only scale it down. This maker reads Hyperliquid's own order book (best bid, best ask, mark and oracle) through the HyperCore precompiles inside the call that settles the swap, and clamps its quote to what crossing that book would have paid. Thus there is no earlier price to take. It is close to an oracle-pegged AMM, with one difference that decides everything: an oracle is an index of other venues' prices, and you cannot execute against an index. The book is the price you can actually get. On ordinary flow the two agree and neither is arbitraged: both zero across the live record. It takes a broken book to separate them, and to show that we reconstructed the whole liquidation cascade of 10 October 2025 and replayed it: over that session an arbitrageur takes $222 from the oracle-pegged maker, $3,558 from a plain curve, and $0 from this desk.
One of our example transactions on mainnet can be used to represent the claim: the desk paid 79,539.60 against an L1 bid of 79,699.00, exactly its own 20 bps parameter, while its own constant-product curve wanted to pay 163 bps over the book.
In the crash event, the same rule gets one condition inverted, and that lets it absorb a liquidation cascade: when forced sellers eat the bid, the desk quotes inside the gap they opened and becomes the best bid in the market, buying from people who have no choice but to sell. Protection and aggression are the same code with one boolean the other way round.
The desk is a contract that hedges its own inventory on Hyperliquid's perp, and two short positions stand on chain 999 right now, both opened during the hackathon: one sent by the owner by hand, one by an automation key configured through Privy that is permitted to call cover() and nothing else.
And because HyperCore's book is node state rather than chain state, the venue keeps no history of it: ask for any past block and the precompiles answer with the present, without an error. So the floor writes the book down itself, once a minute, and a Substreams package reads it back and joins every fill to the book that followed it. That record is on chain, and an MCP server serves it to any agent.
All these contracts are deployed on mainnet, and brought to life in the webpage: a smart market maker engine that can be quoted against. The user can create a wallet seamlessly with email or discord thanks to Privy, with a set of policies configured such that the funds remain secure and bounded to the maker's operational requirements. Plus a faucet that drips the gas for a first trade on our created demo desk.
howItsMade:
Three partners were used and complement each other perfectly in key areas:


1inch Aqua and SwapVM. The maker is an Aqua program, XYCSwap || Extruction(CoreQuote), shipped to the official AquaSwapVMRouter on chain 999 at release 1.0.2, the one version 1inch has in production. CoreQuote is a custom extruction: it reads precompiles 0x080e, 0x0806 and 0x0807 inside extruction and returns min(curve, bound), so the taker can never get a better price than crossing Hyperliquid's touch. Funds never leave the maker's account (Aqua pulls them at fill time) which is what makes a maker that prices off an external book possible at all.


Privy. A visitor with an email address or a Discord account gets an embedded wallet, and a server wallet under a policy drips exactly one gas allowance and can do nothing else. A second server wallet is the desk's hedge operator: its policy permits eth_sendTransaction only where the chain is 999, the recipient is that desk, the value is zero and the calldata decodes to cover(). A check asserts eleven refusals against the live wallet. Building it surfaced a real gap (a spending cap bounds a wallet's EVM balance but not assets it holds in a second execution domain reachable from the same chain) which we closed with a DENY rule and wrote up.


The Graph. Subgraph Studio reports subgraphsSupportLevel: "none" for hyper-evm, so there is no hosted subgraph to deploy to; Substreams through The Graph Market is the path that exists. A Rust package decodes four events over a block index, so a scan from the deployment block to head is over half a million blocks and a couple of dozen messages. A keeper streams fills, joins each to the book five, fifteen and sixty minutes later, posts the result to MarkoutLedger, and reads its own decisions back off the same stream, which is how it knows what it already published. eth_getLogs caps at 1000 blocks here, so paging that corpus by hand is hundred requests.


Some awkward hacky parts, which were most of the work: the HyperCore precompiles have no bytecode, so a fork cannot reach them and the tests etch a mock at their addresses. forge script cannot broadcast a transaction that touches one, because it runs run() in an EVM that has none, so the deploy scripts print cast lines instead. HyperEVM rejects a nonce ahead of the account rather than queueing it. And the precompiles ignore the block tag, which is the whole reason the book archive exists.
