Around 700 tests across the server and the browser. Integration tests run against a real
PostgreSQL through testcontainers, never a mock, because half of what a repository does lives
in SQL, constraints and transactions.

name: ProofStream
description: ProofStream turns live DEX data into portable Merkle receipts anyone can verify.
projectDescription:
ProofStream is a verification layer for blockchain data APIs. It fetches live DEX activity from The Graph, including recent swaps, pool activity, and wallet-origin activity across supported networks. The raw GraphQL response is converted into readable records and sealed into a Merkle tree using the MerkleForge Framework.
Users can select any activity record and generate a compact cryptographic receipt containing the record, dataset root, and Merkle proof. The receipt is verified locally in the browser without downloading the complete dataset or trusting the application’s backend. If the selected record is modified, verification fails immediately.
ProofStream includes editable GraphQL and JSON views, human-readable activity cards, token information, tamper testing, developer-level proof details, and downloadable JSON and PDF receipts. Graph API keys are used only in browser memory and are never stored.
The project demonstrates how wallets, dashboards, AI agents, light clients, and data providers can make indexed blockchain responses independently verifiable. ProofStream proves that a record belongs to a specific sealed dataset; it does not claim that the upstream indexer or blockchain data source is independently correct.
howItsMade:
ProofStream is built as a TypeScript and Rust workspace. Its interactive web application uses React 19, TypeScript, and Vite, while its proof engine is built with Rust and the MerkleForge Framework.
The browser connects directly to The Graph Gateway through editable GraphQL queries. I created schema-aware presets for Uniswap V3, Aerodrome, SushiSwap, ApeSwap, Trader Joe, and compatible deployments across multiple networks. ProofStream also integrates Messari’s standardized DEX AMM schema, allowing SushiSwap, ApeSwap, and Trader Joe to share the same GraphQL query and normalization pipeline. Only the live Subgraph deployment ID changes between these protocols. Users can request recent swaps, activity from a particular pool, or records associated with a wallet address.
The Graph is a load-bearing part of the project: it supplies the live indexed blockchain data that ProofStream converts into verifiable receipts. The application does not rely on mocked or static data for its live demonstration.
After receiving a GraphQL response, ProofStream normalizes each swap into a deterministic, human-readable row containing the protocol, schema version, token pair, token addresses, amounts, USD value, transaction hash, wallet origin, pool, and block number. These exact normalized rows become the leaves of a Merkle tree. Deterministic normalization is essential because even a small change to a committed field must produce a different hash.
The proof layer uses domain-separated Keccak-256 hashing. Leaf data and internal nodes receive different prefixes before hashing, preventing the two node types from being interpreted interchangeably. ProofStream combines the leaf hashes into a binary Merkle tree, produces one dataset root, and generates a compact sibling path for the selected row.
The browser then performs stateless verification using only the selected row, its index, the helper hashes, and the expected root. It does not need the complete dataset or access to the source database. If a user changes an amount, address, token pair, or any other committed value, the browser computes a different root and rejects the receipt.
The Rust implementation uses merkle-core, merkleforge-hash, and merkle-variants from MerkleForge. It constructs a BinaryMerkleTree<Keccak256> and produces a serializable proof packet. I implemented the same proof algorithm in TypeScript so judges and developers can run the complete verification flow in a browser without installing Rust, operating a backend, or trusting a server-side verification result.
The interface separates the workflow into Query, Dataset, and Receipt views. Users can inspect and edit the GraphQL request and raw JSON response, while the same data is translated into readable activity cards. Receipts can be downloaded as structured JSON for software integrations or as a plain-language PDF generated with jsPDF. Token metadata and artwork improve readability but are deliberately excluded from the canonical data used for hashing.
For privacy, Graph API keys remain only in React memory while the page is open. They are sent directly to The Graph in the request authorization header and are never written to local storage, session storage, the repository, or a ProofStream database.
A particularly useful part of the implementation is that ProofStream preserves both representations of the data: the original API response remains inspectable, while the normalized version becomes cryptographically strict. Users can edit the JSON, rebuild the dataset, modify a selected claim, and immediately observe how each change affects the Merkle root and verification result.

name: Aquara
description: Autonomous system that manage positions across 1inch Aqua strategies via EIP-7702.
projectDescription:
Aquara is an autonomous system that manages concentrated liquidity positions on 1inch Aqua on Base, delegated through a scoped, revocable EIP-7702 session key so it can act without ever taking custody of the user's funds.
The problem: once a concentrated strategy drifts out of its band, or was deployed into a pair with no flow, it earns exactly zero while the capital still looks "invested." Take a $3,000 LP split across two strategies: one band drifts out of range, the other sits in a pair nobody trades, and both show $0.00 volume every morning. The fix is a multi-leg operation (verify on-chain truth, get sane quotes, sequence approvals, dock, swap, ship), and every leg carries its own gas cost, revert risk, and stale-data trap. So instead of babysitting it daily, most LPs just leave it idle for weeks. Existing tooling doesn't help either: manual rotation demands 24/7 monitoring, custody-based vaults take away direct ownership, and one-shot scripts trust a single quote and fail cryptically on the first stale read.
Aquara replaces that manual loop with a deterministic rotation cycle that runs on a 15-minute cron:

Evaluate: every position gets a verdict (healthy, depleted, side-depleted, oor-suspect, thin-allowance, inactive) from live chain reads, layered with trash rules and a gain gate. Proven dead capital skips both gates and rotates immediately.
Snapshot: raw balances and decimals are read straight from chain before docking, so under-backed positions are caught before anything moves.
Preflight + approve: swap routes are quote-checked with zero gas spent before committing; any quote priced more than 25% off spot is rejected outright, and missing approvals land in one batched transaction before docking starts.
Dock, merge, deploy: intents are cancelled (Aqua is allowance-based, so docking moves nothing), everything is merged into USDC using measured, not estimated, amounts, and one deploy call ships fresh positions into the current top earners.

Each stage executes as a single atomic Calibur batch, with the relayer paying gas. Tokens never leave the user's wallet, every batch is simulated before it's sent, and every dollar is reconciled afterward, flagging anything beyond 3% drift between what was snapshotted and what actually got redeployed.
howItsMade:
Stack: a Bun 1.4 monorepo with web/ (Next.js 16, React 19, wagmi/viem) for the dashboard and API, rotator/ and taker-bot/ as separate Bun/Hono services, and Postgres/Prisma for jobs, decisions, and per-maker settings. No new smart contracts were written; the whole system is TypeScript orchestrating existing on-chain primitives, which is exactly why it was shippable in a 12-day window.
The pieces are glued together as a shared library, not as APIs between services. The rotator cron imports web/lib/rotation.ts (the verdict engine), web/lib/oneinch-quote.ts (the quoter), and web/lib/calibur-agent.ts (execution) directly by relative path. That means the dashboard's manual "deploy" button and the autonomous cron run the literal same code path and can never disagree about what a position's state is or what a fair quote looks like.
Partner technologies and what each bought us:

1inch Aqua: its allowance model is the entire custody story. Strategies are virtual intents and tokens never leave the wallet, so docking moves nothing and rotation needed zero vault code. strategies/makers and strategies/overview give positions, bands, and performance windows; leaderboard/makers (with strategies/opened as a fallback) gives rotation targets.
1inch Swap API v6.1: every merge and cover leg goes through one shared quote-then-swap function, so we never hand-rolled a router integration or slippage math, and both the dashboard and the cron inherit the same pacing, retries, and off-market sanity check for free.
1inch Price API v1.1: the single source of spot truth, used three ways: proving a position is actually out of range (band vs. spot, not vibes), sizing USD budgets, and reconciling snapshot dollars against deployed dollars after every rotation.
Calibur / EIP-7702: one signature creates a scoped, 30-day, revocable session key. The whitelist (Aqua ship/dock, token approvals, the 1inch router) is the entire access-control layer; zero contracts deployed, zero custody surface to audit.
Base: gas cheap enough to make 15-minute cron ticks, per-leg simulation, and $1 demo positions make economic sense. The architecture assumes reverts are basically free, which would not hold on mainnet L1 gas.

name: Graphitti
description: A visual workflow builder for onchain and offchain automation
projectDescription:
Graphitti is an execution layer for AI agents with a visual workflow builder for onchain finance . You connect triggers,  actions and plugin nodes  on a canvas, run the workflow in the browser, then publish that same workflow as  a paid marketplace listing. New users stay on the canvas. Developers and agents  call it over HTTP or MCP. Teams share a Privy org treasury. The app never holds the private key.
Watching the chain, sending USDC, and letting an agent call the flow still happen in three places. Ops checks Uniswap or a vault on a dashboard, signs from another wallet, and pastes an API key into Slack if a bot should run it. Someone either clicks every transfer, or the bot has no spend cap. Graphitti puts that work in one workflow.
Kelp's April 2026 rsETH incident is what that looks like in practice. A forged LayerZero message released about 116,500 rsETH from the Ethereum OFT adapter with no matching burn on the source chain. Circulating supply went up. Collateral in the LRT vault did not. Unbacked rsETH was still being used as lending collateral while people compared dashboards.
Graphitti does not patch Kelp. It watches the same invariant. From-scratch Substreams index mainnet backing and Arbitrum OFT supply every block and write the rows to Supabase backing_snapshots. The workflow reads the latest row. If supply is more than 50 bps above backing, it pages ops on Telegram so they can pause rsETH as collateral. If the numbers still match, it sends a backing-OK heartbeat so you know the monitor ran.
Shipped examples include Uniswap large-swap Telegram alerts, the Kelp backing monitor, Arc DeFi treasury readiness, FPL top-two USDC payouts on Arc, Stripe invoices into Privy USDC, gasless contractor payroll, an Aave/Uniswap USDC keeper, and payroll that auto-sends at the cap then queues an intent. Eliza OS plugins (plugin-the-graph, plugin-privy) can search subgraphs and call the same listed workflows. Payroll and intents run on Base Sepolia USDC. Arc is Testnet for CCTP preflight and x402 marketplace settlement.
howItsMade:
The app is a Next.js 16 / React 19 canvas on React Flow, with Postgres and Drizzle for workflows, integrations, and Better Auth sessions.

A Privy embedded wallet is bound to that user.
Teams get a Privy org wallet on top, with a payee book, a 10 USDC auto cap, and transfer intents for anything larger.
Graphitti stores wallet ids, not keys.
Plugin steps talk to APIs with fetch.

The same graph then runs from the browser, an HTTP route, MCP (search_workflows / call_workflow), or a Hub listing.
The Graph is the read path.

Uniswap large-swap alerts hit Gateway GraphQL against a live Uniswap V3 Ethereum subgraph, so we did not have to index that protocol ourselves.
Kelp is the from-scratch piece. We wrote Substreams in Rust that, every Ethereum block, compare mainnet rsETH supply and LRTDepositPool collateral with Arbitrum OFT supply (the same invariant the April 2026 forged LayerZero mint broke).
Graph Studio would not take a Substreams-powered subgraph for that package, so we did not ship a fake subgraph. Two SQL sinks write into Supabase. A Postgres trigger merges the rows into backing_snapshots and sets should_alert above 50 bps.
The canvas only reads the latest row and Telegram-pages ops.

Writes and settlement are split on purpose.

Payroll and intents use Privy wallet-actions on Base Sepolia USDC.
Bridge preflight and prize-pool sends use Circle CCTP and Arc Testnet (eip155:5042002).
Arc has two USDCs, which we had to treat separately: native gas USDC is 18 decimals, marketplace USDC is the 6-decimal ERC-20.
Paid listings return HTTP 402 with Circle Gateway nanopayments over x402. The caller signs EIP-3009 TransferWithAuthorization against GatewayWalletBatched and retries with PAYMENT-SIGNATURE. No long-lived API key. Owner wfb_ keys skip the payment gate so we can test our own listings.

Eliza OS plugins (plugin-the-graph, plugin-privy) wrap the same catalogs we published as @graphitti/graph-core and @graphitti/privy-core, so an agent can search subgraphs and call a listed workflow without a second integration.

Stripe, Telegram, and the FPL API sit on that same plugin bus.
Docs are Mintlify. The production app is on Vercel.

name: finity
description: Give your AI agent Ledger-approved pocket money to buy services within rules it cannot break.
projectDescription:
AI agents need to buy APIs, data, compute, and other services—but giving a model unrestricted payment access is unsafe, while approving every purchase destroys autonomy.
Finity lets an owner delegate procurement authority, not control of a wallet.
The owner clear-signs a human-readable spending mandate once on a Ledger device. It defines which providers, services, methods and assets the agent may use, together with per-request limits, total budgets, data-sensitivity rules, expiration and escalation requirements. The agent can then make many purchases inside those boundaries without further wallet prompts, but it never receives payment keys or provider credentials.
For each request, Finity’s deterministic broker discovers services registered on Hedera, obtains signed quotes and evaluates every term against the mandate. If authorized, it reserves the amount in the on-chain MandateRegistry, issues a single-use capability and settles through x402 using native HBAR. An isolated Connector Vault supplies credentials only for that approved request.
The demo sends two otherwise identical requests to the same paid service. One satisfies the mandate, completes a real HBAR payment and returns the service result. The other changes one policy-controlled field and is refused before reservation, credential access or settlement—producing zero payment.
Both outcomes create signed, hash-chained decision receipts committed to Hedera Consensus Service. Anyone can independently verify what the agent requested, which rules were evaluated and why money did or did not move.
Ledger grants authority, deterministic code enforces it, the vault isolates secrets, and the AI only expresses intent.
Finity turns a hardware wallet into a programmable root of trust for autonomous commerce.
howItsMade:
Finity lets a Pi-based AI purchase paid services autonomously without ever receiving a payment key or blanket spending authority.
A Ledger owner clear-signs one bounded mandate; every later purchase is deterministically authorized, settled through x402 in native HBAR, and independently auditable on Hedera.
Finity is a pnpm monorepo centered on strict TypeScript, with a Solidity registry deployed to Hedera EVM.
Its architecture follows three trust boundaries: the Pi-based AI produces structured purchase intent, finityd makes deterministic authorization decisions, and an isolated Connector Vault holds payment keys and provider credentials
.
Every purchase follows one explicit state machine:
INTENT → DISCOVERY → SIGNED QUOTE → POLICY EVALUATION → RESERVATION → CAPABILITY → x402 PAYMENT → DELIVERY → RECONCILIATION
The agent never receives a payment key or plaintext credential. The vault accepts only single-use capabilities, restricts outbound hosts, injects secrets inside the approved request and redacts sensitive output.
Human policy starts in the mandate compiler, which converts provider, service, method, asset, budget, expiry and data-sensitivity rules into EIP-712 typed data plus a human-readable Ledger display model. The owner clear-signs this mandate once. Ledger signs authority changes—mandates, amendments and revocations—but never individual purchases.
The pure policy engine evaluates signed quotes and current policy state in a fixed order. Unknown or malformed inputs fail closed.
MandateRegistry.sol verifies the Ledger authority on Hedera EVM, tracks mandate status and consumption, reserves budget before payment, finalizes or releases reservations and binds each mandate to an HCS audit topic. Hardhat tests cross-check its EIP-712 digest against ethers.
Services are published through a provider SDK built on @x402/core, @x402/express and @x402/hedera.
It generates signed manifests, quotes and usage receipts. finityd discovers these records through HCS, selects a quote deterministically, reserves the amount, mints a capability and asks the vault to settle native HBAR through Blocky402. SQLite makes the workflow resumable across failures.
Each authorization, refusal, payment and reconciliation event becomes a signed, hash-chained receipt committed to HCS. The independent verifier reconstructs the chain, checks signatures and policy state, confirms HCS inclusion and correlates the x402 settlement.
The hackiest integration problem was Pi’s jiti loader crashing on a static Ledger signer import with Cannot redefine property: module.exports. I reproduced it by bisecting the Ledger imports and moved SDK loading into the signing path. The complete EIP-712 mandate hash also exceeded Solidity’s normal stack limit, so the registry is compiled with viaIR.

name: RouteCO2
description: Autonomous carbon offsets settled in USDC the instant a plane lands via 1inch Aqua on Arc.
projectDescription:
RouteCO2 is an autonomous flight emissions reconciliation protocol bridging real-time aviation transponder telemetry (ADS-B) directly to zero-custody on-chain carbon offset settlements.
The global aviation industry operates under strict environmental mandates (ICAO CORSIA and EU ETS), yet airline carbon offsetting remains an opaque, 45-to-90-day manual nightmare. Corporate dispatchers currently lock millions in broker escrow accounts, wait months for third-party flight fuel audits, and pay up to 15% in brokerage overhead just to purchase and retire carbon credits.
RouteCO2 solves this by turning real aircraft transponders into autonomous on-chain economic actors. Operating continuously across European and global flight corridors, our autonomous agent monitors live aircraft transponder telemetry (altitude, true airspeed, and vertical climb rate) directly from the OpenSky Network and global ADS-B receiver grids. Utilizing certified ICAO Doc 9889 fuel consumption benchmarks (scaling across Narrow-body, Wide-body, and Heavy airframes), the system computes instantaneous fuel-burn and metric tonnes of CO₂ emitted.
When an aircraft's landing gear compresses on touchdown (Weight-on-Wheels signal: on_ground: true), the autonomous Circle Agent immediately triggers an atomic wheels-down settlement on Arc Testnet.
Through our custom 1inch Aqua integration, airline corporate treasuries maintain 100% self-custody of their funds—zero upfront capital is locked in third-party escrow. In a single atomic transaction block, 1inch Aqua pulls the exact USDC offset fee from the airline's self-custodial wallet and pushes verified carbon retirement credits directly into the corporate treasury, producing an immutable, cryptographically verifiable ICAO Doc 9889 audit certificate on ArcScan in under one second.
howItsMade:
RouteCO2 was built from first principles under a strict Live-RPC architectural mandate across a three-layer decentralized stack:


Smart Contract & Liquidity Layer (1inch Aqua App on Arc Testnet): We developed and deployed SkyRouteVault.sol and AquaCore.sol on Arc Testnet (Chain ID 5042002). Unlike traditional escrow vaults where airlines must deposit float upfront, our contract acts as a custom 1inch Aqua App. When a flight manifest is settled, the contract invokes IAqua.pull(treasury, usdcAmount) and IAqua.push(treasury, co2Credits) atomically in one block. This guarantees zero-custody shared liquidity—funds never leave the airline's wallet until the physical landing transponder signal is cryptographically verified on-chain.


Autonomous Economic OS (Circle Agent Stack on Arc): The autonomous background agent is built with Viem and TypeScript. It ingests live ADS-B radar state vectors (altitude, ground speed, vertical rate) from OpenSky Network, with automatic sub-50ms failover to the global community receiver network (api.adsb.lol). The agent's embedded ICAO Doc 9889 engine continuously calculates burn rates using certified category benchmarks (2,400 kg/h for A320, 6,500 kg/h for A350, and 10,200 kg/h for A380) and applies the standard 3.16 kg CO₂/kg Jet-A emission factor. Transactions are dispatched natively using USDC as the gas token on Arc Testnet, achieving sub-second finality with deterministic gas efficiency.


Enterprise Identity & Frictionless UX (Privy): Flight operations dispatchers authenticate in under 3 seconds using Privy embedded passkeys (FaceID/WebAuthn), provisioning an enterprise smart wallet without seed phrases. Privy session policies enforce bounded corporate security: transactions are strictly whitelisted to the SkyRouteVault contract and capped by per-flight budget limits, eliminating mid-flight wallet popups during high-tempo dispatch operations.


Notable Hack & Engineering Feat: Ingesting volatile live ADS-B telemetry into deterministic on-chain execution required solving the "transponder flicker" problem. ADS-B transponders occasionally bounce false ground flags during flare maneuvers. We engineered a temporal sliding-window state machine that validates barometric altitude descent curves (< 15m), rate of descent stabilization (< -0.5 m/s), and true ground rollout speed before triggering the atomic settlement transaction.
The frontend is built with Next.js 15, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet radar canvas, and Emil Kowalski interaction physics, featuring an interactive Multi-Flight Replay Engine and an exportable executive ICAO audit certificate modal. All 11 smart contract Foundry tests and 33 Vitest agent integration tests pass directly against live RPC forks.

name: ArcAsset
description: Agents that service tokenized private credit on Arc and sell the repayment data they generate.
projectDescription:
Private credit is large, illiquid, and serviced by hand. A small originator who wants to fund a receivable on-chain hits three walls. Issuance is bespoke: every note is a one-off legal and technical artifact. Servicing is manual, and at small ticket sizes that labour costs more than the spread. And the repayment behaviour that would let the next lender price the next note stays trapped inside whoever serviced the last one.
ArcAsset is three things stacked.
A note primitive. A verified-human issuer mints a note with a principal, a coupon rate and a period schedule. Lenders fund it in native USDC. Repayments land in a vault and are claimable pro-rata; the note itself is an ERC-20, so one token is one unit of principal contributed and transfers move future claims with it.
An autonomous servicing agent. For every note it has been delegated, the agent advances periods, marks missed payments delinquent past their grace window, triggers distributions, and posts every action on-chain. It is paid a servicing fee in basis points out of each repayment it processes. It runs unattended — the demo shows a period settling with nobody touching anything.
An intelligence storefront. Everything the agent learns doing that job — repayment punctuality per issuer, cohort delinquency curves, cure rates, and whether a missed payment was cured by the issuer or by somebody else — is sold per query, settled in USDC on Arc.
The third piece is the point. The agent's job produces a dataset as a byproduct, and the dataset is the durable asset. Servicing pays for itself; the data compounds.
World Selfie Check gates issuance, not lending. Repayment history is worthless without an identity anchor: without one, an issuer defaults, walks away, and reappears at a fresh address with a clean record, and past behaviour predicts nothing about a one-transaction-old address. One human, one issuing identity.
Out of scope and we say so: no secondary market, no multi-tranche waterfalls, no legal wrapper, no collateral liquidation. A default is recorded, not enforced.
howItsMade:
Contracts are Solidity 0.8.24 on Foundry: IssuerRegistry, NoteFactory, RWANote, RepaymentVault and ServicingRelay.
Arc. Notes settle in Arc's native currency, which is USDC at 18 decimals. Settling natively removes the ERC-20 approve step entirely — funding and repayment are one transaction, not two — and it reduces the paid-API payment check to a single value field on a receipt, instead of parsing a Transfer log that a hostile token contract could spoof. The cost is that every payout now hands control to the recipient, so payouts use call{value:} rather than transfer, because transfer's 2300-gas stipend would break any lender that is itself a contract; checks-effects-interactions became load-bearing rather than stylistic; and the vault's own accounting is authoritative rather than address(this).balance, which can be inflated by a force-send via selfdestruct. Cheap settlement is also what makes a $0.50 per-query price viable at all — that is why the data product is on Arc and not behind a Stripe page.
The Graph. The subgraph is not a reporting layer bolted on at the end; it is the agent's decision surface. The agent keeps no database. It queries the subgraph, decides, and acts — so if the agent dies, state is intact on-chain and a replacement holding the same delegation resumes from the same index. The same subgraph is the read path for the web UI and the source for the paid API: one index, three consumers. Delinquency counts, punctuality and cohort rollups are maintained incrementally in handlers, so no query needs a full scan of the repayment history to answer.
World. Selfie Check gates issuance and nothing else. Lending stays permissionless — adding friction to the capital side to fix a problem on the issuance side would be a straightforward mistake. A nullifier verifies at most one address, ever, and is deliberately not reassignable: a "move my verification to a new wallet" path is precisely how a defaulting issuer would escape their own history. It is not KYC and we do not describe it as such; it proves a live human, not an identity.
The agent is Bun and Hono. Its decision function is pure — period state and clock in, action out — so it is unit tested with no chain and no network. The rails around it exist because the key is hot: actions are bounded per tick, so a subgraph bug cannot produce ten thousand transactions before a human notices; every action is idempotent by contract rather than by memory, since settling an already-settled period reverts and local state is lost on restart; and it confirms by transaction receipt, never by the subgraph, because the indexer lags and polling it to learn whether your own transaction landed is how you double-send. It skips a tick entirely when the indexer is more than 200 blocks behind rather than acting on stale data. ServicingRelay is written so a fully compromised agent key can grief but not steal: the servicing fee goes to a recipient fixed at issuance, never to msg.sender, and the relay cannot mint, change terms, or move funds to an arbitrary address.
The intel API is HTTP 402. A request without payment returns a quote; the buyer sends native USDC with the quote id in calldata and re-requests with the transaction hash. Hashes are single-use and quotes expire. No accounts, no API keys — payment is the auth.
One detail worth flagging because it is easy to get wrong and quietly misleading: cohort delinquency curves divide by the number of notes that actually reached each period, not by the original cohort size. That denominator shrinks, and dividing by the original count would understate late-period delinquency. Buckets with fewer than five notes return null instead of a rate, because three notes do not make a rate.
Frontend is Next.js 16 App Router with wagmi and viem. Money is bigint integer math end to end and truncates rather than rounds — at 18 decimals a single USDC exceeds 2^53, so a float anywhere in a money path is a correctness bug, not a rounding one. Every view handles loading, empty, error and stale explicitly, and a banner shows indexer lag rather than silently serving old data.

name: xmbl agent contracts
description: XMBL Contract Lab: build, prove & deploy private smart contracts — zk + homomorphic
projectDescription: XMBL's smart contracts are agentic and privacy-first with a visual Contract Lab at its disposal. Take an example need — a treasury that must prove a payment was authorized without revealing its signing key, move balances no observer can read, and never hand funds to a custodian — and build the contract for it three ways: drag sentence-like statement rows, write it in code, or import existing Solidity. Every call runs against live ledger state in the browser, so you watch state change as you test. When it's ready, deploy a content-addressed instance to the XMBL network, or transpile it to EVM to run on Ethereum (obviously this doesn't work with zk or he bc eth is lol). Confidential amounts stay encrypted end-to-end via homomorphic encryption, authorization is proven with zero-knowledge proofs, and identity and delegation are post-quantum. This is a devnet prototype: the cryptography is really implemented and running — but it is unaudited and not quite mainnet-ready.
howItsMade: https://handoff.lol clinched this work allowing multiple swarms to build at the same time. Honestly I don't know how you people AI without handoff. Anyway. The core is @xmbl/contracts: the LNG language and the XCL agentic-contract runtime, which compile a contract to real WebAssembly in the browser and execute it in-page against a byte-pointer state ABI that stands in for the Verkle-tree commitment. Privacy comes from three real modules — @xmbl/zero-knowledge for authorization proofs, homomorphic encryption for confidential balances, and @xmbl/identity built on cubic-LWE lattice cryptography with delegation certificates and custodian-free sealing. A Solidity importer and EVM transpiler let existing contracts move onto XMBL or back out to Ethereum, with USDC as the settlement asset. The frontend is a Vue 3 MV3 browser extension — the XMBL Console — that hosts the crypto capabilities, wallet, node and config, alongside a single-file Contract Lab miniapp. Contracts are agentic and are published as content-addressed miniapps to the handoff agent mesh, where every agent authenticates with single-shot Ed25519 signed requests (X-Agent-Id / X-Signature / X-Timestamp) so no key ever crosses the wire. The hacky-but-notable part: the entire compile → WASM → run → deploy loop runs client-side, and the same signed-request identity that publishes an app is what lets autonomous agents operate the deployed contracts.

name: Tenor
description: Tokenised securities lending on Hedera with atomic settlement and self executing maturity.
projectDescription:
Tenor is a compliance gated lending desk for tokenised securities on Hedera.
A borrower uses a tokenised bond as collateral and receives USDC from a lender. The lender first signs an EIP-712 quote off chain, defining the principal, repurchase price, maturity and haircut. The borrower accepts that quote and calls openRepo once. Cash and collateral are moved atomically, so the trade cannot settle only one side.
The important part is what happens next. At the moment the repo opens, Tenor schedules its maturity settlement through Hedera's HIP-1215 Schedule Service. No keeper, cron job or liquidation bot is required. At maturity, Hedera calls closeRepo automatically. If the borrower has repaid, the collateral returns. If they have not, the lender receives the collateral. Early repayment is also supported.
The collateral is a real ERC-1400 security issued through Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio, with identity and compliance modules implemented by us because ATS requires them but does not provide them. Transfers are therefore compliance gated by the token itself, not just by our frontend.
The cash leg uses USDC through Hedera Token Service's ERC-20 facade. The complete lifecycle has been proven on Hedera testnet with real ATS collateral and real USDC: atomic opening, early repayment and a scheduled maturity execution have all succeeded. The scheduled maturity execution required nobody to be online and the settlement contract paid its own scheduling fee.
Tenor also records lifecycle events through a Hedera Consensus Service audit trail. The frontend is built with Next.js, React and Tailwind, with wallet support through WalletConnect and Rabby or MetaMask, while Privy provides email based onboarding and wallet access for users who do not already have a wallet.
The result is a complete on chain lifecycle for lending against regulated tokenised securities: RFQ based price discovery, atomic settlement, compliance enforced by the asset, and a maturity event that the network executes itself.
howItsMade:
Tenor is built as a Solidity settlement layer on the Hedera EVM, with a Next.js frontend and a small off chain service for indexing quotes and publishing the audit trail.
The core contract, TenorSettlement.sol, handles the complete lifecycle: opening a repo, verifying the lender's EIP-712 quote, moving USDC, escrowing the security, scheduling maturity, early repayment and default settlement. The quote is signed off chain, so the lender does not need to submit a transaction just to make an offer.
For collateral, we used Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio to issue our own ERC-1400 security on testnet. ATS requires an identity registry and compliance module but does not ship them, so we implemented minimal versions and wired them into the token. This means a non compliant counterparty cannot simply receive the security by bypassing our frontend.
For cash, we use USDC through Hedera Token Service's ERC-20 facade. For maturity automation, Tenor calls Hedera's HIP-1215 Schedule Service directly from openRepo, creating the future close operation as part of opening the trade.
The frontend is Next.js 16 with React 19 and Tailwind CSS. Wallet integration uses wagmi, viem and WalletConnect with Rabby and MetaMask. Privy is used for email based onboarding, allowing users without an existing wallet to reach the product while retaining access to their account. Quotes and repo data are indexed in SQLite, and lifecycle events are mirrored to a Hedera Consensus Service topic to create an independently timestamped audit trail.
We used Foundry for Solidity development and testing. The repository contains hand written interfaces for the Hedera services and ATS, periphery contracts for the required compliance components, a HIP-1215 measurement probe, 29 contract tests and a step by step testnet flow.
The hackiest part was integrating Hedera precompiles with Foundry. forge script --broadcast locally simulates the script before broadcasting, but its local EVM does not implement Hedera's 0x16b Schedule Service or 0x167 HTS facade. That made apparently valid scripts fail before reaching the network. We worked around this by constructing and signing the exact calldata separately and submitting it directly with cast, allowing the real Hedera network to execute the precompile calls.
Another deliberate design choice is that closeRepo must never revert because a scheduled transaction executes only once. Settlement logic therefore treats default as a normal business outcome and uses a nested self call to keep the cash and collateral legs atomic while allowing the outer scheduled call to complete successfully.
Everything important is therefore demonstrated against the actual Hedera testnet rather than only against mocks.

name: Cubic
description: Cloudflare for agent actions. Agents get capabilities - credentials never leave
projectDescription: Cubic is an authorization gateway for AI agents - "Cloudflare for agent actions." It sits between an agent and its tools and deterministically decides every action: the agent's tool call is normalized into a structured intent, evaluated against onchain identity, live reputation, task budget and tenant policy, and answered with ALLOW, DENY, or ESCALATE. Allowed actions get scoped, 5-minute capabilities instead of reusable credentials. Every step — intent → decision → capability → execution → payment → result — is recorded as an audit event and fingerprint-anchored to Hedera Consensus Service, so anyone can verify the record wasn't rigged. The LLM drafts then the policy decides.
howItsMade:
We built Cubic, an authorization gateway for AI agents, in TypeScript. The gateway sits between an agent and its tools. When an agent wants to do something, the gateway turns that request into a structured intent and runs it through a deterministic policy engine - a set of written rules, not another LLM judgment - which answers allow, deny, or escalate. Five developer tools are exposed through the standard MCP protocol, and every decision, execution, and payment lands in a Postgres audit trail that shows the full story of what the agent did and who authorized it.
Each agent has its own identity registered onchain under the ERC-8004 agent-identity standard. We read their reputation live from The Graph's Agent0 subgraph - one of our agents is a contractor with real negative feedback onchain, so the gateway escalates its every move; a page in our console shows the exact query and The Graph's raw response to prove the number comes from the indexer that tracks immutable data.
When an agent needs to spend money, it doesn't get a wallet key. Instead, a paid security-scanner service quotes $0.25 over the x402 payment protocol; the gateway checks the agent's task budget, then settles the payment in HBAR on Hedera testnet through the Blocky402 facilitator. The receipt is a real transaction anyone can open on Hedera's HashScan explorer.
Dangerous actions like merging code, moving funds are blocked until a human signs off. The approver signs with their own wallet, our server cryptographically verifies the signature, and that signature becomes part of the event's fingerprint, which we anchor to Hedera's Consensus Service. If anyone later asks "who approved this AI decision, and can I trust the record?", the answer is on-chain.

name: SwarmProof
description: Decentralized smart-contract auditing powered by AI agents that collaborate
projectDescription:
Smart contract security is critical for protecting user funds, but for independent developers and early-stage teams, traditional audits can often be cost-prohibitive and take weeks to complete. SwarmProof is an open, decentralized security auditing protocol where an autonomous swarm of specialized AI agents collaborates to inspect smart contracts in real time.
When a Solidity contract is submitted, specialized agents (focusing on Reentrancy, Access Control, Business Logic Invariants, MEV, and Static Bytecode) concurrently analyze the contract's AST call graph. To prevent false positives, findings undergo a consensus quorum and are deterministically tested inside an automated Sandbox PoC verification environment.
Once consensus is finalized, an immutable cryptographic audit certificate is anchored onto Hedera Consensus Service (HCS Topic: 0.0.10417469), making every proof publicly verifiable on the Hedera Mirror Node. SwarmProof natively implements the HTTP 402 Payment Required (x402) standard, programmatically streaming micro-bounties directly into each participating agent's Hedera account. Anyone can build, test, and register their own sovereign AI agent to join the swarm and earn bounties.
howItsMade:
Smart contract security audits are essential for protecting user funds, but for independent developers, high costs and multi-week turnaround times can slow down shipping. We built SwarmProof as an open protocol where any developer can spin up an autonomous AI agent, prove its competence, and collaborate in a decentralized security swarm.
Architecture & Open Agent Economy: We structured SwarmProof as a TypeScript monorepo using pnpm workspaces with Hono (API Gateway) and Next.js 15 (Frontend). Our baseline specialists run on DeepSeek V3 / Flash models via Fireworks AI (apps/api/src/app.ts#L484-L520). Anyone can register an external agent by requesting an on-chain cryptographic challenge (apps/api/src/app.ts#L1556-L1605) and passing an automated benchmark (apps/api/src/app.ts#L1618-L1770) to earn a sovereign W3C DID (did:hedera:testnet:<topicId>_<agentId>) on Hedera (packages/hedera/src/identity.ts#L226-L320). An automated virtual sandbox reproduces exploits before any finding is accepted (apps/api/src/app.ts#L2100-L2250).
Hedera & x402 Micropayments: When an audit is initiated, the client escrows the bounty in HBAR using the HTTP 402 standard (packages/mcp/src/index.ts#L210-L290). Upon consensus settlement, funds are automatically split and streamed to each contributing agent's Hedera wallet (apps/api/src/taskPool.ts#L360-L425). The entire audit certificate is hashed, EIP-191 signed, and immutably anchored onto Hedera Testnet HCS Topic 0.0.10417469 (packages/hedera/src/consensus.ts#L60-L140).
The Graph & Interactive Visualizer: Deployed subgraph QmXcvJ1j4xRrnVzUqPzE9jTKn6cR1vT4a on The Graph to index agent reputation scores (0–100 PoR), payout distributions, and live protocol TVL/telemetry (apps/api/src/app.ts#L663-L695). We also built a Three.js WebGL visualizer and AST Knowledge Graph (apps/web/app/graph/page.tsx#L445-L520) allowing developers to inspect AST subgraphs and run real-time Cypher/GraphQL queries.
Developer Experience: Published swarmproof-mcp to npm (packages/mcp/src/cli.ts#L10-L160) so developers can audit contracts via MCP directly inside Antigravity, Cursor, or Claude Desktop without leaving their IDE.
Web Application: https://swarm-proof-web-steel.vercel.app/
API Endpoint: https://swarm-proof-api.vercel.app
NPM Package: https://www.npmjs.com/package/swarmproof-mcp

name: Aqueduct
description: A DeFi maker's real risk is every strategy added up, not one trade — we gate live on that number.
projectDescription: A DeFi maker's liquidity can look safe strategy-by-strategy while being dangerously overcommitted in aggregate — the "multiplier effect." Aqueduct adds _exposureGate1D, a new SwapVM instruction that reads a maker's live, cross-strategy exposure from an on-chain oracle and derates or halts their fill — monotonic by construction, so it can only ever make a fill more conservative, never better. A Uniswap v4 hook (AquaV4Hook) sources v4 swaps from that exact same gated strategy, so the identical safety guarantee holds on both a direct SwapVM swap and a Uniswap v4 swap — proven bit-for-bit identical on real Base Sepolia transactions. The Graph aggregates the maker's exposure across every strategy they've shipped, feeds the oracle, and re-exposes real swap data in a standardized Messari DEX-AMM schema plus an MCP server so AI agents can query it directly. Every number shown is live on Base Sepolia, independently verified on-chain — not mocked, not simulated.
howItsMade: Built in Foundry against real, unmodified 1inch Aqua/SwapVM and Uniswap v4-core/v4-periphery — no forks, no mocks. _exposureGate1D is appended to stock AquaOpcodes at a fresh index, alongside OraclePriceAdjuster (1inch's own instruction, wired into AquaOpcodes for the first time here) composed into a three-instruction "Strategy P" position reading a real Chainlink ETH/USD feed. On the Uniswap side, we extracted a reusable AsyncLiquidityHook base solving v4's flash-accounting settlement-order problem (a working-capital float: mint claims, fund from the hook's own balance, settle, sweep later) — proven generic with two independent implementations — then added a second, independent v4 capability: a risk-adjusted dynamic LP fee via LPFeeLibrary/updateDynamicLPFee, mirroring OpenZeppelin's uniswap-hooks patterns. The Graph side runs a custom subgraph plus a trimmed Messari DEX-AMM standardized layer (same entity/field names as messari/subgraphs) and a zero-dependency MCP server exposing exposure and safety-verdict tools over stdio. Frontend is Next.js + ethers, reading live contract and subgraph state with no personal RPC key shipped client-side. 49 Foundry tests, including a 128,000-call stateful-fuzz invariant suite proving committed-balance accounting holds under arbitrary sequences of pushes, pauses, and swaps.

name: TrueCollective
description: Redefining NFTs by linking ownership, utility, and revenue. A transfer-linked rights runtime.
projectDescription:
TrueCollective is a live transfer-coupled rights runtime on Hedera Testnet. When a RightsNFT moves from A to B, A’s free access ends, B’s begins, eligible purchased licenses remain valid, and future revenue is allocated to the creator and B. AI clients can discover, purchase with native HBAR through x402 and Blocky402, decrypt, and analyze licensed data through MCP.
When ownership changes, separate mechanisms are still required to determine how the previous owner’s access should be revoked, how already-purchased usage rights should be handled, and who should receive future revenue. ERC-721 itself does not define rules for these usage rights or revenue distribution.
Now that the initial hype around the NFT market has cooled, we believe the key question is: 「what kind of ongoing utility can NFTs provide beyond simply holding and trading them?」
Connecting the record of ownership to actual usable rights and recurring revenue is the starting point of TrueCollective.
TrueCollective is a “transfer-aware rights runtime” that connects ownership, usage rights, and revenue to redefine what NFTs can represent. It manages an owner’s privileges and a purchaser’s usage rights separately, and updates each of them according to predefined rules whenever the NFT is transferred.
When an NFT is transferred from A to B, A’s free access as the owner is revoked, while B’s free access becomes active. At the same time, usage rights that were purchased under terms allowing them to survive a transfer remain valid within their defined conditions, such as expiration dates or remaining usage counts.
Revenue from new payments made after the transfer is then distributed between the Creator and the new owner, B. Revenue allocations that were already finalized remain unchanged.
This makes it possible to preserve a purchaser’s existing usage rights while transferring the owner’s privileges and the right to receive future revenue.
This mechanism is implemented on Hedera using two independent permission-management systems. Owner Epoch updates owner privileges on every transfer, while License Epoch and Rights Receipt manage the conditions and revocation of purchased usage rights.
The Access Gateway checks on-chain state every time an access request is made and controls whether decryption key material is provided to a client that satisfies the required conditions.
In addition, x402-based native-HBAR payments are combined with Privy wallet functionality, enabling external AI clients to discover, purchase, and decrypt data through MCP. Verified live on 2026-09-08: an MCP-connected Claude Code session discovered the asset, paid 0.1 testnet HBAR, decrypted nine rows and correctly answered a question about the data.
Our initial use case is managing licensing and revenue distribution between companies that own IP, such as characters or brands, and companies that want to use that IP.
For example, imagine Company A owns a character IP and sells Company B, an apparel company, a license to use that character for a specific product series for six months. Company B can access authorized official images and design assets and use them for product development.
Later, if responsibility for managing the IP moves from Company A to Company C due to a business transfer or similar transaction, the license already purchased by Company B can remain valid until its expiration date, as long as the contract specifies that it survives the transfer.
Meanwhile, revenue from newly sold licenses is redirected to the new managing entity, Company C, while preserving the predefined allocation to the Creator. Revenue distributions that were already finalized in the past are not changed.
TrueCollective provides the infrastructure required for this type of operation: even when the company managing an IP changes, previously authorized usage continues while future access privileges and revenue distribution switch to the new manager.
By associating the NFT with the entity currently responsible for managing the IP while recording purchased licenses separately, the system can treat a change in management independently from existing usage permissions.
For this MVP, we focus on the foundational mechanisms required to support this model: access control for digital assets, usage rights with expiration dates or usage limits, persistence of purchased rights after ownership transfer, and switching the recipient of future revenue.
Legal permissions for commercialization, advertising use, and similar activities are assumed to be governed by separate contractual agreements. Transferring the NFT itself does not automatically transfer copyright, nor does the system attempt to automatically control how an asset is used after it has been obtained.
howItsMade:
TrueCollective combines rights management through EVM contracts deployed on Hedera Testnet with an off-chain Access Gateway API server, a web application, and an MCP interface for external AI clients.
At the core of the design is the independent management of two types of permissions using separate generation counters.
RightsNFT, an ERC-721 contract, increments the Owner Epoch whenever the NFT is transferred. Meanwhile, RightsRegistry maintains a separate License Epoch for policy changes and revocation.
Because these two epochs are managed independently, a purchased Rights Receipt configured to survive ownership transfers does not become invalid simply because the NFT owner changes.
Rights Receipts use EIP-712 typed data to bind usage rights to the purchaser, target asset, permitted operations, policy, expiration date, maximum usage count, and information recorded at the time of purchase.
Individual usage events are recorded separately from the purchase itself. This allows a single usage right to support multiple accesses while preventing the replay of the same payment proof from being treated as a new purchase.
The Access Gateway is built with Hono on Cloudflare Workers. When evaluating an access request, it reads the current owner, epoch values, and receipt status directly from the blockchain.
A self-hosted Graph Node indexes events for asset discovery and audit interfaces, but indexed data is not used as the source of truth for authorization decisions.
To prevent concurrent reuse of the same usage right, the system combines Durable Object-based coordination, unique constraints in PostgreSQL, and on-chain usage records.
For payments, TrueCollective uses native HBAR through x402 and the Blocky402 facilitator.
Hedera acts as the shared state layer for ownership, usage rights, and revenue distribution. Privy provides signing functionality for both the embedded wallet used in the web application and the server wallet used for MCP-based payments.
Spending limits and callable operations are restricted through policy controls, and the architecture is designed so that the Gateway never holds the raw private key of the payment wallet.
Encrypted datasets are decrypted on the client side. Before releasing the required key material, the Gateway's KeyGate verifies that the requester has the necessary access rights.
The MCP server exposes the following tools:
discover_assets
buy_access
decrypt_content
Actual data analysis is performed by the connected AI client itself.
During development, we used Spec Kit extensively for requirements definition and system design. We also standardized the implementation around shared TypeScript domain definitions and API types generated from OpenAPI.
The development process is fundamentally based on Spec-Driven Development (SDD) and Test-Driven Development (TDD).
For validation, we focus not only on the expected end-to-end flow from purchase through ownership transfer, but also on abuse scenarios such as reusing a previous owner's session after transfer, applying usage rights to a different asset, and concurrently consuming the same usage right multiple times.

name: Reckn
description: Agent-payment escrow where a disputed delivery is re-executed, not judged. Reproduce, or refund.
projectDescription:
When one AI agent pays another, the hard question is not which chain to deploy on. It is: when the payment is disputed, who decides — and does that decider belong to a chain? Every answer on offer is a party with a key: an operator inside a TEE, a bonded resolver, a quorum of voters. Each of those is per-chain — you redeploy the judge and re-earn the reputation on every chain your agent touches.
Reckn's answer is that the decider should not be a party at all. A disputed delivery is re-executed: the pre-state is pinned, the disputed work is replayed against it, and the predicate the deal was funded against is evaluated. Reproduce, or refund. Because re-execution is deterministic anyone can redo it and reach the same verdict, and because it is a computation rather than an authority, it does not live on a chain.
IT IS RUNNING. On Arc testnet, one escrow has settled four times in real USDC — and TWO OF THE FOUR WERE DECIDED BY PROOFS ABOUT WORK PERFORMED ON SOLANA, one releasing the seller and one refunding the buyer. The asset never left the chain it was funded on. Only the proof crossed, and there was no bridge and no light client anywhere on the path that chose the payout. Your own browser can read those four settlements off Arc at psyto.github.io/reckn without installing anything and without a wallet.
WHAT EXISTED BEFORE THE EVENT (built July–August 2026; the disclosure below is exact)
The disputed work is re-executed inside an SP1 zkVM and a real Groth16 proof settles the escrow directly. RecknZkEscrow has no owner, admin, resolver, pause or upgrade path, and settleWithProof is permissionless: the right to move money comes from a proof verifying and nothing else. That is enforced as a build condition — scripts/no-keys.sh fails the build if a privileged role, an unlisted state-changing function, or a msg.sender gate appears.
The same re-execution runs on two deliberately dissimilar runtimes. On EVM, every account and storage slot is MPT-verified against the committed state root before real revm executes the seller's committed CALL in-guest. On Solana, the block bank_hash is recomputed with the SIMD-0215 lattice hash, the real transaction is signature-verified, and its transfer is re-executed. Two state models with nothing in common, and one generic on-chain verifier accepts both proofs.
WHAT WAS BUILT DURING ETHONLINE (Continuity Track) — all of the following has LANDED


VERDICT DOMAIN SOUNDNESS. On day one we found a soundness bug in our own proof: the guest judged the balance delta on the low 64 bits while the off-chain engine used the full U256, so a DECREASE — pre = 2^64, post = 2^64 - 1 — proved as a maximal credit and released to the seller. A false release, found by writing the specification rather than by a test failing. Verdict values are uint256 on both sides now, the guest runs under a committed hardfork and block environment whose fields are bound into dealBinding, and every vector is decided twice — replayed off-chain and executed in-guest — and required to agree.


CROSS-VM SETTLEMENT — the headline, and it is done. One escrow settles an EVM proof and a Solana proof. The adjudicating program is named by the FUNDER, per deal, and pinned by its codehash; settleWithProof has no parameter with which a settler could name an adjudicator, and the dispatch is view-typed, so funder-chosen code runs under STATICCALL and cannot write state. The escrow lost its constructor, so any deployment of the same source is behaviourally identical. No resolver, no bridge, no light client on the path that decides who gets paid.


ARC / USDC — and it went to a public chain. The contract needed no change to settle in Circle's USDC, because a deal names its payment token at funding; what it needed was evidence in USDC's own units and semantics — six decimals, revert rather than a false return, and a blacklisting token. Then it was deployed to Arc testnet, where four settlements moved real testnet USDC: a proof released the seller, a proof of a decrease refunded the buyer, and TWO OF THE FOUR WERE DECIDED BY PROOFS ABOUT WORK PERFORMED ON SOLANA.


A KEYLESS TIMEOUT. Before it, a funded deal whose prover never appeared stayed funded forever. refundAfterDeadline returns it to the buyer after 30 days, permissionless — anyone may call it, and calling it gives the caller nothing. The waiting period is fixed in the protocol, chosen by no deployer and no funder.


THE BUILD CONDITION GREW. The script enforcing "no key can move a funded escrow" now reads two files rather than one, because the verifier the escrow calls carries the same authority. Its entry-point check became a CLOSURE rather than a list of forbidden names — a fallback() draining any funded deal passed all four of the old checks.


WHAT WE DID NOT PLAN, AND KEPT. The first live settlement reverted with "Blocked address": Circle's USDC blacklists well-known compromised keys and the first deal had named one as its seller. That deal still holds 1.000000 USDC and can never release, because the seller is fixed at funding — and it is not lost, because the keyless timeout returns it. It is on the live page and in the repository rather than quietly redeployed around.
WHAT IT REMOVES IS NOT A FEE — IT IS THE PERSON
In a machine economy the binding constraint is human attention, not cost. An escrow that a person approves is a serialisation point: agents run continuously and in parallel, and every release queues behind somebody reading something.
x402 has processed 165 million payments across 69,000 active agents. At the dispute rate card payments actually run at — about 0.5% — that is 825,000 decisions, or 14 to 34 person-years of reading depending on whether you allow two minutes each or five. That figure is DERIVED: the transaction count and the dispute rate are cited, the minutes-per-decision is an assumption, and it is stated so you can move it. Halve it and the shape is unchanged, because transaction count is the thing that grows and human attention is the thing that does not.
Reckn's release condition is fixed BEFORE the work begins and evaluated by a computation both parties can run. Nobody reads anything, nobody approves anything, and nothing queues behind anybody. That is the point; the money below is what it costs to do it.
A decided payment dispute costs a merchant $110 to $128 all-in today against a $20-50 processor fee — the rest is people reading conflicting stories. That cost exists because somebody has to decide.
Settling a dispute here costs 0.0070-0.0077 USDC — measured on Arc against our four live settlements at the real gas price. Verifying a Groth16 proof and paying out is under a cent, and it does not grow with the size of the dispute.
The number that constrains us is the other one: the average x402 payment is $0.52, and you cannot re-execute a fifty-cent API call under a zkVM and come out ahead.
And it does not prevent disputes — it makes them not matter. The seller can insist, the buyer can deny, both can write at length, and the money moves the same way regardless. There is also no approval step: if anyone approved after seeing the re-execution, that approver would be a key. The proof's public values carry the outcome and the contract sends the money where the outcome says. Nothing decides in between. What counts as "reproduced" is fixed at funding, before the seller starts work, so the discretion is never created rather than being taken away from a judge.
There is no dispute process here to invoke, either. The escrow has three states — None, Funded, Settled — and no Disputed one, because re-execution is not a remedy that a dispute triggers: it is how settlement works, every time. Money reaches the seller through exactly one function and that function requires a proof. There is no cheap happy path and there cannot be one, because "the buyer voluntarily releases" is a key moving a funded escrow, which is the thing this whole design exists to make impossible.
So the comparison set is not every agent payment. It is the payments that would otherwise need an escrow at all — and nobody escrows a $0.52 API call either. Those payments are priced as a PERCENTAGE today — Upwork takes 20% falling to 5%, effectively 10-12%, plus 3-5% from the client; Fiverr a flat 20% from the seller and 5.5% from the buyer. Fiverr also charges a $2.50 surcharge under $75, which is an incumbent conceding that below a threshold a percentage does not cover the cost of standing behind the trade.
Reckn charges a FIXED cost instead: one proof plus $0.007. Fixed and percentage cross at roughly a $10 delivery if a proof costs $1, or $50 if it costs $5. Above the crossover a $1,000 job pays $100-200 to a platform today at those rates, or a proof plus two thirds of a cent here — and what neither fee table prices is the operator: an arbiter who can be lobbied, subpoenaed, acquired or simply wrong, and who has to be re-established on every chain.
What we deliberately do not quote is a dollar cost per proof. Succinct's network prices proofs by reverse auction and we have never bought one — we prove locally, 335 seconds for a fixture. That figure is unknown rather than estimated, and it is the one an adopter has to price.
(And Solana holding 49% of x402 volume is why cross-VM settlement is not a stunt: for half of this market the money and the work are already on different chains.)
WHAT CROSSES, AND WHAT DOES NOT
The common misreading is that Arc verifies Solana, or that something is bridged. Neither is true. The work happens on Solana; the JUDGING happens inside an SP1 zkVM, which verifies the signatures, recomputes the block bank_hash and re-executes the transfer; and what reaches Arc is a Groth16 proof and nothing else. No bridge is needed because no asset moves — the USDC is on Arc at the start and on Arc at the end, and Arc never runs a Solana VM; it checks that one program executed correctly over public inputs. No light client is needed because Arc is never asked what Solana's state IS; it is asked whether a computation over a committed state is valid.
What this does today: settle USDC on Arc conditionally on the re-executed result of work performed on Solana, with no bridge, no light client and no adjudicator anywhere on the path that decides the payout.
What it does not do today: prove the committed inputs came from Solana mainnet. The guest recomputes a bank_hash over the account set THE DEAL NAMED — internal consistency, not provenance. A fabricated account set hashes just as well, and a test asserts exactly that. Closing it needs a light client, or an oracle with its trust model written down.
Both halves or neither: without them a reader cannot tell this apart from a bridge, a light client, or an oracle, and the boundary is the interesting part rather than the hidden one.
WHAT IS NOT TRUE YET
STILL OPEN, AND NAMED, so you do not have to go looking: the adversarial key gauntlet is stopped at a hard stop; the live adversarial-input feature has a round-3 specification and no implementation; the real ERC-20 workload is not started. None of those three is load-bearing for anything claimed above, and all three are in the README rather than in a footnote.
A proof carries the verdict's authority. It does not by itself prove the committed pre-state was the chain's real state: on EVM that anchoring lives in an off-chain layer, and on Solana the provenance of the committed bank_hash is not proven on-chain — a fabricated account set hashes just as well, and there is a test that says so. "No bridge, no light client" is true of the ADJUDICATION and not yet of the anchoring. Cross-VM settlement also created a new risk for the seller: a buyer can name a verifier that always returns Failed, and on-chain that is indistinguishable from an honest failure, so sellers must read the deal's verifier before working. Our open gaps are in the README, not in a footnote.
HOW YOU WOULD USE IT, AND WHERE THAT STOPS
Two calls. fund opens a deal; settleWithProof closes it. The second is permissionless — the key that pays the gas has no bearing on where the money goes — so there is no integration step where you hand us authority, because there is nothing to hand.
Built during this event, for the half that had no tooling at all: a TypeScript package and a starter. createDeal opens a deal. sellerPreflight answers "what am I about to work on?" before you do the work, and it exists because a buyer can name a verifier that always fails. submitProof settles. verifySettlement decodes what happened from the chain rather than from our report of it, and it distinguishes a payout a proof authorised from the 30-day timeout refund, which the escrow emits as a separate event precisely so nobody has to infer which kind it was. reckn terms turns YOUR transaction into deal terms with one read-only call and no key — the step that previously meant reading a Rust crate and assembling an anchor, a plan and a predicate by hand. It refuses five kinds of terms that open a deal cleanly and then never settle, including a predicate satisfied by doing nothing, which pays the seller in full for no work.
reckn terms needs an endpoint that answers eth_createAccessList and eth_getProof, and Arc's public testnet RPC answers neither — measured 2026-09-09. So on Arc you can compute a binding and fund against it, which needs one block header; what you cannot do from that endpoint is simulate the call or capture the witness. We would rather say this here than have you find it.
WHERE IT STOPS, SAID PLAINLY. Settlement is complete and permissionless. Proving is not self-serve: a proof needs the SP1 toolchain and minutes of CPU — measured on one laptop, 335 s for the shipped fixture and 497 s for a real mainnet Uniswap v3 swap, which is 32x the cycles for 1.49x the time. So using Reckn on YOUR OWN job today means proving it with that toolchain; what you can do without it is fund and settle against a workload already proved. Nobody outside this project has used any of this, and nothing here claims otherwise.
HOW TO CHECK ANY OF THIS WITHOUT TRUSTING US. Open https://psyto.github.io/reckn/ — your browser reads Arc directly and compares the deployed bytecode against the source in this repository. RecknZkEscrow has no constructor, so the same source always produces the same deployment, which is what makes that comparison mean anything.
SUBMITTING FOR: Arc — Launch on Arc Testnet & Push to Mainnet (primary), and Arc — Best DeFi or Agentic Application. Arc mainnet is not deployed and the reason is not ours: Circle had not published Arc mainnet contract addresses as of 2026-09-06, so the bounty's "deployed OR deployment-ready" is met on the second branch, and the same script deploys there unchanged once that address list exists.

WHAT EXISTS BEFORE THE EVENT (BUILT 2026-07-26 → 2026-08-02)

Pre-existing components:

Three SP1 zkVM guests (program/, program-revm/, program-svm/) committing identical public values to one on-chain verifier; RecknZkEscrow, which settles escrow on a verified Groth16 proof with no resolver. 12 tests, including a real Groth16 proof settling to the seller on-chain.
