Total: ~140 tests. All of the above is pre-existing and is not offered as work done during ETHOnline.
Also pre-existing (added 2026-09-03, before the event begins): an autonomous development harness (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .claude/agents/, scripts/no-keys.sh) and the planning documents in docs/ethonline-2026/. These are tooling and planning, not product features, and none of the five items in section 3 is implemented by them. They are disclosed here so that the repository history before 2026-09-04 is fully accounted for.


WHAT WILL BE BUILT DURING THE EVENT (2026-09-04 → SUBMISSION)


Keyless timeout for RecknZkEscrow. The keyless escrow currently has no deadline: if no proof is ever produced, funds lock permanently. A permissionless, deadline-based refund closes this without reintroducing any privileged key.


Adversarial key gauntlet. A test suite and UI that publish every participant's private key and demonstrate that no key can move a funded escrow.


Live adversarial dispute input. (Amended 2026-09-07 — see Amendments.) Open the seller's delivery claim to free-form input, so any observer can write whatever they like about what was delivered — and watch it change nothing. The claim is that prose does not move re-execution, and it is stated without reference to any judge, because a judge we wrote ourselves being "persuaded" would be evidence of nothing.


Real ERC-20 workload. Extend the in-guest re-execution from the current single-slot SSTORE fixture to a real token-credit predicate, with measured cycle counts.


Sponsor integration: Arc. (Amended 2026-09-07 — see Amendments.) Reckn's keyless escrow settles in Circle's USDC on Arc with no change to the contract — a deal names its payment token at funding, so a chain whose money is USDC needs evidence rather than adaptation. Built during the event and deployed to Arc testnet, where four settlements moved real testnet USDC: a proof released the seller, a proof of a wrong execution refunded the buyer, and two of the four were decided by proofs about work performed on Solana — one escrow, two virtual machines, no bridge and no resolver in the path that chose the payout. A fifth deal is frozen at 1.00 USDC because Circle's USDC blacklists its recipient; it is refundable by the keyless deadline and by nothing else, and it is recorded rather than hidden. (At application time Arc and Hedera were both listed as conditional, because the full prize list was not yet published. Arc is the only sponsor integration attempted; Hedera and World AgentKit were dropped by ruling on 2026-09-06.)


Verdict domain soundness. The zkVM guest takes its balance delta on limb 0 of a U256, so a decrease from 2^64 to 2^64−1 is accepted as the largest possible credit — a false release. The guest also sets only chain_id, leaving the spec and block environment out of sync with the off-chain re-execution, which uses the full U256. Both are closed, with tests.


Cross-VM settlement. A proof of work performed on Solana settles an escrow funded on Ethereum. Today the SVM verdict is verified on-chain by the same general verifier, but only EVM proofs reach settleWithProof. This closes that gap with no resolver, no bridge, and no light client in the adjudication path.


HOW THE BOUNDARY IS ENFORCED



All event work lands in commits dated within the event window, pushed continuously — no single squashed commit.
Event work is confined to identifiable paths and is summarized in a CHANGELOG entry that names the pre-event baseline commit.
All new parts remain open source, permanently.


HONEST LIMITS OF THE PRE-EXISTING ENGINE

Carried from zk-verdict/README.md so nothing is overstated: verdict values map to u64 (closed by item 6 above); the guest proves one CALL plus one delta check (a full block or arbitrary contract set is more cycles, same architecture); and the state_root-to-block-header binding remains an off-chain layer.
On precompiles, this document said until 2026-09-04 that c-kzg and ecrecover are disabled in-guest. That is false, and it was inherited from the same sentence in zk-verdict/README.md. revm-precompile falls back to pure-Rust backends when the native features are off — k256 for ecrecover (secp256k1.rs:1-8, preference order secp256k1 → k256) and arkworks for KZG (kzg_point_evaluation.rs:87-101). Nothing is missing in-guest. The true limitation is narrower and worse to state loosely: the guest and the off-chain engine run different implementations of the same precompiles, and equivalence has never been checked. Corrected here rather than left standing, because a disclosure that carries a false sentence is not a disclosure.
howItsMade:
The re-execution engines are Rust. On EVM, reexec-evm drives revm 38 and verifies each account and storage slot against the committed state root with alloy-trie before replay; on Solana, reexec-svm replays a committed signed transaction against a committed account snapshot under LiteSVM. Both emit the identical VM-neutral ReplayRecordV1 through one shared codec, which is what makes the trace hashes comparable across VMs at all, and a cross-VM router replays either kind through a single interface.
The keyless path runs that same re-execution inside an SP1 zkVM. The EVM guest MPT-verifies the prestate in-guest with alloy-trie and then runs real revm over the seller's committed CALL (406,715 cycles, measured); the Solana guest recomputes the block bank_hash from the committed accounts with solana-lattice-hash, signature-verifies the real transaction, and re-executes its transfer (986,097 cycles). Both commit the same public values, and one generic verifier contract checks either Groth16 proof against SP1's canonical verifier. Settlement contracts are Foundry/Solidity; the Solana escrow half is Pinocchio.
ARC IS THE PARTNER TECHNOLOGY, AND IT IS DEPLOYED. On Arc, USDC is the native gas token and Circle predeploys an ERC-20 face over the same balance at six decimals. Reckn's escrow settles against that face with no contract change at all, because a deal names its payment token when it is funded — which is the whole reason a chain whose money is USDC needed evidence from us rather than adaptation. Adding a payable path would have been the easy move and was refused: the function surface is part of the central claim, and widening it to chase a chain's ergonomics would have cost the thing the project is for. The escrow is live on Arc testnet with four settlements behind it.
The part worth calling out is not a library. Our whole claim is "no key can judge", and a claim like that decays the moment someone adds one privileged field — so it is a build condition rather than a promise. scripts/no-keys.sh fails the build if a privileged role appears, if the state-changing surface grows beyond the enumerated functions, if any msg.sender gate is introduced, or if any deployment-time configuration exists at all — and it is itself tested against negative controls. During the event it grew from a denylist of forbidden names into a property: every call-shaped token in the audited files must belong to a closed allowlist, and the verifier contract is pinned to a 43-token vocabulary and a fixed twenty-piece skeleton — so approve, permit, low-level calls and inline assembly are each rejected by a rule that never mentions them. The old check said "the constructor does not store msg.sender"; after the constructor was removed entirely that sentence would have matched an empty range and passed vacuously, so it was replaced. An observer that watches nothing is not an observer.
Development runs through a harness that writes a spec with mechanically checkable acceptance criteria, has a second independent model review it adversarially, and only then implements. Every spec and every review verdict is committed, including the ones that failed. That process is why the soundness bug above was found on day one rather than after shipping, and why we know things like: both test runners exit 0 on a filter matching nothing, so criteria that only check exit status pass with no tests written; our one-command demo discarded its suite's exit status; and regenerating one Groth16 fixture takes 335 seconds, not the 34 the repo advertised for a different guest.
The gates repaid the effort in a way worth reporting, because it is the opposite of a success story. Three full acceptance runs were red before one was green, for three different reasons, and two of them were the same defect wearing different clothes: a correct sentence in a specification sitting on top of code that enumerated names. One specification said its mutation witness covered a narrow glob; the gate globbed wider and swept in a sibling task's files. Another said a sandbox holds "this task's scripts only"; the script implemented "only" as a list of two filenames. Both were invisible while exactly one sibling gate existed — landing a second one exposed both in a single run. The second is the one worth reading twice: the mutant that exists to prove a discovery rule is a closure was itself defeated by one new name.

name: Inlet
description: A deposit and exit rail for DeFi protocols. One signature in, one signature out, USDC on any chain.
projectDescription:
Inlet is deposit and exit infrastructure for DeFi protocols. A protocol mounts it beside its own deposit and withdraw controls, and its users come in from any chain and leave to any chain, native USDC, one signature each.
Today every protocol rebuilds the same onboarding: bridge the USDC, swap or unwrap whatever arrived, switch the wallet to the right network, then sign the deposit. Four steps, two or three signatures, gas on two chains, a wrapped asset somewhere in the middle. And the way back out is left to the user.
With Inlet you pick a destination, Aave on Arbitrum, Compound or a Morpho vault on Base, a Uniswap v4 position on Unichain, and you sign once on whatever chain your USDC already sits on. The USDC arrives as the position itself, in your name, on the chain the protocol lives on. No bridge, no swap, nothing wrapped, no network switch, no gas on the far side. Inlet charges no fee; the only cost is Circle's transfer fee, shown before you sign.
Arc is the settlement hub, not a stop on the way. A hub contract on Arc derives a deposit address from every parameter of the intent: who you are, how much, which chain, which protocol, which beneficiary, which deadline. Change any one and it is a different address, so the address itself is the promise. Circle Gateway or CCTP V2 brings the USDC to that address on Arc, the hub escrows it, every sweep burns from Arc toward the destination, and every refund returns through Arc.
Everything after your signature is permissionless. Anyone can call sweep. Anyone can call refund after the deadline. If the destination protocol reverts, the USDC waits in the receiver, claimable by you. There is no path where funds are stuck and no privileged party who has to act. The relayer we run makes it fast, about thirty seconds end to end, but it makes it fast rather than possible.
The way out is the same trick in reverse. Sign once on the position token and it becomes native USDC in your wallet on the chains you choose, in the amounts you choose, five to Base and the rest to Ethereum. The approval names as spender an executor address derived from every parameter of the exit, so it can only ever produce the exit you described, and anyone can submit it.
Live on testnet: seven destinations across five protocols and five chains, and six sources, five EVM testnets and Solana Devnet, where the same deposit is one transaction signed in Phantom. Thirteen deposits and five withdrawals are recorded with their hashes, the fastest deposit at sixteen seconds, the fastest withdrawal at thirteen, the Solana deposit at twenty nine. A Privy email wallet with no extension and no gas has made the same deposit. You can make a real one on the site or replay a recorded one.
It ships as a kit, not an app. Three lines mount the widget, one Solidity function adds a protocol, the docs state what a protocol needs to be a destination and to be withdrawable, and an MCP server lets an agent do the whole thing from a sentence. From any chain into any position, and back.
howItsMade:
Contracts, Foundry. A hub on Arc holds the destination registry and derives per intent deposit addresses. A receiver on each destination chain validates that Circle actually minted the message before it calls an adapter. Adapters are one function each: ERC 4626, Aave V3, Compound III, and Uniswap v4 single sided liquidity. 43 tests across 8 suites, three of them fork tests against the live protocols on Arbitrum Sepolia, Base Sepolia and Unichain Sepolia.
Circle rails only, native USDC only. Circle Gateway gives the one signature path: a burn intent is a plain EIP 712 signature with no chain in its domain, so the widget signs it on whatever network the wallet is already on and never asks for a switch, spending a unified balance with no gas. CCTP V2 fast transfer is the self contained path when there is no unified balance, and it is the only path on Monad, where Gateway is not deployed. Circle's Iris API supplies the attestations and the fast transfer fee quotes.
Arc is the settlement hub, not a stop on the way. Every deposit address lives there, every sweep burns from there, and every refund returns from there. One chain holds the commitment and the escrow while five other chains hold the positions.
Privy carries the wallet. Email login creates an embedded wallet, and that wallet signs the Gateway burn intent directly, so a user with no wallet extension and no gas anywhere completes a real cross chain deposit into a real lending market. The widget also takes any external wallet through wagmi, so Privy is the default rather than a requirement.
Uniswap in two places. The v4 adapter mints a real single sided ETH/USDC position on Unichain Sepolia from inside the receiver, which needs the raw action encoding, a Permit2 double approval, and tick rounding toward minus infinity. The Uniswap Trading API is proxied through our relayer so the widget shows the live pool price before you commit.
The exit rail. An InletExit contract on each destination chain creates a one shot executor per exit intent with CREATE2, salted by the intent's EIP 712 hash, so the executor address is known before anyone signs. The user's EIP 2612 permit on the aToken or the vault shares, or the allowBySig authorization on the Compound Comet, names that address as spender. The executor runs entirely in its constructor: it delegatecalls the exit adapter, which applies the signature and redeems the position, then burns one CCTP V2 message per leg toward the chain and recipient in the intent, the last leg taking the remainder. Three exit adapters, one per protocol, each a single function.
Relayer, Fastify and SQLite on Azure Container Apps. It watches for funded deposit addresses, sweeps, fetches the attestation, and executes on the destination. For exits it submits the execute call, waits for Circle to attest every leg, and mints each leg on its own chain. Every chain it serves comes from a config file, so a new chain is configuration rather than code. It manages nonces locally because a public RPC once handed us a stale one.
Frontend, Next.js on Vercel. The live widget sits in the hero, so the first thing on the page is a real deposit you can make. There is a flow instrument that follows a deposit by hash and replays recorded ones.
Agents get the same surface. An MCP server exposes quote, create, submit and status, plus a single deposit tool that takes a sentence and returns a position. One of the twelve recorded runs was made by the agent, into Compound III, in sixteen seconds.
The hardest parts were not the contracts. Gateway balances are per chain and a burn intent needs to expire about a week of blocks ahead. CCTP fast transfer deducts its fee at mint, so the intent amount is a floor rather than the burn amount. Public RPCs lag behind themselves, so approvals must be visible before the burn and reads need retrying. Monad has CCTP V2 but no Gateway, which we confirmed by reading localDomain from the MessageTransmitter rather than trusting a table.

name: SIngIt
description: An agent that buys things for you, and asks your Ledger before it pays a stranger.
projectDescription:
SingIt is an AI purchasing agent that helps people buy digital products and access paid services through a conversational interface. Users interact with a Telegram bot to find products, review prices and approve purchases, with USDC payments settled on Base.
The project addresses a practical problem with AI agents: an agent may understand what a user wants, but that does not mean it should have unrestricted permission to spend their money. SingIt separates the agent’s request from payment authorization. An existing spending-policy library remembers previous payments, checks spending limits, detects changes in a merchant’s payout address and asks for human approval when a payment needs review.
This ETHOnline Continuity submission extends the existing product with two main integrations: Ledger and The Graph.
Ledger adds hardware-backed purchase approval. For supported paid API purchases, the gateway creates a persistent order before requesting approval. The owner reviews a compact message on their Ledger showing the purchase, amount, network and recipient. A cryptographic reference binds the approval to the complete order. The gateway verifies the signature, rechecks the payment conditions and executes the approved purchase. Repeated requests return the saved result without submitting another payment. The Ledger signs the approval; the gateway wallet executes the payment. An optional Ledger Key Ring integration also protects the gateway’s wallet-encryption key on enrolled hosts.
The Graph supplies paid blockchain data for the agent. The integration retrieves Uniswap V3 pool prices on Base through The Graph’s x402 gateway. Each query passes through the spending policy, and its payment receipt and answer are recorded in the journal. Repeating the same query within the cache window returns the stored answer without another payment. Answers identify their source pool, indexed block and cache status.
The Graph adapter is published as a reusable open-source Python library, so other agents can use it independently of SingIt.
Verification includes a real Ledger-approved API purchase, a separate hardware check of the final readable approval format, and a real WETH price query costing 0.01 USDC. That price was independently checked against the pool’s contract state, and two subsequent requests returned cached data without additional payments.
These additions were developed and tested on the hackathon branch. The submission documents the pre-existing product, the new implementation and the evidence supporting each integration.
The ETHOnline 2026 implementation is on the ethonline branch of bubon-ik/SingItAI. Please review that branch for the hackathon changes.
https://github.com/bubon-ik/SingItAI/tree/ethonline
howItsMade:
SingIt combines a Python gateway, a Telegram interface and a Node.js payment service. For ETHOnline, I extended the existing application with Ledger approval and The Graph integration, building on its existing spending-policy library and Base USDC payment infrastructure.
The Python gateway coordinates purchase requests, policy decisions, approvals and receipts. The Node.js service uses Coinbase’s CDP SDK and an x402 client to access paid resources. The spending-policy library is maintained in a separate open-source repository, allowing other agents to reuse it independently.
For Ledger, I used the Device Management Kit and Ethereum signer SDK through a local Node.js client. The gateway freezes the purchase details and stores an encrypted operation record in SQLite before requesting a signature. After approval, it verifies the signature, rechecks the quote and spending limits, and atomically consumes the operation before invoking the payer. Completed requests return their stored result on retry.
One practical challenge was device readability: the initial typed-data approval displayed technical fields instead of a useful purchase summary. I switched to compact EIP-191 personal_sign messages containing the purchase, amount, network and recipient. A 43-character base64url SHA-256 reference commits to the complete order, including its resource, owner and expiry. This keeps the device review short while preserving the binding to the full purchase. Ledger signs this off-chain approval; the gateway wallet signs the payment.
I also added an optional wallet-cli ring backend for decrypting the gateway’s wallet-encryption key on enrolled hosts. Startup fails if decryption cannot complete.
The Graph integration sends parameterized GraphQL queries to the Uniswap V3 subgraph on Base through its x402 gateway. The reusable adapter fingerprints the deployment, query and variables, then checks the journal before accessing the network. Identical queries within the default 300-second cache window reuse the stored answer without another payment. The chat integration includes the source pool, indexed block and cache status.
Live testing exposed two integration bugs: the gateway rejected Python’s default User-Agent, and the receipt handler expected a different transaction-hash field from the CDP client. Both were fixed and covered by regression tests. I verified the paid WETH query independently by reading the pool’s token addresses and slot0 state through Base RPC at the same block, then confirmed that cached repeats survived reopening the database and running in a separate process.

name: Preflight
description: A pre-sign firewall that explains wallet approvals in plain English and blocks malicious ones.
projectDescription: Preflight intercepts a wallet transaction before it's signed and explains what it actually does in plain English instead of raw calldata. It decodes approve, setApprovalForAll, and permit calls, flags unlimited or repeatable access, and cross-checks the counterparty against on-chain approval history indexed by a live Graph subgraph. The final verdict is computed inside a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow using a secret that never leaves the enclave. If a transaction is judged malicious, a Privy wallet policy blocks it from being signed even if a user tries to force it through, so the protection holds at the wallet level, not just in the UI.
howItsMade: Frontend is Next.js (App Router, TypeScript) with Privy for embedded wallet auth and pre-sign transaction interception via sendTransaction with showWalletUIs:false. Backend is Express/TypeScript, decoding calldata for approve, setApprovalForAll, and permit into plain English and applying explainable ALLOW/DENY/MANUAL_REVIEW thresholds. A subgraph deployed on The Graph Studio indexes Approval events and wallet first-seen timestamps, giving the verdict logic live on-chain history instead of guesses. The verdict is also computed inside a Chainlink CRE confidential workflow, so the rules that decide ALLOW/DENY run against a secret that never leaves the enclave. As a backstop, a Privy wallet policy denies known-malicious addresses and unlimited-approve calls at the signer level, so a forced transaction is blocked even if the UI is bypassed. Contracts and seed transactions run on Sepolia.

name: AlphaScanner
description: Explainable Uniswap v4 pool checks for agents: PASS, REJECT, or UNKNOWN.
projectDescription:
AlphaScanner is an existing product that collects crypto calls, scores token candidates, and delivers cards. Its separate execution layer can trade on BNB Smart Chain. Neither private system is part of this public submission.
For ETHOnline, I built v4-pool-index: a new open-source module that asks a different question before a signal or execution decision: what do we actually know about a Uniswap v4 pool? It captures pool identity from Initialize events, then uses deterministic checks and available token metadata to return PASS, REJECT, or UNKNOWN with a reason for every result. Nonzero hooks are rejected because creation-event data cannot bound their behaviour. Missing volume stays UNKNOWN, not "no market." The new module is not yet integrated into AlphaScanner, and that boundary is explicit in the repository.
howItsMade:
The project is built around a Rust Substreams producer that emits typed Uniswap v4 pool identity: pool ID, currencies, raw fee, tick spacing, and hooks. The same module is configured per network through its manifest. A second published Substreams package imports the producer by registry name instead of copying the decoder. This proves the module can be reused as a component, not only run as one application.
A separate Node.js assessment path enriches Base token data with the Pinax Token API and applies explicit rules for hooks, fees, tick spacing, metadata, and missing fields. It is available through local MCP tools and a loopback-only x402 HTTP endpoint. A recorded Base Sepolia run shows the full HTTP 402, payment, HTTP 200, and returned verdict path. The rules are deterministic: an LLM does not decide whether a pool passes.

name: LatticePrime
description: A Hedera bond market with sealed orders, ZK eligibility, and verifiable disclosure receipts.
projectDescription:
Lattice Prime is a tokenised bond marketplace on Hedera that brings sealed-order trading, privacy-preserving eligibility, coupon payments, and collateralised financing into one platform. It tackles a core challenge of on-chain finance: making market activity verifiable while controlling what the venue reveals about participants’ trading intentions.
At its core, Lattice Prime features:
🔒 Sealed-Order Markets: Investors commit orders before revealing their terms, then trade through uniform-price auctions with partial fills, collateral backing, cancellation, and expiry. A built lender-interest board adds selective liquidity discovery without exposing an entire lending strategy.
🎩 Zero-Knowledge Eligibility: Participants prove that credentials satisfy KYC, jurisdiction, and validity requirements without publishing the underlying credential details. Eligibility grants are account-bound and expire with their authorised epoch.
💰 Coupons and Repo Financing: A complete coupon lifecycle covers payment calendars, funded distributions, Merkle-backed entitlements, and protected claims. The financing module supports funded lending offers, bond collateral, haircuts, repayment, margin calls, collateral top-ups, and default recovery.
💠 Accountable Disclosure: Policies define what information the venue may publish, at what detail, and when. Budgets account for repeated disclosures, while verifiable receipts and a Hedera consensus audit trail make both publication and deliberate silence inspectable.
🔭 Oracles and Observatory: Valuation and reference-rate feeds support pricing, coupons, and margin checks. State-based monitoring surfaces risk even when events are withheld. Scheduled actions support lifecycle obligations and oracle finalisation.
⚖️ Explicit Market Rules: A versioned rulebook, transparent fees, Merkle-backed policy commitments, governed updates, trading halts, transfer pauses, and targeted freezes make market controls accountable.
🤖 Lattice Claw: A companion trading private-agent prototype adds constrained execution and verifiable decision evidence, with its public interface remaining a preview (prototype style only).
The web app connects these capabilities through Markets, Portfolio, Financing, Eligibility, and Issuer screens. Built extensions are distinguished from enabled functionality, including financing that requires a compatible vault deployment.
Lattice Prime also addresses a subtle market failure: silence must not trap funds or hide risk. Its demonstrated cancellation flow preserves refunds when disclosure budgets run out, while the observatory tracks obligations independently of published events. The result is a bond market designed to account for its money, its rules, and its silence.
howItsMade:
The core idea came from an observation in private marketplace institutions the runners on that idea I kept seeing that what is to be private in a trade, or why are products just toggling shut information using ZK? That drove the core concept, what if privacy was abstracted into a scaled concept?
Not a "lets make another dark pool", I drew privacy as a scale. I started with a ZK outline, then shaped it around a marketplace for Hedera ATS bonds, where disclosure becomes an explicit policy decision. The scope was the information the venue publishes, with rules people could inspect and verify. Cryptography is strict. ZK is strict. Smart contracts are strict. Privacy could still have degrees.
That became the disclosure lattice. So I went ahead and vibecoded an entire regulated institutional finance and not just DeFi, that Hedera can run.
Governed disclosure limits and per-epoch budgets. Around it, I built commit-reveal orders, uniform-price auctions, and repo financing using ATS partition holds for bond collateral. Circom and snarkjs generate PLONK eligibility proofs, verified onchain against credential and policy requirements. Merkle proofs support coupon entitlements and committed policy parameters, while Hedera Token Service supplies the coupon cash token.
The hardest question was what happens when the disclosure budget runs out. Blocking someone’s cancellation refund because the venue cannot publish another event would be a terrible outcome. I separated recovery from publication and built an observatory that reads contract state, because an unpublished margin call still matters. HCS records the disclosure evidence, while Node.js, the Hiero SDK, and Mirror Node tooling independently check it against transactions. The clearest demo became two cancellations: both refunds succeed, but only the first publishes a venue event.
There were practical surprises too. An early deployment mixed Ethereum-style value units with Hedera’s tinybars, making the required deposit enormous. I measured the conversion and corrected the parameters. The oracle combines auction evidence, a valuation model, signed dealer quotes, and reference-rate data. HSS handles scheduled lifecycle actions and bounded oracle checks, with retries and manual fallbacks.
The frontend uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and ethers, with generated deployment bindings and Vercel hosting. I checked the system through Foundry tests, fuzzing, client checks, and Hedera testnet runs, including failed proofs, stale feeds, and exhausted disclosure budgets.

name: NameGraph
description: ENS-named agent that queries The Graph (Uniswap + ENS) and returns answers with receipts.
projectDescription: NameGraph is an ENS-named onchain research agent. Users chat with namegraph.eth in natural language. The agent resolves its own ENS identity, routes each question to the right Graph subgraph (Uniswap V3 or ENS), charges a credit for the query, and returns a plain-language answer plus a query receipt showing who paid, which subgraph was used, intent, and timing. It is not a Uniswap trading dashboard — it is the agent interface to The Graph, with ENS as the agent's name and Privy as the wallet rail for paid queries.
howItsMade: Frontend is Next.js (App Router) with a product workspace UI: sidebar for namegraph.eth identity, live status, and credits; main pane is a chat transcript with receipts. Backend is FastAPI: intent routing in the agent layer, GraphQL clients to The Graph gateway for Uniswap V3 and ENS subgraphs, ENS resolve via public APIs for the agent card and lookups like vitalik.eth, plus a credits ledger (demo top-up now; Privy wallet session next). Every paid ask returns a receipt tying the answer to a subgraph ID. Built From Scratch during ETHOnline with Cursor allowed per AI_USAGE.md.

name: Rovaulta
description: The safety gate for robot software before it reaches the real world.
projectDescription: Rovaulta is a security gate for autonomous robot software. Before a build can be released, Rovaulta verifies the exact software against private safety policies, records a public cryptographic clearance, and uses an AI agent to prepare the deployment. The AI can investigate and prepare a release, but it cannot approve or authorize it. Sensitive safety evaluation stays confidential through Chainlink CRE, public clearance context is verified through The Graph, and high-risk authorization is protected by a human Ledger approval boundary. Rovaulta brings confidential verification, blockchain-backed release integrity, constrained AI, and human control into one deployment workflow.
howItsMade:
Rovaulta is built as a TypeScript/Bun monorepo with a Solidity smart-contract layer and integrates Chainlink CRE, Ethereum, The Graph, Gemini, and Ledger.
Robot builds are evaluated against private safety policies inside a Chainlink Confidential Workflow using handlerInTee, keeping sensitive safety logic and results inside the TEE.
A Solidity-based Ethereum registry records public clearance and exact bindings between the site, robot, build, and evaluation result.
A custom Subgraph indexes that registry, allowing the AI deployment agent to query live blockchain state through The Graph before preparing a release. Gemini operates through tightly scoped tools: it can inspect context and prepare a deployment intent, but it cannot sign, authorize, or bypass the security model.
Ledger DMK/Signer Kit and Speculos provide the human authorization boundary for high-risk actions. The system is organized as a Bun/Turbo workspace with TypeScript, Solidity/Foundry, automated tests, and end-to-end verification. The core design is simple: private rules stay private, public clearance is cryptographically anchored, AI can prepare, and a human remains in control of authorization.

name: AgentTether
description: x402-metered event webhooks for AI agents on Substreams, billed per processed block; oneshot pull.
projectDescription: AgentTether lets autonomous AI agents provision and pay for conditional, asynchronous webhooks for future blockchain events — priced per block, escrow-free, and settled pro-rata. It is application-layer middleware bridging the x402 HTTP payment standard with The Graph's Substreams: instead of locking capital in smart contracts, agents sign a single Permit2 upto voucher whose ceiling is the quoted cost of their monitoring window; the backend holds it until the condition fires or the window expires — then settles exactly the blocks it processed.
howItsMade:
One Node/TypeScript process streams Ethereum mainnet through a sha256-pinned Substreams package (the vendored Pinax ERC-20 spkg), resuming from a persisted cursor with undo-aware reorg handling; metering, capture and cursor commit atomically per block. A single Postgres row enforces single-writer streaming, and the supervisor retries until a dead holder's lease goes stale. The Python/LangGraph agent sleeps at interrupt() until the webhook thread resumes it; its narration renders as agent rows on static flow-charts. Hedera payments ride Blocky402's facilitator, which co-signs our partially-signed TransferTransaction, with the rails discovered live via /supported.
Payment mechanics are deferred, not upfront: at watch creation the facilitator verifies the upto voucher (balance, allowance, ceiling match, Permit2 deadline ≥ TTL + 120s buffer) but deliberately does not settle. The voucher's authorized amount is held server-side while the stream meters blocks, and settlement happens at window end via the hosted facilitator's upto proxy, which pulls exactly the blocks-processed amount from the agent. The facilitator absorbs transient rejections (nonce staleness, congestion) and retries inside the voucher's validity window; only structural rejections go terminal, though a drained wallet yields an honest SETTLE_FAILED with nothing delivered, since the webhook is fail-closed. Permitted amounts are single-use (the Permit2 nonce is consumed on settle), which is why the agent's continuity path is its own re-issue loop: decide to keep listening, sign a fresh voucher.

name: Memento
description: Gift an ENS name by email. They choose the name, and you cover registration.
projectDescription:
Memento lets you gift someone an ENS name. Set a budget in USDC, choose a registration period, and add their email and a note. They receive a claim link, sign in with their email, and choose an available name.
The gift pays for registration, and Memento covers gas fees. The recipient does not need ETH or USDC. The name is registered to their wallet, and they can set it as their primary ENS name. The demo runs on Sepolia.
howItsMade:
The frontend uses React, Vite and ensforge. Privy handles email login, embedded wallets and sponsored transactions. A Solidity contract holds the sender’s USDC, pays for registration and returns unused funds to the sender.
Claiming uses two transactions: an ENS commitment, followed by registration after the required wait. ensforge prepares the calls, and Privy sponsors the recipient’s gas fees.
The backend uses TypeScript, Effect and PostgreSQL to track gifts, verify claims and send invitations. Emails use React Email and Resend.

name: Argus4626
description: Real-time ERC-4626 vault monitoring that detects attacks before they become lost funds.
projectDescription:
ERC-4626 vaults can be affected by donation/inflation attacks, liquidity drains, share-price crashes, and unbacked minting. I built Argus4626 as a real-time watchdog that detects these patterns directly from on-chain activity and exposes actionable alerts through a live dashboard and GraphQL API.
Argus currently monitors four attack patterns: abnormal asset growth without matching shares, withdrawals consuming more than 35% of available liquidity in a short window, sharp asset or share-price drops without a matching withdrawal, and supply growth without sufficient backing assets.
I validated the system against a real first-depositor donation attack on a deployed Sepolia vault. The attack used a direct ERC-20 transfer that bypassed the vault’s own events, and Argus still detected it through the underlying asset’s Transfer event and produced a CRITICAL alert end-to-end.
howItsMade:
I built Argus with Rust, The Graph Substreams, Subgraph Studio, Next.js, TypeScript, and GraphQL.
The core Rust Substreams module decodes ERC-4626 Deposit and Withdraw events together with ERC-20 Transfer events directly from Firehose blocks. Store modules maintain per-vault asset and supply deltas, while rolling 60-second withdrawal buckets measure sudden liquidity outflows. A separate Rust module evaluates the security invariants and emits alert entities for a standard EVM Subgraph.
The detection logic avoids floating-point arithmetic and division. Threshold comparisons use a custom U1024 type so uint256-scale multiplication cannot overflow.
To validate the project, I deployed an ERC-4626 vault and asset on Sepolia, executed a real first-depositor donation attack, and confirmed the resulting CRITICAL alert through the live Subgraph and dashboard.

name: Unisafe
description: Personal Uniswap V4 position manager with ai-operator support
projectDescription: Every unisafe Manager is the same NFT-owned contract non-custodial wallet: a Stable manager for pegged pairs on a range you set once, or a Volatile manager for any other Uniswap v4 pair, where you pick the range each time you allocate.  Also unisafe ships an agent skill and an MCP server. Start with the skill — it takes no keys and no configuration — and add the server later if you want the agent to actually place transactions.
howItsMade:
Solidity + Rust + TypeScript.
CONTRACTS (Solidity). unisafe managers are NFT-owned smart wallets holding Uniswap v4 liquidity: the
NFT holder owns the capital, an appointed operator may rebalance it and has no path to withdraw —
structural, not a check. The deliverable is moveLiquidity: free a position in one pool, re-deploy it
in another inside a single v4 unlock, settle once?  with amazing Uniswap v4 custom accounting.
CHAINLINK is what makes an operator role possible: every operator swap is priced against a feed, and
after an audit during the event the same guard covers liquidity adds — swapless operations deployed
principal at raw spot, which a compromised operator can skew first.
THE GRAPH replaces the engine under an existing index. Our Substreams package (Rust
→ WASM, six modules) filters by address in a map step and builds its manager registry from the
factory's own deployment event, so it works for any manager that factory produced, on any supported chain.
SPLIT AGENT. The MCP server had grown to carry history and yield maths next to the keystore, so it
was cut in half. The local half keeps key, policy, simulation and calldata, and now makes no
outbound HTTP call except RPC — "a remote service cannot hand you calldata to sign" becomes
architecture instead of a promise. The hosted half (no keys by construction) serves MCP over HTTP
and REST, ranks a manager's pools by fee APR and returns a move as plain numbers — pool id, two
ticks, an amount.

name: SKNYDipping
description: Live on-chain risk scoring for DeFi pools — concentration and cross-chain fragmentation.
projectDescription:
DeFi developers and depositors deal with a real, unsolved problem: security and risk of pool and token ownership. When liquidity is concentrated in few wallets — or spread thin across chains — a pool can look deep on a dashboard and still be fragile in practice. SKNYDipping measures the two signals that expose this.


Concentration — the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index applied to LP positions. An HHI of 0.33 means a pool behaves like it's owned by about 3 equal-sized people, even if 40 wallets technically hold a balance. If one of those three withdraws, the market moves.


Fragmentation — the same HHI formula applied across chains. A token's liquidity is often scattered across Ethereum, Arbitrum, and Optimism in uneven slices, so "deep liquidity" on mainnet can coexist with a thin, fragile market elsewhere.


Every score is computed live from The Graph's Messari-standardized subgraphs and comes with a one-sentence AI explanation of what the number means in practice. Connect a wallet, pick a protocol, and get a real risk report.
howItsMade:
Frontend is Vite + React 19 with Tailwind and shadcn/ui components, React Router for the /info explainer page, and Dynamic Labs for wallet connection. Serverless functions in Vercel (api/*.js) proxy all data queries so the Graph API key never touches the browser.
Data comes from The Graph's Messari-standardized subgraphs for Uniswap v3, Curve Finance, and Balancer v2. Every HHI computation runs on live on-chain LP positions pulled at request time — no mocks, no cached datasets. The fragmentation layer reuses the exact same HHI function but feeds it per-chain TVL instead of per-LP balance, which is why one query pattern spans both protocols and chains.
The AI explanation layer uses Gemini 3.6 Flash. It receives the raw computed numbers (HHI, LP count, chain breakdown) and returns a short plain-language sentence about the practical implication for a depositor. The AI is a reasoning layer on top of live Graph data, not a template generator.
Notable hacky bits: every subgraph query rejects implausible values (like $0 or >$1B TVL on a single USDC/WETH pool) rather than silently returning corrupted sentinel data — this caught real bugs during development. Curve pools need manual token ordering because their subgraph doesn't return tokens in a standardized order, which is why custom pool input is disabled for that protocol.

name: Standby
description: Protocol-enforced future execution capacity from shared AMM liquidity.
projectDescription:
Institutions increasingly hold productive onchain assets such as tokenized cash-management assets, but their future settlement needs may be denominated in assets such as USDC. When a known liquidity-risk window approaches, their choices can include holding idle settlement balances in advance, relying on issuer redemption, or depending on whatever acceptable secondary-market spot or RFQ liquidity happens to be available when the need materializes.
Standby introduces another liquidity instrument: a finite-duration commitment to bounded future secondary-market execution capacity.
Instead of reserving settlement assets for a beneficiary, Standby uses qualifying shared AMM liquidity to back the commitment. That liquidity can continue supporting compatible ordinary trading while the commitment is outstanding. The beneficiary therefore gains protocol-enforced access to a bounded amount of future execution capacity without requiring the corresponding assets to sit segregated and idle.
Standby is designed to complement, not replace, immediate cash, issuer redemption, RFQ liquidity, and ordinary secondary-market execution. An institution could use committed capacity selectively during identifiable future liquidity-risk windows as one layer of a broader liquidity strategy—reducing dependence on both fully pre-positioned settlement balances and uncommitted future market liquidity.
The Uniswap v4 implementation makes this enforceable by tracking Supporting Capacity (S) against Capacity Obligation (O) and preserving the invariant S ≥ O. Compatible ordinary activity continues while sufficient backing remains, but a pool transition that would destroy the backing for an admitted commitment is rejected.
The canonical demo proves this distinction end to end: a 50,000 USDC commitment is admitted against 80,000 USDC of supporting capacity; an unrelated trader successfully uses 15,000 USDC from that same shared capacity; a subsequent trade that would reduce supporting capacity below the outstanding obligation is rejected; and the beneficiary ultimately exercises the full 50,000 USDC entitlement through actual Uniswap v4 AMM execution.
The broader idea is to give DeFi shared liquidity a new coordination role: not only providing execution now, but supporting enforceable commitments over execution capacity needed later.
Standby doesn't reserve liquidity. It protects capacity.
howItsMade:
Standby is implemented as a Solidity protocol on Uniswap v4. StandbyHook is the enforcement boundary around shared AMM liquidity: it derives supporting capacity from authoritative pool state, tracks outstanding capacity obligations, admits commitments only when they are supportable, and prevents ordinary pool transitions from violating the S ≥ O backing invariant.
The exercise path uses an ExerciseRouter and hook-owned causal context so an authorized beneficiary can exercise an outstanding entitlement through actual Uniswap v4 execution. An onchain EligibilityRegistry provides the permissioning predicates used by the demo. The canonical fixture uses MockUSTB and MockUSDC, while execution runs through the real Uniswap v4 PoolManager stack.
The contracts and tests are built with Solidity, Foundry, and Anvil. Verification includes unit, integration, fuzz, and stateful invariant testing. The final suite has 590 passing tests, with 99.42% line coverage and 100% function coverage for the Standby protocol core.
A minimal frontend provides demo instrumentation by reading authoritative contract, PoolManager, and token state rather than maintaining separate economic state. The canonical demo deterministically reproduces the complete commitment → shared use → protection → fulfillment sequence.

name: Rialto
description: Oracle-free lending for tokenized securities on Hedera.  HIP-1215 scheduled call closes the loan.
projectDescription:
A tokenized bond is a real asset that no lending market will take as collateral, because
it has no price. It was never listed, and every on-chain money market needs a feed before
it will lend. So an owner who needs cash for a month has one option: sell the bond they
wanted to keep.
The usual fix is to invent a price, and invented prices get attacked. Rialto never asks
what the bond is worth.
A borrower locks the bond and says how much cash they want and for how long. Underwriters
read the bond's own offering document, form a credit opinion, and bid a repayment figure.
Lowest bid wins, the cash goes straight from lender to borrower, and that number is fixed
for the life of the loan.
Fixing it at auction removes everything a lending market normally needs to stay solvent.
No price feed, so nothing to manipulate. No margin call, because nothing is ever marked.
No liquidator, because a funded loan has two endings: repay on time and the bond goes
back, or miss the date and it goes to the lender. And no loan-to-value parameter: the
contract never checks a ratio, so the lender prices the cushion instead of a governance
setting.
A lender still has to trust three things, and each is held by a different Hedera service.
Collateral. A real ERC-3643 security minted through Hedera's Asset Tokenization Studio.
The issuer stores the offering document's hash on the token's ERC-1643 facet, and opening
a loan reads that hash off the security and freezes it into the request — all 29 loans
took it from the token, not from the borrower. Your browser re-fetches the document and
re-hashes it, so swapping the file mid-auction shows up as a mismatch.
Reasoning. The lender publishes why it is bidding to a Hedera Consensus Service topic
before the bid, and the bid carries that message's hash. Consensus timestamps the
reasoning before the outcome exists, so nobody can rewrite their story once they know
they won. Lenders can be people; here one is an AI agent, and its limits live in a mandate
contract the market checks on every bid, so a stolen key cannot exceed them.
Settlement. Awarding a loan asks Hedera's Schedule Service, in the same transaction, to
call the market back after maturity, with the market contract as payer. Settlement is
permissionless and takes only a loan id, so a scheduled call is exactly as powerful as a
passer-by. It only removes the need for one to show up.
29 loans have run end to end on testnet -  11 repaid, 11 defaulted, 7 cancelled because
nobody bid, 46,000 dUSD funded  and Hedera has executed 16 scheduled calls into the
market with the contract itself paying the fee. Market
0x9040986Da679d00F0AA93ca21E1c9Aa2143121a4, topic 0.0.10367534, and every settlement is a schedule on Hedera's public mirror node showing the second it was booked for and the
second it ran.
howItsMade:
Four Solidity contracts, no proxies, no admin keys, nothing upgradeable. Once deployed
there is no address anywhere that can alter a live loan.
RialtoMarket holds the lifecycle: open, bid, award, repay, claim. Mandates is a
separate registry where an underwriter declares its limits and binds an agent key, so an
agent's authority is enforced by a contract the market calls on every bid, not by the
agent's own code. ComplianceLens exists because a blocked ERC-3643 transfer reverts with
nothing at all: it checks paused(), then frozen / not-on-control-list / no-KYC for both
the escrow and the beneficiary, and returns which of the six it was. CouponPassThrough
routes income the bond pays while locked back to the borrower, who still owns it.
ATS. Opening a loan staticcalls getDocument on the token's ERC-1643 facet and reads the
issuer's own document hash out of the return data -  the second word, lifted with assembly
rather than decoded, so a malformed return cannot revert the open. That hash is frozen
into the request, and the contract records whether it came from the token or the borrower.
Every external call is a raw call with a returndata check, never an interface, because a
native HTS token has no EVM bytecode — eth_getCode returns 0x — so a high-level call
reverts on the extcodesize check before it is even attempted. That single decision is what
lets a native Hedera token be collateral at all.
HCS. The agent publishes its opinion to topic 0.0.10367534 and passes the message hash
into bid() as reasoningRef. Messages over 1024 bytes are chunked, so verification
reassembles them before hashing. script/verify-reasoning.sh reads reasoningRef off-chain
from the contract first and then finds the message that hashes to it  the reverse of the
obvious direction, and necessary, because a request can carry more than one opinion.
HIP-1215. award() checks hasScheduleCapacity, then calls scheduleCall on 0x16b to book
claim() sixty seconds past maturity with 1.2M gas and this contract as payer. repay()
deletes that schedule in the transaction that closes the loan early. Both calls are
wrapped, including the capacity staticcall, and every failure path is a no-op that falls
back to a manual claim: the second may be full, the contract may hold no HBAR, the chain
may not be Hedera at all. A funding market must never fail to fund because a convenience
could not be arranged.
Three behaviours we found on testnet that are documented nowhere, and what each one
changed:


Hedera permits one scheduled call per transaction. An award that books its own
settlement and then a coupon record date is rejected outright with
NO_SCHEDULING_ALLOWED_AFTER_SCHEDULED_RECURSION, and the loan does not fund at all —
found when awards that had worked all day began reverting the moment a coupon fell inside
the term. So settlement is booked at award, because it is the one that must not be
forgotten, and a coupon record date is a second transaction that anyone may send.


forge script cannot reach 0x16b. The Schedule Service has no EVM bytecode, so forge's
local simulation refuses the transaction before it is ever sent — with or without
--skip-simulation. Everything that touches the precompile is a shell script driving cast.


Freezing an address on an ERC-3643 security is setAddressFrozen(address,bool), but a
frozen account still reads isFrozen == false. The freeze shows up as removal from the
control list. That is why ComplianceLens reports standing from isInControlList rather than
isFrozen — reading the obvious getter would have told a lender a frozen counterparty was
fine.


The agent is TypeScript on viem: it polls open requests, verifies the document, forms an
opinion, publishes to HCS, then bids — in that order, so the reasoning is timestamped
before the outcome exists.
The document is untrusted input, because the issuer chooses the URL. The system prompt
treats it as evidence, not instructions: any instruction or claim of authority found
inside it is a finding to flag and lower confidence on, never to obey. The reply is then
type-checked field by field, the repayment must be a decimal integer string, and the bid
is re-derived against the same mandate the contract enforces. The model proposes; the
contract decides.
Every revert the agent can receive is mapped to a plain-English refusal by selector, so a
rejected bid reads as an underwriting outcome rather than a crash.
Frontend is Next.js 15 with wagmi and viem over batched multicall reads. No server
component touches a key.
463 tests, all passing: 245 in Foundry across 19 suites, 139 on the agent, 79 in the web
app. The contract suite carries 10 invariants over a randomized handler and a mutation
pass  deleting a guard has to break a test, and where it did not, the assertion was
strengthened rather than the code.

name: Aqua Mux
description: AquaMux atomically builds token baskets and registers shared-liquidity Aqua LP strategies.
projectDescription:
AquaMux is a local-first EVM liquidity-management application for 1inch Aqua shared-liquidity positions. It  helps a wallet owner create, review, and manage versioned LP plans that reference inventory already held in their wallet. One wallet's inventory may back multiple strategies, so fills in one position affect the inventory available to others.
The Next.js app supports Ethereum, Arbitrum, BNB Chain, and Robinhood Chain. Its managed workspace covers strategy configuration, observed positions, activity, browser-bound management runs, pause and close planning, and review history stored in local SQLite. Plans can contain one to six token pairs, pair-specific fees, reserve amounts, price denomination, ranges, and optional expiry.
AquaMux separates planning, review, signing, broadcast, receipt recovery, and confirmation. The owner must explicitly confirm fund-moving actions. External-wallet execution is restricted to a named, tested adapter, while ordinary browser wallets remain manual-signing only.
The project also retains a basket swap flow that can compose one input token into two to six outputs, with wrapping, token approvals, 1inch Classic Swap routing, and supported EIP-5792 wallet batches.
howItsMade:
AquaMux is built as a TypeScript monorepo with a Next.js 16 and React 19 frontend. Tailwind CSS handles styling, Base UI provides accessible primitives, Lucide supplies icons, and TanStack React Query manages client-side server state. Zod validates API input and DTOs at every trust boundary.
The EVM layer uses viem, wagmi, and 1inch's Aqua SDK, SDK Core, and SwapVM SDK. The app maintains its own reviewed network and token configuration for Ethereum, Arbitrum, BNB Chain, and Robinhood Chain rather than trusting browser-provided contract addresses or metadata. It uses bigint for on-chain quantities, builds immutable transaction inputs, and separates simulation, approval, signature, submission, receipt recovery, and confirmation.

name: Overdraft
description: On 1inch Aqua, makers quote depth they can't back. Overdraft measures the gap and ships the fix.
projectDescription:
On 1inch Aqua, the liquidity you see isn't always liquidity you can trade.
Aqua's trick is virtual balances: one wallet can back many positions at once, so a maker can quote far more depth than it could ever pay out. Great for capital efficiency, but it means quoted depth is a promise, not a guarantee, and nobody was checking how much of that promise is real.
Overdraft checks. For every live position on every chain, it works out how much is actually backed (coverage = min(wallet, allowance) / committed), indexes it on The Graph, and reads the backing straight off-chain. On Ethereum right now: about $25.3M quoted against $1.6M backed. That's 6.3% real, $23.9M phantom, spread across 1,046 under-backed positions.
Then it goes past a dashboard. We proved the gap actually bites (a real position quotes 15,818 1INCH; the fill reverts at settlement) and shipped SolvencyGuard, a SwapVM instruction that makes a position refuse to quote past its real backing. Funded makers are never blocked; overquotes revert before a single token moves.
This isn't a knock on Aqua, which has been audited eight times. It's the coverage and monitoring layer those audits don't touch. Every number is live and reproducible, cross-checked against on-chain rawBalances.
howItsMade:
Indexing: one Subgraph schema deployed per chain (Ethereum + Base) on Subgraph Studio, plus a Rust Substreams module to reach Firehose-only chains a subgraph can't. Both read Aqua's Shipped/Docked events off the same schema.
Coverage engine (Node + viem): it enumerates positions from The Graph, then reads min(balanceOf, allowance to Aqua) live on-chain, prices in USD via DefiLlama, and flags positions that quote more than a token's entire supply.
Contracts (Foundry): SolvencyGuard is a custom SwapVM instruction (opcode 0x22) plus a modified AquaSwapVMRouter, tested against 1inch's real swap-vm on a mainnet fork (4 passing tests).
Agent layer: an MCP server and a reusable SKILL over the subgraph, so any agent can ask about Aqua solvency in plain English.
Site: one static page (no framework) with a live dashboard and an interactive guarded-swap demo that reads real backing via eth_call.
A few hacky bits worth mentioning: we rebuild each position's Order from raw Shipped bytes to match its on-chain strategyHash; the router shifts opcode bytes down by one through an array trick, so the guard actually runs at byte 0x22; and enumeration falls back to a keyless Blockscout sweep when public RPCs gate eth_getLogs.

name: Arclet
description: Arclet is an agentic wallet that turns natural-language trading intents into onchain execution
projectDescription: Arclet is an agentic wallet on Arc that turns natural-language trading instructions into structured, autonomous onchain actions. Users define intents like “buy cirBTC when BTC drops 4%, but keep at least 1,000 USDC liquid.” Arclet monitors live blockchain data, evaluates the strategy, and executes only when the user’s approved rules are satisfied.
howItsMade: Arclet is built with Next.js, TypeScript, Bun, Tailwind, Drizzle, Postgres, Privy, Circle Agent Stack, Arc, The Graph, and a provider-agnostic LLM layer supporting cheap models like Qwen3. The Graph provides live market signals, the LLM converts intents into structured strategies, and deterministic TypeScript checks enforce limits before Circle executes USDC-based actions on Arc.

name: thelema
description: Impact markets on Arc. Trade how an event moves any asset like stock, BTC, oil not just yes/no.
projectDescription:
most prediction markets answer one question: will something happen?
thelema asks the next one: okay, but what does that event actually do to an asset?
the demo explores whether allowing advanced AI-chip sales to china could affect a synthetic nvidia index. it shows the probability of the event, the asset’s value in the YES world, its value in the NO world, and the impact gap between both futures.
users can express a view on either the event or the asset using test USDC on Arc. sNVDA is only a synthetic testnet index—there are no real nvidia shares, real-world custody, or investment promises involved.
howItsMade:
thelema runs two connected markets on Arc Testnet. one prices the probability of the event with binary YES and NO tokens. the other prices the synthetic asset separately in each possible world. the app combines those pools to show probability, asset-if-YES, asset-if-NO, and the difference between them.
the contracts are written in solidity and use USDC for collateral, liquidity, gas and settlement. each complete asset set includes an explicit residual claim, so the full collateral stays accounted for instead of disappearing when the final index is below its cap.
the frontend uses react, typescript and viem, with users signing Arc transactions directly from their wallet. the graph provides live cross-protocol ETH market context from uniswap v3 and sushiswap through the same standardized messari DEX schema. it is clearly labelled as context—not fake sNVDA pricing.
chainlink CRE handles the confidential order-size design, where a private maximum controls how much of a requested trade can become public. the workflow compiles to WASM and was run through the official CRE simulator. live remote deployment is still waiting on chainlink access, so we document that boundary honestly instead of mocking a successful execution.

name: x402 Health Oracle
description: x402 micropayment-gated oracle serving real-time L2 health metrics across 12 chains
projectDescription: x402 Health Oracle is a pay-per-query infrastructure service that provides real-time Layer 2 network health data behind HTTP 402 micropayment gates. It continuously probes 12 L2 chains (Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, zkSync, Scroll, Blast, Linea, Mode, Polygon zkEVM, Mantle, Casper, Taiko) measuring RTT latency, revert ratios, and cross-chain temporal correlations. Each API endpoint costs $0.01 USDC on Base via the x402 payment protocol — no API keys, no subscriptions. Autonomous agents and DeFi protocols can programmatically purchase chain health data to make informed routing and execution decisions. The oracle detects anomalies like revert spikes and congestion events in real-time, enabling downstream systems to avoid degraded chains before transactions fail.
howItsMade: The backend runs Python probes that measure RPC round-trip times every 2 seconds across 12 L2 chains via primary and fallback RPC endpoints. Data is distributed over a WebSocket feed with BLAKE3+Ed25519 integrity signing and Isolation Forest anomaly scoring. The x402 payment layer uses Coinbase Developer Platform (CDP) for payment validation — clients send a BASE USDC payment header, the gateway verifies settlement on-chain, then serves the data. Cross-chain correlation is computed as a 12x12 Pearson R_xy matrix from accumulated measurements. The API is served behind nginx with WebSocket proxy support. No API keys needed — the payment IS the authentication.

name: Forfait
description: Turn a 60-day invoice into cash today — non-recourse receivables financing on Hedera.
projectDescription:
Freelancers who invoice clients abroad wait 30 to 60 days to get paid, and have no way to
borrow against that invoice while they wait. Banks won't underwrite a $2,000 receivable
from a sole trader in Malang — the diligence costs more than the loan.
Forfait tokenizes an unpaid invoice as a zero-coupon bond using Hedera's Asset Tokenization
Studio. Face value is the invoice amount, maturity is the due date. A funder buys it at a
discount today; when the client pays at maturity, settlement and distribution execute
automatically. Every state change — submitted, verified, funded, paid, settled — is written
to the Hedera Consensus Service as a tamper-evident audit trail, while the invoice document
itself stays off-chain and only its hash is published.
This is forfaiting: the non-recourse purchase of cross-border receivables at a discount. It
is a century-old trade finance instrument. Forfait makes it work at ticket sizes where the
paperwork used to cost more than the deal.
howItsMade:
The security token is issued through Asset Tokenization Studio (ERC-1400) on Hedera's EVM
layer, using the ATS SDK rather than hand-rolled contracts — so compliance controls like
control lists, KYC gating, pause, and transfer restrictions come from audited code rather
than from me.
Maturity settlement uses Hedera Scheduled Transactions with setWaitForExpiry, so the network
itself executes the payout on the due date. No cron job, no keeper bot, nothing to keep
running. The 62-day ceiling on scheduled transactions is why the product accepts invoices
with terms of 60 days or less.
The audit trail runs on the Hedera Consensus Service: one topic, one message per lifecycle
event, ordered and hash-chained by consensus. Invoice documents never touch the ledger —
only a SHA-256 hash, so a funder can verify the document they were shown is the one that was
financed, without the pricing becoming public.
Privy provides authentication and embedded wallets, so a freelancer signs in with an email
and never handles a seed phrase. Reads go through the Hedera Mirror Node REST API.
Fees are why this works at ticket sizes banks ignore: I measured a transfer at $0.0001 and
an HCS message at $0.00017 on testnet. Financing a $2,000 invoice costs a fraction of a cent
in ledger fees.

name: Cresnex IntentLock
description: Security and outcome enforcement for autonomous onchain agents.
projectDescription:
Cresnex IntentLock is an open-source security layer for autonomous and AI-agent-controlled smart accounts. It lets an owner authorize an agent using signed EIP-712 intents and binds execution to explicit constraints such as spend limits, recipient restrictions, minimum output, token approval limits, expiry, and replay protection. Unsafe outcomes can be rolled back while preserving violation evidence and agent containment state.
This is a Continuity Track project. The core IntentLock prototype existed before ETHOnline 2026. During the hackathon, I am extending it with new context-aware security functionality and sponsor integrations, while keeping the pre-hackathon repository history public so the new work can be reviewed separately.
howItsMade:
IntentLock is built with Solidity and Foundry for the smart-contract security layer, OpenZeppelin primitives for standard security components, and a Next.js/TypeScript frontend using wagmi and viem for wallet and contract interaction. Owners sign structured EIP-712 intents that bind an authorized agent, call data, nonce, validity period, and execution policy. The contracts execute permitted calls in an isolated flow and verify post-execution financial constraints before allowing the outcome to persist. Foundry tests cover signatures, access control, nonce replay, spend/output limits, approval containment, rollback, strikes, quarantine, and recovery.
During ETHOnline 2026, I am adding the hackathon-specific integration layer rather than presenting the existing prototype as new work. My primary focus is using live blockchain data as a load-bearing risk input for IntentLock decisions, with additional sponsor integrations only where they materially improve agent authorization or execution safety.

name: Predex.Fun
description: Launch USDC prediction markets on Arc with instant liquidity and  autonomous trading agents.
projectDescription:
Predex is a prediction-market launchpad for people and automated agents.
Anyone can create a market around a question they care about, trade on
its outcome, and change their position as new information comes in.
Users can discover markets, follow prices, and keep track of their
holdings and trading activity.
Agents are part of the project too. Our creator agent can take proposed
questions, check for duplicates, and create new markets. Our trading
agent discovers markets, looks for opportunities, and places orders
within configurable spending and inventory limits. Developers can review
its planned trades in a dry run before enabling execution.
We’ve kept the app playful and mobile-friendly, with a cartoon-style
interface that works in desktop and mobile browsers. MetaMask is the
main wallet option, with optional email login through Privy. The current
demo runs on Arc Testnet using test USDC, giving people a place to try
prediction markets and experiment with trading agents without using real
funds.
howItsMade:
We built Predex with Solidity contracts on Arc Testnet and a mostly
TypeScript application stack. The contracts handle outcome tokens,
initial LMSR trading, market graduation, and settlement, with Foundry
used for contract testing. Arc lets us use USDC for both collateral and
gas, keeping the funding flow simpler for users and agents.
The frontend uses Next.js, React, wagmi, and viem. MetaMask is the main
wallet option, while Privy adds email login and embedded wallets. We
connected Privy to the existing wagmi signing flow so it uses the same
account and transaction code. A shared TypeScript package holds the
ABIs, API types, and transaction builders used by the website and agent
SDK.
The backend uses Fastify, PostgreSQL, Prisma, and a viem indexer. It
reads contract events and builds the market, position, and activity data
shown in the app. Redis caches market reads and distributes updates to
WebSocket clients. Browser-to-chain subscriptions were unreliable, so
the backend serves the books and reconnecting clients fetch a fresh
snapshot. On-chain and Hybrid books stay separate; Hybrid trading uses
signed off-chain orders with settlement on Arc. Qdrant helps suggest
duplicate markets, with an optional OpenAI embedding and comparison
provider.
We built separate creator and trading agents on top of the SDK. The
creator checks proposed questions for duplicates before creating
markets. The trader discovers opportunities, reads market-derived
pricing signals, and checks current chain state before signing. Trading
defaults to dry-run mode, with configurable spending and inventory
limits. Our subgraph in The Graph’s Subgraph Studio indexes market
lifecycle events and settled trades for agent discovery, while the
backend supplies live orderbooks.
Circle Gateway and x402 provide an optional pay-per-request path for
market signals. This lets agents purchase data with USDC without a
manual checkout. World AgentKit adds a human-backed access policy to
that flow: the backend checks an agent’s AgentBook registration, and
agents backed by the same anonymous human share three free signal
requests. PostgreSQL tracks the allowance and prevents replayed requests
from claiming extra access. Once the allowance is exhausted, or an agent
is unverified, the existing Circle payment path applies.
One practical shortcut was reusing the responsive web app inside a thin
Flutter mobile shell, keeping wallet and trading logic in one place.

name: Agentic Risk Manager
description: An institutional-grade, non-custodial crypto portfolio risk manager that delivers real-time risk.
projectDescription:
Crypto Risk Manager bridges the gap between traditional quantitative finance risk management and Web3:
Zero Private Key Custody: Connect securely via Privy, World ID, or standard Web3 wallets.
Automated Multi-Chain Discovery: Index on-chain token balances and derivative holdings seamlessly through The Graph subgraphs and RPCs.
Institutional Multi-Asset Modeling: Manage Spot Crypto, Tokenized Real-World Assets (RWAs), and Perpetual Futures in one unified portfolio.
Deterministic Math Engine: Analyze single-deal metrics (Beta vs. BTC, Delta, Volatility, Std Dev, Sharpe, Treynor) and portfolio aggregates (Net Delta, Net Vega, Net Gamma, Variance-Covariance matrix, VaR, Expected Shortfall).
Consensual Rebalancing: Formulate mathematical rebalancing proposals and execute them exclusively upon explicit user confirmation via Uniswap and 1inch EVM routes.
howItsMade:
Frontend & UX: Modern TypeScript, React / Vite, Vanilla CSS with curated dark-mode palette and progressive disclosure design patterns.
Authentication: Privy (embedded wallets & social authentication) and World ID (sybil-resistance).
On-Chain Indexing: The Graph protocol subgraphs and ethers.js / viem EVM read-only RPCs.
Oracles & Pricing: Chainlink decentralized price feeds planned however, had to paired with Coingecko API for CEX/DEX historical data feeds with timestamped provenance.
Execution Routing: 1inch API & Uniswap V3/V4 SDK with strict user consent gates. Since it is mainnet-only, simulation exists instead of actual routing
Quantitative Engine: Pure, deterministic TypeScript mathematical library with zero side effects and automated test fixtures.

name: Tool402
description: Agent-ready APIs with x402 payments and tokenized funding on Hedera.
projectDescription:
Tool402 is a Hedera Testnet marketplace prototype connecting API providers, backers and software agents. Its goal is to help finance the creation or improvement of specific tools through a capped share of their paid usage, rather than a guaranteed yield.
The prototype combines machine-readable tool discovery, an x402 consumer payment client, provider campaign workflows using Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio, and HBAR backing for open offerings. RiskScan Quick is our first example tool: it checks supplied disclosures about identity, pricing, limitations and evidence. Optional World Selfie Check adds a wallet-bound human-presence signal alongside MetaMask authentication.
We keep payment confirmation, token allocation and revenue distribution separate. Backing records can be checked server-side against Hedera transaction evidence, but a confirmed transfer does not automatically issue tokens or distribute revenue. The project demonstrates the foundations of agent-driven API commerce and tool-specific financing, not a live investment product.
howItsMade:
Tool402 is a strict TypeScript monorepo with separate web, consumer-agent, core and backend packages. The interface uses Next.js 16, React, Tailwind CSS and nuqs, while Convex stores application records and workflow state.
The consumer agent is a Node.js CLI built with @x402/core and @x402/hedera. It discovers RiskScan, evaluates the quoted network, asset and amount against an explicit spending policy, and handles the signed payment request and response validation. Blocky402 is the intended Hedera Testnet settlement facilitator.
MetaMask handles wallet approvals and signed commands. Server-authenticated requests connect Next.js to Convex. For tokenization, we use the official Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio Factory contract artifacts with viem to encode deployBond and decode deployment events.
A key engineering focus was making transaction evidence durable and preventing duplicate use. Backing verification checks the sender, recipient, amount and successful receipt, binds each transaction hash to one funding attempt, and supports status recovery without sending HBAR again. World IDKit provides optional Selfie Check, with server-side verification and a signed, wallet-bound cookie.

name: Koven
description: Credit and policy infrastructure for autonomous x402 agents on Hedera
projectDescription:
Koven gives AI agents financial autonomy without placing wallet keys in the model’s hands. An agent receives a mission, discovers paid x402 services and ranks providers using price, reliability and reputation. If it lacks funds, competing lender agents can offer working capital and Koven selects the best valid offer.
Before any HBAR payment is signed, an isolated restricted signer verifies a Groth16 proof showing that the payment respects the mission’s spending cap and approved recipient policy. The provider settles the x402 payment on Hedera, returns the paid result, and an authenticated completion flow allows the loan to be repaid after settlement is independently confirmed.
A live dashboard exposes the mission lifecycle, lender offers, provider selection, policy proof, payment status and Hedera transaction evidence. Koven combines agentic procurement, credit, policy enforcement and verifiable settlement into one end-to-end protocol for autonomous commerce.
howItsMade:
Koven is built as a TypeScript and pnpm monorepo containing a consumer agent, competing lender agents, an orchestrator, an x402 resource server, an isolated restricted signer, shared protocol packages and a Next.js dashboard. Services communicate through typed HTTP contracts validated with Zod, while SQLite provides durable mission, loan, idempotency, nonce and event storage.
Payments use x402 v2 with the exact Hedera scheme and HBAR settlement through Blocky402. The Hedera SDK is also used to inspect and independently verify funding, payment and repayment transactions instead of trusting HTTP responses alone. Transaction IDs and signed bytes are persisted before submission so interrupted or uncertain operations can be reconciled safely without sending a duplicate payment.
The wallet private key exists only inside the restricted signer. The consumer and orchestrator can request typed operations but cannot access or export the key. Before signing, the signer verifies a Groth16 proof generated with Circom and SnarkJS. The proof is bound to the mission, amount, recipient, resource and nonce, enforcing the spending policy at the wallet boundary even if the agent’s prompt is compromised.
Provider ranking combines price, latency and event-derived reputation, while lender selection compares independently signed credit offers. Authenticated completion callbacks trigger an idempotent repayment workflow after Hedera settlement has been verified. The React and Next.js dashboard polls typed APIs to display the complete mission, credit, proof and settlement trail.

name: Keryx
description: Keryx pays cited sources and settles evaluated AI research jobs in USDC on Arc.
projectDescription:
Keryx turns a question and a USDC budget into an inspectable research job. Its agent discovers sources, explains BUY/SKIP/CACHE decisions, buys selected content through x402, and produces a cited answer. Creators receive weighted USDC rewards for cited contributions that pass the evidence checks.
For ETHOnline, we extended an existing research engine with a buyer workspace and an independent buyer client.
