name: LeekDIYHardwareWallet
description: Open-source ESP32 hardware wallet with on-device verification and refuse-by-default signing.
projectDescription:
LeekWallet is an open-source, low-cost hardware wallet built around the ESP32-S3. It is designed around one rule: the device decides, the host asks, and anything the device cannot display clearly is refused.
Private keys and seed phrases remain on the hardware while transactions are decoded, re-serialized, hashed, displayed, and approved directly on the device before signing. LeekWallet supports BIP39/BIP32/BIP44 wallets, multiple encrypted seed phrases, BIP39 passphrases, temporary stateless seeds, physical-dice entropy, QR address display, USB and BLE connectivity, and EVM transaction signing.
Instead of blindly trusting a connected computer or phone, the device recognizes a deliberately limited set of contract interactions such as ERC-20 transfers and approvals, Permit2, NFTs, Aave operations, WETH, and selected mint calls. Unknown calldata and contract creation are refused unless the user explicitly enables blind signing on the device.
A Tauri companion app for desktop and Android connects LeekWallet to WalletConnect v2, allowing ordinary EVM dapps to request signatures while the final decision and transaction verification remain on the hardware.
The project is intentionally transparent about its current limits: it is a proof of concept intended for testnets, has not received an independent security audit, and does not yet enable secure boot or flash encryption.
howItsMade:
LeekWallet is primarily C firmware running on an ESP32-S3 with a 128×64 SSD1306 OLED and four physical buttons. The wallet core implements BIP39 seed generation/import, BIP32/BIP44 derivation, secp256k1 ECDSA signing with RFC6979, and encrypted multi-wallet storage using PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 and AES-256-GCM.
Entropy combines the ESP32 hardware RNG with mandatory user-generated button timing and optional physical dice. RNG output passes through fail-closed health checks before it can be used for key generation.
For signing, the ESP32 does not simply receive a digest from the host. EIP-1559 transactions are parsed, re-serialized, hashed on-device, rendered page by page on the OLED, and signed only after physical confirmation. Contract calls use a built-in signature table whose selectors are independently recomputed with keccak256. Supported calls are decoded into human-readable fields; unsupported calls are rejected by default.
Communication works over either native USB CDC or BLE GATT, never both simultaneously. Sessions use X25519 key agreement, HKDF, a commit/reveal handshake with a passkey verified on the wallet's own display, and ChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypted frames.
The companion application is built with Tauri v2, Rust, TypeScript and viem and runs on Linux, macOS, Windows and Android. WalletConnect v2 allows existing EVM dapps to communicate with LeekWallet without requiring an embedded dapp browser.
A particularly important part of the project is its testing architecture. Most firmware logic is compiled natively on a desktop and exercised through 19 host-side test suites, including crash-injected PIN changes, entropy tests, transaction encoding, calldata decoding, protocol conformance, BLE chunking and device wiping. Additional testing uses sanitizers and QEMU's ESP32-S3 emulation, including emulated eFuses. Builds are reproducible and releases include SHA-256 hashes and GPG signatures.
The same firmware source also targets the Firefly Pixie ESP32-C3. Rather than rewriting the UI, I implemented a display compatibility shim that maps the wallet's existing monochrome 128×64 framebuffer onto the Pixie's 240×240 display, letting the same wallet logic and security flows run on a second inexpensive hardware platform.

name: scope402
description: Payment is not Auth. x402 proves an agent paid. Scope402 proves what that payment lets the agent do.
projectDescription:
Payment is not authorization.
x402 gives AI agents a native way to pay for services, but successful payment still leaves an important question unanswered: what exactly did the agent buy permission to do?
Giving an autonomous agent a reusable API key or broad credential after payment creates unnecessary authority—especially when that agent can make repeated calls or delegate work to other agents.
Scope402 turns an x402 payment into bounded permission.
Before paying, the agent can inspect the exact authority being offered: the resource, allowed actions, call budget, expiry, and agent identity. After settlement, it receives a signed capability enforcing those limits.
The agent can use that capability itself or delegate a strictly smaller capability to another worker without sharing its wallet or root credential.
We built two proofs of the same primitive:
AuditLab lets an agent pay for repository analysis and receive limited follow-up access.
Tessera lets a principal agent purchase a region of a shared world and delegate a smaller region to another agent. Valid actions succeed; wrong-key, replayed, expired, and out-of-scope actions are rejected.
Our thesis is simple:
x402 can be the payment layer for agent commerce. Scope402 adds the permission layer that comes after payment.
howItsMade:
Scope402 uses x402 v2 with real native HBAR settlement on Hedera testnet through Blocky402.
The key design choice is that the payment terms and permission terms are bound before the agent signs.
A merchant first returns an HTTP 402 quote containing the payment requirement plus a Scope402 policy describing the exact subject, resource, tools, call budget, expiry, and policy hash.
The agent validates those terms and explicitly approves payment. Once Hedera settlement succeeds, the merchant issues a signed capability carrying the same payment and policy lineage.
Every later protected action is independently signed by the agent. Our authorization kernel checks the subject key, resource, tool, arguments, expiry, replay counter, remaining budget, and original payment lineage before allowing the underlying operation.
Authorization and the merchant action are committed atomically in PostgreSQL, so failed or unauthorized requests cannot partially mutate the resource or incorrectly consume permission.
We also implemented capability delegation. A principal agent can sign authority for a different P-256 worker key, but the child capability must remain inside the parent's resource, tool set, lifetime, and remaining call budget. Delegation can reduce authority, never expand it.
AuditLab and Tessera both use this same authorization kernel, demonstrating that Scope402 is infrastructure rather than application-specific access control.
External agents can integrate through the TypeScript reference client or documented HTTP/OpenAPI interface: inspect resources, prepare a quote without spending, approve payment, perform authorized work, and delegate narrower authority to another worker.
The browser is only an inspection surface; payment keys and capability signing keys remain outside it.

name: AquaGhost Protocol
description: Self-custodial MEV & JIT defense for LPs via Uniswap v4, 1inch Aqua, Chainlink CRE & The Graph
projectDescription:
AquaGhost is a confidential, MEV-resistant liquidity defense engine designed to protect decentralized finance liquidity providers (LPs) from toxic flow and predatory Just-In-Time (JIT) fee-sniping.
The Problem
Passive LPs on concentrated-liquidity AMMs (like Uniswap v3/v4) consistently bleed yield to sandwich bots, arbitrageurs, and JIT attackers who front-run swaps, extract transaction fees, and immediately withdraw capital. While next-generation protocols like 1inch Aqua enable self-custodial liquidity provisioning, automated defense strategies traditionally fail on public blockchains: publishing stop-loss triggers, tick boundaries, and rebalance algorithms directly to the mempool allows MEV searchers to front-run the protection itself.
The Solution
AquaGhost resolves the transparency-versus-protection paradox by decoupling sensitive strategy evaluation from public execution:
Confidential Strategy Isolation: Proprietary anti-sniping heuristics, customized LP risk thresholds, and private stop-loss levels execute inside a hardware-isolated Trusted Execution Environment (TEE). Public mempools never see the LP's private boundaries.
Continuous Market Ingestion: An autonomous sentinel streams live pool depths, tick distributions, and historical volatility across multi-chain liquidity venues.
Verifiable, Self-Custodial Execution: Once the enclave identifies an imminent sniper vector or volatility threshold breach, it signs a verifiable execution payload that instructs automated on-chain contracts to defensively pull, widen, or adjust liquidity ranges without depositing user funds into custodial third-party vaults.
howItsMade:
AquaGhost brings together hardware-enforced privacy, decentralized data indexing, and cutting-edge AMM primitives to form an autonomous defense loop:
Architecture & Partner Technologies
Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE) & Confidential Workflows: The engine core is built as a CRE Workflow using handlerInTee in TypeScript. Sensitive risk parameters, private volatility thresholds, and authenticated off-chain CEX/DEX benchmark feeds execute exclusively inside a hardware-isolated TEE enclave. This ensures algorithmic alpha and stop-loss triggers cannot be inspected or front-run by block builders or MEV searchers.
The Graph (Subgraph MCP & Standardized Subgraphs): The workflow continuously queries live on-chain AMM state—specifically tracking pool tick liquidity, fee growth global counters, and rapid borrow/swap volume changes across Uniswap and 1inch liquidity pools—to identify anomalous swap patterns indicative of JIT attacks.
1inch Aqua: Built as an autonomous Aqua App, enabling automated yield protection while strictly maintaining self-custody over the LP’s assets without relying on custodial balance transfers.
Uniswap v4 Hooks: Implemented a custom reactive hook interface that parses cryptographic enclave attestations produced by the CRE workflow to dynamically alter pool fee tiers or lock swap interactions during detected predatory attacks.

name: Conflict as a Bug
description: Private mutual understanding first; then conflicts become semi-public bugs for solvers and backers.
projectDescription:
Conflict as a Bug (CAB) treats conflicts as problems that can be made explicit, understood, and solved. Instead of jumping directly to judgment or compromise, CAB first asks the parties to state their perspectives, paraphrase each other, and confirm mutual understanding.
This hackathon version begins with a private conflict between two people. Their exchange remains end-to-end encrypted. Only after both consent does CAB create a limited public summary and turn the conflict into a bug listed for solvers. A solver can propose a concrete resolution and, when money could help make it possible, request backing for one of the parties.
The PoC completes that path with a clearly labelled simulated audit and a transfer from a single backer. The broader vision is a platform where interpersonal, community, organizational, and other conflicts can be exposed at the appropriate privacy level and approached as resolvable bugs.
howItsMade:
CAB is built as a Next.js 16 application with TypeScript and Tailwind CSS, deployed on Vercel. Privy provides email authentication and embedded Ethereum wallets, allowing the parties, solvers, and backers to participate without first configuring an external wallet. Privy access tokens are verified server-side and mapped to the authenticated user’s Ethereum wallet before protected actions are accepted.
The private case flow is end-to-end encrypted: perspectives, requests, and paraphrases are encrypted in the browser before persistent storage. The backend handles encrypted content and workflow state, while a lightweight set of Solidity contracts on Sepolia anchors the case, the parties’ wallet identities, their consent, and public resolution and backing events without placing the private conversation onchain.
Once both parties confirm mutual understanding and consent to publication, a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow processes the private case inside a trusted execution environment and produces the limited summary shown in the public solver list. This lets solvers work from useful context while the raw private history remains protected during processing.
A solver can submit a free-text proposal and indicate that the solution needs financial backing for one of the parties. The PoC then passes the request through a clearly identified simulated audit before allowing a single backer to complete an onchain transfer. This deliberately constrained implementation demonstrates the entire path from private disagreement to shared understanding, confidential publication, an external solution, and funded action.

name: Shielder
description: Traders don't blow up on the trade. They blow up on the top-up after. Shield refuses that top-up.
projectDescription:
Open the demo link. It analyses a real Hyperliquid mainnet trader's public history — not ours, not a mock — and replays their worst session. They were down $1,302. They added another $13,894. Fifty-seven minutes later that session was down $53,485, and it ended at minus $117,089. Then it shows what Shield would have done: released $3,750, the limit that trader's own numbers imply, leaving $10,144 out of reach. It also says plainly that it could not have undone the loss. It could only have kept that money out of the session.
That is the whole product. Traders don't lose their money to hacks. They lose it in the ten minutes after a red session, sending one more deposit to win it back. Every wallet ever built will sign that deposit, and no exchange can credibly be the one to refuse it — an exchange holding your money against your own stated wish owns a liability, so it builds an appeals path, and an appeals path is exactly what destroys a commitment device.
So Shield is a contract with nobody to ask. ShieldVault.sol is deployed and immutable on HyperEVM testnet at 0xDaA8B6a85391d54397c3847F006a49A16d0F37b3 — no owner, no proxy, no upgrade path, including for us. You set rules while calm: a protected floor, a rolling 24-hour release limit, a loss trigger. Tightening any of them takes effect in the same block. Weakening one waits 24 hours and must be confirmed again tomorrow, and any tightening in between cancels it, so tilt cannot pre-load an escape.
v3 adds a risk ladder — NORMAL, REDUCED, LOCKED — where the drawdown that moves you down a rung is private. The chain holds a salted hash of it; the plaintext exists only inside a Chainlink confidential workflow. A verifier can move you down the ladder, never up, and only to a rung you wrote yourself.
Everything in the demo is real and checkable. The trader is a public mainnet account. The contract is deployed. The loss that fires the rule is a genuine Hyperliquid testnet loss. scripts/verify-trader.ts re-derives the headline number straight from Hyperliquid's own API and tells you whether it agrees.
Honest limits, stated up front: the vault is on testnet, the Privy release evidence is on v1 rather than v3, and The Graph has no HyperEVM testnet entry so the live Substreams rows come from a Sepolia twin of the same bytecode. All of that is in the repo rather than left for a judge to find.
howItsMade:
Contract. ShieldVault.sol v3 at 0xDaA8B6a85391d54397c3847F006a49A16d0F37b3 on HyperEVM testnet (chain 998), immutable, one contract holding many vaults keyed by authority address. Money leaves through five gated paths only. 64 Foundry tests, including 6 regressions pinning three defects our own review found in v1 and fixed in v2, and 15 for the v3 ladder. 70 more tests on the server and client.
Chainlink CRE — Best Confidential Workflow. handlerInTee from @chainlink/cre-sdk with [{ tee: "nitro", regions: ["us-west-2"] }]. Two secrets are read in-enclave via runtime.getSecret: the verifier key, and — the one that makes this a confidential application rather than confidential plumbing — the user's private risk ladder, the trailing drawdown at which their own reload budget shrinks. The chain holds only keccak256(thresholds ‖ salt). The enclave recomputes that hash, fetches the venue's fills over the TeeRuntime HTTP overload, and emits exactly {tier, ladderHash, nonce, expiry}: no threshold, no dollar figure. On chain that verdict moved a live vault down its ladder. The evidence transcript includes two negative controls — breaking the verifier secret kills the run before any HTTP call, withholding the ladder secret stops the CLI outright — which is what converts "a secret is present" into "the secret is load-bearing".
The Graph — Composable products. substreams-evm/ builds five modules composed on The Graph's foundational [email protected], whose index_events is the declared blockFilter for both maps. The standards leverage is measurable rather than asserted: our entire EVM package is 268 lines of Rust in one file, we never wrote a log scanner or a block index, and the diff between the HyperEVM manifest and the Sepolia manifest is six substantive lines driving those same 268 lines across two unrelated chains. All three packages are published and resolve by name — substreams gui [email protected] runs the pipeline with no clone. The Shield server consumes it live: /api/health reports source.mode "substreams" and the vault is discovered from the stream by store_vault_registry with no RPC log scan.
Privy — Best Financial Flow. The embedded wallet is the vault's authority, not a login: the contract reverts for every other address. Created with createOnLogin "users-without-wallets". The financial flow is a $5.00 release from the vault into a Hyperliquid perps account in a single transaction, through Circle's CoreDepositWallet to the HyperCore system address, signed by the wallet itself. Structurally, Privy is where the funnel earns the ask — the wallet is not requested until the user has seen their own reload history, the replay of their worst session, and the plan Shield proposes from it.
Rest of the stack. Bun server: indexer (Substreams or a labelled RPC fallback), behaviour engine, policy, EIP-712 verdict relayer. React + Vite app. The onboarding analysis runs on the hosted URL with no backend at all, because server/hyperliquid.ts has no imports and uses only global fetch, so it drops into a Vercel function with no keys, no chain access and no state — about 1.3s for an arbitrary mainnet address.

name: presence gate
description: Presence-gated drops: claim a limited unit only by proving you're a live human, right now.
projectDescription:
Presence Gate is a hosted claim gate for allocating scarce things by presence rather than by speed.
The problem. Almost everything scarce online is allocated first-come, first-served on a link: limited drops, capacity-limited sessions, event perks, workshop seats. That rule doesn't allocate to the people it's meant for. It allocates to whoever's script is fastest, and to whoever the link got forwarded to. The offline alternatives — wristbands, QR codes, staffed lists — are bearer instruments: they work for whoever is holding them, not for the person they were issued to.
What we built. An organiser configures a drop: an item, a number of units, a release instant, and a claim window. Anyone with the link can claim, but a claim only counts if a live human completed a Selfie Check inside that window. Units are allocated in real time on a live board showing claims landing, remaining capacity, and funnel drop-off.
How Selfie Check is used. We use the selfieCheckLegacy credential via IDKit v4. The RP request is signed server-side and — critically — the signing endpoint is gated on the drop window, so no proof can be generated before the drop opens. Proofs are verified server-side against the World verifier, and the returned nullifier is stored under a UNIQUE (drop_id, nullifier) constraint, which is what enforces one claim per credential per drop. We reuse a single action across all drops deliberately, because nullifiers are action-scoped and per-drop actions would silently break recognition.
Why this credential fits this problem. Selfie Check attests that a live human was present at a moment, and returns a stable anonymous handle. In this use case the moment of verification is the moment of value — there's no window between the check and the thing being protected for someone to hand off, automate, or substitute into. We make no uniqueness claim and no identity claim, because Selfie Check provides neither; we allocate on presence, which is exactly what it does provide.
What it changes. Scarce capacity stops being transferable at claim time, which is what makes it farmable. It's a drop-in replacement for bearer instruments — any organiser can point it at their own claim page.
howItsMade:
Presence Gate is built with Next.js App Router, TypeScript, and React. World ID's @worldcoin/idkit (v4) powers the Selfie Check flow through the selfieCheckLegacy credential. RP requests are signed server-side with @worldcoin/idkit-core/signing; proofs are forwarded byte-for-byte unmodified to World's verifier at /api/v4/verify/{rp_id}, and only the returned nullifier is persisted. Drops, claims, and funnel events use SQLite locally with a Postgres production adapter; nullifiers are stored as NUMERIC(78, 0) since they're 256-bit field elements. The live board uses Server-Sent Events with a polling fallback.
The most important design decision was window-gating the signing endpoint. The obvious attack on a timed drop is generating a proof in advance and submitting it the instant the drop opens. Because the RP request must be signed by our backend, we simply refuse to sign outside the drop window — so a valid proof cannot exist before the drop is live. The window and capacity are both enforced server-side; client time is never trusted, and allocation happens inside the same transaction as the claim insert so concurrent claims at T can't over-allocate.
The notable subtlety is reusing one World ID action across all drops. Nullifiers are RP- and action-scoped, so giving each drop its own action would return unrelated handles with no error — recognition would silently break and look like a matching bug. With one action, each person's handle is stable across drops, and per-drop uniqueness comes from a UNIQUE (drop_id, nullifier) constraint rather than the UNIQUE (action, nullifier) pattern the docs prescribe. That deviation is deliberate: the documented constraint allows one claim ever, and we need one claim per drop. Replay protection is the constraint violation itself — we never upsert.
Anonymous handles on the board are a short non-reversible hash of the nullifier, so returning participation is visible without exposing raw credentials. We surface no identity and make no uniqueness claim; the trade-off is that one action means we can correlate handles across drops, which we state openly rather than hide.

name: ARCADE
description: Publish any skill or agent as a paid endpoint on Arc; agents hire agents, settled per call in USDC.
projectDescription:
ARCADE is a marketplace where anyone publishes a skill or an agent as a paid endpoint on Circle's Arc, and buyer agents pay per call in USDC.
The problem: an agent that needs a specialist, say live wallet data for a risk report, normally waits for a human to connect that service, arrange the key and the bill. ARCADE lets the agent hire the skill itself. It reads the price and input schema, authorizes exactly that amount, and the hub dispatches the job to the seller's runner, checks the output against the declared schema, and settles on Arc only on success. A failed job leaves the buyer's balance untouched.
What makes it a marketplace for agents rather than an API directory:

Sellers publish an Agent Skill (the open SKILL.md standard), an MCP tool, or an OpenAPI operation. The hub only ever sees the public part: price, input and output schemas. Code, prompts and credentials stay on the seller's machine, inside a runner that connects out to the hub.
Buyers are agents. A skill can hire another skill while it works. Every hire carries a hub-signed capability tied to its parent job, the root sets a budget the children cannot exceed, and the receipt tree is committed on chain at settlement. A live three-hop run on Arc testnet settled three payments and refused an attempted self-hire without a fourth payment.
Discovery is standard: a generated OpenAPI 3.1 document, /.well-known/x402, an MCP server with eight tools, a public receipts feed, and ENSv2 names on Sepolia that publish a skill's endpoint, payee and chain so a buyer can hire by name and refuse a conflicting challenge before signing.
Listings are pay-tested: the hub makes scheduled one-cent canary purchases and delists a skill that stops delivering, then relists it after a paid pass.
Every seller has an ERC-8004 identity on Arc testnet with validation requests and receipt-backed feedback recorded on chain.
A subgraph on The Graph (arcade-ledger-arc-testnet) indexes ARCADE settlements and receipt trees on Arc testnet; the hub queries it for receipt-tree lookups, and the counterparty-graph skill applies a bounded evidence policy to indexed ERC-8004 identity, validation and feedback data.

Live now: marketplace https://arcade-web-production-8dc4.up.railway.app, hub API https://arcade-hub-production.up.railway.app/healthz, nine skills listed on Arc testnet. The demo video shows a real one-cent purchase signed from the owner's MetaMask and settled at https://testnet.arcscan.app/tx/0x87519ca045968f5ae4f45f55447f46d8fdc13375f0bb56f0a4726412db789554.
Continuity: ARCADE existed before ETHOnline (the Encode x Circle Programmable Money build, July 25 to August 7, 2026). Everything after the September 4 planning baseline is ETHOnline work. docs/CONTINUITY.md in the repo dates each move and states its evidence limit, and the README carries a reproducible Git snapshot of that boundary.
howItsMade:
Bun + TypeScript, with Effect throughout (Effect Schema, HttpApi and Socket from @effect/platform, bun:sqlite via @effect/sql). TanStack Start for the web app. Solidity for FeeSplitterV2, tested with Forge.
Secrecy boundary. A schema transformation in packages/core projects a seller manifest into a public listing; anything that would send engine config, entry points, secrets or system prompts to the hub is rejected at the type level.
Pull-model runner. The seller's machine runs the arcade daemon, which dials the hub over WebSocket, so the seller needs no public endpoint. Jobs run in a sandbox; a sub-purchase wallet is held by the runner, not the skill, and the skill gets a per-job HMAC token to hire, so an injected agent can spend the declared budget and not a cent more.
Payments on Arc. x402 challenges with EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization: the buyer signs offline and pays no gas; a facilitator broadcasts. Settlement happens only after output validation. FeeSplitterV2.settleWithTree commits the receipt-tree hash on chain and splits seller and platform fee in one transaction. Circle Gateway nanopayment sessions are a second rail advertised in the same 402. Arc's USDC is both the native gas token (18 decimals) and the ERC-20 (6 decimals), which shaped every amount path.
Authenticated hiring. The hub issues a signed lineage capability per hire with parent, hop count and ancestor set; cycle and depth checks plus a per-tree reservation ledger in SQLite enforce the root budget before dispatch.
Hardening found by adversarial review during the hackathon. Authorization replay was closed by claiming each EIP-3009 nonce at acceptance and persisting the claim; a broadcast-but-unconfirmed settlement now records an unresolved transaction instead of telling the buyer they were not charged; the browser flow selects the payment route by EIP-712 domain so a listing advertising two rails still works.
Identity and naming. ERC-8004 identity, validation and feedback registries on Arc testnet. ENSv2 namespaces on Sepolia with expiry used as liveness and a payee/chain lock verified by the buyer before signing; the production name usdc-flow-check.scf821769ed.arcade.eth resolves to the live hub.
Indexing. A Graph subgraph on Subgraph Studio maps FeeSplitter settlements, receipt trees and ERC-8004 events on Arc testnet; the hub reads it with bounded, cached queries that never affect settlement.
Web. Marketplace with filters and a public receipts feed, an assistant that quotes and prepares purchases but cannot spend (the visitor signs in their own wallet with a hold-to-approve card), My jobs with a receipt-tree explorer, and a seller studio with pay-test history. Last full gate: 5,396 Vitest and 1,885 Bun tests plus strict typechecks; 31 Forge tests.
AI usage, disclosed per the rules. Codex (OpenAI) implemented and tested most of the ETHOnline continuation, rebuilt the web app, produced the diagrams and drove the screen capture and edit of the demo video; its commits carry Co-Authored-By: Codex trailers. Claude (Anthropic, Claude Code) acted as conductor and planner: research, the design spec and plans under docs/superpowers, adversarial review of the payment paths, the early settlement-core commits, the ENS operations, deployments, the video direction and the voiceover script; its commits carry Co-Authored-By: Claude trailers. GPT and Grok took part in the design debate recorded under docs/superpowers/research. The owner set direction, approved every spend and deployment, signed the demo purchase from their own wallet, reviewed the work, recorded the narration in their own voice and made this submission. Specs, prompts, plans and progress records are in docs/superpowers; no text-to-speech was used.

name: Space Object
description: Enables AI agents to discover, negotiate, hire, and transact with another seamlessly.
projectDescription:
Space Object is agentic commerce infrastructure on Arc. Enables AI agents to discover, negotiate, hire, and transact with another seamlessly.
Three standards carry the protocol layer.

ERC-8004 gives an agent an on-chain identity. It registers, publishes a profile with its service endpoints and collects reputation feedback against the identity.
ERC-8183 is job escrow. A client agent creates and funds a job in USDC, a provider agent submits the deliverable, and an evaluator agent signs off before payment releases.
For per-request agent services, it charges with Circle Nanopayments (x402).

What we built on top of those standards:

Open-source subgraphs, ERC-8004 (https://github.com/spaceobject-ai/erc-8004-subgraph) and ERC-8183 (https://github.com/spaceobject-ai/erc-8183-subgraph), indexing Arc Testnet and published to The Graph's decentralized network.
A hardened fork of the ERC-8183 base contracts, deployed on Arc Testnet, with an extended event ABI that makes jobs actually indexable from logs.
A read-only HTTP API and an MCP server over the subgraphs, so any agent can search registered agents, inspect their services and reputation, and track escrow jobs.
Agent skills (npx skills add spaceobject-ai/skills): markdown skill documents that teach any skill-capable agent (Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex) to act as one of three roles. Clients: find and hire agents, Providers: register and get paid for deliverables, Evaluators: watch for submitted jobs naming them and complete or reject.

The agent brings its own wallet, Circle Agent Wallets work out of the box, and signs its own transactions.
You tell your agent to fetch and follow https://spaceobject-web.luckzivanius.workers.dev/SETUP.md and it installs the skills, connects to the MCP server, sets up a wallet, and starts working.
howItsMade:
Contracts
We forked https://github.com/erc-8183/base-contracts into https://github.com/spaceobject-ai/erc-8183-contracts and deployed on Arc Testnet (0x85A21c175655BeBc21F4727bE480Fec57Cd18b1a). We deliberately did not use the ERC-8183 deployment from https://docs.arc.io/arc/tutorials/create-your-first-erc-8183-job because it targets an older version of the standard.
The fork changes the event ABI. Upstream JobCreated omits providerAgentId and description, and when the provider is set at creation you cannot recover it from logs at all. Our fork emits both. Every value-moving event (JobFunded, PaymentReleased, PlatformFeePaid, EvaluatorFeePaid, Refunded, Disbursed, Settled) now indexes the ERC-20 token, so an indexer no longer has to join against BudgetSet.
The ERC-8004 registries were already live on Arc Testnet at the vanity 0x8004... addresses. We use those as-is.
Subgraphs
We evaluated Agent0's ERC-8004 subgraph (https://github.com/agent0lab/subgraph) first and decided against it. It hasn't had a commit since March 2026 and custom services get flattened into a lossy hand-serialized JSON string instead of queryable entities. Fields like mcpTools and a2aSkills exist in its schema but are never populated. Fine for a demo, not for a discovery API.
So we wrote our own, both open source:


https://github.com/spaceobject-ai/erc-8004-subgraph indexes the Identity and Reputation registries. Entity IDs are chain-scoped ({chainId}:{registry}:{agentId}). It decodes data: URI registration files into structured AgentRegistration and AgentService entities and exposes fulltext search over agent profiles.


https://github.com/spaceobject-ai/erc-8183-subgraph keeps a main branch for the upstream ABI, where the mapping has to make an eth_call on every JobCreated to backfill missing fields, and a spaceobject branch that indexes our fork's extended events with no calls needed. The spaceobject branch is what's deployed.


Both are published to The Graph's decentralized network

ERC-8004: https://thegraph.com/explorer/subgraphs/9mRRNdskhxtPAVKbMrU51KrrvpCJB3STGhHTzxNsFtxM
ERC-8183: https://thegraph.com/explorer/subgraphs/Fc5gpvTtrJdiie7REMhNx9PD3NM3vxD7JgRLNGzyu4Ud

Packages
apps/api is Hono with @hono/zod-openapi on Cloudflare Workers. GraphQL Codegen introspects the live gateway schemas and generates typed SDKs, so every subgraph query is checked at build time. apps/mcp wraps the API with @modelcontextprotocol/sdk over streamable HTTP.
Partner technologies

Arc: Everything is deployed on Arc Testnet, jobs are funded in USDC, and Circle Agent Wallets are the supported signer in the skills.
The Graph: Both subgraphs run on the decentralized network.

Future work
Every piece of this stack assumes both parties sit on the same chain. In practice they won't. An agent's funds live on one network, the agent it wants to hire lives on another, and the moment payment crosses that boundary you're into bridges, wrapped assets, and gas on a chain the agent has never touched. An autonomous agent can't stop mid-task to solve a bridging issue.
So the next phase is handling the chain boundary for them. When client and worker sit on different chains, we settle the payment and execute the contract calls on the right networks. From the agent's side it stays one flow: find, hire, pay.
Rollout order: Arc today, then Base, Arbitrum, 0G, Monad, and X Layer. After that we go for non-EVM like Solana and Sui. Same identity and escrow model, new chain adapters underneath. One agent, every chain.

name: Project Handoff
description: Your agent pays a certified human to review it's work. Money in escrow, verdict signed on Hedera
projectDescription:
Handoff is an on-chain protocol for buying human judgment. AI agents produce most professional output today — reports, filings, contract reviews — but nobody qualified has looked at it. Handoff closes that gap: a requester agent posts an order, funds lock in escrow, a credentialed human expert claims it, reviews the work, and publishes a signed attestation. Payment releases on the signature, whatever the verdict — you bought judgment, not approval, so a reject is a delivered product and gets paid.
The protocol runs two separate payment rails that are never conflated. The service fee is an x402 micropayment (0.5 HBAR) settled through the Blocky402 testnet facilitator — this is the HTTP 402 gate on the handoff_verify MCP tool that any AI agent session can call. The order value (e.g. 100 HBAR) is the price of the human judgment itself, locked in a threshold-key escrow account on Hedera. Different rails, different accounts, different sizes.
The lifecycle is: POSTED → CLAIMED → DELIVERED → SETTLED. Orders and claims are published as HCS messages carrying only hashes — task content and expert notes stay off-chain in a content store, with the on-chain hash as the commitment. The expert signs the attestation by submitting an HCS message from their own Hedera account — the account signature is the attestation signature, and the platform is never in the signing path. After validation, the platform co-signs a transfer from the escrow to release payment.
What ships: the x402 payment gate via Blocky402, threshold-key escrow with fund lock, HCS attestation signed by the expert's own account, a full expert web app (inbox → review workspace → sign), the handoff_verify MCP tool as a published npm package (@hedera-handoff/mcp-client) that any Claude Code session or Desktop apps can install without cloning the repo, and mirror-node settlement reads with transaction IDs threaded through to Hashscan.
Known limits:
Certification is an allowlist this week — the issuers and the scarcity are not here, only the interface (even though we're getting certification ID during onboarding)
Disputes are stubbed — a rubber-stamp attestation gets paid, with m-of-n jury as the production answer.
howItsMade:
ARCHITECTURE:
We have monorepo for this project that has following:

Libraries in packages/
Deployables in apps/.
packages/schema is the treaty — it owns every zod schema, the schema_version constant, canonical hashing (deterministic serialization before hashing so two implementations produce the same digest), the money module (tinybars as bigint internally, strings at every boundary, all conversion in one tested module), the ChainAdapter interface, and MockChainAdapter.

Nothing else in the repo imports the Hedera SDK directly — only packages/chain does. This seam let three people build in parallel from day one: the mock satisfied the same interface the real adapter would, so the MCP tool and the expert app never waited on chain work.
HEDERA (PARTNER TECHNOLOGY — THE ENTIRE SETTLEMENT LAYER):
HCS carries order envelopes and attestations as hash-only messages. The escrow is a 2-of-3 threshold-key account — platform verifier, schedule admin, and a guard key — so no single key can move funds. The expert's attestation is an HCS message submitted from their own Hedera account; the account signature is the attestation signature, keeping the platform out of the signing path entirely. Consensus timestamps are the source of truth for claim priority — UIs render optimistically but defer to the mirror node. Every Hedera call surfaces its transaction ID, threaded through to the client so settlement state is read from a mirror node, never inferred from "we sent it."
X402 VIA BLOCKY402 (PARTNER TECHNOLOGY — PRIZE QUALIFICATION):
The handoff_verify MCP endpoint is gated by HTTP 402. The server answers with a PAYMENT-REQUIRED header stating the price; the client builds a Hedera TransferTransaction, partially signs with its own ECDSA key, and retries with the payload in a PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header. The server posts to the Blocky402 testnet facilitator's /verify — verification gates serving, settlement happens last, so an order that fails to post leaves the caller's money untouched. The fee payer is discovered from the facilitator's /supported endpoint at startup, never hard-coded, because a rotated account fails verification silently. We speak x402 version 2 and read both v1 and v2 headers through @x402/core.
MCP:
The MCP client is published to npm (@hedera-handoff/mcp-client), so any agent session on any machine can order from the running service with claude mcp add handoff — nothing to clone. The key never leaves the caller's machine: the client signs locally, only signatures go over the wire, and the server validates the returned bytes against what it asked for.
EXPERT APP:
React, Tailwind, shadcn/ui. The expert pastes their Hedera private key at connect time (main philosophy is not to store the key in the backend, but for the sake of Expert app's UX and smooth flow, we've added email sign-in that we encrypt and keep the Key in our backend. In the future, we'll add secure key management and wrapping for the users). The inbox polls the mirror node REST API for the orders topic. The review workspace shows the document alongside a verdict panel (Approve / Approve with changes / Reject), a defects editor with enforced bounds (max items and max bytes per item, matching the HCS size limit), and a notes field. Signing submits the attestation to HCS from the expert's account and triggers the co-signed payout.
Notable hack: Hedera's Schedule Service cannot debit a KeyList (threshold-key) account — we hit INVALID_SIGNATURE across eight isolated testnet runs while the control (a plain co-signed transfer, same account, same keys) succeeded every time. So instead of scheduled payments, the DELIVERED state co-signs a TransferTransaction directly. The escrow still locks at POSTED and the payout is still committed at claim time, but execution is a direct co-signed transfer, not a schedule firing.
TOOLING:
Five MCP servers checked into .mcp.json — our own handoff tool, Hedera's hosted Agent Kit (testnet), Hedera docs search, Linear for coordination, and Context7 for live SDK docs. A hard rule: never recall a Hedera SDK call from memory, always look it up through the docs servers first. Pre-commit hook runs gitleaks — no secrets in the repo, ever. CI runs typecheck, unit tests, and gitleaks on every push.

name: Aethon
description: Browser Solidity IDE: WASM compile, in-browser EVM, gas heatmap, audit, and live deploy.
projectDescription:
Aethon (CryptP IDE) is Continuity / Extend Open Source. Baseline: an existing browser Solidity IDE (Monaco, WASM solc, @ethereumjs/vm, gas heatmap, audit, MetaMask promote, Supabase workspaces). Live: https://cryptp-production.up.railway.app/ — repo https://github.com/Assassin859/cryptp
Score only ETHOnline work. We extended the deploy loop with three partner integrations:

howItsMade:
React 18 + TypeScript + Vite + Tailwind + Monaco; solc WASM in a worker; @ethereumjs/vm for sandbox; ethers v6 + MetaMask for Sepolia; Supabase for auth/workspaces; Hardhat for contracts/scripts.

name: LitClinic
description: Agentic trust for Web3 healthcare with live onchain context and fail-closed authorization.
projectDescription:
LitClinic is an existing Web3 healthcare product exploring how verifiable onchain context and explicit authorization boundaries can support safer agentic workflows.
For ETHOnline 2026, we built a new agentic trust and onchain context layer that extends the existing LitClinic experience. The new layer gives agents sanitized context, verifies live onchain activity, applies deterministic fail-closed policies, and introduces human-backed authorization before privileged workflows are allowed to continue.
Instead of blindly trusting client input or allowing an agent to act when evidence is incomplete, LitClinic can require stronger approval or block execution entirely. A BLOCKED result is therefore an intentional security outcome, not a failure.
The hackathon extension integrates The Graph for live onchain context and World AgentKit / AgentBook for agent identity and authorization checks, while keeping sensitive clinical information outside public blockchain state.
The existing LitClinic UI predates ETHOnline 2026; the agentic trust and onchain context infrastructure shown in this submission was built during the hackathon.
howItsMade:
The ETHOnline extension is built as a TypeScript/Bun workspace with explicit boundaries between context acquisition, deterministic reasoning, and authorization.
The Graph integration queries live Uniswap V3 Ethereum data and converts it into constrained onchain context, including freshness and observed wallet activity. This prevents the agent from relying only on arbitrary client-provided claims.
A deterministic agent-core evaluates that evidence using a fail-closed policy. If context is missing, stale, inactive, or requires stronger authorization, the workflow returns require_approval / BLOCKED rather than allowing the agent to continue.
For the authorization layer, we integrated World AgentKit and AgentBook. The live AgentBook lookup resolves the agent's registration and human-backed authorization state and feeds that result into the final execution-permission decision.
We also implemented the World ID Sandbox Selfie Check workflow. Android end-to-end verification is currently pending external Google Play Internal Test access approval, so we do not claim completed Sandbox E2E in this submission.
The repository also includes a typed SDK/API layer, sanitized context schemas, validation, secret scanning, deterministic demo modes, and 53 passing tests.
Sensitive clinical data is deliberately kept outside public blockchain state; onchain infrastructure is used for verifiable context and authorization rather than exposing patient information.

name: OpenX
description: OpenX Portal — AI Agent Management & Orchestration Platform . It is the dashboard for AI agents
projectDescription:
OpenX Portal is a context layer for autonomous DeFi lending agents. Instead of making every agent reconstruct market state from raw RPC calls and unstructured data, OpenX uses The Graph to retrieve indexed Aave V3 Arbitrum market data, including hourly deposits, borrows, utilization, and variable rates. It turns that data into a compact, deterministic risk context: LTV, health factor, utilization, kink headroom, 24-hour volatility, risk band, and a recommended action.
The result is available in the Portal UI and through a public Context-as-a-Service API. Other agents can request either a structured vector or a short prompt-ready context card, without receiving wallets, API keys, raw provider responses, or private report data. OpenX explicitly marks unavailable or malformed provider data as degraded rather than presenting synthetic success.
howItsMade:
OpenX Portal combines a Next.js dashboard, a Node.js/Express Gateway, and a Python DeFi lending researcher. The researcher queries The Graph’s Aave V3 Arbitrum deployment through GraphQL and normalizes the live Market and MarketHourlySnapshot schema. It derives utilization from indexed deposit and borrow balances, reads lender and borrower variable rates, and calculates a 24-hour utilization-volatility signal.
The researcher enforces a 40% LTV safety cap before submission and creates a deterministic APSD-L statement with a SHA-256 content hash. The Gateway validates reports with Zod, persists safe projections in SQLite, and exposes a redacted public context endpoint plus a prompt-prefix endpoint for other agents. The Portal renders the resulting report and lets users copy the agent-ready context. We verified the full flow with live Aave data: Graph ingestion returned ok, the Gateway accepted a public statement, and the public context API returned fresh telemetry.

name: Game Over
description: GameOver: human exchange credits expire each sunrise while Ethereum history endures.
projectDescription:
GameOver explores whether economic value can be recorded around participation rather than price or passive holding. When two people exchange goods, services, knowledge or goodwill, an AI-assisted interface structures a shared statement. Both participants must confirm it before Ethereum records a minimal receipt containing the parties, evidence hashes, time and status. No transaction amount is required: the occurrence itself is the unit of record.
The prototype also tests a “Future Commons” model. Each verified participant begins every daily cycle at zero. When an encounter is confirmed, the recipient remains at 0 and the contributor to +1. At the next sunrise, the temporary balances reset, preventing hoarding, while the confirmed encounter history remains. The “infinite depository” is therefore not an infinite reserve of money, but a renewable rule that creates bounded capacity over time.
howItsMade:
GameOver is a solo project by Rudolf Hartwig during ETHOnline 2026. The current MVP combines a standalone browser prototype with a Solidity 0.8.24 smart contract called EncounterLedger. The browser prototype is a single file HTML containing its own interface, CSS and JavaScript. It turns the participants’ input into a structured encounter statement, asks both parties to confirm it, applies the temporary +1/+0 balance movements and displays a simulated chain receipt.
The browser’s internal Web Crypto API creates a SHA-256 digital fingerprint from the structured encounter data and a separate prototype location hash. A QR-like graphic illustrates the intended physical “handshake” between participants. Because a live AI model is not connected yet, a fixed/deterministic local template acts as the AI-scribe placeholder. The demo can recall earlier encounters from its local ledger. In the connected version, an event indexer would allow the AI to retrieve confirmed encounter history directly from Ethereum.
The EncounterLedger contract mimics the actual on-chain process. A verified contributor proposes an encounter and the recipient confirms it in a separate transaction. Only after confirmation, does the contract update their balances and create a permanent EncounterConfirmed event. “Lazy epoch accounting” makes balances from a previous UTC day read as zero without resetting every account individually (instead of looping through the entire population to reset all balances, it checks the day register only once that user interacts again). The current browser version simulates wallet signatures, QR scanning and Ethereum locally. Live AI integration, real wallet signing, a scannable rotating QR code, testnet deployment and event indexing are the next steps.
ChatGPT/Codex assisted with code generation, interface construction, testing and documentation under Rudolf’s direction.

name: postage
description: A forwarding address that holds mail from strangers until they pass World ID or pay in USDC.
projectDescription:
Postage is a forwarding email address that sits between you and anyone you have never corresponded with.
You sign up and get an address like [email protected] that forwards to the inbox you already use. Mail that is clearly expected, such as a receipt or a reply in a thread you started, goes straight through. Mail that looks deceptive is blocked. Everything else, which is most cold email, is held: the message is parked unread, and the sender gets an automatic reply, threaded to their own message, asking one question. Are you a person or a program?
A person answers by completing a World ID Selfie Check on their phone. It is free, and it proves they are one real human without revealing who they are. A program answers by paying a small amount of USDC on Arc. The price depends on how suspicious the message looks and on the sender's track record across the whole network, which anyone can inspect on the public dashboard. As soon as the sender clears the gate, the original message is delivered exactly as they sent it, with their own signatures intact.
The idea is simple: unsolicited email should cost the sender something, a minute of their time or a small fee, rather than costing the recipient their attention. Humans pay with a proof, machines pay with money, and the inbox only sees what was worth sending.
What is live today: all four contracts are deployed on Arc Testnet, the classify, hold, challenge and release loop has run end to end against a real Gmail inbox, and a real Selfie Check has been completed on a phone and recorded on-chain.
howItsMade:
Postage is four independent pieces, each with its own install and no monorepo tooling. The only shared code is one TypeScript type, the gateway verdict.
Contracts (Solidity 0.8.28, Foundry), deployed on Arc Testnet. PostageEscrow holds the USDC payments: a sender submits a price quote signed by the pricing server (EIP-712), the contract checks the signer against EnclaveRegistry, then splits the payment 20% to PostageVault and the rest to the recipient's claimable earnings. HumanRegistry records a World ID verified human as an address derived from their nullifier hash, so nothing on-chain links back to a real wallet. PostageVault routes its share 30% to treasury and 70% to a pool that refunds the relayer's gas; anyone may call refill because the funds can only ever go to one fixed address. The escrow and the registry deliberately use different EIP-712 domain versions so a signature for one can never be replayed against the other, and there is no ReentrancyGuard: every external call happens after state is written and events emitted, with a comment at each site saying not to reorder it. 68 Forge tests. Arc was a natural fit because gas is paid in USDC, so a sender uses one asset for both the postage and the transaction.
Mail path (Cloudflare Email Routing, an Email Worker, Workers KV). Inbound mail hits the Worker, which parses it, posts the fields to the gateway, and parks the raw bytes in KV. Message content never touches a database. When the gateway releases a message, the Worker re-sends the original bytes through Mailgun's raw-MIME endpoint with tracking and re-signing turned off. This is the hack I am most pleased with: Cloudflare's own send_email refuses a From: header you do not own, so relaying the untouched bytes through Mailgun is what keeps the sender's original DKIM signature valid at the far end.
Gateway and UI (Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind 4, viem 2, a small libSQL database for everything except message content). The classifier is Claude (claude-opus-5) reading only the message's own headers, body and SPF/DKIM/DMARC results, and returning one of four tiers; if the API is unavailable a header-only fallback takes over, and it is not allowed to return the "dangerous" tier. Pricing takes the tier and scales it by the sender's history, read from a subgraph on The Graph that indexes all four contracts. The same subgraph powers the public /network page. Privy handles wallets and login, and the server verifies Privy's JWTs against Privy's own JWKS rather than trusting the SDK. Resend sends the challenge email.
World ID is the human lane. The challenge page opens IDKit with a Selfie Check, the server verifies the proof through the Developer Portal, then a relayer signs and submits attest() to HumanRegistry, so the sender never pays gas. One wrinkle worth knowing: Selfie Check currently issues v3 proofs and IDKit v4 rejects those by default, so it takes an explicit legacy opt-in. I wrote that up for the World team in docs/world-feedback.md.
Two honest caveats. The pricing signer is a plain server key registered in EnclaveRegistry under a placeholder measurement; the registry is shaped for a real Nitro enclave later but is not one today. And the deployed Selfie Check runs against World's sandbox, because the production World app does not have Selfie Check enabled yet.

name: NextKey🔑🔒️
description: Secrets handed to a person or an AI-agent, released by ENS rules, confirmed by a human on Ledger.
projectDescription:
You place a secret — a seed phrase, an API credential, a private message. Then you decide two things: who may open it, and under what conditions. Both are enforced by the protocol, not by our servers and not by anyone's goodwill.
Who may open it is answered by cryptography, addressed through ENSv2. Sharing a secret with anna.eth wraps its key to the X25519 public key Anna publishes in her own ENS records — you share with a name, not with 0x7f3a…, and Anna never registers with us. ENSv2 enforces the other half: who may write that grant, revoke it, or delegate the right to. That is state in a registry you own, not a row in our database.
Three independent runs are already on Sepolia, with transaction hashes in evidence/v2-onchain.log: a grant written from a phone with no wallet; one written in a browser on a name outside our own registry and opened from a command line by a key that was never in that browser; and a recovery in which two unrelated signer implementations, MetaMask and viem, reconstructed the same 32 bytes and the chain agreed. Live at nextkey.li — the playground writes real records on Sepolia without asking you for a wallet: a disclosed demo key with roles on a single resolver signs for you.
Under what conditions is answered inside a trusted execution environment. A release agent can propose but never act alone. The condition — a guardian quorum, a time lock, prolonged inactivity — is evaluated in a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow on AWS Nitro, and the verdict carries the hash of the on-chain request it judged, so anyone can recompute it and see that the enclave decided that request and not a modified one. evidence/cre-decision.log has a passing run; evidence/release-loop.log has one where the binding fails on purpose and the release refuses. What leaves the enclave is the verdict and a coarse reason — never how far a request stood from its threshold. Honest scope: the guardian approvals are fixtures. The request is real and on chain; the people around it are not yet.
Where your own key lives is your decision alone — a file on your machine, or a Ledger. The difference is invisible to whoever shares with you, because what they read is a public key in your ENS record and nothing else. On a device, opening a secret costs a deliberate button press, so software running on your laptop cannot do it while you are away from it.
howItsMade:
NextKey is a static site plus a set of Node tools; there is no backend, and that is a design constraint rather than an omission. Everything a server would normally hold is either public on chain or private on your own machine.
The cryptography. A secret is sealed with AES-256-GCM under a content key. That content key is wrapped to the recipient with X25519 ECDH and HKDF-SHA256 — @noble/curves and @noble/hashes in Node, the identical code path in the browser via WebCrypto for AES and the same noble primitives for the curve. A grant made in the playground opens in the command-line tool and vice versa; 26 interop tests assert exactly that, 13 of them inside Chromium.
What ENSv2 does that a database cannot. Three text records carry the whole handover: nextkey.eph, nextkey.secret, and the grant itself. The recipient is addressed by name — we read the X25519 public key she publishes under her own name, so she never registers with us and never learns we exist until she is told. Who may write, revoke or delegate those records is decided by ENSv2 roles on a Permissioned Resolver, so revocation is a protocol write rather than a promise from us. Resolution goes through the hackathon Universal Resolver, with the address overridden explicitly in viem — the built-in default resolves against production and silently returns the wrong answer, which cost us an evening early on.
v2, and the leak it closes. In our first version a grant lived at a record name derived from a hash of the recipient's published key. The ciphertext was never the leak — the record name was: anyone holding Anna's public key could test every name for grants to her. In v2 the wrapping key and the record name are derived from the same ECDH secret, separated by HKDF info strings and salted with ephPub ‖ recipientPub, from one ephemeral keypair per name published once at nextkey.eph. Be precise about what this buys: the records are still public and still countable by an indexer. What is no longer computable is the mapping — whether a given grant belongs to a given person, or to anyone in particular. One scalar multiplication yields both the address and the unwrapping key, which is why a Ledger is asked to sign once instead of twice.
Recovery without a stored file. The ephemeral private key can be re-derived from a deterministic wallet signature, so a name can be recovered with nothing but the wallet that created it. We tested this across two unrelated signer implementations: MetaMask published the key, viem reconstructed it, same 32 bytes, verified against the chain. Determinism here is measured, not assumed.
The release condition, in a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow. An autonomous agent can file a release request on chain under an ENS role that permits that one record on that one name and nothing else — it can propose, and it cannot act. The condition (guardian quorum, time lock, prolonged inactivity) is evaluated inside a Confidential Workflow on AWS Nitro, and the verdict carries the hash of the on-chain request it judged, so anyone can recompute that hash and confirm the enclave decided that request and not a modified one. scripts/release.mjs check performs that comparison and refuses to act when it fails — evidence/release-loop.log is a run where it fails on purpose. What leaves the enclave is a verdict and a coarse reason: quorum_not_met, never 1_of_2, because the distance to a threshold is itself useful to an attacker. Honest scope: CRE protects data during execution, not source code; the workflow is public, as it should be. And the guardian approvals in the fixture are stand-ins — the request is real and on chain, the people around it are not built yet.
The hacky part we are least sorry about. The playground writes real records on Sepolia for a visitor who has no wallet, no account and no ether: a disclosed demo key holds root roles on exactly one resolver, used only by a pool of lent names, and the page says so on its face. That is what makes the on-chain step reachable from a phone in forty seconds.
Where ENSv2 said no. We tried to delegate write access for grants with grantSetterRoles and could not: the role binds to the record key, but a v2 grant's key contains a tag that only comes into existence in the visitor's browser. Reproduced down to the revert selector — EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles, 0x4b27a133. It is written up as Finding 11 in FEEDBACK-ENS.md, together with the rest of our feedback on the beta deployment.
Two things that are unglamorous and saved the demo. A static host caches HTML and JS separately, so a page and its bundle drift; the symptom was Cannot set properties of null, which on a page about cryptography looks like broken cryptography. Every script tag now carries a content hash, and the bundle checks on load that the page matches it. And the site runs in nine languages with a merge tool and a checker, because a hand-edited 365 KB translation file is how one language quietly ends up a sentence short.

name: Coalition
description: Agents pool USDC to acquire shared compute and monetize unused capacity.
projectDescription:
Coalition lets AI agents pool money together to acquire shared compute they could not afford or efficiently use alone. It is a trustless coordination layer for funding, provisioning, and exchanging unused capacity.
The problem is simple: compute infrastructure is usually priced for one owner, while many AI agents only need a fraction of a server. A powerful GPU server can cost around $20/hour, yet several agents may each need only a small share. Renting separately is inefficient, while purchasing the full resource alone may be unaffordable. Coalition makes it possible for agents to coordinate a shared purchase and divide the resulting capacity.
Agents commit USDC toward a shared funding goal. Each commitment is locked in a smart contract, which tracks contributions and pays the compute provider once the pool reaches its target. If the funding goal is not reached before the deadline, participants can be refunded. This removes the need for a human intermediary to hold funds or manually settle a partially funded agreement.
Once the resource is acquired, a Go orchestrator running on the VPS provisions each participating agent with a Docker container and enforces its allocated CPU and memory limits. Agents can therefore share the same infrastructure while retaining isolated execution environments.
Coalition also addresses uneven resource usage. Agents may contribute equally but consume different amounts of the capacity they purchased. Instead of leaving unused capacity idle, an outside agent can purchase access to that spare capacity. The payment is settled atomically to the original participants according to the resale allocation, allowing agents that received less value from their initial contribution to recover more of their cost.
In the current implementation, the funding model uses equal upfront contributions, while resale redistributes value based on unused capacity. A future extension will allow agents to choose between paying upfront for guaranteed access and recovering unused capacity through resale, or waiting for more participants and paying according to their actual allocation.
ENS provides verified, human-readable agent identities tied to their funding wallets. The contract verifies that the ENS name resolves to the wallet participating in the pool, reducing the risk of impersonation or funding the wrong identity.
The Graph indexes pool state and events, allowing the dashboard and participating agents to track commitments, funding progress, settlement, and capacity transactions transparently. Multicall3 is used for atomic resale settlement.
Coalition turns “a group of AI agents want to share a resource” into an enforceable financial agreement: agents pool capital, smart contracts enforce the commitments, providers get paid automatically, unused capacity can be resold, and the economic history remains transparent and verifiable.
howItsMade:
Coalition is built as five cooperating programs: a Foundry Solidity ResourcePool contract on Arc, a viem-based TypeScript SDK, a Next.js dashboard, a stdlib-only Go orchestrator, and a The Graph subgraph.
The entire application is hosted on a VPS. We initially planned to deploy the Next.js application on Vercel, but Coalition requires persistent application-level state, long-running orchestration, access to the agent pool services, and coordination with the shared compute environment. Vercel's serverless and edge-oriented execution model was not suitable for that architecture, so we moved the Next.js application onto the same VPS as the orchestrator and compute services.
The VPS acts as the shared compute resource. Agents do not simply receive an on-chain entitlement; the Go orchestrator converts that entitlement into actual access to the VPS, allowing agents to run workloads inside Docker-enforced CPU and memory limits.
The on-chain core manages funding rounds, participant commitments, exact-fill settlement, deadlines, dropouts, forfeitures, and refunds. Each round is isolated by roundId. The filling commit settles inline and pays the provider automatically, while expired rounds use pull-based refunds. Dropouts forfeit their committed stake, and the contract records ERC-8004 reputation feedback for completion or dropout. The contract has no owner, upgradeability, or pause authority; the provider is only authorized to start rounds.
The TypeScript SDK is the shared integration layer. It uses viem for Arc interactions, keeps all USDC amounts as bigint atomic units, and handles the distinction between Arc's 18-decimal native USDC and 6-decimal ERC-20 USDC. It also integrates ENSv2 for identity resolution and ERC-8004 for agent identity and reputation.
The Next.js dashboard performs all on-chain writes through server-side route handlers. Circle Developer-Controlled Wallets create and control the agent wallets, execute USDC approvals and contract calls, and replace the need for local private-key management. Funding uses parallel approvals but strictly sequential commits so the final commit can trigger inline settlement. The resale flow uses Multicall3 to execute multiple USDC transferFrom payouts in one atomic transaction, preventing partial payment states. Circle App Kit handles treasury transfers, while Circle's x402 Gateway is integrated into a Next.js route through an Express-compatible middleware shim for quota payments.
The Go orchestrator is the bridge between blockchain settlement and real compute. It runs on the VPS, verifies an agent's purchased entitlement, reserves capacity, creates and manages Docker containers, and enforces CPU and memory limits. It maintains a concurrency-safe ledger, meters usage using integer micro-CU/MB accounting, confirms or rolls back reservations, and reaps workloads that exceed their budgets or lose authorization. This gives agents actual, controlled access to the shared VPS rather than merely recording resource ownership on-chain.
The resale market calculates prices from the funding pool's target and ranks sellers by how unevenly their contributed share has been used. It generates a fill plan whose payouts sum exactly to the quoted amount, with division dust distributed deterministically. Once payment is verified, the orchestrator provisions the corresponding compute entitlement on the VPS.
The Graph subgraph indexes pool commitments, settlements, dropouts, refunds, and reputation feedback. It is not just a dashboard data source: pool discovery, roster reads, and the autonomous resale decision loop depend on it. The agent loop fails closed when pool health is unavailable.
Several implementation details were particularly hacky. Because Circle Contracts on Arc rejects Shanghai PUSH0 bytecode, we pinned the Solidity build to the Paris EVM. Because existing subgraph indexing depended on legacy event shapes, we emit both legacy and round-scoped events in the same transaction, preserving compatibility while supporting isolated rounds. Because resale involves multiple payouts that must either all succeed or all fail, we use one Multicall3 aggregate for the USDC transfers, and the Go service verifies the receipt's transfer logs in order. Because floating-point accounting and concurrent reservations can introduce nondeterminism, we use integer metering, explicit NaN/Inf rejection, and last-claimant dust absorption to keep concurrency and refund accounting deterministic.
The result is a full path from agent identity and USDC commitment, through smart-contract settlement, to actual Docker-enforced workloads on a shared VPS and secondary-market resale of unused capacity.

name: T-REX Capital Market
description: Regulated capital markets on Arc, powered by Privy wallets and USDC.
projectDescription:
T-REX Capital Market is a tokenization platform for regulated digital assets, built for institutions, asset managers, issuers, and investors that want to bring financial products onchain while maintaining control over who can participate, hold, and transfer those assets.
Most institutional tokenization is not a purely permissionless DeFi problem. Institutions operate within legal and compliance frameworks, their users are often not crypto-native, and issuers need control over the full asset lifecycle. They need to know who owns an asset, restrict who can receive it, enforce investor limits, onboard legal entities through KYC/KYB, and manage issuance, investment, transfer, and redemption.
T-REX combines ERC-3643 regulated tokens, OnchainID identities, Privy embedded wallets, USDC settlement, and Arc into one institutional workflow.
Users onboard through a familiar Web2-style experience using email and KYC/KYB. Privy creates and manages an embedded wallet for the user, so they do not need MetaMask, seed phrases, or prior Web3 experience.
Once onboarded, an issuer can use the Token Issuance Wizard to configure and deploy an ERC-3643 regulated token on Arc Testnet. The issuer can define compliance rules such as jurisdiction restrictions, maximum investor balance, and maximum investor count. ERC-3643 enforces eligibility at the token layer, so only qualified identities can hold or receive the asset.
Eligible investors can discover an offering, subscribe using USDC, receive the corresponding regulated tokens, and later redeem their position back into USDC.
A wallet that does not satisfy the required identity or compliance conditions cannot participate, demonstrating that compliance is enforced onchain rather than only in the frontend.
USDC is used as the common payment and settlement asset for subscriptions and redemptions.
Arc is an intentional choice for T-REX because USDC is both our settlement asset and the native gas token on Arc. This creates a much simpler institutional experience. A user holding USDC to invest in a dollar-denominated financial product does not also need to acquire and manage a separate volatile gas token just to interact with the platform.
T-REX is not a hackathon-only proof of concept. It is a fully functional product that we intend to launch on Arc Mainnet.
T-REX also includes a wallet-management layer. Users can fund their Privy wallet through a fiat on-ramp and move USDC between Ethereum Sepolia and Arc Testnet using Circle CCTP, giving the platform both traditional and cross-chain capital entry rails.
T-REX is not limited to traditional real-world assets. The same regulated ownership framework can support private-market assets, tokenized funds, managed onchain portfolios, yield strategies, or other financial products that require an identified and permissioned investor base.
The result is a complete regulated capital-market workflow where identity, wallet onboarding, compliance, token issuance, stablecoin settlement, redemption, and cross-chain liquidity work together as one system.
howItsMade:
T-REX Capital Market is a web3 application built with React, Node.js, ERC-3643/T-REX, OnchainID, Privy, Arc, USDC, and Circle CCTP.
The React frontend provides separate issuer and investor workflows for onboarding, KYC/KYB, token issuance, investment, portfolio management, redemption, fiat funding, and cross-chain USDC transfers. Blockchain actions are signed through Privy embedded wallets, giving users a Web2-style experience without exposing private keys or requiring external wallets.
The Node.js backend acts as the orchestration layer between the application database, Privy, and smart contracts. It manages organizations, investors, compliance documents, token metadata, pricing, transaction records, and reconciliation. Application state and blockchain state are kept separate, with onchain activity treated as the authoritative source for asset ownership and transaction state.
The tokenization layer uses ERC-3643/T-REX. Each token is connected to its own IdentityRegistry and ModularCompliance configuration, so transfers, mints, and burns are permissioned based on investor identity and issuer-defined compliance rules.
We implemented reusable compliance modules including:

CountryRestrictModule
MaxBalanceModule
MaxInvestorsModule

These modules are deployed once and configured independently for each token instead of duplicating contract logic for every issuance. MaxInvestorsModule derives the investor count from actual token balances, keeping enforcement tied directly to onchain ownership.
Investor identity is managed through OnchainID. An IdFactory creates deterministic Identity contracts for wallets, while investor eligibility is represented through signed claims. KYC/KYB documents remain offchain, so sensitive personal information is not stored inside token contracts. The blockchain only needs the identity and claims required to determine whether an investor is eligible.
Privy provides email OTP authentication and embedded EVM wallets. Privy's ES256 identity token is verified server-side, and the embedded wallet becomes the signer for blockchain transactions. This allows institutional and non-crypto-native users to interact with onchain infrastructure without managing seed phrases or browser wallets, while Privy's programmable wallet controls provide additional safeguards for institutional workflows.
Purchases and redemptions are coordinated through a TREXPlatformController authorized as a token Agent.
For a purchase:

The investor approves USDC.
USDC transfers directly from the investor to the issuer.
The corresponding regulated tokens are minted to the eligible investor.

For a redemption:

The investor's regulated tokens are burned.
USDC is settled back to the investor using the issuer's approved allowance.

The controller coordinates the asset and settlement legs while ERC-3643 independently determines whether the investor is eligible to hold the regulated token.
T-REX smart contracts are deployed on Arc Testnet. USDC has two responsibilities in the system:

Payment and settlement for investments and redemptions.
Transaction fees on Arc.

This removes the need for institutional users to acquire an unrelated native token simply to pay gas.
The wallet-management interface integrates Circle CCTP for moving USDC between Ethereum Sepolia and Arc Testnet in both directions. This allows users to bring cross-chain USDC liquidity into T-REX and use the resulting balance directly for regulated investments and settlement.
Indexing and reconciliation services track token deployments, identities, claims, purchases, redemptions, and other blockchain events. This allows application state to be reconciled against, and reconstructed from, onchain activity.
T-REX is being built as a production product rather than a hackathon-only MVP. We are extending wallet support beyond Privy with WalletConnect, Safe, and MetaMask to support different institutional wallet requirements. After completing these integrations, the platform can be configured for Arc Mainnet and moved from the current testnet environment into production.
