name: Hunch
description: The prediction market that pays early conviction, not last-second bots. From our whitepaper to Arc.
projectDescription:
I'm Raj, founder of Hunch. This September we published a whitepaper, "The Vested Parimutuel", proposing a new way to settle prediction markets. For ETHOnline we took it from paper to production: the contract runs on Arc, Chainlink resolves it, The Graph indexes it, and humans and AI agents trade it through a live venue.
THE PROBLEM WE FOUND IN OUR OWN DATA
Pool-based prediction markets reward whoever shows up last. In a classic parimutuel pool, a dollar staked ten seconds before close earns the same payout as a dollar staked at open, when the answer was still uncertain. On Hunch's own tape (5,291 markets, 779,549 trades), winners who bet in the final 10% of a market's life took a median 70.1% of the losing pool, and early winners lost a median 38.7% of their payout to them.
THE MECHANISM
Each stake "vests" into the opposing side the moment it lands, and is only accepted up to the amount the other side can still cover. Anything above that is refunded immediately. Your payout is your stake plus whatever vested into your side after you entered, so early capital earns more and late capital earns less.
The paper proves the key properties (payouts sum to the pool exactly, and a stake placed after the last opposing money is paid exactly its principal), then replays the rule on the same real tape:

Last-decile winners' share of the losing pool: 70.1% → 0.08%
Early-winner dilution: 38.7% → 0.00%
Last-second bettors: paid 1.487× → exactly 1.000×
Market creators who seed every outcome: median +248.4% return, negative in 0 of 5,173 markets. Opening long-tail markets becomes a business, not a subsidy.
It settles in constant time: 130k to 315k gas per entry at any book size, against 5.5M for the naive loop at 1,000 opposing positions. We released 118 conformance test vectors with it, and they all pass in our CI.

WHY WE KNOW THIS MATTERS: HUNCH CUP
Hunch Cup is our prediction-market tournament for agents. Season 1 ran four weeks (July 8 to August 5, 2026) with paper money and a real $5,000 USDC prize pool on Base:

1,034,149 trades
7.68 billion pUSDC in paper volume
652,362 wallets, 470,983 of them trading
58,341 markets
469,886 agents vs 1,097 humans: 99.8% of traders were AI agents
Peak of 55,687 daily active wallets

That season taught us two things this project fixes. First, when 99.8% of the flow is agents, a pool that pays latency pays the fastest bot. The vested rule removes that edge. Second, an audit of our top 50 prize wallets found 47 belonged to just 4 operators. So agent identity here is tied to a verified human through World AgentKit: human-backed agents get higher limits, and farms don't.
WHAT'S LIVE

Contracts deployed and verified on Arc, settling in native USDC
Markets resolved by Chainlink Data Feeds, relayed onto Arc by a Chainlink CRE workflow, with no human resolver
A full trading venue: connect a wallet, see exactly how much of your stake will be accepted before you sign, enter, and claim
The Graph subgraphs that serve the book as decision data (remaining capacity, implied odds, projected payouts), plus an ERC-8004 agent-identity subgraph for Arc
An autonomous agent on a Circle Agent Wallet that researches, decides, trades and claims, paying for research with x402 nanopayments
An SDK, MCP server and SKILL so any AI agent can trade the venue
A classic parimutuel behind the same interface, so judges can see the same market settled both ways

The venue never holds user funds. The SDK only returns unsigned transactions, and invariant fuzzing proves no contract lets anyone move another user's money. More than 1,350 tests, one CI gate.
WHERE THIS GOES
Arc mainnet next. Then Hunch Cup Season 2 on this mechanism, settled on Arc, with prize eligibility tiered on human-backed identity. Then Hunch's whole agent API moves onto Arc without changing a single call for existing agents. Our goal is that when agents are most of the market, the market still pays the people who took the risk first.
Links:
Website: https://vpm.playhunch.xyz
Whitepaper: https://playhunch.xyz/vpm-whitepaper
Github: https://github.com/rajkaria/hunch-vpm
X: https://x.com/playhunchxyz
howItsMade:
It's a pnpm monorepo in three layers (settlement, indexing, agents), each usable without the ones above it, behind one gate: pnpm verify, which CI also runs.
FROM PAPER TO CONTRACT
VestedParimutuel.sol is the whitepaper's reference implementation, copied byte for byte. The paper's 118 conformance vectors run against it on every push, so any edit breaks the build. Every property we claim in the paper has a test: Conservation.t.sol proves payouts sum to the pool exactly, Mechanism.t.sol proves late stake is paid exactly 1×, and Gas.t.sol regenerates GAS.md, showing flat entry cost against a naive implementation that grows about 5,000 gas per opposing position.
SETTLEMENT (Solidity, Foundry, Arc)
On top of the mechanism I built:

MarketFactory: opens a market and commits its resolution rules in one transaction, so stake can never land before the rules exist
FeedResolver: feed, strike price, direction and staleness limit are hashed into the market ID, so nobody can change the rules after money is in. Anyone can trigger resolution, and the caller can't influence the result.
ClassicParimutuel: the rule Hunch runs today, behind the same interface, for side-by-side comparison
Swappable oracle adapters
A stale feed refuses to settle instead of voiding, and after a timeout anyone can void, so no market is ever stuck.

ARC + CIRCLE
USDC is Arc's gas token, so the asset you bet with is the asset you pay fees in. One catch I found on-chain: native USDC on Arc uses 18 decimals, but its ERC-20 interface uses 6, so the two views of one balance differ by 10^12. The agent holds funds in a Circle Agent Wallet, and the entity secret is passed in already encrypted, so the raw secret never enters the process. It pays for market research per request with x402 / Gateway Nanopayments.
CHAINLINK (the hacky part)
We started on Stork. Midway through, Stork's Arc testnet feeds stopped updating, and Arc testnet has no Chainlink Data Feeds. So I built a Chainlink CRE workflow: it reads BTC/USD and ETH/USD on Sepolia, reaches consensus across the DON, and delivers one signed report through Chainlink's KeystoneForwarder on Arc to our ChainlinkCreOracle. The adapter accepts only the production forwarder and one named workflow, keeps each feed's own timestamp so staleness reflects real feed age, and can lock its configuration. Oracles sit behind one interface, so the switch needed zero settlement changes. On mainnet, ChainlinkFeedOracle reads published feeds directly. A GitHub Actions keeper settles markets as they close, but anyone can.
THE GRAPH
Our subgraph doesn't just index events. It computes decisions in the mapping: remaining capacity per side, implied odds from accepted stake, vesting so far, and projected payouts. Agents and the venue read answers instead of redoing the math. I also pointed Agent0's standardized ERC-8004 schema at Arc's three registries, so one query covers agent identity and reputation on both Base and Arc. A Rust Substreams package streams market and position tables off the same events.
AGENTS + WORLD
@hunch-vpm/client gives typed reads and viem writes that never hold a key. On top sit three MCP tools and a SKILL that teaches any agent the mechanism. The agent's decide() is a pure function (no clock, no I/O) that returns every option it considered, so every trade can be audited. createArcRail exposes the same four verbs Hunch's existing agents already call (research, quote, positions, trade), so our off-chain book and Arc are swappable by config. World AgentKit checks AgentBook for a human behind each agent. Verified agents get higher rate limits and the full per-market cap, while anonymous agents still trade. This came straight from the Hunch Cup audit where 4 operators held 47 of the top 50 wallets.
FRONTEND (Next.js, wagmi/viem, Vercel)
This contract can accept only part of a stake: offer 1,000 and 340 goes in. No DEX UI handles that, so I designed the pattern from scratch. Before you sign, the stake panel shows accepted, refunded, and which side's capacity limited you. After you enter, the UI shows "the round hasn't closed yet", because the contract only splits stake in a later block. It never claims a fill it can't know yet.
CONTINUITY
Pre-existing: Hunch (live on Base), Hunch Cup, the whitepaper, its reference contract and its conformance vectors. Built during ETHOnline: everything else in the repo, including the Arc deployment, resolver, factory, oracles, CRE workflow, subgraphs, Substreams, SDK, MCP, SKILL, AgentKit tiering, agent, keeper and venue. The README has three commands a judge can run in about 60 seconds each.
More than 1,350 tests across Foundry, Vitest, Matchstick and Rust.

name: ModZero
description: Permissionless content protocol: stake, fingerprint, license & challenge — no moderator, just proof
projectDescription: ModZero is a decentralized content provenance and licensing platform that uses blockchain, fingerprinting, and watermarking to verify ownership, enable content licensing, handle disputes through community challenges, and provide transparent provenance without centralized moderators.
howItsMade: We built ModZero as a full-stack decentralized provenance and licensing protocol. Solidity smart contracts on Ethereum Sepolia handle content registration, staking, licenses, claims, challenges, posts, and wallet-native usernames. A TypeScript/Express backend with SQLite indexes the blockchain state and integrates Hedera HCS for ordered provenance events. The frontend uses React, Vite, Tailwind, wagmi and viem for wallet interactions. We use dHash + invisible LSB watermarking for content matching. A particularly hacky part is binding license payments to contentId + requester at the transaction-data level, then independently re-verifying the payment on-chain before issuing the license, preventing cross-content payment reuse and replay.

name: Glasshouse
description: Glasshouse runs sealed-bid auctions in 1inch SwapVM: highest bidder wins, pays the runner-up price.
projectDescription:
Glasshouse is an on-chain sealed-bid auction mechanism for allocating the right to fill orders based on participant valuation rather than identity or timing.
We compare three allocation gates on the same order: an allowlist, a time-based Dutch auction, and Glasshouse’s sealed-bid second-price auction. In Glasshouse, participants commit a hashed bid, reveal it during a defined window, and the highest bidder wins while paying the second-highest bid. The winner receives an exclusive window to fill the order; once it expires, anyone can fill at the base price.
Across the same participants, the allowlist required 10,000 bps of base, the Dutch auction 10,618 bps, and Glasshouse 9,756 bps. More importantly, Glasshouse was the only mechanism where the participant with the highest valuation received the fill.
The project also emphasizes reproducibility and honest measurement. Every published figure is tied to its underlying computation, with automated linting to prevent unsupported claims. Checks with no applicable data are explicitly reported as “not applicable” rather than treated as passes. The accompanying subgraph deliberately refuses to compute metrics such as market share, concentration indexes, or USD-denominated values when the contract does not emit sufficient data to support them.
howItsMade:
We built Glasshouse as a fully on-chain commit-reveal auction system integrated with 1inch Aqua on Base. GlasshouseBook is a standalone Solidity contract where commit stores a bid hash, reveal validates the bid, and settle determines the winner and second-price payment. It has no owner, admin, or upgrade path, and all parameters become immutable after a round opens. The contract is only 6,149 bytes, with CI enforcing the size limit.
The auction is exposed through a custom SwapVM instruction, opcode 0x2e, in a redeployed AquaSwapVMRouter connected to the official 1inch Aqua contracts. We use Aqua to run Glasshouse alongside its existing identity and Dutch-auction allocation gates, allowing us to benchmark all three mechanisms under identical conditions rather than making theoretical claims.
One of the more interesting engineering decisions was never re-implementing Aqua's order encoding in TypeScript. A Foundry fork test uses the upstream MakerTraitsLib and TakerTraitsLib against real Base state to generate the order encoding, which is then verified on chain before any transaction spends funds. We also use a LIVE_ROUND value in hook data to retry orders without changing semantic auction parameters.
For indexing, we built a Messari-conventions subgraph covering all GlasshouseBook events and added an off-chain derivation of the top-two bidding rule, publishing whether it matches the contract settlement. The subgraph deliberately avoids unsupported metrics such as USD values, TVL, market share, and concentration indexes when the emitted data cannot answer them.
The frontend is a fully static Next.js export with no backend or API key. It reads the contract directly through eth_call, while Vercel rewrites provide clean round and profile URLs. Bidding happens entirely in the browser using commit-reveal, with cryptographically secure salts stored and read back from localStorage before the wallet transaction begins.
Our strongest verification layer is an independent verify-run script that reads raw contract logs from any RPC and reconstructs every auction outcome without importing the contract, subgraph, or frontend implementation. It verified 9 auctions with 8 passed, 0 failed, and 0 not-applicable. A second verifier compared the published subgraph against the same independent replay across 135 fields, with every comparison agreeing. We also added provenance linting, chain-call budget tests, a Uniswap V3 QuoterV2 benchmark as an external pricing reference, and automated contract-size checks. The final test suite contains 97 Solidity tests, 59 JavaScript tests, and the provenance lint, all passing.

name: Mayarin
description: Programmable payments for humans, apps, and agents. Pay with anything, settle your way.
projectDescription:
Mayarin is a programmable payment and clearing platform for internet commerce, built around a simple idea: pay with what you have, settle in what you need.
Today, moving money across digital assets and blockchain networks still requires users and businesses to think about wallets, tokens, liquidity, swaps, networks, gas, and settlement paths. Mayarin abstracts that complexity behind a unified payment flow and simplify fragmented UI/UX for everyone.
A payer whether a human, application, or autonomous AI agent creates a payment intent describing what needs to be paid. Mayarin handles the underlying process of discovering the payment context, determining an appropriate route, executing asset conversion when necessary, and settling the recipient in their preferred asset.
For ETHOnline, we are extending Mayarin with agentic payments and intelligent payment routing. The Graph provides onchain data and context used by the payment flow, Uniswap provides liquidity and asset conversion for execution, and Arc provides stablecoin settlement infrastructure. Rather than treating these as separate integrations, Mayarin orchestrates them as parts of a single end-to-end payment lifecycle.
We are also exploring how autonomous software can transact safely without simply giving an AI agent unrestricted control over a wallet. Mayarin introduces programmable payment authority, allowing applications and agents to operate within defined spending policies while the platform handles execution and settlement underneath.
Our long-term goal is to make the underlying payment rail an implementation detail. Customers should be able to pay using the assets and networks available to them, merchants should be able to choose how they receive settlement, and software should be able to participate in commerce through the same programmable infrastructure.
Mayarin is being developed as a real product beyond ETHOnline. The hackathon is being used to build and validate substantial new capabilities around agentic payments, routing, liquidity execution, and stablecoin settlement on top of the existing Mayarin foundation.
howItsMade:
Mayarin lets a payer pay with whatever supported asset they hold while the merchant receives the exact stablecoin amount they configured. The core abstraction is the PaymentIntent, which keeps four concerns separate that most payment systems collapse into one: the payer's asset, the payment network, the execution route, and the merchant's settlement asset.
The engineering core is the exact-output cross-asset flow. The merchant's settlement amount is locked first, Uniswap derives the payer-side maximum backwards from that fixed output, and the payer signs a bounded input with any residue refunded. A payment only advances after the on-chain receipt is read back and matched against the expected token, recipient, and amount successful transaction submission is never treated as proof of payment.
Partner integrations
The Graph, the settlement indexer queries Subgraph Studio with typed GraphQL for PaymentCompleted, ResidueRefunded, and rail observations, tracking _meta.block.number as its cursor instead of relying on direct RPC log scans. This matters most on Arc Testnet, where fast block production and RPC log-range limits make naïve polling unreliable.
Uniswap, the liquidity and execution layer. Both V3 and V2 venues implement one SwapVenue port: on V3, QuoterV2's quoteExactOutputSingle prices the leg and Mayarin encodes SwapRouter02.exactOutputSingle; on V2-style pools — including the Arc Testnet EURC/USDC pair — getAmountsIn prices it and swapTokensForExactTokens executes. Either way the merchant's settlement amount is the fixed side and the payer's spend is the bounded one.
Arc, supported as a stablecoin payment and settlement rail: chain configuration, USDC decimal behavior, wallet balances, deposit monitoring, PaymentRouter execution, and settlement confirmation on Arc Testnet.
x402 agent payments, an AI agent receives a machine-readable payment requirement, signs one EIP-3009 authorization, and Mayarin verifies, broadcasts, confirms, and settles it through the same clearing engine. No account creation, no gas management on the agent side.
Architecture, ports and adapters. Domain packages own the payment-intent lifecycle, quote locking, routing, clearing, the double-entry ledger, idempotency, and the settlement state machine. RPC providers, wallets, subgraphs, liquidity venues, and databases plug in as replaceable adapters.
Stack are Bun, Hono, Zod, PostgreSQL + Drizzle, viem. Solidity and Foundry for the PaymentRouter, deposit forwarders, and settlement flows. Astro and React for the merchant dashboard and checkout.
The flow that happens in the behind :
payer asset → quote and route → bounded execution → confirmed settlement → ledger and merchant receipt

name: Copy Check
description: Is that wallet worth copying? Scored after gas, and only on trades it makes after you find it.
projectDescription:
Copy-trading tools rank wallets by win rate and total PnL. Both mislead.
One wallet we tracked closed 68 trades at a 38% win rate and still showed +0.033 ETH after gas. Remove its single largest winning trade and it became -0.083 ETH — to copy it profitably you had to be inside one specific trade, which is a timing problem, not a wallet-selection problem. Another wallet sat at -0.00001 ETH before gas and -0.00197 ETH after: 99% of the loss was gas.
Copy Check scores a wallet under three rules the code enforces rather than merely documents:


Forward-only. Registering a wallet pins the current block, permanently. Trades before that block are discarded and counted separately. A score computed over a wallet's past is a number you chose after seeing the answer.


Gas is measured, not estimated. Measured gas per swap ranged 0.000030-0.003157 ETH, a 104x spread. Receipts that fail to fetch stay null and are counted — never filled with zero.


Drop the single best trade. If a wallet only survives with its best trade included, it is reported as one-hit dependent, not as a pass.


The tool also refuses to answer. It returns "withheld" when gas was not retrieved, "too few" under 20 closed round-trips, and skips bots entirely. A judgment without evidence is worse than a wrong one, because you cannot tell it is wrong.
howItsMade:
Python standard library only — no framework, no database, no server. The boundary that matters: verdict.py knows nothing about data sources. It takes a list of swaps, so it runs and self-tests with no API key and no network.
Data comes from The Graph. We query the Uniswap v3 Ethereum subgraph for a wallet's swaps, then translate raw amount0/amount1 sign pairs into buy/sell decisions. Several things only measurement revealed: urllib's default User-Agent is blocked by Cloudflare with error 1010 before authentication is even reached; nested filters (transaction_: {blockNumber_gte}) take 40s and fail with "bad indexers" where timestamp_gte returns in 1.7s; ascending order silently truncates busy wallets, so we page newest-first and stop at the pinned block; and skip is capped at 5000, so the candidate scanner pages by timestamp cursor instead.
transaction.gasUsed ships as 0, so tx hashes come from The Graph and gas comes from public RPC receipts with 12 parallel workers — 8.7 minutes of sequential lookups became 8.7 seconds. Per-wallet scoring went from 270-450s to 4.5-7.4s.
The UI is a single static HTML file generated from the verdict JSON, with inline SVG icons and zero external requests, so it deploys anywhere and opens offline.
Added during ETHOnline: a candidate finder that is blind to past profit by construction (it never reads prices, and counts round-trips by quantity alone), bot-fleet detection by token-basket fingerprint — found after seven addresses turned out to trade an identical basket to stay under the per-address bot threshold — a public live page, and daily automated re-scoring.

name: Wizard
description: Confidential B2B Campaign Factory using Privy and Chainlink Workflows on Base
projectDescription:
The problem:
Cross-brand co-marketing ("spend $10 at Brand A, earn Y redeemable at Brand Z") gets negotiated constantly and built bilaterally, and every new partner pair means a new integration. That's months of engineering per partnership, upfront cost turned into permanent CapEx, and lock-in to whichever partner's API you built first. It also forces two competitors to share raw customer transaction data or stand up a joint PII pipeline just to answer "did this customer qualify?". And even when the integration exists, someone still reconciles receipts by hand at period end, against a ledger of record that belongs to one of the two companies, so neither side gets a proof the other has to believe.
Blockchain doesn't obviously fix this. Public chains are a non-starter: purchase data is personal data, it can't sit on a public ledger, and per-customer claim events leak the customer graph. Permissioned chains demand infrastructure most brands don't run, and still leave the ledger in somebody's custody.
What we built:
Wizard replaces the bilateral integration with one shared on-chain factory plus confidential verification in a hardware enclave. A master CampaignFactory  on Base Sepolia is the campaign clone generator: every campaign is an EIP-1167 clone of a shared CampaignEscrow, with terms fixed at launch, such as reward mechanic (percent rateBps or flat value), minimum spend, per-user cap with a calendar-anchored reset window (lifetime / day / week / month / year, span-N periods, anchor weekday, reset time-of-day), per-transaction cap, campaign-wide issuance cap, allowed days of the week (UTC bitmask), campaign start/end window, redeemable cashback vs. discount proof-of-savings, and a 2-party operating-cost split in basis points.
Purchase payloads don't go to a partner's server or a shared database. They're submitted to a Chainlink CRE Confidential Workflow by HTTP trigger into an attested TEE enclave. Inside the enclave the workflow reads the campaign's terms on-chain from the factory at request time (so new campaigns are picked up with zero workflow redeploys), evaluates the payload against them using the same clamp order the contract uses (per-tx cap → per-user cap → campaign-wide cap), and holds the one partner-held secret the Vault DON releases into the enclave: a master key used to derive a single-use claim nullifier H(HMAC(master, campaignId) || userAnchor || timestamp). Raw payload facts, such as spend amount, item detail, prior earnings never leave the enclave. Only the verdict does (runtime logs currently exist, in production they wouldn’t).
On approval the enclave submits an execution proof via evm.write  through the CRE Forwarder to the campaign's escrow on Base Sepolia. The escrow is not a passive log: it independently re-derives the earn and reverts InvalidReport  unless the delivered points match bitwise, mints the ERC-1155 reward to the customer's wallet, and burns the nullifier, so a forged, replayed, or float-corrupted report cannot settle. Company B never sees Company A's customer records or transaction logs. It sees a settled on-chain claim against an escrow whose terms it agreed to, and it authorizes redemption on its own campaigns. Customer identity is a Privy embedded wallet created from an email OTP, so the customer manages no seed phrase and the merchant stores no password; the deposit handshake (each company funding its share of the operating deposit) is verified on-chain by exact sender, recipient, and wei amount before the campaign contract is ever deployed.
Why the alternatives don't work:
Bilateral APIs: CapEx per partner, vendor lock-in, and full data sharing. CDP/loyalty SaaS (Segment, Braze, mParticle, LoyaltyLion): they unify customer data beautifully by requiring the data to move into a shared processor, which is exactly the thing two competitors can't agree to. Affiliate/offer networks and receipt-parsing reward apps: they can verify a purchase without a bilateral integration, but the trust sits in the network's own database, reconciliation is still manual, and settlement isn't programmatic. Public-chain settlement: leaks personal data. Permissioned chains: infrastructure burden, and a single custodian. Zero-knowledge proofs: the right cryptographic answer and the wrong 2026 economics at retail volumes, where there are proving cost, circuit work per campaign shape, plus you still need a trusted path for the input data. Confidential workflows are the practical middle: the privacy claim is honest and bounded (pseudonymous-but-linkable, not zero-knowledge; the enclave's trust assumption is hardware attestation), and the settlement side gets a proof that neither brand has to be trusted to produce.
Where it goes (how the app would look like in production):
(1) N-party campaigns. The contracts already accept an arbitrary participant set and per-participant fee shares; the wizard exercises the 2-party case today. (2) One reward token across many campaigns, so a brand's points are a single fungible balance instead of campaign-scoped coupon tokens (the ERC-1155 minter role is already per-escrow, so this is an authorization change, not an architecture change). (3) Batch settlement at the merchant ingress to allow one DON consensus round for N receipts instead of N rounds, with a multi-claim report format on the escrow; this is what makes retail-volume economics work at all. (4) A merchant SDK that mirrors the rule gates client-side so obviously-ineligible transactions are never submitted (advisory only, the enclave stays authoritative). (5) Redemption privacy: batchRedeem(bytes32[] commitments) so the chain enforces supply conservation without learning who redeemed what. (6) Production gas: an ERC-4337 paymaster (e.g. CDP or Coinbase Developer Platform) sponsoring gas and settling in USDC, so companies never hold ETH, plus per-campaign workflow deployments for pause/upgrade isolation and per-campaign blast radius on trigger keys. (7) Production identity and authorization. Privy access tokens verified server-side and wallets bound to authenticated company accounts which also kills the demo's first-mover deposit-spoofing hole plus policies as enforced spend limits, and B's wallet as the escrow's authorized redeemer. Beyond that, Privy key quorums are what turn the platform's single relay key into a real org authorization model: an m-of-n threshold over authorization keys and user identities, enforced inside Privy's TEE infrastructure, with one level of quorum nesting so a "Brand Finance" quorum can sit inside an "Org Admins" quorum. Concretely, the demo's redemption authority (one EOA) becomes a 2-of-2 quorum, the reward company's wallet and the platform's server key must both co-sign, so neither side can unilaterally move reward funds, and the genuinely high-value operations (launch with a new fee split, raise a nearly-exhausted redeem cap, migrate a live campaign) become quorum-gated rather than single-signer. This composes with the on-chain story rather than duplicating it: Privy gates who may instruct the wallet, the escrow still gates what the chain will accept.
How it makes money:
Primary: a per-settled-redemption platform fee on volume tiers (e.g. $0.02 → $0.012 as monthly redeemed volume goes 5k → 625k+; more detail in project README.md), billed monthly in USDC. The per-claim cost is nearly fixed (DON consensus is the dominant term, not gas), so the discount is real margin management, not a pricing lever. Secondary lines: a dedicated-workflow premium (own registry entry, keys, and execution lane; the prerequisite for per-campaign pause), settlement-speed tiers (Standard 2,000tx/30min as the default batch, up to Real-time per-transaction at a ~2.5× multiplier), a flat campaign-migration fee for amending a live campaign (pause → redeploy with amended terms → migrate ledger → resume, $50–250), an opt-in per-campaign analytics add-on ($20–50/campaign/month, gated on explicit company consent, built from the verdict lifecycle data the platform already observes for billing), and an optional managed ingestion service for companies with no message broker. Operating deposits are custody, not revenue. Unspent balances are refunded, net of any covered debt.
howItsMade:
Stack at a glance:
Solidity 0.8.28 + Foundry + OpenZeppelin v5.1 (EIP-1167 clones, ERC-1155) for the contracts; Chainlink CRE (@chainlink/cre-sdk 1.18, TypeScript) for confidential verification; bun + Hono + postgres.js + zod for the backend; Vite + React + TypeScript for the frontend; Postgres 16 in Docker locally and Neon in the deployed environment; Base Sepolia for settlement; Privy for identity and wallet signing. Deployment is split frontend/backend on Vercel with Neon as the database. Everything is wired through one Makefile (make db-up, make test, make typecheck) so a fresh clone runs with three commands.
The request path, end to end:
A purchase starts as a JSON payload {campaignId, userAnchor, merchantId, amountSpent, timestamp, earnedInWindow}. The backend relays it, signs it, sends using CRE HTTP trigger, which fires an attested enclave. Inside the enclave, the workflow reads the campaign's terms live from the factory on-chain (evmClient.callContract → factory campaigns(id) → escrow), so new campaigns need zero workflow redeploys; if the campaign has a campaign-wide cap it also reads campaignTotalEarned()  from the escrow rather than trusting any caller-supplied number. It then evaluates eligibility: window, min-spend, day-of-week, per-tx cap, per-user cap, campaign cap; in exactly the clamp order the contract uses, derives the claim nullifier from a Vault-released secret, and crosses back to the DON for consensus. The DON signs the report and writeReport  pushes it through the Chainlink forwarder to the escrow's onReport, which re-derives the earn itself and reverts InvalidReport  unless the delivered points match bitwise, mints the ERC-1155 reward, and burns the nullifier. The frontend then confirms by reading the escrow's on-chain ledger rather than trusting any HTTP response.
Chainlink CRE and how it's actually used:
This is the part I'd call the heart of the project. The workflow is a single HTTP-triggered cre.handlerInTee(...)  handler running on { tee: 'nitro', regions: ['us-west-2'] } (currently deployed to Chainlink private registry), serving every campaign from one binary via a campaigns map in config. Three CRE capabilities do the work: runtime.getSecret()  pulls CAMPAIGN_NULLIFIER_MASTER  from the Vault DON straight into the enclave (never exposed to node operators or workflow-DON memory); the EVM client does the on-chain term reads; and runtime.usingTheDons() → donRuntime.report({encoderName: 'evm', signingAlgo: 'ecdsa', hashingAlgo: 'keccak256'}) → writeReport()  produces the DON-consensus, DON-signed report. The confidentiality is structural: raw purchase facts (amountSpent, items, earnedInWindow) are evaluated inside the enclave and never leave it, only the verdict and a one-way nullifier are written on-chain. Trigger auth is ECDSA: every request must carry an authorized-key signature (KEY_TYPE_ECDSA_EVM), so merchants authenticate to the platform with API keys and never touch a key.
What CRE bought us:
Before confidential workflows, the honest options for cross-brand verification were "share the data" (a non-starter between competitors) or "stand up a ZK proving pipeline" (real cryptographic cost per campaign shape, plus a trusted input path). CRE lets a purely stateless evaluator hold a partner-held secret and produce a settlement-grade proof, without the platform ever seeing the raw data. It also gave the project its cleanest architectural constraint: because the enclave can read on-chain state, the campaign rules live in one place (the factory), and the workflow never needs redeployment to learn new campaigns.
Privy and how it's actually used:
Privy covers the entire identity-and-money surface. Customers and companies onboard with email OTP and get an embedded wallet, meaning no seed phrase, and no password stored anywhere. Two flows ride on it: the deposit handshake, where each company connects its Privy wallet and sends its share of the operating deposit via eth_sendTransaction  (40:60 split → A sends 0.004 ETH, B 0.006 ETH), and the backend verifies each deposit on-chain, like the exact sender, exact recipient, exact wei, confirmed receipt, all before the campaign contract is even deployed; and the reward redemption, which is personal_sign  over a human-readable statement ("Redeem 1.40 points from 0x… on campaign #5 (DayOfWeek Test) as Globex Books"), verified server-side by recovering the signer. The escrow does not exist until both deposits land, which makes Privy the actual activation switch for a campaign rather than a login screen.
What was particularly hacky:

Hand-rolling the CRE trigger JWT. Before the SDK exposed a client for firing deployed workflows, I reverse-engineered the gateway's signing scheme and reimplemented it byte-identically: alg: 'ETH' JWT, digest = sha256  of the body with keys sorted lexicographically at every nesting level, r||s||recoveryId  base64url with yParity normalization. It's the difference between workflows.execute  returning ACCEPTED and returning nothing at all.
Discovering the report encoding the hard way. Wrapping the payload in onReport(...)  calldata made the escrow see a 356-byte "report" that failed its length check; the working shape is a bare abi.encode(nullifier, recipient, amountSpentWei, eligible, pointsWei).
A verdict transport that doesn't exist on Vercel. Execution status lives behind the cre CLI, which can't run in a lambda. So the frontend was rewired to confirm claims by watching the escrow's own Claim  events, with a backend probe that detects CRE-CLI availability and skips polling when it's absent. The on-chain ledger became the source of truth.
Two id namespaces. Postgres row ids and the factory's sequential on-chain campaign ids are different numbers, and the workflow only knows the latter. So the payload route forwards the on-chain id, and the campaigns list verifies factory membership (escrow address match) to hide stale rows from superseded factory generations.
The contract suite enforces calendar-anchored cap windows (day/week/N-week/month/year) with Hinnant's civil-date algorithm implemented in uint256 to avoid an oracle, and the escrow advertises IReceiver  via a bare 0x805f2132  interface id (inherited IERC165  functions are excluded from type(IReceiver).interfaceId)

Tools and AI disclosure:
Built with Hermes Desktop as the harness, using GLM 5.3 Flash (code writing, README) and DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 (technical spec and demo outline consolidation), full breakdown in AI_ATTRIBUTION.md. AI did the writing, cross-layer inconsistency checking between frontend/CRE/contracts, contract logic, test cases, and frontend boilerplate; I did the project and rule design, scope boundaries, naming, test-case design, production roadmap, and the CRE workflow deployment. Testnet ETH came from the ETHGlobal faucet. Local state runs Postgres 16 in Docker (docker compose up -d, port 5433); the deployed app runs on Vercel with Neon Postgres.
Verification, so the claims are checkable:
67 Foundry tests (claim, caps, window resets including N-week anchors and DOW gates, redeem, redeemer whitelist, factory wiring), 27 workflow tests (3 demo campaigns × 5 payloads), and a backend suite covering launch validation, DOW-mask mapping, and wei conversion — all run by make test. The earn→redeem loop is live on Base Sepolia, with the relay authorized per-campaign via the factory's setCampaignRedeemer passthrough.

name: Barker ALM Engine
description: Yield-backed automated liquidity: v4 take-profit ladders on Arc + a vault-backed 1inch Aqua maker
projectDescription:
A market maker's backing capital normally sits idle — it has to be there to honour a quote, so it does nothing else. Barker ALM Engine attacks that from two directions, on two venues, with one engine.
Arc leg — Uniswap v4 on Circle's Arc. A one-sided concentrated liquidity range is an execution primitive, not a yield position. Funded only in the base asset and placed above spot, it is an automatic take-profit ladder: as price rises through it, the position converts to USDC — and it collects trading fees the whole time it waits, which a resting limit order does not. A fully crossed range sells at the geometric mean of its bounds, which is worse than a limit order at the top; the fee is what pays for the difference. For exact-input swaps a crossed range realises geometricMean / (1 − fee). On Arc testnet we measured +0.3008% over the geometric mean on a 0.30% pool, against a predicted +0.3009% — exact to one part in a million.
The Arc leg runs on Arc testnet: a position manager, a dynamic-fee v4 hook, and an unattended keeper. Three full lifecycles are on chain; the second was closed by the keeper on its own key, with the USDC paid straight to the owner. The keeper also found a real bug in our hook: it billed one trade 2.46% for the previous swap's price impact, made four days earlier. We fixed it, redeployed, and replayed the same move on chain — charged 0.30%. Mainnet deployment follows Arc's mainnet launch on Sep 16.
Aqua leg — 1inch SwapVM. A maker whose inventory sits in an ERC-4626 vault (steakUSDC) earning yield while it quotes. A solvency guard caps every quote at what the vault can actually redeem, and settlement hooks redeem just in time for a payout and re-deposit what comes in, inside the swap. Return = vault APY + spread, and the maker never quotes a fill it cannot settle. Proven on an Ethereum mainnet fork against live steakUSDC.
Both legs are on one live dashboard: https://barkermoney.github.io/barker-alm-engine/
This is a Continuity Track entry. Prior work is documented rather than hidden: a pre-hackathon feasibility probe sits unmodified in the initial commit, clearly marked, and everything after it is hackathon work visible in the git history. The proprietary strategy parameters are deliberately not in the repository — what is open is the execution layer. We kept feedback logs for Uniswap and 1inch as we built, including three of our own claims that we retracted in public when our indexer proved them wrong.
howItsMade:
Uniswap v4 is the execution primitive, not a bolt-on. BarkerV4Positions drives the PoolManager directly through unlock/unlockCallback into modifyLiquidity, settling with flash accounting (sync/settle/take) and deriving each position's salt from a registry id so two positions on the same range never collide. We deliberately built without v4-periphery.
Two safety properties are the point of the contract. One-sidedness is enforced, not assumed: open rejects a range straddling spot by comparing against the live tick, then re-checks after the fact that the pool debited only one asset — the pool's own accounting, not ours. Custody stays with the position owner: a keeper may close and collect, but can never name a different recipient, so the worst a compromised keeper does is close a position early into its owner's own wallet.
BarkerDynamicFeeHook carries AFTER_INITIALIZE | BEFORE_SWAP, deployed via CREATE2 salt mining with our own miner (HookMiner lives in periphery, which we do not depend on). In beforeSwap it measures the previous swap's price impact, dates it to the block that swap happened in, and returns an LP fee override that decays linearly over 300 blocks. The constructor checks its own address against the required flags, because a mis-mined salt otherwise yields a hook that deploys, verifies, and is silently never called.
Automation is a TypeScript keeper (viem) over a v4 event indexer. v4 keeps every pool in one singleton, so a pool's history is Initialize/ModifyLiquidity/Swap plus extsload of slot0. The exit rule is a pure function of a snapshot, must hold for three consecutive observations, and runs on its own key. The dashboard runs the same indexer code in the browser (Vite + viem, no backend, no wallet).
Arc (Circle) shaped the tooling. Arc pays gas in USDC, and its USDC is a native precompile behind an ERC-20 shell that Foundry's EVM does not implement. Since forge script simulates the entire script before broadcasting, a USDC-touching script broadcasts nothing while printing success. So Foundry does the arithmetic and the pure deployments, and cast sends everything that moves tokens. Arc's public node also caps eth_getLogs at roughly 25–30k blocks, so the indexer halves its page on rejection.
1inch Aqua / SwapVM is extended through its two official extension points rather than forked. An Extruction guard caps quoted depth at min(virtual reserve, liquid + redeemable, allowance) and scales both reserves together, so it trims depth without moving the price — SwapVM's ship() does not itself verify that a maker can cover its quote. IMakerHooks does redeem-on-fill and redeposit-on-receive against the ERC-4626 vault. It runs on the signature track, because capital held in the Aqua ledger stops earning. Because SwapVM is source-available copyleft, that code lives in its own directory under SwapVM-1.1, while everything else stays MIT.
103 tests: 43 Foundry tests against a real PoolManager, 45 on SwapVM (11 on an Ethereum mainnet fork against live steakUSDC), 15 for the keeper. The notable part is what the tests missed. Our indexer and dashboard, reading real data, caught errors every test had passed: a feesOwed view off by 2^128; a hand-copied figure that had us crediting a 0.048% gap to "v4 rounding" (there was no gap); our claim that v4's Swap event omits an overridden fee (it carries it); a solvency guard that moved the price instead of the depth; and the fee-hook bug above. Each is fixed or publicly retracted in FEEDBACK.md and FEEDBACK-1INCH.md.

name: two field
description: Developers' AI agent hires other specialist agents for specialized tasks.
projectDescription:
twofield is an agentic marketplace where the buyers' existing coding or research agent hires specialist agents for scoped jobs, instead of working on those projects themselves. A mistake in a specialized research task, which the buyers' agent is not skilled at, can lead to a series of incorrect assumptions and decisions.
Instead, a developer can provide a buyer agent with a budget for specialized tasks and the agent browses specialists, files a brief, and funds an ERC-8183 escrow on Circle's Arc testnet. The specialist does the work, submits it, and the developer or the developer's agent rates it.
A good rating pays the specialist agent at once. A poor rating holds escrow for a human review by twofield, and the verdict lands on the ERC-8004 Validation Registry under the specialist's onchain identity.
Every specialist carries an ERC-8004 identity and an onchain reputation score built from real ratings, and a specialist can also be tried for a few cents through a metered x402 preview before you commit to a full job. The buyer never touches a seed phrase, a gas fee, or a private key.
howItsMade:
The frontend is Next.js with TypeScript and Tailwind. Route handlers under the same app act as the backend, since Privy's server SDK is Node only. Neon Postgres with Drizzle ORM tracks agents, jobs, ratings, and receipts.
Every buyer and seller agent gets its own Privy server wallet, owned by an app controlled authorization key so the backend can sign for agents without holding a private key itself. Each wallet carries a Privy policy that whitelists exactly the contract calls that agent may make, capped by its budget, the real enforcement layer rather than trust.
On Circle's Arc testnet, hiring opens an ERC-8183 escrow job, the specialist submits a hash of its work, and the buyer rates it 1 to 5. A good rating settles escrow at once. A poor rating holds funds and hands the case to a review queue, whose verdict is written to the ERC-8004 Validation Registry under the specialist's identity, so a dispute outcome is not just a database row. Ratings also feed the ERC-8004 Reputation Registry, so a specialist's score is real onchain history, not a marketing claim.
The metered preview uses x402, settled by an in process facilitator since public facilitators do not yet cover Arc, with the platform wallet as relayer. Deliverables come from the specialist agent, from the brief and any files the buyer attaches.

name: Frely-Network
description: From know-how to revenue. Frely turns prompts, Skills & Agents into a business.
projectDescription:
Many domain experts, especially experienced developers, have accumulated valuable Prompts, Skills, Agents, and professional workflows, but these capabilities are difficult to turn into revenue. Creators either publish their work for free and risk having it copied and repackaged, or keep it on personal devices and in private environments, where it cannot serve more users. As a result, AI capabilities that create real productive value lack an effective path to commercialization.
Frely aims to solve this problem by helping creators turn their Skills and Agents into paid services while keeping their core Prompts, code, and workflows private. Creators sell access to their capabilities rather than giving away their intellectual assets. Users and AI Agents can discover these capabilities, purchase access, and use them in their own workflows.
Frely and Frely Swarm already provide the Web2 infrastructure for capability execution and service delivery. For ETHOnline, we are building Frely Network, the Web3 commercial layer that enables open and verifiable identity, service, and transaction relationships between creators, users, and Agents.
In a Web2 marketplace, the identity of AI capabilities, transaction relationships, and marketplace data exist inside a platform’s private database. Frely Network makes these commercial relationships verifiable, queryable, and usable across applications. It also allows AI Agents to act as independent participants that can discover and purchase capabilities from other Agents.
The project integrates ENS, Hedera, x402, and The Graph to provide Web3 infrastructure for the identity, transactions, and discovery of AI capabilities.
Our goal is not to build another Skill-sharing website. We want valuable AI know-how to generate commercial returns and give creators a reason to connect their professional capabilities to the broader AI ecosystem.
howItsMade:
Frely Network is built on top of the existing Frely and Frely Swarm infrastructure. Frely provides the user-facing service access and product layer, while Frely Swarm hosts and executes Skills, Agents, and workflows. For ETHOnline, we built Frely Network as an open network layer for onchain identity, service registration, capability discovery, payments, and commercial relationships.
We do not move the Agent itself onchain. Skills, Prompts, Agent code, and runtime environments remain in the existing offchain execution layer, while the blockchain stores identity and service information that should be publicly verifiable. This protects the creator’s core capability while giving Provider identity, service endpoints, capability claims, and payment results a verifiable foundation.
When a creator publishes a Skill or Agent, Frely Network generates a validated Provider Manifest, writes the relevant information into ERC-8004 Registration Metadata, and stores the service endpoint in the ENS Resolver. ENS provides readable names for Providers and Agents, while ERC-8004 stores the Agent ID and registration information. The Network cross-checks ENS, ERC-8004, and the public Agent Card to verify that the discovered service, onchain identity, and Agent all refer to the same Provider.
The payment layer uses Hedera and x402. We treat AI capabilities as network services that can be paid for per call. When a user or Agent requests a paid capability, the system first retrieves a quote and checks the available budget, then uses x402 on Hedera to verify payment conditions. Settlement happens after successful execution, and every execution uses a unique execution ID to prevent duplicate payments. This allows an Agent to act as an independent consumer and complete the full “discover → verify → pay → invoke” flow without a traditional subscription or checkout page.
The Graph indexes onchain registration data. Frontends and Agents can search for candidate Providers based on capability and registration metadata without scanning the chain directly. The Graph is used for candidate discovery, the ENS Resolver is an important verification source for service endpoints, and the Agent Card describes supported protocols, input types, and invocation methods. If a Graph query fails, identities do not match, the service endpoint is invalid, or the Agent Card cannot be verified, the system fails closed and does not continue with the service call or payment.
After verification and payment checks, Frely passes the request to Frely Swarm, which executes the actual Skill or Agent. Settlement is completed after successful execution, and the result is returned to the caller. The system is therefore split into two parts: the offchain layer securely hosts and executes private AI capabilities, while Frely Network handles open and verifiable identity, discovery, payments, and commercial relationships.
One notable design choice is that creators do not need to rebuild an existing Skill or Agent as a full Web3 application. A private Skill can keep its existing execution model and connect through Frely to gain onchain identity, discovery, and payment capabilities. To the consumer, it still behaves like a normal AI service. To an Agent, it becomes an external capability that can be discovered, verified, purchased, and composed.

name: lpTOKEN.fun
description: LP positions you can trade like tokens. One token, two ways to trade it. Built on Uniswap v4.
projectDescription:
lpTOKEN.fun makes a Uniswap v4 LP position tradable like a token. That gives traders two ways to trade one token. Hold the token itself for price. Or hold its lpTOKEN, a share of the pool. It still moves with price, and it also collects the pool's trading fees into its NAV. One asset, two positions, and you pick the side.
Under the hood, a vault owns one full range v4 position, and the vault contract is itself the lpTOKEN ERC-20. Every share is a claim on the same position, so shares are fungible. Mint with both sides, zap in with one asset, redeem anytime, or send it like any other token.
Before ETHOnline, lpTOKEN.fun was live on Robinhood Chain and Base, including stock token markets, so lpAAPL is a position you can hold instead of AAPL. During the event we took the stack to Arc mainnet. Arc's native currency is USDC, so an lpTOKEN there is dollar denominated. That needed a new zap router: on Arc, native USDC and ERC-20 USDC are one balance with different decimals, and there is no WETH style wrapper. More than a dozen new lpTOKEN markets went live during the event, including the first ones on Arc.
Ethereum mainnet is still in development as we submit. Our plan is to ship it before the hackathon ends, so existing v4 pools on Ethereum can get an lpTOKEN too.
howItsMade:
The whole problem is making a Uniswap v4 position behave like a token. Everything else follows from that.
A market is one static fee v4 pool. On a platform launch the pool is opened behind a hook that declares exactly one permission, beforeInitialize, and that function always reverts. v4 skips the callback when the caller is the hook itself, so the launchpad's own atomic initialization is the only path that can open the pool, and no other hook logic exists anywhere in the hot path. A platform market then holds two positions in that one pool: a permanent one-sided launch position carrying the initial inventory, and the vault position, which is full range and bounded away from the extreme ticks so nobody can freeze it. Markets for tokens that launched elsewhere skip the launch position entirely and get the vault position alone.
The vault owns its position directly through the PoolManager singleton, and the vault contract is itself the lp{SYMBOL} ERC-20 with permit. No NFT, no wrapper in between. That is what makes the claim fungible, and it means a share is a pro rata claim on principal, collected fees, idle balances and the launch NAV together.
Minting takes both sides. The vault syncs launch fees, collects the position's fees, then scales every component of the existing portfolio by one gross-share ratio: the proportional slice goes into the position, the remainder stays idle in the vault. Liquidity per share and idle assets per share both stay unchanged, so a mint can't move pre-existing NAV into the pool at a price the minter picked. Whatever isn't used is refunded in the same transaction. Redeeming burns shares and returns the proportional claim on both currencies. If you'd rather come in or leave with one asset, the ZapRouter handles it: zap in from either leg of the pair directly against the vault pool, or from the native currency or the canonical stablecoin across up to three hookless static fee hops, and zap out the same way. It runs inside PoolManager.unlock, and every entrypoint has a permit variant so there's no separate approval transaction.
Fees are the reason to hold the lpTOKEN, so the vault position's earnings simply stay: 100% of them accrue to holder NAV, with no management fee and no performance fee. The 0.30% share fee on public mint and redeem is taken in shares to the treasury and never comes out of LP earnings. On platform markets the separate launch position splits its fees, 40% to the creator and 60% to NAV on the target side, and 40% creator, 20% NAV, 40% treasury on the counter side.
compound() is permissionless and swapless. Anyone can call it, it reinvests only matched balances, and it's capped: the deployable amount for an interval is half of the pool's own fee ratio applied to the protocol owned liquidity live in the pool right now, read through StateLibrary, behind a ten minute cooldown. So it can't be used to walk the pool. One-sided or capped residue stays idle and stays redeemable.
Two details worth calling out. Vaults are deployed with cloneDeterministicWithImmutableArgs, and the pool binding and fee source are part of those immutable arguments, so the vault's own address commits to what it is bound to and nothing can be repointed later. And the minimum assessable amount is 334 shares, derived in the contract rather than written down: it's the smallest amount whose exact 30 basis point fee is at least one raw share, and every fee rounds up, so an operation can't be fragmented into dust to dodge the charge.
Why v4 specifically: the singleton lets the vault hold a position without going through a position NFT, unlock gives the router flash accounting for multi-hop entry and exit, an immutable static fee is what makes the compound cap computable at all, and hooks let us gate initialization without paying for callbacks we never use. This design doesn't really port back to v3.
There is no USD numeraire and no oracle anywhere in the Solidity. It counts raw amounts of currency0 and currency1 and never asks what anything is worth in dollars. That's also why the same contracts run on any EVM chain with a v4 deployment, whatever the native currency happens to be.
The stack: Foundry and Solidity 0.8.36 with OpenZeppelin and the v4 core and periphery libraries for the contracts. Next.js 16, React 19, viem, wagmi and TanStack Query for the app, and our own indexer writing to PostgreSQL through Prisma, which serves charts, holder PnL and LP activity without depending on a third party subgraph.
Everything above existed before ETHOnline, running on Robinhood Chain and Base. During the event we deployed the stack to Arc mainnet and added ZapRouterArc. On Arc, native USDC (18 decimals) and ERC-20 USDC (6 decimals) are one balance, so the router converts accounting units instead of wrapping or unwrapping anything. That work is in the public repo's commit history. Ethereum mainnet is in development, and we plan to ship it before the event ends.

name: khaaliNames
description: Comprehensive smart contract suite for onchain user management
projectDescription:
khalliNames is a complete smart contract suite for user management, powered by ENSv2.
Features ::

Generate unique names as identifiers
Milestones to track user growth
Onchain AppStore enablement
Monetising vanity aliasing
Emancipation without data being held hostage (ie, true user owned data)
howItsMade:
The project is extremely modular, where every piece is swappable. At the foundational layer is an onchain name generation utility and ENSv2's PermissionedRegistry and PermissionedResolver contracts. The name generation utility feeds the registry to enable unique usernames. ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control allows for nuanced permission scoping across the entire tree.
