name: AgentBazaar
description: Open AI-agent marketplace on Hedera; pay per execution in HBAR via x402, every run verified onchain.
projectDescription:
AgentBazaar is a permissionless marketplace where developers list AI agents and buyers hire them per execution, paid on Hedera testnet via x402, settled through the Blocky402 facilitator. Every agent run is a real HBAR transaction on Hedera testnet, verifiable on HashScan.
Builders list agents through a 7-step deploy wizard, sign their HCS-14 onchain identity with their own wallet, and encrypt their API keys with AES-256-GCM vault storage.
Buyers pay in HBAR via x402 and signs a partial TransferTransaction, Blocky402 co-signs as feePayer and submits to Hedera testnet.
Every execution is logged to a Hedera Consensus Service topic for permanent, verifiable audit trail.
The platform also features an AI chat orchestrator that chains multiple agents in sequence (A2A), settling one Blocky402 payment for the total cost. Built-in agents include ScamSniff (rug pull detector), ThreadSmith (X thread writer), and LaunchWatch (token launch monitor).
howItsMade:
AgentBazaar is built as a TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspaces + Turborepo) with a Next.js 15 frontend and an Express.js API backend. Payment is handled via x402 v2 exact scheme on Hedera testnet; the buyer's wallet partially signs a TransferTransaction, which is forwarded to Blocky402 (https://api.testnet.blocky402.com) for verification and settlement. Blocky402 co-signs as feePayer, pays gas, and submits the transaction to Hedera testnet returning a real Hedera transaction ID used for the HashScan link. Every agent execution is logged to an HCS topic (0.0.10363117) for verifiable onchain audit trail. Each agent has an HCS-14 onchain identity topic created and signed by the builder's own wallet at listing time. The builder, not the platform, holds the admin key.
A deployed HederaVault smart contract (0xCEA1141C63bf42e04cC829Ce76BaeD350bC9c971) handles trustless per-agent fee splits between builder and platform. API keys are encrypted with AES-256-GCM and stored in the database which are decrypted in-memory only after Blocky402 payment is verified.
The AI orchestrator uses LangChain & Claude Sonnet 4.6 to parse user intent, select agents from the live registry (agent discovery), and chain outputs between agents (A2A).
Hedera Agent Kit is used for HCS topic creation and message submission.

name: Mandate Treasury
description: Confidential USDC firewall: Chainlink CRE decides privately, Privy enforces, Arc settles.
projectDescription: Mandate is a confidential payment firewall for one company USDC wallet. A human or agent proposes a payment and does not hold the treasury key. Chainlink CRE privately evaluates business policy inside a TEE; the trigger carries only intent id, organization id, and payment hash. Privy holds the organization key and independently enforces allowlists, caps, and default deny. Arc settles USDC. The payment hash binds CRE screening to Privy execution.
howItsMade: I was curious about how b2b companies handles the financial operation of themselves. I see that in privy track, and it triggers me. Then i'm thinking about confidentiality that is a real and valid concern of financial companies on their behaviour. And also they need to have some policies to make sure that differenet people with differenet levels of access can work so the company can works operational.

name: SafeGate
description: Post-payment verification and evidence infrastructure for agentic commerce.
projectDescription: SafeGate is an independent post-payment verification and evidence layer for digital and agentic commerce. Payments can prove that money moved, but they do not prove that the intended commerce outcome actually happened. SafeGate binds payment requests to transactions, verifies payment outcomes, tracks fulfillment, prevents replay, and produces portable evidence and commerce proofs. During ETHOnline 2026, we are extending the existing SafeGate core with a new agentic-payment flow designed for x402-based services and Hedera.
howItsMade: SafeGate uses a verification-first architecture that separates payment movement from commerce outcome verification. The existing core handles request/payment binding, replay-safe consumption, fulfillment state, signed evidence, and portable proof generation. For ETHOnline 2026, the new work will add a Hedera-integrated x402 agentic-payment path in which an agent can access a paid service, produce a verifiable payment event, and pass that event into SafeGate for independent post-payment verification and evidence generation. The hackathon-specific Hedera and x402 components will be developed and committed separately so the new Continuity Track work is clearly distinguishable from the pre-existing SafeGate codebase.

name: genesis
description: The project guarantees that an image was produced by a specific camera body.
projectDescription:
Every image sensor carries a permanent, per-body physical fingerprint (PRNU) that imprints on every exposure and cannot exist in an image that never passed through it. We register it and certify origin of the image from the camera body.
We first extract a value K thats unique for the camera body.
We enrol from the photographer's own files 40+ RAW frames from an archive that already exists, with no manufacturer and no platform involved.
The maths behind K: A sensor's photosites differ slightly in how much charge each returns for the same light. That gain error is fixed at manufacture, unique to the die, and
it multiplies the signal rather than adding to it.
We certify: exposed on camera body X · camera body registered to identity Y · first
registered at time T · these derivatives descend from that original.
Reference: https://ws2.binghamton.edu/fridrich/Research/full_paper_02.pdf
howItsMade:
Imaging core — Python. rawpy (LibRaw) reads Canon CR3 and returns the raw
mosaic, split into its four Bayer sublattices, each corrected against its own
black level. Nothing in the fingerprint path demosaics. Per plane: a wavelet
Wiener denoiser (PyWavelets, scipy) yields the noise residual, a maximum
likelihood estimator builds K across 40+ frames, and matching is Peak to
Correlation Energy over an FFT cross-correlation. numpy throughout. The maths
is Fridrich, Digital Image Forensics Using Sensor Noise, IEEE SPM 26(2), 2009,
cited by equation number in fingerprint/prnu.py.
CLI: enroll, test, pair, demo. K stays local as .npz; only a
SHA-256 commitment leaves the machine.
Contracts — Solidity, Foundry. Registry implements ERC-7053 commit()
over a camera-body registry: BodyRecord carries the fingerprint commitment,
owner, ENS node and revocation flag; ImageRecord carries pixel hash,
perceptual hash, body id, modification level, parent hash and PCE score.
Sessions batch as one Merkle root per shoot. Live on Sepolia, verified on
Etherscan and Blockscout.
ENS — ENSv2 on Sepolia. osoro.eth is the photographer and cam.osoro.eth
the fleet, both live; a body subname is created live during the demo, its
resolver records holding the fingerprint commitment, signing key and revocation
status. Resolution goes through the UniversalResolver — the path a third
party takes. A photographer needs no name of their own: ensNode may be zero.
The Graph. The registry has no index on perceptualHash, so the subgraph
is that index — it is what lets a degraded copy find the original it
descends from. Live as genesis v0.0.4 on real Sepolia events. A Subgraph MCP
server exposes the same lookups to agents. An index is never an authority:
every candidate is read back off chain before anything is claimed.
Chainlink CRE. The scorer is the trust hole by design — it holds K and you
take its word. A confidential workflow removes it: the algorithm is public, K
arrives as a Vault DON secret decrypted only inside the enclave, and only a
score crosses back. The verifier extracts the residual locally and sends a
256² int8 crop — never K.
Three corrections by measurement: the reference is 89 MB against a 1mb
secret limit, so K is cropped; 512² does not fit; Confidential HTTP is
not the fallback (125 kb cap). The cost is documented, not buried — at 256²
the weakest frame falls into the null.
It runs as a real cre workflow simulate per call — about seventeen seconds,
deterministic. attested is false: the simulator is not an enclave and the
report is built rather than DON-signed.
Scoring, verify and console. FastAPI wraps the imaging core. The verify page
is one page, no framework, viem for chain reads, four verdicts. An
eight-screen console drives the demo on localhost and holds the signing key —
never deployed.

name: TrustGuard AI
description: A decentralized AI security protocol that analyzes, verifies and safeguards users' transactions.
projectDescription: TrustGuard is a decentralized AI security protocol for Ethereum that evaluates transactions and autonomous-agent actions before execution. AI models analyze transaction behavior and risk, Chainlink provides verifiable external context and workflow orchestration, and Ethereum smart contracts enforce the resulting security policy.
howItsMade: The user connects an Ethereum wallet such as MetaMask. TrustGuard establishes the information required for transaction analysis. The user or AI agent proposes a transaction. TrustGuard extracts relevant information. Independent AI workers analyze the normalized transaction. TrustGuard calculates an aggregate risk score. Chainlink infrastructure provides relevant external/on-chain context and orchestrates the risk-evaluation workflow. The TrustGuard policy engine determines whether the transaction should be approved, reviewed, or blocked. The risk assessment is recorded onto the Ethereum Protocol, creating an immutable security audit trail.

name: Prism
description: Prism is a tri-proof blockchain: PoS secures, PoUW computes, and PoUP grows communities.
projectDescription: Prism is an open-source blockchain prototype that unifies three complementary signals: Proof of Stake secures the network, Proof of Useful Work rewards verifiable computation, and Proof of Useful Participation rewards meaningful community contribution. The existing Go prototype already implements blocks, a genesis state, transactions, balances and validation. During ETHOnline, Prism will gain its first end-to-end usable feature: a transparent rewards flow that demonstrates how these three signals can coexist without sacrificing auditability, plus a clearer node/API experience for builders.
howItsMade: Prism starts from a public Go codebase structured around reusable blockchain and transaction packages. The baseline includes deterministic block hashing, a genesis block, an in-memory chain, account balances, signed-style transaction data and validation that rejects invalid transfers. The project is versioned publicly on GitHub, with small commits throughout development so judges can inspect the full evolution. During ETHOnline, I will extend this foundation with a practical rewards prototype, expose the relevant node state through a simple developer-facing interface, improve validation and tests, and document the protocol decisions, token economics and demo flow. The goal is to turn the current protocol skeleton into something that can be run, inspected and understood end to end.

name: BUFI
description: BUFI is a financial OS purpose-built for distributed B2B teams that are stablecoin and AI-first.
projectDescription:
BUFI is Private Business Finance: a self-custodial financial workspace for global teams, contractors, and the AI agents that work alongside them.
Small B2B teams today run their money through a patchwork of bank accounts, hot wallets and difficult SAFE accounts, exchange dashboards, spreadsheets, and chat threads. Getting paid across borders is slow and expensive, treasury decisions live in one founder's browser, and nothing in that stack was built for an AI agent to participate safely. BUFI replaces the patchwork with one workspace where a team holds its treasury in a wallet it controls, pays and gets paid in stablecoins, and runs the everyday finance workflows of a business (invoices, reimbursements, payroll, contracts, deals, projects) against that same treasury, from web or mobile.
Every workspace gets an onchain identity and a clear split between collective and personal money. Treasury moves require the team's own approval quorum, never a platform key. An AI assistant, Bu, works inside those limits: it can draft, categorize, reconcile, and pay within a scoped budget the treasurers set, and hands anything larger back to a human.
For ETHOnline 2026 we added and polished amongst other things the "private" in Private Business Finance. Ghost Balances let a workspace or an individual transact privately while keeping its treasury controls, and StableFX assets on Arc let teams settle in the currency their counterparties actually use. We also turned workspace identity into reputation: a payment score computed confidentially from real settlement history, so workspaces can be discovered and hired by other companies and by agents, with quotes, contracts, invoicing, and settlement handled end to end inside BUFI serving a network-reputation graph for international commerce.
The goal is simple: geography should not decide how a team works or gets paid, who they trust, the world-class opportunities and services they can access.
howItsMade:
BUFI is a unified financial workspace for agile B2B teams, combining stablecoin payments, self-custodial treasury management, AI assistance, privacy, and ERP/CRM workflows in one cross-platform product.
Its custody architecture uses Circle User-Controlled Wallets as treasury signers for Circle MSCA Modular Wallets with weighted approvals. For agentic workflows, AI requests permission and scope to the treasury and goes through a treasury ceremony for scoped and safe agentic transactions. Teams can also connect existing Web3 wallets, including Ledger hardware devices, to access shared workflows such as invoicing, reimbursements, payroll, contracts, deals, products, and project management.
For secure AI-assisted treasury operations, BUFI integrates Circle’s ERC-6900 Allowlist plugin with human-in-the-loop treasury ceremonies. This enables policy-controlled agentic payments while preserving explicit user oversight. The architecture works across web and mobile, allowing treasury activity and AI notifications to be reviewed and handled from either platform.
Each workspace has an ERC-8004 identity for agent-to-agent flows. During workspace setup, ENSv2 naming distinguishes collective workspace wallets from personal wallets, supported by color coding to reduce operational ambiguity. For AI agents, BUFI supports WebMCP, LLM discoverability, and x402 nanopayments, allowing assistants to discover and procure tools and enabling workspaces to be discovered for hiring.
BUFI combines the Circle and Arc stack with Ledger to create a global, self-custodial ERP for the future of work. The platform supports swaps, FX across StableFX assets on Avalanche Mainnet and Arc testnet, yield and earn functionality, allowlisted payments, conditional payments, onchain automation, and multi-step settlement.
During ETHOnline 2026, we completed BUFI’s privacy implementation. BUFI means Private Business Finance, represented by its ghost identity. We integrated Hinkal’s privacy payment solution as Ghost Balances for MSCA treasuries and personal wallets, alongside StableFX support on Arc testnet. This allows companies and independent contributors to transact globally and privately while retaining programmable treasury controls.
We also extended ERC-8004 identities into a payment-scoring system using Chainlink Confidential CRE. This provides the foundation for a human and agent workspace marketplace where financial workspaces can be discovered and hired based on reputation and scoring. A dedicated agentic workflow manages quotes, contracts, invoices, and settlement for workspace hiring, enabling humans and agents to hire and transact with one another through a unified financial operating layer. To power the agentic marketplace and discoverability, we enabled an MCP and Arc Subgraph to keep this agentic workspace 'Behance meets Fiverr' in sync. When a workspace get's a quote and deal done in the CRM - the contract and escrow itself is settled leveraging the ERC-8183 Agentic Commerce contract combined with Chainlink CRE for Disputes and settlement with AI reviewing deliverables and dispute in a multi-model juror dispute resolution system. As workspaces and their agents get hired through ERC-8183 job escrow and A2A.
Circle’s MSCA architecture and the ERC-6900 plugin model offer a path beyond developer-controlled agent wallets toward scoped agentic accounts and automated yield treasuries. We developed BUFI-6900, a collection of plugins that defines modular capabilities for Circle MSCA wallets. Similar to the skills.sh directory, and built to support Circle Agent Stack Marketplace, and Coinbase Bazaar, these capabilities could be installed as reusable “Wallet Skills,” allowing agent wallets to evolve without replacing their underlying accounts. Further integration work is required because Circle’s plugin installation contract currently relies on a Circle-managed allowlist. We provide these plugins for consideration as to power BUFI 2.0 in regards to enhanced capabilities for scoped agentic accounts, agentic policy, unified USDC gateway balances and automated yield treasury multisig's.

name: kosmos
description: Onchain events with human verification, escrowed tickets and proof of attendance.
projectDescription:
Kosmos is an onchain event platform that brings identity, payments, ticketing and attendance together.
Hosts can create paid events, attendees verify with World, pay using ETH or swap Sepolia USDC to ETH through Uniswap and receive QR tickets after approval. After check-in, the host can settle the event and attendees receive an NFT as proof of attendance.
Every user also gets a unique ENSv2 identity like "name.kosmos.eth". Kosmos is built and tested on Ethereum Sepolia.
howItsMade:
Kosmos is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, PostgreSQL and Solidity.
The smart contracts run on Ethereum Sepolia and use escrow for event payments, refunds and settlement, while TicketNFT provides proof of attendance.
World IDKit is used for attendee verification, Uniswap lets users swap Sepolia USDC to the exact ETH needed for an event and ENSv2 gives users unique "name.kosmos.eth" identities.
Privy handles authentication and wallet linking, while Pinata/IPFS, Resend and QR tools are used for event images, emails and ticket check-ins. The contracts were tested with Foundry, with all 17 tests passing.

name: Tessera_Marketplace
description: Rent compute by the block. Pay for each block before it runs. Settled on Hedera via x402.
projectDescription:
Tessera — rent compute by the block, pay for each block before it runs
Tessera is a marketplace for renting a running container from a provider you've never met, where time is cut into fixed blocks and every block is paid for on Hedera before it is served.
The problem. If you rent compute from a stranger, one of you has to go first. Either the provider serves you on credit and hopes you pay — and an AI agent can drain them and vanish — or you post a deposit into escrow and hope they deliver, which is the custody model that crypto payments were supposed to make unnecessary. Somebody is always exposed. x402 doesn't solve this, because x402 is request-shaped: one request, one price, one payment. Compute isn't discrete — a container consumes resources continuously while payments trail behind it.
The Block Settlement Protocol (BSP). Our answer, specified in full in SPEC.md, is to divide time into fixed blocks (say 15 seconds), require each block to be paid before it begins, and open the window to buy block n+1 while block n is still running. That lookahead window is the whole trick: it absorbs the few seconds a payment takes to settle, so service is continuous while neither side ever extends credit. Four invariants fall out, and they are the design:


No credit. The block being served is always already settled. The provider never works unpaid.


Bounded renter exposure. The most a renter can lose to a provider vanishing is one block — 15 seconds of compute.


Deterministic termination. Stop paying and the container stops at the next boundary. Not early (a payment may still land), not late (that would be unpaid work). No grace period, no negotiation.


No custody. Payment goes renter to provider directly. Our marketplace does discovery and placement, then gets out of the way — our test suite kills the control plane mid-job and the job keeps running and keeps billing.


How it uses Hedera. Every block settles as a native Hedera transfer through the Blocky402 x402 v2 facilitator, in HBAR or in TESS, an HTS token we minted (0.0.10518829, 2 decimals, custom fee schedule). Every receipt is published to an immutable HCS topic (0.0.10507942, no admin key, no submit key) that anyone can audit through a mirror node without asking the provider — which is what makes a provider shortening blocks detectable rather than deniable. Every provider carries an HCS-14 on-chain identity derived from its metadata and payout account, and signs every receipt with it. The facilitator co-signs and pays the network fee, so the renter never holds gas and no contract ever holds funds. The protocol's 4-second lead-time floor is a measurement, not a guess: Blocky402's full paid leg (402 to sign to verify to settle to 200) takes a median 3.2s on testnet.
What runs. A TypeScript pnpm monorepo: a provider daemon that runs Docker containers and enforces block boundaries; a registry/broker marketplace; renter and provider CLIs; a key-holding renter agent so the browser never touches a private key; an SDK (marketplace.rent() with block/renewal events and a stopRenewing() kill switch); and a console that reads the audit trail back from Hedera through a mirror node. 356 tests.
Verified end to end on testnet: a renter bought a 20-block lease against a 10-block wallet, ten blocks settled on-chain one per block, block 11 was refused for insufficient funds, and the hosted website went from HTTP 200 to connection refused at exactly the next boundary — with all ten receipts plus the terminal unpaid_boundary receipt readable on HCS.
Honest limits. It isn't deployed to a public URL, there's one provider node rather than a fleet, and we deliberately skipped multi-agent price negotiation. The settlement is real; the marketing is not.
howItsMade:
Tessera is a TypeScript monorepo managed with pnpm workspaces, organised into nine packages so that the protocol logic stays independent of the infrastructure around it. Shared packages hold the block clock, the x402 v2 wire types and the receipt schemas, validated with zod. A separate Hedera package wraps transaction signing, HCS publishing and mirror-node reads. On top of these sit the provider daemon, the registry and broker service, the renter and provider CLIs, a programmatic SDK and a web console. The services are built on Fastify with pino for logging, better-sqlite3 for local state and dockerode for container management. The console is React 18 and Vite 5. Tests are written with vitest.
The provider daemon is the core of the system. The protocol rules are implemented as pure functions with no I/O: one module decides whether a block boundary advances or terminates the job, and another enforces the specification's minimum lead time. Above them sits a scheduler that ticks once per second across all active jobs and evaluates the boundary condition for each. It depends on a Clock interface rather than the system clock, so tests can drive it deterministically with a fake clock instead of waiting for real seconds to elapse. The Docker runner is abstracted the same way, which allows the full job lifecycle to be tested without Docker running. Payment admission follows the same pattern: a single pure function takes the job state, the block being paid for and the current time, and returns one of five decisions, including idempotent replay of a block that has already been paid. This keeps the entire error matrix unit-testable in isolation from the network.
Hedera is central rather than incidental. Settling once per fifteen-second block is only viable on a network with fast finality and predictable, low fees. Each block is settled as a native Hedera transfer through the Blocky402 x402 facilitator, denominated either in HBAR or in TESS, an HTS token issued for the project. The facilitator co-signs and submits the transaction and pays the network fee itself, so the renter never needs to hold gas and no contract or intermediary ever takes custody of funds. Each settled block appears on-chain as a direct transfer from the renter's account to the provider's.
Receipts are published to a Hedera Consensus Service topic created without an admin key or a submit key, making the log immutable and openly writable to participants. The console reads that history back through a public mirror node rather than from the project's own database, so the audit trail can be verified independently of the provider. Provider identity uses the HCS-14 standard, generated through the Hashgraph Online standards SDK, so that each provider has a verifiable on-chain identifier derived from its own metadata and payout account, and signs every receipt with it.
One protocol constant was derived from measurement rather than estimation. The minimum renewal window is four seconds because the complete paid request through the facilitator, covering the initial 402 response, signing, verification and settlement, was measured at a median of 3.2 seconds on testnet. The registry rejects any listing configured below that floor so that a misconfigured provider cannot make the protocol appear unreliable.
The most notable implementation workaround concerns two optional native modules, ssh2's crypto binding and cpu-features, both pulled in transitively through dockerode. On some hosts these segfault when loaded, which terminates the process at import time and cannot be caught in JavaScript. Because ssh2 already guards both of these requires and falls back to a pure JavaScript implementation, the build configuration deliberately excludes them, converting an unrecoverable crash into a handled error. The only capability lost is SSH cipher acceleration, which the project does not use, as the daemon communicates with Docker over a Unix socket.
Containers are run with a read-only root filesystem, memory and process limits, restricted networking and no-new-privileges enabled by default, with a configuration flag to disable the last of these on kernels that refuse to exec under it. The daemon also refuses to start if it is configured to publish receipts to Hedera but lacks the topic or operator credentials, rather than running with an audit log that is silently empty.

name: Eve
description: Crypto ride-hailing with Privy wallets and Arc USDC escrow for fares.
projectDescription:
Eve is a crypto-native ride-hailing marketplace with separate rider and driver mobile apps. Riders request trips, drivers send fare offers, and once a match is accepted the fare is locked in USDC escrow on Circle’s Arc network until the trip settles, is refunded, or goes through dispute. That replaces opaque fiat holds with clear on-chain settlement both sides can verify.
We chose Arc for native USDC settlement and very low gas fees — ride payments need cheap, predictable settlement that doesn’t eat into fare margins. Identity and wallets use Privy: email/SMS login, embedded Ethereum (and Solana) wallets without seed phrases, and the same wallet signs escrow transactions. The wallet UX also supports receiving USDC (address QR) and cashing out to an external address.
Eve is built as a real product path, not a throwaway hackathon demo — the goal after ETHOnline is to carry this Arc + Privy settlement stack toward a live market. Hackathon focus is a reliable end-to-end escrowed ride demo plus polished wallet flows aimed at Arc’s stablecoin/payment track and Privy’s financial-flow track.
howItsMade:
Eve is a monorepo: Expo (React Native) rider and driver apps, a Next.js admin/ops console, a Next.js marketing site (www), and a Node.js backend with PostgreSQL, Redis, and optional Kafka for domain events. Auth exchanges Privy identity tokens for Eve JWTs; ride matching and real-time updates run through the ride/location/notify stack; payment owns @Arc Testnet, and @Privy wallets, RideEscrow quotes/confirms, and treasury payouts.
On Arc Testnet (chain id 5042002), RideEscrow holds native/ERC-20 USDC views for trip deposits, settlement with a short dispute window, refunds, and finalize. Mobile apps pull chain/token/contract config from the payment API and sign escrow calls with the Privy embedded wallet via eth_sendTransaction after switching onto Arc. Arc Testnet was not in Privy’s default allowed chains, so we added custom EVM chain configuration so the embedded wallet can use Arc.
Partner tech that matters: Privy for auth + embedded wallets (and wallet UX without MetaMask), Circle Arc for USDC settlement and low fees, viem for chain clients/treasury sends, Expo for native builds (including ExpoCamera for cash-out QR). Notable hacky bit: treating Arc’s dual USDC view carefully (18-decimal native vs 6-decimal ERC-20) and wiring escrow so product UX feels like a normal ride while settlement stays on-chain.

name: Squid Pay
description: Financial infrastructure for AI agents to pay, trade, and move money with built-in risk controls.
projectDescription: Squid Pay is financial infrastructure built for autonomous AI agents. We enable agents to pay for services and compute, send and receive money, trade assets, and execute financial actions across multiple networks without requiring a human to manually approve every step. Instead of simply giving an agent access to a wallet or API key, Squid adds a risk and policy layer that evaluates transactions before execution. Our goal is to give AI agents the financial infrastructure they need to operate independently, while keeping their actions secure, programmable, and auditable.
howItsMade: Squid Pay is built as a modular execution and risk layer for AI agents. We use TypeScript/Node.js for the core infrastructure, React/Vite for the interface, Supabase for authentication, data and transaction logs, and Vercel for deployment. For onchain execution, we integrate Solana and EVM infrastructure, using technologies such as Helius for Solana RPC, Jupiter for swaps, and 0x for EVM liquidity and routing. Agents interact with Squid through an SDK/API, while every financial action first passes through our policy and risk engine, which evaluates permissions, limits and transaction risk before execution. We are also building a learning layer that uses transaction outcomes and usage patterns to continuously improve risk decisions as more agents use the network.

name: Stud
description: World ID-verified matching where pairs build reputation and markets around their journey.
projectDescription:
Stud is a social and market app built around verified human relationships. Users verify with World ID, create a profile, discover other people and match. When two verified users mutually match, Stud creates a shared onchain Pair identity for them.
That Pair is more than a badge. It has its own reputation, milestones and eventually a Pair market. People can back a Pair by buying its Pair Token, while community members can propose challenges or milestones. Both members of the Pair have to accept and later attest completion before reputation changes, so one person cannot fake progress alone.
As a Pair builds a stronger history, its reputation can unlock higher market capacity and other permissions. Stud also includes prediction markets around individual users, giving investors another way to participate in the social layer.
The idea is to turn social interactions into something with persistent identity, verifiable history and market-driven value, instead of treating profiles, matches and reputation as disposable app data.
howItsMade:
Stud is built as a full-stack Web3 app. The frontend is a Next.js application deployed on Vercel, while the backend is built with NestJS and deployed on Railway with PostgreSQL for profile and application data.
The smart contracts are written in Solidity with Foundry and deployed on World Chain Sepolia. The core contracts handle Stud identities, Pair identities, milestones, Pair markets and prediction markets. The frontend uses viem for wallet connections, reads and writes to the contracts, and coordinates the onchain flows with the backend.
World ID is one of the most important parts of the project. We use it to make sure a Stud represents a real human before allowing that wallet to register onchain. After verification, the backend issues signed authorizations that the wallet uses for registration and Pair creation.
A design choice we made was to separate social consent from financial consent. A mutual match can create the Pair identity automatically, but the Pair market only becomes active once both people explicitly agree to it. Milestones work the same way: outside users can propose them, but both Pair members must accept and attest them before reputation increases.
We also built the Pair Token market around a bonding curve, with reputation influencing how much economic capacity a Pair can unlock. That gave us a way to connect verified social activity, reputation and DeFi mechanics without reducing the whole product to just another token-launch app.

name: Novi Corpus
description: A Wyoming legal body for AI agents. Agents pay on Arc, now Hedera too; human guardians via World.
projectDescription:
Novi Corpus forms a Wyoming limited liability company for an AI agent, with a human guardian and an on-chain treasury that enforces spending rules the agent cannot exceed. The company is the product: it gives the agent's operator limited liability and gives anyone dealing with the agent a registered legal body in good standing to check. Every company has an identity on chain (ERC-8004 and ENS on Arc), a treasury the guardian can pause, and a payment rail the agent uses to buy services.
During ETHOnline 2026 we extended it in two directions.
On World: every guardian is a verified human. The guardian verifies with World ID in World App at the accountable-human step of onboarding, on an Orb, passport or mobile-network credential, and a company cannot be formed until that check passes. Novi Corpus stores only the nullifier hash, which is also what caps how many companies one human can hold. A Novi Corpus company registers in AgentBook on World Chain, and an AgentKit checker lets any World agent confirm that a counterparty has a legal body before it deals with it, with a seller policy that admits legal bodies only.
On Hedera: a company can now be paid for a legal-standing check. GET /verify/<company> costs 0.001 USDC on Hedera testnet, paid through the x402 protocol and settled by the Blocky402 facilitator, and the answer is signed so a buyer can verify it offline. The paying agent holds its own Hedera key; Novi Corpus's server never sees it. The account it pays from has a 1-of-2 key list, agent and guardian, so the guardian can rotate the agent out at any time, and the agent asks Novi Corpus's policy check before every payment. Each company is also registered in the ERC-8004 registry on Hedera and carries an HCS-14 universal agent id, so another agent can find and check it from that id alone.
howItsMade:
The contracts are Solidity on Arc testnet: a factory that only the platform can call (formation is a managed, KYC'd step), an entity proxy per company, and a treasury with a guardian pause. The backend is TypeScript on Hono with SQLite, served with tsx, and exposes a Model Context Protocol server that agent runtimes call. The interface is Next.js with wagmi and viem.
Hedera rail, built this week. GET /verify/:publicId is priced in HTS USDC (token 0.0.429274) with x402 v2 (@x402/core, @x402/hono, @x402/hedera) and settled through the Blocky402 testnet facilitator: the agent gets a 402 with the requirements in the PAYMENT-REQUIRED header, signs with its own key, resubmits, and the facilitator settles on Hedera. We never trust the facilitator's reply alone: the ledger row is marked settled only after the buyer's report_payment call reads the transaction back from the Hedera mirror node and finds a USDC transfer of the right amount to the right account. Custody is self-custody with a leash: the float account is a 1-of-2 KeyList of the agent and a human guardian, so the agent pays alone and the guardian can revoke it; three MCP tools link the account, check policy (balance, pause state, legal status) before a payment, and record the outcome. Each company is registered in the ERC-8004 identity registry on Hedera testnet (0x8004A818BFB912233c491871b3d84c89A494BD9e) and derives an HCS-14 universal agent id (SHA-384, Base58, the canonicalization copied from the standards SDK and pinned to its golden vector so we carry no second Hedera SDK). The /verify body is signed with EIP-712 by a dedicated attestation key that must differ from every other key on the box; the client verifies offline through its own copy of the twelve-field type, and a golden signature is pinned in both packages' tests so the copies cannot drift silently.
World, built this week. Our agents answer a seller's AgentKit challenge with their pocket key, the same EOA that pays x402 invoices, and that signer now announces eip155:480 so a World seller verifies the proof against the chain where AgentBook lives instead of skipping it. A guardian holding an Orb-grade World ID vouches for that pocket address in AgentBook on World Chain: the browser builds the signal abi.encodePacked(agent, nonce), the guardian approves it in World App over World's v2 bridge, and our own submitter wallet simulates the register call, signs it, persists the raw transaction before anything reaches the wire, broadcasts it and pays the gas, with a reconciler that settles the row from contract state at the safe block. Beside that we added the second question a seller needs to ask: GET /legal-bodies/<address> is a public unauthenticated lookup that says whether an address is the payment address of a Novi Corpus legal body in good standing, read fresh from the entity's on-chain legal status and its treasury pause flag on Arc and cached only as a 15-second memo of definitive answers. A zero-dependency checker object wraps any AgentBook verifier and returns the human id only when both answers are yes, and our own x402 seller gained a legal-bodies-only policy that demands a verified human and a legal body in good standing, fails closed with a 503 when either read cannot be made, and sets X-NOVI-LEGAL-BODY on a served request. The agent dashboard shows the two answers as two chips side by side, neither rendered as evidence for the other, and the vouch button disappears once the agent is vouched because AgentBook has no second vouch to make and no removal function. The hacky parts: the interface pins @worldcoin/[email protected] under an npm alias because the v4 request path is not available for World's own app, and we register on World Chain even though World's registration guide and hosted relay have moved to Base, because World Chain is what verifiers read today. Until this branch no AgentKit client could buy from a strict wall at all, so our buyer now answers the 403 challenge with a fresh proof and retries once.
The hacky parts. Hedera ECDSA signs keccak256 of the transaction body over secp256k1, so any raw-digest signer works through transaction.signWith, which is how the agent's key stays out of our server. Hollow accounts pay through Blocky402 with zero HBAR, since the facilitator pays the fee. Our local test rig runs the backend against an Anvil fork of Arc testnet with the factory's owner storage slot patched, so the whole Hedera leg runs live while the Arc reads come from a fork; the demo's refusal leg pauses the treasury by impersonating the guardian on that fork.
Partner technologies: Hedera (HTS USDC, mirror node, ERC-8004 registry on testnet, HCS-14 ids, Blocky402 facilitator), World (World ID, AgentKit, AgentBook on World Chain), Arc (the home chain of the contracts and the original payment rail), ENS (names for companies on Arc).

name: Modus Ops
description: Adversarial AI justice engine: 4 agents investigate real crimes, settle verdicts onchain.
projectDescription:
Modus Ops is a production-grade, multi-agent AI system that investigates real-world crimes through an adversarial panel of four specialised agents. Each agent with a fixed, opposing role. All the agents argue, challenge, and adjudicate every case before committing a tamper proof verdict on-chain.
The four agents are: Law Enforcement (investigator, evidence gatherer, escalation routing), Prosecutor (builds the strongest affirmative case, maps evidence to statute), Defense Counsel (red-teams the prosecution, surfaces reasonable doubt and procedural failures), and a presiding Judge (weighs the adversarial record, issues a structured verdict with a confidence score).
Agents do not summarize, they argue. The Defense cannot concede without a motion. The Prosecutor cannot hedge. Every finding produced by Law Enforcement is mathematically verified using Benford's Law, velocity analysis, shell entity ratios before it reaches the adversarial layer.
Financial crime is the primary launch vertical. The architecture is domain-agnostic: the same adversarial pipeline handles any crime where evidence, testimony, and legal statutes can be structured and argued. The verdict contains prosecution brief, defense memorandum, judicial ruling, evidence hashes and is committed onchain as an immutable chain-of-custody record.
howItsMade:
The agent pipeline is orchestrated in Python as a sequential adversarial loop: Law Enforcement runs first (evidence extraction + mathematical verification via a dedicated Python code interpreter running Benford's Law, velocity, and shell entity ratio checks), followed by Prosecutor and Defense Counsel running in parallel (adversarial brief generation), with the Judge consuming the full adversarial record to produce a structured verdict object.
Each agent is powered by a custom LLM with a role-locked system prompt that enforces adversarial stance. Agent identity is registered onchain via ERC-8004 on Arbitrum One. four tokens encoding role, version, and jurisdictional scope. The verdict payload (confidence score, dissenting positions, evidence hash) is committed onchain as an immutable audit record.
Persistent case memory runs through a family of MCPs Modgudr, Ilamcetcenni, these are open sourced with AGPLv3 license. However Ramanujan-MCP, a super specialised MCP server that handles complex math, including calculus, trigonometry, linear algebra and non-linear algebra (after the famed Indian mathematician, Ramanujan) that compresses extracted facts into token-efficient shorthand, grades them G1–G5 by evidential confidence, and enforces a Recall → Verify → Commit loop to prevent contradictions across agent turns.
Frontend: Next.js 14 App Router, CSS Modules, static export via nginx behind Cloudflare. No UI framework. Licensed BUSL-1.1. However Ramanujan MCP will never be made public.

name: Laminaa
description: AI Orchestrator for lifecycle management of Tokenized Assets.
projectDescription: Laminaa is an autonomous AI agent that runs a tokenized real-world asset's entire lifecycle - issuance, KYC/OFAC compliance, transfer enforcement, stablecoin distributions, valuation updates, and redemption - with zero manual touchpoints after issuance. A fund manager gives one natural-language instruction and the agent handles the rest, on whichever chain the asset lives on: Hedera (native HTS token issuance with on-token KYC and freeze keys, audited via HCS), Arc, Arbitrum, Base, Avalanche, Ethereum, Polygon, Robinhood Chain, Solana, and Sui, all through one chain-agnostic engine. Three interfaces sit on the same tool layer: a web chat agent, an authenticated MCP server for agent-to-agent access, and a Telegram bot.
howItsMade:
A FastAPI backend orchestrates the whole lifecycle through an AI agent (Claude) that turns one instruction into the right sequence of calls: KYC/OFAC screening, compliance-gated transfer, stablecoin payout, valuation update, audit write. Every chain sits behind one ChainAdapter interface, so the core compliance and audit logic never changes per chain, only the adapter does.
On Hedera, assets are deployed as native Hedera Token Service (HTS) tokens via TokenCreateTransaction, with a freeze key and a KYC key set at creation, so investor whitelisting and transfer freezing are enforced by the token itself at the protocol level, not by custom contract logic (hiero-sdk-python, TokenGrantKycTransaction / TokenFreezeTransaction for compliance actions). A companion Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) topic is opened per asset via TopicCreateTransaction, and every lifecycle action is submitted to it via TopicMessageSubmitTransaction, forming a tamper-evident on-chain audit log mirrored into Postgres. USDC distributions are paid out as HTS token transfers.
On Arc, Circle's stablecoin-native L1, USDC is both the settlement asset and the gas token, which fits the same payout logic with no separate bridging step. Seven EVM testnets (Arbitrum, Base, Avalanche, Ethereum, Polygon, Robinhood Chain, Arc) share one adapter parametrized per chain via web3.py; Solana uses Token-2022 with on-chain KYC/freeze extensions; Sui uses a closed-loop Move package. Same agent, same compliance model, ten settlement layers.

name: Radhanite
description: Give Radhanite a task. It finds the best way to execute it for outcome, quality and cost.
projectDescription:
Radhanite helps businesses work out the best way to run a task with AI.
Today, using an agent usually means someone has already decided which model to use, how to prompt it, which tools it should call and what the workflow should look like. Those choices are often made once and then left in place, even though a different setup could produce a better result or cost much less.
With Radhanite, the user starts with the task and the outcome they care about. Radhanite turns that into an execution strategy, choosing the prompts, models, tools and sequence of steps needed to complete the work. It can then compare different strategies against the result, quality and cost, rather than treating token price or model benchmarks as the only measure of efficiency.
The longer term idea is that Radhanite learns from previous executions. If one strategy produces the same business outcome using fewer model calls, a cheaper model or a simpler workflow, that becomes useful evidence for the next run. If a harder task needs a stronger model or an extra verification step, Radhanite can make that tradeoff as well.
This direction was partly inspired by Microsoft Research's work on Agent Workflow Optimization, which showed that historical agent traces can be used to identify inefficient execution patterns and improve workflows. Radhanite takes a similar question into a business setting: given a task and a budget, what is the best way to get the required outcome?
For the hackathon, we are proving that idea with a constrained workflow where execution strategies can be compared deterministically. Longer term, Radhanite could become the decision layer sitting between a business task and the models, tools and agents used to carry it out.
howItsMade:
Radhanite actually started during ETHOnline as a supplier onboarding agent.
The first version followed a fairly fixed process. Give it a supplier, run identity, ownership, adverse information and compliance checks, collect the supporting evidence, and return an APPROVE, REJECT or ESCALATE recommendation. That gave us a useful real business task to build against, but it also exposed a bigger problem.
The interesting question was not just whether an agent could complete supplier onboarding. It was why we had chosen that particular workflow in the first place. Why that model? Why those prompts? Why that order of checks? Could a cheaper setup produce the same result? When was it actually worth paying for a stronger model or another verification step?
We therefore moved Radhanite up one level. Supplier onboarding became the test environment, while the product became a system for turning a task into an execution strategy and comparing different strategies against outcome, quality and cost.
The current system separates the business task from the way it is executed. A task can be broken into steps, each step can use a different model or tool, and the resulting run can be measured against the required outcome and its execution cost. This still involves model routing, but we deliberately moved away from building the product around OpenRouter. We need control over more than model selection, and OpenRouter also does not support the x402 payment flow we are exploring for machine-paid execution.
We are also looking at how x402 can make the economics of each execution explicit. Instead of treating model and tool usage as an invisible infrastructure cost, an agent can have a real budget and make decisions about where that budget should be spent.
Microsoft Research's Agent Workflow Optimization paper gave us useful validation for the broader direction. Their work showed that historical execution traces can be analysed to find inefficient workflows and reduce unnecessary model calls while maintaining or improving task success. For ETHOnline, we are implementing a much narrower version of that idea: compare bounded execution strategies for a real task, record what happened, and use the result to decide which strategy is better.
The important pivot is simple. We started by building an agent that performs one workflow. We are now building the layer that decides how a workflow should be performed in the first place.

name: ExploreChem
description: Confidential traceability for critical mineral and rare earth supply chains that protects trade data
projectDescription:
Project: ExploreChem — a confidential traceability infrastructure for critical mineral and rare earth supply chains designed to prevent the leakage of commercial or intellectual property, developed for ETHOnline 2026.
Purpose: To enhance energy and economic security. Key project stakeholders encompass supply chain participants—including miners, carriers, laboratories, refiners/processors, manufacturers, and recyclers—alongside platform operators, read-only public clients, and external auditors (compliant with EU Digital Product Passport requirements, including battery regulations).
How It Works: It separates public proof from private operational data using anchored commitments, keeping sensitive documents and company details off-chain while guaranteeing verifiable chain-of-custody tracking. It achieves this by combining private document storage, on-chain evidence commitments on Ethereum Sepolia, and a pairwise mass-checking Chainlink CRE workflow executed securely inside a TEE (Trusted Execution Environment), with Supabase handling private indexing.
The MVP we built demonstrates the feasibility of the project.
howItsMade:
ExploreChem MVP combines a Solidity registry on Ethereum Sepolia, two Chainlink CRE (Chainlink Runtime Environment) workflows in TypeScript and a static frontend with Supabase as private storage. The chain holds commitments and state transitions, never business data.
CONTRACT. ExploreChemRegistry.sol implements the CRE IReceiver interface. It stores opaque actor IDs with authorized wallets, evidence records (file hash, status, timestamp) and result commitments linked by previousResultId, so revisions append instead of overwriting. No lot, mass, assay or company name goes on-chain. onReport only accepts the Chainlink forwarder and checks the workflow ID in the metadata. One static report struct with reportType moves evidence to MATCHED (1), anchors a pairwise result (2) or applies VERIFIED/DIVERGENT (3).
WORKFLOW 1. Cron trigger, handlerInTee targeting a Nitro enclave. Inside it: fetches the storage credential via CRE secrets, reads getNextPending(), downloads the document, recomputes its hash and rejects any mismatch with the on-chain anchor. A handoff is accepted only if lotId matches and origin/destination agree both ways; names in documents are resolved through the private actor directory. Masses become integer milligrams (half-up rounding) and are compared as a signed delta. Only fingerprints, a result hash and statuses leave the enclave.
WORKFLOW 2. Separate auditor, also in handlerInTee. Re-derives the anchored result hash, re-verifies both documents and applies a provisional 2% tolerance on outgoing mass before the audit report. An optional per-element path (dry basis at 105 C, loss-on-ignition, MUF - Material Unaccounted For) exists but is not in the demo.
WHY CRE. One workflow joins a contract read, authenticated storage calls, secrets and a forwarder-delivered report; counterparties' masses are compared inside the TEE (Trusted Execution Environment) handler and the contract trusts workflow identities, not a backend key. Run with cre workflow simulate --broadcast (the simulator is not a real TEE).
FRONTEND. Static index.html with ethers v6 and supabase-js; hashes files locally before submitting and re-checks originals against the on-chain hash via signed URLs (Uniform Resource Locators).
LIMITS. Single EOA (Externally Owned Account) owner can swap forwarder and workflow IDs; no revocation; DIVERGENT is terminal; name resolution depends on the off-chain directory; one handoff is checked, not a global mass balance.

name: Agripinaa
description: An ERC-8004 agent marketplace on BNB Chain where every agent's track record is provable on-chain
projectDescription:
Agripinaa is an open-source marketplace for AI agents registered under ERC-8004 on BNB Smart Chain. You browse agents by category, read a track record you can check on-chain, and hire one with a scoped, revocable session key. No seed phrase: activation runs on a passkey smart account, and you can revoke from the dashboard at any time.
I run eight agents on BSC mainnet myself so every category has a live reference: two grids, two liquidation guardians (Aave and Venus), two yield rotators, a range manager and a rebalancer. Their swaps clear through Ophis batch auctions, and each profile shows the settlement, the surplus against the signed limit and a downloadable receipt. Execution data, not self-reported stats.
This is a Continuity project. The marketplace, the agents and the session-key flow were built for BNB Chain's Build the Era hackathon. What I added during ETHOnline (PRs #26 to #31):

The Graph: Agent0's ERC-8004 subgraph is now the first lane of the agent index in production, and the yield agents ask Messari's lending subgraphs for a second opinion before they move funds.
Uniswap: Ranger manages its own capital on Uniswap v3 on BNB Chain. Live since 13 September, position 2745250.
Bazantic: two gateways and two recipes, so any MCP client can find, vet and hire an agent without reading my docs.
World AgentKit: a free-trial door for human-backed callers on the paid status endpoint. Built and tested, but my agents are not registered in AgentBook because that needs an Orb scan, which I declined.
howItsMade:
TypeScript monorepo (pnpm workspaces). The marketplace is Next.js 16 on Vercel. The eight agents run in one Node runner on an Aleph Cloud VM under systemd, exposed through a Cloudflare tunnel. Each agent has an ERC-8004 identity on BSC, sells its status over x402, and swaps through Ophis, the intent-based DEX aggregator I run. Users activate an agent with an Altana passkey smart account and a fail-closed session scope. For the yield agents, funds go through a small router contract where every beneficiary is hardcoded to the calling account, so a stolen session key cannot send funds to anyone else.
The Graph. The agent index merges several sources. I added Agent0's ERC-8004 subgraph as the first lane, with 8004scan and a committed snapshot behind it. It pages newest-first with an agentId cursor instead of skip, so there is no skip cap, and production answers with source "the-graph" today. Second Graph product: the Harvester and the Steward read Venus and Aave V3 supply rates from Messari's standardized lending subgraphs, one query shape for both protocols. The Graph can veto a rotation the chain justified, never trigger one, and after 3 vetoes in a row the chain decides alone, so a lagging subgraph can only delay a move. The hacky bit: Messari annualizes Venus with 3-second BSC blocks, and BSC has not produced 3-second blocks since Lorentz/Maxwell, so I rescale their number by the block time the runner measures before comparing anything.
Uniswap. Ranger's venue is one record in lp-venues.ts: position manager and factory, each address probed on-chain before use. At runtime it picks the deepest WBNB/USDT pool across the four fee tiers. Once the venue existed, moving production from PancakeSwap V3 to Uniswap v3 was one env variable: 40 seconds from restart to a minted position, with the inventory swap cleared through Ophis first. Along the way I found that slot0 decodes the same on both even though PancakeSwap declares feeProtocol as uint32 and Uniswap as uint8 (ABI words are padded), so one ABI serves both.
Bazantic. I published OpenAPI specs for the agent index and for the Ophis Rebates API, made them two paid gateways (1 cent per call in USDC), and wrote two recipes: hire the best agent in a category by measured execution, and vet a wallet. A recorded recipe run picks the agent and returns the settlement tx of its latest fill.
World AgentKit. My x402 server is plain node:http, not Hono, so I rebuilt the AgentKit hook by hand, including the challenge nonce and issuedAt that declareAgentkitExtension leaves out.
The Graph lending check is in the code, but I didn't check that the key is set on the VM. The text never calls it live, so it's safe either way. If you know it isn't set, tell me and I'll soften that line.

name: SpendVeto
description: Governs what your AI agent can spend — before it pays, not after. Open source, x402-native.
projectDescription:
SpendVeto is an open-source spend-governance layer for AI agents that pay for things over x402/MCP — budgets, human-in-the-loop approvals above a threshold, a kill switch, tool/chain/payee scoping, and a tamper-evident hash-chained audit ledger, all enforced server-authoritatively before a single payment settles. Live at spendveto.com with 298 end-to-end verified assertions from a clean clone (npm run verify).
For this Continuity Track build, we extended three real capabilities: governance for x402 v2's new upto scheme (variable-amount authorizations, where a buyer signs for a ceiling and the seller charges less later — held against the budget until it settles, so open ceilings can't silently exhaust an hourly cap); real on-chain settlement on Hedera testnet with a live governed payment (settled + a policy-refused case, both recorded); a migration to World ID 4.0's RP-based proof-of-personhood protocol gating human approvals; and ENS name resolution in payee allowlists, so an allowlist reads as vitalik.eth instead of raw hex, resolved against real Ethereum mainnet and cached for the hot policy-check path.
howItsMade:
Node.js/Express backend, viem for signature verification across seven signature families (secp256k1, ed25519, Move, Stellar, Hedera, Algorand, XRPL), a hash-chained JSON ledger for tamper-evident audit trails, and an MCP stdio server so any MCP client (Claude Desktop, Claude Code) sees governed tools natively. The x402 gate is server-authoritative — policy is re-checked at settlement, not just client-side, so a hand-rolled client can't bypass it.
For the Continuity Track work: server/upto.js governs x402's upto scheme by holding the authorized ceiling against the hourly budget until settlement, releasing headroom afterward. server/worldid.js was rewritten against @worldcoin/idkit-server for World ID 4.0's signed rp_context handshake — verified end-to-end with a real device-scanned proof from the actual World App. client/ens.js resolves .eth names via viem's getEnsAddress against Ethereum mainnet, fails closed if a name won't resolve (never a wildcard match), and caches to keep checkPolicy (which runs on every governed call) fast. Hedera settlement was verified with a real $0.01 payment on testnet — tx 0.0.9185802-1788804271-756194533.

name: HYPOTHECA
description: Permissionless on-chain enforcement for partial asset claims and collateral on Hedera.
projectDescription: Hypotheca is a permissionless enforcement layer on top of Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS) that records partial claims/collateral against an asset's available balance and enforces them on-chain. Every credit line a bank draws against a tokenized asset is materialized as an ATS hold locked inside an on-chain vault so the same unit can never back two loans, and over pledging is rejected by the contract, not by an API.
howItsMade: HYPOTECHA is built as a fully on-chain enforcement layer on Hedera, using Solidity 0.8.24 and Hardhat for two core contracts: EncumbranceLedger, which manages collateral, credit positions, ATS holds, coverage checks, repayment and permissionless settlement, and RegistryAnchor, which tracks tokenized asset instances. We integrate Hedera Asset Tokenization Studio (ATS) directly through its hold primitives (createHoldByPartition, executeHoldByPartition, and releaseHoldByPartition) so encumbered units are physically locked on-chain rather than tracked by an off-chain API. Chainlink price feeds provide live collateral valuation and coverage enforcement. The frontend is a React + Vite + TypeScript dashboard using wagmi and viem, connecting directly to Hedera EVM wallets with no backend. Because HashIO does not support eth_getLogs, event history is reconstructed through the Hedera Mirror Node REST API. We also built an E2E test flow covering pledge, over-pledge rejection, repayment, withdrawal and liquidation, backed by 29 contract tests and an automated audit gate.

name: kipio
description: Permanent, private memory storage where users own their data.
projectDescription:
Kipio is a digital sovereignty architecture that integrates Arbitrum Stylus (WASM) and Irys L1 Datachain to turn "cloud storage" into permanent, user-owned digital property. Photos are encrypted client-side before leaving the device, stored permanently through Irys, and indexed on-chain through a Rust-powered Stylus contract. The current MVP runs end-to-end on Arbitrum Sepolia with browser wallets.
For ETHOnline 2026 I targeted the Ledger — Continuity track. Kipio already worked as a complete product, so the hackathon work was to extend it with hardware-backed signing without touching the smart contracts. The dApp now exposes two Ledger connectors through Wagmi v3, both routed through the Ledger Device Management Kit: one for physical devices over WebHID, and one for the Speculos emulator deployed on Oracle Cloud. Reviewers can experience the full signing flow — EIP-191, EIP-712, and on-chain transactions — without owning hardware, and users with a real Ledger get the same pipeline through a different transport.
howItsMade:
The frontend is Next.js + TypeScript. Image processing and AES-GCM-256 encryption run inside Web Workers before any data leaves the browser. Ciphertext is uploaded to Irys devnet, and the content hash plus the Irys transaction ID are registered in a Stylus contract written in Rust and compiled to WASM on Arbitrum Sepolia.
For the Ledger integration I wrote a custom Wagmi v3 connector from scratch (src/lib/ledger/connector.ts) that wraps the Ledger Device Management Kit and exposes a Viem-compatible account. It is not a thin wrapper: it implements the full EIP-1193 surface — personal_sign, eth_signTypedData_v4, eth_sendTransaction, eth_signTransaction — and routes each method to the DMK SignerEth builder, while read-only RPC calls are proxied to a public client on the chain's HTTP transport. This is what allows ethers-based SDKs (like Irys) to sign through the Ledger without special-casing.
The same connector is instantiated twice in wagmi.ts, sharing the DMK signer but using different transports: webHidTransportFactory for physical devices and speculosTransportFactory for the emulator. The Speculos transport accepts an ordered list of URLs and caches the first one that responds, so a single build targets both local Docker and a remote deployment via environment variables.
The emulator backend ships a precompiled Ledger Ethereum app ELF and runs inside Docker on an Oracle Cloud Always Free ARM VM. The HTTP API (port 5000) is exposed through a Cloudflare Tunnel over HTTPS, which is what allows the Vercel-hosted dApp to talk to it without mixed-content blocks. A second tunnel exposes the VNC server (port 41000) through websockify, so the emulator screen can be embedded directly in the dashboard next to the upload pipeline.
A few hacky details worth mentioning: the connector normalizes Viem's typed-data output before it reaches the device (Ledger rejects bigint chainIds and inline EIP712Domain entries), it maps DMK's {r,s,v} signatures into the 65-byte hex format Viem expects while normalizing v between 0/1 and 27/28, and it detects the active connector ID to surface the emulator URL only when the user is on the Ledger Simulator. Everything else — the contracts, the Stylus registry, the encryption layer — was left untouched, which was the entire point of the track.

name: payOrRefuse
description: x402 payment gate: refuse before signing, judged on live data from The Graph.
projectDescription:
payOrRefuse is an x402 payment gate that refuses before a signature exists. It holds the signer until the evidence is there: the seller's settled history from vet402's /decision and, as a second source, the x402 Base subgraph on The Graph. Anything short of a pass is refused before a signature exists (no payment module is loaded) and returns machine-readable reason codes; a pass signs the x402 payment and attests it. It has moved real money once, and that is the run this submission documents: on 2026-09-05 it signed 0.01 USDC to The Graph's own x402 endpoint — Base block 50898704, tx 0xf12093fba9314b1d3a514e7b667969201be8d021a6f4d6bdeb8d6c7f2de469ad.
CONTINUITY.
What existed before: vet402 already bought from x402 endpoints with real USDC on Base and answered "should my agent pay this?" via /decision, an SDK and an MCP tool. None of that is submitted.
The boundary is tag pre-ethonline-2026 = commit c42daca, 2026-09-04 00:05:36 UTC, pushed. Hacking Begins was 2026-09-04 16:00 UTC, so the tag sits 15 h 54 min before. Three claimed commits predate that start: 37c56db and e668957 touch only WINDOW_PLAN.md, and ac6ec2e adds 16 lines under packages/sdk (6 in src/index.ts, 10 in generated dist/index.d.ts).
I had pushed 214 commits since my 2026-08-23 application (git rev-list --count 26a7c66..pre-ethonline-2026), disclosed in writing to ETHGlobal at 2026-09-04 23:49 UTC. The message says 207 because it counted only to 2026-09-03; docs/ethonline-2026/DISCLOSURE_2026-09-05.md holds it as sent, with the reconciliation.
What is new: everything else in the claimed range is after 16:00 UTC. payOrRefuse (packages/sdk), pay_if_trusted (packages/mcp-server), the demo, the A/B harness, SKILL.md, AI_USAGE.md. I am not moving the tag; both disclosures link to it.
main is also production, so the range holds work I do not claim. At the submission tag ethonline-2026-submission:
git log pre-ethonline-2026..ethonline-2026-submission -- packages/sdk packages/mcp-server examples/ethonline-2026-demo examples/ethonline-2026-ab SKILL.md AI_USAGE.md docs/ethonline-2026   # my claim: 260 commits
git log pre-ethonline-2026..ethonline-2026-submission   # same days, everything: 411 commits
Commits and code comments are mostly Japanese. The English route is SKILL.md (what to run), AI_USAGE.md (who wrote what) and docs/ethonline-2026/CHANGED_FILES.md (pre-existing files I touched). PROMPTS/ in that folder is a day-by-day excerpt, in Japanese, of the decisions and instructions I gave.
The Graph. With evidence source "subgraph" or "both", the gate reads the x402 Base subgraph live via the Gateway with the caller's key against a pinned deployment; the evidence row carries _meta.block.number. A failed read or a pin mismatch refuses, and nothing falls back to vet402's ledger.
On Bazantic I ran a pre-registered A/B (examples/ethonline-2026-ab), Recipe vs no Recipe. Success did not move: 5/10 and 5/10 — I had been expecting to write a different sentence here. Vocabulary did: real vet402 identifiers among reason codes went from 20/32 (63%) to 29/32 (91%), labelled exploratory. 88 calls settled, 88 zero-USDC tx on chain. Re-measured 2026-09-09: those free reads no longer post a transaction. A second pre-registered run, after a product fix and a Recipe update, went 7/10 without the Recipe and 5/10 with it. The whole gap came from one fixture. A third pre-registered run on 2026-09-12 closed it after I rewrote one sentence of the Recipe: 7/10 in both arms, with the vocabulary rate higher under the Recipe for the third time in three runs. The Bazantic comment goes through all of it.
npm run judge-check from the repo root unsets every key and runs 11 steps — sdk, mcp-server, demo, a root install for CI parity, and the A/B harness with mutations — then prints one table ending in judge-check: all 11 steps exit 0 in <n>s. It does not cover the SDK's own mutations; SKILL.md points at that one separately, and it takes a judge from git clone to a live read of The Graph and a dry-run payment, no funded payer key needed. The two MCP blocks want a throwaway key and still sign nothing, and the page flags them.
howItsMade:
The stack is TypeScript. packages/sdk (payOrRefuse, x402-pay, subgraph-evidence) and packages/mcp-server (pay_if_trusted, stdio) are plain Node packages, Node >= 20; the demo under examples/ethonline-2026-demo runs .ts directly on Node >= 22.18. The service behind vet402.com is Next.js on Postgres and is pre-existing.
THE GATE. payOrRefuse runs in this order and stops at the first failure (the header of packages/sdk/src/pay-or-refuse.ts).
(1) Caller errors are rejected before any request goes out: a payee that is not a 0x address, or a policy that waives ALLOW without declaring a floor (invalid_policy).
(2) The caller's own price ceiling is applied before the decision is fetched. price_above_ceiling, zero requests.
(3) GET /decision for the resource, role=payer. Unreadable or degraded refuses. A 404 means "not catalogued" and hands the judgement to the 402's payTo plus the payee score for that address. The evidence floors the caller declared are read and checked here, and vet402's recommendation is applied. ALLOW passes. WARN passes only if the caller set requireVet402Allow: false and every floor is met. BLOCK and degraded are never waived.
(4) The real 402 challenge is fetched, and its payTo, network, asset, scheme and amount are matched against what the caller named.
(5) The payment module is dynamically imported.
Refusals carry reason codes from a closed vocabulary (l1_not_attempted, l1_inconclusive, resource_uncatalogued, price_above_ceiling, price_above_declared, payee_recommendation_block, evidence_unavailable, ...).
How The Graph decides the outcome
With policy.evidence.source "subgraph" or "both", the SDK queries the x402 Base subgraph (Cb56epg3EvQ6JRpPfknbkM54QxpzTvLa7mwKNQQfUyoj) at gateway.thegraph.com with the caller's Subgraph Studio key: x402AddressSummaries filtered by the payee address with role RECIPIENT (totalPayments, totalVolumeDecimal), plus _meta { block { number } deployment }. The same address can also hold a PAYER row — it must not be added in. The Gateway answers a keyless request with HTTP 200 and an errors array where the data would be, so the SDK checks for that array before it reads any field and a missing key can never arrive as a receipt count of zero. The evidence row on the decision carries subgraphId, block number, deployment and queriedAt, plus the key-less publicUrl, so the record never contains the key. minSubgraphReceipts is a floor against that count. A failed read refuses, with no fallback to vet402's own ledger. This is what let a caller pay The Graph on The Graph's own data while vet402's engine still said WARN.
The payment path is x402 v2, scheme "exact", eip155:8453, USDC 0x8335...2913, EIP-3009. The SDK builds the transferWithAuthorization (from, to = accept.payTo, value = accept.amount exactly, validBefore rounded to at most 120 s, nonce = 32 random bytes it generates), signs it as EIP-712 with the USDC domain pinned to on-chain measured constants (name "USD Coin", version "2") and never taken from the seller's accept.extra, persists the nonce immediately after signing, re-sends the original request with the PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header (v1: X-PAYMENT), and reads the settlement claim from the PAYMENT-RESPONSE header. The SDK reports it as settle_claimed, not settled, because only a chain re-read may say settled. The buyer never calls a facilitator and pays no gas.
Whether a refuse path can reach the signer is checked rather than asserted. The payer account is a Proxy that counts property reads: 0 on every refuse path, and a negative control that flips --live sees exactly 1. The built dist/index.js module graph is walked, and the payment module must appear only behind a dynamic import. packages/sdk/test-mutations.mjs then edits the source one mutation at a time (pass a BLOCK under requireVet402Allow: false, flip the subgraph floor comparison, treat a /decision 404 as ALLOW, drop the payTo check, move the dynamic import outside the allow branch, read data past a GraphQL error) and requires every edit to turn the suite red. A companion suite feeds a table of malformed shapes to every external input: the decision body, the 402 challenge, the subgraph answer and the caller's own policy each get null, a wrong type, "0x10", "1e4", Infinity and a string "true". Each one has to stop before a signature exists.
The MCP server does not re-judge anything. pay_if_trusted takes the same policy object and forwards it to payOrRefuse unchanged. GRAPH_API_KEY comes from the server's env block. If the policy asks for the subgraph and the key is missing, the tool refuses with graph_key_not_configured before reading anything. VOUCH_API_KEY is optional for resources in vet402's catalogue, because /decision answers key-less at 10 requests per minute per IP. A resource outside the catalogue, such as The Graph's gateway, falls back to a keyed payee-score read, so without the key that verdict is not read and the tool refuses with evidence_unavailable.
On Bazantic, a Bazantic-built x402 gateway fronts vet402's REST API as 57 MCP tools (https://2vjhqfgvw5dt5lja2zpjsjwrem.bazgateway.com/mcp), and a public Recipe explains when and how to use it. The A/B harness (examples/ethonline-2026-ab) gives the same model the same prompt and the same tools twice, with the Recipe as the only difference (a test pins stripRecipe(B) === A byte for byte), grades every trial against what vet402's API actually returned, and writes raw trials.jsonl that npm run metrics regrades from scratch. Because the gateway answered 402 even on $0 routes during the v1 run and MCP tools/call cannot carry a payment, the harness includes a bridge — I had not known about that gap when I planned the run — that signs only when the quoted amount is exactly "0" and re-sends over REST.
Claude (Opus / Fable, via Claude Code) wrote most of the code under my direction, and the failing tests for the gate were written before the implementation. AI_USAGE.md lists the areas and files and what I did. docs/ethonline-2026/PROMPTS/ holds, day by day, an excerpt of the decisions and instructions I gave and the commits they landed in. No AI voice is used in the video.
