name: Ether Hunter
description: Ether Hunt: agents pay $0.01 for Graph-grounded USDC allowance audits (x402 · Arc).
projectDescription:
Ether Hunt is a pay-per-scan on-chain allowance auditor built for ETHOnline 2026 Classic (from scratch).
An agent—or the web UI’s buyer proxy—pays $0.01 USDC for one audit. Settlement is real, not mocked: Hedera ExactScheme x402 via Blocky402 on testnet (HTTP 402 → USDC transfer → 200), or Circle Agent Stack Gateway nanopayments on Arc Testnet (eip155:5042002, GatewayWalletBatched). Unpaid calls stay gated; local “free” scans never count as prize proof.
After payment, the API queries our From-Scratch The Graph Studio subgraph (ether-hunt-approvals). Mapping folds USDC Approval logs into live allowance state—Allowance, Account, and Spender entities with unlimited/revoked flags and blast-radius aggregates—so detectors read structured risk, not prose. While v0.0.2 resyncs, a tip-synced v0.0.1 fallback keeps Case Files reviewable. Rule findings plus a cite-only LLM may only reference real evidence IDs.
The dossier shows Graph LIVE mode, the exact GraphQL that ran, an allowance threat graph, ranked revoke targets, Verifiable rails (HashScan / Arcscan), PDF export, and share. Judges can verify without installing anything: open published HashScan settle txs and Arcscan agent/seller links in the README.
howItsMade:
Ether Hunt is an npm monorepo: Vite/React web app, Hono audit-api, shared report types, agent-consumer CLIs, and a From-Scratch AssemblyScript subgraph under subgraphs/token-approvals.
Payments sit in front of the audit. Hedera uses @x402/hono + ExactHederaScheme and Blocky402’s testnet facilitator: unpaid POST /audit returns HTTP 402; the agent (or /scan/hedera proxy) settles $0.01 USDC HTS, then retries. Arc uses Circle’s Gateway facilitator and circle services pay (GatewayWalletBatched on eip155:5042002) against POST /audit/arc. Both rails stamp sources.payment.rail / settled / explorer links so the UI’s Verifiable rails panel can open HashScan or Arcscan without trust-me slides.
Evidence is Graph-first. We deployed ether-hunt-approvals to Studio: the mapping folds Approval logs into mutable Allowance state plus Account/Spender aggregates (live unlimited counts, peaks, re-approvals) so risk is computed at index time. The API probes allowance-state GraphQL, caches schema mode per endpoint, and if the subject is empty mid-resync falls back to tip-synced v0.0.1 approval-events—still live Graph, not fixtures. Nine Case Files are warmed on API boot for async judges. Detectors read structured links/metrics and a spender registry (Permit2, Morpho, Balancer, Curve, …); DeepSeek (or other LLM) synthesizes only with citeable evidence IDs.
Notable glue: overlapping Graph warm with x402 settle to hide latency; Prove-the-gate decodes the raw 402 challenge in-browser; PDF export uses a Blob URL print sheet (noopener blank windows broke document.write); HashScan URLs normalize mirror tx ids to @seconds.nanos. Partner tech is load-bearing: without Blocky402/x402 and Circle Gateway there is no pay-per-scan; without our subgraph the AI has nothing honest to cite.

name: Iqia - App
description: DeFi savings where your money works but never leaves your wallet. Powered by 1inch Aqua
projectDescription: Iqia is a non-custodial savings app on 1inch Aqua where your money never leaves your wallet. Unlike traditional DeFi pools that lock your funds, Aqua records an allowance your balance stays spendable while earning fees from swaps. The pricing strategy is an on-chain SwapVM bytecode program anyone can disassemble and verify. Backed by the same capital across multiple markets, achieving 3x capital efficiency.
howItsMade: The stack is a monorepo with three layers: Solidity smart contracts (Foundry), a TypeScript SwapVM encoder/decoder, and a React frontend. The contracts extend 1inch's official SwapVM with two custom opcodes: SolvencyGuard (reads real wallet backing on every swap to auto-reprice shared capital) and ExclusiveFill (full 20-byte address comparison for private orders, not the weaker 10-byte version SwapVM ships). The TypeScript encoder builds bytecode programs that are tested byte-for-byte against the Solidity implementation in golden vector tests. The frontend uses React + viem + wagmi to read on-chain state, build transactions, and let users ship positions through the official Aqua registry  all without any custody or helper contracts. Deployed on Ethereum Sepolia against the real 1inch Aqua contract.

name: Sovereign-MCP
description: Your agent hires other agents. Pays per call in USDC on Arc, reputation earned on-chain.
projectDescription:
Sovereign is a marketplace where an AI agent hires other agents to do work, pays a few cents per call in USDC, and can tell beforehand whether the one it is about to hire is any good.
The reason to buy rather than derive is context. An agent that answers a question by fetching twenty web pages burns tens of thousands of tokens and fills its window with noise. A specialist returns the same answer in three hundred tokens for a few cents. But that saving is only real if you can skip checking the result, because re-deriving it to verify spends exactly what you saved. So the hard part is not payments, it is trust.
Sovereign's answer is receipts. Before hiring, the buyer writes down what they expect to get back. After the call they grade the result against that statement, and the grade goes on chain: delivered or not, how long it took, met or partially met or not met. Those receipts aggregate into a public track record, so the next buyer sees how often a worker met what people actually asked of it, how many buyers came back, and how fast it answers. Scores use a Wilson lower bound, which means two perfect calls rank below five hundred good ones instead of topping the leaderboard.
Sellers list an agent on chain with a price and an endpoint. It can already speak x402, or it can be an ordinary webhook that Sovereign wraps in a paywall on the site itself, which is how a seller with an n8n workflow and no interest in payment protocols becomes a paid worker in about two minutes. Before a listing goes live the app probes that endpoint once, unpaid, and requires a 402 response quoting the same payout address and the same price the listing claims. That single request catches dead URLs, endpoints that serve for free, and listings whose advertised price is a lie. Each seller is bound to a unique human with World ID Selfie Check, because a reputation system is worthless if a seller with bad reviews can mint a fresh identity for nothing.
Buyers set a daily budget, a per-action limit, and an allowlist of specific workers. Every hire is checked against that policy server-side before anything is signed, so an agent spends autonomously inside limits its owner set once, and never has to stop and ask. The limits are the permission.
The whole loop runs from Claude Code. One command pairs a terminal with a Sovereign account and installs an MCP server that searches the registry for free, reads a worker's track record, hires it, and pays inside the call. Afterwards it asks the buyer whether the work met what they asked for and files that verdict on chain, signed by the wallet that paid: you cannot review work you did not buy, and one payment gets one receipt. The buyer states the grade. The agent never grades the work it commissioned.
howItsMade:
Contracts (Arc testnet, chain 5042002). Three Solidity contracts. AgentRegistry holds listings: slug, owner, payout address, price in USDC-6, metadata and endpoint. Receipts is append-only graded work, one receipt per (buyer, settlement reference) so nobody can farm a score by re-filing. Verifications records World ID proofs, attestor-signed over EIP-712, binding one nullifier to one account. The trust model is documented in the Receipts header rather than glossed: the contract cannot verify that the payment it describes happened, so it records an attributed claim, and off-chain scoring cross-checks the settlement reference against real transfers and discounts buyers funded by the seller. Verifying settlement on chain would need payments routed through a contract, which is the rigorous upgrade and deliberately not what this does.
The Graph. A subgraph indexes all three contracts and rolls receipt aggregates forward onto each Agent entity: delivered count, met score, distinct buyers, repeat buyers, cumulative latency. Aggregating on write rather than deriving at query time matters because a buyer's agent choosing between workers in milliseconds cannot afford to fan out. Discovery is a single query that returns listings already carrying their track record.
Circle and Arc. Payments run over x402 and settle through Circle Gateway using @circle-fin/x402-batching. The seller's worker is gated by createGatewayMiddleware, which answers an unpaid request with a 402 carrying signable requirements and then verifies and settles the retry. The buyer signs an EIP-3009 authorization against the Gateway wallet contract. This is the partner choice that makes the product possible rather than merely convenient: card rails cannot clear a few cents at all, and Arc being USDC-native means no separate gas token, since gas is paid in USDC. Batched settlement keeps it gasless for the buyer.
Privy. Embedded wallets, so a buyer never manages a key, plus server-side session signers so the marketplace can sign an x402 authorization for a paired terminal that holds no key at all. One thing worth flagging for anyone building this: createOnLogin: 'users-without-wallets' silently breaks external-wallet logins, because connecting MetaMask already counts as having a wallet, so those users get no embedded wallet and every send path fails with an error that names the wrong thing. Sovereign is email-login only for exactly this reason.
World ID. IDKit Selfie Check with the proof bound to the seller's wallet as the signal, verified server-side against both the action and the signal hash. The server then signs an EIP-712 attestation that Verifications.sol accepts, so the nullifier-to-account binding is enforced on chain rather than in app logic. A buyer reading a seller's profile can see the guarantee; before this it lived only in the verifier's own browser.
MCP. sovereign-mcp is published on npm. Pairing is one command: link --spend binds a terminal to a Sovereign account, so the agent can pay and file grades from that account's wallet with no key on the machine. The notable detail is the MCP instructions field, returned on initialize and injected into the model's context by the client. Without it the failure is silent and total: the tools are loaded, the user asks for exactly what the marketplace sells, and the agent web-searches instead because nothing ever told it when to look. Shipping the guidance with the server means discovery works with no install step at all. Ranking is relevance first then track record, so an unproven worker sorts below a proven one of equal relevance.
Designs. The logo and banner designs are public on this Figma Community page (https://www.figma.com/community/file/1678041140667171975)

name: REKT FLY
description: Learn DeFi risk in a 3D fly-brain survival game, then protect a real Sepolia testnet loan.
projectDescription:
REKT FLY turns liquidation risk into something you can see, play, and explain. It is a 3D DeFi survival lab for beginners who find collateral ratios and lending dashboards intimidating.
A player starts with a virtual loan backed by ETH and must survive a falling market while using limited reserves. Adding collateral preserves the loan but commits more capital; repaying debt improves safety while reducing the loan. An interactive price lesson, readable activity graph, pause controls, and an observation log make each tradeoff visible.
The distinctive controller uses a reduced fly escape circuit: 316 real neuron identities and 10,711 recorded connections. Two threat-sensor populations feed an escape alarm. Simulated activity drives a deliberately simple, public protection rule. Players can block sensor outputs and replay the same seed to test the circuit’s causal contribution. Scientific names are optional details, so no neuroscience background is required.
The browser experience works without a wallet. A separate MetaMask panel bridges the lesson to the official Ethereum Sepolia lending challenge: registration, live position reads, a health-factor calculator, exact token approvals, collateral deposits, and debt repayment. A successful onchain registration has been verified. The practice pilot never signs wallet transactions.
Use cases include beginner DeFi education, classroom demonstrations of risk and feedback, and reproducible experiments for builders exploring interpretable controllers. The anatomical fly and inspectable circuit make the lesson memorable without presenting simulated results as investment advice.
Current scope: kinematic 3D body animation, reduced neural simulation, local practice, and explicit Sepolia wallet actions. Full closed-loop MuJoCo locomotion and confidential CRE automation are not deployed.
A live Uniswap V3 exit-liquidity lesson connects the practice to real Ethereum mainnet markets. Compare WETH-to-USDC quotes across two fee tiers and see how slippage affects minimum received and hypothetical debt coverage. It is read-only, requires no wallet, and clearly separates live USDC quotes from practice dollars and Sepolia tokens.
howItsMade:
The frontend uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, and direct Three.js, deployed on Vercel. React updates controls independently of the 3D render loop. We kept the stack small: no database, paid LLM dependency, agent framework, or custom token contract.
The fly asset is derived from Apache-2.0 NeuroMechFly/FlyGym meshes and rigging, converted to a browser GLB with an original preparation pipeline. FlyWire-derived annotations/connectivity provide 104 LC4, 210 LPLC2, and two DNp01 cells; the background points are anatomical context only. Data provenance, pinned sources, transformation steps, and required notices are included. FlyWire data remains CC BY-NC 4.0; original application code is MIT.
An original reduced leaky-integrate-and-fire implementation uses published model parameters, signed delayed connections, a seeded input generator, and an explicit market-danger encoder. The browser advances 20 milliseconds of neural time per 100 milliseconds of game time. The anatomical body uses a designed kinematic gait; it is not driven by inferred biological leg torques.
Viem handles Sepolia reads, contract configuration checks, two-decimal token accounting, transaction simulation, exact-amount approvals, receipt verification, and account/network changes. The official challenge registration was verified onchain. A separate bounded Modal CPU experiment loaded and stepped the articulated MuJoCo fly with finite state and no numerical warnings; it is not a live cloud game backend.
Twelve tests cover circuit integrity, deterministic replay, ablation, accounting, lifecycle, activity history, and protection math. In the seed-42 automated practice comparison, the intact pilot survives 180 seconds with six interventions, while both visual outputs blocked causes liquidation at 64.5 seconds. This is evidence about the game model, not biological validation or financial returns.
OpenAI Codex assisted implementation in web/src, scripts, simulation, tests, configuration, and documentation. The participant supplied the idea, product direction, platform constraints, reuse requirements, and feedback, and performed the MetaMask registration. Existing libraries/assets and newly developed behavior are distinguished in the README. Confidential CRE execution is unfinished and no confidential-workflow prize qualification is claimed.
Uniswap V3 powers the exit lesson through the official Factory and QuoterV2 contracts. A Next.js server route uses viem simulateContract to quote 0.05% and 0.3% WETH/USDC pools at one block, with bounded RPC fallback and explicit errors instead of mock data. Integer base-unit arithmetic rounds minimum output down. The UI exposes verified pool links, block/time, fees, slippage and remaining hypothetical debt. FEEDBACK.md records developer feedback. No swap is sent, and the two-pool comparison is not a best-route aggregator.

name: GlobalPay
description: The financial operating system for AI agents to discover, verify, and pay for services.
projectDescription:
GlobalPay is an AI-native financial operating system for autonomous agents. It gives every agent a programmable financial identity through a managed wallet, scoped API credentials, and the ability to hold and transfer USDC.
GlobalPay enables two sides of an agent economy. Providers can create agents and publish AI-powered services with defined capabilities, endpoints, pricing, permissions, and subscription options. Consumers can discover these services through the marketplace, evaluate providers using human-backed identity and on-chain payment evidence, and purchase services with USDC on Arc.
A custom subgraph built with The Graph indexes Arc settlement activity and powers the Trust Engine, which evaluates payment history, settlement volume, success rate, buyer diversity, recency, and risk signals. World ID and AgentBook connect agent identities to verified humans or organizations.
After payment, the consumer agent invokes the selected service, receives the result, and records usage for billing, invoices, analytics, and future trust evaluation. GlobalPay also includes AI recommendations, autonomous commerce workflows, API access, webhooks, and optional x402 support for HTTP-native pay-per-call payments.
GlobalPay turns payments, service discovery, identity, and trust into programmable infrastructure for an autonomous agent economy.
howItsMade:
GlobalPay is built as a React and Express full-stack application with a PostgreSQL database. The frontend provides dashboards for organizations, agent creation, wallet management, service publishing, marketplace discovery, trust evaluation, autonomous commerce, billing, and analytics. The backend exposes REST APIs secured through session authentication, scoped developer API keys, and agent API keys.
Each agent receives a managed MPC wallet and its own blockchain identity. Arc Testnet handles USDC payment settlement, while a custom subgraph built with The Graph indexes payment events and supplies data for the Trust Engine. The Trust Engine evaluates providers using settlement success, payment volume, buyer activity, recency, and risk signals.
World ID provides human-backed verification, and AgentBook links verified organizations to their agents. AI Recommendations combine service capability, pricing, policy, and trust data to rank providers. After payment, agents invoke services and record usage for invoices, analytics, and future trust evaluation. Optional x402 support enables HTTP-native pay-per-call payments.

name: Agent FUEL
description: stake wNEWS tokens as leverage to power other agents that can grow their business
projectDescription: Agent Fuel is outcome-financed AI capacity for small businesses that already have customers. Small companies rarely get a revolver — the line of credit a PE-backed company draws when it's short — so they end up in merchant-cash-advance loans at effective rates that can reach 1,500% APR. Agent Fuel replaces that with a staged, evidence-gated facility on Base: wNEWS holders stake into one specific, time-boxed intervention inside a business (clear an onboarding backlog, open a channel, relieve a bottleneck); the business pays a small fee now and a premium only on attested lift; AI agents do bounded work under limits the business and the funder set for themselves. Price and market depth come from the canonical wNEWS/USDC Uniswap v3 pool, indexed by a The Graph subgraph and served to agents through an MCP built for this event. Agent-to-agent payments settle on Arc by Circle through a capped wNEWS bridge (testnet today, mainnet to follow), and every contract's admin key lives on a Ledger — it can pause inflows or attest a settlement, never touch a stake. Capital is released in steps: at each evidence date the decision is stop, hold, continue, or accelerate, and declining costs nothing. Every funding event is one canonical intervention record rendered six ways — business, operator, agent, customer steward, capital supporter, auditor — so no party is shown different economics. Live now: the stake contract on Base mainnet and the first real stake, made from a phone through a Telegram mini app.
howItsMade: Contracts are deliberately small Solidity 0.8 with no dependencies, Slither-clean, and hardware-administered. On Base mainnet: EngagementStake — stake, on-chain per-wallet auto-approve cap, exit that can never be paused, admin-attested settle, immutable. On Arc by Circle (testnet; mainnet when Circle publishes parameters): the wNEWS bridge pair — BaseLocker vault and WNewsBridge with a hard 100k mint cap and pause-never-blocks-exits — plus AttestedPrice and ServiceLedger for goal-attributed agent-to-agent payments; Arc's USDC-native gas is what makes small agent payments practical. A Ledger holds the admin role on every contract and the treasury; the deployer key has no post-deploy power, and an ERC-7730 clear-signing descriptor for the stake contract is in the repo. The Graph: a subgraph on the canonical wNEWS/USDC Uniswap v3 pool computes spot and "credibility" (the largest sell that printed under 5% impact), cross-checked against the Messari standardized subgraph; a TypeScript MCP server written during the event (Streamable HTTP on Cloud Run) exposes it as agent tools — credibility, company status, threat report, allocation quote, intervention response, and a six-audience intervention statement. The human side is a Telegram bot plus a React/Vite mini app (Reown AppKit, wagmi, viem): wallets are proven by a signed message, several per person, the page pins the contract address and decodes the calldata before it lets you hold-to-sign, and every read goes through Telegram-authenticated endpoints — no client-side database. The listener (Node, Firestore, Cloud Scheduler) confirms every approval against the chain receipt and keeps an append-only event log for playback. Hacks worth noting: a nonce-per-attempt link flow so chat buttons never go stale, and a native-scheme-first deep link because Telegram's webview swallows WalletConnect's redirect.

name: BLOCKNDRIVE
description: Secure, AI-powered decentralized document vault with blockchain ownership and privacy.
projectDescription: BlockNDrive is a decentralized document vault that combines blockchain, encryption, decentralized storage, AI, and programmable access control to give users greater control over their digital documents. When a user uploads a document, it is encrypted locally using AES before being stored, ensuring that the plaintext file is never sent to storage. The encrypted document is uploaded through Lighthouse to IPFS/Filecoin-backed storage, while its CID, cryptographic hashes, owner address, and timestamps are recorded on an Ethereum smart contract. Chainlink CRE orchestrates the document-analysis workflow to extract metadata and generate an AI-based risk score, with the analysis result and its integrity hash recorded for verification. Lit Protocol provides owner-based access control for the encryption key, allowing only the authorized user to decrypt and download the document. BlockNDrive aims to make document storage more private, verifiable, intelligent, and user-controlled.
howItsMade: BlockNDrive is built as a Next.js web dApp connected to an Ethereum Sepolia smart contract using ethers.js and MetaMask. Documents are encrypted client-side with AES before being uploaded to Lighthouse for IPFS/Filecoin-backed decentralized storage. The smart contract records the document CID, cryptographic hashes, owner address, and timestamps, providing verifiable integrity and ownership records without storing the actual document on-chain. Chainlink CRE is used to orchestrate the document-analysis workflow, including metadata extraction and AI-based risk scoring, while Lit Protocol is designed for programmable, owner-only access to the encryption key. This architecture combines Ethereum, Chainlink CRE, Lighthouse, AES encryption, and Lit Protocol to create a privacy-focused decentralized document vault.

name: Oscillon
description: Uniswap v4 hook for stable LP inventory: tax dumps vs last $1 print, cap size if no price
projectDescription:
Oscillon is a Uniswap v4 hook and testnet UI for stable–stable pools (USDe/USDT-class).The LP problem: when one stable trades cheap vs $1, vanilla 3 bps pools absorb the weak asset. LPs see it on withdraw. Static fees give that spread to arbs.The hook’s rule (as of the Sep 13 policy):If Chainlink has a usable print (age ≤ 24h heartbeat + 1h buffer), depeg is that print vs $1. Drain (weak coin in) can pay more than 3 bps. Restore stays at base fee.
Heartbeat silence is not a depeg. A last print still ~$1 is treated as $1.
If there is no usable Chainlink (past heartbeat, floor, revert), we do not use pool TWAP as $1 and we do not charge max fee. Base fee + size cap.
What we learned building it: push Chainlink stables usually update at ~50 bps or ~24h. Our backtest’s 3–20 bps USDe band almost never produces a new print, so a per-swap fee in that band cannot run on this feed. That is an infrastructure limit, not a missed if-statement. StablePair prices pool mid vs a reference for the same reason — that input exists every swap.The project is an experiment plus a path to an LP Health view (what a $10k position actually holds). It is not a claim that Oscillon beats official USDC/USDT StablePair or that LPs earn extra yield on quiet 8 bps tape.Testnet UI + Sepolia hook. Tests: 42/42 including 128k-call invariants.
website: https://beta-testnet.oscillon.xyz/swap
howItsMade: Uniswap v4 hook (beforeSwap / afterSwap) on Sepolia. Solidity: OscillonHook, ChainlinkOracleAdapter (AggregatorV3 + heartbeat-aligned MAX_ORACLE_AGE), OscillonPriceEngine, OscillonFeePolicy (base 3 bps + drain surcharge), OscillonTwapOracle (pre-swap tick write so a swap cannot paint its own window). TWAP is not used as USD when Chainlink is down.Frontend: Next.js swap UI (wallet, quote, depeg/fee readout). Foundry tests + fuzz/invariants (128k calls). Chainlink-compatible feeds on testnet (RedStone-shaped aggregators where we needed them).Hacky / notable: first version treated 1h silence as stale and could max-fee a quiet book. We replaced that with heartbeat-aligned trust and “blind → cap, not max fee.” A 20 bps Chainlink-vs-TWAP disagreement guard still lives; a large fresh print while the pool is still at $1 can be zeroed — documented, not hidden.Partner tech: Uniswap v4, Chainlink-style feeds. No Data Streams in this submission (pull+verify is a different product than a 3 bps stable swap).

name: Iter
description: Onchain CLOB+pool DEX: LPs set their own price tolerance, so sandwiche attacks stop
projectDescription:
Iter is a decentralized spot exchange that separates the two questions every trading venue has to answer: who supplies the tradable inventory, and how a trade is priced and settled.
Every AMM fused those into a single bonding curve. That is why a Uniswap LP cannot decline a price — the curve fills their capital at whatever price the market pushes it to, all the way down. Onchain order book DEXes fixed settlement but abandoned inventory: their liquidity still comes from professional market makers, not permissionless LPs.
Iter answers both. Settlement is a fully onchain central limit order book, with price-time or size priority chosen per pair at listing. Inventory is a pool layered on top that converts permissionless LP capital into ordinary limit orders on that same book, rather than a second pricing primitive. Every position carries its own slippageLimit, so an LP sets the worst price they will accept. At slippageLimit = 0 a position only ever executes at the reference price, which bounds its worst-case impermanent loss by construction.
Pool trades are priced against a TWAP reference rather than instantaneous spot, so the price an attacker can manufacture inside one block is not the price the pool trades at. In our simulation this cuts same-block sandwich extractability by roughly three orders of magnitude — to negative attacker profit once gas is counted.
Because settlement is an order book, a trade can also add liquidity: it settles whatever it can match and the remainder rests as the trader's own limit order, instead of an AMM route's all-or-nothing revert.
The costs are real and we state them: occasional partial fills when tolerant liquidity is thin, and roughly 6x Uniswap v2's gas per swap, which makes Iter an L2 protocol by construction.
howItsMade: CONTRACTS (Solidity 0.8.24, Foundry). MatchingEngine + Orderbook are the settlement layer: a fully onchain order book in 8-decimal fixed point (DENOM = 1e8), with price-time or size priority selected per pair at listing. src/swap holds the inventory layer — BandPool, PoolBands, BandPositionManager, BandSwapRouter. A "band" is a price tolerance anchored to the orderbook TWAP. The whitepaper described this as a per-position slippageLimit; in the shipped contracts we hoisted it into discrete buckets, because a continuous per-position tolerance had no bucket to be fungible inside. Band is a uint32 tolerance packed alongside shares and an open flag, so a band costs no extra storage slot.

name: Slope
description: Split a big swap into non-custodial scheduled slices along a curve you choose
projectDescription: Existing on-chain execution limits large taker orders to two patterns, and both carry cost. A single market transaction absorbs the entire price impact at once, while manual slicing reintroduces the coordination problem the split was meant to solve, one approval and one transaction at a time, and scheduled alternatives run on a fixed clock regardless of market conditions. Slope introduces a taker-side execution position in which a single order is itself a bounded, executable time curve. A user declares a budget, a duration, and a pace shape (aggressive, neutral, or conservative), plus hard price rails, and the curve determines how much of the budget is authorised at each point in time. A flat pace reduces to ordinary linear TWAP, so the conventional schedule is a special case rather than a separate mode. The schedule lives on-chain: the SlopePosition contract computes how much each slice may sell, measures price impact with a dual-quote probe, enforces the price rails, and pulls tokens per fill with no escrow, so an unexecuted budget never leaves the owner's wallet, and a terminal clamp settles the exact remainder after the window closes. Execution is delegated through a Privy session signer scoped to exactly what the position declared: the contract address, the function selector, the position id, a per-transaction cap, and an expiry. The keeper triggers fills repeatedly without further approval and can never exceed what the schedule authorises; the contract enforces the budget and the schedule, and the Privy policy enforces the scope. The system refuses to act when conditions are wrong: prices outside the declared band, impact above the limit, or an emptied allowance are each recorded on-chain with their reason, and the keeper reads that history back from The Graph to decide whether to retry or park. Realised execution is measured against a linear-TWAP benchmark computed in the subgraph, so the value of adapting to market conditions is a number users can verify. The live application supports creating schedules from the browser, an execution staircase that fills in real time, per-fill deviation against the benchmark in basis points, an Aqua protocol trace decoded per fill with @1inch/aqua-sdk, and a CSV export of the full event stream, all on Base Sepolia.
howItsMade:
Slope is a TypeScript and Solidity monorepo. The onchain system uses Solidity 0.8.30 with Foundry and via-IR, and the keeper and interface are TypeScript on Node 24.
A fixed-point curve kernel compiles each schedule's budget, duration, and pace shape into an  authorised amount per instant. It covers the linear branch, a square-root front-loaded branch, and a squared back-loaded branch, with boundary conditions exact by construction. Custody is pull-per-fill: tokenIn is pulled from the owner at fill time and never escrowed, so a cancelled schedule needs no refund path, and a terminal clamp settles the exact remainder after the window closes so integer-division dust cannot strand a position.
Price impact is measured with a dual quote on the same router in the same call: a small probe approximating spot, and the real fill size, where the difference is the fill's own footprint. Below a decimals-derived probe floor the check cannot measure anything, and the fill event records impactChecked=false rather than claiming a check that did not happen.
The official 1inch Aqua and SwapVM contracts serve as the shared-liquidity and settlement layer on Base Sepolia, where no official deployment exists: the registry and SwapVM router were self-deployed from the v1.0.2 source, whose build requires via_ir with the Cancun EVM target since the function-pointer opcode table breaks without IR codegen. The shipped 1inch strategies embed a KYC gate opcode that only KYB-verified resolvers can pass, so Slope ships its own ungated strategy.
Privy carries the delegation layer. A per-position P-256 keypair is registered as a 1-of-1 key quorum bound to a policy that allowlists the exact contract, the exact selector, the position id, a per-transaction cap, and an expiry matching the schedule. Cumulative spend aggregations are tracked at sign level only, so the keeper signs via eth_signTransaction and broadcasts the raw transaction itself. A policy containing an aggregation reference condition was found to reject every signing request regardless of operator or value format, established by bisecting a live policy where an identical policy without the reference passes immediately; rate limiting therefore lives in the keeper, and the budget invariant lives in Solidity where it belongs.
The Graph is load-bearing in the execution path, not just the dashboard. Each tick the keeper queries the subgraph to decide what to work on: which positions are active, what is already indexed as executed, and whether a recent skip means a position should be parked. Candidate state is re-verified on-chain before signing, because indexing lag must never be the final
authority on a financial decision. If the subgraph is unreachable the tick is skipped and logged; there is no fallback path and no cached substitute. The subgraph also computes a BenchmarkComparison snapshot per position, realised VWAP against the linear-TWAP counterfactual, which powers the per-fill deviation in bps shown in the interface. The application runs no database of its own: the subgraph, queried exclusively through its GraphQL endpoint, is the single structured data source for both the keeper's decision-making and the frontend, and the only local persistence is a JSON file holding per-position delegated signing keys.
The interface uses React, Vite, viem, and Tailwind, with every curve drawn on the Canvas API rather than a charting library, so the time ruler, the planned-versus-actual divergence, and the fill and skip marks stamped along the axis are one consistent instrument. Email onboarding runs through Privy embedded wallets, an Aqua protocol trace is decoded per fill with @1inch/aqua-sdk, and an awaiting-index state covers the window while the subgraph catches up with a fresh schedule. The frontend is hosted on Vercel, the subgraph on The Graph Studio, and the keeper runs under systemd on a VPS.
Testing includes Foundry unit, integration, and fuzz suites with simulated time, cross-validation against an independent TypeScript reference model through committed vectors spanning all three pace shapes across five durations including asymmetric-decimal price normalisation, and Vitest coverage on the keeper and shared model.

name: TrustDrop + VDS
description: Verifiable dataset sampling before purchase; payment bound to verifiable delivery.
projectDescription:
TrustDrop is a protocol for turning delivery into verifiable evidence that contracts can act on. A seller publishes an encrypted payload on Walrus, VSS proves that the buyer receives recoverable key material, and VDD binds the committed key, original Walrus blob ID, and ciphertext Walrus blob ID into one verifiable encryption relation.
For this hackathon, we extended TrustDrop with verifiable dataset sampling. Before this work, a buyer’s knowledge of the original asset stopped at its commitment. Our new SP1 programs derive challenge-selected samples from a committed chain-intelligence dataset: one complete minute of token-flow data and three complete wallet-cluster records with their underlying transfer evidence. Walrus openings authenticate the selected source bytes, and each proof commits the reconstructed sample CID.
This gives buyers verifiable evidence about the original asset before purchase, while TrustDrop handles verifiable key distribution, encrypted delivery, and settlement afterward.
howItsMade:
TrustDrop uses Rust, Walrus, SP1, Solidity, Arbitrum Sepolia, The Graph, IPFS, and a Vite/TypeScript frontend. Its existing SP1 programs prove access-key sharing and encrypted data delivery, while The Graph indexes marketplace activity and supports complex queries without a separately hosted database.
Proof modules can define their own schema, sampling rules, zk program, verifier, certificate, and presentation. For this hackathon, we built a chain-intelligence dataset containing token flows, wallet clusters, and supporting transactions, then implemented two deterministic samplers.
One sampler selects a time-aligned flow interval; the other selects multiple cluster IDs and their supporting transfers. SP1 guests authenticate the required Reed–Solomon slivers against the source commitment, reconstruct the exact samples, and commit their IPFS CIDs. Succinct generates Groth16 proofs, standalone Solidity contracts verify them, and the marketplace displays each certificate with verification results and interactive sample viewers.

name: SwipeFi
description: Gamified Telegram Mini App building sophisticated DeFi yield positions via 1inch Aqua & SwapVM
projectDescription:
SwipeFi transforms complex decentralized finance into an intuitive, gamified Telegram Mini App designed to bring retail users into Web3. Traditional DeFi platforms overwhelm everyday users with intimidating candlestick charts, manual multi-step interactions across protocols, and complex order routing. SwipeFi distills asset discovery and yield generation into a familiar binary experience: swipe left to skip, or swipe right to automatically execute a sophisticated, multi-step DeFi position in a single interaction.
Each token card presents a dark-mode glassmorphic interface showing the asset's identity, a 24-hour price trend, and AI-generated project insights. Beneath its seamless UI, SwipeFi relies on 1inch Aqua and SwapVM to package complex end-to-end trading and yield strategies into a single transaction. Instead of performing basic swaps, a right swipe triggers SwapVM to execute an atomic "Zap & Yield" flow—swapping USDC for an underlying token and instantly depositing it into yield-generating protocols (such as liquid staking), maximizing execution efficiency while eliminating user friction.
howItsMade:
SwipeFi is built as a lightweight, high-performance Telegram Mini App designed for mobile responsiveness. The frontend uses Next.js, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS to deliver a glassmorphic dark-mode interface, paired with Framer Motion to drive 60 FPS touch-gesture physics for card swiping.
The core financial architecture relies directly on 1inch's Aqua Protocol and SwapVM. Using the @1inch/aqua SDK, SwipeFi constructs custom execution instructions targeting SwapVM smart contracts. When a user swipes right, the application calls a Next.js API Route Handler that compiles a unified SwapVM call. This single instruction atomically routes USDC into a target token via 1inch liquidity and immediately deposits the acquired asset into Lido (or similar yield protocols) to issue yield-bearing tokens (e.g., stETH) back to the user.
For the live demonstration and testing environment, the smart contract execution was validated on a local Mainnet Fork powered by Hardhat, simulating live state, whale token impersonation, and on-chain token balance transfers. To overcome Telegram's in-app webview constraints, we bridged the Telegram Web Apps SDK directly to an injected provider context to ensure smooth, single-tap transaction sign-offs.

name: Reckon
description: An agent manages a treasury under rules it can't forge. Refusing it is the whole point.
projectDescription:
If you hand money to an agent, you're trusting it not to do something dumb while you're asleep. Right now that trust sits in the agent's own code — an if-statement it can talk itself out of.
reckon replaces that with a document. The owner writes a mandate in plain terms, signs it, and the agent holds a copy it can't alter. Six clauses: keep 60% in stablecoins, never more than 15% in one asset, max $500 a trade, only tokens older than 90 days with real liquidity, an hour between trades, and Uniswap only. What gets signed is the readable text plus a hash of the exact numbers, so every decision the agent makes can point back to the rules that were live at the time.
Every clause is then enforced in three independent places. The evaluator checks the portfolio-wide limits against live data. Those same clauses compile into a Privy wallet policy, so the agent physically can't sign a transaction outside them — that refusal happens in Privy's signing enclave, not in our code. And anything the mandate merely bounds, rather than forbids, escalates to the owner, who signs an EIP-712 override good for one action, one token, one hour.
Clause four is the one a price feed can't answer, so it comes from two Graph products composed together. The Uniswap v3 subgraph gives token age and the trough of daily TVL across thirty days — not today's number, because a pool that dropped to $40k last Tuesday isn't liquid however healthy it looks now. The Token API gives holder concentration. That second one taught us something: the top ten holders of WETH on Base own 52% of supply, but nine of the ten are bridges and protocol contracts, and real wallets hold 0.93%. The obvious metric rejects WETH for a reason that isn't real, so §4 counts wallets and the receipt records both figures.
Execution is Uniswap v3 through SwapRouter02. The subgraph ranks fee tiers by TVL but doesn't get to set the price: we quote all four through QuoterV2 and take the best fill, which is about 0.6% better on WETH/USDC, with the winner flipping from 0.01% to 0.05% around $5,000.
Four decisions in the demo, all against a fork of Base mainnet — real pools, real prices, real Privy signatures, fake funds. A $5 WETH rebalance clears every clause and executes. $5 of DEGEN is refused: trough liquidity was $493,000 against a $2M floor. A $12 WETH buy would put 34% into one asset against a 15% ceiling, so it stops and waits. Then the owner signs, the policy is widened for that single action, it executes, and the original policy goes back.
Every decision appends a receipt: what it saw and where the data came from, what it wanted to do and why, which clauses it cleared or broke with the observed values and the limits, who authorised it, what it did on chain, and the hash of the mandate in force. The dashboard is that ledger and nothing else — no charts, no dials.
One thing to be straight about: the planner that decides what to propose is written but not wired in, and has never been run — we had no API key. The four proposals in the demo are fixtures we wrote. So what exists is the layer that constrains an agent, with the decision-maker sketched in but not plugged in. It's called out in the README rather than left for someone to find.
howItsMade:
TypeScript throughout, Next.js 16 for the dashboard, viem for anything touching a chain, zod for validating the mandate before it's ever hashed.
The mandate is an EIP-712 document. What gets signed is a readable sentence per clause plus a keccak of the canonicalised clause values — keys sorted recursively, so the same rules always hash the same way. Every receipt cites that hash. Change one number and the hash changes, which is the whole point.
Privy is where the mandate stops being a promise. We compile the clauses into wallet policy rules: §6 becomes a to allowlist of the Uniswap router, §3 becomes an amountIn ceiling, §4 becomes a tokenOut allowlist — and those last two are ethereum_calldata conditions, meaning Privy decodes the swap arguments with the ABI and compares them inside the enclave. That's what makes "the agent physically cannot" true rather than aspirational.
Four things cost us real time there, none of them documented where we looked:
A catch-all {method: "*", action: "DENY"} rule silently disables the entire policy. We added it as a safety net and every transaction started failing, including compliant ones. Bisecting it: a minimal policy with one ALLOW rule passes; add the catch-all and the same transaction is refused. A matching DENY overrides every ALLOW regardless of order, and policies are already deny-by-default, so the "safety net" only removes function. The failure is silent — policy_violation looks identical whether your conditions are wrong or an extra rule is eating them.
Constraining only eth_sendTransaction leaves a hole: the agent can call eth_signTransaction and broadcast the signed payload through any RPC it likes. We emit rules for both.
Rule names must be under 50 characters. chain_id conditions take a string, not a number. Calldata fields are "functionName.argumentName" — exactInputSingle.params.tokenOut, not params.tokenOut. Each of those was a 400 with a different message.
And PrivyClientOptions takes appId while the internal client type uses appID. Passing appID type-errors but works at runtime, because the SDK silently falls back to process.env.PRIVY_APP_ID. That sent us debugging a perfectly good app for a while. We ended up reading the SDK's .d.ts files directly rather than the docs, which is how we found the calldata condition shape too.
The hacky bit worth mentioning: our signer asks Privy to sign and then broadcasts the raw transaction through our own RPC, rather than letting Privy send it. That was originally so we could execute against a local fork — Privy would have sent it to real Base. But it's better in production too: the policy is exercised at signature time, so it holds no matter which RPC is in play.
The owner override uses the same trick in reverse. A valid EIP-712 override still isn't enough, because Privy will refuse anyway — so reckon compiles a widened policy containing one extra ALLOW rule for that specific token and amount, attaches it, executes, and restores the base policy in a finally. The widening lasts one transaction and the receipt cites the override hash.
The Graph is two products, and they authenticate separately — a Graph Studio key returns 401 against the Token API with no WWW-Authenticate header to tell you why. The Token API also 500s on roughly one call in five (we measured: 500 200 200 200 200), which matters because our risk gate fails closed. A flaky third-party turned into "the agent refuses to trade" three times in a row during a demo run. Retry with backoff, cache for 15 minutes, and prefer a stale answer over null.
The subgraph gives token age and poolDayDatas. We take the minimum TVL across the window rather than an average — an average hides the day a pool got drained, which is the exact risk the clause exists to catch. Worth knowing: the community Base deployments report broken numbers, one WETH pool claims $34bn TVL, so we aggregate across pools and take minimums.
Uniswap — the subgraph proposes a fee tier ranked by TVL, and we don't trust it with the price. Quoting all four tiers in parallel through QuoterV2 (which reverts internally, so it goes through simulateContract) is about 0.6% better on WETH/USDC, and the winner flips from 0.01% to 0.05% around $5,000. TVL ranks candidates; the quoter decides.
Testing runs against a fork of Base mainnet: real pools, real prices, real signatures, fake money. We used a Tenderly Virtual TestNet with chain id 8453 deliberately, so the wallet policy is byte-identical to one guarding a real mainnet wallet, and burned through the free-tier cheat-code quota twice; anvil is the fallback and has no limits. The agent wallet has never been funded on real Base, which is what makes the replay warning moot.
Receipts are one JSON object per line in an append-only file. No database. The file is the ledger, and keeping it as one plain readable file was deliberate.

name: speculum
description: Checks whether an AI agent's stated intent matches the transaction it is about to sign.
projectDescription:
In 40 consecutive Ethereum mainnet blocks on 13 September, speculum decoded 7,299 transactions. Of the 203 approvals that carried an amount, 59 were unbounded, nearly three in ten signatures granting a ceiling no token supply can ever reach. That traffic was not written for this project. It is what ERC-20 approval looks like on a normal morning.
An agent says it will approve exactly 100 USDC. It emits calldata. The signer signs bytes that nobody ever compared against the sentence. Nothing in that flow is malicious and nothing reverts, which is why it keeps happening.
speculum makes the agent declare what it is doing before it signs, then decodes the calldata on its own and compares the two. The decoder never sees the declaration, so the check cannot be circular. A match passes. A divergence blocks and escalates to a hardware confirmation. When the calldata cannot be decoded at all, speculum refuses rather than guessing, and says which of the two failures happened.
Fifteen named divergence classes so far. Wrong recipient, wrong token, wrong spender, an amount larger than the one declared, an approval that came out unlimited when a specific figure was stated, native currency riding along undeclared, and calls that transfer ownership or upgrade a proxy behind an otherwise ordinary looking transaction.
Simulators already tell a human what state will change. They do not know what the agent claimed, so they cannot tell you that the two disagree. That gap is the whole product.
howItsMade:
The engine is Node and viem. decode takes a transaction and nothing else and returns what the bytes actually do. compare takes that plus the declared intent and returns a verdict with every reason attached. Calldata in the tests is encoded with viem rather than written by hand, so the bytes under test are real bytes and not strings that happen to parse.
Two bugs came out of the tests rather than out of reading the code. The branch separating an unknown selector from unreadable arguments was structurally always true, so every unrecognised call was mislabelled. And the bitfield that crosses from JavaScript into the Solidity event needed a test of its own, because a silent disagreement there would have miscounted every indexed verdict without ever failing loudly.
The contract stores nothing and emits everything, because the consumer is an indexer rather than another contract, and a check that costs twenty thousand gas is a check that gets skipped. It holds no funds and routes no calls, so it cannot become a point of failure inside a transaction it is judging. It also enforces one invariant: a clean verdict carrying findings, or a flagged verdict carrying none, is rejected rather than indexed as a contradiction.
On AI use, since the rules ask for it. Claude was used to do some work here, including this text, since English is not my first language and I did not want mistakes in it. What it could not do is establish that any of it was true. Every fact in the repository README came from running something: the Ledger needing a physical confirmation and returning 0x6985 when refused was established by pressing both buttons and then pressing reject on a real device, eth_simulateV1 was probed across five endpoints and works on two, and the contract was funded and deployed by hand to Base Sepolia. The model had asserted several of those confidently before they were checked, and was wrong about some. Three errors were caught by eye rather than by tests, including a co-author still showing on the repository after the model declared the history clean, because it had verified commit messages instead of the page a person actually looks at. The problem, the decision to build from scratch, the partner choices and the name are mine.
The root of the service negotiates on the Accept header, so an agent gets the JSON descriptor it needs to discover the price and a browser gets a page, one URL with no second copy to drift. The consumer is in the repo too: hedera/agent.js sends the unpaid request first on purpose, takes the price from the 402 rather than anything hardcoded, signs, and refuses to sign the check it was told to block.

name: Semantic ABI
description: Ethereum type-checks bytes; Semantic ABI type-checks what evidence is allowed to mean.
projectDescription:
Semantic ABI is a type system for what one protocol’s evidence is allowed to mean when another protocol consumes it. Ethereum has an ABI for how contracts compose at the byte / execution level — but nothing checks meaning-level composition. A commitment, an attestation, a state-inclusion proof and an independent recomputation can each return true and carry completely different authority; today those distinctions live in prose and implementation discipline, and compositions silently upgrade one into another.
Semantic ABI makes it machine-checkable. Every component declares a typed EvidenceClaim — authority_class, claim_type, scope, and a temporal boundary — plus an explicit does_not_establish set naming what it deliberately does not prove. A semantic linker checks a composition and throws a meaning-level TYPE ERROR, with a minimal counterexample, whenever an edge would upgrade authority with no evidence. A two-level runner keeps three values distinct that systems routinely collapse into one green light: the expected pair outcome, what a backend observed, and whether the backend conformed.
The proof isn’t “we built X.” It’s that independently-built systems declare into the same schema and are checked by the same runner with no shared checker code — invinoveritas’s adapter is wired and reproduces a real historical bug live (a signed-commitment collapse), and the Vértice gateway maps the same real endpoints. Don’t trust it — recompute what you can, and label honestly what you can’t.
howItsMade:
The core is a zero-dependency Node/ESM engine (runs on clone, no install): a manifest loader + JSON-Schema, a semantic linker, and a two-level protected-relation runner, using node:crypto for content-addressing. Evidence is typed as EvidenceClaim<claim_type, authority_class, scope, issued_at | verification_time>. The linker’s one deliberate cross-class edge — recomputation → semantic verification — is claim- and scope-specific, never global; a global version would be the exact authority over-claim the tool exists to catch, so we refused it in the type system itself.
Each system under test is wrapped by an adapter authored independently by its owner, mapping real endpoints to manifest declarations: invinoveritas (/review, /verify-proof, /ledger, a Bitcoin freshness beacon) and the Vértice gateway (EIP-712 L4 attestation, a Base-Sepolia anchor, a /verify recompute endpoint, ERC-8373 post-quantum key binding). There is no shared checker between adapters, so “N systems conform” means N genuinely independent systems, not one checked N times.
Conformance vectors include negatives that must fail (prove-can-fail). The flagship reproduces a real, git-verifiable historical bug — invinoveritas pre-v18, where two structurally different REJECT verdicts (evidence-against vs merely-insufficient) produced the same signed commitment — as a live FAIL, fixed post-v18 as a PASS.
It composes with the trustless-ai standards family it grew out of: WYRIWE / ERC-8299 (input provenance), ERC-8281 (on-chain anchoring), and a companion recompute-kit recipe that folds a genuine-enclave TEE inference (0G Compute) into an 8281 anchored manifest as an “attested, not recomputed” leaf. The notably-hacky-in-the-best-way part: during review the suite caught a real gap in its own checker — it gated the “not recomputed” disclaimer but not the “not judged correct” one — found by running the mirror case against itself. The thesis applied to itself; now fixed, with a proving negative.

name: BlotChain-MEVShield
description: 3D WebGL control plane detecting MEV sandwich threats & enforcing EIP-712 policies via v4 hooks.
projectDescription:
BlotChain-MEVShield is a 3D WebGL Spatial Control Plane and real-time threat monitoring dashboard designed to protect DeFi transactions on Arc Testnet and Uniswap v4 from MEV exploits, specifically sandwich attacks and mempool front-running.
Users submit intents through an immersive 3D spatial interface built with React and Three.js. As intent payloads enter the system, our risk engine analyzes transaction paths, mempool activity, and pool states indexed by The Graph. When a high-risk sandwich attack scenario is detected, the visual HUD instantly highlights the targeted Uniswap v4 Hook node in red, calculates safe slippage parameters, and generates a cryptographically signed EIP-712 execution policy. This policy is verified on-chain within the Uniswap v4 hook before Swap trigger, neutralizing predatory bots before execution.
howItsMade:
BlotChain-MEVShield is built using a modern decoupled architecture engineered for high availability and low latency:
• Frontend & 3D Engine: Built with React, Three.js, @react-three/fiber, and Tailwind CSS for the glassmorphic spatial control plane UI, hosted on Vercel.
• Backend & Risk Engine: Node.js/TypeScript backend utilizing Viem and Wagmi for EIP-712 signature generation, combined with custom Subgraphs on The Graph to query real-time DEX pool states.
• On-Chain Hook: Uniswap v4 Custom Hook written in Solidity and deployed on Arc Testnet. The hook validates the EIP-712 execution policy inside the beforeSwap() function to enforce maximum slippage limits and prevent front-running.
• API Proxy & Resilience: Configured vercel.json rewrites for seamless API routing with zero CORS hurdles, supported by an automatic multi-tier fallback architecture to guarantee 100% UI availability.

name: Usenami
description: Live, signed market data from The Graph as the trust anchor for an AI trading agent's spend policy.
projectDescription:
Usenami Signer seals exchange API keys inside an AWS Nitro Enclave. The signing secret never leaves the enclave, and every signing request is checked against policy before a signature exists. That policy engine isn't new for this hackathon — it's a Continuity project, live today, gating trade size and blocking withdrawals. We've proven it with real money: completed trades on Binance and Hyperliquid mainnet, and the full signing path proven on OKX.
For ETHOnline we're extending it with a new input: live market data from The Graph. An agent reads Uniswap V3 pool state through The Graph's x402 gateway — no API key, no account needed. The indexer's own response comes back signed, tied to the exact request and exact bytes: EIP-712, verified against the live on-chain DisputeManager and the indexer's real stake of 604,359 GRT. We build a canonical snapshot from that signed response and sign it ourselves, with a key whose address is published in our attestation. That snapshot is the designed input for the enclave's policy — the piece that lets "is this order priced sanely" become something a machine can check, not just a human watching a screen.
The layer that actually enforces a price bound from this data ships in the rotation after submission. What ships in the window is the producing half: read, pay, verify the indexer's signature, build the signed snapshot the enclave will consume next.
howItsMade:
The core signer already runs a hard architectural boundary: the enclave has no network access at all, it only talks to its parent over vsock. Any external data - including a subgraph response - arrives from an untrusted party by construction. Trust can't come from "it's on-chain" or "The Graph served it"; inside the enclave that provenance is unobservable, only bytes are. Trust has to come from a signature the enclave can check with a baked-in key.
We read Uniswap V3 pool state (canonical, immutable factory 0x1F98431c8aD98523631AE4a59f267346ea31F984) through The Graph's x402 gateway — GraphQL directly, USDC on Base, $0.01 per query, no API key. The gateway response carries a graph-attestation header: an EIP-712 signature over (requestCID, responseCID, subgraphDeploymentID). We verified that signature end-to-end against two live paid responses. responseCID matched the exact response bytes on both. ecrecover against the current Horizon DisputeManager - 0x2FE023a575449AcB698648eD21276293Fa176f96 on Arbitrum, the address changed in a recent protocol migration and we caught the stale one before trusting it — resolved to an allocationID, and SubgraphService.getAllocation() resolved that to a real indexer staking 604,359 GRT on the exact subgraph deployment we queried. That signature proves integrity and binding - these exact bytes, for this exact request - not correctness; even a genuine indexer signs what it answered, not that the answer is true, and we treat it that way.
Beyond the new data path, the base signer already proves something most policy engines can't: a refusal is a signed receipt, not a log line you have to trust. It carries a request hash, a sequence number and a boot ID, tying it to one specific request and one specific running image. The response itself carries decided_by: enclave. The refusal happens before a signature exists - a bypass of the outer check runs straight into an independent inner one. That's the target the new market-data input plugs into: what ships in this window is the producing half, and the enforcing half - checking the snapshot's freshness and computing a price bound from it inside the enclave - starts after submission. It isn't part of what we're claiming today.

name: Faultline
description: Cross protocol liquidation contagion solver. Shock one protocol, see who else breaks.
projectDescription:
Every lending protocol reports solvency in isolation. Aave shows Aave health factors. Compound shows Compound collateral ratios. Neither can see that a wallet leveraged against an asset on one protocol and a completely unrelated wallet leveraged against the same asset on another protocol are exposed to each other through the market, with no direct link between them.
Faultline builds that cross-protocol exposure graph from live Aave v3 and Compound v3 positions, applies a price shock, recomputes health factors, liquidates breaches, and prices the forced collateral sale against real Uniswap v3 tick liquidity, iterating to a fixed point. It's a deterministic solver, not a model: every liquidation mechanic is a published protocol parameter, not a prediction.
Live proof, not a synthetic example: a 43.67% oracle shock to wstETH liquidates a real Aave v3 wallet. Because the wstETH/WETH Uniswap v3 pool's liquidity falls to under 5% of its starting depth after just 4 ticks, that wallet's forced 196 wstETH sale alone crashes the pool price from $1,718.78 to $0.50, a near total collapse independently verified against Uniswap's own QuoterV2 contract. That crashed price liquidates a second wallet sharing no protocol and no debt asset with the first; its own forced sale drives the price down to a final $0.0028.
howItsMade:
Python/FastAPI backend, React + react-three-fiber frontend. No ML or LLM anywhere in the solve path, a hard rule from day one: liquidation mechanics are published protocol parameters, so we solve the system deterministically instead of predicting it.
Data layer: live positions pulled from Aave v3's and Compound v3's own subgraphs via The Graph. Three of our first four subgraph IDs, pulled from search results with plausible display names, turned out dead or pointed at a completely different schema (Messari-standardized instead of the protocol team's own). We rebuilt the rule after that: every subgraph and contract ID now comes only from the protocol's own docs or README, verified live before use.
Live balances were harder than expected to get right. Aave's UserReserve.currentVariableDebt and Compound's PositionAccounting.baseBalance both look like live numbers but are snapshots written only on a wallet's last interaction, understating real debt by however much interest accrued since. We derive live values ourselves (scaled amount times the reserve's current index), verified to four decimal places against DeBank on real wallets. A second bug: Aave's eMode liquidation thresholds only apply to assets that specific eMode category lists as eligible, and our first query for that list silently truncated to GraphQL's default first-100 rows across the whole deployment, dropping a real eligible asset that happened to land outside the window. That produced a plausible-looking wrong health factor before we caught it.
Uniswap v3's tick-level liquidity is what prices the forced sale for real, not a flat slippage assumption. We implemented the actual v3 constant-liquidity-within-a-tick-range swap math ourselves and verified it against Uniswap's own deployed QuoterV2 contract via a raw eth_call, matching our simulation to four significant figures. That check caught a real off-by-one in our own tick-crossing boundary (excluding the pool's current tick from a downward walk, producing impossible negative liquidity). Pool selection is address-verified too, not sorted by raw reported TVL: Uniswap's subgraph doesn't sanitize that field, and a real query surfaced a spam pool claiming ~$1.1 trillion TVL. We only treat a pool as eligible if both its tokens are governance-listed reserve assets already pulled from Aave or Compound.
The solver is a fixed-point cascade: apply a price shock, recompute every wallet's health factor across both protocols, liquidate anything under 1.0 using Aave's own close-factor and seizure formulas straight from LiquidationLogic.sol, price the resulting forced sale against the real pool depth above, repeat until nothing new breaches. The reference case is externally reconciled against DeBank on both wallets.
The frontend renders that cascade live with react-three-fiber: a shock slider calls the real solver on every drag, not a replay, and a wallet-lookup feature runs the full pipeline against any address typed in. Its honest-failure path (an asset with no Aave oracle price configured) was verified against a real wallet holding COMP as Compound v3 collateral, since COMP isn't a listed Aave v3 reserve at all: the app reports "health factor not computed" by name instead of showing a number built on an incomplete price.
Partner tech: The Graph is what makes composing two independent lending protocols' full position state into one cross-protocol query pattern possible at all, that's the actual product. Uniswap v3's tick-level depth is what turns "the price moved" into an actual, mechanically-priced forced sale, and is what surfaced the concentrated-liquidity finding that became the second half of the demo.

name: SPRY Finance
description: Dynamic-fee Uniswap v4 hook that turns arbitrage-driven IL into LP revenue.
projectDescription:
Spry is a non-custodial Uniswap v4 hook that replaces flat swap fees with dynamic, per-swap pricing designed to better protect liquidity providers from impermanent loss and LVR. Instead of charging every trade the same rate, Spry measures how much a swap moves the pool and applies a four-zone fee curve: ordinary flow stays near a low base fee, while larger price-moving arbitrage and MEV trades progressively pay more. The additional fees accrue to LPs through Uniswap v4's native fee accounting.
To prevent traders from bypassing the curve by splitting a large trade into smaller swaps, Spry tracks cumulative pool movement over a block window and prices each swap across that path using integral-based pricing. The mechanism is designed to be path-independent and splitting-resistant. Spry uses five fee tiers for different asset classes, requires no external oracle, makes no external calls from the hook, and never custodies user funds.
Ref.: https://spry.fi/Spry-Whitepaper.pdf
howItsMade:
Spry started from a simple problem: impermanent loss has always made LPing feel risky, especially when large arbitrage trades extract value from pools.
When Uniswap introduced hooks, we saw an opportunity to change how swap fees work at the pool level. We built a hook that measures how much each swap moves the pool and adjusts the fee dynamically, so normal trades stay cheap while larger, more harmful trades pay more.
The contracts are written in Solidity and tested with Foundry (covering unit, integration, attack scenarios, fuzz/invariant behavior, and fork tests).
The hook is non-custodial, uses only on-chain pool state, and does not rely on external oracles.

name: fuda
description: Membership as an on-chain right — issued in seconds, verified at the door with no server to trust.
projectDescription:
🎫 Membership as an on-chain right. A venue issues a right, the member saves a standard pass to Apple Wallet, Google Wallet or the browser, and a scanner checks admission through fuda's API against the on-chain record. +Private adds a separate browser flow: unlock with a passkey, discover your rights and sign to enter. The right's on-chain validity can be checked independently of fuda.
🚀 Try a standard pass — no crypto wallet setup, no member account, no app install

Claim your ETHOnline 2026 pass: https://app.fuda.sh/@ethonline2026/pass →
The display a venue puts on its counter (scan it with your phone): https://app.fuda.sh/@ethonline2026/home →
